# Patrologia Latina, vol. 140

Volume front matter

Series title page

## The Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library

A complete, uniform, convenient, economical collection of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived from the first twelve centuries of the Church, prepared from the most accurate editions, collated with one another and with certain manuscripts, and corrected with the greatest diligence; continually illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by the discovery of all works brought to light after the extensive editions owed to the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume and each author of any importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; augmented with works both doubtful and apocryphal, and also with works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it is readily apparent to the reader which Fathers commented on the texts of the individual books of Scripture, and in which places in their works they did so.

A most accurate edition, and one easily preferable to all others if consideration is given to the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the works reprinted, the very convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the whole work, the low price, and especially this collection—single, methodical, and chronological—of six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, but now gathered for the first time in our library from works concerning every age, place, language, and form.

## Second Series

In which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III.

Prepared by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or Complete Courses in the individual branches of ecclesiastical learning.

Patrology was printed in two editions, one Latin and the other Greek-Latin. Two hundred volumes of the Latin edition were sold for one thousand francs; three hundred volumes of the Greek-Latin edition for eighteen hundred francs. The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the Eastern authors, however, are presented in it only in Latin translation.

# In the Year of the Lord 1024, Saint Henry, August Emperor

## Acts

[Col. 0009] # Preliminary Commentary on Saint Henry the Emperor at Bamberg in Germany

*(In the Bollandists, July, vol. III, on the 14th day.)*

## § 1. The Saint’s Lineage, Name, and Surnames

### 1

[Col. 0009A] Gaspar Bruschius has briefly, but not inelegantly, touched upon the praises of the bishopric of Bamberg; the city itself has been described more than once in our Acts. It rejoices in Saint Henry as the patron and founder of its Church—a man who, the honor and glory of his Caesars, Germany sent to heaven on this day, or rather on the preceding day; the second King of that name in succession, but the first Emperor, whom nevertheless, in the more usual reckoning, we shall call Henry II. He was a man distinguished by an altogether remarkable holiness, renowned for preserving virginity within marriage, and unequalled in beneficence toward the Church.

We shall not here discuss his continual internal wars, in which throughout the whole period of his kingdom and empire he was harassed even by those nearest to him and most deeply bound to him: [Col. 0009B] he defended the interior regions of Germany splendidly against rebels, while he pursued external enemies—the Slavs, Bohemians, Poles, and others—with unconquered arms. He also carried his victorious standards into the most opposite regions of Europe, Apulia and Flanders.

I have said that we have not undertaken here expressly to excavate these matters. We are chiefly concerned with what we judge to belong to his singular virtues, worthy of a Christian and truly holy prince; to his miracles; and to his veneration, deservedly spread throughout the whole Catholic Church. We shall listen especially to those writers who have recounted his brave deeds on behalf of the faith and religion, his generosity in building and restoring churches, and the other proofs of his undefiled sanctity.

These, then, will be the principal subjects of this preliminary treatment, though we shall arrange them here [Col. 0009C] in such a way that we omit nothing by which the whole course of his life may be illuminated. Although many have wondered at this, certainly no one has yet dared to level the tangled forest of events. But first we must carry out what we proposed in the title.

### 2

[Col. 0010A] Among these matters, the first that presents itself is the Saint’s lineage, stock, origin, or family. I would have had no doubt about it after reading so many and varied testimonies of contemporary writers, had not our Matthew Rader, in his *Holy Bavaria*, vol. I, p. 103, compelled me to examine the matter somewhat more carefully.

There Rader attempts to refute the more widely accepted ancestry of Saint Henry, according to which he descended from the same stock as Otto I, namely Henry the Fowler. He was connected with his predecessor Otto III in the third degree of consanguinity through two Henrys: one the brother of Otto the Great, the other the paternal cousin of Otto II. His genealogical tree would therefore be immediately and perfectly clear at first sight.

On the following page, 104, Rader substitutes another line, taken from Hofmann, [Col. 0010B] as though it proved that Saint Henry was by birth not a Saxon but a Bavarian. Hofmann himself, however, denies this in the recent edition of Ludwig, col. 56, after prefacing his table with these words:

> “When he [Saint Henry] had died without male offspring, imperial dignity fell away from the Saxon line of Henry the Fowler and passed to the East Franks.”

Whatever may be the obscurity of that table of Hofmann’s, it is clear that he himself departs from Rader’s opinion. We must acknowledge the clearer genealogy, which Rader vainly attacks, bringing forward various insignia in an equally futile effort; for these ultimately establish only what is not disputed: that Saint Henry was duke of Bavaria.

### 3

It is neither necessary nor worthwhile to discuss at greater length the table proposed there by Hofmann [Col. 0010C] and reproduced by Rader. It will be more than sufficient to bring forward the testimonies of the ancients, from which it is evident that Saint Henry’s relationship with Otto III was so close that he must himself have belonged to the family of Otto the Great.

The witness to this is Adelbold, [Col. 0011A] bishop of Utrecht, a contemporary writer and one beyond all exception, in his account of the deeds of Saint Henry, preserved by Gretser, p. 432, and to be given below in our new edition, no. 5. After first lamenting the premature death of Otto III, he adds:

> “The grief would also be incurable if the glorious Duke Henry had not survived him, a man vigorous enough to assume the kingdom. At that time he held the duchy in the Bavarian kingdom; he governed the people peacefully, enlarged peace, increased the resources of the churches, and magnified laws and religious observances. At length he lived in the duchy in such a way as to please everyone, so that he was transferred from the duchy to the kingdom and raised from the standard to the hereditary throne. We call it hereditary because, as we heard from those who knew how to calculate genealogies, on his father’s side he possessed the seventeenth line of descent from Charlemagne, [Col. 0011B] and on his mother’s side the sixteenth. Moreover, after the death of Otto III [the text reads “the third Otto”; perhaps read “of the third Otto”] he was elected king, and he and Otto III stood in the third degree of consanguinity with each other.”

This is what he says there.

### 4

Adelbold speaks again in the same sense shortly afterward, on p. 434. After listing Saint Henry’s rivals, among whom was Theodoric of Lorraine, he says of him that, “knowing Duke Henry to be the heir to the kingdom, he did not wish to begin what he could not finish.”

I pass over here what Hofmann and others assert concerning the reduction by Otto III of the election of the Empire and of the King of Germany—as they then called it—to seven electors. It seems sufficiently certain that hereditary succession remained in force down to Saint Henry. The Saint, however, could not have acquired the kingdom by that right [Col. 0011C] unless he had descended from the Ottonian line, a fact that Adelboldus states here most clearly, once and again.

Ditmar does not obscurely agree, when in the prologue to his fifth book he asserts that Saint Henry was born from the stock of kings. At the beginning of that fifth book, in Leibniz, p. 365, he plainly acknowledges the hereditary right, when the great multitude of nobles responds with one voice:

> “Henry, by Christ’s help and by hereditary right, shall reign.”

Add Sigebert of Gembloux, whose words under the year 1002 are these:

> “For Saint Henry was the son of Duke Henry, who was begotten by Henry, brother of the first Emperor Otto.”

From this Mabillon’s error in the Benedictine *Annals*, p. 159, no. 25, must be corrected. He writes that Saint Henry was “[Col. 0011D] the son of Duke Henry, the brother of Otto the Great.” From what has been said it is plainly evident that one should read: “the nephew of Otto the Great through his brother.”

To this may be added the Saxon Chronicler’s account under the same year, 1002, in sufficiently explicit terms:

> “The aforesaid Duke Henry, the king’s nephew, was elected to the kingdom.”

### 5

I shall not pile up more testimonies here, which recur in the same Chronicler under the year 983 and elsewhere, since those already cited seem fully sufficient to provide the true and exact account of Henry’s lineage that we intend to give here, whatever Rader or others may argue against it on the basis of the various insignia existing at Bamberg or elsewhere.

I have not seen our Saller’s treatise on the lineage of Saint Henry, [Col. 0012A] nor the other authorities usually cited in that discussion. Their authority cannot be compared with that of Adelbold, Ditmar, Sigebert, and the Saxon Chronicler—at least not by those who know how properly to weigh the decisive evidence of historical truth.

As for the surname Hezilo, added to Henry the Bavarian, the parent of Saint Henry—whom one might more accurately call the Quarrelsome, but also the Pious, whatever he may have plotted against Otto II, as you will find in the *Life of Saint Godehard*, 4 May, no. 7, p. 504—I have no quarrel concerning the name Hezilo. Among the ancients this appended designation is entirely absent. From the writers cited above it is wholly beyond doubt that he must be called the nephew of Otto the Great through his brother, and therefore Saint Henry the great-nephew of that same Otto in the same line.

[Col. 0012B] This is relevant to a diploma of Otto II, in Gretser, p. 13, where he calls Henry, duke of the Bavarians and the father of the Henry under discussion, his “dear nephew.” Understand “cousin,” as Gretser correctly explains on p. 84, where he also splendidly confirms our genealogy.

Not to speak at greater length about a matter already established, consult the *Life of Blessed Matilda*, 14 March, chap. 5, p. 366, written at Saint Henry’s command and dedicated to him. There you will find a clear genealogy of our Saint, together with a prophecy concerning his empire. All these things make it impossible to doubt that Saint Henry traced his origin from Henry the Fowler through a father and grandfather bearing the same name.

### 6

I shall therefore pass over many other matters here, nor do I wish to introduce or refute at greater length everything devised by various people more from national spirit [Col. 0012C] than from a zeal for truth.

Rader himself, after collecting so much in favor of the Bavarians from heraldic insignia and other sources, finally, in the fourth volume of his *Holy Bavaria*, p. 34, yielding at last to the evident facts, did not hesitate to insert these words:

> “For we now wish Saint Henry to have been a Saxon by origin, as is clear from Ditmar,”

and also from the other authorities whom we have already sufficiently presented.

Those who try to reconcile the two opinions—I do not know whether seriously—either accomplish nothing or merely play with words, reducing everything to empty changes of terminology.

We are not here disputing his homeland, as the cities of Greece dispute Homer. We readily and willingly grant that Saint Henry was born in Bavaria, at Abudia. But we deny just as firmly that he derived his ancestry by ancestral blood [Col. 0012D] from the earlier Bavarian dynasts or dukes, as it is certain that the lineage of Emperor Charles V, surviving in our Most August Emperor Charles VI, must be acknowledged as Austrian and German by origin, not Spanish.

From here we may safely proceed to the remaining matters set out in the title of the paragraph.

### 7

The etymology of the name Henry, as Gretser correctly noted from Aventine on p. 80, is Germanic, from *Dain* or *Daim*, meaning “at home,” and *Reich*, meaning “rich,” “kingdom,” and “empire.” Hence *Dainreich*, *Daimreich*, and so forth.

The ancients called him *Honoricus*. But the name in use is *Henricus*. The Hungarians, Gretser continues from Aventine, call it *Haemericus*, and, without aspiration, *Aemericus*.

Saint Emeric (*Haemericus*, or, without aspiration, *Aemericus*) was the son of Saint Stephen, king of the Hungarians, and of [Col. 0013A] Gisela, sister of Saint Henry the Emperor.

This name signifies a prudent and good head of a household, and one who cultivates a kingdom and an empire.

Under the name Henry are known seven kings of Germany, or Emperors; four kings of France, with the name refined into *Henri*; eight kings of England; and the name even passed into Spain, where four kings bore the corresponding name *Henrique*. The Italians pronounce it *Errico*.

Gretser further notes that the Emperor Henry had surnames: “saint,” from his holiness; “pious,” from his piety; and “lame,” from his dislocated thigh.

It is commonly known that such names were frequently added to kings and Emperors. Thus Henry the Fowler, the great-grandfather of Saint Henry, was so called because he delighted in fowling; he was also called “the Humble,” because he declined the imperial crown.

[Col. 0013B] Otto II retained the surname “the Red”; Otto III was called “the Boy,” because he had begun to reign as a child. Henry III was called “the Black,” while his father Conrad was called “the Salian.”

Nor were surnames lacking in France, as may be seen in the case of the Charleses—Charles the Bald, the Fat, the Simple, the Wise, and so on—not to mention the Greeks, among whom there was no less freedom in giving additional names to their Emperors.

### 8

The matter is established concerning the surnames “Pious” and “Saint,” which were bestowed on Saint Henry. Indeed, the principal, or rather the only, question concerns the designation “Lame.” Writers relate in marvelous ways how it was given to him. Among them was, I suppose, the monk who wrote some sort of life of the Saint, although he remains anonymous in the Bamberg fragment down to this point. In an addition to chapter 22 he relates a long story.

I do not wish wholly to ridicule it, but I would prefer it to possess greater weight of authority [Col. 0013C] and to be supported by broader agreement among the ancients. Other writers, cited by the aforementioned Gretser, report that Saint Henry, during the Lombard war against Arduino or Hardwig, was “captured; and when he had escaped after deceiving the guards, he threw himself from a wall, dislocating or breaking his leg, and afterward limped, from which he acquired the surname ‘the Lame.’”

If you wish, add what Hofmann collected on the same matter in his *Annals*, cited above, cols. 38–39, and most recently Burchard Struvius in the first part of his *Syntagma of German History*, p. 372.

Nor should the aforementioned Gaspar Bruschius be passed over. In his volume *On the Monasteries of Germany*, on p. 87, when describing the Monks’ Mountain—about which we have spoken sufficiently in the Acts of Saint Otto on 2 July—he introduces still other details, [Col. 0013D] even less credible. The very different circumstances attached to the same event, narrated in different ways, force anyone, even unwillingly, to remain uncertain about the truth.

### 9

I do admit that he limped, but, to speak truthfully, I am not greatly inclined toward any of the causes advanced by those writers. I prefer what our Browerus says in *Fuldensian Antiquities*, book III, chapter 15, p. 255:

> “I see that inquiry is being made into why this same Henry [the Saint] bore the surname ‘the Lame.’ Nauclerus reports that, according to a story preserved by popular tradition, this happened because of a heavenly vision shown to the King. When at Rome, in the church of Saint Mary Major, he saw Jesus Christ, the supreme Priest, performing the sacred rites while surrounded by his Mother and a [Col. 0014A] choir of Saints, he also saw, as soon as the Gospel had been read, a book being brought to him by an angel for him to kiss according to custom. At that apparition he lost control of his mind, his senses being deranged; and while he himself did not know what was happening to him, the angel, having praised his chastity and devotion to purity, touched the sinew of his thigh, and from that moment he began to limp.

> “But I have found in the manuscripts of the church of Fulda, in those passages where his royal generosity is described, that at the beginning of his reign, while he was engaged in hunting, he was seriously wounded by a wild beast. From this, according to popular proclamation, he acquired the name *Duffchols*—“a stilt-walker” or “one who hops on a wooden support”—that is, ‘the Lame.’ Therefore, with our elders, it is more reasonable to believe that he limped from this attack [rather] than from an angel’s touch, if the [Col. 0014B] vision is granted its own credibility as testimony to marital abstinence and chastity.”

These things are clear, straightforward, and sound. Nor was there any need for miracles to make Saint Henry, who had previously walked correctly, lame—as is so common among mortals.

We now proceed to the Saint’s age, death, and veneration.

## § 2. The Saint’s Age, the Year and Day of His Death, His Veneration, and His Eulogies

### 10

It is clear that the age of Saint Henry cannot be recovered from either Adelbold or Ditmar. The former’s work is incomplete, ending in the year 1004; the latter did not outlive the Saint, having been prematurely taken from the living in 1018.

The anonymous monk whom we suppose to be the author of whatever sort of Life it is says in chapter 30:

> “Thus, when the most blessed servant of God had died in the twenty-fourth year of his reign, the fifty-second of his life, and the ninth of his empire,”

and so forth.

[Col. 0014C] But in the first figure there was an error, since he had previously placed the beginning of the Saint’s reign in the year 1001. From 6 June 1002—the eighth day before the Ides—to the day of his death, 13 or 14 July, only the twenty-third year, in its beginning, can be found. For this reason others say, using a round number, that he reigned for only twenty-two years, but as Emperor for ten years.

All this is easily understood. It is not equally easy to understand the claim that he died in the year 1022, as many writers have stated. There is no time here either to list or refute them, nor those who place the beginning of his reign in the year 1000.

The authority of the author of the *Life of Saint Meinwerk* may here stand for all. In our edition, under 5 June, chapter 13, no. 101, we read:

> “Saint Henry, amid the immeasurable grief of all Christendom, died in the fifty-second year of his life, the twenty-second of his reign, the tenth of his empire, and the year 1024 of the Lord’s Incarnation.”

[Col. 0014D] This is fully confirmed by the Saxon Chronicler under the year 1024, and more explicitly by the Hildesheim Annals, whose entry is as follows:

### 11

> “1024, Indiction 7. Emperor Henry honorably celebrated the Nativity of Christ at Bamberg, Easter at Parthenopolis [Magdeburg], and Pentecost at Goslar. Afterward he came to Gruna, where he was seized by illness and took to his bed. Amid the grief of the whole kingdom, alas, alas, on the third day before the Ides of July, he laid down his human life. But he had reigned for twenty-two years, five weeks, and one day. May his soul rest in peace. May he who governs all things everywhere grant rest to his soul.”

The calculation is correct if 6 June, on which he was proclaimed king, and 13 July, on which he died, are excluded. There remain thirty-six days, which, divided by seven, [Col. 0015A] yield exactly five weeks and one day.

These matters are sufficiently clear and evident. The entire period of his life is extended to his fifty-second year, and, counting backward, the year of his birth must unquestionably be placed before June of 972.

Thus Gretser correctly calculated the matter in his notes on chapter 30 of the aforementioned Life, as follows:

> “Emperor Henry died in the year 1024, on the third day before the Ides of July. He was born in the year 972 at Regensburg”

Rader noted another place not far distant from it, Abudia, at the location cited above—

> “on the day before the Nones of May, as Fabricius notes from Ditmar in his *Saxon Origins*.”

It is pointless to discuss further here what is not in doubt.

### 12

[Col. 0015B] The additions to Usuard’s Martyrology and the more recent Martyrologies might raise a question about the day of his death. In some of them Saint Henry is marked on the third day before the Ides, while in others on the day before the Ides. The latter date is stated most explicitly in the present Roman Martyrology:

> “At Bamberg, Saint Henry, the first Emperor of that name, who with his wife Cunegund preserved perpetual virginity and led Saint Stephen, king of the Hungarians, together with almost his entire kingdom, to receive the faith of Christ; his feast is celebrated on the following day.”

This plainly suggests that he left this mortal life on that day.

In favor of Gretser, however, besides the ancient writers already praised above and others whom I consider it unnecessary to list, stands the same *Life of Saint Meinwerk*, which, at the place cited, records this epitaph:

> [Col. 0015C] Henry Augustus, just through the offspring of his virtues,  
> whose entrails this decaying earth preserves;  
> he was the splendor of laws, the mirror, light, and jewel of kings;  
> he went to heaven—he did not die, but departed.  
>   
> On the third day before the Ides, July had taken him,  
> still bearing the burden of the flesh, into the heavenly realm.

### 13

These words seem to settle the entire dispute, whatever the veneration of Saint Henry may perhaps have been in various places on 14 July. All the more recent writers announce him on that day with virtually unanimous agreement. Elsewhere, whether on this day or on the following, 15 July, we have referred everything concerning the Saint to the dates in question, following the Roman Martyrology just cited.

In that Martyrology the Office of the holy Emperor [Col. 0015D] has now been postponed to the aforementioned 15th because of the more solemn feast of Saint Bonaventure. It could not conveniently be restored to its proper day, since it would be impeded by the feast of Saint Anacletus.

I do not know why the Martyrologies have varied in assigning the Saint’s natal day. But, unless I am greatly mistaken, the person who wrote that Saint Henry died during the very night between 13 and 14 July has resolved the whole difficulty quite appropriately. This would easily have provided the occasion for assigning different days to his passing—unless, perhaps, the solemnity of his canonization or some other consideration intervened.

However that may have happened, although the Church at the present time, as we have said, consistently commemorates the Saint’s solemnity on the following day, 15 July, we have judged that his Acts [Col. 0016A] should be illuminated by this more widely accepted celebration. We shall here pursue the matters belonging to his deeds and veneration, first presenting certain additions to Usuard’s Martyrology in which we find him placed on both 13 and 14 July. For among the ancients there could have been no record of a Saint whom we know to have first flown to heaven in the eleventh century.

### 14

For the rest, it is sufficiently certain that the fame of Saint Henry’s virtues, piety, and miracles was so illustrious and spread throughout the entire Catholic world that soon after his death he began to be regarded as a Saint and venerated by the faithful. This was especially true among the people of Bamberg, who, I believe, immediately pressed for their founder to be enrolled among the citizens of heaven.

Yet, as often happens, because of various intervening circumstances the matter was postponed until the following century. [Col. 0016B] In the meantime, there may have been in use the special Masses once transcribed by our Janning, customarily celebrated for the holy spouses who remained virgins. Their prayers were as follows:

> “Be merciful, we beseech you, Lord, to the soul of your servant Henry, and grant that he who in this place, from your gifts, prepared daily services for your name with vigilant care may deserve to enjoy everlasting gladness with the Saints. Through our Lord.”

Secret:

> “May this offering, we beseech you, Lord, bring salvation to him whose support has enlivened and sustained our service to you in this place.”

The Postcommunion and the rest also refer to him.

The prayer concerning Saint Cunegund reads:

> “Grant, we beseech you, almighty God, that the soul of your servant Cunegund, [Col. 0016C] released from the bonds of all her sins, may deserve to enjoy everlasting gladness with all your Saints,”

and so forth.

From these prayers it is certainly clear that during that period pious clients refrained from rendering to them the honors due to Saints themselves. Nor is it likely that Saint Henry’s name had been entered into the sacred calendars before his canonization—first on 13 July and then on 14 July—as the examples appended here will make clear.

### 15

Among our manuscripts, the first to mention “Saint Henry on 13 July” is the Hagenau manuscript, written in Germany, in these words:

> “At Bamberg, Saint Henry, Emperor and confessor.”

The Utrecht Carthusian Calendar is briefer:

> “Henry, Emperor.”

The Lübeck-Cologne edition composed the following eulogy:

> “In the city of Bamberg, the deposition of Saint [Col. 0016D] Henry, the most Christian Emperor, who reigned for twenty-two years, in the year of the Lord 1000. Saint Cunegund was betrothed to him, the daughter of the Count Palatine of the Rhine, a most devout virgin. Both of them, vowing their virginity to God by a common pledge, secretly remained virgins until the end of their lives.”

Grevenus speaks somewhat differently, erring in the year of his death:

> “At the city of Bamberg, Saint Henry, the most Christian Emperor, the first of this name among the Emperors who received the imperial blessing or crown. His wife Cunegund, a most holy virgin and exceedingly beautiful young woman, induced her husband to agree that by their common vow they should preserve perpetual virginity between them. In this state Saint Henry, serving Christ, rested in a blessed death in the year of the Lord [Col. 0017A] 1021, shining with miracles.”

Canisius expanded this same eulogy. Molanus also did not omit it from his additions, although he condensed everything more briefly:

> “At Bamberg, Saint Henry, Emperor and confessor.”

Thus far, then, the evidence correctly belongs to 13 July. One could add the longer prayer of the *Florarium of the Saints*. It is therefore astonishing that the following day, 14 July, later became so prevalent.

### 16

In favor of 14 July, among our Usuardine manuscripts, only the Brussels manuscript recurs, with this brief phrase:

> “Saint Henry, Roman Emperor and confessor.”

Molanus repeats him on this day:

> “On the same day, Saint Henry II, Roman Emperor and confessor, who died in the year 1021.”

Read, as above, “in the year 1024.”

The anachronism passed into Maurolycus, [Col. 0017B] who on this very day writes:

> “At Bamberg, Saint Henry II, most holy Emperor, who with his wife Cunegund preserved virginity. By them the church of Bamberg was founded and endowed, and he died in the year of salvation 1021.”

He is marked in nearly the same terms by Felicius. But Galesinius entirely omitted him, both on this day and on the preceding one.

Brautius, bishop of Satsin, who inserted the praises of the Saints in verse, sang of the Saint on this day:

> “Henry the First, king of the kings of the whole world,  
> adorned his marriage-bed with his wife’s virginity.”

What he adds about Hungary’s conversion through Saint Henry requires explanation, which we shall provide below in its proper place:

> “Henry brought the kingdom of Hungary, with its faithful king Stephen, under the service of Christ.”

[Col. 0017C] I pass over the other more recent writers, as well as Bucelinus with his lengthy eulogy, to which I have preferred to substitute the more ancient and more accurate accounts.

### 17

Among these sources none can be suggested as older or more authentic than the verses Ditmar prefixed to his fifth book. They are hexameters, though not always exact in meter:

> Henry ascends, after overcoming youthful things,  
> to the heights of virtue, born from the stock of kings.  
> His father was Duke Henry, and his mother  
> Gisla, who in her merits equaled the footsteps  
> of the king, Conrad her father, who held the Burgundian kingdoms  
> (*Burgundiae*, “of Burgundy” [variant: *Burgundica*, “Burgundian”]).  
>   
> Bishop Wolfgang nurtures the illustrious pupil,  
> who follows the Lord Christ with all his strength.  
> After the killing (*necem*) [variant: death, *mortem*] of his father, he succeeded as hereditary ruler,  
> [Col. 0017D] and the empire too looks from afar toward his helm.  
>   
> The greater part of the kingdom, ravaged by the cruel (*crudeli*) [variant: ferocious, *feroci*] Slav,  
> greatly rejoices that through this man’s peace it enjoys  
> its longed-for dwelling-places, the rapacious enemies having been justly driven far off by arms  
> and subdued by divine law.  
> He crushes all the puffed-up enemies who oppose him,  
> soothing all his allies with pleasant speech.  
>   
> If he commits even a small fault, he immediately repents;  
> with worthy fruits he heals the wounds of the flesh.  
> Serviceable to the Church, he has compassion on all everywhere.  
>   
> Merseburg, if you knew his pious vows, you would long  
> for the coming of so great a ruler; you would praise  
> Christ’s illustrious gifts and render worthy recompense.

### 18

[Col. 0018A] The Saxon Chronicler follows Saint Henry’s virtues and deeds through various years and chapters. It will be sufficient to extract a few passages from him under the year 1004:

> “Therefore King Henry, an illustrious cultivator of justice and an outstanding devotee of divine religion, whatever affairs of the kingdom had been left by his predecessor—who was, as it were, a child and had also been overtaken by premature death—in a less carefully ordered condition, himself endeavored to restore and arrange justly according to the fear of the Lord.”

Let the passages found there be consulted concerning what the most holy King piously and religiously contributed toward restoring the bishopric of Merseburg.

Here is a small fragment:

> “After the King had fulfilled the vow of his blessed desire, he returned to Magdeburg. So that he might not be accused of having inflicted any loss on the archbishop through this institution, he transferred to him by lawful [Col. 0018B] testament an estate belonging to him, together with all its appurtenances, situated in the province of Zeudici.
>
> “For the King himself, a man of great devotion in the Lord, took no small portion of the relics of the blessed Mauritius from his chapel. At that time winter happened to be raging with renewed cold, and the earth was covered with icy harshness and snow. From the mountain of Saint John the Baptist, where the relics were kept, he carried them into the city barefoot, as is said, being animated by the warmth of piety. This occurred on the thirtieth day after the deposition of Gisilharius, the archbishop. Everyone received them with the festal rite, as was proper. He offered them upon the holy altar together with the donations mentioned above, and instituted the celebration of that day in honor of the aforesaid Martyr in his church, as it is still observed.”

19. A commendation of the holy Emperor not much unlike this, [Col. 0018C] but briefer, was composed by the author of the Lorsch Chronicle, cited by Freherus, p. 72:

> “When Emperor Otto III had died at Rome and had been buried at Aachen by Heribert, Archbishop of Cologne, and Duke Godefrid, Duke Henry of Bavaria, having taken up the reins of imperial power, was elected king and solemnly ordained at Mainz. How great were his distinctions of justice and piety is testified by that noble Babenberg church which he founded and in which he was buried. For he was so devoted to the love of religion that he was called the father of monks. Indeed,” says Mabillon in *Acta Benedictina*, sixth century, part 1, p. 434, “that he truly was their father and patron is proved by the ancient documents repeatedly issued in their favor”—see these there, together with the list of the saints whom the pious Emperor honored during his lifetime, and indeed the whole eulogy, which would deserve to be inserted here if it were not settled that only the more ancient materials should be collected, such as also that found in the author of the *Life of Saint Meinwerk* among our materials, ch. 2, no. 9, p. 515:

> “Henry, Duke of Bavaria, exceedingly wealthy according to the dignity of the age, and not inadequately instructed in literary studies, and—what is greater than these—a man outstanding in every ecclesiastical perfection.”

I pass over many other passages, especially those sufficiently common in the writers of the *Life of Saint Meinwerk*, since no one has mentioned the holy Emperor without deserved praise. The remaining matters concerning the cult of the holy Emperor will be supplied in what follows.

§ III. The canonization, elevation of the sacred body, and translations

[Col. 0019A]

20. Whether the vision which the anonymous monk inserted into his *Life*, ch. 28, contributes greatly to displaying Saint Henry’s merits or procuring him glory, I leave to others to examine. The Almighty, glorified in his saints, furnished posterity with more illustrious proofs when he willed that Henry himself should become renowned through several outstanding miracles. At length, moved by these, Egilbert, ninth Bishop of Bamberg, brought the matter to the point that the sacred heavenly honors were decreed to the holy Emperor. I shall first establish in what year this occurred; then I shall proceed with the rest.

The entire determination of the matter depends upon the period of Egilbert’s episcopate, since the aforesaid canonization was procured chiefly through his efforts, and the diploma of Pope Eugenius III was addressed to him personally, as will shortly be produced. The *Catalogue of Bishops*, most recently published and, unless I am mistaken, abridged from Hofmann, assigns Egilbert’s episcopate only a “five-year” duration, during which “he presided over the church with truly paternal solicitude, worthy of a longer life. He died,” however, “in 1146 and was buried in the imperial church”; Eberardus of Bavaria succeeded him, having been elected in that same year.

Since, therefore, the entire prosecution of this cause belongs to the aforesaid Egilbert, and Eugenius’s rescript was addressed to him, Saint Henry’s canonization cannot be postponed beyond Egilbert’s time. It consequently follows plainly that we must abandon Baronius’s reckoning. It is astonishing that he deferred the aforesaid canonization until 1152, since he had before his eyes the letters of Eugenius [Col. 0019C] from some Bamberg chronicle of unknown provenance.

21. Thus he writes under the year 1152, no. 3, drawing from Otto of Freising’s *Deeds of Emperor Frederick*, book I, ch. 63:

> “But since that same Otto here mentions Henry the Emperor as having been enrolled among the saints, there exist in the Bamberg Chronicle letters of Pope Eugenius concerning this matter.”

Baronius appends them there, and we shall give them below. But, in my opinion, he was misled by Otto of Freising when, under that year 1152—the final year of Conrad III—and on the occasion of Conrad’s burial, he writes in the cited passage:

> “Beside the tomb of Emperor Henry, founder of that place, who recently, by the authority of the Roman Church, had been raised to the holy places and was regarded as a saint, the Bamberg church buried him with royal honors.”

That is, the Bamberg church, which had not permitted Conrad’s body to be transferred elsewhere. The distinguished Baronius understood the word “recently” far too narrowly; the sequence of events clearly shows that it must extend over several years. Thus the canonization must have been decreed at Rome while Egilbert was still alive, most probably in 1145, and then celebrated more solemnly, together with the elevation and translation of the sacred body, by Egilbert’s successor Eberardus in 1147. This is decisively established by the previously demonstrated date of Egilbert’s death: the diploma of Eugenius could certainly not have been addressed to him after he had died. Let Hofmann be heard, asserting this more explicitly in the *Bamberg Annals*, col. 121.

22. “In the following year (1145), a great light of holiness shone forth at Bamberg. For Saint Henry the Emperor confirmed his sanctity by many miracles performed at his tomb and proved that he had been received into that heavenly fellowship of God and the saints. Consequently, Bishop Egilbert thought that an embassy should be sent to Rome and that Pope Eugenius should be carefully informed of everything. After learning these things and hearing the report of the envoys, the Pontiff, filled with religious devotion, enrolled Saint Henry the Confessor among the number of the saints by his solemn decree in that same year—that is, in the one hundred and twenty-first year after Henry’s death. Concerning this he sent letters from Rome, on 14 March, to Bishop Egilbert and the other leaders of the church.

“The monk Nunnesius relates that a certain Cardinal John, who vigorously opposed and resisted the canonization of Saint Henry, was deprived of his sight and seized by an intolerable pain in his limbs, thereby paying the severest penalties for his rashness. Finally, after invoking the name of that same confessor, he was restored to his former health.”

That punishment is narrated by Gretserus in ch. 39, and appears among the miracles below as no. 9.

23. Hofmann does not produce the canonization diploma—though he dates it to 1145—and I confess that I do not know the chronicle of Hofmann cited by Baronius. Gretserus, however, supplied the omission from some Bamberg copy of an anonymous document; from it we append the bull here:

> “Eugenius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Egilbert, bishop, and to his beloved sons, the canons of the Bamberg Church: greeting and apostolic blessing.
>
> “As we remember having informed you by letters and messengers, venerable brothers, we have delegated from our side to those regions N., Bishop of Santa Rufina, and N., Cardinal Priest, for various affairs; and we have instructed them orally to visit your church, inquire carefully into the truth concerning the life and miracles of King Henry, and report it to us in their letters.
>
> “Now, on the testimony of these same brothers of ours and of many religious and discerning men, we have learned much concerning his chastity; the foundation of the Bamberg church and of many others; the restoration of certain episcopal sees; his many and abundant almsgiving; the conversion, with the Lord’s cooperation, of King Stephen and of all Hungary through him; his glorious death; and the many miracles divinely displayed after his death in the presence of his body.

24. “Among these matters, we have paid particular and most careful attention to the memorable fact that, although he had received the diadem and scepter of the empire, he lived not imperially but spiritually. Even while occupying a lawful marriage-bed—a condition which we read was true of very few—he preserved the purity of chastity until the end of his life.

“Considering all these things together, and carefully weighing your devotion and that of the Bamberg church, which is known to be subject solely to the Holy Roman Church, although such a petition is not ordinarily admitted except in general councils, nevertheless, by the authority of the Holy Roman Church, which is the foundation of all councils, we assent to your petitions. Having taken counsel with our brothers, the archbishops and bishops who were present, we decree that the memory of this illustrious man, whose exaltation you request, is henceforth to be numbered among the saints, and we establish that his anniversary is to be solemnly celebrated.

“It is therefore your responsibility to persevere in obedience and fidelity to the Holy Roman Church, and to respond to her with services of worthy devotion, so that you may be found deserving of the greater grace of blessed Peter and of ourselves.

“Given across the Tiber, on the day before the Ides of March.”

No other chronological indication was added by which the precise year could be established. Baronius’s error can therefore be more easily excused, since he apparently did not turn his eyes to the succession of the Bamberg bishops.

25. As I was just saying, that solemn enrollment of Henry among the saints was followed by the elevation of his sacred body and its translation to a more fitting place. Hofmann, cited above, briefly describes these events under the year 1147, col. 123:

> “In those same days the bones of Saint Henry the Emperor were translated with solemn ceremony. The matter was carried out in this way: Bishop Eberardus, having summoned Eberardus, Archbishop of Salzburg, and Hermann, Bishop of Brixen, and together with the abbots, religious men, and the leading citizens themselves, went to the place where the body had been buried. After removing the earth, he raised the sacred bones from there, transferred them into a marble tomb, [Col. 0021C] and secured it with keys.”

You find the same account, somewhat abridged, in the episcopal eulogies, p. 6:

> “Eberardus II, Duke of Bavaria, was elected in 1146, under Pope Eugenius III and likewise Emperor Conrad III. He transferred Saint Henry’s bones with great solemnity to a more honored tomb and adorned them with the marble monument still visible today.”

I do not yet see clearly how far the word “today” is meant to extend. This must be gathered from the notes of our Father Johannes Gamansius, so often praised in our *Acts*, who had them copied from a manuscript catalogue of the Bamberg bishops at Saint Michael’s in Bamberg. I thought it worthwhile to cite them here, since they supply what is lacking in Hofmann.

[Col. 0021D]

26. This writer, who brought his *Annals* only down to the year 1440, after briefly mentioning in the year 1379 the rebellions of the Bamberg citizens against Lambertus, the thirtieth bishop, adds:

> “By these words Lambertus was thrown into great fear, and had recourse to imploring divine aid. In the following year, after clergy and people had been summoned, he opened Saint Henry’s tomb and brought out his sacred relics.”

From these words it is scarcely, or perhaps not at all, possible to understand what was then done. The following, fuller account is from the note of Gamansius, which I reproduce on his authority:

> “Under that most reverend father in Christ and lord, Lord Lambertus, in the year of our Lord 1380, Indiction III, on 8 July—the feast of the holy martyrs Kilian and his companions—during the sixth year of his administration, in the presence of the honorable men and lords, the canons of the Babenberg church, Lord Berthold of Henneberg, son of Count Henry of Henneberg; Lord Ulrich of Thunfeld, Scholasticus; and Lord Frederick Zotner of Halberg; after mature and prudent deliberation by the lords of the chapter of the Babenberg church, and in order to obtain a more certain and sounder knowledge of the sacred relics of the holy father and founder of the Babenberg church, Lord Emperor Henry, the sarcophagus of the aforesaid confessor was opened. It had previously been securely closed, locked, and sealed with the great seal of blessed memory of Lord Eberardus, the ninth bishop of the Babenberg church—elsewhere called the tenth.”

27. In that sarcophagus were found relics consisting, as it were, of nearly all the venerable bones of the sacred body, except the head, which is venerated separately in another gilded reliquary. Acting on sound advice and with careful security, they reserved only the jaw, an arm, and two ribs, together with some small additional bones from the aforesaid relics, to be honorably stored outside the sarcophagus and committed to secure custody—not without reasonable cause and particular devotion.

Finally, they carefully enclosed Saint Henry’s relics once more in the same sarcophagus, sealing it with the seal of the aforesaid chapter, which those lords use in legal matters. At that time the same lords, the canons mentioned above, found two old notes attached to the inner reliquary. One of them contained the following writing:

> “Lord Eberardus, first bishop of this Babenberg church, buried the aforescribed Saint Henry the Emperor. Egilbertus, ninth Bishop of Babenberg, canonized Saint Henry himself—namely, through Pope Eugenius III—and Eberardus, Duke of Bavaria and tenth Bishop of Babenberg, transferred the aforesaid father and founder of the church, Saint Henry, and commended him for veneration in holy places, in the year of our Lord 1147, on 13 July, in the presence of the venerable princes and lords Lord Eberardus, Archbishop of Salzburg, and Hartmann, Bishop of Brixen, together with many other religious, faithful, and God-devoted persons.”

28. The opening of the sarcophagus should be sought in the rear section beneath the back of the image of the Blessed Virgin Mary, where these words are written:

> “THE GOLDEN GATE OF HEAVEN.
>
> PLACEMENT OF THE RELICS ON SAINT HENRY’S FEAST AT HIS SARCOPHAGUS.”

The writer of the Catalogue then proceeds to enumerate several distinguished Bamberg relics, in the order in which they are arranged there in the cathedral church:

> “The head of Saint Henry is placed in the middle before the sarcophagus, at the altar of the Holy Cross, toward the east. On the right, as one leaves the choir of Saint Peter, are the head of Saint Cunegundis and the image of the Blessed Virgin Mary. On the left are Saint Margaret and the head of Saint Kilian. On the right, as one leaves the choir of Saint Peter, are the heads of Saint Theodore and Saint Dionysius; and toward the east, a silver head. On the left are the heads of Saints Cosmas and Damian, and a silver head. Toward the choir of Saint Peter are the head of Saint Otto and the head of Saint Pius, pope and martyr.”

The Gamansian document then records a miracle concerning the complete restoration of an ivory image of the Crucified Christ. It is said to have been brought to Bamberg from distant lands by Saint Henry, and to have been shattered and crushed into extremely small pieces by a stroke of lightning on 10 May 1515; the continuation of Hofmann by Ludwig gives the year as 1516. However this may have happened, the matters more directly relevant to our subject are those which the cited document adds concerning the proper translation of the sacred relics, as follows:

29.

> “In the year of our Lord 1513, Indiction I, on 11 September, the ancient sarcophagi of the saints Henry and Cunegundis, the founders, were opened in the body of the church behind the altar of Saint Cunegundis by our most reverend lord aforesaid of Limburg, on account of the new burial, sculpted from marble, for the aforesaid holy patrons.
>
> “In the ancient sarcophagus a single old chest was found, containing ashes from the body of Saint Henry, one part of his shoulder blade, together with certain pieces of leather and silk in which Saint Henry’s body had been wrapped.
>
> “In Saint Cunegundis’s sarcophagus a bronze casket was found containing relics from Saint Cunegundis’s body, two ribs, and certain other relics of hers.
>
> “In both sarcophagi ashes from the bodies of both saints were collected. These relics were carried with honor and reverence in their caskets to the great sacristy by the aforesaid Bishop Georgius, his suffragan Lord Caspar, and Lord Johannes, abbot of the monastery of Saint Michael’s Mount.
>
> “Afterward, on 9 September, namely on the feast of the translation of Saint Cunegundis, the aforesaid relics were divided into four new caskets and, by divine arrangement, carried to the new sarcophagus, where they were reverently placed and enclosed by Bishop Georgius and his suffragan Lord Caspar. Present there were Lord Johannes, Abbot of Banz; Lord Georgius Stiber, dean of the cathedral church; Lord Wilhelm Schenk, Baron of Limburg, cantor; Lord Leonard of Eglofstein, doctor and Scholasticus; Lord Sebastian of Kungsberg, cellarer; and the other capitular canons of the said Babenberg church, with as much of the clergy and people present as the cathedral basilica could contain.”

30. This, then, is the penultimate solemn translation of Saint Henry’s sacred relics. I now add the remaining material collected in the same Gamansian document:

> “This writing on a parchment note was placed beside the leaden casket. In this stone sarcophagus, formerly raised above the ground with its stone cover, the body of Saint Cunegundis, virgin and Empress, was once enclosed, before her translation. Now, because of the construction and erection of the new sarcophagus, as it is seen today, this sarcophagus was placed beneath the ground, containing Saint Henry the Confessor and Emperor, founder of this church.”

There is something here that you may wish clarified:

> “Moreover, the altar of Saint Cunegundis, which had recently been demolished and broken apart, was renewed and erected and was consecrated by Lord Caspar, the suffragan, on that same day after the relics had been placed there, with all those mentioned above still present.
>
> “The courtyard before the Babenberg church, from the Gate of Adam and Eve to the Gate of Grace, was paved with stone in the same year mentioned above, and was enclosed all around by a breast-high wall of hewn stones, constructed with masterly craftsmanship in the shape and form of a crown, lest innocent blood should be spilled there if someone fell.”

Thus far the document. As a concluding addition, it includes what is found in the continuation of Hofmann, col. 242. Let us proceed with other proofs of religious devotion.

§ IV. The Bamberg relics, sacred treasures, the Henrician mausoleum, ecclesiastical offices, and the ancient Mass

[Col. 0024B]

31. Concerning the Bamberg relics, sacred monuments, and treasures, since apart from what has recently been supplied from Hofmann and the Gamansian notes I had nothing at hand, I thought it necessary to return to the source itself, so that I might obtain more certain and reliable information than from what Ludwig had published.

Nor was my expectation disappointed. Through the assistance and support of the Reverend Father Nicolaus Pottu, our College’s rector there, the noble, distinguished, and highly learned Lord Joannes Franciscus Xaverius Eppenauer, archivist—as they call him—of the Most Eminent Elector of Mainz and Bishop of Bamberg, and the Very Reverend Father Lord Otto Schugentius of the Order of Saint Benedict at Saint Michael’s Mount, known to us and our friend through his longstanding kindness and through the many forms of assistance he once provided for the illustration of the *Acts of Saint Otto*, supplied many learned observations. Assisted by their subsidiary efforts, I was able to insert into the commentary already prepared here certain matters which otherwise would have had to be omitted altogether.

There also arrived from the generous clients of the most holy patron and founder the necessary assistance by which various objects were drawn there and engraved here on copper; these could therefore be displayed to everyone’s eyes and to pious curiosity.

32. To arrange the individual matters in order, I begin with those more closely concerning the sacred relics, and first with the portions that are reverently preserved either in the cathedral church itself or in other Bamberg churches.

We recently noted that, at the first elevation and exaltation of the sacred body, the honored head was separated from the rest of the body and exposed for the veneration of pious worshipers, as was also indicated in the preceding section.

The distinguished Eppenauer describes it as follows. The head is of a suitable proportion to support a gilded silver imperial crown, heavy and adorned with many large oriental gems, with golden treasures set around it here and there. Its diameter is eight inches of a foot, and its height nearly six inches; from this the size of the head may easily be inferred. He says that, crowned in this manner, it is held upon the imperial orb in the right hand of a silver image approximately equal to human stature down to the navel. I conceive this image as not greatly unlike the Roman one to be exhibited below, except that the latter represents arms.

From the illustrated crown you may judge its cost and elegance, and you will laugh at the Bamberg account, which, following Ludwig, imagines that there were two crowns from Saint Michael’s—one used on solemn occasions and the other on ordinary days. Schugentius assured me that there is not even the slightest basis for this claim. Only a drawing of our crown was sent to me, and I reproduce it in a reasonably successful engraving.

[Col. 0025B]

33. Eppenauer described the other relics in nearly these words:

> “The jaw, with its teeth, enclosed in a gilded-silver reliquary, is decorated with eight precious stones; a ninth, at the top, is a sapphire as large as two inches. He likewise says that the throat is enclosed in transparent crystal, but without precious stones.
>
> “In the monastery of Saint Michael’s there is, in a certain wooden reliquary, a small bone fragment from Saint Henry’s body.
>
> “In the Bamberg monastery of Saint Anne, belonging to the Reverend Friars Minor of the Seraphic Order of Saint Francis, two very large and intact bones from Saint Henry’s feet are kept on both sides of the tabernacle of the high altar. Each is nearly one foot and ten inches long. This,” he says, “is clear evidence of the great stature mentioned above, so that his height approaches fully seven feet.”

This is Eppenauer’s account. From it I was unable to learn when those two bones were removed from the tomb; below it will become clear that they are Roman relics obtained from there, which we shall discuss shortly.

Here Lambertus, the bishop in 1380, made no mention of “the arm and two ribs, together with certain small bones, which were to be honorably stored outside.” Yet perhaps those relics originated from them—the relics which we shall discuss in the following section.

34. Nor should the other sacred treasures of the most holy patron of the Bamberg people, carefully guarded there with the greatest reverence, be passed over. The two principal ones are the famous cross, which Henschenius testifies that he saw in his *Acts of Saint Cunegundis* and which is kept on the monks’ mount, or at Saint Michael’s; and the mantle, as they call it there, or cloak, worked with marvelous craftsmanship and deposited in the treasury of the cathedral church. These will be explained with particular care in an appendix following the *Acts*.

Eppenauer further reports four other Henrician silk mantles or cloaks of blue color, one of them adorned throughout with a great cross. He also reports:

> “Saint Henry’s own sword, double-edged, though without a sheath, was generously given at Augsburg by the Lord Bishop of Augsburg to the newly consecrated Bishop of Bamberg, Johannes Godefridus of Aschhausen, at the beginning of the preceding century. It has an elliptical hilt of curled boxwood, nearly three feet long and one and a half inches wide.”

The remaining details may be given in the words of that distinguished archivist:

35.

> “There is,” he says, “an iron spearhead, double-edged, supposedly a surviving part of his (Saint Henry’s) military standard, two and a half feet long and two inches wide.
>
> “There is also a similar but smaller standard spearhead, one foot long and more than one inch wide. According to tradition, it is said to have been miraculously given by Saint George to Saint Henry for the defeat of the pagans.
>
> “Finally, there is a certain short sword with a cheap sheath and attached belt, possessing only one cutting edge and an angular ivory hilt encircled by a small silver ring toward the sword. Four signs of the Evangelists are engraved upon it with a shining stylus. It is piously believed that this sword is now the instrument of the martyrdom of Saint Adrian. Its total length is one foot and seven inches, and its width is one inch and a quarter.”

Thus far the report, which adds that all these objects are kept in a certain dome of the cathedral church and that “most of them are customarily displayed for public veneration on feast days at the altar of Saint Cunegundis, near the tomb.”

There are also sacred books, such as Missals, Graduals, and others of the same kind, covered with great expense and adorned with their paintings. They are said to have been left by the most holy patron for the church he founded, and will later be displayed together with the Cross.

But the tomb itself, as the clearest proof of the cult of both most holy spouses, must now be examined somewhat more attentively and described by the pen of the distinguished man so often praised above.

36. Here we must briefly repeat—or at least recall—the matters more fully related in the preceding section from the Gamansian documents: first, the “some sort of marble monument” erected by Bishop Eberardus II for the Saint as a public memorial; and then the “new burial,” “sculpted from marble” in 1513.

Those who, on the basis of some unknown tradition, became convinced that the Henrician monument still standing today was the same monument said to have been erected for the Saint by Eberardus II failed to pay sufficient attention to these matters. They further believed that the earlier monument had stood in the middle of the church’s nave, enclosed by iron railings, and had eventually been raised by several steps in the choir of Saint George.

I had already observed that these things were being circulated in the wrong order. The Reverend Father Rector cited above instructed me more reliably from a German inscription found in the archive and translated into Latin as follows:

> “It should be known that the marble tomb seen in the cathedral church above the grave of Saint Henry and Saint Cunegundis was constructed and secured with iron grilles in the year 1518; this number of years is expressed below at the foot of the tomb.”

It is unsurprising that this note is now absent, since the tomb has been placed upon a new base. That the German writing incorrectly gave the year 1518 instead of 1513 is proved by the Gamansian document already cited; a diligent collaborator sent me a similar, recently discovered document while this material was being prepared for the press. The differences between the two notes are not important enough to deserve mention; indeed, once the type had been set, they could not be noted.

37. The generous restorer of the present tomb, Bishop Melchior Otto, died before the splendid new work was completed. He was taken from this life in 1653, but had already designated the resources necessary to finish the entire undertaking. The work is therefore attributed solely to him, as is made entirely clear by the inscriptions soon to be reported.

Thus the final translation, or rather transposition, of the sacred remains of both most holy spouses—into the marble tomb removed from the middle of the church’s nave and restored in the choir of Saint George—was finally carried out with the greatest solemnity and festivity by his successor, Philippus Valentinus Voit of Reineck, on 9 September 1658.

For this distinguished celebration, the suffragan of Würzburg, four Bamberg abbots, and parish priests from the surrounding area as far as four miles away were invited. In their presence he placed and enclosed the sacred relics. A feast was proclaimed throughout the entire diocese, and the said suffragan honored it with a panegyric addressed to the densely assembled people, no less devout than elegant, in praise of Saints Henry and Cunegundis, under the theme:

> “David and all the house of Israel brought up the ark of the covenant of the Lord with jubilation and the sound of the trumpet” (2 Samuel 6:15).

An inscription sent to me from the Bamberg archive, written in capital letters, exists concerning this matter. I reproduce it here:

> “In the year of Our Lord 1649, on 2 September, by order of the Most Reverend and Most Illustrious Prince and Lord, Lord Melchior Otto, the marble tomb of Saints Henry and Cunegundis was transferred from the middle of the church’s nave to the choir of Saint George, as a more conspicuous location.
>
> “The sacred relics, enclosed in four wooden boxes and temporarily kept in the sacristy, remained there until the Most Reverend and Most Illustrious Prince and Lord, Lord Philippus Valentinus, with magnificent care and expense, assisted by Lords Franciscus Conradus of Stadion, provost; Georgius Henricus of Kunsberg, dean; Joannes Philippus of Egglofstein, coadjutor of the deanery; Martin of Seckendorff the elder; as well as the suffragan of Würzburg, five abbots, and the other capitular members, together with all the clergy and people, arranged for them to be transferred with the greatest religious solemnity in a procession through the city specially instituted for this purpose, and reburied them in this renewed marble monument in 1658, on 9 September.”

38. Having prefaced these remarks concerning that last translation of the sacred remains, I present the tomb itself divided in such a way that its individual parts may be seen, adding the dimensions communicated to me by Eppenauer. I reproduce these, as well as the other relevant details, in his own words:

> “It is seven feet and eleven inches long—one Nuremberg foot being divided into twelve inches—three feet and two inches wide, and four feet and five inches high. On the exterior it contains five scenes, which above are enclosed by a cover bearing the design numbered I. It depicts Saints Henry and Cunegundis in human stature, skillfully fashioned by the sculptor’s hand in that century.”

We must ask whether these were made in the twelfth century or rather in the sixteenth.

> “At the feet of both saints lie two heraldic lions. The first, on Saint Cunegundis’s right, has, besides the lozenges, two small crowned lions; the one on the left, besides the lozenges surrounding the Duchy of Bavaria, has two uncrowned double-headed eagles. Father Raderus displays these two insignia excellently engraved in copper in his *Holy Bavaria*, volume 1, folio 103 verso.”

Indeed he does. Yet Raderus later judged that the objects he had considered to be made from them should be recalled elsewhere; consequently, we must admit that nothing can be concluded from the insignia placed there.

[Col. 0029]

[Col. 0031A]

39. Nor among those scenes sculpted there in relief are there lacking representations that cannot withstand the scrutiny of exact truth. The first, numbered 11 and situated on the front facing the nave of the cathedral church, depicts the death of Saint Henry and indicates a surviving virgin. Raderus expressed it somewhat more elegantly, and in its proper place we defended it against the calumnies of detractors.

I do not approve equally of the scene on the side, which represents a balance and an outweighing chalice. Concerning it Eppenauer candidly observes that the story “rejoices more in the simplicity of its own age than in theological precision,” as we have also explained sufficiently elsewhere.

The next scene, on the same side of the tomb, represents with rather crude workmanship the miraculous liberation from a kidney stone through the aid of Saint Benedict at Monte Cassino; its accompanying details have likewise been treated in their proper place.

On the other side of the tomb, under number III, Saint Cunegundis treads unharmed upon glowing ploughshares. A more vivid image of this event is also found in the aforementioned Raderus.

The final scene concerns the renewal of the memory of the miraculous distribution of the daily wage to the laborers engaged in the construction of Saint Stephen’s church. The money was customarily placed for payment by the holy Empress in a dish. On this matter Henschenius should be consulted at 3 March, § 4, no. 25, of his Commentary.

I shall complete the remainder in Eppenauer’s words.

40.

> “The inscription of Bishop Melchior Otto of Bamberg completes the five scenes of the tomb. It is enclosed in bronze treasures—or rather tablets—on the final face, under number III, facing the high altar of the choir of Saint George the Martyr, with these words:
>
> “On face A:
>
> **THIS GLORY BELONGS TO ALL HIS SAINTS.**
>
> “On face B:
>
> **TO GOD, THE BEST AND GREATEST; TO JESUS CHRIST, THE REDEEMER OF THE HUMAN RACE; TO THE FOUNDERS, PROTECTORS, AND PATRONS OF THIS CHURCH, THE DIVINE HENRY AND KUNEGUNDA, IMPERIAL AND VIRGINAL SPOUSES, HE CONSECRATED, ERECTED, AND SET UP THIS ALTAR, TROPHY, AND MONUMENT. M. O. E.**
>
> “These are simply capital letters, of which the final three designate Melchior Otto, Bishop.”

It remains to add a few words concerning the ecclesiastical offices.

[Col. 0031D]

41. We have indicated above that Saint Henry’s feast was formerly celebrated on various days and with various Offices, according to the received rite of particular churches. Nor would it now be useful to enumerate each one, since an Office is today prescribed in the Roman Breviary for the whole Church, and the Saint’s name is entered in the Martyrology on 14 July and, because of the transfer of the aforesaid Office, entered again on the following day, the 15th—although we have shown above that he died on neither day.

What is common to the holy spouses, after the example of the holy Apostles Peter and Paul, was long ago explained by Henschenius in the preliminary Commentary on the *Acts of Saint Cunegundis*, no. 9, where he adduces certain passages from the *Life* printed at Brussels in 1484; what else would it be to repeat them here than to do what has already been done?

Among our papers are manuscript Offices customarily recited at Passau and elsewhere; but they are of no great authority, being infected with errors. Nor is the present Roman Office altogether free from such errors, having, I think, been taken from Saint Michael’s at Bamberg. In it the following final words of the first lesson must be brought to a suitable sense: “He received Benedict VIII, from whom he had received the imperial crown, when he was an exile, and restored him to his See”; as also these words in the second lesson: “He brought Pannonia, still unbelieving, to the faith of Christ, after giving his sister in marriage to King Stephen and after Stephen had been baptized.”

[Col. 0032B] **42.** For even on the hypothesis that Saint Henry received Benedict VIII as a fugitive—which still does not seem plausible to me—in that hypothesis, I say, it cannot properly be said that he received him as a fugitive “from whom he had received the crown”; for Benedict is supposed to have fled in 1012, whereas the Saint first received the crown in 1014.

Moreover, the statement that Stephen was led to the faith by Saint Henry must be understood in a somewhat broader sense, since Stephen, born to Géza, who was already a Christian, was baptized as an infant. Indeed, he had already fought more than once on behalf of the Christian faith before marrying Gisela. That the affinity contracted between the saints contributed greatly to the conversion of the Hungarian kingdom is certainly beyond doubt; but here we are examining the passages as they stand.

There is also a proper Office of Saint Henry in the Bamberg Breviary, printed at Dillingen in 1575. Yet nothing particularly new occurs in it, since the lessons are taken from the Anonymous Legend, while the antiphons, responsories, and other such pieces are either almost common forms or clearly bear the mark of the same source. It contains the following proper prayer:

> “O God, who, after Saint Henry had been distinguished by earthly imperial power, placed the blessed man in the heavenly dwellings, grant, we beseech you, that the one whom we see shining through signs of miracles may be felt by us as an intercessor in our troubles.”

This was taken from an old Bamberg Missal, from which the Reverend Father Rector Nicolaus Pott, whom I have already praised, sent me the proper Mass; I shall describe it briefly here.

**43.** It is from the Common of a Confessor who is not a Pontiff, whose Introit is *Os justi* (“The mouth of the just”). The prayer already mentioned follows, immediately joined to a proper prayer for Saint Cunegund. The Epistle is *Justus cor suum tradit* (“The just man gives his heart”).

Attached to the Gradual is this distinctive verse:

> “O [perhaps ‘this’]! You have obtained and firmly ruled the sceptre of the whole monarchy; on this day, Henry, you have reached the shining summit of heaven. We beseech you on this day, kneeling with bent knee, that you lead us to the kingdom of the hierarchy, illustrious King.”

Then follows this sequence:

> “Let every spirit praise Christ, who by divine power crowned the glorious confessor with glory; this church venerates him as its patron and founder.
>
> The old man, in sins, received the first garment of renewal together with the ring. Let everyone, with a purer mind, applaud with the hand and sing with the mouth, worthily for God’s servant.
>
> After reading six, the King doubts what meaning the truncated prayer should bear. The sixth year rolls around, and the problem is solved: the crown is doubled.
>
> The virgin, vindicating the chastity of the Virgin, cleanses the mark of crime. She purges adultery, feeling none of the heat of the fiery ploughshares.
>
> On Mount Cassino, after a long oppression, he feels Benedict’s care for the suffering of the stone; although the body was nowhere touched, everyone marvels that it was nevertheless drawn out from there.
>
> A mighty angel fights in the camp, crowning the victor with glory after the enemy has been put to flight.
>
> He persists in frequent prayers, free from worldly concerns and often devoted to God, while the world is at peace.
>
> As he was departing this life, the hermit learned from the demon the end of the matter: nothing was found worthy of death—not hay, not wood, nothing human in the man.
>
> Such was the one who served Christ; such is the servant and friend of Christ who, living for Christ, lives in the eternal homeland. May your grace, O God, console us through our Henry.”

**44.** You will find that these statements are not sufficiently exact with respect to historical truth; I have discussed them in their proper places.

The Gospel is *Homo quidam nobilis* (“A certain nobleman”). The Offertory is *Posuisti, Domine* (“You have set, O Lord”). The Secret is:

> “Look, we beseech you, O Lord, upon these gifts with such serene mercy that they may be infused with the blessing of the Holy Spirit, and that they may pour into our hearts that strong love by which Saint Henry, your confessor, overcame every impediment of the body.”

The Communion is the same as the Offertory, *Posuisti, Domine* (“You have set, O Lord”).

The Completion, or Postcommunion, is:

> “May your people, O Lord, be magnified by the glorification of Saint Henry, your confessor, and, with him always praying, deserve to have you as their ruler. Through the Lord.”

There is another prayer for the Saint:

> “Attend to our supplications, almighty God, and, to those who have confidence in the mercy they hope for, …”

From the folio of the aforesaid Missal, sent directly to me, it is clear that it was printed in fairly elegant large German type, with various rubrics suitably interspersed. At its end, in accordance with the custom of that age, the following inscription is added:

> “In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1499, on the fourth day before the Kalends of June, this Missal, printed with the utmost diligence in the city of Babenberg by Master Johann Pfeyl, a resident of the aforesaid city, in praise and glory of the holy and indivisible Trinity and of the undefiled Virgin Mary, happily comes to an end.”

This is sufficient concerning the Bamberg monuments, Offices, and ancient Mass. Let us now investigate the sacred relics transferred elsewhere.

### § V. Relics transferred elsewhere, especially to Rome, to the church of the Professed House of the Society of Jesus

**45.** From what has already been established, it is sufficiently clear that the principal sacred remains of the most holy married couple, Henry and Cunegund, are still preserved in the Bamberg mausoleum itself, although some portions have been transferred elsewhere for veneration; I am not in a position to enumerate them individually.

The Gamans document cited above records a pious exchange of sacred relics, made in the year of the Lord 1501, Indiction I—it intended to say IV—on 18 July, between Gabriel, Bishop of Eichstätt, and Vitus of Bamberg. According to it, Gabriel gave the Bambergers:

> “A portion of the arm of Saint Willibald, bishop and confessor, and of Saint Walburga, on the very day of Vitus’s consecration,”

while, “conversely,” the same Lord Vitus, with the consent of the lords of his chapter, gave Bishop Gabriel:

> “One piece, or portion, of the relics of Saint Henry; likewise a portion from his throat; likewise a portion of Saint Cunegund,”

in the presence of the venerable and distinguished lords Charles of Seckendorff, dean; George of Schwinburg; and Frederick of Quedwiz, senior capitulars and canons appointed by the chapter for this matter.

It is not unlikely that pious exchanges of this kind were made with other German churches, from which relics of Saint Henry may have reached them, although I find nothing about them recorded in public documents.

[Col. 0034B] **46.** Nothing would be more natural than to suspect this in the case of Würzburg, unless it were otherwise established that the sacred relics of Saint Kilian had existed at Bamberg, and that this Saint had even been regarded as its patron before the time of Saint Henry, as the charters demonstrate: in them Saint Kilian, in Saint Henry’s own age, is associated with Saint George.

In any event, the notable—certainly very ancient—translation of a part of the sacred body to Merseburg must be much earlier than the exchanges mentioned above. The Anonymous speaks of it so explicitly in Gretser, chapter 41, and in our work among the miracles, no. 11, that anyone who says it occurred not long after the Saint’s canonization will not have strayed far from the truth. The same writer reports it in nearly this order:

> “At the time when Volcmar, venerable abbot of the church of Merseburg, brought the relics of Blessed Henry the Confessor into the land of Saxony.”

That they passed as far as Poland may be understood from the miracles below, no. 18. Whether, and in what manner, the aforesaid Merseburg relics perished, I do not know. But from a document sent to me by the distinguished Eppenauer mentioned above, it will clearly appear that other relics were sent there, doubtless to replace those that had been lost.

**47.** These are letters from Adolf, Bishop of Merseburg and prince of Anhalt, to George, Bishop of Bamberg, dated “the Friday within the feast of Saint Martin,” namely 13 November 1517. In Latin translation they read as follows:

> “Our friendly services first: Venerable Father in God, especially beloved lord and friend. Since Your Love, in response to our petitioning request, has granted certain sacred relics of Saint Henry the Emperor, we have received the same relics sent by Your Love with veneration and a grateful and benevolent heart.
>
> And although we acknowledge ourselves bound to Your Love and to our church by the gift granted to us—so valuable that no temporal price can equal it—we are in no way able to discharge that obligation. Nevertheless, we trust in the holy patrons of our church, and especially in our beloved Saint Henry the Emperor, that by praying for Your Love to obtain the happiness desired in this temporal life and, above all, with God in eternal life, they will repay this gift a hundredfold.”

How long this treasure continued to be valued and duly venerated there after the epoch marked by the fatal Lutheran apostasy is not so easy to investigate.

**48.** I am convinced that other churches also received portions of these precious remains, although the documents by which we could learn more about them are not presently at hand.

That they penetrated even into Spain is attested by our colleagues Pinius and Cuperus. While examining the library of Saint Lawrence at the Escorial, they encountered the remarkable treasury of relics gathered there by King Philip II, founder of that most magnificent palace, monastery, and church—an occasion which I consider sufficiently well known.

In that reliquary they found three small fragments of the sacred remains of Saint Henry, two of them joined to other relics, and, moreover, a larger portion of his skin, about four fingers long and two wide. The *Lipsanologium*, or catalogue of relics, does not state how these came there.

The aforementioned Eppenauer also informed me that, under the administration of the Most Reverend and Most Illustrious Prince Peter Philip of Dernbach, Bishop of Bamberg, certain relics of Saint Henry were sent to Florence between the years 1672 and 1683, at the request of the Grand Duke of Tuscany.
