I do not know, however, where they are now displayed or with what honor they are venerated.

**49.** I shall not undertake here a longer investigation of the other sacred pledges transmitted in every direction. But the exceedingly devoted veneration of our Society for the most holy Emperor cannot be passed over. Moved by it, the Fathers of the German Assistance, just as the French Fathers had obtained the sacred remains of Saint Louis the King, tried various approaches and finally achieved their purpose through the efforts and authority of His Most Serene Highness Maximilian, Elector of Bavaria, the foremost supporter and patron of that same Society.

The whole undertaking appears to have been promoted and brought to a successful conclusion by the Reverend Father Gualterus Mundbrott, who at that time was serving in Rome for Germany as Assistant to the Most Reverend Father General Mutius Vitelleschi. Since he enjoyed influence and favor with the Most Serene Elector, he induced him, through his good offices, to request relics of Saint Henry from the Most Reverend and Most Illustrious Francis, Bishop of Bamberg and Würzburg; and in the end he obtained them with the desired success.

I was unable to obtain the letters of the Most Serene and never sufficiently praised Maximilian, Elector. But from the replies of Bishop Francis, which bear witness to the precious treasure granted, the substance of the prayers that had been presented can readily be gathered. Translated from German into Latin, they read:

**50.**

> “Most Serene Prince,
>
> I would have complied as quickly as possible with Your Serene Highness’s recent request, by which you wished to receive a portion of the relics of Saint Henry, patron and founder of my Bamberg church, if the relics of my aforesaid cathedral had been at hand.
>
> Since, however, they had necessarily been transferred to Villach in Carinthia before the first incursion of the enemy, for the sake of their preservation, and since they have not yet been able to be brought back because security remains unsettled, I nevertheless made diligent inquiry whether something of that Saint might perhaps be found in other churches.
>
> At last I discovered here among the Franciscan Fathers a fragment of the thigh bone of my aforesaid holy Patron, which had been preserved in their church for several hundred years with the greatest veneration. At my request they gave me a substantial part of it, which I entrusted to the Capuchin Provincial Father, who was going there for other reasons, to offer to Your Serene Highness.
>
> I therefore amicably beg Your Serene Highness to regard it favorably and to deign to keep me and both my cathedral churches commended on every occasion.
>
> Bamberg, 3 November 1641.
>
> Your Serene Highness’s most dutiful and obedient servant,
>
> Francis, Bishop of Bamberg and Würzburg.”

**51.** The same relics, received as a gift from the Most Serene Elector, were sent that same year, on 5 December 1641, by the Reverend Father Rector of our Munich college, George Spadser, to Rome, to the aforesaid Reverend Father Gualterus Mundbrott. This is more clearly understood from the words of his letter written at that time. He writes:

> “Reverend Father in Christ,
>
> I am taking advantage of the Elector’s mail, through which I am sending Your Reverence a fragment of the thigh bone of Saint Henry the Emperor.
>
> I am also enclosing a letter from the Most Illustrious and Most Reverend Bishop of Würzburg to our Most Serene Elector, furnishing testimony concerning these relics that is beyond all objection.
>
> The Most Serene Elector graciously sends his greetings to Your Reverence and, through me, transmits the aforesaid relics, obtained with no small effort and labor. He orders Your Reverence to regard this undertaking of his favorably.
>
> He had indeed hoped for something greater from the Bishop, especially after the most ample and repeatedly renewed promises; but for the present he must be content with this, and in turn asks that Your Reverence not disdain the smallness of this gift.”

**52.** Father Mundbrott by no means disdained the most precious gift. In the following year, in September, he presented those very relics for approval to the Most Illustrious Lord Giovanni Battista Altieri, Bishop of Camerino and acting deputy for the Cardinal Vicar of Rome—later Pope Clement X. After everything had been duly examined, the bishop graciously granted approval on 7 September in the following terms:

> “To all and each who shall inspect these present letters, we attest and certify that today there was brought before us by the Reverend Father Gualterus Mundbrott, Assistant of the Society of Jesus for Germany, a certain portion of the thigh bone of Saint Henry the Emperor, for whose authenticity and validity he showed us sufficient attestations.
>
> Since we have approved this sacred relic as genuine, belonging to the aforesaid Saint, we grant and impart in the Lord to the same Reverend Father Gualterus permission and authority to give it to others and to place it in a church, so that it may be venerated by devout faithful.
>
> In testimony whereof, etc.
>
> Given at Rome, on this seventh day of September 1642.
>
> J. B., Bishop of Camerino, acting Vicar.”

[Col. 0037]

[Col. 0039A] **53.** Once this permission had been obtained, it was not long before the aforesaid relics of Saint Henry were honored with due veneration and worship in the Roman church of the Professed House, dedicated to Jesus the Savior.

A remarkable silver reliquary was soon prepared—or perhaps had already been prepared—such as you see depicted here. It is approximately six feet high and nearly four feet wide, skillfully made by the most accomplished craftsman of that age. The Reverend Father Franciscus Wenzel, now Substitute of the German Assistance, rightly wonders whether Rome currently possesses anything equal to it. To his care and benevolence I owe thanks for nearly all the information given here, together with the drawing from which the same object has been engraved in copper, for the glory of the holy Emperor and as proof of the Society’s worship and reverence toward him.

[Col. 0039B] Lest you think that Saint Henry’s memory is honored there with less devotion than expense, every year, when the Saint’s anniversary feast returns, the reliquary is accustomed to be displayed on the altar of our holy Father Ignatius, with candles burning more abundantly than usual. On that day the more senior Fathers of our house perform the sacred rite there.

At other festivals throughout the year, it is placed on the principal altar together with the relics of Saint Louis, so that, in the capital of the world, the venerable memory of both most holy princes has in a sense been restored.

Having now sufficiently dealt with the worship accorded to the Saint, we proceed to his deeds and their writers.

### § VI. Writers of the Life and others who discuss Saint Henry

**54.** An Anonymous author wrote the Legend of Saint Henry according to the custom of his age, namely the twelfth or thirteenth century; he appears to have been a monk. He was, I believe, the same man who later committed the deeds of Saint Cunegund to memory, which Henschenius illustrated under 3 March.

I say, according to the custom of those times, because he chiefly recounted particular virtues, generosity in building and restoring churches, miracles, and similar matters, without observing any order of events or chronology. He also mixed in material that bears only a very remote relation to the Saint’s life.

That he himself lived in the twelfth century, after Saint Henry’s canonization, and that the work therefore cannot at all be attributed to Adelbold, Bishop of Utrecht—formerly a monk or cleric of Lobbes, first counselor and chancellor, then raised to the episcopate and dying three years after the Saint—is demonstrated conclusively by Gretser in his notes, page 80. The Anonymous mentions several things that occurred a full century after Saint Henry’s death. He speaks of the miracles as an old matter received from his ancestors, which cannot possibly suit Adelbold.

Moreover, he writes about matters that occurred long after Adelbold’s death: the charter of King Henry III, the Bulls of Clement II and Leo IX, and the fourth and sixth Bishops of Bamberg. Thus there can be no doubt that Adelbold preceded this compilation by a full century or more.

**55.** The distinguished and often praised Henry Canisius first brought this Life to light in volume VI of the *Antiquae Lectiones*, beginning at page 383, from a manuscript codex of Windberg monastery. It was not, as Gretser says, especially complete. Later Gretser found another copy in the monastery of Rebdorf, which he published in 1611 among the *Bamberg Saints*, collated with a Bamberg copy, from which he expanded and corrected several passages, as he explains at greater length in the notes already cited, beginning on page 79.

The same Legend of Gretser appears in the posthumous edition of Surius, though the frequent chapter headings have been omitted; we too judged that they should be shortened according to our practice.

Our superiors obtained a copy of the Rebdorf codex, from which, together with Surius, we shall provide the complete Legend below, supplying lacunae or gaps from Gretser’s edition. We shall relegate to this Commentary or to an appendix whatever seems less relevant to the thread of the history, such as chapters 16, 17, 18, and 19, which enumerate not the deeds of Saint Henry but the privileges of the Bamberg church.

Johann Peter Ludewig recently revised Gretser’s entire work in a new form and inserted it, in 1718, into his volume on the Writers of Germany, which chiefly contains material relating to the Bishopric of Bamberg. He added individual notes to their respective chapters. We have not considered it useful to employ his work, since the original source has been opened to us, from which everything could be drawn in a purer form.

**56.** This Legend of Saint Henry, however imperfect, is now extremely widespread and well known, and therefore we have not departed from it. Yet I also found another Legend, written by some fairly recent and ignorant author, joined to a Life of Saint Cunegund. Henschenius likewise mentions it in the place cited above. At the end of both works the following inscription is appended:

> “To the praise and glory of almighty God, the glorious Virgin Mary, and all the Saints, the Legends of the saints Henry the Emperor and Cunegund the Empress, virgins and spouses, come happily to an end. They were printed with the utmost diligence in the famous city of Brussels by the Brothers of the Common Life at Nazareth, in the year of the Lord 1484.”

I read and reviewed the whole work more than once. It is written in a crude style, confused and inelegant, divided into fourteen chapters. From no indications could its author be determined.

I found Henschenius noting that Nonnosius, custodian of the monastery of Momperg, composed a German Legend, and that this might be the very work translated into Latin. But if Hofmann and others are right, the aforementioned Nonnosius was the author not of this Legend but of another German one. Some fragments of that work, sent to me, easily satisfied my thirst for the remainder.

In any event, there is absolutely no proof, indeed not even an indication, that this Brussels Legend was translated from German.

**57.** Its value should be judged as follows: it is, as I had begun to say, an unformed compilation by a more recent writer, since he cites Vincent of Beauvais in the *Historical Mirror* as though he were some ancient witness to Saint Henry’s deeds. Vincent, as we know, flourished and wrote in the middle of the thirteenth century; the work therefore most probably reflects the century in which it was printed, namely the fifteenth.

You may understand how exceedingly verbose the writer is from the fact that he fills fourteen pages merely in assembling his prologues, mixing many doubtful and false statements with the true. He goes astray at the very beginning of the Life, asserting that Saint Henry was unanimously elected by the princes in 1003, but that he reigned for twenty-two years and five months. I did not consider hundreds of similar statements—false or badly arranged—worthy of citation, much less of correction.

I may safely say that in this entire jumble, together with the appended lessons of the Office, nothing is found that is not explained somewhat better in the commonly received Legend. In that Legend there are already so many difficulties to be excavated that no new ones need be imported from elsewhere.

By “difficulties” I mean chiefly those arising from the fact that such Legends lack the proper light of history. Our principal labor must therefore be to attach each event to its distinct time and, as far as possible, arrange those times in order. The whole of our effort will chiefly be devoted to directing the remaining sequence of the Saint’s life.

**58.** Adelbold’s excellent work would have freed us from this burden, had the injustice of time not deprived us of most of it. It must be judged to have perished badly, since only a fragment has reached us, published by Gretser among the aforesaid *Bamberg Saints*. Gretser explains on page 428 where he obtained it; concerning the author he transcribed the following from Trithemius:

> “Adelbold, Bishop of Utrecht, formerly a monk of the Order of Saint Benedict, etc., a man devoted to and learned in the divine Scriptures, and exceptionally instructed in secular letters; subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech, outstanding in life and conduct, and, on account of these virtues, held in great esteem at the court of Saint Henry the Emperor. He wrote several booklets of by no means contemptible learning, through which he made his name known to posterity. Among them is one book on the Life and Deeds of that same holy Emperor Henry; one book on the Praises of the Holy Cross; likewise one book on the Praises of Saint Mary. He also published various sermons in praise of the Saints, and other works both in verse and prose, which have not come to my attention. He died under the Emperor Conrad II, in the year of the Lord 1027, Indiction X, in the twenty-second year of his episcopate, on the fifth day before the Kalends of December.”

“These are the words of Trithemius,” Gretser says, adding that whether this is the Life written by Adelbold or not, it is certainly to be wished that it were not mutilated. We too have long wished this, and continue to wish it most fervently.

**59.** The beginning of Adelbold’s episcopate is expressed more clearly in the Hildesheim Annals, in Leibniz’s *On the Writers of Brunswick*, volume I, page 722, where under the year 1010 they state:

> “Ansfeld, bishop of the church of Utrecht, died, and Adelbold succeeded him.”

From this beginning it is perfectly clear that what Trithemius reports is correct: Adelbold was taken from the living in the eighteenth year of his episcopate, since he lived until 27 November 1027.

Moreover, it seems fairly clear from the words of the aforementioned Trithemius that Adelbold’s work existed in his time and was known to him. I can scarcely persuade myself that all copies of it disappeared within the span of only two centuries.

If that did happen, the loss of the distinguished Acts is irreparable. It leaves us with an even greater longing, since the surviving fragment clearly shows that the entire sequence of Henry’s Life must have been composed with the utmost precision, if it was carried through to the end in the same order, method, and diligence. It was written by an eyewitness to all the events, and by an entirely upright bishop. Concerning his administration, his buildings, virtues, and writings, see John of Beka, page 37, and William Heda, page 107, rather than Vossius, who wrongly confused the Anonymous work published by Canisius with Adelbold’s.

In vain—as I may say once and for all—our superiors have sought this most desirable history, and in vain have we sought it until now. If anyone can unearth it from somewhere, he will bind both us and all lovers of sacred history to himself with everlasting gratitude.

**60.** Gretser was the first to bring to light the fragment he possessed. Leibniz consequently included Adelbold among his Brunswick Writers, volume I, beginning at page 430. In his Introduction he remarks:

> “What is lacking from Adelbold can in good part be supplied from Thietmar; and where Thietmar ends, a gleaning should be made from various historians, although of lesser weight, after the harvest has been lost.”

The very learned man offers sound advice, but it is not equally easy to construct a patchwork even from Thietmar himself and bring it into conformity with exact chronological calculations, since both manuscript and printed copies of his work sometimes depart manifestly from the truth.

To make a gleaning from various other historians will be still more difficult, since they scarcely touch upon Saint Henry’s deeds, contenting themselves for the most part with general statements and a confused heap of events and times. It will not be easy for anyone to emerge successfully from this material.

Let the learned reader consult the writers of the nearby centuries—Otto of Freising, Hermann the Lame, Lambert of Hersfeld, the Abbot of Ursperg, Marianus Scotus, and any others. Unless I am mistaken, he will experience what happened to us: those scattered fragments are extremely difficult to bring into conformity with a correct history of Saint Henry.

Vincent or others will provide no assistance; nor will that Vitus Arnpeck, in his *Chronicle of the Bavarians*, which the very learned Bernard Pez inserted into the third volume, part 3, of his latest *Thesaurus of Anecdotes*, beginning at column 157. At the very beginning, in chapter 12, he assigns to the year 1014 events that must have occurred a full decade earlier, to say nothing of the other matters in which he is more prolix than accurate.

**61.** Wherever you turn, you will encounter equal or greater obscurities, which kindle our longing for Adelbold more and more.

It is not, however, the purpose of our undertaking to compose histories of this kind. We have been accustomed to examine the monuments as they have reached us and to restore them intact, illuminating them with the proper light.

For this purpose, then, it will be sufficient here to arrange the chronology from the aforementioned Thietmar, the Saxon Chronicle, the Hildesheim Annals, and other writers, bringing it into conformity with chronological calculations according to our custom. Thus our effort may serve as a guiding light for those who have both the leisure and the enthusiasm to carry out the history itself.

A particularly serious difficulty in those German chronicles is that they often diverge from one another by one year, or even by several, as is clearly evident in Adelbold, the Saxon Chronicler, the Hildesheim Annals, and others.

The matter can readily be tested by comparing Adelbold, the Saxon Chronicler, and the aforesaid Annals with Thietmar. The former connect Saint Henry’s first expedition into Italy explicitly with the year 1004; Thietmar, in equally explicit words, records it in the following year, 1005, together with most of the other writers whom modern authors generally follow along with Baronius. On this point, however, we consider Thietmar must be entirely abandoned, as will be demonstrated somewhat more fully and clearly below.

**62.** To understand how imperfect Thietmar still remains today, even as he was recently edited by Leibniz and ennobled by the splendid title *Thietmar Restored*, consider what our Janning indicated briefly in volume VI of the June Acts, page 38. He left observations and annotations on many other similar points.

Even if all these matters had been corrected by the editor Leibniz, there would still be no easy way to continue a coherent history of Saint Henry from Thietmar unless someone first devoted painstaking effort to dividing that Chronicle into its chapters, paragraphs, and numbered sections, and to shedding a more laborious light upon it, so that the individual periods of the years might be properly and suitably distinguished from one another.

In this way the work—otherwise highly esteemed—could be carefully rescued from its many confusions and scattered errors. After a long examination of the work, I myself found this so necessary that, had I not been occupied with countless other matters, I would by no means have shrunk from undertaking the task.

I trust that others will have more leisure to adorn the republic of letters with so worthy a service, so that the work might rightly be called the distinguished Chronicle “Thietmar Restored and Illuminated.”

But let these remarks be regarded as incidental. Difficulties remain to be explained in the Anonymous author. I have already touched above on some of them, namely those concerning the Saint’s lineage, name, surname, age, year and day of death. I shall resolve a few others here and defer the remainder to the following paragraphs.

[Col. 0043D] **63.** I have suggested more than once that many things are found in the work of that Anonymous monk which I would prefer to see arranged more correctly in historical order and more accurately organized after extraneous matters had been removed.

I do not wish here to pursue in order each of the matters that have been sufficiently indicated in scattered fashion and will be indicated further, lest the discussion limp from a cause fetched from so far away, which we discussed above.

The statements concerning the vision of demons and the handle of the chalice are scarcely credible. They are closer to a pious dream than to sincere truth, as the Bambergers themselves will not deny today, whatever we may have reported in the monument of the most holy married couple mentioned above.

Something was also said in passing about Nonnosius. Because the work itself is lacking—which, I understand, is carefully guarded—it has not been possible for me to investigate precisely what particular contribution he made to the Saint’s glory.

But since he lived in the sixteenth century and, according to what has been written to me, died in February 1529, it can readily be inferred how much credibility his German history of Saints Henry and Cunegund, published, as they say, in 1511, can deserve—especially in those matters that he thought should be added to our Anonymous author.

We know of no others who have treated the life and deeds of Saint Henry expressly. Nor do we wish to heap together fragments or eulogies by various authors, lest repeated accounts of the same matters bring the reader weariness rather than pleasure, while we hasten toward matters of somewhat greater usefulness.

### § VII. The Life of Saint Henry published at Dillingen in 1648

**64.** The matters discussed thus far and those discussed subsequently throughout this preliminary Commentary on the deeds of Saint Henry had long since been prepared for the press when an Anonymous Life of the holy Emperor came to our attention. It was printed at Dillingen in 1648 by some priest of our Society, at the Academic Press.

To obtain it in time, I left no stone unturned, writing to friends in Germany. The result was that, with the ever-ready assistance of the Reverend Father Nicolaus Pott, Rector of our Bamberg college—whom I often and deservedly praise for the diligent and unwavering service he rendered—I obtained a copy.

I shall first say a little about its author, then about his purpose and the value of the entire booklet. Finally, I shall review whatever I consider worthy of notice here and there for illustrating the Saint’s deeds, especially where the same matters are treated that are mentioned by Adelbold or by our Anonymous author, whom we have undertaken to illuminate.

To make the character of the work clear from its very beginning, here is its title:

> “Saint Henry the Emperor Augustus, thirty-first Duke of Bavaria, distinguished for religion, prudence, fortitude, chastity, clemency, and other heroic examples; recently proposed for admiration and imitation by a certain priest of the Society of Jesus. Dillingen, at the Academic Press, 1648.”

**65.** The Bambergers and others commonly call the writer Anonymous, because his name is not displayed on the title page. Yet it is so easy to point him out that, scarcely having read two pages, I immediately discovered that the work was composed by our Melchior Inchofer, a native of Vienna, admitted into the Society at Rome in 1607 and commended in the *Bibliotheca of Writers* for his “manifold learning.”

From elsewhere he is known as a man of somewhat acute intellect, much labor, and extensive writing, but whose style—because of excessive concision and frequently pointed, highly compressed sentences—is too involved and consequently rather obscure. This is immediately apparent, at least in the work under discussion.

That he himself composed the aforesaid Life is entirely clear from his frequent citations of his own works, especially the *Ecclesiastical Annals of Hungary*, cited by us elsewhere. He published its first and only volume at Rome in 1644. In that same year, following a recommendation from his friend Leo Allatius, he obtained permission from the Reverend Father Hyacinthus Serronus, companion of the Most Reverend Master, to publish a Life of Saint Henry.

Why this was not done at Rome I do not wish to conjecture. Anyone can easily understand that it would not be worthwhile to investigate the matter at greater length for the purposes of the work now before us.

66. Nor was it possible to ascertain whether he himself had sent the autograph manuscript to Germany for printing, with his name suppressed, or whether the editors had obtained it elsewhere and, whether by accident or design, made no mention of the author, dedicating it instead under the name of the Dillingen college to the most illustrious and reverend Melchior Otto, bishop of the imperial church of Bamberg and prince of the Holy Roman Empire, to whom the little book is truly inscribed. However this may have happened, in that same year, 1648, the author ceased to live at Milan on 28 September. I am surprised that, among his many other works—some published under other names, others said to have been prepared by him for the press—this work on Saint Henry was omitted from our Bibliotheca: whether Allegambe and Sothuellus were unaware of it, or whether they did not think the little work worth much, I leave others to investigate. For my part, throughout the entire booklet I found absolutely nothing that would compel me to depart even slightly from what I have already examined, discussed, and defined with whatever degree of probability was possible. I do not deny that I disagree with him on certain points, but I judged that no weight should be assigned to his assertions except insofar as they rest upon the authority of ancient writers. Since, therefore, we have drawn our material solely from those sources, I do not see how his opinions can contribute greatly to settling the controversies that arise here and there. From the whole plan of the booklet it will be easy to perceive what Inchofer intended.

[Col. 0045C] 67. He seems to have kept this in view—not to present a historical and chronological account of the saint’s life and deeds, but a mere Legend, of the kind that we see many of them adorned in these later centuries. These might not improperly be called exhortations to Christian holiness, by which examples of virgins are set before virgins, of married people before married people, of widows before widows, and thus incentives appropriate to people of each individual order are offered. He seems, I say, to have kept this in view: to paint, with a more florid brush, urgent stimuli for Catholic princes in so illustrious a mirror of outstanding virtues. He expresses this sufficiently clearly in his very title, where he presents Saint Henry as “illustrious in religion, prudence, fortitude, chastity, clemency, and other heroic examples, for admiration [Col. 0045D] and imitation.” In every other respect Inchofer far surpassed the Anonymous author in this: he arranged the saint’s deeds in at least some sort of order, whereas the other left them entirely confused. Moreover, he subjected to a more exact critical examination matters that the Anonymous author, sometimes too credulously, did not distinguish adequately from popular traditions, as you will find us observing in more than one place. What I miss in Inchofer is this: although he is accustomed to cite certain writers, he nevertheless asserts many things about which one may reasonably doubt whether they rest upon sufficiently reliable evidence. Through the division of the entire work into its chapters, together with our annotations on them wherever necessary, I shall enable you to form a clearer idea of it.

68. We have already said enough about the title, dedication, and Roman approbation [Col. 0046A]; other permissions are also appended, namely that of the Most Reverend Father Mutio Vitelleschi, Superior General, granted at Rome on 12 September 1644, and that of Father Laurentius Keppler, Provincial of Upper Germany, granted at Munich on 18 February 1648. Here now is the order of the chapters. First, then, there is an account of “Saint Henry’s homeland, birth, and education.” This does not concern us; enough has been said elsewhere about the other matters. Inchofer notes as something unusual that the saint was born in 972, on 6 May, “on the second feria” [Monday]. This is sufficiently detailed and sufficiently exact: for in the year 972, when the Dominical Letter was F, 6 May fell on the “second feria.” But we need not quarrel over such minutiae. Whether he was born on that day or another matters little to our purpose, since we are chiefly concerned with elucidating the Anonymous author, whose account, as also Adelbold’s Henry Legend, begins not with the life but with the beginnings of the reign; hence the following chapters do not concern us either, and it will be enough to set out their titles here:

“Chapter II. Henry, placed by his father in charge of the government, administers the realm with extraordinary prudence and piety.

“Chapter III. Henry, binding himself in marriage in accordance with his parents’ vow, preserves his virginity.”

We shall discuss this fully in its proper place.

“Chapter IV. The death of Saint Wolfgang and then of the elder Henry; the succession of the younger Henry and his pursuit of peace.”

69. He divides Chapter V into two parts. The first concerns the fact that “Henry was rebuked by Saint Benedict,” of which the Anonymous author nowhere makes mention. Nor does our author cite the source from which he obtained it, as though the story were sufficiently well known from Leo of Ostia’s *Chronicon*, Book II, chapter [Col. 0046C] 45. In the second part Inchofer rightly disagrees with the Anonymous author, who writes that Saint Wolfgang’s famous prophecy, “POST SEX S. Henrico” [“after six, to Saint Henry”], had already been announced to the king, and applies it so explicitly to his coronation as emperor at Rome that the event would consequently have had to occur around 1007 or 1008. As we also said in its proper place, this seems to indicate clearly that the Anonymous author’s interpretation of the oracle is not very satisfactory. Inchofer therefore judges—and much more correctly—that “when Saint Henry was going to Italy with Otto, in 996, Saint Wolfgang miraculously foretold the kingdom to him.” Let us hear his words on page 22:

“Those who refer this to the empire after he had obtained the kingdom do not consider that there would have been no need for conjecture. For what great thing beyond his hope would it be to foretell the empire so obscurely to a king and Caesar already crowned? The man himself would have named the day on which he would be inaugurated. But since there was no immediate hope of this, while King Otto was still flourishing in life, age, and fortune, and was shortly to be called Emperor in the city, Wolfgang could not have foretold the kingdom to Henry except by the will of Him who holds the times in his hands.”

70. As for what he records in Chapter VI about the determinate votes of the electors, supposedly circumscribed by a definite law under Pope Gregory V and Otto III and applied, at least in Saint Henry’s election, we admit that we cannot accept it for that period. We have explained this sufficiently against Hofmann and others, demonstrating that the saint attained the summit of imperial power by hereditary right of succession. Henschenius set out his own and our view of the origin of the seven electoral princes in his Commentary on Saint Heribert, 16 March, no. 7. Chapters VII and VIII likewise do not concern us. As we have said again, only Adelbold and the Anonymous author need to be elucidated; but everything that Inchofer has in chapters 9, 10, 11, 12, and 13 is accurately described by that author, so we may omit listing it here. Part of Chapter 14 is also taken from Adelbold; to this Inchofer adds “the reform of the churches in Germany” and “the Polish and Flemish war,” which we have tried to connect with their proper periods from Thietmar and others. Chapter 15 proceeds through the monasteries and churches founded or adorned, and through the elevation of the city of Bamberg into a bishopric. On this erection he argues quite appropriately. Nor would I deny that the saint bestowed many gifts upon the convents of Neuburg and Nunburg [Col. 0047B] near Salzburg, although here the author departs from the chronological sequence. But when, on page 65, he relates the previously unknown miracle of Saint Erentrudis’ ashes enclosed in a ring and hung around the neck, although I do not think it should simply be denied, it is certainly surprising that nothing related to this matter appears in the saint’s own Acts, illustrated in volume V of June, beginning on page 580. Inchofer ought certainly to have secured the credibility of the claim by producing evidence for the matter asserted.

71. He pays no more attention to chronological order when he prefaces Chapter 16 with this title: “Henry, accusing Queen Cunegund of adultery, is corrected by a miracle of her innocence.” The event itself has been sufficiently vindicated from the slanders of enemies; but I confess that I have not yet been able to determine with certainty at what particular time it occurred. I leave to his authority whatever he collected in Chapter 27 concerning Gunther and his dealings with Saint Henry. Many matters are connected in Chapter 28 that we have distinguished somewhat more orderly. Chapter 19 pleases me even less, where he brings Benedict VIII into Germany to invite Henry to oppose the rebels and to settle some schism whose origin I do not know; our opinion on these matters is given in § 12, no. 128. Chapter 20 treats of the monastic life embraced at Cluny and Verdun. Since these matters are not alien to Henry’s sanctity, what we have reported from Alberic is sufficient for us. In Chapter 21, among other things, Inchofer reveals his opinion concerning “the prodigious victory attributed by some to the auspices of Saint Henry.” This may considerably clarify what we conjectured in its proper place concerning that famous [Col. 0047D] battle mentioned by the Anonymous author in Chapter 4, which Thietmar deliberately passed over and which we are not yet persuaded to accept. From Chapter 22, the principal point to note is the admonition of Poppo, abbot of Stavelot, by which he turned Saint Henry away from watching theatrical performances and gladiatorial games, while he was paying overly curious attention to such spectacles at Nijmegen. This event, and others of the same kind, deserved to be corroborated by the authority of writers.

72. Next, in Chapter XXIII, comes the arrival of Benedict VIII in Germany. This rests on the testimony of ancient writers with proportionately greater strength, while the earlier journey—or should I say the suppliant flight—of that same pope to the empire for Saint Henry’s assistance rests on weaker and more uncertain foundations. Chapter 24 explains the reconciliation with Saint Heribert of Cologne, and Chapter 25 his prophecy concerning Saint Henry’s death, together with other matters relating to them, which are more fully recorded in the Acts of Saint Meinwerk. The prophecy itself, however, is not there recorded; Rupert of Deutz reported it in the *Life of Heribert*, chapter 8, no. 31, under 14 March, page 488, in these words:

“For you should know that, after my death, he will not complete the course of three years.”

Saint Henry lived until 13 July 1024, while Saint Heribert died on 16 March 1021. Inchofer saw the difficulty; to resolve it, he is forced to move Saint Heribert’s death, contrary to historical fact, to the year 1022. We believe he is plainly mistaken in this. Whether the prophecy is correctly expressed there is not for us to decide; it is certainly absent from the Acts that we are illustrating here. In Chapters 26, 27, 28, and 29 he is occupied at length with the circumstances of the final Italian war, which do not concern us any more, or at least are sufficiently reported in our chronological sequence, as is also the encounter with Robert, king of France, which he describes in Chapter 30. For the deeds of Saints Henry and Meinwerk in Chapter 31, see the chapters assigned elsewhere in Meinwerk’s Acts.

73. The most devout death of the holy emperor follows in Chapter 32. But Inchofer strangely twists both the facts and the words in order to calculate the various periods of Henry’s life, and errs in most of them. Let us give his words:

“He lived thirty years before his reign; twelve years and five months in his reign; ten years as emperor, and as many days beyond four months; to God and himself fifty-three years, if three months with twenty days are subtracted; he died in the twenty-fourth year of the eleventh century, on the second feria.”

I willingly agree with his first and last calculations. He would have expressed the remainder correctly and clearly by saying that the saint lived “in his reign” from 6 June 1002 until 14 February 1014. In that interval there elapsed no more than eleven years, eight months, and as many days. He enjoyed the title “emperor,” or “of Emperor,” from 14 February 1014 until 13 July 1024; from this there arise exactly ten years and five months, less one day. But why Inchofer wishes only “three months with twenty days” to be subtracted from the fifty-three years of his life, I entirely fail to understand. Let him remember that he himself fixed the epoch of the birth in the year 972, “on 6 May, the second feria.” If he consults and counts the figures from that point, he will find two full years beyond fifty-two years of life, with two months and seven days additionally elapsed, so that nearly ten months should be subtracted. But enough has already been said about this above in § 2.

74. Five chapters remain, namely Chapter 33, where, unless I am seriously mistaken, Inchofer counts among fables “the appearance of a demon at the funeral,” or at the final struggle of the dying saint, “and the accusation before the tribunal of God.” Add to these the weighing of Saint Lawrence’s chalice and similar matters, which we discussed in their proper place. These seem more akin to the pious dream of a good and simple hermit than to historical truth, and are supported by no ancient authority. Perhaps, through poetic license, painters or sculptors symbolically sketched such things—examples of which are exceedingly common—and, according to the understanding of those centuries, subsequently gave them the appearance of genuine history, worthy of representation in the very mausoleum of Saints Henry and Cunegund.

In Chapter 34 are recounted certain “public monuments of piety and religion that were erected,” together with other pious works performed by Henry. All these matters, as well as “the illustrious miracles performed by the saint after death,” his “apparitions,” the diploma of his canonization granted by Pope Eugene III, and the remaining material collected in the last three chapters, have been reported and explained by us somewhat more fully in their proper places. Let what has been said about Inchofer’s work suffice. In the paragraphs that follow we shall present in order the thread of our Commentary, which we began and carried forward some time ago, after first setting out those matters that deserve somewhat more careful examination and more forceful confirmation in order to vindicate the saint’s principal crown of glory.

§ VIII. Saint Henry’s chastity preserved in marriage with the holy virgin Cunegund

75. Although I said above that there are many things in the Anonymous author of the *Life of Saint Henry* that I do not consider wholly admissible, I certainly cannot tolerate having what he relates in chapters 21 and 27 attacked: namely, that the chief and most enduring glory of the most holy couple, “Henry and Cunegund,” throughout so many centuries has been that both carried undefiled and unblemished virginity with them to the tomb and to heaven.

I do not undertake here to mention or refute the ancient songs of lament and the old satires of heterodox writers against this miracle of continence. One must contend with arguments, not calumnies or insults. I turn to more recent opponents. Leibniz unjustly disparaged this part of the history in § 30 of his Introduction to the *Brunswicenses Scriptores*, in these words:

“We cannot doubt that [Saint Henry] was a great and good man; his deeds do not permit us to do so. Later writers have reported that he practiced voluntary virginity in marriage with his wife Cunegund, but his contemporaries do not exhibit even the slightest trace of this opinion, so that it cannot be trusted to any considerable degree.”

Struvius praises Leibniz and agrees with him on page 388; I agree with both. It is plainly evident that Leibniz treated the matter very superficially, since he wrongly attributes Saint Henry’s canonization to Innocent III—perhaps so that he might remove the papal testimony concerning his preserved virginity to the thirteenth century. But it has already been shown above that the holy emperor obtained the honors of the saints nearly sixty years earlier, namely in 1145.

76. But “his contemporaries do not exhibit even the slightest trace of this opinion.” Whom can Leibniz mean by “contemporaries” here? Perhaps Adelbold? But only a fragment of that work survives. Thietmar? The learned man knew that Thietmar died six full years before Henry, and thus that, while the saint was alive, this matter could not have come to his attention if it was first disclosed at the end of Henry’s life. It would not be easy to produce other contemporary writers.

If he appeals to the chronographers who followed soon afterward—Otto, Hermann, and the others named elsewhere—he does an injustice to the saint by wishing Henry’s affairs to be judged by witnesses who scarcely, as the proverb goes, tasted them with their first lips. But, they say, the Saxon Chronographer is silent about this matter, and the Hildesheim Annals are silent as well. Certainly they are. Yet the silence of these and other writers of the twelfth century is confronted by the positive assertion of a writer of that same century, namely Gotfrid of Viterbo, in Pistorius, volume II, column 484; his verses will be found at the end of this treatise.

It is also confronted by the most positive declaration of the same period by the pope, expressed in explicit terms in the canonization bull recently cited, which testifies that “Saint Henry, even while lying in a legitimate marriage bed, preserved the integrity of chastity to the end of his life.” The pontiff would certainly not have declared this had he not received legitimate proof of it from the people of Bamberg. Therefore, the silence of that chronographer and ten others of the same kind can do no harm, since it is outweighed by an older and better attested assertion.

77. If Leibniz places less trust in the papal diploma, I have something he cannot reject: the explicit testimony of Leo of Marsica, otherwise Cardinal-Bishop of Ostia, in the *Chronicle of Cassino*. It is much older than the cited diploma, indeed close to the age of Saint Henry himself, since its author was a writer of the eleventh century. Angelo de Nuce, the most recent editor of the *Chronicle*, says that Leo “began his account from the foundation of the monastery and carried it down to the time when the church was dedicated and inaugurated by Alexander II.” This occurred, they report, in 1071. Thus you can clearly see how little removed from the saint was the writer whose speaking authority we judge far more weighty than the silence of all the writers of that and the following century.

Hear Leo’s words, Book II, chapter 46:

“Beyond all the other goodnesses or virtues that the same emperor is said to have possessed from God, he is reported to have lived most chastely, so that, when he came to the moment of death, in the presence of the bishops and abbots and of the relatives of Cunibunda [Cunegund], his wife, and having handed her over to them, he is reported to have said—or rather, may he be reported to have said: ‘Receive back the virgin whom you entrusted to me.’”

Leibniz himself praises the author of the *Life of Saint Meinwerk*. “The *Life of Meinwerk*,” he says, “although written only in the following century—and therefore in the twelfth—nevertheless contains much useful material for learning about the affairs of the bishop’s contemporaries and for understanding the deeds of emperors and princes, since it does not omit synods and other ecclesiastical matters.”

78. If this most diligent writer deserves belief in all the matters that pertain to “learning about the deeds of emperors and princes,” I do not think he should be rejected in that part where he gives, in very explicit words, testimony concerning the most chaste marriage of Saints Henry and Cunegund, being equally close to all the events he narrates. Here, then, is not merely a “trace” of the opinion rejected by Leibniz, but a new testimony faithfully “exhibited.”

This is how he speaks in our edition, Chapter 2, no. 9; in Leibniz’s work, no. 12, page 521:

“In that same year—namely 1002—when the new king was celebrating the Nativity of Saint Lawrence in the city of Paderborn, Lady Chunigund, who was thought to be his wife but in reality was his sister in the pursuit of chastity, received there from the aforesaid Willigis, archbishop of Mainz, the royal consecration.”

These words are extremely clear and, unless I am greatly mistaken, decisive. They are not arguments “handed down by later writers,” as Leibniz claimed, but evidence “exhibited” by contemporaries and near-contemporaries. The silence of contemporary writers, if any should perhaps still survive somewhere, could not harm them in the slightest. Thus Leibniz’s cold phrase, “later writers have reported,” as though it meant that this pious belief had first arisen in recent centuries, is thoroughly weakened and overturned.

79. I shall say no more here, since what has already been alleged is entirely sufficient to refute the statements—put forward, to speak as mildly as possible, rather carelessly—by that distinguished scholar, who was also our friend while he lived. They would have been better omitted there, since they were intruded at an inappropriate point, apparently to display learning, especially since in the work under discussion there—namely the work of Adelbold, bishop of Utrecht, which we described above—I found not a word concerning “voluntary virginity” practiced by Saint Henry “in marriage with his wife Cunegund.”

It would certainly be desirable that all sacred ecclesiastical history should be consolidated and established upon foundations so firm that the slanders of hostile critics might be barred and utterly extinguished. For a long time now, non-Catholic scholars have learned, from this work of ours on the Acts of the Saints, that historical truths are distinguished so carefully from matters admitted at times with excessive readiness on the basis of light popular tradition that they may safely trust our sincerity: we will not rashly admit anything that has not been established on solid historical foundations.

Therefore, let holy Mother Catholic Church remain in possession of this claim, and may she never cease to exalt and proclaim to her faithful children that rare example of virginal continence amid so many temptations—or rather, that miracle of divine grace—which Saint Edward of England likewise exhibited in the same century.

80. Having thus discussed and established these matters modestly and without giving offense to the most illustrious and renowned man, whom we esteemed highly, I ask forgiveness if I do not receive with equal moderation the “leisure”—or, more correctly, the “Gundlingian dreams”—which I hear were printed in German in 1706. I was able to read the summary, received from a friend, only with indignation, execrating and wondering that in Saxony itself a Saxon professor should have exposed to the eyes of the common people, in the vernacular, such immodest jests against the most august Saxon prince, contrary to the clearest historical evidence and to the consistent testimony of so many centuries. I believe that even Lutherans themselves, at least those of sound judgment, must detest them as foul inventions fit only for Vulcan.

The man, as I hear, though not uneducated, dares to abuse his “leisure” in order to spew forth, with an insufficiently disciplined pen, calumnies against heavenly Augustuses and to stain their most chaste marriage with certain filthy sarcastic attacks. He describes the holy emperor “as a sick, impotent man, etc., a good and simple man, granting everything at the prayers of his ambitious and cunning wife with disgraceful complaisance.” He attacks Saint Cunegund with various insults and quite openly represents her as an adulteress who, while her husband was absent on military expeditions, used the damnable familiarity of certain bishops, “etc.”

81. Marvel, I beg you, at these “Gundlingian leisures.” Let us call them mere idleness, vulgar jokes, old-womanish satires, trifles and nonsense more empty than Sicilian boasts. All learned people to whom we write this—and even non-Catholics—will surely acknowledge them as such. Among them, these little songs of abuse deserve pity rather than applause, just like the latest historical thesis of another Lutheran—or rather, the most foolish little fable imaginable—namely: “The marriage of Saint Henry the Emperor with Saint Cunegund was not virginal at all times.” What is delirium, if this is not?

“But,” he says, “documents are found from which it is clear that public prayers were ordered to obtain fertility for Henry’s marriage bed.” What then? What if the people of Bamberg freely admit and acknowledge this? Why should that have been forbidden in Saint Henry’s case more than at another time? Has he ever read anywhere that the continence of the most chaste couple was publicly known, since Saint Henry himself, already close to death, was the first to disclose it, returning his virgin wife to her relatives?

One imposture drives on another. He has unearthed, apparently, authentic documents by which it could be demonstrated that a daughter was born from Saints Henry and Cunegund. A new monstrosity—or rather, a tasty dish—which should be thoroughly chewed not by me but by the “idle Gundling,” so that he may at least learn from his fellow countryman that the most holy emperor was not impotent, as he impudently portrays him.

82. Closely related to that illustrious miracle of preserved virginity in marriage is the matter that the Anonymous author relates in Chapter 21 concerning Saint Henry’s jealousy and the proof of her innocence by his holy wife through glowing ploughshares. This too could be gnawed at by malicious people with almost the same contrived argument as above, on the basis of the silence of contemporary writers.

But in truth this matter was sufficiently vindicated long ago by the often-mentioned Hofmann in the *Bamberg Annals*, columns 52 and 53, and by Henschenius on 3 March, in the preliminary Commentary on the Acts of Saint Cunegund, § 2. To them, so that I do not repeat what has already been done, I refer the readers—and above all Gundling, that savage scourge of the most chaste empress.

The only point that stricter critics might miss in this story is that the precise time cannot be identified, nor the place where the event occurred. Hofmann designates Bamberg itself, the delight of both saints, as the arena of the triumph; and he assigns the year 1017, which I suspect he derived from Bamberg documents. Whether everything fits that year most appropriately may be gathered, to some extent, from the chronological sequence of Saint Henry’s life that we shall shortly set out. For us it is enough that the event itself should not be so easily called into question, since, as Hofmann testifies, such authentic records of it survive to this day. Since I do not see them being so strongly challenged, it is enough to have vindicated the credibility of the Legend in this part as well.

83. I did not think that the principal controversy discussed above—concerning the undefiled continence preserved in marriage by both most holy spouses—could be left at that. I had noticed that it could be attacked, or at least assailed, by Koelerian plausible quibbles: on the one hand, by the alleged or genuine prayers for marital fertility, and on the other by the supposed mention somewhere of royal offspring, if heaven wills it. I therefore thought that nothing should be omitted to silence not only heterodox detractors but also more audacious Catholic slanderers. I did not stop until I had completely uncovered the source from which, as I finally discovered plainly, such varied, contradictory, and poorly connected claims had flowed.

For this purpose I had all the archives, registers, obituaries, and choir books of the Bamberg church examined, to determine whether the older writings offered any occasion for so enormous a calumny. Here again, because of his outstanding devotion to Saint Henry, the often-praised Reverend Father Rector Nicolaus Pottu diligently contributed his assistance. From his letter to me, written this year, 1723, I shall make you understand the matter as clearly as possible and enable you to see, more clearly than in midday light, that the story about prayers for fertility is a pure invention, and that “royal offspring” did not then exist in reality any more than it does now.

I shall present the whole matter exactly as it occurred, in Pottu’s own plain and candid words.

84. When he had learned from my letters of the calumnies that had been raised, he replied in these very words:

“After receiving your Reverendness’s previous letter, my first concern was to investigate the prayer which certain malicious persons falsely imagine and claim to have been composed and prescribed at the command of Saint Henry himself, to implore and obtain fertility for his marriage, so that by this means they might attack the perpetual chastity of him and his holy wife.

“I found in the custody of the imperial church a very ancient book, written—as all the signs show—while the holy emperor was still alive. The enclosed sheet shows the form of the book. The outer front part of the cover represents the image of Saint Peter the Apostle; the back represents Saint Paul. The pages are parchment. The title of the book is *Libellus Gradualis* [Little Gradual Book]. Then follow the Graduals, beginning with Advent.

“When one comes to Easter, there are Litanies written in the same form and with the same type of letters as the enclosed sheet displays. In those Litanies, after an invocation had been made for the supreme pontiff, Emperor Henry, and Queen Cunegund, an invocation is also made for the most noble royal offspring.

“But it is clear that the calumny receives no support from this invocation”—as will shortly be demonstrated somewhat more fully, in order to silence the mouths of malicious chatterers.

The letter continues:

85. “I could find no other prayer for obtaining fertility for the marriage of the most holy emperor, although, together with the Reverend Custodian, I carefully examined the second part of the Gradual, various Missals and Breviaries written in Saint Henry’s time, and some written after his blessed passing. Nor could Mr. Eppenauer find anything at Saint Michael’s Mount.”

Here, then, is the sole source of all these inventions, exposed from every side and easily disposed of. The whole matter could not be reported with greater candor and sincerity than in these familiar letters written back and forth, whose words we are setting out.

I can scarcely bring myself to believe that the cited codex belongs to Saint Henry’s own age, although I readily admit that it may have been copied from some older exemplar. Indeed, I believe that the formulas of prayer inserted into the aforesaid Litanies—the point on which the whole matter turns—are much older than the saint himself and were used in German churches both in the preceding centuries and in those that followed. Thus other prayers are now in use besides those received by the universal Roman Church and by other churches.

Pottu rightly observes, however, that no support for the common calumny remains in these formulas, however much the opponents of Henry’s chastity may seem to wrangle from them. We therefore freely offer them everything that, even remotely, provided material for disseminating and embellishing these calumnies, without concealing a single detail. For this reason we reproduce the Litanies themselves here, insofar as this was possible in our printing, to be explained in the following paragraph.

**LITANY AT MASS ON HOLY EASTER DAY**

86. **Christ conquers. Christ reigns.**

Christ commands. | |

Hear us, O Christ. | Life to the supreme pontiff and universal pope. |

Savior of the world. | Help him. |

Saint Peter. | Help him. |

Saint Paul. | Help him. |

Saint Andrew. | Help him. |

Hear us, O Christ. | Life and victory to Henry, crowned by God, the great and peaceful emperor. |

Redeemer of the world. | Help him. |

Saint Michael. | Help him. |

Saint Gabriel. | Help him. |

Saint Raphael. | Help him. |

Saint John. | Help him. |

Saint Stephen. | Help him. |

Hear us, O Christ. | Salvation and life to Queen Cunegund. |

Saint Mary. | Help her. |

Saint Radegund. | Help her. |

Saint Gertrude. | Help her. |

Hear us, O Christ. | Salvation and life to the most noble royal offspring. |

Saint Clement. | Help him. |

Saint Vitus. | Help him. |

Saint Pantaleon. | Help him. |

Hear us, O Christ. | Salvation and life to N., the peaceful leader. |

Saint Maurice. | Help him. |

Saint Lambert. | Help him. |

Saint Gereon. | Help him. |

Hear us, O Christ. | Salvation and life to N., the bishop, and to the entire congregation of N. |

Saint Sylvester. | Help him. |

Saint Martin. | Help him. |

Hear us, O Christ. | Life and victory to all judges and to the entire army of Christians. |

Saint George. | Help them. |

Saint Emmeram. | Help them. |

Saint Sebastian. | Help them. |

**Christ conquers, Christ reigns, Christ commands.** | |

King of kings. | Christ conquers; Christ reigns. |

Our glory. | Christ conquers; Christ reigns. |

Our mercy. | Christ conquers; Christ reigns. |

Our hope. | Christ conquers; Christ reigns. |

Our help. | Christ conquers; Christ reigns. |

Our victory. | Christ conquers; Christ reigns. |

Our light, way, truth, and life. | Christ conquers. |

Our strength and justice. | Christ conquers. |

Our prudence and temperance. | Christ conquers. |

Our deliverance and redemption. | Christ conquers. |

Our unconquerable weapons. | Christ conquers. |

Our impregnable wall. | Christ conquers. |

Our defense and exaltation. | Christ conquers. |

To him alone be dominion, glory, and power through immortal ages of ages. Amen. | |

To him alone be praise, honor, and rejoicing through endless ages of ages. Amen. | |

To him alone be virtue, strength, and victory throughout all ages of ages. Amen. | |

Christ, hear us. Three times. | |

Lord, have mercy. | |

§ IX. The Bamberg Litanies vainly attacked

[Col. 0055C] 87. You now have the alleged mystery of iniquity exposed and revealed to the world: the malicious enemies not only of Henry’s continence but of all chastity, so highly esteemed in the Roman Church, have vainly persuaded themselves that it lay hidden in the Bamberg Litanies.

All the characters have been reproduced, at least insofar as this was possible, after abbreviations were excluded from the typography. It did not seem worth the trouble to cut them in copper, since the crux of the controversy does not depend upon them. This little Gradual Book is oblong and of a narrow format, only slightly exceeding the columns set out here; all the words have been arranged according to syllables and lines, with no mark omitted or transposed.

The entire Litany fills approximately three pages, and from it all the material for these suppositions and calumnies has been drawn. We could not divide it here according to the format of the little book; it was sufficient to reproduce it faithfully in its entirety.

The title mentioned above, *LIBELLUS GRADUALIS*, is neatly painted on the first page in large rubricated letters, as they are commonly called. The letters differ little from modern forms, except for E, G, A, and D. The interior title is likewise rendered in red capitals, insofar as our types permit. Thus all the initial letters are illuminated, as is also the letter X whenever the name of Christ the Savior occurs, whose monogram we believe to be sufficiently well known.

Anyone who takes the trouble to inspect the autograph itself at Bamberg and compare it with this edition will be able to testify that we have discharged our duty of fidelity completely.

88. Furthermore, I examined the draft sent to me and printed here [Col. 0056A] so rigorously, point by point, that I left nothing untouched without immediately bringing it to the attention of the Bambergers. In the first place, although these Litanies are still preserved at Bamberg, they do not appear to have been written for the use of that church itself, since invocations of its founder and foundress would undoubtedly have been added. Moreover, Saint [Henry] is incorrectly designated “emperor crowned by God,” while Cunegund is given merely the title of queen, although it is certain that both were inaugurated by Pope Benedict VIII at Rome on the same day, in 1014, with the imperial diadem placed upon them.

But Koeler’s chief argument for the existence of “most noble royal offspring” I have continued to press still more sharply, concluding against the Bambergers, as they say, ad hominem, by something like the following reasoning: It is no less certain that in these Litanies God is invoked for “the salvation and life of the most noble royal offspring” than it is certain that He is invoked for the life and victory of Saint Henry and for the salvation and life of Saint Cunegund; and the latter is undisputed among you—why, then, should not the former be so as well? Prayers for the spouses, as living persons, are there offered to God; therefore “the most noble royal offspring” must also have been living, together with the conclusions Koeler draws from this.

Pottuvius, as we say, took up these propositions—put forward by me for the sake of exercise—and learnedly disentangled and dissolved them, clarifying everything in three responses, so that Koeler has grounds for accepting the result. I shall also reproduce his words faithfully.

89. “If Koeler wishes to infer from the words of the Litanies found in the manuscript Gradual, ‘SALVATION AND LIFE OF THE MOST NOBLE ROYAL OFFSPRING’ [Col. 0056C], that at least a daughter was born from the marriage of Saints Henry and Cunegund, he does not infer this correctly.”

Here is his first response: “Because these Litanies had very probably already been in use before the time of Saint Henry in the churches of Germany, as common formulas for making supplication for the Pope, the Emperor, the Empress, and so forth. We do not indeed deny that they were written or copied out in Saint Henry’s time; both the form of the letters then in use and the expression of the names Henry and Cunegund, for whom supplication is made as living persons, persuade us of this. We say only that, after the erection of the Bamberg church, they were copied or transcribed from another exemplar, with the names of Henry and Cunegund then added as those actually reigning [Col. 0056D]. Nor do we say this without grounds, since the entire Gradual Book—of which there are two parts, one winter and the other summer—was copied from exemplars customarily used in churches. We therefore rightly maintain that the Litanies, which are part of the Gradual, were likewise common to other churches at that time and were taken from exemplars belonging to them. It does not, therefore, follow correctly from these Litanies that at least a daughter was born from the marriage of Saints Henry and Cunegund, since they are merely a common formula.”

90. Pottuvius presses the point appropriately, and insists on it still more in the following manner: “But if you contend that these Litanies were not taken from other exemplars, but were first composed for the Bamberg church itself, let us grant [Col. 0057A] that this was so—although you do not prove it. Even so, I show from the Litanies themselves that the saintly spouses had no child at the time when the Litanies were written. For if they had had one, either the child’s name would have been expressed in the Litanies, just as the names of Henry and Cunegund were expressly given, or at least the sex would have been indicated, whether it was a son or a daughter.

“For just as in the supplication for Saint Henry it says, ‘Help him,’ and in the supplication for Saint Cunegund, ‘Help her,’ so, if a royal daughter had then existed, it ought to have said, ‘Help her.’ Since the abbreviated form alone is given—‘Help ill.’—and ‘ill.’ signifies neither him nor her, but is indifferent to either, this is a sign that at that time there was neither daughter nor son. It therefore remains that this is a common formula [Col. 0057B], capable of applying equally to a male or a female. This is confirmed by the formulas that follow in the same Litanies, where N. is used; these are common formulas for making supplication for any dukes, bishops,” and so forth.

91. “Furthermore,” Pottuvius continues in the same vein, “even if a supplication for ‘THE MOST NOBLE ROYAL OFFSPRING’ is found in the Litanies, how do you prove that, when no child existed, that supplication was sung, rather than omitted in such circumstances? Certainly, although these Litanies contain a formula of supplication for an Empress, nevertheless, if the Emperor had not yet married, or had become a widower, the formula of supplication for the Empress would unquestionably be omitted in either case.

“Thus, even if a formula for the most noble royal offspring is included in the Litanies, when there was no offspring it seems that this formula was omitted in the singing of the Litanies [Col. 0057C]. Unless, perhaps, there had been some expectation or indication of the marriage’s fertility: for then faithful subjects are accustomed to hope and pray to God that the fruit may ripen on the tree and the bud in the shell. The Bambergers, however, could have hoped for this and rightly offered such good wishes for spouses of such distinction, whose vow of continence they did not know.”

It may be added that the formula immediately following, “salvation and life for N., the peaceful leader,” must unquestionably be passed over when the emperor himself is commanding the armies. In the same way, no one would dream that the second formula, for the local bishop, or the first, for the Roman Pontiff, was sung when either see was vacant. Let Koeler consult the Church’s present practice, which has remained constant for so many centuries, and he will see that what has been said here [Col. 0057D] is entirely true.

92. Pottuvius does not stop here, but presses another response or argument in the following terms: “Without imputing dishonor to the most holy and prudent Emperor”—Koeler, together with Gundling, will not deny these predicates—“it cannot be asserted that he fathered at least a daughter by his marriage. For either he fathered her before the foundation of the Bamberg bishopric, or after it; neither alternative can be asserted without dishonoring the Emperor.

“In the first place, it cannot be said that he fathered her before the foundation, which occurred in the sixth or seventh year after the millennium. This is gathered from the address of Saint Henry that he delivered at the assembly in Frankfurt to Saint Willigis, archbishop of Mainz, and the other archbishops and bishops present [Col. 0058A], as reported by Bishop Ditmar of Merseburg, a contemporary historian, in Book VII, p. 67: ‘For the sake of future recompense,’ said the holy Emperor, ‘I have chosen Christ as my heir, since no hope remains for me of acquiring offspring.’

“But if Saint Henry fathered a daughter before the foundation of the bishopric, how could he truthfully say that no hope remained for him of acquiring offspring? Could not the assembly of the Fathers have objected: ‘How can no hope of acquiring offspring in your present marriage remain to you, when in the few years during which you have lived in marriage you have fathered a daughter?’ He therefore poorly serves the dignity of the holy Emperor who attributes the procreation of offspring to him before the foundation of the bishopric.

[Col. 0058B] 93. “Furthermore, without disgracing that same Saint, it cannot be asserted that a daughter was born to him after the foundation of the bishopric. In clear and explicit words, before that most celebrated assembly of prelates, he affirms that no hope remains for him of acquiring offspring. Who, then, without dishonoring so wise and circumspect an Emperor, would say that he nevertheless fathered a daughter after such a solemn affirmation?

“Unless a strong reason is brought forward—and none is brought forward—the dignity of so great an Emperor requires us to believe that he spoke truthfully when, in a solemn declaration, he affirmed that no hope remained for him of acquiring offspring. But who deprived him of all hope? Who, except he himself, by a voluntary vow of continence made in honor of God and ratified by his most chaste wife? He could say with Jephthah (Judges 11:35): ‘For I have opened my mouth to the Lord, and I cannot do otherwise,’ than to preserve perpetual continence.

“What else do the words immediately following, spoken by the Emperor at the assembly, imply: ‘And what I possessed as my chief treasure, and myself, together with what has already been acquired or is to be acquired, I offered long ago in the secret of my mind as a sacrifice to the Father unbegotten’? What else, I ask, do those words imply than a vow of chastity, by which the most holy Emperor, following the Savior’s counsel (Matthew 19:12), ‘made himself a eunuch for the sake of the kingdom of heaven,’ and offered to God as a sacrifice his inclination to leave behind him one like himself? In this he may be compared with the great Abraham: Abraham was ready to sacrifice Isaac, his son already born to him, whereas this Emperor sacrificed to the Most High, with the innermost devotion of his mind, the hope of a son and heir who might be born to him?”

94. We refer all these questions, sufficiently concise and pointed, back to Koeler, so that in his forthcoming historical theses he may provide suitable answers. Yet Pottuvius does not end here; this is his third response:

“If Saint Henry fathered a daughter and arranged for public prayers to be instituted for her in the Bamberg church, as Koeler seems to wish to prove from the cited Litanies, it is morally impossible that the universal conviction could have prevailed in the world, and especially at Bamberg—as in fact it did—that Saints Henry and Cunegund had preserved perpetual virginal continence in their marriage.

“For if Koeler is so perceptive that, after seven hundred years, he can scent royal offspring in these Litanies, how is it that the Bambergers, who sang those Litanies in Saint Henry’s time and in the following years down to the present, who retained them in the Gradual Book, examined them repeatedly, and displayed them for examination by others—how, I ask, did none of them ever think of such a daughter or draw that conclusion from them?

“Were they all, for seven centuries, so foolish that no one grasped the mystery hidden in the Litanies, which Koeler now at last reveals to the world? And if the Bambergers knew of Henry’s daughter in Saint Henry’s time and publicly prayed for her in the Litanies, how and when could they have slipped into the belief that Saints Henry and Cunegund had mutually agreed to preserve perpetual continence in their marriage?” [Col. 0059A]

95. Pottuvius is an importunate questioner. “How,” he asks, “could the entire empire and the whole Christian world over so wide an area have been brought to the same opinion? How could the celebrated Order of Saint Benedict, after Saint Henry’s death, have received Saint Cunegund into the monastery of Kaufungen as a virgin, and thereafter consistently treated and honored her as such, if it knew—as it could not have failed to know—that she had been the mother of a royal daughter in her marriage?

“In what century, and around what year, was the memory of this daughter obliterated, and in its place the belief in the spouses’ virginal continence arise? From a rescript of Eugenius III it is clear that by the twelfth century it was already believed, and confirmed by legitimate testimony, [Col. 0059C] that Saint Henry, even while joined in a lawful marriage, preserved the integrity of chastity until the end of his life. If, in the immediately preceding century, Saint Henry fathered a daughter in his marriage and public supplication was made for her in the Litanies, who could persuade himself that in so short a time the memory of the most noble royal offspring could perish among everyone, and that the fertile spouses could come to be regarded as virgins?

“Even if offspring never appears in a particular marriage, people are nevertheless with difficulty brought to believe that such spouses are childless through the virtue of perpetual continence; rather, they attribute it to natural sterility or to other natural impediments. Still less would people close in time to the holy spouses have allowed themselves to be led to believe in their perpetual continence if they had received a daughter in their marriage, since this could certainly not have remained hidden from people so close to that age.” [Col. 0059D]

96. “It must therefore be admitted that the apostolic legates sent by Eugenius III to Bamberg in the twelfth century to investigate the truth of the matter, as well as the many religious and discerning men, could not have been led to believe and attest to the integrity of Saint Henry’s chastity until the end of his life if he had either fathered a daughter in his marriage or if they had lacked certain, entirely trustworthy signs, testimonies, and proofs of that integrity—proofs in which Christian piety could rightly rest and could enjoy the memory of so illustrious an example with consolation.

“But since the enemy of the human race most indignantly endures the public presentation in the Church of such illustrious images of continence for veneration and imitation, he acts in fury and envy to obscure them with hideous colors, just as he once attempted through the iconoclasts to remove the images of Christ and the Saints from human eyes, lest people, by looking upon them, should be stirred to imitate the excellent deeds of those Saints.” [Col. 0060A]

What effrontery, my Koeler! Yet it is you alone whom these darts strike, since you rashly cast this matter into the midst of the discussion, and the other arguments have already amply refuted it above. You alone are wounded by these darts, and everything debated in this entire paragraph is directed at you: you kneaded this dough yourself, and you must eat it all. For us, what remains is to arrange chronologically, according to our purpose, the principal deeds of the most holy Emperor.

§ X. The principal deeds of Saint Henry restored to chronological order, from the beginning of his reign to the foundation of the Bamberg church.

[Col. 0060B]

97. As for what was done by the most holy Emperor before he assumed the reins of government, since neither the writers of the Lives nor Ditmar or any others have recorded it, it is futile for us to seek its order. Our sequence begins with the death of Otto III. Nor do we scrutinize every detail, but only the principal or more illustrious events—those relating to the Saint’s holiness and to the other affairs carried out throughout the period of his reign and empire—which have indeed been partly remembered by the compiler of the well-known Life, or rather panegyric, the Anonymous, but so confusedly interwoven that nowhere does it appear to which year they should be assigned. The author was so inattentive to chronology that, when he gives a year, he usually departs from the correct sequence.

An example occurs at the very beginning of the Life just mentioned, which he starts in this way: “In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1001, in the year 1752 from the founding of the City, when Otto, still a boy, died at Rome and the throne of the kingdom was vacant, while discussion was taking place about appointing a successor, everyone’s votes, by divine direction, inclined toward the man who was then regarded as the most powerful in the kingdom.”

Almost all the chronological data here are wrong. Otto III did not die in 1001, but in 1002; nor was it the year 1752 from the founding of the City, but more probably 1754; and this Otto did not die at Rome, but at Paterna or Paternus, a fortress in Roman Campania, in the territory of the Church and on the coast, along the Tyrrhenian shore, where there had formerly been the younger Pliny’s villa, according to Holstenius, whatever slight deviation from the site may be found in other writers.

98. From such an opening it is easy to understand what may be expected concerning the arrangement of the sequence of events [Col. 0060D]. Our chief concern will be to restore the truth of events to a correct chronological order, insofar as this can be done, occasionally adding and assigning to their proper years the Emperor’s very generous donations and privileges to churches and monasteries. Since several writers have already recorded these, it will be enough for us to touch on them in passing.

You will find an indication of this almost lavish imperial generosity from the beginning of his reign in Mabillon’s Benedictine Annals under the year 1002, p. 159, no. 26, where he gave a certain plot within the walls of Regensburg to the monastery of Altaich. In the following years he bestowed still more numerous and greater benefits upon the same monastery, the charters for which Gretser prints at the end of the widely circulated Life, beginning on p. 65.
