Nor are there lacking examples of Henry’s munificence in Hund’s Salzburg Metropolis; see p. 140 and elsewhere. The privileges and donations of Saint Henry relating to Westphalia or Saxony have been distributed among their respective years and explained more fully and carefully by our Nicholas Schaten in the Paderborn Annals, Book IV, beginning on p. 362; it is enough to have indicated this here. The Life of Saint Meinwerk lists the gifts themselves rather than the instruments. The aforementioned Mabillon has further material on p. 161. We shall now begin the sequence outlined above.

99. As regards the first three years of Saint Henry’s reign, there will be no great difficulty, since the aforementioned Adelbold, bishop of Utrecht, an eyewitness to almost all the events, has distinguished and ordered the events of that period quite appropriately [Col. 0061B]. I therefore do not think Alberic’s Chronicle should be heeded at all when, in that year 1003 alone, while the older authorities are silent, it seems to invent rather than truthfully narrate extraordinary stories about the pagan Wends or Winids, peoples supposedly subjugated by Saint Henry at that time. Alberic applies the following anecdote to their kings:

“Henry made these peoples tributary, so that at every solemn occasion on which he was crowned, four of their kings carried to the kitchen on their shoulders, by means of two poles inserted through four rings, the cauldron in which the meats were cooked.”

Let the responsibility for this rest with its author.

Much sounder are the matters carefully recorded by Adelbold, who comprehensively treated all the deeds of the holy Emperor from the death of his predecessor Otto III up to the Slavonic war, reviewing the Acts of Saint Henry after his first expedition into Italy. If only these had been transmitted to us in the same method and with the same reliability all the way to the end of his life! It is regrettable even in this respect that our fragment is lacking in the material relating to the aforementioned war. [Col. 0061C]

100. Hofmann did not consult this source when, in his Bamberg Annals, beginning at col. 35, he mixed together many matters wholly alien to truth and correct chronology. These are completely overturned by comparison with Adelbold’s account, just as is the fictitious election of Saint Henry by the seven Electors of the Empire, who were unknown in Germany at that time and for many years afterward. We leave the discussion and refutation of these matters here to others.

He is somewhat more accurate in reviewing what he reported, beginning at col. 40, concerning the most munificent foundation of the Bamberg church; we shall examine this more fully below. We return to Adelbold, whose account calls for special attention because, within the span of three years—namely 1002, 1003, and 1004—he compresses events that others, following Ditmar, whose manuscripts were perhaps corrupted by copyists, extend over four years, down to 1005. In their accounts, that first Italian expedition undertaken by Saint Henry, during which miserable Pavia was almost reduced to ashes, is incorrectly assigned to 1005. Adelbold, the Saxon Chronicler, and the Hildesheim Annals most clearly assign it to 1004 [Col. 0062A], as is evident from their celebrated texts. This is also confirmed plainly by the festival celebrations held throughout the first three years of Saint Henry’s reign, which can likewise be extracted from Ditmar himself.

101. Meanwhile, he himself begins his sixth book in the following way:

“After the life-giving birth of the undefiled Virgin, when the line of the millennium had been completed and in the fifth place of the cardinal order, at the beginning of its fourth week, in the month of February, which is called purgatorial, a bright morning dawned upon the age. And Henry, king by divine grace, wishing to cleanse the stain of his predecessors and merit eternal forgiveness, having arranged according to his own will all matters pertaining to this, proceeded to his house, where he was accustomed always to refresh himself bodily and where he might be refreshed somewhat in spirit by the food he had long desired. Then, summoning to himself all the leading men of the kingdom, he gave the bishopric of the holy church of Merseburg to his own chaplain Wigbert.”

Ditmar continues by indicating the matters that the Anonymous records in chapters 3 and 4. From his account, the victory won by Saint Henry over the Slavs should be placed before the restoration of the Merseburg church, since that restoration resulted from a celebrated vow made before the victory. It is remarkable that Ditmar does not mention this more explicitly, although he seems to allude to it in the final three lines of the panegyric given above.

Accordingly, in that same year 1004—or perhaps the preceding year, as others maintain—the aforementioned victory was obtained, and the restoration of the Merseburg church followed it. Thus Hermann the Lame speaks under the year 1004:

“King Henry, setting out for Italy, subjugates it to himself. On the very day on which he was crowned, he broke into Pavia and subdued it with sword and fire. Returning from there to Saxony, he subjugated Bohemia and Boleslaus, duke of the Slavs, together with his entire people.” [Col. 0062C]

102. I will not conceal that I have never approved the entire narrative adorned by the Anonymous in chapter 4 and cloaked in so many marvelous portents. Above all, I am compelled by the most urgent argument arising from these circumstances: Ditmar, an eyewitness and writer of all the events then taking place, records with such care and precision the destruction of his Merseburg church, the alienation of its property, and finally its restoration by Saint Henry, yet says nothing of the many miracles gathered there by the writer of the Life. He was never accustomed to conceal in silence matters that he thought might contribute to the glory of so outstanding a benefactor. It must therefore seem almost miraculous that, if such a distinguished victory was won in this manner, he should have passed it over.

To speak frankly about what I think, I suspect that the Anonymous, a good man, transferred to Saint Henry certain matters that perhaps belong to others, or fitted events to dates that do not suit them. Certainly he could never persuade me of the little story in chapter 28 concerning the weighing of the Saint’s merits in a balance. Nor do I approve the other account concerning lameness, found in chapter 24 of the Bamberg copy. All these matters, to put it as mildly as possible, I judge should not be so readily accepted by sensible and learned men [Col. 0063A].

103. I return to Ditmar. After the matters already mentioned, he records a brief winter expedition against the rebellious Boleslaus, the restoration of the rebellious Henry to Henry’s favor, and the flight of his brother Bruno to Saint Stephen, king of Hungary and his brother-in-law. Through Stephen’s intercession Bruno was eventually restored to favor.

Ditmar connects these events with what was done by the Saint at Clusae and in the rest of Lombardy, and brings him back through Alemannia and Alsace into Saxony, hostile to Boleslaus. At that time he undoubtedly attacked Boleslaus in war, though this was not the campaign mentioned by the Anonymous in chapter 4. The aforementioned Ditmar gives a far better and fuller account of the expedition beginning on p. 378.

All these events are most correctly assigned by Adelbold and the other authorities cited to the year 1004 [Col. 0063B]. Accordingly, an error must be acknowledged in Ditmar, notwithstanding that Baronius and later writers have generally followed him in this matter. This removes the otherwise inextricable difficulty of properly distinguishing the deeds performed by Saint Henry in the two years 1004 and 1005.

For the Saxon Chronicler has nothing under the year 1005 except the invasion of Poland, during which “alas, he lost many men, returning from there with the bodies of dead commanders and bringing them along with his army.” The Hildesheim Chronicle reports that in that year 1005 the King “stayed for a time in the regions of Saxony” during Lent, but celebrated Easter at Aachen. Add to this what is related in the Life of Saint Meinwerk, chapter 2, no. 11, p. 515, and by Schaten beginning on p. 372.

Whatever else Saint Henry may have done in 1005, it nevertheless seems certain that the beginning of the cited sixth book is thoroughly corrupt, as we shall attempt to demonstrate below from Ditmar himself [Col. 0063C].

104. The Hildesheim Annals, or Chronicle, preface the year 1004 as follows: “And Bruno, the king’s brother, through the intervention of his mother, Lady Gisla, obtained favor”—which is precisely how the aforementioned Life of Saint Meinwerk also speaks at the cited passage.

In my opinion, these events are correctly placed in that year. Against the opinion of Adelbold and others, however, they attribute this to “the intervention of Gisla his mother,” whereas those writers attribute it instead to “Gisela his sister,” who was married to Saint Stephen, king of Hungary. I have so far sought in vain among contemporary writers for the definite year of this marriage.

It was therefore necessary to consult the Ecclesiastical Annals of that kingdom, compiled by our aforementioned Melchior Inchofer. Yet it was impossible to accept his account, since he asserts there that the marriage was contracted in 1005, the twentieth year of Stephen’s reign—a claim that cannot at all be reconciled with the narrative of Adelbold and others. It should rather be said that this Gisela, the Saint’s sister, entered Saint Stephen’s marriage bed in 1004 at the latest.

I prefer what the aforementioned Inchofer adduces to soften somewhat the harsher statements of the German writers, who repeatedly insist that the aforementioned Gisela was granted to the king of Hungary on no other terms or conditions than that he should renounce paganism and receive Christian worship and baptism [Col. 0064A]. From this Saint Henry earned the title “Apostle of the Hungarians.” Here are Inchofer’s words:

105. “Others also wrote with insufficient consideration that Stephen, captivated by Gisela’s beauty as conveyed through messengers and painters, sought her hand in marriage. Yet they say that she rejected him unless, after abandoning the worship of idols, he gave his name to Christ. The king of Hungary accepted the condition in order to obtain the most beautiful girl, and soon, together with his entire kingdom, approached the rites of Christ, taking the name Stephen. Henry, because he had given his sister in marriage and labored for the conversion of the nation, was called the apostle of the Hungarians.

“Among others, Sigebert, Albert Krantzius, and John Cuspinianus seem to have agreed with this story, failing to observe that Stephen, descended from Christian parents of long standing and called by divine prompting, had kept far from such a bargain, while Henry, moved by love for his virtue, willingly favored so advantageous a marriage, which would contribute greatly to the advancement of religion among a people already converted.

“Although there is no doubt that Gisela’s and her brother Henry’s piety and zeal greatly assisted in bringing many more people who were not yet devoted to Christ over to the faith, so that for this reason he may retain the name of Apostle of the Hungarians and she that of their most faithful helper.”

As an incidental observation, it may be noted that from this and other passages of the same history one must refute the disgraceful and unspeakable accusations that Alberic dared to attach to this Queen Gisela under the year 1010.

[Col. 0064C] 106. Finally, concerning the two years just mentioned, 1004 and 1005, I wish that what Struvius not long ago proposed in the Syntagma cited above were true. To resolve the knot that he saw himself unable to untie, he joined the events together in this way, volume I, p. 379:

“Having settled affairs in Germany, he entered Italy in the year 1004, summoned by the Italians. Although Harduinus carefully guarded the approaches, he reached Verona; proceeding from there as far as Brescia and Pavia, where he was kindly received by the entire population, he was crowned king of Italy in the year 1005 by common agreement. After calming the disturbance of the Pavians that had been stirred up against the Germans, he returned to Germany.”

One would say that the first expedition undertaken by Saint Henry lasted almost two full years. Yet, according to Adelbold and Ditmar, it was very brief. The holy Emperor spent Holy Week at Clusae until Easter; then, after rapidly completing his affairs, following the coronation and the disturbances at Pavia, “having celebrated holy Pentecost with devout spiritual piety . . . he hastened to return to his homeland, keeping in mind the injury inflicted upon him by Boleslaus . . . and on the vigil of Saint John [the Baptist] he held a meeting with the Alsatians . . . After this the King came to Mainz, where with his customary devotion he solemnly celebrated the feast of the Apostles.” From there he set out into Saxony against Boleslaus.

The whole sequence of events makes it perfectly clear that his first excursion into Lombardy lasted, from his departure from Bavaria, scarcely three complete months [Col. 0064D].

107. What the same Struvius says, following Sigebert, under the year 1005 is less objectionable: “When Duke Otto died, the duchy of Lotharingia was entrusted to Count Godfrey, son of Godfrey of Ardennes.” Other writers agree sufficiently on this point.

But what he reports under the guidance of that same Sigebert—namely, that in 1010 the Hungarian people, hitherto devoted to idolatry, were then first initiated into baptism together with their king, a claim that so many others have incorrectly followed Hofmann in repeating—must be explained entirely according to the sense of what was said above.

A somewhat more careful investigation of the Bamberg bishopric will be undertaken in the next two years. The synod of Tremonia properly belongs here. Ditmar speaks of it on p. 380; from the beginning you may gather almost everything else:

“A great synod was also held at a place called Throsmunini [Tremonia], where the King, in the presence of his fellow bishops and all those present, complained of many matters pertaining to the holy Church. By their common counsel he then decreed that these things should henceforth be prohibited, and, by the excellent decree of this new institution, that he should be relieved of the heavy burden of his sins, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1005, and in the fourth year of Lord Henry II’s reign, on the day before the Nones of July.”

Leibniz, or rather one of his copyists, supplied from our manuscript codex the names of the bishops and the matters decreed there. Through the copyist’s inadvertence, however, the note from the earlier edition was left standing: “The decree of the synod of Tremonia is lacking,” although the decree itself has been placed immediately beforehand.

Let this be the first period of the Life of Saint Henry.

§ XI. The Bamberg bishopric founded by Saints Henry and Cunegund.

[Col. 0065C]

108. Here we encounter the most outstanding monument of the most holy and munificent Emperor: the erection from its foundations of a new cathedral church and its richly endowed foundation. For the holy founder himself this brought no small amount of care, trouble, and even warfare. Serious difficulties arose from the neighboring bishops of Würzburg and Eichstätt over the determination of the boundaries of the new diocese. Hatred, envy, conspiracies, and even wars were also stirred up by the brothers of his most holy wife, since the wealthy patrimony—and even the dowry assigned to their sister Cunegund, which they hoped would return to them—was being squandered, as they themselves put it, in lavishly enriching communities of canons and monks [Col. 0065D].

We shall not fail to indicate below, in their proper places, how far these conflicts extended. Yet Saint Henry’s most chaste religious devotion, steadfast piety, and proven courage overcame all these obstacles. Armed with these virtues, he both vindicated the diocese for his Bamberg church and restrained the efforts of his ungrateful relatives, if not with deserved vengeance, at least with Christian forbearance.

The Anonymous writer of the Life treats the foundation itself, as the principal subject of his work, in many chapters. Yet, as I explained sufficiently above, it yields little that can be extracted for a chronological sequence, so that this sequence must be derived and arranged from elsewhere.

109. The order of events in Ditmar requires us to understand that, after the synod of Tremonia, of which we have now said enough in the preceding paragraph, the remainder of the year was spent in military efforts against Boleslaus. When he learned of the schemes of Baldwin, count of Flanders, which Ditmar describes on p. 383, he turned his arms against him in the immediately following year, 1006, as Sigebert testifies.

There Ditmar connects together the events of the two years 1006 and 1007, again taking up on the same page the matters belonging to the already mentioned year 1006. Jacobus Meyer, in the Annals of Flanders, carefully and accurately described what Saint Henry attempted in this Flemish war against our Count Baldwin, though with varying success. He explained the cause of the conflict and several other details of considerable interest [Col. 0066B], which are not found so distinctly elaborated elsewhere. See his account under the years 1005, 1006, and 1007.

It is enough for us to have assigned each event to its proper calculation. Mabillon assists us here on p. 185, where, from a charter of the year 1006, he shows that in that very year a meeting took place between Saint Henry and Robert, king of France, by which their somewhat weakened friendship was restored. See the same Mabillon, p. 188, nos. 88 and 89, where he records the king’s settlement concerning the Italian monasteries.

110. We again follow Ditmar. In his account, “when these regions had then been pacified, the King held a general council at Frankfurt.” In that council the institution of the Bamberg bishopric, long contemplated, and the various difficulties debated there are sufficiently clear to everyone [Col. 0066C].

The principal question here is whether all these events took place in 1006 or 1007. On this matter I find the authors as sharply divided as they are concerning the Saint’s first Italian war. Since Ditmar did not distinguish his events with sufficient chronological precision, Baronius begins the year 1006 as follows:

“In the year 1006 of Christ the Redeemer, Indiction IV, a synod was held in Germany at Frankfurt, at which, among other matters, the erection of the Bamberg church as an episcopal see was discussed. Ditmar treats of it at length,” and so forth.

Pagius counters him for the same year with the letter of Pope John quoted in volume IX of the Councils. At its end we read:

“Written by the hand of Peter, notary and archivist of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of June, Indiction V.”

“That is,” he says, “in the year of Christ 1007. A great number of bishops unanimously approved this privilege at the synod held at Frankfurt and confirmed it with their subscriptions, as may be read at the end of the aforesaid apostolic rescript. Therefore,” he continues, “that council was not convened in this year, as Baronius supposed, but in the following year,” and so forth.

111. Pagius corrected Baronius in part, not unsuccessfully, though in another respect Pagius himself requires no less correction. For both seem not to have paid sufficient attention to everything connected with the matter of this bishopric, which was treated over a longer period; and, unless I am very much mistaken, the first source of the confusion was taken from Thietmar, who in a certain way conflated into a single year events that must certainly be divided between two different years. The aforementioned Baronius rightly assigned a Frankfort synod [Col. 0067A] to the year 1006, since Thietmar describes it quite accurately as having taken place in that year, deservedly extolling that remarkable humility of Saint Henry toward the fathers of the council: he prostrated himself at their feet and performed other acts of comparable humility, which we have indicated to the reader there. Baronius was at fault in omitting a second synod, for which the first may be called a kind of preparation. Pagius, for his part, rightly argued from the diploma cited from Pope John in favor of a synod in the year 1007, but wrongly accused Baronius, as though everything that required explanation concerning the establishment of the aforesaid bishopric had been settled in the same year. Here, if anywhere, the proverb applies: distinguish the times, and you will reconcile the writings [Col. 0067B] that Labbe presents to us in the cited ninth volume of the Councils. An exact distinction of the events alone will clarify—and perhaps settle—the whole controversy.

112. Three documents are reported there in the following order: “First, the Frankfort Council concerning the raising of the church of Bamberg to an episcopal cathedral, held in the year of the Lord 1006, in the time of Pope John XVII,” which is taken entirely from Thietmar. The second document is placed out of its proper position and bears no true title: “Acts of the same Frankfort Council from the archives of the church of Bamberg.” The item that follows, “the diploma of Pope John XVI,” ought, in the proper sequence of events, apparently to have been placed second; from these materials the correct order [Col. 0067C] would be established. Saint Henry had hoped to soften Henry, bishop of Würzburg, so that, after some exchange had been made, he would permit a portion to be detached from his diocese and assigned to Bamberg. But the latter had attached other conditions that were by no means pleasing to the Saint; and, so as not to be compelled to come to the announced synod, he had fled elsewhere—I think to Cologne, to Saint Heribert—so that everything Thietmar records there took place in his absence. From these events it is clearly understood that, in that first council, the principal matter was that, notwithstanding Henry of Würzburg’s evasion, the church of Bamberg should be raised to cathedral rank, and that “its pastoral care should be entrusted by the King to Eberard, then Chancellor.” This the Council obtained, with Tagmo presiding, “and all those present then affirming and subscribing to his speech” [Col. 0067D]; yet Eberard’s ordination, which Thietmar appends there, must be deferred to the following year.

113. Let the prayer of the holy Emperor himself be heard:

“For this reason I appeal to your most serene piety, Fathers of the entire synod, lest the absence of this man, Henry of Würzburg, who through me wished to obtain what I was not permitted to grant him, should be able to impede the purpose of my will. For it is clear from his staff, as a sign of our mutual confirmation, that he has fled not for the Lord’s sake but because of his grief at being unable to attain a dignity. Let what he has attempted through his ambition move the hearts of all present: to nullify the increase of holy mother Church [Col. 0068A] through a trifling embassy [nugigerula legatione]. If at any time the bishop deigns to come and accept what was promised, he will unquestionably find me prepared to do everything that seems good to you.”

There follows a protest made in the name of Bishop Henry:

“When such addresses had ended, Bernigerus, the chaplain of Bishop Henry of Würzburg, arose. He testified that his lord had not come here because of fear of the king, and that he had never approved of any harm being done to the church entrusted to him by God; and he beseeched all those present, for the love of Christ, not to allow such things to be done in his absence, lest they become an example for him in the future. His privileges were then read aloud.”

But, as we have already said, these things did not prevent the holy king from obtaining his wishes [Col. 0068B]. Hence afterward “Bishop Henry, with the help of his fellow bishop Heribert, secured for the king the favor and fulfillment that pleased him.”

114. All these events must have taken place either toward the end of 1006 or at the beginning of 1007, when “the most glorious King Henry, having attained the fulfillment of his wish, sent two of his chaplains, namely Alberic and Louis, together with letters from Bishop Henry of Würzburg, all the way to Rome, so that what had been well begun here might advance to something better through Roman authority.” The Anonymous author recounts these matters at length in chapter 10 of the Life, as does the Bamberg document, which may properly be called a report of the completed undertaking. In it, I think, the actual substance of the proceedings rather than their chronological order is set out and ought to be understood in this way [Col. 0068C].

Once the disputes between Saint Henry and the bishop of Würzburg had been settled, the aforesaid envoys were sent to Rome, as the Pontiff testifies:

“For this reason the most glorious King Henry II sent his messengers to us, who told us all these things and appealed to us for the confirmation of this see.”

Let the remainder of the papal bull be read. From it, it is clear that they were graciously heard and that the entire matter was strengthened by the authority of Pope John. The diploma, moreover, was issued “by the hand of Peter, notary and scriniarius of the Holy Roman Church, in the month of June, Indiction V,” and therefore in the year 1007. It was then, finally, that the Frankfort synod must have been held, of which, as we said, the Bamberg document makes mention:

115. “In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1007, Indiction V, on the Kalends of November, while the most pious and serene Henry II was reigning, in the sixth year of his reign, for the welfare and increase of holy mother Church, a great synod was held and celebrated in the place called Frankfort” [Col. 0068D]. It was not now, as the author of the document seems to imply, held to discuss the establishment of the bishopric of Bamberg, but—as the Anonymous author observed out of sequence in chapter 12—so that “this privilege of the Apostolic See might be received with due veneration.”

The clause reads as follows in Labbe:

“This privilege, therefore, the venerable Fathers assembled in the aforesaid synod held at Frankfort, constituting a general council, received with the greatest veneration by reading it, and, obeying Apostolic authority, praised it with devout minds by subscribing to it [Col. 0069A], and unanimously confirmed it.”

There follow the names of thirty-five bishops. Among them, I suspect, Henry of Würzburg was omitted; had he been included, he would have made the thirty-sixth, which the Legend declares were the number of bishops present at that council, in the chapter 12 cited above. Thus, I think, the events connected with the foundation and confirmation of the see of Bamberg have been restored to their proper order and calculation. Had these matters been observed by the younger Pagius, there would have been no reason to accuse the Bamberg document of falsity in the *Breviarium Pontificum Romanorum*, volume II, page 285. We have already said enough about that document, from which the Anonymous author’s chapter 10 seems to have been taken—or conversely.

116. I think that matters otherwise extremely tangled [Col. 0069B] can be reconciled in this way, since the Anonymous author is always unsteady in chronological matters. He does indeed acknowledge two synods; but when he wishes the first to be the one about which the Bamberg document speaks, it becomes necessary to place the preparatory synod—the one in which Saint Henry prevailed in his dispute against the bishop of Würzburg—in the same year, 1007, around the Kalends of November. By then, however, the confirmation of that bishopric would have to be supposed to have been obtained from Pope John in the month of June, and I entirely fail to see how these things can be combined.

Hofmann treats this matter at length, almost according to our own method, beginning at column 40; but I do not know whether he deliberately passed over this difficulty untouched. He correctly assigns Eberard’s ordination to the year 1007, whatever Thietmar connects and inserts in one continuous account, placing everything in the synod of 1006, by which arrangement, as we have said above, he confused the events. For I plainly consider it established that such a consecration must have required the prior confirmation of the bishopric by the Pontiff. In the meantime, I am quite willing for someone else to produce a more precise solution. Furthermore, Hofmann carefully lists the rich endowment and splendor bestowed by the Saint upon the Bamberg church so often mentioned, at column 43. I leave to his authority the remaining matters that he laboriously collected, beyond our subject, concerning its officials and the electors of the Empire.

§ XII. Continuation from the Stabilization of the Church of Bamberg to the Imperial Coronation Received at Rome from Pope Benedict VIII

117. I begin this paragraph by resolving another extremely intricate difficulty [Col. 0069D], from which I recently said that the copies of Thietmar’s Chronicle, both manuscript and printed, must be convicted of an obvious error at the crucial point in question. The events of Saint Henry that Adelbold, the Saxon Chronicler, the Hildesheim Annals, and various other sources most correctly attach to the year 1004 are transferred by Thietmar, at the beginning of his sixth book, to the later year 1005, with a somewhat fuller phrase but in the clearest possible terms. How this can be demonstrated from Thietmar’s own Chronicle, a single example—without examining the others here—will clearly establish.

The aforementioned Saxon Chronicler, together with ancient and more recent writers in many places, with no one, so far as I know, dissenting, assigns the death of Wigbert, bishop of Merseburg, and Thietmar’s own succession to the year 1009 [Col. 0070A]. His words are:

“Wipert, bishop of Merseburg, died, and Thietmar succeeded him.”

But Thietmar himself writes on page 385:

“This venerable man, Wigbert or Wicbert, sat in the episcopate for five years, six weeks, and five days. After often making his confession amid lamentation, and receiving absolution from Bishops Wigo and Henry, who visited him in his final illness, he departed happily, as I hope, from this light to Christ at Merseburg, on the ninth day before the Kalends of April, a Tuesday.”

118. Compare this with what we quoted from Thietmar himself in paragraph 10, number 101, where he expressly states that “at the beginning of the fourth week in February [Saint Henry] gave the bishopric of the holy church of Merseburg to his own chaplain Wigbert” [Col. 0070B]. You will readily conclude that Wigbert could not have ascended that see in 1005 if he held it for five full years, six weeks, and five days; consequently, its beginning must be moved back entirely to February of the preceding year, 1004.

So that no doubt may remain in this matter, Thietmar himself proves it once again most plainly on page 422, toward the end, in these words:

“This year in which I entitled this book”—he entitled it in 1018—“is the fortieth or somewhat more of my life; but in the month of April, on the fifth day before the Kalends of May, the tenth year of my ordination entered.”

Thus the ninth year had been completed, having begun in that very month of April, after the aforesaid Wigbert had departed this life nine years earlier, on the ninth day before the Kalends of April, that is, 23 March [Col. 0070C]. By following the same line of succession upward, it is again plainly established that Wigbert died in 1009 and was ordained a full five years earlier, in 1004. What is finally concluded from this is that Thietmar’s sixth book was improperly, to use his own term, “entitled” in the year 1005. With these matters established, let us continue the chronology set before us.

119. The “vision offered to Saint Henry at Regensburg at the tomb of Saint Wolfgang” is commonly assigned to the year 1007 or 1008. The Anonymous author speaks of it in chapter 2: his former instructor in morals appeared to him standing there and addressed him in these words:

“Look carefully at the letters written on the wall beside my tomb.”

There, as it appeared, was written only:

“POST SEX” [“AFTER SIX”].

We do not deny that in that year, 1007, according to the Saxon Chronicler and Thietmar himself—if he is speaking consistently—Saint Henry celebrated the Lord’s resurrection in that city, at which time he could have understood the celebrated prophecy. But the good Anonymous author arranged the matter incorrectly here; he should have referred more properly to the beginning of Henry’s reign than to his imperial coronation, for Henry was free to receive the latter whenever he wished.

In any event, however one understands the prophecy, it is sufficiently explained in the Life itself and adequately established for the circumstances. Thus it cannot serve here as a purely negative argument, by which Leibniz and others have dared to challenge the perpetual virginity preserved in marriage by both spouses, Saint Henry and Cunegund, on the ground that Thietmar or other contemporaries did not mention the matter clearly enough [Col. 0071A]. We consider it already sufficiently defended.

That Thietmar was ignorant of the aforesaid vision is nothing remarkable. Otherwise he would scarcely have kept silent about it, since he relates that something similar occurred elsewhere and is in no way averse to such revelations, as you will see abundantly from page 387 alone.

120. The war of Metz, or of Trier, belongs to the year 1008. Concerning it, the Saxon Chronicler writes under that year:

“Adalbert, a cleric and brother of the queen, having been made an adversary of the king, stirred up many abominations against all right and law. He seized Trier for himself and his followers, and then withdrew. When the king learned of this, he immediately gathered his forces and arrived [Col. 0071B]. He besieged in the palace the Lotharingians who resisted him, remaining there for sixteen weeks.”

Thietmar gives the cause of the war on page 384:

“When the king heard this, mindful of the earlier matter, he rejected Theodoric, the brother of this same man, together with his beloved wife and all his household, who were anxious to obtain that bishopric, because the arrangement had not been considered beforehand; and he gave the same office to Meingard, chamberlain of Archbishop Willigis [lacuna]. Because of this, the fury of the treacherous faction was kindled.”

Here Thietmar, both in this passage and frequently elsewhere, hints at the hatred of Saint Cunegund’s ungrateful brothers toward Saint Henry, a hatred that seemed to pour itself out upon the churches, especially that of Bamberg. Henry seemed to be scattering, with excessive religious scruple, among the churches—especially Bamberg—the possessions for which they themselves greedily hungered, so that the duchy of Bavaria had to be taken away from Henry, the other brother [Col. 0071C], although he later recovered it through the favor of the holy king.

To this may be added what Alberic noted for this year: that the holy Emperor gave “Jopilia, near Liège,” to Henry, bishop of Verdun. He was always and everywhere generous toward churches.

121. Nor should we pass over the celebrated monastery of the Mount of the Monks near Bamberg, about which we have spoken at greater length in the Life of Saint Otto. In this same year it was founded by the holy Emperor “and by his consort, Saint Cunegund, Palatine and Empress, in honor of Saint Michael the Archangel, together with almost the entire bishopric of Bamberg,” as Bruschius says in his *On Monasteries*, page 87.

He adds “the reason for its foundation”: while the Saint was once praying more devoutly in a certain secluded chapel, the archangel Michael appeared to him. Touching the king’s thigh—whence he is said to have become lame, though he had previously walked upright—and offering him an Evangelical book to kiss, he consoled him in these words [Col. 0071D]:

“Do not fear, chosen one of God. Rise quickly and receive this sign of peace sent to you from heaven, and continue zealously to spread the worship of God. Afterward, when you return from Apulia to Germany, having successfully concluded the war there, and lie ill at the monastery of Cassino because of the stone,” [lacuna].

Anyone who tries to reconcile all these details of Bruschius with the beginnings of this monastery as they have just been dated will sweat profusely. We have already said enough about Saint Henry’s lameness and its more probable cause. This much certainly cannot be disputed: the most generous Emperor enriched the monastery dear to him with many estates and broad lands, all of which he confirmed by a splendid diploma in the year 1015. See the same Bruschius at the cited page [Col. 0072A].

122. “MIX. The king celebrated the Nativity of Christ at Salzburg, but Easter at Augsburg.” These are the words of the Hildesheim Annals.

The Saxon Chronicler devotes himself entirely to describing the calamities of that year: the extraordinary overflow of waters; drops of blood that fell upon people’s garments on Palm Sunday; the obscuring of the sun; and unusual fires, all of which were followed by severe pestilence and mortality.

Apart from these matters, and passing over what concerns Saint Henry, he accurately records Thietmar’s succession to the bishopric of Merseburg, about which we have just spoken. He could also have added the appointment of Saint Meinwerc to Paderborn [Col. 0072B], which is sufficiently described in the Hildesheim Annals and in his Life. In that Life you will also find, for this year, the deeds splendidly and royally performed by Saint Henry.

Thietmar writes on page 388 that “the king tested various dispositions among the western peoples and attempted to calm them, lest they be disturbed in their customary ways.” He thereby shows that his constant concern was to do good to all his subjects, of every sex and rank, and “to hasten, with fear removed, toward the unfailing crown of honor; and, while laboring especially on journeys and in other necessities to obtain it, he made friends into enemies, justly hating them.” This means that he suffered persecution because he administered justice [Col. 0072C].

For other donations of this year, see Gretser, pages 69 and 71. To these may be added the Chronicle of an anonymous monk of Schuttern, recently published by Abbot Johann Friedrich Schannat in the first collection of his *Literary Vintage*, where it is listed as the fourth work in order.

123. The Saxon Chronicler describes the year 1010 as follows:

“King Henry, gathering his forces for an expedition in search of Boleslav of Poland, but not reaching the destination toward which he was proceeding, turned back halfway because a serious illness came upon him [lacuna]. Theodore, bishop of Metz, grieving that the dowry and patrimony of Queen Cunegund, who was his sister, were being assigned by the king to the Church of Bamberg, rebelled against him.”

Thietmar recounts these same events somewhat more lamentably on page 388, mixing together and transposing several matters [Col. 0072D] that I wish had been distinguished more accurately. For, unless I am greatly mistaken, the war against Boleslav, which he continues on the following page, 389, ought to have been placed before the other Moselle expedition, which continued up to the year 1011. Concerning that expedition, the Saxon Chronicler speaks under the year 1011:

“The king besieged the city of Metz and the aforesaid Bishop Theodore until, through the intervention of justice, peace was established between them.”

Yet I do not deny that the various expeditions may have been taken up again more than once. Indeed, toward the end of the entire narrative, on page 390, Thietmar writes:

“The king again visited the western regions, and, taming the wavering minds of their inhabitants with the bridle of wisdom, celebrated the feast of the Lord’s Nativity with festive joy at Palthi” [Col. 0073A].

All this could not possibly have happened in 1010; at the very least, it marks the end of the year 1011, immediately followed by the dedication of the church of Bamberg.

Assign to the year 1010 the restoration of the monastery of Saint Mary at Regensburg, which Mabillon discusses on page 218, number 52.

124. Moreover, that most celebrated dedication did not take place in 1011, as many assign it with Baronius, but in 1012. This is proved by the Saxon Chronicler, the Hildesheim Annals, and other ancient sources together with Hofmann, whatever may be alleged against them by the brief Chronicle of Würzburg preserved by Baluze.

One should note Struve’s incompetence in matters relevant to our subject. After incorrectly asserting on page 384 that the foundation of the bishopric of Bamberg was confirmed by Pope John XXII, he soon adds still more ineptly:

“This bishopric, too, in the presence of Pope Benedict VIII, after the construction of the greater church had been completed, was finally consecrated in the year 1012.”

He could have been better instructed if he had paid even slight attention to the words of Thietmar that he himself quotes. Thietmar speaks as follows on the already cited page 390:

“When the greater church in the city of Bamberg had been completed, and it was the king’s birthday, and he was already beginning his thirty-fifth year, on the sixth day before the Nones of May the entire primacy gathered there for the dedication of that hall, and this bride of Christ was dedicated by the hands of John, patriarch of Aquileia, and more than thirty other bishops” [Col. 0073B].

The Chronicler adds: “consecrated through the ministry of thirty-six bishops.” The Hildesheim Annals agree with this. Yet in all these sources there is not a word [Col. 0073C] from which anyone could infer that Pope Benedict attended the dedication. More probably, he had not yet been elected when the ceremony took place. Whether he came to Germany in that year, however, we shall investigate below.

125. Thietmar adds:

“After this a great synod was held here, in which Gebhard, bishop of the church of Regensburg, was accused by his own archbishop, and Theodore, bishop of the church of Metz, was rebuked by the king because in a letter of his he had unjustly accused the king before the Pope. But all these matters and many others were settled by prudent counsel [lacuna]. When all business in eastern Francia had been completed, the King visited the city of Merseburg again and celebrated there the holy solemnity of Pentecost. At first light on the Lord’s Day, when the Holy Spirit filled the holy Apostles, Archbishop Tagmo began to fall ill [Col. 0073D]. Shortly afterward, on the fifth day before the Ides of June, he did not die,” says that same Thietmar, “but happily departed to Christ, whom he had always loved.”

I wished to set all these events out together so that it might be more evident that the dedication of the Bamberg church took place, as we have maintained, in the year 1012, in which Tagmo’s death is certainly attested by the Saxon Chronicler and the Hildesheim Annals. This is especially worth observing in order to demonstrate another error of Thietmar, who had just said that Saint Henry celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Palthi, or Palithi, immediately before the consecration of the Bamberg church. The cited Annals, however, more distinctly record that the Saint celebrated two other Nativities of the Lord in between, from which the year begins: “in the year 1011 at Frankenford,” and “in 1012 at Thornburg,” in which year the aforesaid dedication is correctly recorded there [Col. 0074A].

126. From these matters it is again clear what I have said more than once above: Thietmar’s Chronicle must be used with the greatest caution when arranging its chronology.

As for the rest, the aforementioned Thietmar recounts at greater length throughout the remainder of his sixth book the other labors of the holy Emperor in settling the affairs of the Empire—whose various regions he could not fail to inspect each year—and in diligently securing peace with the Slavs and other enemies.

On page 397 he enters the year 1013, in which Henry celebrated Epiphany at Alstedt and the Purification of the holy Mother of God at Magdeburg. “He celebrated the Paschal feast [Col. 0074B] with Meinwerc, who was especially close to him, at Paderborn with due veneration, but Pentecost with us,” that is, at Merseburg. On the vigil of Pentecost, Boleslav came with the hostages left in his keeping under safe protection and was received most favorably. Thus Henry wished to make everything secure on that side before undertaking his planned Italian journey, for which preparations were then being made.

That year was not very favorable to the men of Fulda, since “Abbot Bronnag was deposed, and then this monastery, with the brethren dispersing far and wide, was changed from its former condition.” These events are expressed somewhat more harshly by the Saxon Chronicler under the same year 1013:

“The king, corrupted by the counsel of fools, plundered the possessions of the monastery of Fulda in a remarkable manner,” [lacuna].

But they may be found explained more mildly by Mabillon on page 252, number 88.

127. Thietmar continues:

“The king, proceeding toward the western regions, arranged his journey to Lombardy, and returned to us again; and departing from there on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October, he hurried through the territories of the Bavarians and Swabians to a place called [Col. 0074C; lacuna]. An army gathered here from every direction, and from there the King came all the way to Rome without hesitation, accompanied by the queen.”

There follow new crimes of Boleslav and secret plots against Saint Henry, which nevertheless did not prevent him from bringing the rebellious Lombards back into order and finally from being invested with the imperial crown in the imperial city.

Before these events, however, must be placed—if they belong anywhere here—what Thietmar inserts near the end of his sixth book, while treating a plainly different matter, on page 399 [Col. 0074D], concerning the arrival, as some understand it, of Benedict VIII in Germany, because of the intrusion, as they think, of a certain Gregory.

Hear Thietmar himself:

“For Pope Benedict prevailed over a certain Gregory in the election. Because of this, this man”—who is meant?—“came to Palithi at the Nativity of the Lord with all the Apostolic apparatus, making his expulsion known to everyone through lamentation.”

From this Baronius concluded, under the year 1012, that Benedict, expelled from Rome by Gregory, had fled to Germany to Saint Henry to seek his help. All more recent writers follow him in this, including Francis Pagius most recently in his *Breviary of the Roman Pontiffs*, volume II, page 291, although he rightly observes that not one of the ancient German writers mentions Benedict’s expulsion or the schism that supposedly arose on that account [Col. 0075A].

128. This is certainly not surprising, for, unless I am very much mistaken, the eminent annalist did not correctly grasp Thietmar’s meaning. I shall say nothing for the moment about the fact that the entire matter concerning a supposed schism after the death of Pope Sergius IV is wrongly attached to the year 1012; it seems instead to belong to the following year, 1013, whose beginning Saint Henry celebrated at Palithi, counting from the Nativity of the Lord.

You should therefore note that Thietmar is treating entirely different matters in that passage, matters concerning his own church, and that he introduces this affair there only incidentally. It certainly deserved to be explained differently if Benedict himself, the legitimate Pope, had journeyed to Germany; without doubt the Saxon Chronicler, who abridges Thietmar in many matters, and the Hildesheim Annals, as well as other contemporaries or near-contemporaries, would not have kept silent about it [Col. 0075B].

To make my meaning clear, translate Thietmar’s words in whatever way and order you wish, and examine everything else, both what precedes and what follows, seeking even a single word by which he might imply that the holy Emperor ought to have taken Benedict’s side, or to have defended or assisted him in any way, or that he afterward proceeded to Rome in order to restore him to the see by whatever means.

However obscurely you may think Thietmar spoke, either he said nothing of this kind, or he indicated clearly enough that the fugitive was not Benedict but Gregory, “over whom Benedict prevailed,” since Benedict held sway more powerfully than all his predecessors. Indeed, the well-known power of the Tusculan counts at that time could very easily have prevailed even by force against a man of lesser reputation, Gregory, who was compelled to seek foreign assistance but was not heard by the Saint.

129. In brief, Thietmar is not discussing there the election of a Pontiff or a schism arising from it. Rather, he is chiefly considering what the Roman Pontiffs and Saint Henry, competing with one another, contributed to the increase and splendor of the Church.

These are the final words with which he concludes his sixth book:

“For King Henry increased our church with many benefactions, above all with sacred furnishings; and from all the estates that he possessed in Thuringia and Saxony he gave us two households. He gave an Evangelium adorned with gold and an ivory panel, a golden and jeweled chalice together with a paten and a tube; likewise two crosses and covers made of silver [Col. 0075D], and a large chalice of the same metal, together with a paten and a tube. Whatever in the estates had been neglected by my predecessors, he renewed by command.”

Thus he deserves to be called not only the restorer but also the founder of this church, just as of the church of Paderborn, which in this same year, 1013, while he was lying ill at Werl, he enriched with many other benefits in addition to the rich estate with which he endowed it. With his customary generosity he also bestowed an entire county upon Saint Bernward, bishop of Hildesheim [Col. 0076A]. Schaten, our author, records the documents of these donations beginning on page 402.

One might say that the holy Emperor wished through so many pious gifts to obtain from God a prosperous Italian journey. From this point we shall begin another period of his life, indeed another epoch of his imperial rule.

§ XIII. The Coronation of Saint Henry at Rome and the Events That Followed It, up to the Arrival of Pope Benedict VIII in Germany

130. Thietmar begins his seventh book as follows:

“When thirteen years had elapsed from the Lord’s Incarnation after the completion of the thousand-year number, and in the second month and third week of the following year, in the thirteenth year of his reign, on a Sunday and on the sixth day before the Kalends of March”—read “the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March” under Sunday letter C—[Col. 0076B]“Henry, the illustrious king by the grace of God, accompanied by twelve senators, six of whom proceeded shaven-bearded and the others with long beards, mystically carrying staffs, came with his beloved wife Cunegund to the church of Saint Peter, while the Pope awaited him. Before he was admitted, the same Pope asked him whether he wished to be the faithful patron and defender of the Roman Church and faithful in all things to him and to his successors. He replied with a devout profession; and then from the same Pope he received anointing and a crown, together with his consort. He ordered his earlier crown to be hung above the altar of the Prince of the Apostles. On that same day the Pope provided them with an abundant dinner at the Lateran.”

It is not relevant here to describe what disturbances arose in Rome eight days later, or by whom they were stirred up. The Saxon Chronicler gives a concise account of what happened afterward, bringing the Emperor back to Pavia by the Lord’s Resurrection. The Cassino Chronicle, book II, chapter 31, assigns the Roman coronation itself to that occasion, but we have already refuted this elsewhere [Col. 0076C].

After restoring the disposition of the Lombards at Pavia as best he could, Henry returned to Saxony. Matters concerning the monks of Corvey are then added; as with the disputes of the men of Fulda with the Saint, I prefer to read about these in Mabillon’s *Benedictine Annals* rather than recount them more laboriously here.

131. More closely relevant here is what Rudolf Glaber relates in book I, chapter 5 of his History: Benedict, the Pope, is said to have offered Saint Henry a golden apple or globe surrounded with precious gems and adorned above with a golden cross, as a symbol of worldly power. But Saint Henry “immediately sent it to the monastery of Cluny in Gaul, which at that time was considered the most religious of all the others, and to which he had also presented many other gifts of ornaments,” as the aforementioned Glaber says in the same place [Col. 0076D].

But if what the Legend reports in chapter 26 is true, there was no need for that dispatch, since, as will appear in the Life, the holy Emperor himself went to Cluny and offered not only the globe but also a golden crown, together with many other gifts mentioned in both Lives of Saint Odilo published by our predecessors under 1 January: the first on pages 18 and 26, and the second at numbers 6 and 21.

Thietmar, the Saxon Chronicler, and other contemporaries say nothing about this pilgrimage. Mabillon nevertheless inferred it not implausibly from the Life of Saint Meinwerc, in book LV of the Annals, page 241. I do not see why he assigns to the year 1015 what, if it occurred at that time, most probably belongs to the year 1014, when Henry passed through Burgundy into Alsace and from there “through Liège and Trier,” as the Anonymous author says in the cited chapter [Col. 0077A].

132. What Mabillon relates there deserves to be reported:

“The Anonymous author who wrote a book about the deeds of blessed Meinwerc of Paderborn indicates clearly enough that Emperor Henry, on his return from the city of Rome after his coronation, stopped at the monastery of Cluny with Lord Bishop Meinwerc and a few attendants, because of his religious fervor and because of the site’s particular renown. Perhaps Abbot Odilo, who had accompanied him on that journey, escorted him there. Having seen for himself the things he had learned by report about that sacred monastery, he offered a most precious golden crown at the Mass called the Mass of the Chair of Saint Peter, and, having humbly sought and received admission to the brotherhood of the monks, commended himself to the prayers of all the brothers [Col. 0077B].”

For these and further details concerning other benefits bestowed by the Saint upon that monastery, and concerning the monks taken from there for the founding of the monastery of Abdinghof, see 5 June, chapter 4, number 26, page 521.

These matters have led us somewhat farther from those gifts that the newly inaugurated Augustus, after the Roman coronation, bestowed upon the Roman Church itself. These are explained in Pagius’s *Breviary*, beginning on page 293. Add to them other benefactions of the most generous Caesar in the aforementioned Mabillon, pages 237 and 239, and finally the gifts he made for his beloved church of Bamberg, listed by Hofmann at column 49.

133. Nor should we pass over [Col. 0077C] what Thietmar reports—as I return to him—about the bishopric of Bobbio, established by Saint Henry before he left Italy.

“In these regions,” he says, “the Caesar constructed a bishopric, the third ornament of his devoted work, in the city of Bobbio, where the bodies of the holy worshipers of Christ and illustrious confessors Columbanus and Attala rest. He did so by common counsel and with the permission of the bishops of the province, because the greatest necessity, and the charity of Christ that surpasses it, urged him to this. Here, with the greatest prosperity and glory, he overcame the Alpine difficulties and entered the pleasant regions of our land, because the qualities of the air and of the inhabitants do not agree with those of our regions.”

I omit what Thietmar says here in a more offensive manner against the Lombards and others. It is enough to conclude this year, 1014, with him and to begin the next with these words:

“But the Emperor, having crossed the Alps and traversed the neighboring provinces in his rule, celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Palithi. After this, coming to Merseburg, he made known to his faithful men Boleslav’s loyalty and assistance, and unanimously requested that Boleslav be summoned by them to offer an excuse or make restitution for the matter brought against him.”

These events have thus been correctly arranged and properly assigned to their respective years, although some writers have greatly confused them by mixing and combining them with other matters.

134. This author of the *Life of St. Meinwerk* must be numbered among them. In chapter 4, no. 22, he records that “St. Henry, after subduing all the cities that had attempted rebellion and reducing them to surrender, celebrated the approaching Christmas at Pavia,” and from there leads him into Apulia, over which he had appointed Ismael after its subjugation; then to Monte Cassino, where he was freed from the stone; and finally, in no. 23, he says that Henry “entered Rome with Lady Cunigund, in great triumph, where he was kindly and honorably received by the blessed Pope Benedict . . . and, with a solemn blessing and the immeasurable rejoicing of all the people, was consecrated Caesar and emperor.” Clearly, two Italian expeditions of St. Henry have been confused here: this one, in which the coronation alone was accomplished within a short time, and another, to be explained somewhat more fully below. The writer would easily have noticed this had he marked the day of the coronation—namely, 14 February—more explicitly. For who could readily conceive that St. Henry celebrated Christmas at Pavia, then subjugated Apulia, and lay sick at Monte Cassino, yet in the meantime reached Rome early enough to receive the imperial inauguration on that 14 February? These events have not been assigned very appropriately to their proper times. Hofmann also falsely referred all of them here in column 50. I shall more readily accept what he reports there in no. 79, and then what follows concerning the disputes over the boundaries of the church of Bamberg, settled during this period with Gundekar of Eichstätt.

135. Immediately after the words of Thietmar just quoted, other material is inserted that might somewhat disturb the chronological sequence, unless the distinct type used on page 402 made it clear that the holy emperor celebrated Easter at Merseburg in the year 1015. In that year the Vigil of the Resurrection fell on 9 April, the date explicitly marked by him; Easter itself fell on 10 April. “On Maundy Thursday,” Thietmar says, “I unworthily blessed the chrism in his presence.” The Saxon Chronicler gives the following account for that year:

> “Emperor Henry spent Palm Sunday at Wallbeck and bound the envoys from Italy to himself by oaths. Departing from there, he celebrated the Easter festival at Merseburg, where he lost all the gifts he had sent to Boleslav, together with his favor, when he provoked him by an arrogant embassy.”

These events paved the way for repeated expeditions and for the almost uninterrupted wars then vigorously waged against Boleslav. The fortunes of war varied, as may be read more fully there and in Thietmar. Since these matters are no more relevant to our purpose than the renewed, lamentable disputes with the monks of Corvey recorded by Thietmar on page 403, I shall not pursue them here. Mabillon, in the Annals cited above for this year, page 242, has investigated somewhat more distinctly the fact that St. Meinwerk, bishop of Paderborn, played some part in provoking them; to that work we refer the reader.

136. The Saxon Chronicler begins the following year, 1016, as follows:

> “The emperor celebrated Christmas at Paderborn with festive rejoicing. Afterward he appointed Poppo, son of Margrave Liutpold and provost of the Bamberg church, to the city of Trier. Since he was to be consecrated by Erchenbald, archbishop of Mainz, at the emperor’s command and with the permission of the bishop of Verdun—who was first in rank among these brethren—Theodoric, bishop of Metz, repeatedly and humbly attempted to prevent this, because the appointment ought more properly to have been made by him. For the emperor did not heed Theodoric, although he produced written evidence and forbade the matter under penalty of ban; and he caused the anointing to be completed.”

Add to this the various conflicts among individual princes, quieted either by arms or by friendly settlement, and Boleslav’s constant incursions, which Thietmar recounts up to page 406. To the same year must also be assigned what he adds there concerning “the approaching joy of Palm Sunday,” which the emperor “completed with Henry, the venerable bishop of Würzburg, and the Lord’s Supper and Passion, together with the joyful celebration of Easter, honorably observed at Bamberg,” and so forth. Read there what follows concerning Rudolf, king of Burgundy and the saint’s uncle, who transferred his kingdom to him by gift; this was confirmed two years later with the consent of the nobles. Other events, including some English affairs, are also recorded, but there is no time to enumerate them. Thietmar returns to St. Henry on page 412, writing as follows:

137. “In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1017, the emperor departed from Palithi, where he had celebrated Christmas, and solemnly kept the Epiphany of the Lord at Alstedt.” A little farther on:

> “The envoys arriving here from Italy returned home rejoicing.”

They may have been the envoys who brought from Pope Benedict VIII “a portion of the golden head ornament, set with gems,” belonging to the Saracen queen who had been beheaded at Rome; the portion was “valued at one thousand pounds,” as Thietmar had mentioned on the preceding page, 411. The envoys “returned rejoicing” because the emperor had promised the requested assistance against the Saracens and Greeks, although this could not be supplied until five years later.

> “The emperor’s journey to the west was postponed because of the difficulty of the road. The emperor approved what had been requested of him on Boleslav’s behalf: that his princes had come to him, and that, if Boleslav wished to offer him anything good, he would gladly accept it with their counsel. Envoys were sent back and forth, and a truce was established.”

Meanwhile:

> “The emperor celebrated with us the Purification of the holy Mother of God. Afterward the bishops and counts arrived sorrowfully because Boleslav had scorned and deceived them, and by open embassies they inflamed the emperor’s mind. There they then deliberated concerning the future expedition.”

See the whole passage on page 413, including the many benefactions of St. Henry to various churches—benefactions from which, clearly, he never knew how to desist.

138.

> “The king celebrated Palm Sunday at Mainz and Easter at Ingelheim; never in these regions had he been honored with greater magnificence and authority. Since, because of so great a solemnity, many matters could not be concluded there, an assembly was arranged at Aachen. There, with the counsel of Archbishop Heribert, he reconciled Theodoric, bishop of Metz, and Henry, his brother. Queen Cunigund, however, departing from the emperor at Frankfurt, fell ill when she reached a place called Kapaun, and there promised the Lord that she would build one monastery to his praise.”

On page 414:

> “When the emperor heard that his wife was somewhat better and had made a vow to the Lord, he gave heartfelt thanks to Christ.”

A little farther on:

> “The emperor, however, proceeding eastward, ordered the empress to come to him at a place called Paderborn. From there they both traveled as far as Magdeburg.”

They then proceeded together to other places until, “after the empress and many others had returned, he himself”—the emperor—“advanced in companies,” namely, as he threatened Boleslav with a huge army and pursued him through almost the rest of the year. I have drawn these events out somewhat more fully here so that it may be clearer how improperly Hofmann thought that the famous ordeal of St. Cunigund by means of red-hot ploughshares should be assigned to this year, 1017. It seems more suitably to belong to another year. For the rest, see above and under 3 March.

139. Just as St. Henry wished no year of his life to be without benefactions worthy of a Caesar, so he also made the year under discussion illustrious, as Thietmar testifies on page 316. I shall quote his words:

> “On the following Sunday, that is, 3 November, the emperor gave to our brethren serving Christ at Merseburg an estate called Bogalici, which he had acquired in an exchange acceptable to himself from the soldier Hathold; and he assigned for their use a certain place purchased from Hager, the brother of the aforesaid lord, for ten talents of silver, ordering it to be secured by his own charters. He also granted me three churches situated at Leipzig, Oschatz, and Gossna. During this spring he had likewise ordered a golden altar to be made for the adornment of our church, toward which I contributed six pounds of gold from the cost of our old altar.”

The emperor first reached Bamberg around the middle of December. There he “restored Henry, formerly duke of Bavaria, who had been deposed through his own fault for eight years and almost as many months, to his former honors on Sunday.” No one could say that, at this time, Henry’s sister Cunigund could have been summoned to the ordeal. “To conclude the year with Thietmar,” I shall add a confirmation from the saint concerning the monastery of Kemnade: estates were given to the church of Paderborn, along with other grants of the same kind, whose documents Schaten presents from page 422 onward.

140. Thietmar provides the beginning of the year 1018 when, on page 418, he says that the emperor, “departing from Bamberg after a very brief stay, came first to Würzburg and finally to Frankfurt, and there celebrated Christmas with festive rejoicing.” Then, passing to the eighth and final book of his *Life* as well as of his *Chronicle*, he begins in this way:

> “In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1018, indiction 11, and in the sixteenth year of the Lord Henry, the august emperor, and the fourth year of his empire,” the Circumcision of the Lord and the Epiphany were reverently celebrated by him in the aforesaid city. Afterward, at his command and at the unceasing supplication of Duke Boleslav, peace was confirmed by oaths in a certain city called Bautzen, through Bishops Gero and Arnulf . . . on 30 January—not as it ought to have been, but as it could then be accomplished. After selected hostages had been received, the aforesaid lords returned.”

These repeated settlements with Boleslav did not bring lasting peace to the empire, as Thietmar demonstrates at greater length in what follows—matters that do not belong here, any more than the detestable pagan superstitions concerning which it is said on page 420 that “the emperor sighed heavily.” There he finally adds the material we recently touched upon:

> “Now,” says Thietmar, “I turn away from these matters and shall speak of the prosperity that has recently arisen for our emperor. For his uncle, Rudolf, king of Burgundy, granted him his crown and scepter, together with his wife, stepchildren, and all his nobles. The confirmation of the oath was renewed, and this was done at Mainz . . . and on 16 March a great synod was held at Nijmegen.”

The rest must be read in the source.

141. As Thietmar approaches the end of his work, he does not cease to testify to his most grateful disposition toward the emperor. On page 422, he enumerates other distinguished benefits bestowed by him upon his church:

> “You ought to know the manifold benevolence shown by our king and emperor Henry toward our church. I have included part of it above, but I considered it best now to write down the greater part, which I left unexamined. See that by constant remembrance he may be renewed as your benefactor and remain our unfailing helper in those times when hope is lacking to the wretched and to the church of Merseburg . . . . And because there is no time to recount individually the things you will be able to see confirmed by his charters, I record only those whose lack of documentary authority makes me fear that they may perhaps perish in the future: a portion of the most victorious holy Cross, together with other relics of the saints; a golden altar honorably adorned with gems; a golden pyx decorated with precious stones; a collectary, embellished at his own expense as well as ours, with two censers and a silver beaker. With a generous hand the emperor gave these to our church . . . . But since I am wholly unable to say enough about his honey-sweet piety, I eagerly desire, as I proposed, to explain his conduct in orderly fashion.”

Would that he had been able to explain it himself; he ended his life in that year. I think it was near its end, for he carried his *Chronicle* beyond September.

142. To pass briefly over the remaining matters belonging to this year: on page 423 Thietmar says that the emperor, “after a long residence at Nijmegen,” where several excellent statutes were enacted, “carefully celebrated the solemn days of Rogations at Aachen . . . and Pentecost at Ingelheim,” from which “he hastened into Burgundy.” The empress, however, having arranged a monastic life at Kapaun, “enthroned” her brother Duke Henry, mentioned above more than once, at Regensburg.

After inserting many other matters, including events carried out by Boleslav, he finally adds this concerning the saint:

> “Let my account now turn to our emperor, who, returning from the expedition he disliked—I think the Burgundian one—received nothing of what had been promised, but harmed those who resisted him only slightly.”

Here are his final words:

> “When our emperor had become certain of all these matters, which had found little favor, he held an assembly in Swabia concerning the commonwealth, and soon descended anxiously along the Rhine. For most of his assistants and pillars of his kingdom, alas, had fallen, and those who secretly resist him through outsiders strive, while pretending fidelity, to impose upon him a grave hidden burden, so that he may not rule with the freedom proper to him or diminish their unjust arrogance in any respect.”

This is the end of the *Chronicle*, and with it we conclude this period of the *Life of St. Henry*. Elsewhere we shall seek whatever will help arrange the remaining years of his life. The most troublesome point is that the Saxon Chronicler seems here to have combined two years into one, producing the confusion that must be discussed next. The charters concerning the saint’s unfailing generosity are found in Schaten from page 438 onward.

## XIV. The Remaining Years of St. Henry’s Life up to His Blessed Death in 1024

143. Since Thietmar is now entirely lacking, the material that can be arranged concerning the final period of St. Henry’s life will be poorer. It is especially regrettable that, at the very beginning, the Saxon Chronicler departs from the true chronology for a whole year. He wrongly transferred to the following year, 1019, what Thietmar correctly and certainly assigned to 1018, as you will already understand from his first and last words:

> “The emperor,” he says, “traveling from Bamberg, came through Würzburg to Frankfurt, where he celebrated Christmas in royal fashion.”

He is mistaken here. We have shown from the sequence and course of events, and from Thietmar’s clearest chronological markers in the preceding paragraph, that the holy emperor celebrated the Circumcision of the Lord and the Epiphany at Frankfurt not in 1019 but in 1018. Moreover, it is universally acknowledged among writers that Thietmar ended both his life and his writing at the time already mentioned. Yet the same Saxon Chronicler adds at the end of the year he calls 1019:

> “Thietmar, bishop of Merseburg, of pious memory, departed to Christ.”

Nevertheless, the whole matter can be preserved if the years alone are transposed—perhaps having been wrongly marked through the carelessness of copyists. This may be thought to have arisen from the confused preceding canon of which we recently spoke.

144. But the error does not stop there. Proceeding in the same manner, the events belonging to the true year 1019 were placed under the heading of the following year, 1020—namely, the arrival of Pope Benedict VIII at Bamberg to visit the emperor. It is established with complete certainty that this occurred in 1019, as is shown by the Hildesheim Annals, the brief Chronicle of Würzburg, Hermannus Contractus, Lambert of Hersfeld, Marianus Scotus, the *Life of St. Meinwerk* in the *Acta* for 5 June, page 538, no. 82, and many earlier writers together with Hofmann. Baronius rightly followed them, against Sigebert, Alberic, and a few others, although these too have their own followers.

In the meantime, Schaten, drawing on the *Life of St. Meinwerk*, chapter 11, no. 81, explains what Caesar did that year against Bernard, duke of Saxony, before the august meeting. There one may again—and indeed throughout the entire Legend—observe the empress’s exceptionally strong beneficence toward the church of Paderborn, demonstrated by the documents cited by Schaten.

We regard it as beyond dispute that Pope Benedict was received at Bamberg by St. Henry in the year just mentioned, 1019. The Legend describes his arrival and the solemn events surrounding it in chapter 23. It is chronologically unfortunate once again, however, that it places St. Henry’s final expedition into Italy before the arrival of Pope Benedict in Germany, although that expedition preceded it by almost three full years, as will become clear from what follows. The matters recorded in that *Life* need not be described by us here. Some of them are explained here and there by Hofmann in column 54.

145. The Saxon Chronicler gives the matter briefly:

> “Pope Benedict is said to have duly celebrated the Lord’s Supper and the Easter festival with Emperor Henry at Bamberg. There, having been honorably presented with the emperor’s and the princes’ appropriate acts of service and with an abundance of wealth, he returned rich and safe to Rome, the mistress of the world.”

I do not know how long the pontiff remained at Bamberg or precisely when he returned to his own lands. He must have returned before November, since Baronius produces a charter issued in that month.

As for what Henry did throughout the rest of that year, which the Chronicler embellishes with innumerable marvels, gather it from the *Chronicle* of Sigebert appended to that year: “On 5 August, in a second hostile incursion, King Henry’s army entered Ghent.” These are Alberic’s exact words, together with several matters concerning Rudolf, king of Burgundy, which he copied from Sigebert, although other writers refute them.

Regarding the Ghent expedition, Meyer explains it in his *Annals* as follows:

> “In August, Emperor Henry again made a hostile expedition as far as Ghent into Flanders. In it, I read, Eppo and Canon, the emperor’s nephews, fell.”

I confess that I have considerable doubt whether this account of St. Henry’s nephews is sufficiently certain, nor is it possible to investigate where Meyer read it.

146. The final event of this year may be filled out by what Alberic, I do not know on what basis, attaches to it:

> “It is reported of Emperor Henry, and found written, that he made profession to Richard, abbot of Verdun, and committed himself entirely to his counsel, wishing to become a monk at St. Vanne. But the holy abbot Richard, by the virtue of obedience, enjoined him not to abandon the empire as long as he lived, and thus sent him back to the empire.”

Something similar is read in the epitome of the *Life* taken from Menard and Wasseburg, under 6 June, page 1003, no. 6; the author of the *Life* given first, however, does not mention it.

Mabillon seems to accept the account on page 301. There, from the epitome just cited, St. Henry is introduced as one who, upon entering the monastery, uttered this verse of the Psalmist:

> “This is my resting place forever and ever; here I shall dwell, for I have chosen it.”

It is not said there that he made a profession, but only that he expressed a desire to assume the monastic habit. To this the holy abbot replied: “We wish and command you to return to govern the empire entrusted to you by God.” The emperor obeyed, and thereafter was more devoted than before to St. Benedict and his Order.

I do not reject the account, although I know that others have rejected it. It may be said that the year or time when the event occurred remains uncertain.

147. The events narrated by the author of the *Life of St. Meinwerk*, chapter 12, page 539, are correctly assigned to the following year, 1020:

> “In the following year, after Christmas, the emperor, having mobilized his army, besieged a certain Count Otto, a man of considerable distinction in worldly rank, in the fortress called Hammerstein, situated above the bank of the Rhine.”

This was because of the various crimes he had committed against the archbishop of Mainz and others, as you will find explained more fully there.

St. Heribert of Cologne was summoned to that war. After excusing himself because of the severe fever with which he was struggling, all the events arose that may be seen both in the cited passage and in the *Life of St. Heribert* itself, under 16 March, pages 472 and 485. Nothing further need be said here about them.

Schaten adds that in this year—although the Hildesheim Annals assign it to the following year—Bavaria was shaken by a violent earthquake, and that the church of Basel was severely damaged by a major disaster:

> “Wishing to repair this damage, Henry came to Basel in the following year, 1021, moved the entire structure of the church fourteen paces from the bank of the Rhine, restored it in a much more beautiful and stronger form, and, according to Münster, furnished it most abundantly with new territories, peoples, and fortresses.”

The same Hofmann also records that Henry provided for the church of Bamberg with equal munificence. Schaten likewise confirms this by producing documents—documents that would scarcely seem credible in the *Life of St. Meinwerk*.

148. The Saxon Chronicler returns to the correct calculations, although his text is mutilated in several places. The first indication of this is that he begins the year we have now entered, 1021, as follows:
