> “The emperor, praising the Lord God of gods for the victory granted him by divine providence, hastened to Saxony to celebrate Palm Sunday at Wallbeck and to celebrate the Easter joy at Merseburg with due devotion. On this journey he learned, through a swift messenger, that the venerable Archbishop Heribert had departed this life in a blessed course . . . . Having completed the journey he had begun, the august emperor—while all the leading men of Europe, so to speak, flocked to him, and envoys of various nations hastened from every direction to attend upon his imperial majesty—celebrated the sacred joy of the Lord’s Resurrection with extraordinary glory, while the whole world already smiled. When all these matters had thus been suitably completed, the emperor proceeded to Parthenopolis and most gloriously spent the sacred days of Pentecost with Gero, the celebrated archbishop of that city, in no lesser devotion and with worthy veneration. From there he returned to the royal court called Alstedt. After holding an assembly there amid the gathering of the entire senate and people, soothing the good with a very gentle kindness, terrifying the guilty with strict severity, and fortifying his homeland with every effort, he happily spent the whole year within the cities of this province.”

Here the account stops, without a word about preparing the army for the famous Italian expedition against the Greeks, among whom the saint is placed in the middle of the following year, as we shall soon say.

149. “There follows,” says Baronius, “the year of the Redeemer 1022, indiction 5, in which Emperor Henry, encouraged by the embassies of the Northmen, as we have seen, and by the Roman pontiff himself, went into Italy against the Greeks, who had already become objects of fear to the Roman Church because of their power. He himself was a terror to the enemy with the powerful army he led.” See the fuller account there, including the conversation with St. Romuald and other matters relating both to the war and to St. Henry’s commemoration at Monte Cassino, drawn from Rudolf Glaber and Leo of Marsica.

We shall give a briefer account from the Chronicler, whose text is again mutilated for this year. He begins to speak of the emperor as follows:

> “As the emperor proceeded from place to place, he first brought his warlike army against the strongly fortified city of Troy—whose native inhabitants he had learned, through an embassy from the province, to be rebellious against royal authority.”

Glaber describes the siege more fully in book 3, chapter 1.

> “Although he subdued it through a long siege and the exertions of his men . . . he either consigned the inhabitants to death or ordered those captured to be bound—those who had previously opposed him with stubborn resolve—and afterward rejoiced, with God’s help, that they had been subjected to his rule.”

To establish the chronology, I ask that the following be carefully observed: according to Glaber, the siege of Troy lasted a full three months and more. It is therefore not easy to reconcile all the events that writers record as having taken place in that year. Let us give the rest from the Chronicler.

[Col. 0085D]

150.

> “Yet he was not lifted up by these successes. Rather, endowed with God’s mercy and attributing this victory not to his own but to the Lord’s powers, he hastened to the summit of the Roman See. After remaining there for some time, having bound the nobles of that kingdom to himself by peace and favor, he crossed the snowy peaks of the Alps with swift progress. A mortality then followed so great that it can scarcely, or perhaps not at all, be explained by signs of the voice or even by the functions of writing. Escaping this disaster, the august emperor, overshadowed from heaven but accompanied by only a few soldiers—apart from those whom Mother Europe had admitted to him by meeting him—reached the German territories and held a great synodal assembly in the western regions, with bishops from various lands gathering there.”

No council can be indicated here other than the one noted by Baronius, namely, the council of Seligenstadt. If St. Henry attended it, he must have returned to Germany before August, at the beginning of which it was held, as may be seen in Labbe’s collection, column 844.

See volume 3 of the June *Acta Sanctorum*, page 78, for what the saint bestowed that year upon Saints Aureus and Justina.

To reduce all the foregoing to a correct chronology, it is necessary to say that the imperial forces were sent ahead into Italy near the end of the preceding year under Poppo, archbishop of Trier, and Pilgrim, bishop of Cologne. The holy emperor followed them at the beginning of this year, after celebrating Christmas at Thorneburg, as the Hildesheim Annals record.

151. I therefore think that our Schaten is mistaken when, in his Paderborn Annals under this year, he writes:

> “The Italian expedition this year was memorable, undertaken at the urging of Pope Benedict through his legates. For this purpose, they say, the emperor summoned a synod at Aachen, according to Sigebert, with bishops gathering from all Germany. But the expedition was not undertaken until the end of the year, with a great military apparatus.”

I do not yet dare to determine what should be concluded concerning that synod. It seems certain to me that the emperor could not have remained at Aachen during this year, which the Italian expedition occupied for so many months; and we know from a charter issued at Benevento that he was there on 10 March 1022.

This is even more opposed to Schaten, who postpones the expedition to 1023. For that year he presents the emperor signing four charters of donation at Paderborn in January and February. Thus Henry could not conveniently have reached Italy—at least Apulia—before the end of March or the beginning of April. If he then spent three months or more on the siege of Troy alone, afterward lay sick at Monte Cassino, and then “remained for some time” at Rome, it is wholly impossible to suppose that he accomplished all these things and returned to Germany in July, unless one invents miracles. I see no need to summon such miracles here.

The matter appears otherwise concerning the cure of the stone obtained there through the aid of St. Benedict. Although I do not at all wish to dispute it, I certainly wish that it were reported by the writers with more unanimous agreement.

152. In chapter 22 of the Anonymous Life, no. 26 in our edition, St. Benedict opened with the medicinal knife he was holding the part of the body where the stone lay; after gently extracting the stone, he restored the opening of the wound by an instantaneous cure.

But the account of Leo of Marsica is entirely different, although both accounts agree in affirming that St. Benedict’s body was present in that chief monastery when the miracle occurred. The principal controversy between Leo, book 2, chapters 43 and 44, and the Gallic and other writers concerns not so much the cure itself—whose enduring memorial is customarily shown to all who visit the place and which we ourselves once saw with our own eyes—as the accompanying circumstances. These circumstances have been embellished in various ways by different writers, and thereby made doubtful to some.

I am not acting as judge here. Those who wish to know these matters should consult Mabillon in the *Annals*, page 288, no. 15, and the *Acta Sanctorum of the Order*, volume 6, part 1, beginning at page 452. For me, it is enough that these events most probably occurred in the year already mentioned, 1022.

For the precious gifts and other distinguished benefits generously bestowed by the holy emperor on the monastery of Monte Cassino on that occasion, see the cited passages of Leo of Marsica. The monastery at Benevento also belongs to this question, if St. Henry ever founded or endowed it, as some maintain. For from the charter in Ughelli, volume 8, column 115, it is established only that the saint confirmed all the estates and property previously granted to the monastery of St. Sophia. This is the charter we said was issued on 10 March 1022.

What St. Henry arranged with St. Romuald on his journey there or back is reported by John Damian and Jerome of Prague, cited under 7 February.

153. From here we return to the Chronicler, with whom we begin the year 1023:

> “At Merseburg, Henry the emperor duly celebrated the Albas and the Easter festivals, while princes flocked from every direction in companies. He was gratified by the dedication of the same church three times—something that seems rare or entirely unheard of.”

The writer does not explain how this is to be understood, nor do I think it necessary to investigate it at length.

The *Chronicle* of Sigebert suggests a memorable event of that year:

> “Emperor Henry and Robert, king of the Franks, met over the River Cher at Evosium, to deliberate concerning the condition of the Church, the kingdom, and the empire. They agreed that, in order to confirm these matters, both should meet the Roman pope at Pavia at a suitable time. The emperor bestowed such generous gifts upon the king and his men, and upon many others who had gathered merely to admire the emperor’s majesty, that the emperor’s munificence could be compared with the wealth of the kings of Persia and Arabia.”

Rudolf Glaber describes all this somewhat more fully in book 3, chapter 2, from which Baronius derived his account. See also what is recorded as having taken place at the council in volume 9 of Labbe’s collection, column 854.

We have already mentioned the holy emperor’s constant and perpetual beneficence toward Christ’s servants, demonstrated by the four charters of donation issued in this year and reported by Schaten. In addition to these, the above-mentioned Schannat drew my attention to another charter issued at Bamberg on 1 August 1023. In favor of his “confessor,” Abbot Theobald of Saints Ulrich and Afra, the emperor showed that monastery the greatest possible generosity.

Our chronology now reaches the final year of the saint’s life.

154. The Chronicler briefly summarizes the events of 1024 as follows:

> “The emperor celebrated Christmas at Bamberg. A crowd had gathered there without pastors, because all remained in suspense as to whose provident care they would be entrusted by imperial authority . . . . The emperor, afflicted by various pains, prolonged his stay there through frequent and protracted illness. At last, having recovered his strength, he resolved to go at a swift pace to Parthenopolis. Finally, after long deliberation over the difficult journey, he solemnly celebrated Palm Sunday at a place called Alstedt. On the day of reconciliation, because the severity of his illness required it, he withdrew from himself the assembled multitude and, accompanied by a few men, celebrated the Lord’s Supper at Neuburg. On Holy Saturday, having summoned an assembly of the entire senate and accompanied by his wife Cunigund, he came to Parthenopolis, where he was received with great honor. He also celebrated the joy of the Lord’s Resurrection with solemn honor. Then, after receiving many gifts of gold and silk from the bishop of that place, he went to Halberstadt. From there he proceeded to Goslar, where, after spending ten days, he hastened to a certain place called Grona. There, overcome by a severe illness and intoxicated by the cup of bitter death, he gave up his vital spirit.”

The matters that follow there concerning the efforts of Bruno, bishop of Augsburg, are found in chapter 32 of the *Life*. They will be described below, at the beginning of the miracles, from the Anonymous author. Here we place the crown upon the chronology of Henry.

[Col. 0087]

# Fragment of Adelbold, Bishop of Utrecht, Concerning the Deeds of St. Henry the Emperor

## From the Edition of Jacob Gretsers

[NOTE.]

[Col. 0087]

We call this a fragment because it scarcely comprises two complete years of the reign or imperial rule of St. Henry. Yet it is such a work that one can discern in it the author’s fidelity, skill in handling historical material, and exact diligence so clearly that one cannot sufficiently lament the loss of the remainder of the work.

All our efforts to excavate this precious treasure from elsewhere proved fruitless, as was sufficiently stated above in section 6, where more will be found concerning the author. Here I wished briefly to indicate the principal way in which I have divided the aforesaid fragment: not into chapters, but rather into years, according to which the author himself seems to have distinguished his work, as will be evident from the surviving context.

I place this section of the Anonymous compilation first, both because it is genuinely historical and because it agrees much more suitably with our Commentary. I almost wonder whether it would not have been preferable to begin the chronological sequence of St. Henry’s *Life* with it. Nevertheless, in accordance with the practices and judgments of our predecessors, it seemed better not to depart from them.

Thus anyone may make this his starting point who judges that the order of events should be followed rather than the confusion of the author of the Legend. From Adelbold’s prologue alone, it is easy and straightforward to form a judgment concerning his skill and learning as a writer.

## Concerning the Deeds of St. Henry

### The Author’s Prologue

[Col. 0089A]

1. In writing deeds, two things must be kept in view: that the writer preserve truth in his account, and that the reader derive benefit from his reading. But the writer cannot preserve the truth unless he has either firmly avoided or to some extent banished from his mind four things: hatred, carnal affection, envy, and infernal flattery. Hatred and envy either wholly suppress good deeds, pass over them cursorily in their narration, or maliciously distort them. Conversely, they recount, enlarge, and magnify evil deeds. Carnal affection and infernal flattery, knowingly ignorant of evil deeds and pretending ignorance, conceal the truth; but, seeking to please those who have done good, they describe their deeds at length and magnify them beyond what is just. [Col. 0089B] Thus, through these four influences, whether in good deeds or in evil deeds, truth vanishes, while falsehood shines with an overlaid coloring. Spiritual affection, however, the friend of truth, neither conceals evil deeds nor pompously enlarges good ones; for it knows that evil deeds often serve correction, while good deeds frequently do harm when they are turned into pride. It is better to restrain the mind through adversity than to be insolently inflated by prosperity. Nor can the reader derive benefit unless he has either attended carefully or thoroughly understood why good things happen to the good, evil things to the evil, good things to the evil, and evil things to the good.

2. Why good things are granted to the good can be understood in two ways. Some are good in such a manner that, through the trials of this age, they need neither testing nor purification [Col. 0089C]; others are good in such a way that, if they were assailed by trials, they might perhaps be made worse according to the measure of their simplicity. Thus [Note: [Col. 0089D] The reading should undoubtedly be *tales* (“such”), since the verb *foedantur* has a plural subject.] they are not defiled by their life in the mire of this world, so that through what they suffer they may either be summoned to correction or, if they refuse to repent, understand that by enduring evils they must be condemned both here and in the future. Evils sometimes come upon the good [Note: [Col. 0089D] The verb *obveniunt* or *accidunt* is missing.] not so that they may deserve them, but so that their merit may be increased through torment and their reward enlarged through merit. At other times a slight fault lies beneath them, for which they are lightly chastised here, lest they be tortured more severely in the future. Good things are granted to the evil so that they may either recognize God’s mercy in this way and repent of their perversity, or so that what they refused to recognize—the giver of their benefits—may be reserved for their reproach. [Col. 0089D]

3. We believe that what we have set forth is useful in every account both to the writer and to the reader. We know, moreover, and hear very often, that in all writings antiquity is revered with indulgence, while novelty is rejected with disdain. Yet what is accepted as ancient would not be ancient unless it had first been new. [Col. 0090A] Novelty therefore precedes, so that antiquity may follow. It is foolish to despise what precedes and not to accept what follows, and what derives from what precedes its very existence. A thirsty person rarely asks for the stream when the spring is at hand. We say this not so that antiquity may be rejected, but so that novelty may be accepted. Indeed, in every writing, if truth and usefulness are present, novelty and antiquity have equal value. Perhaps someone will say: “What usefulness can there be in reading accounts of deeds?” We answer that whoever reads another’s deeds, if they are good, finds something to follow; if they are bad, he has something from which to take fright. To read another’s deeds is to look into a mirror. [Note: [Col. 0089D] He alludes to Terence’s *Adelphoe*, Act III, scene IV, verse 53.] If you see in it anything that displeases you, correct it in yourself; if anything that pleases you, imitate it. Let the preface end; what the preface has introduced now follows. [Col. 0090B]

## THE YEAR OF CHRIST 1002, THE FIRST YEAR OF SAINT HENRY’S REIGN

4. In the thousand and second year from the Lord’s Incarnation, in the twelfth Indiction [Note: [Col. 0090D] He meant to say the fifteenth; perhaps some copyist wrote what another altered from XV to XII, as will become clearer in the following year, which is marked by Indiction I.], the Emperor Augustus Otto III died at Paterna, which is a castle in Romagna. In bodily beauty he was flourishing, in moral integrity modest, in age indeed young but in natural intelligence mature, and remarkable for his kindness. I would be eager to write an account of his deeds if I either remembered them myself or had a reliable informant. This alone I know: although in the earliest part of his life he had done many childish things, in his final years he lived irreproachably. He loved God, feared him through loving him, pleased everyone, and displeased no one [Col. 0090C] except perhaps unbelievers—for it is innate in the good to displease the wicked and to please the good. At last, what his former life had been, those who were present were able to see in his death. Whoever witnessed it could understand from his devotion that he did not die but departed toward his singular desire. As a faithful creature, he hastened to return to the Creator in fulfillment of his vow. His death—or rather his passing—was for all who were sound in mind a remarkable mourning and an unbelievable lamentation.

5. The grief would also have been incurable had there not survived him the glorious Duke Henry, a man vigorous enough to assume the kingdom. At that time he held the duchy in the Bavarian realm, ruled the people peacefully, enlarged peace, increased the resources of the churches [Col. 0090D], and magnified laws and religious observance. At length he lived in the duchy in such a way that he pleased everyone, so that he might be transferred from the duchy to the kingdom and raised from the standard to the hereditary throne. We call it hereditary because, as we heard from those who knew how to calculate genealogies, on his father’s side he stood in the seventeenth line of descent from Charlemagne, and on his mother’s side in the sixteenth. [Col. 0091A] Moreover, after the death of Otto III, he was elected king [Note: [Col. 0091D] Gretser correctly observed that this passage is corrupt; it is sufficiently clear that the words should be read after “the death of Otto III.”], and he and Otto stood to one another in the third degree of kinship. His mother, moreover, was the daughter of King Conrad [Note: [Col. 0091D] Namely, of Burgundy.].

6. From these predecessors a noble successor arose, was elected, and was desired by all to become king. But how he was invited to the kingdom by those who were sound in mind, and how envy—the companion of good men—tried through its agents to prevent this, it is neither tiresome for me to say nor superfluous for others to hear. Do not be surprised that I have called envy the companion of the good: wherever vigorous deeds abound, envy also abounds. Accordingly, when a certain Philosopher was asked by his disciple how he might live [Col. 0091B] so as to avoid the gnawing attacks of the envious, he replied: “Do nothing well, nothing vigorously, nothing prudently, and know that in this way you can avoid the slanders of the envious.” Either be foolish, then, and avoid envy; or act prudently, and endure envy.

7. When the most glorious Emperor Otto had died, the Cisalpines who had been with him—the Archbishop of Cologne, the bishops of Liège, Augsburg, and Constance, Otto son of Charles, the Counts Henry and Juncmann, and many others acting faithfully—were carrying his body back with the greatest difficulty and amid many dangers through Verona and Bavaria. The most noble Duke, accompanied by the Bavarian bishops and counts, came to meet them. He received the body of his lord [Note: [Col. 0091D] *Senior* is used for “lord”; this usage is extremely common here, as it is in Thietmar and others, whence the French *seigneur*.] [Col. 0091C] and of his kinsman with the reverence that was fitting, received the entire army with the generosity that was required [Note: [Col. 0091D] Gretser says that perhaps *refecit* (“refreshed”) should be read, although it may also be understood that the army was won over by his generosity and thus received.], and conducted it through his land with the convenience that was appropriate. At last, when he reached Muneborg, he carried the Emperor’s body into the city on his own shoulders, displaying an example of piety and performing the duty of humanity. He made the army halt for the day, so that they might confer about the welfare and consolation of the kingdom and so that their horses, wearied by the length of the journey, might recover. There he gave royal gifts to each of the better men and bound to himself in friendship those whom he would later receive into his service.

8. Then, proceeding with the body as far as Augsburg, he had the Emperor’s entrails buried most honorably in the basilica of Saint Afra, beside the tomb of Saint Ulrich, and [Col. 0091D] granted that church one hundred hides from his own hereditary property for the Emperor’s soul. There, taking leave of the others, he returned to his own lands. The Emperor’s body, transported honorably to Aachen, was buried—as it can still be seen—in the middle of the church of Saint Mary. The same most gracious Emperor had both loved this church uniquely and endowed it with very extensive resources.

9. At that time, after the magnificent Duke Henry, [Col. 0092A] the leading men in the kingdom were Duke Benno in Saxony, Duke Hermann in Alemannia, Theodoric in the Lotharingian kingdom, and Margrave Eckehard in Thuringia. Benno, being wise, did not aspire to the kingdom, knowing that Henry was stronger than the others in obtaining it. For it is the mark of a wise man to disdain desires in matters where he knows attainment is impossible. Theodoric likewise, knowing that Duke Henry was the heir to the kingdom, did not wish to begin what he could not finish. Hermann, however, was a powerful man and prudent in other matters, but in this he was not wise: he believed himself capable of what he later proved himself incapable of. As for Eckehard, I do not know whether he retained hope of obtaining the kingdom or was contemplating rebellion. At the royal court called Poleda [Note: [Col. 0092D] This was a famous palace at that time, often visited by Saint Henry, as is clear from Thietmar and the Hildesheim Annals.], he went out by night from his enemies [Col. 0092B] and was killed while fighting bravely. The struggle remained between the most glorious Duke Henry and the most powerful Hermann, but it was brief and soon destined to end. For the two differed from one another in nobility and wisdom, resources and bodily elegance.

10. As June began, Duke Henry, soon to be king, came to Worms on the Rhine with a considerable host gathered from Bavaria and East Francia. He wished to cross there and proceed to Mainz to receive the royal blessing. But Duke Hermann, having assembled the Alemanni, certain Franks, and the Alsatians, hastened to Worms to prevent the crossing, and allowed no one to cross there. He could easily resist, since he had the Rhine [Col. 0092C] as his ally. With Duke Henry, however, were illustrious and most wise men: the Archbishop of Mainz, the Archbishop of Salzburg, the Bishop of Brixen, the Bishop of Würzburg, the Bishop of Regensburg, the Bishop of Strasbourg, the Bishop of Batavia, the Bishop of Friesland, the Abbot of Fulda, and many other abbots and counts.

11. After taking counsel with these men, the Duke pretended to return to Bavaria and, as though despairing of crossing, came to Lorsch. From there, hurrying toward Mainz, he crossed without hindrance. There, on the eighth day before the Ides of June, he was elected king, acclaimed, blessed, and crowned. There the Franks and Mosellans [Note: [Col. 0092D] Understand “those of the Moselle,” that is, those who dwell along the Moselle River.] gathered, became the king’s men, and duly venerated his majesty. After celebrating the days of his installation and receiving all who came into his service, the King crossed the Rhine again and hastened with a very large force through East Francia into Alemannia, so that Hermann, having heard of the devastation of his land, might desist from the rebellion he had begun and submit his head, like the others, to royal majesty. Thus the King remained in Alemannia for several [Col. 0093A] days, devastating the land both unwillingly and willingly.

12. But Hermann, hard of heart and stubborn of neck, angry with the Bishop of Strasbourg because he had acted wisely and chosen the better side, joined by his son-in-law Cuno, went to Strasbourg. Since the Bishop’s soldiers did not resist faithfully, he breached the city walls, seized considerable booty, entered the church by force, and impiously violated it. Meanwhile the King, who was in Alemannia, was celebrating the Nativity of Saint John at Reichenau. Fearing no one, he was conducting himself with confidence when he was informed that Hermann wished to come to meet him and end their dispute in battle. This proposal pleased the King. He departed from Reichenau and reached certain very extensive meadows suitable for [Col. 0093B] combat. There he awaited the Duke’s arrival, refusing to decline the judgment of battle [Note: [Col. 0093D] Gretser restored *iudicium*; read: “not refusing to undergo the hazard of battle.”], and celebrated the feast of the Apostles. But Hermann, following sound advice, refused to meet the King and judged that it would be safer for himself and his men to lie hidden than to come face-to-face with him.

13. While the King was waiting in this way, certain men of imprudent mind advised him to go to Constance and there repay Hermann for what he had deserved at Strasbourg. The bishops of Chur and Constance were with Hermann, choosing him for the kingdom not so much from their hearts as from fear of his proximity and uncertainty about the outcome of the dispute. But the King, being prudent and secure in his control of that city, answered them gently and graciously: “Far be it [Col. 0093C] from me that, because of Hermann’s madness, vengeance should be turned against him from whom the crown of the kingdom has been granted to me. Perhaps, even if I devastated Constance for Strasbourg’s sake, I would not lessen my loss but double it. Moreover, he poorly acquires a kingdom who, in obtaining it, places the ruin of his soul second. God crowned me not for the violation of churches but for the punishment of those who violate them.” After waiting for a long time in the meadows and finally recognizing that Hermann would not come, he departed and began to travel through Alemannia, devastating the Duke’s courts everywhere [Note: [Col. 0093D] *Curtis* is used for a palace, as we have already said concerning Poleda or Polithi; compare French *cour*, Dutch *hof*. Here it seems to mean estates, lands, or possessions.].

14. At last the excessive outcry of the poor grew and reached the King’s ears. The King could not endure it for long, knowing that they had done nothing wrong against the Duke’s harshness [Col. 0093D] and had therefore suffered more than was just. Moved by compassion, he consequently withdrew from Alemannia and came to Francia [Note: [Col. 0093D] Namely, East Francia, or Franconia.], a land especially dear to him, certain that the Duke, willingly or unwillingly, would have to bow his neck and eventually bear the yoke.

15. I do not think it should be passed over that, before the King left Alemannia, Hezelo, son of Berthold, [Col. 0094A] whom he had enriched above all the kingdom’s counts during his own time as duke, sent to him the best envoys he could select from the army and unwisely asked him to grant him the Bavarian duchy. But an ill-considered question receives a considered answer, and a hurried petition is met with a deliberation carefully weighed. After patiently hearing the embassy, he said: “Those whom I have always held foremost among all peoples, and whom I have always loved with the whole affection of my mind, now that I have obtained the royal blessing, I neither wish to diminish in their law nor, while I live, will I allow them to be diminished. They have their law, and by that law they possess the power to choose a duke [Note: [Col. 0093D] This must be understood with qualification. It is not likely that the Bavarians possessed a full right of election; indeed, Saint Henry himself gave them Henry, the brother of Saint Cunegund, as duke, and deposed and restored that same man at his own discretion, as you have in the preliminary Commentary.]. Shall I be the one to break it? Whoever attempts to break it will have me as an enemy. Nor have they deserved anything bad in this campaign [Col. 0094B] that I should grant them to anyone without their own election. They are still serving with me under an uncertain outcome, and should I hand them over against their will to any mortal? Let him wait until I return to Bavaria. If they elect him there, I will elect and approve him; if they refuse, I will refuse. Nor do I think him so foolish that he would seek to increase his own honor through my disgrace.” Having received this answer, Hezelo conceived the spark of rebellion, which after a year he brought forth, to his own grief.

16. The King, therefore, after spending only a few days in Francia, went to Thuringia. There, Prince William of the Thuringians came to meet him with the others without delay and became the King’s man. Proceeding from there into Saxony, the King reached Merseburg [Note: [Col. 0094D] Also, and better, *Merseburch*.]. Duke Benno of the Saxons, Bulizlaus, Duke of the Slavs [Col. 0094C], Liebzo, Archbishop of Bremen, Bishop Benno of Hildesheim [Note: [Col. 0094D] I do not know who this Benno, Bishop of Hildesheim, was. I think Saint Bernward, the Bishop of Hildesheim, is meant; he was faithful and dear to Saint Henry.], Rather, Bishop of Paderborn, Arnulf of Halberstadt, the other bishops of Saxony, and many counts came to meet the King on the feast of Saint James. They received him with acclamation and praise, and, having praised him, each in turn rendered his hands to him; having rendered their hands, they promised their faith by oaths; with their faith promised, they crowned the King; having crowned him, they placed him on the royal throne; and, having placed him there, they venerated him with due rejoicing.

17. These matters having been vigorously completed, Bulizlaus departed from there and, from the very day on which he had promised his faith and confirmed that promise by oath, began to contemplate evil and, as far as he could, to contrive what he had contemplated. For he and Hezelo held a conversation with one another; each was touched by the other’s poisonous counsels, and both began to do what each was later ashamed to have brought to a bad end. Meanwhile, as the King was hurrying from Saxony into the Lotharingian kingdom, his wife, Lady Cunigund by name, already present but soon to be queen in fact, met him at Gruona. [Col. 0094D] From there she came to Paderborn and, on the feast of Saint Lawrence, was acclaimed, [Col. 0095A] blessed, and crowned, becoming *Kunigunda Kuninga* [Note: [Col. 0095D] The author alludes to the name *hunig*, which in German means “king,” and *hunige*, “queen.”], which can be interpreted in Latin as “queen, queen.”

18. But just as serenity is never found without cloudiness following it, so joy rarely exists without adversity accompanying it. For while everyone was rejoicing at the queen’s blessing, the Bavarians—for it is their custom to want in another’s land what they want in their own [Note: [Col. 0095D] I would prefer to read *nolunt* (“do not want”), since neither the Bavarians nor anyone else is accustomed to plundering in his own land.]—began irrationally to gather crops around the city and, wishing to defend their own peasants, to behave. This provoked the locals and also emboldened them to resist strongly. Thus the King’s household and the natives, as the quarrel grew stronger, streamed together, clashed, and met. A serious battle arose. One young man from the King’s household was killed, namely the brother of Lord Filbert, who at that time was Chancellor [Col. 0095B] and later became Bishop of Friesland. Deeply angered by his death, all the King’s faithful men began to pursue the citizens and, in pursuing them, to rage insatiably. Unless they had been restrained by royal authority, they would have pursued them all the way to annihilation [Note: [Col. 0096D] It is quite clear that the intended word was *internecionem* (“destruction”).].

19. When the tumult had finally been quieted with great difficulty and those whose folly had caused the sedition had been punished, the King hurried from there to Dinsberg and awaited there the arrival of the Lotharingians. First the bishops of Liège and Cambrai arrived, doubting neither the King’s prudence nor his faith. The Archbishop of Cologne also arrived, but, the richer he was, the more slowly he came. There was also a reason [Col. 0095C] for his delay: he had received the crown of blessing at Mainz. These men together became the King’s subjects, promised faith, and sealed their promise by oath. With them the King reached Aachen, where, when the other Lotharingians had gathered on the Nativity after the Virgin’s delivery, he was elected, praised, raised to the royal seat, and glorified. But beneath that glorification some offered applause, others shed tears. Those who wept mourned the loss of Otto and did not recognize Henry as the one who had been received.

20. Thus, having been received in each of the kingdoms of his predecessor, except Italy and Alemannia, and praised unanimously by all, the King returned to Francia so that, after passing the severity of winter there, when spring [Col. 0095D] restored its pleasantness he might lead an army into Alemannia and teach Hermann, who refused to follow the counsels of the prudent, to bear the yoke after being afflicted by various devastations. But Hermann, who by following the counsels of young men and holding an empty hope had been beside himself, gathered himself together and came to meet the King at Brusellae on the feast of Saint Remigius [Note: [Col. 0096D] In the territory of the Bishop of Speyer; elsewhere called Bruchsal. The remaining sense is easier to understand than to explain.], knowing that it was better not to have caused harm beforehand [f., than to repent]. He presented himself to the King barefoot with faithful intercessors, asked pardon for his wrongdoings, sought grace [Col. 0096A] to possess his property by royal grant, and, in order to obtain these things, bent his knees to the ground.

21. He was immediately received kindly, and what he sought was granted to him with complete humility. Only the terms of a certain condition were woven into the arrangement; although burdensome at present, it was nevertheless beneficial to him in the future. He was received into favor on the condition that the church of Strasbourg should be restored by him to its former state after the losses it had suffered. He did not refuse this, but at the King’s command and with his advice he handed over the abbey of Saint Stephen to the said church as compensation for the damage he had inflicted. Once this condition had been confirmed by the giving of hands and oaths, he became the King’s man and rejoiced that he had thus brought the badly begun dispute to an end. When these matters were completed, the King decided to return to Bavaria, his native land, [Col. 0096B] unwilling to favor new faithful men in such a way that, by setting the old ones aside, he would dismember them.

22. At Regensburg, therefore, while celebrating the solemn feast of Saint Martin, he bestowed the Duchy of Bohemia on a certain Slav named Blademar and, to make him more acceptable to the others, honored him beyond what was just in words and deeds. He remained in Bavaria for several days, administering justice to those who sought it and showing due honor to those who came to visit him, according to each person’s worth.

23. At that same time, a certain bishop-killer named Harduin was not reigning in Italy but was serving the vices that reigned within him. When they heard of the Emperor Otto’s death, the Lombards—deaf and blind, and making no provision for the future—elected this man [Col. 0096C] and, hastening toward repentance, crowned him king for themselves. At that time, as I have said, he ruled in servitude, and, constantly awaiting the arrival of King Henry, guarded with sufficiently prudent care the entrances to Lombardy, which the natives call the Cluses. This too was a true judgment of God: he honored the bishops, who in his election had burned and thirsted above all others, as bullock-drivers and treated them as swineherds. One day the Bishop of Brixen came to him and wished to argue some matter—I do not know what. As soon as the argument began to displease him, Harduin seized him by the hair and threw him to the ground like a most worthless oxherd. He conducted no business with the older men but arranged everything with the young. What was most grievous of all, under him [Col. 0096D] perjurers, violators, and devastators held power, while lovers of the laws and worshipers of God were oppressed. Greed was his counselor; avarice, his chamberlain; money, his lady and queen. With these attendants he held adulterous scepters.

24. Therefore, some who had repented of his coronation sent envoys, others letters, to King Henry, humbly begging him to aid a land subjected to so grievous a burden. They also instructed him that, if he himself were occupied with other matters, he should at least send them some prince of his own with a small force [Col. 0097A]. In this desire some were open and some concealed. For Margrave Tiebold, the Archbishop of Ravenna, and the bishops of Modena, Verona, and Vercelli openly remained faithful to King Henry. The Archbishop of Milan and the bishops of Cremona, Piacenza, Pavia, Brixen, and Como made their wishes known. Yet all together desired King Henry and invited him through petitions delivered by envoys and letters.

25. At last Otto, Duke of Carinthia, who also held the county of Verona, was chosen by the King to fulfill the Lombards’ petition and was sent into Italy with a small force, relying on the trust of those mentioned above. Otto, son of Heribert, [Col. 0097B] was also attached to him, together with Ernest, son of Margrave Tietbold. When these men had gathered among the mountains that separate Bavaria and Carinthia from Italy, on the river called the Brenta, the Carinthians and Friulians came to meet them in small numbers, as though relying on the promises of the Italians and thinking nothing of battle. Meanwhile the Archbishop of Ravenna and Margrave Tiebold, together with the other openly faithful supporters of King Henry, had gathered their men, intending to meet the Germans and receive them safely into Italy. Harduin, learning of this, hastened to come to Verona with a very large force, intending both to intercept there the Italians who were hastening to assist the Germans and to storm the Cluses, which were guarded by the Bishop of Verona. This he did.

[Col. 0097C] 26. After the Cluses had been stormed, Harduin heard that the Germans had gathered in the plain of Trent and hastened there with all his men. But, finding no Germans there, he withdrew into the countryside of Verona and celebrated the Nativity of the Lord in a certain little castle. Yet, coming from such a man, this celebration should more properly be called an abuse of celebration. Meanwhile the Germans, having advanced in the vicinity of a certain mountain called Ungarius—for I do not know for what reason—and knowing that Harduin had already occupied the Cluses, sent their envoys to Harduin and asked him either to yield to them until they had passed or, if they yielded to him, to come to them. When Harduin heard the embassy, he turned to a deceitful stratagem and said: “Stay with us through the night; tomorrow, after taking counsel with our faithful men, we shall be able to give you an answer.” [Col. 0097D]

27. While the envoys did not understand the ambush, Harduin went around his camp throughout the night, warning his men to be ready to engage the Germans on the following day. At daybreak, when the envoys came to receive the answer, they saw all the Lombards armored and prepared for battle and asked Harduin what this meant. He, spewing forth a wicked plan, said: “Perhaps your departure will last only for a time.” He then moved his army and at midday reached Mount Ungarius. That army was estimated to consist of 1,015 men. [Col. 0098A] The Germans, however, scarcely numbered five hundred; and of these some were scattered in search of fodder [Note: [Col. 0097D] They had been sent out to forage, for *fodrum* means fodder or provisions, necessary for human beings as well as animals; see the glossaries for more on the word.], while others had been sent to guard the roads. When they perceived Harduin’s arrival, they suddenly armed themselves and prepared as best they could to resist, choosing the fame of courage and setting life second.

28. Meanwhile Harduin came upon them with the Lombards. Otto advanced to meet him with the Germans. They engaged, fought, and inflicted very heavy slaughter on both sides; and the Germans, although far fewer, would almost have won the victory if they had not been hindered by the flight of Otto, brother of the Bishop of Regensburg. When he fled, the German battle line was weakened and, attacked again by many, was defeated. At last the victory belonged to the Lombards, [Col. 0098B] but it was purchased at the cost of a very great slaughter of their own men. The Germans withdrew, confused for the moment but destined eventually to repay the injury in kind. Meanwhile the King, having returned from Bavaria to Francia, celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Frankfurt, received embassies from many, and sent envoys back with gifts and appropriate replies. Hermann too, who had previously been unwilling to bear the yoke, attended that celebration and, as was fitting, obeyed royal majesty in everything.

## THE YEAR OF CHRIST 1003, THE SECOND YEAR OF HENRY’S RULE

29. In the year 1003 from the Lord’s Incarnation, in the first Indiction, King Henry resolved to go into the district of the Moselle, which he had not yet entered, knowing that a land which the king does not visit very often abounds in the cries and groans of the poor. He therefore came to Thionville and held there a general assembly with all the Mosellans. At this assembly the dukes Hermann and Theodoric, who ought to have been defenders and assistants of the laws, were conscious of their own guilt, opposed them, and wished to be their attackers. But when the King learned this, the more stubborn he saw them against justice, the more ardently he pressed the matter; and, by administering the law to all who complained—even against the dukes themselves—he strove to set things right. At last, discovering that one of the Duke’s castles, called Mulsberg, was harming the inhabitants of the district, he ordered it to be demolished and warned that it must not be rebuilt as a powerful fortification. [Col. 0098C]

30. After holding the assembly with authority, he resolved to go to Aachen, so that there he might commemorate the Emperor’s anniversary with due devotion and strengthen the Lotharingians, who were flocking to him, in loyalty to himself and in the interests of the kingdom. Meanwhile he was struck by a very serious illness, and, although he was King, was reminded that he was a man. Nevertheless, he completed the journey he had begun and reached Aachen. There, after commemorating his kinsman and lord [Note: [Col. 0098D] Otto III, whom he also called his lord above.] with the deepest devotion, he heard much [Col. 0099A] about the holiness of Saint Servatius and went to Maastricht, both to implore the intercession of the Saints resting there and to organize a place and a way of life for the service of God by canons. There he first heard of the battle fought between the Italians and the Germans and, as is characteristic of a wise man, bore it with equanimity, knowing that the sky cannot always remain clear and that human affairs cannot prosper without interruption.

31. From there, not undervaluing the merits of Saint Lambert, he came to Liège. There he suffered most severely from a colic illness inherited from his predecessors; he who through royal power was raised above the ordinary experience of human frailty [Col. 0099B] was restrained through bodily suffering by paternal chastisement. He returned again to Aachen and venerated the Purification of the Holy Mother of God with the most celebrated devotion. Having granted the Lotharingians permission to depart, he came to Nijmegen. There he remained for several days of Lent, rendering to God what belongs to God and doing for human beings what belongs to them. Meanwhile Duke Blademar of Bohemia died, and Bulizlaus attempted to spew forth the poison of disloyalty, drunk from the spring of his own iniquity, against the King. For he invaded Prague, the capital of Bohemia, through deceptive payments [Col. 0099C], false promises, and extremely cunning frauds. He also subjected Milzavia, the march lying between Saxony and Poland, to his own misfortune through the ambushes in which he was skilled.

32. When this was reported to the King, he was neither inflamed nor angered, nor was he stirred to vengeance by sudden impulses, knowing that anger and haste are always enemies of deliberation. Concealing his knowledge of the invasion in question, however, he sent word through wise and eloquent envoys that Bulizlaus should not invade the land that had recently been deprived of its prince and that, if he wished, he could acquire it with the King’s favor and voluntary grant. When the wretched Bulizlaus heard this embassy, he rejected the gentle commands, destined at some time to suffer bitter blows. For Hezelo was with him, digging a well of rebellion from which he was destined to drink the water of disloyal confusion; he was also weaving nooses into which he himself would fall. When Lent had ended, the King celebrated Easter at Theleborg [Note: [Col. 0099D] Understand Quedlinburg, or, as the Hildesheim Annals read it, *Quidelingaburg*, a place as well known at that time as Palithi.], and, like a wise man, deliberately ignored Bulizlaus’s violence. He also honored Otto and Ernest, who then came to meet him after returning from the Italian battle, with royal gifts for having received wounds and for the confusion of their necessary flight, and relieved them with due consolation [lacuna] He also received those who had until then been hostile to the Saxons, but who came of their own accord [Note: [Col. 0099D] Leibniz rightly observes that Adelbold must here have indicated some people of the Slavs.], and, with benevolent discernment, made them most faithful to himself.

[Col. 0099D] 33. After these events, during the days of the Rogations, he remained at Meresburg [Note: [Col. 0100D] Read, as above, Merseburg.], where he was informed of the defiance of Bulizlaus and Hezelo. Pretending not to believe it, he departed from there and came to Halberstadt to celebrate Pentecost. He then headed into Bavaria, wishing to learn whether what was being said about Hezelo was true. When he arrived and discovered that Hezelo’s fury had been irrationally kindled around the neighboring regions, and learned that Hezelo relied on Bulizlaus’s aid, he reserved retaliation against Bulizlaus [Col. 0100A] for the future and decided first to uproot the root of the implanted plague from the bosom of his kingdom, so that, once inward quiet and peace had been restored, he might more easily extinguish disturbances on the outside afterward. He did not fail to recognize that it is the mark of a foolish man suddenly to heal the skin over a wound and conceal a bruising of the flesh beneath the healing of the skin. For the treatment of a wound, when it is carried from within outward, is more firmly completed at the surface.

### 34

Meanwhile Ernestus [Note: “Ernesto,” “Ernestio,” and “Ernestus” are to be understood as referring to the same person.] also joined the same rebellion—not compelled by any injury, but either seduced by the ardor of youth or misled by the suggestion of those seeking through him to enlarge their own advantages. The lord Bruno as well, King Henry’s brother and a bishop, joined them: young in years and, because of his youth, easily led astray. It was a source of pride to the faithless that they had the King’s brother in their region. Thus this conspiracy, the younger and more foolish its recruits, failed all the more disgracefully and feebly. For it is said: “The gathering of fools is the dispersal of counsel; and the dispersal of counsel is the enervation of action.”

### 35

King Henry therefore gathered some Lotharingians, Franks, and Bavarians and, at the beginning of August, led an army into Francia against Hezelo. He devastated Hezelo’s possessions and forced him, together with Lord Bruno and Ernestus, to hide in the forests. At last Hezelo withdrew to the fortifications of castles which neither he feared could be captured nor anyone else believed could be taken. At the first assault, Mertula was destroyed, and Hezelo’s soldiers captured there were permitted, through the intercession of the princes, to depart unharmed. But the Slavs [a] sent by Bulizlaus to his aid were distributed among the army as slaves.

### 36

After this the King besieged Crucina [Note: Leibniz advises reading “Crossen,” perhaps Creussen in the Upper Palatinate of Bavaria.], where Hezelo’s wife and sons were, together with whatever could be dearer to him. During the siege, those who imprudently went out, especially after the distribution of provisions, were wounded, captured, and killed by Hezelo and his other associates. When the King learned of this, he assigned four hundred guards each day to accompany those who went out, so that they might protect them and lay ambushes for those who were setting ambushes.

When Hezelo and his companions heard this, he withdrew into a certain valley into which there was no entrance except by a single path. There he pitched his tents; there, for—I do not know—three or two nights, he lived almost safely from the plunder of the poor. When the guards learned this from one peasant, they secretly descended into the valley around the sixth hour, when Hezelo and his men were taking things more easily because of the heat of the day. They went around many places, carefully searching for Henry’s camp.

### 37

At last one of them, seeing the tents, hurried too eagerly to summon his companions and began shouting, “Kyrie eleison” (“Lord, have mercy”), repeating it frequently so that they might come more quickly. When Hezelo perceived this, he abandoned the tents and even his weapons, took flight, and with difficulty escaped the hands of those arriving. Lord Bruno too, having shamefully abandoned the small shield which he was accustomed to use when placed outside himself [i.e. when acting independently], fled from those whom he could have commanded had he remained with his brother; and he became an object of ridicule, though he ought to have been an honor and distinction.

But these were the actions of youth. For it is said: “Whoever is led in youth without the bridle of knowledge is often driven headlong into the narrow places of disgrace.” That this was indeed an age of youth was later shown by the maturity which made him both more useful to himself and more faithful to his brother. Ernestus was captured and brought before the King.

### 38

Some immediately advised the King to order him struck with the death sentence, so that through him later generations might be chastised and might not attempt, without cause, to incur the King’s anger. But the Archbishop of Mainz, who held the highest position with the King for obtaining whatever one might request, came forward as an intercessor, rescued the young man from the law, and saved him from death.

At last Crusina was captured, destroyed, and burned by the King. He permitted Hezelo’s wife and her companions to depart, granting this to her through the intercession of her brother Otto. When Hezelo heard that Crusina had been captured, he reached by flight one of his own fortifications called Erana. There he encountered a certain Saxon named Sigefrid, a participant in the perverse conspiracy.

### 39

But Hezelo too, having no hope of resisting the royal anger, himself set fire to that same fortification; and, unable to conceal his misery, showed how utterly desperate he was. When the Saxon Sigefrid perceived this, he fell away from the hope of the rebellion he had begun. He who had swollen with confidence borrowed from another against royal majesty burst, struck by the bitterness of another’s disgrace.

He was ashamed, therefore, to have come there, and returned to his own lands as quickly as he could. Hezelo, however, fled with Lord Bruno to Bulizlaus, as though to his one refuge; and, what is most grievous to anyone, he learned to live like a beggar on another man’s bread. Meanwhile, when the King arrived at Erana, he found that the purpose of his coming had already been accomplished by the hands of his enemy. He had come to destroy, but they had destroyed themselves, lest he find anyone whom he would have to destroy.

### 40

After Hezelo had been driven away and his castles destroyed, the King returned to Baveberg, a place especially dear to him. There, granting leave to the army, he celebrated the Nativity of the holy Mother of God [the feast of the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary].

From there he came into the forest called Speicheshart [Note: Leibniz says that it is otherwise called “Speteshart,” and today Spessart: a wooded and rather difficult mountain passage situated between the territory of Mainz and farther Franconia. Thus the text seems almost certainly to contain an error, unless Bavaria at that time extended as far as Swabia.], which separates Bavaria from Francia. After the exertion of the campaign, he enjoyed the pleasure of hunting. He spent the autumn there; there he provided himself and his companions with abundant recreation and delight. From there, passing slowly through Francia, he came into Saxony and announced to the Thuringians and Saxons a future expedition into Milzavia. He then celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Poleda.

## The Year of Christ 1004, the Third Year of Henry’s Reign

### 41

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1004, in the second indiction, the King was invited by the Archbishop of Magdeburg, named Giselarius, who, having been afflicted with paralysis for many years, was unable to leave the metropolitan city. Moved by pious affection, he willingly obeyed and set out to visit the Archbishop at Magdeburg.

When he arrived there, the Archbishop had already entered the way of all flesh; he who had been awaiting the King had migrated at the command of the King of Kings. In his place Tageno [Note: Otherwise Tagino or Tagmo; Thietmar says more about him in various places.] was immediately elected, the King’s chaplain, and, with the clergy and people acclaiming him, was raised to the episcopal seat. From there the King proceeded to Merseburg, where he venerated the Purification of the holy Mother of God with due reverence. There Tageno was also consecrated Archbishop by his suffragan bishops.

### 42

After this, having gathered the Thuringians and Saxons, the King entered Milzavia, wishing to storm the fortifications which Bulizlaus had occupied. But the severity of winter interrupted this plan and denied the royal will an outcome which could easily have been achieved in summer. Abandoning the fortifications, therefore, he devastated the land, assigning this guilt to its inhabitants: that, corrupted by money, they had not resisted Bulizlaus in accordance with their pledge of fidelity.

From there he returned to Merseburg, stationing margraves along the course of the Elbe, so that they might guard both Saxony and against Bulizlaus’s predatory incursions, and themselves inflict upon Bulizlaus the troubles of his continual disturbance.

### 43

Meanwhile Hezelo began to regret what he had undertaken. He was ashamed to live longer on another man’s bread, and weary of wandering alone in exile among strangers. He therefore preferred to risk death rather than continue living in this way. At last he returned and, having sought trustworthy intercessors, surrendered himself at Merseburg to the royal majesty.

Thus, kicking against the goad, he felt the sting twice: he lost his possessions and handed himself over to another’s power. Lord Bruno, however, finding no consolation with Bulizlaus, fled to his sister, the Queen of Hungary; and, recognizing his own fault, he sought her intercession [Note: These events, composed in 1004, show that Gisela had been married before the year 1005, as we stated in the preliminary commentary.].

### 44

Meanwhile the King, mindful of the injury which the Italians had inflicted upon the Germans, departed from Saxony and came into Bavaria. There he granted the Bavarian duchy to Henry, the Queen’s brother, on the feast of Saint Benedict.

At last, when he was coming to Augsburg, situated on the borders of Bavaria and Alemannia, the Lotharingians, Franks, and Alemanni came to meet him, volunteering to avenge the injury inflicted upon the Germans and prepared in every way to serve the royal honor. Proceeding from there with them in order to assemble the army, he halted at a place called Omuga [Note: Leibniz thinks that Otting is indicated.].

There Lord Bruno, having returned to the King, came to meet him together with the Hungarian envoys of the King, who had come to intercede for Bruno. Humbly requesting pardon for his offenses, he moved his brother’s heart and quickly inclined him to forgive. For there is a proverb: “A brother’s tears quickly move the heart of every moderate man; and a kinsman’s calamity becomes one’s own anxiety.”

He therefore received Bruno with the piety that was fitting, and, having received him, attached him to himself with the familiarity that was due. From there he advanced the army through barren places, rugged mountains, spacious forests, and slippery roads, and reached the city of Trent. There, on Palm Sunday, he had his men spend the day with the solemnity that was appropriate.

Foreseeing his arrival, Harduinus, the false king, sent guards to the Claustra, whom he considered utterly faithful to him, and hastened as much as he could to assemble an army.

### 45

Harduinus then came to the plain of Verona, hoping that the outcome of what followed would resemble the first event. When King Henry perceived this, he turned to other roads—not to avoid battle, but to seek an easier entrance for himself. For it was impossible to pass through the Claustra beside the Adige, which Harduinus defended with a very large multitude.

Meanwhile he sent ahead a certain chaplain of his named Hemilgerus [Helingerus] to the Carentani, ordering him to seize in advance the Claustra, set far from the direct road, which Harduinus guarded less carefully. No one could believe that the royal army would either wish or be able to pass along roads so difficult and narrow.

The Carentani obeyed the King’s commands and, at Helinger’s urging, divided themselves into two groups. Before sunrise, one group abandoned its horses and secretly occupied the mountain above the Claustra. The other, once daylight had appeared and having heard the signal from those who were on the mountain, hurried to storm the Claustra.

The guards, unaware of those who had occupied the mountain, approached to resist the attackers at the Claustra. Suddenly those hiding on the mountain sprang out and attacked the defenders of the Claustra fiercely from the rear. The guards, realizing that they had been deceived, some took flight, some threw themselves over the precipice, and others into the flowing river Brenta. After this assault, the Carentani, holding the Claustra, awaited the King.

### 46

When the King learned this through the chaplain whom he had sent ahead, he hurried to the Claustra. Leaving behind the baggage and taking with him those prepared for battle, he crossed with the greatest difficulty. Then, coming to the plain, he ordered tents to be pitched beside the Brenta, so that there he might venerate the solemn days of Holy Week with worthy devotion.

It did not seem good to him that during those days, in which the Founder for the founded, the Creator for creatures, and the Lord for servants had willed, as a revelation of his charity, to be seized, scourged, crucified, and buried, any engagement should be proclaimed from which a violent shedding of Christian blood might result.

There, therefore, the consecration of the chrism was performed by the Archbishop of Cologne, something greatly needed in those regions at that time. For in twelve bishoprics around the entrance to Italy, on that day, because of the present confusion, there was neither a bishop nor consecrated chrism.

There the Lord’s Supper was most devoutly commemorated by the entire army; there Good Friday was observed; there Holy Saturday was celebrated with pious devotion. Moreover, the Lord’s Pasch was celebrated with worthy veneration and honored with pious observance.

### 47

After this the King ordered the Count Palatine to proclaim throughout the entire army, under the royal ban, that flight was forbidden. He was also to add that anyone who dared to flee should know that he would be punished by the death sentence.

When this ban had been proclaimed throughout the army, the King crossed the river on the Tuesday of Easter week and ordered tents to be pitched there again, awaiting the messengers whom he had sent ahead to investigate the place where Harduinus was staying with his men.

Meanwhile, for a reason I do not know, the unity of the Lombards was broken, and, divided in their resistance, they all hastened to return to their own homes. Whether fear caused this, or love of King Henry, or hatred of Harduinus, I leave to the knowledge of those who were present.

This alone I know: the providence of Him was not absent whose benevolence grants each person what he wills without dispute and, for hidden reasons of judgment, consents that what he wills be decided through battle.

### 48

The entrance was therefore open to King Henry; what had been expected to come through labor was granted through rest by true Rest. He came to Verona, was received by the citizens, acclaimed, praised, and crowned. Margrave Tietbold came out to meet him, as did many others, rescued from the jaws of fury and restored to the hope of freedom.

From there he proceeded to Brescia and was received with every expression of joy by the bishop and citizens. There the Archbishop of Ravenna, together with his own men and those from neighboring territories, came out to meet him and surrendered hands not yet stained by adulterous dominion to the long-awaited elder.

From there the King came to Bergamo and received the Archbishop of Milan through the surrender of hands and the taking of oaths. From there he went to Pavia. There he was received with worthy acclamations by a very great multitude of Lombard nobles who had assembled to welcome him, and with the rejoicing of the entire city he was led to the church of Saint Michael.

There the clergy, there the assembly of nobles, there the common people of both sexes—all in agreement and with one voice—acclaimed and praised King Henry, and, having praised him, indicated their approval by raising their hands.

### 49

Having been praised, he was crowned; having been crowned, he was duly honored by everyone. He was then escorted back to the palace with every expression of joy.

At last, as the day was already declining, the devil—envious of peace, hostile to concord, and an ardent sower of discord—by whose prompting Judas, after receiving the mystery of the Lord’s body and blood, swelled up to perpetrate an unspeakable crime and, persuaded by that same devil, burst into eternal punishment—stirred up the citizens against the royal majesty.

They had surrendered their hands, promised faith, and secured their safety by oath, and had not been compelled by any injury that could reasonably be alleged. Nevertheless, after the poison of drunkenness had been introduced, the devil moved them against the King.

At his persuasion they armed themselves; at his goading they were incited; under his leadership they hastened to the palace; at his direction they surrounded the walls. Some instigators were also among them [the text’s *interrant* is uncertain], men troubled by their own consciences who preferred to wander under Harduinus through illicit plunder rather than be restrained under Henry by the bridle of justice and law.

A clamor arose and a din broke out; it was immediately heard in the palace. But because no one could believe such things after the faith promised on that very day, they were not understood at once. The King nevertheless ordered an investigation. The city’s fury and the madness of the common people were reported.

The Archbishop of Cologne, who was with the King, hoping that he could restrain this fury, looked out through a window and began to inquire into the causes of so great a frenzy. But stones and arrows came upon him, and he was scarcely allowed to finish the speech he had begun. For the anger of the Lombards was burning fiercely, and from the outcome of the war against Duke Otto it still possessed strength for defiance.

### 50

The Lombards therefore pressed on to break into the palace. The King’s household resisted, although they were few. Some of the Germans were with their horses, some were staying in lodgings, and some were in castles neighboring that district.

The King immediately boiled over in indignation into anger and wanted to go out armed with those who were with him, making up the number of his soldiers through hope in heavenly grace. But the Archbishop of Cologne, with all the force he could summon and together with those who were of sound mind, held the King back, knowing that once the head was lost, no hope of escape would remain in the limbs.

Meanwhile, as the shouting grew stronger, the Germans assembled. Joining their companions, they advanced toward the palace and for a while restrained the Lombards from their unbridled fury. At last the darkness of night thickened, and the missiles of stones and arrows became extremely dangerous for the Germans.

Necessity seized counsel and, in order to provide missiles, very quickly produced a fire. With much exertion the Germans attacked the city walls; with much fear the Lombards fought for their lives.

### 51

Then a certain young man, the Queen’s brother, named Gislebertus, was wounded by the Lombards. Because of his mortal wound the Germans were enraged, and, blinded by fury against the missiles, stormed the city walls. Breaking in, they hastened to avenge the young man’s blood, which was the spur of their rage.

One of them, more ardent in spirit than the rest, named Voleramus, threw himself into the midst of the Lombard ranks. Drawing the sword with which he was girded, he courageously drove it into one of the Lombards who was raging more insanely than the others, from the sharp point of his helmet down to his throat; and, quicker than words can tell, he withdrew unharmed among his own men.

Thus a fierce battle was fought throughout the night. Suspended between two possible outcomes, it made now one side and now the other bolder and more active in hope of victory. At times the Germans, forming a tortoise with their shields, broke into the Lombard ranks and brought some of them whom they had captured alive before the King.

### 52

Meanwhile the palace, which was at times the Germans’ one refuge when they were exhausted, was set alight and burned, and threatened to collapse. But when the hope of refuge had been removed, their courage was kindled more strongly, and they were driven more fiercely to engage the Italians again.

When daylight had fully come, while the Alemanni, who had learned of these events later, were breaking through the city walls far from the palace, the Lotharingians and Franks began once more to pursue the Lombards heavily before the palace and forced them to flee as far as their own walls.

But unable to endure for long the density of the missiles coming from the rooftops, they were compelled to set fire to the houses; with sword and flame they inflicted a pitiable slaughter upon the citizens.

At last the anger of the Germans, which was not easily satisfied, was sated by a great massacre. Then, when no one any longer resisted, they turned to plunder. But when the fire had grown excessively strong, the King was moved from the rigidity of his mind and, prompted by compassion, ordered his men to desist from what they had begun.

He could scarcely restrain them, and, unable to bear the stench of the burning any longer, withdrew to a certain small fortified place called the Golden Cell of Saint Peter. The citizens, scarcely able to breathe, followed the King and earnestly begged him to forgive their drunkenness. Forgiveness was granted them; indulgence was granted them.

But indulgence is easy after punishment has exceeded the offense. Thus those whom war against Otto had made swollen with pride were made suppliant and subject by the humility they had newly assumed.

### 53

When Pavia had thus been subdued, all Italy was shaken, and all the natives came to the King without being summoned, obeying his commands in every respect. Even cities to which the King had not yet come voluntarily sent hostages and promised the required fidelity by oaths.

When these matters had been completed, the King came to a certain place called Long Bridge. There an innumerable multitude of Lombards assembled and subjected themselves entirely to obedience to the royal majesty.

After holding a conference there and setting aside [Note: It is quite clear that *dipositis* should be read instead of *depositis*.] the affairs of the kingdom, he turned aside to Milan, moved by love for Saint Ambrose, whose freedom of speech and excellence of character he loved.

Having sought the intercession of that saint and of the other saints at rest, he returned to the meadows of Long Bridge. There he consoled the Lombards, who complained about his sudden departure, with the promise of a speedy return. From there, coming to Chromo [Note: Gretser says that perhaps *Cremam* should be read.], he celebrated Holy Pentecost with devout piety. As he departed from there, the Tuscans came to meet him, and each in order surrendered his hands.

### 54

After this the King, keeping in mind the injury inflicted upon him by Bulizlaus, hastened to return home. He proceeded through Monte Celer [Note: No one explains *Montem celerem*. It is sufficiently certain that he did not enter Savoy by way of Mont Cenis, since he is said to have hastened into Alemannia. Perhaps, therefore, we should read “swiftly through the mountains.”] into Alemannia.

He knew that a land subject to the rule of a child often uses the reins too loosely and, through the tumultuous diversity of its own will, is swept along various precipices. For Duke Herimannus had already died, and his son had been appointed by the King in his place to the duchy; but, still excessively young, he did not know how to govern even himself.

At a place called Turegum [Note: It is not implausible that Zurich in Switzerland is indicated here. If so, *montem celerem* might perhaps be understood as the mountain now called Saint Gotthard.], the King held a conference and compelled everyone, from the least to the greatest, to swear to preserve peace and not consent to robbery.

Having thus established all Alemannia under the tranquility of peace, he came into Alsace. While he was holding a conference with the Alsatians in the city of Strasbourg on the vigil of Saint John, the house in which he was sitting to administer law and justice suddenly collapsed. It broke the bones of the leg of a certain priest who was accustomed to remain with a certain excommunicated lady.

He alone died; the others suffered nothing except fear. But through his death they learned what they had often heard through the Psalmist: “With the chosen you will be chosen, and with the perverse you will be perverse.”

### 55

After this the King came to Mainz, where, in his customary spirit of piety, he solemnly celebrated the feasts of the apostles. Then, passing through Eastern Francia, he hastened into Saxony, intending to relieve his heart, weighed down by indignation against Bulizlaus, through a powerful act of vengeance.

An expedition was announced to the Saxons, Bavarians, and Eastern Franks. A date in mid-August was set for the advance, so that, after the crops had first been gathered, abundance might accompany the army.

Accordingly, in the middle of August, the Saxons assembled at Merseburg. The King did not wish to reveal to any of his intimates whether he intended to go into Poland or Bohemia, since he knew Bulizlaus’s winding cunning, by which, through certain secret friends, he was accustomed to learn even royal secrets.

Nevertheless, ordering ships to be assembled from Magdeburg as far as Zeitz, he pretended that he intended to go into Poland and simulated that this would be the route of passage. While everyone expected this, he suddenly led the army into Bohemia, seeking first to recover what was his own and then, in vengeance, to invade what belonged to others—not entirely foreign possessions, however, since they ought to bear the yoke of his kingdom.

### 56

It is worthwhile to insert something which, once heard, makes it clear that there is rarely a fault which is not followed by vengeance, unless repentance has forestalled it.

When the elder Bulizlaus, the Bohemian duke and uncle of the Bulizlaus now under discussion, died, he left three sons surviving him. The eldest, named Bulizlaus, having obtained the duchy after his father, began to live more cruelly than that land either wished or was able to endure.

The natives, therefore, cursing him for his excessive cruelty, he began to fear that he might be expelled by one of his brothers, with the people of Prague inciting them to do so. Suspicion, conceived from a bad conscience, incited him to a most wicked crime and led him to an abominable deed. For he castrated one of his brothers and attempted to suffocate the other in a bathhouse.

Those two men—one castrated, the other half alive—fled to Bavaria, excluded from their paternal inheritance.

### 57

King Henry, moved by this impiety, gave the Bohemian duchy to Blademarius, whom we have already mentioned. After Blademarius died, Bulizlavus, the son of Bulizlaus, attempted to retain the duchy against the King’s will, having brought Bulizlaus, the son of Mesecon, into the conspiracy as his associate.

A false friendship therefore arose between those two Bulizlauses, and a deceitful alliance. One frequently invited the other; they often feasted pleasantly at one another’s expense, although a hidden fire lay beneath the ashes.

At last Bulizlavus, the son of Mesecon, preferred the pleasures of Prague and the loveliness of Bohemia to the friendship that had been promised. So that, by whatever means, he might expel his nephew and possess the rule of so great a land, he searched out the innermost reaches of his schemes.

He invited him to banquets and provided various kinds of food, intending finally to offer him bitter cups. After he had been satisfied with food, he entrusted him to his soldiers and, by nods of the eyes—teaching them to do likewise—signaled that he should be led out and blinded.

### 58

The commands of impiety were fulfilled and the works of iniquity were carried out. Thus he who had castrated his brother perished, led to his death by his kinsman and associate. He who had refused to have his brother as an equal partner in the principality was made, through the punishment he suffered, his equal in condition and still more useless.

After this man had been blinded, Bulizlavus, the son of Mesecon, as I said above, through winding frauds and perverse cunning that always followed in his footsteps, and through endless promises, invaded Prague and all Bohemia. Having acquired dominion in this manner, he fortified extremely strong castles throughout the places accessible to the royal army.

### 59

Meanwhile the King, coming with the Saxons, entered Bohemia with the greatest difficulty over a certain mountain on which Bulizlavus had already established a fortification to block the entrance. He sent the margraves ahead by night.

When the Bohemians perceived his entry, some, overcome by fear of the royal presence, surrendered one castle, together with themselves, to the King. The King immediately granted it, with the greatest goodwill, to the eunuch Laramerus [Note: Jaremiro.], the brother of the blind Bulizlavus, whom he was bringing back with him out of compassion to his native land.

Then, extending his journey, he proceeded through that land, awaiting the Bavarians, for whom the entrance into Bohemia was not the same as it had been for the Saxons.

### 60

But when the Bavarians prolonged their arrival, the King reached, with the Saxons alone, a certain city called Satiza [Note: Today Saaz, according to Leibniz.]. When the citizens saw his power, they were greatly disturbed and immediately began considering how they might seek peace and obtain the King’s favor.

They opened the city gates at once, inserting the condition that they might obtain favor. They expelled the Poles whom Bulizlavus had placed there to defend the site.
