In expelling them, they mutilated some by cutting off their limbs, threw some down from very high places, and killed others, both to avenge the injuries inflicted upon them by the Poles and to satisfy the royal honor in every respect.

At last the heat of this cruelty struck the King’s heart, and his innate compassion inclined him to oppose such madness. The survivors were now led out alive and brought before the King in the church. After this the entire city surrendered to the King. As it was required to do, it bound itself by a promise of fidelity through oaths and by hostages.

Meanwhile rumor flew that Bulizlavus had been killed by the people of Prague, who were bound together by the tie of conspiracy. Although the rumor was false, it nevertheless terrified Bulizlavus’s faithful followers.

## The Life of Saint Henry

### Preliminary Notice to the Following Life

As has already been observed more than once in the Commentary, the following point must once again be placed before the eyes of readers: the work presented here by the anonymous author is not a Life, that is, a historical narrative of Saint Henry’s deeds, but merely a compilation of various matters relating to his sanctity and his generosity toward churches. You may rightly call it very poorly arranged, since it gathers various materials from places where they do not belong and inserts charters granted long after the Saint’s death to the people of Bamberg by Popes Clement II and Leo IX and by Emperor Henry III. These documents occupy chapters 16, 17, 18, and 19 in Gretser, but we have, as noted above, relegated them to an Appendix, since they disrupt whatever sequence of events there may be.

No less ineptly, the letters of Benedict, Pope VIII, have been inserted into chapters 24 and 25: one addressed to the Saint concerning the confirmation of the bishopric, and the other to Eberard, the first bishop of that church. At least the former should have been placed immediately after chapter 15.

Therefore, so that these documents may not delay the reader, we shall first reproduce them in the said Appendix, while leaving the rest untouched. Let what follows, then, proceed.

## The Life of Saint Henry by an Anonymous Author

Published in Surius, from Jacob Gretser’s *Bamberg Saints*.

### Chapter One

**Saint Henry’s succession to the empire, the appearance of Wolfgang, his generosity toward churches, his victory over the Slavs, and the restoration of the bishopric of Merseburg**

### 1

In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1001 [Note: The author is mistaken at the beginning, as has been sufficiently noted above, and persists in the same error below in section 12, where he connects Saint Henry’s seventh year with 1007, three days before the Kalends of November.], but, according to the foundation of the City, in the year 1752, when Otto the boy had died at Rome and the throne of the kingdom was vacant, and the matter of appointing a ruler was being considered, everyone’s wishes, by divine direction, turned toward the man who at that time was regarded as the most powerful in the kingdom.

For at that time Henry was Duke of the Bavarians, distinguished both by royal goodness and by nobility, and illustrious in every moral excellence. He fully followed the beginning of wisdom, the fear of the Lord. He was thoroughly instructed in every branch of literary study and wholly Catholic in faith and conduct.

He was therefore summoned by everyone with equal desire [Note: How far the native wishes of the princes of the empire extended is better shown by Adelboldus.] and common agreement, by the ordering, of course, of divine clemency, so that through the height of a temporal kingdom he might reach the summit of the heavenly kingdom. For, just as earthly goods, through bad use, impede some people’s salvation, so through good use they advance others toward salvation.

### 2

Although he had not yet attained the dignity of Caesar or emperor, Wolfgang appeared to him at Regensburg in a dream vision of the following kind [Note: This material is taken from the Life of Saint Wolfgang in Surius, 31 October, section 39. Thietmar, moreover, states that Saint Wolfgang was Saint Henry’s instructor: “The illustrious bishop Wolfgang nurtures his pupil,” and so forth. The other matters relevant here have been discussed in the Commentary.].

It seemed to him that, while remaining in the church of Saint Emmeram, he went for the sake of prayer to the tomb of blessed Wolfgang, situated in that same church. As he was striving there to entreat the holy lord Wolfgang with intimate prayers, it suddenly seemed to him that the Saint himself stood before him and addressed him in these words:

“Look carefully at the letters written on the wall beside my tomb.”

There, as it seemed, was written only: “After six.”

When he awoke, King Henry turned the very brief writing of this vision over in his mind for a long time. At first he supposed that he would die after six days, and he distributed many gifts to the poor. When the number of six days had passed and he felt no bodily discomfort, he thought that it referred to six months.

When that period too had passed, and he had suffered no illness, he supposed that the number referred to six years; and he therefore began to fear the things mentioned above. When the full number of six years had passed and the day of the seventh year had arrived, on that very day he received the dignity of Caesar through the Apostolic entreaty.

Then at last, understanding what his vision had meant, he gave thanks to God and to Saint Wolfgang, who had deigned to reveal such exaltation to him.

### 3

Having therefore been anointed king, the most blessed servant of God, not content with the confines of a temporal kingdom, resolved to serve the supreme King—for whom to serve is to reign—in order to attain the crown of immortality. He also applied the greatest diligence to enlarging the worship of religion: he began to enrich churches with possessions and increase them with immense ornaments.

He restored the episcopal sees of Hildesheim—where he had been raised from childhood and taught his letters—Magdeburg, Strasbourg, Meissen, and Merseburg, which had been devastated by the barbarous savagery of the neighboring Slavs [Note: This should have been explained, if the confused writer intended to say anything; he omits Paderborn, to which the Saint contributed the principal gifts.].

He bestowed innumerable possessions and ornaments both upon that church and upon the other bishoprics throughout the kingdom. To the people of Hildesheim he appointed Saint Godehard [Note: See the Acts, 4 May, p. 508, no. 18.], instructed by divine revelation.

What he contributed more particularly to the church of Merseburg than to the others, we wish to make known in part for the benefit of those to come. For this church, in the time of the great Otto—I mean the Otto who defeated the Hungarians at the river Lech under Saint Ulrich the Confessor and hanged their kings, Laelius and Assur, at Regensburg, when the princes had adjudged that this should be done [Note: The victory is described in the Life of Saint Ulrich, 4 July, p. 110, no. 46.]—had been reduced to nothing by the Slavs’ constant incursions and hostile devastation.

4. And because it could not withstand the violence of the neighboring nations, it began to decline completely in its possessions, its religious life, and everything pertaining to episcopal dignity. It happened, however, that at the same time the Archbishop of the church of Magdeburg entered upon the way of all flesh, and the bishop of Merseburg—because of the wisdom bestowed upon him by God and the many virtues with which he was adorned, on account of which he was also exceedingly pleasing to Otto the Great—was appointed to the see of Magdeburg, through the action of the aforementioned King.

[Note: What is related here concerning the possessions of the bishopric of Merseburg transferred to Magdeburg should be attributed not to Otto I but to Otto II. The punishment that followed upon him is therefore described in the Life of Saint Adalbert, 23 April, chapter 190. See there the cited notes of Thietmar, who treats in several other places of the restoration of the same bishopric by Saint Henry.]

It came to pass that the bishopric of Merseburg was utterly destroyed, and that the more valuable properties of that church—its estates, ministeriales, and ornaments—were transferred into the jurisdiction of the church of Magdeburg; while, from whatever remnants of its possessions remained to Merseburg, an abbey was constructed there. This arrangement remained unchanged until the time of the pious confessor Henry.

When that same King had summoned the princes of his kingdom and held a court at Quedlinburg, all agreeing in the same purpose, he resolved to wage war against Poland, Bohemia, and the other neighboring regions of the Slavs, which were laying waste the borders of his kingdom.

5. Having therefore assembled his army, he led it in battle against the aforementioned nations. As he passed through a place called Walbeck, he took the sword of Saint Adrian the martyr, which had long been kept there as a relic.

[Note: Gretser recorded further information about Walbeck and the sword of Saint Adrian, which may be consulted in his work.]

Girded with it, he cried out with all his heart and said:

“Judge, O Lord, those who assail me; fight against those who fight against me. Take up arms and shield, and rise to my aid.”

Proceeding from there, he pitched his camp in the field where the church of Merseburg is situated. When he saw the place desolate and reduced to nothing, he groaned and said:

“Blessed Lawrence, martyr of Christ, if through your intervention I subdue to the Roman Empire and to the Christian religion these barbarian nations against whom I am marching, then, by the favor of divine grace, I shall restore this desolate place, consecrated to your name, to its former dignity.”

When the princes of Poland and Bohemia, together with the leaders of the other Slavic peoples, learned that the Roman Emperor was approaching with an army to defeat them, they gathered an innumerable multitude and advanced to meet him in battle. The pious King soon learned of this through his scouts and, as he was accustomed to do in all his difficulties, took refuge in the weapons of prayer. Having invoked over himself the name of the Lord, he commended himself and his army, with the utmost devotion, to the protection of the blessed martyrs Lawrence, Saint George, and blessed Adrian.

6. When all had been strengthened by receiving the body and blood of the Lord, they came to the place of battle. There the blessed King, having roused the courage of each man through exhortatory words to act bravely, saw the innumerable multitude of the adversaries and cried out to the Lord:

“O God, who crushes wars from the beginning, raise your arm against the nations that devise evil against your servants. Scatter them by your power and destroy them, my protector. Make them like a wheel and like chaff before the face of the wind.”

As he said this, his eyes were opened, and he saw the glorious martyrs—namely, George, Lawrence, and Adrian—preceding his army with the angel who was striking down the enemy, and driving the enemy ranks to flight. And just as the army of Sennacherib was crushed and perished by the striking angel, so this entire multitude of barbarians, terrified by the power of God, threw down its arms and sought refuge in flight, without the shedding of Christian blood.

When the holy King saw this, he raised his eyes and hands to heaven, blessed the God of heaven, and said:

“I bless you, King of heaven and earth, who resists the proud and gives grace to the humble; who guards those who love you and is glorified among the nations because of the victory given us from heaven.”

After the barbarians had been defeated and whatever could contribute to future peace had been secured by the firmest treaty, the blessed man and his men returned home in peace, glorifying and praising God, who saves those who hope in him.

7. When the most Christian King had made Poland, Bohemia, and Moravia tributary, he began, out of reverence for Saint Lawrence the martyr, to regard with pious compassion and kindness the trampling down and destruction of the church of Merseburg. Since it had been reduced to nothing in its buildings, ministeriales, secular possessions, and ecclesiastical ornaments, he labored to restore it to its former rank of episcopal dignity, just as he had vowed to God and Saint Lawrence. Nor did he cease from works of mercy until he had completely brought it back to its ancient state of dignity and its former religious honor.

8. Finally, he founded the bishopric of Bamberg in its entirety within his own domain.

[Note: The various meanings of *domas* may be found in the glossaries; here it means jurisdiction or possession.]

He exchanged territories with the neighboring bishoprics by a lawful agreement. Having founded the bishopric, he entrusted it by special right to the holy Roman Church, dedicating it to the princes of the Apostles, Peter and Paul, and to the most precious martyr George. In this way he both rendered to the First See the honor due to its dignity and strengthened his own foundation more securely through such great patronage.

On the southern side of the city he built a monastery in honor of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr under the canonical order. On the other side, that is, to the north, he established another monastery under the monastic rule, in honor of Saint Michael the Archangel and Saint Benedict the abbot.

[Note: This monastery is treated in the Acts of Saint Otto, 2 July.]

For himself and for his city, founded upon the Rock of apostolic firmness and fortified and adorned with walls and strongholds of the merits of Saint George and the other saints, he prepared, against the assaults of vices, a tower of strength in Stephen, and, against the cooling blasts of him who resolved to establish his seat in the north, whence every evil spreads, a sure refuge in the protection of the angels. Thus, surrounded on the right and on the left by the weapons of justice, the adversary would be unable to prevail against it in anything.

9. To these three churches a fourth was later added by Gunther, the fourth bishop of the same see of Bamberg, and by a certain Reginold, a nobleman, in honor of Saint Mary, the Mother of the Lord, and of Saint Gangolf the martyr. It was situated outside the city toward the east, at a place called Teuverstat, under the canonical order and possession.

[Note: None of this belongs to the Life of Saint Henry.]

Finally, Herimann, the sixth bishop of the same see, began, opposite the city toward the west, a church under the canonical order in honor of Saint James the Apostle, son of Zebedee. Otto, the eighth bishop of the same see, a humble lover of Christ’s poor, completed and dedicated it with the assistance of Eberhard the provost, and suitably arranged there the community and order of those serving God.

Thus the place of Bamberg, fortified on every side by churches dedicated to the patronage of the saints in the form of a cross, celebrates and performs daily and assiduous worship and service for Christ Jesus crucified, on behalf of its first founder, the most pious Emperor Henry II, and all his collaborators, successors, and benefactors. And so that greater tranquility, security, and reverence in supplicating God might continue among those serving the Lord there, the aforementioned five churches were situated in such a way that they are most suitably separated from almost all the noise and disturbance of the marketplace and the populace.

10. But so that it may shine more clearly before everyone with what vigilance the most blessed man provided for the goods of peace and tranquility belonging to his new church, even for succeeding ages, we insert here several letters of confirmation issued both by bishops and by kings. Since there are two things by which this world is chiefly governed—pontifical authority and royal power—we wish to show that, supported by both, and defended on the right and left, it remains forever secure against every troublesome attack.

For the Lord and Savior says that two swords suffice for the Church: one penetrates for the defense of soul and spirit; the other subdues and restrains inflexible and hardened hearts by its severity. Whatever is fortified here and there by the authority of those same swords plainly cannot be shaken from the uprightness of its status by any assault of evil.

First, however, we set down here the charter of the Emperor Otto III.

[Note: Gretser demonstrates at length that this diploma belongs to Otto II; we too discussed it in the Commentary, including the title “nephew,” which the Emperor Otto gives to his cousin Henry, duke of Bavaria and father of Saint Henry.]

Thus those who wish to know how the place of Bamberg came into the jurisdiction of the holy King may gather it from that same written document.

11. In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity: Otto, by divine providence Augustus Emperor.

Let all our faithful, both present and future, know how, at the intervention of our most beloved mother Adelheid, we have granted and firmly donated, by our imperial power and for perpetual ownership, to our dear nephew Henry, Duke of the Bavarians, a certain estate belonging to our right—namely, the city called Bamberg, with everything pertaining to it, and Nemkin Uraha, situated in the county called that of Count Berthold Volckfelt.

We have granted these possessions together with slaves of both sexes, buildings, churches, cultivated and uncultivated lands, and everything legally and rightfully pertaining to the aforementioned estates, on the condition that he thereafter enjoy free discretion to hold, exchange, give away, leave to his descendants, or otherwise do with them whatever he wishes.

And so that this decree might remain more stable and firm, we ordered this charter to be written and, having sealed it with a ring, strengthened it with our own hand.

Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of July, in Indiction I, in the fourteenth year of the reign of our Lord Otto, and the seventh of his Empire.

## CHAPTER II. The foundation of the church of Bamberg, the synods concerning it, and its approval by the Supreme Pontiff

12. In the year 1007 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in Indiction V, on the third day before the Kalends of November, a great synod of bishops and other Fathers was held and celebrated in the royal village of Frankfurt, through the agency of the great and peaceful King Henry, in the seventh year of his reign.

[Note: The inexperienced writer is mistaken and confuses the events; we have attempted to restore them in the Commentary. His connection of the year 1007 with the seventh year of Henry’s reign follows from the first error noted above.]

For while that same King, devoted to God, was pondering deeply in his mind by what work above all he might more easily gain the mercy of God, inspired by the prompting of divine counsel he resolved to choose God as his heir, to record this in writing, and to establish the bishopric of Bamberg, as has been stated, from his hereditary possessions, so that paganism among the Slavs might be destroyed there and the memory of the Christian name might remain celebrated forever.

But since he did not possess a parish belonging to that see, and in the same year of his reign was celebrating holy Pentecost at Mainz, he acquired from Henry, Bishop of Würzburg, by firm and lawful transfer, a portion of the Würzburg diocese—namely, the county called Raterzgewe and part of the district called Wolcvelt, situated between the rivers Uraha and Ratenza.

[Note: From the Viennese codex, Gretser writes *Ratenzgonui*, and shortly afterward *volcfelt*. It is not worthwhile here to investigate these places and others more precisely.]

In exchange, he gave to the church of Würzburg 150 hides in a village called Memmigun and in the neighboring places. Henry of Würzburg and Willigis, archbishop of the metropolitan church of Mainz, together with many archbishops and bishops who were present, agreed to and joined in this arrangement, strengthening this lawful exchange by their testimony and signatures.

[Note: Gretser reports some names from the Viennese codex. Yet the times and councils must be distinguished; see the fuller discussion in the preliminary Commentary, where everything that might be noted here has been explained.]

When the most glorious King had obtained the fulfillment of his desire, he sent two of his chaplains, Alberic and Ludwig, together with letters from the Bishop of Würzburg, to Rome, with the consent of the Fathers mentioned above, so that this good beginning might advance to something better through apostolic authority.

The Roman Pontiff, the universal Pope John, rejoicing in the devotion of the most pious King, held a synod in the Basilica of Saint Peter for the confirmation of the bishopric of Bamberg. He ordered a privilege to be written and confirmed by apostolic authority, replying to all the bishops of Gaul and Germany that they too should strengthen the aforementioned bishopric by equal and common authority. A copy of that privilege follows in these words:

13. “John, Bishop, servant of the servants of God.

“It is the duty of our office to consider generally the interests of all the holy churches of God, and especially of those which are subject in a particular way to the jurisdiction and dominion of our Roman Church: to remove any disadvantage, lest, neglected because of their serious difficulties, they should become contemptible, or, having found some opportunity, should be deprived of the solemnity due to them.

“Therefore we wish it to be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God, present and future, that our beloved spiritual son, Henry, the most glorious and invincible King, inspired by divine clemency, established a bishopric at the place called Bamberg from his own hereditary possessions, for the sake of his own soul and those of his parents, with perfect devotion of faith and charity, in honor of the most blessed Peter, prince of the Apostles. He did so after making a lawful and legal exchange with Henry, Bishop of Würzburg, concerning a certain portion of the parish of his bishopric.

“Therefore the aforementioned Bishop also sent us his letter, so that, with his consent, the newly established bishopric might be founded by the privilege of our apostolic authority. For this reason the most glorious King Henry II sent his messengers to us, who told us all these things and appealed to us for the confirmation of this see.

“Looking upon his most holy example with paternal and heartfelt affection, we therefore decree that all the possessions which he has lawfully gathered and bestowed upon the blessed Peter, prince of the Apostles, in the aforesaid place, shall be confirmed by the privilege of our authority. The Bishop of that place, and all who shall succeed him forever, shall possess them in secure tranquility and shall have free power to administer, arrange, and even augment the possessions and properties of that church; but they shall have no power to dissipate or disorder them.

14. “By our authority we likewise decree that within the boundaries and possessions of that church there shall be no assault by tyrants or by any other wicked men, whether in the city itself of Bamberg, or in its castles and villages, its male and female servants, tributaries, tithes, forests, woods, fisheries, hunting grounds, mills, fields, meadows, pastures, cultivated and uncultivated lands, or anything else that now belongs to it or may be acquired in the future. All this, strengthened by the privilege of our authority, shall remain in secure peace.

“No count or judge shall presume to make law there except such as the Bishop of that place may choose by concession of the most glorious King Henry or his successors. No foreign power shall invade it by force.

“Thus shall that bishopric be free and secure from every external power, subject only to Roman protection.

[Note: It is also called *mandiburgum*; it means protection, defense, or guardianship.]

“This is so that the Bishop may devote himself more effectively, together with his canons, to the service of God, and may perpetually preserve the memory of the first founder and restorer of that place. Nevertheless, let him remain subject and obedient to his metropolitan.

“Whoever observes these decrees shall receive divine recompense and apostolic blessing. But whoever proves contemptuous of them and violates them shall be subject to the condemnation of perpetual anathema, unless, repenting, he attains satisfaction.

“Written by the hand of Peter, notary and archivist of the holy Roman Church, in the month of June, Indiction V.”

15. When a general council was again held at Frankfurt, presided over by the venerable Archbishop Willigis of Mainz, all the archbishops and bishops who were present, thirty-six in number, received this privilege of the Apostolic See with due veneration. With unanimous and devout hearts they praised it and confirmed it by ordering it to be written.

Concerning the aforementioned boundaries of the parish exchanged with the church of Würzburg, so that no complaint or doubt might arise in the future, they ordered the following document to be written. It was first subscribed by Henry himself, Bishop of Würzburg, and then by nine provosts or priests of that same church.

16. “We wish it not to remain unknown to all the faithful of the holy Church of God, both present and future, how the most glorious King Henry, moved, as we believe, by the stimulus of divine admonition, desired to increase the service of God by establishing a bishopric from the estates that, by God’s grace and by hereditary right from his parents, had come into his possession.

“Desiring to accomplish this lawfully and reasonably, he began earnestly to request Henry, the venerable administrator of the church of Würzburg, to transfer from his own jurisdiction into the King’s jurisdiction a certain place called Bamberg, together with the district called Raezengevum, which appeared to belong to the status of his diocese, so that this purpose might be fulfilled.

“Since these seemed to be just and reasonable causes, Henry, yielding to the petitions of that most august and invincible King, and acting with the common counsel and consent of his clergy and soldiers, as well as of the entire people, transferred the aforementioned place and district to the King’s authority, excluding three parish churches with their adjacent territories, whose names are Wachenrode, Lonerstat, and Mulehusen, with all contradiction henceforth removed.

“Of the other district called Volefeld, in which the aforementioned place is situated, he granted to the same King that portion extending from Bamberg to the river Uraha, from Uraha to the river Ratenza, and then along the course of that river to the Main; from there to the stream Wichibach, then to the head of that same stream; and from there by the shortest and nearest route to the Uraha.

“Done in the city of Würzburg, in the presence of the most serene Emperor Henry, on the condition that the church of Würzburg retain the tithe from the newly cleared lands already cut down and measured into hides, together with the old tithe, which was not exchanged. But in newly cleared lands cultivated thereafter, the church of Bamberg shall possess the tithe within the exchanged boundary.”

17. John, Patriarch of Aquileia, also embraced with his whole heart so praiseworthy a work of the most excellent King and his pious devotion toward Christ, and wrote to Henry, Bishop of Würzburg, a letter full of congratulations.

“To the most blessed lord Henry, venerable Bishop of the holy church of Würzburg, whom we love with sincere charity: John, patriarch of the church of Aquileia, together with all the bishops of his diocese, sends fraternal love in Jesus Christ our Lord, who loved us first and handed himself over for us.

“Although, reverend brother, the care of fraternal love admonishes us that in all the good works which the Creator of the human race mercifully ordains daily for salvation we ought to give him boundless thanks, nevertheless, whenever and wherever we happen to hear of some magnificent work arising from the advancement, exaltation, or establishment of the holy Church, we ought, with the devotion of boundless affection and the effect of spiritual rejoicing, to praise, bless, and proclaim him whose gifts these are and from whom all good things proceed ineffably.

“He is the one who, among the countless mysteries of his eternal favor, dictates in the hearts of his princes those things which he arranges for the example and salvation of many.

18. “Among these is one which has recently been accomplished by divine action and has generated the greatest joy in our hearts. We have heard that our lord Henry, the most glorious and invincible King, inspired by divine grace, established from his own estates and paternal inheritance, at the place called Bamberg, a bishopric in honor of the most blessed Peter, prince of the Apostles. After an exchange had been made, he lawfully and worthily acquired from your church a certain portion of its diocese, and this exchange was strengthened by a privilege of the Apostolic See.

“This excellent and praiseworthy work, the King’s most worthy generosity, and your charity, which is eminently deserving of praise, are thereby commended: the work is his through its execution, and yours through your love.

“For this we give boundless thanks to almighty God, whose immeasurable glory is shown by the fact that through our King Henry, his good and faithful servant, he grants firm peace to all the churches and, moreover, forms a new church. Through it, with God’s help, he will triumph over the enemy of the human race among the neighboring Slavic peoples and multiply for himself an innumerable family through the washing of regeneration.

“We, together with all the bishops of our diocese, praise this divine work in common; and, rightly consenting to it and subscribing below, we confirm it forever.”

19. “Henry, by the mercy of God’s prior ordinance, King, to all the sons of the Church, present and future.

“We are instructed and forewarned by the most salutary teachings of sacred Scripture that, leaving behind temporal goods and setting aside earthly advantages, we should strive to attain eternal dwelling places in heaven that endure without end. For present glory is fleeting and vain while it is possessed, unless one thinks within it of something belonging to heavenly eternity.

“But God’s mercy provided a remedy for the human race when it made earthly substance the price of a share in the heavenly homeland. Therefore, not forgetful of this clemency, and not unaware that we have been exalted to royal dignity by the free regard of divine mercy, we deem it fitting not only to enlarge the churches built by our predecessors but also to build new ones for the greater glory of God and to exalt them with the most welcome gifts of our devotion.

“Therefore, not giving deaf ears to the Lord’s commands and attending obediently to his divine exhortations, we desire to store in heaven the treasures bestowed upon us by the generosity of divine abundance, where thieves neither break in nor steal, and where rust and moth do not destroy; where, whenever we recall all that has now been amassed, our heart may repeatedly be stirred by desire and love.

20. “Accordingly, we wish it to be known to the entire community of the faithful that we have raised a certain place of our paternal inheritance, called Bamberg, to the rank and summit of a bishopric. Confirmed by the authority of the Roman See, with the consent of the venerable Henry, Bishop of Würzburg, the will of our beloved wife Cunegund, and the equal and common counsel and decree of all our faithful—archbishops, bishops, abbots, dukes, and counts—and praised by the concordant devotion of our entire kingdom and its princes, we have founded, established, and strengthened it for the honor of almighty God, of blessed Mary ever-virgin, of the holy Apostles Peter and Paul, and also of Saints Kilian and George.

“This has been done so that there may be celebrated there a solemn memorial of ourselves, of our parents, and of the Emperor Otto III, our predecessor, and so that a perpetual saving sacrifice may be offered for all the orthodox.

“Therefore, in the same church beloved by us, for the honor and adornment of the house of God, we have offered objects made from precious metals and stones for various uses of the sanctuary—vessels, vestments, and other ecclesiastical ornaments. We have also bestowed upon the aforesaid episcopal see estates, churches, villages, and settlements with all their appurtenances and attachments, namely, male and female servants, plots, buildings, cultivated lands, roads and trackless places, issues and revenues, things acquired and to be acquired, woods, fishing rights, hunting grounds, meadows, pastures, fields, forests, forest officials, cellars, rents, waters and watercourses, mills, movable and immovable goods, and all other things that can rightly be written or named, whatever their uses may be.

[Note: Elsewhere these words appear as *senegis* and *saginis*. I see no other meaning indicated than the right of fishing. Consult the glossaries.]

“By the present decree of our authority we establish that Eberhard, the Bishop of the aforesaid see, beloved by us in God, and his successors shall henceforth have free power to hold and possess the aforesaid goods with all their appurtenances, or to convert them to whatever uses of the bishopric they may choose.

“As for the canonical brothers serving God there, we confirm by our imperial authority and ownership the possessions that we have granted them, to be possessed for the daily necessities of temporal life.”

21. “This is on the following condition: that the aforementioned canons and their successive provosts shall henceforth have free power, with the consent and counsel of those canons, to exchange these possessions for better uses, increase them, and in whatever way convert them to their advantage, so that they too, kindly remembering us before God, as well as our most beloved wife and partner in the kingdom, Cunegund, and our parents, may in turn respond to our benefits with pious and constant intercession.

“But if anyone—which God forbid—should attempt to destroy or violate the generosity of this donation of ours, or the institution of the Apostolic See, established by the authority of so many venerable Fathers, let him suffer eternal punishment by unquenchable torment on the day of judgment before the eyes of God.

“And lest this occur, but so that this grant and decree may remain inviolable forever for all, we have strengthened this charter, drawn up for that purpose, with our own hand, and ordered it to be marked with the impression of our seal.

“Nor only during the remaining life of the most glorious King, but even more after his passage from death to life, did his fortunate plantation—the church of Bamberg—receive growth from day to day, watered by the showers of divine grace, often nourished and satisfied at the breasts of pious consolation by its holy and special mother, the Roman Church, and nobly and firmly exalted forever by the authority and privileges of successive kings.”

[Note: These matters have nothing whatsoever to do with the Life of Saint Henry; as we have already said, they should therefore be placed in the appendix.]

We have already stated in the preface that these privileges should be relegated to the Appendix.

## CHAPTER III. Bruno’s hatred of his holy brother; Saint Cunegund’s innocence; the healing of the stone on Mount Cassino; and the cause of Saint Henry’s lameness

22. Let what we have said, taking the opportunity to do so, concerning the foundation and confirmation of the holy church of Bamberg suffice. Now let us turn our mind and pen back to the narrative already begun concerning the deeds of the blessed man.

The King’s brother was Bruno, Bishop of the see of Augsburg.

[Note: Adelbold gives a somewhat fuller account of Bruno; see the correction below at the first miracle.]

Envious of his brother’s successful deeds, Bruno inflicted upon him as many injuries and adversities as he could. Where he could not do so personally, he joined those who were inflicting them, or encouraged others to inflict them by applying the goads of wicked incitement. His brother, however, not only failed to repay him in kind but, instructed by brotherly love, strove to overcome him in goodness by ignoring everything and patiently enduring it.

23. How great his generosity was, and how great his liberality toward God, both in that church of Bamberg and in many other places, is shown by clear evidence of his works. He chose God alone as his heir, so that God might deign to admit him into the fellowship of the eternal inheritance.

For he neither had nor expected children according to the flesh, since it has been established that he never knew Cunegund, whom he appeared to have as his wife.

How this became known should not be passed over, for the common edification of all, so that we may be instructed by examples of chastity and moved by wonder at divine secrets, understanding how all things work together for good for those who love God.

For such great and extraordinary virtues could not be without temptation. The devil, envious of every good, when he could not wound the unblemished marriage bed, resolved to defile it with the stain of jealousy and at least damage the reputation of her whom he could not inflict with the wound of corruption.

Thus, at the devil’s instigation, she who knew no stain of corruption was made suspect of the crime. But because the person who neglects reputation is cruel, she chose, for the sake of clearing herself, that judgment by means of glowing plowshares which is known to have been instituted because of human hardness.

When she, beloved by God, was led to that judgment like a sheep to the slaughter, she groaned and said:

“Lord God, creator of heaven and earth, who tests the reins and hearts, judge my judgment and deliver me. For today I call upon you as witness and judge, because I have never known in carnal union either this present Henry or any other man.”

After she had spoken these words, while all who were present stood astonished and weeping, she stepped barefoot upon the glowing plowshares and passed over them safely, without the pain of burning.

Thus almighty God preserved the bond of chaste love, proved her innocence, and added the protection of humility to her integrity.

24. Meanwhile, the glory of the most blessed Prince advanced more and more, and the grace of God was with him. His shield did not turn away from battle, nor was his spear withdrawn.

He recovered Apulia, long held by the Greeks, for the Roman Empire, and appointed Ismael duke over that province. Ismael later died at Bamberg and rests in the Lord, buried in the chapter house of the greater monastery.

He founded the monastery of Benevento and enriched it with every adornment. As he passed through the cities of Apulia and prudently arranged within them whatever pertained to the usefulness and honor of the kingdom, he began to suffer from the illness of the stone.

The holy man endured the affliction of this disease with such patience that he declared the sufferings of the flesh to have been bestowed upon him by God for the preservation of humility, and affirmed that the scourge of correction was the surest sign of love.

He nevertheless had remedies applied for his healing, but no medical skill could free him completely. As the pain grew worse, he ascended Mount Cassino, seeking that through the intercession of blessed Benedict and Saint Scholastica God might grant him the remedy of health.

25. When he came to the place where the relics of the saints had been deposited, he poured out his soul before the Most High and, through the intercession of the saints—namely Benedict and Saint Scholastica—asked God with prayers and tears to grant him health of body and soul. And what is said through the Prophet was fulfilled: “I sought the Lord, and he heard me, and delivered me from all my tribulations.” For he asked, and he was heard; he perseveringly knocked at the door of merciful power, and was admitted.

Meanwhile the King began to consider what he had heard concerning the translation of Saint Benedict; and because it was said that Benedict’s relics had been secretly taken away and transferred elsewhere, the holy man doubted whether he was physically present there. After completing his prayer, therefore, the man of God went to his lodging and, exhausted and weakened, lay down on a little bed. As he slept, he saw Saint Benedict standing beside him and holding in his hand a surgeon’s instrument suitable for making medicinal incisions. Benedict said to him:

“Because you have placed your hope in God and in his saints, behold, I have been sent by God so that through my treatment you may be freed from your illness. Behold, I am the one whose bones you thought had been secretly carried away; I present my presence to you, and as proof of the truth I shall heal your sufferings.”

Saying this, he opened with the surgical instrument he held in his hand that part of the body where the stone lay; and, gently extracting the stone, he restored the wound’s opening by an immediate cure, then placed the stone he had removed in the hand of the sleeping King.

[Note: This matter, together with related and other stories, has been discussed in the Commentary.]

26. After this, the most Christian Emperor awoke. Reflecting upon what Christ’s Confessor had done for him, and seeing the stone that he held in his hand, he summoned the attendants who, according to royal custom, were always present with him and said to them:

“Call the bishops and the princes of our kingdom to me, so that they may know and see the wonders of God which his ineffable mercy and indescribable power have worked in me.”

They quickly carried the King’s command to the princes and brought them to him. The King greeted them, and, having been greeted in return, addressed them:

“My brothers and fellow soldiers, magnify the Lord with me, and let us exalt his name together, for he is a great Lord and exceedingly worthy of praise, and there is no end to his greatness. He strikes, and he heals; he scourges sinners and has mercy on the penitent. He humbles one and exalts another, for there is a cup in the Lord’s hand, full of unmixed wine.”

“Behold, I who yesterday was near death appear to you today healthy through the mercy of God; and the sting of death, which yesterday I bore enclosed within my body, I now visibly show to your eyes.”

27. Saying this, he showed them the stone that he held in his hand, and, displaying the scar of the wound, related in order, before all who listened, everything that had happened to him through Saint Benedict.

When they saw and heard the wonders of God, they were astonished beyond what can be believed. Blessing God and acclaiming him for a long time, they rejoiced in the King’s recovery. The King again said to them:

“What acts of thanksgiving, or what gifts worthy of such great benefits, can we offer to our physician Benedict?”

They all judged that Benedict was worthy of royal munificence. Therefore, on the advice of his princes, the King bestowed immense gifts upon Saint Benedict’s church: estates, gold, silver, and very many ornaments. After bidding farewell to the brothers who presided over that church, he departed from Monte Cassino cheerful and healthy.

From that time onward, he devoted himself with a particular love and veneration to Saint Benedict and to all who practiced the monastic life, and he proved himself a kindly and devoted Father in enlarging and protecting ecclesiastical possessions. These things are recorded at Monte Cassino so that people of the present may keep the mighty works of God in memory, and so that, with the passage of time, they may not fall into oblivion among posterity. And if anyone wishes to know why the most glorious Emperor Henry limped, let him learn this reason: he had first been entirely healthy in body.

28. Once, when he had come to Apulia to arrange affairs of state, he reached Mount Gargano. At its foot lies a city, and on the mountainside, in a hollow rock, there is a basilica not built by human beings or dedicated by any human being, but constructed through divine activity or power. Indeed, by a wondrous act of divine blessing it was reverently consecrated. The Archangel Michael is the patron of this basilica.

In this church, angelic singing is said to be heard every week by those who are worthy of it. The man devoted to God therefore entered this basilica with the other faithful of Christ for the sake of prayer. When they had celebrated the divine praises there and had offered the vows of their prayers to God with great devotion, the time had come when the heavenly host was to enter this sacred temple to render praises to God.

Thus, when everyone was leaving and those who lingered were being compelled to go out, the holy man asked that he be permitted to remain inside. After all the others had departed, he alone, trusting in the mercy of God, dared to remain there. He continued prayer after prayer and repeated his genuflections. With many tears he entrusted himself to divine clemency and earnestly commended his soul to the blessed Archangel Michael.

29. As the devout King’s incense [Note: Understand “the incense of the prayers that he poured out to God.”] rose to the Lord, God of Israel, who is always wondrous in his saints, deigned to show him a wondrous vision. He saw a great multitude of angels, radiant like the sun, entering the holy temple; two of them solemnly adorned the principal altar. Then he saw countless companies of the heavenly Virtues, shining like flashing lightning and escorting, with the greatest glory, one who seemed to be their prince; there is no doubt that this was the standard-bearer of the heavenly army.

Finally, he was permitted to see the King of the angels himself coming with great power and might. The innumerable heavenly host served him, and his splendor was incomparable, for by his nod all things heavenly and earthly are governed.

At last, the choir of the new Jerusalem, gathered in the basilica mentioned above, solemnly celebrated the divine service. When this had been completed, one of the chief angels, carrying the sacred text of the Gospel with the greatest reverence, [lacuna] brought it to the person; and when he had kissed it, he indicated to the angel that it should be carried to the Emperor to be kissed, in a corner [lacuna]. When the angel had fulfilled the command given to him, the aforesaid servant of Christ began to tremble in spirit and to shake in all his limbs at the unfamiliar sight of such majesty and glory, as though he were saying with the Prophet: “My heart is broken within me; all my bones tremble.”

30. When that angel saw this, he gently touched his thigh and said:

“Do not fear, chosen one of God. Rise quickly, gladly receiving the sign of peace sent to you from heaven.”

Immediately his thigh withered, and from that time throughout the rest of his life he limped. An event exactly similar is read of blessed Jacob, whose thigh withered at the touch of the angel wrestling with him.

To tell the truth, I did not find this in the writings, but through the report of truthful and venerable men I learned that it was true. For Conrad, the powerful Chancellor of the Bishop of Würzburg, who suffered persecution for righteousness’ sake, firmly asserted that he had read these things and recounted them before many hearers while he was present in the Church of Bamberg. One of those hearers, a man familiar to me and himself entirely truthful, faithfully related the matter to me and earnestly begged me to write it down, although I wished to suppress it in silence. At last, moved by the petitioner’s insistence and the diligence of his admonition, I faithfully recorded it, so that it might be told to a later generation.

I would rather rest in sleep than write false or frivolous things about the saints of God, especially since those who have deserved to be adorned with signs and wonders have no need to be exalted by false praises. Let this suffice concerning so glorious a miracle.

As clear testimony to this sign, an image of Saint Henry himself appears before the monastery door, on the right side beside the choir of Saint George, [lacuna], with a pillow placed beneath it, opposite the luminous images of Adam and Eve.

[Note: This entire account of the lameness was added from the notes of Gretser, where he also adds other material, about which we have said enough in the Commentary.]

## CHAPTER IV  
### The Arrival of Pope Benedict VIII in Germany; the Saint’s Pilgrimage to Cluny; His Deeds on Behalf of the Church and Empire; His Most Blessed Death and a Remarkable Vision Concerning Him

31. From there he journeyed to Rome, where he was kindly and honorably received by Pope Benedict. He told him how many acts of compassion and benefits the Lord had bestowed upon him through Saint Benedict. Pope Benedict gave thanks to God for all his benefits and offered a sacrifice of praise for the King’s health and that of the entire Catholic people.

At that time, as stated above, the holy King surrendered the estate of Bamberg, with all its appurtenances, to blessed Peter and entrusted it from then on and forever to the Apostolic Prelate for protection. In memory of this agreement, he decreed that each year a white ambler [Note: Namely, a white horse, about which Hofmann has more in his Annals; he also notes that one hundred marks of silver should have been added, but that this payment was remitted by Pope Leo IX through an exchange. This belongs to the period of the Pope’s arrival in Germany; the usual confusion.] with trappings should be given to the Roman Prelate.

He also obtained this from the Lord Pope through humility and devotion: that he should come to Alemannia and visit the estate of Bamberg, the new plantation. This was done. For in the following April he entered Alemannia, and, after traveling through all the cities of that region, arranged to visit Bamberg at the appointed time.

Accordingly, he came on the Thursday of Holy Week, at the sixth hour, dressed in the sacred pontifical vestments, as though he were about to proceed to celebrate the mysteries of God and the solemn office of that day. He was received with the greatest glory by the Emperor, by all the princes who were present, and by the entire clergy and people, amid an immeasurable outburst of rejoicing.

32. So that, at the arrival of so unusual and greatly desired a guest, a pleasing and fitting praise might be offered to our God, the wisest of kings suitably arranged four choirs of singers to meet him: the first on the bank of the river, the second nearer at hand, the third before the city gate, and the fourth in the church courtyard. There the King himself, first of all, took the Pope by the hand and led him into the house of the Lord; while divine hymns resounded melodiously [lacuna], he seated him in the episcopal chair.

The Apostolic Pontiff celebrated the proper office of this most sacred day with twelve assisting bishops, and likewise celebrated the offices of the following days with the greatest devotion. On the holy Sunday of Easter, during the morning office, the Patriarch of Aquileia read the first lesson, the Archbishop of Ravenna the second, and the Apostolic Pontiff himself the third. Since the solemn rites were being performed with every adornment and elegance of procession, as befitted Apostolic dignity and Imperial magnificence on the solemnity of solemnities, who would not judge that such a religious celebration, unprecedented in our regions, deserved to be perpetually preserved in the knowledge of all the sons of the Church of Bamberg, and that its memory should never be abandoned to the ages?

During those same days, on the eighth day before the Kalends of May, the same venerable Pope consecrated a basilica in honor of Saint Stephen [Note: Here this Anonymous writer is rightly opposed to Leo of Ostia, who represents it as a church consecrated in honor of Saint George by Pope Benedict, although it had long before been dedicated, as you will understand more fully from the Commentary.] and adorned it with precious gifts, which are still preserved there. During the celebration of the Mass, with the cooperation of seventy-two bishops and the unanimous consent of the princes, he established that the bishopric should be free from all secular power. By the authority of his presence, the attestation of his privilege, and the force of his ban, he confirmed everything appropriate to pontifical dignity and utility.

The confirmation of this privilege is as follows: it is to be found first in the appendix.

33. To return to the earlier subject from which we have digressed for a little: after the holy man, while staying in Rome, had obtained from the Lord Pope everything he requested, and had been strengthened by the Apostolic blessing, he crossed the Apennine Alps and, sending his army into his own land, went with a few companions to Cluny for the sake of prayer, because he had heard much about the religious life and condition of that place.

There, when he had seen very many signs of religion and holiness, he was kindled by the fire of the Holy Spirit. He offered at the Mass celebrated from the chair of Saint Peter a golden crown adorned with the most precious jewels. Receiving the brotherhood of the monks, he commended himself to their prayers with the greatest humility and contrition of heart. To supplement their necessities, he also surrendered to that community excellent estates in Alsace.

From there, journeying through Liège and Trier, he passed through those regions and enriched the communities serving God there with very many gifts and estates.

[Note: It cannot apparently be denied that Saint Henry went to Cluny at some time; but we have explained elsewhere how poorly our author arranged this and other matters, so that no further observations need be made here.]

34. It is remarkable that the man of God, who burned with such zeal for ecclesiastical interests on behalf of the salvation of his soul, neglected the advancement of the kingdom in nothing. Rather, without shedding blood, by piety and wisdom he enlarged the boundaries of his kingdom and increased and adorned the Imperial dignity with glory and honor.

He conquered and subjected Bohemia; he received Burgundy into submission; he also united Pannonia to the Catholic faith and to the Roman Empire. Victorious over other nations, he became the Apostle of the Hungarians.

For while they were all still unbelievers, the Emperor Henry drew them to the confession of the faith. To make this easier, he joined his sister Gisela in marriage to King Stephen, according to the Apostle’s saying: “The unbelieving husband is sanctified through the believing wife, and the unbelieving wife is sanctified through the believing husband.”

After King Stephen had been baptized [Note: This too has been restored to a sensible meaning in the Commentary], all Pannonia received the word of life and, through the astonishing novelty of events, was incorporated into the holy Catholic Church by royal apostles.

How splendid was the fellowship of such great apostleship; how worthy of honor and veneration was the holiness of both, through whom so many were saved and sanctified. The aforesaid King of the Hungarians, religious and devoted to God, afterward persevered in the practice of good works. Divine mercy demonstrated this after his death by unmistakable signs and miracles performed at his tomb.

35. The victory over the Burgundians, too, was divine rather than human. Although they were equipped with arms and every resource of war, and were men highly trained in warfare, they laid down their weapons—not from fear of a human being, but at God’s command—and, asking for the things that make for peace, gave their right hands.

Just as the Lord granted a peaceful conclusion to the war in celebration of the merits of blessed Martin the Confessor, so now he deigned to display a similar power through the merits of his servant. Thus he made him like the saints in glory.

And just as Moses triumphed more by prayers than by weapons, so the most glorious Prince, through the weapons of righteousness, successfully completed all his wars and always achieved a victory that was neither deadly nor bloody.

Finally, after completing most gloriously the labors of this life, after he had caused the fragrance of a good reputation to spread far and wide, and had brought the place he loved, together with the other monasteries, to perfection by enriching, adorning, and cultivating it, he was called by the Lord from the prison of the flesh to receive the unfading crown.

When he saw that the day of his death was approaching, he summoned the parents and relatives of the most blessed Empress Cunigunde, together with some of the leading men of the kingdom. Taking her by the hand, he entrusted her to them in these words worthy of remembrance:

“Behold, I received this virgin of yours from you—indeed, through Christ—and I now return her, a virgin, to Christ our Lord and to you.”

36. At his passing, while the earth wept, heaven rejoiced, as the Lord deigned to reveal through his mercy. At the very hour of his death, a devil is said to have appeared in human form to a servant of God dwelling in solitude [Note: Gretser should be consulted concerning this somewhat uncertain vision, p. 94 onward; we have explained elsewhere the remaining matters pertaining to the saint’s most blessed death.].

The man of God immediately recognized him through the spirit and said:

“Where are you going?”

He replied:

“I am going to the Prince’s funeral.”

The servant of God answered:

“Go and complete your business, insofar as the Lord permits you. Nevertheless, when you have completed your duty, adjured by the living God, return to me, so that through you I may learn the outcome.”

After a short time he returned and stood before the servant of God lamenting. In a querulous voice and with a great howl he said:

“Alas, alas! We have been deceived; we have labored in vain; indeed, we departed confounded by the angels of God. For while we and the angelic spirits stood on either side, the merits of the soul were justly weighed in the balance; and as bundles of sins pulled it downward, our side had almost become the heavier.”

37. Then suddenly a certain scorched figure arrived carrying a golden dish. He loaded the pan on the right-hand side, and in a wondrous manner it outweighed our side so greatly that, when the dish itself collapsed to the ground, the impact of its fall left a visible mark.

Thus the victorious angels, rejoicing, carried away the soul that had been snatched from us into their fellowship.

Although these things are reported as having occurred bodily, they must nevertheless be understood as accomplished through spiritual power. Spiritual realities are expressed through bodily images; when one thing is done or said outwardly, something else is signified as occurring inwardly.

The aforesaid servant of God, who deserves frequent remembrance, had presented a golden chalice to the Church of Merseburg in honor of God and in memory of Saint Lawrence the martyr. It is believed that, through the martyr’s special patronage, he was aided before God and delivered at the very hour of his death.

It is judged worthy of all reverence and wonder that at that same hour the chalice was locked away in a secure place, yet nevertheless received the material mark of the collision described above.

38. We have judged it worthwhile to disclose to the memory of future generations what we truly heard from the report of religious men concerning this same chalice.

When the aforesaid Confessor of Christ, Henry, had come to Marsipolis to arrange affairs of the kingdom, it happened that one day he listened most attentively to Mass at the altar of Saint Lawrence. When it had been completed, as he was always accustomed to do, he wished to consume the ablution of the chalice, but because an important matter of the kingdom, which the holy man had undertaken, intervened, this could not be done at that time.

He therefore summoned the church custodian and said, “I asked him to place the chalice with its ablution in a clean place and guard it with every care until, freed from his affairs, he could find a suitable time and place to consume it.”

But as his business and engagements multiplied, he was occupied throughout that entire day and could not free himself. On the following day, after Matins, he secretly entered the monastery with a few of his secretaries. For a long time, kneeling and shedding abundant tears, he prayed to God. Then he summoned the custodian and ordered him to bring him the chalice with its ablution.

When it had been brought and uncovered, they found that the ablution had been changed into the form of true blood.

This wondrous event soon became known to all who were present, and the whole Church will recount it to its successors, now and always, for the praise of God and the glory of his Confessor.

39. Therefore, you rich people of this age, learn to make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that, when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings.

It is not fitting for the tongue of flesh to remain silent about the praises of this most glorious and blessed Father, at whose passing heaven rejoiced while the angels triumphed.

When the most blessed servant of God died, in the twenty-fourth year of his reign, the fifty-second year of his life, and the eleventh year of his Empire, his body was honorably buried in the church of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul at Bamberg. Later, the Lord glorified it through many miraculous powers.

# THE MIRACLES OF SAINT HENRY

## Preliminary Observation Concerning the Book of Miracles

Gretser noted on page 81 that, in the Bamberg copy of the Life of Saint Henry, he found this title: “Here begins the first book concerning the life and deeds of Saint Henry, Emperor and Confessor.” In that same copy, however, there appeared nowhere “either the conclusion of the first book or the beginning of the second,” unless, he says, this should perhaps be understood to begin with the account of the miracles that God performed through the holy Emperor after his death.

We think this must be precisely the case, since chapter 30 is called an exhortation and epilogue, while the following chapter, 31, begins with miracles—namely, with the vision through which Bruno, Bishop of Augsburg and the Saint’s brother, was deterred from overthrowing the bishopric of Bamberg.

The miracles extend from the said chapter 31 through chapter 54, twenty-four in number. The first ten seem to have occurred before the canonization, for chapter 41 is prefaced by this title: “Prologue to the miracles performed at the translation of Emperor Saint Henry.” No one would say that his relics were translated before the sacred body had been raised from the earth, which, as we showed above in section 3, occurred in the year 1147.

I do not deny that the translation of Saint Henry might also be understood as referring to the time when his sacred body was brought back to Bamberg from the place where he died. Nevertheless, the circumstances speak as though they should be restricted to some translation of the relics carried out after the Saint’s canonization.

It therefore seemed best to divide the entire history of the miracles according to our method, so that the first ten should form the first part and the rest the second, describing them from Surius while omitting Gretser’s divisions into chapters. Let it therefore stand as follows.

## The First Part of the Miracles of Saint Henry

1. In the year 1025 from the Lord’s Incarnation, and 1776 from the founding of the City, Conrad, one of the leading men of the kingdom—but previously hostile to the kingdom through rebellion, while the princes were divided over his election, though Aribo, Archbishop of Mainz, and Eberhard, Bishop of Bamberg, supported him—received the kingdom in the eighty-fifth place after Augustus and reigned for fifteen years.

After he had been elevated to the royal throne, he planned, on the advice of Bruno, Bishop of Augsburg and brother of the Emperor Henry—who, as stated above, always envied Henry’s successful deeds—to destroy the bishopric of Bamberg. For Bishop Bruno had promised Queen Gisela that he would transfer to her son Henry all the estates that belonged to her by hereditary right.

A place and time were therefore appointed for an assembly at which this matter was to be brought to completion. On the night before the day on which these matters were to be discussed, Bishop Eberhard secretly approached Bruno’s tent. Sitting beside his bed, he earnestly addressed him at length concerning this matter, admonishing and imploring him, and impressing upon his mind the memory of his brother.

Since a considerable part of the night had already passed, Eberhard withdrew, and Bruno, troubled by what he had heard, was overcome by sleep. He seemed to see his brother, the Emperor Henry, standing beside his bed and presenting his face to him, disfigured by having one side of his beard shaved away.

When Bruno, astonished and bewildered, asked who could have dared to do such a reckless thing to him, Henry said:

“You did this—you who intended to strip me and the saints of God, whom I endowed with the possessions granted to me by God. Beware of persisting any further in such audacity, lest you pay for what you have begun with great misfortune.”

At this he awoke, very frightened by the vision, and was also severely affected by trembling and terror throughout his body.

When morning came, and Bruno did not come to the assembly of the nobles, although he had long been expected, the queen, anxious for her son, sent messengers and urgently begged him to come and fulfill his promise. But he declared that he was burdened with such an illness that he could neither rise from his bed nor move his foot anywhere.

When he was asked whether he would allow himself to be carried in his bed to the assembly, so that even in this way the promise might be fulfilled, he rejected the proposal entirely and finally proclaimed openly that he had sinned against God and his saints.

Thus divine mercy, through the merits of its servant, restrained all the machinations of that wicked conspiracy, lest Bruno should be defrauded of the hope he had placed in him. By confirming what had been well begun through him, it thereafter continually advanced it toward better things.

2. But let us now turn to the miracles that the Lord worked after his blessed passing, around the burial of his glorious body, to reveal the distinction of his merits. We shall transmit a few of them to the knowledge of posterity: those that have reached us through the truthful or unquestionable report of our elders, or that we ourselves have verified and witnessed in recent times.

A certain woman lived in the city who was so contracted and bent over that she could not straighten herself at all to walk, but rather crawled on her hands than walked on her feet. As she frequently devoted herself to prayer, she was divinely inspired to approach the memorial of the most blessed man and implore the mercy of almighty God with greater earnestness.

It happened that the anniversary of the aforesaid Father of our Lord was to be celebrated with appropriate observance. As the people customarily flocked to the church and the clergy celebrated the evening vigils, that bent and contracted woman also arrived. Full of faith and devotion, she approached the place of the tomb, saying with the Prophet:

“I will pay my vows to the Lord in the presence of all his people, in the courts of the house of the Lord.”

Spending the night there in prayer, she offered to the Lord all that she had—namely, a contrite and humbled heart—and watered Christ’s feet with tears in the faith of Christ, wiped them with the hair of her head, and anointed them with ointment.

Since the persistent prayer of a righteous person is very powerful, she continued without weariness in such sacrifices until daybreak. Around the third hour, during the solemn celebration of the Mass, while the Alleluia was being sung, “Praise of God among human beings” was fulfilled in the deed itself.

Suddenly, in the sight of all who were present, the woman seemed to fall into an ecstasy. Then, little by little, the nerves that had been rigid began to loosen, and all the limbs of her body began to stretch, cracking as they did so. Thus, in due order, the entire deformity of her bent body was restored to its proper beauty, so that the woman, standing upright, fully recovered both the use of walking and the other functions of her limbs.

This was known with the greatest certainty, on the testimony of reputable brothers who declared that they had been present at and witnessed this miracle.

3. Nor does this seem something to be neglected or passed over in silence: antiquity has handed it down and commended it to the memory of many through truthful report.

A certain sacristan, a lay member assigned to guard the church, began to become accustomed to theft and secretly removed from the church whatever he could. But just as wicked people, by misusing God’s good things, turn—or rather pervert—the very good things of God toward evil as far as they are able, so, conversely, the supreme craftsman sometimes turns the evil of the wicked to their own good.

To return to the matter at hand: the man assigned to the ecclesiastical guard, having made the ingrained habit of vice into something like a law of sinning for himself, was mercifully visited and corrected by the Lord, according to the saying:

“If they profane my statutes and do not keep my commandments, I shall visit their iniquities with a rod and their sins with blows.”

One night, while he was sleeping in the church itself, a servant of God of terrifying appearance appeared to him. He harshly rebuked him, saying:

“Appearance deceives you, and desire overturns your heart. Why did you do this and that? Know that you have committed an iniquitous deed.”

Having said this, he dragged him from his bed and left him beaten and bloodied after many blows.

He suffered these things while dreaming, but after waking he displayed clear marks of the blows and confirmed the words by the evidence of the beating. Thus pulled back from a dreadful precipice, he afterward remained in his ministry in the church until advanced old age, and many were corrected through his correction, glorifying God, who through his servant, already crowned in heaven, still works such things on earth.

4. On one occasion, by an uncertain accident, it happened to someone that his natural organs became separated from one another, his jaw was displaced from its proper place, and it obstructed the function of his mouth and disfigured the natural arrangement of human beauty.

The distress of pain and deformity was added to his suffering; we can properly appreciate it in another person if we turn our minds to the infirmity of our own bodies. Surrounded by such troubles, he cried out to the Lord and, as one dependent upon divine mercy, implored his help.

Therefore, so that the works of God might be manifested in him, he approached the Blessed One’s tomb while many stood by and watched. Placing his head upon it, he persisted in prayer until, through the merits of God’s servant, he received the health he desired.

For what else could happen? Those who obey the Lord of all creation must necessarily have every creature obey them, by the power of almighty God and according to the fixed laws of reason.

5. We also truly heard that at another time it happened that someone was afflicted by paralysis to such an extent that he lost the use of his arm. Warned by divine prompting, he was told to approach the burial place of the Saint’s body and, prostrating himself in prayer, invoke the mercy of almighty God through the merits of the most blessed man resting there.

He therefore prostrated his entire body and devoted himself to prayer. What happened then? Christ, the Son of God, who while walking on earth healed the man with the withered hand, now seated at the right hand of the Father, performed the same miracle when invoked and freed this suppliant through the merits of his beloved servant.

He rose from prayer healed and glorified God as his reconciled Lord in remembrance of the Saint. A cry rose to heaven, and all who stood by sang a hymn of glory to almighty God with fitting thanksgiving.

6. We have also taken care to report to our successors what we know to have truly happened at the tomb of the aforesaid Confessor during the days of the Rogations.

A certain priest, with the people entrusted to his care, was carrying a cross with hymns and songs to the monastery of Saint Peter and Saint George during the Rogation days. A certain blind man, led by another’s hand, was coming with them.

When he reached the tomb of Christ’s Confessor, he asked Saint Henry with all his heart that, through his intervention, the sight of his eyes might be restored. After he had long knocked at the door of the merciful Confessor with prayers and tears, his sight was restored by the grace of the Almighty, while everyone looked on and acclaimed the praise of God.

In a wondrous manner, the blind man who had followed the Lord’s cross led by another’s hand now returned home illuminated, carrying the cross with his own hands and guiding the people with praises of Christ.

7. Another miracle of divine power is also known through widespread commemoration and certain testimony.

There was a sick man, known to everyone in the city, whose entire lower body from the loins downward was completely dead. He could not support himself on his feet at all; rather, suspended from a device fitted with four little wheels, he clung to it and, as far as the craftsman’s construction allowed, pushed the weight of his body along with his own hands.

He was accustomed to visit the little coffin containing the most holy body frequently. Through God’s mercy, in order to celebrate the merits of his servant, he obtained such great grace that his deadened limbs were given life again. Thereafter, with staffs placed beneath both shoulders, he touched the ground with his feet and walked upright.

8. In modern times also, a certain cripple, who is still alive in the flesh, was healed in that same place and recovered the natural use of walking. Besides these things, many other proofs and manifestations of holiness have frequently been seen in that place: the weak have been cured, the blind enlightened, demons visibly driven from possessed bodies; many have very frequently been freed there from various illnesses, the Lord testifying how great is the glory in heaven of the Saints whom he permits to shine on earth with such powers of miracles, so that those who are proved to be exalted before God by their merits may not be held in low esteem among human beings.

9. For when the Lord was declaring the holiness of his Confessor through the testimony of miracles, the prelates of the Babenberg Church, as the signs multiplied, went to Rome with the commands and letters of King Chunrad and the princes, and announced to Pope Eugenius and the Roman Curia how many great wonders God worked through his Confessor. They, rejoicing and glorifying God for the sweetness of so great a reputation, began carefully and diligently to confer among themselves about the canonization of the holy King Henry, so that he might be inscribed in the Catalogue of the Saints, who was proved by virtues and signs to have been taken up into the heavenly kingdom.

A certain Cardinal, named John, began vehemently to oppose this canonization and, casting aside the fear of God, did not hesitate to disparage the aforesaid Confessor in every way he could. But divine vengeance suddenly restrained the detractor with a heavenly blow; and while he was tearing apart the reputation of the blessed man, the power of God deprived him of the light of his eyes. Struck and humbled by the affliction of blindness and by the consciousness of his guilt, he began to be tormented; and he publicly confessed how, by sinning against the Confessor of Christ, he had deserved this punishment. In a wondrous manner, the man whom previously he had torn with the teeth of detraction he now exalted with praises and commendations to the stars.

Thus converted to penance, he obtained swift pardon and was again enlightened through the intercession of the Confessor of Christ, by whose vengeance he had been blinded according to the just judgment of God.

10. In a similar manner, when at Babenberg, where the aforesaid Confessor had been buried, a celebrated report was circulating about his canonization, a certain religious man began to doubt the signs that were being performed through him and to grieve inwardly over the alteration of the funeral rites that were solemnly celebrated on his anniversary. He was soon struck by such darkness of the eyes that, after being healed through the Confessor of Christ, he experienced in that cure how much his holiness could accomplish before God.

It is greatly to be wondered at that anyone could have doubted the holiness of so great a man, since he had preserved, with the highest devotion and to the end of his life, the holiness of his conduct, the integrity of his chastity, the generosity of his almsgiving, the guardianship of humility, and every work of justice. But, as it is written: “No prophet is accepted in his own country.”

The man mentioned above, therefore, burdened by the loss of sight, fled to the protection of the Saints, begging that through their intercession the health of his eyes might be restored. When, exhausted by sorrow and exertion and by the continual bending of his veins, he had grown weary, he restored his tired body through sleep.

While he slept, Saint Wolffgang appeared to him—because he had held him as one familiar in his prayers—and said to him: “Pray to the Confessor of Christ, Henry, and he will free you, because this plague of blindness has come upon you on account of the fact that you diminished his holiness.”

After this vision he awoke trembling with awareness of his offense and hurried with swift steps and devout mind to the tomb of the Confessor of Christ. Prostrating himself on the ground, he asked the Confessor of Christ for pardon for his excesses with tears and prayers. He was immediately heard and restored to his former health, and he rendered thanks to God and to Saint Henry. He himself related to the religious men who reported it to us the great things that God had done for him.

Let the inhabitants of this world, therefore, beware of disparaging God’s household members and the citizens of the Saints; for those who habitually speak against and envy the good works of the Saints must necessarily perish here and forever.
