Although, then, this is not now a time of miracles—for signs are owed not to the faithful but to unbelievers—nevertheless, whenever anything happens to us beyond the ordinary course and order of nature, it must be embraced with every reverence, so that he himself, who is wondrous in his Saints, may be honored, and our sluggishness may be kindled toward all better things by such displays of virtue; through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

## PART TWO

[Col. 0133]

11. At the time when the venerable abbot Volcmarus of the Church of Merseburg brought the relics of the blessed Confessor Henry into the land of Saxony, a crowd of both sexes, having heard the report, came out to meet them. Some were drawn by the hope of recovering health, others by the fervent devotion that they had long held toward the name of that King, because from the accounts of their forebears they had learned that he had restored the condition of their land, which had been shaken by frequent pagan incursions.

But the praises of his merits began to be declared during the journey itself by evident signs of miracles. To recount individually how many people, oppressed by various kinds of illnesses, were restored to their former health would perhaps cause weariness to the writer and tedium to the reader. Nevertheless, this must not be left unmentioned: at many places of healing, as a testimony to the virtue divinely displayed, not very large heaps grew up, piled together through the zeal of the common people, so that, on seeing them, posterity might show reverence to the man through whose merits it saw so many benefits conferred upon his people.

Leaving these matters aside for the moment, however, those events should be related that are still remembered by many today.

12. Among the sick multitude that accompanied the relics in search of healing, a certain youth, bent and twisted by an unmistakable contraction of his limbs, was carried by his parents [in a sedan chair]. Having obtained nothing along the way, he was brought as far as the threshold of the church.

A choir of monks and clerics came out to meet the relics with fitting reverence—not only from that place but also from other churches, where they had gathered together. Then, as is customary, amid the mixed singing of the people and clergy, the procession returned. The solemnity of the Mass was also begun with a more festive rite in honor of the blessed Henry.

That cripple, scarcely brought into the church amid the crowd pressing forward, was laid down near the altar where the relics had been placed. You would have seen fulfilled in him that saying of Isaiah: “The lame man shall leap like a stag, and the tongue of the mute shall be clear.” For the bonds of his sinews began to loosen, and his feet and legs to stretch out. Leaping forward before the eyes of everyone, he proclaimed, with all the strength of voice he could summon, the power that had been wrought in him.

Thus the ability to walk, which habit had denied him from the very beginning of his birth, was restored by the grace of Christ through the merits of the blessed Henry. A cry of praise to God rose high from both sexes. The healed man was stationed before the altar to receive Communion, and then returned home with his parents.

13. Three demoniacs—one man and two women—were cured in that same place. They had frequently repeated the name of Henry while blaspheming it, but at last they abandoned the seats they had occupied with a terrifying shriek.

One of them, more stubborn than the others and long resisting the invocation of the holy name, learned that the relics were being brought to him. “Now, when Henry himself comes, I will not remain,” he said. Immediately, with a great cry, he abandoned the possessed man. These events occurred on the very day the relics arrived, during Mass.

14. In the territory of Merseburg there was a woman who had long been blind. With relatives guiding her steps, she hurried beyond her strength to meet the relics, hoping to recover her sight. Since she had received no healing along the way, she attributed this to the obstacle of her sins. For three days, remaining awake and indefatigable in prayer, she knocked at the door of Christ’s mercy; and at last, through the merits of the blessed Henry, she obtained the aid of the desired light.

She lived for a long time afterward in the same village where she had previously lived. This kind of miracle became so famous throughout that entire land that it could scarcely have been unknown to anyone, especially to those who lived at that time.

15. Likewise, among those coming from the more distant parts of that land, a certain woman who was deprived not only of the ability to walk but also was deformed and twisted in the miserable appearance of her whole body, was dragged in a vehicle by her companions [1. traveling companions]. Trusting in the protection of the blessed Henry, because the distinction of his virtues had by now been proclaimed everywhere, she continually invoked his name while extending her eyes and hands.

Thus she deserved to find, while still on the journey, what she had sought with the whole desire of her soul. For when her sinews had been loosened, her hump straightened, and her whole body restored to a serviceable form, she poured forth a proclamation of the power displayed in her. The passersby were filled with astonishment. She left the vehicle and, rejoicing herself, went ahead toward the church, while those around her rejoiced in God’s great works.

Having already obtained the health for which she had come to make her vows, she remained there for three days and fulfilled them.

16. In the city of Halle, which is two miles from Merseburg, there lived a matron of no mean standing. She was afflicted almost continually by toothache, so that, as the strength of her teeth gradually wasted away, the persistence of the pain denied her any hope of recovery.

When, at the beginning of one night, the severity of the illness tormented her more violently, she burst out with a deep sigh: “O blessed Henry, who comes to the aid of the needs of all who seek you, do not despise me, a sinner who invoke you with full faith; but grant that, through your patronage, I may enjoy at least one night’s rest.”

After saying this, she leaned her head back for a little while and, overcome by exhaustion, fell asleep. Immediately all the pain with which she had long struggled vanished completely.

17. In the Monastery of Saint Peter, adjoining the city of Merseburg, the following event occurred. Almost the whole community remembers it, and the brother concerned in the matter, who is still alive and was questioned, is accustomed to recount it with a groan.

When all the churches throughout that land, far and wide and with common devotion, received the feast of the blessed Henry for celebration with a more festive rite, the church mentioned above, being the nearer one and therefore the more ready to praise him, began, as far as it could, to be more splendidly adorned.

But because it is impossible for anyone, however just or holy, to escape envy in prosperity, a certain brother, driven by the goad of envy, did not fear to disparage his holiness and to resist his glory by every means within his power. He went so far that, since he was then serving as sacristan, he concealed all the more precious objects on that day and hindered the sounding together of the great bells.

But that brother did not long escape punishment for his offense against God and the blessed Henry. For suddenly he began to be deprived throughout almost his whole body of the function of the five senses. Then, when the rigidity of his mind had relaxed, he openly declared before everyone God’s judgment against himself; and, although not yet perfectly healed, he was restored somewhat toward improvement.

18. What I am about to relate I learned, with God as witness, from the Bishop himself, the person about whom I shall speak.

When Poland, being a rebellious and fierce people, and trusting more in the inaccessible wildernesses and marshes of its forests than in the strength of its forces, strove to shake the yoke of imperial rule from its neck, the glorious Emperor Frederick resolved to repress its insolence.

When a general expedition had been proclaimed and an army had been assembled in large numbers from various parts of the kingdom, the princes of that land and the whole people were seized with fear. They saw the forces of the kingdom being moved against them, while they themselves recognized that they were unequal to the task and inexperienced in the art of war. They therefore sent ambassadors to appease the king’s anger and promised in every way, by renewed submission, to correct the error of their former dissension.

For this purpose they chose Wernher, Bishop of the Church of Płock, a man of reverend character and remarkable wisdom. With gifts befitting royal magnificence, they sent him to the Emperor, who was staying at Aachen and storing the bones of Charlemagne, which had been raised from the tomb, in coffers made of gold and jewels.

After being rejected by him for a long time, he was finally admitted to favor through the intervention of the princes. Having completed his embassy according to his wishes, he returned with relics of Saint Henry and other gifts received from the Emperor. In the forest lying between the borders of Xurbia and Poland, at midday, he ordered the tents to be pitched.

After food, when he had given his tired limbs over to rest, a certain man appeared to him in sleep, clothed in royal garments and holding a scepter in his right hand. He stood beside him and addressed him in these words:

“Why are you overcome by sleep in this vast solitude? What are you carrying with you without knowing it?”

When the Bishop, terrified, asked who he was, he replied: “I am Henry, founder of the Babenberg Church, who during the course of temporal life earned from the Lord the short path to immortality. Therefore, in the place where you are lying, build a church in my name as circumstances permit. Know without doubt that, as time proceeds, divine worship will be increased there.”

The Bishop immediately arose and, as the servants rushed eagerly to bring him timber, built a church in a suitable form. But, troubled by the lack of stones—which were accustomed to be heard there but not seen—he went around anxiously. By chance, when he planted the staff he was carrying into a mound of heaped earth, he discovered an abundance of stones in the form of squares.

Thus he constructed an altar and dedicated it to the name of God, the blessed Henry, and the holy King Sigismund. A larger church is now being built there, with many people supporting it, and the Order of monastic profession is being begun. What he had foretold already appears to be coming to fulfillment.

On this occasion, therefore, the name of the blessed Henry began to be held in veneration among those nations.

19. Once, when a considerable multitude of poor people oppressed by various illnesses had gathered in the church at Merseburg, asking not only for bodily health but also insistently for alms, the people who had come for the sake of prayer extended the hand of mercy to each one as their means allowed.

A certain peasant from a nearby village, stained by greed, pretended to have a contraction of the sinews and sat down among the sick with his foot bent backward. When concern for his household affairs forced him to return, and he had already crossed the church threshold leaning on a staff and walking with a feigned gait, he sought a suitable place so that, with his foot bent, he might reach his destination more easily.

But when God and the blessed Henry imposed upon him a punishment worthy of his merits, he began to feel the misery he had previously feigned, his foot now fixed fast by an unbearable pain [the printed reading is uncertain].

What was he to do? Shame and pain struggled equally in his mind. Shame prevented him from revealing what had happened; pain compelled him to confess. Fear nevertheless prevailed. And when everyone heard this, a great fear seized them.

By this sign it became clear to all that God’s servant was present not only to the devout prayers of those who sought him, but also opposed with severity those who presumed to attempt such things. From then on, such presumptuous fraud by the faithless ceased.

20. There is a parish church adjoining the Church of Blessed Peter in the Old Castle. Near it lived a certain blind man who heard the singing of the people rejoicing with the greatest devotion at the recovery of a certain sick man.

This blind man was from the land and nation of the Slavs. Among them, simplicity—or rather irrationality—was so natural, through a certain perversity of mind, that they seemed scarcely to possess even a faint spark of faith.

He therefore asked the reason for such singing. When he was told that it was taking place because of the healing of the sick man, he said: “Since this Henry is a German, he grants the assistance of his grace only to Germans; but he has never bestowed any benefit upon me or upon the people of my nation.”

Those present burst into laughter. Others, however, being of sounder mind, urged him to go to the church and ask for health.

He was accordingly led to the place where the relics of the blessed Confessor were kept and was prostrated on the ground. Soon afterward the Slav himself experienced the mercy of the German whom he had complained was denying it to him. For the whiteness on his eyes began to peel away like scales, and the desired aid of light was restored to him.

Thus that people, which, as I said, imagined itself despised because of its rustic simplicity and smallness of faith, regained confidence and hope through this benefit and thereafter venerated the blessed Henry with more devoted zeal than all the others.

21. The event I am about to relate has almost as many witnesses as there are brothers who were living at that time and can now be found at the aforesaid Church of Blessed Peter. They testify that they came to know it all the more faithfully because they knew it all the more truly.

In one of their villages, near the city, a certain peasant was struck by a serious illness and lost the use of one foot. He wasted away so greatly, with his sinews dried up and his flesh almost dead, that it seemed impossible both to him and to all who looked upon him that human skill or effort could restore his health.

Therefore, what he despaired of receiving from human beings, he sought from him for whom nothing is difficult and who alone restores all things. Through the patronage of the blessed Henry, with firm faith and solid hope, he knocked persistently at the door of God’s mercy with tears and frequent fasts, and at last deserved to be restored to the form of his former gait.

22. In a certain village one mile from the Castle of Merseburg, there lived a woman who had been deaf and mute from the beginning of her birth. Her relatives and fellow citizens cherished her in the bosom of mercy.

They brought her to the church and, by nods and signs, insofar as it was possible to communicate with her, instructed her to prostrate herself before the relics of the blessed Confessor. But, like an irrational beast, she knew neither how to ask anything on her own behalf nor even what the relics were or what was happening.

Nevertheless, the prayer and faith of the faithful, who were collectively beseeching God for her health, came to her aid. Through the intercession of the blessed Henry she deserved to be completely restored in both functions of the body, as she herself later testified.

23. Since the faithful kept sacred vigils without interruption around the incomparable treasure, so that, as some departed and others arrived, the doors of the church were not closed day or night, the church custodian, considering that wolves hiding beneath sheep’s wool could not easily be recognized, feared that the relics might be secretly carried away.

To prevent this, he placed them in a sufficiently suitable repository made of squared stones. He also fitted it with a small door of pinewood, which could be closed and opened when circumstances required.

One night, while more carelessly placing a lamp near it during the course of Matins, he entered the choir that he attended more diligently than the others. Shortly afterward, sensing smoke and suspecting inwardly what had happened, he hurried back to the place. He found the little door touched by flame and giving off smoke, but not damaged.

To whose merits could this be attributed, if not to the one whose relics were kept there? Through his intervention, they could indeed have been preserved from theft without enclosing them in wood and stone. But the devout Confessor of God did not wish the labor and zeal of those who served him devotedly to be wasted, lest they should be saddened even by a small loss to the door. Therefore, in the wood suitable for use as fuel, he obtained from God’s power that the fire should forget its force.

24. A woman possessed by a demon was brought before the aforesaid repository with her hands bound by ropes, although she resisted vehemently. While the demon uttered a bellow into the air and she cried out that she was being tormented by Henry, she herself was sufficiently tormented and was freed.

As she later reported in the presence of others, it seemed to her that a certain man with gray hair, a long beard, and a royal garment had come forth from that same place and had driven the evil spirit from her with blows and threats.

But if I wished to pursue in detail all the miracles that occurred day after day, time would leave me before the material did—especially since the church custodian himself, who was present at almost all of them, declared that, although they exceeded the possibility of being counted, he had been able to commit only a few of the many to memory.

This alone must not be omitted here: people suffering from fever are cured by drinking water or another liquid from the golden chalice mentioned above, which the same Emperor had ordered to be made for blessed Lawrence as a special sign of his devotion.

Through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with God the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout endless ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0139]

## APPENDIX

Of those matters that chiefly concern the more recent benefits of Saint Henry, the mantle, the cross, and other sacred treasures; the present solemnity; renewed offices of devotion; and the churches and chapels erected, in addition to the preceding Life written by an Anonymous author.

## CHAPTER ONE  
### On the charters transferred here from the Life

[Col. 0139B]

1. We have transferred here the charters of the Life of Saint Henry that were not sufficiently fittingly attached to the various chapters of which we have spoken above.

The first place here belongs, in chronological order, to the two letters of Pope Benedict VIII: one addressed to Saint Henry, not yet crowned at Rome, and the other to Eberhard, first Bishop of Bamberg, concerning the confirmation of his church. The former is said to have been written in the month of June, Indiction XI, but dated “the twelfth day before the Kalends of February, in the first year of the pontificate.”

It is not easy to determine the end of the pontificate of Sergius IV or the beginning of that of Benedict VIII, as Baronius correctly observes under the year 1012, although he himself places the death of the aforesaid Sergius in that year, and therefore also Benedict’s entrance into the Roman See.

For if all the details of this charter are correctly dated, Benedict could not have ascended the chair of Peter before the year 1013, Indiction XI, which is the chronological indication of that year. Since the charter was both written and dated in the first year of his pontificate, it follows that this first year must still have been in progress in January—that is, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of February of the following year, 1014. It is not the place here to investigate this matter further.

2. From this one might perhaps reasonably conclude that this charter, written in the preceding year, 1013, seems to have been carefully preserved by Pope Benedict so that it might be presented to the Emperor himself, already crowned or about to be crowned, at the beginning of the year 1014 in the city of Rome, although it bears only the title of King.

This is a conjecture, and I will readily allow myself to be refuted. I observe in passing that toward the end the Supreme Pontiff no longer addresses Saint Henry but turns his speech to the “most beloved brother” alone, and therefore to Bishop Eberhard alone. But we do not undertake to examine even this matter more closely here.

The second charter, addressed only to Eberhard, bears no date. Gretser correctly observes, however, from Benedict’s statements that certain events occurred in his presence at Bamberg, that it was issued after he himself had come to Bamberg—namely, in the year 1019, when he consecrated the Basilica of Saint Stephen on the eighth day before the Kalends of May, as stated in chapter 23, number 32 in our work. Perhaps it was issued in the city of Bamberg itself, before he returned to Italy.

Of the three other later charters, of Clement II, Leo IX, and the Emperor Henry III, there is nothing that needs to be explained at length here.

3. One matter remains to be indicated on this occasion while we are discussing the charters: the form in which the seals of Saint Henry appear is somewhat varied.

This was brought to my attention by a Henrician charter, expanded on a very large sheet and written according to the model of the autograph, which was found among our papers. It reads: “Given on the sixth day before the Nones of April, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1003, Indiction I, in the second year of Lord Henry, King I. Done at Quedlinburg.” I would reproduce it here in full, indeed engraved in copper, if that were worthwhile. These matters have long been known, and the distinguished Schaten mentioned above reproduced the whole document long ago in his Paderborn Annals under the year 1003, page 367.

[Col. 0140D]

[Col. 0141A] Nor am I concerned here with the monogram, nor do I examine the script, since these matters have been amply discussed elsewhere. But the seals display a diversity that deserves to meet the eyes of those curious about treasures of this kind.

I observed it by comparing the seal of the aforesaid copy with another Bamberg seal, formerly sent to us. I shall append impressions of both here.

Thus Saint Henry is represented in the Quedlinburg charter. Its detached seal, already reproduced here and applied to the other, was noted long ago by Papebrochius, volume III of June, page 79; we reproduce it from our own copy.

4. The other seal differs considerably from this form. In 1699 it was drawn for us by the above-mentioned Joannes Franciscus Xaverius Eppenauer, then sworn substitute registrar of the Bamberg archive, as he himself signed and wished to attest on 18 May of that same year, in these words:

“I, the undersigned, attest in my own hand that I have faithfully drawn the seal of the present form according to the original—written in the Emperor Saint Henry’s own hand and authenticated with this wax seal on the Kalends of November, at Frankfurt, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1007—by virtue of which, as the formal Latin words state, he elevated his paternal inheritance, called Babenberg, with the consent and at the request of his most beloved wife, Queen Chunigunda, into the seat and dignity of a bishopric.”

The seal of Saint Henry is somewhat different in form from the preceding one and is represented as follows:

[Col. 0141C]

[Col. 0141D] 5. From these two examples alone, I do not see how anything certain can be decided about the greater or lesser authenticity of either. It is enough for me to have displayed both, lest either should subsequently perish here, so that those who have more material at hand may undertake a more exact investigation.

Now receive the promised charters, transferred here from the Anonymous author’s work. It will be enough to reproduce them fully as they were published by the Anonymous author, since only the first two concern the time of Saint Henry and have already been sufficiently explained. Apart from the annual pension customarily paid to the Roman Pontiff, concerning its exchange with the territory of Benevento, see Baronius’s Annals under the year 1053, number 1; this matter can easily be passed over here.

### Confirmation of the privileges of the Church of Bamberg by Pope Benedict VIII  
*To be read in chapter 24.*

6–9. Benedict, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved in Christ, always his lord, the most serene King Henry, crowned by God, and his spiritual son; and also to Eberhard, his brother and bishop, namely the venerable bishop of the holy Church of Babenberg: eternal salvation in the Lord and Apostolic blessing.

“Among all …” The remainder may be seen in our edition under Benedict VIII, in the *Patrologia*.

### Letter of Pope Benedict to Eberhard, first Bishop of the Church of Bamberg  
*To be read in chapter 25.*

[Col. 0142B]

10–12. The same Pope Benedict also wrote a letter to Eberhard, first Bishop of the Church of Babenberg, concerning the confirmation of that bishopric, in the following form:

“Benedict, Bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved son in the Lord Jesus Christ, Eberhard, venerable bishop of the holy Church of Babenberg: perpetual salvation. Whenever the pious assistance of our Apostolic confirmation is requested …” and so forth. See the passage cited above.

### Letter by which Pope Clement II confirmed the privileges and immunities of the Church of Bamberg  
*To be read in chapter 16.*

13–17. Clement, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to our most sacred Church of Babenberg, in its sons and daughters—namely, its clergy and people—perpetual salvation in the Lord.

“The dispensation of the ages …” See the *Patrologia* under Clement II.

### Diploma of Leo IX concerning the privileges of the Church of Bamberg, especially the Pallium and the occasions on which the Bishop may use it  
*To be read in chapter 17.*

18–20. After the happy passing of Clement, of pious memory, when Pope Damasus—formerly Poppo, Bishop of Brixen—had occupied the See for only thirty days, Leo IX, also called Bruno, elected by the aforementioned Emperor Henry III and appointed the one hundred and fifty-second Pope, sent the Pallium from the Apostolic See to Hartwic III, Bishop of Bamberg, as a sign of the benevolence he had toward the Babenberg church. He wrote him a letter in these words:

“Leo, Bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Hartwic, venerable Bishop of the Church of Babenberg: perpetual salvation in the Lord Jesus Christ. If shepherds of sheep …” and so forth. See the passage in our text under Leo IX.

### Leo IX’s arrival in Germany. The privileges of the Church of Bamberg are confirmed by him  
*To be read in chapter 18.*

21–26. The same Apostolic Prelate, invited by the Emperor Henry, came into the German lands and reached Regensburg. He raised Saint Wolfgang, the Bishop of that city, from his tomb; then at Bamberg, in the presence of the Emperor himself and the people, he ordered the privileges to be proclaimed and confirmed them by his authority.

The text of this confirmation is as follows:

“Leo, Bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Hartwic, Bishop of Babenberg, and to his canonical successor in the episcopal see in perpetuity: eternal salvation in the Lord. Since pastoral care requires …” and so forth. See the passage cited above.

### Constitution of the Emperor Henry II, King III, by which the privileges of the Church of Bamberg are confirmed  
*To be read in chapter 19.*

27. Nor did the aforesaid King Henry III, son of the Emperor Chunrad, appointed King long before while his father was still alive, fail to act. In the twelfth year of his appointment and the first of his reign, he ordered the privilege reproduced below to be written for the confirmation of the Babenberg bishopric, while Eberhard, the first Bishop of that see, was still alive.

“Henry, by the favor of God’s clemency, King. In the judgment of God, who sees all things, we believe that the merit of the giver and of the confirmer will be equal. We also believe that it belongs to our royal majesty to consider the concerns of the whole kingdom, and especially the welfare of all the holy churches of God, and to abolish with all speed everything adverse to them, lest they become degraded by serious disadvantage or, through any occasion arising from our fault, withdraw from their former worship and religion.

Thus, while we faithfully perform these things out of love and equally out of fear of God, we may share in the merits and glory of those who have bestowed these gifts upon God with pious affection.

Therefore, we wish it to be known to all the faithful in Christ, both present and future, that, in hope of this, through the intervention of our most beloved mother, Gisila, Empress Augusta, and also out of love for our beloved and faithful Eberhard, first bishop of the holy Church of Babenberg, we decree, with the consent of our faithful, that the same place—which the divine Emperor Henry II, through divine inspiration and with perfect faith and devotion of charity, elevated into a bishopric in honor of the Prince of the Apostles Peter and the holy martyr George, for the sake of his own soul and those of his kin—shall remain so established.

Removing every contradiction, we confirm it by the authority of our royal majesty. We also confirm all the movable and immovable property of that holy Church of God which the divine Emperor himself, in his ardor for the heavenly homeland, generously bestowed there, so that our faithful Eberhard, the first Bishop of that place, and his successors forever may possess them in secure tranquility and may have free power, with the consent of the clergy and people, to arrange, regulate, and enlarge the goods and properties of that church.

28. “We also decree by our authority that, in the abbeys, monasteries, counties, courts, markets, mints, ferry dues, tolls, castles, villages, settlements, plots of land, male servants, female servants, tributaries, tithes, preserves, forests, hunting grounds, fisheries, mills, waters and watercourses, fields, meadows, fishponds, cultivated and uncultivated lands, books, silver and gold, gems, vessels, ornaments, or any utensils bestowed there for the worship and religion of God, and in all the boundaries and possessions of that church, or whatever at present belongs to it or may be increased from these things, there shall be no harassment by tyrants, no power shall invade by violence, and no count or judge shall presume to impose law there except the Bishop of that place.

Let every possession of those serving God there be regarded as protected by immunity. Let that bishopric be free and secure from every external and unjust authority, so that those serving God there may worthily celebrate the memory of its first founder, and may be able and willing to commend us, its supporters and confirmers, to God in their prayers.

And so that this grant of our authority may remain firm and unshaken, we have ordered this privilege, written for that purpose, to be confirmed by our own hand and marked with the impression of our seal.”

## CHAPTER TWO  
### On the more recent patronage of the Church of Bamberg through Saint Henry

[Col. 0144B]

29. Having prefaced this with the earlier miracles of the holy Emperor, I append the following account, which the Reverend Father Nicolaus Pottu, praised so many times above, the most worthy Rector of our Bamberg college, carefully collected and arranged in its entirety, for the glory of the most holy married couple, founders of the Bamberg church, and for the deserved commendation of two most distinguished prelates, their clients. I had asked him whether the Bambergers had kept any account of miracles performed by the Saints during these latter centuries, a list of which might also be appended here. In a wordless response, so to speak, he submitted the aforesaid appendix [Col. 0144C], or treatise. Although he left it entirely to my discretion, I judged that it should be reproduced untouched and complete, since it had been composed from those records to which I believed nothing should be added or removed. And although the favors granted by Henry, considered separately from the others, could have been condensed into fewer words, they nevertheless seemed such outstanding examples of virtue, presented to the Catholic world by two Bishops of the Bamberg church, chiefly through the assistance of St. Henry, that they deserved a place here. From the narrative itself, properly arranged by Pottu, the whole structure of the matter becomes clear; the following title has been prefixed to it:

**Favors granted from heaven by St. Henry to two Bishops of Bamberg**

[Col. 0144D] 30. “During these latter centuries, when heresies spread through Germany and also infected a large part of Franconia, St. Henry, together with his virginal wife, appeared to take special care of the Bamberg church which he had once founded. He showed extraordinary favors to several Bamberg Bishops, especially two who were singularly devoted to him—namely, Nythard, the forty-sixth Bishop, and John Godefrid, the forty-eighth—and by the same work, through the zeal of these two prelates, rescued the Bamberg church from the most wretched servitude to heresy and wickedness.

“What is related here is drawn chiefly from Fridericus Fornerus, a writer contemporary and personally acquainted with those Bishops. Some information about this man is supplied by the inscription on his tomb in the parish church of St. Martin at Bamberg, which reads as follows:

“‘The Most Reverend Father in Christ and Lord, Fridericus Fornerus, Doctor of Sacred Theology, Bishop of Hebron, Suffragan of Bamberg, and there Vicar General in spiritual matters; counsellor to His Sacred Imperial Majesty and to the Most Serene Duke of Bavaria; known to the world for the integrity of his life, zeal for religion, embassies undertaken, prudent counsel, living eloquence in the word of God, and published books; piously fell asleep in the Lord in the year 1630, on 5 December.’”

31. “A handwritten history of the Society of Jesus college at Bamberg, written in that same year, 1630, agrees with this eulogy. Among other things it says of him: ‘He was a man who loved the common good and was highly commended for virtue and learning . . . . Under the mitre he led a religious life.’

“This Suffragan therefore published a little work entitled *Two Mirrors of an Ecclesiastical Prince*, composed and arranged chiefly from the illustrious deeds and heroic virtues of two most praiseworthy prelates and princes: John Godefrid, who died most piously on 29 December 1622, and Nythard, who died on 26 December 1598. It also contained four funeral sermons, delivered in the vernacular and written down in Latin, preached at their tombs and funerals in the cathedral church of Bamberg, and was issued and published for public reading and imitation by Fridericus Fernerus, etc. Ingolstadt, printed by Gregorius Hoenlin, in the year of Christ 1623.

“Most of what is cited here has been taken from this author. Whatever has been drawn from other sources is indicated in its proper place. We begin with Nythard, who was earlier in age.

32. “Nythard, of the noble Franconian family of Thüngen, after having already discharged the office of dean in the cathedral church at Würzburg and then serving as provost of that same church, having placed residence at his very extensive provostship in the last place and taken leave of it and, by divine providence—with Saints Henry and Cunigunde, to whom he was specially devoted, certainly interceding—moved his residence to Bamberg. There he began his first residence as though he were a junior canon; after completing in nearly one and the same year the probationary period of residence, as it is called, he was enrolled among the chapter, elected dean of the cathedral church, and, after the death of Bishop Ernest, was elected Bishop on 14 November 1591, by the unanimous consent of his fellow canons, without a formal ballot, through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, while the entire people, from the highest to the lowest, rejoiced.

33. “And—something astonishing to see and hear—so that he might properly prepare himself for this highest governance of souls, as soon as he arrived at Bamberg he changed the former, less seemly dress of the canons and entirely renounced his former manner of life. He began to differ so greatly from his former self that, by everyone’s judgment and assessment, he was believed to have been transformed into another man, created according to God, and thus made most capable of receiving the heavenly gifts that descend [Col. 0146A] from the Father of lights.

“This rare change in his clothing, manners, household, domestic magnificence, daily intercourse, and every form of conducting business seemed miraculous to all who had previously known him. From that time the efficacy of the patronage of Saints Henry and Cunigunde became known, for he devoted himself wholly to their worship and imitation. He not only read their lives constantly, but also himself copied both of them from an ancient manuscript codex, acting as a transcriber in his own hand.

34. “Encouraged by the examples of these patrons and relying on divine assistance, he undertook a task altogether arduous and, in the circumstances of those times, judged even by great men to be impossible: namely, the reformation of the Bamberg church, which heresy had almost entirely occupied and shamefully polluted.

“For, first of all, in the city of Bamberg itself the entire civic senate, with only two exceptions, not only defended the Lutheran sect with the greatest obstinacy, but approximately fifty of the principal and wealthier nobles of the whole community of citizens had conspired, declaring that they would rather transfer their residence elsewhere with all their possessions than submit. In most of the other cities and towns of the diocese not even a single Catholic citizen could be found. Nevertheless, in order to rescue this Imperial church—the noble daughter of Saints Henry and Cunigunde—from the jaws of wolves, this pastor, no less prudent than courageous, left nothing unattempted.

[Col. 0146C] 35. “After first communicating the matter to Matthias, Emperor of the Romans, to William, Duke of Bavaria, to several other orthodox princes, and to his cathedral chapter, he expelled before all else the preachers who, through I know not whose connivance, had occupied a number of parishes belonging to the Bamberg territory.

“Next he acted against the schoolmasters. Just as they were infected with heresy in most cities and towns, so too they instilled heresy into the children: sometimes by drilling Luther’s catechism into them, sometimes by corrupting them with little songs rejected by the Catholic Church, and in a thousand other ways inserting perverse doctrines. He therefore removed these deadly corrupters of flourishing youth and substituted Catholics for them.

“Proceeding still further, he removed all prefects, all tax-collectors, all local judges, all *Schultheissen*, all consuls, and all civic senators who refused to submit to the Catholic religion and profess it, and replaced them with others.

36. “With this as a kind of prelude to the whole drama, he prudently began the conversion of his subjects and pursued it courageously for many years amid innumerable complaints, contradictions, disturbances, uprisings, and threats and persecutions from non-Catholic princes.

“And since this great undertaking required considerable expense, lest the sinews of successful action be lacking, he reduced expenditures on his own person, wherever he could, in a manner rarely seen. He cut the number of court servants down to such a small figure that he scarcely seemed able to maintain the dignity of an Imperial prince. He rejected all pride and display and lived with such frugality—especially when dining or supping privately—that, content with at most three ordinary dishes, he resembled a religious in a cloister more than a Bishop and Prince in a palace.

37. “On the other hand, whenever divine worship or the restoration of souls was concerned, he spared no expense. Thus, to kindle and promote among the young an eagerness to learn Christian doctrine, he spent a vast sum from his own treasury merely on catechetical gifts: Canisius’s catechism and his little books on preparation for confession and Communion, forms of prayer, rosaries, images [Col. 0147B], and other things of this kind.

“I was an eyewitness, indeed a fellow worker, when on one occasion he sent three thousand florins to Augsburg for this purpose, so that nothing other than such sacred amulets and stimulating gifts for children should be purchased. When they arrived, he distributed everything most generously throughout all the parishes of this church within the space of a single week, adding letters of instruction.

38. “There were moneylenders who grumbled that excessively large sums were being spent on reforming the diocese, since everything could be accomplished at less expense if undertaken at a more suitable time. To them he gave an answer worthy of an ecclesiastical prince:

“‘The temporal goods of my church,’ he said, ‘will never be dispensed more usefully than when they are spent on increasing the glory of God and promoting and extending the salvation of souls. For what other purpose did St. Henry enrich his church so greatly?’

“Through this pastoral vigilance and generosity, as well as his unconquerable endurance of labor and opposition, this most praiseworthy prelate accomplished so much that within seven years the heretical plague had been driven from almost the entire diocese and orthodox faith restored to it. Thus many thousands of people—not only those then living but also their descendants—were rescued from destruction.

39. “How pleasing this zeal of the prelate was to St. Henry, and how meritorious it was before God, may be inferred from the fact that the heavenly Master of the household deigned, toward the evening of this faithful laborer’s life, to call him through the holy Emperor himself and his most holy wife to receive the eternal reward of so outstanding a labor.

“Fornerus relates this memorable event on page 110 in the following words:

“‘I shall relate to you a truly astonishing yet entirely true matter, from which it will become clear who foretold to him his impending departure from this life. In the year 1598, which proved fatal to him, on the feast of the Emperor St. Henry, after he had celebrated the sacred rites in the morning according to the pontifical rite, he was reading the life of that Saint after dinner, seated in his oratory. He had opened the windows facing the cathedral church to admit the air. While reading, it happened that he looked toward the bell tower where the larger bells of St. Henry and St. Cunigunde hang. There, through the upper windows, he saw immense images of St. Henry and St. Cunigunde, in imperial dress and crowns as they are painted, flashing with extraordinary light; and he saw St. Henry actually beckoning to him with his hand.

40. “This vision initially struck him with the greatest terror. But when he had gathered himself somewhat and earnestly commended himself to those holy patrons, an inward consolation that came over his mind immediately drove away and wiped out the fear.

“Yet, in order to investigate the truth of the matter thoroughly and ascertain it more certainly, he sent first one chamberlain and then another there with the sacristan, so that they might discover who was in the tower. After searching everywhere, they reported that they had seen absolutely no one there. Nevertheless, the vision remained while they were present, although they felt nothing anywhere except an unusual kind of dread and did not understand what the Bishop wanted.

“When the same apparition had shown itself a third time, it finally disappeared altogether.

“It happened in the evening that, as was customary, I was walking with him through the garden and reciting the prayers of Matins with the praises before supper. When these had been completed, he addressed me in these words: ‘I have a question for you, Doctor Fornerus. If a Saint appears to someone and, as though beckoning with his hands, calls him to himself, what do you think it signifies?’

“‘I consider it a very good omen,’ I replied [Col. 0148C]. ‘It is a sign that the Saints will soon adopt the person whom they are calling into their company.’ This may also be gathered from various apparitions of the Saints related by St. Gregory the Great in his books of the *Dialogues*. Thus the holy Apostles Peter and Paul appeared to the priest Ursinus and summoned him to the heavenly realm.”

41. “Thus St. Juvenal and St. Eleutherius, Martyrs, foretold the day of death to Probus, Bishop of Rieti. Thus the Archangel St. Michael foretold the day of death to Arnulf, Bishop of Soissons. Thus, according to St. Gregory of Tours, St. Martin and others appeared to Aredius and invited him to the joys of the blessed.

“These were the histories that came to my mind at that time. To this he replied: ‘You have judged correctly. I shall tell you what happened to me a few hours ago, still on this very day.’ And he explained the whole matter in order, just as we have now recounted it.

“After he had clearly explained the interpretation of the vision as referring to his imminent death, he himself finally added:

“‘I hear that a similar vision was once offered to one of my predecessors, Wigand Redwitius. He was the fortieth Bishop of Bamberg, at the time when heresies were ravaging the whole of Germany. He resisted Luther and his followers with the greatest vigor—if anyone ever did—and drove their paradoxes from the fold of this church by every remedy within his power. He, moreover, died in that same year. You will see,’ he said, ‘that the same thing will happen to me. For I shall not survive into this year.’ He spoke, and the event answered his words shortly before the end of that same year, 1598.”

[Col. 0149A] 42. “Meanwhile his sole and supreme concern was to make himself worthy of the company of the holy patrons, by whom he had been most graciously invited to join them. At that time several towns still remained—such as Höchstadt, Herzogenaurach, Oberscheinfeld, and Burgkunstadt, together with some villages—in which reform and the return of those in error to the unity of the Church had indeed begun but had not yet been brought to the desired conclusion.

“Therefore, believing that he would be most welcome to the holy Founders if he could present to their sight the church founded by them without the stain of heresy, he applied all the strength of his efforts to completing this work. He achieved what he desired, the Lord favoring the efforts of his most faithful servant and cooperating with evident [Col. 0149B] helps of divine grace.

43. “Moreover, since he believed that St. Henry, beckoning to him with his hand from the tower, had announced the words of 4 Kings, chapter 20: ‘Give orders for your house; for you shall die, and you shall not live,’ he began to set everything in order, both with respect to temporal matters and with respect to the state of his soul.

“Desiring to redeem his sins through almsgiving, he sent the most generous donations to all the churches and monasteries of poor religious, to hospitals and infirmaries; he also arranged for money to be distributed without number to other poor people of Christ.

“After he had fallen ill at Würzburg, where he had gone on business as provost of that church, he granted both to me and to the others who attended him throughout his illness the free authority to distribute at our discretion, for the sake of his soul, to the poor and to pious places, as much alms as we wished from all his goods in his granaries, storerooms, and available cash. He often repeated these words: ‘Whatever alms you distribute for my soul, I shall approve.’

44. “He repeated this several times even in the presence of two prelates of the Imperial church of Bamberg, who had gone down to Würzburg to visit and console him during his illness. He added more than once:

“‘My sins are exceedingly grave and almost infinite in number; they must therefore be washed away by many and great alms.’

“He expressed his final wishes as follows:

“‘I wish all my goods, over which I can dispose as my own property, for the most part inherited, to be divided into three parts. The first shall be given to the Church; the second shall be spent for the needs of the poor; the third shall go to my relatives. Among these I especially wish those who are still engaged in their studies to be included, as well as the underage sons of my brother, so that they may be raised in the Catholic religion.

“‘I would not wish to grant anything from the goods of the Church to those related to me by blood, unless it were available from my own patrimony, so that I might benefit them; for I know that ecclesiastical goods are not owed to them.’

“He added at the end that he wished to be buried in the cathedral church of Bamberg, without pomp and at the least possible expense.

45. “Fornerus explains over several pages how exactly he prepared himself for a blessed death and how piously he met it. Finally he concludes:

“‘I confess frankly, and declare what is true. I have attended at the final moments of many people who were believed to have departed this life with great piety. But to this day I have seen no one—indeed, I have scarcely even heard of anyone—with a piety like that of this dying man, with which he closed his final day.

“‘Such was the importance and efficacy for dying well of the patronage of Saints Henry and Cunigunde, and of their gracious apparition, by which they invited their devoted client to blessed eternity.’

“It also seems appropriate to mention here another vision offered to this prelate several hours before his death, by which he was informed about a future successor who would vigorously continue what he himself had rightly begun for the good of the Bamberg church.

“The frequently praised Fridericus Fornerus relates this prophecy in the cited treatise *Two Mirrors of an Ecclesiastical Prince*, and in the second funeral sermon for John Godefrid of Aschhausen, p. 60, where he writes as follows:

46. “When the Most Illustrious and Most Reverend Nythard, Bishop of Bamberg, of most praiseworthy memory, had attended the sacrifice on the morning of the feast of St. Stephen in the year 1598—the very day on which he ceased to live—I, who was always with him, introduced our John Godefrid, who had returned home from France the day before yesterday, to him as he lay in bed, in the presence of many people.

“When he saw him entering, he turned to me and said: ‘What sort of Bishop are you bringing me?’

“I answered: ‘Most Illustrious Lord, he is the young Canon John Godefrid of Aschhausen, returned home from France a few days ago.’

“Then, taking him by the hand, he said: ‘This man, after a few years, will adorn the episcopal see of St. Otto.’

“After these words he remained silent and thoughtful for a while; finally he congratulated him on his return. Our most illustrious John Godefrid, of pious memory, often remembered these words, but forbade them to be made public.

47. “Thus far are Fornerus’s words on page 60. Earlier, on page 11, he had related that his most pious mother, Brigitta of Zobel, when her little son was still lying in his cradle, saw him one night—after she had received the Holy Eucharist the previous day and had commended her son more devoutly to Christ and his Mother—standing before her adorned with a mitre and pontifical vestments and shining with a wondrous radiance.

“The young man praised above was then twenty-four years old. He was specially devoted to St. Henry and, as may rightly be believed, especially dear to that Saint, not only because of the tenderness of his devotion, but above all because of the likeness of his chastity. In this virtue the young man shone beyond the ordinary measure and, not long before, had given at Würzburg, where he was engaged in study, an example of that virtue worthy of immortal memory.

“Fornerus relates it in this way in his first funeral sermon, p. 26:

48. “‘I shall relate to you something admirable, yet entirely true. John Godefrid of Aschhausen, as everyone knows, was in his youth exceedingly handsome and attractive, with a very elegant bodily constitution. The hereditary enemy of the human race seized upon this circumstance and, by this stratagem, laid snares and set traps for his virginal purity.

“‘Certain women from the household of a person of great name and illustrious rank, having been captivated by his remarkable appearance and beauty at the instigation of an evil demon, invited him to a banquet under the pretext of honor. There, after deliberately making the man who was officially responsible for his care drunk, while he suspected nothing evil, they ordered that he be taken to bed.

“‘That night they also wished to keep the young man with them. Since he too suspected no evil and had already gone to sleep, those lustful instruments of the devil secretly and silently approached his bed and began to entice him to wicked acts, both with lascivious words and with every kind of stimulation they could devise.

“‘What did the most chaste young man do? Crying out in horror, he sprang from the bed as he was, dressed in linen stockings and a shirt; he broke free from their hands, hurried to the door of the house, and, leaving all his garments behind him, came to the house of a certain friend. There, giving thanks to God for the victory of chastity he had obtained, he quietly passed the remainder of the night . . .’

49. “After he had finally been ordained a cleric, he judged that he must watch over the chastity of body and mind with greater care, and that all the more diligently because corruption was then widespread everywhere . . . . . . . In our age scarcely anyone like him has been found who preserved the law of the Most High with such zeal for virginal purity.

“St. Henry therefore seems to have been delighted by the fragrance of this chastity and of the other virtues that usually accompany it, and to have chosen John Godefrid and obtained him from God as a Bishop for his Church, or as a particularly suitable instrument for restoring modesty, which had collapsed in a pitiable manner not only among the people but also among the clergy.

“Thus, when in the year 1609 the forty-seventh Bishop was at the point of death, the virginal married couple, Saints Henry and Cunigunde, once again allowed themselves to be seen in the tower of the cathedral church, concerned about the election of a new prelate.

50. “This is related in the work entitled *The Public Lament of Franconia for the Untimely Death of John Godefrid*, published by the college of the Society of Jesus [Col. 0151D] at Würzburg in 1623, p. 3, in these words:

“‘Saints Henry and Cunigunde were seen shortly before his election looking out over the city from the tower.’

“The poet expresses this apparition as follows:

> Rumour, untainted, reports that Henry,  
> the Father of his homeland,  
> a weighty member of the heavenly host,  
> with his virginal wife  
> joined to his side,  
> obtained this bishop among the venerable men,  
> when he appeared, from the towered house,  
> to cast his gaze about  
> his own city,  
> at the time when savage fates  
> pressed upon the departure of the prelate still alive.

[Col. 0152A] 51. “At that time no one imagined that John Godefrid would emerge from the electoral urn, both because he was one of the younger members of the chapter and because the votes were converging on John Christopher Neustetter, called Sturmer, dean of the Imperial church.

“But St. Henry’s vote with God in favor of his client John Godefrid ultimately prevailed. Consequently, although the aforesaid dean had been elected Bishop at once in the first ballot, he nevertheless refused to accept the dignity. Although the entire chapter earnestly begged and pressed him to consent, he refused not only a second and third time but even a fourth.

“When this struggle had continued for a long time, finally, with the dean himself leading the way, through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit and the unanimous consent of the lords of the chapter, John Godefrid of Aschhausen was acclaimed Bishop of Bamberg on 21 July 1609.

“It was the common conviction of the learned that this election had been arranged and ordered by the special providence of God for the good of the Bamberg church, which was in great need of assistance.

52. “The Most Eminent Cardinal Bellarmine, in his first letter to John Godefrid, the newly elected Bishop of Bamberg, dated 4 November 1609, writes as follows:

“‘Most illustrious and most reverend Lord, this has been done by the Lord, and it is wonderful in our eyes. The news of Your Most Illustrious and Most Reverend Lordship’s election gladdens the whole city of God.

“‘We grieved over the oppression of the noble Bamberg church; and when no suitable remedy came to its aid, we prayed the Lord for assistance. But the merciful Lord did far more abundantly than we could ask or understand.

“‘It now remains that he who began the good work in you should himself complete it, and that through you the Bamberg church should receive its glory in the present life, so that on the day of the Lord you too may receive from the Prince of Shepherds an immortal crown of glory.’”

53. “On the same day and in the same year, writing to the Most Serene Duke Maximilian of Bavaria, the same Cardinal said among other things:

“‘But what shall I say about the Bishop-elect of Bamberg? I certainly experienced incredible joy of heart and gave the most humble thanks for so manifest a grace of God.’

“Thus he wrote.

“A history of the Society of Jesus college at Würzburg, written in that very year, 1609, speaks as follows of the recently elected Bishop of Bamberg:

“‘From among the members of the Parthenian sodality, John Godefrid of Aschhausen was divinely given as prelate to the Bamberg church: a man learned in philosophy and in human and divine laws, in whom there was no pride or affectation; whose manners were formed for humanity; whose age was flourishing and, astonishingly, nearer to adolescence; an image of ancient integrity and stricter holiness, etc.’

54. “Just as so distinguished a Bishop was given to the Bamberg church at an exceedingly dangerous time through the care of St. Henry, so the same Bishop, with the same holy Emperor as his patron, undertook great works for God and the Church as soon as he assumed pastoral care—both in restoring divine worship [Col. 0153A] and in correcting the morals of clergy and people.

“By the very greatness of the works he accomplished, he made it clear to everyone that he had been raised to the episcopate for the good of the Church not so much by human as by heavenly suffrages.

“When these outstanding deeds could not remain unknown at Rome, the Most Eminent Bellarmine again wrote to John Godefrid in 1610 as follows:

“‘What I did in the matter . . . although I acted with great willingness, was not of such importance that it was necessary to tire myself by writing to a Bishop so occupied with more serious affairs. Yet since I was pleased to write, it is also a great pleasure for me to reply to a man whom I suspect to have been sent, as it were, from heaven.

“‘I do not know the Bishop and Prince of Bamberg, Godefrid, by sight, but from his outstanding works, by which he is very well known, I love and venerate him greatly. I continually pray God that he whom, at so opportune a time, he deigned to place over the tottering Bamberg church may graciously preserve him safe for a long time, guide and protect him, and finally crown him gloriously, full of days and merits.’”

55. “Writing in 1612, on 12 February, to Fridericus Fornerus, Suffragan of Bamberg, the same Cardinal added the following:

“‘But setting these matters aside, I give immense thanks for what you wrote to me about the remarkable progress of your excellent prince and Bishop, whom not human wishes or efforts but God himself, in his infinite goodness, gave to his Church.

“‘For my part, I am so bound to him by genuine affection that, if I could take up the wings of a dove, nothing would hold me back from flying at once to embrace him. Would that we had many like him not only in Germany but also in Italy and throughout the rest of the Christian world! For we would immediately see the Lord’s vineyard wonderfully flourishing again, entrusted to such good cultivators.

“‘From my heart I pray for him the length of life necessary for the reform of the Church, etc.’”

56. “The praised Cardinal has many more such statements in his letters, pointedly extolling the greatness of the benefit that divine goodness bestowed upon the tottering Bamberg church by providing it with a Bishop ‘who upheld his house during his life and strengthened the temple in his days; who cared for his people and delivered them from destruction’ (Ecclesiasticus 50).

“That this must be credited to the merits and intercession of Saints Henry and Cunigunde is demonstrated by their constant concern, mentioned above, over the election of this Bishop, as well as by the Bishop’s singular devotion and confidence toward the holy founders. An example of this devotion and confidence follows:

57. “As soon as John Godefrid assumed the episcopal burden, he had to struggle not only against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places—namely, against heresy, magic, sorcery, demonic idolatry, the foulest corruptions of the flesh, and innumerable monstrosities of wickedness—but also against the terrifying armies of heretical princes, which continually threatened Franconia.

“Understanding that he needed heavenly assistance against them, he fled to the patronage of St. Henry [Col. 0154A]. And, in order to obtain a pledge of his assistance, he secured from Eberhard, Bishop of Augsburg and his consecrator, the sword which the holy Emperor had once used in battle to subdue the enemies of the Church.

“He received this holy sword as a gift sent by God, by whose power he might repel the adversaries of his people, who were many and powerful: especially Frederick V, Count Palatine of the Rhine, invader of the Bohemian crown; Mansfeld; the Margrave of Durlach; the Duke of Anhalt; Christian of Brunswick, or Halberstadt; and their associates. They had openly designated the Bamberg diocese, as well as the Würzburg diocese, as their prey in printed broadsheets and had already devoured it in expectation.

58. “Although they attempted several incursions into both dioceses, John Godefrid—who in the meantime had also been made Bishop of Würzburg—partly frustrated the enemy’s efforts by strategy and partly broke them by force, opposing them with his own troops, which he had enlisted, together with auxiliary forces supplied by the Most Serene Duke of Bavaria.

“While the soldiers fought at the borders of the country, he himself, day and night, lay prostrate on the ground, like another Moses, pouring out prayers to God for his people. What he could not sometimes accomplish during the day because of the interruptions caused by envoys and military commanders coming and going, he made up in the middle of the night: rising, greatly shortening his sleep through vigils before dawn, and spending entire hours conversing with God.

“With these weapons, the devoted client of St. Henry preserved his Church, throughout the whole period of his government, unharmed by enemy incursions, plundering, and fires—and even by the plague, which had previously raged in Bamberg every year.

59. “John Godefrid experienced the supreme favor of St. Henry before his death: the holy Emperor appeared to him together with his virginal wife and announced his death to him, as is related in the manuscript Life of this prince.

“From that time he did not cease to prepare himself as carefully as possible for his happy departure from this life. His entire life, especially the life he led in the episcopate, had indeed been a continual preparation for a blessed death; but after receiving this heavenly indication concerning it, he devoted his cares still more intensely to that final task.

“In the very year in which he died, while, at the doctors’ prescription, he was staying at the castle of Waldaschach to restore his health, throughout that entire period, whether he dined or supped publicly or privately, he always ordered one of his chamberlains to read aloud from the book on eternity by Jeremias Drexel, S.J. During that time he went through the whole work three times.

“Meanwhile, whenever he was using the baths or taking treatments to induce sweating, he relaxed his mind with other pious books, especially histories of the deeds of the Saints.

60. “I remember that someone, in my presence, advised him that books dealing with pleasant matters rather than gloomy and melancholy subjects—death, hell, and the eternal punishments of the damned—were more suitable for the time when his health was being restored.

“He replied: ‘I know that I shall die soon. I stand before the door of eternity, etc.’

“At that very time he repeatedly spoke to me of his death, which he often said was near, and discussed with me the arrangement of his final wishes.

“Shortly beforehand he had likewise hinted at similar matters while going to Lanckheim to give the abbot his blessing and while returning, when I was sitting alone with him in the carriage. He firmly asserted that he would not live long; and that, if the journey to Regensburg did not have to be hastened, he would spend several days doing nothing other than arranging his household, as though he were soon to die.

“On the evening before his departure toward Regensburg, where obedience and his singular love and respect for the Emperor summoned him to the imperial diet, he was to set out on the journey early the next morning. As he bade me farewell, he said: ‘We shall see each other again; if not here, then, God willing, in heaven.’

[Col. 0155B] 61. “From these facts it may be gathered that John Godefrid was warned from heaven twice of his impending death: once before undertaking the journey to Regensburg, when he learned only that his death was near, without any definite indication of time; and a second time at Regensburg, where he additionally learned that he would die before the beginning of the new year. He had repeatedly affirmed this many days beforehand to various people and had therefore ordered that his will be brought from Bamberg to Regensburg.”

62. “Furthermore, that this announcement was made to him at Regensburg by Saints Henry and Cunigunde is stated in his own manuscript Life. Nor should anyone find it surprising that these holy patrons took such exceptional care for the happy passage of their client from this life, since he had earned their special favor by his special devotion to virginal chastity, so greatly loved by them. For he had defended this invincibly not only in his youth, as was related above, but also throughout the whole course of his life, against every temptation of the flesh and of Satan. Indeed, by the illustrious examples of his most chaste life he persuaded certain members of Luther’s sect that the claim was worthy of belief that Saints Henry and Cunigunde had preserved virginal continence in marriage by mutual consent—something that men who understood nothing beyond the flesh rejected as a fable, attributing to natural sterility and impotence what ought to have been attributed to virtue and grace. They further boasted that not even priests, much less married people, could be continent.

63. “On this subject John Seller of the Society of Jesus, preacher of the cathedral at Regensburg, relates something memorable in the funeral sermon that he delivered there for John Godefrid during the imperial diet, on 12 January 1623. When a certain non-Catholic prince observed that John Godefrid relentlessly persecuted the abominable concubinage of clerics and the license of a lustful life in his diocese, depriving the incorrigible of parishes and benefices and expelling them from the diocese, he argued in a private conversation with the Bishop that marriage ought to be permitted to priests, since it was impossible for them to maintain continence. The Bishop, on the contrary, demonstrated by firm arguments that this was possible with divine grace. But when the non-Catholic prince could not be persuaded by any argument, the Bishop said:

“‘I do not ordinarily confirm my statements by oath; nevertheless, on this occasion, by my priestly faith and dignity I affirm that it is possible, through God’s grace, to live chastely. For I myself have never touched a woman throughout my entire life, nor have I felt any impulse to do so.’

“The non-Catholic prince asked: ‘Is it truly as Your Lordship says about yourself?’

“‘It is truly so,’ replied the Bishop; ‘and I solemnly affirm it again by my episcopal faith.’

“Deeply moved by these words, the non-Catholic prince reverently kissed the virginal hands of John Godefrid, declaring at the same time that these hands were worthy to offer sacrifice.

64. “Finally, the virginal chastity that John Godefrid, under the protection of Saints Henry and Cunigunde, preserved unharmed and without the smell of fire amid the dangers of youth and the rest of his life—as though in the midst of Babylon’s furnace—he likewise brought happily into eternity under the patronage of those same Saints. ‘I call you yourselves to witness,’ says Fornerus in the funeral sermon delivered at Bamberg, ‘all of you who are present here: can his entire life not be called an outstanding mirror of priestly chastity? Do not doubt that this most chaste Bishop carried with him from this life into the next, to the tribunal of Christ the eternal Judge, the undefiled flower of virginity—which, as he confided to me on the last journey I made with him, as on many earlier occasions, he had preserved to the end . . . . The noble athlete and hero of Christ, John Godefrid, fought courageously and triumphed gloriously, carrying away the aureole of virginity with flesh and limbs intact, as Saint Jerome says.’

65. “The most praiseworthy Prince died at Regensburg on 29 December 1622. Just as he had been honored in life and death by extraordinary favors from the holy Emperors Henry and Cunigunde, so too, not content with the veneration he had shown his holy patrons during his lifetime, he wished his funeral to stand as a monument to his reverence for them. For the most humble Prince, deeming himself unworthy of burial together with those Saints, ordered that his body be buried in Bamberg Cathedral—not, however, in the church itself, where the Saints rested, but beneath it, in the dark crypt beneath the choir of Saint George the Martyr; there, in 1658, the bones of those Saints were later transferred. But God in turn deigned to honor his humble servant in his lifeless body.

66. “For when, fifteen days after his death—that is, on 12 January 1623, the day on which his solemn obsequies were celebrated at Regensburg in the Imperial Chapel in the presence of the nobles of the Empire—his body, dressed in episcopal vestments, was displayed to everyone’s view in an elevated tomb, his whole face appeared lively and ruddy, just as if he were still alive. Thus testifies the historical protocol of the city of Regensburg for the years 1622 and 1623. And when six further days were then spent conveying his body to Bamberg, where it was finally committed to the earth on 19 January, it retained the same grace, as Frederick Fornerus, an eyewitness, asserts on page 59, saying: ‘Not resembling a dead man but a sleeping one, it retained a pleasant and most vivid countenance after so many days of travel, right up to the hour of burial.’

67. “Such beauty God imparted to the lifeless body of John Godefrid, which during his life he had disciplined with so many hardships, so many vigils, so many fasts even on bread and water amid the principal meals, so many scourges, hair shirts, kneelings, and prostrations upon the ground; and, moreover, after his death, for the greater contempt of himself and the greater exaltation of Saints Henry and Cunigunde, he ordered it to be buried in a deep and dark crypt, which few people ordinarily enter! Yet although he had despised and concealed himself and his own merits, the splendor of his virtues could not be so hidden that many did not recognize and esteem them. The annual letters of the College of the Society of Jesus at Regensburg for the year 1622 report that Ferdinand II, Emperor of the Romans, bore the death of this Bishop heavily and said, among other things: ‘In this Prince we have lost a faithful friend, both bishoprics a good shepherd, and his subjects a father.’

68. “The Most Illustrious Lord Carlo Caraffa, Bishop of Aversa and Apostolic Nuncio, who was then present at Regensburg, wrote a book entitled *Germania sacra restaurata*. In it, among other matters, he describes what took place at Regensburg in the assembly of the Electors and Princes of the Empire convened there by Ferdinand II in 1623, where the question was discussed of substituting the Bavarian Maximilian for the rebel Frederick V, Elector Palatine. Concerning our John Godefrid he writes:

“‘John Godefrid, Prince and Bishop of Würzburg, had once been of such a mind that Germany saw no Prince more inflamed by zeal for God. He was the father of soldiers, the model of priests, the glory of Princes, the protector of Catholics, a despiser of himself, and a most ardent and prudent worshiper of the Roman Church and of the Imperial Majesty. He sighed for nothing except a Catholic Elector; amid these sighs, to the supreme grief of us all, he departed this life.’

69. “We conclude this account with the encomium bestowed upon John Godefrid by an orator of the Society of Jesus, apparently president of the Marian sodality, in a funeral oration delivered in the church of the Fathers of the Society of Jesus at Bamberg on 18 January 1623. Near the end he speaks as follows:

“‘Nothing distinguished can be conceived by the mind of which some exceptional portion was not divinely granted to our John Godefrid. He was a model of virtues upon which all Bishops, all Prelates, and all Princes may gaze. He was a model of perfection, according to which ecclesiastical men ought to shape their morals and their lives, as upon a shining and perfectly polished mirror. God wished to show the world, in one and the same Bishop and Leader, a model complete in every respect, demonstrating what consummate virtue can accomplish when joined with the greatest honor and dignity . . . . I congratulate you on your happiness. I know that you will be celebrated not only throughout your own Franconia but throughout the entire world, in the languages and writings of all peoples. All ages will gaze upon you; every memory will recall you; all posterity will venerate you, etc.’

70. “The things thus far brought forward concerning the distinguished deeds and virtues of the two Bishops of Bamberg pertain not only to their praise but also to the greatest glory of Saints Henry and Cunigunde. Through them we learn more clearly how great is the weight of those Saints’ intercession with God and how great their solicitude, charity, and beneficence toward the church of Bamberg. That these two men, in a most dangerous period, were raised to the episcopate by the wondrous providence of God; that, clothed with power from on high, they set aside every earthly advantage and, despising every difficulty, accomplished such great things for God and their subjects; and that they rescued their homeland of Bamberg, which had almost wholly fallen shamefully into heresy and depravity, from destruction with such courage and prudence and restored it to the way of salvation—all this was effected by the favor, patronage, and assistance of those Saints, as their extraordinary vigilance and solicitude toward these two Bishops leave us no room for doubt.

“Bamberg owes much to its Saints because, through their piety and generosity, it was adorned with an episcopal see and an Imperial church; but it should persuade itself with complete certainty that it owes them still more because, after almost the whole homeland had rashly submitted itself to the yoke of heresy, it was not abandoned in that most wretched condition—as happened to many other dioceses in neighboring Saxony and in other northern lands—but, through the solicitude, patronage, and protection of Saints Henry and Cunigunde, it was delivered from the most destructive evil of heresy, despite countless difficulties and the ambushes and attacks of hostile forces, and thereafter preserved in the bosom of the Catholic Church.”

## CHAPTER III  
### Concerning the Mantle of Saint Henry, as it is called, preserved at Bamberg in the Imperial Church

71. Besides the sacred treasures discussed above in § 4 of the Commentary, we said that other monuments of this kind survive, especially two: namely, the most precious Cross in the famous Benedictine monastery of Mount Saint Michael, which we discussed in the Acts of Saint Otto and which is customarily used on certain more solemn feast days; and the *Mantele* or *Mantum*, as the people of Bamberg call it—that is, a very broad robe or cloak, as you see here, shaped like an ancient chasuble without lateral openings—stored in the treasury of the Imperial church. They believe it was made by Ishmael, whom the Anonymous Life mentions, given to the holy Emperor, and used by him like an imperial military cloak on more celebrated ceremonial occasions. It is adorned with numerous precious signs woven in Phrygian work and distinguished by various inscriptions, with a sufficiently astonishing mixture of sacred and profane elements. Ingenious minds are said to have labored in vain until now to arrange or explain these inscriptions in an intelligible sense. I was certainly able to experience this in the observations of a most learned man, which will be given below and which I have so far been unable to approve.

“Both monuments appear, if one may speak so, mysterious. Since the first of them—the Cross—has already been printed and is open to everyone’s eyes in the work of Ludwig cited elsewhere, it might have been left to critics for examination; nevertheless, we too shall provide it. Here we first present the Mantle, together with some explanations by the distinguished Eppenauer, which anyone may replace with others according to his understanding and learning.

[Col. 0159]

72. “I readily confess that, after contemplating and examining the whole work—not lightly or superficially, but as it was drawn at my request—and its individual parts, I have been entirely unable to determine what the inventor or craftsman of this mantle, cloak, or robe intended finally to indicate or signify by the combination of such disparate elements.
