Perhaps he later added certain sacred features to an object originally intended for secular use, so that it might more easily be transferred to the use of the most holy Emperor or at least to ecclesiastical use.

“I shall refrain from conjectures and be content with the description of the distinguished man. He says that the Mantle is of blue silk, and that its very minute characters, whether genuine or defective, have been faithfully reproduced according to the form of the original.

“‘It is four and a half feet and two inches long,’ he says, ‘and was arranged by Ishmael, a relative of Saint Henry, buried at Bamberg. He was his sister’s son, once raised by Saint Henry to be duke of Apulia, as is clear from the inscription of the Mantle immediately above the fringe of red silk interwoven with gold thread, as though in thanksgiving to Henry:

“‘PAX ISMAHELI QUI HOC ORDINAVIT.’

“‘Peace to Ishmael, who arranged this.’

“Could anyone detect in this formula, ‘Peace to Ishmael,’ something Jewish in the craftsman? Rather, he seems deliberately to have concealed something and, through affected or genuine ignorance, to have entangled it in enigmatic expressions.

73. “No one will adequately guess what the little figures between the words ‘Sun’ and ‘Moon’ signify, or what the others signify on the other strip. The square placed beneath the sun and moon represents, unless I am mistaken, the symbols of the four Evangelists, surrounded by a little figure to which the inscription is fitted:

“‘Superne usie sit gratum hoc Cesaris donum.’

“‘May this gift of Caesar be pleasing above.’

“Would a religious craftsman have placed this for the eternal and indivisible Trinity, or at least for the eternal incarnate Word? For what is *οὐσία* (*ousia*) except supreme essence expressed in a metaphysical concept? Why is holy Mary, renowned as the Star of the Sea, not called the Mother of God? Which Saint John does he indicate—he who is also ‘the grace of God’?

“We continue with our guide, who asserts that all the figures are purely golden, woven in Phrygian work. The signs of the Zodiac and other constellations are sufficiently evident, arranged, as he believes, according to the manner of that period.

“‘For it is established,’ he says, ‘that Otto III, Saint Henry’s immediate predecessor in the Empire, possessed a similar Mantle, with which he was covered when crowned, and which he had with the Apocalypse inscribed upon it. This was probably the Mantle with which Saint Henry was clothed at his imperial coronation.’

“Let my friend forgive me if I am unwilling to assent so readily. Apocalyptic signs could appropriately have been embroidered on Otto’s cloak; but I do not yet allow myself to be persuaded that Saint Henry was clothed at his coronation in the military cloak of which we are speaking. Here are a few other letters, more or less accurately rendered, together with the explanation of the distinguished man.

74. “Here one must certainly play the role of Oedipus in extracting the twisted meaning of:

> AQVILA PPTVE IOCITAE VOIATVS IER ASTRA

“He renders it:

> ‘The eagle, continually placing itself among the stars by its flights,’  
> on account of the constellation of the eagle flying with outspread wings.

“For Ishmael,” he says, “appears to have been devoted to astrology, because near the right shoulder of the Mantle, by his arrangement, these words are read:

> Astrologus hic sit cautus.  
> Let the astrologer here be cautious.

“There is another inscription on the other part of the Mantle, which reads:

> VIRGINITASP APBATE MIREME RE.

“To him this sounds like:

> Virginitas approbate miremur terrae.

“‘Let us admire virginity approved on earth.’

“Once the faulty metathesis has been removed, it seems to allude to Ishmael’s reference to the chastity of Saint Henry, perhaps in this sense:

> ‘Let us admire virginity approved on earth.’

“I very much wish to agree with the most learned man; yet if he persuades himself that Saint Henry used this Mantle at his Roman coronation, as he said most recently, he must admit that Ishmael already knew at that time of the virginal continence of the most holy married couple. I undertook above to defend that continence, but I consider it absolutely certain that no one knew of it before the Saint’s final illness.

“For the rest, whether the hand of Orion is gnawing the Bull; whether he was an imitator of the law; whether the Serpent-Bearer is said to be Aesculapius the physician; whether Pegasus is asserted in these signs to be a horse consecrated to music; and other matters of this kind—I do not think they should be traced to anything more than that obscure, or perhaps poetic, craftsman. The chief knot remains: whether the learned interpreter has combined the confused characters of the lowest inscription more successfully. I shall transcribe his words exactly:

75. “‘The fringe of this Mantle is ornamented with letters fashioned with singular diligence by the craftsman—each individual letter being made separately, or independently, with gold thread and then fixed by means of silk thread in its appointed place—skillfully executed in Phrygian work, together with very many twisted golden ornaments that produce obscurity in the reading. The letters are of considerable length and placed so close together that the reader is left in the greatest uncertainty as to where the reading should begin in the circular chaos. Moreover, they lack all punctuation; hence, to the present day, although many have attempted the reading in vain, they have remained unknown, as I hear—especially on account of several other small and obscured inscriptions.’

“He then proceeds to an explanation that no one has yet approached more closely:

“‘The words of the fringe are literally these, with a faulty metathesis:

> O Decus Eeropae Cesar Heinrice beare  
> Angeat impreium ibmi Rexque rena bene.

“The lowest circumference of the Mantle is equal in length to sixteen feet and two inches.’

76. “‘Here it should be noted that Ishmael intended something unusual by the letter X in the word *Rex*, since this one and only letter among all the others stands out in artificial size and is somewhat separated from the E before it and the Q after it. Hence I not unreasonably conclude that, because of the abundance of the words running beyond the available space, he wished to preserve a connected expression and arranged this congratulation for Saint Henry in the following sense:

> Rexque millies ibi regna bene.  
> And may you, O King, reign there a thousand times well.

“‘For X, as is well known, is the number one thousand among the Greeks. Nevertheless, as I have said, this is submitted in every respect to the better judgment of others, for such refinements were common among the ancients.

“‘He then warns that it should be noted that certain letters are missing from the verses of the Mantle’s fringe: in the word *REGNA*, the letter G; and in the word *WENE* or *BENE*, the letter E. For the letter A is hidden in N, since N, as it is formed there, denotes both N and A among the ancients. Conversely, after the word *Imperium* there is an unnecessary letter M, perhaps to be substituted for the intended M, or else to be omitted entirely at that time; beside it, three *IBI* are visible after the letter Q. Likewise, in the word *ANGEAT*, the letter V is reversed and therefore appears as N.’

77. “Thus far the distinguished friend, who adds that four other silk Mantles, likewise blue in color, are preserved there; it is unnecessary to discuss their uses here. Let us meanwhile examine the explanation already given.

“I clearly see the first four words expressed on the fringe:

> O decus Eeropae Cesar Heinrice.  
> O glory of Europe, Caesar Henry.

“It is not so easy to find *BEARE*, since B is read for R; nor can *ANGEAT* be extracted, since the final letter is not T but rather Y. *Impreium* is not found intact, since the final letter appears double and is both E and the Greek Λ. In this matter it cannot be argued very openly that the M after *Imperium* is superfluous, since I am forced to admit that no superfluous M—or indeed even necessary M—can be found from which *Imperium* or *Impreium* might be formed. Nor are the three *IBI* so clearly visible; and there is no basis for concluding that N is reversed, from which *AUGEAT* could plausibly arise. *IBMI* yields no meaning. *REXQUE*, or *REX QUI*, is present; but the rest requires more than an Oedipus, and no one could easily extract from it a complete construction.

“I say this only so that the reader may understand that we have neglected nothing, and so that my most friendly assistant may observe that the enigma concealed in these letters has not yet been solved in every respect. ‘You should substitute something better,’ you will say. I would rather honestly confess ignorance than waste oil and effort in investigating these matters. Nevertheless, without any risk to myself, I shall not hesitate to bring forward the thoughts of another most learned man, as they were communicated to me.

78. “To begin with, he differs from the opinion of the people of Bamberg in denying that the aforementioned Mantle can be assigned to the time of Saint Henry; he also denies that the title ‘Caesar’ was in use during that Saint’s lifetime. He therefore considers the work to belong to the fourteenth century and believes that those confused words indicate Henry VII of Luxembourg, Emperor of that name, who, after the murder of Albert of Austria, King of the Romans, committed in 1308, was crowned at Aachen on 6 January 1309.

“He argues that the address of the fringe is directed to this Henry, beginning its sequence with *CESAR HENRICE* and connecting to it *BEA*. He takes the following B and E to represent the Bamberg Church, and from the adjacent letters forms *ANGELV*, with U marked. He then proceeds in this way, nearly restoring the words from the letters:

> IMPerium REgere Injuste Volens, EΛ  
> Wishing to rule the Empire unjustly, EΛ—

“with the Greek lambda used for the Latin L, from which he derives:

> EΛectus Invitis, vel Inimicis Bambergensibus, Miserabiliter Interiit REX Qui.  
> Elected against the will of, or by the hostility of, the Bambergers, he miserably perished, the King who—

“Finally, from *RE* and other contracted letters he forms *REGNAVIT*, ‘he reigned,’ and from the following character, no less hieroglyphic, he constructs:

> ANTE TE, O DECUS EEROPAE.  
> Before you, O glory of Europe.

“This is his explanation. I refrain from adding others, since both the signs and the words are so entangled that they carry individual observers in different directions.

“I think this explanation, drawn from so far away, will strike all the people of Bamberg no less than it does me. It may be criticized for forming the word *ANGELU* for *angelum*, since the penultimate letter is not L but A, as in *Ces Ar* and *be A*; while the final letter is more likely Y or V than a marked U. But we are rubbing our brows here in vain. It is enough to have supplied curious investigators with material for further inquiry and, as far as our principal purpose is concerned, to have omitted nothing concerning Saint Henry and his monuments.”

## CHAPTER IV  
### Concerning the celebrated Cross and the other sacred treasures of Saint Henry among the people of Bamberg

[Col. 0165B]

79. Henschenius spoke briefly of this most precious Henrician Cross when he illustrated the Acts of Saint Cunigunde on 3 March. In 1695 the Reverend Father John Risse, then rector of our Bamberg college, sent its drawing to Papebrochius. Later John Peter Ludewig published another version engraved on copper and inserted it into his volume on the writers of the history of the bishopric of Bamberg.

“After comparing this printed exemplar with the Rissian drawing, I easily observed that they differed so greatly from one another that neither image reproduced the prototype with sufficient accuracy. It was therefore necessary to return to Bamberg so that the defects occurring in them could be properly corrected. The distinguished Otto Schugentius, whom I have often praised, accordingly undertook an entirely new drawing, expressing also the colors both of the precious stones and of the other ornaments. The most discerning eyewitness inspectors—especially the often-mentioned distinguished Eppenauer and the Reverend Father Nicholas Pottu, whose merits cannot be adequately praised—testified that nothing was lacking in it. Furthermore, the engraver attempted to reproduce the colors as far as his art permitted. Those who compare the Ludewigian image with our engraving will readily notice more than one difference. I have therefore decided first to present here the image of the aforesaid Cross, to which other treasures have been added and which will likewise be described in their proper order.

80. The words of Henschenius should be prefaced here. While enumerating the sacred monuments of Saint Cunigunde that he had personally seen, he speaks as follows in § 4, no. 25, of his Commentary:

“‘I am pleased to add what we saw at Bamberg itself on Mount Saint Michael, in the abbatial church: namely, the dowry or *morgengabe* given by Saint Henry to Cunigunde; a golden Cross of the most ancient Greek workmanship, as could be recognized from its inscriptions and images. This, according to the most widely accepted tradition among the people of Bamberg, is the celebrated Cross, valued at many thousands of gold pieces, which the holy Bridegroom gave to his holy Bride, Saint Cunigunde, on the day after their wedding. Hence among the Germans it is called *MORGHENGABAM*, which is to be rendered in Latin as “morning gift”—concerning which you will find more in the glossaries of Spelman, Du Cange, and others. The most holy Empress herself left it to the monastery that she had founded with her most devout husband, as an enduring monument of her generosity. To this day it is customarily carried in procession on certain more solemn feast days, mounted on a silver-plated handle extending to five Nuremberg feet, which we have wished to show in the image.

“‘That the Cross itself was originally made by a Greek, or at least by a Greek-influenced craftsman, seems sufficiently clear; and I should judge that the Latin inscription running around it was added later. Why the verb is inflected in the future, I frankly confess that I cannot determine, unless, while he was still alive, it was made the subject of a fideicommissum.’

81. There are many other things there that rightly make one long for clarification; many were fashioned according to the artist’s ingenuity and discretion, while others seem deliberately concealed, and no one has yet known how to explain them. So much so that I have sometimes considered setting aside this monument, however distinguished, rather than leave some of its parts untouched and unobserved.

“I consulted very learned men, some of whom criticized it with harsher judgment and others with somewhat milder judgment, yet none of them properly solved those features which I have openly declared, even to the people of Bamberg, to displease me. It must be acknowledged that a historian cannot be required, when describing ancient monuments of this kind, to explain every detail minutely or determine individually what each thing signifies. It should be enough, as philosophers say, to determine that a thing exists, though not always what or of what kind it is—especially where certain features appear to be intricately entangled like riddles.

“That the object exists is absolutely certain. But to disentangle its age, craftsman, reason and purpose of manufacture, and all its other circumstances—this is the task, this the labor, these are the difficulties. I have found that no one has yet even touched upon them, much less solved them. The already-cited Ludewig was content to reproduce the Cross and certain other objects in print, leaving their explanation to others to investigate. It will be useful to attempt something, at least to the extent that more experienced students of such monuments may advance our effort.

82. “Our Janningus, now deceased, discussed at length ancient Crosses, both those that are, so to speak, bare and those representing the human figure of Christ affixed to them, in his treatment of the Vatican Basilica, volume VII of the June Acts, beginning on page 141. Among others he describes one sufficiently similar to ours, at least as regards the formation of the Cross itself and the image of Christ, and he assigns other comparable examples. Lambecius likewise has examples not very different from it in his *Caesarea Vindobonensis Library*, book 2, page 482 and elsewhere, so that it is unnecessary to debate the matter further here.

“We are chiefly seeking the period in which this Henrician Cross can be considered to have been made. It must have been produced at least in the tenth century if the holy Emperor offered it to his holy Consort as a *morgengabe* at the very beginning of the following century. Only in this way can the Bamberg tradition be reconciled with the sequence of Henry’s life, whatever learned critics may object and however much they may argue that this mixture of Greek and Latin letters points to later centuries. Solid additions, coins, and other features are commonly judged to belong to a more recent age, as are the Leonine verses, which they demand should be shown by other evidence to have been in use in the tenth century.

83. “Allow me to state my opinion, or conjecture, frankly. I see nothing that so strongly prevents us from assigning the Cross itself, insofar as it is wholly Greek, to the tenth century—whether it was made in ancient Greece, in Magna Graecia or Apulia, or by Greek craftsmen in Germany itself—and from supposing that it came into the hands of Saint Henry as a sacred and precious treasure before he was raised to the throne.

“Let him himself have given it to his most holy Consort; and let her, either by testament or by another donation, have wished it to be kept among her Michaelite monks—Greek up to that point, and perhaps not yet assigned to sacred uses. Later, some abbot may have judged that the most precious monument could be carried in processions according to Catholic rite, and accordingly fitted it with a silver handle or shaft upon which it could be mounted. To renew continually the memory of the most holy founders, he may have caused these Latin verses to be inscribed around it:

> Jesu Christe bonum clemens Crucis accipe donum,  
> quod dabit Heinricus pius Caesar atque secundus.

> Kind and good Jesus Christ, receive the gift of the Cross,  
> which the devout Caesar Henry, the second, will give.

“Here the only thing that displeases me is that, instead of *dabit*, ‘will give,’ he did not write *dedit*, ‘gave,’ as he certainly ought to have done if he ordered it to be written when he had received the Cross. In this way the difficulties are avoided—although the people of Bamberg believe that they can solve them in another manner as well.

84. Nor is it so very abhorrent to find Greek and Latin letters mixed in this way, since even in those obscure centuries the itch to imitate Greek became so strong that expressing names adopted by the Latins in those letters seemed to display a certain learning.

“You have an example in the object represented under the letter D: the cover, binding, or outer case of a very large parchment volume containing the written Gospels running throughout the entire year, as we say. The ornament of this case is no less admirable than it is precious; and what is most important, and most relevant here, it closely resembles the ornament of the entire Cross. There you see Greek and Latin mixed together, as though it might be considered a sacrilege to express the names of the holy Apostles in Latin letters.

“In the center is an ivory panel on which the mysteries of Christ buried and rising again are elegantly carved. The remaining ornament, on the broader borders surrounding the panel, corresponds exactly to the panel itself in both material and workmanship. The borders consist of gold, or gold plates, worked in encaustic and mosaic technique, with precious stones also set into them.

“All the figures, whether one considers their material, their form, or their characters, are extremely similar to those represented on the Cross, so that they seem unmistakably to indicate the same craftsman, or one close to him in date. That this Gospel book existed in Saint Henry’s time is proved clearly enough by the verses written in larger gold letters on its first face, of the kind represented by *GRAMMATA QUI SOPHIAE*. They are written in this manner:

> Rex Heinricus ovans, fidei splendore coruscans,  
> Maximus imperio fruitur quo prosper avito;  
> Inter opum varias prono de pectore gazas,  
> Obtulit hunc librum divina lege refertum:  
> Plenus amore Dei, pius in donaria templi,  
> Ut sit perpetuum decus illic omne per aevum  
> Princeps Ecclesiae, coelestis claviger aulae,  
> O Petre, cum Paulo gentis doctore benigno,  
> Hunc tibi devotum prece fac super astra beatum,  
> Cum Cunigunda sibi conregnante serena.  
> Hoc Pater, hoc Natus, necnon et Spiritus almus  
> Annuat aeternis semper Deus omnibus unus.

> King Henry, exulting and radiant with the splendor of faith,  
> enjoys the greatest imperial power, prosperous in his ancestral realm.  
> Amid the various treasures of wealth, from a devoted heart  
> he offered this book, filled with the divine law:  
> full of love for God, devoutly among the temple’s offerings,  
> so that it might be an everlasting ornament there through every age.  
> Prince of the Church, keeper of the keys of the heavenly court,  
> O Peter, together with Paul, gracious teacher of the nations,  
> make this man devoted to you blessed above the stars by your prayer,  
> together with serene Cunigunde reigning jointly with him.  
> May the Father, the Son, and likewise the Holy Spirit,  
> one God, always grant this for all eternity.

85. Consider these verses as much as you wish: nothing seems capable of being extracted from them that does not unmistakably suggest Saint Henry while still living and surviving. From this the people of Bamberg rightly argue that there is nothing in the Greek portion of the Cross that compels us to assign it to a later century, since everything comparable is found in the Gospel case.

“To the critics’ repeated claim that the title ‘Caesar’ and the additions ‘second’ or ‘devout’ did not belong to Henry’s century on coins, or at least that no such coins are found, the defenders of the Cross reply—and rightly—that it is sufficient for those titles to be explicitly expressed in charters, so that the craftsman or the person who added them cannot be blamed for adorning Saint Henry with those titles, even though he ought properly to have been called not the second Emperor of that name but the first.

“Likewise, the surname ‘Pious’ given to the holy Emperor during his lifetime is proved by the distinguished Eppenauer from charters or privileges granted at that time. In one of them, dated 1017, he cites the following terms: ‘under the patrimony of the most pious Emperor Henry,’ and so forth.

“These points are more than sufficient, since the entire antiquity of the Greek Cross is preserved even if one supposes that the Latin inscription was added later. Concerning the reverse side of the Cross, it is enough to mention that Saint Henry is represented standing beneath the Lamb of God, on which rests the figure marked with the letter F, with the title ‘Emperor Augustus’ among the four symbols of the Evangelists. The people of Bamberg themselves, unless I am greatly mistaken, will readily concede that these elements were added later.”

86. Some suspect that the craftsman of this Cross was unskilled and inexperienced in correctly rendering Greek, since instead of ΥΙΟϹ he writes ΥΟϹ, and instead of ΝΙΚΟΛΛΟϹ he puts ΝΙΚΟΛΛΟϹ; and perhaps that he was not sufficiently Christian, wishing, under the specious guise of religion, to conceal something impious, since he depicts the saints without the familiar prefatory formula ὁ ΑΓ (“the Saint”), which he claims to be unusual among Greek Christians. He is more displeased by the little figure on the right side of the Cross, whose inscription is accurately reproduced in Schugentius’s drawing as Ο θῶ ΛΙΓΟϹ—with Λ written for Γ and almost Υ for Ϲ—which is extremely difficult to explain, whether one joins θῶ to ΛΙΓΟϹ or supposes that separate words are intended. If they are joined, it will signify nothing; if they are separated, ΛΙΓΟϹ could be taken as ΛΟΙΓΟϹ, which are alike in pronunciation, and would then contain a notable blasphemy—a matter I shall refrain from explaining here, since I believe it never entered the craftsman’s mind. I would rather accuse him of ignorance than of monstrous wickedness. Why should we not recognize here Saint John the Evangelist, θῶ ΛΟΓΟϹ (“the Word”), already old, although he is represented as young in the middle? Certainly this is made probable by a similar little figure of the same Saint from the Gospel-book case, where nearly the same inscription is found, as you can see clearly enough here in the enlargement of the larger image under the letter E.

Let us, I beg, make some allowance for the crudity of that age, and admit that the craftsman was not so skilled in Greek orthography that he did not stumble here and there through excess or omission, as you see in the very little figure just cited, in which it is difficult to join the syllables correctly. In any event, that the same Saint is represented in both places, and with a radiant head, is not absolutely certain but at least highly probable.

87. The little figure placed at another end of the Cross, namely the left, is represented correctly neither in Rissius’s drawing nor by Ludewig; nor are the accompanying letters—or rather abbreviations—properly rendered as OAP and HI. Schugentius restored them more successfully, showing an angel extending his outspread wings upward, as though in a gesture of astonishment at the Son of God suffering on the Cross for the human race. The letters inscribed beside him indicate by OAP the archangel, and by MI Michael, commander of the heavenly host and defender of the Church.

I consider the remaining Greek, although it too is not very exact, sufficiently clear, since the little statues of the most blessed Virgin and Saint John the Evangelist placed on either side of the image of Christ plainly suggest that the words refer to both: “Behold your son; behold your mother.” Why, however, the place of the skull below is indicated there so explicitly, let those explain who have found more monuments of this kind elsewhere. I neither wish nor have time to fetch similar examples from far away.

Nor is the question here to be debated of whether the Savior’s body was affixed with three or four nails, a matter often disputed elsewhere. Consult Angelus Rocca, Cornelius Curtius, and Papebrochius’s *Responses to the Exhibition of Alleged Errors*, article XX, from no. 2 onward.

88. If someone meanwhile asks me what the craftsman ultimately intended by such a collection and combination of objects, I shall readily confess that I do not know. Nor shall I be displeased if I can learn from elsewhere why Saint Nicholas, rather than some other saint, was represented at the summit; why Saint John the Evangelist, or perhaps another figure, and Saint Michael the Archangel appear in the outer circles; or what more relevant purpose was served by the lowest compartment, now empty, which appears filled in Rissius’s drawing.

I acknowledge all these uncertainties; yet the enormous price of the Cross itself, said to be made of pure gold, does not alarm me, whatever the critics may argue, namely that gold was extremely rare in Henry’s century. The Bambergers will reply that precious gifts made to the churches of God in that and earlier centuries were not so rare, and they will cite the golden cross of the Emperor Constantine, weighing one hundred and fifty pounds, and countless other objects of the same kind with which the history of Anastasius the Librarian concerning the Roman pontiffs is filled. The sections relating to the aforementioned Constantine and Charlemagne alone will satisfy the curious.

Why, then, could the holy and munificent Emperor of that age not have acquired this Cross, when he deposited so many other most precious gifts—of which we have placed not a few before your eyes—in his Bamberg church, consecrated to God, to say nothing of many others?

89. The images of sacred treasures presented here under the letters A, B, and C are accompanied by examples of similar objects preserved in the Bamberg treasury, with no less piety than care, in memory of its most holy Patron and Founder. You may suppose that they were made either while the Saint was still alive or shortly afterward, from the resources he left for that purpose. There are several other sacred books of this kind, highly esteemed for their workmanship, antiquity, and value.

The two upper sections, under the letters A and B, are displayed on one and the same page and follow the verses cited above in the Gospel-book. The upper part, A, clearly denotes the justice of the most equitable Emperor; how greatly he excelled in administering it is too well known to require explanation here. The lower part, or B, speaks for itself, since the entire territory of Bamberg professes itself subject to the excellent Prince. I see no serious objection to these representations, since such paintings, or symbols of justice and equity, do not appear incompatible with the modesty of Saint Henry while he was still alive.

In the other section, C, where Saints Ulrich and Emmeramnus somehow present a spear and sword to Saint Henry, certain features are embellished so as to approach the indications of sanctity. Some, however, may not so readily admit that these were depicted while the Saint was still living. Even so, they cannot invalidate what has been argued concerning the antiquity of the Cross, its case, and the Gospel-book.

90. The aforementioned section C, taken from a Missal that is also extremely precious, requires no lengthy explanation, since all the verses, however crude, can conveniently be understood on their own. There is one that may delay readers: the uppermost verse on the left, which alludes to the Saint’s sword. If I distinguish the words correctly, it seems to be read as follows:

> “Here too he fits the sword, which, by foretelling, inspires fear.”

The two verses beneath the Saint’s arms are to be begun at the lower little cross beside the right foot:

> “Behold, by divine power, pious King Henry is crowned and blessed,  
> glorious in the lineage of his ancestors.”

I believe this alludes to his great-grandmother, Queen Matilda, and to other men and women of his family distinguished for holiness, whom he calls *polosi*, that is, “blessed.” On these matters see our *Acts* for 14 March, volume II, page 356.

We leave the remainder for the curious to examine and weigh, bringing this ambiguous inquiry to an end. We dare hope that we have satisfied the desire of the Bambergers. We shall always desire, however, that the soul of the entire matter—namely, the *Acts* written by Adelbold—may at last be brought to light from somewhere, so that they may be published in the appendix or Supplement to the entire month and fully elucidated.

# CHAPTER V  
## On the present-day glory of Saint Henry in the annual Bamberg celebration, customarily conducted festively throughout the entire octave according to Catholic usage; and on the Office of devotion and the churches and chapels erected to the Saint

[Col. 0175A]

91. From what has already been said, I think it is abundantly evident with what tireless zeal, care, and diligence the often-praised Reverend Father Rector of Bamberg, Nicolaus Pottu, labored so that nothing might be omitted that he judged conducive to the glory of Saint Henry. He himself added this crowning section, gathering with the greatest accuracy those things that especially concern the present celebration of the most holy Patron. It seemed appropriate to give them a place here both in deserved praise of the Bambergers, for the advancement of the Catholic religion, and as an example for other churches to imitate in celebrating the solemnities of their saints.

That this celebration was extremely ancient, and, I believe, perpetual, at Bamberg is demonstrated by an older description of the annual celebration and procession from the year 1379, which our most energetic collaborator recently appended as well. But, lest the same or at least similar material have to be repeated here, to the annoyance of readers, it will be enough to set before their eyes the present celebration that we have mentioned. To this will be added the most recent embellishment, appended this year through the devout diligence of the same Pottu, and finally the proper Office of the Saint, reprinted on the same occasion, together with the churches founded in his honor.

Here, then, are the proofs of the Bambergers’ illustrious veneration for their Protector, outlined in Pottu’s own words as follows.

### § I. Preparations preceding the festival

[Col. 0175C]

92. “On the preceding day, the altar placed above the tomb of Saints Henry and Cunegund is furnished with the most solemn worship and adornment, especially with truly distinguished and abundant relics. Since these are extremely precious and, in fact, for the greater part acquired by Saint Henry himself with vigilant care and imperial authority, and generously donated by him to the church he had recently founded, they deserve to be described more distinctly here, together with the rest of the altar’s adornment. This is especially so because, although mention is made of them in the preliminary Commentary on the Life of Saint Cunegund, under 3 March, a more exact description is deferred to this place, as may be seen there.

93. “The altar just mentioned, therefore, which is erected above the tomb itself in the form of a kind of mausoleum ending as though in a pyramid, is arranged so that, through its middle, where an arch has been hollowed out, the marble tomb of the Saints is visibly exposed from an elevated position. This altar, I say, both its upper surface and its sides, is covered with three hundred cubits of precious red Damascus cloth.

“Placed at the very summit of the altar is a most precious cross, approximately six feet high, skillfully worked from pure silver and lavishly adorned with gems and pearls. Enclosed within it and visible at the front through clear crystal is a distinguished and splendid fragment of the holy and saving Cross, nearly a span in length. In the cathedral archive there is an authentic Bull of Benedict II, Supreme Pontiff, concerning its authenticity. It states that this sacred fragment, together with the genuine iron nail of the holy Crucified One mentioned below, was given as a gift to Saint Henry by the Duke of Burgundy and King Rudolph; and by papal authority it is recognized and declared genuine.

94. “Directly beneath this stands a statue of Saint George, the church’s secondary Patron, seated on a horse. It is somewhat smaller than life-size and likewise skillfully fashioned from silver. A little lower, on either side, stand two distinguished statues, also made of gilded silver and representing half the human body: one of Saint Cunegund, holding a glowing plowshare in her hand; the other of Saint Henry, equal in size and material. On either side of each statue is placed its imperial crown, the very crowns with which the Saints, who had once been married on earth, were crowned.

“Between these two statues, in the middle, rises a statue of equal size, likewise half-length and elegantly fashioned from gilded silver, of the Blessed Virgin embracing the divine Child in her arms. These statues are illuminated by several silver candlesticks placed among them, with burning candles.

95. “Next come various relics of various saints, placed around the middle part of the altar. Namely, on either side are two cushions, one supporting part of the skull of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite, the other the intact head of Saint Margaret. Then, on both sides, there are eight small coffers or smaller sarcophagi, or gilded reliquaries, containing the bodies of saints or their principal remains, namely:

1. the body of Saint John the Martyr;
2. Saint Isaac the Monk;
3. Saints Dulcissimus and Carissimus, disciples of Saint Peter;
4. Saints Caius and Pius, Roman Pontiffs;
5. Saint Hermes, Martyr;
6. Saints Herculanus, Bishop and Martyr, and Remaclus, Bishop;
7. Saint Theodore, Martyr;
8. Saint Brictius, Confessor.

96. “Among these rise four distinguished silver pyramids, richly endowed with truly precious relics of eminent saints, namely relics or bones of Saint John the Baptist; Saints Paul and Bartholomew the Apostles; Saint Stephen the Protomartyr; Saint Lawrence the Martyr; Saint Pantaleon the Martyr; Saint Achatius the Martyr; and others; Saint Mary Magdalene; Saint Cecilia, Virgin and Martyr; and others.

“There is also displayed among the other objects a portable altar, as it is called, which Saint Henry is said to have used during military service for preparing an altar for the sacrifice of the Mass. This portable altar is enclosed in a precious case marked with gems and pearls. Besides a fragment of the Holy Cross, it contains relics of Saints George and Stephen the Protomartyr, Christopher, Pancratius, Sebastian, and Lawrence, as well as a piece of his gridiron.

97. “In addition, four Gospel-books stand prominently on both sides. They are precious codices bound in silk cases generously decorated with gold and gems, and commending themselves by their antiquity, since they were offered by Saint Henry himself as a gift to the cathedral church, worthy of so great and pious an Emperor.

“Thus crowned by such magnificent adornment above, in the very middle of the altar, through the hollowed arch as described, appears the marble tomb of the holy married couple. It is covered with a most precious black silk carpet, richly interwoven with pearls and gold in Phrygian work. Forty candles of virgin wax burn around it and illuminate it magnificently. Sixteen gilded-silver lamps on either side of the arch add their light, together with four hanging silver candlesticks, each shining with two candles. All these things together contribute splendidly to the glory of the Saints.

98. “To these are added, in the lowest part of the altar, other relics no less important than those already listed: namely, the iron nail with which Christ the Savior was fastened by the hands to the Cross, concerning whose authenticity the authentic Bull cited above bears witness; likewise, a thorn from the crown of the same Savior; and, in addition, a gilded-silver cross containing a fragment of the Holy Cross and a finger of Saint Gertrude. With this cross Saint Henry is said to have given his virgin bride Cunegund her betrothal pledge.

“Six silver candlesticks, with a silver crucifix between them, further adorn and illuminate this part of the altar. At the foot of the altar are placed two other silver candlesticks, seven feet high. Thus much concerning the magnificent adornment of the tomb and altar. What follows concerns the solemnity of the Feast itself and of the succeeding Octave.”

### § II. Its institution and continuation

99. “On the day before the Feast, at the very vigil, at the first hour the bells are rung for First Vespers with the solemn pealing of the great bells mentioned above. The Feast is episcopal and of the Pallium, at which the officiant is the Bishop. Vespers begin at the third hour with the most solemn rite, according to the Roman Ceremonial. Throughout the entire Octave, likewise, the rest of the divine Office is celebrated not in the ordinary choir but in the nave of the church before the tomb of Saints Henry and Cunegund. When Vespers have ended, Compline follows. Canons of the three collegiate churches are present.

100. “On the following morning the divine Office begins at the sixth hour, again preceded by the ringing of the bells. After Matins, Lauds, and Prime have been solemnly sung, a panegyric sermon on the Saint follows at the eighth hour. When it is finished, None, Terce, and Sext are sung.

“When the Bishop enters the church, he is received by one of the cathedral canons, who awaits him with a cross resembling an archiepiscopal cross, as a sign of the prerogative of the Bamberg bishopric, which enjoys the Pallium and is immediately subject to the Roman Pontiff. The Bishop is then led to the sacristy, where he is vested in pontifical garments for celebrating the solemn Mass. When Sext has subsequently ended, he proceeds from the sacristy in the following order.

101. “1. The sacristan, wearing a surplice and carrying a silver staff, goes first.  
2. Four acolytes follow him with two censers and two incense-boats.  
3. Four other acolytes carry candlesticks with lighted candles and lead in their midst a cathedral canon vested in a cope and carrying the cross.

“Two canons of the cathedral church, in deacon’s dress, assisting the Bishop, follow. After them proceeds the subdeacon who will sing the Epistle, then the deacon; both are cathedral canons, and the latter walks on the left of the assisting priest, who is vested in a cope.

“The Bishop follows in pontifical vestments, with the Pallium and pastoral staff. He is followed, together with the other court chaplains, by the master of ceremonies. Two canons from the collegiate churches, vested in copes and serving the mitre and pastoral staff, receive him.

102. “When the divine Office has been completed in this manner before noon, at the first hour after midday the first sodality of young craftsmen, under the title of the Blessed Virgin Conceived Without Sin, is led in solemn procession from its oratory to the cathedral church. There, after another panegyric sermon on the merits of the Saint, Vespers begin at the third hour.

“When these, together with Compline, have ended, and the hymn of Saint Ambrose, *Te Deum*, and so forth, has been sung at the conclusion, and solemn benediction has been given with the Venerable Sacrament, the celebration of that day concludes. On the following day and on the other days throughout the Octave, the solemn High Mass is celebrated by the Reverend Lord Suffragan and by the cathedral canons, together with the deans of the collegiate churches.

103. “On the day before the octave day, after the great bells have given the signal at the first hour as above, Vespers are celebrated at the third hour by the Most Reverend Lord Dean of the cathedral church, in the presence of the Bishop and the entire Most Reverend cathedral chapter, according to the Roman rite and with the prescribed solemnity. Compline follows. After Compline, at the sixth hour in the evening, Matins with Lauds is anticipated, with the same Most Reverend Lord Dean officiating.

“On the following morning, at the middle of the sixth hour, the remaining Hours are sung up to and including None. At the sixth hour there is a panegyric sermon. At the first hour a most solemn procession through the city is arranged, whose description seems to demand a place here. It is as follows:

104. “One of the sacristans of the principal church, dressed in a surplice and carrying a silver staff, gives the signal for the beginning. Four banners follow. Between them walks a priest vested in a cope, carrying the aspergillum. After him proceed, two by two, the scholars of the principal church; likewise two guilds of craftsmen, the butchers and the fishermen, carrying large candles. They are followed by the vocal choir of singers.

“Religious orders follow, distinguished by their respective crosses: first the Capuchin Fathers, then the Carmelite Fathers, then the Franciscan Fathers, then the Dominican Fathers, and finally the Benedictine Fathers of Mount Saint Michael. As a sign of the imperial foundation made by Saint Henry, a silver staff with two silver crosses is carried before the Benedictines.

105. “These are followed again by a sacristan of the cathedral church, in a surplice and carrying a silver staff; then by two white banners. After them come two silver crosses, carried by two domicellar canons, the first resident in copes; then twelve so-called brothers of the seats, in blue mantles, and four brothers of the knights—they are laymen who enjoy lay prebends.

“These are followed by the gentlemen vicars of the cathedral church, as well as the canons of the three collegiate churches, namely Saint James, Saint Gangolph, and Saint Stephen. The Most Reverend cathedral chapter follows.

“Then come statues carried on biers by religious of various orders, dressed in dalmatics:

1. the precious Cross mentioned above, carried by four Capuchins;
2. a statue of Saint Gregory, carried by four Carmelites;
3. a statue of Saint Cunegund, carried by four Franciscans;
4. a statue of Saint Henry, carried by four Dominicans;
5. a statue of the Blessed Virgin, carried by four Benedictines.

“A musical instrumental choir intervenes, followed by another choir of young people dressed theatrically as angels with cymbals.

106. “Next follow two priests in copes, carrying the Gospel-book and a stole for singing the Gospels at the appointed stations; then two acolytes carrying candlesticks with lighted candles. Four men in dalmatics follow with incense-boats and censers, continually censing the Most Holy Sacrament.

“After them come the subdeacon and deacon, and finally, beneath a baldachin, the Most Reverend Dean of the cathedral church carrying the Venerable Sacrament. The Bishop and the Provost of the same cathedral church flank him on either side, equipped with white torches.

“Eight young men carrying torches surround the baldachin, as do the three guilds of bakers with their large candles. Next follow the gentlemen of the secular state, the court nobility, then the Most Illustrious Lord’s councillors and the remaining officials from the various departments, each in his proper order. The people and common crowd close the procession.

107. “The procession stops at four stations. The first is near the church of the Capuchin Fathers; the second is in the parish church of Saint Martin; the third is in the marketplace near the church of the Fathers of the Society of Jesus. There citizens appear under arms, divided into four companies, and receive the procession.

“Returning to the cathedral church, the procession makes its fourth and final station in the open square before the Prince’s palace. There two other companies of citizens take their place, joining the four earlier companies. Afterwards, with a festive discharge of cannon repeated at the Gospel and at the elevation, they increase the solemnity of the High Mass. The same Most Reverend Lord Dean celebrates it, and, after solemn benediction with the Venerable Sacrament at the end, concludes the celebration before noon.”

### § III. The addition made this year, 1723

108. The established and most constant veneration of all the Bamberg orders for their most holy Patron, as most devout clients, has been described above. You will understand from the accompanying letter of Pottu, which I reproduce here as well, that a new addition was made this very year. It reads as follows:

“This worship of Saint Henry has hitherto been customary and ordinary. This year, 1723, the Congregations established at the Bamberg Academy under the direction of the Fathers of the Society of Jesus, kindled by the desire to increase, to some degree, veneration for the holy Emperor, who deserved so greatly of this homeland, and to merit by some special devotion the powerful intercession of this Saint, whose most sacred body they possess, chose several days within the Octave on which they would approach the sacred tomb in the manner of supplicants and implore the Saint’s patronage with united minds and voices.

“On one day the Angelic Sodality came forth, comprising the three classes of Grammar. On another day came the Middle Sodality, formed by the Poets and Rhetoricians. On the third came the Major Sodality, also called the Academic Sodality, in which the Philosophers and Theologians have their place.

109. “On each appointed day, without loss of lessons, at the time of its customary Mass, each sodality proceeded from the school. Drawn up in orderly fashion and following its banner, amid the devout singing of litanies, it went to the cathedral church. There it was received by the very Reverend Lord Subcustos with the ringing of bells and, at the entrance to the door, with the sprinkling of holy water.

“Then, prostrate before the altar and sacred Tomb, and having received the blessing of the Most Holy Sacrament, they heard Mass. During it they recited aloud the Office of Saint Henry in alternating verses, with the president leading. After the consecration, accompanied by the organ, they sang the very ancient and devout hymn concerning the same Saint, *Let every spirit praise Christ, who [acts] divinely, etc.*, and finally concluded their devotion by repeating their adoration of Eucharistic Christ, who blesses them.

110. “The parents, delighted by this piety of their children toward the holy Emperor, arranged that the civic sodality should offer a similar service of veneration to the aforementioned holy Patron. It did so notably on the Sunday within the Octave, with a very numerous company of gentlemen and citizens.

“The Most Excellent Lord Dean, observing this inclination of the Bambergers toward the worship of Saint Henry, wisely used it to celebrate the octave of the holy Emperor also in the afternoon, with the devotion that was proper, and to conclude it with an excellent outcome. Until then the Bambergers, after expending their efforts in the morning on preparing and carrying out the procession, had been accustomed to devote the afternoon to relaxation, visiting friends or strolling in gardens and pleasure grounds.

111. “Therefore, so that not even a portion of this good day might pass without spiritual fruit and public veneration of the holy Patron, the aforementioned Most Excellent Lord took care that the praise of our Saint, gathered from the youth of all the catechisms and elementary schools of the entire city, should finally be completed.

“Accordingly, after an invitation had been issued, a very large number of young people, together with the heads of the schools, gathered after midday in the church of the Fathers of the Society of Jesus. There a procession was arranged, which in a long and beautiful order, amid pious songs, reached the cathedral church toward the end of Vespers.

“And because, by order of that same Most Excellent Lord, it had been announced from the pulpit that after Vespers not only was the procession of the children to be led there, but that a panegyric sermon on Saint Henry was also to be delivered there, the church was already so filled with people of every rank and status that the procession could find no room there.

112. “Nevertheless, a passage was opened for it before the sacred Tomb, so that every child might at least venerate his holy Patron with devout reverence.

“A panegyric was then delivered. On that occasion, and because of the many supplications that the Bambergers had instituted at the tomb of Saint Henry throughout the course of this Octave and that the children had now completed for the last time, the preacher graciously brought forward that memorable procession in which children once proceeded as suppliants in Apulia from the city of Troy, which was under the tightest siege, to the camp of the angry Emperor. They moved him to mercy, so that he would spare the city, already reduced to the utmost extremity, and so forth.

“The entire celebration concluded with the singing of the Ambrosian hymn and solemn benediction of the Most Holy Sacrament, to the great consolation of the whole city, rejoicing in the notable increase of the worship of its holy Patron.”

### § IV. The newly revised devotional Office of Saint Henry

For the honor and love of Saint Henry, Roman Emperor, Apostle of the Hungarians, Founder and Patron of the Imperial Bishopric of Bamberg; published at Bamberg in 1673 with the permission of the Superiors; now reprinted there to renew devotion to the same Saint. Printed by Georg Andreas Gertner, printer to the Most Reverend Chapter. 1723.

O God, lover of integrity, who, in order to commend the beauty of chastity to the whole human race, wished it also to shine conspicuously in the august marriage of Blessed Henry: grant, we ask, that we may be so fortified by his prayers with the antidote of heavenly delights that we may know nothing at all of the wounds of earthly corruption. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, forever and ever. Amen.

## OF SAINT HENRY

From the Bamberg Annals, in Gretser, p. 426.

**124.** Hail, offspring of the Saxons; summit of the Bavarians; honor of the Palatines of the Rhine; glory of Germany; splendor of the Empire; singular ornament of the Church; and astonishing miracle of the whole world: most holy Emperor Henry, look upon those who love you, and by your merits and prayers make them worthy to become your devotees and, as far as possible, imitators of your virtues. Thus, clinging to your footsteps, may we rejoice here always in your protection, and at last in heaven in blessed companionship with you. Amen.

## VERSES OF GODFREY OF VITERBO ON SAINT HENRY, CALLED “THE LAME”

[Col. 0187A]

**125.** Hear solemnly the merit of Henry the Lame,  
whom it is fitting to applaud, whose verses I offer in praise:

Taken from the citadel of the sun, he reigns in the citadel of heaven.  
With a virgin wife, he himself remained a virgin.  
He gave nearly a thousand Catholic churches.  
To the poor and widows he was hope, way, and life.  
Now on the altar we see his bones consecrated,  
and, in salutary fashion, solemn rites worthy of them prepared;  
many bodies of the infirm are granted healing.

**126.** We mentioned above, in the preliminary Commentary, no. 76, this metrical encomium by the Viterbian, which embraces the chief virtues of Saint Henry. There, when we discussed the virginal [Col. 0187B] chastity of Saint Henry preserved in marriage, we referred the reader to the author’s own words; by them we also vindicated this singular distinction of the most holy Emperor. Some matters concerning the exposition of the Bamberg relics, customarily celebrated every seven years, were proposed; but since these things are sufficiently common elsewhere, and seem no more relevant to the holy spouses than to other saints, it was not worthwhile to discuss them at greater length. I preferred to place a crown upon the entire treatment by briefly enumerating the churches and chapels erected in honor of the most holy spouses, which Pottuvius listed as follows.

### § V. Churches and chapels erected in honor of Saint Henry and Saint Cunegund, apart from the one mentioned above, no. 18, among the miracles

[Col. 0187C] **127.** “At Prague there is seen a distinguished church of Saint Henry, which Emperor Charles IV, King of Bohemia, built in honor of this saint in the year 1333, while he was still Margrave of Moravia and governor of Bohemia, and raised to the status of a parish church. To this day it is one of the principal served basilicas of New Prague, equipped with numerous foundations, especially for supporting musicians assigned to the service of the church.

**128.** “The parish church of Burkunstadt, a city of the diocese of Bamberg, was dedicated several centuries ago to Saint Henry the Emperor, whose patronage is solemnly celebrated each year.

[Col. 0188A] **129.** “At Bamberg, in the year 1654, the church of the Reverend Capuchin Fathers was built in honor of Saints Henry and Cunegund. In that same year, on 28 June, the Most Reverend Lord Johannes Melchior, Bishop of Domitiopolis and suffragan of Würzburg, dedicated it with solemn rite under the patronage of the same saints.

**130.** “Bottenstein, a city of the diocese of Bamberg situated in the mountains toward Voitland, has outside its walls a chapel dedicated to Saint Cunegund the Virgin and to her holy Husband. There, as a consistent tradition received from our ancestors testifies, a memorable event occurred which must not be passed over in silence. When the Hussites, in the year 1430, after devastating Voitland and capturing and burning Kulmbach and Bayreuth, entered the mountainous region of the diocese of Bamberg [Col. 0188B] in divided bands and approached Bottenstein unobserved, suddenly an unusual sound of bells was heard in the chapel of Saints Cunegund and Henry. Awakened by it, the inhabitants hastened to the chapel; they found the doors closed and no trace of any person who could have rung the bells. At the same time, however, they saw the hostile troop approaching nearby. Having gained a very brief but highly opportune delay in which to attend to their affairs, they quickly prepared themselves both in the city and in the adjacent fortification to repel the hostile force. Thus, with the help of their guardian Patrons, they happily escaped the disastrous destruction by which many neighboring cities, towns, and villages then miserably perished. In perpetual and grateful memory of this benefit, a procession is held every year from the parish church to the said chapel.

**131.** “In Styria, at the foot of Mount Piri, there is a chapel in honor of Saint Henry the Emperor, built by Frederick of Huffses, Bishop of Bamberg, around the year 1436.”

**132.** I faithfully deliver what I have received; nothing remains for me to add to what has just been said. I dare trust that everything relevant to commending the most holy Emperor and his most pious clients is clear from the foregoing. See the Dillingan Life, chapter XXXIV, p. 161.

[Col. 0187]

## ADDITION TO THE ACTS OF SAINT HENRY

*(Monumenta Germaniae Historica, Scriptores, vol. IV, p. 816.—“Another history of Saint Henry and his wife Cunegund, appended to the Life of the holy Emperor, written quite elegantly by someone unknown at the beginning of the thirteenth century but full of fables, is presented as Book III by a manuscript of the library of the Leipzig Senate, no. 194, parchment, thirteenth century. It was copied for our use with the utmost diligence by the distinguished Naumann, prefect of the library,” says G. Waitz in his preface to Saint Henry.)*

[Col. 0187C] **1.** The Psalmist admonishes us that it is good to conceal the secret of a king, but honorable to recount the works of God, saying: “Praise the Lord in his saints” (Psalm 150:1). Therefore, what we have learned as clearly as daylight concerning the glorious Emperor and Confessor of Christ, Henry, and his praiseworthy and glorious wife, though a virgin, we propose to proclaim, in an unpolished but truthful style, for the glory of God who works in his saints, so that what seems to be lacking in their legend may be found here more fully.

If anyone desires to know why blessed Henry, the Confessor of Christ, and blessed Cunegund, before they came together, had offered to God, as a sweet fragrance, a vow of virginal continence, and why afterward they entered into a marital union, let him know that the reason was this. When the fame of the illustrious prince was spread everywhere, when through him the enemies of the faith were subjected to the yoke of Christ, when new churches were being built and those first destroyed were being rebuilt, and when this glorious and victorious emperor was increasing and exalting the commonwealth just as a timely rain usually waters the earth, all the princes rejoiced together in his glory and applauded the abundance of peace which they enjoyed through him.

[Col. 0188C] Consequently, if it had been possible, they wanted him to reign forever. But because the human condition does not permit this, the prudence of the princes, looking ahead to the future of the commonwealth, endeavored to suggest to the illustrious emperor that he should take a wife to propagate offspring, so that, once the virtuous emperor had entered the way of all flesh, virtuous offspring might nevertheless receive the government of the kingdom by hereditary right and rule it virtuously, emulating their father’s virtue.

But the Confessor of Christ, mindful of his vow and a lover of chastity, could not readily consent when the princes urged him to take a wife. Since they continued to press their advice opportunely and importunately, and wanted to deprive him of the kingdom if he did not consent, he was compelled, though reluctantly, to agree. But he entreated God, for whom nothing is impossible, with unspeakable groanings, asking him to arrange matters so that he might satisfy the will of the princes and nevertheless preserve his vow of continence inviolate.

[Col. 0189A] Thus the gracious God, who is always ready to hear pious supplications, deigned to grant him the desire of his soul. The king, trusting in the Lord, gave this answer to the princes: “I am indeed ready to obey your will, but I wish to associate with myself in marriage no woman unworthy of royal majesty; and even this matter I entrust to your prudence.”

When the pious king’s promise had been gratefully accepted, all the princes rejoiced greatly. They deliberated with much care whom they should unite to him in marriage, yet they could find no one except her whom divine foreknowledge had ordained long before the ages.

There was a Count Palatine on the Rhine named Sifrid, who had a wife called Hedewih. Both were distinguished by a very illustrious lineage, being descended from the most noble line of emperors; they were also notable for their great wealth and, what is more praiseworthy, devoted themselves to virtue. At an early age they had a daughter who shone like a jewel set upon gold, since she was added to ancestors already illustrious. She was beautiful in face and adorned with excellent character, but above all chastity held first place in her. For, as was said above, she had devotedly vowed virginal continence to God.

[Col. 0189B] Therefore, since she was noble both by birth and by character, and no other like her could be found, it pleased the illustrious princes to join her above all others to the glorious emperor in lawful marriage.

Accordingly, they sent honorable envoys to her, or to her relatives or friends—for she had already been deprived of both parents—and began discussions with them concerning the marriage. But the most chaste maiden, whose mind was directed elsewhere, hearing that marriage with her was being discussed, began to grieve beyond measure and to resist with all her strength. From sorrow her eyes poured streams of tears, because she, who had already chosen the King of angels as her bridegroom, refused to marry the King of the Romans, illustrious though he was.

Her relatives, however, thinking that it would bring glory and great distinction to their family if their kinswoman reigned together with the Roman emperor, soothed her in her distress with flattering words. They sometimes advised her, and in advising earnestly entreated her, not to refuse to marry so glorious an emperor, but rather to do so gladly.

[Col. 0190A] Meanwhile the maiden’s mind wavered amid various movements of thought, like a ship lying on the open sea and driven about by powerful winds. At last, however, fixing the anchor of her hope in divine assistance, she commended her salvation to the Lord in constant prayers, trusting without doubt that he, who can do whatever he wills, could preserve the flower of her chastity from withering even when she was placed in marriage.

Strengthened by this hope, the exceedingly wise virgin surrendered herself to the will of her relatives, though not with a willing heart. The envoys of the princes, rejoicing at this, brought the new bride to their lord with the greatest celebration. Her relatives and friends accompanied her, and a considerable crowd formed in her procession.

Thus all the princes rejoiced beyond measure at the marriage of the king and queen—but in vain. For they did not marry in the manner of carnal people, as they had hoped; instead, they remained virgins.

[Col. 0190C] When, strengthened by the blessings of the bishops, they had entered the privacy of the bridal chamber, the most chaste bridegroom, together with his no less chaste bride, began, not without embarrassment, to speak about chastity. “For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.” He therefore burst forth in these words:

“My dearest bride, know that I have never experienced the love with which carnal spouses take the greatest delight and are joined to one another; nor do I wish to experience it, because I chose the celibate life and long ago bound myself to the Lord God by this vow.”

When she heard this, the glorious queen, the blessed virgin, was overjoyed beyond measure and began ardently to love the bridegroom. She gave him this answer:

“Your word, my lord and king, is sweet in my heart, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb; and the purpose of chastity is pleasing to my spirit. If I were given a choice, I would prefer it to many kingdoms. For I too confess that I offered the vow of my virginity to the Lord God as a most acceptable gift. If anyone should presume to take it from me—which God forbid—he would incur the anger of the heavenly Judge and suffer eternal damnation.”

[Col. 0190D] The king rejoiced at what had been said to him. Since everything loves what is like itself, the virgin embraced the virgin and the chaste man the most chaste woman with chaste love. Taking her white hand and placing it in his own, he addressed her in these words:

“O my beloved, my bride, my immaculate one, truly the Lord is in our midst. He has caused us to come together in his name with one will and one purpose; he is our refuge and our strength. With unanimous consent, let us now offer ourselves to him, promising that for love of him we shall live a celibate life all the days of our lives.

“And I promise you, under the testimony of Christ, that I shall always honor you as a glorious empress and love you as my own body. I shall firmly keep the marital bond with you; and although I shall never touch you with carnal love, I shall diminish nothing of the affection or honor appropriate to your dignity. Rather, I shall love you above all, as is just, and honor you in everything.”

[Col. 0191A] While such and similar exceedingly sweet conversations passed between them in turn, a blazing fire arose in their hearts, as they loved one another intensely; for there was in them one spirit and the same fervor of charity.

Indeed, I consider it superfluous to dwell long on the royal wedding, especially since anyone can easily infer that the same wedding was celebrated solemnly with great generosity, as befitted royal excellence, with honorable bishops and all the princes of the kingdom attending with great devotion, and countless persons of both sexes and of various ranks invited to the royal wedding.

Although we have not read this in the sacred books, we nevertheless confidently affirm that, among the other more honored guests who were invited, one guest superior to all was invited: namely, the Son of the Virgin, who first changed water into the most excellent taste of wine at a wedding. Indeed, although he was not visibly present in his own person, he was present in the persons of his members, even the least of them, at the same wedding, and in them he was most excellently refreshed by the finest food. For he himself will say: “Whatever you did for one of the least of mine” (Matthew 25:40), and so forth.

[Col. 0191C] The glorious emperor honored the illustrious empress, his partner in kingdom and bedchamber, in every way, as he ought; and all the affairs of the kingdom were arranged at her command. She herself, the noblest flower of married women and the brightest mirror of all women, adorned with varied virtue, shone like a star.

To make it easier for these blessed spouses to appear before human beings to have a marriage, they customarily rested in one bridal chamber, according to the practice of carnal spouses, and nevertheless preserved undefiled continence. A wondrous thing, unheard of in our times.

There are indeed many virgins of both sexes, but, so that they may preserve the seal of virginity undefiled, it is fitting that men and women live separately. “Who can hide fire in his bosom without burning his garment?” Among human beings this is impossible, but not with God.

[Col. 0191D] Therefore these people of whom we speak, dwelling more familiarly than other mortals under the protection of the God of heaven, sometimes lived together and nevertheless remained undefiled virgins. Since, apart from the shedding of blood, there are two kinds of martyrdom—namely, chastity in youth and abstinence amid abundance—we confidently believe that these blessed spouses, whose praises we do not silence, were crowned with a double crown of martyrdom, since throughout their whole lives they strove with the utmost care to preserve both chastity and abstinence.

## 2. How He Began to Limp

[Note: This chapter was inserted in the copy of the Bamberg manuscript possessed by Gretser after chapter 24 of the Life, with certain words altered.]

If anyone wishes to know why this glorious emperor began to limp, although at first he had been sound in his entire body, let him know that the cause was as follows.

When he had come at a certain time to Apulia to arrange the affairs of the commonwealth, he reached Mount Gargano. At the foot of the mountain lies a city, and on the mountainside, in a hollowed rock, stands a basilica not built by human beings or dedicated by a human being, but wonderfully constructed by divine operation or power and venerably consecrated by divine blessing. The patron of this basilica is Michael the archangel. It is also said that angelic singing can be heard in this church every week by those who are worthy.

This basilica, therefore, the man devoted to God entered with the other faithful of Christ for the sake of prayer. When they had celebrated divine praises there and offered to God the vows of their prayers with great devotion, the time had already come when the heavenly army was to enter this sacred temple to render praise to God.

[Col. 0192B] Accordingly, when everyone was leaving, and those who delayed were compelled to go out, the holy man asked that he be allowed to remain inside. When everyone else had departed, he alone, trusting in the mercy of God, dared to remain there. He continued prayers with prayers and repeated his genuflections. At one moment, with many tears, he entrusted himself to divine clemency; at another, with much supplication, he strove to commend his soul to the blessed archangel Michael.

As the pure prayer of the pious king rose like incense before the Lord, the God of Israel, who is always wondrous in his saints, deigned to show him a wondrous vision. He saw a great multitude of angels, splendid like the sun, entering the holy temple. Two of them solemnly adorned the principal altar.

[Col. 0192C] Then he saw countless other companies of heavenly powers, shining like flashing lightning and escorting, with the greatest glory, as it were, their prince. There is no doubt that this was the archangel, standard-bearer of the heavenly army.

Finally, he was granted the sight of the very King of angels, the Lord, coming with great power and might. The innumerable heavenly army attended him, and his splendor was incomparable; by his nod all things heavenly and earthly are governed.

At last, the choir of the new Jerusalem, gathered in the aforesaid basilica, solemnly celebrated the divine service. When it had been completed, one of the angels present brought the sacred text of the Gospel, with the utmost reverence, before the person of the Lord. After kissing it, he signaled to the angel to carry it to the emperor, who was hiding in a corner, so that he too might kiss it.

[Col. 0192D] When the angel had fulfilled the command given to him, the aforesaid servant of Christ began to be terrified in spirit and to tremble in all his limbs at the unfamiliar sight of such majesty and glory, as though he were saying with the prophet: “My heart is broken within me; all my bones tremble” (Jeremiah 23:9).

Seeing this, the angel gently touched his thigh and said: “Do not fear, chosen one of God. Rise quickly and gladly receive the sign of peace sent to you from God.”

Immediately his thigh withered, and from that time onward he limped throughout the whole period of his life. A similar event in every respect is read concerning blessed Jacob, whose thigh withered at the touch of the angel with whom he wrestled (Genesis 32:32).

[Col. 0193A] To tell the truth, I did not find these things in Scripture; but from the report of truthful and venerable men I learned with certainty that they are true. Indeed, the powerful chancellor and Bishop of Würzburg, named Conrad, who suffered persecution for righteousness, firmly affirmed that he had read these things and, while residing in the church of Bamberg, had recounted them before many hearers.

[Col. 0193B] One of those hearers, a familiar acquaintance of mine and himself a thoroughly truthful man, faithfully reported the matter to me. When I wanted to suppress it in silence, he earnestly begged me to write it down. At last, moved by the petitioner’s persistence and by the earnestness of his exhortation, I wrote it faithfully, so that these things might be recounted to a later generation.

I would rather rest in my sleep than write false or frivolous things about the saints of God, especially since those who have deserved to be adorned by divine signs and wonders have no need to be exalted by false praises.

[Note: Let what has been said about so glorious a miracle suffice. As visible testimony to this sign, an image of Saint Henry appears clearly before the monastery gate, on the right side near the choir of Saint George, with [lacuna], a single pillow placed beneath it, opposite the images of Adam and Eve. GRETSER.]

Let us omit this and return to the history.

## 3.

The faithful servants of Christ mentioned above, and often to be mentioned, lived together in the kingdom. They had one heart and one soul, and were two not so much in one flesh as in one spirit. They had the same willing and the same refusal, to such an extent that whatever one of them began, the other diligently endeavored to complete. They had an equal will toward everything that belonged to virtue, piety, and religion.

Whatever the emperor was about to do, he entrusted to the counsel of his beloved wife; whatever he had done, he confirmed with her approval. Although they loved each other so tenderly and nevertheless preserved virginal continence, their spiritual love was known to God alone and almost unknown to human beings.

The devil, the enemy of every good, observed their chastity, envied it, and wasted away. Just as a blacksmith continually intensifies the fire needed for his work, so Satan endeavored by his suggestions to inflame their chaste hearts toward lust.

[Col. 0193D] When that thousand-skilled artificer gained nothing by this method, he tried by another cunning to overthrow those whom he could not drive into sin. Therefore, with God permitting it—he permits his own to be tested by temptations, not rejected—the devil attempted by this stratagem to disgrace the blessed spouses, who were nevertheless virgins.

One day, at the rising of the dawn, when blessed Cunegund was rising from her undefiled bed, that most cunning one, having assumed the appearance of a soldier, appeared to leave the queen’s chamber. The empress’s attendants who were present saw him and, suspecting that he had slept with blessed Cunegund, were astonished, since such a report had never before been heard about her. They all whispered to one another about the matter: some grieving over the disgrace, others maliciously gnawing at her reputation.

[Col. 0194A] The thousand-skilled artificer was not content with this single occasion. On the following day, and again on the third day, he pretended to leave the chamber of the most chaste matron, seen by far more people than on the first day. In a strange way, it seemed to those present that they recognized him, although they did not know who he was.

“Immediately the swift rumor reached the open ears of the people—no evil is swifter than it.”

—Virgil, *Aeneid* IV, 174–175

From then on, men with women, old with young, the small with the great, slandered the glorious empress. She became a story for everyone: some deeply grieving on her behalf because of her many virtues, others maliciously defaming her. Many heaped reproach and insult upon her, although she had never caused them trouble.

Her heart, however, had confidence in the Lord, because she knew her innocence. She foresaw that distress and hardship were approaching; and although she possessed the treasure of a good conscience, she could not refrain from tears. As has been said, all good people sympathized with her, while the malicious—and especially wicked little women, as though trying to cover their own misdeeds through her—defamed her, saying: “See how cunningly she has until now cloaked her disgrace beneath this appearance of sanctity.”

[Col. 0194B] As these and similar insults were directed against the innocent woman, the breeze of the evil rumor struck the ears of the emperor, who was far away. [Col. 0194C] His heart also trembled within him, and he said, deeply distressed: “God forbid—yes, God forbid—that this wickedness should come from my most beloved wife!” For he suspected nothing evil concerning the woman he loved, since he confessed that he had never known a woman so sober and so chaste.

At last, when one person after another confirmed the same story, he, credulous enough, was touched by an inward grief of heart and resolved within himself that, for as long as he lived, he would never see her again.

Meanwhile, after the emperor had successfully arranged the affairs for which he had departed, he returned to Bamberg with a grieving mind and neglected to greet his once-beloved wife in the customary manner. The prudent empress clearly understood that she had been defamed in his hearing. Her soul was therefore greatly troubled, and, wounded by love for her beloved, who was offended with her without cause, she ardently desired to see him.

[Col. 0194D] Seizing an opportunity, she approached him full of charity and love, and she received him most kindly and greeted him with the deepest affection. But he did not deign to return her greeting, or even to look at her.

She, the gentlest of women, wishing to appease the one who was offended with her, said in a tearful voice: “My most desired lord, why do you not speak to me? Why do you turn your face away from me?”

He answered with downcast eyes: “It is not fitting for me to answer you about this matter. Return to your conscience, and you will find the cause of my offense.”

[Col. 0195A] She replied confidently: “My conscience is clean, and my witness is on high, for he plainly testifies on my behalf that I have never committed this most wicked deed of which I am accused. I beg you, my lord king, to act manfully and to grant me your patience.
