“The honor of the entire empire seems to have been diminished through me, but, if God wills, it shall very soon be restored through me. If it is agreeable to you, I shall briefly explain how this may be done.”

Hearing this, the emperor was somewhat softened. At last he ordered her to sit down and explain how the matter could be resolved.

She answered: “Let your Majesty, my lord, command all the princes, both bishops and laymen, to assemble at the royal court. In the presence of all, let the case in question be examined according to judicial procedure; and whatever they advise may be done, with your honor preserved. I hope in the divine mercy that it will rescue us from the mire and misery of this filth.”

[Col. 0195B] Since these words of the prudent empress pleased the prince greatly, the princes assembled at his command. While they were sitting in judgment with the emperor, the fearless empress entered and sat beside the feet of the man who had once loved her. She was “black but beautiful,” a daughter of Jerusalem [Col. 0195D]: black through defamation, beautiful through innocence, and truly for that reason a daughter of Jerusalem, since she commended both herself and her case to divine providence.

Then the king addressed all the princes in a tearful voice:

“O my beloved and glorious princes, I think it cannot be hidden from your nobility that for several days I have endured reproach and that shame has covered my face. For this reason above all I wished you to assemble, so that by the counsel of your wisdom I might be freed from the impending troubles.

“Now, therefore, I ask your affection: what judgment should be imposed upon a matron who, having rejected her lawful husband, has presumed to bring another man over him? I beg you—and by begging command you—to recall the laws and decrees of our ancestors and pronounce sentence as justice dictates.”

[Col. 0195C] Hearing this, both the princes and the entire assembly wept abundant tears, pitying the empress for the punishment they thought she would suffer, since they knew her to be endowed with virtue of singular kind. Therefore, unwilling to pronounce sentence against her, they bought time with various conversations.

She prudently perceived this. Inserting a manly spirit into her womanly breast, she rose and stood in the midst of them. Silence was granted her, and all listened to her reverently. She argued eloquently, saying:

“O princes worthy of every honor and dear to me, long ago it pleased all of you to exalt my beloved lord and husband to imperial dignity, and you wished me to share his kingdom. By the grace of God and by your constitution, we seemed superior to other human beings.

“Since, therefore, I appear to be superior among women, but am now accused of the most wicked crime, it is necessary that by the harshest judgment—namely, twelve glowing plowshares—I clear myself of this disgrace in your presence.

“Yet I offer your serenity boundless thanks, because your gentleness, out of mercy toward me, was unwilling to pronounce a severe sentence against me.”

Having said this, she sat down.

[Col. 0196A] All those present, hearing this, discussed the matter with one another, saying: “If awareness of a crime committed were pricking our lady’s conscience, she would certainly not propose this most severe ordeal for herself; rather, she would reject it if proposed by others.”

Meanwhile, the plowshares, heated until they glowed, were carried into one basilica. There blessed Cunegund was led by two more distinguished bishops like a sheep to sacrifice, and the Confessor of Christ followed immediately behind her.

When he saw the plowshares breathing sparks and vaporous fire, remembering mercy in his anger and also recalling his former love, he said to her:

“Stop, my most beloved lady; stop, most desired by me. Spare yourself, I beg you, and do not enter this judgment, terrible even to hear about. For I believe that you are free from every crime.”

[Col. 0196B] She answered him with a serene face:

“If I escape this judgment for the present because you are sparing me, I shall not escape the reproach that, though innocent, I have endured until now. Therefore it is necessary that I hasten to clear myself by this examination, terrible though it is, so that those who have defamed me until now may at last be given another subject on which to speak about Cunegund.”

Having said this, she approached confidently. Raising her eyes to heaven, she said:

“Lord, my helper and protector, do not abandon me. Hasten, Lord; do not delay, but assist your handmaid in this present tribulation. You, Lord, before whose eyes all things are naked and open—you, I say, Lord, I call today as my witness: I have known neither this present Henry nor any other man through carnal intercourse.”

[Col. 0196C] When he heard this, the king growled. Wishing his secret to remain hidden, and therefore striving to silence the mouth of the woman who was speaking, he violently compressed her mouth. A copious stream of blood flowed from it.

When the emperor saw this, he was suddenly overcome by repentance. He wept bitterly and grieved over her as one grieves at the death of a firstborn child. For his beloved wife was a bundle of myrrh to him. He therefore withdrew and waited, groaning, for the outcome of the matter.

Meanwhile, the holy woman placed her hope in the Lord,

and bent her knee; repeating her prayer, the pious woman said:

“O King, maker of the world, bring help to wretched Cunegund.”

And when those present trembled greatly as they looked on,

she trod upon the glowing ploughshares as though they were flowers.

Having traversed the eleven ploughshares, she was not harmed at all,

[Col. 0196D] Standing venerably upon the last ploughshare, she praised

the supreme King, through whom she had overcome Satan. Thus, when the illustrious empress had been quite plainly cleared of the charge brought against her, the emperor, wishing to soothe her spirit with conciliatory words, fell prostrate at her sacred feet and said:

“Be reconciled, my lady; be gracious to me, and do not reject me from your favor or affection. Indeed, I confess that I sinned and acted foolishly in troubling you; now I repent. May my tongue cleave to my throat if I do not henceforth make satisfaction to you for as long as I live.”

But she, possessing dove-like simplicity and extraordinary patience, forgetful of the injury and mindful of mercy, said to her beloved:

[Col. 0197A] “My lord, it is God’s favor rather than mine that you ought to seek. In order that you may deserve fully to obtain it, fear God and observe his commandments. As for my devotion toward you, it neither has ceased nor will ever cease.”

Indeed, when the virtues and signs that were taking place there had been witnessed, the assembled crowd rejoiced greatly in the Lord. The sorrow of those who had grieved with the empress was turned into joy, and those who had wept with her now rejoiced with her rejoicing. Therefore all, with one voice, offered hymns of thanksgiving to the ruler of all, who does wondrous things and, in a gracious dispensation, permits his chosen ones to be tested, so that, just as spices, the more finely they are ground, produce the greater fragrance, so the elect, tested by tribulations, may be [Col. 0198A] the good fragrance of Christ before God in every place. Truly true is the saying that the Lord spoke: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden, nor do they light a lamp” (Matthew 5:14), and so forth.

That burning lamp had been placed under a bushel.

For previously everyone thought that this woman was married,

and at last they considered her corrupted through adultery;

but that she preserved her virginal flower forever

was clearly demonstrated by the judgment that bore witness.

That Henry was pious, and that the virgin was chaste,

was made manifest, although it was not pleasing to him.

The most evil fabrications of Satan were annihilated.

When a woman, though fragile, is tested under Satan’s temptation,

the devil, hateful to all, is condemned through her.

# THE LIFE OF SAINT CUNEGUNDIS, EMPRESS AND VIRGIN

[Col. 0197]

## PRELIMINARY OBSERVATIONS, CONCERNING SAINT HENRY THE EMPEROR AND HIS WIFE

*(In Mabillon, Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict, sixth century, part II, p. 451.)*

### 1. An illustrious pair of spouses and virgins

The Benedictine Order rightly claims as its own an illustrious pair of spouses and, at the same time, virgins: namely, the emperor Henry and Cunegundis Augusta, his wife. The former, bound by the obedience that he had vowed to the Rule, remained in the world; the latter, after her husband’s death, assumed the monastic habit and ended her life in holy religious observance at the monastery of Kaufungen, which she herself had built from the foundations. Both therefore deserve to be counted among the disciples of the holy Father Benedict.

### 2. The scope of these observations

It is not my purpose here to discuss the ancestry of either of them or the antiquity and nobility of their families; nor do I have room to set forth at greater length their distinguished achievements in the administration of the commonwealth. That belongs to those who devote themselves to writing the annals of the Roman Empire, a task already amply performed by many. It will therefore be enough for us to recall those matters by which our Order is bound to those pious rulers: namely, the splendid and immense benefits that they conferred upon the Benedictine Order, or the distinguished deeds and pious works by which they brought it renown.

For this reason, it did not seem worthwhile to reproduce here the whole Life of blessed Henry, since it contains much that is entirely foreign to our purpose. We shall, however, give below the Life of his holy wife, as it was published by Gretser and Bollandus for 3 March, collated with several manuscript copies, since it contains almost exclusively what she did in the monastery of Kaufungen, where, after completing a course of several years in the exercises of the religious life, she ended her earthly existence.

### 3. Henry’s support of the Church and the servants of God

Henry, formerly duke of Bavaria, was made emperor in the year 1002 after the death of the emperor Otto III. He regarded nothing as more important than to support the Church and men devoted to God’s service, not only by his authority and protection, but also by enriching them abundantly with every kind of property. In this matter he had Cunegundis not merely as an assistant but also as an encourager, since she was no less zealously than her husband devoted to whatever concerned God.

Accordingly, bishoprics are frequently mentioned as having been either newly established, restored, or certainly enlarged by them with new possessions. There was scarcely any monastery in the Roman Empire during those times that was not either restored through their beneficence or confirmed in its possessions and enriched with new ones.

Among their distinguished works, the establishment of the bishopric of Bamberg particularly excelled. In this undertaking they spared neither expense nor labor—labor that was indeed considerable, both because of the bishop of Würzburg, who was reluctant to see part of his diocese separated from the Church entrusted to him, and because of their own relatives and princes, who rebelled against the holy emperor on the pretext that their family’s property would thereby be dissipated. But Henry overcame and conquered all these difficulties with remarkable courage and incredible patience.

### 4. The monastery of Saint Michael at the Monks’ Mount

But so that the clergy of the new see would not lack a monastic community, they erected on a mountain situated beside the city to the north—a mountain thereafter called the Monks’ Mount—a distinguished monastery under the patronage of Saint Michael and the other angels. They endowed it with many possessions and estates, freed it from every external authority, and subjected it to the Benedictine Rule.

[Col. 0198D] Trithemius records its dedication in the year 1021 in the new edition of the *Chronicle of Hirsau*, and he states that it was carried out with the greatest devotion by Eberhard, the first bishop of the Church of Bamberg.

[Col. 0199A] Precious relics are still preserved in the treasury of that monastery, gifts presented to it by Cunegundis. Among them the Bollandists list, in the prolegomena to her Life, no. 25: “A golden cross of very ancient Greek workmanship, as may be gathered from the inscriptions and figures; the belt of blessed Cunegundis, together with two of her crowns made of gems.”

The same author also observes that several men distinguished for learning and holiness flourished there. “Many,” he says under the year 1007, “in the course of time, very famous men flourished under the monastic habit in that same monastery, bringing honor to the holy Church by their learning and the merit of their lives.”

In the following century, when regular observance had grown somewhat lukewarm in that place, Saint Otto, bishop of Bamberg, restored it after rebuilding the structures to their former splendor. In this undertaking he employed the work of monks from Hirsau, who at that time were bringing distinction to the Benedictine Order throughout Germany both by the holiness of their conduct and by their careful observance of the Rule.

The distinguished monastery of the Mount of Saint Michael still continues to this day; our Bucelinus supplies a catalogue of its abbots in *Sacred Germany*.

### 5. Henry’s foundations in Italy

When Henry went to Italy to vindicate the Church against the Greeks, “he founded a monastery at Benevento,” which, as the author of his Life reports in chapter 22, “he enriched with every adornment of beauty.”

From Book VII of Dithmar’s *Chronicle* we learn that the same ruler established a bishopric in the city of Bobbio, [Col. 0199C] “where the worshiper of Christ and the illustrious holy confessors Columbanus and Attala rest bodily,” and that he did so “with the common counsel and permission of the bishops of the province.”

Trithemius adds in the *Chronicle of Hirsau* under the year 1007 that this new see was endowed by the same emperor. The cathedral church, he says, was located at no other place than the monastery that blessed Columbanus had built, inhabited by a multitude of monks serving God; for that reason Henry appointed these monks as electors of the bishop. Thus far Trithemius.

Later, however, the arrangement established by the blessed man was altered: the cathedral church was separated from the monastery, and a separate superior was appointed for each place. This caused great disputes between the bishops and abbots of Bobbio, which were scarcely brought to an end by the authority of the supreme pontiffs.

### 6. The healing of Henry at Monte Cassino

Nor may we omit the remarkable miracle that took place during this Italian expedition through the merits of the blessed Father Benedict. The emperor, who was deeply devoted to the Order, was suffering terribly from stone. At the very monastery of Cassino, to which the pious ruler had ordered himself to be carried, Benedict restored him to health.

The matter should be reported in the words of the author of the emperor’s Life, who narrates in chapter 22 that it happened as follows:

“When Henry was passing through the cities of Apulia and had prudently arranged in them whatever pertained to the welfare and honor of the kingdom, he began to suffer from the disease of the stone. The holy man endured the distress of this illness with such patience that he declared the sufferings of the flesh to have been bestowed upon him by God for the preservation of humility, and affirmed that the scourge of correction was the surest sign of love.

“He nevertheless ordered remedies to be applied for his healing, but no medical skill could free him completely. As the pain grew worse, he climbed Mount Cassino … and there, through the intercession of blessed Benedict and Saint Scholastica, he sought from God with prayers and tears the health of body and soul. What is said through the Prophet was fulfilled: ‘I sought the Lord, and he heard me, and delivered me from all my tribulations’ (Psalm 33). For he asked and was heard; he perseveringly knocked at the door of merciful power, and he was admitted.

“Meanwhile the king began to think about what he had heard concerning the translation of Saint Benedict, and since it was said that his relics had been secretly taken away and transferred elsewhere, the holy man doubted whether Benedict was bodily present there.

“When his prayer was complete, the man of God went to the guesthouse and, exhausted and weakened, lay down on a small bed. As he slept there, he saw Saint Benedict standing beside him and holding in his hand an iron instrument suitable for making medical incisions. Benedict said to him:

“‘Because you have placed your hope in God and in his saints, behold, I have been sent by God so that through my medicine you may be freed from your illness. Behold, I am he whose bones you thought had been secretly taken away; I present my presence to you, and as proof of the truth I shall heal your sufferings.’

“Having said this, he opened with the medical instrument that he held in his hand the part of the body where the stone lay; after gently extracting the stone, he restored the opening of the wound by an instantaneous healing, and placed the stone he had removed in the hand of the sleeping king.

“When this had been done, the most Christian emperor awoke. Reflecting upon what had been accomplished around him through Christ’s confessor, and seeing the stone that he held in his hand, he summoned the attendants who, according to royal custom, were always in attendance upon him. He said to them:

“‘Call the bishops and the princes of our kingdom to me, so that they may recognize and see the wonders of God, which his ineffable mercy and unspeakable power have wrought in me.’

“They promptly carried the king’s command to the princes and brought them to him. The king greeted them, and when they had returned his greeting, he addressed them as follows:

“‘My brothers and fellow soldiers, magnify the Lord with me, and let us exalt his name together, for he is a great Lord and greatly worthy of praise, and there is no end to his greatness. He strikes and heals; he scourges sinners and has mercy on penitents. He humbles one and exalts another, for “in the hand of the Lord is a cup full of pure wine mixed”’ [Psalm 74:9].

“‘Behold, yesterday I was near death; today, through God’s mercy, I appear to you healthy. The sting of death that yesterday I carried enclosed within my body I now visibly display before your eyes.’

“Having said this, he showed them the stone that he held in his hand and, displaying the scar of the wound, related in order to all who were listening everything that had been done around him through Saint Benedict.”

### 7. The emperor’s gifts to Saint Benedict

“But when they saw and heard the wonders of God, they were amazed beyond belief. Blessing God and loudly praising him for a long time, they rejoiced in the king’s recovery.

“Again the king said to them: ‘What thanksgivings, or what gifts worthy of such great benefits, can we return to our physician Benedict?’

“They all judged him worthy of royal generosity. Therefore, on the advice of his princes, the king presented enormous gifts to the church of Saint Benedict: estates, gold, silver, and many ornaments. After bidding farewell to the brothers who presided over that church, he departed cheerfully and healthy from Mount Cassino.

“From that time onward he devoted himself, with a special love and reverence, to serving Saint Benedict and all who practiced the monastic religion, and he showed himself a kind and devoted Father in enlarging and protecting ecclesiastical possessions.

“These things are found written on Mount Cassino, so that people of the present day may keep the mighty works of God in their memory and so that, with the passage of time, they may not fall into oblivion among later generations.”

Henry immediately went to Rome, as the same author of his Life relates, and informed Pope Benedict of his recovery.

### 8. Leo of Marsi’s account of the miracle

I would readily persuade myself that the writings which the author of Saint Henry’s Life praises here and says were preserved in the monastery of Cassino were none other than Leo of Marsi’s *Chronicle*, unless the miracle performed by the holy Father Benedict—described in those writings in precisely the manner in which the author himself relates it—were reported differently by Leo. For Leo narrated this miracle in such a way that it would provide the strongest possible argument for asserting that the Cassinese possessed the body of the holy Father.

He writes in Book II, chapters 42 and following, that the emperor Henry visited the monastery of Cassino together with Pope Benedict VIII, in whose presence Theobald, the elected abbot of Cassino, was consecrated by the pope.

At that time, he continues, Henry was afflicted by an extremely sharp pain in the groin. While neither completely asleep nor fully awake, blessed Benedict appeared to him. To Henry, who doubted whether Benedict’s body truly rested on the sacred mountain, he said:

“‘I know that until now you have doubted whether I rested here. But so that you may no longer doubt in any way, and may most certainly believe that my little body rests in this place, this shall be a sign for you: as soon as you rise today, you will urinate three stones, not small ones, and from that time onward you will suffer no more from this pain.’

“Henry immediately awoke and rose, and in the manner foretold by the holy Father recovered his health. When morning came, he went into the chapter house and related what had happened to all the brothers, together with many other details that the author sets forth at length. He is entirely concerned to prove from this miracle that the relics of the blessed Father were never brought to Gaul—a conclusion that is certainly not easily drawn from the Life of Saint Henry.”

### 9. The possibility of an apparition

I do not, therefore, wish to call so illustrious a miracle into question. For the holy Father could have shown himself visibly to the sleeping emperor on Mount Cassino even if his bones had been lying in Gaul, just as he is said to have done elsewhere, in places that he had never illumined by the presence of his body, whether alive or dead.

Leo himself supplies us with an example of this in chapter 45, where he relates that the same Saint Benedict once appeared with a threatening expression to Henry, before Henry had been raised to the imperial dignity, because he had allowed his horses to spend the night in the cloister of a certain monastery:

“That same night,” he says, “Father Benedict appeared to the same duke with a very grim and terrifying gaze, threatened him with many things because he treated his house in such a manner, and struck him in the side with the rod that he carried in his hand. From that time onward he began to suffer the most severe torment from pain in the groin.”

Certainly the author of the Life of Saint Meinwerc also relates this very miracle of Henry’s healing near Mount Cassino. But he does not include what the holy Father says to Leo concerning the presence of his body; we therefore conjecture that this detail was invented by Leo himself.

### 10. Henry’s offerings

The same Leo, in chapter 43, lists the precious gifts that Henry offered to blessed Benedict at that time in gratitude for the recovery of his health:

“Namely, a Gospel book, covered on the outside on one side with the purest gold and most precious gems, and on the inside magnificently decorated with uncial letters and golden figures, as they say; a golden chalice with its paten, adorned with gems, pearls, and excellent enamels; a *diapistin* chasuble decorated with golden bands, together with a stole, maniple [*mappula*], and belt, each woven with gold; also a *diasprum* cope with bands woven in gold, and a tunic of the same, adorned with golden woven work, together with a *diapistin mappula* likewise decorated with gold; also a silver bucket and a silver cup of considerable size, from which the brothers might drink on the principal feast days.

“Moreover, he redeemed from the Jews a garment from the altar of Saint Benedict, which had once belonged to King Charles and which those Jews held in pledge for five hundred gold pieces; also a large Saxon silver chalice with its paten, which Theodoric, king of the Saxons, had formerly sent to blessed Benedict.

“He placed all these things together upon the altar of blessed Benedict in the presence of the brothers and offered them. He asked the aforesaid pope to make a written grant of all these things at that place, with the bond of apostolic anathema attached to the document, so that no one might ever presume to take away either the things we have mentioned or anything else that the same emperor might thereafter grant to this monastery.”

### 11. Gifts of Pope Benedict and Archbishop Piligrinus

Pope Benedict and Piligrinus, archbishop of Cologne, also presented their own gifts. Leo records them in the same place:

“The same apostolic pope, greatly rejoicing in the emperor’s recovery, also offered blessed Benedict on that day an excellent blue chasuble, suitably decorated with golden bands, and an excellent stole embroidered with gold, together with its maniple.

“Piligrinus, archbishop, likewise offered blessed Benedict, in gratitude for the emperor’s recovery, an excellent purple chasuble adorned around its border with golden bands bearing the signs of the twelve months, together with a stole with gold and a cope.

“After this, the most Christian emperor, still considering that he had done very little in view of his excessive love for this place, was advised by Piligrinus and by his chancellor Theodoric. On the following day he issued a charter of grant to this place concerning Rocca, called Vantra, whose possessors, like a band of brigands, very frequently harassed this monastery. He therefore snatched it from their hands and granted it for the perpetual use and possession of the servants of God in this place.

“He also issued another charter concerning all the possessions of this place throughout the world, in accordance with the provisions of his imperial predecessors. By this charter as well, he confirmed by imperial authority to this monastery the monastery of Saint Mary at Canneto, in the territory of Termoli.

“Having thus commended himself greatly to Father Benedict and all the brothers, he returned home with their blessing. And so that he might not appear in any way to forget the favor of so great a benefactor, as soon as he returned home he took care to send here to blessed Benedict, with the greatest expressions of thanks, an excellent *diarodina* chasuble beautifully decorated with golden bands, together with an alb, belt, stole, and maniple, such as it would be fitting for an emperor to send.

“His devotion toward this holy place thereafter became so great that, if he had lived somewhat longer, he promised that, leaving behind the dignity of the empire, he would serve God here under the monastic habit.”

### 12. Henry’s monasteries and foundations

Henry’s affection for our people was so great that, according to the author of the *Chronicle of Lorsch* under the year 1000, he was commonly called “Father of the Monks.” And the ancient documents issued for their benefit everywhere prove that he truly was their father and patron.

Gretser provides nine of these in his book *On the Saints of Bamberg*: eight for the monastery of Altaich and the ninth for Tegernsee, almost all granted through the initiative and encouragement of Saint Cunegundis. The *Cassinese Bullary*, volume II, presents five others for various monasteries in Italy. Many more are found in other books, but there is no time to list them individually.

Besides the monastery of Bamberg, mentioned above, and that of Kaufungen, which was chiefly endowed by Cunegundis, Henry restored from the foundations, enlarged, and enriched with many possessions the monastery of Schuttern in the diocese of Strasbourg, which had been almost completely destroyed, as Trithemius testifies in the *Chronicle of Hirsau* under the year 1007.

The monastery of Saint Vito at Verdun was restored at his expense. Nor should we pass over the noble convent of holy virgins that the same emperor founded together with Cunegundis at Neuburg in Bavaria, on the very bank of the Danube.

In that place, renowned for wealth and religious observance, the Benedictine Order continued until the end of the previous century. At that time, as Lutheranism gained strength throughout the region, after the death of Magdalena Hundtin of Lauterbach, the abbess, and with a new election forbidden, it later became unlawful to admit virgins to the monastic profession. Indeed, the remaining women were permitted to marry, but all of them steadfastly rejected the permission.

“All of them,” says Bucelinus in *Sacred Germany*, “sustained until death on the bread of tribulation, proved and commended themselves magnificently to the Deity amid adversity.”

After conditions had later been pacified, no virgins were restored there, and the monastery fell into the hands of the Fathers of the Society of Jesus. The same Bucelinus provides a catalogue of the abbesses in the place cited.

### 13. Henry’s devotion to holy men

Henry honored men distinguished for virtue and holiness no less than he honored sacred places. He continually made use of their assistance and counsel in promoting the salvation of himself and his subjects.

Such men included Wolfgang, bishop of Regensburg, who is said to have been his tutor in early youth; Godehard, first abbot of Altaich and later bishop of Hildesheim; Heribert of Cologne; Poppo, abbot of Stavelot; Richard of Verdun; Odilo of Cluny; William of Dijon; Pandulf of Agaunum; and many others who at that time brought distinction to the monastic Order.

Peter Damian certainly states that Saint Romuald once approached Henry, who was then in Italy. Romuald, he says, spoke to him at some length about restoring the rights of the churches, the violence of the powerful, the oppression of the poor, and so forth. The emperor did not take this in bad spirit; rather, out of reverence for the man’s holiness, he handed over to Romuald’s congregation the monastery of Saint Amiatus, where regular observance had grown lukewarm.

For Henry delighted in associating with religious men. Thus, on his return from Italy to Germany, he dismissed his army and went with a few of his household companions to Cluny,

“where,” says the author of his Life in chapter 26, “when he had seen very many signs of religious devotion and holiness, inflamed by the fire of the Holy Spirit, he offered a golden crown adorned with the most precious gems at the Mass celebrated from the chair of Saint Peter. He received the brotherhood of the monks and, with the greatest humility and contrition of heart, commended himself to their prayers. He also granted to that congregation excellent estates in Alsace to supply its necessary resources.

“Proceeding from there, he passed through Liège and Trier and enriched the congregations serving God in those places with very many gifts and estates.”

### 14. Henry becomes a monk in spirit

The author of the Life of blessed Richard relates that Henry once visited Verdun to see blessed Richard, with whom he often associated on intimate terms. As he toured the buildings of the monastery of Saint Vito, over which Richard presided as abbot, he entered the cloister and immediately recited this verse of the Psalm:

“This is my rest forever and ever; here I shall dwell, for I have chosen it.”

The bishop of Verdun, Heymo, who was present, was troubled by this. He secretly warned Richard not to allow Henry to become a monk among them, since this could not happen without the empire’s suffering incredible loss.

The following day, while Henry was standing before everyone in the chapter house, Richard asked him whether he wished to become a monk and to obey him completely in all things as his own abbot, according to the precept of the Rule. When the emperor had promised this and had been received as a monk, the abbot said:

“Therefore we wish and command that you return to govern the empire entrusted to you by God.”

Thus the pious emperor, bound by the Rule, spent the remainder of his life in the practice of the virtues and truly honored blessed Benedict as his Father.

A similar event occurred in the monastery of Gellone in the twelfth century, where Berengar of Mayrosio likewise vowed obedience to Richard, abbot of Gellone. This is clear from the document of his profession, which seemed worth reproducing here from a manuscript of that monastery:

“In the year 1162 from the incarnation of the Lord, in the name of the Lord, I, Berengar of Mayrosio, wishing to renounce earthly things and pursue heavenly things, place myself in the hands of Lord Richard, abbot of Saint William, to be received into the monastic habit whenever it pleases the lord abbot. Moreover, at the present time I promise obedience according to the Rule of God and of blessed Benedict.”

The golden plaque that, according to various authors, Angelus de Nuce reports in his notes on Book II, chapter 43, of the *Cassinese Chronicle*, was seen in the great church at Basel, which Henry had restored, also proves Henry’s devotion to Saint Benedict. Four angels were depicted there with Saint Benedict, and Christ the Lord was represented in their midst; at Christ’s feet Henry and his wife Cunegundis were shown prostrate.

Henry died on 14 July 1024 and was buried in the church at Bamberg. He was later enrolled in the catalogue of the saints by Pope Eugene III and began to be publicly celebrated throughout the Church.

### 15. Cunegundis enters the monastery

After her husband’s death, Cunegundis was entirely free to embrace whichever state of life she preferred. She chose above all the monastery of Kaufungen, into which she withdrew in the manner described in her Life. Since we shall reproduce that Life in full, it would be unnecessary to speak at greater length here about her deeds.

Hofmann states in the *Bamberg Annals* that her Life was written by a certain monk named Nonnosius. But it is uncertain when he flourished or whether this is the same work that has come down to us. It certainly seems clear that whoever the author of the Life may have been, he lived in a place endowed by blessed Cunegundis. For in section 5 he says that it would be unworthy for him to deprive her of the service of his mouth, since through her providence he received daily nourishment for his body.

He does not reveal his own age very clearly. Nevertheless, in section 5 he indicates that he wrote after Saint Henry’s canonization, which was carried out by Eugene III in 1152, when he says that writings concerning the blessed emperor had been accepted by the Church.

Moreover, since he says that on that occasion it came to his mind to write about blessed Cunegundis, it may be inferred that he lived at the very time when the matter of publicly enrolling the blessed emperor among the saints was being considered. Yet it must be admitted that he did not write until near the end of the twelfth century, unless we say that the miracles placed after the Life were described by another author.

Besides the miracles that we have published below, the Bamberg copy also contains another book of miracles, which we omitted because it contains almost nothing beyond what we have already presented. If anyone nevertheless wishes to read it, he may consult Gretser in *On the Saints of Bamberg*, or Bollandus under 3 March, where it is given in full.

### 16. The later history of Kaufungen

The monastery of Kaufungen, which Dithmar calls *Capungum* in Book VII and which is commonly called Kauffungen, not far from the renowned town of Kassel in Hesse, continued in regular observance until the previous century.

At that time, however, when the entire region was moving toward the Lutheran party, the nuns were finally expelled under Landgrave Philip, around the year 1531, and the Catholic religion was completely abolished there. Our Adolphus Overham offers further observations about this monastery in a note on section 86 of the Life of blessed Meinwerc, bishop of Paderborn.

### 17. Cunegundis’s feast

The memory of Cunegundis is commemorated not only in the Benedictine calendars but also in most of the particular martyrologies of Germany and Belgium, together with the Roman Martyrology. Her feast is celebrated on different days for different reasons.

The principal day is 3 March, on which she certainly departed this life. This occurred in the year 1040 or the following year, if she spent fifteen years in the monastery after one year of widowhood, as the author of her Life asserts. Lambert of Hersfeld, however, recorded her death under the year 1030, and Trithemius, following Marianus Scotus, under the year 1038.

[Col. 0205]

# THE LIFE OF SAINT CUNEGUNDIS BEGINS

[Col. 0205D] ### 1. The Empress Cunegundis, married

From the illustrious blood of their parents and the rank of Augustan nobility, two flowers of unfading glory shone forth upon the world: namely, Saint Henry, called the Pious, the most glorious ornament of the Roman Empire, and his most worthy *contectalis*, Cunegundis Augusta and empress, of pious memory.

The blessed and God-beloved Cunegundis was bodily joined to an earthly emperor [Note: [Col. 0206D] Gretser, together with manuscript 1, reads *copulariter*, “conjugally.”], but not carnally; she consecrated her virginity to the heavenly King and, with the consent of her chaste husband, preserved it to the end, God bearing witness.

Afterward, so that this testimony of the Divinity would not remain a light hidden in darkness, God revealed it by granting that she walk upon burning ploughshares and emerge unharmed, in order to confound the enemy of virginity and close the mouths of those speaking lies against Christ’s virgin.

[Note: [Col. 0205D] Several manuscripts read *collectalis* instead of *contectalis*; but our reading is better, since they lived under the same roof (*tectum*), not in the same bed (*lectus*). Indeed, Henry himself uses the same word in various charters.]

### 2. She proves her virginity by a miracle

How this happened should not be passed over, for the common edification of all, so that we may be instructed by examples of chastity and moved by wonder at divine secrets, understanding how all things work together for good for those who love God.

Such great and excellent blessings could not be without temptation. The devil, envious of every good, was unable to wound the immaculate marriage bed; so he planned to defile it with the stain of jealousy and at least injure the reputation of the woman whom he could not wound with corruption.

Thus, at the devil’s instigation, she who knew no stain of corruption was suspected of a crime. But because one who neglects his reputation is cruel, she chose, for the sake of clearing herself, the judgment of the glowing ploughshares, which is known to have been instituted because of human hardness.

When the woman beloved of God was led to that judgment like a sheep to the slaughter, she groaned and said:

“Lord God, creator of heaven and earth, who tests the kidneys and hearts, judge my judgment and rescue me. For today I call upon you as witness and judge, because I have never known either this present Henry or any other man through carnal intercourse.”

After she had spoken these words, while all who were present stood amazed and wept, she trod upon the glowing ploughshares with bare feet and passed over them confidently, without the pain of burning.

Thus almighty God preserved the bond of chaste love, proved her innocence, and joined the protection of humility to her integrity.

### 3. He establishes and endows holy places

Having assumed the imperial insignia, she strove to conceal the glory of her continence beneath the mantle of earthly empire, so that, with all the greater zeal and effectiveness, she might promote the works which, with God’s inspiration and help, she had conceived for his praise.

Finally, after the church of Babenberg, the new planting of her most fruitful foundation—which she had built with that most zealous collaborator of hers, Henry, at Babenberg, with the greatest elegance, as it is still seen today, under the patronage of the prince of the apostles Peter and of Saint George the martyr—she constructed a monastery under the Rule of Saint Benedict to the north, in honor of Saint Michael the Archangel [Col. 0207D], sparing no less care in estates and gifts of various ornaments. At last, toward the south, under the order of canons and under the title of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr, she founded from her own patrimony a church small in design but greater in workmanship.

To dedicate it, she asked Pope Benedict [Note: [Col. 0207D] Benedict VIII, who succeeded Sergius IV in the year 1012] to come—the pope whom the aforesaid God-worthy Emperor Henry had summoned to confirm the bishopric of Babenberg. She herself, chanting with him the Psalmist’s words, “Lord, I have loved the beauty of your house” (Psalm 25:8), presented that church with various gifts, in keeping with imperial munificence, for its various ornaments [Col. 0208A]. On that very day the apostolic lord himself confirmed all these things by the severe binding of his ban, with the authority also of the seventy-two bishops [Note: [Col. 0208D] The Bodecensis Codex has “forty”] who were present there, so that the memory of its foundress might always flourish in that place and so that the gifts might never be removed from it by fraud, violence, or theft.

Likewise, she magnificently built a monastery in honor of the holy Savior and of his most victorious cross at a place called Confugia, and most suitably organized there a community of maidservants of God serving God according to the Rule of Saint Benedict. Moreover, with the imperial majesty assisting her in all things, she adorned that monastery with every kind of ornament. Before the principal altar she set up an image of gold and of the most precious stone [Col. 0208B]; she gave that church golden and silver chalices, basins, pitchers, altar cloths, chasubles, veils, curtains, and copes woven with gold and precious gems, together with the other utensils and vessels of the ministry, with such care and at such lavish expense that all who behold them cannot cease greatly to marvel at the royal magnificence and the wonderful devotion to God of both emperor and empress.

### 4. She restores what has fallen into ruin

Besides these principal foundations and first-ranking churches of theirs, what collegiate church or monastery does not glory in their benefaction, whether enlarged with estates or adorned with ornaments? They rebuilt some that had collapsed through age, and restored others that had been destroyed and reduced to nothing to their former or even better condition [Col. 0208C]. Like prudent virgins, they poured out the oil of their mercy upon many, so that they might rightly say: “We are the good odor of Christ in every place” (II Corinthians 2:15).

O marriage joined not by pleasure but by good will! O holy matrimony, in which there was one faith in inviolate chastity, one spirit of mercy and truth, the same willing of virtues and the same rejection of vices! In which neither the one nor the other could be distinguished, since the second wished what the first did; in which one equal mind displayed, through manifold effects of works, equal affections in both!

I do not know what I should call such a marriage. I know only that our age now knows no such thing, since they, making themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven and awaiting no offspring of earthly fertility, received from God a celibate generation, from whose mouths the praise of God will never fail [Col. 0208D]. This is the generation of those who seek the Lord, who seek the face of the God of Jacob: living in Christ, putting their members to death for Christ, dying upon earth, yet now reigning with Christ and seeing the good things of their Lord in the land of the living.

### 5. The author undertakes the life of Saint Cunegund

Since the holy Church has received a sufficiently full and worthy account of the life and virtues of the pious and holy Henry, most Christian emperor, of the various acts of mercy he performed in the house of the Lord, and also of the signs and miracles that God worked through him after his passing [Col. 0209A], it now moves me, and comes to mind, briefly to set forth the life of our memorable virgin Cunegund and commend it to writing, so that all virgins and all true widows, looking to her example, may regard her way of life as the standard of a perfected life.

For we considered it unworthy of us, yet more worth the labor, not to withhold the service of our speech from her through whose providence we receive the daily nourishment of the body.

### 6. After her husband’s death, Saint Cunegund devotes herself to pious works. Her letter

When her Henry, ever the most patient guardian of her chastity, being at the point of death, entrusted her as a virgin to his own people—as he had led her into Christ—and, having been transferred to the heavenly joys for which he had continually sighed [Col. 0209B], she devoted herself entirely to the Lord, as always. She did not cease to call upon him to be present for her chastity, her needs, and her salvation; for her churches; and for the sons whom she had gathered to him in Christ. She summoned him through vigils, persisted in prayers, lived by day the active life with Martha and by night the contemplative life with Mary.

Whoever wishes to know with what generosity of almsgiving and with what persistence in prayer she labored for the soul of her blessed deceased husband may learn it from the following page, which she herself composed and wrote—for she was as skilled in distinguishing letters as in the other arts, and in embroidering sacred vestments with gold and gems:

> **Cunegund, by divine dispensation empress in name only, to the especially beloved congregation at Confugia, whatever is proper to just affection.**
>
> I think I would more easily bear the burden of my own adversity if I saw your affairs safe and unharmed. For although my mind is shaken on every side by the stormy waves of cares, the anchor of remembrance of you is not torn from the depths of my heart. And although you are far removed from my eyes, you never depart from my mind.
>
> “Who will separate us from the love of Christ?”—the occurrence of grief, or the distance of separation? Indeed, if the use of my lost resources were granted to me, this will would be proved by the display of a deed. Yet we do not wish the little that, by God’s will, we still possess to be foreign to your admonition, so that the greatness of devotion may be relieved through sharing our smallness.
>
> For when a mother has little, she gives little to her children. Behold, these small gifts of modest expense are sent to you for the refreshment of the flesh, so that you may refresh the soul of your elder Father by the continual nourishment of prayer; for the prayers of so many righteous people, continued with one accord before God, can greatly avail, as James testifies: “The persistent prayer of the righteous is very powerful” (James 5:16).
>
> That just Lord, who loved righteousness, does not refuse to hear an equitable supplication. He will give you, indefatigable intercessors who keep the aforesaid beloved man in remembrance, the reward of salvation that he himself promised when he said: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” [Col. 0210A] (Matthew 10:22).
>
> You see that it is also pleasing in God’s sight if you pray not only for those who, placed in this life, have done you much good, but also for those who have done none. I beg you, therefore, never to cast from your hearts him who loved you as his own and wished this place to flourish through your service.
>
> Also remember my need, always merciful with a cheerful heart, according to the Apostle’s words: “Love without pretence” (Romans 12:9). May your minds, too, grow more and more firm in a certain solidity of mutual charity, so that on the day of tribulation the ears of him who says, “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in their midst” [Col. 0210B] (Matthew 11:20), may hear your cry.
>
> I urge you to merit this in every way, through the one who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

### 7. She puts on the monastic habit. Her pious exercises

Finally, when Conrad succeeded her in the kingdom [Note: [Col. 0209] In that very year, 1024, in which Henry had died], she, relieved of secular cares as she had long desired, summoned the archbishops and bishops on the anniversary of the death of Saint Henry to the dedication of the church at Confugia. There, during the solemn celebration of Mass, most suitably adorned in every imperial garment, the virgin devoted to God came forward before the principal altar and offered to God an incomparable treasure: the cross of the Lord’s wood, small indeed in its material but most great in its power.

When the Gospel reading had been read, in which a little man, climbing the tree, deserved to receive Jesus looking upon him and a blessing from him, she removed the royal purple and, after receiving the priestly blessing, put on the garment of religion—a darker tunic which she had made for herself with her own hands. While many wept for themselves but rejoiced for her, who had now condemned the world in her clothing, her hair was cut—the hair that is still preserved in the same monastery in her honor—and a veil was placed upon her by the bishops. Betrothed with the ring of faith, she joyfully sang:

> “He placed a sign upon my face, and my Lord Jesus Christ betrothed me with his ring.”

Thus consecrated as Christ’s bride to Christ the Bridegroom, when she had joined herself to the most holy fellowship of her daughters, she did not set herself above them as a mother above daughters, but in every service showed herself a servant. Yet, while doing everything, she avoided displaying any individual deed, lest she receive her reward in the present age.

She worked with her hands—for no one was considered her equal in distinguishing vestments with gold and gems, or in making stoles and girdles—knowing that it is written: “If anyone will not work, neither let him eat” (II Thessalonians 3:10). For the Bridegroom she either prayed or sang psalms. She hastened to the thresholds of the church almost unseen. Nothing was more pleasing than her severity, nothing more severe than her pleasantness: sad in laughter, gentle in sadness.

She compensated for the brief span of life with everlasting remembrance. The same place was both her place of prayer and of rest; her manner was always the same, her body unadorned, since she knew that bodily delights must be rejected by the body which shortly afterward would be worked over by worms. You would always see her reading or listening to someone reading.

She showed great devotion toward her companions, frequently visited those lying ill, and anxiously consoled the poor. Moreover, we believe that she performed many more miracles, but that they were suppressed because she always shunned human praise and the oil of flattery. This, however, must be attributed to the negligence of writers or the passage of time, not to any lack of virtues. We have nevertheless judged it worthwhile to insert here the few miracles that we have found in writing or learned from the truthful report of the nuns among whom she served Christ.

### 8. She is illustrious for miracles. She extinguishes a fire

When, after frequent prayer, the handmaid of Christ had surrendered her limbs to sleep on a bed not built up with feathers but spread with sackcloth, a consecrated girl who customarily sat beside her was reading the sacred books. When her reading had continued almost until midnight, she closed her dimming eyes, and the lamp slipping from her hands caught the straw and, with its crackling, awakened the sisters lying nearby.

When the cry caused by the gathering of people arose, Christ’s virgin was shaken from sleep. Seeing the flames wrestling and crackling around her, she turned to the weapons of prayer and, by the sign of the cross, averted the fire without any injury to her garments.

These are your works, Christ, who once confounded the Babylonian king in his fury and, by your power, extinguished the Chaldean fires so that your children might be delivered unharmed [Col. 0211C].

### 9. Concerning her niece Jutta, the abbess

It has seemed appropriate to append here another miracle, as astonishing as it is marvelous, from which you may learn the constancy of her spirit and the severity of her discipline.

She had with her her sister’s daughter, named Jutta [Note: [Col. 0211D] Manuscripts vary in writing this name. The older printed editions have Vitha; manuscripts 2 and Vtham; Hofmannus, Juditha. Miraeus, in *Notitia ecclesiarum Belgii*, p. 148, mentions Juitha, Cunegund’s sister married to Wolfo, and Juta or Muta, her niece and wife of the count of Limburg]. She had raised this girl from her earliest years and instructed her in every discipline, including knowledge of secular letters. The girl followed and consecrated herself to her maternal aunt no less from love of religion than from affection.

When Cunegund saw that she was fully instructed in all things—observing her vigilance in prayers, perseverance in fasts, and patience in everything—she placed her, with the consent and at the request of all, as the first abbess in that very monastery.

Then the virgin mother, receiving her daughter, admonished her for the sake of salvation, repeating the exhortations of the Fathers formerly given to her: she should often speak what was useful and pleasing to God, frequently listen, not abandon the accustomed paths of the religious journey, and trample ever more firmly upon the byways of error and the devil’s fabrications.

She taught that among God’s servants there could be no fellowship between light and darkness, truth and falsehood, disgrace and honor. She warned her carefully lest, by pursuing vanities, she cease to be the temple of God, become a dwelling place of demons, and turn into a monument of the demon [Col. 0212A]. She instructed her to fix her eyes upon God’s gaze and to be the first to do what she taught, so that, with God’s help, she might herself find the fruit of her teaching in heaven.

Repeating these and similar teachings to her again and again with maternal devotion, she began to venerate her as a teacher, as though she were already perfect in every respect.

But once she had obtained premature freedom, the girl gradually fell away from her former strictness. She began to desire softer clothing and richer food, which are nourishment for vices; she became last in the choir, first at table, eager to take part in the girls’ gossip, and more lax in everything.

Because of such frivolity, the holy woman frequently rebuked, entreated, and reproved her, privately among themselves and publicly before everyone, according to the Apostle’s command. But the girl, vainly relying in some way on her aunt’s protection or familiarity, did not reform at all.

One day, while Cunegund herself was following the cross with the community—for it was Sunday—the abbess was absent [Note: [Col. 0212D] That is, she did not take part in the procession which is still customarily held in monasteries before the principal Mass on Sundays]. Cunegund searched for her and found her dining with her peers in a room. Armed with the zeal of piety, she struck her right cheek with her hand, together with a word of correction. The cheek received the shape of her fingers like a kind of seal, and she never lost that mark throughout her life.

It is clear that she endured this deed not only for her own sake but also for the correction of others, so that the sight of it might benefit them and turn them back from their vices to a better way of life.

### 10. A sunbeam supports her glove

This, too, may perhaps seem fabulous to detractors and unbelievable to unbelievers: that the silent elements proclaim her holiness, which she herself wished to conceal from people for the sake of humility.

After the Gospel reading, when she approached the altar according to her solemn custom to offer the sacrifice, she removed the glove from her right hand. Since no one was present to receive it, she threw it aside. A sunbeam entering through the narrow openings of the window caught it and held it up as though serving her, until she returned after the sacrifice and received it.

Something similar is also recorded as having once been shown by divine power in the garment of the blessed man Goar [Note: [Col. 0212D] You will find the *Life of Saint Goar*, where this miracle is described, in the second Benedictine century, around the year 649 (*Patrologia* 121, in Wandalbertus]. Although he was despised by Rusticus, bishop of Trier, he was honored by the supreme majesty through the service of a greater luminary. Thus he was capable of every merit, since he deserved to have as judge the one who is judge of all virtues.

### 11. Her final illness. She rejects royal funeral rites. She dies [Col. 0212D]

She lived fifteen years beyond that holy commitment, admired by all both for her humility and for the reverence of her religion. At last, because of excessive abstinence from food and her unbelievable perseverance in prayer and vigils, her body began to grow weak, and as the illness worsened she gradually failed.

But while her limbs were contracted outwardly by pain, she was strengthened inwardly in spirit, for the praise of God was always in her mouth. She called upon the holy angels, whose life she enjoys here and whose fellowship she now enjoys there. She entreated the apostles and confessors, whose faith and confession she had always maintained. At her departure she summoned the choir of Christ’s virgins, whose emulation had enabled her, while living in the flesh beyond the flesh, to preserve her bed undefiled for Christ. She prayed that all who serve God would be present and come to her aid.

Truly, what is written—“For those who fear God, all things work together for good” (Romans 8:28)—we saw confirmed in the death of so great a virgin. She had not yet breathed out her spirit, nor had she returned her soul, owed to Christ, and already flying rumor, heralding so great a sorrow, was gathering for the funeral not only consecrated virgins and men of various orders but also the populations of the entire city.

Psalms resounded, and the litany for the departing soul shook the entire house [Col. 0213B], where her holy little body lay placed in the midst upon that noble sackcloth of hers.

Meanwhile, as was customary, royal funeral rites were prepared for her as an empress, not the rites owed to a poor little sister; golden coverings were brought forth to be spread over the bier. Then you would see her turn her pale face—which she had formerly shown joyful when her Bridegroom came to her—toward them and refuse them with her hand:

> “This covering,” she said, “is not mine; take it away from here. This ornament belongs elsewhere. With these I was joined to an earthly bridegroom; with those, to a heavenly one. Naked I came forth from my mother’s womb, and naked I shall return there. Wrap this vile material of miserable flesh in these things, and place my little body beside the tomb of my brother and lord, Emperor Henry, whom I now see calling me.”

After saying this, she commended her spirit into the hands of the Lord, and her soul flew back to its creator and ascended, after a long pilgrimage, into its former possession. The earth wept because it had lost a common mother, while heaven rejoiced because it had received a fellow citizen into its fellowship.

### 12. She is buried at Bamberg

At last, when that sacred body had been placed upon the bier, with a long procession of nobles preceding it and many people streaming together from every direction, the joyful funeral procession reached the place at Babenberg destined for her burial, accompanied by that fellowship of the poor who had always been especially familiar to her.

Then you would see people rushing together from everywhere—from abandoned cities, empty countryside, and desolate towns: mothers carrying their little ones in their arms, the sick lying on stretchers hoping to receive the gift of health, and each person considering himself fortunate if he could be joined to the bier or if its shadow happened to fall upon him [Col. 0213D].

At last the body was carried, not without difficulty, into the church of the blessed apostle Peter. There she received a three-day funeral service worthy of her merits and benefits. Her sons, whom she had gathered there into unity in Christ, now secure regarding their mother’s peace but anxious for themselves, sang psalms without ceasing. They rejoiced that, though she had been taken from them for a time, they had received her without fear of loss, in the hope of her perpetual intercession. The mother, looking down from heaven, rejoiced at the affection of her sons.

Thus the sacred body, veiled and clothed in sacred garments, with Christ’s diadem placed upon its head, was laid in its own tomb on the right side, where it is still venerated [Note: [Col. 0213D] Much is inserted here in the Brussels edition concerning a voice heard from heaven when the tomb was opened, commanding Henry to yield the place to Cunegund] [Col. 0214A].

O happy church of Babenberg! You have received the treasure that you had lost. The presumptuous and malicious tongue of detractors was refuted by the testimony of the eyes, since her virginity was proved by facts and her holiness was visibly attested by radiant signs.

### 13. Miracles after her death

Let the faithful Church, which advances the Christian religion—the Church that, as the Lord’s voice testifies in the Gospel (Matthew 12), is called by grace both the mother and daughter of God: mother because, through the example of holy works, she generates children for the Lord; daughter because, through the Son of the Virgin, incarnate for the salvation of the world, she is daily generated by the instruction of the holy Fathers—let her perceive with the ears of both mind and body the salvation sent by the Lord, full of the healing effects of the heavenly chief physician [Col. 0214B].

The creator of the world’s structure, grieving over the human race fallen through disobedience, wished to graft into it a new planting producing the fruit of eternal life, namely the primitive Church, and therefore deigned to send patriarchs and prophets into the world. They fulfilled faithfully the service entrusted to them: using the five senses of the body and the sixth, which is the spirit of prophecy, they proclaimed the mystery of Christ’s incarnation and all that was to be announced concerning him; some through austerity of life, others through various deaths by punishment, serving the one whom they foretold.

Christ, the boundary and fulfillment of these things, proceeded from the womb of the undefiled Virgin according to the counsel of the eternal Father, in order to free humanity. Then, through apostles sent throughout the world, he built upon the planting already begun a new Church, fashioned from the blood poured forth from his body [Col. 0214C]. Imbued with faith in the Holy Trinity and cleansed by the grace of baptism, it offered as its first fruits martyrs, confessors, and virgins of the weaker sex but steadfast in spirit.

Among these was blessed Cunegund, the flower of the church of Babenberg. Together with Saint Henry, who held the Roman Empire, she served the immortal Bridegroom under the appearance of marriage, with the honor of chaste virginity.

Thus the merits of her holiness now appear manifest throughout the world through evident proclamation, because at the place where her holy body rests, the sick, whatever illness afflicts them, receive health.

But so that we may be most cautious witnesses in all things, and so that those who succeed our age and carefully investigate what we write may know at what time the works of healing performed by the aforesaid empress began, we wish, with the Lord’s generosity, to explain as best we can [Col. 0214D].

### 14. A possessed man is freed, and others from various illnesses

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1189, in the second indiction, under Tietmar, the thirteenth bishop of the church of Babenberg, in the fourth year of his pontificate, at the Chains of Saint Peter, we were assured by experience of signs, lest we doubt the holiness of the virgin mentioned above.

For when the people had gathered at the aforesaid place, as usual, for prayer and vigils, there was present a certain demoniac from a village called Dierrut [Col. 0215A] [Note: [Col. 0215D] The Leuven edition has Beyrent; other copies have Beyrrent]. He recognized neither pity nor shrank from crime, and had burned his own son in a fire. Bound with strong ropes, he began to grow so gentle at the tomb of Saint Cunegund that, freed from his furious illness, he praised almighty God. Together with the crowd that stood present, he proclaimed the due praises of her whose merits he recognized as having brought this about for him.

While these things were being performed with solemn devotion by both clergy and people, three contracted persons were placed upon the tomb of the blessed virgin, and by the hand of divine healing all three were raised from the pain of their affliction: one from the suburb, from the hospital of Saint Giles [Note: [Col. 0215D] It was founded at the foot of the Monks’ Mountain by Blessed Otto, bishop of Bamberg, as related in Book I, chapter 27 of his *Life*; according to the following chapter, the monastery was subject to it]; another from the house of Chunrad, provost of the major church; and the third likewise from the house of Otto, a canon of the same church [Col. 0215B].

A paralytic woman, another woman—a nun—who limped on one foot [Note: [Col. 0216D] In the Bamberg transcript she is not called a nun, but a woman who had indicated a secular condition by a mourning garment], and a lame man from the castle called Giet were cured during the very night, after a prayer scarcely completed. A boy whose limbs were so soft that he could almost have been thought to lack bones, and another from Lincendorf, consumed by disfiguring emaciation, received the use of walking and speech, of which they had been entirely deprived.

A girl suffering from sciatica, from Gisenuelt [also Gisfeld], before she had even been brought to the sacred tomb because of the crowd; a boy deprived of the use of his feet through contraction of the nerves; a girl from Nuornberc [Note: [Col. 0216D] The Bamberg copy has “Nuremberg”], whose sole was bent upward and whose knee was contracted; and likewise a girl from the same village who had a withered hand were cured amid prayers and vigils.

### 15. A hanged thief is delivered

A certain man was sentenced to hanging for a horse stolen at the River Werra [Col. 0215C], in a village called Wasegen. Placed in torment, he called upon the ears of the blessed virgin Cunegund with whatever voice he could muster, and perceived that her speedy help was present to him.

By divine power, after the people had departed, the bonds on his hands were loosened. He removed the noose himself, returned to the city, and explained to everyone his deliverance, giving glory to God and to his savior. Brought to us through the faithful testimony of those people, he was entered for a payment of five denarii by his parents, who had vowed it for him earlier, when he was condemned.

Among us, too, a similar sign appeared in the case of a certain servant boy who, while bound, had been thought dead by everyone. For after he had discharged urine—which is a sign of death in such torments [Col. 0215D]—he was restored to the health and life breathed into him, in the presence of all who stood by.

In the same way, two men delivered at Rottenburg, an imperial castle, have reached us through the testimony of many.

### 16. A dead boy is restored to life

I am about to relate things marvelous, though nothing is impossible for God, and perhaps incredible to our age; yet the entire city of Bamberg was not without knowledge of this event.

A woman from the nearby village of Elrin placed her crying infant, who had died within forty days without baptism [Col. 0216A], upon the tomb of the blessed virgin, not without hope of resurrection. I call to witness the one who is the firstborn of the dead and who raises the dead: when the miserable mother, grieving before all, poured out many tears while repeatedly invoking the name of the holy virgin Cunegund, she lifted alive from the tomb the child whom she had placed there lifeless.

Who could restrain himself from tears? Who from praise? There was one voice from everyone, as a great crowd had gathered on Saturday:

> “What is this? How holy she is, how beloved by God! She makes the lame run, the blind see, the mute speak, and even extinguished limbs live again! Blessed is the womb that bore her; blessed by the Lord are the breasts that nursed her!”

From her blessing, so many gifts of grace have flowed into this world now passing away—[Col. 0216B]

### 17. Likewise, a suffocated child

Another sign, similar to this but occurring in a different way, was performed upon a three-year-old boy in the village of Grunberc. He had lain suffocated in a muddy pond from morning until evening. Found and lifted out by women beneath bundles of flax, he was carried all the way home amid the great company of those who wailed.

There, while his parents performed mournful funeral rites throughout the night, a priest came in the morning to complete the duty owed to the dead. The people present, who had already seen and heard many things concerning the signs of the blessed Cunegund, begged with great hope of being heard that her presence might be with them.

In a wondrous manner the boy began to move his ring finger and, to everyone’s astonishment, rose healthy after the space of one hour. The priest himself first came to us as a witness of this event under the stole; then eight soldiers [Col. 0216C] came under oath, with the boy placed in their midst, together with the entire gathered population of his parish.

### 18. Likewise, a girl

A seven-year-old girl in the parish of Liuberstat was accidentally drowned while heedlessly drawing water from a spring. When the people had returned home from the processions with the crosses—for the Rogation days were approaching—they lifted her lifeless from the spring. After a vow had been made in memory of the blessed Cunegund, whom they had shortly before mourned as dead, they marveled to find her alive, not without giving divine praises.

In these three resurrections of the dead, when we have also learned, through the most trustworthy approval of witnesses and the presentation of the children themselves, that two other bodies were restored to the same life at the invocation of the holy empress, who but the Holy Trinity appears to have performed these works? According to the signs that it performs, it later promised its own people that it would perform these and even greater works [Col. 0216D].

### 19. A mute receives his voice

We have judged it not unworthy to hand down to human memory another most renowned event, performed before the eyes of all concerning a mute, with the foremost nobles of the kingdom standing present.

For Christ wished to make the event so clearly manifest through his handmaid that it could scarcely remain hidden from anyone [Col. 0217A]. King Philip [Note: [Col. 0217D] He was born to Frederick Barbarossa and succeeded his brother Henry. He was elected in 1198, though some opposed him and elected Otto [Col. 0218D]. After Philip was killed in 1209, the kingdom remained with Otto], had summoned an assembly for his own confirmation—or meanwhile, as he believed would win him greater favor, for the translation of the blessed virgin.

A certain mute servant boy had gathered with a company of reputable men from Pogen, carrying their vessels, since they too were penitents. As the queen was proceeding to the church, when she was solemnly received by the clergy according to custom, a confused clamor of the people arose: they were shouting praises, not for a man destined to die, but for one already living with his Christ.

I call Christ and his apostles to witness: this man, who previously, being mute, had known no tongue, answered each question fluently in the language proper to him.

### 20. The wolf grows gentle

What shall I say about a brute animal whose innate greed for rapine, while it was carrying off prey, seemed to sense that the name of Cunegund had been invoked against it and therefore caused it to cease from its fury?

At evening, a wolf, roaming around the sheepfolds according to its nature, carried a little child incautiously left before the doors into its lair. The child’s mother, awakened by the cries of the others who had been terrified by the wolf, struck her breast with clasped hands and, through many wails, stirred all her fellow citizens to grief.

Although everyone judged it useless to pursue the beast because night was approaching, the mother fled to the church. After the bells had been struck three times, as though for a dead person, she did not cease throughout the night from calling upon the ears of the virgin there for the preservation of her son.

When morning came, the wolf, emerging from the forest, brought back unharmed the little child it had carried away and placed him carefully wrapped in his own skin in a furrow where oxen had plowed the previous day [Col. 0217C]. It sat beside him and kept watch.

When it saw the peasants and plowshares already approaching, it departed gently, as though secure that the child was resting safely. The peasants pursued it with shouts, as is customary. A servant driving the oxen, seeing the skins, said:

> “Look—the covering of the child whom the wolf carried away.”

They ran up and found the little boy sleeping, untouched, with a radiant face. Considering this with great astonishment, they reported it to the citizens and to the mother.

She hurried forward and, bursting into tears of joy, asked where and how he had been. In the simplicity appropriate to his age, he replied:

> “That dog which carried me away gently licked me, laid me in its lap, and made me sleep there all night” [Col. 0217D].

### 21. Miracles omitted

These are the miracles we have just related briefly, together with many others that we pass over because of the fault of excessive length. We do not wish, like a leech, to kill by draining him dry and making him weary the reader whom we have held attentive up to this point. We shall now explain a sign performed by divine action upon a servant boy of about sixteen years.

Although the rest of his limbs were well arranged according to nature, he was afflicted in the principal part, the head, by such a severe disorder that without interruption he struck it against the wall whenever one was near. He beat his chest with his chin and struck his shoulders from time to time. He never remained in the same position, nor did he ever manage to take food or drink except perhaps occasionally; at times he poured out words.

If he happened to fall asleep, you would see him collapsed in such a way that sometimes his head struck the earth and sometimes the sky. And, pitiable to say, although everyone fled from him because he was horrible to look at, each person wished to see him.

Known by reputation before he was known by sight, he came to us and was supported for some time by receiving alms from house to house. When the ruler of the synagogue saw him, he said to the Christians:

> “If your Cunegund cures this man, she will be able to attach me to Christ and to your faith.”

But what the Apostle says—“Jews demand signs” (I Corinthians 1:22)—was demonstrated in this Jew. On the Tuesday of the Lord’s Resurrection, while the sufferer was held in healing sleep upon the tomb of the life-giving virgin [Col. 0218B], he was touched by an invisible hand and, healed there, departed amid the greatest astonishment and praise of all.

But the unhappy Jew did not depart from his unbelief, and for it he would suffer the eternal fires.

22. Approved by a Pope.—I shall add one final matter, although it was not the last of her signs. For the earth around her tomb, collected by the faithful, was often transformed into the appearance of the brightest incense, or even of the purest grain. Concerning this, Pope Innocent, in a sermon delivered to the people in the Lateran palace, recalled the merits of her life and the distinction of her miracles, and added:

“Rightly, dearest brothers, is the dust with which the clod of this most holy virgin, buried in accordance with the due of humanity, is covered transformed into incense and grain. For, while she lived, restraining herself from what was permitted despite her fragile sex and abstaining from what was forbidden, she offered the Lord an undefiled holocaust; rich toward Christ but poor for herself, she daily feeds Christ’s poor under the profession of various orders and sexes. Rightly, therefore, she is to be inscribed in the catalogue of the saints, since she always strove to imitate the life of the saints. Accordingly, we have appended to this sermon of ours the Collect that we composed, together with the office of the entire Mass, and by apostolic authority have ordered it to be sung in all churches in honor of so great a virgin.”

23. The Author’s Epilogue.—It is enough, most prudent charity of yours, to have said these very few things from among the innumerable virtues and signs of the most holy virgin Cunegund; if anyone were to review them fully, the page itself would run out before the subject.

O blessed woman, worthy of praise, who despised the kingdom of the world and all the adornment of the age for heavenly adornment! She chose Christ as her bridegroom, legally joined to a royal husband but not carnally joined. She trod upon fire to prove her virginity among royal marriage chambers and to clear herself of the charge of disgrace cast upon her by the envious. Since she did not await offspring destined to die, her chaste generation endures, never to suffer the loss of succession, since the Church in her children continually receives increase in divine praise through her almsgiving. Many signs declare that she lives even after death with her Christ, whom she loved, in whom she believed, and whom she cherished. In memory of her, the blind receive sight, the dead life, the mute speech, and obstructed ears hearing.

24. How great, then, do we believe that woman to have been who, while alive, practiced these things alone and without a witness, avoiding vainglory, when we have seen with everyone looking on that she performed such great signs after death?
