Let us therefore transfer inwardly to ourselves these signs that we marvel at outwardly; let us correct our life and conduct, so that, if we are not worthy of the company of the virgin, we may at least receive this reward through the virgin: that, after descending along the paths of vice, we have escaped so great a punishment of sins.

This little book teaches the deeds of the virgin Cunegund.

Yet it is silent about more that should be said, while it fears that the boat may be submerged in the stream,

and that the beast that touches the mountain dies.

[Col. 0219B] But what the tongue is silent about, signs speak on behalf of the virgin;

signs so frequent speak of her fame and praise,

when the desired care of salvation comes to the blind,

the mute, and the lame; when sickness departs and fever withdraws,

life returns, and mottled skin recovers its color.

[Col. 0220A] He who can grant all things to virginity was able to do this,

he who can move mountains for faith.

Under the law of a husband, married to a man, the virgin wishes to remain hidden;

betrothed and pledged, yet inviolate to her bridegroom,

she chose Christ as the husband whom she would have within her heart.

The virgin keeps faith; the matter became clear when tested by fire.

Learn marriage, celibate one, where there is no pleasure:

those who keep the laws without mingling,

esteem as nothing all things that will soon collapse,

here sowing seeds in the hope of fruits amid sorrow,

will reap long joys and follow the Lamb in white garments.

We pray you, most holy virgin, most glorious empress: you who sprinkled the earth with the works of your mercies and the heavens with the flowers of your virtues, assist your people who are tossed about in the world; drive away the stormy tempests of those who oppose them by your prayers; and, when vices have been driven away, grant all devoted to you to rejoice perpetually in your benefits and merits. Grant also that all who write or read this text of the faithful’s lesson may not be deprived of the fruit belonging to their share of devotion. Amen.

[Col. 0219]

## Pope Innocent III’s Bull on the Canonization of Saint Cunegund

Innocent, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Theumo [Note: Thiemo succeeded Poppo, or Potto, in 1192, and relinquished the see in 1201], bishop, and to his beloved sons, the chapter of Bamberg: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Since, according to evangelical truth (Matt. 5:15), no one lights a lamp and places it under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, so that all who are in the house may see it, it is both pious and just that those whom God crowns and honors in heaven for the merit of their holiness should be praised and glorified by us on earth through the duty of veneration—since it is rather he who is praiseworthy and glorious in his saints who is praised and glorified in them. For piety has the promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come, as the Lord says through the Prophet: “I shall give you to all peoples for praise, glory, and honor” (Deut. 26:19); and as he promises in his own words: “The righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. 13:43).

For, in order wonderfully to manifest the power of his virtue and mercifully to accomplish the cause of our salvation, God frequently honors in this world the faithful whom he always crowns in heaven, producing signs and wonders at their memorials, through which heretical perversity may be confounded and the Catholic faith confirmed. Therefore, dearest ones, we give almighty God as many thanks as we can, though not as many as we ought, because in our days he visibly renews signs and powerfully works miracles for the confirmation of the Catholic faith and the confusion of heretical perversity, causing those who have maintained the Catholic faith in heart, mouth, and deed to shine with miracles.

Among these was Cunegund, of blessed memory, Augusta, empress of the Romans, who once lived in the world and excelled in great merits, but now, living in heaven, shines with many miracles [Col. 0220B], so that her holiness may be proved by certain indications.

Although, for someone to be a saint before God in the Church triumphant, final perseverance alone is sufficient, as the Truth testifies, saying: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 10:22); and again: “Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life” (Rev. 2:10), nevertheless, for someone to be regarded as a saint by human beings in the Church militant, two things are necessary: the virtue of conduct and the virtue of signs—that is, merits and miracles—so that each may bear witness to the other. For neither merits without miracles nor miracles without merits fully suffices to provide testimony of holiness among human beings. Sometimes, after all, Satan’s angel transforms himself into an angel of light, and some people perform their works so that they may be seen by human beings. The magicians of Pharaoh once performed signs, and the Antichrist will eventually perform wonders, so that, if possible, even the elect may be led into error. But when sound merits precede and evident miracles follow, they provide a sure indication of holiness, so that they lead us to venerate the person whom God displays as worthy of veneration both through preceding merits and through subsequent miracles. These two things are more fully gathered from the words of the evangelist, who, speaking of the apostles, said: “They went forth and preached everywhere, while the Lord worked with them and confirmed the word by the signs that followed” (Mark 16:20).

When the merits and miracles of the aforesaid empress had come, through your report, to the hearing of Pope Celestine [Note: This is Celestine III, created on 14 April 1191; he died on 8 January 1198 and was immediately succeeded by Innocent III], my predecessor, so that he might gain fuller knowledge of them, he entrusted their investigation by apostolic letters to our venerable brothers, the bishops of Augsburg and Eichstätt and the bishop of Würzburg, of blessed memory, and to his beloved sons, the abbots of Ebrach, Langheim, and Heilbrunn [Col. 0221A].

[Note: Ebrach, commonly called Ebrach, is a most distinguished Cistercian monastery of Franconia, situated in the diocese of Würzburg. Langheim likewise belongs to that order, but lies in the diocese of Bamberg itself. It was founded by Saint Otto, bishop of Bamberg, as was the following monastery, Heilbrunn, also of the Cistercian order.]

After his death, miracles began to become so manifest and so numerous that, through both their evident character and their frequency, her holiness was proclaimed by everyone as virtually notorious, as was recently disclosed to our apostolate by many testimonial letters from bishops, abbots, provosts, princes, and many others.

Accordingly, your beloved sons D., abbot of Michelfeld [Note: Michelfeld, otherwise called *Michaelis Campus*, is a distinguished monastery of our order founded by the same holy Otto. Bucelinus gives a catalogue of its abbots in *Germania sacra*, from which it is clear that at that time Adalbert was abbot of the place. Hence the letter D may here signify *domnum*, “lord”], Gundel, dean, Conrad, custodian, Mark, archdeacon, Herman, senior subdeacon of your principal church, Lupold, deacon of Saint Stephen, Burchard, deacon of Saint Mary, Henry, priest of Saint Michael, and Henry, subdeacon of Saint Mary, came from your side to the apostolic see and humbly petitioned us and our brothers that, from the fullness of the power that Jesus Christ granted to the most blessed Peter, we might deign to inscribe the aforementioned empress in the catalogue of the saints and decree that henceforth her memory be celebrated among the saints by all the faithful, since this sublime judgment belongs only to him who is the successor of blessed Peter and vicar of Jesus Christ.

We therefore recognized that this judgment truly had to be considered more sublime than all other judgments, and in examining it we wished to exercise complete caution. For this reason, we bound the aforementioned men by the sanctity of an oath, so that they might tell us the pure truth about the matter. Having sworn, they said that, as they knew from widespread report and solemn written testimony, blessed Cunegund had been married to Saint Henry the emperor, but had not been carnally known by him. Therefore, when the emperor was at the point of death, he said concerning her to the princes and relatives:

“As you entrusted her to me, so I return her to you. You gave me a virgin, and I return her a virgin.”

She therefore consecrated her virginity to the Lord and kept it undefiled. Thus, when at some time, through the instigation of the enemy of the human race, a suspicion had arisen against her, she walked barefoot over red-hot plowshares in order to demonstrate her innocence, and came away unharmed.

Likewise, the holy emperor Henry and this distinguished empress Cunegund founded and endowed the church of Bamberg from their own resources. Out of the fervor of their devotion to the apostolic see, they offered it, with all its appurtenances, to blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, paying him an annual census as a sign that it belonged by right to the Roman Church [Col. 0222A]. They also bestowed many other benefits upon pious places and venerable churches, making Christ their heir.

They reported these and other matters concerning her merits. Concerning her miracles, they asserted that, in their presence and before their eyes, the blind at the memorial of this virgin recovered sight, the lame walking, the mute speech, and the deaf hearing; that those afflicted by other illnesses frequently and visibly obtained complete health; and that—a wonder of extraordinary novelty and a new miracle—the dust taken from her tomb was often changed into grain.

We, therefore, having been made more certain of her many and great merits and miracles not only by testimonies but also by witnesses, and since, according to the Prophet, God is to be praised in his saints, with the counsel of our brothers and of many bishops present at the apostolic see, inscribed the blessed virgin Cunegund in the catalogue of the saints and decreed that her memory should be celebrated among the saints.

Therefore, we admonish and exhort your whole community in the Lord, commanding by apostolic letters that you humbly and devoutly observe what we have solemnly and carefully established, so that through her merits and prayers we may obtain indulgence from the most merciful Judge. We have also issued the Collect and the other prayers to be said in her commemoration, which we have thought proper to append on this page:

### Prayer

Almighty and merciful God, who exclude no sex from your glory and reject no condition, we humbly beseech you: just as, after the height of earthly imperial power, you granted your blessed virgin Cunegund the throne of the heavenly kingdom, so, through her merits and prayers, grant also to us, your servants, the rewards of eternal happiness. Through the Lord.

### Secret

We offer you, Lord our God, this sacrifice of praise, imploring your clemency, so that through the power of this sacrament, with your blessed virgin Cunegund interceding, you may both free us from sins and protect us from dangers. Through the Lord.

### Postcommunion

May the sacrament of human redemption, which we have offered to you, Lord, in honor of blessed Cunegund, make us acceptable to you, so that through this gift—which we have received from what is yours and which you have accepted from what is ours—we may always live in union with you, who are with the Father.

Given at the Lateran, on the third day before the Nones of April, in the third year of our pontificate.

[Col. 0223]

## Addition to the Life of Saint Cunegund

*Monumenta Germaniae historica*, *Scriptores*, vol. IV, p. 791.—“In the Munich manuscript among the Ranshofen manuscripts, no. 40, parchment, thirteenth century, the following items concerning Cunegund, who had possessed the estate of Ranshofen, and concerning her family are read. They were copied by the distinguished Föringer and contain much that is new and highly worthy of notice.” Thus D. G. Waitz in the prolegomena to Saint Henry.

[Col. 0223A]

On the sixteenth day before the Kalends of March: the ordination of the emperor Henry and the empress Cunegund.

On the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March: the empress Gisila, mother of Saint Henry the emperor, died.

On the sixth day before the Kalends of March: the arrival of the holy Cross at Confungen.

On the third day before the Kalends of March: Henry, duke and brother of the empress Cunegund, died.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1033, in the third indiction, on the fifth day before the Nones of March, the lady Cunegund, Augusta empress, of worthy memory, died.

On the sixth day before the Nones of May: Theoderic, bishop of Metz and brother of the empress Cunegund, died.

On the sixth day before the Nones of May: Ermindrut, her sister, abbess, died.

[Col. 0223B] On the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June: Gisilbert, brother of the empress Cunegund, was killed and died at Pavia.

On the second day before the Nones of July: Conrad, Augustus emperor and father of the emperor Henry, died.

[Col. 0224A] On the third day before the Ides of May: Liukart, countess and sister of Cunegund the empress, died.

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1024, in the seventh indiction, on the third day before the Ides of July: the passing (*transitus*) to the translation of Saint Henry the emperor. On the same day, the church of Confungen was dedicated, when the lady Cunegund, Augusta empress, was veiled.

On the fourth day before the Kalends of April: Dietmar, father of the abbess Uota, died.

On the thirteenth day before the Kalends of October: Abbess Uota, daughter of the sister of the empress Cunegund, died.

On the second day before the Ides of October: Henry, son of the brother of the empress Cunegund, died.

On the fifth day before the Kalends of November: Count Sigefridus Kunuz, father of the empress Cunegund, died.

[Col. 0224B] On the Ides of December: the lady Hedwig, countess and mother of the empress Cunegund, died.

On the same day, the empress Agnes, her kinswoman, died.

# The Laws and Constitutions of Saint Henry, Emperor Augustus

(*Pertz, Monumenta Germaniae historica*, Laws, vol. II.)

[Col. 0223]

## Note

With the help of Muratori, we have collated the laws of Henry II from the Ambrosian, London, Florentine, Viennese, Veronese, and Este manuscripts. There was uncertainty about the year to which they should be assigned; we preferred 1019, on the authority of the Ambrosian manuscript, which indicates the third indiction, rather than the other year that could be taken into account, 1023, which follows more closely upon the Italian expedition of the years 1021 and 1022.

[Col. 0223]

## Laws and Constitutions

Textual apparatus for the preface (the readings are retained because several concern wording rather than merely typography): at *Heinricus*, L, V, Vn, and E have the verse “Husbands rejoice in King Henry’s law”; the whole preface is absent from Fl. At *Dei gratia miserationis*, L omits the words, while V, Vn, and E read *gratiae miseratione* (“by the grace of mercy”). L reads *probabiliumque* (“and of worthy persons”) for *probabilium*; at *acceptione* it has alternatively *actione* (“action”). Amb. has *optumni* in the margin, identified as indiction III, for *auctumni*. Vn has *haerisantiae* and E *erisantiae* for *Elisantiae*. L has *demoraremur* (“were remaining”) for *moraremur*. A has *Straburge*, L *transburgie*, and V, Vn, E *transburg* for *Strasburge*. A has *prolatum*, while L reads *perlatu ad nos relatum est* (“it was reported to us by a report”), for *perlatum est ad nos relatione*. A reads *Trauerensis* and V and Vn *Rauenensis* in the list of archbishops. Vn supplies in the margin “*episcoporum quoque … Vercellensis*.” The name *Januensis* is restored from L. E omits *Vulterensis*. A has *uas . . sorum*, corrected to *vasuassorum*, “sub-vassals.” A reads *et* for *ut*, Vn *hominibus* for *omnibus*, and A, V, Vn, E *nostri imperii* for *nostro subjectis imperio*. L omits *jubemus*.

[Col. 0223C] Henry, by the grace of God and by the mercy of the [divine] compassion, Augustus, emperor of the Romans. We wish it to be known to all our faithful, present and future, that, always providing for the commonwealth, we arrange what is fitting with the assent of worthy persons faithful to our empire. When, in the autumn season, *auctumni* [Note: Amb. has *optumni* in the margin, identified as indiction III] in the region of Alsace, *Elisantiae* [Note: Vn has *haerisantiae*; E *erisantiae*], we were staying in the city of Strasbourg, which is called by the common name Strasburg [Note: A has *Straburge*; L *transburgie*; V, Vn, and E *transburg*], for the manifold benefit of our kingdom, many reports were brought to us that at that time there were many people suffering from these dangers. Therefore, coming to the aid of all with appropriate provision, with the testimony of praise of very many faithful who were present with us—namely, the archbishops of Milan and Ravenna [Note: A has *trauerensis*; V and Vn *rauenensis*], and also the bishops of Strasbourg [Note: Vn supplies in the margin *episcoporum quoque … vercellensis*], Piacenza, Como, Vercelli, Parma, [Col. 0225A] Aquae, Genoa [Note: The reading *Januensis* is restored from L], Luni, and Volterra [Note: Absent in E], as well as the Italian margraves and counts, and many nobles, vassals [Note: A originally has *uas . . sorum*, corrected to *vasuassorum*, “sub-vassals”], wise men, and judges—we inserted, among the many matters that concerned the commonwealth, three chapters. In order that they may be observed by all subject to our empire [Note: A, V, Vn, and E read *nostri imperii*, “of our empire”] and held by firm observance, from now and henceforth we establish, order [Note: Absent in L], and firmly command. These are the things that we command to be observed inviolate.

### Chapter 1

Whoever, of whatever nation, has taken a lawful wife [Note: A, V, and Vn read *acceperunt*, “have taken”; in the London manuscript *accepit*, “has taken,” is inserted by a second hand], or shall take one [Note: V and Vn read *acceperint*, “shall take”], if she should happen to die without children of them both [Note: A reads *filiis, filiabus*, “sons, daughters”], the husband shall succeed to his wife and receive all her property.

[Col. 0225B] 2. Whoever, out of greed for property, kills his father, mother, brother, sister, nephew, or any of his relatives [Note: L reads “or another”], either personally or through another, shall have the inheritance of the slain person pass to his other legitimate heirs. But the inheritance of the murderer shall be confiscated to the treasury. He himself shall be subjected to public penance as the bishop orders [Note: L reads “shall perform public penance”]. If the person accused of the crime wishes to deny it, he shall fight personally; nor may he provide a champion (*campionem*; L, V, and Vn spell it *camphionem*) in his place, unless advanced age, youth, or illness prevents him from fighting [Col. 0225C].

At Muratori’s text, old formulae are appended to chapter 2, which we have thought it worthwhile to reproduce here:

“Peter, Martin, who is advocate for the public party, accuses you of having killed Marquard, your father, out of greed, or of having caused him to be killed. This does not please God. Do you wish to challenge him? I do. Let the battle be formally assigned. The pledges for this proceeding must be made with sureties and a tacit penalty. The oaths of that proceeding should be as follows. The advocate shall swear: ‘Concerning the matter of which I have accused you, knowingly I have not accused you wrongfully.’ The accused shall answer: ‘Concerning the matter of which you have accused me, you have accused me wrongfully.’ This response is to be made only until the advocate challenges him to battle.

“But if the advocate does not wish to challenge him, then the accused shall defend himself by oath according to his law, without the advocate first swearing. This is the custom, and it is to apply to all accusations. Both alternatives may be used. If only oaths are to be used, then the accused shall swear according to his law without the advocate’s oath.

“Peter, Martin accuses you of having killed Marculph, his father and your father, out of greed, or of having caused him to be killed. ‘You have accused me wrongfully.’ ‘Do you wish to challenge him?’ ‘I do.’ ‘And do you wish to defend yourself?’ ‘I do.’ Let the battle be formally assigned.

“If the accuser does not wish to challenge him, then he shall swear as stated above, and the accused likewise as above. The compurgators shall swear: ‘What the accused has sworn, he has sworn truly—so help me God.’

“The following penalty threatens both parties: for the defeated advocate, that he lose his hand or redeem it; and likewise for the relative; for the accused, that he not have the inheritance of the slain person; that he lose his own property, pay the ban, lose his hand or redeem it—that is, pay the *widrigild*—and be subjected to public penance as the bishop orders. But if the dispute is ended by oaths on both sides, no penalty shall threaten them. If the advocate or relative has sworn and the defendant has not dared to clear himself, then he shall suffer the aforementioned penalty, except for the *widrigild*.”

3. Whoever [Note: Omitted in A] kills a person within a truce or after the kiss of peace has been given [Note: L places *vel*, “or,” after *datum*, “given”], and wishes to deny it, shall fight personally; nor shall he provide a champion (*campionem*; L, V, and Vn have *camphionem*) in his place, unless he is as stated above [Note: V omits *sit*; E has *sicut*; A has *nisicut*, corrected to *nisi ut*; L reads *superius*, “above”]. If he is convicted, he shall lose the hand with which he committed the homicide [Col. 0226B].

Old formulae:

“Peter, Martin accuses you of having killed Donatus, his father, within a truce or after the kiss of peace had been given. ‘You have accused me wrongfully.’ ‘Do you wish to challenge him?’ ‘I do.’ ‘And do you wish to defend yourself?’ ‘I do.’ Let the battle be formally assigned.

“The oaths of that proceeding are as follows. The accuser shall swear: ‘Concerning the matter of which I have accused you, namely that you killed my father Donatus within a truce or after the kiss of peace had been given, knowingly I have not accused you wrongfully—so help me God.’ The accused shall answer: ‘Concerning the matter of which you have accused me, namely that I killed your father within the truce, you have accused me wrongfully—so help me God.’

“If the accuser does not wish to challenge him, then the dispute shall be ended by oaths, as we said above. A penalty threatens both parties: the accuser, if defeated, shall lose his hand or redeem it; the accused shall pay the ban, lose his hand, and make compensation for the homicide according to the law.”

[Col. 0225]

# The Pavia Laws of Saint Henry

(1 August 1022.) They survive in the acts of the synod of Pavia held by Benedict VIII, inserted by Cossart from a codex damaged at the end, in volume IX of the Paris collection of councils, 1671.

## The Pope’s Address

[Col. 0225B]

“Common honor, common grief, etc. … Therefore, with God as author, and with our princes Peter and Paul, while our most glorious son H., ever Augustus, flourishes, and with the approval of our brothers and all our fellow priests, let us remove this error from the world and instill this understanding in every age, banishing all doubt, so that this plague may never again sprout up at any time, nor may posterity ever doubt without cause in matters of this kind. And so that what we establish may henceforth remain firm and reach the ends of the earth to be preserved, the entire substance of this judgment will be confirmed by this form of our decree, with our brothers and fellow bishops subscribing.”

1. That no one in the clergy may touch a woman. No priest, no deacon, no subdeacon, and no one in the clergy may admit a wife or concubine, since no layman either is permitted to know a woman except his wife. If anyone does so, let him be deposed according to ecclesiastical rule. Nor, according to the human laws long established and received, should anyone have any place of honor in the people [Note: Perhaps “any administration,” according to Cossart].

2. That a bishop may have no woman and live with none. Just as a bishop shall have none, so he shall live with no woman at all. If he does so, then, in accordance with both our regulations and the secular laws, he shall be deprived of the honor of which he has made himself unworthy.

3. That the children of clerics, who are servants of the Church, shall be servants of the Church with all acquisitions. The sons and daughters of all clerics of every rank, born from any free woman to whom they may have been joined in any manner, shall, together with all property acquired through anyone’s hands, be the personal servants of their own church, and shall never leave the service of the Church.

4. That no judge may promise freedom to the children of clerics who are servants of the Church. Whoever judges that the children of clerics who are servants of the Church, born of any free woman, are free, let him be anathema, and let him have in judgment what he has done, because he has taken from the Church what he did not give.

5. That the servants of the churches may acquire nothing through the hands of a free person. No servant of the Church, whether in the clerical or lay state, concerning whom it belongs to us and our brothers to judge, may purchase or acquire anything in any way through the hands or under the name of any free person. Whoever does so shall be beaten without possibility of evasion [the supplied text has *in evasibiliter*], and shall be held in prison until the entire Church receives the written instruments [Note: One manuscript reads *omnis*, “all,” rather than *omnes*, “the entire”].

6. That the person through whose hands the servant receives a charter shall make settlement with the Church. That evil free man, who has been made the devil’s servant, through whose hands the Church’s thieving servant acquired whatever it may have been, shall either provide the Church with complete security or be regarded as accursed among the Church’s thieves and sacrilegious persons.

[Col. 0227D] 7. That no judge or notary shall write charters by which the servants of the Church acquire property through the hands of a free person. Judges or notaries who write such unlawful charters and presume to register in the name of some free person property purchased for the price of Church servants or bestowed through some gift shall be struck with anathema. Nor shall the person who was not ashamed to attack the Church, the mother of the palace, be honored at court.

We wish this testament of the Church of God, a God-authorized sanction against evil-doers, to be confirmed and strengthened by the law of the edict of our beloved son H., Augustus, and to be inserted and recorded in the human laws. We all jointly pray and beseech that throughout the breadth of his empire it may be received, maintained, and judged at all times by public authority. For, God willing, it will endure forever if what ecclesiastical authority prohibits is destroyed by public force. Nor will factional persons conceal knowledge of this decree, which, inscribed in everyone’s books, will fly from mouth to mouth; nor will they think it safe to attempt with impunity what they know to have been condemned by public severity.

I, B., pope [Note: Benedict VIII], have subscribed this synodal statute of the eternal City.

I, A., archbishop of the holy Church of Milan [Note: Aribert], have subscribed.

I, R., bishop of the Church of Pavia [Note: Raynaldus], have subscribed.

I, A., bishop of Como [Note: Albericus], have subscribed.

I, L., bishop of the Church of Turin [Note: Landulfus], have subscribed.

I, P., bishop of the Church of Tortona [Note: Petrus], have subscribed.

I, Leo, catholic bishop of the Church of Eusebius [Note: That is, the Church of Saint Eusebius of Vercelli. The same Leo subscribed in a placitum of the same year and elsewhere: “Leo, servant of Eusebius,” in Muratori, *Scriptores*, I.II, p. 498], have subscribed.

[Col. 0228C] Enacted at Pavia, on the Kalends of August, while our lord H., most glorious Augustus, was reigning, through the hand of our brother, the bishop of Vercelli.

## The Emperor’s Reply

I can deny you nothing, most holy Pope B., to whom through God I owe everything, especially when you ask what is just, offer what is honorable together with your just brothers, and summon me into the fellowship of holy solicitude so that we may share not only the labor but also the joy. Therefore I rightly owe abundant thanks to your holy episcopate, which both beneficially orders the Church and has vigilantly begun the work of correction against the incontinence of the clergy, from which all evil has arisen over the earth as though from the north.

Everything that your fatherhood has synodally established and reformed as necessary for the restoration of the Church I, as a son, praise, confirm, and approve. And, so that everyone may be more ready, with God’s help I promise to observe it inviolate. By this authority of ours, before God and the Church, together with the senators of the land, the members of the palace, and the friends of the commonwealth, we strengthen it so that it may endure forever, always be received among the public laws, and be solemnly inscribed in human laws, while the Church lives and is destined through God’s grace to prevail.

## Chapters

1. That no one in the clergy may touch a woman. No one of any rank in the Church may presume to have a wife or concubine, nor dare to live in one house with a woman. If he does so, preserving the equity of Augustus Justinian (Novella 123, chapter 14), he shall be handed over to the curia of the city of which he is a cleric. For he will rightly remain in the curia—that wretched man whom the rule of the Church, after deposing him, has expelled from the Church.

2. That no bishop may have a woman or live with her. A bishop shall never share a roof with any woman, nor share a bed with one. If he does so, he shall be deposed in accordance with the Church’s ancient and modern judgment. The greater the rank, the graver the fall will be.

3. That the children of clerics, who are servants of the Church, shall be servants of their own church with all acquisitions. The children of all clerics and of servants of every ecclesiastical rank, born of whatever woman to whom they may have been joined in whatever manner, shall be servants of their own church, together with all acquired property. Since they are and will remain servants, they must never leave the service of the Church. Whatever they acquire through the hands and written instruments of any free person, we restore to the Church as its own property. For the Church shall claim as its own right everything that a servant of the Church has acquired by any device; nor shall it grant to anyone, according to fictitious pretenses, the adulterous freedom that drags the body into disgrace and the soul into servitude.

4. That no one may presume to judge the children of clerics, servants of the Church, free. Whoever henceforth judges them to be free, gives judgment on their behalf against the Church, fails to receive this chapter established by the authority of the holy Church [Note: Cossart conjectured this reading; the manuscripts have *nostrae*, “our” or “of us”], fails to write it in his books, and fails to judge according to this chapter that the children of clerics from the household of the Church are its own servants, with the Church’s customary right always prevailing, shall be stripped of his property and condemned to perpetual exile. There, just as he will never have any law by which to judge, so he will have no hope of returning.

For it is not surprising, but entirely just, that the man whose office has been lost should live in bodily exile, when the Church, because he has lost God, has struck him with anathema. Their mothers, however, who sell their freedom through adultery, shall first be punished in the forum and made an example, and afterward shall be exiled by the judgment of the Church and of us. For if they remain in the neighborhood, their wickedness will scarcely ever or never cease.

5. That the servants of the Church may acquire nothing through the hands of a free person. Servants of the Church may, as our own servants, acquire things justly, and they have been permitted to do so; but at no time will they be permitted to contract any written instruments through the hands of a free person. If anyone does so, he shall be restrained by the judgment of the Church as its servant. If the matter belonged to our judgment, he would be assigned as a fugitive.

[Col. 0230B] 6. That judges or notaries shall not write charters by which the servants of the Church acquire property through the hands of a free person [Note: This has been corrected by Cossart; the manuscripts read “inscribe”]. As for judges and notaries, whose conduct is our concern, if henceforth they produce such writings, we cut off the right hand that wrote against the Church. Thus the man who refused, while whole, to judge the truth at the palace shall, maimed in the forum, correct others concerning falsehood.

7. That the person through whose hands the servant of the Church received charters shall make settlement and provide security to the Church. That man, accursed by God and human beings, through whose powerless hands and empty name the servant of the Church fraudulently received written instruments, shall, under oath and upon returning those same instruments, be compelled to make complete settlement with the Church according to what is established, so that the weapons of all lawsuits may be laid to rest. Immediately the pen of proscription will pursue him, whom our mother and teacher, the Church, has wounded with the sword of malediction.

### Subscription

I, H., by the grace of God Augustus emperor, have established, confirmed, and decreed that this constitution of perpetual law shall always remain valid, with the counsel of our lord Pope B., at the urging of a very large gathering of bishops, with God as author; and I have asked the leading men of my empire to confirm it.

I, O., margrave, was present and confirmed and praised this law, entirely necessary to the world and restoring to the Churches the eyes that had been taken away.

I, R., margrave, was present and praised it.

Ego O., count palatine, was present and approved. [Note: [Col. 0229D] The remaining names have perished.]

[Col. 0229]

## Constitution of Saint Henry of Rimini. (Dated 4 April)

(Apud Mansi, *Councils*, vol. XIX, col. 357.)

[Col. 0229D] Since it is provided by the laws that no cleric should presume to swear an oath, while elsewhere it is found written that all principal persons must, at the very beginning of a lawsuit, undertake the oath against malicious prosecution, the matter has come into doubt for certain legal experts: whether clerics ought to give an oath, or whether it is permissible to delegate this duty to other persons. For that constitutional edict in which clerics are forbidden to swear appears to have been promulgated by the Emperor Marcian [Marcianus] for the clerics of Constantinople; therefore it is not believed to pertain to other clerics.

Therefore, so that this doubt may be completely removed from everyone, we have decided to interpret that constitution of the divine Marcian [Marcianus] so that it is judged generally to apply to the clerics of all churches. For since the divine Justinian rightly decreed that the canons of the Fathers ought to have the force of laws, and since certain canons of the Fathers are found to provide that clerics should not dare to swear, it is fitting that the entire clerical order should, beyond doubt, be considered exempt from giving an oath. Accordingly, while preserving the intention of both divine and human law, we decree that neither a bishop, nor an abbot, nor a presbyter, nor a cleric of any order, nor any monk or nun, in any controversy—whether criminal or civil—shall be compelled by any means to undertake an oath; rather, they may delegate this duty to their suitable advocates.

### Doubts

[Col. 0231]

## Judgment of Saint Henry concerning the marriage of clerics. (In the year 1019, March)

### [Note]

We present it from the manuscript of the ducal library of Wolfenbüttel, among the Helmstedt manuscripts no. 32, in parchment folio, in which it is recorded by a hand of the eleventh century; from there Mader also published it in his *Brunswick Antiquities*. Since, however, it should be regarded not as a charter written in proper and formal form, but only as a record of an event, composed after Henry had already died, we have decided to include it especially in this place. The year 1025 indicated in the charter conflicts with Bernward’s earlier death; accordingly, we have judged that the matter, also discussed at the assembly of Pavia, should be assigned to the year 1019, when Henry stayed at Goslar in March. From the same manuscript one may add Bernward’s constitution of the year 1020, written by an eleventh-century hand.

[Note: [Col. 0231B] In the name of the holy Trinity. Bernward, humble bishop of the holy church of Hildesheim, sends greetings of salvation and peace to all brothers and venerable fathers devoted to good cooperation. The legislators have decreed, through synods and public councils, that the several useful ordinances of the holy Church should be established, and have likewise approved that what is right and lawful should be arranged in an equally salutary manner.

Therefore, in the year 1020, on the sixth day before the Ides of October [ [Col. 0231D] M. XX. VI. ID. OCTB. in the manuscript], believing that we were making use of sounder counsel, we judged it fitting to mark everywhere, in the places under our jurisdiction, a memorial of our undertaking, so that, piously accommodating ourselves to one another, we might support one another unanimously in the fear of Christ. For at the present time, alas, because our well-deserved sins require it, no one takes thought or exercises moderation concerning the many evils beneath which the world, endangered more and more each day, is collapsing.

Therefore, so that we might lighten somewhat, as far as possible, the burden of our offenses, we have established publicly and privately that, at the four seasons of the year, when the lawful decrees of the synod are to be enacted, all those belonging to our diocese should assemble from every quarter, gathered within its boundaries, in shared agreement and participation in so great a work, namely those to whom this business is rightly entrusted. For such a decree is recognized as more salutary and more powerful when it is issued with the support of many.

[Col. 0231D] We do not, however, decree that everyone be individually summoned together in one place, since we are well aware that this cannot be done because of many obstacles; especially since human frailty necessarily requires that each person attend daily to the practices by which his livelihood is secured. Thus, for example, there are peasants, upon whom, through various labors, daily service is imposed at home and outside it, so that our own necessary supplies of food may also be provided.

Moreover, there are certain clerics and nuns distinguished by regular observance. Both careful consideration of the weakness of their way of life and the legitimate strictness of their monastic vocation advise against their coming out individually in public or appearing in crowds; still less should they be compelled to wander outside as though by the force of such a statute and thereby be induced more easily to deviate from their accustomed spiritual rigor. Rather, they should strive to labor in the customary service of God.

Having also warned them beforehand with diligent watchfulness, we jointly urge them that, on the appointed days, each according to sex and age, should devote themselves earnestly to the sacred duties of prayers and offerings. Above all, they should implore the supreme Divinity with complete contrition of spirit that he himself may deign to be present at our assembly—he who promises to stand among two or three gathered in his name—and that, by his gracious pardon, something may emerge from our deliberation which may benefit the salvation of those now living and serve suitably for the imitation of those to come. In addition, may the commonwealth be governed well and vigorously, and may the holy Church, fortified until now by the protection of the blessed and glorious Mother of God, be strengthened. May that same Church be defended everywhere from the attacks of the enemy and of those who serve him, whether pagans or wicked Christians.]

[Col. 0231B] The architects of Catholic teaching, laying down what ought to be followed as the foundations of faith, are clearly known to have approved this, whether collectively or separately, so that we may glory in the praise of Christ. Therefore, in the year 1025, at the royal assembly convened at Goslar, specifically in the church adjoining the southern side of the same place, a gathering of the faithful was assembled to consider a matter proposed as salutary and beneficial.

Henry, who at that time was vigorously governing the monarchy of the commonwealth, had taken his place at the head of this assembly. Surrounded on every side by a gathering of bishops—namely, Gero, archbishop of Parthenopolis; Unwan, archbishop of Bremen; Arnolf, bishop of Halberstadt; Benno, bishop of Slavonia [Note: [Col. 0232D] That is, of Aldenburg.]; Thioderic, bishop of Minden [Note: [Col. 0232D] He held the see from 1018 until 19 February 1022.]; Thioderic, bishop of Mimigardevord [Note: [Col. 0232D] He died on 23 January 1022.]; and Ekkihard, bishop of Schleswig—he weighed right and wrong alike in the balanced scales of judgment.

Among the questions debated back and forth, Bernward, bishop of the holy church of Hildesheim, of pious memory, whose office required him to lead this important business, investigated a certain point of uncertainty, namely:

If any bishop, or anyone of whatever rank, having promoted one of his own dependents to the priestly grade, had allowed him to remain subject to his authority according to his will, and had moreover acquired for himself, through gracious kindness, a church belonging either to himself or to another; but if that man, after prosperity had followed, had raised himself above his station through the arrogance of greater merit, and had turned the gift divinely bestowed upon him into a shameful profit, so far as, inflamed by the nobility of his birth, to take a free woman in marriage, on the condition that he should in some way alienate from the service of the lord under whose dominion he himself had been placed the offspring born from her—what, above all, should the unanimous agreement of those men decree concerning the matter?

After these points had been introduced, each of the nobles, according to his assessment of his own ability, engaged in lengthy alternating deliberation concerning the proposed matter. At last, however, when the emperor took the lead in resolving this hesitation, the entire assembly rose in favor of such a decision, and all acclaimed that it was lawful for both the woman herself and her offspring to be subjected to the same yoke of servitude under which he himself had fallen.

They added that the decree of the present compact, sanctioned by the majesty of the Roman Empire, should in no way be dissolved in perpetuity, especially since, with the approval of the universal pope, it promotes the welfare of the holy Church.

[Col. 0233]

## Pact of Saint Henry with Benedict VIII. (Year 1020, April)

### [Note]

The authentic document, which is said once to have been preserved in the Vatican archive, no longer exists. But the first copy of the constitution is found in the canonical collection of Cardinal Deusdedit. Therefore it is useful to reproduce the supposed transcript of the authentic document, which was prepared at the Council of Lyon and reprinted by Borgia in his *Brief History of the Temporal Dominion of the Apostolic See*, appendix, pages 40–43.

The charter closely follows the Ottonian pact, so that only one sentence in particular, copied in Vatican manuscript 1984, departs from it; hence the same judgment must be made concerning both.

[Note: [Col. 0233C] The manuscript reads as follows: “Concerning this, we confirm to you, blessed Apostle Peter, and through you to your vicar, Lord Benedict, supreme pontiff and universal pope, the monastery of Fulda and the consecration of its abbot, together with all the monasteries, estates, and villages which Saint Peter is known to possess in the transalpine regions, except Antesna, Guinneringa, and Wilinbach, which were transferred from the church of Saint Peter to the bishop of Bamberg by a deed of exchange. In return for these, we grant and confirm to the aforesaid church of blessed Peter all that land which we held between Narni, Terni, and Spoleto. Furthermore, we place under the protection of blessed Peter, of you, and of your successors the aforesaid bishopric of Bamberg. Therefore we decree that you shall receive annually from the bishop of that place, by way of tribute, one white horse equipped with a caparison.

And below: ‘In the election of the Roman pontiff, neither free man nor slave should presume to come to it in order to cause any hindrance to those Romans whom the ancient custom established by the constitution of the holy Fathers has admitted to this election. If anyone should presume to act against this constitution of ours, let him be handed over to exile. Furthermore, we absolutely prohibit any of our agents from daring to devise any obstruction at all in the aforesaid election. For we have also determined in every way that those who have once been received under the special protection of the apostolic lord or under ours should rightly enjoy the protection they have obtained. If anyone should presume to violate it against any of those who have earned this protection, let him know that he will incur danger to his life.’ And Henry the emperor subscribed, together with thirteen bishops, four abbots, three dukes, nine counts, and nine nobles.”]

The date of the charter, which was of such importance, could not have been omitted; therefore it is hardly credible that the authentic document reached the Council of Lyon. Moreover, since the charter speaks of the exchange of the estates of Antesna, Wieneringa, and Wilinbach, which is known to have taken place on 8 February 1018, it seems preferable to assign the charter to the meeting of the emperor and pope at Bamberg in April 1020. This is supported by the fact that among the witnesses, Macelinus or Meginhardus was promoted to the bishopric of Würzburg on 2 December 1018, while Heribert, archbishop of Cologne, died on 16 March 1021.

[Col. 0233B] In the name of the Lord God Almighty, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. I, Henry, by the grace of God august emperor, pledge and promise, by this pact of our confirmation, to you, blessed Peter, prince of the apostles and holder of the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and through you to your vicar, Lord Benedict, supreme pontiff and universal pope, that, just as your predecessors until now have held and governed in your power and jurisdiction, so I confirm to you the city of Rome with its duchy, suburbs, all its villages and territories, both mountainous and maritime, its coasts and harbors, and all the cities, castles, towns, and villages in the regions of Tuscany:

Porto, Centumcellae, Cere, Pletia, Marturianum, Sutri, Nepi, Castellum, Gallese, Orte, Polimarzio, Amelia, Todi, Perugia with its three islands, namely the Greater and Lesser islands, Pulvensis [Note: [Col. 0233] Borgia reads *Pulverisim*], and the lake; Narni and Otricoli with all the boundaries and territories belonging to the aforesaid cities; and also the Exarchate of Ravenna in its entirety, with its towns, cities, settlements, and castles, which the lords Pippin, Charles, Louis, Otto, and likewise his son Otto, our predecessors, in pious memory, long ago granted by deed of donation to the blessed Apostle Peter and to your predecessors.

That is: the city of Ravenna, Emilia, Bobbio, Cesena, Forlimpopoli, Forlì, Faenza, Imola, Bologna, Ferrara, Comacchio, Adriano, and Gabello, with all the boundaries, territories, and islands belonging by land and sea to the aforesaid cities; likewise the Pentapolis, namely Rimini, Pesaro, Fano, Senigallia, Ancona, Osimo, Humana, Jesi, Fossombrone, Montefeltro, Urbino, and the territory of Balva; Callis [Note: [Col. 0235] Borgia reads *Collis*], Luciolis, and Gubbio, with all the boundaries and territories belonging to those same cities.

In the same way, the Sabine territory, in its entirety, as it was granted by deed of donation to the blessed Apostle Peter by the aforesaid emperors, our ancestors, namely [Note: [Col. 0235] Borgia adds *et*] in the regions of Tuscany of the Lombards, the castle of Felicitas, Orvieto, Bagnoregio, Ferento, Viterbo, Orte, Martana [Note: [Col. 0235] Manuscript B reads *Martani*], Pletia, Tuscania, Sovana, Populonia, and Roselle, with their suburbs and villages and all their territories and maritime towns, or all their boundaries.

Likewise, from Luna with the island of Corsica, to Suriano, then to Mount Bardone, then to Berceto, from there to Parma, then to Reggio, from there to Mantua, and then to Monte Silicis and the province of Venice; Istria; and also the entire duchy of Spoleto and the duchy of Benevento, together with the church of Saint Christine situated near Pavia, by the Po, four miles away.

Likewise, in the regions of Campania: Sora, Arce, Aquino, Arpino, Teano, Capua, and also the patrimonies belonging to your power and jurisdiction, namely the Beneventan and Neapolitan patrimonies, and the patrimonies of Upper and Lower Calabria. As for the city of Naples, with its castles, territories, boundaries, and islands belonging to it, as they appear to pertain to that same city; and also the patrimony of Sicily, if God delivers it into our hands.

In like manner, the city of Gaeta and Fondi, with all their appurtenances.

Furthermore, we confirm to you the monastery of Fulda, the consecration of its abbot, and all the monasteries, estates, and villages which Saint Peter is known to possess in the transalpine regions, except Antesna, Winiheringa [Note: [Col. 0235] Borgia reads *Vurniteringa* or *Viullmbach*], and Willinbach, which were transferred from the church of Saint Peter to our bishop of Bamberg by a deed of exchange. In exchange for these, we transcribe, grant, and confirm to the aforesaid church of Saint Peter all the land which we held, from our share of the kingdom, between Narni, Terni, and Spoleto.

Moreover, we place the aforesaid bishopric of Bamberg under the protection of Saint Peter, of you, and of your successors. Therefore we decree that you shall receive annually from the bishop of that place, by way of tribute, one white horse equipped with a caparison.

[Col. 0235D] Furthermore, we offer, confirm, and strengthen to you, blessed Peter, and to your vicar, Lord Benedict, and to his successors, just as was done by our predecessors the Ottos for Pope John of blessed memory and his successors, the cities and towns with their fisheries: Rieti, Amiternum, Forcone, Norcia, Valva, and Marsica; and elsewhere the city of Terni with its appurtenances.

We confirm all the provinces, cities, towns, castles, villages, territories, and patrimonies mentioned above to your aforesaid church, blessed Peter, and to your vicar Benedict and his successors, for the preservation of our kingdom and of the entire Christian people, until the end of the age, in such a way that they may hold them in their own right, sovereignty, and jurisdiction.

In the same way, by this pact of our grant, we confirm the donations which Pippin, king of pious memory, and afterward the most excellent emperor Lord Charles, and subsequently the most devout Ottos, freely bestowed upon blessed Peter, the apostle of Christ. We also confirm the tribute, rent, and other payments which used annually to be brought to the palace of the king of the Lombards, whether from Tuscany or from the duchy of Spoleto, as is contained in the aforesaid donations and as was agreed between Pope Hadrian of holy memory and Lord Charles the emperor, when that pontiff confirmed for him, by his own authority, the aforesaid duchies, namely Tuscany and Spoleto, in such a way that each year the aforesaid tribute should be paid to the church of Saint Peter, while our domination over those duchies in every respect, and their subjection to our side, remains intact.

Moreover, as we have said, we have strengthened all the aforesaid names on our side by this pact of our confirmation in such a way that they remain under your right, sovereignty, and jurisdiction, and that neither by us nor by our successors, through any device or contrivance, your power over any part of them shall be diminished or anything taken away from you—namely from the provinces, cities, towns, castles, villages, territories, and patrimonies written above, as well as from the rents and tributes.

Thus we shall neither do such a thing ourselves nor consent to anyone wishing to do it. Rather, we testify that, insofar as we are able, we are defenders of all that is written above—provinces, cities, towns, castles, lands, patrimonies, islands, tributes, and rents—for the church of the blessed Apostle Peter and for the pontiffs residing in his most sacred see, so that they may firmly retain that jurisdiction for their use and administration.

Our power and that of our descendants remain intact in all respects, according to what is contained in the pact, constitution, and binding promise of Pope Eugenius and his successors: namely, that all the clergy and the entire nobility of the Roman people shall bind themselves by oath, on account of the various necessities and the unreasonable harshness which the pontiffs exercise toward the people subject to them, so that these may be restrained; and that the future election of the pontiffs may, insofar as each person’s understanding permits, take place canonically and justly.

The person elected to this holy apostolic government shall not be consecrated pontiff before he has made, in the presence of our agents or of the whole community, a promise for the satisfaction of all and for future preservation such as our spiritual father, the lord and venerable Pope Leo, is known to have freely made.

Furthermore, we have judged that other lesser provisions should be inserted into this work: namely, that in the election of the pontiffs neither free man nor slave should presume to come forward in order to cause any hindrance to those Romans whom the ancient custom established by the constitution of the holy Fathers has admitted to this election. If anyone should presume to act against this constitution of ours, let him be handed over to exile.

Moreover, we prohibit any of our agents from daring to devise any obstacle whatsoever in the aforesaid election. For we have also determined in every way that those who have once been received under the special protection of the apostolic lord or under ours should rightly enjoy the protection they have obtained. If anyone should presume to violate it against any of those who have earned this protection, let him know that he will incur danger to his life.

We also confirm that they are to render just obedience in all things to the apostolic lord, as well as to his dukes and judges in the administration of justice.

For we have recognized that this provision must necessarily be appended to the present constitution: agents of the apostolic lord or of ours are always to be appointed who can report to us annually how each duke and judge administers justice to the people and how they observe this imperial constitution.

We decree that these agents shall first bring to the attention of the apostolic lord all complaints found to have arisen through the negligence of dukes or judges. He shall then choose one of two alternatives: either the wrongs shall immediately be corrected through those same agents, or, after our agent has reported the matter to us, they shall be corrected through agents sent by us.

So that this pact of our confirmation may be believed firm by all the faithful of the holy Church of God and by your people, we have strengthened it by the mark of our own hand and subscriptions, and have ordered it to be authenticated by the impression of our seal.

+ Sign of Lord Henry, most glorious august emperor of the Romans.

# Ecclesiastical Diplomas of Saint Henry, August Emperor

## I. Precept granted by Henry, king of Germany, to the monks of Saint Remigius. (Year 1002)

[Marlot, *Metropolis of Reims*, II, 58.]

[Col. 0237D]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, king by the gracious favor of God.

Since it is acknowledged to be the duty of royal dignity that monasteries dedicated to God and his saints should, for the preservation of the state of holy religion, always be fortified by new privileges against the attacks of all aggressors, therefore we, through the intervention of our beloved wife, namely Queen Cunegund, and also of our faithful bishop Nother, have decided to strengthen by the authority of our royal name the royal document or precept granted by the great Otto to the monks serving God and the holy Remigius, eminent teacher of the Franks, under regular discipline in the suburb of Reims; this we confirm by the royal authority granted to us by God.

Therefore we desire and firmly command that the estate called Cosla, with all its appurtenances belonging by right and ownership to the same blessed Remigius, situated within the boundaries of our kingdom, which in all former times under our predecessors had been held as a benefice, and which the same great Otto, for the security and welfare of his kingdom or empire, assigned to the use of the aforesaid monastery, just as we now restore and release it, shall be held and possessed without anyone’s opposition by the monks serving God and Saint Remigius there. Whatever benefit arises from it, they may add to their own uses as they wish.

No judge or advocate shall have the power to demand anything from it, except what the abbot or monks of the same monastery may have given or permitted. And so that this precept of our authority may remain firm and stable, we ordered this charter to be written and marked with the impression of our ring, and we confirm it below with our own hand.

Sign of Lord Henry, unconquered king.

I, Egilbert, chancellor, acting in place of Willigis, archchancellor, have examined this.

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of September, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1002, indiction I, and in the first year of Lord Henry’s reign. Done at Aachen.

## II. King Henry II grants Godehard, abbot of Niederaltaich, a plot of land situated at Regensburg. (Year 1002, 13 July)

[Ried, *Diplomatic Code*, I, 115.]

[Col. 0239C]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, king by the gracious favor of God.

Let it be known to all our faithful, present and future, how, attending to the pious petition of Abbot Godehard—for he had served us faithfully and was worthy to be rewarded—we have granted by this royal precept, to be held in perpetual right, a plot of land belonging to us, situated within the walls of the city of Regensburg, measuring forty feet in width and eighty in length.

On one side it borders the street leading to the river, and on the other the plot of a certain man named Ruozi. We have granted it to the monastery of the martyr Saint Maurice, over which the same venerable abbot is known to preside at the place called Altaha, together with its boundaries, its rights of exit and return, and all other appurtenances which can rightly and legally be called by any name.

This is granted on the condition that the aforesaid Abbot Godehard or his successors thereafter have free power over the same plot, to possess it or to do with it whatever they wish for the benefit of the monastery. And so that the authority of this grant of ours may remain stable and unshaken, we have strengthened it with our own hand and ordered it sealed with our image.

Sign of Lord Henry, unconquered king. (Monogram.)

[Col. 0240A] I, Engilbert, chancellor, acting in place of Willigis, archchaplain, have examined this.

Given on the third day before the Ides of July, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1002, indiction XV, and in the first year of Lord Henry’s reign.

Done at Bamberg, happily in the name of God. Amen.

With the seal of the majesty intact, impressed within.

## III. King Henry II grants the monastery of Tegernsee a plot of land situated at Regensburg. (Year 1002, 12 November)

[Ried, as above, p. 116, from *Monumenta Boica* VI, 156.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, king chosen by the heavenly governing clemency.

Since it has been granted by God to all mortals, according to the individual will of each person, to be able to store up future goods for their own happiness and enduring hope, therefore we wish it to be known to all the faithful, present and future, that, for the prosperity of our kingdom and the earning of eternal life, at the petition of the venerable Abbot Eberhard, we have given to the monastery of Saint Quirinus one estate in the city of Regensburg, situated beside the market, near the place called Ahachircha, in the county of Ruodpert.

And so that this royal grant of ours may remain firmly with that monastery in perpetual right without any opposition, we have subscribed the sign with our own hand on this charter and ordered it to be authenticated by the impression of our seal.

Sign of Lord Henry, unconquered king. (Monogram.)

[Col. 0240C] I, Egilbert, chancellor, acting in place of Willigis, archchaplain, have examined this.

Given on the second day before the Ides of November, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1002, indiction I, and in the first year of Lord Henry’s reign. Done in the city of Regensburg.

## IV. King Henry grants to the Old Royal Chapel, restored by him, his own village of Duveninga with its appurtenances. (Year 1002, 16 November)

[Ried, as above, p. 116.]

C. In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, king by the gracious favor of God.

If we repair holy places that have collapsed through age or neglect, and if in those places devoted to divine worship we piously provide some means of livelihood, we have no doubt that this will benefit us both in this life and in the eternal life. Therefore let it be known to all our faithful and those of Christ, present and future, how we, together with our beloved wife, namely Queen Cunegund, inside the city of Regensburg, in the royal estate, raised from its foundations a certain chapel which formerly was called the Old Chapel, in honor of the holy Mother of God, and granted it royal freedom by a precept.

To the congregation of canons instituted there in the service of God under an abbot or provost named Tagino, among other provisions for their support, we have granted and by this mark of royal majesty confirmed a village belonging to us, named Duveninga, situated in the Kelsgau and in the county of Magenes, with all the lawful appurtenances of that village, movable and immovable: male and female servants, plots, buildings, cultivated and uncultivated lands, meadows, pastures and common pastures, woods, hunting rights, waters and watercourses, fisheries, mills, roads and trackless places, rights of exit and return, things acquired and to be acquired, and all other things which may rightly be called by any name, together with its equipment and appurtenances.

This is granted on the condition that the congregation of the aforesaid place thereafter have free power over the same estate to do, by common decision, whatever it wishes for its own needs and those of the aforesaid mother church. And so that this grant of ours may remain stable and unshaken, we have strengthened this page of our precept with our own hand and ordered it to be impressed with our seal.

Sign of Lord Henry, unconquered king. (Monogram.)

I, Egilbert, chancellor, acting in place of Willigis, archchaplain, have examined this.

Given on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1002, indiction I, and in the first year of Lord Henry’s reign.

Done in the city of Regensburg itself.

The seal, impressed within, remains intact.

## V. King Henry II grants the bishop of Brixen a plot of land situated at Regensburg. (Year 1002, 16 November)

[Ried, as above, from Resch’s *Annals of the Church of Säben*, III, 701.]

[Col. 0241C]

C. In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, king by the gracious favor of God.

We wish it to be known to all our faithful, present and future, how, because of the intervention and devoted service of our faithful Albwin, venerable bishop of Säben, we have given in ownership to the church of Saint Ingenuinus one farmstead in the province of Bavaria, situated in the city of Regensburg, in the county of Ruotpert, possessed by three men named Azo, Lanzo, and Gotti.

It measures eleven and a half perches in length and six in width. We have granted it with all rights of exit and return and with everything legally and rightfully belonging to the same farmstead, on the condition that the aforesaid bishop and all his successors have power over that farmstead for the use of the aforesaid church, without any opposition from malicious persons, to hold it, exchange it, and do with it whatever they wish.

And so that this grant of our authority, made in accordance with God’s will and for the remedy of our soul, may become firmer, more stable, and more enduring, we have strengthened this page with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed.

Sign of Lord Henry, unconquered king. (Monogram.)

I, Egilbert, chancellor, acting in place of Willigis, archchaplain, have examined this.

[Col. 0242A] Given on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1002, indiction I, and in the first year of the reign of Lord Henry. Done in the city of Regensburg.

With the seal of the majesty intact.

## VI. The royal protection of King Henry II granted to the Lower Monastery. (Year 1002, 20 November)

[Ried, as above, p. 118.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, king by the gracious favor of God.

Just and pious royal consideration ought, wherever opportunity permits, to accommodate something to the churches of God, so that from this they may more readily obtain the rewards of eternal recompense. Therefore let it be known to all our faithful, present and future, how the venerable abbess Ouda, through the intervention of our beloved wife, namely Queen Cunigunda, approached our majesty, humbly requesting that we receive into our royal protection and the safeguard of royal immunity, together with all its appurtenances, the monastery of nuns over which she then appears to preside within the city of Ratisbona. Our revered grandmother, Judith, once raised this monastery from its foundations as an abbey in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God, and enriched the place, among other things, with gifts of estates.

Therefore, assenting to her pious petition for the love of God, by this insignia of our majesty we subject the aforesaid monastery to the perpetual royal and imperial protection of ourselves and of our successors after us. Moreover, we endow it with that excellent liberty which the other royal monasteries throughout the lands of our kingdom are seen to enjoy, so that the nuns devoted there to the monastic life under the rule of Saint Benedict may henceforth preserve more freely and devoutly the life they have undertaken, without disturbance from royal officials or intruding persons.

Accordingly, by royal word and command, we order and firmly prohibit that henceforth any duke, margrave, count, viscount, bishop, or anyone under a bishop, or any public judge or royal exactor, or any judicial person, greater or lesser, exercise any public authority within or outside the aforesaid monastery, or over its places, people, or anything belonging to it; nor may anyone presume to usurp for himself, or for us or our successors, anything from the nuns’ property, except through the advocate whom the present abbess and her successors shall choose and appoint for this purpose. Even he shall impose no other office of authority upon himself in the monastery or its places, nor exact any service, except what the abbess and her holy sisters prescribe for him.

We also confirm to the same monastery whatever was ever transferred or granted there by kings and emperors under the force of a royal charter, or by dukes or other faithful Christians, in whatever county or jurisdiction, together with estates and small holdings, buildings, slaves, mills, watermills on both banks of the Danube, the river flowing before the city, along with all implements and appurtenances belonging to the places. Their names, in part, are these: Schirelinga, Lirundorf, Roggingun, Biberbahe, Linthart, Heroldeslinthart with all their appurtenances; Hardkiricha with its tithes collected from villages everywhere; Salla with the Forest, water, mills, and other appurtenances; in Sinzingun, all that utility belonging there to the aforesaid monastery; Deggindorf with its tithes and customary dues; Berge, situated beside the river Philisa; and Budelshuson with waters, watermills, mills, and plots of land on the rivers Isara and Walechenesbah, with their bridges and all their adjacent lands.

The nuns shall also have the free power, at the death of an abbess, to choose from among themselves an abbess whom, by God’s favor, the rule of a reputable life and conduct has shaped, with the contradiction of all authorities and persons removed. And so that this transfer, confirmation, or liberty of ours may remain stable and unshaken, we have ordered this page of our command to be strengthened by our own hand and impressed with our seal.

Sign of the lord Henry, the unconquered king. (Monogram.)

Egilbert, chancellor, recognized this in place of Willigis, archchaplain.

Given 20 November, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1002, indiction I, in the first year of the reign of our lord Henry. Done in the city of Ratisbona itself.

With the seal of the majesty intact.

### VII. King Henry grants the collegiate church at the Old Chapel of Ratisbona the village of Walchina, situated in the Nordgau. (Year 1003, 20 November.)

[Ried, as above, p. 120.]

[Col. 0243C]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, king by the gracious favor of God.

If we restore holy places that have collapsed through age or negligence, and devoutly provide those devoted there to divine worship with some means of livelihood, we have no doubt that this will benefit us both in this life and in the eternal one. Therefore let it be known to all Christ’s faithful and our own, present and future, how we, together with our beloved wife, namely Queen Cunigunda, raised within the city of Ratisbona, in the royal estate, a certain chapel—once called the Old Chapel—from its foundations as a mother church in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God. Having granted it royal liberty by charter, and having established there a congregation of canons devoted to God under an abbot or provost named Tagino, we transferred among other gifts, for their support, and by this insignia of royal majesty confirmed, one village belonging to us, Walehinga, situated in the Nordgau, in the county of Henry, together with all its lawful appurtenances, movable and immovable: male and female slaves, plots of land, buildings, cultivated and uncultivated land, meadows, pastures and common pastures, woods, hunting rights, [Col. 0244A] waters and their courses, fisheries, mills, roads and trackless ways, incomes and outgoings, things acquired and to be acquired, and all other implements and appurtenances that may properly be called by any name.

This is granted so that the congregation of the aforesaid place may henceforth have free power over the same estate to do whatever, by common decision, it wishes for its own needs and those of the aforesaid mother church. And so that this transfer of ours may remain stable and unshaken, we have ordered this page of our command to be strengthened by our own hand and impressed with our seal.

Sign of the lord Henry, the unconquered king. (Monogram.)

Egilbert, chancellor, recognized this in place of Willigis, archchaplain.

[Col. 0244B] Given 20 November, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1002, indiction I, in the first year of the reign of our lord Henry. Done in the city of Ratisbona itself.

The seal of the majesty, impressed within, remains intact.

### VIII. King Henry II grants the village of Teign, near Ratisbona, to the bishop of Brixen. (Year 1002, 24 November.)

[Ried, p. 121, from Resch’s *Annales Ecclesiae Sabionensis* III, 704.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, king by the gracious favor of God.

Let it be known to all our faithful, present and future, how we, through the intervention of our beloved wife, namely Queen Cunigunda, transferred to our faithful Albuvinus, bishop of the church of Sabiona, a certain estate belonging to us—that is, whatever we have so far been seen to possess on our behalf in the village of Tiginga—together with everything lawfully belonging to it, movable and immovable: male and female slaves, a church, tithes, plots of land, buildings, cultivated and uncultivated land, meadows, pastures and common pastures, woods, waters and their courses, roads and trackless ways, incomes and outgoings, things acquired and to be acquired, and appurtenances and implements of every kind that may properly be named.

This is granted so that the aforesaid venerable bishop Albuvinus and his successors may henceforth hold the aforesaid estate with free authority, convert it to the perpetual uses of their church, and possess it without contradiction from any person or authority, having permission to exchange it and to do with it whatever they please. And so that this transfer of ours may remain stable and unshaken, we have ordered this page of our command to be strengthened by our own hand and sealed.

Sign of the lord Henry, the unconquered king. (Monogram.)

Egilbert, chancellor, recognized this in place of Willigis, archchaplain.

Given 24 November, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1002, indiction I, in the first year of the reign of our lord Henry. Done at Ratisbona.

With the seal of the majesty impressed within.

### IX. Charter of King Henry II by which he grants to Burchard, bishop of Worms, the entire estate that Duke Otto held in that city. (Year 1002.)

[Schannat, *Episcopatus Wormatiensis*, p. 35.]

[Col. 0245A]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, king by the gracious favor of God.

If we enrich the churches of God with goods granted to us by divine providence, we wisely understand that this benefits not only the happier and more stable condition of our kingdom, but we also have no doubt that it greatly assists us in attaining the eternal joys of paradise. Therefore let all our faithful, present and future, know how, for the salvation of the soul of our most beloved lord, the emperor Otto Augustus of blessed memory, and also for the church of Worms, at the worthy petitions of Cunigunda, our beloved wife, and of the venerable bishop of that same church, namely Burchard, we transferred by this royal charter into the proprietary right of the church consecrated in honor of Saint Peter, and of the venerable bishop of that church named above and his successors, the entire estate and ownership which we received as our own right through the firm transfer of our beloved kinsman Otto, also a duke, just as he is seen to have held it within that same city, namely Worms.

This was together with everything lawfully and legally belonging to the same property: plots of land, buildings, roads and trackless ways, incomes and outgoings, waters and their courses, fisheries, mills, and slaves of both sexes, except for the three servants of the aforesaid Duke Otto—namely Syggelone, Ebo, and Hezilino—with their wives, sons, and daughters. The grant is made on the condition that the aforesaid Bishop Burchard and his successors have free power to do with the things written above whatever they wish for the benefit of the Church.

And so that the authority of this transfer of ours may remain stable and unshaken, we have ordered this page, written for that purpose, to be signed with the impression of our seal, having strengthened it with our own hand.

Egilbert, chancellor, recognized this in place of Willigis, archchaplain.

[Col. 0245D] Given 3 October, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1002, indiction I; in the first year of the reign of our lord King Henry.

Done at Bruchsal.

### X. Charter of King Henry II by which he grants the royal ban to the church of Worms in the forest of Forehichi. (Year 1002.)

[Schannat, as above, p. 34.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, king by the gracious favor of God.

Whatever we grant and donate to the churches of God for the love of God, we undoubtedly believe will benefit us in the present and future life. [Col. 0246A] Therefore let the judgment of all our faithful, present and future, know how, at the intervention of Willigis, venerable archbishop of the see of Mainz, and Henry, illustrious bishop of the church of Würzburg, and also at the petition of our beloved nephew Duke Otto, we granted to our faithful Burchard, venerable bishop of the church of Worms, because he had often served us with devoted spirit, the royal ban in the forest called Forehahi:

from the village called Elmeresbach, situated beside the Rhine, as far as Heriveldon; from there to Bibiloz; thence by the straight road to Otterestat; from there by the straight road to the church situated at Bezcingun; thence by the straight mountain road to Herbestat; from Herbestat, by the straight mountain road [Col. 0246B] to Bosinesheim; thence by the entire mountain road to Winenheim; from Winenheim by the straight mountain road to Sericzesheim on the Lobdengau; from there down to the river Neckar; from the river Neckar to the Rhine; thence along all the banks of the Rhine downstream as far as Elmersbach.

All these places, from Elmersbach to Winenheim, lie in the Rheingau, in the county of Count Gerung; the remaining places lie in the Lobdengau, in the county of Count Mezingozi. We grant this aforesaid forest, with its full integrity and all the uses belonging to it, by our royal authority to Saint Peter of the church of Worms, so that no person, small or great, may presume to hunt, capture, or pursue any wild animal or beast in that forest without the permission of the above-mentioned Bishop Burchard or his successors.
