If anyone should presume to do this—which God forbid—then, while he remains alive in the flesh, he shall unwillingly pay to the bishop and his successors both the royal ban and the peace-fine that he ought to have paid to the royal treasury. The ban and peace shall remain, as has already been granted by kings or emperors in the case of other forests, under the perpetual right of the church of Worms and the bishops presiding over it.

And so that this grant of our concession may remain firm throughout the ages to come, we have ordered the text of this charter to be signed with our seal and have strengthened it with our own hand, as appears below.

Sign of the lord Henry, the unconquered king.

Egilbert, chancellor, recognized this in place of Willigis, archbishop.

[Col. 0246D] Given in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1002, indiction XV, on 10 June, in the first year of the reign of our lord King Henry.

Done successfully at Worms.

### XI. Charter of Saint Henry granted to Lady Godesdihui, abbess of the monastery of Herford. (Year 1002.)

[Dronke, *Codex diplomaticus Fuldensis*, p. 57.]

C. In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, king by the gracious favor of God.

If we strive to exalt the churches of God through our royal power, we undoubtedly believe that this will benefit both the present condition of our kingdom and the reward of eternal blessedness. Therefore we wish it to be known to all our faithful, present and future, how, through the intervention of our beloved wife and queen Cunigunda, with the counsel of the honorable Willigis, archbishop of the church of Mainz, and of Duke Berenhard and our other faithful, we followed the wishes and petitions of Lady Godesdhiv, venerable abbess of the monastery of Herford, and of the entire congregation of Saint Mary entrusted to her.

By our royal authority we confirm to that monastery, according to the custom of our predecessors, three churches in the counties called Bursibant and Scopingon, built in the villages of Hreini, Wadiringas, and Stochheim, together with all their goods and tithes, which Emperor Louis transferred to the aforesaid monastery of Herford for the salvation of his soul. This is on the condition that the said Lady Godesdhu the abbess, and all who succeed her in that office, may henceforth freely dispose of and govern, according to ecclesiastical order and with their ministers, the aforesaid ecclesiastical properties and all other things transferred there by kings and emperors through a charter, with the contradiction of all persons removed.

Moreover, under the same confirmation we include whatever has now been transferred, or shall in future be transferred, to the often-mentioned monastery of Herford by religious and God-fearing persons. And so that this confirmation of our royal donation may from this hour onward remain firm and unshaken, we have ordered this confirmation of our donation, written for that purpose, to be marked with the impression of our seal and have strengthened it with our own hand, as appears below.

Sign of the lord Henry (royal monogram), the unconquered king.

Egilbert, chancellor, in place of Willigis, archchaplain, recognized it.

Given 12 August, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1002, indiction XV, in the first year of the reign of our lord King Henry.

Done at Aruitdi.

### XII. Charter of Saint Henry for New Corbie. (Year 1002.)

[Dronke, as above, p. 58.]

[Col. 0247D] C. In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, king by the gracious favor of God.

Let it be known to all our faithful, present and future, how the venerable abbot named Hosat approached our excellence, humbly asking that our magnificent generosity look favorably upon the monastery over which he appears to preside. It is built on the river Weser, in a place called New Corbie, in honor of God and of Saint Stephen, the first martyr, where the precious relics of Saint Vitus the martyr are also known to be preserved.

Granting his reasonable petition out of love for God and reverence for the blessed martyrs, we ordered these lines of our serenity to be prepared concerning that monastery, [Col. 0248A] by which we decree and order that no public judge or anyone exercising judicial authority—except only the administrator of that place and the advocate of the aforesaid monastery—may ever enter the churches, places, fields, or other possessions of the aforesaid monastery which it appears currently to possess justly and lawfully, in whatever bishoprics, counties, or territories they may lie, or whatever may have been granted there for the love of God and reverence for that holy place, for the hearing of cases, the collection of fines, the provision of lodging or transport, the taking of sureties, the demanding of any payments or unlawful services, or the unjust coercion of the monastery’s people, whether free or enslaved or otherwise dependent.

Nor may anyone presume wholly to demand or exact the things mentioned above. Rather, those serving God there may live and reside in peaceful order under the protection of our immunity, so that they may be more pleased at all times to implore God’s mercy more attentively on behalf of us and our wife, and for the stability of the entire kingdom granted to us by God.

Moreover, they shall hold and administer the tithes and tithe-churches in the various bishoprics in the same way as they are seen to have held and administered them under our predecessors, namely kings and emperors, according to their charters. To the bishops, however, they shall pay each year, at the time of their circuit, the service and lodging dues they owe, according to their written obligations.

And so that this authority of our concession and confirmation may be regarded as more secure, and may be more readily believed and more carefully preserved by all the faithful of holy God’s Church, present and future, we have strengthened it below with our own hand and ordered it to be marked with the impression of our seal.

Sign of the lord Henry (royal monogram), the unconquered king.

Egilbert, chancellor, in place of Willigis, archchaplain, recognized it.

Given 25 August, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1002, indiction XV, in the first year of the reign of our lord King Henry. Done at Nijmegen.

### XIII. Charter of Saint Henry for the church of Paderborn. (Year 1002.)

[Dronke, same work.]

C. In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, [Col. 0248D] Henry, king by the gracious favor of God.

Let it be known to all our faithful, present and future, how, grieving as was fitting over the disastrous burning of the church of Paderborn, and assenting as was proper to the petition of our faithful Rethar, the venerable bishop who now appears to preside over that see, we grant as an addition to the aforesaid church, and confirm by this royal charter, the forest that begins at the river Lutter and extends through Osnig and Sinidi to the road that leads to Horohusen.

We also decree that none of the men of the aforesaid bishop, whether free or enslaved, shall be compelled by any judicial authority except before the advocate whom the bishop himself chooses, with the contradiction of us, all our successors, and all mortals removed.

And so that this confirmation may remain more secure for all time, we have strengthened this page with our own hand and ordered it to be marked with the impression of our seal.

Sign of the lord Henry (royal monogram), the unconquered king.

Egilbert, chancellor, in place of Willigis, archchaplain, recognized it.

Given 15 September, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1002, indiction I, in the first year of the reign of our lord Henry. Done at Bochbardon.

### XIV. Charter of Saint Henry for the same church. (Year 1003.)

[In Dronke, *Codex diplomaticus Fuldensis*, p. 59.]

C. In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, [Col. 0249B] Henry, king by the favor of heavenly mercy.

If we are seen to restore, adorn, and once again exalt a place devoted to divine worship that has been consumed by sudden fire, together with its ornaments and charter documents, we know and are certain that this deserves not only to be proclaimed with human praise but also to be rewarded with divine recompense.

Therefore we wish it to be known to all the faithful of God’s Church, and to our own people now present and to come, that, grieving exceedingly over the burning of the church of Paderborn, we renew and confirm once again in this charter the commands of our predecessors and the offerings of the faithful belonging to that see. Among these are: one concerning the constitution of the bishopric; then one concerning the protection and royal guardianship of the same church; one concerning all property belonging to that church; and one concerning its people, both free and enslaved, who are not to be compelled by any judicial person except before the advocate whom the bishop himself chooses.

Moreover, we renew and confirm to the see already possessed the counties over the districts of Paterga, Aga, Threveresga, Auga, and Sorehtfeld, granted in connection with the tithes of New Corbie belonging to the monastery; the property of clerics, if any of them should die without an heir, granted to the same church; three hides at Duisburg and at Dortmund; and the forest that begins at the river Delme and extends through Ardenna and Sinedi to the road that leads to Herisi.

All these things written above, and whatever that see was seen to hold and possess on the day when it was burned, we donate in proprietary right to the often-mentioned see of Paderborn and restore by the firmest transfer. This is done on the condition that Lord Rethar, the venerable bishop of the aforesaid see, and all his successors, may securely possess everything that belongs to the bishopric by any lawful grant, with the contradiction of us, all our successors, and all mortals removed.

And so that this renewal and confirmation may remain more secure for all time, we strengthen this page with our own hand and order it to be marked with the impression of our seal.

Sign of the lord Henry (royal monogram), the unconquered king.

Egilbert, chancellor, in place of Willigis, archchaplain, recognized it.

Given 3 April, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 0250A] 1003, indiction I, in the first year of the reign of our lord King Henry. Done at Quedlinburg.

### XV. Saint Henry bestows the abbey of Nonantula upon Sigifred, bishop of Parma. (Year 1003.)

[Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, II, 161.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, king by the gracious favor of God.

We wish it to be known to all the faithful that Sigifred, venerable bishop of the church of Parma, our faithful, approached our clemency; and through the intervention of our faithful Theobald, margrave, the said Sigifred, bishop of the church of Parma, did so in order that, strengthened in faith, he might serve us zealously, and receive from the eternal Rewarder, who abounds in all good things, the recompense of eternal reward: [lacuna] that we should grant the abbey of the monastery called Nonantula, in honor of Saint Sylvester, confessor and bishop of God, to him and to his church of Parma in proprietary right, together with all its adjacent lands and appurtenances, in their entirety and for all time, except for the land that we granted to our faithful Bishop Hubert, which lies beside the river Adige.

Listening favorably to his entreaties and considering his most devoted loyalty toward us, we ordered this charter of our imperial authority to be written for him and for his church of Parma, dedicated in honor of Saint Mary, Mother of God. By it we grant, donate, and bestow upon him the aforesaid abbey called Nonantula of Saint Sylvester, confessor and bishop, together with all its adjacent lands and appurtenances, estates, chapels and their buildings, lands, fields, meadows, vineyards, woods, male and female slaves, movable and immovable property, in their entirety, and everything else belonging to the aforesaid abbey that may be spoken or named, by our imperial grant, so that he and his successors may have, hold, and perpetually enjoy it for the benefit of his often-mentioned church, and may do with it whatever, according to eternal judgment, they shall deem best. Whoever, however, acts against this donation of ours, etc.

[Col. 0250D] Sign of the lord Henry, the unconquered king.

Aubert, chancellor, recognized it in place of Archbishop Videchi.

Given 2 March, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1003, indiction I, in the first year of the reign of our lord Henry.

Done at Nijmegen.

### XVI. Charter of Saint Henry for the church of Hamburg. (Year 1003, 25 May.)

[Lappenberg, *Hamburgische Urkundenbuch*, p. 62.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, king by the gracious favor of God.

If we bring the pious petitions of priests to fulfillment with willing devotion, we undoubtedly believe that this will benefit us both for the condition of the present life and for attaining the rewards of eternal blessedness. Therefore let the judgment of all our faithful, present and future, know how the venerable man Liebizo, archbishop of the holy church of Hamburg, caused to be presented before our eyes a charter of our blessed predecessor Otto III, emperor Augustus. In it was contained how he, for the love of God, had granted by imperial authority liberty and protection to the monasteries situated in his bishopric. Liebizo asked our highness that we should likewise confirm those monasteries and everything belonging to them by a new charter of ours.

Assenting to his just and reasonable petition, with the intervention of our beloved wife and consort in the kingdoms, Cunigunda, and to the honor of holy Mary, Mother of God, to whom that place, Hamburg, is consecrated, we grant to the aforesaid place all the concessions which the emperors of pious memory—namely our grandfather and father—granted to the monasteries belonging to this diocese, namely Bremen, Bücken, Ramsloh, Birkach, Haselünne, and Rüdesholt. This is on the condition that they shall always remain perpetually under our protection, and that whatever they now possess or may in future acquire in any way shall freely serve them and their bishop, with every judicial authority removed.

Moreover, we grant to the aforesaid archbishop and his successors permission to establish a market at the place called Bremen, together with the ban and toll, as well as a public mint of standard weight and pure silver, and full [lacuna] authority to choose a bishop from among themselves, or from elsewhere if necessity requires, subject nevertheless to the king’s equal consent. And so that this [lacuna] may be strengthened, we ordered it to be marked with the impression of our seal.

Sign of the lord Henry (monogram), the unconquered king.

Egilbert, chancellor, in place of Willigis, archchaplain, recognized it.

Given 25 May, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1003, indiction I, in the first year of the reign of our lord King Henry.

Done at Gebehildehuson.

### XVII. Diploma of Saint Henry, king of the Romans, for the convent of Mulenbech, by which he confirms the privileges granted to it by the emperors Arnulf and Otto II, grants the free power to elect an abbess, and so forth. (Year 1003.)

[Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, I, 363.]

[Col. 0251D]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, king by the gracious favor of God.

If we strive to enlarge places dedicated to divine worship through our assistance, we clearly trust that by this we shall obtain a portion of the eternal kingdom. Therefore let the judgment of all our faithful, present and future, know how a certain venerable abbess named Bertheid presented before our eyes certain imperial charters, granted by our predecessors Arnulf and Otto II for the immunity of her monastery. The monastery had formerly been built from its foundations at a place called Mulinbeche by certain noble persons, Hildiburga and the priest Folchart. She humbly begged our clemency that we too should receive that place, together with its appurtenances, into our royal protection and defense for the redemption of our soul, and that we should strengthen in writing, by the authority of our charter, the agreement and grant found recorded in her documents.

Therefore, with the intervention of Duke Bernhard and Bishop Thiederic, in whose diocese this nunnery was built [Note: [Col. 0251D] Of Minden, as is clear from the diploma of Otto II.], for the increase of divine reward we received the monastery itself, together with its adjacent lands and all its appurtenances, into our royal protection, confirmed everything according to the order of the earlier charters, [Col. 0252B] and strengthened it with this royal insignia.

We firmly enact that, at the successive deaths of abbesses, the nuns devoted to God there may freely choose from among themselves the best woman they know and set her over themselves as abbess, with the consent of their bishop communicated. Moreover, in memory of our name, we grant that no count, judicial official, or person exercising royal exaction may henceforth demand from the people of the aforesaid church, who are subject to its uses and to the service of the servants of God, the royal or imperial tribute that used to be paid from there.

No count, public judge, or powerful person may dare to disturb the people of the aforesaid church in his own court by imposing a ban upon them or by demanding any justice from them in any way, except only the law which the advocate of the bishop presiding over that church is accustomed to claim from them, and that provision of law by which, if something necessarily needs to be completed and judicially determined before the duke on account of a capital crime, it may be brought to conclusion there.

And so that this authority of our concession may be regarded as more secure, we ordered this command of our dominion, strengthened by our own hand, to be marked with the sign of our image.

Sign of the lord Henry, unconquered king in Christ.

Egilbert, chancellor, in place of Willigis, archchaplain, recorded it.

Place of the seal, which is entirely intact.

Given 13 March, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 0252D] 1003, indiction I, still in the first year of the reign of our lord Henry.

Done at Minden.

### XVIII. Saint Henry, emperor, confirms the possessions of the monastery of Saint Bavo of Ghent, of the order of Saint Benedict. (Year 1003.)

[Miraeus, *Opera diplomatica*, I, 347.]

Henry, king by the gracious favor of God.

If those things which our faithful [lacuna] Therefore let the judgment of all the faithful of holy God’s Church and of our own people, present and future, know that the venerable man Erembold, abbot of the monastery of Ghent, situated where the river Scheldt joins the river Lys, built by Blessed Amandus the bishop in honor of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, where the distinguished confessor of Christ, Bavo, also rests, presented to us the charter of immunity of our predecessor, namely Otto, the unconquered emperor.

In it was inserted how he, for the love of God and the reward of eternal recompense, restored to the same monastery the properties of certain goods unjustly seized by the tyrannical invasion of certain persons, strengthened this by a written confirmation of his own, and had the grace of fraternal association granted to him in that monastery; it also stated how he had remitted all toll exactions.

[Col. 0253B] For the sake of strengthening its security, the aforesaid Abbot Erembold asked us to renew that charter, namely so that, through such a guarantee of firmness, we might also add our authority. Gladly assenting to his petition, we decreed that a charter of royal dignity should be made, namely that the same monastery should quietly possess its property, whose names are these:

In the county of Baagbat, the village of Suolmam [Note: [Col. 0253D] Suolmam, today Muninex Swolm, a village near Zottegem.] with two churches and all its adjacent lands; and the village of Holthem [Note: [Col. 0253D] Holtem, commonly Hanthem, a village at the third milestone from Ghent, in whose parish basilica the body of Saint Livinus, bishop and patron of Ghent, was formerly buried; there still appears to be there a large burial mound with an underground chamber, as I explained more fully in the *Fasti Belgici* under 12 November.]; and Mereshem; and Fliethersele [Note: [Col. 0254D] Fliethersele, today Vliedersele, or commonly Vlierzeels, at the second milestone from Aalst.], with their churches and all their appurtenances; and, in the same county, villages called Merem, Lietheka, Setteka, and Cranihom; and, in Rien, Boholt [Note: Bocholt, Bouchout, a village in the district of Rien near Lier, mentioned above, p. 29.].

With their individual churches, woods, and all their proper appurtenances. These villages, together with other properties unjustly seized by the hostile plundering of certain persons, our glorious predecessor, the lord emperor, restored by right and piously returned.

And at Rien, the estate of Frunethe, with its church and all its appurtenances. And the woodland of Summi Gerotha; and at Wilrika, a church with its appurtenances. Also, in the district of the Scheldt, the holding called Erika, and Papingolant with its church and all its appurtenances; and at Odrorstiet, land on which five hundred sheep can be fed; and whatever is known to be contained in Bevelanda [Note: [Col. 0254D] Bevelanda and Walacra, islands of Zealand, Beverlant and Valcheren], and in Walacra, and in Bruinsela, from the jurisdiction of Saint Bavo; and at Essperia, land on which four hundred rams can be pastured, and in another place two hundred; and at Holfcols, on the river Iora, four hundred.

Therefore, with the fullest integrity of all the possessions belonging to it [Col. 0253D], we confirm this perpetually for the use of the brothers of the aforesaid monastery, under the perpetual protection of immunity and by a charter of our majesty. By it we order and command that no count, public judge, vicar, advocate, or anyone exercising judicial authority dare enter, in our time or in that of our successors, the churches, places, lands, or other possessions of the aforesaid monastery—which it now justly and legally possesses in whatever regions and territories within the jurisdiction of our empire, or which divine piety may hereafter wish to increase in the right of that holy place—for the hearing of cases, the collection of fines, the provision of lodging or provisions, the taking of sureties, or the coercion of the people of that place, whether free or enslaved, residing on its land; nor may anyone presume to demand any dues or unlawful exactions or pretexts whatsoever.

Moreover, for the aforesaid monastery, in the hope of eternal blessedness and so that this may contribute to the salvation of my soul in eternal rest, we wish and grant that, with the fines remitted, all tolls and toll exactions be forgiven and released, as is contained in the charter of my predecessor. Thus, whenever it happens that people must travel through various places of our empire for the benefit of the monastery and its brothers, both on their outward journey and on their return, they may conduct their business without any troublesome harassment, so that those servants of God who minister there may continually delight in imploring God’s mercy for me and for the welfare of the kingdom granted to me by God. And so that the authority of this renewal and confirmation may possess greater force in the name of God, I have confirmed it below with my own hand and ordered it to be marked with the impression of my ring.

Sign of the Lord Henry, the most unconquered king.

I, Egilbert, chancellor acting in place of Willigis, archchaplain, have recognized this.

Given on the Nones of February, in the year 1003 of the Incarnation of the Lord, in the first indiction, and in the second year of Lord King Henry II.

Enacted at Aachen Palace.

### XIX. Charter of King Henry II granting Count Adalbero the ban over wild game. (Year 1003, 30 June.)

[Ried, as cited above, p. 122.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, by the favor of divine clemency king.

Let all our faithful, present and future, know how, considering in every respect the faithful service of our beloved count, namely Adalbero, and attending to his petition through the intervention of the venerable bishop Gotescalch, we granted him, as he had requested and as we were legally able to do, the royal ban over wild game between the two rivers Ysara and Liubasa—both over the land belonging to the aforesaid Adalbero himself and over the lands of episcopal houses or monasteries in the abbacies belonging to us there, as well as over the lands of all those people who now or in the future shall approve such an arrangement with him [Col. 0255A]—in the county of Frederick, who judges at Hachingun, in the district of Sundergau: first, from the mouths of the aforesaid rivers, up the Ysara as far as Hohenberg; from there to Huggenberg, then to Cumizdorf; from there to Carphse and Winidowe; and, following the course of the river Liubasa (the Loisach), as far as Wolveradeshusun.

Therefore, by our royal authority, as prescribed above, we have transferred to him and by this charter granted him the ban over wild game between the aforesaid rivers and boundaries. By royal word we strictly forbid that, within this circuit and without his permission, anyone thereafter dare capture by any device or kind of hunting those wild animals which are placed under the ban in other royal forests. And so that the authority of this grant of ours may remain stable and unshaken [Col. 0255B], we have strengthened this page of our charter with our own hand and ordered it impressed with the sign of our image.

Sign of Lord Henry, the most unconquered king. (Monogram.)

I, Egilbert, chancellor acting in place of Willigis, archchaplain, have recognized this.

Given on the second day before the Kalends of July, in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1003, in the first indiction, and in the second year of the reign of Lord Henry II. Enacted at Regensburg.

With the seal for the most part broken.

### XX. The privilege of Saint Henry granted to Abbess Frederuna. (Year 1004.)

[Dronke, as cited above, p. 60.]

[Col. 0255C]

C. In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, by the favor of divine clemency king.

Let the entire body of the holy Church of God and of our faithful, present and future, know how the venerable lady Frederuna, abbess, and her sister Imma, countess, with the assistance of Count Gerone, built a certain monastery dedicated to the honor of Mary, the holy Mother of God and perpetual Virgin. To it they transferred, with the greatest goodwill, their entire inheritance, namely: Keminetan, Haegen, Barigi, Tundiriun, Othere—these are in Tilithi—Varstan in Auga, Rothe in Wikanavelde, Bardenwic, Hotmannessun, Witthorp [Col. 0255D], Britlingi, Biangibudiburg, Addunesthorp, Hatherbiki, Bodanhuson, Sutherburg; in Bardanga, Claniki; in Drevani, Wigmannesburstal; Bennedestorp; in Mosidi, Widila and Waldersidi; Kokerbiki; in Heilanga, Holana and Aun; in Hogtrunga, Setila, Hepstidi, and Sinigas—and all the estates mentioned above.

These possessions are situated in the county of Duke Bernhard. Therefore they approached our royal majesty and humbly requested that we receive the monastery under our protection and grant it such precedence of liberty and law as Gandersheim, Quedlinburg, and Herford appear to possess [Col. 0256A]. Let the entire body of the faithful know that we did this at the petition of Theodric, bishop of Minden. Furthermore, we decree that the aforesaid monastery and abbey shall remain, by our grant, in the power of the aforesaid abbess and of her sister the countess for the duration of their lives; but after the death of both of them, the same abbey shall belong perpetually by right to our public authority.

Moreover, we wish that no person, great or small, of our kingdom may hold a court in that abbey, inflict any disturbance upon it, or exercise any public function there, except the advocate of the abbess and the holy nuns. We also grant this to the same abbey by our royal authority: after the abbess’s death, the holy nuns of that monastery shall have permission to choose another woman suitable for the office [Col. 0256B]. And so that the charter of our authority may remain firm forever, we have strengthened this page with our own hand and ordered it marked with our seal.

Sign of Lord Henry, the most unconquered king.

Egilbert, chancellor, acting in place of Willigis, archchaplain, has recorded this.

Given on the fourth day before the Nones of November, in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1004, in the second indiction, and in the third year of Lord Henry II, king. Enacted at Magdeburg.

### XXI. Charter of Saint Henry granted to the monastery of virgins at Keminad. (Year 1004.) He receives the monastery under his protection and grants the nuns the power to elect an abbess.

[Martene, *Amplissima Collectio* I, 365.]

[Col. 0256C]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, by the favor of divine clemency king.

Let the entire body of the holy Church of God and of our faithful, present and future, know how the lady Frideruna, abbess, and her sister Imma, countess, with the assistance of Count Gerone, built a certain monastery dedicated to the honor of Mary, the holy Mother of God and perpetual Virgin. To it they transferred, with the greatest goodwill, their entire inheritance, namely: Keminadam, Hogen, Barigi, Tundivium, Othere—these are in Tilichi—Warstan in Auga, Rohten in Wakenafalde, Bardewik [Col. 0256D], Hottmannessum, Wintorp, Britlingi, Biangi, Budiburg, Addunestorp, Hatterbiki, Bodenhusen, Suterburg; in Gardanga, Clomkey; in Drevan, Wigmannesburgscal and Bennestorp; in Mosidi, Widila, Waldersidi, and Kokerbiki; in Heilanga, Holana and Aunsetila; in Hostrunga, Hepenstidi and Sungad—and all the estates of theirs mentioned above.

[Note: [Col. 0255D] In the course of time this monastery was converted into a provostship of New Corbie, with the support of Emperor Conrad II and Pope Eugene III; it eventually passed to the dukes of Brunswick.]

These possessions are situated in the county of Duke Bevardi. Therefore they approached our royal majesty and humbly requested that we receive the monastery under our protection and grant it such precedence of liberty and law as they saw Gandersheim, Quedlinburg, and Herford possess [Col. 0257A].

[Note: [Col. 0257D] Gandersheim, the most distinguished Benedictine monastery of virgins in the Duchy of Brunswick, was founded around the year 852 by Liudolf, duke of the Saxons, and his wife Oda.]

[Note: [Col. 0257D] This monastery was founded by Queen Mathilda, wife of Henry the Fowler, king of the Germans; she led a religious life there while retaining secular dress. It is situated in the diocese of Halberstadt, and she rests there together with King Henry.]

Let the entire body of the faithful know without reservation that we did this at the petition of Theodoric, bishop of Minden. Furthermore, we decree that the aforesaid monastery and abbey shall remain, by our consent, in the power of the aforesaid abbess and of her sister the countess for the duration of their lives; but after the death of both of them, the same abbey shall belong perpetually by right to our public authority.

Moreover, we wish that no person, great or small, of our kingdom may hold a court in that abbey, inflict any disturbance upon it, or demand any public service, except the advocate of the abbess and all the nuns. We also grant this to the abbey by our royal authority: after the abbess’s death, the nuns of that monastery shall have permission to choose another woman suitable for the office [Col. 0257B]. And so that the charter of our authority may remain firmer forever, we have strengthened this page with our own hand and ordered it marked with our sign.

Sign of Lord Henry, the most unconquered king.

Egilbert, chancellor, acting in place of Willigis, archchaplain, has recorded this.

Given on the fourth day before the Nones of November, in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1004, in the second indiction, and in the year of Lord Henry the king . . . .

Enacted at Magdeburg.

### XXII. Saint Henry confirms the privileges of the Church of Como and increases its possessions. (Year 1004.)

[Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, V, 280.]

[Col. 0257C]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, by the favor of divine clemency king of both the Franks and the Lombards.

Let all our faithful know that, through the intervention of Bishop Everard of Como, out of reverence for God, for the benefit of our most glorious predecessors, the emperors, and for the advancement of our kingdom, we have given in full and in perpetuity to Saint Abundius that entire part of the castle of Bellinzona which belonged to our public authority, both within and outside it, with all its appurtenances and dependencies, with its markets, tolls, all public revenues and services [Col. 0257D], and also the gate itself, which until now has served the public use, so that Bishop Everard of Como and all his successors may freely, securely, quietly, and peacefully possess and hold it with full authority, and may devote to divine worship whatever their will shall decree.

For the castle of Bellinzona, with everything belonging to it within or outside it, we transfer and give entirely from our right and lordship, and from every public claim, into the right and lordship of Saint Abundius [Col. 0258A]. We grant and donate it so that, without any reservation and without any public disturbance, they may hold, judge, and administer all the aforesaid appurtenances, with male and female servants, just as the other properties which the church of Saint Abundius acquired and held a hundred years ago.

For it is fitting, and it increases our kingdom, to donate from the things God has given, and to return honor to him who freely honors and from whom all honor proceeds. Let us therefore honor the saints, enrich the places of the saints, and have the saints themselves as helpers and intercessors with God. Through this our predecessors greatly pleased God; through this we too hope for the salvation of our lives, the advancement of the kingdom, and the honor of peace and prosperity.

Therefore we order that no duke, margrave, count, viscount, no Latin, no German, and no great or small person of our kingdom dare henceforth at any time or by any device interfere with the aforesaid castle of Bellinzona, or with any of its dependencies, whether within or outside it; nor may anyone presume to dispossess the church of Saint Abundius of it, or seek to disturb or harass our most faithful bishop Everard of Como or any of his successors on that account, or to burden him with a court hearing.

If anyone does so, let him pay one thousand pounds of the finest gold, one half to us and the other to Saint Abundius. Let this charter remain firm for all time. And so that it may be believed more truly and observed more carefully, we ordered this charter to be written, confirmed it with our hand [Col. 0258C], and ordered it marked with our seal.

Sign of Lord Henry, the most unconquered king.

Egilbert, chancellor, acting in place of Willigis, archchaplain, has recognized this.

Given on the second day before the Ides of June, in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1004, in the second indiction, and in the third year of the reign of Lord Henry II. Enacted at Lacunavara, happily in the name of God. Amen.

### XXIII. Charter of Saint Henry by which he generously grants the estate of Pipinesdorff to the Church of Worms. (Year 1004.)

[Schannat, *Episcopatus Wormatiensis*, II, 36.]

[Col. 0258D] In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, by the favor of divine clemency king.

If we exalt the places of the saints through the generosity of royal munificence, we openly confess that this benefits us both in the course of the present life and in the state of future glory. Therefore let all the members of the holy Church of God and our faithful know how Burchard, the venerable bishop of the holy Church of Worms, humbly approached our royal excellence, asking that we deign to grant to his bishopric and to the holy Church of Worms, dedicated in honor of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, the estate which we appear to possess in the village called Pipinesdorff [Col. 0259A], for the remedy of our soul.

Accordingly, granting assent to his petition through the intervention of our beloved wife, namely Queen Cunigunda, and for the increase of our future reward, we have granted by this royal charter the aforesaid estate, situated in the village of Pipinesdorff, in the district of Mulselgau and in the county . . . . . , in its entirety with all its appurtenances—namely, plots, buildings, male and female servants, cultivated and uncultivated lands, meadows, pastures, woods, hunting rights, and so forth—to the already mentioned church of Saint Peter and to its rectors who may be appointed there in due course. We have transferred it from our right [Col. 0259B] into its right . . . . . . And so that this authority of ours may obtain inviolable stability in the name of God, we have strengthened it with our own hand and ordered it marked below with our seal.

Sign of Lord Henry, the most unconquered king.

Egilbert, chancellor, acting in place of Willigis, archchaplain, has recognized this.

Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of January, in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1004, in the second indiction, and in the third year of the reign of Lord Henry II.

Enacted at Dornburg, happily in the name of God. Amen.

### XXIV. Concerning immunity. (Year 1004.)

[From Ludewig, *Scriptores rerum Germanicarum* I, 330.]

[Col. 0259C] In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, by the favor of divine clemency king.

Because, if we lend a kindly ear to the pious petitions of those who serve God, we confidently believe that the remedy of supreme salvation thereby arises for us, let the religious community of all the faithful of the holy Church of God know that, both considering the welfare of our soul and complying with the petitions of our beloved Godehard, abbot, we have received under the protection and guardianship of our immunity the venerable abbey dedicated to the martyr Saint Maurice, called Altaha, together with everything in any way attached to that aforesaid abbey.

This includes the villages called Iserahoff, Suartzaha, Coella, Gunzia, Munichdorff, Puechoff, Oberanhaus, Usterlingen, Gotzzolting, Otilingen, Richerisdorff, and Boltheringa [Col. 0259D], together with all other advantages and useful resources of every kind; households, tributes, tribute-payers, movable and immovable goods, roads and trackless places, woods, fattening grounds, waters, fisheries, millstones, mills, pastures, common pastures, or bee pastures, things acquired and to be acquired, and all appurtenances belonging by just acquisition to the aforesaid abbey.

Therefore, by royal authority, we proclaim and command that no duke, margrave, count, viscount, *schuldheiß*, *Schöffe*, or any great or small person presume to disturb, harass, or dispossess the same abbot or his successors with respect to the aforesaid properties. If anyone should prove to be a violator of this charter of ours—which God forbid—let him know that he must pay one hundred pounds of the finest gold [Col. 0260A]. And so that it may be believed more truly and observed more carefully by all, we have strengthened this charter, written for that purpose, with our own hand and ordered it marked with the impression of our seal.

Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of February, in the second indiction, in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1004; and in the third year of Lord Henry II, king. Enacted at Altötting, happily in the name of God. Amen.

### XXV. King Henry grants to the old chapel an estate belonging to him in Nortgau, together with whatever he possessed in the two villages of Durnin and Mantalahi. (Year 1004.)

[Ried, as cited above, p. 123.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, by the favor of divine clemency king.

[Col. 0260B] Let all our faithful, present and future, know how we have transferred by perpetual law, through this royal charter, to the royal chapel within the city of Regensburg, which we restored in honor of the most sacred Virgin Mary, Mother of God, an estate belonging to us, situated in Nortgau and in the county of Count Oudalscalch, and likewise whatever we appear to possess in the two villages called Durnin and Mantalahi. This was done through the intervention of Tagino, archbishop of the Church of Magdeburg and formerly provost of the same chapel.

We grant it with all its appurtenances and revenues: plots, buildings, male and female servants, fields, open country, cultivated and uncultivated lands, meadows, pastures and common pastures, woods, hunting rights, waters and watercourses, mills, fisheries [Col. 0260C], roads and trackless places, outgoings and incomings, things acquired and to be acquired, and all other appurtenances whatsoever, for the perpetual use of the church and of the congregation canonically serving God there. And so that this transfer of ours may remain stable and unshaken, we have strengthened this charter with our own hand and ordered it impressed with our seal.

Sign of Lord Henry, the most unconquered king. (Monogram.)

Egilbert, chancellor, acting in place of Willigis, archchaplain, has recognized this.

Given on the sixth day before the Ides of February, in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1004, in the first indiction, and in the second year of the reign of Lord Henry II.

Enacted at Vuarim.

The seal is intact, impressed on the inside.

### XXVI. King Henry II grants the lower monastery an estate in the courts of Regensburg—that is, in the Regensburg *Burgfrieden*. (Year 1005.)

[Ried, ibid., p. 124.]

[Col. 0260D]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, by the favor of divine clemency king.

If we grant the petitions of those who piously serve God, we undoubtedly hope thereby to obtain the remedy of eternal reward. Therefore let all the members of the holy Church of God and of our faithful, present and future, know how we, both for the welfare of our soul and also at the tender desire of our most beloved consort, namely Queen Cunigunda, and through the diligent intervention of the venerable abbess of Regensburg, namely Uota, have transferred and donated as property to the monastery of Saint Mary at Regensburg—commonly called the lower monastery—and have established as a firm donation for the increase of the sustenance of the nuns living there under the Rule of Saint Benedict, an estate belonging to us which the cleric Macelinus, while alive, appeared to possess by right of investiture at the courts of Regensburg, called Ekmulla, in the county of Count Roudbert.

We grant it with all the implements and appurtenances of the same estate: movable and immovable goods, households of both sexes, plots, buildings, cultivated and uncultivated lands, meadows, pastures and common pastures, roads [Col. 0261B], trackless places, outgoings and incomings, things acquired and to be acquired, waters and watercourses, and all other advantages that can rightly be named or written in any manner whatsoever. We grant it on the condition that the aforesaid abbess and her successors henceforth have free power to possess, exchange, cultivate, lease, or do with the same estate whatever they wish in every way for the benefit of the nuns.

And so that the authority of this transfer may remain stable and unshaken forever, we have strengthened this charter, written for that purpose, with our own hand and ordered it marked with the impression of our seal.

Sign of Lord Henry, the most unconquered king. (Monogram.)

I, Eberhard, chancellor acting in place of Willigis, archchaplain [Col. 0261C], have recognized this.

Given on the fourth day before the Ides of June, in the third indiction, in the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1005, and in the fifth year of the reign of Lord Henry II.

Enacted at Puozinesheim. Amen.

With the seal of the majesty.

### XXVII. The monastery of Stein, transferred from Duellium, is endowed by Henry II, King of the Romans, and placed under the Church of Bamberg. (Year 1005, 1 October.)

[Newgart, *Codex diplomaticus Alemanniae*, from the original in the archive of the Republic of Zurich.]

[Col. 0262A]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, by the favor of divine clemency king.

Since the Lord has made us princes and defenders of the churches, so that we may not appear ungrateful for his grace, we ought to increase his service, multiply the churches, defend those well and suitably built, and restore those that have been destroyed. Therefore, in our own time we arranged for the construction of a distinguished monastery in these regions of Alemannia, beside the bank of the Rhine, at a place called Stein [Note: [Col. 0261C] Stein is a town of the Republic of Zurich on the right bank of the Rhine above Schaffhausen. It is connected by a bridge to Thurgau], dedicated to Saint Mary and to the holy martyrs George and Cyril.

Their relics are known to have been transferred there from Mount Duellium [Note: [Col. 0261C] Duellum, Duellium, Dwiel, Hohentwiel, a mountain fortress in Hegau, subject to the most serene Duke of Württemberg [Col. 0261D]. According to Goldast, it received its name from a battle. For an old glossary says: “*Duellum*, battle, as if *dubellum*. *Duellium*, a place where battle is waged and where soldiers persist steadfastly in war; it is formed from *duo* and *bellum*, as if *dubellium*, because battle is conducted within and without.”], from the site of the older monastery [Col. 0262B].

Previously, there, through the efforts of Duke Burchard and his wife Hadewiga, fairly honorable but not very commodious dwelling places for monks had been built [Note: [Col. 0261D] An anonymous writer of Petershausen mentions this foundation, or rather restoration, in his *Chronicle*, in P. Ussermann, *Germania sacra prodromus*, vol. I, p. 319; Ekkehard the Younger also mentions it in *On the Disasters of Saint Gall*, chap. 10, in Goldast.]. But after their possessions came under our rule, and after deliberation with the bishops and princes of the kingdom, it seemed to us more expedient to transfer the monastery to another site, in accordance with the wishes we had heard expressed by the monks of that place and the inhabitants of the very steep mountain, who complained of its difficulty.

Now, therefore, so that the memory and honor of the former lords of the place—our faithful kinsmen—may be established, it has pleased our serenity to assist their religious undertaking by our royal authority in such a way that, through our arrangement, the servants of God may obtain the tranquility of the more suitable site they desire [Col. 0262C].

Let it therefore be known to all the Church of God that, with the present support of our bishops and abbots, and especially through the efforts of Warinher, abbot of Reichenau [Note: [Col. 0261D] Warinher, also called Werinher or Wernher, succeeded Alawic as abbot of Reichenau in the year 1000; he in turn succeeded Widerold, bishop of Strasbourg, who died in Italy. See Hermann the Lame, under this year; compare *Gallia christiana*, V, p. 986], and of Duke Hermann [Note: [Col. 0261D] Hermann II assumed the duchy of Alemannia in 997], together with the other princes of Swabia, we transfer to the monastery called Stein estates belonging to our inheritance, situated in various districts, counties, and places: Arola [Note: [Col. 0262C] Arlen, on the river Aach between Stein and Duellium], Ezzewilare [Note: [Col. 0262C] Ezweil, in the Black Forest Albgau on the river Alb toward the Rhine], Hiltesinga [Note: [Col. 0262C] Hiltisen, near the Arola mentioned above], Nagelta [Note: [Col. 0262D] Nagold, a town in the Duchy of Württemberg on the river of the same name], Epfendorf [Note: [Col. 0262D] Epfendorf, below Rottweil], Phisgina [Note: [Col. 0262D] Fischingen, below the town of Sulz, where there is now a saltworks], with its salt spring, Vfeninga [Note: [Col. 0262D] Today Avingen, in the Munsingen district of Württemberg], Affraninga [Note: [Col. 0262D] Effringen, near Wildberg], Rahtfelda [Note: [Col. 0262D] Rotfelden, between the towns of Nagold and Wildberg], Sindelstetta [Note: [Col. 0262D] A place unknown to me, unless it is Zindelstein, a ruined castle near Fehrenbach in the Black Forest, in the Fürstenberg territory, or Saenstetten in the Heidenheim district of Württemberg], Hoenstetta [Note: [Col. 0262D] Honstetten, between Tuttlingen and Stockach, in Hegau], Rieden [Note: [Col. 0262D] There are several places in our diocese bearing this name], Suaninga [Note: [Col. 0263D] Swaningen, in the Black Forest Albgau; I cannot readily say whether Sweningen in the old Bertholdsbar is intended], Purch [Note: [Col. 0263D] Burg; there is an old castle of this name in Hegau, a village in Breisgau, and another place of that name in Bertholdsbar], together with churches and tithes, villages and rent-paying dependents, people and bondsmen of both sexes, cultivated and uncultivated lands, pastures, meadows, woods, things acquired and to be acquired, movable and immovable goods, and ministerial vassals with all their possessions.

We therefore grant and lawfully confirm these properties, with all their appurtenances and whatever else may still be named, to the relics of the saints of the church at Stein, so that in succeeding ages the abbot who is promoted to the governance and care of that church may rule over them and, with his monks, not neglect continually to implore divine mercy for us and our predecessors.

Furthermore, we wish to make known to the fidelity of all that we are now undertaking to raise the castle called Bamberg [Col. 0263B], situated in the part of East Francia, into an episcopal see. Therefore we must enrich and enlarge it by donations of estates and by resources obtained from every source. We have accordingly resolved and firmly determined to transfer there the estates that came to us by hereditary right in these regions of Alemannia after the death of Hadewiga, the widow of Duke Burchard.

We also wish to subject the monastery of Stein, whose status and arrangement we have now addressed, to the bishops of the see of Bamberg. This is to be done, however, on the condition that none of those bishops or other powerful persons presume to inflict upon that place, its abbots, administrators, or possessions the burdens or damages of any unjust exaction or construction, nor demand a rent, nor subtract anything from their uses [Col. 0263C].

We grant only that, when the abbot of that congregation dies, whoever is canonically elected by the monks—whether from among themselves or from another known monastery—to succeed him shall have the care of the monastery entrusted to him by the bishop of the aforesaid see. The abbot shall thereafter obey that bishop in living well, governing his monks according to the rule, and arranging everything accordingly; and he shall fear him, lest he presume to dissipate the property of his church or recklessly grant benefits from its possessions to free persons or to any outsiders.

Moreover, we have heard that many of those appointed advocates of churches greatly abuse the authority entrusted to them, so that those who ought to be modest defenders have shamelessly become rapacious and unjust exactors [Col. 0263D]. Therefore it has pleased our foresight to place this perpetually in the power of that abbot and his brothers: after taking the counsel of wise men, they shall choose, from among the powerful of the world whom they know to be more devoted to equity and moderation, advocates and defenders suitable for their respective places. No one else may presume to claim this authority for himself or seize it as though it were hereditary, except by appointment of the abbot [Col. 0264A].

The ministerial vassals whom we have transferred to the same church shall also be permitted, together with those whom we have decided to assign to the aforesaid episcopal see, to live according to the customary honorable manner of fellowship, to give their daughters in marriage to one another by common consent, and to receive daughters in return. Their offspring shall remain securely, on either side, as property of the church to whose jurisdiction the women are transferred through the marital union.

Therefore, so that these decrees of our transfer and the confirmation of our authority may be held more firmly in the years to come and observed more carefully, we have confirmed them with our own hand and ordered them sealed with our seal.

Sign of Lord Henry, second emperor.

[Col. 0264B] Sigefridus [Note: [Col. 0263D] Sigefridus, bishop of Münster], chancellor, acting in place of Bruno [Note: [Col. 0263D] Bruno, Sigefridus’s successor in the bishopric of Augsburg [Col. 0264D], and brother of King Henry. Both Sigefridus and Bruno are absent from the list of chancellors and archchancellors in Malinkrot], archchancellor, has recognized this.

Given on the Kalends of October, in the third indiction [Note: [Col. 0264D] The third indiction corresponds to the year 1005], in the year 1005 of the Incarnation of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0264D] That is, 1005. For the I with a transverse line at the top, which the original displays, indicates the numeral for one thousand], in the fourth year of Lord King Henry. Enacted at Ulm, happily.

### XXVIII. Emperor Saint Henry confirms the foundation of the college of canons at the Church of the Holy Cross in Liège, established by Notger, bishop of Liège. (Year 1005.)

[Miraeus, *Opera diplomatica*, II, 808.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, crowned by God through divine providence and gloriously raised to the kingship by all the people.

Whoever among the Catholics . . . . . .

Therefore we wish it to be known . . . . . how a man of great holiness and sufficiently worthy reverence, Lord Notger, bishop of the Church of Saint Mary and provider and guardian of Saint Lambert the martyr, inflamed by devotion to divine love, built from the foundations a certain church in the city of Liège [Note: [Col. 0264D]

The collegiate church of the Holy Cross at Liège was built at the expense of Notger, bishop of Liège. He consecrated it on 23 October 979 and instituted and founded there fifteen canons. Wazo, bishop of Liège, later increased their number in 1044 to twenty-five; it eventually rose to thirty, with a provost and dean. The provost must be chosen from among the canons of the cathedral church of Saint Lambert. The abbot of Belliredit, of the Premonstratensian order, holds one of the prebends at Liège; the Jesuit Fathers hold another in return for the obligation of teaching the humanities [Col. 0266D].

Moreover, Notger arranged for this church to be built on the highest point of the city, so as to prevent the construction of a fortress which a certain powerful man, skilled in arms, was planning to erect there; from it the city could have been attacked, and the clergy and people oppressed by its inhabitants.]

—to the memory and praise of the wood of the Holy Cross. There he established a community of canons and, to earn eternal life, suitably furnished and adorned the building at his own expense for those serving God in that place, so that, following the institutions of the holy Fathers, they might serve day and night, offer unceasing prayers to God for the peace of our kingdom, for our safety and that of our most beloved wife, and for the unity of the Christian faith; eat together, sleep together, and devote themselves entirely to divine worship.

[Col. 0264D] Therefore the same aforesaid bishop approached our dignity in person, humbly asking that what episcopal prudence and diligence had wisely arranged might remain firm and indissoluble through the strength of the royal hand.

We have assigned to the same Church, through the intervention of the aforementioned bishop, certain estates for the congregation to administer as circumstances require, namely, in the Ardennes district, the estate of Berthonia, etc. [lacuna].

And so that this grant, devoted to divine service, might by right remain inviolable and indissoluble according to the aforesaid determination, we ordered it confirmed by the proclamation of our ban and commanded these letters of our majesty to be issued concerning it. Through them we decree and command that no one henceforth, touched by any impulse of malice, dare oppose this conveyance made under our charter.

But just as it was ordered by the aforesaid bishop according to God’s will, so throughout all succeeding generations let it obtain, in God’s name, unchallenged and unimpaired, an irrevocable stability by the decree of our firmness. We have authenticated it with our royal right hand and ordered it marked with the impression of our seal.

Given on the Nones of April, in the thousand and fifth year of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the third indiction, in the third year of the reign of Lord Henry II.

Done at Aachen, successfully, in God’s name. Amen.

## XXIX. Saint Henry grants certain estates to the monastery of Altaha at the request of Abbot Godehard (1005)

[At Ludewig, *Script. rer. Germ.* III, 331.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, by the favor of divine clemency, king.

It is fitting for the majesty of royal excellence mercifully to grant reasonable petitions made to it by the Lord, so that through their continual prayers it may be crowned, both in this temporal and peaceful life and eternally, with the diadem of the heavenly prize. Therefore let the diligence of all our faithful, present and future, know how a certain venerable man, Godehard, abbot and administrator of the monastery of Altaha, approached the eminence of the power granted to us by God, humbly requesting that, since he had been struck by no small grief at losing what he seemed justly to have possessed, we might graciously restore to that monastery a certain estate called Flinspach, situated in the district of Sweinichgou and in the county of Count Tiemo, formerly belonging to the aforesaid monastery.

Believing that his worthy petition ought to be granted, we restore and return the same aforementioned estate by our royal conveyance and charter to the aforesaid monastery of Saint Maurice, built at Altaha; we grant it, donate it, and, subscribing with the greatest firmness, consolidate it for the construction, restoration, and walling of the aforesaid monastery, together with its other churches and the community of the brothers. The aforementioned abbot requested this because the land is sandy and useful for masonry.

Therefore, conveying to Saint Maurice, and to the abbot subscribed below as well as to his successors, as their property, whatever appears to lie between Winter and Hoffkirchen, or whatever otherwise belongs there to the aforesaid monastery, together with all movable and immovable things: cultivated and uncultivated lands, vineyards and vine-plots, mills, roads and trackless places, buildings, outgoings and incomes, woods, hunting rights, meadows, pastures, common pastures, or bee pastures, waters and their courses, fisheries, households of both sexes, those acquired and those yet to be acquired, and everything else that can be named or written, within or without, among its appurtenances and useful resources.

And so that the authority of this conveyance of ours may remain stable and unshaken, we have strengthened this charter written concerning it with our own hand and ordered it marked with the impression of our seal.

Given on the Nones of November, in the first indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1005, and in the fourth year of the reign of Lord Henry II. Done at Werda, successfully, in God’s name.

## XXX. Saint Henry II, emperor, renews the immunities and privileges granted to the monastery of Saint Maximin (1005, 9 April)

[Hontheim, *History of Trier: Diplomatic Documents* I, 350.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, by the favor of divine clemency, king.

Since the foresight and solicitude of our royal predecessors have always piously watched over the construction of God’s churches and the strengthening of those already built, for this reason, through the most kindly mercy of Christ—in whose hand the hearts and rights of kings rest—their reign was strengthened and flourished in peaceful security. Therefore, as we piously and beneficially consider the condition of our kingdom and desire to imitate their devoted solicitude, we have decided, through our authority also, to strengthen the privileges granted or assigned by our royal or imperial predecessors to the monastery of Saint Maximin, which rests in the suburb of Trier, at the intercession of our most beloved wife, namely Queen Cunigunda. Thus the benevolent piety of our predecessors, not neglected by us, may not be weakened, and the tranquility of the monks serving God there may not be disturbed by any person intruded among them.

The arrangement is that the same monastery, where the aforementioned holy bishop rests and where the venerable Abbot Ofderath now appears to preside—

[Note: “The impression of our seal.” The seal of the present charter, not published by Zyllesius, is distinctive in that the emperor’s right hand extends not a scepter, as elsewhere, but a cross, while his left holds a globe bearing no cross. Abbot Ofderath is thereafter found inscribed in no ancient record. The final day of his life—for nothing is known with certainty about the year—is given by the Maximinian calendar as: “16 Kalends of July: Oftradus, abbot of our congregation.” He was succeeded by Vinrichus, inaugurated on the Nones of March, in whatever year that may have been.]

—may stand under our authority, protection, and defense, just as under those of our predecessors; and may be subject to no see or church, except our royal power and that of our successors, as a servant, dependent, or beneficiary. We also grant them the free choice of electing among themselves an abbot worthy of such an honor and suitable for that office, so that through him they may fulfill their divine ministry with greater security and more earnestly implore the aid of the supreme Majesty on our behalf.

Furthermore, we grant that the same abbot, the congregation entrusted to him, and their successors shall have the power to give the advocacy of their monastery to whomever they wish and to withdraw it from whomever they wish.

And no person of any judicial rank shall presume to hold a public court in their estates; no one shall exact a toll from their ships; their household shall pay a ban or penalty to no one except the abbot; and it shall attend the public court of no one except the abbot or those appointed by him. In every royal or prefectural city they shall have free power to enter and leave, to sell and buy, to pasture and water their animals; and we wholly remit to them every royal or comital service.

And so that this authoritative charter of ours may remain firm and stable, we have strengthened it with our own hand and ordered it marked with the impression of our seal.

Sign of Lord Henry, the most invincible king.

I, Egilbert, chancellor, in place of Willigis, archchaplain, have examined and authenticated this. Given on the fifth day before the Ides of April, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1005, in the third indiction, and in the third year of the reign of Lord Henry II. Done at Aachen, successfully, in God’s name. Amen.

## XXXI. Saint Henry confirms the privileges of the Church of Como and increases its possessions (1006)

[Ughelli, *Sacred Italy* V, 281.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, by the favor of divine clemency, king.

When we incline the ears of our piety to the petitions of our faithful for the increase of our fidelity, we judge it much better if we willingly grant something of our possessions to God’s churches, through whose assistance greater advancement is bestowed upon us and the eminence of our kingdom is strengthened. Therefore let the entire assembly of our faithful, present and future, know that, for the remedy of our soul and that of our wife, and for the stability of our kingdom, through the intervention of Egilbert, bishop of Freising, we have donated to Eberard, bishop of Como, and to his successors, for the portion of Saint Mary and Saint Abundius, the whole half of the vice-county of Valtellina. We have entirely transferred whatever belongs to that half, whether on this side of Lake Como or at Bellagio, from all our public rights, and have given it as property to the aforesaid bishop and his successors, both within the district and in *precantia* and *erimaria* [uncertain administrative terms], and in every appurtenance that now appears to belong to us. We transfer and grant it to Eberard, bishop of Como [the text also reads “Gumano,” probably an error for *Cumano*], and to his successors, from our share to the portion of Saint Mary and Saint Abundius.

Therefore we decree and command that no one subject or to be subjected to our authority—namely, duke, margrave, bishop, count, vice-count, or any great or small person—dare disturb, molest, or dispossess the aforesaid bishop or his successors. If anyone should presume to do so, let him know that he must pay one hundred pounds of the purest gold, half to our treasury and half to the aforesaid bishop and his successors.

And so that this may be believed more truly, we have strengthened it with our own hand and order this charter to be marked with the impression of our seal.

Sign of Lord Henry, the most invincible king.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1006.

## XXXII. Charter of Saint Henry II confirming all the possessions of the Church of Worms and adding others to them (1006)

[Schannat, *The Bishopric of Worms* II, 36.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, by the favor of divine clemency, king.

We believe that nothing can contribute more suitably to the honor of our high position and the strengthening of our rule than our taking care of God’s holy churches and striving to preserve their endowments unshaken. Therefore let the diligence of all the faithful of God’s holy Church, present and future, know that, for the benefit of divine recompense and for the veneration of the blessed chief of the apostles, Peter, in whose honor the bishopric of Worms is known to have been founded, and also at the admonition and request of Burchard, the most devoted bishop of that see, we confirm by this charter of our grant everything that our royal and imperial predecessors, or we ourselves, have bestowed upon the same Church.

The arrangement is that the aforesaid bishop and his successors shall have, hold, and firmly possess all that was granted to their Church, as we have said, free from the molestation and opposition of everyone. So that this may be believed as true and observed more carefully by all, we have strengthened this charter written concerning it with our own hand and ordered it marked with the impression of our seal, as appears below. From our own property we also transfer to the Church one church situated in the suburb and another one mile from the city [lacuna], for the use of the brothers’ prebend.

Sign of Lord Henry, the most invincible king.

I, Eberard, chancellor, in place of Willigis, archchaplain, have examined and authenticated this.

Given on the second day before the Nones of March, in the third indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1006, and in the fifth year of the reign of Lord Henry II.

Done at Ladenburg, successfully. Amen.

## XXXIII. Saint Henry II, emperor, confirms to Notger, bishop of Liège, and his successors the abbeys and collegiate churches of Lobbes, Saint Hubert, Brogne, Gembloux, Fosses, Malonne, Namur, Dinant, Maaseik, Mechelen, Tongeren, Huy, and Maastricht (1006)

[Miraeus, *Diplomatic Works* III, 11.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, by the favor of divine clemency, king.

We believe and know that it will benefit us both in passing through the present life and in happily obtaining the future one if, in accordance with the just petitions of our faithful, we have freed ecclesiastical possessions from the judicial jurisdiction of every authority, increased those already freed, and firmly established that the increased possessions are to be protected by the security of a royal charter.

Therefore we wish it to be known to all our faithful, future as well as present, that the venerable Notger, bishop of Tongeren or Liège, presented to our sight a certain charter belonging to Otto II, our emperor and kinsman, confirmed by his hand and marked with his seal. It stated that not only Otto himself and his father—namely the first Emperor Otto in power and name—but also their predecessors, the Frankish kings Pepin, Charles, Louis, Lothar, and the other Charles, as well as the remaining kings who were their predecessors and successors, had granted by their authoritative charters to the same Church of Saint Mary and Saint Lambert, over which that bishop presides by God’s authority, that both it and its dependencies—namely Lobbes [note: Lobbes, in French *Lobbes*, a powerful Benedictine abbey on the River Laubach, whose abbot administers the bishopric of Liège in pontifical matters when the see is vacant. See Miraeus for many charters concerning this abbey], the place called Saint Hubert [note: Saint Hubert, formerly Andain, a powerful Benedictine abbey in the Ardennes forests in the diocese of Liège, famous for the miraculous healings performed through the relics of Saint Hubert, bishop], Brogne [note: Brogne, also called Saint Gerard’s, a Benedictine abbey in the county and diocese of Namur, united to the episcopal table of Namur], Gembloux [note: Gembloux, also called Gemblacum, a Benedictine abbey in French Brabant and the diocese of Namur; its abbot is the first count and holds first place in the assemblies of the Brabant nobility], Fosses [note: Fosses, a chapter of canons dedicated to Saint Foillan, not far from Namur], Malonne [note: Malonne, an abbey of regular canons near Namur], Namur [note: Namur, an episcopal city and the principal city of the county of Namur. It has the cathedral chapter of Saint Alban and a collegiate chapter of canons of the Blessed Virgin Mary; there was also formerly a chapter of Saint Peter in the castle], Dinant [note: Dinant, a town on the Meuse, where there is a collegiate church dedicated to the Blessed Virgin Mary], Ceumaco [note: Ceumacum, also called Cinacum, a chapter of canons dedicated to the Virgin Mary], Edla [note: Edla, also called Cyka and commonly Maseyck, a town in the diocese and Campine of Liège, where there is a collegiate church dedicated to the holy virgins Harlindis and Relindis], Tongeren [note: Tongeren, the most ancient city of the diocese of Liège, formerly the seat of the kings of Tongeren and of the earliest bishops. There is a collegiate church of the Blessed Virgin Mary], Huy [note: Huy, commonly Huy, a city on the River Meuse, with a collegiate church of the Blessed Virgin Mary], Maastricht [note: Maastricht, on the River Meuse, commonly Maestricht, a very strongly fortified city, now under the authority of the States General of the Netherlands. There are two collegiate churches of canons there, one dedicated to Saint Servatius and the other to the Blessed Virgin Mary], Mechelen [note: Mechelen, an archiepiscopal city in the Belgian province. It has a metropolitan church dedicated to Saint Rumold, in which a chapter of canons was founded in 996 by Saint Notger, bishop of Liège. Some attribute its original foundation to Saint Rumold himself, bishop and martyr, who died around 774], or any other places, together with all the things and people belonging to them, should remain free in themselves and protected and secure from every disturbance by judicial authority.

The aforementioned venerable bishop requested that we confirm this authority of security, promulgated in this way by our predecessors, by adding our assent out of love for God and reverence for the same Church.

We willingly inclined our ear to his just and reasonable petition and decided to issue this charter of our authority for the protection of that Church, out of love for divine worship and for the salvation of our soul. Through it we most firmly command that henceforth no count and no judge, except one to whom the bishop has entrusted the matter, dare enter the aforesaid places or their territories—whether in any districts within the jurisdiction of our kingdom that they now possess or are to possess in the future—to hear cases, collect fines, bans, tributes, or tolls from ships stationed there, or to exact tolls for any other reason, or to exercise any business of coercive jurisdiction over the people residing there, whether free or servile. Nor may anyone dare attempt anything there against the will of the bishop and his successors, now or in the future.

But it shall always be permitted to that bishop and his successors to possess peacefully the aforesaid properties and those subject to them under the protection and immunity of our defense, with all disturbance by judicial authority removed; to obey our imperial authority; and, together with the clergy and people subject to them, continually to implore God’s mercy for our safety and that of our wife, and for the condition and perpetuity of our kingdom. Whatever right the treasury could exact from the aforesaid ecclesiastical properties shall belong to the aforesaid Church, so that it may henceforth become an increase and supplement for carrying out God’s service.

Therefore, so that the authority of this charter may possess fuller force in the name of Him who granted us the power to command, and so that it may be preserved more carefully by the faithful of God’s holy Church and by our own faithful, we have confirmed it with our own hand and ordered it marked with the impression of our seal.

+ Seal of Lord Henry, the most invincible king.

## XXXIV. Henry II, king of Germany and Italy, receives Landulf, bishop of Cremona, under his protection (1007)

[Muratori, *Italian Antiquities* I, 991.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, by the providence of divine favor, king.

It is always the duty of royal dignity to provide for God’s churches, etc. Let everyone know that, having learned that in Italy the possessions of churches were being plundered after the death of their bishops, and that the holy Church of Cremona had recently suffered the same thing after the death of its pastor, we have received under the protection of our *mundeburdium* the venerable Lord Landulf, bishop of that same holy Church of Cremona and our most beloved chaplain, together with all his clergy and households.

We command likewise that no person great or small in our kingdom, after his death or that of his successors, dare disturb or molest the aforesaid Church, its clergy, or its servants. If anyone—which we do not believe—should become a violator of this protection of ours, then, if he is a knight of that Church, he and his heirs shall be deprived forever of every benefice that he has held from that Church, and he shall undoubtedly know that he must pay one hundred pounds of pure silver, half to our public treasury and half to the aforesaid Church.

If he is a citizen or suburban resident, let him know that he will lose all his estates and possessions, half to the public treasury and half to the aforesaid Church. If any other person in the kingdom should act against this, let him undoubtedly pay one hundred pounds of the finest gold, half to us and half to the aforesaid Church. And so that this may be believed more truly, etc.

Henry’s monogram is absent.

I, Everard, chancellor, in place of Willigis, archchaplain, have examined and authenticated this.

[lacuna] In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1007, in the fifth indiction, and in the sixth year of the reign of Lord Henry II, king. Done at Polede, successfully. Amen.

## XXXV. Saint Henry II, emperor, grants the estate of Kircheim to the monastery of Stein (1007, 1 November)

[Newgart, *Alemannic Diplomatic Code*, from the original in the archive of the Republic of Zurich.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, by the favor of divine clemency, king.

We are instructed and admonished by the saving teachings of sacred eloquence to despise temporal advantages and strive to obtain in heaven eternal dwellings that will always endure. Therefore, giving no deaf ear to the Lord’s commands and applying ourselves to obedience to divine exhortations, we elevated a certain place of our inheritance, called Bamberg, by raising it to the seat and summit of a bishopric, and magnificently exalted it with estates and various gifts of property.

We also entrusted the bishop of that see with the governance and administration of certain monasteries. Among them is one in Alemannia, situated beside the bank of the Rhine, called Stein, built and administered by our arrangement; we wish it to be subject to his care.

The administrators and prelates of this monastery therefore approached the presence of our serenity and, complaining of the poverty of the aforesaid place and the smallness of the possessions belonging to it, humbly requested that some support and an increase of estates be granted and added to it. When the favor and counsel of our faithful—namely bishops and abbots, dukes and counts—had strongly joined their petition, we graciously received their wishes and decided to fulfill their request for the increase of divine reward.

Therefore let the diligence of all our faithful, present and future, know that we transfer to the aforesaid monastery a certain place belonging to our jurisdiction and property, called Chilichheim [note: Kirchen, Kircheim on the Rhine below Basel], situated in the district of Prisichgowe and in the county of Count Adelbero, together with all its appurtenances: churches, estates, male and female servants, plots of land, buildings, people and rent-bearing lands, and the tributes and tolls from ships traveling along the Rhine, or whatever right our treasury ought to exact or might hope to exact from anywhere around that place.

We therefore transfer and convey all this to the same monastery in perpetual firmness, together with all its other dependencies that could still be named, so that any abbot who succeeds there may possess it in his power without opposition. He shall not be permitted to grant any portion of it as a benefice to any powerful free man, or in any way to alienate it from the use of the brothers serving God there.

And so that this gift of our authority may be held more firmly, believed more truly by all our faithful, and preserved more carefully, we have confirmed it beneath with our own hand and ordered it sealed with our seal. If anyone—which God forbid—should oppose this sanction of ours and remove what we have given or diminish it by any fraud, may he, unless he repents, burn eternally in unquenchable fire as the companion of the traitor Judas.

Sign of Lord Henry, the most invincible king.
