I, Eberard, chancellor [note: bishop of Bamberg], in place of Willigis, have examined and authenticated this. Given on the Kalends of November, in the fifth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1007, in the second year of Lord Henry.

[Note: The second year of Henry’s reign in Lombardy was still running, counted from the common year 1004, when he was crowned at Pavia on 14 May.]

## XXXVI. Charter of Saint Henry II, emperor, by which he grants the county of Cambrai to the metropolitan Church of Cambrai, to Bishop Erluin, and to his successors (1007)

[*Gallican Christianity* III, documents, p. 1.]

Henry, by the favor of divine clemency, king.

We wish it to be known to all the faithful how, both for the welfare of our soul and through the intervention of the venerable Heribert, archbishop of Cologne, we have granted the county of Cambrai as property to the Church of Cambrai, built in honor of Saint Mary, by this charter of our authority. We command that Erluin, bishop of the aforesaid see, and his successors shall henceforth have free power to hold the same county for the use of the aforesaid Church, to choose its count, to possess its bans, and in every way to do with it whatever may please them.

Sign of Lord Henry, the most invincible king.

I, Eberard, chancellor, in place of Willigis, archchaplain, have examined and authenticated this.

Given on the eleventh day before the Kalends of November, in the fifth indiction, in the year 1007, in the sixth year of the reign of Lord Henry II. Done in the palace at Aachen.

## XXXVII. Letter of Saint Henry concerning the bishopric of Bamberg established by him (1007)

[Ludewig, *Script. rer. Germ.*, 282.]

Henry, king by the preordination of divine clemency, to all the sons of the Church, future as well as present.

We are instructed and forewarned by the saving teachings of sacred eloquence to leave behind temporal things, set aside earthly advantages, and strive to obtain in heaven eternal dwellings that will endure without end. Present glory is fleeting and empty while it is possessed, unless some thought of heavenly eternity is entertained within it. But God’s mercy provided a remedy for the human race when it made a portion of the heavenly homeland the price of earthly substance.

Therefore, not forgetful of this mercy and not unaware that we have been elevated to royal dignity through the gratuitous regard of divine mercy, we judge it fitting not only to enlarge the churches built by our predecessors but also to build new ones for the greater glory of God and exalt them with the most welcome gifts of our devotion.

Therefore, giving no deaf ear to the Lord’s commands and applying ourselves to obedience to divine exhortations, we desire to store in heaven the treasures bestowed upon us by the munificence of divine generosity, where neither thieves break in and steal, nor rust or moth destroy; and where, whenever we recall all that has now been gathered, our heart may turn again and again in desire and love.

Accordingly, we wish it to be evident to the whole community of the faithful that we have elevated a certain place of our paternal inheritance, called Bamberg, to the seat and summit of a bishopric; that it has been confirmed by the authority of the Roman See; and that, with the consent of the venerable Henry, bishop of Würzburg, the will of our beloved wife Cunigunda, and the equal and common counsel and decree of all our faithful—archbishops, bishops, abbots, dukes, and counts—and with the harmonious devotion of all the princes of our kingdom, we have founded, established, and strengthened it in honor of almighty God, blessed Mary ever-virgin, and the holy apostles Peter and Paul, as well as Saints Kilian and George.

This was done so that there might be celebrated there a solemn memorial of us, of our parents, and of our predecessor, Emperor Otto III, and so that a perpetual saving sacrifice might be offered for all the orthodox.

Having therefore offered to God in this beloved Church of ours, for the honor and adornment of the house of God, vessels, vestments, and other ecclesiastical ornaments made of precious metals and stones for various uses of the sanctuary, we have moreover granted to the aforesaid episcopal see estates, churches, villages, and settlements, with all their appurtenances and attachments: male and female dependents, plots of land, buildings, cultivated and uncultivated lands, roads and trackless places, outgoings and incomes, those acquired and those yet to be acquired, woods, fishing nets, hunting rights, meadows, pastures, fields, forests, forest-rights [the printed text has *praestariis forestariis*, uncertain], cellars, rents, waters and their courses, mills, movable and immovable property, and all other useful resources that can properly be written or named in any manner.

By this edict of our authority we establish that Eberard, the bishop of the aforementioned see, beloved by God and by us, and his successors, shall henceforth have free power to hold and possess the aforesaid goods with all their dependencies, or to convert them to any use of the bishopric.

For the canonical brothers serving God there, we confirm, by our imperial authority and as their property, the possessions that we have transferred for the daily support of temporal life. The arrangement is that the aforesaid canons and their successive provosts shall henceforth have free power, with the consent and counsel of those canons, to exchange them for better uses, increase them, and turn them to their advantage in whatever way they can, so that they, remembering us kindly before God, as well as our most beloved wife and partner in the kingdom, Cunigunda, and our parents, may in turn answer our benefits with pious and continual intercession.

But if anyone—which God forbid—should attempt to destroy or violate this munificent gift and institution of ours, confirmed by the authority of the Apostolic See and of so many venerable Fathers, let him pay eternally on the day of judgment before God’s eyes with unquenchable torment.

To prevent this from happening, and so that this conveyance and decree may remain inviolable forever for all, we have strengthened this charter written concerning it with our own hand and ordered it marked with the impression of our seal.

## XXXVIII. Saint Henry II, emperor, benefits the college of noble canonesses at Thorn on the Meuse, at the request of Notger, bishop of Liège (1007)

[Miraeus, *Diplomatic Works* I, 507.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, by the favor of divine clemency, king.

We believe and know that it will benefit us both in passing through the present life and in happily obtaining the future one if, in accordance with the just petitions of our faithful, we confirm that ecclesiastical possessions, increased and still to be increased, are to be protected by the security of a royal charter.

Therefore we wish it to be known to all our faithful, future as well as present, that, through the intercession of the venerable Notger, bishop of Tongeren or Liège, we have granted to the monastery of Thorn, subject to the bishopric of that same bishop, the market of that place, its toll, and its coercive jurisdiction.

Moreover, through the intervention of the same venerable bishop, we have assigned, by the authority of our consent, to the jurisdiction of the said monastery the churches of Britte, Chamaritte, and Avesate, which that same bishop granted to the monastery for the enlargement of its ecclesiastical resources and the accumulation of heavenly reward.

And so that the authority of this charter may possess fuller force in the name of Him who granted us the power to command, and so that it may be preserved by the faithful of God’s holy Church and by our own faithful, following the custom of our predecessors, we have confirmed it with our own hand and ordered it marked with the impression of our seal.

Sign of Lord Henry, the most invincible king.

I, Heribert, chancellor, in place of Willigis, archchaplain, have examined and authenticated this.

Given on the eleventh day before the Nones of June, in the fifth indiction, in the thousand and seventh year of the Lord’s Incarnation, and in the fifth year of the reign of Lord Henry II.

[Note: From the letter-forms of the year in this charter it seems possible to conclude that Notger, bishop of Liège, died only in 1008, and not in 1007, as Bucherius and others calculate.]

Done at Mainz, successfully. Amen.

## XXXIX. Henry II, emperor, grants the abbey of Kitzingen to the archbishopric of Bamberg (1007)

[Ludewig, *Script. rer. Germ.*, p. 1112.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, by the favor of divine clemency, king.

We are instructed and admonished by the saving teachings of sacred eloquence to leave behind temporal goods, set aside earthly advantages, and strive to obtain in heaven eternal dwellings that will endure without end. Therefore, giving no deaf ear to the Lord’s commands and applying ourselves to obedience to divine exhortations, we elevated a certain place of our paternal inheritance, called Bamberg, by raising it to the seat and summit of a bishopric. By the authority of Rome, by that of the venerable Henry, bishop of Würzburg, and through the pure and common counsel and decree of all our faithful—archbishops, bishops, and abbots, as well as dukes and counts—we established and strengthened it in honor of holy Mary, God’s mother, and the holy apostles Peter and Paul, as well as the martyrs Kilian and George, so that a solemn memorial of us, our parents, and Otto our elder might be celebrated there and that a perpetual saving sacrifice might be offered for all the orthodox.

Therefore let all our faithful, both the present generation and posterity to come, know that we donate and grant as property, by this charter of our authority and as firmly as we can, a former possession of our jurisdiction, the abbey called Kitzingen, situated in the district of Gotzfeld, to the same aforesaid episcopal see, together with all its appurtenances and attachments: churches, tithes, woods, hunting rights, and all useful resources that can in any way be named or written, with every opposition removed.

Therefore we command that Eberard, the bishop of the aforementioned see, beloved in the Lord, and his successors shall henceforth have free power to hold and possess the same abbey with all its dependencies, or to do with it in every way whatever may please them.

If anyone, which God forbid, should presume to destroy or violate this munificent gift of ours, let him pay with unquenchable torment before the eyes of God on the Last Day. To prevent this, and so that this conveyance of ours may remain uncorrupted for all, we have strengthened this charter written concerning it with our own hand and ordered it marked with the impression of our seal.

Dated on the Kalends of November, in the fifth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1007, and in the sixth year of the reign of Lord King Henry II. Enacted at Frankfurt, successfully. Amen.

## XL. Foundation by Saint Emperor Henry of Furth, at Frankfurt during the assembly (Kalends of November 1007)

[Ludewig, *Scriptores rerum Germanicarum*, 1281–82.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, king by the favor of divine clemency.

We are instructed and admonished by the most salutary teachings of sacred eloquence [Col. 0276D] that, abandoning temporal advantages, we should strive to attain dwellings in heaven that are eternal and destined to remain without end. Therefore, obeying the Lord’s commands with attentive hearing and applying ourselves to obedience to divine exhortations, we elevated a certain place of our paternal inheritance, called Babenberg, to the dignity and summit of an episcopal see. By Roman authority, with the consent of the venerable Henry, bishop of Würzburg, and by the counsel and decree of all our faithful, both archbishops and bishops and abbots, [Col. 0277A] as well as dukes and counts, we established and confirmed it in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God, and of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, as well as of the martyrs Kilian and George, so that there might be celebrated there a memorial of us and of our parents, and also of Otto III, namely our imperial predecessor and lord, and so that a perpetual saving sacrifice might be offered for all orthodox Christians.

Therefore let all our faithful, both the present generation and posterity to come, know that we grant and establish as property, by this page of our authoritative charter, as firmly as we can, with all contradiction removed, a place formerly belonging to us, called Furth, situated in the district of Nordgau and in the county of Count Berengar, for the support of the canons serving God in the same aforesaid episcopal see in community, together with all its appurtenances and attachments, namely villages, estates, churches, male and female servants, plots, cultivated and uncultivated lands, roads and trackless places, exits and entrances, things acquired and to be acquired, woods, forests, pannage, hunts, waters, fisheries, mills and millworks, movable and immovable property, and all other useful things that can properly be written or named in any way.

We therefore command that our dearest brothers in Christ, the Bambergers, henceforth have free power, by our right, to possess the same place called Furth with all its appurtenances, and also to choose for themselves a suitable advocate over the aforesaid place, or [Col. 0277C] to do with it in every way whatever they may wish for the use of the monastic brotherhood. If anyone, which God forbid, should presume to destroy or violate the munificence of this our donation, let him eternally pay the penalty of unquenchable torment before the eyes of God on the day of judgment. To prevent this, and so that this our grant may remain inviolate by all forever, we ordered this charter, written concerning it, to be authenticated by our own hand and marked with the impression of our seal.

## XLI. King Henry II gives and establishes as property, for the support of the canons serving God in the episcopal see of Bamberg which he established, a certain place of his property called Pferingun, situated in the district of Chelesgau and in the county of Count Berengar, together with all its appurtenances or attachments—namely villages, estates, churches, male and female servants, plots, buildings, cultivated and uncultivated lands, roads and trackless places, issues and revenues, things acquired or to be acquired, woods, forests, pannage, hunts, waters, fisheries, mill-sites, mills, movable and immovable property, and all other useful things that can properly be written or named in any way—with all contradiction removed; on the condition that the aforesaid canons henceforth have free power to hold and possess the said place Pferingun with all its appurtenances, to choose for themselves a suitable advocate over the said place, or to do with it whatever they please (1007)

[Ried, ibid., p. 125.]

So that this our grant may remain inviolate by all forever, we ordered this charter, written concerning it, to be authenticated by our own hand and marked with the impression of our seal. In addition, at Regensburg we gave and confirmed, for the use of the brothers—the Bamberg canons—three plots within the city beside the Danube, two at Brunnelaite, and two at Reginhusen.

Sign of Lord Henry, the most invincible king. (Monogram.)

I, Eberhard, chancellor, have reviewed this on behalf of Willigis, archchaplain.

Dated on the Kalends of November, in the fifth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1007, and in the sixth year of the reign of Lord Henry II. Enacted at Frankfurt, successfully. Amen.

## XLII. King Henry gives to the Church of Bamberg, which he established, an abbey belonging to him, or an ancient chapel, as its property (1008)

[Ried, ibid., p. 126.]

[Col. 0278B]

C. In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, king by the favor of divine clemency.

We are admonished and instructed by the divine and saving teachings of the Holy Scriptures to enrich the churches of God with generous benevolence and not to cease enlarging them with the greatest devotion. Therefore let the diligence of all Christ’s faithful and of our own know that, through the intervention of our most beloved wife Chunigunda, we give as property, with the greatest and most generous devotion, a chapel or abbey belonging to us, situated within the city of Regensburg, in the district of Tuonogau and in the county of Count Ruodpert, to the holy Bamberg Church [Col. 0278C] consecrated in honor of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and Saint George the martyr, together with all its appurtenances, namely its issues and revenues, cultivated and uncultivated lands, and all useful things that can in any way be written or named.

This is on the condition that the venerable bishop Eberhard of the aforesaid Bamberg Church, and his successors, henceforth have free power to hold and possess it and to do whatever pertains to the use of the aforesaid church, with all contradiction removed. And so that the authority of this our donation may remain stable and unshaken, we ordered this charter, written concerning it, to be authenticated by our own hand and marked with the impression [Col. 0278D] of our seal.

Sign of Lord Henry, the most invincible king. (Monogram.)

I, Gunther, chancellor, have reviewed this on behalf of Willigis, archchaplain.

Dated on the Kalends of June, in the sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1008, and in the seventh year of the reign of Lord Henry II. Enacted at Merseburg, successfully.

The seal is impressed inside.

## XLIII. The charter of Saint Henry by which he assigns to the Church of Worms whatever Count Becelin possessed as a benefice (1008)

[Schannat, *Episcopatus Wormatiensis* II, 37.]

[Col. 0279A] In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, king by the favor of divine clemency.

If we strive to improve the places of God’s churches by an increase of some advantage, we have no doubt that this will greatly benefit us. Therefore let the whole body of all Christ’s faithful, present and future, know how we, for the salvation of the soul of Emperor Otto III, as well as of our own soul and those of our parents and of Chunigunda, our most beloved wife, through her intervention and at the request of Burchard, the venerable bishop, grant and bestow in full, by this page of our charter, upon the bishopric and Church of Worms, built and dedicated in honor of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, whatever Count Becelin has hitherto had and held from us as a benefice, together with all its appurtenances [Col. 0279B] or attachments, and all useful things that can in any way be named or written, situated in the district of Lahnau and in the county of Count Gerlai. We transfer it entirely from our right into his right and dominion, on the condition that the aforesaid Burchard, bishop of the holy see of Worms, and his successors, henceforth have free power over the aforesaid estate and its appurtenances to hold, possess, or do whatever they wish, with every contradiction removed.

And so that the authority of this our donation may remain stable and unshaken for all time, we ordered this charter, written concerning it, to be authenticated by our own hand and marked with the impression of our seal.

[Col. 0279C] Sign of Lord Henry, the most invincible king.

I, Eberhard, chancellor, have reviewed this on behalf of Willigis, archchaplain.

Dated on the fifth day before the Ides of May, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1008, in the fifth indiction, and in the sixth year of Lord Henry’s reign.

Enacted at Tribur, successfully. Amen.

## XLIV. Diploma of Emperor Henry II by which he transfers Meiningen and Walldorf to the Church of Würzburg in exchange for other possessions granted to the new bishopric of Bamberg in the district of Ratenzgau (1008, 7 May)

[Ussermann, *Germania sacra* III, *Preuves*, p. 16.]

[Col. 0279D] In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, king by the favor of divine clemency.

We wish it to be known to all Christ’s faithful, present and future, that, hoping for divine reward and making the Lord our heir, we raised and elevated from our hereditary possessions a certain place belonging to us, called Babenberg, into the dignity and headship of a bishopric distinguished by the honor of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles. From Henry, bishop of the same church, with the consent and approval of the clergy and people, we acquired by a firm and lawful exchange a part of the diocese of Würzburg, namely the county called Ratenzgau, excepting the three churches of Wahenrod, Mulinhusen, and Lonerstat with the chapels pertaining to those churches, and a certain part of the district called Volckfeld: namely, from the place where the river called Vraha flows into the Ratenza, [Col. 0280A] downstream along the Ratenza as far as the river Main, downstream along the Main as far as the place called Fiheriet, then upstream along the stream that flows past and divides the same village as far as the head and source of that stream; and from the head of that stream, by the most direct and nearest route possible, back to the aforesaid river Vraha.

In return, we transfer to the same Bishop Henry and to his church, by right of ownership, places situated in the district of Grabfeld and in the county of Count Otto, called Maynunga, the march of Maynunga, and Walahdorf, together with all their appurtenances, namely villages and male and female dependents, churches, tithes, woods, hunts, waters [Col. 0280B] and watercourses, fisheries, mills, meadows, pastures, cultivated and uncultivated lands, things acquired or to be acquired, roads and trackless places, exits and entrances, and all useful things that can be named or called by any name. We transfer them from our right into the right of the aforesaid church, on the condition that Bishop Henry and his successors henceforth have free power over the aforesaid places to possess, exchange, or do whatever they wish with them, with all contradiction removed.

And so that the authority of this our exchange or donation may remain stable and unshaken for all time, we ordered this charter, written concerning it, to be authenticated by our own hand and marked with the impression of our seal.

[Col. 0280C] Sign of Lord Henry, the most invincible king.

I, Eberhard, bishop and chancellor, have reviewed this on behalf of Willigis, archchaplain.

Dated on the Nones of May, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1008, in the fifth indiction, and in the sixth year of the reign of Lord Henry II. Enacted at Würzburg, successfully. Amen.

## XLV. Privilege of Saint Henry for the Church of Vicenza (1008)

[Ughelli, *Italia Sacra* V, 1, 40.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, king by the favor of divine clemency.

If we care for the churches of God and strive to enlarge them, we have no doubt that the condition of our kingdom is thereby increased. Therefore let the whole body of the holy Church of God, present and future, know how Jerome, bishop of the holy Church of Vicenza and our familiar associate, approached our clemency, requesting that, for the love of God and the salvation of our soul, we forgive and grant, by the generosity of our royal authority, the castles of his bishopric which until now had been devastated and trampled down through the burden of the *fodrum*.

Granting his requests, as we can justly and lawfully do, we forgive to the aforesaid Bishop Jerome and his successors, just as it was granted and forgiven to him by the blessed-memory Lord Otto Caesar Augustus, that no *fodrum* be paid or granted from all the castles belonging to his aforesaid bishopric—namely Barbarano, Salvatiano, [Col. 0281A] Nosceta, Albetine, Aureliano, Custodia, Grancona, Grumodo, Vicenza-Brendulis, Altavilla, Montedigno, Corvedo, Valle Coturnica, Cucullo, Vello, and Arserio—or by any dependents living or residing in the territory of the aforesaid bishopric, to any man, whether duke, margrave, count, or any person of high or low rank. Rather, by this charter, it shall be permitted to the aforesaid Bishop Jerome and his successors, as written above, peacefully and quietly to defend and protect all the aforesaid castles and their inhabitants belonging to the aforesaid bishopric, or residing on its territory, from every *fodrum*, with all contradiction removed.

If it should happen that we come into those parts, the aforesaid Bishop Jerome or his successors, personally or through their faithful agents, shall collect the *fodrum* and prepare services for us according to their ability. This shall be done in such a way that no duke, patriarch, margrave, count, viscount, *sculdasius*, *gastald*, or any great or small person of our kingdom may dare or presume to disturb, harass, or trouble the aforesaid Bishop Jerome or his successors concerning the forgiveness and grant of the *fodrum* from the castles listed below.

If anyone, which we do not believe, should attempt to violate this our charter, let him know that he shall pay five hundred pounds of pure gold, half to our treasury and half to the aforesaid Bishop Jerome [Col. 0281C] and his successors.

[Note: [Col. 0281D] The same Jerome was deposed by the same Emperor Henry as a perjurer and apostate, and his property was confiscated. What he possessed in the county of Pavia was granted to the Church of Como; this is mentioned in a diploma granted in 1026 by Conrad II, Henry’s successor, to the same Church of Como.]

And so that this may be regarded as more certain, we ordered this page to be authenticated by our own hand and marked with our seal.

Sign of Lord Henry +, the most invincible king.

Eberhard, archchaplain, has reviewed this.

Dated on the thirtieth [lacuna], in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1008, in the sixth indiction, and in the fifth [read: sixth] year of the reign [read: kingship] of Lord Henry. Enacted at Mulind [lacuna], successfully. Amen.

## XLVI. Saint Emperor Henry grants Bishop Baldric of Liège and Count Baldric the ban over game in the woods they possessed (1008)

[Miraeus, *Opera diplomatica* II, 53.]

[Col. 0282A] In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, king by the favor of divine clemency.

Let it be known to all our faithful, present and future, how, through the intervention and request of Heribert, archbishop of Cologne [Note: [Col. 0281D] Saint Heribert, archbishop of Cologne, passed to the better life on 16 March 1021. He was buried opposite the city of Cologne in the monastery at Deutz, which he himself founded. Rupert, abbot of Deutz, wrote his life; it was published by Surius.], we grant and bestow by this page of our charter our ban over game, in their own woods, to Baldric [Note: [Col. 0281D] Baldric, bishop of Liège and founder of the abbey of Saint James in the city of Liège, ceased to live in the year 1017, etc.], bishop of the holy Church of Liège, and also to Baldric [Note: [Col. 0281D] Baldric was Count of Liège. I suspect that formerly many episcopal cities, such as Cambrai, Arras, Amiens, and others, had their own counts.] the count, situated between those two rivers both called Nithe [Note: [Col. 0282D] Both are called Nithe. Two rivers are indicated here that still bear the name Nithe or Nettre in Brabantine Campine and converge at the town of Lier: namely, the Greater Nethe and the Lesser Nethe.], and the third called Thila [Note: [Col. 0282D] Thila, or Thilia—Thy in French, Dilia or Dyle in German—is a river rising near Genappe in French Brabant. It waters the Cistercian monastery of Villers, then, enlarged by the Fura stream at Leuven, flows into the Demer and finally into the Scheldt.], and belonging to the villages called Heiste [Note: [Col. 0282D] Heiste is a municipality in the district of Rijen, still known today as Heist-op-den-Berg.] and Heisten, as well as Badfride and Maclines [Note: [Col. 0282D] The village of Maclines. Perhaps this is Mechelen, *villa* in medieval writers, meaning the same as the French *village*.]. The whole area is called Waverwald and is situated in the county of Count Gozilo, which is called Antwerp [Note: [Col. 0282D] Antwerp, in the county of Count Gozilo. The reader should note here the county or march of Antwerp.].

We grant and bestow this by our charter [Col. 0282B] and transfer it from our right into their right and dominion, on the condition that the aforesaid Baldric and Baldric have free power henceforth to do whatever they please concerning the aforesaid ban and its benefits, with the contradiction of all men removed.

And so that the authority of this our donation may remain stable and unshaken for all time, we ordered this charter, written concerning it, to be authenticated by our own hand and marked with our seal.

Sign of Lord Henry, the most invincible king.

I, Eberhard [Note: [Col. 0282D] Eberhard was appointed in 1006 as the first bishop of the Church of Bamberg, founded by Saint Henry the Emperor.], chancellor, have reviewed this on behalf of Willigis, archchaplain.

Dated on the day before the Ides of September, in the sixth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1008, and in the seventh year of the reign of Lord Henry II [Col. 0282C]. Enacted at Trier, successfully. Amen.

## XLVII. King Henry II grants the Niederaltaich monastery a parish church at Mundraching with its tithes, a mansus there, three mansus at Siffenkofen, and a mill at Mangolting (1009, 6 April)

[Ried, *Codex episcopatus Ratisbonensis*, from *Monumenta Boica* XI, 137.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, king by the favor of divine clemency.

If we strive to enrich or elevate the churches of God by an increase of some gift, we have no doubt that this will benefit us. Therefore let the diligence of all Christ’s faithful and of our own know how, for the salvation [Col. 0283A] of our soul and through the intervention of our beloved abbot Godehard, in consideration of his constant and devoted service, we grant and bestow by this page of our charter upon his monastery called Altaha, for the service and use of the brothers serving God there: in the village called Mundriching, one church with its endowment-mansus and two parts of the tithes belonging to the same church; and in the same village another mansus with the dependents Frudun, his wife, and their children.

At Siffenkofen, three mansus with the dependents living on them; and at Mangolting, the aforesaid mill-site together with the mill, situated in the district of Duonagau and in the county of Count Ruotbert, together with all appurtenances or useful things that can be named or called. [Col. 0283B] We transfer them entirely from our right and dominion into their right and dominion, on the condition that the aforesaid abbot and his successors, together with the brothers serving God there, henceforth have free power over the aforesaid property and its equipment to do whatever they wish for the common use of the brothers, with the contradiction of all men removed.

And so that the authority of this our donation may remain stable and unshaken for all time, we ordered this charter, written concerning it, to be authenticated by our own hand and marked with the impression of our seal.

Sign of Lord Henry, the most invincible king. (Monogram.)

I, Gunther, chancellor, have reviewed this on behalf of Willigis, archchaplain.

[Col. 0283C] Dated on the eighth day before the Ides of April, in the eighth indiction, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1009, and in the eighth year of the reign of Lord Henry II.

Enacted at Regensburg, successfully. Amen.

## XLVIII. King Henry II grants the monastery of Prüf, near Regensburg, a royal mansus in the village of Genstall (1009, 20 May)

[Ried, cited above, p. 128.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, king by the favor of divine clemency.

If we strive to elevate the places of God’s churches by an increase of some gift, we have no doubt that this benefits us and the condition of our kingdom. Therefore let the whole body of Christ’s faithful, present and future, [Col. 0283D] know how, moved by divine love, for the salvation of our soul, and at the intervention and request of Boniface, abbot of Prüf, we grant and bestow by this royal page one royal mansus—which we had previously granted to Waltrico—in the village called Genstall, situated in the district of Tunagau and in the county of Rupert, upon him and his monastery, built and dedicated in honor of Saint Bartholomew the apostle, together with all its appurtenances, roads and trackless places, cultivated and uncultivated lands, issues and revenues, things acquired or to be acquired, and all useful things that can in any way be named or written.

We transfer it entirely from our right and dominion into his right and dominion, on the condition [Col. 0284A] that, if any bishop of the Church of Regensburg, which God forbid, should presume to destroy the same monastery or violate the monastic life there, the aforesaid mansus shall return again to royal hands. But if the aforesaid monastery remains firm and inviolate, the aforesaid Abbot Boniface and his successors shall have free power to do with it whatever they please for the benefit of their church, with all contradiction by men removed.

And so that the authority of this our donation may remain stable and unshaken in this manner, we authenticated this charter, written concerning it, with our own hand and ordered it to be marked with our seal.

Sign of Lord Henry, the most invincible king. (Monogram.)

[Col. 0284B] I, Gunther, chancellor, have reviewed this on behalf of Willigis, archchaplain.

Dated on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of June, in the seventh indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1009, and in the seventh year of the reign of Lord Henry II.

Enacted at Regensburg, successfully. Amen.

## XLIX. King Henry II grants the Church of Bamberg the place called Lichtowa, situated in the district of Nordgau (1009, 2 July)

[Ried, *Codex episcopatus Ratisbonensis* I, 129.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, king by the favor of divine clemency.

Giving attentive hearing to the Lord’s commands [Col. 0284C] and applying ourselves to obedience to divine exhortations, we elevated a certain place of our paternal inheritance called Babenberg into the dignity and summit of an episcopal see, and by Roman authority established and confirmed it in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God, and of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, so that there might be celebrated there the name of us and of our parents, and of Otto III, namely our emperor and predecessor, and so that a perpetual sacrifice might be offered for all orthodox Christians.

Therefore let all our faithful, both the present generation and future posterity, know how we grant and establish as property, by this page of our charter, as firmly as we can, with all contradiction removed, a place belonging to us called Lihtowa, situated in the district of Nordgau and in the county of Count Henry, to the same aforesaid episcopal see, together with all its appurtenances or attachments, namely movable and immovable property and all other useful things that can in any way be written or named. [Col. 0284D]

And so that this grant of our authority may remain firm and unshaken, we ordered this page, written concerning it, to be authenticated by our own hand and marked with the impression of our seal.

Sign of Lord Henry II, the most invincible king. (Monogram.)

I, Gunther, chancellor, have reviewed this on behalf of Erchanbald, archchancellor.

Dated on the sixth day before the Nones of July, in the eighth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s [Col. 0285A] Incarnation 1009, and in the ninth year of Lord Henry’s reign. Enacted at Ingelheim, successfully.

The seal of majesty is impressed inside.

## L. Charter of Saint Henry for the Church of Cremona (1009)

[Ughelli, *Italia sacra* IV, 594.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, king of the Franks and Lombards by the favor of divine mercy.

If we strive to assist the distress and oppression of the holy churches of God and labor to provide the support of our majesty, we have no doubt that the condition of our kingdom will be strengthened and that the reward of eternal recompense will be repaid to us. [Col. 0285B] Therefore let it be known to all our faithful, present and future, that the venerable Landulf, bishop of the holy Church of Cremona and entirely our most faithful servant, reported to our moderation that a certain abbey subject to his bishopric, dedicated in honor of Saint Lawrence and situated near his city, was being diminished by a certain abbot named Lampert through granting benefices and making harmful written instruments. On this account, the provisions of the brothers were being withheld, and thus the prayers and alms that ought to have been offered for the soul of the man who built it and for the souls of all Christians appeared to be diminished.

Struck inwardly with grief of heart because of this matter, we began to consider what should be done about it. Therefore, with divine grace inspiring us and with the salutary counsel of our most beloved wife Chunicunda [Col. 0285C] intervening, we ordered a charter of our royal authority to be made, to be held inviolably forever, on the condition that neither the present abbot nor future abbots should henceforth have any power to diminish the property belonging to the aforesaid abbey, whether by granting benefices, making exchanges, or issuing leases or hereditary grants, without the permission of the present bishop and his successors who shall hold office in due course.

If any abbot should thereafter presume to act against this authority and charter of ours, the writings and investitures he has made shall remain invalid, void, and without force; the abbot shall be deprived of his office and [Col. 0285D] dignity; and those who presume to accept an investiture or any written instrument shall know that they must pay one hundred pounds of the finest gold, half to our treasury and half to the abbey to which he attempted to cause damage and diminution. To make this more firmly believed and more carefully observed by all, we ordered this charter to be authenticated by our own hand and marked with the impression of our seal.

Sign [lacuna] of Lord Henry, the most glorious and invincible king.

I, Egilbert, chancellor, have reviewed this on behalf of Wilibisi, bishop and archchancellor.

Dated on the seventh day before the Ides of October, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1009, and in the seventh year of King Henry I.

Enacted at Magdeburg, successfully. Amen.

## LI. Charter of King Henry II for the monastery of Classe of Saint Apollinaris (1009, seventh day before the Kalends of May)

[*Annales Camaldulenses* I, 190, from the original charter of Classe.]

[Col. 0286A]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, king by the favor of divine clemency.

If we incline the ears of our serenity to the petitions of our faithful, we have no doubt that they will thereby become more ready and devoted in our service. Therefore let the discernment of all the holy Church of God and of our faithful, present and future, know that Bon, priest, monk, and abbot of the Ravennate monastery of Saint Apollinaris, which they say was long ago founded in the city called Classe, [Col. 0286B] and our most devoted faithful, entreated our highness in every respect that, for the love of God and the perpetual salvation of our soul, we should strengthen, establish, found, and determine, by our most gracious generosity, for perpetual confirmation, through this inviolable page of our charter and pragmatic instrument, all the properties and possessions that the aforesaid Church of the aforesaid monastery appeared to possess in full by whatever guarantees or grants.

Graciously and willingly assenting to and approving his sacred petitions and just desires, we strengthen and confirm them, and transfer them from our right and dominion into his right and dominion: namely, whatever belongs to the monastery, both in the *monarchia* and in the individual places of our kingdom. [Col. 0286C]

In the county of Forlì and in that of Pesaro or Rimini, the village called Sala with all its appurtenances in full; the title-church of that monastery, situated beside the wall, in honor of Saint Felicula and the holy martyrs Mark and Marcellian; the church of Saint Mary, Mother of God, in the aforesaid village and estate of Sala; and the church of Saint Martin called Aqualonga.

All these in full, with all their appurtenances, attachments, and underlying lands adjoining Sala on every side: on the first side, the river called Pisciatellus; on the second side, Vedrita and Paverianus; on the third side, the boundary called Arzer, running from Paverianus as far as the small road; and the stream called the stream of Fabrica, [Col. 0286D] ending and flowing down to the sea, together with as much of the seashore itself as appears to belong to me, in full.

We also grant Sala Nuova in full with all its appurtenances, and whatever is royal property at Castancto, Bulgaria, and Branchisi. Again, we grant that it may make, in the city called Forlì, a postern in the public wall at the place where they have their own land within and outside the wall, and build a church beside the wall called Dapenna.

We also grant and command, establishing it by statute, that no duke, archbishop, margrave, count, viscount, *sculdasius*, *gastald*, or any public exactor may dare or presume to demand or exact, under any title of coercion, a toll or any public levy from any estates and possessions situated throughout any places of our kingdom, [Col. 0287A] or from the people dwelling or residing upon them; nor may anyone attempt in any way to carry out or inflict any invasion, diminution, or reckless presumption.

If anyone, which God forbid, should attempt by reckless audacity in any way to violate this page of our guarantee, definition, grant, and voluntary distribution, which is to remain inviolable always and everywhere, let him know that he must pay one hundred pounds of gold or one thousand [silver pounds], half to our treasury and half to the aforesaid monastery of Saint Apollinaris. To make this more firmly believed and more carefully observed by all, we authenticated this page with our own hand and ordered it to be marked below with the impression of our seal. [Col. 0287B]

Sign of Lord Henry, the most invincible king.

I, Eberhard, chancellor, have reviewed this on behalf of Willigis, archchaplain.

Dated on the seventh day before the Kalends of May, in the seventh indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1009, and in the seventh year of the reign of Lord Henry II.

Enacted at Niven [lacuna], successfully. Amen.

## LII. Privilege granted by Saint Henry to Abbot Godehard (1009)

[Ludewig, *Scriptores rerum Germanicarum*, 333–34.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, king by the favor of divine clemency.

[Col. 0287C] If we strive to enrich or elevate the churches of God by an increase of some gift, we have no doubt that this will benefit us. Therefore let the diligence of all Christ’s faithful and of our own know how, for the salvation of our soul and through the intervention of our beloved abbot Godehard, in consideration of his constant and devoted service, we grant and bestow by this page of our charter upon his monastery called Altaha, for the service and use of the brothers serving God there: in the village called Mundriching, one church with its endowment-mansus and two parts of the tithes belonging to the same church; and in the same village another mansus with the dependents Frundun, his wife, and their children; at Siffenkofen, three mansus with the dependents living on them; and at Mangolting, the aforesaid mill-site together with the mill, situated in the district of Wonaulgau and in the county of Count Ruotbert, together with all appurtenances or useful things that can be named or called.

[Col. 0287D] We transfer them entirely from our right and dominion into their right and dominion, on the condition that the aforesaid abbot and his successors, together with the brothers serving God there, henceforth have free power over the aforesaid property and its equipment to do whatever they wish for the common use of the brothers, with the contradiction of all men removed.

And so that the authority of this our donation may remain stable and unshaken for all time, we ordered this charter, written concerning it, to be authenticated by our own hand and marked with the impression of our seal. [Col. 0288A]

Dated on the eighth day before the Ides of April, in the seventh indiction, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1009, and in the eighth year of the reign of Lord Henry II. Enacted at Regensburg. Amen.

### LIII. Privilege of Saint Henry for the same church. (In the same year.)

[Ludewig, cited above.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, king by the favor of divine mercy.

If we have endeavored to enrich the churches of God, or those serving in them, from our possessions, we firmly believe that we shall thereby receive an unfading reward in the future. Therefore we wish it to be known to all our faithful, present and future, how we, inflamed by the desire for eternal life, both for the salvation of our soul and those of our parents, and also at the intervention of our beloved wife Chunigunda, and in return for the most pleasing service of Godehard, the beloved abbot of Altach, have by this royal charter conferred and granted upon the same church, over which he is seen to preside, for the use of the monks serving God there, a perpetual right to exact the toll from both travelers and those traveling by water at the market held in the county of Count Thiemo, near the monastery, in the village called Helnigerimperk. Whoever removes anything from that place shall be answerable at the future judgment. And so that the authority of this conveyance of ours may remain stable and unshaken, we have ordered it to be sealed with the impression of our image, after strengthening it with our own hand.

Given on the seventh day before the Ides of June, in the seventh indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1009, and in the eighth year of the reign of our lord Henry II, king.

Enacted at Merseburg, successfully. Amen.

### LIV. He grants many estates to the church of Northwald, “situated in the wilderness.” (Year 1009.)

[Ludewig, cited above, pp. 331–32.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, king by the favor of divine grace.

Just as a shoot of any planting, grafted onto a green trunk, is watered the more often by surrounding waters, so much the sooner, as its branches grow, it is raised into a tree. Therefore, by this comparison, if we support the churches of God, newly planted wherever they may be, by applying our goods with somewhat greater kindness, we confidently trust that they will more quickly flourish successfully in divine praise, and that we shall thereby establish more firmly the summit of our empire.

Therefore we wish it to be known to the whole community of all God’s and our faithful, how we, at the intervention and petition of our beloved wife Chunigunda, august empress, and of Bruno, bishop of the church of Augsburg, and of our other faithful, Eberhard, bishop of Regensburg, and Bennon, bishop of Passau, have granted and confirmed as their property, for the use of the brothers serving God there under the rule of Saint Benedict, everything we possessed belonging to the church situated in the wilderness called Northwald, constructed by the monk Gunther, who first led the eremitical life there, and dedicated in honor of the most victorious holy Cross, of holy Mary, Mother of God, and of blessed John the Baptist:

from the spring of water called Leipfliusa to the place called Swartawinchill; from there to the mountain called Ekkirischbuch; then onward to the water called Forchenbach; from there to Holerenberch, until one comes to Plecentenstein; from there to Grachenbach, and thus to the spring of that water; then by the water called Flinsbach, and from there, as it has been marked out, to the river Regin; along the descent of the river Regin as far as the village called Piberach, which the two Piberachs flow through midway; then upward along that same Piberach to the place on Mount Hanawich; from there along the course of the water called Sebach; and thus from there, as it has now been marked out, to the place where Kelbirbach falls into the white Regin; then to Aflaltresbach; from there to the great stone lying on the eastern side near the road that leads toward Bavaria; then along the road to the black Regin; upward along that same river to the place where the water Fladinz flows into it; from there to the spring of that water; and thus as far as Nauffinna—

together with all appurtenances: courtyards, buildings, cultivated and uncultivated fields, meadows, pastures, woods, hunting rights, waters and watercourses, fisheries, millstones, mills, roads and trackless ways, exits and entrances, things acquired and to be acquired, and every profit that might in any way arise from them.

We have granted and confirmed all this by this charter of ours as their property, on the express condition that henceforth no one, without the permission of the administrator of that cell and his successors, shall have the power to make new clearings, fish, trap wild animals by any device, or exercise any authority whatsoever within the boundary prescribed above. And so that the authority of this donation of ours may remain stable and unshaken for all time, we have ordered this charter, written for that purpose and strengthened below with our own hand, to be marked with the impression of our seal.

Given on the seventh day before the Ides of June, in the seventh indiction, in the year of the Lord 1009, and in the seventh year of the reign of our lord Henry II.

Enacted at Merseburg, successfully in the name of God.

### LV. King Henry II grants to the nunnery of Obermunster the estate of Salach, after completing it from its foundations and consecrating it in his presence on 17 April. (17 April 1010.)

[Ried, *Codex episcopatus Ratisbonensis*, I, 130.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, king by the favor of divine mercy.

If we have endeavored to exalt or improve the places of God’s churches by increasing their possessions through some gift, we have no doubt that this will greatly benefit us and the condition of our kingdom. Therefore let the knowledge of all Christ’s faithful, present and future, learn how we, moved by divine love, for the salvation of our soul, and of our predecessor, namely the emperor Otto, and of our beloved wife Chunigunda, queen, and of our parents, and also for the welfare of our kingdom, granted and transferred in full to the monastery at Regensburg called Oberenmunester, dedicated in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God and ever-virgin, on the very day when we caused it, completed by us from its foundations, to be consecrated in our presence, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, an estate belonging to us called Salaht, situated in the county of Count Ruotpert, in the district of Duonochgowe, with all its appurtenances and belongings: villages, settlements, households of both sexes, courtyards, buildings, fields, meadows, pastures, woods, hunting rights, waters and watercourses, fisheries, mills, exits and entrances, roads and trackless ways, things acquired or to be acquired, and every utility that can in any way be stated or named.

By this royal charter of ours we have granted and delivered it to the same monastery for the use and support of the nuns serving God there, and have wholly transferred it from our right and lordship into their right and lordship. This is on the condition that the abbess Wicpurg, who now appears to preside over the aforesaid monastery, and the abbesses succeeding her, shall henceforth have free power over that property—but only for the use of the monastery and of the nuns serving God there—to do whatever they wish, all contradiction or disturbance by anyone being removed. And so that the authority of this donation and confirmation of ours may remain stable and unshaken for all time, we have ordered this charter, written for that purpose, to be marked with the impression of our seal after strengthening and confirming it with our own hand.

Sign of our lord Henry, the unconquered king. (Monogram.)

I, Gunther, chancellor, have recorded this in place of Willigis, archchaplain.

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, in the eighth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1010, and in the eighth year of the reign of our lord Henry II. Enacted successfully at Regensburg. Amen.

The great seal was impressed inside and is broken for the most part.

### LVI. King Henry II grants the estate of Tharissa to the church of Bamberg. (1 June 1010.)

[Ussermann, *Germania sacra* III, *Preuves*, p. 16.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, king by the ordering of divine providence.

Let it be known to all Christ’s faithful, present and future, that after, by the inspiration of divine grace, with the authority of the Roman power and by the unanimous counsel of all our faithful, we had elevated the place of our property called Bavenberc into the seat and dignity of a bishopric, with the consent and petition of our most beloved wife Cunigunda, queen, we give and establish, by this charter of our authority, for the same episcopal see of Bavenberc, an estate called by people today Tareisa, but by the ancients Sinthorishusun, situated in the district of Volcfelt and in the county of Count Tietmar, together with all its appurtenances: villages, settlements, churches, chapels, male and female servants, courtyards, buildings, cultivated and uncultivated lands, roads and trackless ways, exits and entrances, things acquired or to be acquired, woods, pannage, hunting rights, waters, fisheries, millstones, mills, movable and immovable goods, and all other utilities that can properly be written or named in any way; and, removing all contradiction, we establish it as their property.

We command that Eberhard, beloved of God, the first bishop of the aforesaid see, and his successors, shall henceforth have free power to hold and possess the said estate with all its appurtenances, or to do with it in every way whatever they please for the use of the bishopric. If anyone, which God forbid, should presume to destroy or violate the generosity of this donation of ours, let him pay for it on the day of judgment with unquenchable torment before the eyes of God. And so that this may not happen, but that this conveyance of ours may remain perpetually inviolate, we have ordered this charter, written for that purpose, to be marked with the impression of our seal after strengthening it with our own hand.

Sign of our lord Henry II, the unconquered king.

I, Gunther, chancellor, have recorded this in place of Willigis, archchaplain.

[Note: [Col. 0291] Therefore he had not yet died on 23 February of this year, as some maintain.]

Given on the Kalends of June, in the eighth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1010, and in the eighth year of the reign of our lord Henry II.

Enacted successfully at Mainz. Amen.

### LVII. The privilege of Saint Henry for the church of Altach. (Year 1011.)

[Ludewig, *Scriptures of German Affairs*, I, 335–36.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, king by the favor of divine mercy.

If we have endeavored to enrich the churches of God, or those serving in them, from our possessions, we firmly believe that we shall thereby receive an unfading reward in the future. Therefore we wish it to be known to all our faithful, present and future, how we, inflamed by the desire for eternal life, both for the salvation of our soul and those of our parents, and also at the intervention of our beloved wife Chunegunda, and in return for the most pleasing service of the beloved Godehard of Altach, have by this charter granted to the same church, over which he is seen to preside, for the use of the monks serving God there, ten royal hides in the march and county of Margrave Henry, bounded by these terms:

in the east, from the ditch and the two trees commonly called Felevun, below the village called Abbatorf, to the river Danube; from there again in breadth to the western side, to the boundary of the district of Sigimar’s Weride; and in length, from the Danube to Wagreim toward the north.

We grant these lands together with all appurtenances belonging to them: courtyards, buildings, cultivated and uncultivated lands, meadows, pastures, watercourses, mills, fisheries, hunting rights, woods cleared or still to be cleared, and all equipment that can be stated or named. We wholly transfer them from our right and lordship into his right and lordship, on the condition that the aforesaid abbot and his successors shall henceforth have free power to hold, exchange, or do whatever they wish with them for the use of the aforesaid brothers. And so that the authority of this donation of ours may stand firm and secure, with all contradiction by anyone removed, we have strengthened below with our own hand this charter written and signed at our command.

Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of July, in the ninth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1011, and in the tenth year of the reign of our lord Henry II. Enacted at Regensburg.

### LVIII. Diploma of Saint Henry the emperor issued for the monastery of Tegernsee. (Year 1011.)

[Pez, *Codex diplomaticus historico-epistolaris*, from the Tegernsee library.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, king by the favor of divine mercy.

We wish it to be known to all our faithful, present and future, how we, for the salvation of our soul and those of our parents and from the desire for eternal life, and also at the intervention of our beloved Godehard, abbot of Altach, received by exchange into our right certain estates belonging to a certain craftsman, Perengarius, which pertained to the monastery of Saint Quirinus at Tegernsee, because that man was a servant of the same church and they had been granted to him by Emperor Otto, our predecessor, in Francia and Thuringia.

In exchange, beyond the river Ainzim, in the county of Margrave Henry, in a suitable place beside the estate of that church called Creberbach, on the southern side of the public road commonly called Hochenstrassa, we grant by this charter of ours to the aforesaid monastery of Tegernsee, for the use of the monks serving God there, a part of the forest called Enisiwalt, comprising sixty royal hides. We wholly transfer it from our right into their right and lordship, together with all equipment that can be found or prepared there; and if they are not found there in their entirety, they are to be supplied from a nearby estate of ours.

This is on the condition that the abbots of that place shall henceforth have free power to do with it whatever they please for the use of those monks, all contradiction by anyone being removed.

And so that the authority of this donation of ours may stand firm and secure, we have strengthened with our own hand this charter written and signed at our command.

I, Gunther, chancellor, have recorded this in place of Erchambald, archchaplain.

Given on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the ninth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1011, and in the tenth year of the reign of our lord Henry II. Enacted at Randesbura.

### LIX. Diploma of Saint Henry by which he adds an entire county in the district of Lobedengowe to the remaining possessions of the church of Worms. (Year 1011.)

[Schannat, *Bishopric of Worms*, II, p. 38.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, king by the ordering of divine providence.

We wish the diligence of all the faithful of the holy church of God, of either sex, living under the authority of our kingdom, to know how Burchard, venerable bishop of the holy church of Worms, faithful to us in all things, approached our lordship and asked that we remember the fidelity and various labor which he had continually expended for love of us. Granting his petition and mindful of the fidelity promised to him, and at the intervention and petition of our beloved wife Cunigunda, queen, we have ceded by this royal charter the county situated in the district of Lobedengowe, with everything belonging to it, and transferred it from our right and lordship into his jurisdiction.

This is on the condition that the aforesaid bishop shall henceforth have power to enjoy, hold, or do whatever he pleases with the said county and its revenues, all contradiction by anyone being removed. And so that this may be believed more truly and observed more carefully by all, we have ordered it to be marked with our seal after strengthening it with our own hands.

Sign of our lord Henry, the unconquered king.

I, Gunther, chancellor, in place of Erkanbald, archchaplain, have recorded this.

Given on the seventh day before the Ides of May, in the eighth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1011, and in the tenth year of the reign of our lord Henry II.

Enacted successfully at Bamberg. Amen.

### LX. Privilege of Saint Henry for the church of Paderborn. (Year 1011.)

[*Codex diplomaticus of the history of Westphalia*, p. 61.]

C. In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, king by the ordering of divine providence.

The mercy of divine compassion, which raised us to the height of royal majesty, wished us to reign for this purpose: that we might assist in strengthening and consolidating the order of the churches, especially those places founded by our predecessors, kings and emperors, but which, because of the demands of their sins, now appeared almost destroyed.

Therefore we wish it to be known to the diligence of all our faithful, present and future, how we, moved by divine love, for the salvation of our soul and those of our parents, and also of the emperor Otto III, of blessed memory, at the intervention of our beloved wife Cunigunda, queen, and at the request of Meginwerc, venerable bishop of the holy church of Paderborn, have granted and given as their property, by this royal charter, to him and to his holy church—founded long ago by Emperor Charlemagne, but in our time afflicted by fire, and dedicated in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God and ever-virgin, and of Saint Kilian, martyr, and Liborius, confessor—the county which Count Hahold held during his life, situated in the following places:

Haverga, Limga, Thiatmalli, Aga, Patherga, Treveresga, Langaneka, Erpesfeld, Silbiki, Matfeld, Nihterga, Sinatfeld, Ballevan near Spriada, Lambiki, Lession, and Sewardeshusun,

together with all legal authority.

This is on the condition that the aforesaid bishop Meginwerc and his successors, presiding over the aforesaid church, shall henceforth have free power to do with the said county and its revenues whatever they please, for the benefit of their church, with every disturbance removed. And so that the authority of this conveyance and confirmation of ours may remain stable and unshaken for all time, we have taken care to strengthen this charter, written for that purpose, with our own hand and have ordered it to be marked with our seal.

Sign of our lord Henry (L. M.), the unconquered king.

I, Gunther, chancellor, in place of Erkanbald, archchaplain, have recorded this.

Given on the fourth day before the Ides of April, in the ninth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1011, and in the ninth year of the reign of our lord Henry II.

Enacted successfully at the royal estate of Tribur. Amen.

### LXI. Conveyance of King Henry. (Year 1012.)

[Dronke, *Codex diplomaticus Fuldensis*, p. 343.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, king of the Romans by the favor of divine mercy.

It is clear that, by God’s disposing grace, we surpass other mortals; therefore it is fitting that we strive in all things to obey the will of him by whose gift we excel. Accordingly, we wish it to be known to all worshipers of the Christian faith and to our faithful, present and future, how the venerable abbot Branthoh of the monastery of Saint Boniface, called Fulda, together with his monks, petitioned our majesty that the men belonging formerly to the Roman Empire who dwell upon the lands of their monastery—whom the lord Louis, of divine memory, king, and likewise the lord Otto, emperor, the first of that name, granted and confirmed to the scholars of the monastery of Fulda and their successors, for the nourishment of boys and their instruction in scholastic disciplines, so that divine worship might be increased more abundantly—we too might deign by royal authority to convey and confirm to them and to their monastery, together with the province called Sarowe and a certain village in Thuringia called Holzhus, which a certain count from Bohemia named Thacholf bequeathed to them in his testament, choosing burial among them.

In addition, they requested the other goods which our predecessors—emperors, kings, princes, and other faithful persons—offered to them within the Roman Empire out of devotion.

Therefore, for the love of God and reverence for that holy place, we convey by these letters of our serenity and perpetually confirm by royal authority to the aforesaid abbot Branthoh, his successors, and the monastery of Fulda all goods, movable and immovable, with abbeys, counties, hundreds, jurisdictions, tolls, mints, banns, districts, forest jurisdictions, and every kind of jurisdiction, which the same monastery of Fulda possesses within the kingdom divinely granted to us, or which it may in the future acquire by the Lord’s concession, together with the aforesaid men of the empire and all who dwell upon their lands and, according to their condition, ought to pay a census to the royal treasury, as well as the testament of the aforesaid Count Thacholf.

Furthermore, we most strictly prohibit our agents or the officers of the empire from taking, carrying off, or invading anything from the household goods or property of abbots who die. Everything is to be reserved for the successor; nor is anything to be demanded from a newly created abbot for the investiture that ought to be performed by the royal scepter. Rather, everything is to be arranged for the liberty of that holy place in such a way that the worship of the Lord may perpetually endure there.

And so that no one in future times may dare to act against this conveyance or confirmation of ours, we have had these letters, written for that purpose, strengthened with our own hand and marked with our seal.

Sign of our lord Henry (M), the unconquered king.

I, Erkanbald, archchaplain, have recorded this.

Given on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of January, in the eleventh indiction, in the year of our lord 1012. Likewise in the eleventh year of the reign of our lord Henry II. Enacted successfully at the monastery of Fulda in the name of the Lord. Amen.

### LXII. Conveyance of King Henry concerning the forest of Zunderenhart. (29 December 1012.)

[Dronke, cited above.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, king by the favor of divine mercy.

If we have endeavored to exalt or improve the places of God’s churches by increasing their possessions through some gift, we do not doubt that this benefits us and the condition of our kingdom. Therefore we wish it to be known to the diligence of all our faithful, present and future, how we, moved by divine love and also at the intervention and petition of Abbot Branthoy, have granted as property, by this royal charter, to him and to his holy church, constructed and dedicated in honor of God’s Mother and Saint Boniface, archbishop and martyr, a forest belonging to our royal right, lying within and enclosed by these boundaries:

from Biberaho to Wolfeshart; from there, proceeding straight across, through Rodenmannum and Byochineberge to Calbaho and Fliedenu; from there to Langenaho and Widenaho; then to Guncenaho and Mosebrunnen; from there, proceeding straight across, through the places Ufecreginfelt, Warmuntessneida, Iliwineshusun, and Heribrahteshusun, and also Slierefa downward to Slidesa; then downward as far as Fulda—

together with the ban and all its appurtenances.

We grant it as property by this royal charter and wholly transfer it from our right and lordship into his right and lordship, on the condition that the aforesaid Abbot Branthoh and his successors shall henceforth have free power to do with the aforesaid forest and its appurtenances whatever they please, but for the use of the church, all contradiction by anyone being removed. And so that the authority of this conveyance of ours may remain stable and unshaken through future ages, we have ordered this charter, written for that purpose and strengthened with our own hand, to be marked with our seal.

Sign of our lord Henry (M), the unconquered king.

I, Gunther, chancellor, in place of Erkanbald, archchaplain, have recorded this. (S.)

Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of January, in the tenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1013, and in the eleventh year of the reign of our lord Henry II.

Enacted successfully at Polida. Amen.

### LXIII. Conveyance of King Henry II concerning the march of Lupence. (Year 1012? 30 December.)

[Dronke, cited above.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, by the favor of divine mercy, august emperor of the Romans, sends grace and salvation in Christ to all our faithful, present and future.

We wish it to be known to the memory of all the Catholic faithful how, at the intervention and petition of Chunigunda, our beloved wife, august empress, we grant by this charter of our imperial authority to the holy church of Fulda and to Lord Boppo, its abbot, and his successors, in perpetuity, our ban over wild animals of every kind within the boundaries and limits through which the march of Lupence extends in every direction, with the consent and will of Erkenbald, archbishop of Mainz, and also of Arnold, abbot of Hersfeld, and of Count Willehelm and his brother Boppo, and likewise of Sigimar, the advocate, and of all the inhabitants in the surrounding area who are known to possess estates nearby.

This is on the condition that the aforesaid holy church of Fulda, and our faithful Boppo, its venerable abbot, and all who shall succeed him in the present church of Fulda in future times, may within the aforesaid boundaries, by this imperial conveyance, obtain from the other inhabitants of the region and those living around them the same protection and security in exercising forest rights as those churches, and the other churches, have until now appeared to possess which have received charters from us or from our predecessors, emperors and kings, concerning the exercise of forest rights over such forests.

And so that this concession of our ban may always remain stable and unshaken, we have ordered this charter, written for that purpose, to be marked with the impression of our seal after strengthening it with our own hand and confirming it with the character of our name.

Sign of Henry, the most glorious august emperor.

I, Gunther, chancellor, have recorded this.

Given on the third day before the Kalends of January.

Enacted successfully at Fulda.

Let it be known to all the faithful how, making an exchange with the church of Fulda, we gave to Saint Boniface a place belonging to us in the march of Lupence, and received in return other places, namely Wazerlosen and Eibingen.

These, moreover, are the boundaries and limits of the march of Lupence:

from Truchenebach to Steinenbrunnen; from there to Birkinen solen; from there to Holcbiberen; from there to the other Biberen; from there to Hattenbach; from there to Leingruben; from there to Cumbelum; from there to Lyopbergun; from there to Horsuerzum; from there to Brestinesbrunnen; from there to Hohen eihcholcen; from there to Merenlinden; from there to Habechental; from there to Steininen strazen; from there to Weidenbrunnen and Nazaha below, to Steinenbrunnen; from there to Widinen solen; from there to Marcsteinen; from there upward to Neptale and below Neptale; from there to Setensteten by the chapel; from the chapel to Hurselen; from there to Ottereswag; from there to Horwiden; from there to Lachweige; from there to Kabenbuhele; from there to Wartbergen, at the spring; from there to Zugenturnen; from there to Madungen; from there to Gerwinessteinen; from there to Alviges sol.; from there to Suarzbach; from there to Alinde, and below Alinde to Merrith; from there to Liggenhoug; from there to Drinhougen; from there to Rotensolen; from there to Gotdedah; from there to Ahorne; from there to Kubach; and from Kubach below into Werraha; and from Werra below into the aforesaid Truchenebach.

### LXIV. Charter of King Henry by which he settles the dispute between the church of Worms and the monastery of Lorsch concerning the forest of Odenwald. (Year 1012.)

[Schannat, *Bishopric of Worms*, II, 38.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, king by the ordering of divine mercy.

We wish the diligence of all the faithful of the holy church of God living in our kingdom to know how the venerable man Burchard, bishop of the church of Worms and faithful to us in all things, approached our lordship and lodged a complaint concerning the frequent dispute between his church and the abbot of the church of Lorsch over certain revenues in the district of Lobedungowe. The aforesaid abbot wished, by arbitrary authority, to dispossess the church of Worms of all woodland rights in the forest of Odenwald and claim them entirely for his own church.

On account of this dispute he presented for our examination a charter of Dagobert, the most famous king of the Franks, in which it is written how King Dagobert granted to the basilica of Saint Peter the Apostle, constructed at Worms, the fortress of Ladenburg, situated in the district of Lobedungowe, with all equipment belonging to it and all woodland rights in the forest of Odenwald. He also produced before our eyes the charters of Dagobert’s successors—namely Pippin, Charles, Louis, and Otto I, most illustrious kings or emperors of the Franks—in which it is found how they renewed by their charters the conveyance and confirmation of the aforesaid king.

But, for the security of the matter, he entreated our mercy to put an end to the frequent litigation. Readily assenting to his petitions, for the love of God and in view of his faithful service, we sent Boppo, count of the aforesaid district, by authority of our empire to settle the ancient dispute. We ordered Sigebodo, a man of Worms, and Werner, a man of Lorsch, together with the assessors of the aforesaid count, to distinguish under oath the march of Lobedunburg, over which they were disputing, from the march belonging to Epfenheim.

These are those who swore concerning that march: Sibodo, Siguin, Wazzo, Auduom, Reolfreging, likewise Siguin, Hartmann, Hetzel, and Eskrih.

They distinguished the aforesaid marches by these boundaries: from Hegisurum to Flichenbach, and thus to the possession of Homathoni; upward along that possession to Enthelen Wichelstein; from there to the eastern spring; from there to the foaming pond; and thus into the Ulmena; from there to the roaring Egkam; from there from the dunes of Wichental; from there into the eastern Ulmena; and thus as far as Richeresvinda. From there into the Nevara, and thus downward along the Nevara to Niwenheim. They stated nothing specific there, except Colegenberg and the forest called Eugizunforste.

Therefore we have decreed that this charter of our authority be made for the same church, by which we command that no person cause any impediment to the aforesaid possessions of the church belonging to Bishop Burchard or his successors. We add this: if anyone, acting arrogantly, violates this agreement or charter, he shall pay three pounds of gold to our treasury or that of our successor, and whatever he has begun shall be held invalid.

And so that this authority of our confirmation may remain firm and secure, we have ordered it to be marked with the impression of our ring and have noted it below with our own hand.

I, Gunther, chancellor, in place of Erkanbald, archchaplain, have recorded this.

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1012, in the tenth indiction, and in the tenth year of the reign of our lord Henry II.

Enacted successfully at Nierstein. Amen.

### LXV. The Florennes abbey, a Benedictine house in the diocese of Liège, founded by Gerard I, bishop of Cambrai and Arras, is confirmed by a diploma of Saint Henry. (Year 1012.)

[Miraeus, *Diplomatic Works*, I, 675.]

*(The beginning is missing.)* Therefore we make known to all Christ’s faithful and to our own, future as well as present, that Gerard, a venerable man, at first our chaplain, but afterward, by the favor of God and through our appointment, made bishop of Cambrai, together with his brothers Godefrid and Arnulf, an abbey situated in the district of Lomac, at Florennes, for the salvation of their souls and those of their parents.

[Note: [Col. 0299D]

Florina, commonly Florenne, a small town of the diocese of Liège situated between the Sambre and the Meuse, six and a half miles from the town of Philippeville in Hainaut and five miles from Mariemont. Formerly quite prosperous, but repeatedly devastated by the French.

There is a Benedictine abbey there, concerning which see more in the *Benedictine Origins*. There is also a chapter of ten canons, founded in honor of Saint Gengulphus the martyr by a certain abbot of Florennes, who reserved for himself and his successors the title of provost together with the right to confer prebends, and acquired the archdeaconal right over the town of Florennes and its district.]

They built it.

At their intervention we received that abbey, together with all goods belonging to it, present and future, into our perpetual protection and guardianship.

Therefore, with the common consent of the brothers, the advocacy of this abbey constructed by them was granted to Godefrid.

And so that no dispute might arise between it and the abbey, the same Godefrid explained in our presence the right of advocacy which he retained, as follows: “From each market . . . . .”

But if any of his successors should arrogantly bring any further trouble against the church by reason of this advocacy, let Balderic, bishop of Liège, now present with us, and his successors, act in our place as judges and avengers with stronger authority, so that our grant may remain effective. . . . .

Therefore we publicly command, in full assembly, that the labor expended should not perish, but that the monastery constructed in honor of blessed John the Baptist should remain secure and defended; and, so that those dwelling there may continually entreat God’s mercy for our safety, for that of our wife, and for the stability of our empire, we have decreed that this charter of our authority be made.

These are the names of the free witnesses:

Burchard, bishop of Worms.

Heribert, archbishop of Cologne.
