### CXIV. Likewise, “a certain forest belonging to our property.” (In the same year.)

[The same, p. 80.]

C. In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, by the favor of divine clemency emperor Augustus of the Romans.

[Col. 0352A] If we enrich and exalt the places of the holy churches of God with goods granted to us by God, we hope not only to increase the length of our life but also the prosperity of the kingdom. Therefore, let the whole community of the faithful of the holy Church of God and of our own faithful, present and future, know how, for the remedy of our soul and those of our predecessors, and also for the welfare of our beloved wife, the empress Augusta Cunigunda, and through the intervention of Gero, archbishop of Magdeburg, and of Count Duticho, we firmly and permanently give and grant to the holy church of Paderborn, over which the venerable and beloved bishop Meinwerk presides, a certain forest belonging to our property, situated in the county of the same Duticho, with every benefit that may in any way arise from it.

It begins at Rothalmingahusun and extends in a straight course to the river Wisara; from there it ascends to the river called the Fulda, and then continuously maintains its upward course beside the same river Fulda as far as the stream called Grumelbichi.

[Col. 0352B] It also extends toward the settlement called Holthusun, proceeds together to Othilanham and Rechinherishusun and to Rothiereshusun, then goes to Rikillahusun and to Beverbiki; from there it extends to the road leading to Vulfredeskirchun, and likewise to another road extending to Gunnesburin and Vuicmonneshusun; then, making a circuit, it surrounds a road that reaches as far as the aforesaid settlement of Rothalmingahusun.

We give and grant it firmly and permanently to the holy church of Paderborn, over which the venerable and beloved bishop Meinwerk presides, for the altar and relics of the holy Mother of God Mary, of Saint Kilian the martyr and bishop, and of Saint Liborius the confessor, with every benefit that may in any way arise from it. We transfer and delegate it from our right and lordship into the right and lordship of the same holy church of Paderborn, on this condition: that no one presume to dispossess or disturb the bishop of the aforementioned church or his successors concerning the aforesaid forest.

And so that this page of our authority may remain stable and unshaken, strengthening it with our own hand, we have ordered it to be marked with the impression of our seal.

The sign of our lord Henry, most serene and unconquered emperor Augustus of the Romans (L. M.).

Guntarius, chancellor, examined this in place of Archbishop Ercumbald and the chief chancellor.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1020, indiction III, [Col. 0352D] in the nineteenth year of the reign of our lord Henry, Emperor Augustus Henry II, and the seventh of his empire.

Done successfully at Chuofunga on the eleventh day before the Kalends of June. Amen.

### CXV. Decree of the emperor Henry for the abbey of Pratalia. (Year 1020, on the third day before the Kalends of December.)

[Camaldolese Annals I.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, by the favor of divine clemency emperor Augustus of the Romans.

If we give our goods to places dedicated to the Lord and his saints, and confirm what was given by our predecessors, we do not doubt that this will benefit our soul eternally. Therefore, we wish it to be known to all our faithful, present and future, how, through the intervention of Theuzo, our faithful monk, for the remedy of our soul, we rightly and lawfully grant and give to the monastery of Saint Mary and Saint Benedict, which is situated in the Alps called Pratalia, beside the stream named the Bident, at the foot of the mountain called Acutus, which divides Tuscany and Romagna, certain manses belonging to the right of our kingdom.

Namely, one mansus commonly called Nibli of Soci; another held by the son of the priest Alprand of Soci; and Leo of Soci; and the fishery and Barricule of Soci, which Margrave Hugo had given to the aforesaid monastery by a *libellus*; another mansus called Theuzo’s Brussatus, which the same margrave likewise gave; also the mansus of the sixth, concerning which the margrave drew up a *libellus* for Winizo the castald; likewise the mansus of Ventrina, which the margrave had given to Leo by a *libellus*, together with three manses of Caprena; also the mansus of Linaro, for which Bonizo held one *libellus*; and the mansus of Tejano, which Winizo holds by a *libellus*, together with part of that vineyard.

We give these from the right and lordship of our kingdom and transfer them into the right and lordship of the aforesaid monastery of Pratalia, Saint Mary and Saint Benedict, and of the Bident, in perpetuity, with all their appurtenances that can be said or named: lands, fields, houses, vineyards, meadows, pastures, woods, waters and watercourses, and all movable and immovable property.

[Col. 0353C] On this condition: that the aforesaid Theuzo, rector of that monastery, and the abbot-successors may have the power to do with them whatever the law prescribes for the benefit of that monastery.

Therefore, we order and command that no duke, margrave, count, viscount, bishop, castald, or any great or small person of our kingdom presume, without lawful judgment, to divert or disturb the rector of the aforesaid monastery or his abbot-successors concerning everything written above.

If anyone should become a violator of this decree of ours, let him know that he will pay one hundred pounds of the finest gold, half to our treasury and half to the aforesaid monastery.

So that this may be believed more truly and observed more diligently by all forever, confirming this page of our donation with our own hand, we have ordered it to be marked with the impression of our seal.

The sign of our lord Henry, unconquered emperor Augustus of the Romans.

I, Piligrinus, chancellor, have examined this in place of Egerard, bishop and chief chancellor.

Given on the third day before the Kalends of November, indiction III, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1021, in the eighteenth year of the reign of our lord Henry II and the seventh of his empire.

Done at Amersten.

### CXVI. Decree of the emperor Henry Augustus by which he grants the estate of Butenhart to Hilderad, abbot of the monastery of Prüm. (Year 1020.)

[Marten, *Amplissima Collectio* I, 380, from the Prüm cartulary.]

[Col. 0354A]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, by the favor of divine clemency, emperor Augustus.

If by a gift of our generosity we confer some benefit upon places dedicated to God and relieve ecclesiastical needs through our assistance, we clearly believe that this will benefit us both in passing through mortal life temporally and in obtaining eternal life successfully. Therefore, let it be known to all the faithful of Christ, present and future, how [Col. 0354B] we, for the remedy of our soul and of our beloved wife Cunegunda, and through the intervention of our beloved abbot Hilderad, granted and gave as property to the monastery of the Savior of the world, situated in the place called Prüm, for the use of the brothers serving God there under the rule of Saint Benedict, the estate called Butenhart, situated in the district of Hulpia and in the county of Count Hezelin.

This estate came into our royal and imperial hands, by right and by law, after the death of Eppo. We grant it with male and female servants of both sexes and with all its equipment, lands, cultivated and uncultivated property, fields, meadows, pastures, woods, waters and watercourses, fisheries, mills, roads and pathless places, exits and entrances, and all appurtenances, things sought and yet to be sought, that can be said or named.

[Note: The people of Prüm report that Hilderad descended from the counts of Burgundy and, having been especially dear to the emperor Henry, died after eight years of rule, in the year 1026.]

We grant and give all this as property so that, throughout the entire course of succeeding ages, it may remain firm and stable forever for the same monastery, without contradiction from any mortal.

And so that this transfer of our grant may remain stable and unshaken at all times, we have ordered this page of the imperial decree to be written for that purpose and, confirming it with our own hand, to be marked with the impression of our own seal.

The sign of our lord Henry, unconquered emperor Augustus of the Romans.

I, Witharius, chancellor, have examined this in place of Archbishop Erchanbald.

Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of October, indiction III, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1020, in the eighteenth year of the reign of our lord Henry [Col. 0354D] II and the seventh of his empire.

Done successfully at Hamerstein. Amen.

### CXVII. Immunity of the emperor Henry II. (Year 1020, 3 May.)

[Dronke, *Codex diplomaticus Fuldensis*, p. 347.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, by the favor of divine clemency emperor Augustus of the Romans.

It is evident that, by the dispensation of divine grace, we surpass other mortals; therefore, it is fitting that we strive in every way to obey the will of him by whose gift we excel. Accordingly, let the diligence and welfare of all our faithful, present and future, know that the venerable abbot Richard, from the monastery called Fulda, situated in the district of Grapfeld and built in honor of Saint Boniface, martyr of Christ, where that glorious martyr rests bodily, approached the excellence of our highness and presented to us an authority of our predecessors—namely Pepin, Louis, Conrad, Henry, and also the emperor Augustus Otto.

It contained how those illustrious princes had placed the aforesaid monastery, with the monks serving God there and with the property and people lawfully belonging to it, under their protection and fortified guardianship.

[Col. 0355B] The aforesaid abbot earnestly asked that we likewise place that monastery, with the monks serving God there and with the property and people legally belonging to it, under our protection, and join our authority to the authority of our fathers.

Since we judged his petition to be just and indeed reasonable, we willingly granted it and assented to the benefit he requested. Therefore, for divine love, out of veneration for that holy place, and for the tranquillity of the brothers residing there, we decreed that this authority be made concerning the monastery.

By it we establish and command for the future that no public judge or anyone exercising judicial power dare enter, in our time or in that of our successors, the churches, villages, places, fields, or possessions that the aforesaid monastery presently holds justly and reasonably within the kingdom divinely granted to us, or that divine piety may henceforth wish to increase for the right of that place, in order to hear cases according to judicial custom, exact fines from anywhere, impose lodging or transport obligations, take sureties, or distrain the people of the monastery, both free and enslaved, who reside on its land.

Nor may anyone seek any other payments or unlawful pretexts, or presume to demand any of the things mentioned above. Rather, let the aforesaid abbot and his successors be permitted to possess the property of the monastery, with all subject to it, under the protection of our immunity and faithfully obey our imperial command.

Whatever the treasury could have demanded by right from the aforesaid properties, we have granted to the aforesaid monastery and its monks for eternal recompense.

And whenever, by divine calling, the aforesaid abbot or his successors depart from this life, so long as the monks themselves can find among their number men capable of governing that congregation according to the rule of the pious father Benedict, let them have by this authority of ours the consent and permission to elect abbots.

And so that this authority may possess fuller firmness in the name of God, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be marked with our seal.

The sign of our lord Henry, unconquered emperor Augustus of the Romans [Col. 0356A] (M). I, Guntherius, in place of Erkanbald, chief chaplain, have examined it (S).

Given on the fifth day before the Nones of May, indiction III, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1020, in the nineteenth year of the reign of our lord Henry II and the seventh of his empire.

Done at Fulda.

### CXVIII. Saint Henry grants certain estates to the Church of Paderborn. (Year 1021.)

[Codex diplomaticus Historiae Westphaliae, p. 80.]

XP. In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, by the grace of God emperor Augustus of the Romans.

[Col. 0356B] The clemency of divine mercy, which brought us to the summit of imperial majesty, willed us to rule for this purpose: that we might assist in strengthening and consolidating the order of the churches—especially those places founded by our predecessors, kings and emperors, but which, because sins required it, now seemed almost destroyed.

Therefore we wish it to be known to the diligence of all our faithful, present and future, how we, moved by divine love, for the remedy of our soul and those of our parents, and also of Emperor Otto III, of blessed memory, through the intervention of our beloved wife Chunigunda Augusta, and at the request of Meginwerc, venerable bishop of the holy church of Paderborn, grant and bestow upon him and his holy church—once founded by the Emperor Charlemagne [Col. 0356C] but in our time afflicted by fire, and dedicated in honor of holy Mary, ever-virgin Mother of God, and of Saint Kilian the martyr and Liborius the confessor—the county which Count Dodico held during his lifetime, situated namely in the places called Hessiga, Netga, and Nihterga, with every legal right, as property, through this imperial charter.

This is granted on the following condition: that the aforesaid Bishop M. and his successors, presiding over the aforementioned church, shall thereafter have free power to do with that county and its revenues whatever they wish, provided that it is for the utility of the church and with every disturbance by others removed. And so that the authority of this transfer and confirmation may remain stable and unshaken for all time, we have confirmed this charter, written for that purpose, with our own hand and ordered it to be marked with the impression of our seal.

Sign of Lord Henry, most victorious Emperor Augustus.

Guntherius, chancellor, acting on behalf of Herkembald, archbishop of Mainz and archchaplain, has authenticated it.

Given on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of March, in the fourth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1021, in the nineteenth year of the reign of Lord Henry II, and the eighth of his empire.

Enacted at Paderborn, successfully. Amen.

### CXIX. Saint Henry confirms to the monastery of Saint Emmeram all its goods in general, removing from the bishop and others the power to alienate them. (Year 1021, 3 July.)

[Ried, *Codex diplomaticus Ratisbonensis*, I, 135.]

[Col. 0357A]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, by the favor of divine clemency, Roman Emperor Augustus.

We know that the excellence of our imperial name requires—or rather greatly contributes to the stability of the kingdom and the salvation of our soul—that we should strengthen with the support of our generosity those who love divine service, so that they may persist without complaint in the praise of God, and especially those whose devotion in labor keeps more vigilant watch than others over divine service.

Therefore let the whole community of all Christ’s faithful and ours know how we, moved by hope of divine reward, and also admonished through the intervention of our beloved wife Cunigunda, Empress Augusta, and of the venerable Richolf, abbot, confirm forever through this imperial charter, and grant as property without contradiction from anyone, to a certain church of God constructed within the city of Regensburg in honor of the precious martyr of God, Hemmeram—where his venerable body is demonstrably at rest, as miracles declare—all the goods that have hitherto been granted and bestowed by our predecessors, kings or emperors, and by all the faithful of Christ, whether within the city of Regensburg itself, in its suburb, or anywhere else.

This is granted on the condition that neither the bishop of that place, nor any judicial or ecclesiastical person, shall have any power to take away the aforementioned goods from the aforesaid church or alienate them from the uses of the brethren serving God there under monastic discipline. Rather, the aforesaid Richolf, abbot of that place, and his successors shall thereafter have free power to do with them whatever they wish, solely for the benefit of the brethren serving God and Saint Hemmeram there under the rule of Saint Benedict. And so that the authority of this confirmation and grant may remain stable and unshaken for all ages, we have strengthened this charter, written for that purpose, with our own hand and ordered it marked with the impression of our seal.

Sign of Lord Henry, most invincible Roman Emperor Augustus. (Monogram.)

Guntherius, chancellor, acting on behalf of Erkenbald, archchaplain, has authenticated it.

Given on the fifth day before the Nones of July, in the third indiction, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1021, in the twentieth year of the reign of Lord Henry II, and the eighth of his imperial rule.

Enacted at Cologne, successfully. Amen.

The seal of the majesty remains intact.

### CXX. Saint Henry confirms to the monastery of Saint Emmeram the transfer of the estate of Ruita (Vogtareut), made by Count Warmund. (Year 1021, 3 July.)

[Ried, cited above, p. 136.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, by the favor of divine clemency, Roman Emperor Augustus.

We know that the excellence of our imperial name requires—or rather greatly contributes to the stability of the kingdom and the salvation of our soul—that we should strengthen with the support of our generosity those who love divine service, so that they may persist without complaint in the praise of God, and especially those whose devotion in labor keeps more vigilant watch than others over divine service.

Therefore let the whole community of all Christ’s faithful and ours know how we, moved by hope of divine reward, and also admonished through the intervention of our beloved wife Cunigunda, Empress Augusta, and of the venerable Richolf, abbot, grant as property through this imperial charter to a certain church of God constructed within the city of Regensburg in honor of the precious martyr of God, Hemmeram—where his venerable body is demonstrably at rest, as miracles declare—a certain estate belonging to us, called Riute, situated in the district of Chiemgau, in the county of Count Pabo, which a certain nobleman, Count Warmund, bestowed upon the same monastery, together with all its appurtenances: namely, villages, plots, fields, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, fords, mills, fisheries, entrances and exits, roads and trackless places, acquired and to be acquired, woods, hunting rights, male and female dependents, and all other utilities that can in any way be spoken or written of and that legally and lawfully pertain to the same estate. We also confirm Count Warmund’s transfer to the aforesaid church in perpetuity.

This is granted on the condition that neither the bishop of that place, nor any ecclesiastical or judicial person, shall have any power to take the aforementioned estate away from the aforementioned church or alienate it from the uses of the brethren serving God there under monastic discipline. Rather, the aforesaid Richolf, abbot of that place, and his successors shall thereafter have free power to do with it whatever they wish, solely for the benefit of the brethren serving God and Saint Hemmeram there under the rule of Saint Benedict, with all human contradiction removed. And so that the authority of this grant and confirmation may remain stable and unshaken for all ages, we have strengthened this charter, written for that purpose, with our own hand and ordered it marked with the impression of our seal.

Sign of Lord Henry, most invincible Roman Emperor Augustus. (Monogram.)

Guntherius, chancellor, acting on behalf of Erkenbald, archchaplain, has authenticated it.

Given on the fifth day before the Nones of July, in the third indiction, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1021, in the twentieth year of the reign of Lord Henry II, and the eighth of his imperial rule. Enacted at Cologne, successfully. Amen.

The seal is extant, somewhat damaged.

### CXXI. Saint Henry confirms to the monastery of Saint Emmeram the estate of Eiterhoven. (Year 1021, 3 July.)

[Ried, cited above, p. 137.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, etc., as in the preceding document—he grants, concedes, and perpetually confirms through this imperial charter, as property, a certain estate belonging to us, called Eitterhoven, situated in the district of Tunegau, in the county of Margrave Adalbert, which our grandfather, Duke Henry of pious memory, had previously bestowed upon the same monastery, together with all its appurtenances: namely, villages, plots, fields, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, mills, fisheries, entrances and exits, acquired and to be acquired, woods, hunting rights, dependents of both sexes, and all other utilities that can in any way be spoken or written of and that legally and lawfully pertain to the same estate.

This is granted on the condition that neither the bishop of that place, nor any church or judicial person, shall have any power to take the aforementioned estate away from the aforesaid church or alienate it from the uses of the brethren serving God there under monastic discipline. Rather, the aforesaid Richolf, abbot of that place, and his successors shall thereafter have free power to do with it whatever they wish, solely for the benefit of the brethren serving God and Saint Hemmeram there under the rule of Saint Benedict, with all human contradiction removed. And so that the authority of this grant, concession, and confirmation may remain stable and unshaken for all ages, we have strengthened this charter, written for that purpose, with our own hand and ordered it marked with the impression of our seal.

Sign of Lord Henry, most invincible Roman Emperor Augustus. (Monogram.)

[Col. 0359C] Guntherius, chancellor, acting on behalf of Erkenbald, archchaplain, has authenticated it.

Given on the fifth day before the Nones of July, in the third indiction, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1021, in the twentieth year of the reign of Lord Henry II, and the eighth of his imperial rule. Enacted at Cologne, successfully. Amen.

The seal of the majesty remains intact.

### CXXII. Saint Henry grants to the upper monastery two plots of land (*plaetze*), within and outside the walls of the city of Regensburg, toward the south. (Year 1021, 12 November.)

[Ried, cited above, p. 138.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, Roman Emperor Augustus.

[Col. 0359D] If we strive to console lovers of the Christian religion and angelic way of life through the benefit of our generosity, so that they may serve God more securely, we confidently hope that we shall become participants with them in eternal rewards. Therefore let it be known to all Christ’s faithful and ours how we, through the intervention of Henry, Duke of Bavaria, grant and concede as property through this imperial charter, with every legal right, to a certain church constructed within the city of Regensburg in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God and ever-virgin, commonly called Obermünster, where the venerable abbess Wichpurg appears to preside over virgins serving God under monastic discipline, a certain plot of land within the aforementioned monastery, adjoining its courtyard and lying along the public street that leads from the gate of Saint Hemmeram to the church commonly called Ahachiricha, within the city, measuring twenty perches in length and ten in width; and another plot lying immediately outside the wall, likewise measuring twenty perches in length and eight in width, in the county of Count Ruodpert.

This is granted on the condition that the aforesaid abbess and all women who succeed her in that place in the same order and dignity shall thereafter have free power to do with it whatever they wish for the benefit of the aforementioned monastery and of the sisters living there in monastic observance. And so that the charter of our authority may remain stable and unshaken for all ages, we have confirmed this charter, written for that purpose, with our own hand and ordered it marked with the impression of our seal.

Sign of Lord Henry, most invincible Roman Emperor Augustus. (Monogram.)

Guntherius, chancellor, acting on behalf of Aribo, archchaplain, has authenticated it.

Given on the second day before the Ides of November, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1021, in the twenty-second year of the reign of Lord Henry the Emperor, and the eighth of his empire.

Enacted at Augsburg, successfully. Amen.

The seal of the majesty is missing in its middle part.

### CXXIII. Saint Henry’s charter granted to Amatus II, archbishop of Salerno, by which he confirms all his rights. (Year 1022.)

[Muratori, *Antiquitates Italicae*, I, 193.]

[Col. 0360C]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, by the favor of divine clemency, Roman Emperor Augustus.

If we strive not only to preside over just places and places dedicated to God, but also to benefit them, we do not doubt that we shall find support in the present life and a remedy for the eternal one; and if we endeavor to restore them to their former condition, we unquestionably believe that we exalt the summit of our empire. Therefore let the whole community of all the faithful of the holy Church of God and of ours, present and future, understand how, through the intervention and petition of Theoderic, our beloved chancellor, by this present page of our charter, insofar as we can do so justly and lawfully, we newly grant and confirm inviolably and perpetually to the church of the holy see established in honor of the blessed apostle Matthew, where due praises are sung daily to the supreme Trinity, and to Amatus, archbishop of that aforesaid church and our faithful, all the possessions and properties granted to this church by the ancient princes of the aforesaid city, and also those which Prince Gisulf and his wife Gemma offered there for the remedy of their souls—both those which it appears to possess within the same city and those outside it, together with the lands beyond the Tuscian River that appear to belong to the aforesaid church as far as the river called the Siler, as well as those in the county of Capua and Dulcaria, and in all other places belonging to the aforementioned church that can be spoken of or named.

Moreover, we grant the castle of Libani with all that is adjacent to it, just as that church anciently held and ruled it by charters and whatever documents, namely the castle of Libani, which was unjustly seized by Grimoald and Alfanus, brothers. Finally, we grant and confirm to the same church all the property of the dead that is or will be in that bishopric or among its possessions, and all movable and immovable goods offered there from ancient times by God-fearing people, and all grants made to the same holy church by princes, dukes, or kings.

We order that all the tenants owing rent to the same church be subject to its authority, so that the aforesaid bishopric may exercise dominion over them, without anyone’s opposition, as it did in ancient times. By our imperial authority we grant and confirm to it the right that the portion belonging to the same bishop may appoint within the same city five butchers, wherever it wishes, to sell meat.

We also decree, grant, and confirm to it all those possessions removed without reason or justice from the jurisdiction of the same bishop after the death of Peter, of holy memory, the venerable bishop of that church, by Bishop John, who held the same see improperly. If any document previously written by that John should be produced, we judge it void and without effect as a grant, because he abandoned his see contrary to canonical authority and went to another; this could in no way be done according to the regulations of the canonical authorities.

We decree that the portion belonging to the aforesaid bishop shall exercise jurisdiction over all foreign priests belonging to him and over the clerics, and over all their dependents—namely, those who live in the diocese of that bishopric. We wish him to judge and exercise jurisdiction without any opposition from the public authority, and to have them in his service, as the canons command.

We confirm to him all the possessions mentioned above, together with lands, vineyards, fields, meadows, woods, pastures, mountains, valleys, plains, waters and watercourses, banks, mills, fisheries, forests, hunting rights, male and female slaves, male and female dependents, *ancariae*, rents, leases, chapels, castles, villages, and everything that can be spoken of or named and that justly and lawfully belongs in full to the aforesaid church.

Therefore we strictly order that no lord, prince, *stratigo*, margrave, bishop, count, viscount, nor any great or small person of our kingdom, presume to disturb or molest the possessions or bishop of the aforesaid church, or to deprive him of them in any way without legal judgment. Rather, let the aforesaid Archbishop Amatus be permitted to hold and possess the possessions of the aforementioned bishopric and, by this charter of ours, to acquire the aforesaid possessions for the benefit of his church, with all human contradiction removed.

But if anyone—which God forbid!—should prove a presumptuous violator of this authority of ours, let him know that he shall pay one thousand pounds of pure gold, half to our treasury and half to those governing the same bishopric. And so that this may be believed more firmly and carefully observed by all, we have strengthened this page with our own hand and ordered it marked with our seal.

Sign of Lord Henry, most serene Emperor Augustus.

Theoderic, chancellor, acting on behalf of Eberard, bishop and archchancellor, has authenticated it. . . . . . .

Given on the day before the Kalends of June, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1000 [lacuna], in the fifth indiction, in the year of the reign of Lord Henry II [lacuna], and in the ninth year of his empire.

Enacted at Troyes, successfully. Amen.

### CXXIV. Saint Henry confirms to the venerable Romuald, founder of the Camaldolese hermits, the abbey of Saint Benedict situated in the Alps at Bifurcus. (Year 1022.)

[Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, II, 493.]

[Col. 0362B]

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, Henry, Roman Emperor Augustus.

It seems fitting for our imperial clemency justly and reasonably to comply with the appropriate petitions of religious men. Therefore let the diligence of all the faithful of the holy Church of God and of ours, present and future, know how we, for the remedy of our soul and those of our parents, for our salvation and that of our most beloved wife Cunegunda, Empress Augusta, and through the intervention of the religious man Romuald, monk and hermit, establish an abbey constructed on property belonging to us in honor of Saint Benedict, in the Alp called Bifurcus—an abbey customarily invested only by kings or emperors—and decree that it shall remain under the provision and discipline of that venerable man Romuald and of his successors who persist in that hermitage and observe his way of life and religion, provided that this provision and discipline do not oppose the rule of Saint Benedict.

We confirm to the church of Saint Benedict of the same monastery the lands that it now holds, whose names are these: a church with three mills and three hides at Domicuicrolo; at Galiano, two hides and one church; at Partisidia, one church, two hides, and one mill; at Casale, two hides; at Mistriano, one hide; at Drimano, one hide; at Dipidano, one hide; at Monte Martino, one hide; at Africo, two hides; in the mountains of Saint Gaudentius, five hides; and everything that it now justly and lawfully possesses, or shall possess in the future, or shall acquire, or has acquired, so that it may have and hold these things in full with all their appurtenances.

Let it possess them by proprietary right, in such a way that neither the abbot now in office nor his successors may sell, alienate, or place the lands of the church under a precarious tenure without our permission; rather, they shall remain solely for the use of the monks serving there according to the rule of Saint Benedict. Moreover, we confirm the entire inheritance of the goods of that monastery and its monks, so that it may hold them in the manner in which it now holds them.

We therefore decree that the aforesaid monastery shall be subject to no margrave, no count, no archbishop, no bishop, and no individual person, unless that person exercises imperial or royal authority. We therefore wish and decree that Romuald and his successors, and the abbot of that monastery and his successors, may summon any bishop to consecrate churches and perform every consecration.

We also wish that, around the monastery and hermitage, the church possess land bounded on the east by the stream from the lake, on the west by the Alpine ridge, on the north by Ceresio, and on the south by the hill of Gimelli.

Therefore we strictly order that no duke, margrave, count, or any great or small person whatsoever attempt to violate this imperial charter of ours. But if anyone—which God forbid!—should attempt to infringe it, let him know that he shall pay two hundred pounds of refined gold, half to us and half to the said monastery. And so that this may be believed more firmly and preserved unshaken, we have subscribed it with our own hand and ordered it marked below with our seal.

Sign of Lord Henry, most invincible Emperor Augustus.

Theoderic, chancellor, has authenticated it.

Given in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1022, in the tenth indiction, in the twenty-first year of the reign of Lord Henry II, and the eighth of his imperial rule.

Enacted at Ravenna on the day before the Kalends of January, successfully. Amen.

### CXXV. Saint Henry’s privilege for the monastery of Saint Sophia at Benevento. (Year 1022.)

[Ughelli, *Italia sacra*, VIII, 76.]

[Col. 0363C]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, by the favor of divine clemency, Roman Emperor, ever Augustus.

If we devote ourselves with every effort to the churches of God’s saints, we do not doubt that this will advance our empire. Therefore let the whole community of the faithful of the holy Church of God and of ours, present and future, diligently understand how Henry, venerable bishop of the Church of Parma, approached the exalted majesty of our throne, earnestly requesting that, for the love of God and the remission of our sins, we might deign to confirm and thoroughly strengthen for the monastery dedicated to the church of Saint Sophia, constructed in the city called Benevento, where the venerable abbot Gregory appears to preside, everything granted to that monastery by our predecessors and by other worshipers of the Lord, and everything that the same monastery has held since it was founded—whether by charters of our predecessors, or by precarious grants, releases, offerings, investiture, or any instruments of charters or title of any written document.

We, considering his petition with grateful mind and inclining our spirit to his prayers, confirm and strengthen through this charter, insofar as we can do so justly and lawfully, all the possessions and properties of that monastery, namely: at the place called Pentano, with its appurtenances and with a chapel in honor of Saint Benedict; another in honor of Saint Vitalis with all its appurtenances; another in honor of the archangel Saint Michael, called at Holibola, with all its appurtenances; and at Pallaria, one chapel in honor of Saint Mary; also the church of Saint Bartholomew on the hill; the estate of Nuriano at Petra Furmina, with houses and woods; the estate of Lapiso, an inheritance; the church of Saint Felix at Burto; at Cortiano, a chapel in honor of Saint Peter; at Cerreto, a chapel in honor of Saint Martianus with its appurtenances; a chapel in honor of Saint Sylvester at Corneto, in the county of Capua, at the place called Juliano, with a chapel in honor of Saint Mary at Bivine on the Beletro River; in the city, a chapel in honor of Saint [Col. 0364A] Martin; within the city of Ascoli, churches, and outside it, the entire inheritance; in the territory of Cauno, the church of Saint Julian; in the county of Frignano, the estate of Pazano with its olive groves; in the county of Siponto, a fishery; in the county of Lesina, a fishery; the estate of Delania; the estate of Calaza; Saint Roseo with Sessa and its territories; in the territory of Capua, at Saint Paul and Saint Stephen, with their territories; in the field of Marrini, in the territory of Tremons, at Saint Adiutor beside the Volturno River, with its territories.

Moreover, as is written above, we confirm to the same monastery the church of Saint Magnus in the castle of Magnus with its appurtenances; the church of Saint Angelus on the highest point above the Biferno River, in the territory of the field of Morano, together with that church; also the church of Saint John with all its possessions at the house of Pollux; an inheritance measuring two miles in length and one mile in width; the church of Saint Peter in the territory of Laureto with all its appurtenances; Saint Angelus at Palumbara with all its appurtenances; Saint Michael of Sessola with all its appurtenances; the Holy Cross within the city of Naples with all its appurtenances; in the field of Sinarcum, land three miles in length and one in width; the church of the Holy Trinity beside the Biferno River with all its appurtenances; and the church of Saint Marcianus in the castle of Mosano with all its appurtenances; and the church of Saint John on Mount Tabenna with all its appurtenances; also the church of Saint Bartholomew, which is beside the church of Saint John, with all its appurtenances; the cell of Saint Angelus beside the city of Trianum, with all its appurtenances; the cell of Saint Gregory in the county of Frigento, with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Bittus in the county of Vulturara; the church of Saint Stephen, the first martyr, within the city of Cucheri, with all its appurtenances; the church of Saint Donatus lying at Leone with all its appurtenances; and the church of the Holy Cross at Nola with all its appurtenances—namely, in full, all lands, buildings situated upon them, vineyards, meadows, fields, waters and watercourses, mills, fisheries, houses, demesne lands, castles, villages and chapels, male and female slaves, mountains and plains, hazel-groves (*hasulis*; reading uncertain), brushlands, cultivated and uncultivated lands, movable and immovable goods, male and female dependents, their provisions and household goods, together with all the adjacent properties that truly and lawfully belong or pertain to this named church of Saint Sophia, in their entirety, both within the Italian kingdom and in the regions of Apulia.

Therefore we strictly order that no margrave, duke, prince, archbishop, bishop, count, or any great or small person presume to interfere with, bring a claim against, or molest the aforesaid abbot Gregory or his successors concerning anything belonging or appearing to belong to the aforesaid monastery, whether possessions or dependents.

But if anyone violates this charter in any respect, let him know that he shall pay one hundred pounds of gold [lacuna] of the purest gold, half to our treasury and half to the aforesaid abbot or to our and his successors. And so that this may appear certain and be observed by all, we have strengthened this page with our own hand and ordered it sealed.

Theoderic, chancellor, acting on behalf of Ethard, pope, bishop of the Church of Brescia, and archchaplain, has recorded it. Given on the sixth day before the Ides of March, in the year 1022, in the fifteenth indiction, in the twelfth year of the reign of Lord Henry, and the ninth of his empire.

Enacted at Benevento, successfully.

### CXXVI. A writing of Saint Henry addressed to Pope Benedict in favor of the abbey of Monte Cassino. (Year 1022.)

[Tosti, *History of the Abbey of Monte Cassino*, I, 253.]

[Col. 0365C]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, by the favor of divine clemency, Emperor Augustus, to Benedict, most holy pope of the city of Rome, and to his successors canonically appointed to the apostolic see, forever.

It belongs to the care of the Roman Empire to provide, throughout the whole world, assistance for the defense of the churches established throughout the Roman world by imperial authority, so that, through its aid, they may be protected from the attacks of unfaithful or wicked men. Therefore, in providing for the Church of Cassino, Benedict, pontiff of the apostolic see—which more particularly pertains to the Roman Empire and has existed as the treasury of our predecessors from the very beginning of its construction, and which has remained immune and free from the domination of all mortals—we commend to your fatherhood that the same church, enriched by imperial munificence, suffer no injustice through the force of any authority, except for what appears specially and uniquely to pertain to the Roman Empire beyond all other churches.

For since every church is free from every conditional or servile bond, and the Church of Cassino is especially free after the dignity of the Roman See, and since all our predecessors, the emperors—namely Pepin, Charles, Louis, Lothar, Otto, and the other emperors—possessed their own special treasury, it ought to enjoy the distinction of liberty.

Therefore we commend the aforementioned monastery to your fatherhood, so that you may be its collaborators and defend it from every attack, not destroy it, except in what pertains to our empire. We also grant to you and your successors the consecration of the abbot of Cassino. From the revenues of that place, when going to and returning from Benevento, we establish that one meal be prepared for the pontiff of the apostolic see. We do not wish the Roman pontiff to have any other authority or lordship over the monastery of Cassino; rather, just as it has always remained uniquely and specially under the rights of the emperor from the beginning of its construction, so we wish it to remain forever.

When the abbot of Cassino dies, in accordance with the rule and the precept of the holy canons, an abbot shall be chosen from among all the brethren on the basis of merit of life and knowledge of doctrine, and shall be canonically, not simoniacally, ordained. He shall immediately be made known to us, and they shall give him their consent by an edict of pragmatic sanction; only then shall he be presented to the Roman pontiff for consecration without any venality.

But if this should be done otherwise, let them prevent the consent of wicked men from prevailing; and let the emperor who is in office at the time, together with the brethren of the same monastery, appoint to its governance a suitable abbot, whom he finds to be the better and more worthy, and faithful to the Roman Empire, without anyone’s disturbance or opposition.

If anyone should presume to violate this constitution of ours, let him know that he shall pay one thousand pounds of pure gold, half to our treasury and half to the aforesaid monastery, and let this grant remain firm forever. And so that this may be believed more firmly, we have resolved to strengthen it with our hand and mark it below with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Lord Henry, most serene Roman Emperor Augustus.

I, Conrad, duke and cousin of the lord emperor, have subscribed. Theoderic, chancellor, acting on behalf of Edon, bishop of Paderborn and archchancellor, has authenticated it. In the year from the incarnation of the Lord 1022, in the fifth indiction, in the twenty-second year of the reign of Lord Henry, most excellent and most invincible Roman Emperor Augustus, and the ninth of his imperial rule.

Enacted on Monte Cassino, successfully. Amen.

### CXXVII. Saint Henry II, Emperor, grants to the Church of Bamberg the estate of Hormunze in the archdiocese of Trier, which he had received from Archbishop Poppo. (Year 1022, 11 November.)

[Hontheim, *History of Trier: Charters*, I, 357.]

[Col. 0366D]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, by the favor of God’s clemency, Roman Emperor Augustus.

Since, through the loss of temporal goods, we ought to hope for a reward that remains without end, let it be known to all our faithful how we, for the remedy of our soul and those of our predecessors, and also for the salvation of our most beloved wife C., namely the Empress Augusta, grant in perpetuity to the altar of Saint Peter, chief of the apostles, for the use of the bishop possessing the episcopal see of the Church of Bamberg, and transfer entirely from our jurisdiction to his jurisdiction, an estate such as Archbishop Poppo of Trier gave us, [Col. 0367A] situated at Hormunze.

[Note: [Col. 0367C] It is situated at Hormunze. It is now called Ormiz or Urmiz, situated on the left bank of the Rhine, approximately halfway by road between Koblenz and Andernach, in the district of Megin. Today the Church of Urmiz, with its tithes and right of appointment, still belongs by direct lordship to the provostry of the cathedral church of Bamberg, which has the nobles von Scheben of Cronfeldt as its vassals there.]

The estate lies in the district [lacuna], in the county of Count [lacuna], together with plots, buildings, fields, vineyards, meadows, pastures, woods, waters and watercourses, fisheries, roads and trackless places, entrances and exits, male and female slaves, acquired and to be acquired, and all implements that can either be written or named, to be held perpetually.

Therefore, by the same imperial authority that the kings and emperors before us have hitherto exercised, we order that no one dare violate this transfer of ours. And so that this authority of ours may remain stable and unshaken, we have had this page written for that purpose, strengthened it with our own hand, and ordered it marked with our imperial sign.

Given on the third day before the Ides of November, in the fifth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1024 [rather 1022], in the twenty-first year of the reign of Lord Henry II, and the eighth of his empire.

Enacted at Augsburg, successfully. Amen.

### CXXVIII. Saint Henry II, Emperor, confirms to the monastery of Echternach the right of coinage. (Year 1023, 18 June.)

[Hontheim, *History of Trier: Charters*, I, 858.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, by the favor of divine clemency, Roman Emperor Augustus.

The whole assembly of Christ’s faithful and our own faithful should know how we, for the salvation of our soul and those of our parents, and also through the intervention of [Note: Henry, illustrious duke of the Bavarians. Henry, the eldest son of Count Sigefrid of Luxembourg, the first count of Arlon and also count of the Ardennes, and advocate of the abbeys of Saint Maximin and Echternach; Henry II, the emperor, who had married his sister Cunigund, made him duke of Bavaria in 1002.] Henry, illustrious duke of the Bavarians, grant, renew, and confirm by this imperial document to the monastery called Echternach the mint granted by our elder nephew and predecessor, namely Otto III, emperor Augustus, in which good-quality coins may be struck, as in other places subject to royal authority, for the use of the Church and of the monks serving God and Saint Willibrord the confessor day and night.

We further decree that henceforth this mint shall remain under the perpetual right of the aforesaid Church, its abbot now living and his successors, without being held as a benefice; and that from now on no person, great or small, clerical or lay, shall have any authority over it except the abbot of that Church and his successors, and the monks who will serve God and Saint Willibrord there, for the adornment of the Church and the increase of their provision, so that God may be more pleased to hear their prayers for our salvation and for the deliverance of the souls of all our parents and of all the faithful departed.

And so that this decree of our confirmation, written out for this purpose [something is omitted here], might be marked with the impression of our seal, we ordered it signed and strengthened with our own hand, as appears below.

The sign of Lord Henry, the invincible emperor Augustus of the Romans.

Gunther, chancellor, recognized this in the place of Aribo, archchaplain.

Given on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July, indiction VI, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1023; in the twenty-second year of the reign of Lord Henry II, and the tenth of his empire.

Done at Neuss, successfully. Amen.

## CXXIX. Saint Henry II, emperor, receives 6,656 hides from the abbot of Saint Maximin as a benefice, which he granted as benefices to Count Palatine Ezzon, Duke Henry, and Count Otto. (Year 1023, 10 December.)

[As above.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, by the favor of divine clemency emperor Augustus of the Romans.

Although no one is permitted to depart from ecclesiastical institutions or paternal precedents, it is nevertheless especially and particularly our right to change for the better whatever burdens our faithful within our kingdom, or whatever causes the Churches of God to suffer harm rather than benefit. Therefore we wish it to be known to the prudent attention of our faithful, both present and future, how we received from the abbey of Saint John the Evangelist and Saint Maximin, situated in the suburb of Trier, where Abbot Haricho appears to preside, certain [Note: Courts and territories, villages and possessions. Tolner, who published this diploma from Zyllesius, note a, thinks that the castles of Cochem, Klotten, and other places along the Moselle are meant here. But since these can never have belonged to Saint Maximin—as is also apparent from the fact that, despite the great abundance of royal and imperial confirmations, including those issued by us, in which the monastery’s more notable estates and acquisitions are recounted with the utmost care, there is complete silence concerning them; [Col. 0368C] and since nowhere else in the extremely well-supplied archive of Saint Maximin does even the slightest information about such possessions survive—I would rather understand the estates meant here as lying across the Rhine [Col. 0368D] and around it. They are mentioned in charters of Otto the Great from the years 945 and 966, of Otto II from 973, and of Otto III from 992.] courts and territories, villages and possessions, namely [Note: Six thousand six hundred and fifty-six hides. Above, in the note to the charter of Megingaud from the year 929, we said, on the authority of Caesarius of Prüm, that an ingenual hide consisted of 160 jugera. The hide is then found in the same Caesarius as containing twelve bunnuaria, called bonniers by the French. Everyone generally agrees that a hide contains as much land as can be plowed in one year by a single yoke of oxen, and as much as is sufficient to support one peasant household. Experts in agriculture, however, hold that one yoke of oxen is sufficient each year to plow sixty-four jugera. If we apply that calculation to the 1,656 hides taken from the people of Maximin, we arrive at 48,984 jugera—a scarcely credible extent of land.] 6,656 hides, as could be more accurately calculated, from the aforesaid abbot as a benefice. We then grant these as benefices to our faithful, namely to Count Palatine Ezzon [Note: Namely to Count Palatine Ezzon. They consider Ezzon, or Erenfrid, later founder of the monastery of Brauweiler, to have been the son of Count Palatine Hermann by Mathilde. Compare Tolner, cited above, p. 22, note c.], to Duke Henry [Note: To Duke Henry. It is sufficiently established that this duke of Bavaria was Henry, son of Count Sigefrid I of Luxembourg by Hadewich, brother of Empress Cunigund, and advocate of Saint Maximin.], and also to Count Otto [Note: To Count Otto. By this name Tolner, in the cited work, note e, understands Ezzon, the son of Erenfrid, the Rhenish count palatine, and his father’s successor in the Palatinate in 1035. Others prefer to identify this Otto as the lord of Hammerstein, the fortress of Trier situated on the Rhine. Shortly before this year, inflamed by love for a certain concubine named Irmingard, he attacked Archbishop Erckenbold of Mainz, who had severely chastised him for his forbidden embraces. Later, out of fear of Emperor Henry and respect for Aribo, archbishop of Mainz, who had pronounced curses against him, he abandoned his unlawful schemes and ceased his madness. See John of Mainz, *Rerum Moguntiacarum*, vol. I, p. 461.], on this condition: since the aforesaid abbot, now worn out by old age, could not conveniently serve us at home or in the field, he and the heirs who hold these benefices shall perform court service and go on campaign in place of that abbot and his successors; but the abbot and his successors shall be entirely free from court service and every military expedition, unless, compelled by some necessity, they are summoned to the city of Mainz, Metz, or Cologne for a general council or conference.

And lest we suffer harm to our souls if we should appear unjustly to take away what has been handed over or granted by Christ’s faithful to that most sacred place, we have, out of fear of God and reverence for Saint John and Saint Maximin, and through the intervention of Aribo, archbishop of Mainz, Piligrim, archbishop of Cologne, and Poppo, archbishop of Trier, all venerable archbishops, as well as our other faithful, remitted and forgiven—and, in forgiving, have permanently pardoned—the service [Note: Service. A fixed sum of money. Compare, however, Spener, *Jus Publicum*, book II, chapter XI, § 6, note a.] that was delivered to us and to certain of our predecessors every second year from the same abbey.

And lest any of our successors, kings or emperors, should henceforth demand that same service at the peril of our soul and his own, unless he first fully return or restore the goods which we have taken from that place not so much for our own service as for theirs, we decree by our imperial authority and confirm by this decree.

We also order and forbid the aforesaid abbot and his successors forever to grant as benefices, or in any way alienate from their right, any of the remaining courts, churches, or possessions that our predecessors, kings and emperors—namely Dagobert, Pippin, Charles, Louis, Arnulf; likewise Charles, Zwentibold, and also the three Ottos—up to our own time, and we ourselves as well, assigned and granted for the particular provision of the brothers serving God there, to any of the powerful, free men, or servants of another Church or of another household.

These are the places: Swabheim, Hesinesheim, Brizinheim, Eversheim, Weldinstein, Albucha, Gosolvesheim, Bingen, Holzhusa, Apula, Alsontia, Sceringesfelt, Hakinesheim, Bukinheim, Siemera, Mannendal, Karheim, Folemaresbach, Proverstervoth, Gracha, Decima, Vallis with its dependencies; Rateresdorff, Bikendorff, Meisbrath, Ebeno, Arnolfesbere, Lieznich, Okisheim, Rivenacha, Loavia, Windingis, Lukesingis; and in the district of Sallingowe, Dincriche, Juolkurt, Bisangis; and in the city of Metz and its surrounding area, houses, vineyards, fields, and small plots; and in these places: Diedenhown, Wilare, Besiaco, Luzelenkiricha, Tavena, Druhdilingis, and Murmiringa; Meroldivilla, Wimareskiricha, Straza, Crufta, Seranna, Markidith, Krische, Billich, Curmiringun, Brunnacha, Haniwileri; moreover, in the district of Drachere [Note: In the district of Drachere. There is no doubt that this is the ancient territory of Tricoria, bordering the Rhine.] a place called Gunthereshusun; and also in the district of Einriche another place called Prichina, with all things lawfully and legally belonging or pertaining to them.

We have specifically established and confirmed that these two courts are to be used for nourishment [Note: For nourishment. The ancients called *sagina*, or *sagimen*, moderate luxury, by which ascetics, weakened by perpetual devotion to divine worship, periodically restored their exhausted bodies.] and breeches, as well as for the cloaks and tablecloths of the brothers, for the care of the sick and weak, for receiving guests, and for the refreshment of the poor and pilgrims, just as our predecessors established.

And we have given the firmest command that from these places and churches no abbot, nor any other person, great or small, dare grant anything as a benefice to any free or outsider, as we said above, or alienate anything in any way from the brothers’ provision. Rather, the abbot and his successors may use their resources to restore the church lamps, repair the buildings, and provide only what is necessary for the brothers.

As for the churches and all the tithe of willows throughout the abbey, we permit no benefice whatsoever to be granted to anyone, but establish and decree that they remain perpetually for the use of guests, the poor, and pilgrims.

We further establish and confirm by this imperial authority that if any of those to whom we have granted the goods and possessions of Saint Maximin as benefices, or any of their descendants, should die without an heir, the benefice—or whatever he appears to have held from that place—shall return and pass under the right and dominion of the aforesaid saints, the abbot, and the brothers of that monastery. It shall remain without any opposition for the enlargement of the community and also for royal service, to the extent that the abbot can properly accomplish this without harming the Church’s other possessions.

Moreover, we grant and command that the same abbot and his successors have the power to appoint advocates for their monastery wherever they wish and to remove them by lawful judgment. And we order that advocates dare not appoint anyone after themselves who may be called a sub-advocate, nor presume to hold more than the three courts legally owed in the abbey; nor may any of them burden anyone by violence, or forcibly take away their mounted transport animals [Note: *Paraveredi*. *Veredi* are beasts of burden stationed at intervals for speed, the word being derived from animals used to draw carriages.], their livestock, or anything else; nor may they impose anything over the officials, ministers, householders, or any of the abbot’s rights.

And so that this decree of our authority, written out for this purpose, may always remain firm and stable, we have not only strengthened it with our own hand and ordered it marked with the impression of our seal, but, so that it might possess still firmer authority, we have also obtained for the aforesaid monastery a privilege written by our most blessed father, namely Lord Benedict, bishop of the apostolic see, and confirmed by apostolic authority.

Thus, if—which God forbid!—any of our successors, kings or emperors, corrupted by diabolical greed, should attempt to diminish anything that we have established for the repose of the brothers of the aforesaid monastery, the abbot who then presides there and the brothers may freely and confidently appeal to the apostolic see, to which this most sacred place is known to have been attached in ancient times, under the emperor Constantine and his mother Helena, and flee to it as sons to their mother. Supported by it, as is fitting, they may either recover their goods that we have taken away, or, strengthened by apostolic authority, obtain what we have arranged and confirmed for their repose in compensation for the many goods and possessions of Saint John and Saint Maximin taken away by us.

The sign of Lord Henry, the invincible emperor Augustus of the Romans.

Gunther, chancellor, recognized this in the place of Aribo, archchaplain.

Given on the fourth day before the Ides of December, indiction VI, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1023 [Note: But the year of the reign of Lord Henry is given as 1023. [Col. 0372D] The year 1023 is placed here instead of 1022, as occurs in several other charters reported in the *Chronicle of Gottwic*, vol. I, p. 242. This can be excused by saying that the remaining months of the year 1022 were counted as a full year, and then additional months of the year 1023 were again counted as an entire year. We remember having noted elsewhere that this was by no means unusual among notaries and chancellors.], but in the twenty-third year of the reign of Lord Henry II, and the tenth of his empire.

Done at Tribur, the royal villa, in the public palace, in the name of God. Amen. Amen.

## CXXX. Diploma of Saint Henry II, emperor, for the abbey of Mouzon. (Year 1023.)

[*Ecclesiastical and Civil History of the Diocese of Laon*, p. 602.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, by the favor of divine clemency emperor Augustus of the Romans.

It is fitting that the benevolence of royal excellence and imperial sublimity should enrich with great gifts the churches built throughout the world in honor of God, and should especially assist in every way those distinguished by the rule of Saint Benedict, defending them, according to its ability, from wicked usurpers by the strength of royal power. Therefore I wish it to be known to the faithful of the Church, present and future, that a certain venerable abbot of the church of Mouzon, named Boso, approached our serenity, humbly asking and requesting that we prohibit by the authority of our decree anyone disloyal to God—from whom may this be absent!—from alienating or unjustly oppressing the estates situated in the kingdom, by God’s clemency, under our authority, which are known to have been devoutly handed over by God’s faithful to the aforesaid church of Saint Mary of Mouzon.

Following the custom of our predecessors, the Roman emperors Augustus, we granted his requests and by a decree of our authority—however small it may be—confirmed everything given by God’s faithful in the name of the Lord to the aforesaid church of Saint Mary. We strengthened it so that the church of Saint Mary might hold these things forever in peace and without any claim being brought against them.

Namely: three churches, situated in the villa of the same monastery, dedicated to Saint Denis, Saint Martin, and Saint Genevieve, with their lands and all their appurtenances; half of the market of the same place; and the jurisdiction and ban over those men and women who, in the same villa, belong from their origin to the monastery of that place; and four villas whose names are these: Breveliacum with its church, Secia with its church, Odunt with its church, and Remiliacum with its woods and all its appurtenances.

In the villa of Allicurt, one hide with all its appurtenances. In the villa of Duziacum, a church with two chapels and two hides. In Titania, one hide. In the villa of Hercumbre, a church with three chapels. On Mount Saint Remigius, a church. In Hermannis, a church with one chapel. In Villare, one church. In the villa of Sedens, three parts of a church with its lands. At Butoni Court, a church with a chapel. On Mount Rudini, half a church. On Mount Amblini, one church. At Givunna, four hides and a third part of a church. In Upper Purio, one church. On Mount Evrini, one hide. In the villa of Hannonia, an allod with a mill, woods, and all its appurtenances, given by Helgodus. At Bertoldi Court, an allod with a mill, woods, and all its appurtenances, given by Amalric for the soul of his brother Olo. In the place called Villa, an allod given by the same Amalric for his mother. In the villa of Falisia, an allod with a mill, woods, and all its appurtenances, given by Wiricus the cleric. In the villa called Nonas, an allod with a mill, woods, and its appurtenances, given by Jozbert the cleric. At Eomloncare, an allod with mills, vineyards, and all its appurtenances, given by Emma, the wife of Dudo. In the villa of Hairicurte, an allod with half a church and all its appurtenances, given by Hanno, son of the aforesaid Dudo. In the same villa, an allod given by Dada, together with a certain portion of a church, in the villa called Bar, with all its appurtenances. In the villa of Sommoya, an allod given by Lielther for his son Heribert, with all its appurtenances.

At Gunhericurte, an allod with mills, woods, and all its appurtenances, given by Fulcrad and Hamedeus. In the aforesaid villa of Secia, one hide given by Hilbert. In the villa of Flaveio, one church with an allod, given by Hamedeus and his niece Molimdis, with all its appurtenances. In the villa called Urgan, one fiscal hide, given by Duke Frederick for the soul of Otto, with all its appurtenances. In the villa called Ouvelais, one hide. In the villa of Enemente, one hide. On the Moselle River, in the villa of Rozerolax, ten hides. In the villa called Castellum, two hides.

Moreover, we confirmed to the aforesaid monastery the estates that Count Godefrid and his wife Mathild established for the soul of his brother and granted and handed over for the salvation of their souls and those of their parents: namely, in the villa of Madringas, five hides with one demesne hide and half a church; at Rotela, seven hides and a third part of a mill, with cultivated and uncultivated lands; and at Bretenacum, sixteen hides and a certain portion of a church, with all the appurtenances of the aforesaid churches, hides, and estates: pastures, fields, vineyards, meadows, slaves of both sexes, woods, fisheries, mills, cultivated and uncultivated lands, and everything that can be said or named, which now belongs to the aforesaid monastery or which in the future, with God’s favor, will belong to it from anyone.

Let him and his successors in the same monastery have and hold all the things prescribed, so that they may serve God securely, with all human disturbance removed.

If anyone, however—which God forbid!—should become a violator of this confirmation of ours, let him know that he must pay one thousand pounds of gold, half to the palace and half to the brothers of the aforesaid monastery. And so that this may be believed more firmly, we have confirmed it with our own hand and ordered it sealed with our seal.

The sign of Henry, the invincible emperor Augustus of the Romans.

Gunther, chancellor, recognized this in the place of Aribo, archchaplain.

Given in indiction VI, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1023; in the twenty-second year of the reign of Lord Henry II, and the eleventh of his imperial rule.

Done successfully at Yvois. Amen. So be it.

## CXXXI. Saint Henry confirms the privileges of the Church of Bergamo at the request of Bishop Ambrose. (Year 1023.)

[Ughelli, *Sacred Italy*, IV, 441.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, by the favor of divine clemency emperor Augustus of the Romans.

Let the understanding of all the faithful of God’s holy Church and of our own faithful, both present and future, know that Ambrose, venerable bishop of the holy Church of Bergamo, presented to our clemency the decrees and charters of the most pious emperors, kings, and all our predecessors who have reigned from the time of the blessed memory of Charlemagne the Great up to our own present time. All of them raised up and strengthened the aforesaid Church by the protection of their immunity and generosity. He requested that we add our authority to their charters.

We most willingly assented to the prayers of his devotion and ordered this document to be written. By it we decree that whatever the ancient emperors and kings, as well as the empresses and queens of the Romans, Lombards, or Franks, and also the other God-fearing people, bestowed upon the aforesaid holy Church of Bergamo by their decrees and testaments, and whatever the most excellent kings and Augusti later confirmed by their authority, shall remain perpetually stable and inviolate, in our time and in that of our successors, under the right and power of that Church.

No count, judge of the public authority, gastald, or any other person shall dare or presume, in the monasteries, guesthouses, baptismal churches, cardinal churches, or oratories, or any possessions that the aforesaid Church of Bergamo is known to have held anywhere within the kingdom of Italy from the time of Charlemagne the Great up to the present, or that divine mercy may thereafter increase for it, to summon anyone before a court to hear cases judicially, demand fines, require lodging or provisions, forcibly take post-horses or sureties, harm the clerics of that Church in their persons or houses, exercise coercive authority over the freeborn, leaseholders, or slaves living in the possessions or dwellings of that Church, or impose or inflict any public exactions, unlawful pretexts, or forced services, so that they may be able to pray continually and peacefully to the Most High Lord for our safety and the stability of our kingdom.

Moreover, we command and decree that wherever the aforesaid Church is known to have had a lawful investiture from the time of the aforementioned Charlemagne, no one may presume to diminish it unless the matter has first been determined judicially in our presence.

We further order and decree that all exchanges which the Church of Bergamo is known to have lawfully made from the time of the aforementioned great emperor Charles up to the present, whether with a portion of our palace or with other bishoprics, abbeys, counties, public guesthouses, or public institutions, it shall retain inviolate and possess perpetually, without any future contradiction or public claim, with the right of that Church preserved and untouched.

But whoever is found and proved to have violated this decree of ours, we grant that he shall be compelled to pay to that Church the penalty of immunity, in the amount of thirty pounds of gold.

And so that this confirmation, concession, and grant of immunity of ours may retain unimpaired strength in future times, we have strengthened it with our own hand and ordered it sealed with our seal.

## CXXXII. The decree of Saint Henry the emperor granted to Degenhard, abbot of Morbach. He confirms the monastery’s privileges and the right to elect an abbot. (Year 1023.)

[Marten, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, I, 143, from the Morbach cartulary.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, by the favor of divine clemency emperor Augustus of the Romans.

If we enrich places devoted to divine worship for the love of God, and bestow suitable benefits upon those serving Him in those places, we confidently trust that God will repay us with the reward of eternal recompense. Therefore let all our faithful, present and future, know that the venerable Degenhard, abbot of the monastery of Morbach, which was built in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God and ever-virgin, and of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, and of Saint Leodegarius, martyr and bishop, brought before us the charters of immunity of Lord Otto II, emperor of the Romans. These contained the provision that the monastery itself, with the goods and people lawfully subject to it, should, for the love of God and the tranquility of the brothers residing there, be held under their fullest defense and protection of immunity.

For the complete security of the matter, our most beloved consort Cunigund, and the count-bishop of the city of Strasbourg, Verinhard, petitioned us to renew and confirm by this authority of ours such immunity of ours toward that monastery, out of reverence for that holy place.

We willingly assented to the petition, for the love of God and the increase of our reward, and ordered this decree to be written. By it we grant and strengthen for them, by our imperial authority, all the places which, either in the time of Eberhard and Luidefrid, were granted for their use, and which are now held in their possession, for their own property; and whatever is known to have been unjustly taken away, we likewise grant and confirm to them in its entirety. We also freely grant them the right to elect from among themselves an abbot capable of presiding over the brothers’ possessions whenever necessity requires.

Moreover, we decree by the imperial scepter that no count, judge, or any powerful person dare maintain residences in those places or demand provisions, but that they may live in peace and serve the Lord according to the rule. Likewise, in accordance with the ancient grants of our predecessors, no toll shall be collected or demanded from them or their people anywhere within the borders of our kingdom—not in a city, on a road, at bridges, or at any other narrow passage.

And so that this decree of our confirmation may remain firm and stable, we have signed it below with our own hand and ordered it marked with the impression of our seal.

The sign of Lord Henry, the invincible emperor Augustus of the Romans.

Gunther, chancellor, in the place of Aribo, archchaplain, recognized this.

Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of October, indiction VI, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1023, in the twenty-second year of the reign of Lord Henry II and the eleventh of his empire.

Done successfully at Basel. Amen.

## CXXXIII. The decree of Saint Henry the emperor by which he puts an end to the grave dispute that had arisen between the Church of Worms and the monastery of Lorsch. (Year 1023.)

[Schannat, *Bishopric of Worms*, II, 43.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, by the favor of divine clemency emperor Augustus.

Let it be known how continual complaint disturbed our ears because of the long-standing and frequent disputes and the unwithering enmities that had always existed between the bishop of Worms and the abbot of Lorsch, and between the households of both Churches. These had grown so powerful that innumerable murders were even committed between them, and each Church suffered the greatest harm from this.

Therefore, after consulting my faithful, I resolved to regulate the matter. First, I ordered—and sent my messengers to carry this out—that every injustice which had remained uncorrected on both sides for so many years should be completely remedied by their advocates on either side. Thereafter they were to take care that such matters did not become similarly entrenched among them. If any new dispute should remain between them—which God forbid!—I established this decree:

If anyone from the household of Saint Peter of Worms pursues anyone from the household of Saint Nazarius, or conversely anyone from the household of Saint Nazarius pursues any servant of Saint Peter, and with reckless boldness and armed force breaks into someone’s court or house in order to kill or plunder it, and attacks him, but that person escapes or in any way frees himself from his attacker, then the skin and hair of the man who was the leader and chief of this audacity and invasion shall be removed; moreover, on both his cheeks he shall be branded and burned with a specially made iron, heated until glowing. His other followers shall be deprived of their skin and hair.

But if he kills him there, all who participated in such murder or invasion shall, after losing skin and hair, be marked with the aforesaid burning; and the author of the murder shall pay the *weregeld* of the slain man to his lord and make compensation with the relatives of the murdered man, and so forth.

Gunther, chancellor, in the place of Aribo, archchaplain, recognized this.

Given on the fourth day before the Ides of December, indiction VI, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1023.

Done successfully at Tribur, the royal villa. Amen.

## CXXXIV. Saint Henry grants the estate of Steini to the Church of Paderborn. (Year 1023.)

[*Diplomatic Code, History of Westphalia*, p. 87.]

C. In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, by the favor of divine clemency emperor Augustus of the Romans.

If we strive to enrich and exalt the venerable places of God’s Churches, we have no doubt that this will benefit us, the salvation of our souls, the souls of our parents, and the condition of our kingdom. Therefore let the whole assembly of Christ’s faithful and our own faithful know how, taking account of the intervention of our most beloved wife, Cunigund, empress Augustus, who constantly admonished us and unceasingly brought to our remembrance that Meinwerk, venerable bishop of the Church of Paderborn, had labored in our service with continual devotion more than our other faithful, we grant and bestow by this imperial document upon that Church of Paderborn, dedicated in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God, and Saint Kilian the martyr, as well as the precious confessor Liborius, over which that same beloved bishop of ours appears to preside, a certain estate of ours called Steini, situated in the district of Westphalia and in the county of Count Bernhard, with all the appurtenances of that estate: cultivated and uncultivated lands, court-buildings, plots, buildings, slaves of both sexes, meadows, pastures, woods, hunting rights, waters and their courses, fisheries, mills, roads and roadless places, exits and entrances, things acquired or to be acquired, and all other utilities belonging to that estate which can in any way be said, written, or named.

We transfer it entirely from our right and dominion into the right and dominion of that Church, on this condition: that the aforesaid bishop M. and those who succeed him thereafter shall have free power over that estate and its appurtenances to do whatever they wish for the use of the Church, with the opposition of all persons in our kingdom removed.

And so that this authority of our generosity may remain stable and unshaken for all time hereafter, we have confirmed this imperial decree written out for this purpose with our own hand and ordered it marked with the impression of our seal.

The sign of Lord Henry, the invincible [L. M.] emperor Augustus of the Romans.

Gunther, chancellor, in the place of Aribo, archchaplain, recognized this.

Given on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of February, indiction VI, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1023, in the twenty-first year of the reign of Lord Henry II and the ninth of his empire. Done successfully at Paderborn. Amen.

## CXXXV. The privilege of Saint Henry for the same Church. (In the same year.)

[Ibid., p. 83.]

C. In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, by the favor of divine clemency emperor Augustus of the Romans.

Since the mercy of divine favor has raised us, through the magnificence of its boundless goodness, to govern the affairs of the entire commonwealth, above all we must labor for this: that we, who glory in the crown of earthly rule, may not be deprived of that immeasurable glory of joy.
