This is most certainly believed possible if the places assigned by Christian men to ecclesiastical service are confirmed and strengthened by our authority, so that, once every external disturbance has been removed, those devoted to divine praises there may delight in serving the Lord in peace and quiet, and so that we, who are burdened with worldly cares and business, may be freed from the bonds of our sins through the prayers of those who meditate on his law day and night.

Therefore let the whole community of Christ’s faithful and of our own people know how our beloved and venerable Meginwerc, bishop of the Paderborn Church, approached our highness, humbly entreating that the monastery founded by him in the western part of the suburb of Paderborn, in honor of the holy Mother of God and perpetual Virgin Mary and of all the saints, might be confirmed by our imperial authority, so that the brothers of that monastery, intending to remain continually in divine service, might be removed and protected from every secular violence and harassment, and might run the way of God’s commandments all the more swiftly because no impediments of earthly inconvenience stood in their way.

Rejoicing in the intention of this praiseworthy undertaking, and freely assenting to the just petitions of our most beloved wife, Cunigunda, namely the empress Augusta, and of our other faithful men, we have decreed by imperial authority that everything granted to that monastery by us or by the venerable bishop himself from his inheritance, or elsewhere by exchange or lease, or by those worshipers of God, namely: territories, villages, plots, estates, buildings, male and female slaves, cultivated and uncultivated lands, meadows, pastures, fields, waters and watercourses, mills, millworks, fisheries, woods, hunting grounds, outgoings and revenues, traveled and untraveled ways, things acquired and to be acquired, together with every advantage and entirety that may in any way arise from them, shall be held and possessed by the abbot of that monastery with his brothers, by right of ownership and with full authority; and, with the bishop’s permission, he shall do whatever they wish for the common use of the Church.

Moreover, we decree firmly and permanently, by perpetual right, that no duke or count, nor any person, small or great, presume to disturb, harass, or dispossess any abbot of that monastery with his brothers concerning those same goods, or to intrude by any judicial power, except the Church’s advocate, elected by the abbot and the brothers as their defender and appointed by the bishop. This is to be understood in such a way that, content with the Church’s right, he shall do and arrange everything according to the abbot’s command and counsel.

But if anyone should attempt, with any presumption, to violate this decree of our imperial confirmation, let him be fined one hundred pounds of refined gold, measured according to our standard: fifty pounds to be paid to our treasury and fifty to the same Church which he has rashly presumed to disturb. And, so that this confirmation may more truly be believed and may remain stable and unshaken for all time, we ordered this page of the imperial decree to be written out and, having confirmed it with our own hand, to be marked with the impression of our seal.

The sign of Lord Henry, the most invincible emperor of the Romans, Augustus (L. M.).

Gunther, chancellor, recognized this in place of Aribo, archchaplain.

Given on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of February, indiction VI, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1023, in the twenty-first year of the reign of Lord Henry II, and in the ninth year of his empire.

Done successfully at Paderborn. Amen.

## CXXXVI. Saint Henry grants certain estates to the Paderborn Church. (In the same year.)

*[Ibid., p. 84.]*

**C.** In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, by the favor of divine clemency, emperor Augustus of the Romans.

[Col. 0379C] If we strive to enrich and exalt the venerable places of God’s Churches, we have no doubt that this will be of the greatest benefit to us and to the condition of our kingdom. Therefore let the whole community of Christ’s faithful and of our own people know how we, for the remedy of our soul and of that of our most beloved wife Cunigunda, namely the empress Augusta, and also for the souls of our faithful whose bodies rest there, namely Count Erpho and Cono, have granted to our monastery called Cofunga, built in honor of the Lord Savior and of his holy Mother, and also of the most victorious cross and of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, for the use of the holy women serving God there, an estate belonging to our right called Hardinghuson, [Col. 0379D] situated in the district … and in the county of Count …, with all the appurtenances of that estate: namely cultivated and uncultivated lands, estate buildings, plots, buildings, male and female slaves, meadows, pastures, woods, hunting grounds, waters and watercourses, fisheries, millworks, traveled and untraveled ways, outgoings and revenues, things acquired or to be acquired, and all other things that can in any way be said or written, together with the advantages belonging to that estate; and we wholly transfer it from our right and lordship into its right and lordship.

This is done on the condition that the venerable abbess Ota of that church, and those who shall succeed her thereafter, may freely have the power to do with that property and its appurtenances whatever they wish for the use of the church, all contradiction from the people of our kingdom being removed. And, so that this authority of our liberality may remain stable and unshaken for all time hereafter, we ordered this imperial privilege to be written out and, having confirmed it with our own hand, to be marked with the impression of our seal.

The sign of Lord Henry, the most invincible emperor of the Romans, Augustus (L. M.).

Gunther, chancellor, recognized this in place of Aribo, archchaplain.

Given on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of February, indiction VI, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1023; in the twenty-first year of the reign of Lord Henry II, and in the ninth year of his empire.

[Col. 0380B] Done successfully at Paderborn. Amen.

## CXXXVII. Decree of the Emperor Saint Henry II. (Year 1024, 9 March.)

*[Dronke, Codex diplomaticus Fuldensis, p. 348.]*

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, by the favor of divine clemency, emperor Augustus of the Romans.

We desire it to be known to all the faithful, both present and future, how continual complaint troubled our ears on account of the countless and frequent disputes that always existed between the household of Fulda and that of Hersfeld. These grew so strong that innumerable murders were even committed among them, and from this each Church suffered the greatest loss.

Therefore, so that the audacity of such a grave and great presumption might not remain longer between the two households without deserved punishment, with the consent and counsel of both abbots, Richard of Fulda and Arnold of Hersfeld, and of our other faithful men, we have established the following decree by the command of this document:

First, every injustice that had remained uncorrected on both sides for many years shall be fully corrected on either side by their advocates and provosts. Thereafter, if anyone from the household of either Church pursues one of the servants of Saint Boniface or Saint Wigbert, breaks into his estate or house with rash intent and armed force in order to kill or plunder, and attacks him—and if that man either flees, or happens not to be at home, or in any way frees himself from his power or attack—then the skin and hair of the man who was the leader and chief of this audacity and invasion shall be stripped from him; moreover, both his cheeks shall be thoroughly scraped and burned with an iron made for that purpose and heated red-hot. His remaining followers shall be deprived of skin and hair.

If he is killed there, all who have participated in this murder or invasion shall be subject to the punishment stated above. And if the man who is killed and those who kill him belong to the same household, each of them shall pay individually to his own Church the weregild of the slain man and every debt, as they have done until now. But if the man who is killed belongs to one household and those who kill him to the other, the author of the murder alone shall pay the weregild on behalf of all.

And wherever someone from either household is killed, unless the man who committed the homicide has credible witnesses or can prove by means of the red-hot iron that he did not do it for any other reason than that, during the attack upon him, he could not otherwise have escaped alive, he shall be subject to the punishment stated above. But if he can prove this, he shall suffer nothing except what that Church has hitherto held to be the legal penalty.

The advocate in whose jurisdiction this has occurred shall faithfully carry out this provision, with the knowledge of both abbots and in the presence of their messengers. But if the advocate, whether hired for payment or moved by pity, should attempt by any deception to evade this decree, let him be deprived of our favor and of his advocacy, unless he dares affirm over the holy relics that he nowhere can obtain the murderer or invader, and nevertheless obtains him as quickly as he can.

And if the man in whose jurisdiction this has occurred is unable or unwilling to obtain the accused, the faithful men of the other abbot shall obtain him, if they can, and present him for the aforesaid punishment in the presence of the messengers of both abbots.

Concerning the chamberlains, cupbearers, and other honored servants of both abbots, we establish that if any one of them commits such an act, he shall be subject to the aforesaid punishment according to the abbot’s judgment, or shall redeem it with ten pounds of denarii.

And I firmly will and command this: once a matter has been well and rightly determined, no one shall dare repeat or renew it. But if the aforesaid abbots wish to annul this decree, each of them shall pay me or my successor two pounds of gold, yet they shall not accomplish their attempt.

And, so that this constitution may remain stable and unshaken, we ordered this charter to be marked with the impression of our seal.

The sign of Lord Henry, the most invincible emperor of the Romans, Augustus (M) (S).

Odalric, chancellor, recognized this in place of Aribo, archchaplain.

Given in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1024, while Emperor Augustus Henry had reigned twenty-two years, and in the eleventh year of his empire, indiction VII.

Given on the seventh day before the Ides of March.

Done successfully at Bamberg.

## CXXXVIII. 738. Grant of the Emperor Henry II. (Year 1024, 26 June.)

*[Dronke, in the work cited above, p. 349.]*

[Col. 0381D]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, by the clemency of divine grace, emperor Augustus of the Romans.

Since it is our duty, from the goods bestowed upon us by God, above all to enrich the holy churches, our will is ready in the Lord for that same devotion, even if the gifts are very small yet pious—for he gives rewards for good will.

Therefore let the whole community of Christ’s faithful and of our own people know how we, for the remedy of our soul, through the intervention and petition of our beloved wife Cunigunda, empress Augusta, and also of our faithful Richard, abbot of Fulda, have given the county of Stoddenstat, situated in the district of the Maingau, to the altar of Saint Boniface at Fulda, with such right and under such arrangement as it ought to have, and as it has been held in the power of the aforesaid abbot from the beginning by all prelates to whom it was pleasing, without anyone’s contradiction.

This is done on the condition that he and his successors, as with the other goods of the same abbey, shall thereafter have free authority to issue commands concerning it in any manner, or to do from it whatever may be useful to the aforesaid Church.

Let the abbots of the aforesaid monastery take care of this one thing: that neither the religious observance of monastic custom be abolished in their time, nor the care of the souls entrusted to them be endangered, nor the provisions of those serving God there diminish. This is especially important because patrimonies granted to God and tithes handed over to the hands of laymen are polluted, and those men are found guilty before God who regard as nothing the fact that they have laid the sins of men upon themselves.

Those who confer earthly patrimonies upon God and the saints are relieved of their sins; but those who receive the offerings of the faithful, and once more grant what is owed to God and entrusted to God’s service for the exercise of worldly pomp and pride, double the burdensome sins upon themselves.

Therefore we advise and command that a measure and limit be imposed upon these things. Yet there is one middle course. There ought to be many resources in the churches, and especially in Fulda, because from the one to whom more has been entrusted, more is demanded. For it must render many services both to the Roman and the royal court, since it is written: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.”

Therefore let them take thought for themselves and forestall scandals before they arise; let them retain among themselves the things offered to God and not cast them away to no purpose. For the time will soon come when the world receives back what it gave to God, and the monasteries that are now in abundance will be first in plunder, so that what the Savior says may come to pass: “When iniquity abounds, the love of many will grow cold.”

We therefore command, under the strict judgment of God, that all grants of kings, apostolic decrees, and offerings of the faithful be kept in secure custody and faithfully observed.

And, so that this authority of grant and command may remain stable and unshaken for all time, we ordered this document to be written out and marked with our seal.

The sign of Lord Henry, the most invincible emperor Augustus of the Romans.

Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of July, indiction VI.

Done successfully at Goslar. Amen.

## CXXXIX. Saint Henry confirms and enlarges the privileges and possessions of the Novara Church. (Year 1024.)

*[In Baronius, Ecclesiastical Annals, under the year 1014.]*

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Henry, by the ordering of divine clemency, emperor Augustus of the Romans.

When we grant assent to the petitions of the faithful of our imperial highness, we have no doubt that they become much more ready and devoted to our service. Therefore let the prudence of all the faithful of the Catholic Church and of our own people, both present and future, recognize that Peter, a venerable man, bishop of the holy Church of Novara and our faithful servant, who for the sake of our loyalty endured many hardships—hunger, thirst, heat, and cold, and moreover icy crags and very rugged hills, which he overcame barefoot while fleeing from his pursuing enemies—has now also suffered many losses while Harduic ravaged the land.

For his churches have been plundered, his fortresses shattered, his houses overturned, his vineyards cut down, his trees stripped of bark; moreover, his people and estates have been given by Harduic as benefices to his own enemies. He approached our imperial excellence so that, in recompense for his labor and for the restoration of his losses, we might grant to the aforesaid Church of Novara a certain small county, known to lie in the valley of Auxula within the parish of that bishopric, together with all the public dues belonging to that county.

He also asked us to restore to his Church a certain parish which it once lost through evil procedure and unjust dealing, situated in the village called Trecate, not very far from the city, and also an estate called Gravanola, formerly belonging to that bishop, but now evidently seized unjustly.

It is therefore fitting that the aforesaid bishop should receive from us a recompense for his labor. And since it is just that the parish named above and the estate already mentioned should be restored to his bishopric, and since other faithful men of ours, learning of this, may thereby be made more firmly devoted to our loyalty, we have granted his petitions.

We wholly transfer the said small county from our right into the power of his Church and grant it; and by this privilege of our authority we return and grant the aforesaid parish and estate to the aforementioned Church of Novara, together with all jurisdiction and tolls, and fisheries in the river Toxo, specifically in those places where that Church holds land on both sides of the river; and together with hunting grounds and all things that can be demanded from the same county for the public treasury, with chapels, a house, a small estate, tenant holdings, cottages, building sites, fields, meadows, vineyards, pastures, [Col. 0383D] woods, stables, willow groves, marshes, waters, watercourses, mills, fisheries, cultivated and uncultivated lands, divided and undivided property, boundaries, grants, fishponds, purchased properties, and every other payment or due, together with male and female slaves and male and female dependents of intermediate status, with everything that can be said or called as belonging or pertaining to the parish or estate already mentioned.

Also the port of Bestagno, belonging to the same parish, which our most glorious uncle Otto the Elder granted to that see by a privilege. Thus no margrave, count, viscount, his sculdahis, or any other person, great or small, may dare to distrain the people of the aforesaid county, parish, or estate, or presume to exact or compel anything within that county, or acquire any dues; rather, the aforementioned bishop and his successors shall be permitted to hold the said county, together with the aforesaid parish or estate, and to distrain all the people of that county, or of that parish or estate, personally or through their representative, just as they would be distrained by us or by our envoy.

And he shall have, hold, and firmly possess everything belonging to the public treasury from that county, or that can be exacted from it, together with the aforesaid parish of Trecate and estate of Gravanola, with all their appurtenances and pertinences—both he himself and his successors who, by God’s favor and disposition, shall receive the chair of that see—without any contradiction or diminution from us, our successors, kings and emperors, or any other people.

If anyone, therefore, should presume to violate this privilege of our grant by a wicked and rash act, he shall be compelled to pay one hundred pounds of the finest gold, half to our palace and half to the Church of Novara and its rector, whoever at that time shall be in charge there.

And, so that this may be believed more truly and observed more diligently by all, we ordered it to be marked, having confirmed it below with our own hand and with the impression of our seal.

The sign of Lord Henry, the most serene and most invincible emperor Augustus.

Given in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1024, indiction XII, in the thirteenth year of the reign of Lord Henry, emperor Augustus, and in the first year of his empire.

[Col. 0384D] Done successfully at Trucate. Amen.

[Col. 0383]

# Sermon of Saint Henry

Delivered at the council of Frankfurt, held in the year 1006 for the establishment of the bishopric of Bamberg.

*(Mansi, Councils XIX, 289.)*

[Col. 0383D] Lords and Fathers, you have been summoned here by my smallness, and I shall explain why I summoned you; I beg the mercy of all of you that, in these matters which divine grace, as I hope, has inspired in me, you may favor me for love of it.

Since I have no hope of having offspring, I have chosen Christ as my heir. I have long desired to establish a bishopric at Bamberg, with the permission of my bishop, and today I have decided to accomplish it. For this reason I appeal to your most serene piety, lest, because of the absence of the man who wished to obtain from me what I was not permitted to grant, my purpose should be impeded.

Behold the staff, in which the sign of mutual confirmation shines forth; he fled not because of the Lord, but because of grief over a dignity that could in no way be attained. [Col. 0386A] Let the hearts of all present be moved by the fact that he dares to nullify the increase of Holy Mother Church with a foolish embassy.

Behold, the generous goodwill of my present wife and of my only brother and co-heir supports these things; and let each of them know for certain that I shall restore them to them by a restitution pleasing to them. If the bishop deigns to come and accept what was promised, he will find me ready for whatever you may approve.

# In the Year of the Lord 1025. Thangmar, priest of Hildesheim.

[Col. 0385]

# Life of Saint Bernward, Bishop of Hildesheim

By Thangmar, priest.

*[In D. Pertz, Monuments of German History, Historical Writers, vol. IV, p. 754.]*

## Notice

[Col. 0385B] Thangmar, a Saxon by birth [Note: [Col. 0385B] Chapter 1: “of the distinguished blood of our people.”], at the end of the tenth century and the beginning of the eleventh, a priest of the cathedral church of Hildesheim [Note: [Col. 0385B] He calls it “our monastery”; for example, in the year 1000, chapter 18; in 1007, chapter 43.] and first teacher of the boys’ school, and in the eleventh century dean of the church, nurtured Bernward, who had been entrusted to him for instruction in letters and training in character, with such affection that thereafter, throughout his life, he bound him to himself as a son to a father [Note: [Col. 0385B] He is also said to have educated Benno, later bishop of Meissen, in the Chronicle of Saint Michael of Hildesheim, Leibniz II, p. 400.].

When Bernward was advanced to the bishopric of Hildesheim, Thangmar himself, as dean [Note: [Col. 0385B] Chapter 33.], librarian, and notary [Note: [Col. 0385B] Prologue.], took a very large part in the administration of affairs. In the Gandersheim matter in the year 1000, he was sent as an envoy, together with others, to Archbishop Willigis [Note: [Col. 0385B] Chapter 18, “they command through us”]. In the same year he accompanied his bishop to Rome [Note: [Col. 0385B] Chapter 25, “a priest”; compare chapter 34.] and returned with him from Italy. In August of the year 1001 he attended the Frankfurt synod together with Eggehard [Note: [Col. 0385B] Chapter 33.]; then [Col. 0386B] he revisited Italy alone as envoy to Otto III and Sylvester II [Note: [Col. 0386B] Chapters 34–37.]. At the council of Todi he conducted the affairs of his Church; soon afterward, richly rewarded by the emperor who was already near death, he returned home in the year 1002 and lived with Bernward for the remainder of his life [Note: [Col. 0386B] Prologue, at the end.].

Since he lived in the greatest intimacy with the bishop and indeed seems to have been his confessor [Note: [Col. 0386B] Who but a confessor would say this: “Nor in all the zeal of his life could anything defraud my conscience, so that I did not know it fully”?], he undertook to collect his splendid deeds [Note: [Col. 0386B] Prologue.]. With difficulty, and only at length, he composed the work with Bernward’s consent, and completed it after the death of the beloved man [Note: [Col. 0386B] In chapter 22, he speaks of Henry II in such a way that one sees that Henry was then still alive; therefore the book was completed before the year 1024.].

The work agrees in many places with the Hildesheim Annals, which I therefore stated above seemed to have been written by our author [Note: [Col. 0386B] Historical Writers III, p. 20 (Patrology, vol. CXLI, in Lambert of Aschaffenburg under the year 1039). Thangmar must be considered to have brought his account to an end in the year 1022, when writing of Bernward’s death; there, in the account of the dedication of the monastery of Saint Michael, another hand begins. He also seems to have known the old Halberstadt Annals, part of which survives in the Hildesheim and Quedlinburg annals; compare chapter 12.]. The reader will readily observe that nearly everything he relates was either seen by him in person or at least well known to him. In such a man, one could hardly doubt his devotion to truth.

After completing the work, he seems not to have lived long; at least, we read that Tadilo was already dean in the year 1027 [Note: [Col. 0387D] Life of Godehard, chapter 32.]. The book, preserved in the Hildesheim Church to the great advantage of history, was enlarged at the beginning of the twelfth century by miracles attributed to the power of the blessed bishop, and, when offered to Celestine III in 1193, caused Bernward to be numbered among the saints [Note: [Col. 0387D] History of the canonization of Saint Bernward, Leibniz I, 469–474.]. In our own age, too, it will make itself highly acceptable to readers, because it rescued from oblivion many things worthy of knowledge concerning Otto III, whose teacher and friend Bernward is known to have been, and concerning the reign of Henry II. It also unfolds from the beginning the fabric of the Gandersheim dispute, in settling which the emperor and the bishops labored for many years, as we know.

It is written in a simple and lucid style. Like the Hildesheim Annals, it begins the year at the Nativity of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0387D] For example, chapter 36.].

Not long after it appeared, Wolfher used the work in his twofold Life of Bishop Godehard and inserted many excerpts from it into his own writing. At the beginning of the twelfth century it became known to the author of the Chronicle of the Bishops of Hildesheim, and toward the end of that century to the author of the History of the Translation of Saint Bernward.

After the invention of printing, Surius first published excerpts from a certain Hildesheim manuscript in the Acts of the Saints under 20 November. Brower, however, published in the Stars of Germany the books *On the Life, Death, and Translation of Saint Bernward*, and *On the Translation of Saint Epiphanius*, with scholia, using a fifteenth-century manuscript [Note: [Col. 0387D] For in the final chapter it contains a miracle in which the duchy of Mecklenburg is mentioned, although it is known to have been established only in the year 1348.], but one that had been interpolated, with the order of the narrative reversed and the language corrupted.

Mabillon, in the *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, sixth century, part I, p. 202, [Col. 0387C] and Leibniz, in *Brunswick Historical Writers* I, 441, repeated Brower’s text; Leibniz, however, added a few readings from the Wolfenbüttel manuscript and from the Saxon version, which follows the Browerian text.

Our edition is based on:

**1. C. Royal**, formerly belonging to the monastery of Saint Michael of Hildesheim, founded by Bernward. Written in the eleventh century, it is decorated throughout with gold, silver, and various colors, formerly adorned with precious stones, and held in great veneration in the monastery.

The Life itself is completed in five gatherings. A sixth, written by a hand of the beginning of the twelfth century, contains miracles; a seventh, written by the same hand, contains a revelation of Saint Michael and several readings; an eighth, written by a hand of the twelfth century, contains charters issued by Benedict VIII, Henry II, and Provost Bodo in favor of the monastery of Saint Michael, together with some material from a later period. [Col. 0387D] This book, of great authority and at the same time of the best quality, has been reproduced by me almost letter for letter; a specimen of its script is provided in the accompanying plate. It agrees very closely with:

**2. C. Royal, Dresden Library, manuscript in quarto**, written by two eleventh-century hands, but rather frequently interpolated by Wolfher, author of the *Life of Godehard*, with the same sentences that we encounter in the First Life, and enlarged with notices concerning Bishop Godehard that agree with his First Life down to chapter 26. On the other hand, several chapters in the middle of the book are omitted.

At the beginning it is defective. The learned V. cl. Mauritius Haupt, professor at the University of Leipzig, collated the book with the printed editions for our use and reported the following concerning it:

> “The codex, transferred in the year 1832 from the secret archive of the Kingdom of Saxony to the Royal Library at Dresden, contains twenty-three square-format leaves of moderate size. Each page contains twenty-five lines. The book was written by two hands, the first of which continues to the end of the nineteenth recto leaf. On the verso of that same leaf the second hand begins with these words: ‘These things having been so arranged,’ which are read in Leibniz, chapter 41 (now 44). Both hands belong to the eleventh century, and a third, not much more recent, occasionally filled out abbreviations of names above the lines and more than once wrote in the margin [lacuna] (note), and here and there added summaries or annotations, which I did not neglect in collating the codex.

> “I collated this book—and indeed in such a way that, apart from the interchangeable use of the letters *ae* and *e*, I omitted not even the smallest orthographical details—with Leibniz’s edition.

> “The Dresden codex is mutilated. It begins on folio 1 [Col. 0388C] verso, after several worn-away syllables, with the words ‘of the place and congregation,’ which are read in Leibniz, chapter 13, line 14, *Historical Writers of Brunswick*, vol. I, p. 447 (now chapter 12). The first page of this leaf is covered with pasted-on papyrus. Very recently the learned V. cl. Gersdorf, director of the University Library of Leipzig, most generously presented a second copy of the codex, made in his own hand.”

Around the end of the thirteenth century or the beginning of the fourteenth, Thangmar’s book was transcribed anew for the use of Sifrid II, bishop of Hildesheim [Note: [Col. 0387D] Here is the preface to the little book:

> “Here begins the epistle for the legend of the blessed Bernward, bishop and confessor. To his reverend father and lord Sifrid, by the grace of God bishop of Hildesheim, the least of all God’s servants sends his wish to follow the footsteps of the most holy man Bernward, so that he may be able with him to possess the serene joys of the blessed.
>
> “The fountain of the wisdom of God the Father—the Word begotten in his heart—is thus eternally generated; its nature is goodness, its work mercy: redeeming those whom it created, placing the wandering little sheep upon its own shoulder, it led them all the way to the fold of the angels. He does not abandon the vineyard which he brought out of Egypt until the consummation of the age. That vineyard is the Saxon people, long blinded in the darkness of unbelief and wandering without a shepherd, whom he himself, the good shepherd, transferred to the radiance of faith.
>
> “In his natural goodness, he was not content with this, but made the aforesaid vineyard fruitful with the blessed offspring of a holy progeny above the many regions by which it is surrounded; [Col. 0391B] and he raised up for them a prophet from among their own brethren, namely the blessed Bernward, who alone from the Saxon people has been entered in the catalogue of the saints—a fact which no neighboring region can demonstrate from its own blood.
>
> “This man of God, Bernward, bearing a senile heart from childhood, sought the author of all life. Diligently imitating Samuel’s service concerning holy things, he likewise continued the most devout disposition of holy Daniel in the desire for chastity. Running along the paths of justice and the ways of the saints, he did not depart from the Lord’s tabernacle—that is, from the governance of the Church militant—but subjected the flesh to the spirit and sensuality to reason. Having become one spirit with God, he strove to proceed into him through ecstasy of mind, while through the pursuits of sober compassion he did not withdraw from love of neighbor.
>
> “This shepherd of the divine flock not only governed holily the flock entrusted to him, but also enriched the whole holy universal Church by his merits and examples, and confirmed the faith of the weak through rare and wondrous signs. For, besides the works of his holiness, by which he gave forth a sweet fragrance while in the flesh, and besides the many miracles that occurred on the very day of his translation, he healed many illnesses of bodies and souls. Not only on dry land but also at sea, when all hope had been abandoned, the rudders and equipment taken away, and tears nevertheless shed as people hastened to his patronage, he powerfully delivered them more than once.
>
> “And although many of his miracles have been buried through negligence, nevertheless some—fifty-four of them, namely, sufficiently remarkable ones—shine forth in his legend. But because dark Egypt—alas—despises the bodily and spiritual benefits of this true Joseph, the mother of all vices, ingratitude, which dries up the fountain of divine mercy, so many things are found in this saint that scarcely can their like be discovered throughout all Germany.
>
> “For, to say nothing of the parishes of the church of Hildesheim, how many collegiate churches are there which will be unable to show even a single word about his most holy life in all their books, although God says publicly: ‘Ask your father, that is, your spiritual father, and he will tell you,’ and so forth? Alas, by now even a peasant has learned by hearsay from his parents many signs and marvels concerning the blessed Bernward which, through the negligence of certain people, are not contained in his deeds!
>
> “Oh, if the Italian people [the translation into German has: ‘the people of the Walen’] had this saint born from their own flesh, or if the English people had him, would they not zealously urge our entire universal mother, [Col. 0392B] the Church, to join them in praising him? Oh, if the hard Saxon hearts preserved all the words of the holy Gospel as they preserve this one: ‘No prophet is without honor except in his own country!’
>
> “If, therefore, you review in your mind the various regions, scarcely is a man found so cruel that he does not love his own people more than another’s. Hence every true Saxon ought to be greatly disturbed by the fact that many saints are held in such great reverence, while this man has now been exalted and there is no one who grasps it in his heart.
>
> “Since, therefore, the holy Bernward of God always bestowed many benefits upon his neighbors on earth, and now in heaven continually intercedes with the strict Judge for those who love him, your reverend fatherhood, which is vigorous in natural intelligence and powerful in moral virtues and examples, and which has surrounded the church of Hildesheim with many fortifications [the German translation: ‘fortify it with castles and towns’] and strongholds [cf. the Chronicle of the Bishops of Hildesheim in Leibniz, Scriptores rerum Brunsvicensium I, 757 and 774]—for unless the Lord guards it, the watchman keeps watch in vain—should now take care that we summon the most holy Bernward to new praises, so that he may guard us with his Church both in life and in death.
>
> “For his name, Bernward, is interpreted as meaning ‘one who guards well.’ Therefore, so that we may always be able to contemplate God’s face with him, let us rouse the lukewarm to his praise, so that now in life he may preserve us from falling, and in death, through his prayers, free us from wicked enemies and gladden us eternally with his joyful presence.
>
> “Let your fatherhood therefore receive this legend, which briefly embraces his life, although it is itself very long, and read it with devotion, so that from it you may be able to advance to greater devotion.”]

—but with the style altered, with very many sentences and words added, removed, or changed, and with a continuation of the miracles added down to those times. It is clear that the explanation for this text’s great departure from the authentic one must be sought only in what has been added. It is read in three manuscripts, namely:

[Col. 0389]

1. **Alpertus.** Royal manuscript of Hanover (fol. 2).

2. **Life of Saint Bernward.** Royal manuscript of Hanover (fols. 2, 41).

3. **Life of Bernward and Godehard.** Royal manuscript of Dresden (fols. 10, 20).

[Col. 0391A] 3. A manuscript formerly belonging to Saint Michael’s, now belonging to the distinguished Hermann Adolf Lüntzel, whom we mentioned above on p. 248, also presents an account of the translation of Saint Bernward and was printed by Brower in *Sidera Germaniae*. Closely related to it is:

4. The ducal Guelferbytanus manuscript, formerly Heiningensis, now marked no. 353, on paper, fifteenth century, in folio. At its end miracles have also been added to the history of the translation, though not all those found in no. 3; and:

5. The ducal Guelferbytanus among the Augustan manuscripts, nos. 19, 26, and 7, on paper, in quarto, fifteenth century. In 1470 Henninghus Papetranus, parish priest of Goslar, gave it as a gift to the nuns at Frankenberg. Leibniz used this book [Col. 0391B] III in volume I of the *Scriptores rerum Brunsvicensium* when publishing the *Life of Bernward* and the *History of his Translation*. We examined it, as well as the other Guelferbytanus, through the kindness of the distinguished Schoenemann, its librarian.

A translation of this text, even more interpolated and rendered in the Saxon dialect, appeared in quarto in 1540 from the press of Jaspar van Gennep [Col. 0392A]; Leibniz used it in the notes to his edition.

6. In Brussels, in the Royal Library, manuscript no. 8950 contains a copy of the parchment manuscript of Böddeken, which, according to Bethmann, presents only excerpts from the book, omitting, for example, Leibniz’s chapters 11–42, 46–48, 50, 52–58, 60–65, 67, and the rest.

I used these aids as follows: after transcribing the royal manuscript [Note: [Col. 0392D] I nevertheless restored the diphthong in *prae*, *saepe*, *quae*, *laetus*, *moerens*, *aestimo*, and similar words, which was sometimes written simply as *e*], I recorded all the readings of the Dresden manuscript, while taking the others into account only in a few places where this seemed likely to offer some advantage. Following the royal manuscript, I established a division of the work different from that of earlier editors, adding numbers only. I have reserved for another place the history of Bernward’s translation, first added by Brower from manuscript 3. I decided to omit the very brief *Life* published by Leibniz, since it belongs to a much later period [Note: [Col. 0392D] Apart from spurious information—that Henry II was raised by Bernward and, at his command, instructed by him in sacred letters in the church of Hildesheim, and that the dying Otto II entrusted his son, wife, and kingdom to Bernward’s care—it contains nothing that is not found in Thangmar’s *Life*.].

The miracles of Bernward written at the monastery of Saint Michael at the beginning of the twelfth century [Note: [Col. 0392D] “By a certain brother of ours,” chapter 10; in chapter 12 Abbot Conrad is mentioned] were enlarged over the course of time, as can be seen in manuscript 3.

## PROLOGUE OF THANGMAR [Note: [Col. 0393D] *Tanmari* in manuscript 1] THE PRIEST ON THE LIFE OF THE HOLY BERNWARD, BISHOP AND CONFESSOR

[Col. 0393]

[Col. 0393A] Human reason neither clearly grasps nor adequately marvels at the wise and wondrous ordering of divine providence. For we are sustained by the marvelous benefits and daily blessings of divine clemency, so that it appears a grave fault to remain silent about God’s praises, since it is written most plainly: “It is good to conceal the king’s secret, but it is honorable to reveal and confess the works of God” (Tob. 12:7).

Persuaded—indeed compelled—by these angelic utterances, I, the sinner and unworthy priest Thangmarus, also the humblest librarian and notary of our holy church, undertook to collect the splendid deeds of a memorable man, namely our lord Bishop Bernward. God is my witness that I was moved not by the pride of vanity, but so that, if anything worthy of imitation shone forth in them through God’s clemency, I might proclaim to posterity the grace of divine mercy, [Col. 0393B] from whose dew it flowed, and [Col. 0394A] urge them by such an example toward advancement in virtue.

And because I knew that it was rash to undertake this without his knowledge, I hesitated for a long time to discuss the matter openly with him. At last, when I found an opportunity, I attempted an approach. At first he resisted me with firm authority, for he avoided all boasting and popular acclaim as deadly poison. But when I repeatedly insisted that it was a grave sin to conceal good works, lest others make progress through such an example, since the Lord says, “Let your light shine before men” (Matt. 5:16), and so forth, he yielded to my judgment and left to me the task of composing what I should write. For he had been with me from childhood into young manhood, clinging to me and living with me familiarly, like a son with his father; nor could anything in the whole course of his life escape my knowledge, so that I knew it all most completely [Col. 0394B].

## HERE BEGINS THE LIFE OF BERNWARD, BISHOP AND CONFESSOR

[Col. 0393]

### 1

[Col. 0393B] The boy Bernward, therefore, born of an outstanding character and of the noble blood of our people [Note: [Col. 0393D] The German translation calls his father Theoderic, count of Sommerschenburg], from the daughter of Athelbero, count palatine, is said to have been entrusted by his devout maternal uncle, the deacon Folcmar, to our bishop, Lord Osdagus [Note: [Col. 0393D] Bishop in the years 985–989; therefore either Otwinus, who occupied this see in 954–984, is intended, or—what seems more likely—the boy was entrusted to Osdagus before he became bishop, or else to Folcmar, who was already bishop]. Later Folcmar also became bishop of Utrecht [Note: [Col. 0394D] In the years 977–990]. Through the diligence of both men, Bernward was assigned to my care for instruction in letters and morals, since I was then in charge of the school for boys as *primicerius*.

Having received him with complete devotion, I judged that the capacity of his understanding should first be tested on the divine page with its lighter milk. Immediately, therefore, as we read of holy Daniel (Dan. 1:20), I found in him ten times as much understanding in every matter as in all his peers. For, in a wondrous manner, his tender age, irradiated by heavenly light, continually searched out the inner meanings of divine wisdom through subtle meditation. Sometimes he read publicly with the others; sometimes he drew aside those whom he saw to be more diligent in holy contemplation and took them into closer companionship. By setting questions before them, he sifted every difficulty to the marrow.

Like a most prudent bee, he listened attentively from a more distant place to each lesson that I expounded in the schools from various books. Yet afterward, sitting among the boys, he taught these lessons perfectly by a fortunate theft and impressed them upon their understanding. With rejoicing affection I embraced the boy who applied himself to learning by this fortunate theft [Note: [Col. 0393D] Missing in manuscript 1], and thereafter I labored much more vigilantly [Note: [Col. 0393D] Missing in manuscripts 3] to rouse his intellect to knowledge of true wisdom.

The venerable Lord Osdagus, foreseeing in him—by a kind of presage of his future merit—that he would become a great man, ordained him an exorcist and repeatedly urged me to take charge of him more diligently [Col. 0394B]. When I sometimes went beyond the monastery in the service of the lord bishop, I also took him with me, so that I might examine and discuss his intellect more subtly and carefully in private. Among the multitude of boys I could neither distinguish it nor probe it according to my desire, but once they had been removed I could do so with undivided attention. In a wondrous manner I found him sprinkled, beyond his years, with the varied colors of every virtue.

Often we wore away the entire day in study while riding: sometimes reading a lengthy lesson, no less than if we had devoted ourselves to it in the schools; sometimes playfully composing verse in meter along the road; then alternating our exercise with the arena of prose; at times discussing an argument in simple exposition; and often sweating over sophistical disputations. He too frequently questioned me—modestly indeed, but with sharp questions drawn from the innermost approaches of philosophy.

His eager intellect responded to me with such ease that scarcely any hour, not even the hour of meals, showed him to be idle. And although he burned with the most lively fire of spirit in every liberal science, he nevertheless also devoted himself to the lesser arts called mechanical. In writing he particularly excelled; he practiced painting with refined skill; and in the crafts of metalworking, gem-setting, and every kind of construction he wonderfully surpassed others, as he later became renowned for doing in many buildings which he composed with splendid magnificence. In domestic affairs and matters pertaining to the management of the household, he was a most energetic executor, skilled as though he had been trained in them from childhood.

Through the grace of such a disposition, pleasing to God and acceptable to men, he became worthy and familiar to the lord bishop in whose household he lived, and he was held in the highest esteem by his relatives. His grandfather, Athelbero, count palatine, a man distinguished by the greatest praise for his virtues, discharged the administration of the office entrusted to him more from a sense of duty than from personal ambition. When he was blessed with abundant offspring of both sexes, he adopted this distinguished youth, flourishing in the first promise of youthful beauty, as a son. Because he found in him a most salutary source of sound counsel, he brought him into still closer association, so that he did nothing, however insignificant, without consulting him.

### 2

Having received from the venerable Archbishop Willegis the rank of subdeacon, Bernward spent some time in his company. When Willegis perceived in him the advancement of religion through the uprightness of his conduct and the probity of his life, he ordained him deacon. After a further, not very long interval, he raised him to the honor of the priesthood.

When Bernward returned to the aforementioned count, his grandfather, the latter received him with the greatest affection and repeatedly begged him not to leave him. Bernward readily consented. He served him with such humility and devotion that, while the others sometimes withdrew for rest, he alone remained constantly at his side day and night, tirelessly enduring the weakness of the sick old man worn down by age and accommodating himself to his ways. He moved between the count and his household, instructing them daily by salutary admonitions in what they should do and frequently attending to their concerns with vigilant kindness before the count.

He gave himself wholly to the count’s children with paternal affection and won great favor among them. And although envy easily creeps into such intimacy, he avoided it in most matters with the greatest caution. He often went back and forth as intermediary between the father and son, namely the lord bishop [Note: [Col. 0395D] That is, Folcmar, manuscript 3], and fostered a great bond of affection between them.

He pleased the bishop so greatly that the bishop wished to place him in charge of the monastery at Deventer as his representative. Thus a pious contest arose between the bishop and the count over so promising a young man, as each intended to adopt him for himself on account of his excellent character. Bernward, however, preferred to support the weakness of his infirm grandfather rather than seek the comforts of an episcopal household. He labored in faithful devotion with him until the day of his death.

When his grandfather died (987), Bernward went to the palace, entering the service [Col. 0395D] [Note: [Col. 0395] “He became a learned court secretary, tutor and chief secretary of Otto III”; below, chapter 51] of the emperor Otto III, who, still a boy of seven, governed the affairs of state together with his venerable and most wise mother, the empress Theophanu.

The empress received the venerable young Bernward with the greatest kindness, and within a short time he obtained a position of the highest intimacy with her. She therefore recommended, with the consent of all the nobles, that he instruct the lord king in letters and train him in morals. In this he excelled so greatly—although he was attacked by the envy of certain people—that the imperial boy made marvelous progress in learning, while Bernward’s intellect nevertheless remained occupied with every liberal activity needed for affairs abroad.

While others served the boy king by flattering him, even persuading him to engage in amusements and in whatever his tender age demanded, the empress, fearing that her son’s affection might be taken from her, had been softened by such favor to the point that she herself agreed with the greatest pleasure to everything the boy’s age urged him to do. Bernward alone persisted with such skill that he restrained the boy through fear from doing what ought not to be done, while at the same time binding his heart to himself with the fullest affection.

### 3

Meanwhile, the empress Theophanu died at Nijmegen in the midst of the greatest grief for the affairs of the whole kingdom (991, June 16). The lord king, thus deserted by both parents, entrusted himself entirely to the guidance of his most faithful teacher. By his counsel he examined whatever others tried to persuade him to do through flattery, for although he indulged in childish pursuits at the beginning of his reign, he nevertheless foresaw, through deeper prudence, the pretenses of certain people.

He embraced his teacher with exceptional intimacy and did not treat him as inferior to anyone. He revered him as a man adorned with the full splendor of virtues.

### 4

At about this time, when the venerable Bishop Gerdag died (993, January 15), this devout young man Bernward was elected to the episcopate by the unanimous desire of all. Although many noble clerics, after long contending in the service of the palace, sought release from that service, the agreement of all nevertheless united upon this young man chosen by God.

Accordingly, by common election, he was ordained bishop of the holy church of Hildesheim [Col. 0396C] by Archbishop Willegis (Annals of Hildesheim, year 993), in the year 993 of the Lord’s incarnation, the sixth indiction, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of February.

### 5

After attaining the episcopate, he compelled his youthful body toward the summit of virtue with such self-restraint that it cannot be expressed, embracing above all moderation in everything he did, in accordance with the saying of the wise man (Terence, *Andria* 1.1.34): “Nothing in excess.”

By the gravity of his conduct he wonderfully surpassed even old men, so that he trained his subjects in many matters to act under the censure of discipline. No one can adequately praise his frugality in seeking delicacies of food. He moderated his drinking so strictly that after dinner, before going to bed, he drank only once, unless the presence of members of his household or guests compelled him otherwise; often he abstained from drinking altogether.

Once he had been placed in bed, he sometimes devoted himself to reading around cockcrow. Often interrupting his sleep, he gave himself to secret prayer until the clerics rose for the morning hymns. When the hymns had been completed, he very often prolonged the chanting of psalms until daylight; then, resting for a little while, he refreshed his small body until at dawn he again performed the canonical office of Prime in the church.

After completing it, as one placed regularly under discipline, he went with the brothers who lived with him to the chapter house. He also ordered the weekday and the lunar date, as well as the names of the brothers whose annual commemoration was approaching, to be recited every day.

When prayer had been completed, around the third hour he proceeded with festive celebration to the solemnities of Mass and poured out his whole self to the Lord with great contrition of heart. Then, going out into public, he briefly examined legal cases and the affairs of the oppressed, for he was exceptionally skilled in intelligence and eloquence.

He then awaited the cleric who was in charge of almsgiving and the poor. Their number—one hundred or more—he fed most abundantly each day; he also relieved many with silver or other forms of assistance, as his resources permitted [Col. 0397B].

From there he went around the workshops where metals for various uses were made, weighing the work of each person, until, when everything had properly been completed around the ninth hour, he sat down at table, surrounded by a large company of brothers and common people, with fear and the blessing of the Lord. He did not dine with pomp, but in religious silence, while all attended with the most honorable discipline to the reading, which was not brief and continued during the meal.

To sick brothers and those worn out by old age he cheerfully sent a blessing from his own hand, while ensuring that no needy person in the city or suburb whom he knew was deprived of such kindness. Thus, in accordance with the Apostle (1 Cor. 9:22), he desired to become all things to all people, so that he might win them all for Christ.

### 6

It is difficult and arduous to touch upon his daily labor in words, for, as God is his witness, he persisted with every effort in divine matters throughout the day and night. Nevertheless, he also drove all who adhered to him toward such work, so to speak, beyond their strength. There was no art that he did not attempt, even if he could not bring it to perfection.

He fostered scriptoria not only in the monastery but also in various places, and thus amassed a rich library of both theological and philosophical books [Note: [Col. 0397D] Among the books written at his command are a missal from 1014, a Bible, and three Gospel books, one of them from 1011 and bearing the name of the scribe Guntbald; all are decorated with paintings and are still preserved in the episcopal church of Hildesheim. There is also a “Mathematical Book,” which Bernward is said to have used in instructing Otto III. See Kratz, *Der Dom zu Hildesheim*, 1840, vol. II, pp. 104–128. An alchemical book perished in the seventeenth century; vol. III, pp. 11–12.].

He never allowed painting, sculpture, metalworking, gem-setting [Note: [Col. 0397D] The art of enclosing gems in metals], or anything more elegant that could be devised in such an art [Note: [Col. 0397D] Manuscripts 3, 4, and 5 add: “or discovered by anyone”] to be neglected. Thus, from vessels brought from overseas and from Scotland as exceptional gifts to royal majesty, he would not allow anything rare or excellent that he found to pass by unworked.

He took with him to court, or wherever he traveled farther away, ingenious boys [Note: [Col. 0397D] The candlestick bears this inscription: “Bishop Bernward ordered his boy, in the first flowering of this art, to cast this candlestick—not in gold, not in silver, and yet, as you see.” See Kratz, vol. II, p. 32] and boys of exceptional character [Col. 0398A], and drove them to practice whatever more worthy work appeared in any art.

He also devoted himself to mosaic work in the decoration of pavements and, without anyone demonstrating the method to him, fashioned bricks suitable for roofing tiles through his own ingenuity. To put it briefly, he never let a moment pass idly; rather, as a faithful steward of the Lord’s household, he faithfully supplied his fellow servants with the necessary resources.

And although he gathered with faithful devotion whatever he knew to be suitable into Christ’s treasury, he nevertheless rendered to Caesar what was Caesar’s, according to the Gospel. For he served the emperor Otto III with the most devoted spirit, as far as he knew and was able. Consequently he stirred up against himself the envy of many, who were indignant that he conducted the affairs of the state with such vigilant zeal.

### 7  
*(Annals, years 994 and 995)*

Saxony, for the most part devastated by the savagery of pirates and other barbarians, lay continually exposed to the unceasing incursions of robbers. Bernward always strove to drive this plague from the state at great danger to himself and his people; sometimes he attacked them with others, and sometimes, even with his own men, he rushed upon them alone and beat them down with courage.

But when such attacks could in no way be brought to an end—for the barbarians who held both banks of the Elbe and all the ships under their power could, by naval transport, pour themselves with the greatest ease throughout Saxony—the most vigilant pontiff of God, concerned for the people entrusted to him, was deeply troubled as he considered how he might rescue God’s people from the savagery of the barbarians.

They were extending the fury of their attacks almost as far as Hildesheim and were promising themselves that the holy place itself would become their prey. Therefore, by divine inspiration, almost at the extremity of his bishopric, where the rivers Aller and Oker meet, he built a very strongly fortified little fort [Note: [Col. 0398D] Mundburg; cf. the confirmation of Henry II in 1013, *Origines Guelficae* IV, 435]. After stationing troops there, he repelled the barbarians’ attack and freed God’s people from enemy savagery.

Through God’s grace such security of peace was bestowed upon the faithful in those places through him that afterward they suffered no loss or danger from the barbarians. Once the barbarian tumult had been driven out of those places through the industry of Christ’s priest, the barbarians raged more fiercely against the surrounding regions.

Therefore, as a type of Christ his Lord, the most vigilant shepherd of the divine flock placed himself against the adversaries of the Church, rejoicing to run his course like a strong giant [Col. 0398D]. In the place called Wirinholt, where their safest station had been, he established a most strongly fortified stronghold, making the place free from the incursions of robbery wherever they might direct the ambushes of their treachery [Note: [Col. 0398D] It does not seem to be either Wiringen or Warenholz, since both villages were separated from their mother churches only much later. Varenholz below Rinteln was not situated in Bernward’s diocese].

He made it extremely secure with ditches and channels of water flowing through a stream, and he stationed there an abundance of troops supplied with food, arms, and all other necessities. By divine grace he made this extremely dangerous place peaceful and tranquil for God’s people, so that, once every foulness of diabolical and barbarian treachery had been expelled, he transformed the abyss of invasion and hostile incursion into a place of prayer and consecrated an oratory of Saint Lambert, bishop and martyr, to God.

From that day onward, once the Church of Christ had been restored to profound peace, God’s people, through the industry of their most vigorous protector, enjoyed complete rest from every hostile attack.

For these and the other benefits which he exercised with the most devoted zeal for the state and the faithful people, he aroused against himself the envy and indignation of many, especially of princes. Consequently he suffered many grievous attacks from the archbishop of Mainz, as we shall explain more fully below. Bearing the latter’s hostility with the greatest patience, he administered divine and royal affairs with the utmost kindness.

### 8

Although he expended very great sums abroad to repel barbarian savagery, it nevertheless cannot be said how much he contributed within the bishopric for the use of his church.

In estates he accumulated so much that he acquired thirty or more principal farmsteads, outstanding for their splendid buildings, together with the households of the tenants and cultivators, while in countless other places he transferred ten hides, or eight, or more or fewer, into the possession of his church, according to the circumstances of each case [Note: [Col. 0399D] Compare Bernward’s charter of donation for the monastery of Saint Michael].

The ancient places possessed by his predecessors, which he found uncultivated, he illuminated with the finest buildings. Among these he interspersed certain structures with more elegant designs in white and red stone, and with varied mosaic painting he made them into a work of great beauty.

What should I say of the zeal and expense with which he ennobled our holy place and the principal church, since he preferred to devote himself and everything he could possess to its use? His works testify to this [Note: [Col. 0399D] There remain a gold cross, a silver cross, two candlesticks, a bronze column, and the bronze doors of the cathedral church. Another cross is preserved at Heiningen and a paten at Hanover [Col. 0400D]. For the other lost objects, see Kratz, cited work, p. 38], speaking clearly to future generations of the pious desire of his heart [Note: [Col. 0400D] That is, “speaking”].

He ardently strove to adorn the church with extraordinary zeal. Thus he decorated both the walls and the ceilings with refined and luminous painting, so that one would think the old church had become new.

For solemn processions on the principal feasts he made Gospel books resplendent with gold and gems, as well as thuribles of magnificent value and weight. He also made several chalices, one of onyx and another of crystal, with marvelous skill. In addition, he cast one golden chalice of the purest gold for liturgical use, weighing twenty pounds according to the public standard.

He also suspended before the façade of the church a crown radiant with silver and gold and of remarkable size, along with many other objects which we have thought best to pass over, lest we cause weariness through excessive length.

With the greatest determination he also undertook to enclose our holy place within a circuit of walls. He began the work with towers arranged around it and with such prudence that, in both beauty and defense, as is evident today, you will find nothing like it throughout all Saxony.

He also built a very splendid chapel outside the walls in honor of the life-giving cross. There he deposited a portion of the cross, encased in brilliant gems and the purest gold, with the assistance of the lord emperor Otto III Augustus [Col. 0400A] [Note: [Col. 0400D] This cross is now preserved in the church of Saint Magdalene]. There, too, divine mercy displayed many signs of its own mercy through evident miracles performed by the power of the holy cross.

### 9

Among these, I would like to insert one unique event by which the Lord deigned to console the devotion of our bishop.

The venerable Bishop Bernward prepared a splendid reliquary of gold and gems in which to enclose the life-giving wood. When he attempted, if it could be done, to cut a fourth piece from three fragments of the holy wood, so that he might place one portion in each of the four apses, the thinness or smallness of the wood for whatever reason would not permit it to be cut. As the most devoted servant of God was wavering in mind, behold, suddenly a fourth fragment of the most sacred wood appeared between the hands of the bishop himself, brought there, as is believed, by angelic ministry.

The bishop immediately rejoiced and prepared the holy wood for the four apses. Oh, how many people who drank from it afterward repeatedly extinguished the burning heat of the most violent fever through the power of the holy cross! Many times the faithful, cleansing themselves and their possessions with this life-giving wood, calmed the pestilence that had arisen from an imbalance of the air.

We also drove away an excessive drought by bringing this singular wood out in public, as though commanding the rains. Through the power of this most holy triumph, many daily cures are performed, while each grieving person who prostrates himself there receives ready consolation.

### 10

He dedicated the chapel of the holy cross, completed with varied ornament, on the fourth day before the Ides of September, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 996, the ninth indiction, in the thirteenth year of the reign of the most glorious emperor Otto III, the first year of his empire, and the fourth year of Bernward’s ordination.

He made the place, once terrifying with thickets and brambles, into an everlasting source of consolation for the neighboring inhabitants through the gifts of your baptism, O Christ—glory to you!—of burial, and of anointing.

### 11.

For such and other acts of pious devotion, by which he labored with every effort of mind and body for the benefit of the church [Col. 0400D], the bishop of blessed memory was most acceptable both to God, who presided inwardly in his heart, and to the church, which approved the result of his work outwardly. Therefore it followed that this blessed man—of whom, as it is written concerning holy Job (Job 1:8), it was then thought that there was no one like him on earth—should, through the trials of temptation, be shown to all as remarkable not only for his other virtues but also for the renown of his humility and patience.

In the eighth year of his ordination [Col. 0401A] (1000), he was openly attacked by Archbishop Willegis with grievous troubles and persecutions concerning the territory of Gandesheim, plainly contrary to ecclesiastical sanctions; yet he was not at all moved from his customary, steadfast observance of humility and patience. Nevertheless, the prudent man opposed what the archbishop was attempting—not so much by executing a just claim as by presuming upon unrestricted power—with firmness of authority, not rash audacity. In accordance with Paul’s statement, “As long as I am the apostle of the Gentiles, I will honor my ministry” (Rom. 11:13), for as long as he presided over Christ’s church in the capacity of shepherd, he took the greatest care to preserve the rights of his bishopric in their proper state of honor; and, with God’s approval, he achieved this, though only after much labor.

But lest a similar controversy should later arise concerning Gandesheim church itself [Col. 0401B], I have thought it useful to insert here the entire course of the dispute between the archbishop of Mainz and the venerable lord Bernward [Note: [Col. 0401] “lord” in witness 1.]. I think it necessary to investigate and recount these matters from somewhat earlier, though this should not be burdensome to the reader, since perhaps it will be useful to posterity in many respects.

### 12.

The territory of Gandesheim, situated in the district of Flenithi, together with the neighboring villages, is certainly subject to the administration of the bishops of Hildesheim, from the time when the bishoprics were first delimited throughout Saxony. This is made perfectly clear to all who wish to know it by the fact that, from the very beginning of the Christian faith of our people, even before the construction of the monastery mentioned above [Col. 0401C], it belonged to the care of our bishop.

In the time of Lord Altfrid [Note: [Col. 0401] “lord” in witness 1.], the fourth bishop of our church, Duke Liudolf and his religious wife Oda [Note: [Col. 0401] The codex has a lacuna, evidently to be supplied with contectali (“wife”); a recent scribe nevertheless inserted contectrice (“female companion”), a reading also found in witnesses 3, 4, and 5.], inflamed with great zeal for divine worship, went to Rome on the advice of the aforesaid bishop. There they were magnificently received by Pope Sergius; and when he learned of their devotion to divine things, he dismissed them with relics of the holy bishops Anastasius and Innocent, together with his blessing.

Thus, having reached their homeland by God’s grace, on the advice of Lord Altfrid they first established a convent of virgins dedicated to God at Brunesteshusen. They also entrusted their daughter, Lady Hathumod, then twelve years old, to the aforesaid bishop so that she might be placed in charge. This took place in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 852 (cf. the Annals of Quedlinburg), while Rabano presided at Mainz. They committed the entire administration of the aforesaid place [Note: [Col. 0401] witness 2 begins with this word.] and community to Lord Altfrid. [Col. 0401D]

After several years had passed, when Karolo succeeded Rabano, in the year 856 of Christ’s singular birth, he himself began work on a certain site above the river Ganda, which he named Gandesheim after the river [Note: [Col. 0401] “Gandesheim” in witness 2.]. There, with the duke’s consent, he began construction of the monastery on a larger scale, while Liudbert of Mainz was bishop; Liudbert had succeeded Karolo. The site seemed more suitable for the dwelling of those who serve God because of the beauty of its meadows and woods, and also safer because of the density of the forests and the protection afforded by the marshland.

Before the construction of the church at Gandesheim was completed [Note: [Col. 0401] “Gandeshemensis” in witness 2.], both the duke and Lady Hathumod died and were buried in the old church at Brunesteshusen [Note: [Col. 0401] “Brunisteshusum” in witness 2.]. Lady Gerburgis [Note: [Col. 0401] “Gerbergis” in witness 2.] was then placed in charge as the first [abbess; Note: [Col. 0401] “prima” is written by a second hand in the margin of witness 2.], sister of Lady Hathumod [Note: [Col. 0401] “Hathomod” in witness 2.], through the agency of the venerable Bishop Altfrid, with Liudbert of Mainz [Note: [Col. 0401] absent in witness 2.], who had succeeded Karolo, as archbishop.

Not long afterward, after only two years had elapsed, the venerable Lord Altfrid died. He held office under the bishops of Mainz: Rabano [Note: [Col. 0401] “Hrabono” in witness 2.], Karolo, and for twelve years under Liudbert [Col. 0402B]. He completed with every adornment the church of Hildesheim, which he had built from its foundations, and, after it had been consecrated by God’s grace, he died full of good works.

Marcwardus succeeded him, the fifth bishop [Note: [Col. 0401] absent in witness 1.] of our church. He held office for only four years and laid the beams of the church [Note: [Col. 0401] “four” in witness 1.]. After him Lord Wicbert succeeded as the sixth bishop. He completed the construction and also consecrated the church.

He began and completed all the religious observance and discipline at the aforesaid place together with Lady Oda and Gerburga [Note: [Col. 0401] “Gerberga” in witness 2.], the abbess; they arranged and carried out everything according to his counsel. Lady Gerburgis [Note: [Col. 0401] “Gerbergis” in witness 2.] presided over the community for twenty-two years. She was placed in the new church beside Lady Hathumod [Col. 0402C] [Note: [Col. 0401] “Hathumoðam” in witness 2.].

Her sister Cristina was admitted and consecrated to the administration by Lord Wigbertus. Lady Oda died in the 107th year of her life, after all her children had preceded her in death; only Cristina survived. She was buried beside her daughters. Cristina herself survived her mother by only six years and then departed to the Lord by a blessed death.

Lord Wigbertus held office under the bishops of Mainz, Liudbert, Sunderaldus, and Hatto. After him Walbertus succeeded as the seventh bishop. He admitted to the administration Rotsuitha, a venerable woman chosen from that same community. He also performed the consecrations in the aforesaid church, the veiling of the handmaids of God, and the other matters pertaining to ecclesiastical ministry.

After Walbertus [Note: [Col. 0401] “Uualtbertum” in witness 2.], Sehardus, a venerable man, was ordained the eighth shepherd of our church [Col. 0402D]. Without any opposition, he administered at the aforesaid place whatever pertained to ecclesiastical ministry.

Ninth after Sehardus, Thiethardus [Note: [Col. 0401] “Thiuthardus” in witness 2.] was placed over us as bishop, while Frithericus presided as archbishop at Mainz [Note: [Col. 0401] “Mogontia” in witness 2; “Frithericus, archbishop of Mainz,” written by a second hand in the margin of witness 2.]. He consecrated the new church where the nuns now serve Christ, and properly administered everything episcopal [Col. 0403A] at the aforesaid place, without anyone opposing him.

Tenth after Thiethardus [Note: [Col. 0403] “Thiothardum” in witness 2.] was Lord Otwinus. He appointed and consecrated Lady Gerburga [Note: [Col. 0403] “Gerbergam” in witness 2.] the second [Note: [Col. 0403] “by a second hand” in witness 2.] to the administration, and faithfully provided everything episcopal, with Lord Willehelmus [Note: [Col. 0403] “Uuillihelmo” in witness 2.], the son of the great Otto, opposing him in nothing. Likewise Hatto and Rodbertus, opposing him in nothing, held him in the greatest friendship.

Willegisus, succeeding him, feared the old age and gravity of such a man. He publicly honored him greatly, but secretly, with a certain resentment of spirit, contended against him somewhat more sharply. Nevertheless, he showed nothing harsh, either in words or deeds, in the administration of the aforesaid monastery [Note: [Col. 0403] “or” in witness 2.].

I have therefore set out these matters so that everyone may understand with what frivolity and rashness a custom was violated which, for nearly two hundred years [Col. 0403B], had endured strengthened by the concord of such venerable fathers, the bishops of both places, and fixed and confirmed by all canonical authority [Note: [Col. 0403] “so many” in witness 2.].

### 13.

But the daughter of the second Emperor Otto—if I may speak plainly, the source of this kind of dissension—when she refused to receive the sacred veil from her own bishop, Lord Osdagus, sought Willegisus, considering it unworthy unless she were consecrated by a bearer of the pallium. He willingly agreed, giving no thought to how greatly he was violating the ancient statutes of the canons [Note: [Col. 0403] “institutions” in witness 2.]. Nor did he seek an approach through brotherly charity; instead, he commanded his brother and fellow bishop to appear on the feast of Saint Luke the Evangelist for the veiling of the handmaids of God.

When Lord Osdagus found an appropriate opportunity, he asked the archbishop privately by what authority he was acting. When the latter replied with a threatening expression and sharper words that the matter belonged to his own diocese, he promised that on the appointed day he would veil the handmaids of God and remove all episcopal authority from that place.

When the appointed day arrived, Lord Osdagus resisted him with full authority, in the presence of King Otto III, together with his mother, the empress Lady Theuphanu [Note: [Col. 0403] absent in witness 2; “Theofanu” in witness 2, consistently.], and with the bishops Retharius [Note: [Col. 0403] “Hretharius” in witness 2.], bishop of Paderborn; Milo, bishop of Minden; Hildebaldo [Note: [Col. 0403] “Hildibaldo” in witness 2.], bishop of Worms [Note: [Col. 0403] “Wormacensis” in witness 2.], together with the other princes who had assembled for the solemnity of veiling the virgins.

When the lengthy dispute had taken place, Lord Osdagus, a man of simple character, moved by divine prompting, ordered the episcopal chair to be placed at the altar’s apse. By this protection he defended the place and its administration for himself [Col. 0403D], with almost everyone supporting him, since although they concealed their feelings out of fear of the archbishop, his hostility displeased them all.

The archbishop, deprived of the support of the multitude, had earlier promised that everything belonged to his right. Only with Lady Theuphanu and the bishops exerting themselves on his behalf, and with the archbishop himself pleading beyond what could be believed, did he obtain permission to perform the sacred rites at the principal altar on that day—specifically, to conduct the veiling of Lady Sophia [Note: [Col. 0403] “Sophyae” in witness 2, frequently.] [Col. 0404A] together with Osdagus, while Lord Osdagus alone oversaw the others who were to be veiled.

An unprecedented event then occurred, one never before seen by us: two bishops sat together at the side of the altar, solemnly wearing the episcopal vestments and mitres.

The consecration of the handmaids of God then took place. During the Mass, the bishop who had previously feared that he would be deprived of episcopal right, suddenly raised up by God’s grace, first humbly asked the lord king whether he consented to the veiling of his sister, and then asked the other guardians. When they declared their consent, he first asked Lady Sophia whether she professed subjection and obedience to the see of Hildesheim and to its successors, and then asked the other women who were to be veiled.

They confessed their religious commitment and subjection with unanimous consent [Col. 0404B]. It was publicly announced to all the clergy and people [Note: [Col. 0403] “It was also publicly announced” in witness 2.] that the archbishop claimed no right for himself in that church [Note: [Col. 0403] absent in witness 1.] except with the consent and permission of the bishop of Hildesheim.

When everything had been properly completed, they departed in complete peace and concord. Unity continued under Lords Osdagus and Gerdagus and for several years under Lord Bernwardus [Note: [Col. 0403] “years” in witness 2.], to such an extent that Bernwardus consecrated certain churches there in the presence of the archbishop. He also held a great synod in the presence of Lord King Otto III [Note: [Col. 0403] abbreviated “Lord Otto, third king” in witness 2.], while the aforesaid archbishop was likewise present; yet the archbishop decided nothing by his own authority except that he gave his consent, equally with the other brothers, to Lord Bernwardus, who presided over the synod.

Those present included Islarius [Note: [Col. 0403] “Islarus” in witness 2.], archbishop of Magdeburg; Liudolfus [Col. 0404C] [Note: [Col. 0403] “Liudulfus” in witness 2.], archbishop of Trier; Milo, bishop of Minden; Hildebaldus, bishop of Worms [Note: [Col. 0403] “Hildibaldus, bishop of Worms” in witness 2.]; and Hugo, bishop of Zeitz.

Yet this concord did not remain firm, because certain matters emerged which destroyed the love that was beginning to grow, like weeds of falsehood [Note: [Col. 0403] “thus” in witnesses 1 and 2.].

### 14.
