It is indeed hateful in our time to identify anyone by the truth, as someone said: “Truth breeds hatred.” But for writers it is a grave fault either to state falsehoods or to omit the truth. Therefore, with everyone’s peace, let it be said that what it is a crime to conceal must be disclosed.

That illustrious community of handmaids of God was established with such zeal and devotion by our lords, the fathers of our homeland, dukes and kings, through Altfrid and his successors, that at the beginning they flourished as an example of humility and charity for all to imitate. They listened to, honored, and loved their own bishop, appointed over them by God, as though he were God’s messenger and father. They welcomed all who came with exceptional kindness, as was appropriate to each person.

This was their custom and this their devotion. These qualities brought reverence to that holy place and gained them favor among all. Through this privilege of humility, whenever they were summoned to the palace on church business [Col. 0404D], they came in clothing that was either exceedingly neat or very plain, and were regarded and venerated by all as true handmaids of God.

But after luxury and excess arrived, insolence of character entered; obedience grew sluggish; reverence for the bishops was rejected; whatever pleased each person was treated as permissible.

The prolonged illness of Lady Gerburgis, the most venerable mother of that monastery [Note: [Col. 0405] Witnesses 1 and 2 read venerabillimae (“most venerable”); witness 1, in the same hand, also reads venerabilissimae (“most venerable”).], also contributed to the increase of evil. The Lord had bestowed upon her many distinguished virtues. The religious sisters who had been formed under the care of the ancient discipline also died.

A numerous group of young women had grown up in the training of Christ. Brought up more delicately and ignorant of the limits of the former discipline and severity, they deviated after their vows, as is human [Col. 0405B].

Sophia too, against the will and strong resistance of Lady Gerburgis, went to the palace through the faction of Archbishop Willegisus. There she remained for a year or two, following a dissolute way of life and spreading various rumors about herself.

The venerable Bishop Bernwardus could not tolerate this, since he had always honored her with the greatest love and affection. By gentle admonitions he persuaded her to return to the monastery. Although at first she scarcely admitted his words through outward hearing, he repeatedly urged her more familiarly to return to the convent.

At first she avoided his visits and conversation; then she fled to the archbishop as though seeking his protection. She provoked Bernwardus’s anger with harsher words and annulled with empty speech the agreement made at her veiling, saying that she had been veiled by the archbishop, not by the bishop of Hildesheim; that she did not belong to the administration of Bishop Bernwardus; that the Gandesheim monastery belonged to his diocese; and that she had found many people who could truthfully testify to this.

By these and similar words [Note: [Col. 0405] “such words” in witness 2.] she seriously stirred the archbishop’s mind against Lord Bernwardus. Afterward she returned to Gandesheim [Note: [Col. 0405] “Gandeshem” consistently in witness 2.] and spread various accusations about the bishop among the sisters. She was preparing, by whatever effort she could, to drive him from the place and alienate him.

### 15. (1000)

Meanwhile, when the bishop learned that such things were being plotted against him, he came to Gandesheim. He deeply resented being alienated, receiving none of the charity or honor that had been shown to his predecessors, and being treated as an outsider bishop, although innumerable benefits had been bestowed on the holy place by his predecessors [Col. 0405D]. Many tithes, moreover, had been contributed from his side both in ancient times and recently; yet, in return for these benefits, injury and insult were repaid to him, the payments due for the tithes were reduced and often fraudulently withheld.

With humility he urged them to sacrifice obedience—which no offering is more pleasing to God—upon the altar of the heart. He said that he could patiently endure everything, but that they should fear offending Christ in him, since he acted in Christ’s place. Whatever they might inflict upon him, he held to be deserved according to his merits [Note: [Col. 0405] witness 2 reads “his own merits”]. Nevertheless, he did not dare through his own fickleness to neglect the obedience, charity, and reverence that their foremothers had shown to his predecessors [Col. 0406A].

When he had pleaded these matters with a father’s heart, their sins impelled them to stir up greater hatred against him, with Sophia pressing the matter on behalf of both the archbishop and the community.

### 16.

The hour was approaching when Lady Gerburgis had requested that the church she had built be consecrated. Since she, exhausted by prolonged illness, was entirely unable to undertake the solemnities of so great a festival, Sophia, with the consent of her lady and mother, had assumed the burden of this great labor.

As was their custom, they set aside and rejected their own bishop [Note: [Col. 0405] absent in witness 1]. The archbishop was summoned, and under his direction everything pertaining to the dedication [Col. 0406B] was arranged. They fixed the day of consecration as the feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross (September 14).

A messenger was also sent from the abbess, who was to invite Lord Bernwardus to the dedication and announce the day to him. Although many reproached him for having been anticipated by the archbishop’s summons, he endured this with a gentle spirit and promised that he would come on the appointed day.

Meanwhile, for a reason unknown, the archbishop changed the arrangement, abandoned the appointed day, and announced the same dedication for the feast of Saint Matthew the Apostle (September 21). He sent Lord Bernwardus a delegation with the same authority that he had once sent the venerable Lord Osdagus for Sophia’s veiling, ordering him to appear before him without delay for the dedication on the aforesaid feast.

Bernwardus himself sent his messenger and a written reply back to the archbishop, explaining that he was bound by imperial commands and occupied with certain serious matters, and that he could not appear before the archbishop for the dedication on that day as ordered.

### 17.

Nevertheless, on the feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross he came to Gandesheim to dedicate the church, just as the abbess had originally arranged. He found nothing prepared; rather, he found certain people gathered who would resist him and drive him out with insults if he should attempt to consecrate the church forcibly with his attendants.

They had spread this rumor, although God was witness that he was attempting or even conceiving nothing of the kind. By then they had fled with all their mind to the archbishop and had entrusted themselves and the place to his protection. Sophia, constantly attached to him and living with him, pursued this purpose day and night.

Lord Bishop Bernwardus celebrated the solemn Mass there on that very day, despite the community’s greatest indignation. Nevertheless, he urged them to offer the oblations [Note: [Col. 0405] “the offerings at Mass” in witness 2.] and receive the blessing.

When the people learned of their bishop’s arrival, they assembled as though for a solemn festival, grieving and bearing beyond what could be believed the fact that the bishop was being driven from the place by its insolence and disobedience.

He consoled them and all who came with polished speech, publicly recalling with tearful complaint that he had been invited that very day to the dedication of the church, but that no honor had been shown him; rather, he had been excluded. Therefore, he forbade all, by canonical authority, to consecrate the church—which belonged to him—without his consent.

At this, the community of sisters became indignant and was inflamed with the fire of still greater indignation [Note: [Col. 0407] the words “of still greater indignation” are absent in witness 2.]. When the time for the offering came, they threw down the offerings in indignation and unbelievable fury, and heaped savage curses upon the bishop.

Struck by this extraordinary tumult and covered with tears, the bishop did not weigh his own injury [Note: [Col. 0407] the words from “not [weighing] his own injury” through “lamenting” are absent in witness 2.], which he considered of little importance. Rather, following the example of the true shepherd who prays for his persecutors, he lamented the ignorance—or rather the malice—of the raging women. He returned to the altar and completed the Mass in its proper order with great contrition of heart. Then he addressed the people, blessed them, and strengthened them [Col. 0407B]. They escorted him away honorably, and he returned to the place from which he had come.

O man worthy of remembrance, to be celebrated by every mouth and embraced inwardly by the devotion of all! In himself he was incredibly humble, yet before God, the examiner of hearts, and before God’s faithful, truly exalted.

Who would have believed that, in such great honor of pontifical dignity, in nobility of lineage, and with such a multitude of attendants, he would have preferred to be protected against the insults inflicted upon him by the shield of patience rather than that of power?

But the blessed man cared nothing for the reproaches of human humiliation. Entirely devoted to divine love, he ardently desired above all to please the eyes of the one whom he loved uniquely.

I have wished to insert these matters as a greatly useful example for the imitation of those who hear them. Now let us return to the sequence of events.

[Col. 0407C]

### 18.

Meanwhile, the archbishop and Sophia diligently prepared all the equipment necessary for the consecration of the new church, without consulting Bishop Bernwardus. Lady Gerburgis attempted to associate him with the proceedings, but, fearing the archbishop, she was afraid to oppose his wishes.

Moreover, on the vigil of Saint Matthew (September 20), the archbishop came to the aforesaid monastery with the bishops Retharius [Note: [Col. 0407] “Hretharius” in witness 2.], bishop of Paderborn, and Berengarus, bishop of Verden [Note: [Col. 0407] “Berngero Uardensi” in witness 2.], and also Duke Bernhardus [Note: [Col. 0407] “Bernwardo” in witness 2.], together with many others, intending to consecrate the church on the following day.

Messengers were also sent to Bishop Bernwardus to invite him to the church’s solemnity. But early on the next day (September 21), the venerable Bishop Eggehardus [Note: [Col. 0407] “Ae,” written by a second hand, “Eggeardo” in witness 2.] came in the place of our lord bishop, together with the elders of our community and certain leading men from our monastery [Note: [Col. 0407] absent in witness 2, which leaves a space.].

When permission to speak had been granted, they greeted the archbishop in the name of Lord Bishop Bernwardus with every honor and devoted service [Note: [Col. 0407] witnesses 1, 3, 4, and 5 read “he greeted him, saying”]. They said that Bernwardus was detained by imperial service and could not be present; yet they expressed great astonishment that, in his diocese and church, which had always been possessed by his predecessors without any opposition, the consecration of a church had been announced without his consent.

With brotherly charity they begged the archbishop to desist from such an invasion [Col. 0408A] and not to intervene except to the extent permitted by the canons. If he thought that some special privilege supported his exclusive right, Bernwardus would not fail to pursue the matter fully through the common counsel of the brothers, wherever the archbishop might choose.

The archbishop, however, inflamed with harsher indignation, ordered Bernwardus to hasten without delay to the consecration of the aforesaid church early the next morning, which was then dawning as Sunday (September 22). If he delayed coming, the archbishop said that he would nevertheless dedicate the church.

The chief cause of this anger and indignation of the archbishop against the revered bishop was Bernwardus’s special intimacy with the emperor. The emperor honored him with exceptional devotion and affection, and Bernwardus bound the emperor to himself through the most devoted service: he carried out with the greatest vigilance everything he knew would be pleasing to him.

For this reason he aroused against himself the hostility and envy [Note: [Col. 0407] “and jealousy” in witness 2.] of many, especially the bishop of Mainz, who was angry that anyone besides himself should have a place of intimacy with the emperor.

As Sunday dawned, the aforesaid Bishop Eggehardus [Note: [Col. 0407] “Ae”; written by a second hand, “Echoardus” in witness 2.] arrived with the venerable council of our brothers [Note: [Col. 0407] absent in witness 1; “assembly and council” in witness 3.], sent in the place of our lord. They opposed the archbishop’s undertaking forcefully, citing canonical authority and the ancient custom of the holy fathers. Thus the consecration of the aforesaid monastery was prevented.

During the solemn Mass, the bishop himself delivered a sermon to the people and announced that he would hold his synod two days before the feast of Saint Andrew [Col. 0408C], with the approval of the ban. Then, returning to the altar and sitting in his chair, he ordered certain previously unknown privileges to be read. These stated that no one should remove from the right of that church whatever it then possessed in tithes, estates, or anything else held in tenure.

He strengthened this also by a ban, and then departed.

The bishops who were present, complaining bitterly about the archbishop’s hostility [Note: [Col. 0407] “also” in witness 2.], sent word through us to their brother and fellow bishop that they were unable to restrain the archbishop’s obstinacy and rash undertaking. They said that the only recourse was for him to approach the apostolic lord and the emperor; that his cause was their common cause; and that they would not fail to write to both—the apostolic lord and the emperor—concerning the matter.

[Col. 0408D]

### 19.

The venerable Father, Lord Bernwardus, therefore took with the utmost concern the fact that even the slightest schism was spreading in the church. He knew that the injected poison could not be suppressed except by an apostolic and imperial antidote. Although he was often weakened by serious bodily illness and such a long journey was entirely contrary to his frail body, he nevertheless did not refuse to undertake it despite his weakness, in order to restore peace.

For some time he had been burning with an extraordinary desire to see the emperor, whom he loved uniquely [Col. 0409A]. Having prepared what was necessary for so great a journey, he arranged to travel through the valley of Tarentus [Note: [Col. 0409D] “Tridentus” in the note.], since that route seemed more convenient [Note: [Col. 0409] absent in witness 2.], carrying with him the letters of all the bishops on this side of the Alps [Note: [Col. 0409] witness 2 reads “the letters of almost all the brothers.”].

Then, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation one thousand [Note: [Col. 0409] the words “in the year of the Lord’s incarnation one thousand” are absent in witness 2.], on the fourth day before the Nones of November (November 2), he left the monastery amid the immense grief of the entire community and people. He was escorted by everyone with great contrition.

Accompanied by God’s grace and with events proceeding according to his wish, he entered Rome on the second day before the Nones of January (January 4, 1001).

When the most humble and devout emperor heard this, burning with extraordinary affection to see his beloved teacher, he nevertheless did not wish to weary him by making him come to his presence. Instead, he hurried nearly two miles from the palace to Saint Peter to meet him. He received him with the greatest kindness, kissed him most familiarly in an embrace, and led him to his lodging.

After conversing with him for a long time, he asked him to come to the palace the following day. He did not permit Bernwardus to spend even the smallest amount of his own property on his service. For the six weeks during which he stayed with him, the emperor ordered everything necessary for him and his attendants to be generously supplied in sufficient measure [Note: [Col. 0409] Witness 2 adds: “The pious host also supplied the natural foods to which he knew Bernwardus had been accustomed in his homeland; anticipating the arrival of his beloved guest, he also prepared mead and beer, and provided vessels, drinking cups, polished dishes, and candles for use during the meal [ [Col. 0410D] You can see that the customs of the eleventh century were not very different from our own.”].].

In the morning he summoned the apostolic lord to meet his beloved guest (January 5). When the apostolic lord came out into the courtyard to meet him, they received Bernwardus most willingly. He was not permitted to return to his own residence; instead, the emperor provided him with a splendid lodging [Note: [Col. 0409] “bedchamber” in witness 2.] beside the place where he himself was staying [Note: [Col. 0409] “stays” in witness 2.].

At times they sat in the emperor’s chamber, at times in the bishop’s, and discussed both legal matters and the necessities of public affairs. News concerning the archbishop and the disturbance that had arisen at Gandesheim had already spread everything before the bishop’s arrival. Therefore Bernwardus had no need to set out each matter in detail; when the emperor asked him, he gave a brief and concise account [Note: [Col. 0409] “gave an account” in witness 2.].

### 20.

But the archbishop carried out in action what he had conceived in his mind. Certain evil men had driven him to it, and Sophia had also pressed him.

Accordingly, two days before the feast of Saint Andrew, he came to Gandesheim for the synod (November 28, 1000), as he had arranged. He brought with him the venerable Bishop Retharius [Note: [Col. 0409] the same reading in witness 2.] and many other outsiders, namely men from Thuringia and Hesse, who had no interest in the matter, as well as some men from his own diocese within Saxony [Col. 0409D].

At the beginning of the proceedings, however, the venerable Bishop Eggehardus [Note: [Col. 0409] “Eggihardus” in witness 2, frequently.] warned the archbishop to withdraw from the synod and not presume to undertake such things in another church, especially since Lord Bishop Bernwardus, to whom the church belonged, was absent [Col. 0410A] and was staying with the apostolic lord and the emperor.

At this the archbishop was inflamed with unbelievable fury. With a grim and threatening expression, he ordered Eggehardus to be silent, saying that such matters did not concern him: “Let him have his own church and govern it!”

Eggehardus replied:

“Because sins have acted, the boundaries of my bishopric have been devastated by barbarous violence; the city is deserted and the church desolate. I have no see. I acknowledge myself a servant of Saint Mary and of the church of Hildesheim, and I shall strive in everything I can to benefit the holy place.”

The archbishop then brought forward the men he had summoned and asked the bishops whether he might compel those men by his ban to swear oaths, since the monastery belonged to his diocese.

Although they feared him, they replied that this could not lawfully be done [Col. 0410B] in the absence of Bishop Bernwardus. Bishop Eggehardus [Note: [Col. 0409] “Ekkihardus” in witness 2.], our brothers, and the people therefore earnestly begged that the oaths be suspended.

Moved by this unanimity of clergy and people, the archbishop threatened Bishop Eggehardus that, unless he kept silent, he would drive him out with insult. Many became indignant at this. Some of those whom the archbishop had brought also became agitated, and a disturbance was almost arising.

At the bishops’ request, Bishop Eggehardus withdrew and invited all the people of Gandesheim and everyone belonging to the diocese of Hildesheim to his synod. At his ban they all departed unanimously, leaving behind only the archbishop and his own men whom he had brought.

When they were questioned about the diocese in connection with the oaths, some asserted that the river Ethrina [Note: [Col. 0409D] “Eder” in the note.]—the river Frideslar—was the boundary of the parish of Hildesheim. They were misled by the name of the river Eder, which flows past Gandesheim [Col. 0410C]. Others affirmed that they knew nothing certain except what they had learned from the reports of others [Note: [Col. 0409] witness 2 reads approbabant, “they were affirming,” for approbant, “they affirm.”]. No one asserted anything worthy of remembrance.

The archbishop nevertheless acted as though everything had been firmly established by truth. He fortified the monastery with a ban, so that no one might remove it from him while it remained bound by oath. Then they departed in unconstrained error.

The people, however, obediently carried out whatever was ordered by the council of Hildesheim.

### 21. (1001)

Meanwhile, a messenger was sent to the bishop in Rome concerning these matters. He also carried letters to the apostolic lord and the emperor, written in a very tearful style.

As a result, both the apostolic lord and the emperor, together with all the Romans, were deeply moved: the authority of the canons and likewise the tradition of the fathers violated; the greatest contempt inflicted upon the Roman see and the apostolic lord, and also upon the emperor, by such presumption; a dangerous scandal able to arise in the church through this insolence [Col. 0411A] [Note: [Col. 0411] witnesses 3–5 read “i. scientes p.” (“knowing that … could”), abbreviated and materially uncertain.]; and such poison to be eradicated completely [Note: [Col. 0411] witnesses 3–5 read “they resolved.”].

22. During this period, the sole glory of the empire, Lord Henry, then its most powerful duke and soon, by God’s mercy, to be king, remained with the emperor. Into him the Lord had poured all the treasures of divine and human wisdom. He always bore heavily the controversy that had arisen over Gandersheim, and earnestly strove to bring peace to the church and to restore those serving under Christ’s standards to charity and grace.

At his urging, therefore, a synod of twenty bishops from Romania was assembled. Several also came from Italy and Tuscany; from our own region as well came Siegfried of Augsburg [Note: [Col. 0411] *sifridus* in 1; *sigifridus* in 2], Henry of Würzburg, and also the younger Hugh of Zeitz. Lord Gerbert the pope presided with the emperor in the palace [Note: [Col. 0411] “in the palace” is absent in 2] [Note: [Col. 0411D] Perhaps *Aspastico*, and therefore a hall for receiving, speaking, or conversation. Brower. Commonly called the *parlatorium*. Leibniz], in the church of Saint Sebastian the martyr; there was also present Lord Henry the duke, a man of singular merit [Note: [Col. 0411] “Henry” in 2], most peaceable, together with the abbots, the priests and deacons standing by, and the entire Roman order.

At the beginning of the proceedings, after the Gospels and certain chapters of the Fathers had been read and the blessing given, when they had taken their seats and silence had been established, the venerable Bishop Bernward advanced a little from his place and, in polished language, humbly set forth the case of his church before the pope, the emperor, Lord Henry the duke, and the entire synod.

When all had been moved by his complaint, the most wise pope asked the council whether it should be called a synod that the archbishop had assembled with those whom he had brought, in a church that had always been possessed by the bishops of Hildesheim [Note: [Col. 0411] “by the bishops of Hildesheim” is absent in 1], especially since the bishop had been absent and had fled to the Roman See for these very reasons; or by what name such a gathering ought to be called.

The holy council asked to withdraw, so that they might confer among themselves more privately about these matters. The most devout pope consented [Note: [Col. 0411] “the pope willingly consented” in 3–5]. The Roman bishops alone went out; afterward they re-entered, and, when they had again taken their seats, the most wise pope said:

“Brothers, what do you decree concerning the synod?”

The holy council replied:

“In another’s church, possessed by others, it had no right; nor could it canonically hold a synod there or establish anything without the consent of its proper bishop. Nor could it in any way be canonically called a synod.”

The most wise pope said:

“By what name, then, may it properly be called?”

The holy council replied:

“A schism fomenting dissensions.”

The most wise pope said:

“Are the things done there to be rejected?”

The holy council replied:

“By canonical authority and the authority of the holy Fathers, the things devised or decreed there must be abolished.”

The most wise pope said:

“By apostolic power and by the authority of the holy Fathers, we disperse, break, and annul the things devised and established by oaths at Gandersheim, in his own diocese, by Archbishop Willigis and his accomplices, while our brother and fellow bishop Bernward was absent.”

He added:

“Our brother and fellow bishop Bernward asks that the vestment taken from him by the archbishop be restored to him. What do you decree, brothers?”

The holy council replied:

“The vestment that the archbishop could not take away need not be returned to him. But since he himself insists on requesting this, if it pleases the lord emperor, let it be restored and confirmed to him by the staff of your apostolate.”

The most wise pope said:

“Let it be done according to your pleasure.”

And he handed him the apostolic staff, saying:

“I restore and confirm to your jurisdiction the monastery of Gandersheim, together with its adjoining villages and boundaries; and by the apostolic authority of Saints Peter and Paul I forbid anyone to resist you, except insofar as the canons permit.”

When these matters had been concluded, the lord pope asked the council what ought to be done. It was answered that, if it suited both rulers, the archbishop should be accused in writing, because a man of the highest dignity had attempted so bold an undertaking, contrary to the canons and the rules of the Fathers. At the same time, he should be warned to desist from such a controversy in the future and not to interfere in anything unless he proceeded canonically. A synod should also be announced to the bishops throughout Saxony, and a representative should likewise be sent by the lord pope to preside over it.

This was agreed. Palithi was designated as the place where the synod should be held, and the eleventh day before the Kalends of July was announced. Fritheric, cardinal priest of the holy Roman Church, later archbishop of Ravenna, Saxon by birth, young in years but advanced in moral integrity, was chosen and sent as the representative of the lord pope, wearing the apostolic vestments and insignia no less fully than if the pope himself were proceeding [Note: [Col. 0411] “the apostolic pope were proceeding” in 2].

[Note: [Col. 0411] From this point through “They assembled,” at chapter 28, no lacuna is indicated; the material is absent in 2.]

23. In those days the lord emperor surrounded the city of Tibur [Note: [Col. 0412D] Tivoli] with a close siege. After engines and many instruments for storming the fortress had been prepared, and ditches of extraordinary size had also been dug in order to divert the water from its channel, he inflicted great pressure upon the citizens but could not force them to surrender. The emperor was therefore summoned.

Without delay he arrived with the pope and the venerable Bishop Bernward. As is usual in such circumstances, some advised that the siege be intensified, while others said that, after such prolonged and burdensome labor, little had been achieved and that it seemed best to lift the siege, provided this could be done honorably. The emperor led Bishop Bernward aside and asked his advice, saying that he was very reluctant to desist from an undertaking begun with such injury to himself.

Bernward replied:

“I will not allow you, my soul, whom I love more dearly than life, to be troubled over this. But now order the city to be surrounded by a tighter siege; for although I long to return to my homeland, I will not depart from your majesty before, by God’s mercy, I see the city and its people subjected to your authority.”

At this the emperor rejoiced and gave thanks to his beloved master. He strengthened the position with a tighter siege, equipped the soldiers for the assault, and by imperial authority forbade everyone to enter or leave.

After several days had passed, Lord Bernward and the pope approached the city. The joyful citizens came out to meet them, received the servants of God honorably, and admitted them into the city. They did not desist until, with God’s help, they had all been reconciled and subjected to the emperor’s dominion [Note: [Col. 0413D] “the pope and Bernward”].

On the following day, after a noble triumph, the bishops approached the emperor. All the leading citizens of the aforesaid city were present, naked except for coverings around their thighs, holding swords in their right hands and brooms in their left as they advanced toward the palace. They declared that they and all they possessed were subjected to imperial jurisdiction, that they would negotiate nothing—not even life itself—and that the emperor should strike with the sword those whom he judged worthy, or, in mercy, order them to be publicly punished with brooms. If it pleased his will that the city walls be leveled to the ground, they were ready and willing to carry out everything, and, as long as they lived, would never oppose any command of his majesty.

The emperor magnificently praised the peacemakers, the pope and Lord Bishop Bernward, with abundant thanks; at their request he granted the guilty pardon. After deliberation, they jointly decided that the city should not be destroyed. The citizens were granted the emperor’s favor and were admonished to conduct themselves peacefully and not to defect from the emperor.

24. Finally, the Romans, indignant that the people of Tibur had made peace with the emperor, secured the gates of their own city with bolts and blocked the roads. Free entry into and departure from Rome were denied, and the buying and selling of merchandise were prohibited. Some of the king’s friends were also unjustly killed.

The palace officials, however, instructed by the salutary admonitions of Bishop Bernward, cleansed by confession as well, and fortified with the sacred Viaticum during the solemnities of Mass, prepared to go out in the opposite direction and attack the enemy courageously.

Bishop Bernward took up the Lord’s spear [Note: [Col. 0413D] See vol. III, p. 322; Liudprand, *Antapodosis* IV.24]. He signed himself and all the others with the protection of the life-giving cross; after giving a public blessing and consoling and strengthening them with life-giving admonitions, he himself, carrying the holy spear as standard-bearer at the very front of the battle line, prepared to go out.

On the following morning, after the solemnities of Mass, the emperor and his men, consoled by the venerable Bishop Bernward with the heavenly sacraments and divine exhortations, prepared for battle against the enemy. The bishop himself, carrying the holy spear, thundered terribly at the front, while with earnestness of heart he humbly implored peace from the author of peace [Note: [Col. 0413D] Compare Richer I.9].

Thus it came to pass that, in answer to the prayers of his devoted soldier, the presence of Christ the peaceful king soon appeared. At his birth, the joys of peace were first announced; afterward, by the evangelical truth, those who love that same peace are designated as sons of God.

By his mercy, therefore, the rebellion of the entire dispute was brought to rest. The enemy asked for peace, threw down their arms, and promised to come to the palace on the following day. In the morning, by God’s clemency, they appeared, asked for peace, renewed their oaths, and promised that they would keep faith with the emperor forever.

25. Meanwhile the most devout and gentle emperor climbed a certain tower with a few companions and addressed them, saying:

“Listen to the words of your father, pay attention to them, and carefully store them in your minds. Are you my Romans? For your sake I left my homeland and also my relatives. Out of love for you I cast away my Saxons and all the Germans, my own blood; I brought you into the distant regions of our empire, where your fathers had never set foot, although they held the world under their dominion—namely, so that I might extend your name and glory to the ends of the world [Note: [Col. 0414D] That is, of the earth]. I adopted you as sons; I preferred you to all others. Because of you, when I placed you before everyone else, I stirred up the envy and hatred of all against me.

“And now, in return for all this, you have cast aside your father, killed my companions by a cruel death, and excluded me, although you cannot exclude me; for those whom I embrace with a father’s affection I never allow to be exiled from my love. I know perfectly well who the leaders of the sedition are, and I point them out with the movement of my eyes; yet they are not ashamed, even though they are publicly marked in everyone’s sight. I consider it monstrous that my most faithful men also—men whose innocence I celebrate—should be stained by association with criminals and that they should not be distinguishable from them.”

Moved by this speech of the emperor even to tears, they promised satisfaction. They seized two men, Benilo and another, beat them cruelly, dragged them barefoot up the steps, and threw them half alive before the emperor in the aforesaid tower.

26. When this sedition had been quelled, the venerable Father Bernward went to Saint Paul’s for the sake of prayer. He opened the sarcophagus of Saint Timothy, concerning which the *Life of Saint Sylvester* gives an account; in the presence of the custodian whom the emperor himself had placed there, he removed the entire arm of the holy martyr. His priest [Note: [Col. 0414D] Thangmar himself; compare chapter 34] also carried a substantial portion of those relics to the camp.

27. The pope and the emperor then departed on the Sunday *Exurge quare* (February 16), and, amid the citizens’ immense tears, pitched their camp not far from the City.

Lord Bishop Bernward, who had already received permission to return to his homeland before they left the City, sent all his men ahead and accompanied the emperor in only a simple garment for two days’ journeys. On the Thursday of that same week (February 20), he was released from the emperor’s service. It cannot be expressed how great the sorrow was, or how many tears were shed by both men, so that they were afraid to appear in public.

The most devout emperor entrusted to his faithful master, as the secret confidant of his mind, to be weighed on the scales of wisdom, those matters that he had hesitated to communicate either in writing or through a messenger. He also sent to Goslar, for Bernward to deposit there in a celebrated place through his own efforts, the relics—namely, the entire body of Saint Exuperantius, martyr and deacon of Saint Sabinus the bishop [Note: [Col. 0415D] Goslar was already famous at that time because its mines had been discovered during the reign of Otto I, and it had been assigned to the diocese of Hildesheim].

The bishop, in sweet speech and with the guidance of a master, recalled everything that ought to be done, just as he had once played with the boy; he urged him to flee vices, to weigh everyone’s conduct in the balance of equity, to cultivate patience as his most familiar and constant companion in all things, and above all not to undertake anything with excessive obstinacy.

After these matters had been completed, the emperor led his devoted master to his lodging and rewarded him with carefully chosen gifts. Then, having summoned the pope and received his blessing, they dismissed their dearest master in the grace of God and in peace, weeping amid embraces. The emperor also sent companions from his own household with him, so that they might escort him, then return to the emperor and report his safety and the success of his journey.

As everything proceeded according to his wishes by God’s mercy, Bernward reached Pavia, where the bishops and counts of all Liguria were awaiting his arrival. He delivered the emperor’s message to them and, taking his seat in their assembly, discussed many matters concerning the welfare of the state. Everyone obeyed his counsel, for they knew how greatly he was loved by the emperor.

Leo, bishop of Vercelli, a man learned in letters and practiced in eloquence, invited him to his city with the greatest honor and affection; he scarcely succeeded in obtaining his consent. Then, going ahead and gathering a very large company of clergy and people, with all singing praises to God and the bells ringing, he received him with no less ceremony than if the pope had arrived. Everything required for his service was supplied with the utmost abundance and splendor, and he honored him with exceptional gifts. He also sent companions with him who provided his lodging in full abundance on the following day.

From there Bernward proceeded through various places and cities, enjoying the kindness of many people in many locations. He passed beyond the fortified gates, crossed the Alps by God’s mercy [Note: [Col. 0416D] Mount Jovis], passed Octodurum [Note: [Col. 0416D] Martinach], and went to Agaunum [Note: [Col. 0416D] Saint-Maurice]. There he was received with the greatest generosity by Rudolf, king of Burgundy. Rudolf granted the bishop three estates below Pavia as a possession, together with a written document, and confirmed it with his subscription and the impression of his ring.

Strengthened by God’s grace, Bernward then turned away and, traveling prosperously by God’s mercy, entered Hildesheim amid the greatest rejoicing of clergy and people on the holy feast of the heroic Supper [Note: [Col. 0416A] April 10]. He deposited the relics of the saints that he had brought with him in the church with great honor and spent an immense amount of money on the service of the altar and for the needs of the poor.

Throughout the entire summer he devoted himself to constructing the walls of the city, whose building Hildesheim had begun. At times he also suffered from a severe stomach disorder.

28. Meanwhile there arrived Cardinal Priest Fritheric, sent by the pope and the emperor in the pope’s place, wearing all the apostolic insignia as though the pope himself were proceeding, and riding horses furnished with a Roman-style purple apostolic saddle.

Letters were also sent by the pope and the emperor to the bishops and the other princes, instructing them to receive the Roman legate with due honor and all to obey his legation without hesitation, as though the pope were visibly present [Note: [Col. 0415] “Here the account continues in 2”].

They therefore assembled at Palithi for the synod on the tenth day before the Kalends of July (June 22), according to the decree previously issued by the pope [Note: [Col. 0415] “The archbishop and those who supported him received the appointed legate with varied feeling” in 2]. They received the legate with differing attitudes: the archbishop and those who supported him despised him with extraordinary indignation and execration. Bishop Bernward, however, and Lievezo, archbishop of Hamburg [Note: [Col. 0415] *lieuizo hammab.* in 2], together with many others, treated him reverently and honored him with exceptional respect.

But once they came to the council, it can scarcely be said how great a disturbance and uproar arose. No suitable place for the apostolic representative to sit was granted; dreadful noise was repeatedly raised; justice and right [Note: [Col. 0415] “and right” in 2] were despised; and canonical discipline was abolished.

The representative sat between the bishops Lievezo [Note: [Col. 0415] *liaurzonem* in 2, frequently] and Bernward. He stated that he had writings and a legation from the pope for the bishops and asked that authority to carry out what he had brought be shown to him.

When silence had finally been obtained [Note: [Col. 0415] “therefore” in 2], he first admonished the bishops in gentle speech concerning peace, charity, and concord. Then he produced the pope’s letter addressed specifically to the archbishop and asked that it be read aloud publicly in the hearing of all. When the archbishop scorned even to touch or look at it [Note: [Col. 0415] “considered it unworthy” in 2], it was read publicly by order of the bishops. In it the bishop himself was openly reproved [Note: [Col. 0415] “criticized” in 2] and admonished concerning fraternal concord and obedience.

Although the representative took great care not to provoke the archbishop, he nevertheless urged him in mild speech to answer obediently, on the advice of the brothers, whatever charges were brought against him, by apostolic authority.

Though indignant at this, the archbishop sought the advice of the brothers, and especially of Archbishop Lievezo. The latter replied that it seemed good to him that, since the injured brother of our lords, the pope and the emperor, had sought their support, he should satisfy them before their representative, according to the judgment of the bishops.

Meanwhile the church doors were thrown open and laymen were admitted. A great uproar and tumult arose. The people of Mainz, exulting [Note: [Col. 0417] “stirring up” in 2], demanded arms [Note: [Col. 0417] “asked for” in 2] and hurled immense threats [Note: [Col. 0417] “they uttered threats, although a large army was present with the representative and Lord Bernward; nevertheless they were not moved by the tumult” in 2] against the apostolic representative and Bishop Bernward.

The legate and Bishop Bernward, neither moved by the uproar nor frightened by the threats, although they had larger forces of soldiers, did not brandish weapons but restrained the sedition. The bishops suggested postponing the matter until the following day, undertook responsibility for it, and promised that the archbishop would come and obediently carry out justice.

29. Meanwhile the archbishop, inflamed with immense fury, went out. The apostolic representative followed him beneath the circle of the brothers and, under penalty imposed by apostolic authority, invited him to the synod in the same church at dawn the following day. Thus that proceeding was dissolved [Note: [Col. 0417] “left unfinished,” corrected to “dissolved” in 2].

At daybreak, however, the archbishop secretly departed with his men, while everyone was unaware. The representative began the second session of the synod on the following day (June 23). At the beginning of the proceedings he sought the archbishop; because he was absent, he suspended him from all episcopal ministry until the pope’s presence.

By apostolic authority he announced to all the bishops that a synod would be held at the pope’s presence on the feast of the Nativity of the Lord. He also sent the archbishop a letter in these terms:

“Because you withdrew from the synod and were disobedient to the commands of the Roman pontiff, know that, by the authority of the holy apostles Peter and Paul and of their representative, Pope Sylvester [Note: [Col. 0417] In the margin: “who is Gerbert” in 2], you are suspended from every priestly office until his presence.”

Thus the second session was concluded [Note: [Col. 0417] “Thus also the second session was concluded” in 2].

30. The representative stayed for some time with Lord Bishop Bernward. He himself and all his companions were rewarded with distinguished gifts and were then dismissed in peace. When he reached the pope and the emperor, he explained the course of his legation.

They were deeply indignant [Note: [Col. 0417] “disturbed” in 2] and ordered all the German bishops to hasten to their presence around the Nativity of the Lord, not merely for a synod but equipped with all their vassals [Note: [Col. 0417D] “A company of vassals”], so that they could proceed to war wherever the emperor commanded.

The aforementioned Fritheric shortly afterward obtained the episcopal chair of Ravenna.

31. Moreover, Bishop Bernward, hoping by God’s grace and through the mercy of both rulers to live in complete peace, planned to visit the abbey of the church of Hilwardshausen, which had been handed over to him by the emperor, consecrated by him with a solemn dedication, devoted to divine service, and enriched by him with many benefits and gifts [Note: [Col. 0417] “The abbey of the church of Hilwardshausen, cultivated and exercised by his predecessors in divine service, and likewise handed over to him by the emperor, where …” in 2]. His maternal aunt was also in charge there [Note: [Col. 0417] In the margin: “Hemma the most holy, through whom the Lord performs many miracles”]. He intended to visit it on the principal feast of its patron saints [Note: [Col. 0417] “their” in 2], and all the equipment necessary for so great a solemnity had been sent ahead as people gathered for it.

When everything was already prepared and Bernward himself was soon to arrive, the archbishop’s men came during the night, invaded and destroyed everything, and left several of the bishop’s household cruelly beaten.

32. After this injury had been endured, the venerable prelate planned to visit the monastery of Gandersheim and correct whatever needed correction, so that it might not be neglected through any fault of his.

An immense multitude opposed him, equipped with weapons no less fully than if they were being summoned to public war. Sophia stirred them up: namely, everyone whom she could summon either from the archbishop’s vassalage or from his household, all her associates and retainers, and a strong force from her own household. They filled the towers and stronger places around the church with armed soldiers and fortified the castle against one unarmed man—namely, their own bishop, who was bringing them his blessing—as though they were preparing to defend themselves in barbarian battle array [Note: [Col. 0417] “They prepare. Nevertheless, they send some men who report that access could not be attempted without great danger and that it would be wiser to withdraw. If he decided to act otherwise, he would plainly cause the greatest harm. After hearing this, the prelate …” in 2].

Thus it seemed that the Apostle’s words had truly been fulfilled in him:

“All who desire to live piously in Christ will suffer persecution” (2 Timothy 3:12).

After hearing this, the prelate asked his men what he should do. They all decided that they must yield to the danger. Men were also sent to investigate the truth carefully; they reported that everything rumor had spread [Note: [Col. 0417] “everything that rumor had spread” in 2] was true, and even worse than this.

33. When these events had taken place in this manner, the bishops, seeing such a controversy raging in the church [Note: [Col. 0417] “c. s. t. v. t. i. et i. i. n. d.” is absent in 2], and grieving exceedingly over the unheard-of and intolerable injuries inflicted upon so great a man, sought an assembly at Franconofurd after the Assumption of Saint Mary [Note: [Col. 0417] *francanafordi* in 2]. The archbishops of Cologne and Trier were also invited.

The day of the council arrived. The archbishops presided: Willigis of Mainz, Heribert of Cologne, and Liudolf of Trier, together with the other servants of God—Rethar of Paderborn, Rodbert of Speyer, Beringer of Werden [Note: [Col. 0417] *berngero* in 2], and Eggehard of Schleswig [Note: [Col. 0417] *sliesuvicensi* in 2].

But because Eggehard himself was lodging at Hildesheim—his city and church having been devastated by barbarous tumult—and Lord Bishop Bernward was prevented by bodily illness [Note: [Col. 0417] “the bishop” in 2], Bernward sent Eggehard as his representative, adding as his companion Thangmar [Note: [Col. 0419] “notary” in 3], a priest and dean of the monastery, who was to be present as an assistant [Note: [Col. 0419] “T.” in 2] in case anything adverse arose from the archbishop’s side.

At the beginning of the first session [Note: [Col. 0419] “of the initial session” in 1], the archbishop, in a milder account, complained to the brothers about the absence of Lord Bernward and declared that, if he had been present, he would have done him justice by fraternal judgment.

In reply, it was explained that Bernward was absent not through rashness or disobedience but because he was hindered by severe bodily illness. Whatever the sacred assembly, enlightened by the divine Spirit [Note: [Col. 0419] “by its position” in 1; “by the Spirit” in 2], might deliberate, decree, or command, he would obediently carry out and observe [Note: [Col. 0419] “and observe. For the more bitter matters that had been enacted on both sides were publicly explained by the brothers sitting together before the procession; they ordered them to be kept silent in the synod, lest they generate a dispute. Thus …” in 2].

Thus, after a mutual blessing had been given, that session ended on the same day.

On the following day the archbishop, uncertain who was urging him on [Note: [Col. 0419] “urged on by someone, he became somewhat more hostile” in 2], advanced to the session more aggressively. Some others, including certain bishops [Note: [Col. 0419] “some, out of fear and favor” in 2], influenced by his favor, advised that Bishop Bernward be publicly summoned before the synod [Note: [Col. 0419] “They also admonished those sent by him, especially the priest, to excuse the bishop by oath. He, presuming nothing of himself, although he had very often attended synodal councils, asked the other clergy of the archbishops and of the other bishops who supported him, men highly skilled in divine matters, to consider the case. He said that he would never undertake the oath demanded of him except by the authority of the canons; finally, he humbly begged and implored the assembly, which they had stirred up against the apostolic synod without any authority, to admonish the lord bishops to restrain the archbishop from obstinacy and hostility. After this, by God’s mercy, the archbishop became more gentle” in 2].

Thangmar the priest, however, admonished the bishops to restrain the archbishop from his stubborn hostility. At last, by God’s mercy, the archbishop became more gentle. Nevertheless, while everyone insisted that Bishop Bernward should possess the vestment of the monastery of Gandersheim, the bishop in no way consented. Instead, he proposed that neither of them should interfere until they came to Fridislare [Note: [Col. 0419] *fridislari* in 2] at the palace on the octave of Pentecost [Note: [Col. 0419] “so that neither of them … should interfere” in 1].

Thus, by God’s grace, the council was dissolved.

34. For his part, Bishop Bernward was burning with a twofold desire to go to Italy: to fulfill the command of the pope and to see his dearest lord [Col. 0419C] the king [Note: [Col. 0419] “the king” is absent in 2], whom he esteemed as more precious than life [Note: [Col. 0419] “whom he esteemed. But, suffering from frequent fever, he was afraid to undertake so long a journey. He sent …” in 2].

He therefore sent Thangmar the priest in his place [Note: [Col. 0419] *Thongmarum* in 2, frequently]. Thangmar had been his companion on the previous year’s journey to the emperor and had devoted himself from earliest youth to old age to scholarly study, applying himself to the education of boys.

Sent to the presence of the pope and the emperor with letters and official mandates, he benefited on the way from the goodwill of many people through the favor of his lord. He found the emperor in the region of Spoleto. The emperor, receiving him most graciously out of respect for the bishop, was awaiting the pope’s arrival.

When they met, Thangmar delivered the legation and the letters, while the emperor graciously pleaded the bishop’s case before the pope. He was then ordered to await the synod that was to be held at the city of Todi [Note: [Col. 0419C] Todi] on the Nativity of the Lord, and he was lavishly supported in every good thing by both rulers [Note: [Col. 0419] “Supported. The Romans, however, resisting imperial commands, were harassed by frequent incursions. The emperor’s forces, besieging the very strongly fortified castle of Paternum, continually afflicted them with assaults, plundering, and the frequent slaughter of many. For Tammo, count and brother of Bishop Bernward, dear to the emperor, together with some vassals whom the aforementioned bishop had sent to the imperial army, held the garrison; military operations were conducted at their direction. Likewise the pope celebrated the unique Nativity of Christ at Todi. In 2; compare chapter 35.”]

35. At the same time, while certain people resisted imperial commands, Tammo, Bernward’s brother, a count dear to the emperor and indeed distinguished by every moral excellence, at the king’s command besieged Paternum, a very strongly fortified castle [Note: [Col. 0419] “I. of Sommerschenburg, paternal [castle], in the erased passage: a correction by an incompetent scribe who, not knowing of Paternum in Italy, thought that the text referred here to Tammo’s paternal castle, which he believed had been Sommerschenburg”] [Note: [Col. 0420C] *Paterno*]. By his skill and diligence, the commonwealth was well safeguarded in those regions.

### 36

> **Source-grounded apparatus:** Retain the source columns **[Col. 0419]–[Col. 0430]** as anchors for this translated run. In chapters 36, 39, 40, 43, and 48, every reading or omission of witnesses 1 and 2 is source content: a witness’s omission is “absent,” and a variant form is kept with its English force rather than reduced to a generic manuscript claim. Paired forms include *missarum / namque* (“of Masses / indeed”), *Urbis / orbis* (“of the City / of the world”), *post / ante* (“after / before”), *aggregati / congregati* (“gathered / assembled”), and *misteria / ministeria* (“mysteries / ministries”). In the Aribo passage the source variants are retained as the particular witness readings attached to that passage, not transferred to a neighboring sentence. In chapter 39 the surviving manuscript-2 notation is **a. g. r. e. m. s. jam erasa**; it is an erased abbreviation and remains unexpanded/uncertain.

> **Editorial corrections:** The abbess is of **Hildeward** (not Hildesheim) in the source wording. The Bernward reference is to *Legum*, vol. II B, pp. 172–173, and concerns the 1020 constitution on four annual diocesan synods.

In the year 1002 of the singular birth of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the fifteenth indiction, the apostolic lord celebrated the Lord’s Nativity with the emperor at Todi. There, on the feast of Saint John the Evangelist (December 27), a council was assembled of bishops from throughout Romania and of some from Tuscany and Italy. From our regions also sat Notger of Liège, Siegfried of Augsburg, and Hugh of Chichester.

During the solemn celebration of Mass, therefore, when about thirty fathers were seated and the lords, the rulers of the City—the pope and the emperor—presided, after the Gospel had been read and certain chapters from the decrees of the holy Fathers had been recited, the venerable Bishop Bernward’s legate was presented to the synod through the official bearing the offerings.

The apostolic lord said to him:

“Tell us why you have come into our presence, and what you have to bring before the synod.”

At once the legate, the priest Thangmar, prostrated himself full-length upon the ground; then, lifted up by the hands of those assisting him, he fell at the feet of both rulers. Rising, he began as follows:

“My lord has offered magnificent thanks for the authority of your apostolate and also for the imperial majesty, on account of all the things in which you have mercifully labored for his church. What your legate has accomplished, however, and what has happened to him during his legation, he himself, since he is present, will explain better.

“After that bishop’s departure, because they were grieved that the dispute and controversy continued to rage for so long, they arranged a meeting at Frankfurt. Since my lord could not come there, hindered by severe bodily illness, he sent me in his place.

“At last the reverend fathers jointly decreed that neither the archbishop nor my lord should interfere in the convent of Gandersheim until after the octave of Pentecost, and that they should then meet at Fritzlar in synod for this very cause. Since this matter, after being brought before the seat of your apostolate, has often been annulled by your letters, it seeks your judgment: let your authority order in what court, or before which judges, the case ought to be settled.

“Nevertheless, my lord sent my lowliness into the presence of this most holy assembly, gathered here through you by the grace of the Holy Spirit, so that the whole senate of the apostolic Church might publicly know that he obeys and agrees with the apostolic lord and the Roman See with the most devoted affection, and that he asks for and will strive with all his ability always to preserve whatever your judgment discovers or decrees.”

At this the apostolic lord greatly praised the obedience, devotion, and zeal of Bishop Bernward. The venerable metropolitan of the Church of Ravenna, Frederick, also spoke, recounting what had occurred to him at Palithi and throughout his legation: the archbishop’s disobedience, injury, and contempt even for the Roman See. Conversely, he described Lord Bernward’s kindness and charity, and reported that Bernward had been treated with particular honor and richly supplied with every good thing.

At this, the archbishop’s arrogance was openly condemned by all the Roman bishops, and the rashness of his presumption was censured. Nevertheless, they all jointly decided to await the archbishop of Cologne and the other bishops who were expected shortly. Messengers were also sent to order them to come into the presence of both rulers on the Epiphany of the Lord.

But when they did not come at all, they were awaited through three adjournments.

[Note: One manuscript adds that they were scattered throughout every region, sitting in counties and marches wherever they could find the necessities of life.]

When it proved entirely impossible for them to assemble, the priest Thangmar pressed with every effort to be released.

[Note: The manuscript continues: “For they were suffering miserably from an immense shortage of every kind of provision. Already the miserable day was near—namely, the death of our most gentle emperor—although he was still in vigorous health and no one perceived in him any sign of illness. On the third day before the Ides of January, he dismissed from him the legate of his dear master, Bishop Bernward, namely the aforementioned priest T., richly rewarded. To the bishop he sent distinguished gifts, among them an onyx vessel of very great value, various medicinal substances, and perfumes. When the priest questioned him about this, he confessed that he was suffering from a slight fever. But as the illness grew worse each day, while bishops attended him and he was fortified with the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, the most gentle and humble emperor, amid the words of a pure confession, breathed out his spirit in the evening twilight on the tenth day before the Kalends of February, to the immense grief of all. After his departure, when Lord Henry by God’s grace had obtained the royal scepter, the agitation of the aforementioned dispute was no less intense. For while the king was celebrating the feast of Saint Lawrence at Paderborn, Lady Cunigunda …” (See below, chapter 39.)]

Thus, on the third day before the Ides of January (January 13, 1002), the emperor dismissed from him the legate of his dear master, Bishop Bernward, namely the aforementioned priest, richly rewarded. He sent distinguished gifts to the bishop, among them an onyx vessel of great value, various medicinal substances, and also various perfumes.

### 37

The grievous day was now close at hand—namely, the death of the most gentle emperor. When the priest questioned him, he confessed that he was suffering from a slight fever. As the illness therefore grew worse each day, while bishops stood around him and he was fortified with the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, amid the words of a pure confession, on the tenth day before the Kalends of February (January 23), the most gentle and humble emperor breathed out his spirit, to the immense grief of all good people.

[Note: The Annals of Hildesheim and Einsiedeln likewise have “the tenth day before the Kalends of February.” The Annals of Quedlinburg, Thietmar, and the Fulda Necrology have “the ninth day before the Kalends of February.”]

Who could express in writing or describe in speech the irreparable grief of those who flocked from everywhere to the funeral rites? The funeral procession of the Germans, after preparing everything necessary for the journey, carried the body of the most pious lord to Aachen. It was received on the holy and festive day of Palm Sunday (March 29) with the ceremonial service of the whole kingdom; all the rulers served at the funeral with extraordinary devotion, and he was buried in the middle of the choir.

### 38

Meanwhile the wishes of the rulers were being dragged in different directions, since many strove to seize the height of royal power without regard for the fear of God. A certain nobleman named Bruno, knowing that the venerable Bishop Bernward was utterly loyal to the most reverend Duke Henry, feared that Bernward would oppose any undertaking of his. He therefore did everything in his power to arm against him anyone whom he could incite to Bernward’s destruction or to the injury of the Church of Hildesheim. From this point he raged everywhere through the bishop’s lands and against his people with plunder and robbery.

Bernward, however, in accordance with his custom, never departed from fidelity, although he was often harassed by many injuries. Like the wisest architect, the prudent bishop began the foundations of the new kingdom with the first beginnings of prayer. He urged all the communities of brothers and sisters who served beneath his banners under the divine scepters to keep watch through earnest supplication in such a great necessity of affairs.

He himself also—which he concealed from everyone—sought the mercy of the Lord through strict abstinence. Thus, by God’s marvelous pity, there came about a union in favor of the chosen one, so that the wishes of the common people anticipated the efforts of the nobles. For wherever public assemblies were summoned, the voice of the common people was one: Lord Henry ought to rule; he, and no one else, ought to preside over affairs.

When all therefore agreed with one voice in his election, Archbishop Willigis and Bishop Bernward, together with the other rulers of the kingdom, led Lord Henry to Mainz with the highest honor. On the octave of Pentecost (May 31), they handed over to him the government and royal power, together with the lordly spear.

[Note: The word “spear” is absent in manuscript 1.]

Then, after everything had duly been completed, they solemnly anointed him by God’s grace amid the greatest rejoicing of all.

### 39

The new king celebrated the feast of Saint Lawrence at Paderborn (August 10), and there Lady Cunigunda received the royal crown and blessing from the venerable Archbishop Willigis.

Sophia, having been elected to govern Gandersheim, as was her custom, had repudiated her own bishop, as though at her sacred veiling. Thus, now also, disdaining to receive governance and consecration from her own pastor and father in administration, she sought, through the king and queen and the rulers, to be blessed by a bearer of the pallium, moved by the swelling pride and vanity of her heart. Lord Bernward, unable to resist, consented.

[Note: One manuscript has a series of words, now erased, concerning the governance of Gandersheim and the request to be blessed by the metropolitan. Another reads “governance” where the principal text has “father of administration.”]

### 40

In the year 1003 of the Lord’s incarnation, the king traveled around the bishoprics and abbeys—holy places where servants and handmaids of God kept watch more religiously in divine service—in order that his kingdom, divinely bestowed upon him, might be protected by their prayers. He greatly desired to visit Hildesheim.

But because no king before him had dared to undertake this out of reverence for the place, he consulted Bishop Bernward, asking by what means he might venture to visit the holy place. Having received permission from him, he visited the aforesaid church before Palm Sunday, which that year fell on March 21.

[Note: The heading is absent from manuscript 2.]

[Note: Palm Sunday fell that year on March 21.]

He was received with solemn honor. He himself also gave a substantial sum for the service of the altar and the brothers, promised to enrich and honor the place, and most graciously fulfilled a large part of this promise.

### 41

In the third year after this, in the year 1006, when the western Gauls were troubling the state, the same Emperor Henry launched an expedition against them. The venerable Bishop Bernward followed his army with a vast company of soldiers, faithfully rendering to God what belonged to God and to Caesar what belonged to Caesar, according to the Lord’s command, and serving with the most vigilant devotion in order to win his favor.

When the expedition was over, Bernward traveled to Saint Martin.

[Note: At Tours.]

He had previously determined this by a vow, though not without royal permission and the fraternal generosity of the bishops. He carefully concealed his planned journey from all his people, fearing that he would be unable to endure their tears. After commending them to the king, he set out with only a small retinue. He stayed for several days at Saint-Denis near Paris, visiting holy places, and offered his whole self to the Lord with great contrition of heart.

From there, traveling toward Tours, he enjoyed the great attentiveness of King Robert along the way. He remained there for a week and, before his pious patron, mourned daily with abundant tears the sins committed by himself and his people.

Finally, honored by the king and bishops with the most precious relics of Saint Martin’s sacred body—for it was considered a very great thing if anyone could receive even a small fragment of the saintly confessor’s vestment or other liturgical garments—he was rewarded with a heavenly treasure. He also received relics of many other saints, and, with the blessing and grace of all, departed from there.

Reaching Paris, he devoted several days to his customary exercise of prayer. He also received from the aforesaid ruler and bishops the most precious and holy relics of the martyr Dionysius and his companions. With their blessing and grace he departed from them and happily returned toward his homeland.

Although everyone’s wishes preferred that he make a swift return after the exceptionally difficult labor of so long a journey, the affection with which he always served rulers nevertheless prevailed, and he went to visit the most gracious king, who was staying at Aachen. The king received him with the greatest affection, for he had long been eager to see him.

For he was planning to establish a new episcopal see at Bamberg, a royal place that belonged to him by hereditary right from his ancestors. Therefore he assembled a synod of all the bishops at Frankfurt, so that the letters and decrees of the Roman pontiff concerning this matter might be approved by common judgment.

The royal majesty first, and then the episcopal dignity, urgently requested that the distinguished servant and bishop of God, Bernward, attend this deliberation. He did not refuse, but honored the lord king with the most willing obedience.

After returning to Hildesheim, he placed the relics of the saints that had been brought to him in a worthy place of preservation. He applied himself daily with even greater care to his customary holiness and guarded the anciently established boundaries of his bishopric with immense labor and vigilance.

[Note: Here manuscripts 3, 4, and 5 contain material based on the Hildesheim Annals under the year 1013, but the expressions “blessed” and “patron of the holy city of Hildesheim” show that these words were inserted in later centuries:

“In those days a grievous mourning arose, forever lamentable to all the sons of holy mother Church, as our sins demanded. On the twelfth day before the Kalends of February, the noble monastery of the Church of holy Hildesheim was almost destroyed by fire through the torches of diabolical deceit and the flames of our crimes. For on that same night, at the time of the first sleep, while all who lived within the city were overcome more by the burden of their sins than by the rest of ordinary sleep, that great grief came upon us wretched people.

“Yet through the intervention of the holy Mother of God, through the pious prayer of our saints,

[Note: Manuscript 4 reads, “through the prayer of Saint N.”]

and through the bitter lamentation of our lord, the venerable Bishop Bernward, that violent fire was extinguished by the pouring out of divine dew. The venerable church remained unharmed, preserved by God’s grace, except for what we must mourn forever: together with the most precious liturgical missal, an indescribable quantity of books perished and left us unarmed in the spiritual weapons of our faith.

“In that same year, the blessed Bernward, patron of the holy city of Hildesheim,

[Note: Manuscript 4 reads, “patron of the Church.”]

on the day following the feast of All Saints, restored and blessed the high altar of the holy Mother of God, which—alas!—because our sins had deserved it, had been shattered by the powerful inundation of fire, as has been said. With the most devoted intention of mind, on the fourth day before the Nones of November he restored it to a better condition and made it more acceptable to God and more praiseworthy among human beings through the splendor of gold, silver, and gems.”]

### 42

Meanwhile Lady Rothegard, abbess of the Church of Hildesheim and a woman worthy of remembrance, the maternal aunt of the venerable Bishop Bernward, chastened by a prolonged bodily illness, recognized that the day of her release—which she had always desired—was approaching, as is believed, through divine inspiration.

Therefore, on the most sacred night of the Lord’s Nativity (December 25), she ordered herself to be carried into the church for the Mass “The Lord said.” There she received the viaticum of the Lord’s body and blood. After everything had been duly completed, she was carried back to her bed. Having summoned the sisters, she began as follows:

“My dearest sisters, I announce to you that today I shall be invited from this life to wherever God commands. But since I know that this will occur during the solemn celebration of the principal Mass, I ask you not to be disturbed when you hear of my death, lest any interruption occur in divine service.

“For I trust that God’s help will be all the more generously present to me if no interruption occurs in his service because of me. Therefore, when the divine solemnities have been completed according to custom, hasten to come as quickly as possible to attend my departure. Take care to commend my soul more earnestly to its Creator through your prayers.

“Always keep your own end before your eyes, and, in that terrible judgment, while it is permitted, strive through good works to be found worthy before God.”

After saying this, she allowed them to depart, exceedingly astonished and amazed. The outcome of the event plainly showed that she had foreseen it through a prophetic spirit. For, just as she had foretold, during the principal Mass, when the sequence began, her holy soul was released from the prison of the flesh.

This makes it plainly understood that this blessed woman had received something more of divine grace than other mortals: not only was she granted so clearly to know in advance the release of her own flesh, but on that very day she also happily escaped the misery of the present life—the day on which the Redeemer of the human race is believed to have come forth ineffably from the inviolate womb of the Virgin in order to endure suffering for the salvation of the whole world.

### 43

In the year 1007 of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, the venerable King Henry, most powerful throughout the whole Roman Empire, celebrated the Lord’s Nativity at Palithi with the greatest glory.

Wherever the most wise emperor turned the face of his most sacred countenance, if he happened to find people at odds, he immediately reconciled them; or, if something prevented him from doing so, he never struck the matter from his mind until he restored the charity that had been violated.

He prudently and persistently tried to do this also then, during the very feast of the singular Nativity. For Archbishop Willigis had conceived an old hatred against Bishop Bernward of Hildesheim for trivial reasons and had nourished it unremittingly in his heart with the fierce goads of anger. The emperor often wished to soothe him, but, overcome by his hostility, he abandoned the attempt.

Nevertheless, in the presence of many bishops and other rulers who had gathered at the palace for that distinguished feast, he confronted him and so broke the obstinacy of his mind with a fitting rebuke, backed by such authority, that Willigis submitted himself and his entire controversy to the emperor’s judgment and to that of the brothers, and would oppose neither the emperor’s commands nor the wishes of the brothers in any matter.

Then the most wise king appointed the long-delayed dedication of the Church of Gandersheim for the vigil of the Epiphany of the Lord, which then coincided with the first day of the week, the day of the Lord’s Resurrection. He also appointed the veiling of the handmaids of God for the very day of the Epiphany.

The venerable Bishop Bernward therefore invited Archbishop Willigis and the other brothers to assist him in consecrating the aforesaid church (January 5, 1007). There was no delay: the sacred solemnity took place. The rites of consecration were arranged at the command of Lord Bishop Bernward. Everything was done in fraternal charity, so that the archbishop held the first place in the sprinkling, with Bishop Bernward beside him.

Within the church, however, Bernward himself—since it was his parish—distributed the rites of consecration among the brothers; he held the first rank.

When, by God’s grace, everything had been completed in fraternal charity, the king went forth with the archbishop and the others before the people and spoke as follows:

“Dearest brothers, today we must lay aside and end the long-standing controversy that has arisen through our sins. For I recognize and know that this church and the neighboring villages have always belonged to the bishops of Hildesheim and have been possessed by them without contradiction.”

[Note: Manuscript 2 lacks the words extending to this point.]

At these words of the emperor, Archbishop Willigis, finally returning to himself through God’s mercy, publicly confessed whatever he had done against God and his holy Mother, whether through his own guilt or through the instigation of others—namely, his unjust invasion of the parish of Gandersheim, which belonged by title to the Church of Hildesheim. He renounced his claim and demand regarding that place, and, as testimony to this renunciation, handed his episcopal staff to Lord Bernward, saying:

“Dearest brother and fellow bishop, I renounce my right to this church. I hand over to you, under the testimony of Christ, our lord king, and our brothers, this pastoral staff which I carry in my hand, as a witness, so that after this neither I nor any successor of mine may bring any challenge or claim concerning this matter.”

[Note: In the margin of manuscript 2, by a second hand: “Note more fully concerning this very matter in the Life of Saint Gotthard.”]

Thus the office of Mass was solemnly completed by Archbishop Willigis, with the consent of Lord Bishop Bernward.

[Note: Manuscript 2 has the feminine form, “completed,” agreeing with the office.]

On the following day, the Epiphany of the Lord, the veiling of the virgins was solemnly performed by Lord Bernward in the presence of the king and all the bishops. Thus, by God’s grace, the affairs having been settled in peace and charity through the wisdom of the most pious ruler, they departed.

[Note: Manuscript 2 continues: “Having remained for some time in Thuringia, he proceeded into Bavaria and began Holy Easter at Regensburg (April 21). The rest of the chapter is absent.”]

After this dispute had been settled, the archbishop freely loved our bishop with every honor and affection. Having honorably acquired a place of brotherhood in our monastery, he showed the greatest love to both the place and the brothers.

### 44

With matters standing thus, the same archbishop, five years later, full of days and also of good works, migrated to Christ on the sixth day before the Kalends of March (February 24, 1011).

[Note: Manuscript 6 has the following expanded account:

“When these things had taken place, at that time, on the sixth day before the Kalends of March, the aforesaid Archbishop Willigis, struck by God’s judgment, yielded to human nature. At the very threshold of death he belatedly repented and confessed whatever he had done against God and the holy Mother of God through his own guilt or through the instigation of others hateful to God—namely, his unjust invasion of the parish of Gandersheim, belonging by title to the Church of Hildesheim.

“Having been worn down by so many synodal decrees, now in the presence of the Roman cardinals sent by the apostolic lord, and also having been opposed by the two emperors, Otto III and the benign Henry, while many archbishops, bishops, and dukes presided, he was overcome. Yet, unable to yield to truth and equity, he left the aforesaid parish to the right of Lord Bishop Bernward, still shameless concerning the injury he had begun but never completed.

“After him Erkenbald was appointed to the government of Mainz, previously abbot of the monastery of Fulda, lacking nothing of the Catholic faith. God advanced him to the archbishopric of Mainz through the anointing and consecration of Bernward, Bishop of the Church of Hildesheim. By divine providence …”]

### 45
