After him, Erkenbald was appointed to govern Mainz. He had previously been abbot of the monastery of Fulda, and nothing was lacking in him of the Catholic faith. Lord Bernward consecrated him at Mainz on the Kalends of April (April 1).

Thus, through divine providence, he rose to be archbishop, because in a time of anger he became a reconciliation. As long as he lived, he set aside the enticements of the former discord. Moreover, he honored his ordainer, who was also related to him by blood, with the devotion owed to a father and treated him with paternal affection.

[Note: Manuscript 2 reads “until” where the principal text has “as long as.” It also reads “his Bishop Bernward” rather than “his ordainer,” and omits the words describing their kinship.]

### 46

Meanwhile the venerable Bishop Bernward, striving to enlarge the service of divine worship in the parish of his episcopate, chose Christ as his heir in expectation of future recompense. He offered himself, together with all the things he had acquired or would acquire, as a sacrifice to the almighty Father, just as he had long before determined in the secrecy of his heart.

He therefore established a monastery on the northern side of the city of Hildesheim, in a place formerly desolate and suited even to wild and brute animals. With complete devotion and suitable preparation he founded it, endowed it with sufficient estates, and assigned it to monks gathered there to serve God.

[Note: Chapter 46 is absent from manuscript 2. Manuscript 2 instead begins here: “Meanwhile Lord Bishop Bernward, after a prolonged illness” (after chapter 48); its intermediate chapters 46, 47, and 49–53 are absent.]

### 47

In the year 1015 of the incarnate Word, the fourteenth year of the reign of Lord Henry, the most pious emperor, the twenty-third year of the ordination of Lord Bernward, the thirteenth indiction, on the third day before the Kalends of October (September 29), the crypt of the same monastery, completed by God’s grace with great splendor, was dedicated by the aforesaid Bishop Bernward, by the honorable Bishop Eggehard of Schleswig, and by the venerable shepherd Thideric of the Church of Minden.

It was dedicated in honor of our Lord Jesus Christ the Savior; of his most blessed and glorious Mother, Mary, perpetual Virgin; of Saint Michael the archangel; and of the entire heavenly army. Sixty-six relics were also reverently deposited there by those same venerable bishops.

[Note: The heading is absent from manuscript 2.]

### 48

Five years later, in 1020, Erkenbald, metropolitan of Mainz, full of days and merits, departed from the peace of the Church of God on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September and breathed out his soul into the hands of the angels.

[Note: Manuscript 2 continues after “breathed out his soul”: “A certain man, Aribo, commonly called Aervo, succeeded him in office and name; in accordance with his name and byname, he resolved to live by toil and tyranny. Through him …” The margin has “Er—,” with the remainder of the name cut off.]

A certain man named Aribo, commonly called Aervo, succeeded him in office. He set himself to live under a corresponding name and nickname through toil and tyranny. Through him the revived weapons of discord were restored—the weapons that, under his predecessor, had lain dormant in the prevailing grace of concord.

When the most worthy Bishop Bernward was to consecrate this future archbishop as a priest, he bound him with the sword of the word of God and anathematized him in the presence of Lord Henry, the most benign emperor, and various bishops, with clergy and people standing by. He did this so that, after receiving the governance, Aribo would not inflict injury upon the holy Church of Hildesheim concerning the parish called Gandersheim.

[Note: Manuscript 2 lacks “Lord” and reads “benign” rather than “most benign.”]

He repeated and confirmed this very thing when the venerable Bishop Eggehard consecrated him as archbishop in Bernward’s place.

[Note: Manuscript 2 reads “him” rather than “that man,” lacks “venerable,” and has the form “Egkih.”]

But what he then promised deceitfully, he later betrayed in the advance of his folly. At the very time of his promotion, he approached Bishop Bernward through his legate under the pretense of peace and, through false words of greeting, attempted to raise a complaint concerning Gandersheim.

Bishop Bernward, instructed by divine inspiration, paid no attention to his empty talk but drew out against him the anathema of his obligation, saying that he had nothing in common with Aribo—if Aribo wished to act rightly—except what belonged to God; as for his parish, there was no doubt that he had conceded nothing to him.

[Note: Manuscript 2 omits the words “if Aribo wished to act rightly” and also lacks “concerning his parish.”]

By this answer the archbishop’s scheme was blocked. He did not dare even to mutter about this matter during the lifetime of the venerable Bishop Bernward.

[Note: Manuscript 2 reads “nor” rather than “and”; it lacks the first “concerning this matter” and adds, “he who dared to mutter during the bishop’s lifetime.”]

[Note: Manuscript 3 adds: “Here Thangmar ends. Meanwhile, and so forth.” This is refuted by the authority of manuscripts 1 and 2. Another ancient author, in the Translation of Saint Bernward, expressly says that Thangmar narrated at greatest length the holiness of Saint Bernward’s way of life, the magnificence of his deeds, and his death. The style also reveals no other author. Leibniz.]

[Note: See Bernward’s constitution concerning synods to be held four times each year in the diocese of Hildesheim, issued in 1020 on the sixth day before the Ides of October, in *Laws*, volume II, pages 172–173.]

### 49

[Note: Chapters 49–53 are absent from manuscript 2.]

In the second year thereafter—that is, in the year 1022 of the Lord’s incarnation, the twenty-first year of the reign of Lord Henry the emperor, the thirtieth year of Bishop Bernward’s ordination, the fifth indiction, on the third day before the Kalends of October (September 29)—the aforementioned monastery, constructed for the benefit of monastic life and completed with manifold adornment, as can be seen today, was dedicated with every devotion of ecclesiastical religion.

It was dedicated by the venerable pontiff Bernward, the provider of that church; by the honorable Unewan, archbishop of the Church of Hamburg; by Eggehard, Bishop of Schleswig; and by Bennon, the most reverend bishop of the Church of Oldenburg.

It was dedicated in honor of our Lord Jesus Christ the Savior; of his most holy Mother and perpetual Virgin, Mary; of the venerable and life-giving wood of the cross, which is to be adored; and for the special protection of Saint Michael the archangel, of the entire heavenly army, and for the praise and veneration of all God’s saints.

### 50

Soon afterward, the habitation of the same monastery was entrusted for governance to Goderam, provost of the monastery of Saint Pantaleon, in the office of abbot.

### 51

Finally, after the blessed man had endowed the Church of Saint Michael with exceedingly rich estates, he confirmed it by the authority of his ban in the presence of a legate of the apostolic lord—namely, one of the cardinals—together with eleven bishops and persons of various orders.

How earnestly he had conceived this work of pious devotion in his mind, with what ardor he undertook it when the opportunity arose, with what vigilance and perseverance he pursued it, with what charity he provided it with sufficient external resources, with what freedom he built it, with what authority he confirmed it, and how much progress he himself made during this time after being touched by the divine scourge—we shall present more fully in his own words.

For he himself says in the privilege granted to that monastery:

> Every creature called man was created by its Creator for this reason: that, according to the order of nature, he should serve his Creator rather than a creature. When the proper condition of this relationship is altered by the varied use of things, it nevertheless always turns the rational mind back toward the path of its condition. But the more the draught of divine inspiration corrects each person, the more divinely each person binds himself to God [Col. 0430B] in all things. And this cannot happen unless the powerful hand of God has drawn each person to himself. Hence, in the desire for grace, the protection of divine mercy takes shape and adapts itself to each person.

> When we consider the proof of this, the divine answer immediately presents itself: after Adam sinned and thereafter endured the long hardships of exile, Abraham believed God, and this was reckoned to him as righteousness. And when, both through divine prevenient clemency and according to the demands of merit, we accept that Moses, the giver of the law, was leader and teacher of the people of Israel, we marvel, by an equal measure of holiness, that Elijah, the worker of miracles, had not yet known the boundary of human life, but had been taken up in a chariot of fire until the final judgment of the ages.

> [Col. 0430C] The mind cannot comprehend, nor will it find an end, if our reasoning should wish to extend itself further concerning these matters and those like them. It is sufficient evidence how great a man David, strong of hand, rose up in battle; and it is brighter than the sun that, after constructing the tabernacle of God, the holy Solomon approached God through how many rites of religion and mystical observances of offerings—no one has ever been found equal to him in the merits of repentance.

> Through all these things God revealed, in accordance with the pattern of their deeds, the secrets of merit: so that temporally, in merit and deed, they might always be different from everyone else, and moreover eternally become equal to the angelic spirits.

> Considering these things, I, Bernward, called bishop by God’s election, not by my own merits, and turning them over in prolonged meditation—by what architecture of merits, [Col. 0430D] or at what price of things, I might purchase heavenly realities—when I was a learned court scribe and instructor of [Col. 0431A] the emperor Otto III of blessed memory, as well as his chief notary, touched by divine grace, shuddering at the excesses of my guilt and desiring divine grace, directed my mind in various ways, asking how I might satisfy eternal mercy and thus obtain a remedy for my soul.

> But because of the lowliness of my condition at that time, whatever I proposed in my mind I feared would either scarcely be begun or never completed. Nevertheless, my spirit labored more and more in the ardor of its holy purpose, although at that time fortune forbade me to begin anything. Then, behold, God’s election and the acclamation of the assemblies chose me beforehand to be enthroned upon the seat of pontifical glory; and, so that the Lord’s flock might not be disturbed without a shepherd, and our mother the Church might not be like a widow, the spirit of peace caused everyone, in the election of the new pontiff, to have one heart and one soul.

> [Col. 0431B] Once enthroned in the Bennopolitan Church [Note: That is, the Church of Hildesheim; see the *Annales Hildesh.* in *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, Scriptores III, p. 22], I wished to complete in deed what I had long conceived in my mind: namely, to commit the renown of my name to blessed memory by building churches, to establish there the offices of those serving God, and to make all my little resources profitable for the Lord.

> And because God’s judgments are hidden, yet always just, with the consent and encouragement of Christ’s faithful I began to establish a new church of God. In it, for the praise and glory of the Lord’s name, I fulfilled the purpose of my vow and provided for holy Christianity by bringing in brothers beloved of God.

> Once the new work had been founded and the qualities of the place had been determined, lest earthly wandering provide an excuse for delaying the work begun—glory to you, O Christ!—I was struck by the affliction of fever and began to be ill for five years. And since nothing is done on earth without cause, the Lord chastised me severely, yet did not hand me over to death, as I believe and trust in the Lord, lest my absence interrupt the fulfillment of my hope.

> To this place, dedicated to God, the holy Cross, the perpetual Virgin Mary, and the holy archangel Michael, I assigned members of the monastic order. I gathered them together for this reason: just as, according to the monastic rule, they were removed from worldly activities, so they would also be free from every impediment of worldly service.

> On the advice, therefore, of my lord, the emperor Henry, and of my teacher, Archbishop Erkenbald—whom I myself, together with the assembly of my brothers, consecrated archbishop—I handed over through the hands of my advocate, for the use of the brothers, whatever earthly possessions I possessed in estates, small holdings, lands, pastures, waters, forests, meadows, churches, relics of saints, books, silver, and gold, and whatever else I possessed by hereditary right or could acquire by secular purchase, except for the many things I had given to the altar of Saint Mary in the principal church: golden crowns, chalices, candlesticks, [Col. 0432A] vestments, and other ornaments of ecclesiastical order.

> I handed over all of it to God and his saints, for the souls of my aforesaid imperial lords, for my own soul, for the souls of all my successors, and for the souls of those whose patrimonies I acquired, so that the servants of Christ, free from every earthly service and protected under the defense and patronage of my successors, might lead peaceful days in quietness and mercy and cling to blessed contemplation for the salvation of the living.

> But if any successor of my order or any secular person should wish to break this arrangement and presume tyrannically to usurp these things for himself, I remove him from God and his saints by the sword of God’s word, so that, when every curse falls upon him, he may lack blessing; and thus, exterminated from heaven and earth, may have his portion with Judas and with those who possess the sanctuary of God as an inheritance.

> Moreover, the heirs, with God’s permission and ours, should strive to reclaim these things for their own use when they see a foreign invader raging among their patrimonies [Note: Witnesses 3, 4, and 5 add: *qui esset pars et haereditas mea*, “who would be my portion and inheritance” [the added fragment has no clear antecedent here].]

### 52

Anyone considering these words of the blessed man will readily perceive how greatly he advanced either in devotion to God or in the degree to which the favor of heavenly regard raised him up. For he who, while engaged in such a work, deserved to be refined by a heavenly scourge was proved by clear signs to be loved by the Lord.

### 53

Having thus conducted himself throughout all his life in these devout pursuits, worthily before God and laudably before men, in the thirty-first year of his ordination, when he already foresaw that the day of his passing—which he had always desired—was approaching, he had the chapel built between the chapel of the Holy Cross and his monastery dedicated in honor of the blessed confessor of Christ, Martin, by the venerable Eggehard, bishop of Schleswig. There, on that same day, changing his former clothing for the advancement of religion, he took upon himself the yoke of the monastic profession.

### 54

Then, struck by his final illness, when he sensed that the hour of his departure had come, he ordered himself to be carried into the same chapel, declaring that it was right for him to meet the end of his life there, where he had been marked by the habit of renouncing the world.

[Note: Here manuscript 2 begins again: “Meanwhile, Lord Bishop B., worn down by a prolonged illness …”]

Thus the most blessed man, worn down by prolonged bodily affliction, “fighting the good fight, completing the course, keeping the faith,” entered upon the way [Note: Manuscript 2 has “ways” (*vias*).] of all flesh and, as we believe, accompanied by divine spirits and guided by the archangel Michael, was presented to blessed immortality. [Note: Manuscript 2 omits “who.”] As long as he lived, he offered himself to the Lord as a sacrifice of righteousness; and thus, distinguished by many marvelous signs [Note: Manuscript 2 has *insignis*, “distinguished,” for *insigniis*, “signs.”], he rests in heavenly peace.

He died on the twelfth day before the Kalends of December (20 November). He had sat [Note: Manuscript 2 has *qui sedebat*, “who was sitting,” for *sedit autem*, “he had sat.”] in the episcopal chair for thirty years. His departure to God made us orphans without a father and our mother, the holy Church of Hildesheim [Note: Manuscript 2 omits “the holy Church of Hildesheim”], like a widow [Note: Manuscript 2 omits the remainder; in its place it adds the following in the *Life of Bishop Godehard*, to be edited: “But lest …”].

For immediately after the passing of so great a father the whole city was shaken and groaned together, and every gathering of both clergy and people grieved in its heart. Everywhere mournful cries arose; inconsolable sorrow was heard from every class. The man whom, while he remained among them, they had always embraced with common affection, they rightly followed at his departure with common lamentation.

Here a crowd of the poor, there of widows and orphans, proclaimed with pitiable wailing that they had lost a father; here the nobility and there the humility of the common people lamented with united grief that they had been deprived of the defender of their homeland, the lover of peace, and the most prudent provider for the whole commonwealth.

In a remarkable way this man had become all things to all people. Between rich and poor, between the exalted and the humble, he walked in the middle with a certain authoritative modesty; and, justly prudent toward both sides, he appeared neither inaccessible to the gentle nor contemptible to the insolent.

Thus, as has been said, the deceased was mourned with common complaint, he who in life had been honored with the common reverence of love. But lest we grieve irrationally like those who have no hope, if we grieve that we have lost on earth one who consoled us, let us rejoice that we have in heaven one who intercedes for us; and let us perform the offices of compassion toward his body in such a way that we also render the due tribute of rejoicing to his spirit, which happily reigns with God.

### 55

While he was still alive, he had ordered that the bier on which his body was carried out for burial should be covered not with a pall, as is customary in the funeral service of such a person, but only with sackcloth. We have thought it should be inserted here so that all readers may see how greatly this man, although exalted by the Lord even in temporal honor, humbled himself; and how the devotion of his living spirit provided such a humble service even for his dead flesh.

After the ecclesiastical rites had been duly celebrated, the body of the beloved bishop was buried in the crypt of the monastery that he himself had founded, before the altar of Saint Mary, with the greatest devotion of Christ’s faithful.

He had himself prepared his tomb with holy devotion and had inscribed upon it the following epitaph in his customary humility:

> I, Bernward, was a part of humankind; now I am enclosed in this  
> dread sarcophagus—look, vile ashes.  
> Alas, because I did not bear the summit of office well!  
> May there be merciful peace for my soul; and you, sing “Amen”!

### 56

What could be sweeter than this gentleness of the blessed man, or more praiseworthy than this abasement? The lower he places himself beneath the bushel of humility, the more brightly he appears upon the Church’s lampstand; and the more unworthy he considers himself, by his own judgment, of priestly honor, the more entirely he is proved worthy by the testimony of a praiseworthy life.

Finally, to anyone who considers devoutly the manner of his conduct and his holy formation from childhood, it will appear clearer than daylight that he possessed great merit, although he himself judged himself very differently. For, according to the Psalmist, the valleys abound in grain—that is, those humble in spirit overflow with the more excellent gifts of divine generosity.

But this devout Father, wholly most worthy of God and the Church, and among the other virtues with which he was adorned a foremost cultivator of humility, reveals what consolation, faith, and hope he conceived from that humility of heart in the inscription that he carved upon the inner sarcophagus:

> “I know [Note: The sarcophagus reads *SCIO ENIM QUOD* (“For I know that”), etc.] that my Redeemer lives, and that on the last day I shall rise from the earth, and again I shall be clothed with my skin, and in my flesh [Col. 0434C] I shall see God my Savior. I myself shall see him, and my eyes shall behold him, and not another” [Note: The sarcophagus has *alium* (“another,” accusative) for *alius* (“another,” nominative).] “This hope of mine has been laid up in my bosom” [Note: The sarcophagus spells this *HEC* for *haec* (“this”).] [Note: This inscription still survives on the sarcophagus; see Kratz, *Description of the Metropolitan Church of Hildesheim*, vol. III, plate 13. The lower part of the sarcophagus bears: “BERNWARDUS, BISHOP, SERVANT OF THE SERVANTS OF CHRIST.”]

These words are believed to have been repeated by him in the same spirit in which they were first spoken, as though he had expressed the matter more clearly in other words:

> “I have fought the good fight, I have completed the course, I have kept the faith; from now on the crown of righteousness is laid up for me.”

[Note: Manuscript 3 inserts the following. Its final words demonstrate that it was not written before the year 1195:]

> “What follows is found in most books and manuscripts concerning the death of the holy bishop. The passing of our most holy bishop, the man of God Bernward, was revealed by God to several people; but, in order to pursue this account, it is useful first to attend briefly to earlier events.
>
> “Once, while the man of God Bernward was still alive, he was sitting with his guests in his hall. A poor scholar stood before the doors asking for alms and called upon the pious bishop to have mercy on him. Hearing this, the prophetic man, full of the Spirit of God, ordered that the bishop of Cologne, who was standing outside, should immediately be brought in.
>
> “The servants ran and reported that no one was outside except the poor scholar. But Saint Bernward, insisting that he was the bishop of Cologne, ordered that he be brought in quickly. Receiving him kindly, he placed the reluctant poor man at the head of the table. After the meal, his face flushed with embarrassment at the honor shown him by so great a bishop, the blessed man foretold that he would become bishop of Cologne, humbly asking him to sing the first Mass that he celebrated in Cologne for the poor Bernward.
>
> “The man agreed to his request with the greatest devotion. After asking for and receiving a blessing, he departed. Having therefore become archbishop [Col. 0433C: Pilgrim], according to the prophecy of the holy man, while Lord Henry of Bamberg was reigning, in the year of the Lord 1023, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of December, the bishop of Cologne himself approached the altar to celebrate Mass. Preceding the singers, and to the astonishment of all who were present, he began a Mass for the dead. Nor, when he came to the canon, did he forget the one who had foretold his future, the blessed Bernward; with the utmost devotion, as he had promised, he commemorated him among the living.
>
> “But during the consecration of the saving victim, the passing of the man of God was divinely revealed to him. Therefore, immediately afterward, he also mentioned his name among the dead; and, when Mass was finished, he made public to the faithful everything that had happened. Wishing to investigate the heavenly miracle more carefully, they sent scouts to Hildesheim and learned with complete certainty that at the very hour when the archbishop sacrificed the host of our salvation, the most holy soul of the faithful and prudent servant of our Lord Jesus Christ entered heavenly joy.
>
> “Nevertheless, twelve Roman miles from the city, in a remote region called Lunda [Col. 0435C: Lühnde, east of Hanover], a devout hermit named Anselm had been enclosed in a certain forest for twenty-six years. While he was pouring out his customary prayers to God, he was immediately in the spirit. On the very day when the soul of the man of God sought the heavenly courts, he saw the heavens opened with immense light, and amid the sweet melody of the blessed spirits he heard the angels repeat this song:
>
> > ‘O happy soul of Bernward, whose merits are still unknown to human beings but are very well known to God and to us.’
>
> “He saw and heard this three times in succession on the day of the burial. As the man of God often turned this revelation over with devotion, while still not knowing where so blessed a man of that name had lived, behold, a venerable figure of lofty stature, handsome of face, sprinkled with gray hair, and clothed in pontifical garments stood before him and said:
>
> > ‘I am Bernward, bishop of Hildesheim, whom you heard praised three times in a vision among the choir of angels. I built a temple for the angels at Hildesheim and made the Son of the Virgin heir to my patrimony; I renounced all the pleasures of the world and assumed an angelic habit. Now also I have received a hundredfold, and in such jubilation as you saw I possess eternal life.’
>
> “After revealing these and certain other things to him, the figure disappeared in great light. For the glory of the holy man, the hermit faithfully reported what he had heard and seen. Thus the holy bishop died in the year of the Lord 1023, as has been said, and was buried in the crypt of his church, which he had built; but he lay hidden beneath the earth for one hundred and seventy-two years. Manuscript 4 records this among the miracles after chapter 7.”

### 57

Nevertheless, on the right side of the tomb, above the columns, the following inscription can be seen [Note: The German translation states that it was composed by Bishop Benno of Meissen]:

> In this tomb’s hollow the bones of Bishop Bernwald [Note: Variant name: *Berwardi*.]  
> are enclosed, a wondrous and magnificent man.  
> He, the glory of his homeland, shining like a clear gem,  
> pleased the Lord and was beloved by the people.
>
> For he was a bishop worthy of the Church,  
> May God Emmanuel and Michael love him.  
> At last, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of the eleventh month,  
> the blessed man changed this life for an angelic one.

[Col. 0435]

# APPENDIX. MIRACLES OF SAINT BERNWARD

### 1

[Note: What follows was added in manuscript 1 by another hand, though one of the early twelfth century.]

It is not for our smallness to explain with how many distinguished miracles the Lord glorified his confessor after these events. But lest we seem to have passed over everything, we shall relate a few from among the many.

### 2

A certain girl from Erpesford, named Hildegard, came to Hildesheim with a great crowd of sick people afflicted by various illnesses. She was miserably contracted throughout her body, so that her knees clung to her chest, her right hand was bent, and, scarcely raised a cubit from the ground, she dragged herself along by crawling.

For six months and more she crawled around the holy places, begging health from God and alms from the people. Then, as she herself reported, she was admonished in a dream, crawled to the tomb of the blessed Bernward, and reached it. When a wax image had been placed upon the tomb, she immediately began to suffer more severely from the stretching of her sinews before the people, a crowd of whom had happened to gather there at that time.

What more is needed? Within two days she was standing upright, so that not long afterward she returned home healthy. Our entire city is witness, for her misery had long made her well known.

### 3

There lived in our city a certain knight of ministerial rank. His little daughter was afflicted by illness, and it was feared that she might not even live long enough to receive the grace of baptism. The anxious father, fearing that her soul might perish without the sacrament of regeneration, vowed to carry a wax image to the tomb of the blessed Bernward, so that through the saint’s merits the Lord might grant the child enough time merely to receive baptism.

After making the vow, he immediately had the image made of wax and went barefoot to the tomb of the most blessed bishop. Returning from there, he found that the child had completely recovered.

### 4

A certain girl in the village of Hanover [Note: Manuscript 4 has “Honovere”] suffered such severe pain in her eyes that it seemed, from the force of the pain, that the eyes themselves would be torn completely from their sockets. After promising an offering at the tomb of the holy bishop, she immediately became well, and the force of the pain subsided.

[Note: This is the earliest mention of our native city; from this it is clear that Hanover was a village in the eleventh and early twelfth centuries.]

### 5

A certain man in Runeberge [Note: Ronnenberg near Hanover] was afflicted by a similar complaint. On the night of the beheading of Saint John the Baptist, when he had entirely despaired of the health of his eyes, he invoked the aid of the same man and fell asleep. At daybreak, when all pain had completely fled, he rose and on that same day came with witnesses of his recovery to give thanks at the tomb of the blessed bishop.

### 6

Bukenem [Note: Bokenem.] is a village three miles from the city of Hildesheim [Note: German miles]. There a blacksmith named Dodo was struck by a severe illness for three weeks, so that he thought his hands and feet, already almost dead, would fall from their joints.

A priest was summoned and came when his case was already considered hopeless. At the priest’s advice, and that of his other relatives, Dodo vowed that if he began to improve within three days, he would visit the tomb of the blessed man Bernward to give thanks.

These things took place on the Wednesday before Rogation Sunday. During the following day and night he recovered so greatly that on the next Friday he came barefoot to Hildesheim by the prescribed route. His face, however, was so sallow that the sight of it itself convinced those who heard him that a miracle had occurred.

### 7

A woman from Goslar named Eilmod was possessed by a demon. When she had come to the memory of the blessed man, she was tormented there in a horrible manner for several days, but was cured through the prayers of the same most holy bishop.

She remained with us for seven or more days, visiting the episcopal tomb every day with the most devout thanksgiving and frequently receiving communion of the Lord’s body and blood there. After departing, she returned six weeks later and, placing upon the tomb wax purchased for two denarii, gave thanks for the continuance of her health.

All Goslar is witness, where she is very well known on account of her business.

### 8

A certain young man in Bohemia, on the most sacred night of the Lord’s Nativity, was keeping vigil at certain games with two brothers and other companions of his age [Note: The manuscript reads *uls*.]. He was handed over to be tormented by a most savage demon. Both his brothers were overtaken by sudden death, while all the others who had taken part in the same ill-fated games were either removed by death or handed over to the torment of demons.

Thus, after three years, while his unhappy affliction continued, the young man, wandering here and there without his parents’ knowledge, finally reached Hildesheim. While compline was being sung there, he entered the monastery of Saint Michael and was tormented so violently before the altar of the Holy Cross that everyone present was left stunned with great horror and pierced with compassion.

He was therefore brought by force, while resisting fiercely, into the crypt to the tomb of the blessed Bernward. There, after being whirled about for a long time in madness and babbling blasphemous words—as certain people who understood his language and happened to be present reported in fearful astonishment—he finally collapsed. Then, with his mouth open and gasping, he belched out the foulest liquid with a terrible stench, and rose unharmed.

The following day he was presented to the people in good health. For approximately fifteen days thereafter he frequently visited the tomb, continually licking and kissing the pavement around it, and gave the one who had freed him devout thanks with tears.

### 9

Certain merchants from Bremen were sailing across the sea toward England when they were overtaken by a most violent storm. The anchor rope broke, the entire ship was shaken, and the sea seemed already to threaten everyone with imminent death.

As a common supplication and tearful cry arose to seek the patronage of the saints, someone suddenly declared that a certain holy bishop named Bernward was shining in Hildesheim through miracles. They therefore requested his assistance by common vow and immediately, amid the peaks of the waves, made their way without difficulty to the harbor in the usual calm. Returning in a smaller boat, they brought back their anchor, which had slipped into the sea.

After returning home, they sent two of their companions, one named Godescalc and the other Elveric, with a wax boat to the tomb of the blessed man on the Tuesday after the Sunday *Laetare Jerusalem*, as an offering of thanksgiving. Later, having again been rescued by him from a similar danger, they offered a silver anchor with their own hands.

### 10

A merchant lived in Hildesheim. On Good Friday his wife was going barefoot around the holy places according to her customary annual practice. She purchased some incense, intending to carry it to the tomb of the blessed Bernward.

On the road leading to the monastery of Saint Michael, she washed her feet in muddy water that flowed through the city toward the city wall, and from there continued to the monastery. When she had climbed into the cemetery of the same church, she realized that the incense she had bought had slipped away.

Greatly distressed in spirit, as she related, she shook out her clothing in case the incense had adhered somewhere, then retraced the road by which she had come, all the way to the water where she had earlier washed her feet. She found nothing and returned to the monastery in deep sadness.

From there she entered the crypt and prostrated herself in prayer before the tomb of the most blessed bishop, weeping copiously. She reasoned within herself that her offering had slipped away because she had been unworthy to carry it to the memory of the holy man.

After finishing her humble and tearful prayer, she rose and found the lost incense in her left hand. Placing it upon the tomb, she departed in great fear and concealed what had happened in silence until, on the fifth or sixth day, it became known through her household.

Later, when one of our brothers asked her to disclose the truth of the event, she was unable to recount it without tears.

### 11

A certain knight named Thietmar, a royal ministerial, lives in the village of Hogen [Note: Hoya], beside the river Weser. His son Machelmus, about eight years old, had been afflicted for five years by a fistula in the left jaw, and all the efforts of the physicians had been useless.

At last he vowed to carry his offering, namely a wax head, to the tomb of the holy bishop, if within nine days health should be restored to him through the merits of the blessed man.

Accordingly, the boy received relief within three days, before the appointed time. On the Tuesday within Pentecost week, he came safely with his father, mother, and grandmother to the memory of the blessed man, bringing the promised vows as testimony to his recovered health.

### 12

The abbot of the monastery of Saint Michael, named Conrad [Note: Abbot, 1102–1124], was traveling one day on business for the monastery. It happened that the horse on which he was riding slipped, and his shin was struck, leaving him completely helpless and tormented by pain. He was carried back in a sedan chair.

He ordered that he be taken to the tomb of the blessed bishop Bernward. There he prostrated himself in prayer and vowed that, for as long as he lived, he would provide a candle there by night and day. Immediately he rose unharmed. The man who had been carried in on others’ hands went out on his own feet.

[Note: Manuscripts 3, 4, and 5 add: “Nor does this seem worth concealing, because many people devoted to God, both men and women, have testified that during the hours of the night’s rest they heard the singing of psalms at the tomb of the blessed bishop, saw lights divinely kindled, and sensed the fragrance of a marvelous odor.”]

### 13

A woman from the province of Moravia, from the city of Olomouc, born of parents of no low standing, had been weak and withered for seven years. The fingers of her left hand were contracted into the palm, and the forearm of that same arm was stiffened and almost attached to her chest. She regularly visited many holy places in search of health.

Exhausted by the great labor of the journey, she came in the morning of the seventh day before the Kalends of June to the tomb of the blessed Bernward. Placed there during the first Mass, she recovered her former health while the people looked on.

Many reliable witnesses were present at the time. They affirmed that they had truly known her previously as a disabled woman. Immediately, therefore, all who had witnessed this miracle, along with many people from the city who came running and were able to learn what had happened, devoutly blessed God in hymns and praises, while the bells also rang out, because he glorifies his servant through such great miracles.

### 14

A certain man in Thuringia had a withered hand, deprived of every capacity for work. He vowed to go with offerings to the memory of the blessed Bernward if he should deserve to obtain health through the saint’s merits. With unexpected speed he received what he had desired.

But because he thought so little of such great grace and neglected to fulfill the vow he had made, he was afflicted anew with weakness in that hand and arm. Compelled by excessive pain, although late, he came to his senses and was not unaware why he suffered this. He began to go with the promised offerings to invoke the aid of the blessed confessor.

Before he had completed the journey, he received perfect health. When he reached the place where the body of the holy bishop rests, he offered worthy thanks to his healer and related to us how this had happened, with many witnesses to his recovery.

### 15

Another man, named Volquardus and well known throughout our city, was afflicted by a similar illness. One day he was brought into the church of Saint Michael and asked that physical medicines be applied to him. A certain priest admonished him that he ought rather to seek health from God and persuaded him to go in hope of recovery into the crypt to the tomb of the blessed Bernward.

After doing so, scarcely half an hour had passed before he came happily out of the crypt and clearly showed everyone who was standing in the church that he had been healed.

Seven days later he was summoned again and questioned about the continuance of his health. After declaring that he felt no pain, he was presented to the people, a large crowd of whom was present at the time. God was glorified by all with great praises for what had taken place.

### 16

A certain peasant lived in a village called Lühnde [Note: Manuscript 1 originally had “Liunine,” corrected to “Liuline” by the same hand] [Note: Lühnde]. He was traveling to Rome for the sake of prayer to Saint Peter when, on that same journey, he began to be detained by a serious illness.

He vowed entirely to abstain from eating meat until he could come to the tomb of the blessed Bernward to give thanks, if through Bernward he should happen to be freed from the danger of death. Immediately he was restored to his former health.

### 17

A little girl named Mathild, born in Bavaria but living among us from almost her earliest years in the village of Tosseim [Note: At the place now called Marienburg, between the south and east of Hildesheim], was supported by the alms of a certain religious man [Note: Manuscript 3 adds: “named Ekbert”]. Her hand was contracted. She came to the tomb of the blessed Bernward and, as soon as she touched it, found the remedy of the health she desired.

### 18

There was also in Bremen a woman of no unknown reputation among her people. As her disease grew worse, her face had swollen so greatly that it had almost entirely destroyed the distinction between her nostrils and eyes.

When her acquaintances invoked the compassion of the blessed bishop Bernward over her excessive affliction, vowing that she would visit his tomb, the pain immediately ceased and her former health returned with unexpected speed.

### 19

There was also in Nitelogon [Note: Nettlingen], a village two German miles [Note: German miles, eastward] from the city of Hildesheim, a girl who for five years had been afflicted by various bodily sufferings and troubles. At last, with almost all her nerves and limbs contracted, she was useless to herself and became a burden to her family.

She was therefore brought by cart on the sixth day before the Nones of May. With the greatest difficulty, leaning on two staffs, she crept into the crypt of our basilica and bent herself over the tomb of the blessed man. There she recovered with marvelous speed from every ailment by which she had suffered.

The following day an incredible multitude of people from our city assembled, along with a considerable crowd of pilgrims and others who had come from various places for the solemnity of the Invention of the Holy Cross celebrated on that day. After receiving testimony from the girl’s parents and fellow citizens concerning what had happened, they devoutly glorified almighty God with public praises in his saint.

The girl returned home unharmed that same day.

[Note: Manuscript 1 ends here, with several blank leaves remaining. Manuscripts 3, 4, and 5 continue as follows:]

### 20

A certain man from the city of Lübeck, named Adelward, had lain paralyzed and helpless for so long that he could neither raise himself in bed nor bring his own hand to his mouth.

The blessed Bishop Bernward appeared in a vision to his wife and instructed her that she ought to vow to God, for her husband’s recovery, a candle made according to the length and breadth of his tomb.

When she awoke from sleep and reflected on the vision, she immediately rose, took two women with her, and prostrated herself on the floor in the entrance hall of her house. After prayer and the promised vow, she returned to her husband and found him giving thanks to God because he had already recovered his health.

From that hour he recovered so completely that not long afterward he visited the holy man’s tomb with his wife to fulfill the vow and became the most reliable narrator of the miracle performed upon him.

### 21

On another occasion, the son of the same head of household, still a little child, was crushed and mangled beneath the collapse of a heavy object falling upon him. He already seemed almost lifeless when his wailing mother fled to the patronage of Saint Bernward, nor was her hope disappointed.

For immediately after she had poured out prayers and tears to God, the boy, under the invocation of the holy bishop, was restored to life as though snatched from the very jaws of death.

22. A certain soldier, Herebord by name, from the village of Horhusen [ [Col. 0441A] So in 4 and 5; in 3, in an erasure, *hornsen*.—This is not Horsum near Alfeld.], wasted by a prolonged illness, had reached his final extremity. While his relatives and friends grieved excessively over the impending loss of their dearest man, the priest of that place suggested that they should implore the patronage of blessed Bernward on his behalf, making a vow that, if he could be restored to life and recover his health, he should come to the saint’s tomb clothed in wool and barefoot, beginning from his own house. When all had faithfully made this vow, the sick man began to improve; and as the gains of his recovery increased, he soon became completely well.

Later, while staying in the city of Brunswick on another matter, he set out from that same place to fulfill his vow, because by taking the shorter route he would be less fatigued in walking. When he reached the city of Hildesheim, however, he began to fall gravely ill. Nevertheless, desiring to complete what he had begun, he made for the church of Saint Michael, where the holy bishop rests; but before the church atrium he fell as though pushed by someone. When his companions took hold of him and led him, and they had reached the basilica’s door, he was struck by overwhelming horror and fear and collapsed in their hands. He could neither rise nor summon the strength to enter the church until, in a public confession before everyone present, he revealed for what offense he was being punished with this penalty.

Having recovered his strength, he returned to his own home and then set out from there, fulfilling the order of his vow with a devotion all the greater because he had been instructed by the divine scourge [variant: *divine*, 3].

23. A certain matron of Bremen, while lying ill, saw standing beside her a man of venerable appearance in priestly dress, who asked her whether she recognized the person she was looking at. She replied as best she could—for the breath of life scarcely stirred in her breast alone—that he was entirely unknown to her. But he declared in the kindest manner that he was Bernward, bishop of Hildesheim, and asserted that he had come for the sake of her health. He also admonished her, once recovered, to offer at his tomb a sum for wine [ [Col. 0442A] That is, the price of wine.] for the celebration of Masses. Having said this, he disappeared.

The woman, who was thought to be near death—for she had lain stretched out on the ground in the manner of the faithful departing this life—raised herself slightly and recounted the vision to all who had gathered to await her departure. From that hour she was restored to health. Later she visited the saint’s tomb and faithfully presented the prescribed offering, becoming an example to other faithful people for following this kind of devotion. Thereafter many, imitating so pious an act, were freed from various illnesses and calamities through the merits of blessed Bernward.

Here ends codex 4 and 5. Codex 3 adds, in somewhat smaller script:

24. A certain soldier from the duchy of Mecklenburg, violently seized by a fever, was admonished at the urging of certain people to make a vow to Saint Bernward, patron of the people of Hildesheim, and not to doubt that he would receive relief and recovery. He readily agreed; and when the vow had been made, as soon as the words had left his mouth he was healed. As evident testimony to this, the same soldier sent a gold florin by two priests to the tomb of the holy bishop; they faithfully testified that the events described above had occurred in this way.

25. A certain peasant from the diocese of Hildesheim, who had been suffering from fever for a long time, asked that water from the holy bishop’s tomb be brought to him. As soon as he began to drink it, the fever departed and did not return after that day; as he himself said, he remained in good health.]

[Col. 0443]

AROUND THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1024. ALPERT, MONK OF SAINT SYMPHORIANUS OF METZ

[Col. 0443]

S. NOTICE CONCERNING ALPERT AND HIS WORKS.

(From Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae historica*, historical writers, volume IV, p. 696.)

[Col. 0443A] Alpert, according to Sigebert [Note: [Col. 0443B] *On ecclesiastical writers*, chapter 143.], a monk of Saint Symphorianus of Metz at the beginning of the eleventh century, composed two short books: one on the bishops of Metz, addressed to Abbot Constantine [Note: [Col. 0443B] Concerning him, see above, p. 658 (Patrologia, volume CXXXIX, under the year 1024).], of which the only surviving fragment [Note: [Col. 0443B] The material reported by Hugh of Flavigny in Book II seems to belong to the lost portion of the work: “Lord Fingenius, descended from the race of the Scots . . . . . Anyone who wishes to know more fully about his arrival, pilgrimage, and conversion can learn it from the *Life of Theoderic*, the illustrious bishop of Metz.”] deals chiefly with Theoderic; and another, which he called *On the Diversity of Times*, addressed to Burchard, bishop of Worms [Note: [Col. 0443B] Meurisse writes in *History of the Bishops of Metz*, p. 349, that it was addressed to Theoderic II, bishop of Metz, perhaps misled by the fact that the final chapter of the sole manuscript concerns Theoderic II.].

In the former work he reports certain matters of the greatest importance for the history of the years 978–984, which he had learned from a man who had once been constantly in the service of Bishop Theoderic I [Note: [Col. 0443B] Chapter 1.]. He adds only a few details about Adalbero II and Theoderic II, and these indicate that our author sided with Adalbero III and Duke Theoderic against Bishop Theoderic, and therefore wrote before the year 1017. The book, following the catalogue of the bishops of Metz shown to Saint Clement, proves that Alpert had at some time lived in the diocese of Metz and had been enrolled among the Metz clergy [Note: [Col. 0443B] He calls Theoderic “our bishop,” chapter 1.]; nevertheless, it was not written at Metz, since it is said to have been sent to Abbot Constantine [Note: [Col. 0443B] Thus, sent rather than presented in person.], not presented to him.

Certainly Alpert composed *On the Diversity of Times* not at Metz [Note: [Col. 0443B] He calls it “Metz in Belgica,” I, 5.], but in the diocese of Utrecht, whose clergy he had joined under Bishops Ansfrid and Adalbold [Note: [Col. 0443B] He calls the clergy of Utrecht “our clergy,” I, 8, 12, 13; see also the account of Ansfrid, I, 11–18, and of the merchants of Tiel and the war against the Frisians, II, 20 and following.], in a church or monastery situated on the left bank of the Rhine [Note: [Col. 0444B] II, 1, 9.], perhaps at Utrecht [Note: [Col. 0444B] I, 14: “There is a hill six miles from Utrecht.”] or Nijmegen. Since he had before his eyes Bishop Adalbold’s book on the deeds of Emperor Henry II [Col. 0444A] [Note: [Col. 0444B] I, 5. See also the praises of Adalbold, II, 2.], he intended to narrate matters concerning the province rather than the empire.

He therefore related events that he had either experienced himself [Note: [Col. 0444B] For example, I, 15: “I heard a certain man,” and so forth.] or heard from men whom he considered trustworthy [Note: [Col. 0444B] I, 18, 12; II, 14.], events that had taken place in the diocese of Utrecht in the time of Ansfrid and Adalbold. He was guided by no partisan zeal [Note: [Col. 0444B] Compare II, 14. Thietmar presents Balderic’s affairs in almost the same way.], but attacked wicked and depraved men vigorously. Book I deals with the affairs of Ansfrid, and Book II with those of Bishop Adalbold. He wrote in 1021 [Note: [Col. 0444B] He began writing when Henry II was already emperor (I, 7), and after Adalbold’s book on Henry II had appeared; he brought his own work down to the year 1021, II, 16, 17.] or 1022, after Balderic had died [Note: [Col. 0444B] In the year 1021.], but before the cathedral church at Utrecht had been consecrated [Note: [Col. 0444B] The solemn consecration of Utrecht cathedral was performed by Bishop Adalbold on 26 June 1023, in the presence of Emperor Henry II and twelve archbishops and bishops. Certainly our author would not have passed it over in silence had he written after it had taken place. He also wrote while Henry II was still alive.].

This highly useful work for understanding the history of that region, together with the history of the bishops of Metz, came into the hands of Sigebert of Gembloux, who was staying at the monastery of Saint Vincent at Metz, and was copied by him [Col. 0444B]. Sigebert perhaps used the same manuscript that I now have in my hands—the only one, at least, that survives—which Eccard says was given to him by Robert Verboeckhorst, provost of Saint Ludger at Helmstedt. In his *Corpus of the Saints of the Middle Ages*, volume I, pp. 91–132, Eccard corrected it in a few places but reproduced it badly in many others.

Yet part of the work—namely, chapters 11–15 of Book I—had already appeared in 1680, without Eccard’s knowledge, under the title “Part of the *Life of Saint Aufrid, Bishop of Utrecht*, by a monk of Saint Paul’s at Utrecht,” in volume I of the May volume, pp. 431–432, of the Antwerp *Acts of the Saints* [Col. 0445A]. It had been transcribed from an old parchment manuscript of Saint Paul’s at Utrecht. Since this manuscript plainly did not derive from the Hanover manuscript, its evidence also had to be taken into account.

The following witnesses therefore served our edition:

1. C. Royal. It consists of six parchment leaves in folio, with two columns per page, written in small, delicate eleventh-century script. Many passages prove that the scribe did not understand the book, whether they were written later by his own hand or by another writer of the same century, perhaps Sigebert, whom I designate by the numeral.

2. I have marked as 2 the corrected readings, although even this witness is sometimes not skilled in discerning the true sense.

3. The edition of chapters 11–15 of Book I in the *Acts of the Saints*, cited above.

With these materials, we present a text restored, as far as possible, to its original integrity.

[Col. 0445]

A SHORT BOOK ON THE BISHOPS OF METZ

[Col. 0445B] 1 [Note: [Col. 0445] I have added the numbers.]. . . . Therefore, in his time [Note: [Col. 0445D] Namely, the time of Bishop Theoderic.]—in the year 978—Lothair, king of the Franks, turned his attention to the Belgian part of the kingdom, which [Note: [Col. 0445] *regnique*, c.] was under the authority of Emperor Otto, intending to bring it under his own rule as far as the Rhine.

For when Otto Caesar [Note: [Col. 0445] C writes *cesar* at times, and similarly *regine, letus, edificia, eger, cepit, presul, cenobium,* and *equavi*; but it writes *e, ae,* and *oe* most often.] happened to be staying safely at Aachen, with every fear removed, to hold assemblies, and this was reported to King Lothair by spies, Lothair hastened toward him by forced marches and unexpectedly approached the camp, leaving the emperor scarcely any opportunity to recover himself. In the haste of flight, many valuables were abandoned, all of which fell as booty to the enemy.

Lifted up by this success, the king increased the confidence of his men and made more frequent and bolder incursions, advancing as far as Metz; but having achieved nothing, he returned in disgrace. And just as insolence arises from success, so from the same source mental negligence can sometimes arise. Bishop Theoderic therefore decided that the king’s foolishness, although his incursions had been fruitless, ought to be restrained.

Accordingly, he sent letters and envoys to Otto Caesar, informing him of these events and saying that, in so extensive an empire, he ought not to endure any longer the insult being inflicted upon him and his peoples. When the emperor heard this, he necessarily judged that the matter demanded his attention. He considered it damaging and dishonorable that the Franks were accustomed to make attacks and plunder his kingdom.

He therefore summoned all the princes and complained of the injuries inflicted upon him by the king. All of them [Note: [Col. 0445] *hi*, 2.], after deliberation, declared that the king must be met with arms. With their unanimous consent he undertook the matter [Col. 0445D], gathered an innumerable army from every part of his empire, even from Italy, marched as far as Paris, ravaged the region, and returned without engaging anyone in battle.

At that time there was in France a man of such holiness and spirit [Note: [Col. 0445] *spiritalis*, c.] that it was divinely revealed to him that all those who had advised that the army be led into France would die within the span of seven years. We understand that his prophecy was fulfilled as follows.

For when he had returned from France, in the second year afterward the emperor led an army in Calabria against the Greeks. There, when he rashly and with excessive speed joined battle, contrary to what the circumstances of war required, all the nobility of our army perished by the sword, by the excessive heat, and by thirst; not one of them survived to report what had happened to posterity (982).

When this rumor reached the ears of Queen Theophanu, who had been left at Rossano [Note: [Col. 0446D] Rossano.] by the emperor, she immediately began, with the insolent speech characteristic of women’s fickleness, to extol her countrymen—for she was Greek—to the heavens, and to turn the outcome of the disastrous battle, with the greatest disgrace, into a reproach against the emperor: he who had so often been praised for his valor [Note: [Col. 0445] “By his hand,” 2.] had so easily been defeated by his own men.

When Bishop Theoderic heard the queen’s insulting words, he was deeply, and deservedly, angered against her. He was also afflicted with the greatest sorrow both by the misfortunes of his most beloved and revered lord and by the deaths of his dear soldiers [Note: [Col. 0445] *delictorum*, c.] and of the other friends who had fallen. Nevertheless, he did not consign the queen’s insolence and insult to oblivion.

Many believed that this had happened through divine vengeance, in accordance with what that holy man had foretold: those who had advised the devastation of the Frankish kingdom were themselves to lack burial in foreign lands and the comfort of all their friends.

Otto Caesar himself, however, hastened recklessly with a few men toward the Greek ships to fight. Surrounded by them, with no place of escape open to him, he leapt into the sea with his horse. He remained mounted upon it until he had cut apart with his sword all the garments he was wearing, so that he could make himself more able to swim.

From a distance he saw a ship and wished with all his strength to reach it—for he was highly skilled at swimming. When the sailors saw him swimming, they dragged him aboard. There was a certain man on the ship, of the Slavic nation, who was known to the emperor. He immediately took off the cloak which he himself was wearing [Note: [Col. 0445] *exiens* corrected to *exuens*, c.], handed it to the emperor so that he could put it on and cover his naked limbs, and indicated by whatever gesture he could that the sailors should not suspect or notice [Note: [Col. 0445] *animaverterent*, c.] who the man really was.

He was also capable of speaking with highly persuasive eloquence [Note: [Col. 0445] Thus Eccard; *persuasioris*, c.], and said that, if they would heed his advice and follow his counsel, they would soon become extremely fortunate. The city of Rossano [Note: [Col. 0447] *rothsan*, 2.] was not far away; all the treasures of Otto Caesar were kept there under the custody of the man who was his chamberlain. They should know for certain that a very large share of these treasures would be given to them if they took him there and allowed him to enjoy his freedom.

When they heard this, and looked at one another and discussed the matter at length, they were finally enticed, as is the custom of human greed, by the hope of money. “If,” they said, “you carry out what you have promised, we shall undertake your proposed plan without delay!”

“I pledge myself and my faith to this promise,” he replied.

Seeing the steadfastness of the promisor, from whose lips they hung, the sailors encouraged one another, saying that it would be the height of madness to let slip from their hands what they had the legal right to receive as the captive’s ransom.

They immediately turned the ship and came to the aforementioned place, the city of Rossano, and moored [Note: [Col. 0447] “And landed,” 1.]. Their guide, seeing everything unfold according to his desire, rose joyfully and addressed the sailors briefly. He ordered them to await his return confidently: he would go in and quickly bring back the captive with the money he had promised [Note: [Col. 0447] “Would arrive,” 1.].

Entering the city in haste, he found Bishop Theoderic, who, when the emperor had departed for battle, had been left there with Queen Theophanu. He disclosed the whole order of events to him, urged him to keep the matter completely secret, and told him to come immediately, bringing no one with him except two soldiers proven in courage, if he wished to receive the emperor alive.

The bishop rejoiced at the safety of his lord the king and ordered his soldiers Liupo and Richezo to accompany him [Note: [Col. 0447] *peragant*, 1.]. He said that he wished to go outside the city walls to inspect the layout of the place and the buildings. When he went out, he caught sight of the ship’s height—for it had been constructed with marvelous workmanship in the Greek manner—examined its entrance with careful attention, and finally, with whatever effort he could summon, laboriously overcame the difficulty of climbing aboard.

He saw his lord sitting far removed from royal honor, and, clapping his hands, shouted in a loud voice. The king immediately leapt out without hesitation.

At first the sailors thought that the captive’s companions had come carrying money. But when things turned out otherwise, contrary to their expectations, they tried to take up arms and resist their enemies. The aforementioned soldiers, Liupo and Richezo, urged the bishop to get out as quickly as possible. Since he hesitated from fear of being drowned, they forced him out of the ship, even tearing his clothing. Then, rushing upon the sailors with drawn swords, they killed some and wounded others. Some hid beneath the thwarts; others threw themselves from the ship in a frantic race and committed themselves to the open sea at the risk of their lives.

The king, fastening spurs onto his bare feet and mounting a horse, brought them all ashore. After generously supplying them with what they needed and enriching them with a very large sum of money, he allowed them to depart in peace.

He himself returned to Rome with Bishop Theoderic and there, falling ill, died not many days later (983, 6 December). He was honorably buried at Saint Peter’s, in the Paradise, beside the oratory of Saint Mary, amid the greatest lamentation of the entire city.

When these events had taken place, Bishop Theoderic, having prepared for his departure, set out on the journey home. Remembering the queen’s insult against Caesar, he began to consider how, under the pretext of his son’s right to rule, he might deprive her of the rights of kingship.

While he was thinking about this, an opportunity occurred which seemed favorable to him, though it happened without God’s predestination. There was a certain Bavarian named Henry, a man of great wealth, who, driven by the desire to rule, approached everyone he could and persuaded them to adopt his cause as their common cause. After giving many gifts, he easily brought them over to his opinion.

Very many, enticed by these promises, surrendered themselves to him and proclaimed him king over them [Note: [Col. 0447] *sub*, c.] [Note: [Col. 0447] *rege*, c.].

When this was reported to the bishop by those who told the story, he turned aside from his journey and went to him. He was received magnificently, and after the matter had long been debated between them, the bishop was deceived by the false king’s stratagems—for he was clever in speech. The false king offered splendid gifts and promised even greater rewards with the highest powers of the kingdom. The bishop therefore made his election and surrender, and returned to the journey he had begun (984).

When this deed spread widely among the peoples, there was absolutely no one, high or low, who did not detest his actions. They said that, since he held such a position of favor with the emperor that no one in the whole kingdom surpassed him in power, counsel, or the king’s familiarity, he ought not, contrary to everyone’s expectations, to commit so great a crime against the king’s son.

Thus it came about that, because he would not take precautions against his sudden rashness, he opened the mouths of many against his own disgrace [Note: [Col. 0447] “Opened,” 1.]. Finally, when he learned that his plan displeased many princes, because he had done all this without their knowledge, he was overcome with great sorrow, confined himself to his house, and, going nowhere, mourned his transgression secretly within himself.

Not long afterward, overcome by illness, he fell into bed and died around the fifth of the aforementioned seven years. He was buried in the monastery of Saint Vincent, which he himself had built and enriched with innumerable and magnificent ornaments [Note: [Col. 0447] Eccard supplied the missing word.].

I have composed this account of what happened during the final period of our bishop’s life from information obtained from one who was constantly in his service. These events do not compare with his earlier deeds, which he carried out most gloriously; but because those deeds were not fully known, we have passed them over.

Nevertheless, some people, moved by a certain compassion of mind, are accustomed to wonder how such a man, endowed with so many virtues as has been described, could so easily have departed from the position of his authority and so suddenly surrendered himself to the aforementioned king without consulting his own people.

Our answer can easily alleviate this wonder by way of excuse. Crushed and afflicted by the recent calamity and by the intense grief with which he was oppressed because of the death of his most beloved and intimate companion, and goaded by the queen’s insults, while at the same time deceived by the assertions of the aforementioned king [Note: [Col. 0449] *asert.*, c.] [Note: [Col. 0449] *set ductus*, c.], he almost forgot himself. With his mind pulled in different directions, he was uncertain what to do.

Yet he was not lacking in the knowledge and rational judgment of the truth, in which he had always excelled above all others. Had he been permitted to live longer, he could soon have repaired the damage and restored himself to his former dignity.

But when I consider the claims of all our distinguished men, I find nothing in them that does not surpass the elegance of his life; and anyone who thinks that he can be compared, by any judgment, with the life of Theoderic incurs the charge of arrogance.

For many became wealthy and famous not through themselves but through the benefits—or even the plunder—of others [Col. 0449B]. Theoderic, by contrast, was renowned in a wholly different way: through the nobility of his parents and the excellence of his ancestors, and also through the great abundance of estates he possessed by inheritance.

Indeed, unless his strength and greatness had grown with him from his earliest age, and the glory of his power had remained with him until the end of his life, this would have been impossible.

How frequent and diligent he was in caring for the salvation of his soul is shown by the oratory of Saint Vincent, mentioned above, which he built with magnificent workmanship on an island in the Moselle outside the walls of the city of Metz. Into it he also gathered, with pious zeal, the bodies of many saints brought from distant regions.

Whatever resources he bestowed upon the monastery and the community devoted to divine service, he confirmed by the authority of the pope of the Roman see, in the presence of Emperor Otto II, under threat of anathema. Finally, the pope ordered a privilege to be written concerning all these matters and, at the bishop’s request, sent a dalmatic and sandals to the abbot of Saint Vincent, so that whenever the bishop was absent, the abbot of that place would always perform the divine office in his stead at the episcopal seat, in the house of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr.

I, Alpert, who ought not even to be counted among the servants of God, have arranged this little work concerning our bishop and sent it to you, holy Father Constantine, for correction [Note: [Col. 0449] “To direct”; I have corrected it to “for correction,” 1.], lest some rival—if there is one who, drowsing, recoils from the vigilance of sacred study and embraces the sluggishness of idle leisure—find something in it with which to detract.

But if, even after correction, he refuses to lay aside his stubbornness [Note: [Col. 0449] *pertinantiam*, c.], let your permission and my affection provide him with the consolation of a dog’s letter, so that, devoted at least in this way to an unsuitable sound, he may furnish a laughingstock to his readers.

2. (Years 984, 16 October; 1005, 14 December.) “Likewise Adalbero, for twenty-two years.” The words of the holy angel are usually brief and obscure, so that pious minds may exercise themselves delightfully in investigating them.

For behold, he says, “Likewise Adalbero,” as though he were saying that this man was similar to the preceding one [Note: [Col. 0449D] Namely, Adalbero I.] both in name and in life, so that he who agreed in name would not differ in conduct.

It is said that both bishops [Note: [Col. 0449D] The two Adalberos.] were exceedingly devoted to the care of the poor and persevered unfailingly in building and governing churches. Therefore they deserved, rightly, to be made equal by the angel in both name and life.

[Col. 0450B] 3. (Years 1006, 1047.) This letter [Note: [Col. 0450D] A.] plainly does not fit the name of the man [Note: [Col. 0450D] Theoderic II.] who has now been substituted in the see. Hence many think that he should not be counted among the bishops, but was substituted because of the people’s transgression; they say that the episcopate would remain vacant until the one who bears the letter marked above should come.

But let us also apply ourselves to our own opinion. We suppose that the A was placed as if to mean *Alter Deodericus*, “another Theoderic.” Here a difficult question troubles us: why did the angel not say, “Likewise Theoderic,” as he had said concerning the preceding men [Note: [Col. 0449] *dixerit*; *dixit*, c.]?

Finally, as we seek to unravel the hidden meaning of this statement, it occurs to us that he may have used “another” because of its two meanings: either according to numerical reckoning, by which we say “one,” “another,” “third,” or to distinguish another kind of life, so that he might indicate that men who would be namesakes would nevertheless be different in life [Note: [Col. 0449] “In name,” 1.].

Yet none of us can examine their lives, because God alone looks into the hearts of mortals; and the deeds even of the great—whom we sometimes venerate out of flattery, affection, or ignorance—are examined before God’s eyes by the sentence of a stricter judgment.

Our Redeemer knows the name of the man whom he knows to preside, in accordance with apostolic dignity, over the sheep entrusted to him, through deeds of praiseworthy conduct and examples of virtue. [Col. 0451]

TWO BOOKS ON THE DIVERSITY OF TIMES

THE PROLOGUE BEGINS

[Col. 0451A] Brother Immo [Note: [Col. 0451C] Eccard suspects that Immo, abbot of Gorze, Prüm, and Reichenau, was Alpert’s brother; but Immo seems to have been a deacon of Worms, to whom the monk of Tiel wrote a letter about the miracles of Saint Walburga, *Acts of the Saints*, February, volume III, p. 548. There too his brother is mentioned: “If you wish to have your brother as a witness to this sign, you will ask him whether the matter is so; he married this woman after her husband had been killed in that miserable slaughter of the Frisians.” Nevertheless, I consider him different from Alpert, who seems to have been a cleric.] came to me out of affection. He reported your holy pursuits, venerable Bishop Burchard, your faith, holiness, and uprightness of conduct, and showed with what authority you built and governed the church entrusted to you by God.

I confess that I not only rejoiced greatly at his reports but also exulted with fitting wonder, giving thanks to God with my whole heart. And when I still desired to learn more about your goodness, he explained how deeply you were occupied with meditation on the Holy Scriptures, with the labor of fasts and vigils, and with the other works of Christ.

Finally, the more fully he spoke of you among us [Note: [Col. 0451] “He has spoken,” 1; “he had spoken,” 2.], the more agreeable and joyful he made the day for us. And because you have become known for such a praiseworthy life, although many splendid and illustrious things had already been heard about you from numerous eminent men [Col. 0451B], in accordance with the words of our Savior, the only-begotten Son of God: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden, nor is a lamp placed upon a lampstand” (Matthew 5:14–15), nevertheless, when your inner way of life has been more openly revealed, it will bind me to the memory of you, which the seal of Christ’s charity has impressed more firmly upon my heart, with perpetual attachment—if I may dare to confess this.

And if the narrowness of my circumstances denies me the means to render services, nevertheless the affection of a pious mind in Christ will always be present for you, supported by the testimony of Scripture, which says: “Good will is sufficient for all things.”

Moreover, I have consecrated to your name this little book, composed about the people of our times, whose title is *On the Diversity of Times*, because different matters seem to have been collected in it. I have not gathered absolutely everything that ought to have been written on the proposed subject, lest I seem more verbose than I should. And, to avoid causing weariness amid your most holy occupations, I have devoted myself to brevity in everything.

But if some rival should perhaps arise against me, wrinkle his brow in envy as he examines these pages with a jaundiced eye, and attempt to criticize me because I have published new material needlessly and in an impudently unpolished style—on the grounds that the books accepted by learned men are sufficient, and that they should be burdened even with these unlearned writings, as with a useless load—and if for that reason he rejects the little book, let him know that it has been sent solely for your judgment, so that, according to your decision, it may either be destroyed or preserved for reading.

For, trusting in your favor, no one will easily divert me from this purpose of mind, so that whatever your judgment approves may, without hesitation, be confirmed by the examination of others as well.

And if I am finally charged with having written things known to everyone, let them weigh, on your advice, my answer: things already known are often heard with pleasure, as happens with songs; when old songs have become tiresome through constant repetition, new ones, repeated more frequently day by day, are heard with greater delight.

In addition, let your dignity know that I undertook to write these things also to avoid idleness and sloth of heart. Since I am not fit for the work of God or for the advancement of any virtue, at least in this little work I might restrain my wretched spirit from empty curiosity.

For this reason, too, it has been presented without the author’s name: if it displeases you, as I said above, you may cut it out or order it to be covered over with earth after a ditch has been dug; but if it pleases you, then, after adding the name, read it happily as an exercise.

THE LETTER OF LORD BURCHARD, BISHOP, BEGINS

[Col. 0451]

[Col. 0451C] Burchard, most humble administrator of the holy church of Worms, to Alpert, his special friend: fullness of grace and abundant health.

I received cheerfully your letter, which you sent in my name, though you were very unknown [reading uncertain] [Col. 0452C]. Out of affection, and also on account of your request, I read it myself and ordered it to be read aloud in my presence. In it I recognized fully and abundantly the devotion of your study [Note: [Col. 0451] “I studied,” 1.] and your will.

But as often as I reread it, I was moved by almost every word and grieved over this matter in the presence of our boys: namely, that in these times there are either no people, or scarcely a very few, who are found capable of studying or whose willingness to study is sufficient. Yet through this occupation each person would be refreshed, his spirit would be suspended for a while from the various tumultuous concerns of the world by his lips, and a praiseworthy example would be handed down with every care to posterity.

But all deceived by the pleasures of the world and exceedingly prone to worse things, they serve the wretched vanities of this age and neither know how to practice nor seek the delightful feasts of souls; indeed, they utterly neglect them, as it is written: “All have turned aside; together they have become useless. There is no one who does good, no, not even one” (Romans 3:12).

Therefore, your devotion to study is not empty in my eyes, nor does it seem deserving of blame, but rather of great praise. For in the thread of your composition, turned diligently on the lathe, you have carefully preserved great and authoritative subjects, with steps that do not falter.

In every authoritative exposition, and in every book [Note: [Col. 0453] “Of morals,” 1.], six different questions ought to be asked and resolved, as Severinus [Note: [Col. 0453] “Prudentibus” was deleted, 3.], the most prudent teacher, established in the preface to his first edition of Porphyry’s *Isagoge*, at the urging of Fabius, saying:

“First,” he says, “they teach what the intention of each work is; second, what its usefulness is; third, what its order is; fourth, whether it is the genuine and proper book of the person to whom the work is said to belong; fifth, what its title is; sixth, they state toward which branch of philosophy the intention of each book is directed.”

You have carefully preserved all these matters in your book, but you have not added the inscription of your name. Since you left the matter to my judgment [Note: [Col. 0453] “You judged,” 1.], I judge—and also command—as follows: add a title to the book, confidently inscribe your name, and let the book be open to everyone who wishes to read it. By my judgment, let it remain stable and unshaken.

If anyone, driven by envy, should vilify us and our work with the murmur of detraction, I answer him and silence him, confounded, with these words:

> You envy our work because you do not know how to produce such things.

[Col. 0453] THE LETTER OF LORD BURCHARD, BISHOP OF WORMS, ENDS.

ALPERT’S *ON THE DIVERSITY OF TIMES* BEGINS.
