BOOK I [Note: [Col. 0453] “Book I” is absent in c.].

Additional textual notes: [Col. 0447] *adiit*, 2; *te*, 1; *eximis*, c; *prosus*, 1; *facnus*, 1; *apperuit*, 1. [Col. 0449] *obliviscetur*, 1; *dari*, c; *et*, c. [Col. 0450] *dms*, c; *uo*, 1. [Col. 0451] *pote*, 1; *taemptaverit*, c. [Col. 0453] *pudentibus* deleted, c; *propriisque*, c.

[Col. 0453C] 1 [Note: [Col. 0453] Eckhart added the numbers.]

Among the Germans who dwell around the Rhine, two exceedingly wealthy men, Wicmann and Balderic, contended with one another for supremacy. Wicmann, however, relied upon the favor and friendship of the king and of many Germans; the other gathered the support of a Cologne priest and likewise of Gerhard of the Moselle, a powerful man. Strengthened by these resources [Note: [Col. 0453] “Strengthened” is feminine in the manuscript.], they considered it disgraceful for either of them to yield to the other in any matter [Note: [Col. 0453] “That matter” in the manuscript.]. At times, even when peace had been made between them, they took pains to preserve not the trust of any genuine friendship but rather deceit.

Balderic married the daughter of the very wealthy and far nobler Wicmann [Note: [Col. 0453D] Count of the district of Hamaland.], whose ancestors held dominion over a large part of Germany, especially along the shores of the Ocean. Wicmann, meanwhile, some years later had taken in marriage the daughter of the prefect Godefrid [Note: [Col. 0453D] Count of the Hattuarii; cf. II, 6.], the maternal uncle of Balderic. Through these marriages both men—this one in Gaul and that one in Germany—had acquired many estates and buildings by right of dowry.

### 2. On the burning of Adela’s castle and on her character

There was formerly a time when Balderic did not even think that he had any hope of winning his wife, because she had a sister named Liutgard, abbess of Elten Mountain [Note: [Col. 0454D] Elten on the Rhine, founded by Wicmann, Liutgard’s father.]. Since Liutgard was unwilling, he did not dare inflict any insult upon his own family through a degrading marriage.

For although he had been ennobled by his position [Note: [Col. 0453] “By nobility” in witness 1.], according to the opinion of some he seemed by birth to be . . . [Note: [Col. 0453] Eckhart supplies “base,” perhaps “of ordinary rank”; see below, II, 8, p. 713]. At that time a certain Godizo as well, son of Richizo, a man of great wealth, had pledged himself, together with Balderic, to Liutgard’s patronage; they had established partnership and loyalty with one another and had obeyed her services and commands. Godizo was related to these sisters. At first he attached himself to the friendship of one of them and offered her his devotion and assistance. But when he observed her fickleness of mind and easygoing character, he withdrew from her acquaintance and joined the patronage of Lady Liutgard.

Two years afterward, because of the many injuries that Adela was inflicting upon her sister, Lady Liutgard, Godizo, having joined forces with Balderic, suddenly burst into Adela’s castle and destroyed it with plunder and fire. When Adela herself learned of their arrival, she fled shortly before midnight with a few companions. But this too is a matter greatly to be wondered at: that these sisters [Note: [Col. 0455] “Sleepers” in witness 1.], born of the most distinguished parents, could have been so different from one another that however many faults were noted in one, just so many virtues were praised in the other—unless we set against our reflections the fact that this was not remarkable, since our first ancestor likewise fathered unlike sons, one of whom, the most savage parricide, killed the other, the gentlest, out of envy.

We must pass over in silence what was said about Adela: that she was loud in voice, wanton in speech, carefully adorned in dress, disordered in mind, and that she displayed the instability of her mind through the gestures of her eyes. We do know, however, that she was skillful at many tasks, possessed great intelligence, and kept numerous chambermaids trained for producing various woven goods; in making costly garments she surpassed nearly all the women of our regions [Note: [Col. 0455D] Nearly the same words concerning the sister of Burchard, bishop of Worms, are found in his Life, chapter 12.]. This alone is the mark of humanity found in her.

### 3. On Liutgard’s character

Liutgard, however, was altogether different from her. She was renowned for honorable conduct and extraordinarily distinguished in every virtue, beyond what can be believed. She was so accustomed to hospitality that she took the greatest pleasure in the arrival of guests; and whenever they were absent—which nevertheless happened rarely—she displayed a kind of sadness in her face.

There is no need to praise her prudence, since not only from the palace but also from distant regions a great number of people gathered to seek her counsel in their affairs [Col. 0455C]. For she possessed both the highest knowledge and the truest ability to resolve the counsels she gave. Affable to all and kind to all, she also gained the greatest renown by giving many things. Thus it came about that everyone celebrated her with the highest honor.

The poor, even from foreign places, visited her continually as though she were their mother; she permitted none of them to depart from her without consolation. It is a wondrous thing that the frailty of the female sex was not burdened even for an hour by such great troubles, but rather—what is more wondrous, as I have said—took pleasure in them. Accordingly, when we often conversed among ourselves [Note: [Col. 0455] Eckhart reads “conversed”; the manuscript has “were placed.”], and considered such great humility amid her glory, I confess that even then we divined what was true: once she had died, no one of such illustrious life would remain in these regions comparable to her.

She also transferred to the church over which she presided all the patrimony that had come to her as her share of the inheritance [Note: [Col. 0455] Corrected from “through her father” to “as her share.”]. Her sister, deeply distressed by this act [Note: [Col. 0455] Corrected from “her sister-sister” to “her sister.”], repeatedly tried to rescind the transfer. But when she could not accomplish this, she plotted Liutgard’s death. After consulting with certain deadly men, they are said to have killed her with poison.

We leave this matter, of which we have learned little in proportion to the enormity of the crime, for popular opinion to chew over. But those who had prepared the poison were captured and condemned to lose their eyes [Note: [Col. 0455] Corrected from “to be beheaded” to “were captured.”].

After her death, while everyone everywhere mourned with grief and lamentation the loss of so great a woman [Note: [Col. 0455] Corrected from “sobriety” to “loss.”], her sister, raging, seized her place and turned to her own power all the patrimony that her pious sister had transferred to the church [Note: [Col. 0455] Corrected from “turned backward” to “turned to her own power.”]. But not long afterward she was expelled in disgrace by order of the emperor Otto III [Note: [Col. 0455] “Otto the Third” in witness 2.], and, considering that she should guard against these adversities, she took counsel with her followers.

After the death of her first husband, she had lived disgracefully and openly, refusing no one who desired access to her. Having long lived in wantonness as a lascivious widow [Note: [Col. 0455] Thus in Eckhart; the manuscript has “lascivious” misspelled.], according to the saying of the holy Apostle (1 Tim. 5:11), she married Balteric, whom we mentioned above, although while her sister was alive neither of them had dared even to conceive in thought a union with the other.

Not long afterward, at her instigation, he suddenly occupied Elten Mountain with an armed force [Note: [Col. 0455] “Etna” in witness 1; “Elten” in witness 2.]. When the townspeople, struck by sudden fear, sought safety in flight, they hid themselves in the monastery. After the monastery had been stormed, and arrows had been shot through the altars, he took captive one man whom he wished to be regarded as his enemy.

But when the king learned of this and was deeply angered by the deed, Balteric’s offense was expiated with money through the assistance of intercessors. The king, however, wishing by a deeper plan to secure the future stability of that place, summoned a council at Nijmegen (18 May 997). Since people came there in great numbers from every direction, he decided that the matter of the aforementioned place should be examined.

Balteric was present with his wife, because the senators had reached the decision that, once convicted, he should, according to the law, be permanently excluded from making any further claim against that church. Thus they secured the stability of the place by charter and privilege [Note: [Col. 0456D] On this matter, see the emperor’s charter in Schaten, Annales Paderbornenses I, 343.].

### 4. On Otto’s death and Balderic’s deceptions

After these events, the emperor Otto III, a young man of good character, died in Italy, and his body was carried to Aachen, where he was buried with royal honor (1002). After his death, Balteric broke faith and, attacking with hostile forces, went against Elten Mountain, tore apart the rampart that surrounded the church like a castle, and compelled the entire household to serve him.

### 5. On King Henry [Note: [Col. 0455] “Henry” in the manuscript at this place.]

When Henry had obtained supreme power, he restored that place once again to its former condition. There would be enough for us to write many splendid things about this man: how easily, by the gift of God’s favor [Note: [Col. 0457] “Granting” in the manuscript.], he reached the summit of kingship [Note: [Col. 0457] “The summit” is misspelled in the manuscript.]; how he compelled illustrious and very powerful men, who were stirring up wars against him, to submit through swift victory; how he made tributaries subject to his rule the kings in the interior regions of Germany who are called Wends [Note: [Col. 0457] This clause is absent in the manuscript but present in Sigebert under the year 1003]; how he devastated Metz in Belgica, which had long been plotting evil against him and had been besieged for many years, nearly to destruction [Note: [Col. 0457] The manuscript has “destruction” in a defective form.] (perhaps 1012), and finally subjugated it after inflicting many hardships upon it.

But since Lord Adelbold, bishop of Utrecht, has fully covered all these events in a single volume written in elegant style, the portion that occasionally necessarily arises in our writings seemed best omitted by us, lest a history produced with such great and beautiful instruction be obscured by us, as though by the barking of an ignorant man.

### 6. On the appearance of a comet, famine, and mortality

Three years after the king had been raised to the throne, a comet of dreadful appearance was seen in the southern part of the sky, casting flames this way and that. In the following year, an exceedingly severe famine and mortality occurred throughout the whole world (1005), so that in many places, because of the multitude of the dead and the weariness of those burying them, living people who still drew breath and resisted as best they could [Note: [Col. 0457] The manuscript has “relented” or “sent back.”] were overwhelmed together with the dead.

### 7. On Wecelin the apostate

In those same days, namely in the reign of King Henry, who afterward became emperor through apostolic blessing, a certain Wecelin, who had been cleric to Duke Conrad, was led astray by diabolical deception and assented to the error of the Jews.

When the king heard this, he was moved, as was just, by exceedingly great agitation. At his command, one of his disciples named Henry—bearing the same name as the king—defeated the aforesaid apostate with the most truthful testimonies of Holy Scripture, as his letter states, proving that he had spoken false words against Christ and his saints. Since this matter has been extended at some length, we have decided to place it at the end of this little book (Book II, chapters 22–23).

### 8. On the arrival of the Northmen [Note: [Col. 0457] “Normans” in witness 1.]

Wicmann, having married the prefect’s daughter, as we said above, resolved to obey her in all things and to preserve faith and friendship with her [Note: [Col. 0457] “Friendship” in the manuscript.]. Frequently invited by one another to banquets [Note: [Col. 0457] “Invited” in witness E; “summoned” in the manuscript.], they had made their interests common.

When the prefect had already been worn down by old age and was so weakened by illness [Note: [Col. 0457] The manuscript has “perfected.”] that he could scarcely walk, pirates from various islands [Note: [Col. 0457] Corrected from “places” to “islands.”] of the Ocean appeared with a great multitude of ships. Carried swiftly along the river Merwede [Note: [Col. 0457] Today the Merwede, a branch of the Rhine or Waal.], they reached the port of Tiel [Note: [Col. 0458D] On the right bank of the Waal.] (1006).

The people who lived along the banks of the river Waal, having learned of the arrival of such a multitude, placed all their hope of safety in flight and left nearly everything they possessed, except their money—for they were merchants—to complete strangers.

The prudent prefect, fearing that the fields, left without inhabitants, would offer the enemy an easier entrance, mounted a horse as best he could and scarcely restrained the fleeing people. The enemy came as far as Tiel, lowered their sails, entered the harbor without resistance, and found a large supply of food. After quickly carrying it away, they devastated the village with fire.

They also broke into the monastery of Saint Walburga. They carried away the sacred vestments placed there by a certain Count Waltger, the founder of the place, and his wife Alberada, worthy of God [Note: [Col. 0457] “Worthy” in the manuscript.]. After stripping the altar and carrying away many other ecclesiastical goods, they left the church unharmed and returned to their fleet.

Immediately, when the prefect had sent messengers in every direction, a very large multitude assembled early the next morning. Since the prefect could not command the army, the war was entrusted to Balteric, whom we mentioned above, and also to Count Unruoch [Note: [Col. 0457] Thus Eckhart correctly emended the text from chapter 16; the manuscript has room for only the syllable *un*.], a vigorous man who, in the army of the emperor Otto III, was considered highly renowned in military affairs in Italy.

When the enemy saw our forces and their swift arrival, they were terrified. They loosened their ships as quickly as possible and withdrew, so that their retreat appeared like a flight. Our men pursued them and, engaging in light skirmishes on both banks of the river, wounded or killed only a few on either side [Note: [Col. 0457] Thus Eckhart; the manuscript has “each.”], while preventing the enemy, in their greed for plunder, from wandering farther from the bank.

After burning the villages near the shore that they were able to reach [Note: [Col. 0457] “Shore” in witness 2.], at the ninth hour of the day they all leapt from their ships and drew up a very tightly packed battle line [Note: [Col. 0457] The manuscript has “very tightly packed” in a defective form.], offering our men the opportunity to fight [Note: [Col. 0457] The manuscript has “our” for “our men.”].

Our men, however, held their position. Since most had been compelled to come from the countryside, and those gathered with them were inexperienced in warfare and harassed by the poverty caused by the previous year’s barrenness, they did not dare to engage in battle.

When the barbarians saw that no one was advancing to fight, they considered that they had done enough to display their courage, returned to their ships, and withdrew without anyone preventing them.

### 9. On the second arrival of the Northmen

[Col. 0458D]

In the following year (1007), some pirates again came with ninety longships by way of the river Lek [Note: [Col. 0458D] The Lek.]. Our men immediately assembled a large force of cavalry and infantry and a few ships [Note: [Col. 0457] “And” in the manuscript.], and, drawn up along the bank with their weapons, awaited the enemy’s arrival.

When the first barbarians saw such a large multitude, they were thrown into confusion. Anchoring their ships in the middle of the river channel, they decided to wait for the others. After they had gathered together and exchanged opinions among themselves, they did not dare to cross in the face of our men. They sent envoys to them, asking that they be allowed to pass through their territory; they said that they intended to go without injury or wrongdoing and begged that they might be permitted to do so with the others’ peace and authorization.

After this permission had been obtained [Note: [Col. 0459] “After it had been obtained” in Eckhart.], they were allowed to pass that day in peace.

On the following day, when they had moved their fleet and the first ships had already entered the Rhine, our men, with a few ships, attacked the last vessels amid a great shout and began to challenge them to battle [Note: [Col. 0459] The manuscript has “to grow weary” in two forms.]. When the others heard the shout, they hurriedly came to the rescue and, stationing armed men along the bank, terrified our men so that they did not dare approach.

After the interval of the night had passed, all our men had been transported across the river, and at dawn a false report reached those of our men who were in the ships [Note: [Col. 0459] This is the manuscript’s construction, peculiar to it.]—namely, that the cavalry had engaged the enemy in a great battle and that some ships had already been plundered [Note: [Col. 0459] “Had reached them” in the manuscript.]—they left nothing undone in their haste.

Filling everything with tumult and shouting, without a commander or any fixed order, each advancing toward the enemy as quickly as he seemed able, they approached them. When the enemy saw this, they gathered into one mass and came to meet them.

But our men who were in the ships, seeing that the Northmen had come against them with their strength intact, abandoned the ships and threw themselves headlong into flight. The enemy pursued them and killed as many in that flight as they were able to overtake.

### 10. On the burning of Utrecht harbor

[Col. 0459C]

The people of Utrecht, informed of the arrival of the barbarians [Note: [Col. 0459] “Utrecht” in the manuscript.], burned the entire harbor themselves, lest it provide the enemy with convenience or assistance for besieging the castle.

After the harbor had been burned, the barbarians complained that such harm had been inflicted. They said that they were planning no evil against the place, especially since Ausfrid, a man of such holiness, was its bishop.

Nevertheless, they asked to be admitted into the castle for religious purposes; they claimed that they wished to venerate the churches with their offerings. The townspeople, assuming a composed expression and standing firm, replied that they could not grant armed men access.

Although the place would have been very easy to capture, they recognized that the holy site and so great a priest might otherwise resist their fortunes. They therefore departed without inflicting any injury upon the city.

Who would not attribute this to the merits of the holy bishop: that the townspeople, contrary to hope, were freed from fear, escaped danger, and preserved that place inviolate? Since this holy man appears in our writings, I am pleased to insert a few things about his life into this work.

### 11. On the blessed Count Ansfrid

Ansfrid was count in the territory of Brabant [Note: [Col. 0459D] Brabant.], a man of the highest justice, so that neither gifts nor presents [Note: [Col. 0459] “Transitory gifts” in witness 3.] could in any way turn him aside from the path of righteousness.

Frequently in councils and assemblies, the judgments sought above all from him were awaited; everyone hung upon his words, and no one was permitted to contradict the decrees of law that he established.

His speech was so tempered with moderation and discretion that it did not exceed the saying of our comic poet [Terence, *Andria* I.1.34]: “Nothing in excess.” This too must be added: from the moderation of his words, his hearers could easily understand the order and integrity hidden in his heart.

Whatever he said in continual and daily conversation [Note: [Col. 0459] “What” is absent in witness 1.], he seasoned gently and mildly with examples from the divine Scriptures. Whenever he happened to be free from secular business, he either considered righteous judgments [Note: [Col. 0459] “Legal judgments” in witness 3.] or devoted himself so earnestly to reading that certain foolish people mocked him as though he were living a monastic life.

This should be considered less surprising because the more eagerly holy men attend to divine works in meditation, the more contemptible they become to the world; and, so that their patience may be tested, they are often dishonored by wicked people with God’s permission, as the secretary of the Holy Spirit testifies, saying: “You have made me a reproach to the fool” (Ps. 38:9).

Great and illustrious men also, whenever some difficult matter had to be debated in the administration of justice, when different people—as commonly happens—held different opinions and judgments seemed to vary, turned to him to learn and ask questions [Note: [Col. 0459] “Sought” in witness 1; “came” in witness 3.].

He was also very frequently present at the emperor’s private councils. Whenever major matters had to be considered, he was held in such authority and dignity [Note: [Col. 0459] “He was regarded as a man of such authority” in witness 3.] that rarely was anything decided without his advice.

He had established this for himself at every age and set this before himself: unlike certain men of our time [Note: [Col. 0459] “Certain” in witness 3.], whom we often see slip from judgment either through pity or envy, he diminished nothing of the truth of right and law [Note: [Col. 0459] “To diminish” in witness 3.].

For these reasons [Note: [Col. 0459] “For this reason” in witness 3.] he was frequently summoned by the king and held dearer than others. By his counsel he restrained the wicked and governed the commonwealth [Note: [Col. 0459] The manuscript reads: “and through him governed the kingdom in peace”; witness 3 has the same.].

He was exceedingly hostile to robbers, by whom the region of Brabant [Note: [Col. 0459] “Brabant” in witness 3.] was especially nourished, and by frequent attacks he thwarted their attempts [Note: [Col. 0459] “Their attempt” in witness 3.].

He also pressed their leader, a desperate man whose name need not even be mentioned [Note: [Col. 0459] “Nor” in witness 3.], nurtured on the blood of citizens [Note: [Col. 0459] “Nurtured on civic blood” in witness 3; the middle of the sentence is missing.], and scarcely escaping through frequent flight. Whenever that man wished to evade the immediate danger, he hid himself either in thickets or in dense marshes overgrown with trees.

He won many victories and waged many wars successfully—not for the destruction of citizens but to restrain the audacity of wrongdoers. Such were the deeds of his lay life.

### 12. How Count Ansfrid became bishop

When Baltwin [Note: [Col. 0461] “Balduin” in witness 3.], the priest of Utrecht, departed this life (995), and the messenger had come to the camp, the king took Ansfrid aside by the hand and began to offer him that priesthood.

When Ansfrid resisted and argued that, now an old man who had spent the whole period of his life in military arms, it seemed altogether absurd for him to undertake clerical duties, the king pressed him strongly and compelled him by force to accept. Realizing [Note: [Col. 0461] “Foreseeing” in witness 3.] that he could not resist the king, Ansfrid asked permission to deliberate on the matter with his companions.

After this was granted and he had received counsel from his companions, he promised that he would do what the king commanded. He took the sword with which he had been girded and placed it upon the altar of Saint Mary, saying:

“Until now I have held this earthly honor and driven away the enemies of Christ’s poor and of widows. From now on I commend myself to this, my lady, Saint Mary, by whose power I may obtain honor and the salvation of my soul” [Note: [Col. 0461] “This honor” in witness 3; “my soul” in witness 3.].

As he said this, tears rising in the eyes of all, the pontifical mitre was bestowed upon him amid the applause of everyone present, in keeping with his worthy merits [Note: [Col. 0461] “With applause” in witness 3.].

One of our men composed verses about these events. I have been pleased to weave them into this little work, so that we might have another witness to our narrative [Note: [Col. 0461] “To attach” in witness 3; “also” in witness 3.].

### 13. Verses on the same matter

O blessed Utrecht, mother chosen above all places,

now you retain a lord who has won universal praise.

Ansfrid, for his merits, is your pontifical glory [Note: [Col. 0461] “Given” in witness 3.],

and he is chosen for the Lord as a gracious and holy confessor.

He who formerly strengthened kingdoms for the people in war

is now the holy priest and guardian of the Church.

Thus the practice of combat is turned, yes, turned to something better:

formerly a warrior, now a lover of peace;

then a participant in wars, now a leader of souls;

formerly he fought, now he governs the hearts of the people;

the soldier’s duty has fallen silent, replaced by prayer.

Now wholly freed from arms in the priest’s vestment,

he took the chalice in his hands and laid aside the sword.

He put down the shield and began to raise the paten [Note: [Col. 0461] “Began” in witness 3; “to wash” in the manuscript.];

he despised the standard, because he wished to chant the Mass [Note: [Col. 0461] “The standard” in witness 3.];

now he sings the Mass and faithfully devotes himself to prayers.

He does these things without hesitation after the example of Peter,

who first sang the Mass and shaved his beard.

Whatever God wishes to come, all things immediately stand ready [Note: [Col. 0461] “Are present” in witness 3.];

here God made a sheep from a dog, as once he did,

when he drew Paul to himself from the lot of wolves,

and afterward commanded him to be a teacher of the Church.

Now he is clothed in white [Note: [Col. 0461] “Taken away” in witness 3.], glorified with his emblem,

and he bears the stole, administering the weapons of virtue,

he who formerly prevailed through many dangers in war.

The glory of the shepherd resounds sweetly in his speech!

### 14. On Ansfrid’s blindness, monastic life, and almsgiving

After assuming the episcopate, he for some time wore canonical clothing—not out of pride, but lest he appear to differ from the conduct of the other priests through suspicion of disdain [Note: [Col. 0461] This sentence is written twice in the manuscript.].

But since the merciful Lord had now called him to his service and entrusted him with the care of the Church, he resolved, in his accustomed and fuller kindness, to draw him still closer to himself.

For although it is impossible for anyone’s life [Note: [Col. 0461] “Of any saint” in witness 3.] to pass without sins, yet those faults that are heedlessly contracted through the frailty of the flesh are customarily cleansed in this world by some bodily affliction, through the abundant mercy of God [Note: [Col. 0461] Absent in witness 3.], as Scripture testifies when it says: “The Lord chastises every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12:6).

Ansfrid lost the light of these shadows [Col. 0462B] in such a way that, while the integrity of his eyes remained, he seemed to see no less than someone who was looking [Note: [Col. 0461] “Seeing and thinking that he saw” in witness 3.]. He endured the failure of sight [Note: [Col. 0461] “Of sight in himself” in witness 2.], but no disfigurement dishonored the man’s face.

I believe this was done through the kindness of our Savior so that, with the desire of the eyes extinguished and the occasion for sin removed, he might preserve the dignity of a bishop’s countenance and thereafter have nothing further to desire.

Nor was he ever overcome or cast down in spirit by this affliction. Rather, with the same expression, the same cheerfulness, and the same joy, he remained with the greatest patience.

Accordingly, returning more earnestly to consideration of God, a saving thought came to him: that the flowers of this world appear as filth before God, and that those things sought at great expense for the adornment of decaying flesh belong not only to harm [Note: [Col. 0461] Absent in witness 3.] but also to the eternal ruin of the soul [Note: [Col. 0461] Absent in witness 3.].

He put aside his more delicate clothing and assumed garments—not, I should say [Note: [Col. 0461] “I should not say” in witness 3.], mean, but rather angelic—in accordance with the institution of Saint Benedict.

There is a hill six miles from Utrecht [Note: [Col. 0461] In the manuscript: “Heilgenberg,” three miles, in witness 3.], later called Heiligenberg [Note: [Col. 0461D] Hohorst, later Heiligenberg, near Amersfoort.]. It is enclosed on every side: on one side a muddy river, and around the remaining area an uninterrupted and very broad marsh, shutting out every approach.

He had a small boat brought there and ordered himself to be carried across that river. Because he wished to avoid the tumult of people for the sake of prayer, he cleared the summit of the hill into a level place by cutting down the trees and bushes. First he built an oratory, then a cell for himself; afterward, once other buildings had been constructed and a cloister established, he placed a small community of monks there [Note: [Col. 0461] “A convent” in witness 3.] and appointed an abbot [Note: [Col. 0461] “And appointed an abbot over them” in witness 3.] [Note: [Col. 0462D] The foundation charter is printed as document V in the *Acta Sanctorum*, May I, 430.].

After audiences with the king, after synods, and after various assemblies, he used to withdraw there. Here he removed from himself the wretched burden of secular business and devoted all his strength to the praises and service of God. He was so intent upon prayers, vigils, and almsgiving that no one of our age could be compared with him.

We shall recount one of the innumerable acts of generosity that he showed to Christ’s poor. While he was staying in the very cell we have mentioned, after completing the customary work of God, following the third vigil he called one of his servants to him, showed him what he wished to be done, and strictly forbade anyone to learn of it.

He took a bucket, inserted a pole, and ordered the servant, carrying him as well, to go ahead and guide his steps to the river. Having drawn water, he returned [Note: [Col. 0463] The manuscript has “he returned”; witness 3 adds “he heated.”], warmed it with fire, and himself poured it into a tub. He stripped a leper whose body was entirely covered by miserable foul matter, placed him in the bath, carefully washed his decaying limbs with his hands [Note: [Col. 0463] “Diligently” in witness 3.], and, once washed, placed him in his own little bed [Note: [Col. 0463] “Bed” in witness 3.]. After clothing him in new garments, he ordered him to depart before dawn, under oath that no one should know of it [Note: [Col. 0463] “To leave” in witness 3.].

If you ask why so great a man, endowed with so many virtues and watered by the grace of the Holy Spirit, did not confer upon that leper the consolation of healing, I shall meet these thoughts easily with the following answer.

### 15. Why Ansfrid did not heal the sick

For we read (1 Cor. 14:22) that signs were given to unbelievers, not to believers [Note: [Col. 0463] “Are given,” with the addition “therefore,” in witness 3.], so that at the beginning of the Church’s birth the hearts of the Gentiles, hardened by the very long practice of idolatry, might be softened toward belief [Note: [Col. 0463] Thus in witness 3; the manuscript has “toward growth.”] when they saw so many wonders.

For who, at that time, when the world stood in the full bloom of its prosperity, would have believed someone preaching another life unless things were displayed that had never before been seen or heard [Col. 0463C]? And what need was there in these last times [Note: [Col. 0463] “Our times” in witness 3.] for the Church of God to be glorified by signs, when there is no place among any peoples—no mountain, no valley, no boundless forest, no immense marsh, no island removed from the inhabited world [Note: [Col. 0463] Thus I have corrected the manuscript’s corrupt reading; the order is reversed in witness 3, and Eckhart conjectures a different form.]—that is not filled with the confession of our Lord Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 0463] The manuscript repeats part of the word “filled.”]?

The man of God did not wish to be raised up by empty human praise. He always strove to conceal within his conscience what good he had done, so that it might be known to God alone [Note: [Col. 0463] Corrected from “did not wish” to “strove.” At this point witness 3 ends.].

Perhaps that leper’s illness was useful to him, so that the weakness of his body might prevent him from repeating what he had committed unlawfully through human frailty [Note: [Col. 0463] Thus in Eckhart; the manuscript has “debts.”].

No one should doubt the holiness of this man, whom even demons confessed. I heard a certain possessed man, while confessing various crimes, add this as well: that he had frequently slandered that holy bishop without cause and had said many shameful things about him while holy religion held him in its embrace; but that he had no charge against him except envy, for the exercise of his own wickedness.

Yet the wretched man, a few days later, while the others were asleep, took his own life by hanging.

I have touched on these matters briefly, lest anyone suppose in his heart that, because of the failure of a proven life, our Lord Jesus Christ was unwilling to grant his servant the power of signs—he who granted him much greater and far more blessed things, namely eternal life in the heavenly kingdom.

### 16. On the death of Bishop Ansfrid
Therefore, when he perceived that the weakness of his strength was increasing and that his body was declining toward its end through illness, he ordered himself to be transferred to the hill mentioned above. While he was there oppressed for some time by the force of his disease, he gave back his spirit to our Redeemer, whom he had served (in the year 1010). Present at his funeral were his venerable daughter, [Col. 0464B] abbess of the monastery of Thorn [Note: [Col. 0463D] Thorn lies on the left bank of the Meuse, above Roermond], and his kinsman, Count Unruoch, of whom we spoke above (chap. 8). His little body was placed in the oratory and regularly attended by the brethren’s offices, with the intention that on the following day it should be buried in that very church, as they had firmly resolved.

Meanwhile, the people of Utrecht had gathered in the greatest numbers and were trying to carry away the dead body [Note: [Col. 0463] thus witness c, i.e. after a procession had been made; *exanime* in E] to be taken to Utrecht. To accomplish this, they prostrated themselves before God in the church beside the bier and prayed with all their groans for his help. Then suddenly, on one side of the hill, a workshop was seized by fire, whether by accident or by God’s command. While everyone rushed to extinguish the fire and was wholly occupied with that matter, the people of Utrecht gently lifted the bier on which the body of the man of God lay and proceeded as far as the river. [Col. 0464C] They placed it in a little boat and began to cross the river. Since the boat could hold only a few, the others followed as long as the ford allowed [Note: [Col. 0463] so E.; *vasum* in witness 1], and thereafter by swimming.

But those who had rushed to put out the fire did not notice their plan until afterward. Although only a very short distance separated them from the point at which the others were drawing the boat toward the opposite bank, they took up their arms and prepared to frustrate what they were attempting. There the abbess whom we mentioned above, with outstretched hands and prostrate on the ground, scarcely obtained by her prayers that they should not pursue those who were departing. Who would not also attribute this to the merits of the blessed man: that armed men, raging in spirit, were so easily calmed, and that the rustic multitude, obstructed while crossing the river, escaped both danger and death?

Thus, both parties, joined together in complete tranquility, carried the very light burden as far as the Rhine with psalms and hymns, and placed it in a ship prepared for this purpose. They reached Utrecht. When the body was brought ashore, it was honored by the gathering of the people and by great offerings; on the following day it was reverently buried in the church [Col. 0465A] of Saint Martin, where he had held the episcopal seat.

These are the things I had to say about the blessed man—not in order to gather completely everything about him that deserved to be commended to memory, but so that this little work, although foolishly composed, might be illuminated by the material of his life as by the sun.

## 17. On the detractors of Bishop Ansfrid

But I would still like to ask where those men are now who used to tear apart Ansfrid’s life with poisonous tongues, wickedly accusing him of having afflicted himself with starvation, and declaring in their pestilential attacks [Note: [Col. 0465] written twice in witness c.] that his withered body had never, amid the great abundance of his bishopric, been refreshed even by a modest meal.

O profane men, glorying only in the fullness of their bellies! O that none of them could be found occupied in such a way of life [Note: [Col. 0465] *ocupatum* in witness c.]! O barren of every form of piety, who, conscious of no virtue in yourselves, envy holy men what you yourselves cannot attain!

I openly admit that he often suffered from fasting, not from starvation, as his detractors barked about in their workshops; and that, wholly turned toward God, he passed the pestilential hissing of the Sirens by with deaf ears. But when we see that many of these detractors have been expelled from their homes by divine judgment, have lost estates, villages, and buildings because their cultivators were gone, and have long begged from other people’s thresholds—or have shamefully acquired their food by theft or robbery—we recognize what became of them.

## 18. Also concerning a certain detractor

I heard one of our faithful report that one of these wretched men, while heated with wine in taverns, mocked the holy man and then burst out with this further miserable utterance: that the human soul was nothing and that, in the final breath, it completely vanished into the air.

Because he did not wish to know God, and moreover did not fear to attack God’s servants with obscene words, God gave him over to a reprobate mind, so that he might do and say things that were unfitting. Thus it also happened that he was handed over to the power whose prompting had led him to act in this way.

For, although some time was granted him for repentance, he did not recover his senses. One day, as usual serving his appetite, he returned home near sunset, as though to satisfy a renewed hunger, and prolonged his banquet far into the night [Note: [Col. 0465] *pertraxit* in witness c.]. At last, loaded with the desired food, he lay down in his bed and joined sleep to sudden death.

He was thrown out for burial and thrust into a large tomb. But when the upper stone was placed over his greatly distended belly and compressed it, the fattest grease poured around through the lips of the tomb, though the skin remained intact—shame upon it! If you had been present, unable to bear the stench, you would have blocked your nostrils with your garment.

But why say so much about a man whose memory ought rather to be passed over than recalled? Clearly, because you see that he was a wretched man who, even in the final period of his life, refused to restrain his tongue from slandering the holy man. At the end of the world, when he sees his glory, he will say:

> “This is the man whom I once held in derision and as an object of reproach. I, senseless as I was, regarded his life as madness and his end as dishonorable. Behold how he has been counted among the sons of God, and his lot is among the holy.”

Let those who serve only carnal desire and pursued the man of God with a similar envy hear this. When they have seen the end of both men, let them receive an example of whom they ought rather to imitate. Let them remember that one of them, not rich in very great resources but running daily from house to house, filling his belly now with threats, now with wretched mockery, finally gave his salvation to the world and his hope to the tomb, like a beast with a fattened carcass.

The other, although every abundance of good things was available to him and he deprived himself of nearly everything for the use of the poor, brought his fruitful labor to completion through the grace bestowed by God. For him, as long as he lived, to live was Christ and to die was gain.

We, meanwhile, while journeying along the road of our narrative, have looked upon pleasant meadows and have not uselessly turned aside from the path. Gazing around at the most beautiful places, we have lingered for a while; and, not yet satisfied with the fragrance of the sweetest flowers, we will often look back as we try to complete the journey we began.

[Col. 0465] **HERE ENDS BOOK I.**

**BOOK II BEGINS.**

## 1. On the conflict between Baldric and Wicmann [Note: [Col. 0465] *wincmani* in witness c.]

After the affairs of the prefects Godefrid and Wicmann had come together in a pact of friendship, and each thought that this arrangement would thereafter provide him with sufficient protection, the prefect died. The prefecture was transferred to his son because of his father’s integrity and because of the exceptional care in counsel by which he had always distinguished himself.

But since he was sluggish, devoid of counsel, and almost entirely without strength, he deliberately resolved to preserve the agreement of friendship that Wicmann had sworn to his father, hoping that, if he had him as an ally, he could easily dominate all his own people. From that time hostility arose between him and Baldric (in the year 1011). Although neither would tolerate the other’s superiority, they nevertheless met with one another frequently and maintained a friendship clouded by suspicion [Note: [Col. 0465] *amiticia* in witness c., frequently].

But Wicmann was hindered in this undertaking by the fact that he did not possess in Gaul the same abundance of estates as Baldric, although he himself held broad territories in Germany and had nothing on this side of the Rhine except what he had received with his wife [Col. 0467A]—yet even this could not be matched with the other’s resources. Therefore, after binding certain people from across the Rhine to himself through familiarity, he explained to them what his plan was [Note: [Col. 0467D] namely, Wicmann].

## 2. On Wicmann’s castle [Note: [Col. 0467] *WINCMANNI* in witness c.] captured by Baldric, and on the fortification of Munna [Note: [Col. 0467] the word is missing, with space left]

There is a marshy pond two hundred paces distant from the river Meuse. Beneath it was a small hill, difficult of access—for it could not be reached at all except by boat, because of the depth of the pond and the obstruction of the marsh. It seemed to offer a man intent on revolution an opportunity to build a castle.

Having learned of this place through friends, Wicmann approached it with ships brought there. After inspecting it, he immediately compelled a large number of armed men, summoned peasants from everywhere, dug a ditch around it, and made the site considerably higher. He surrounded it with a rampart and, raising towers, completed a sufficiently strong fortification. Then, not without arrogance, he ordered the neighboring people to bring supplies to the stronghold. He placed as guards the very men who had given him the advice to build it. He regarded the place as highly suitable for retaining the prefecture in the future and for more easily suppressing Baldric if he attempted anything.

When Baldric heard this, he was greatly disturbed and considered his fortunes to be in extreme danger. He did not doubt that, unless he took the greatest care to forestall these adversities, he would lose the highest honor of his dignity. Accordingly, after summoning his dependents, of whom he had a great number, and sending messengers in every direction, he gathered together Lantbert [Col. 0467C] [Note: [Col. 0467] *lanttbertum* in witness c.], whom we mentioned above, Gerhard, whose singular friendship he had enjoyed, and his other friends. In their presence he explained what was being prepared against him.

After examining the matter [Note: [Col. 0467] *incognita* in witness 1; *cognita* in witness 2], they declared that they would support whatever course he decided upon. After thanking them generously, and at their urging and desire, he approached the fortification [Note: [Col. 0467] *accedit* in witness 1; *accessit* in witness 2] and besieged it insofar as the position of the marsh permitted. Nature did not allow him to surround the whole place, because the inlet of the pond extended farther out.

The townsmen, however, certain that a missile could neither be driven against them across such a distance nor returned from them, kept themselves safely within the rampart and awaited the outcome. But when the attackers discovered that they could not cross by a ford anywhere, they began to build a bridge. Since they persisted in this work for a long time, yet the labor of the workers could produce no result because of the immense quantity of water, they abandoned the attempt [Note: [Col. 0467] *destituerunt* in witness c.].

Finally, they brought in cargo ships, yoked animals, and prepared to drag the ships into the pond, so that they might construct machines upon the ships, approach the fortification, and begin the battle. After spending several days on these works, those inside the stronghold, despairing that they would be freed from the siege by their lord and fearing that, if defeated, they would be treated more harshly—and since their provisions had already begun to fail—sent envoys to Baldric to negotiate surrender.

When he learned their demands, Baldric ordered them to burn and destroy with their own hands the very fortification they had built. When this had been done, he allowed them to depart unharmed with all that belonged to them.

After these matters had been settled, Wicmann, despairing of resisting the strength of his enemies, secretly crossed the Rhine and raised the castle of Munna higher with an embankment and towers. Since it stood upon a mountain, he fortified it so effectively that it could be taken only by siege.

The enemy, however, devastated the villages and neighboring places with frequent raids, by plunder and often by slaughter, so that they would be of no use to the men in the castle.

Baldric’s cause was also helped by the fact that he still enjoyed considerable favor with the emperor [Note: [Col. 0467] *utebantur* corrected to *utebatur* in witness c.]. He also secured the assistance of the priest of Cologne and of Lord Bishop Adelbold, who was held by the celebrated reputation of all our age to be the wisest of men and, in the Latin tongue, by far the most eloquent, as well as a man of the greatest intellectual power.

Gerhard of the Moselle and Lantbert, whom we mentioned above, also declared that they would endure every hardship and danger with him. These two were always prepared to stir up every disturbance and revolt.

## 3. On Aspola [Note: [Col. 0468D] Perhaps Spel, at the confluence of the Rhine and the Lippe] besieged by Bishop Adelbold

After this, an occasion arose on which Lord Adelbold, priest of Utrecht, went to the emperor’s camp. Having accomplished what he had come for, he was carried back by ship along the Rhine [Col. 0468C]. His horses, however, were being led back by his men along the bank of that same river near Aspola. The retainers of Godizo, because they favored Wicmann’s party, intercepted them and distributed them among themselves.

The bishop was necessarily angered by this and, wishing to remedy these injuries as quickly as possible, joined all his forces [Note: [Col. 0467] written twice in witness 1] with Baldric’s. Coming unexpectedly, he besieged Aspola on one side. On the other side it was inaccessible because a marsh and pond lay between them.

Although the two sides fought fiercely for several days and attempted every measure in their effort to storm the place, they could accomplish nothing because of the strength of the site and the height of the towers. When they saw that they were laboring in vain and that their hope of taking the stronghold was slipping away, and also because it was said [Note: [Col. 0467] *dicebantur* in witness 1] that the enemy had arrived with an army [Col. 0468D], they abandoned the assault and withdrew to their own positions.

The bishop, however, for these reasons—because before the siege Godizo had sent envoys to him to seek peace and had promised to make satisfaction in every way for all the injuries inflicted upon him by his men, although the bishop suspected that he was speaking deceitfully and therefore had been unwilling to offer any terms of peace; because he considered that his grief had already been sufficiently expiated by the devastation of the fields and villages; and because he thought that the enemy had already returned to his senses—withdrew from this storm of revolt and began quietly to await the outcome of the affair. Nevertheless, he always gave Baldric his attention and assistance.

## 4. On the peace made between Baldric and Wicmann

After Munna had been built and strengthened, Wicmann resisted more boldly and increased the hopes of his men. Often arriving unexpectedly against the enemy, he put them to flight. But after the enmity between them had continued for a long time, homicides had occurred, ambushes had been laid by both sides, and each had driven the other into flight, at last both were summoned by the king to his camp.

After their cases had been discussed for a long time, and the king could not, without offending many people, show greater favor to either of them in effecting a reconciliation, he ordered them by royal authority to maintain peace with one another. After the peace had been confirmed by an oath, they departed.

Wicmann, thinking that the matter had been placed in a more favorable condition and suspecting no further danger, was preparing to visit the threshold of Saint Peter for the sake of prayer. After gathering what he needed for the journey, he set out for Rome.

While he was on this journey, Baldric’s wife, unable to endure peace and always inclined to stir up novelties, addressed her husband in these words:

## 5. Adela’s speech, Baldric’s wife

“I cannot bear this Saxon as our neighbor, living so close to our buildings; and I do not wish to live if I see him, whom I cannot tolerate as your equal, become your superior. Therefore, I beg you, follow my advice and, setting aside your other concerns, store my words in your mind; for from this you may become the most fortunate of men.

“Look: this enemy of ours, seeing that your nephew is without knowledge or counsel, deceives him day after day with false flatteries and, against your will, has already invaded your dignity. In the end, that fool thinks that he, brought in by true kinship, sincerely favors his interests, rather than doing this so that he may overthrow him in the neighboring principality and, through his excessive cunning, seize his place himself.

“Who could doubt that he has long been plotting wickedly against you? If I were a man, would I allow him to remain in these regions? And if now, after peace has been made, no just opportunity presents itself by which you can contend with him openly, do at least this: approach the king and demand the prefecture, which belongs to you more justly by the line of your kinship and the ancestry of your forefathers. If the enemy stirs up any disturbance against you on this account, he himself will first be at fault, and you, bound by oath, will not be held responsible.

“What stands in your way? What prevents you? Your most distinguished household, your broadest estates, and your numerous soldiers will give you strength and favor, and no one will be more worthy than you of this honor. You will also have no lack of gifts to distribute—gold, silver, and precious clothing. I will give everything without hesitation.”

Desire easily persuades, and, like men who cannot be filled with honors, he undertakes the business—not only to the damage of his domestic affairs but also to the lasting ruin of his salvation. Although serious causes of anger had already existed between them, this became the fuel and beginning of the destruction of both. As Jezebel did with Ahab, so she continually incited him to crimes, giving him advice that he would use to his own ruin, until he became hateful and detestable to everyone.

## 6. On the prefecture given to Baldric

After preparing for his journey, Baldric came to the king, by whom he was kindly received. He presented the things he had brought, explained the reasons for his arrival, and brought the king around to his own opinion.

In the end, the prefecture was given to him, and the strictest prohibition was issued lest civil dissensions arise from this, by which arms might be taken up. As soon as he returned, he occupied the little fortress of Gennep [Note: [Col. 0469] Gennep, at the confluence of the Niers and the Meuse, in the district of the Hattuarii] belonging to his kinsman, the prefect. Through a fugitive servant, who had long before pledged himself to the men in the tower and promised his support, he was introduced by deceit. He expelled the men whom his neighbor had left to guard the tower and placed his own garrison there.

## 7. On the reconciliation of Bishop Adelbold and Wicmann

When it was reported publicly among the people that Baldric had approached the king, seized the prefecture for himself, and invaded the tower at Gennep, such a sudden change took place in everyone that the minds not only of the neighboring people but also of his household were turned so far against him [Note: [Col. 0469] *everterentur* in witness c.] that few remained who did not detest his actions [Note: [Col. 0469] so Eckhart; *detarentur* in witness c.].

While Wicmann was returning across the Alps, he was informed of what had happened and was deeply troubled, wondering what remedy he could find for this misfortune. Fear of the emperor prevented him from beginning the matter openly with arms; therefore he decided that a plan and method had to be sought through courage of spirit.

While he was troubled by these thoughts, an opportunity perfectly suited to his purpose arose. He had heard that all the people were murmuring against Baldric and detesting his actions with every prayer. He therefore decided first to work toward this: he would withdraw from Baldric the assistance of Lord Bishop Adelbold, so that he would have no further hope of taking refuge with him; he would join the bishop’s friendship to his own and, by the bishop’s authority and support, deter the enemy from his undertaking.

But since the bishop did not yet appear favorably disposed toward him, because of the injuries that Godizo had inflicted upon him, Wicmann first decided to test the man through envoys. When he learned that access to the bishop’s friendship was open—because the bishop was not a friend of Baldric on account of the matters described above [Col. 0470D] [Note: [Col. 0471] so Eckhart; *noverat* in witness c.]—he went to him, and when [lacuna: a word has fallen out; Note: [Col. 0471]] he promised, as the opportunity allowed, to submit to his authority and to make satisfaction for the injustices that the bishop complained had been inflicted upon him by Wicmann and his friends [Note: [Col. 0471] *questus* in witness 1; *gestus* in witness 2], they established faith and friendship between themselves.

Baldric was little moved by their agreement. Nevertheless, he was forbidden, by the bishop’s authority, to exercise jurisdiction in the places belonging to the prefecture. The bishop, seeing dissensions increase and lawsuits multiply day by day, feared that the common people might be led astray by their rashness. Hoping that he could lessen the disputes by his authority, he appointed a day for a conference and compelled them to come to it.

## 8. On the arguments exchanged between them

When they had assembled, the bishop began his speech as follows: he said that he was distressed that so many disturbances were growing irrationally each day; that the matter ought to be referred to his judgment and to that of all who wished to decide justly; and that these wicked uprisings, by which the people were harmed and the fields devastated, ought to be suppressed.

If they refused to desist from their obstinacy, he declared that, by the emperor’s authority and with his own forces, he would compel them by force to withdraw from the tumult they had begun.

Wicmann replied that he understood that what the bishop had recalled about the recent tumult was true [Note: [Col. 0471] *veram* in witness c.], that no one felt more grief because of it than he did, and that he promised to submit to the bishop’s authority and make satisfaction in every way if he were accused of any fault.

Nevertheless, he said that he was troubled because, after the friendship between them had been confirmed, Baldric had been the first to stir up the beginnings of war. Baldric had stripped Wicmann’s kinsman, who ought to have benefited him by loyalty and counsel, of every honor and cast him down from his principality. This seemed detestable to Wicmann and to all nations to which the report of such inhumanity could reach.

Unless Baldric withdrew from these injuries and allowed that man free use of his own laws, Wicmann would not neglect his injuries, at least on the basis of the kinship by which Wicmann had married the prefect’s sister. He confirmed that in doing this he would commit no offense against the emperor’s favor, especially since he wished, through his devotion to peace, to interpose himself with the utmost care in every matter from which disputes were increasing and to remove those causes.

Baldric replied to this argument: he had not violated his faith, nor had he done anything by which the friendship ought to have been dissolved. He certainly knew that his kinsman did not possess such knowledge or prudence that he could care for the dignity entrusted to him [Col. 0471D] [Note: [Col. 0471] *illi* in witness c.]. Therefore, he had interfered in his affairs to help rather than harm him. He had wished to do this of his own accord long before, if he had been able to obtain an opportunity to speak with him [Note: [Col. 0471] *se* in witness c.].

But Wicmann had always kept him bound to himself as though under a kind of custody and constrained him by such discipline that he did not dare leave his side even for a moment.

If the emperor’s commands were also to be observed, then no one ought to forbid what the emperor had given him with his own hand. As for Wicmann’s declaration that, because of their kinship, he would not neglect his injuries, Baldric himself was closer to him by blood, since he was the son of his uncle. Therefore, on the side of their ancestors, that dignity more justly belonged to him than to his nephew or to anyone else.

As for his claim that he wished to intervene to settle disputes, no one was more zealous than Baldric himself in caring for the common welfare of the citizens. Proof of this was that he had undertaken the office not at his own discretion but because the emperor had bestowed it upon him [Note: [Col. 0471] *susciperit* in witness 1].

After both sides had put forward these and many other arguments for a long day, the bishop, having learned their disputes more fully, decided to defer the matter to other assemblies. Meanwhile, he resolved that peace should be established between them (in the year 1012).

Baldric, however, remembered that only a few days earlier some men from Wicmann’s side had invaded his sister’s household; after killing some people, one of her sons had barely escaped death inside a church, while another had been seized and carried away by dishonorable men. He therefore declared that he could not have any peaceful friendship with those who had inflicted so great an insult upon him and his people without satisfaction.

Wicmann replied: “If the injuries are to be compared, one of the most unjust was this: a prefect who was traveling securely with only a few men, and who suspected no harm from anyone, was unexpectedly attacked with great insolence by a servile band gathered from the still underage sons of my sister. He was put to flight, took refuge in a sacred building, and was barely rescued from death. No one could be so patient as to allow such a dangerous and insulting deed to pass unavenged [Note: [Col. 0471] *potuisse* in witness c.].”

When Baldric understood more clearly that resistance was being offered to him, he said that the matter would by no means have the outcome they expected.

When this nearly provoked an uprising, someone approached him and said—in a louder voice so that a large part of his men could hear—that he would not leave that territory alive unless he did what the bishop and Wicmann had decided. Terrified by these words, he agreed that peace should be made. Both sides confirmed it by oath on an appointed day.

## 9. On Wicmann’s deceptions

But as I reflect upon so many oaths committed with treacherous intent, I do not know whether I should marvel or grieve that men endowed with the highest honor and dignity descended to such treachery that they did things against justice and the Christian faith which even the lowest common people would not dare conceive in thought.

Therefore, in accordance with the words of the notary of the Holy Spirit, “Let my mouth not speak of the works of men” (Psalm 16:4), I fear to recount the utterly perverse customs of our age, which are established by almost no faith [Note: [Col. 0473] *stabilitas* corrected to *stabilitos* in witness c.], but are driven by blind desire for wretched honor and false power and have forgotten all humanity and goodness [Note: [Col. 0473] *oblutos* in witness c.].

Yet there are some who maintain that Wicmann was the more unjust in these disputes. They take this as support for their opinion: that, since he possessed fewer estates on this side of the Rhine, he tried, with whatever speed of planning he could muster, to equal Baldric’s resources. The outcome of what follows can easily reveal whether this was so.

On the following day, Baldric crossed the Rhine with a few men to visit his sister. When the scouts discovered his arrival, those men whom we mentioned above, who had attacked his sister’s household, came out from Munna and secretly descended along the bank of the Rhine with a large cavalry force. They approached him without being seen until they had come close to the village.

Baldric’s men had released their horses into the fields to graze and, fearing nothing, were behaving carelessly because peace had been established and confirmed between them the day before. But when they saw the enemy making an unusually determined charge against them, they quickly called back their horses, divided the cavalry into two groups, and formed a battle line according to the limited time available. They received the enemy.

After a fierce battle had been fought by both sides, and when matters had reached the point at which Baldric ought to have gained the upper hand, he suddenly turned his horse, contrary to everyone’s expectation, and fled. Reaching the bank, he found a little boat and escaped in it.

When the others saw this, they too began to flee in different directions, and many shut themselves inside a church. Wicmann, who happened at that time to be not far from the place, received news of the battle through a messenger, hurried there, broke into the church, seized those who had hidden inside it, ordered them to be held more severely, brought them to Munna, and threw them into chains.

From this incident the earlier uprisings between them arose again. Although, as we said, Baldric had the more just causes in this dispute, he was nevertheless inferior in this respect: his soldiers, exhausted by repeated expeditions, had received small rewards for such great labor; and his wife, addressing them disdainfully and reproaching them for cowardice and sluggishness, alienated them from his service and made them far more disloyal than before.

She was also so harsh toward her household that for a minor fault she sent some men into exile, while she caused others to appear deformed by having their noses or ears cut off, making their present life hateful to them.

The nobility of her family and the abundance of all her possessions raised her far too high, so that she could justly be marked by the verse of that satirist [Juvenal 6.460]:

> “Nothing is more intolerable than a wealthy woman.”

By such things and others of the same kind, she turned the hearts of many away from their husband’s friendship and intimacy [Note: [Col. 0473] *advertit* in witness c.].

## 10. On the army sent into Bratuspantium and Baldric’s capture

In the dissension that had now arisen, since neither of them could safely guard himself from the other when their estates lay so close together, peace was again arranged between them for an appointed day.

During this interval an occasion arose for the emperor to send an army into the territory of Bratuspantium [Note: [Col. 0473] *mitteretur* in witness c. corrected from *mitterentur*]. He had heard that the region was being devastated by frequent raids by certain troublesome and rebellious men. Bishop Adelbold, Duke Godefrid, and Wicmann commanded this army.

They did not wish Baldric to accompany them because he was a friend of those against whom the army was being led.

After they had departed, Baldric devoted his attention to Gerhard, whom we mentioned above. Gerhard had already besieged the little fortress of Heimbach [Note: [Col. 0473D] Heimbach in the Eifel] for many days. Since it was situated on extremely high cliffs, it was impregnable. Nevertheless, the townsmen, worn down by a very long siege and having consumed everything they had with them, surrendered.

Having learned Baldric’s routes, Gevehard, who had invaded the house of his widowed sister mentioned above, blockaded all the roads and kept watch with all his men, carefully seeking an opportunity to approach Baldric while he was unprepared. Fortune did not disappoint the man’s plan.

Baldric, having sent his retainers here and there to their own places, began a careless journey toward Cologne with only a few men. The enemy soon saw him and pursued him at a rapid pace. Baldric, suddenly terrified and weakened, was captured before he even attempted to mount the horse of the gelding [Note: [Col. 0473] thus witness 1; perhaps “of the eunuch”; *accuratioris* in witness 2] that was being led beside him.

He was treated with every indignity: part of his beard was torn out and his cheeks were battered [Note: *colafis* is materially uncertain]. He was led to Munna, Wicmann’s castle, in the greatest disgrace. There, under threats and the excessive fury of the victors, he was compelled to surrender Aspola unless he preferred to be punished by decapitation.

He asked that a messenger be sent there. When this was granted [Note: [Col. 0473] *imperato* in witness c.], some of his men came to him. Deeply grieved and lamenting his misfortune, he ordered the fortification to be surrendered.

## 11. On Gevehard and Baldric’s ransom

Godizo, whom we mentioned above (Book I, chap. 2), a kinsman of the venerable Liutgard and of Baldric’s wife, when he was dying entrusted Heimbach and Aspola to Gerhard’s [Note: [Col. 0473] *gehardi* in witness c.] protection, because he was his kinsman, so that he might raise and care for his wife and little daughters.

Gerhard, however, entrusted Aspola to Baldric because it was nearer, and ordered that Heimbach be guarded by the widow, assigning his own guards to it [Note: [Col. 0473] *adhibitus* in witness c.].

Agitated by womanly concerns [Note: [Col. 0473] *mulieribus* in witness c.], she admitted Gevehard, whom she had summoned, and joined herself to him in marriage. This man had formerly been Baldric’s soldier. But because he had done all these things without Baldric’s knowledge or counsel, and because Baldric learned that he intended to seek Aspola, which was under his authority, on his wife’s behalf—a possession he did not wish to lose—Baldric rejected his friendship and dismissed the soldier.

Unable to resist Baldric’s power, Gevehard pledged himself to Wicmann and submitted to his commands. This was the cause that inflamed Gevehard against Baldric and produced the breach between them.

While Baldric was held in chains for several days, he asked to be released in exchange for whatever sum of money they wished to accept. Although he was scarcely persuaded to approve this arrangement, they stipulated that within a very short time he would provide two thousand pounds of silver.

He was released on these terms, and he gave hostages as security for the money. While it was being gathered and assembled [Note: [Col. 0475] *conferreretur* in witness c.], and part of it had already been paid, the bishop and Wicmann returned with their army. They learned what had happened from those who reported it, and, moved by the outcome demanded by his many misfortunes and by the excessive submissiveness of his wife [Note: [Col. 0475D] Adela], they took pity on him.

They summoned an assembly, met together, brought in Gevehard, and succeeded in persuading him to forgive Baldric the money except for four hundred pounds of silver. Gevehard confirmed by oath that he would never seek vengeance for any of the things that had been done against him.

## 12. On the death of Wicmann [Note: [Col. 0475D] Cf. Thietmar, *Chronicle* VII.33–34; *Ann. Hild.*; *Lamb.*; *Quedl.*, s.a. 1016.]

Not long afterward (in 1016), Baldric’s and Wicmann’s relatives and friends agreed that henceforth, putting aside every quarrel, a lasting peace and firm loyalty should be established between them. When everyone applauded this with one accord, they all met again on the appointed day. After many discussions, eleven men went over with Baldric and as many with Wicmann; by oath, they bound themselves with the greatest readiness of all to maintain peace, loyalty, and affection between them. Once this had been done, they afterward enjoyed, as some thought, a sufficiently trustworthy friendship without any suspicion.

But when not much time had passed—indeed, before a year was complete (October)—Wicmann invited Baldric to a banquet. When it was over, and the most generous gifts had been offered and graciously received, he dismissed him and accompanied him as he departed. As they were going, Baldric asked Wicmann to return the favor by coming to his house and allowing him to serve him a meal with suitable preparation. At first Wicmann resisted; but when he recalled the great friendship and affection that had been forged between them, he considered it wrong not to yield to Baldric’s wishes. Although his soldiers advised against it, as though already foreseeing his fate, he nevertheless consented and followed the man who was escorting him.

When they had already arrived before the entrance of the castle called Upladium [Note: [Col. 0476D] Not far from Nijmegen and Elten.], Wicmann turned and said to the other man: “Look, against the wishes of my soldiers I am entering this castle, not knowing what is to happen to me there; but I place myself between God and your good faith.” When the other man, greatly astonished at these words, replied that, with God directing matters, no misfortune or hostility would occur, but that everything fitting to Wicmann’s safety and honor would happen to him, Wicmann entered.

Baldric’s wife, proceeding in body alone and not in spirit, received him with many words, as is the custom of flatterers. Indeed, I seem almost in every sentence to take up arms against her, while I am compelled, against my will, to set out in due order what is reported about her. As soon as Wicmann entered, she began plotting the man’s death, and first attempted to destroy him with poison. But when she realized that she was accomplishing nothing by this, she made a plan, without her husband’s knowledge, with two men—one of his soldiers and the other his own servant, both depraved men. By promises and pledges given with clasped hands, she secured their agreement to kill him by whatever means they could.

On the third day, when the banquet was over, Baldric escorted Wicmann as he departed with a large retinue, in joy and merriment. As they set out (October 6), one of Baldric’s party, observing Wicmann’s elegance and the man’s uprightness, said to his companion: “One would not easily find a man so prudent, so adorned with honorable character, and so distinguished by so many virtues.” The other replied: “Wait a little, and you will see the glory of this most envied man perish shortly.” From this it is inferred that a conspiracy had truly been formed against him.

But when they had advanced no more than a mile from the town, and Wicmann, together with one of his household who was traveling with him, had gone a little ahead, while his own men, scattered across the countryside before him, had proceeded without any thought of danger, those wicked men suddenly attacked him without warning, killed him, and swiftly fled. When a crowd gathered, and one person loudly asked another what the disturbance meant, while no one, before the matter was known, could give any certain reply, at last they learned of the killing and saw the corpse lying beside the road, covered with blood. A great cry and lament arose, and everyone unanimously attributed this crime to Baldric, saying that such were his counsel and his faith.

Although he was innocent of this plot, no one among them could be brought to believe that Baldric was free of guilt. Thus, because of his wife’s wickedness, everyone’s common opinion united in hatred of him. When Baldric heard that the count had been killed, he was utterly stricken in spirit, mourning the man’s death with tears and many groans. Fearing that an uprising might be raised against him because of their fresh grief, he quickly withdrew into the town.

### 13. The Destruction of Ubladium

When this matter had been spread everywhere, envoys were immediately sent by Lord Adelbold the bishop, the duke, and their other friends to the emperor, who at that time was staying in Burgundy with his army, so that he might learn from them of Wicmann’s slaughter. Deeply moved by the death of a man who had been his very dear friend and intimate, he ordered them to pursue the author of the killing and seize his property, and announced that he himself would come at once.

Baldric, however, understood that no one would think otherwise than that the man had been killed on his advice, since Baldric himself had invited him into his house, received him in the town, escorted him when he departed, and he had been killed in Baldric’s presence. He was therefore afflicted with profound grief and began considering what answer he could make to the charge. His wife approached him as he grieved and reproved him with many harsh words. She urged him to recover his courage and strength and to abandon his inactivity. She said that such softness of spirit was more fitting for a worthless slave than for him, and taught him to bear the matter with a calmer mind, since it could not be remedied by any means. There was no doubt, she said, that they would judge the count to have been killed by her husband’s plan and will, and that therefore he must certainly expect them to seek vengeance. It was consequently necessary for him to look after the safety of himself and his people and to guard his property with the utmost care.

Moved by these and similar words from his wife, and driven into still greater anxiety, Baldric ordered provisions to be brought into the town, so that, if action were required, he would not lack the means of resistance. He sent messengers to Cologne, to the archbishop under whose protection he stood and from whose generosity he held many benefices, and laid the matter before him. The archbishop promised that his assistance would not be lacking.

Baldric also sent to Utrecht and requested reinforcements from the bishop. The bishop declared that he could not be Baldric’s helper and friend unless Baldric cleared himself, by a faithful satisfaction offered to his lord, the august emperor, of blame for the crime he had committed.

Disappointed in this hope, Baldric summoned to his aid everyone from whom he expected loyalty and friendship. Before he could accomplish this, however, Wicmann’s relatives and all his friends—and especially Adelbold, the bishop of Utrecht, who because of this affair had become his most hostile enemy—judged Baldric to be an enemy and confiscated his property. With the greatest secrecy, so that the matter might not come to his knowledge, they began sending envoys among themselves. Each gathered troops as he could, and they arranged to meet on an appointed night at a fixed place and, if possible, besiege Baldric inside his fortification.

While this was being rapidly carried out by those eager for the undertaking [Note: [Col. 0477] Thus E.; “administeretur” in the codex.], Baldric, following his usual practice, fearing the danger of a siege, left the town with a few men before the first watch had ended. In the darkness, deprived of sight [Note: [Col. 0477] “adepto” in the codex.], he could not see the enemy; but when he heard the tumult of those approaching, he was terrified and escaped by a swift flight.

The castle was besieged [Note: [Col. 0477] “obsiditur” in the codex.], and all the villages and private buildings belonging to it were everywhere devastated; they seized a great number of cattle and other goods. Then they brought out the equipment they had prepared for battle. Both sides fought with the greatest force. But the townsmen were overcome in this respect: although many came forward and others took the place of the exhausted, the small number of defenders made it impossible for them to accomplish anything against the attackers.
