They also placed women along the wall with helmets set upon their heads and made them present the appearance of combatants, so that, when the supposed multitude of armed men was seen, the enemy would despair of taking the town. Exhausted by such hardships, they barely sustained the siege for several days. Their only source of relief was that the site, naturally somewhat sloping upward from the plain, had been greatly raised by an embankment and surrounded by a wall—a rare feature in those regions. They trusted in this strength more than in themselves.

But when they learned that the emperor had drawn near and noticed that his camp was being constructed in the distance, they despaired of their safety and sent envoys to the enemy concerning surrender. Bishop Adelbold and Duke Bernhard granted them pardon and allowed Baldric’s wife to depart with all her possessions. They destroyed the castle, however, tearing down and overturning its wall and consuming it with fire.

### 14. Ruodold, King of the Burgundians

As I said, the emperor was staying in Burgundy with his army during those days for the following reason. Ruodold, king of Burgundy, had been despised by certain of his princes because of his gentleness and blameless life. They therefore attempted to expel him from the kingdom. Compelled by this necessity, he came to the emperor and explained the whole matter to him in order. Since he could no longer endure the burdens and affairs of the kingdom, being already advanced in age, he handed the kingdom over to the emperor and, after receiving very generous gifts, returned to his homeland.

After this, the emperor went into Burgundy, held the assemblies he had appointed, received hostages, issued orders concerning necessary matters, and returned. Those who had previously rebelled, when they saw that the king had been removed from the affairs of the kingdom, that they had been deprived of their former power, and that their authority and favor among the cities in which they had been accustomed to rule had diminished, came to the king, threw themselves at his feet, and surrendered. They promised that they would make satisfaction in every way for their contempt and would never again turn away from this resolve, but would always obey his commands. They begged only one special favor: that he not permit a king of another nation to rule over his people. They said that it was the perpetual law of the Burgundians to have as king the man whom they themselves chose and appointed.

The king was appeased by their speech and accepted their satisfaction. He sent envoys to the emperor, saying that his adversaries had come to him, had asked pardon for what they had committed against him, and had confirmed that henceforth they would obey him without any suspicion. He asked the emperor to grant him this favor and, in his clemency [Note: [Col. 0477] “potentia” corrected to “clementia” in the codex.], to allow him to exercise the former power of his kingdom.

Although the emperor considered this disadvantageous to himself, he nevertheless remembered that his kinsman had come to him under the compulsion of the greatest necessity and had handed over the kingdom not so much willingly as under pressure. In order that he not be thought to have acted too inhumanely toward him, he granted the king’s request, returned the kingdom to him, and ordered his princes to obey him in everything.

But if anyone should contend that, out of regard for the emperor’s honor, I have departed in a few words from the truth of history, although I wrote nothing false according to my conscience but only what I learned from the report of many, let him nevertheless know that this is true by the testimony of all: terrified by fear of the emperor, the Burgundians thereafter rendered their former submission to the king.

Heinricus, returning from Burgundy, entrusted Munna and everything that had belonged to Wicmann to Duke Bernhard [Note: [Col. 0479] “berhardo” in one witness; “bernardo” in another.], so that he might raise his little son until he grew up.

### 15. Munnum Secretly Handed Over

In Munna there was a servant belonging to Baldric’s party, exceedingly skilled at deception. Guilty of some offense—I do not know what—he had been a fugitive from his master for many days. After devising a plan, he secretly came to his master, firmly promising that he could be reconciled to him in this matter if he handed over the castle. He declared that, if his master were willing to follow him, he would lead him safely into the middle of Munna without any danger.

The young man, however, as is the custom of the young, rejoicing excessively in his promise, offered him great rewards and urged him to accomplish the matter as quickly as possible. The servant pledged that he would do so, and at the appointed time, after the gates had been opened, he admitted his master in the early morning.

The townsmen, still weighed down by sleep in their beds, were suddenly awakened by the unexpected shouting of the enemy. As they ran here and there through their dwellings, not knowing where to take refuge, they were captured unarmed. Only one man was killed in the first clash; all the others were driven out of the castle.

### 16. Baldric Expelled and Munna Destroyed

Baldric, expelled from his home and having lost all his possessions (in 1018), went to the priest of Cologne. Taking pity on his recent disasters, the priest assigned him a residence in the city and established a stipend for him. Gerhard of Moselle also lent him Hengibach, so that he would have somewhere to withdraw and could remain safe from his enemies.

But when Munna, as we said above, had been captured by his own men, Baldric’s hope increased, since he hoped through this event to expiate his misfortune and grief and recover his former security [Note: [Col. 0479] “manu” in witness 2.] [Note: [Col. 0479] “hunc” in witness 1; “hanc” in the codex.]. But the matter turned out very differently. For when a council had been summoned at Nijmegen (March 16), and many had arrived, the emperor ordered Munna to be destroyed, lest any harm or plunder should come from that region. He sent Archbishop Heribert, Gerhard of Moselle, and many others for its destruction [Note: [Col. 0479] “misit” corrected to “multos” in the codex.]. They completely demolished all the buildings, set them on fire, and deprived everyone of any hope of establishing a fortification there again.

### 17. The Inquiry Held with Baldric Concerning Wicmann’s Death

After these matters had been dealt with, the emperor began an inquiry with Baldric concerning Wicmann’s death. When many people were present at this assembly, the emperor, having given a public pledge of safety, ordered Baldric to appear.

When the harshest judgments were being pronounced against him, and Baldric desired with the greatest effort to prove himself innocent by every legal procedure the emperor might establish, Duke Godefrid and Bernhard [Note: [Col. 0479] “berhardus” in the codex.] forbade every form of self-purification according to law. They argued that, although peace and faith had repeatedly been confirmed by oath between Baldric and Wicmann, Baldric had always been the first to break the agreement; therefore, his defense should no longer be admitted, since he stood convicted as a perjurer by such manifest evidence [Note: [Col. 0479] “pejurus” in witness 2.].

As Baldric tried to speak, they interrupted his voice so that he could not state his case, and they raged against him, savage over the death of an innocent man and scarcely able to endure the sight of him. The matter had nearly reached the point where he would be torn apart by the hands of the soldiers.

When he saw himself trapped and despaired of escape, he cried out in a loud voice, asking for the king’s help. When the king heard his cry, he rose and, extending his hand so as not to violate the public pledge he had given, snatched Baldric from the hands of the enraged men. He ordered him, now in despair, to withdraw from his presence.

The archbishop took him under his protection and guarded him with great care. After scarcely being rescued from his enemies, Baldric was sent back to Cologne. Three years later he fell ill and died at Hengibach (in 1021). His body was carried to his own estate at Sefluche [Note: [Col. 0479D] Perhaps Sefferen, formerly belonging to the jurisdiction of Prüm.] and buried there.

### 18. How Gevehard Was Led to His Death

After Baldric’s death, the same servant who had handed over Munna came to Gevehard, whom we mentioned above (chapter 11). He promised that, if Gevehard were willing to accept his advice and follow him, he would make him prosperous, lead him to his castle Hengibach—which had come to him by right through his wife’s side—and grant him the unhindered opportunity to enjoy it without injury.

Gevehard, too credulous in the servant’s words and to his own misfortune, followed him without delay. When scouts reported that he had drawn near, Gerhard, as had been agreed, hid a large number of armed men in the workshops and chambers of the town, showed them what his plan was, and himself concealed a further force in the forest around the castle.

When Gevehard had been led into the middle of the fortification like an ox to sacrifice, everyone suddenly leapt out from the towers and dwellings and blocked the gates. A few escaped in the first clash; the rest were killed. Gevehard, however, climbed the wall without delay and, unaware of the ambush outside, threw himself down and was badly mangled in his limbs.

Gerhard also ran up and, stretching out his hand, struck him hard on the neck, saying: “You struck down your lord in the same way; behold, you have what you did!” Then Gevehard was stabbed and killed by the man who had struck down Wicmann, together with a certain servant of Baldric.

Thus, while he sought more, he lost what he had, along with his life.

### 19. An Eclipse of the Moon and Sun, and the Sight of a Comet

One year before the council was summoned at Nijmegen (in 1017), the moon failed after midnight during the winter season. When the king was staying in the same place the following year (1018), an eclipse of the sun occurred during Holy Week. In the third year also (1019), a comet was seen in the northern part of the sky, with extremely long hair and a pale appearance.

Many wars followed this sign, and in numerous nations a great quantity of human blood was shed in battle.

### 20. Meriwido Taken from the Frisians, and the Men of Tiel

Before this portent appeared in the sky, war broke out near the ocean shore (in 1018). The cause of the war was as follows. A part of the Frisians, abandoning their homes, settled in the forest of Meriwido, which we mentioned above (Book I, chapter 8), building dwellings there. After joining themselves to them, robbers inflicted great losses on merchants.

Later, after the robbers had subjected the Frisians, they divided the land among them according to each man’s capacity for cultivation, so that they might clear new fields, ordered them to cultivate it, and made them tributary to themselves.

For this reason the merchants of Tiel—who, even more readily than others, are especially incited to raise every sort of complaint [Note: [Col. 0481] “acceduntur” in witness 1.]—repeatedly appealed to the king, asking him by his favor to defend them from these injuries. They said that, if he did not do so, they would neither come to the island [Note: [Col. 0481D] Britain.] for the sake of trade nor be able to have the Britons come to them, and therefore could not receive their revenues as fully as they ought.

But I wish to insert here a few remarks—not in detraction, but grieving from the depths of my heart [Note: [Col. 0481] “detrahendo” corrected to “condolendo” in the codex]—about the customs and institutions by which these men of Tiel differ from other people [Note: [Col. 0481] I emend thus: “istis” corrected to “vicis” in the codex.].

They are a harsh people, almost unaccustomed to any discipline. They render judgments not according to law but according to their will, and claim that this was handed down and confirmed to them by the emperor in a charter [Note: [Col. 0481] To prevent anyone from supposing that “Karolo” should be read, I point out that the codex has “karta.”].

If someone has received anything from another as a loan or something lent, and the owner later demands his property at the appointed time, the recipient stoutly denies it and immediately swears that he received nothing from him. If anyone is publicly caught in perjury, they maintain that no one may rebuke him [Note: [Col. 0481] “pose” in witness 1.].

If he has held the object in one hand, provided it is small enough to be enclosed in a fist, he will deny it under oath with the other hand. If any one of God’s faithful should intercede with the emperor to prohibit these crimes, lest so many souls perish every day, he may surely hope that God will grant him a great reward.

They do not regard adultery as a fault. As long as the wife remains silent, they consider it permissible for a man to defile himself through wicked crimes, and they hold that no one except the wife ought to bring such a man before a synod.

From early morning they devote themselves to drinking, and whoever there utters obscene speeches in a loud voice to provoke laughter and entice the undisciplined crowd to drink wins great praise among them. Indeed, for this purpose they collect money together, distribute it in shares as prizes, and with it choose whatever drinks [Note: [Col. 0481] “pot’” in the codex; perhaps “potos”?] they see at particular times of the year [Note: [Col. 0481] “cernt” in the codex.], and on the more celebrated festivals they devote themselves, as though solemnly, to drunkenness [Note: [Col. 0481] Thus witness 2; “ebriati” in witness 1.].

### 21. The War Undertaken against the Frisians

Wishing to open the merchants’ routes (in 1018), the emperor summoned Bishop Adelbald and Duke Godefrid to him [Note: [Col. 0481] “adebbaldum” in the codex.] [Note: [Col. 0482D] Cf. Thietmar VIII, 13.] and ordered them to go against the Frisians, drive them from the settlements they had unjustly occupied, and remove the robbers.

After receiving these orders, they assembled an immense multitude. They also took with them distinguished men, especially well trained in military affairs, who throughout their lives had devoted themselves to cavalry service but could do nothing in ships [Note: [Col. 0481] “adciscunt” in the codex.]. When they had gathered together, they placed the entire army in ships and hurried to the place where they had heard that the Frisians were with their assembled forces.

When the men occupying the forest learned through scouts of the army’s arrival, they abandoned their homes and fled to those among whom the robbers had built a small fortification. Our men, however, approached Flaridingun with the whole fleet at high tide. This is the name given to this region of the Frisians [Note: [Col. 0482D] Today only a village of this name remains, Vlaerdingen, which one sees below Rotterdam on the left as the Meuse flows into it from the ocean.].

When the soldiers were landed on its shore, the duke ordered the rest of the multitude to disembark, leaving only a few men to draw the ships back into deep water, lest, when the tide changed again, they should remain on dry land, so that the ships might be freely used if necessary.

When the Frisians saw the enemy boldly filling the field with their ranks, and expected no support from those inside the fortification—since those men, surrounded by so great a multitude, had no means of escape—they gathered at their stations on higher ground and awaited what strategy the enemy would adopt.

One circumstance nevertheless kept them in place: they had learned that the enemy had arrived without horses, while they themselves trusted that, through daily labor and rustic exercise, they were especially strong on foot. If the enemy pressed them, they stood ready and prepared to flee.

They had one circumstance of great advantage: they had dug the entire field through with ditches, either to protect against the greater force of the sea, which is accustomed to rise higher at the full moon, or to impede the enemy’s passage.

Since the duke thought it difficult for so large a multitude to cross them, he ordered those carrying the standards to return and, after passing around the ditches [Note: [Col. 0483] “circutriis” in the codex; “circuitis” in Eckhard. “Circutare” means approximately “to go around,” that is, “to circle around.”], to take up position on level ground, so that, if the Frisians wished to fight, there would be a more convenient opportunity to receive them.

When the duke’s army had begun to withdraw its standards [Note: [Col. 0483] “duos” in witness 1.], a cry arose among the rear ranks from a certain utterly wicked man, a relative of the robbers. He shouted that each man should look to his own life, because the duke, pressed in the front line by the attack of the Frisians, had been defeated and had withdrawn from the battle in flight.

When this false report had spread through the army, everyone turned to flight. They were so terrified that, although no one was pursuing them, they threw themselves into the river (July 29). Many, trusting in their strength, wished to swim to the ships. When they seized them and attempted with all their strength to climb aboard, the ships were sunk by the crowd pressing around them.

In this way even more perished. Each man, seeing his dear one or relative struggling in the peril of death by drowning, wished to help him; but an immeasurable crowd gathered around them, dragged the ships into the depths, and thus all were suffocated together.

A few, seeing this and fearing the danger of drowning—and, as usually happens, since most people in such a disturbance feel no compassion lest they perish in the same way—hastened their flight with vigorous rowing. Many, however, overcome by fear, exhaustion, and the weight of their armor, entered the water upright as they ran and stood lifeless beneath it.

Those who were in the fortification, seeing the crowd rushing about and men throwing themselves headlong from the shore into the water, realized that they had begun their flight in confusion. They immediately began signaling and shouting to the Frisians that the enemy was fleeing.

The duke, seeing the multitude in flight, stood stupefied with his men. Even the bravest, whose hearts had been like those of lions, were so loosened by fear that they could not move from the place where they stood.

Then there occurred—I do not know whether by divine judgment—something like an unheard-of miracle: summoned by the signals of the townsmen, the Frisians came running and killed the men who stood motionless like stones. By God’s command, their limbs were so bound that no one among such a great number of distinguished men raised a hand with drawn sword to resist or held up a shield to protect himself [Note: [Col. 0483] Thus E.; “a dno” in the codex.].

After these men had been killed, the Frisians swiftly reached the shore and stabbed with javelins many who were crawling through the shallow edge of the shore in the water with their hands.

Others surrounded the duke when they saw him standing alone. But he, having exhausted his breath, resisted bravely. He received a spear that had been thrown and, turning his spear backward, pierced the one man who was attacking him from behind [Note: [Col. 0483] “tm” in the codex.]. After that man had been killed, he somewhat restrained the attack of the others.

Meanwhile the robbers, already rejoicing in the town over their victory, suddenly burst out. They trampled over all the corpses of the dead and hurried to the place where they saw the duke surrounded by the multitude.

Recognizing him, and seeing that he had already been wounded in the face and was almost beyond hope, they immediately rescued him from danger. They led him, together with a few captives, into the castle. They threw themselves at his feet, surrendered to him, and begged him to look after their interests and to intercede for them with the emperor and Bishop Adelbald concerning the outcome of the affair.

When he told them that he would do everything they asked, provided only that they allowed him and the other survivors and captives to depart unharmed, they replied that they had incurred the intense hostility of the parents and relatives of those who had fallen. If the duke would confirm by oath that they would never demand vengeance from them for what had happened, they indicated that they would do what he requested.

The duke approved this arrangement, and they fixed the day and place on which all these things were to be carried out. They kept those who had been captured in chains until the agreed truce; they allowed the duke to depart.

After he had gone, they rushed upon the slain and, forgetful of all humanity, stripped every body of its clothing, leaving not even a scrap with which the private parts might be covered.

The following is also reported about them: certain of these bodies, driven far out to sea by the inhabitants because of their stench, remained untouched and unharmed by birds, beasts, and sea creatures, which are exceedingly eager for human corpses. When they were again cast upon the shore by the tide, their whiteness could be seen for two miles or more, as though the shore had been spread with the whitest linen.

This too may be cited as testimony to the event: nine of their bodies, still bound together, were found on a certain bank on the Kalends of December, so intact that scarcely any decay could be detected in them, although the slaughter had taken place on the fourth day before the Kalends of August.

### 22. A Cleric Who Became a Jew

Above (Book I, chapter 7) I promised to report on that apostate who, abandoning his religion, fell from the clerical state into the abyss of the faithless Jews. But in fulfilling that promise I tremble completely, and, with the hairs of my head standing on end, I am shaken with fear that the devil could have persuaded a man to dare to utter such filth against Christ and his saints.

For that most wretched man had written in letters of destruction:

### 23. The Writings of the Apostate

[Col. 0484D]

“Why do you contradict the just man, fool? Read the prophet Habakkuk, in whom God said: ‘I am God and I do not change’ (Malachi 3:6). If, according to your accursed faith, he were changed and united himself with a woman, the beginning of his words would not be truth.

“The Lord said to Moses: ‘For no human being shall see me and live’ (Exodus 33:20). Which son of man did he omit? For the prophet David says: ‘Do not put your trust in princes, in human beings, in whom there is no salvation’ (Psalm 145:3); and Ezekiel says: ‘Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his arm, for he shall be like a tamarisk in the desert and shall not see the fruit when good comes’ (Jeremiah 17:5–6).

“What do you say against these things, you senseless creature? Which son of man did he omit? Peter and John, perhaps, and Martin and the other demons whom you call saints?

“In every place the God of Israel is read of, and there is no God of the nations. Where is your understanding? David says: ‘The Lord will remember his covenant forever, the word that he commanded for a thousand generations, the covenant that he made with Abraham and his oath to Isaac’ (Psalm 104:8–9)—that is, his holy law and circumcision, which he gave to Moses his servant.”

### 24. Heinricus’s Letter to Wecelinus

[Note: [Col. 0485] I have added the heading; see above, line 7.]

“[Col. 0485B] To answer your calumny, O unbelieving Jew, which you have recently spewed forth from your blasphemous mouth against Christ and his saints—and which it would be easy for one trained in Christian warfare to refute, if it were not easier to turn rocks into softness than to split your hearts open to receive the truth—: for even those rocks recognized their creator when he was dying, being split apart [Note: [Col. 0485] *recognovert* in c.], and yet the insensibility of your heart, although shattered and overthrown, still persists in the hardness of an iniquity grown old. And although, through the coeternal Wisdom of God, by whom the world was both wonderfully created and more wonderfully restored, the mouth of those speaking iniquity has been stopped, and your iniquity has lied to itself, while it is made clear throughout the ages and by the words of the prophets and the examples of the saints how the blind impiety of your unbelief has been condemned, and how the weakness of mortality assumed in Christ has been glorified [Col. 0485C], nevertheless, since the obstinate perversity of Jewish malice still does not despair of its schemes, mutters with criminal arrogance against the Christian religion, and, through the examples of the Fathers and the sayings of the prophets, challenges the Church—already so often defeated and utterly overthrown, yet standing and flourishing—to battle once again, let us attack them, with that very Wisdom of God, the Word of God, the Son of God, giving and supplying our aid. Let us first strike their stony hearts with that stone which the prophet Daniel—whom you call your own, but rather ours—saw cut from the mountain without hands and fill the whole world (Dan. II, 34). Concerning it David also says: ‘My heart has uttered a good word’ (Ps. XLIV, 1). And again: ‘The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you’ [Col. 0485D] [Note: [Col. 0485] Here and several other verses are written only with the first letter of each word.] (Ps. II, 7). And again: ‘You made all things in wisdom’ (Ps. CIII, 24). And Solomon: ‘The Lord possessed me at the beginning of his ways’ (Prov. VIII, 22).

But since our discussion with the Jew concerns not Christ’s eternal birth, in which he was always equal to the Father, but his temporal birth, in which, as David cries out, he was made a little lower than the angels (Ps. VIII, 6), let us hear what he says and answer his objection accordingly.

You say, Jew: ‘Why do you contradict the just man, fool?’ First I would like you to answer me: whom do you call just, yourself or the prophet? If the prophet, I agree—but, by showing that I do not contradict him, I shall rightly prove that you have lied. If, however, you call yourself just, although it is clear that you first lied, I do not know how you will obtain justice, since the stain of falsehood has defiled you. Nor can you consistently be both defender and transgressor of your law, which says: ‘You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor’ (Exod. XX, 16).

But if, as I have already stated, I do not contradict the prophet, since he himself speaks on my behalf, then with the very weapons you have prepared against me I shall inflict lethal wounds upon you. For you have borne false witness against your neighbor, contrary to the commandment of the law; you will therefore incur the law’s guilt. Guilt will draw you to punishment, and punishment will lead you all the way [Col. 0486B] to death.

But let us examine what follows. Unhappy Jew [Note: [Col. 0485] *judex* in witness 1.], whom do you call foolish? Do you mean us who believe in the Crucified One, who indeed became for you ‘a stone of stumbling and a rock [Note: [Col. 0485] *petri* in c.] of offense’? ‘For the stone which the builders rejected, this has become the cornerstone. This was done by the Lord, and it is marvelous in our eyes’ (Matt. XXI, 42). Are we therefore foolish and you wise? Yet through the foolishness of preaching the world’s pride has already fallen, and on the foreheads of kings you see the trophy of the cross. ‘For God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the strong’ (I Cor. I, 27). Therefore we gladly embrace the foolishness of Christ’s cross, because we believe that we shall attain Christ’s glory.

But what am I telling a deaf man a story? Or why do I place light before a blind man? Or preach the Gospel to a Jew? Let us return to what follows.

You say: ‘Read the prophet Habakkuk—not in whom, as you say, but through whom God himself says: “I am God and I do not change.”’

I have already stated to you, Jew, that I in no way contradict Habakkuk’s testimony; indeed, I declare that I accept not only Habakkuk’s testimony but also that of all the prophets and the teachings of the law, because I worship him who came not to abolish the law but to fulfill it. God said through Habakkuk: ‘I am God and I do not change,’ and the Christian religion firmly believes this.

But as for what you added—‘If he were changed according to your accursed faith and united himself with a woman, the beginning of his words would not be truth’—what wonder is it, since you are blind, if you do not see that light which is seen only by those who are pure in heart; indeed, since, like a madman, you also recoil from the physician and heap curses and insults [Note: [Col. 0485] *cumuitia* in c.] upon the one who wishes to heal you?

The mysteries of Christ’s incarnation are so lofty and profound that the Word of God, remaining unchangeably with God the Father from eternity, took flesh from a virgin and united our nature to his own. No one grasps these things unless he is spiritually wise; and no one is wise unless, by God’s gift, he grasps them; by that same gift, the one who does not yet grasp them believes. For, says the prophet: ‘Unless you believe, you will not understand’ (Isa. [Col. 0487A] VII, 9).

Thus merit is gathered for the believer, while the reward will be given to the one who sees, because if you see, it is not faith. As long as we journey through the darkness of this world, faith purifies the hearts of those who are destined to see God.

By this faith, through which the Son of God is also proclaimed the son of man, God had long before foretold through the prophet Ezekiel that some of your people would be cleansed, saying: ‘And it shall be in the last days: I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh’ (Acts II, 17), ‘and I will pour clean water over you, and you shall be cleansed from all your defilements; and from all your idols I will cleanse you. And I will give you a new heart, and I will place a new spirit within you; and I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh’ (Ezek. XXXVI, 25–26), and so forth.

These words clearly show that God has removed the veil from the hearts of some among you, so that, with the Spirit of God at work, the hearts of many might be prepared by faith to receive the saving water for the cleansing of all sins; while others would be blinded and remain in the error of unbelief, as it is written through another prophet: ‘Blindly I will blind their hearts, so that they may not see the light’ (Isa. VI, 10).

Therefore, O Jew, since you are blinded by palpable darkness, how do you think you can perceive how God, without any change in himself, united himself to a woman—not as you, faithless man, babble—but fashioned a body for himself from a woman’s flesh? For the divinity of the Word of God would assume it into the unity of his person, so that neither the divinity would pass into the passibility of flesh, nor humanity into divinity [Col. 0487C]; and yet the Son of God would be man because of the man assumed, and the Son of Man would be God because of the God who assumed him.

The prophet foretold to you: ‘Unless you believe, you will not understand.’ Believe, and you will understand; and ask God to remove the veil and take away the heart of stone. We too pray for you, against your will.

But since a Jew accepts neither reasoning nor preaching unless God removes the veil—indeed, I know how exceedingly hard his neck is—let us confront him with the oracles of the prophets, so that either he may believe in this way, or in this way depart in confusion.

That Christ would take flesh from a virgin, Isaiah foretold: ‘Behold, a virgin shall conceive in her womb and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel’ (Isa. VII, 14), that is, ‘God with us’ [Col. 0487D].

That he would be born from the tribe of Judah and be filled with the Spirit of God, the same prophet says: ‘A rod shall go forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root; and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him’ [Note: [Col. 0487] *replevit* in c.] (Isa. XI, 1–2).

That he would live among human beings, Jeremiah foretold: ‘This is our God, and no other shall be reckoned beside him’; and shortly afterward: ‘After this he was seen on earth and lived among human beings’ (Baruch III, 36, 38).

That he would suffer for us, Isaiah likewise said: ‘He was wounded for our iniquities’ [Col. 0488A] (Isa. LIII, 5).

And they uttered many other things about him, by which it is openly taught that the whole conduct of the Lord among us, from the time of his incarnation until his ascension, accords with their testimonies.

What do you say against these things, wicked man? Unless perhaps you offer the lie that comes from your father the devil, as our same Lord Jesus Christ said: ‘You are of your father the devil, and you do the works of your father’ (John VIII, 44).

Behold: by reasoning and examples you have been answered briefly—that God remains unchangeable and yet took flesh from a virgin.

Now let us return to what follows.

God said to Moses: ‘For no human being shall see me and be able to live.’

Here I ask you, Jew, who always follow the letter that kills and not the Spirit that gives life: how do you think it is possible for a human being to see God—or do you think it impossible? If possible, is it with bodily eyes or with the mind? If with bodily eyes [Note: [Col. 0487] *manu* in witness 2.], it certainly seems absurd, since that unbounded Spirit is neither extended by bulk, nor confined by place, nor moved by time, while human sight is so weak in comparison with the one who extends everywhere and encompasses all things.

If with the mind, it is not impossible—provided the mind is pure. For this has been promised to us: ‘Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God’ (Matt. V, 8).

If it is impossible, how will this be true, since David, speaking under the direction of Truth, said: ‘Seek the Lord and be strengthened; seek his face continually’ (Ps. CIV, 4)? Was David not speaking to human beings, whose minds he was stirring up to seek the face of the Lord? Will Truth and the herald of Truth disagree?

Certainly not, for those who understand.

Again I ask: can a human being see God and live, or not? If one can see him and live, how will it be true that God said: ‘No human being shall see me and be able to live’? But if one cannot, so that this may be true, how will it be true that Jacob said: ‘I saw the Lord face to face, and my soul was saved’ (Gen. XXXII, 30); and Isaiah: ‘I saw the Lord Sabaoth with my eyes’ (Isa. VI, 5)? How will Truth and the prophets of Truth proclaim contradictions?

But since your stupidity walked in the oldness of the letter and not in the newness of the Spirit, you blindly stumble over the very thing from which you could have guidance toward the light.

Therefore let us, who have received the truth of eternal light, tear apart the error of Jewish blindness, so that the truth of the question proposed may be revealed to faithful minds, while those who hear do not understand and those who see [Note: [Col. 0487] *videntibus* corrected to *videntes* in c.] become blind.

God said to Moses: ‘No human being shall see me and be able to live.’ This can be understood as follows: as long as a human being lives in this mortal body, which is subject to corruption and weighs down the soul, he cannot see God as he is in the nature of his divinity—neither with bodily eyes nor even with the mind itself, however pure and cleansed from every stain of vice it may be.

Even if the mind is already engaged in divine contemplation, it nevertheless falls short of the highest degree, because it contracts some stain from mortality. Therefore a human being cannot see God and live so long as he lives according to humanity and not at all according to God, and does not die to himself so that he may live to God.

But how could a human being, living mortally in the region of death, as I may put it, see or seek God, who is true Life, unless Life, mercifully bending down, had descended to the dead?

For we were dead from the moment when, through that first transgression in Adam, we all fell from the face of God. Therefore, taking pity on our mortality, deceived by the devil’s fraud [Note: [Col. 0489] *nra* in c.], Life descended to us veiled in flesh. For the weakness of the flesh could not otherwise endure inaccessible light, unless that same Life veiled itself in flesh and, through the interposition of flesh, displayed to us the light of the Godhead. Isaiah foretold this as though it had already happened [Col. 0489B]: ‘For those dwelling in the region and shadow of death, light has arisen’ (Isa. IX, 2).

Thus both Jacob and Isaiah saw this light not with bodily eyes but with spiritual ones. From this vision one of them burst forth into a voice of rejoicing, saying: ‘I saw the Lord face to face, and my soul was saved.’

He had understood God’s saying to Moses—‘No human being shall see me and be able to live’—as though he would have despaired of the salvation of his soul if, through the mystery of prophecy [Note: [Col. 0489] *testimonium* in witness 1.], he had not learned that God, who could not be seen by a human being, could be seen through the assumption of flesh.

Therefore, because he saw, he cried out: ‘I saw the Lord face to face, and my soul was saved’; and from that vision he took up hope of salvation. Through the appearance of assumed mortality, and through the testing of his flesh, he recognized that salvation—the expectation of the world—would come to the world.

He also expressed this by prophecy in the blessing of his sons, saying: ‘The scepter shall not be taken from Judah, nor the ruler from his loins, until he comes who is to be sent, and he himself shall be the expectation of the nations’ (Gen. XLIX, 10).

Isaiah also says of him: ‘Before him kings shall shut their mouths’ (Isa. LII, 15); ‘the nations shall entreat him’ (ibid. XI, 10).

Now why do you contradict this, Jew? Why do you call us animals? Behold, we are his animals, concerning whom Habakkuk said: ‘In the midst of two animals you shall be known.’ We do not, as you reproach us, hiss [*hiscimus*], but answer as rational animals [Col. 0490A].

But as for your further claim that David said, ‘Do not put your trust in princes, in human beings, in whom there is no salvation,’ and that therefore he had omitted no son of man—so that, on the testimony of the prophet, you might appear secretly to insult Christ, while openly blaspheming his servants, as though an insult against a servant did not concern the contempt of the Lord—we answer these things with the prophet: ‘Let lying lips be silenced, which speak iniquity against the just man with pride and contempt’ (Ps. XXX, 19–20).

We place our hope not in a human being but in God and in his Christ, whom we truly believe to be God and man; and we have proved, by the testimonies of your prophets [Note: [Col. 0489] *vestrarum* in c.], that he is God and the Son of God [Note: [Col. 0489] *cum prob.* in c.].

As for Peter, John, and Martin, we faithfully confess that they are not demons but expellers of demons; and we still see this to be true today by clear signs. We do not place our hope in them, but commend our hope to their God through their intercessions.

As for your statement, ‘In every place the God of Israel is read of, and not the God of the nations,’ God refutes you through David, saying to the Son: ‘Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance and your possession to the ends of the earth’ (Ps. II, 8); and likewise to Abraham: ‘In your seed all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed’ (Gen. XXII, 18).

If the nations are God’s inheritance, I do not know how he can fail to be their God, whose inheritance they are.

In this point, then, which you weave together while demanding our interpretation, namely that the Lord should remember his covenant and the word which he commanded for a thousand generations, and which he established with Abraham, our understanding agrees more closely with the truth than yours.

How do you understand the phrase ‘for a thousand generations’? If you count the generations from the beginning of the world, you will not find a thousand. But since in the sacred Scriptures a definite number is often used for an indefinite one, ‘a thousand generations’ must be understood as all generations. Consequently, the oath established with Abraham is truly fulfilled: ‘In your seed all the nations shall be blessed’—that is, in Christ.”

ANNO DOMINI 1026. BURCHARD, BISHOP OF THE CHURCH OF WORMS.

PREFACES.

[Col. 0491]

HISTORICAL AND LITERARY NOTICE.

(Oudin, *Script. eccles.* II, 525.)

[Col. 0491A] Burchard, bishop of Worms, was German by nation, a Hessian by homeland, and was first a monk at Lobbes in Belgium and a disciple of Olbert, monk of Lobbes and later abbot of Gembloux. In 996, at the urging of his master Olbert, he was elected bishop of the Church of Worms, where he remained until the year 1025 or 1026, when he died. Sigebert, in his *Chronicle* under the year 1008, reports that, with his master Abbot Olbert—a man most learned in every respect—cooperating, he produced a large volume of Canons. In his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 141, he says this of him:

“Burchard, bishop of the city of the Vangiones called Worms, compiled with much effort a large volume of Canons, which is named *Burchard* after its author. He authorized it with the testimonies of all authentic councils, the decrees of the Roman pontiffs, and the opinions of almost all Catholic Fathers; from it the decrees of all councils are still authorized.”

What he had written in the *Chronicle* concerning Olbert’s assistance in making this compilation, he confirms in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under Olbert, ch. 142, in these words: “Burchard, bishop of Worms, advanced by the instruction of that Olbert to the point of devoting himself so earnestly to ecclesiastical usefulness, and by his zeal, speech, and hand publishing that great volume of Canons for the common benefit of all.”

Where, and with whose help, Burchard completed this work is taught by the anonymous author who wrote his Life after his death, published with his *Decree*:

“Forestus is a wood two miles distant from Worms, abounding in fir trees; a muddy marsh surrounds it on one side, and in its midst stands a most beautiful hill. The man of God ordered himself to be conveyed there; and because he wished to avoid worldly tumults, he cut down the trees and bushes and levelled the hill. There he first made an oratory; then, after completing the whitewashed buildings, he constructed an excellent cell. There he withdrew after councils and royal conferences, after synodal business and the various noises of the world. There too, casting secular affairs behind his back, he devoted all his strength to God’s service. At that same time he laboured not a little in this cell upon a collection of Canons. For, with the help of Lord Walter, bishop of Speyer, and with Provost Brunicho exhorting and suggesting, he gathered the Canons into one body. He did this from no arrogance, but, as he himself said, because the laws of the Canons and the judgments concerning penitents had been utterly neglected and destroyed in his bishopric; and he divided this body, or Collection, and distributed it into twenty books.”

[Col. 0492A] He himself testifies to the same in the preface to his work. “When, in his diocese, he saw the Canons and the rules concerning penitents confused, indeed divergent, so that they appeared either wholly neglected, or deprived of almost every authority, or only scantily established in ecclesiastical discipline, at the request of Brunicho, provost of the Church of Worms, he began to gather and arrange ecclesiastical laws for the benefit of his Church, because of the negligence and ignorance, as he himself says, of the priests.” He himself indicates the sources and divisions of his work at the end of the aforesaid preface.

“I have gathered,” he says, “synodal precepts and holy ordinances, both from the opinions of the holy Fathers and from canonical writings, with God’s help, into one bundle from the widest world; and, as best I could, I joined them together as though in one body and divided them into twenty books.” And, after some intervening remarks: “God most good will judge with what labours and vigils I have accomplished this, and he is not unaware that I have done it for the need of our Church. Therefore, even if it should not go beyond the bounds of our province, we shall feel no distress whatever, provided that it be worn in the hands of our ministers. Moreover, we desire to persuade those who read it also that nothing of my own has been added in this work, but that every item has been excerpted from the divine testimonies of the Scriptures (what at this time, here and above, were called divine Scriptures and canonical writings will, alas, immediately become evident), and indeed with such fidelity that I do not doubt that they will possess perpetual authority. The following order indicates from which writings I selected them:

“From the Canons called the *Corpus canonum*.

From the Canon of the Apostles.

From overseas councils”—he means Oriental councils.

“From councils held in Germany, Gaul, and Spain.

From the decrees of the Roman pontiffs.

From evangelical and apostolic Scriptures.

From the Old Testament.

From the books of Saint Gregory; from Jerome, Augustine, Ambrose, Benedict, Basil the Great, and Isidore.

From the Roman Penitential; from the Penitential of Theodore; from the Penitential of Bede.”

[Col. 0493A] Burchard divided his work into twenty books, each of which has its own chapters or canons; each chapter contains only one canon, and each canon has a prefixed summary or title. Burchard himself prefixed the following summary of the books.

The first book contains material on the power and primacy of the apostolic see; on patriarchs and the primates of the other sees; on metropolitans; on holding a synod and summons to a synod; on accused persons, accusers, and witnesses; on those unjustly despoiled; on judges; and on every appropriate honour, dignity, various duty, and ministry of bishops.

The second book contains material on the fitting dignity, various formation, maintenance or manner of life, and various duty and ministry of priests and deacons and of the remaining ecclesiastical orders.

The third book contains material on the establishment, worship, and honour of houses of God; on tithes, offerings, and the judgments applicable to individuals; and on which books are to be received in the sacred catalogue, which are apocryphal, and when they are to be used.

The fourth book contains the sacrament of baptism and the ministry of those to be baptized and baptized, and of those to be confirmed and confirmed.

The fifth book contains material on the sacrament of the body and blood of the Lord and on their reception and observance.

The sixth book contains material on voluntary and involuntary homicides, parricide and fratricides, those who kill their lawful wives and their lords, the killing of ecclesiastics, and the observance and penance appropriate to each.

The seventh book contains material on incestuous unions of consanguinity; on the degree in which the faithful ought to be joined and separated; and on the recall and penance appropriate to each.

The eighth book contains material on men and women consecrated to God, those transgressing their sacred profession, and their recall and penance.

[Col. 0494A] The ninth book contains material on unveiled virgins and widows, their abductors and their separation; on the union of lawful marriages, concubines, and the transgression and penance appropriate to each.

The tenth book contains material on enchanters, augurs, diviners, sorcerers, the devil’s various deceptions, cursers, contentious persons, conspirators, and the penance appropriate to each.

The eleventh book contains material on those to be excommunicated and the excommunicated, thieves and plunderers, presumption, contempt, negligence, reconciliation, and their penance.

The twelfth book contains material on perjury and its penance.

The thirteenth book contains material on the veneration and observance of the sacred fast.

The fourteenth book contains material on gluttony and drunkenness and their penance.

The fifteenth book contains material on emperors, princes, and the remaining laity, and their ministry.

The sixteenth book contains material on accusers, judges, advocates, false witnesses, and the penance appropriate to each.

The seventeenth book contains material on fornication and incest of various kinds, and the penance of both sexes and different ages.

The eighteenth book contains material on visitation, penance, and reconciliation of the sick.

The nineteenth book, called the *Corrector*, contains corrections of bodies and remedies for souls; it teaches every priest, even a simple one, how or in what manner he may help each person: ordained or unordained, poor, rich, child, young man, old man, decrepit person, healthy or sick person, of every age and either sex.

The twentieth book is called *Speculations*, for it considers divine providence and predestination, the coming of Antichrist and his works, the resurrection, the day of judgment, the punishments of hell, and the blessedness of eternal life.

This is the summary of the twenty books contained in the *Decree* of Burchard, bishop of Worms.

Burchard’s work *Decrees* was first published at Paris in 1499, again at Cologne in 1548, in octavo, and finally at Paris in 1549. Burchard brought into this Collection much material from Isidore Mercator, that is, from his forged decretal letters. The following examples, accurately collected by the most eminent David Blondel in ch. 18 of the *Prolegomena to Pseudo-Isidore and Turrianus Being Whipped*, will furnish a specimen.

[Col. 0494D] “Accordingly, he takes from Pseudo-Clement, Epistle 1: book I, chs. 124, 125, 126, 127, 133, 137, and 155; book II, ch. 94; book VI, ch. 28; book XIV, ch. 16. From Epistle 2: book III, ch. 216; book V, chs. 11 and 14. From Epistle 3: book II, ch. 93; book III, ch. 59; book IV, ch. 15.—From the first Pseudo-Anacletus: book I, chs. 4 and 59; book II, ch. 154; book III, chs. 71 and 77; book XI, ch. 18. From the second epistle: book I, chs. 1 and 15; [Col. 0495A] book II, ch. 5. From the third: book I, chs. 136, 152, and 178.—From the second Pseudo-Evaristus: book I, chs. 76, 99, 34, and 40; book II, ch. 9.—From the second Pseudo-Sixtus I: book III, ch. 214.—From the first Pseudo-Alexander: book I, chs. 129, 130, and 132; book II, ch. 52; book V, ch. 5.—From the epistle of Pseudo-Telesphorus: book III, ch. 63.—From the earlier Pseudo-Hyginus: book I, ch. 65.—From the second Pseudo-Pius: book II, ch. 29.—From Pseudo-Anicetus: book II, chs. 28 and 63.—From the later epistle of Pseudo-Soter: book III, ch. 215.—From Pseudo-Eleutherus: book XVI, ch. 30.—From the earlier Pseudo-Victor: book I, ch. 176; book IV, ch. 3.—From the earlier Pseudo-Zephyrinus: book I, ch. 154; book XVI, ch. 13.—From the later: book II, ch. 3.—From the earlier Pseudo-Callistus: book II, ch. 38.—From the later: book I, chs. 66, 80, [Col. 0495B] 135, and 171; book III, ch. 49; book VII, ch. 1; book X, ch. 64. See also book IX, ch. 7.—From Pseudo-Urban: book III, chs. 3 and 143; book I, ch. 1.—From Pseudo-Anterus: book I, ch. 77; book IV, ch. 66.—From the second Pseudo-Fabian: book I, chs. 147 and 148. From the third: book I, ch. 183; book II, ch. 10.—From the second Pseudo-Cornelius: book I, ch. 193; book XII, chs. 12 and 19.—From Pseudo-Lucius: book I, ch. 54; book XI, ch. 19.—From the earlier Pseudo-Stephen: book I, ch. 173. From the later: book I, chs. 142, 161, and 177, and book XVI, ch. 19.—From the later Pseudo-Sixtus II: book I, chs. 143 and 192.—From the second Pseudo-Dionysius: book III, ch. 43.—From the first Pseudo-Felix I: book I, chs. 157 and 169; book XVI, ch. 11. From the second: book I, ch. 174.—From Pseudo-Eutychian: book V, ch. 7.—From [Col. 0495C] Pseudo-Caius: book I, ch. 139.—From the first Pseudo-Eusebius: book I, chs. 138 and 165. From the second: book XI, chs. 25 and 27. From the third: book IV, ch. 63.—From the earlier Pseudo-Miltiades: book III, chs. 2, 4, and 5. From the later: book I, ch. 2; book IV, ch. 61.—From Pseudo-Mark: book I, ch. 98.—From the second Pseudo-Julius: book I, chs. 144 and 170; and from the first: book I, ch. 175.—From the earlier Pseudo-Felix II: book I, chs. 141, 163, 167, 180, 221, and 222; book XVI, ch. 11.—From the fifth Pseudo-Damasus: book I, chs. 153, 156, 171, and 179; book XVI, ch. 31.—From the earlier Pseudo-Anastasius: book III, ch. 103; and from the later: book XIX, ch. 129.—From the second Pseudo-Felix IV: book III, chs. 57 and 58.—From the earlier Pseudo-John II: book III, ch. 32.—From the ninth Pseudo-Pelagius II: book III, ch. 69.—From Pseudo-Gregory’s [Col. 0495D] epistle to Felix: book VII, ch. 19.—From [Col. 0496A] Pseudo-Deusdedit: book XVII, ch. 44.

“Moreover, he heaps together many other passages, drawn I know not from where, which he attributes to Evaristus: book III, ch. 17; book XVIII, ch. 16. To Alexander: book I, ch. 59; book XIX, ch. 100. To Sixtus: book IV, ch. 46. To Hyginus: book III, chs. 11, 21, and 39; book IV, ch. 24. To Pius: book III, chs. 72 and 124; book V, chs. 27 and 47; book VI, ch. 37; book VIII, ch. 18; book XII, chs. 4 and 15; book XV, ch. 10; book XIX, ch. 63. To Anicetus: book V, ch. 29. To Soter: book III, chs. 73 and 74; book V, chs. 20 and 44; book XII, ch. 18. To Zephyrinus: book VIII, ch. 40. To Callistus: book XVIII, ch. 2. To Fabian: book IV, ch. 1; book V, chs. 17, 24, 25, and 36; book VII, ch. 21; book IX, ch. 30; book X, chs. 59 and 60; book XII, ch. 40; book XIII, ch. 8. To Eutychian: book I, chs. 91, 92, 93, and 94; book V, ch. 35; book VIII, ch. 17; book IX, [Col. 0496B] chs. 59 and 60; book XI, ch. 30; book XII, ch. 14; book XIV, chs. 2, 3, and 10; book XIX, ch. 105. To Marcellus: book III, chs. 1, 3, and 9. To Eusebius: book III, ch. 99; book VIII, ch. 19; book IX, ch. 13; book XIII, ch. 17; book XIV, ch. 7; book XVIII, ch. 11; book XIX, ch. 110. To Lucius: book XIX, ch. 69. To Julius: book II, ch. 127; book III, chs. 1 and 204; book V, ch. 1; book VII, ch. 7; book IX, ch. 18; book XVIII, ch. 21. To Liberius: book XIII, chs. 13, 14, and 18. To Felix: book I, ch. 51; book XVI, ch. V; book XIX, ch. 62. To Damasus: book I, ch. 25. To Boniface: book I, chs. 73, 131, 184, and 202; book III, ch. 26; book XI, ch. 17. To Silverius: book III, ch. 23; book V, ch. 19; book XIII, ch. 12. To Pelagius: book XII, ch. 9. He also cited the Preface of Pseudo-Isidore, book I, ch. 42.” These materials were collected by the most learned David Blondel in ch. 18 of the *Prolegomena to Pseudo-Isidore and Turrianus Being Whipped*.

[Col. 0496C] Burchard, bishop of Worms, is treated by Sigebert in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chs. 141 and 142; Henry Pantaleon in the *Prosopography of Illustrious Men of All Germany*, part II, p. 46 of my copy, Basel edition of 1565, published by Nicolaus Brylinger, folio; Antonio Possevino, vol. I of the *Apparatus sacer*, under “Burchard, bishop of Worms”; Gerard von Mastricht, *History of Ecclesiastical and Pontifical Law*, nos. 248–254, pp. 280–291, Doesburg edition of 1676 and Amsterdam edition of 1686, octavo; and William Cave, *History of Literature*, under the year 996, p. 593 of the London edition of 1686, [Col. 0496D] folio.

[Col. 0497]

ON THE COLLECTION OF BURCHARD, BISHOP OF WORMS. His practice of ascribing the opinions of certain later writers to synods, pontiffs, or Fathers; and the Penitential of the Churches of Germany, received and enlarged by him.

(From the dissertation of the Ballerini brothers, *On Ancient Collections*, in *Works of St Leo the Great*, vol. III, or *Patrology*, vol. LVI, col. 320.)

[Col. 0497A] 1. Burchard, a Hessian by homeland, was not a monk, as many have believed, but a canon and royal chaplain; later he was promoted to the see of Worms before the year 1002, and held it until 1025, when he departed this life on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of September [20 August]. While bishop, at the urging of Brunicho, provost of the Church of Worms, he compiled a collection of Canons. In §18 of the preface to Antonio Agustín’s books *On the Emendation of Gratian*, Étienne Baluze observes that the true author of this collection ought rather to be called Olbert, monk of Lobbes and later abbot of Gembloux, at whose dictation and instruction Burchard pieced together that great volume of Canons—if the statements read in the book *On the Deeds of the Abbots of Gembloux* are true. [Col. 0497B] But Bartholomew Fisen relates the matter otherwise, on the basis of Gembloux and Liège manuscripts, in the *Flowers of the Church of Liège*, p. 328. Yet, since Burchard employed Olbert as his teacher and intimate associate, it cannot be denied that he used him as assistant in the work. Hence Sigebert writes in his *Chronicle* under the year 1008 that Burchard, with his master Olbert, a man most learned in every respect, collaborating, published a great volume of Canons. The anonymous author who composed Burchard’s Life after his death, inserted in the Cologne edition, mentions another assistant in the same work: “At that same time,” he says, “he laboured not a little on the collection of Canons . . . . . For, with Lord Walter, bishop of Speyer, assisting, and Provost Brunicho exhorting and suggesting, he gathered the Canons into one body.”

The title *Collectarium canonum* [Collection of Canons] deserves notice, for the manuscript codices lack every title. It agrees, moreover, with the preface of Burchard himself, to be given shortly below, at the end of which he calls his collection a *Collectarium*.

### 2

In the same preface he testifies that he composed this work for the use of his own Church of Worms. That it was not begun before the year 1012 is inferred from Book II, chapter 227, where he reports a letter of his own, written to Walter, Bishop of Speyer, in that same year on the Ides of March. That the work had already been completed before Burchard attended the Synod of Seligenstadt in 1023, we learn from the fact that, since he could not insert the canons of that synod into the collection, he appended them all at the end. [Col. 0498A]

Joannes Molinaeus, in his preface to Ivo’s *Decree*, states that much is missing from Burchard’s printed books which he himself saw more fully in the old manuscripts, but that this material was divided into only twelve books, of which the sixth part is the printed book. Hence, as we believe, Joannes Albertus Fabricius, in volume XI of his *Bibliotheca Graeca*, p. 8, reports that Burchard collected twelve volumes of decrees, and adds: “This work itself has not yet seen the light in its entirety, but only excerpts from it, divided into twenty books.”

Yet not only does the manuscript from which the edition was produced ascribe twenty books to Burchard, but so too do those most ancient copies mentioned by Petrus Pithoeus. We likewise saw four complete manuscripts: two in the Vatican Library, numbered 1350 and 1355; one among the Benedictine Fathers in the monastery of Padiliron; and another at Padua in the library of Saint Justina. All of these present the same number of books, ascribed to Burchard. We may add two other ancient Vatican copies, 1356 and 4980: one begins with Book VII, the other with Book IX, and both continue through Book XIX, which, because the manuscripts are mutilated, lacks its ending. Since the series of books and the contents found in them are the same as in other complete copies, these two manuscripts likewise confirm the same number of twenty books.

Moreover, since no manuscripts known to date contain any collection prefaced by Burchard’s name and divided into twelve parts, we fear that Joannes Molinaeus, led by some ambiguity, inadvertently took another, larger anonymous collection divided into the same number of parts for Burchard’s work because of the agreement between them in several respects. Perhaps he had before his eyes the Sorbonne–Modena collection, divided into twelve parts, which we described in chapter ten; and he may have been misled because there is very close agreement between the titles of Burchard’s Books I, II, and the following books, and the titles prefixed to Parts I, II, III, IV, V, and X of that collection.

Certainly, the preface found only in manuscripts that present twenty books names Burchard as its author and confirms the authenticity of those same books. This becomes much clearer from three manuscripts of Burchard—the Vatican manuscript 1355, the Padua manuscript of Saint Justina, and the Padiliron manuscript—in which the preface itself differs from the printed versions and, as we shall soon see, is more authentic than the received text. It not only explicitly approves the same number of twenty books, but also presents their titles inserted into the preface itself, thereby testifying that these, and no others, were arranged by Burchard. [Col. 0498B]

An anonymous writer contemporary with Burchard likewise agrees with him; in his *Life* he states: “He divided this body, or *Collectarium*, and distributed it into twenty books.” Do not these two testimonies—namely, that of a contemporary writer and that of Burchard himself—eliminate the opinion that there were twelve books?

[Col. 0498C]

### 3

In the *Works of Georgius Cassander*, pp. 1091 and 1098, Fabricius reports that the following is found:

“We also came upon a manuscript work of Burchard, which we compared only cursorily with the work printed at Paris in 1549, and discovered that the wording of the letter had been entirely altered.”

We too observed the same thing in the three manuscripts mentioned above, in which we found only the preface. In them the preface differs from the received version not only in wording but also in arrangement. For the material which, in the printed editions, may appear to have been added by others at the end of the preface is inserted into the preface itself in these manuscripts, so that it is unmistakably evident that it was written under Burchard’s authorship. [Col. 0499A]

The agreement of these ancient copies—with which, we do not doubt, other manuscripts that possess a preface also agree—suggests that this is the genuine preface, or letter, of Burchard to Brunicho. The same conclusion is confirmed by the very inelegance of its style and syntax, which is particularly characteristic of that age. We believe, however, that the received preface was altered by the judgment of some learned man who preferred a more elegant style, since it differs so openly from the ancient manuscripts just mentioned.

For the present, we reproduce it here as it is read in the manuscripts.

### 4

“Burchard, Bishop of Worms in name only, to his faithful Brunicho, namely, the provost of that same see: salvation in Christ the Lord.

For many days now, your familiarity, dearest brother, being present with us, has repeatedly urged and suggested that I should carefully gather into one body a little book drawn from various useful sources for the benefit of our fellow priests, both from the teachings of the holy Fathers and from the canons or from various penitentials. This was especially necessary because the laws of the canons and the judgments concerning penitents in our diocese are so confused, diverse, unpolished, and altogether neglected, so mutually inconsistent and supported by almost no authority, [Col. 0499B] that, because of their discordance, they can scarcely be distinguished even by the half-learned.

Consequently, it often happens that no assistance can be given to those who flee to the remedy of penance, both because of the confusion of the books and because of the ignorance of the priests. Why is this? I judge that it happens chiefly because the canons do not prescribe with sufficient care, clarity, and completeness, for each individual crime, the measure of time and the manner of penance to be carried out, stating how each offense is to be corrected; rather, they decide that the matter should be left to the judgment of an understanding priest.

Therefore, since this cannot be done except by the wise and those instructed in divine law, your affection asked me to offer this book, briefly compiled, for boys to learn at last, so that what our fellow workers, being placed at a more mature age, had neglected in our own time and through the sluggishness of our predecessors might now be handed on to the young and to others who wish to learn. Thus they might first become good disciples and afterward pastors and teachers of the peoples, and might receive in school what they would one day have to teach those entrusted to them.

Your desire and request, brother, seem to me just, and I give thanks for such a wish. I also offer many thanks to Him who provided you to me as such a man, since I have learned that you have labored continually for the condition of our Church. But because I delayed for so long the exhortation you repeatedly impressed upon me, I do not want you to attribute this to my laziness, because for two reasons I was scarcely able to undertake it: namely, because of the various and unavoidable ecclesiastical necessities that arise daily like waves; and, in addition, because of the care of worldly matters pertaining to imperial commands, which greatly dull the mind of one who is striving and reaching toward higher things. For everyone’s mind, while it is divided among many things, becomes less capable of attending to each.

Nevertheless, obedient to your holy requests, with God’s generosity I gathered the synodal precepts and holy statutes both from the teachings of the holy Fathers and from the canons, and, as far as I was able, joined them into a single body; and I distributed that same body into twenty books. If any diligent reader carefully examines them, he will find in them many aids for our ministry.

[Col. 0500C]

### Contents of the individual books of Lord Burchard, Bishop of Worms, briefly indicating what each book contains

[Note: [Col. 0499] This title, or at least Burchard’s name, appears to have been inserted at the discretion of the scribes.]

The first book contains material concerning the power and primacy of the apostolic see, of the patriarchs, of the other primates, and of the metropolitans; the holding of a synod and the summons to a synod; accused persons, accusers, and witnesses; those unjustly dispossessed; judges; every appropriate honor and dignity; and the various affairs and ministry of bishops.

The second book contains material concerning the appropriate dignity, the various institution, training, or quality of life, and the various affairs and ministry of priests, deacons, and the remaining ecclesiastical orders.

[Col. 0500D]

The third book contains material concerning the establishment, worship, and honor of the houses of God; tithes, offerings, and the rights of individuals; which books are to be received into the sacred Catalogue and which are apocryphal; and when they are to be added.

The fourth book contains the sacrament of baptism and the ministry of those to be baptized, those baptized, those to be confirmed, and those confirmed.

The fifth book contains material concerning the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, and their reception and observance.

The sixth book contains material concerning homicides committed voluntarily and involuntarily; parricides and fratricides; those who kill legitimate wives and their elders; the killing of ecclesiastical persons; and the observance and penance of each individual.

[Col. 0501A]

The seventh book contains material concerning incestuous intercourse among relatives; at which degree of relationship the faithful may marry and must separate; and the restoration and penance of each individual.

The eighth book contains material concerning men and women dedicated to God who transgress their sacred commitment, and concerning their restoration and penance.

The ninth book contains material concerning unveiled virgins and widows; those who abduct them and their separation from them; the formation of legitimate marriages; concubines; and the transgression and penance of each individual.

[Col. 0501B]

The tenth book contains material concerning enchanters, augurs, diviners, sorcerers, and various deceptions of the devil; those who curse; quarrelsome people; conspirators; and the penance of each individual.

The eleventh book contains material concerning those to be excommunicated and those who have been excommunicated; thieves and plunderers; presumption, contempt, and negligence; and their reconciliation and penance.

The twelfth book contains material concerning perjury and its penance.

The thirteenth book contains material concerning the veneration and observance of the sacred fast.

The fourteenth book contains material concerning gluttony and drunkenness, and their penance.

[Col. 0501C]

The fifteenth book contains material concerning emperors, princes, and the remaining laypeople, and concerning their ministry.

The sixteenth book contains material concerning accusers, judges, defenders, false witnesses, and the penance of each individual.

The seventeenth book contains material concerning fornication and incest of various kinds, and the penance of both sexes and of different ages.

The eighteenth book contains material concerning the visitation, penance, and reconciliation of the sick.

The nineteenth book, called *Corrector* and *Medic*, contains corrections for bodies and medicines for souls. It teaches every priest, even a simple one, how and in what manner he may come to the aid of each person: ordained or unordained, poor or rich, child, young person, old person, decrepit person, healthy or sick, of every age and of either sex.

[Col. 0501D]

The twentieth book is called *Speculations*. For it considers divine providence and predestination, the coming of Antichrist, his works, the resurrection, the day of judgment, the punishments of hell, and the happiness of eternal life.

Therefore, brother, if one of these things is lacking to those who govern their peoples, how will they be able to instruct and teach them? Indeed, the name of priest will scarcely remain among them, because the evangelical threats are exceedingly dangerous, as it is said: “If the blind leads the blind, both fall into the pit.”

But if there is some envious person who, after seeing this, envies me and says that I gather food from another’s threshing floor and make an empty name for myself from another’s labor, so be it. I confess that I gathered it from the labor of others, because it is not permitted to me alone to make canons, but it is permitted to collect them—and that is what I did. God knows that I did so not out of some arrogance, but because of the need of our Church.

To silence the murmur of the detractor, let the book be of whatever sort: let it belong to our people. I do not ask that it cross the threshold of our bishopric; let it remain for our people to learn. But I want you to hear how and from where I collected it; and if there is any sin in it, I leave it to your judgment to decide.

I added nothing of my own except the labor. Rather, from divine testimonies I gathered, with great effort, the things you will find in it. And so that what I had brought together might possess authority, I labored with the greatest care.

For from that very nucleus of the canons—which some call the *Corpus of Canons*—I excerpted what was necessary for our time. Some things from the Apostolic Canon; some from councils overseas; some from German councils; some from Gallic and Hispanic councils; some from the decrees of the Roman pontiffs; some from the teaching of Truth itself; some from the Old Testament; some from the apostles; some from the sayings of Saint Gregory; some from the sayings of Saint Jerome; some from the sayings of Saint Augustine; some from the sayings of Saint Ambrose; some from the sayings of Saint Benedict; some from the sayings of Saint Isidore; some from the sayings of Saint Basil; some from the Roman Penitential; some from the Penitential of Theodore; and some from the Penitential of Bede.

[Col. 0502C]

Moreover, if you find anything useful in this *Collectarium*, attribute it to God’s gifts. But if you find anything superfluous, charge it to my foolishness. Farewell, and I beg you to remember me, a sinner, in your sacred prayers.

Here ends the prologue.”

### 5

In this preface, or letter, of Burchard, the words “I distributed that same body into twenty books” must be noted. It should also be recalled, as we mentioned earlier, that the order and titles of the individual books were inserted into that same preface by Burchard, so that there can be no doubt that the printed work—which agrees perfectly with this number of books and with the same titles and order—has Burchard as its author.

In the received preface, although it differs in many matters, the same number of books is indicated. But the order is different; [Col. 0502D] and certain passages have been cut away from that preface and thrown to the end in such a way that they may appear to have been written and added not by Burchard but by someone else.

For not only has the index of the title of each book been detached from the preface in the received versions, but it is also preceded by a list of the authors from whom Burchard derived the canons—a catalogue likewise torn away from the same preface, with this heading, which cannot have come from Burchard: “From which places and authors’ writings he collected these ecclesiastical decrees.”

The nucleus of the canons, which Burchard praises at the beginning of the catalogue at the end of the preface and says is called by some the *Corpus of Canons*, is the collection of Pseudo-Isidore, from which he transcribed many apocryphal decrees. [Col. 0503A] Stephanus Baluzius demonstrates at length in his preface to Regino that Burchard also excerpted many chapters from Regino, as well as several from the two appendices appended in the manuscripts to Regino’s collection.

In the titles, however, he altered many things, prefixing other titles at his own discretion. Later collectors of canons adopted these titles from him, thereby causing great confusion. Since many passages in Burchard are headed with the names of councils or pontiffs in whose separately published decrees nothing of the sort is found, many believed that Burchard or his copyists had discovered them in lost documents of those councils or pontiffs. Consequently, they were added as precious fragments preserved by them, each in its proper place under the relevant synod or pontiff, in editions of the councils.

Those who undertook to examine the matter more carefully discovered that Burchard attributed to synods, Roman pontiffs, or the holy Fathers chapters which Regino had quoted either from the capitularies of kings, from Hrabanus, from Ferrandus the deacon, or without mentioning any author.

Stephanus Baluzius noted the following concerning the books of the capitularies in the preface mentioned above, no. 22:

“When compiling Regino, Burchard preferred to attribute to certain councils or ancient Fathers the chapters he took from him rather than to our kings, because the designation ‘Frankish’—by which the kings of the Germans still gloried in the age of Regino and Widukind—had ceased to be used in Burchard’s time, and thus all reverence for these capitularies had been stripped away by the Saxons.

“For Burchard cites chapters of Charlemagne only once, in chapters 218 and 219 of Book I, adding that they had been praised by the bishops at Aachen; otherwise, perhaps, he would not have used them.

“It appears, however, that Burchard adopted the practice of citing under another, more celebrated name, rather than under the name of the actual author, chapters taken from authors who were neither supreme pontiffs, nor synods, nor sufficiently well-known and distinguished Fathers.”

This observation will be extremely useful when reading collections later than Burchard’s, such as those of Ivo and Gratian, who received many passages of the same kind from Burchard.

Everyone attributes the following further merit to this collection: that it follows a sufficiently suitable method and, in addition, contains several canons of later German councils which are found either only in very rare manuscripts [Col. 0503D] or even preserve excellent readings from which the received texts can be corrected.

### 6

Finally, we do not wish to omit two points.

First, in the Vatican Library there is an old manuscript, number 4227, entitled *Corrector and Medic*, without the name of its author. Jacobus Petit likewise saw a similar manuscript in the Paris Library of Saint Victor and published an excerpt from it in volume I of Theodore’s *Penitential*, p. 358. [Col. 0504A] This work belongs to Burchard’s collection, in which Book XIX bears the same title, as is clear even from the titles previously described in Burchard’s preface.

Second, Vatican manuscript 3830, from the eleventh century, contains a Penitential in which are found questions to be put by confessors, together with the assignment of penances. All these questions are copied word for word in the same chapter 5 of Burchard’s Book XIX. Only in Burchard’s chapter are there more of them than in the manuscript mentioned.

The paragraphs of questions—which, to avoid confusion, we have counted and distinguished by numbers—number 194 in Burchard. In that manuscript the questions are the same as those in Burchard’s fifth chapter, from no. 1 through no. 59, which begins: “Have you violated a tomb?” [Col. 0504B]

Then the manuscript omits Burchard’s subsequent numbers 60 through 103 inclusive, headed “Concerning magical art,” “Concerning sacrilege,” “Concerning gluttony and drunkenness,” “Concerning irreligion,” again “Concerning magical art,” “Concerning superstition,” and again “Concerning magical art.”

All these numbers are absent from the manuscript mentioned. After no. 59, “Have you violated a tomb?” and so forth, it continues: “Have you lain with your wife’s sister?” and so forth, as in Burchard no. 104, and it continues through no. 152, “Have you believed what some people are accustomed to believe, that there are wild women?” and so forth.

It omits, however, what is added at the end of this number in Burchard: “In all these matters mentioned above, priests ought …” It also omits the following number, 153, which begins: “Have you caused certain women, at certain times, to …” [Col. 0504C]

Soon afterward, although it gives Burchard’s numbers 154, 155, and 156, the manuscript passes over the next six numbers, from no. 157—“Have you done what certain women are accustomed to do, namely, with your little son …”—through no. 162.

It does, however, give no. 163, “Have you killed a son or daughter?” and the following two numbers.
