It lacks no. 166, “Have you tasted semen?” Then, after copying no. 167, “Have you drunk chrism?” it omits the next fourteen numbers, from no. 168 through no. 181, and concludes with Burchard’s numbers 182, “Have you oppressed an infant?” and 183, “Have you found an infant?”

Burchard adds eleven numbers at the end which are not found in the manuscript.

That the Penitential in this manuscript was used in German churches is indicated, among other things, by two numbers in which a German expression is mentioned: in no. 30, what is called *carina* in German; and what is expressed in the manuscript in no. 151 of Burchard as “what common foolishness calls *Wervvolff*” is written thus: “what is called *Werevvlf* in German.” [Col. 0504D]

From what has been said, it can easily be conjectured that Burchard inserted into his collection this Penitential, which was accepted among his own people, and added from other Penitentials what was lacking in it.

[Col. 0505]

# THE LIFE OF BURCHARD, BISHOP  
## Edited by G. Waitz, Ph.D.

*(In Pertz, Monumenta Germaniae Historica, Scriptores, vol. IV, p. 829.)*

## Notice

[Col. 0505A]

A cleric of Worms set forth the life of Burchard, Bishop of Worms, illustrious and famous for his public and private achievements, [Note: [Col. 0505B] At the end of the twelfth century, Hermann, a cleric of Worms, also celebrates his memory in the Worms cartulary. We have decided to reproduce that passage here as well, formerly published together with the *Life*, from the excellent manuscript Cod. membr. s. XII, fol. 25, in the Royal Library of Hanover:

“Here begins the prologue concerning the privileges of Burchard, Bishop of the Church of Worms.

After the times of the venerable bishops, during which they governed the Church of Worms, entrusted to them by God, amid the waves of various storms, with vigilant care according to the duty of their office, and left it enriched in resources and honors either by their own generosity or through the gifts of kings or emperors, we must now approach the entrance of the pious shepherd and the time of Bishop Burchard. His memory is celebrated among men because of the distinction of his merits and is immortal in the sight of the Most High.

How he conducted himself in the episcopate need not be explained in words, since the fame of his virtues is confirmed throughout the world by the testimony of his works. To speak with everyone’s agreement, although many men of wondrous holiness preceded him in the see of Worms, in comparison with his planting and superstructure this Church was, both in spiritual and temporal matters, almost formless.

The clergy testify to this, raised by him with fatherly affection; the city, adorned and enlarged by him, testifies to it; the entire bishopric, enriched in possessions and generous endowments, testifies to it; and the communities of this Church testify to it. Finding them very small, he abundantly enlarged them through his gifts or established them anew. With great labor he gathered the body of the canons into a single form of chaste utterances. He gave a particular law to the household of Saint Peter, as will be seen below. In short, he happily left the Church of Worms shining with all good things in the splendor of midday. Thus, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of September, his place was made in peace, and he was buried at Saint Lawrence.”]

He was a cleric of Worms who had seen him and had been present at his death. [Note: [Col. 0506B] Chapters 20–23.] The author himself explains at greater length in the preface with what purpose and in what spirit he undertook this task. There he dedicates the book to a certain bishop whom he declares to have been Burchard’s closest associate and friend, and his own teacher and almost a second father. I have not been able to discover the man’s name. [Note: [Col. 0506B] It can scarcely have been Azzecho, who governed the Church of Worms after Burchard, since the author nowhere indicates that one succeeded the other. Nor would he have written, in chapter 20, “after he [Burchard] died, no one of equal distinction in so glorious a life would be found in this place,” if the book had been addressed to Azzecho.]

Certainly, he appears to have written several years after Burchard’s death. [Note: [Col. 0506C] Prologue, chapter 2.] But he clearly committed to memory and history a valuable and highly important monument for posterity: “the things he had seen and the good things he had learned about him from the reports of religious men.”

This *Life*, however, appears to have been read by no one throughout the Middle Ages, so far as I know, and is also greatly neglected by more recent scholars. Its rarity is probably due to the fact that it was published only once, in a volume entitled:

1. *The Twenty Books of Decrees of Lord Burchard, Bishop of the Church of Worms. The Work Now Printed for the First Time.* Cologne, from the workshop of Melchior Novesianus, 1548, folio.

Having searched for this book unsuccessfully in both the Royal Library of Hanover and those of Göttingen and Berlin, we received it from that rich treasury of books at Wolfenbüttel, through the customary kindness of the distinguished V. Cl. Schonemann, who acceded to our request. From it I have arranged to reproduce that *Life*, of which I believe no manuscript now survives, since Worms was most disastrously devastated and burned by the French in 1689. The editor, who placed the *Life* after the index of the decree’s chapters, appears to have used a sufficiently good manuscript with considerable accuracy, so that I have attempted to correct only a few minor points.

For this purpose I also used:

2. The *Chronicle of Worms*, which a certain monk of Kirsgarten composed at the beginning of the sixteenth century. He says:

“Burchard was the sixteenth bishop of Worms. Twenty-five years ago we found his history at Saint Paul. Likewise, it is kept in the greater church; and here, for the praise of our city, I wish to append it word for word, just as I find it written.”

Nevertheless, he did not use it with such fidelity. He often altered the wording, added some things, omitted others, and rendered the work quite corrupt. Moreover, both Ludewig’s edition (*Reliquiae manuscriptarum*, II, pp. 43–72) and the manuscripts which the distinguished Bohmer and Petersen kindly communicated to us—the Frankfurt manuscript [Note: [Col. 0506C] *V. Archiv* I, p. 323. Written in the mid-seventeenth century in folio from the library of Johann Maximilian Zum Jungen.] and the Hamburg manuscript [Note: [Col. 0506C] *V. Archiv* VI, p. 244. It appears to have been copied from the Frankfurt manuscript.]—both written in the seventeenth century, are filled with the most disgraceful errors. I do not know whether these should be attributed to the monk of Kirsgarten or to incompetent scribes.

Nevertheless, I have reported in the notes whatever readings appeared to possess some importance—readings I would certainly have omitted [Col. 0508A] had this book not been almost buried in oblivion and deprived entirely of the authority of manuscripts, while still requiring publication.

**G. Waitz**

## Prologue

[Note: [Col. 0507] The entire prologue is absent from manuscript 2.]

[Col. 0507]

[Col. 0507A] [Note: Manuscript 1 reads *charissimi* (“dearest”); the editor has corrected the word to *carissimi*.]

### Supplementary textual apparatus

- **Prologue, “more plainly.”** The printed *planius* means “more plainly”; the editor queries *plenius*, “more fully.”
- **§1, opening and character description.** The printed opening *Erat igitur Burchardus* means “Burchard therefore was [born in the province of Hesse]”; manuscript 2 begins *Erat namque Borchardus*, “For Burchard was [born in the province of Hesse].” In the next sentence manuscript 2 has *quippe*, “indeed,” for printed *nempe*, “certainly.” Manuscript 2 omits the whole description *in justo stabilis*, “steadfast in justice”; it has *quamvis*, “although,” for printed *quamquam*, also “although”; and it omits the entire clause *nec ullum contradicendo aliquando objiceret verbulum*, “nor did he ever offer even a little word in contradiction.”
- **§2, advancement and office.** For printed *ab archiepiscopo sublimatus est*, “he was exalted by the archbishop,” manuscript 2 reads *a Willegiso* (“by Willigis”), while manuscript 1 has *sublatus* (“raised”) for *sublimatus* (“exalted”). For printed *Positisque ad electionem fratrum claustri primatibus*, “and after the leaders of the cloister had been appointed according to the brothers’ election,” manuscript 2 reads *Positis ergo ibi …*, “therefore, after the leaders … had been appointed there.” Where the printed text begins *Ergo religiosissimus Willigisus*, “Accordingly, the most religious Willigis,” manuscript 2 places *autem* after the adjective: *Religiosissimus autem Willegisus archiepiscopus*, “The most religious Archbishop Willigis, however.” For printed *praemia lucratus est sempiterna*, “he gained eternal rewards,” manuscript 2 reads *praemia sempiterna est consecutus*, “he obtained eternal rewards.” In the following causal clause manuscript 2 omits *nec* (“nor”) before “regard for any person.”
- **§§3–4, verbal forms.** In the prediction of Franco’s death, printed *praedixit* means “he foretold,” while manuscript 2’s expanded reading supplies the subject and outcome: “Franco, the venerable man and bishop of Worms, beloved of God, succumbed to nature and paid the debt of death, and his body was buried in peace at Rome by the emperor with great honor.” The apparatus abbreviates *praedixit* as *p.* and ends its variant quotation at *cum*, “with,” before resuming the shared continuation *magno honore in pace sepultum est*, “was buried in peace with great honor”; it does not indicate a manuscript lacuna. In §4 the printed counterfactuals *non vidisset* and *non vixisset* mean “had not seen” and “had not lived”; manuscript 2 has the indicative forms *non vidit* and *non vixit*, “did not see” and “did not live.”
- **§5, the emperor’s report and compulsion.** Printed *rogarit*, “may have asked/has asked,” is replaced by *rogavit*, “asked”; printed *demandarit*, “may have entrusted/has entrusted,” by *demandavit*, “entrusted”; and printed *compulerat*, “had compelled,” by manuscript 2’s *compulit*, “compelled.” Thus the witness changes tense or mood even where the running English sounds similar.
- **§6, the wolves.** Printed *devorassent*, *terruissent*, and *evasissent* mean “had devoured,” “had terrified,” and “had escaped.” Manuscript 2 instead has *devorabant*, “were devouring”; *terruerunt*, “terrified”; and *evaserunt*, “escaped.”
- **§7, Duke Otto’s stronghold.** In place of the printed sequence saying that robbers, thieves, and all who offended against the bishop had a very safe refuge there, manuscript 2 reads in full: “All who offended against the bishop and his faithful men by word or deed withdrew to this stronghold, and thus they had a very safe refuge there; hence also, on account of this, many slayings and murders occurred on both sides.” Manuscript 2 also reads “God’s servant Burchard endured this for a long time” for the printed “the man of God endured this disgrace and these harsh calamities”; it omits *hoc genus hominum*, “this class of people”; and it has imperfect *respuebant*, “were rejecting him,” for perfect *respuerunt*, “rejected him,” of the peaceful young man’s parents and relatives.

When I was deliberating with myself about writing the life and happy deeds of the blessed Father and my dearest senior, Bishop Burchard, you, most pious prelate N., came to my mind, so that I might assign and dedicate what I had written to your name. For your wisdom is known to all, and everyone acknowledges that you exercise the office of a capable man not only in your own affairs but also in the imperial camps. You build and govern with the greatest authority the church entrusted to you by God; you are openly proclaimed a man of supreme virtue; and you are rightly called the consolation of the poor and needy. You showed this most clearly toward me, wretched as I am, when you mercifully received me, worn down by various hardships and despised and cast aside by everyone, and, as became you, fostered me by kindly counsel [Col. 0507B] and care. Such things you did toward one who did not deserve them. For you do not seek what belongs to human beings but, as is evident to all, meditate with a pure mind on what belongs to God; you do not look to anyone’s status, but follow with an unwavering step the straight path of the heavenly journey. Therefore, if I may venture to say so, through an everlasting bond of love for your life, the seal of Christ’s charity has been stamped upon my heart.

Although poverty in my household resources has denied me the means of rendering services, my will toward you will nevertheless always remain devoted in Christ. Hence I have consecrated this little work to your name, composed concerning the deeds of your most intimate and familiar friend. Let your dignity know, however, that these things were not composed out of any pride, but, God as my witness, to avoid idleness and the sloth of the heart, and especially to preserve the memory of his blessed life, so that, when his most pious deeds are read, the wicked mouths of those speaking against him may be stopped. If I have joined anything together disorderly or unskillfully, I have decided to submit it to your correction and authority, hoping that your mercy will correct and defend it. Finally, let this little work also be subject to your judgment: if it displeases you, let it be destroyed; but if it pleases you, let it remain as a testament to the deeds of God’s servant.

This little work, however, took its beginning in the following manner. One day, as I sat in a more secluded place, turning various matters over in my mind and thinking not without sighs, one of my companions came in and addressed me in these words:

“Why,” he said, “my dearest, are you sitting here alone, meditating with a troubled mind? Or why, sadder than usual, do you gaze at the ground with bowed head? If someone has disturbed you by words or deeds, he has already disturbed me along with you. Therefore, if anything troubles your mind, tell me and do not conceal your purpose from me, for whatever you call me to, you shall have my counsel and assistance ready.”

“Dear brother,” I replied, “you have found me here at the right moment, and you have come to me as one whom I greatly desired. For some time I have been thinking of revealing to you, either in writing or by disclosing it in speech, something of what I have in mind. But because many things have hindered my feeling, I have postponed it until now. Yet among these many obstacles the greatest has been this: I hesitated to bring into public view what I had thought out. You yourself know how harmful modern people are, how full they are of various opinions. What if someone, goaded by envy, sees what is written here and, condemning me in these words, brings me to shame—saying, namely, that it is a great act of boldness for me, poor and foolish as I am, to present my little notions to prudent men, notions scarcely put together by a naked and thirsty intellect? Let it be so: I confess that I am poor and foolish. But if I am poor, I am not ashamed to become rich; whereas the rich man is ashamed to become poor, just as we read that the rich steward said: ‘I am ashamed to beg’ (Luke 16:3).”

It is dearer to me to live as a poor man with Lazarus than to be sent with the rich man into eternal fire. We were all born poor and naked. But he who gave the soul also supplies food, and he who created the body provides clothing. He himself possesses these things; he himself will give them to me, because the soul is more than food and the body more than clothing. He does not despise the poor either, but chooses the weak in order to confound the strong. If I am naked and barren in intellect, nevertheless I clothe myself in the boldness of speaking, because I hope in him as helper who said: “Open your mouth and I will fill it” (Psalm 80:11). For in accordance with his promise of mercy he himself will bring to completion, strengthen, and establish whatever I am to do and say.

Therefore I shall postpone speaking further about these matters, and I shall disclose to your affection what the course of our narrative requires to be brought forth. My mind is incessantly impelled by continual promptings to write, according to the measure of my intellect and the testimony of my conscience, the holy and God-consecrated life of our blessed Father, Bishop Burchard, most worthy of all praise. To complete this work I humbly ask both your counsel and your assistance, for I know that you are thoroughly instructed in divine matters, acquainted with these events, and very suitable for this undertaking. For I have not yet forgotten how, at a certain time of conversation, you questioned me at length about the virtues of the aforementioned man; and when I had recounted to you his holy pursuits and uprightness of character, [Col. 0508C] and had explained to you how steadfastly he had persevered in the works of Christ, in the Holy Scriptures, in fasts, vigils, and prayers—this I confess I did not relate without tears—I also told you how, through the constancy of his prayer, he had very often restrained the worldly storms, various adversities, and terrors of the air. Thus we considered the day exceedingly delightful.

“Do you remember?”

“How could I not? For afterward, knocking at the door of holy desire, you urged me day and night, pressing me to bring forth something written about the life or virtues of this man, or to suggest to you material for writing about him. Obeying your pious requests, I shall endeavor, with your assistance, to narrate something of his life, although my compositions are inarticulate, while heavenly grace fills the barrenness of my mind.

“But whenever mention of that most blessed man occurs to me, I am afflicted by weeping and sighs. At such times, dear friend, I can do nothing but pour forth tears and sighs without ceasing and silently turn over these wretched thoughts within me: Who was I, who am I, or who shall I be? I am that man mercifully nourished and miserably abandoned, placed in labor and misery and almost the vilest of all, of lowly stock and sinful parentage, unknown to everyone but conscious to myself. ‘The likeness of the nations and the shaking of the head among the peoples.’ For, as a sluggish man, I am rejected; as something foul, I am spat out; as something rotten, I am despised—and not undeservedly. For every day I, most wretched, rot in the mire of sins, and, miserable, I grow accustomed to carrying heavy burdens unbearable for my neck. Whatever my fleeting spirit desires, like mud untested in any kiln, I soften toward carrying out; and the sins I scarcely once bewail with tears newly arisen, I immediately multiply a hundredfold, forgetting the salvation of my entire soul. Hence my words are full of sorrow.

“I think you recognize this in yourself as well, brother; I know that you too have more than once sweated within similar boundaries [Note: *thermis* (“baths” or “hot springs”) seems to be the reading; manuscript 1 has the word in the margin]. But why all this? Why, dear friend, am I finally leading you through a superfluous argument? By ‘superfluous argument’ I mean what we profess in words but do not accomplish in deeds. For at the beginning of this discussion I was calling you, dear friend, not to sadness but to joy, not to sorrow but to gladness, not to vices but to the virtues that must be brought forth.

“Therefore I return to the thought I began, and I earnestly and humbly entreat your affection either to lead me by questioning and to understand me as I narrate the life of this man, or to correct me when I ask questions and to teach me fully by recounting the virtues mentioned above.”

[Note: Manuscript 1 reads *tuam dilectionemque* (“your affection and”) rather than *dilectionemque tuam* (“your affection”).]

In response, the other, giving thanks, said:

“Your request or admonition, dearest friend, is not to be censured but seems to me greatly worthy of praise. For by asking, you have, as it were, written these things, and by narrating them you have admonished me concerning matters beneficial to salvation; thus you have moved me by saving words. You said that you had not yet forgotten my questioning and your account of the deeds of our senior. I too remember my inquiry and your exposition of his virtues. Therefore I asked, and I ask again, that you write something about his happy deeds, or suggest to me material for writing. For it is shameful to lower the sails when a favorable wind does not cease to blow. Let your promise therefore be fulfilled, and since fortune favors us, let there be no further delay.

“But those heavy burdens and miserable cares of worldly affairs of which you spoke I have hitherto scarcely known even by name, yet now I carry them on my already sloping shoulders to such a degree that, alas, I can neither breathe nor raise my head under the greatness of the weight. The worldly storms, the various assaults of adversity, and the terrors of the air that, while our blessed patron lived, we experienced only rarely, we now endure, because of our deserving sins, as though they were daily or momentary. For while he lived, aided by his pious prayers before God, we were protected from every danger as though by a wall [Note: Manuscript 1 reads *sumus* (“we are”) rather than *fuimus* (“we were”)]. But after we were deprived of his blessed presence, once the shepherd had been struck down, according to the Lord’s saying, we were scattered—like sheep set without an impediment (*offensaculum*, an uncertain reading)—and nearly reduced to nothing.

“Thus, whenever I heard you speaking such things just now, I silently wept at almost every word—not with bare tears, but, as my conscience bears witness, tears congealed from the deepest remorse. Therefore, I beg you, continue by narrating what you promised about this man; and if I can suggest anything to you, brother, I shall not cease to do so.”

“I confess,” I replied, “that we were always protected from dangerous weapons by his pious prayers; and for that reason, in my extreme foolishness, I then thought that I had sinned with impunity, because I knew that he prayed for us without ceasing. For the pious shepherd labored greatly before God on behalf of the flock entrusted to him, and he endured many calumnies and calamities in the world, resisting them manfully with a stout heart.”

All these matters, with God’s help, we shall recount more clearly in their appropriate places. [Note: The editor asks whether *plenius* (“more fully”) should be read for printed *planius* (“more plainly”).] But we must respond to the point at which you admonished us, by examples, that promises must be fulfilled. You said that it is shameful to lower the sails when favorable gusts of wind do not cease. I understand that this is true, but I do not think it should be done carelessly. If someone intends to cross the breadth of the sea, he should first fortify his ship on every side against the threats of the sea; then, by investigating the depth of the water, he should cautiously identify the hidden rocks beneath the waves, so that, when he begins to sail, he may safely have no fear of the dangers of the sea and not strike the concealed rocks, but, directing the ship by a firm rudder, may reach the harbor of salvation with full sails and favorable winds.

In a similar way, for the magnitude of this undertaking, faith must be implored for us; the smallness of our intellect must be sharpened on both sides, so that we do not fall into the condemnation of the envious but reach the end in safety. For an envious man often praises a person’s deeds to his face by flattering him, but in his absence, barking pointlessly like a rabid dog, condemns them.

But because I fear going on to describe the most wicked customs of people, poisoned by the venom of envy and established in no faith, I shall place my finger upon my mouth, so that my mouth may not speak of human works. Therefore, not fearing the envy of flatterers or slanderers, let us undertake, with the help of divine mercy, to recount at least something of the deeds of this just man. Nevertheless, if we ought to narrate what we ourselves saw and what we learned about him as good from religious men, we shall see the day incline toward its end before we have finished. For this reason, touching briefly upon the substance of the matter from his birth, let us begin with divine assistance and thus endeavor, by briefly narrating his deeds, to reach the end.

[VITA]

### 1.

Burchard was born in the province of Hesse to parents who, according to worldly rank, were not of the lowest station. As a boy, he was first brought up in canonical discipline at Confluentes (Koblenz), through the recommendation of his parents [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “educated”]; then he was sent to various places for the sake of study [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “cast down”] [Col. 0511C] [Note: A canon of Liège is named in the continuation of the *Deeds of the Abbots of Lobbes*; I do not know whether correctly; Dachery, second edition, II, p. 744].

Afterward he attached himself to Willigis, the venerable archbishop of the see of Mainz [Note: Manuscript 1 has *Vuilligoso* throughout; manuscript 2 reads “he attached himself to the venerable archbishop of the Mainz see”], and, filled with that man’s salutary wisdom and formed according to his noble character, he avoided vicious deeds by fleeing them, although his youth did not permit it, and gradually turned his mind toward better things. For after the first flower of youth he shone forth illustrious in every goodness: steadfast in justice, faithful in what was entrusted to him, prudent in counsel, not elated in prosperity, not disturbed in adversity, obedient to those of higher rank, compassionate toward the needy, approachable by the miserable, merciful toward his subjects, exceedingly generous, most upright in conduct, and energetic in every work of God [Note: Manuscript 1 omits “of God”]. There is no need to praise his patience, since toward those serving him—even though they often offended against him—he never at any time offered even a word of contradiction [Note: Manuscript 2 omits the entire clause *nec ullum contradicendo aliquando objiceret verbulum*: “nor did he ever offer even a little word in contradiction.”].

### 2.

Strong in these and similar virtues [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “strong in these and suchlike virtues”], he was elevated by the archbishop through the successive stages of advancement to the order of deacon [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “stations”] and was placed in charge of a very poor locality [Note: Manuscript 2 omits this]. With the archbishop’s assistance, he immediately enlarged this place with the greatest effort and adorned it with all his strength [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “destroyed it”]. For there he built both an outstanding monastery and a canonical cloister in honor of Saint Victor [Note: Manuscript 2 adds “outside the walls of the city of Mainz.” The monk of Kirsgarten adds: “This Victor is the companion of Saint Gereon, who rests at Cologne. They suffered on the same day, but Victor with his companions at Xanten, and Gereon with his companions at Cologne.”]

After appointing leaders of the cloister according to the brothers’ election, he ordered the course of the liturgy to be sung and observed at fixed times and according to prescribed signs. Thus, when the ecclesiastical affairs had been properly arranged according to canonical rule, he transferred to this church as its own property many estates and serfs that he had acquired either through the gifts of his parents or through a royal donation [Note: Otto III’s two charters, by which he gave certain properties to Burchard the cleric in the district of Hesse, in the county of Thancmar, properties that Count Hermann had held as a benefice, were published by Schannat, *History of Worms*, II, pp. 32–33].

Through the pious labors of this man, therefore, praises and thanksgivings are offered to our God by the daily office in the place mentioned. Accordingly, the most religious Willigis, recognizing the holy meditation of the man of God, chose him as his closest companion [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “chose him as his familiar”] and appointed him master of his chamber and chief official of the city. In this office he gained eternal rewards not only among human beings but also with God, because neither gifts nor presents nor regard for any person could turn him from the path of uprightness, as we commonly see certain people easily slip from right judgment either through friendship or through envy [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “either friendship or envy, or both”].

As the fame of the blessed man increased through these and many other works of piety, knowledge of him reached the ears of the emperor Otto III. Since the emperor was himself most pious, he loved Burchard greatly, often received him kindly when he came to him [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “received him”], and honorably sent him away laden with various gifts, promising him his future favor.

### 3.

Meanwhile it happened that Hildebald, bishop of the church of Worms [Note: Manuscript 2 omits “of the church”], closed the final day of his life (4 August 998), and in his place Franco [Note: Manuscript 1 has *francko*], the brother of the aforementioned lord Burchard, was appointed bishop. Much could sufficiently be narrated about this man if the smallness of my intellect did not impede me. But since mention of him has entered our account, if we cannot speak of his greater deeds, let us nevertheless say something about the lesser ones [Note: Manuscript 2 omits this sentence].

After receiving the bishopric [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “Then Franco, having received the bishopric”], he remained for some time within the borders of Worms. Then, after he had rationally arranged the ecclesiastical affairs [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “settled”], he set out with the emperor on the Italian expedition [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “with Otto III”]. There he devoted himself for more than a year to the emperor’s service with vigilant attention [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “for a period of more than a year”]. He was often present at the emperor’s secret counsels [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “very often”], and whenever anything concerning important matters had to be discussed, he was held in such familiarity and authority with the emperor, although he was young, that rarely was anything decided without his counsel.

He was approachable to all and kind to all [Note: Manuscript 2 adds “and gracious”], and by giving many gifts he acquired no small glory among everyone. Hence all held him in the greatest honor and affection and already divined him to be almost a saint [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “declared him”]. For this reason he was greatly honored by the emperor and held dearer than others; on his advice the emperor restrained the wicked and governed the commonwealth in peace [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “administered it”].

Thus it happened that the emperor granted the abbey of Lorsch [Note: Manuscript 2 reads *Laurissam* with the remainder omitted] to the church of Worms and confirmed it by a charter and perpetual privilege, and ordered this grant to be read aloud and proclaimed in the assembly and council of the Romans [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “of the Roman provinces.” The diploma has not been found].

At the same time the emperor and the aforementioned bishop [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “Franco”], clothed in hair shirts and with their feet completely bare [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “bare”], secretly entered a certain cave beside the church of Saint Clement, unknown to everyone. There they remained hidden for fourteen days in prayers, fasts, and vigils [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “for fourteen days”] [Note: He did this at approximately the same time as he visited Mount Garganus and Saint Nilus].

Some report that they were frequently consoled in that place by divine visions and conversations. We, however, leave this matter, of which we have little certain knowledge [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “little understood”], to be chewed over by popular opinion.

Nevertheless, we know this for certain: the day and hour of his death had been divinely disclosed beforehand to the bishop. After they had returned home [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “while at home”], he himself announced this to the emperor [Note: Manuscript 2 expands: “The bishop himself disclosed the day of his death beforehand to the emperor”]. Therefore the emperor, greatly saddened, asked him with many tears whom he ought to have in his place or to whom he ought to entrust his bishopric [Note: Manuscript 2 omits the relevant phrase]. At last, as though compelled, he replied:

“I have one brother. If it should please God, I would ask that he be my successor [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “If it pleased God … I would ask”]. Above all this, however, may God provide one man in whom he is well pleased [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “foresee one man”].”

Then the emperor swore by God’s testament that he would give the aforementioned bishopric to his brother. And so that he might remember it better and more easily, he received from the bishop a petitioning letter concerning this matter and placed it in his pouch as a testament [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “as a written testimony”].

Why say more? On the very day and at the very hour that he had foretold [Note: Manuscript 2 expands: “Franco, the venerable man, the bishop of Worms, beloved of God, succumbed to death, paid the debt of mortality, and his body was buried in peace at Rome with great honor”], he succumbed to death, and his body was buried in peace at Rome with great honor (27 August 999).

### 4.

After the bishop’s death, various petitioners immediately appeared, appealing to the emperor concerning the bishopric. Among them, a certain Erpho [Note: Manuscript 2 has “Epho”] was distinguished by the pastoral title [Note: Manuscript 1 reads “assigned”]. But he did not see a fourth day afterward, because he died on the third day.

After his death, not a few others appeared again, continually filling the emperor’s ears with various petitions and promises of money concerning the bishopric. Among them was one named Razo [Note: Manuscript 1 has “Raizo”; manuscript 2 has “Raso”], who, by exerting himself greatly and promising no small amount, received the pastoral staff. Immediately returning joyfully from Italy, he reached a place called Curo [Note: Manuscript 2 has “Chur”], and there ended his life. The messengers returned, brought the staff back to the emperor, and announced his death [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “reported”].

Then at last, remembering his promise, the emperor closed his hand [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “his own hand”] and promised that he would give this bishopric to no one before he returned to his homeland.

Who would not count this among the merits of our blessed Father [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “of our blessed Burchard”], and praise his life for this also—that he had been so chosen by God that he might reveal the failures of those men? It is a most wondrous and astonishing thing that one man, after his election and acceptance of the bishopric, did not see a fourteenth day, while the other did not live to see a fourth day [Note: Printed counterfactual *non vidisset* and *non vixisset* mean “had not seen” and “had not lived”; manuscript 2 has indicative *non vidit* and *non vixit*, “did not see” and “did not live.”]. Here we can understand and also see God’s wonders. For there is no wisdom, prudence, or counsel against the Lord [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “nor”]. What pleased human beings displeased God; what the emperor chose, God rejected; and he chose the weak in order to confound the strong [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “that he may confound”]. For God knew the man who feared him, loved him, and honored him with all his strength [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “worshiped him, feared him, and loved him”]. He called the predestined man, justified the one he called, and glorified the justified man—not by human praise but by his own mercy [Note: Manuscript 2 omits “predestined” and “called”].

### 5.

The emperor, having returned from Italy (1000), entered Saxony and reached a place called Kirchberg [Note: Manuscript 2 has “Kyritzberg”] [Note: [Col. 0514C] *Kirchberg*]. The bishop of Mainz came there to the emperor, and with him came the venerable Burchard. The emperor received the archbishop honorably and explained to him the matter of the bishopric of Worms [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “he explained it”], fully relating the wondrous deaths of the two men.

After much conversation, the emperor, looking out through a window [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “looking”], saw Burchard and immediately called him quickly to himself. Taking him by the hand [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “taking him by the hand”], he led him aside [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “told him”] and carefully explained what his brother [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “Franco”] had asked on his behalf and what he had entrusted to him [Note: Printed *rogarit* means “may have asked/has asked,” while *rogavit* means “asked”; printed *demandarit* means “may have entrusted/has entrusted,” while manuscript 2 has *demandavit*, “entrusted.”]. Then he opened for him the letter that he had kept in his pouch and began to offer him the bishopric of Worms.

When Burchard strongly resisted and insisted that he was unworthy to undertake the episcopal office [Note: Manuscript 2 omits this], the emperor, pressing him vehemently [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “pressed more vehemently and questioned him”], compelled him almost by force to accept it [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “compelled him”]. At last, realizing [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “Then the venerable Burchard, seeing”] that he could not resist a powerful man, he requested that he might deliberate on the matter with his senior, the archbishop [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “he asked that he might”]. Having obtained this permission and received the archbishop’s counsel [Note: Manuscript 2 has a doubtful reading, perhaps “after the archbishop’s counsel had been received”], he promised that he would endure whatever the emperor ordered him to do [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “that he would ultimately do what the emperor ordered”]. As he said this, tears arose in the eyes of all who were present [Note: Manuscript 1 reads “burst forth”], and, in recognition of his most worthy merits, the pastoral staff was entrusted to him.

### 6.

> [Note: Manuscript 2 supplies the rubric: “How Bishop Burchard, having become bishop of Worms, visited Worms, found it desolate, and then …”; it continues: “Burchard, therefore, departing from the archbishop, came to Worms, which he found destroyed.”]

After several days [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “a few days”], having received permission from the emperor, he reached the place called Helingunstat [Note: Manuscript 1 has “Heilegenstat”] [Col. 0515C] [Note: *Heiligenstadt*] with the archbishop, and there received the insignia of the priestly office [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “went to Heiligenstadt”]. On the following day [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “the next day”] he was solemnly consecrated with the anointing of episcopal blessing. Then, after many greetings and various embraces [Note: Manuscript 2 omits “various”], he was honorably dismissed by the archbishop [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “by Willigis, archbishop of Mainz”].

He visited the bishopric entrusted to him and came to Worms, which he found destroyed and almost [Col. 0515B] deserted. For it was suited not for human use but for the lairs of beasts, especially wolves. The level ground of the ditch and the destruction of the wall offered robbers and wild animals an easy entrance.

They say that wolves often devoured livestock there in full view of everyone [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “were devouring”], and that when people wished to prevent this, the wolves boldly terrified them with continual attacks [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “terrified them and”]; finally, although everyone pursued them, they escaped unharmed [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “escaped”].

The robbers, for their part, boasted [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “said”] that this place was perfectly suited for carrying out the wickedness of their will, because neither the fortification of the ditch nor the barrier of the wall ever presented them with any difficulty in entering [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “would offer”]. If any citizen opposed their will in anything, they attacked him by night, carried away with them everything he possessed, and left the man either dead [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “half-dead”] or half-alive.

Such was the peace, such the security, and such the fortification enjoyed by the citizens of Worms in those days. Finally, abandoning the deserted city, they all went outside the wall; there they built houses and buildings necessary for their use [Note: Manuscript 1 reads “houses”], and, as far as they could, fortified themselves and their families against robbers and wild animals with hedges, beams, and other timber.

Therefore [Note: Manuscript 2 adds the rubric “How Bishop Burchard began to fortify the city”], when Bishop Burchard saw the deserted city, he grieved greatly. Having taken counsel with his people, he surrounded the city with a very strong rampart. He rebuilt the wall on every side and ordered the citizens to build and live within the wall [Note: Manuscript 2 adds “houses”]. Thus, in almost five years, he recalled the expelled citizens, established peace in those regions, and properly restored the city, which had been entirely deserted. But this one matter became the greatest impediment to the pious labors of this man.

### 7.

> [Note: Manuscript 2 supplies the rubric: “It follows concerning Duke Otto and his son Conrad.”]

Duke Otto [Note: [Col. 0516C] “The son of Conrad, formerly duke of Lotharingia”] and his son Conrad had within the city a stronghold made extremely secure by towers and various buildings [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “a strong and very well-fortified stronghold with towers and various buildings”]. To this house [Note: Manuscript 2 omits the phrase] robbers, thieves, and all who offended against the bishop [Note: Manuscript 2 expands: “all who committed offenses against the bishop and his loyal men”] had a most secure refuge. For if anyone offended against the bishop and his faithful men by word or deed, he immediately withdrew to that place; and for this reason many slayings and murders occurred on both sides.

The man of God endured this disgrace and these harsh calamities [Note: Manuscript 2 omits “harsh”]; but with a stout heart he always resisted their bold actions as though undaunted [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “Burchard endured this for a long time”]. Hence it happened that this man of God hated this class of people throughout all the days of his life [Note: Manuscript 2 omits the phrase] and rejected them all as invaders of the church of God—except for one young man. His parents and other relatives had rejected this young man in anger because he was peaceable and loved an innocent life [Note: Manuscript 2 has imperfect *respuebant*, “were rejecting him,” for perfect *respuerunt*, “rejected him.”].

The venerable man of God summoned him to himself, taught him both the fear and the love of God [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “taught him to possess the fear and love of God”], and raised him as though he were his adopted son [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “for the best”]. Because he recognized in him steadfastness of mind, he loved him greatly above all others. God later mercifully exalted him to the royal throne [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “placed him on the royal throne”].

When the bishop despaired of resisting the strength of the powerful by other means, he surrounded his own court with a wall like a castle and, within it, diligently raised towers and dwellings suitable for fighting, constructing a sufficiently strong fortification. Once the castle had been secured and built [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “fortified”], he bravely resisted the bold actions of his enemies [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “strong actions”] and increased the hope of his own people [Note: Manuscript 2 adds “and of the citizens”]. Often, too, he terrified the enemies themselves by his fearless words and deeds [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “his own enemies”].

## 8.

Afterward [Note: “true” in 1.], when the uprisings had been quieted and peace had scarcely been established among them [Note: “had been made” in 2.], at the emperor’s command the bishop, together with a large retinue and the Mainz soldiers [Note: “large” in 1.], as well as the abbot of Fulda and the bishop of Würzburg with a considerable multitude, set out for Italy (1001). When they had crossed Tuscany [Note: “tussania” in 1; “justamani” or “nstamani” in 2.] with the greatest exertion [Col. 0517A] [Note: “they crossed” in 2.], they were informed that the emperor had died. As was necessary, they were greatly saddened and returned by the road along which they had come [Note: “came” in 2.] (1002).

Then the people of Lucca [Note: “That city of Lucca” in 2.] and of the surrounding villages, having gathered a very large force of cavalry and infantry [Note: omitted in 2.], blocked the roads on every side and, armed [Note: omitted in 2.] and arrayed as if for battle, awaited the arrival of our men. But our men, seeing so great [Note: “such a great” in 2.] a multitude, were thrown into confusion [Note: “are thrown into confusion” in 2.] and hesitated to cross their territory against their will. At last, after the bishop’s counsel had been taken, they sent envoys and humbly begged them to permit our men to pass peacefully through their borders [Note: “so that they might be thought to permit it” in 2.]. Having scarcely obtained this, they enjoyed peace for that day.

When the interval of night had passed, at first light the enemies, massed together, began with a great shout and light skirmishes to harass the foremost of our men; and, with a few wounded or killed on either side [Note: “and” for “or”; “and or” in 2.], a cry was heard from the others. Accordingly, all quickly arose, seized their weapons, and gathered together. Among them was a certain Thiemar [Note: “Tremarus” in 2, and below], a soldier of the bishop of Worms, an energetic man distinguished above all in every virtue. In this army he was regarded as highly renowned in military matters [Note: “most splendidly equipped” in 1.].

The bishop summoned him [Note: “summons him” in 1.] and asked [Note: “asks” in 2.] him whether, if possible, he could help bring this matter to an end without human bloodshed. He promised to carry out the bishop’s orders and departed; then, after calling together others, he quietly disclosed what he had in mind [Note: “had” in 2.]. Next, with his men, he climbed a mountain exceedingly dangerous to ascend, with the greatest labor and exertion, and secretly went around the enemy force [Note: “went around the hostile hand” in 2.].

Thus, when the enemies saw our men and were terrified by their astonishing arrival, they lost heart and precipitately gave themselves to flight. Our men pursued them and in that flight killed and cut down as many as they were able to catch [Note: “as much as” in 1.]. Disturbed by this slaughter [Note: “the venerable Burchard, disturbed” in 2.], the bishop shed tears and severely rebuked Thiemar for what had happened [Note: “the aforesaid soldier” in 2.]; finally, he sent back not a few coins to the townspeople, as if by way of expiation. Thus [Note: “So likewise” in 1.], with God’s grace assisting them, they returned to their homeland.

## 9.

[Note: In 2 a red heading is added: “How Saint Henry came to Worms and concerning his elevation as emperor,” followed by: “When Otto III had died, Henry …” In 1, “Henry” is lowercase; in 2 it is consistently so, but in 1 only sometimes.]

Meanwhile Henry, duke of the Bavarians, having gathered forces from every side, came to Worms (May–June), and worked very hard to acquire the royal scepter [Note: “so that the summit of the kingdom might adhere to him” in 2.]. There, together with the bishop of Mainz and the bishop of Worms [Col. 0518A], he took counsel concerning these matters [Note: “those matters” in 1.]. He therefore explained to them the reason for his arrival. Then he promised that, if they consented to his will, he would do everything they wished [Note: “their will” in 2.].

For he had promised that he would acquire Otto’s fortified house [Note: “the house of the aforesaid duke Otto, which he possessed at Worms” in 2.] and return it to the authority of the bishop of Worms. Thus, by giving and promising many things, he brought these men to approve his decision. Then he went with them to Mainz (June 6), and there, while all who were present applauded him [Note: “praised him” in 2.], he received the royal scepter [Note: “the royal seat” in 2.].

When Henry had been elevated to the royal throne [Note: “when Henry had become emperor” in 2.], Bishop Burchard, mindful of his promise, urged the king incessantly, day and night, concerning the freedom of his city [Note: “for the freedom” in 2.]. At last the king summoned Duke Otto to him, discussed these matters with him [Col. 0518B], and disclosed his intention [Note: “to him” in 2.].

Otto, being a prudent man, answered prudently: “Father, even if you had told me of a great matter, I would certainly have wished to do it [Note: “I ought to have done it” in 2.]. But I want you to know for certain that, for these deeds, I firmly hope that in God’s eternal kingdom I shall possess an everlasting reward with you.”

By these and similar sayings [Note: “examples” in 2.] the matter was settled [Note: “Thus the matter was completed in this way. For a certain estate, together with whatever belonged to it, was given in exchange for the castle of Duke Conrad at Worms on behalf of this house; it is called Bruchsella. The rest is missing; the following red heading occurs: ‘How Bishop Burchard destroyed the castle and built the church of Saint Paul there.’”]. A certain village called Bruchsella [Note: Bruchsal in 2.], with all its revenues and appurtenances, was given to the duke in exchange for this house (October). In this way Worms, long subjected to an unjust servitude, was liberated through the pious labors of the bishop [Note: “See Henry’s charter dated October 3, 1002, in Schannat, *Historia Wormatiensis*, II, p. 35; and compare what Thietmar sings concerning this freedom at the end.”].

Therefore, on the very day that the duke departed from this fortification [Note: “from his fortification, or from the duke’s castle” in 2.], the bishop, having gathered many people, attacked the same house [Note: “the house, or castle” in 2.] while the duke watched [Col. 0518C], and destroyed it completely, down to its foundations, with eager hand [Note: “so that it might no longer be a snare to the citizens. Then, from the same …” in 2.]. He then built a monastery and cloister from the same material and the same stones, in honor of Saint Paul, and inscribed this title upon it: “A church for the freedom of the city.”

When he had rationally arranged there everything belonging to the canonical rule, he established twenty brothers to maintain the course of worship at appointed times and with appointed signs [Note: “Compare Burchard’s charters in Schannat, *ibid.*, pp. 41–42.”]. In these ways the man of God changed a warlike house into a church of Christ; and what had been a house of strife became a house of reconciliation, in which praises and thanksgivings to our God are offered day and night [Note: “in which now day and night praises to God are offered; ‘and thanksgivings’ are absent in 2.].

## 10.

The forest of Forestus [Note: “a single forest” in 2.] lies two miles [Note: “two thousand” in 2.] from Worms [Col. 0519A], abounds in fir trees, and on one side is surrounded by a muddy marsh encircling it. In its middle there is a most beautiful hill, to which the man of God ordered himself to be transferred [Note: “caused himself to be transferred when the …” in 2.]. Because he wished to avoid worldly turmoil, he cleared the hill by cutting down trees and shrubs [Note: “afterward, having cut down the trees, he had the hill leveled” in 2.; “having cut out the fruits” is another reading], and there he first made an oratory; then, after completing other buildings, he constructed an excellent cell.

After councils, royal conferences, synodal business, and various disturbances of the world, he withdrew there [Note: “he often transferred himself there” in 2.]. There, casting secular affairs behind him [Note: “having put them aside” in 2.], he devoted all his strength to the service of God [Note: “exercised himself” in 2.]. At that same time he labored considerably in this cell on a collection of canons [Note: “collection” in 2.; “in this place,” not “on this hill,” in 2. A red heading is also added: “How Bishop Burchard selected the canons.”].

With the assistance of Walter, bishop of Speyer [Col. 0519B] [Note: “The *Gesta abbatum Gemblacensium* report that Olbert, who was later made abbot of Gembloux, rendered especially valuable assistance to Burchard; see D’Achery, 2nd ed., II, p. 763. [Col. 0519C]], and with Brunicho, the provost, exhorting and advising him [Note: “Compare Burchard’s letter to Brunicho, prefixed to the collection of decretals.”], he gathered the canons into one body—not out of any arrogance, but, as he himself said, because the laws of the canons and the judgments concerning penitents had been entirely neglected and destroyed in his bishopric [Note: “had been” in 2.].

He divided this body, or collection [Note: “or collectorium” in 2.], and distributed it into twenty books [Note: “This work is still preserved at Groß-Frankenthal in a beautiful library, although jurists no longer use it because of Gratian’s work. Words of the monk of Kirschgarten. A red heading follows: ‘Concerning the construction of the new church of Saint Peter, which is now called the cathedral, or major church.’”].

## 11.

Moreover, the man of God [Note: “Burchard, the man of God” in 2.], never ceasing from his pious labors, demolished the church of Saint Peter at the episcopal see [Note: “of the apostle Peter” in 2.], because it had been far too small [Note: “was” in 2.]. Laying its foundations, he marked out a monastery of astonishing size, which he brought almost to completion in only a few years and with such speed that it did not seem to have been built gradually, but rather to have suddenly stood there as if desired into existence.

[Col. 0519C]

## 12.

[Note: In 2 a red heading is added: “Concerning his sister, whom he placed over the nuns at Nonnonmünster in the suburb of the city.”]

In those days he summoned his sister, named Mahilda [Note: “Mahilla” in 2; perhaps “Mahtilda”], a most honorable woman and worthy of every distinction, and cherished her with fraternal affection. This lady was extraordinarily skillful and ingenious in women’s handiwork; she had women trained in the various kinds of textile work [Note: “varieties” in 2.] and surpassed many women in making costly garments [Note: “surpassed” in 2.; “Compare Alpert, I.2, above.”].

Meanwhile it happened that the abbess of the monastery of consecrated women serving God there died. After her death [Col. 0520A] all the sisters, as if with one voice, begged and prayed the bishop [Note: “were praying” in 1.] to give the abbacy to his sister and entrust her with the responsibility of caring for them [Note: “entrust their care to her” in 2.].

The venerable man consented to their petitions [Note: “their,” not “her,” in 1.], summoned his sister, and, exhorting her with various circumlocutions, finally said:

“Most beloved sister,” he said, “you see how fragile and perishable worldly things are, how full of every iniquity they are. For gold and silver and precious stones [Note: “stones” in the text; “precious stones” in 2.], which seem precious to us, what else are they counted as before God but filth [Note: “reckoned” in 2.]? In these things we do nothing but deceive our wretched souls through desire for temporal things [Note: “secular things” in 2.]. Wherever we walk, the shadow of death follows us; and he who today lives securely in delights tomorrow falls unhappily under death [Col. 0520B] [Note: “by death” in 1.]

“Blessed is the one who follows the straight path of the just way, rejects the glory of this world, and receives God’s things within the dwelling of a pure heart. Therefore, my dearest sister, I want you to lay aside bracelets, earrings, and luxurious garments, and accept the sacred veil; thus you will join yourself to the everlasting King [Note: “unite yourself” in 2.].”

When she heard this, she was exceedingly frightened and, wondering beyond what can be expressed, said:

“Holy elder, do you know that throughout all the days of my life I have lived among secular affairs and am entirely ignorant of this office? Except for the Psalter, I know nothing of books at all. I do not know how to carry out this office. How then, lord [Note: “the life of the Lord, without …” in 2.], shall I be able to live in this life without giving offense?”

The man of God replied:

“Stop adding anything [Col. 0520C] to these words, and do not delay in fulfilling my exhortation as quickly as possible [Note: “so that you may add something”; “anything” in 2.]. What hinders you? What obstructs you? Most blessed is the exchange [Note: “the exchange is most blessed” in 2.]: to abandon passing things and happily acquire eternal riches and everlasting life [Note: “and perpetual salvation” in 2.].”

By these and many other exhortations he overcame his sister so completely that at last she vowed that she would do whatever he wished [Note: “would know” in 2.]. When the servant of God heard this, he rejoiced and gave thanks to God with all his heart. Immediately he ordered her to learn the canonical rule, the calendar, the life of the Fathers, the *Dialogues*, and other books suitable for this way of life [Col. 0521A]. She immediately strove obediently to learn and complete everything he commanded [Note: “took care to do so” in 2.].

When the man of God perceived such willingness and such pious zeal in this servant of God, he placed the veil upon her and consecrated her to God’s service. After assembling the sisters, he entrusted the abbacy and care of the sisters to her. Once she had received the veil, she shone forth distinguished by every virtue and honorable conduct; and, as though she had been nourished according to the rule throughout her entire life [Note: “nurtured” in 2.], she offered divine examples to all.

She did not wish to be served [Note: “she did not wish to be served, but …” is absent in 2.], but to serve; nor did she exalt herself above the others in a teacher’s manner [Note: “magisterial” in 1.], but loved and taught them all like a mother. It was a remarkable thing that a secular woman was not burdened by this undertaking even for an hour, but rather took delight in it.

Every estate that she had acquired she transferred to the church over which she presided, with the help of her brother. Moreover, with her brother exhorting and assisting her, she not only renewed the cloister and monastery, which had been almost deserted, but rebuilt them and had them dedicated [Note: “and” in 2.]. She remained day and night in the service of God [Note: “the Lord” in 2.] with the sisters entrusted to her, with a perfectly steadfast heart and mind [Note: “most steadfastly” in 2.], and, with her brother’s assistance [Note: “her brother assisting” in 2.], arranged their life in every respect rationally, as the canonical order requires [Note: “demands” in 2.].

## 13.

Following the examples and teachings of that holy woman [Note: “therefore, following the examples of that holy woman,” with a red heading in 2: “Concerning a certain sister who asked the bishop to lead a solitary life, which he granted.”], one of the same sisters, named Caritas and devoted to God, asked the bishop for the stricter discipline of a higher and more demanding life. Although he affirmed that God’s will could be properly fulfilled in such a life through righteous deeds [Col. 0521C] [Note: “works” in 2.], the virgin of God nevertheless continued to ask him persistently and without ceasing to remove her from secular things and enclose her, since she wished to do greater things [Note: “she did not cease asking him to exclude her more completely from secular affairs and enclose her as a solitary” in 2.].

At last the man of God consented to her petition, ordered her to be enclosed [Note: “to make an enclosure” in 2.], appointed a fixed day [Note: “established the day” in 2.], and came to the monastery of the nuns with all the brothers in order to carry out the will of God’s servant [Note: “to fulfill” in 2.]. When they had arrived there, he summoned the brothers together, placed the virgin in their midst, and said [Note: “said” in 2.]:

“My dearest brothers, you see this virgin, inflamed alike by love and fear of God, rejecting the slippery delights of this world and longing to please God. Receiving the evangelical word not with a deaf ear [Note: “with,” rather than “not,” in 2.], she has rejected father and mother, relatives and friends, houses and fields, and has resolved to unite herself to God alone [Note: “rejecting them, she resolved to unite herself to God alone” in 2.].

[Col. 0521D]

“Be ashamed, old men, and you also, young men, who do nothing similar to this! Why are you silent? Why do you struggle with shame? [Col. 0522A] Behold, this most frail girl, with her banner raised, fearlessly goes before you and does not fear to fight against spiritual wickedness. Behold, clothed in the breastplate of faith and the helmet of salvation [Note: “the girl, furnished with a shield, helmet, and …” in 2.], she is prepared with undaunted spirit to fight against the enemy [Note: “to battle” in 2.]. Therefore, if you cannot precede her or contend alongside her [Note: omitted in 2.], at least strive to follow her by similar examples of piety.”

After these and other divine words, when the offices of the Mass had been completed [Note: “solemn rites” in 2.], he enclosed her in a little cell. Since she had died to secular things through divine compunction [Note: “from secular things” in 2.], he commended her to God according to the order of the dead. There she lived an angelic life for three years in the service of God. Tested by various sufferings [Note: “temptations” in 2.], at last she gave her completely purified soul [Note: “purified” in 2.] back to its Creator, so that God might be honored in all things, he who is always wonderful in [Col. 0522B] his saints [Note: “more wonderful” in 2. A red heading is added: “Concerning the dedication of the major church in the presence of Emperor Henry and many other prelates.”].

## 14.

At that time (perhaps 1009) [Note: omitted in 2.] Emperor Henry intended to go with an army into Burgundy, and on that journey came to Worms [Note: “to Worms” in 2.]. When he saw that splendid monastery almost completed, he repeatedly begged the bishop to consecrate it in his presence [Note: “with persistent prayers” in 2.]. Although the man of God strongly resisted, he finally consented to the emperor’s will, as if compelled.

Therefore, after all impurity had been cast out and all soot wiped away [Note: “driven away” in 2.], on the following day, with the emperor present and ordering it, and with great praise and the greatest rejoicing of clergy and people, while many bishops were present, this house was dedicated to God [Note: “on the following day, the feast of Philip and James” is added in 2. A red heading also follows: “How, after two years, part of that church collapsed.”].

## 15.

After two years (perhaps 1011), a lamentable event occurred in that same monastery [Note: “occurred” in 2.]. For the western part collapsed completely in a sudden ruin one night [Col. 0522C]. Yet this was remarkable: under so great a mass, no bell was broken except one small one.

Disturbed by this event, as was necessary [Note: “the servant of God was greatly disturbed and bore a certain sadness on his face” in 2.], the servant of God wore an expression almost of grief. His disciples [Note: “counselors” in 2.], a considerable number of whom constantly followed him [Note: omitted in 2.], approached him and consoled him with these words:

“We rightly marvel, elder, that you are so greatly disturbed by the misfortune of this work, since in your daily offerings [Note: “prayers” in 2.] you ask that it be completed in the way pleasing to God. For God has heard your prayers and has publicly fulfilled your will. Indeed [Note: the text from “indeed” through “rebukes” is absent in 2.], what pleases God is often proved, as it is written: ‘Whom the Lord loves, he rebukes’ (Proverbs 3:12). For what displeased God, he has rejected, as you asked. Therefore lay aside your sighs and take up the strength of patience. This is praiseworthy and acceptable to God.

“For God, as you know very well, among the other teachings of his doctrine, gave such words of consolation: ‘In your patience you will possess your souls’ (Luke 21:19). Attend to these words, Father, attend to them, and put aside the burden of your cares; forget your sadness, because according to the Lord’s promise your sadness will be turned [Note: “changed” in 2.] into joy.”

Then the man of God, as if roused from his sadness, answered with a cheerful face [Note: “thus he replied with a cheerful face” in 2.]:

“I return great thanks and manifold gratitude to you for such consolation and admonition. For as it pleased the Lord, so he acted. In this I rejoice: that what did not please him, as we asked, he willed to be changed for the better. But now listen, I beg you, while I tell you how I learned these things [Note: “I once foretold these things to you” in 2.; a red heading follows: “How Bishop Burchard, entering his garden, saw the devil there in human form, answering him grimly.”].

“One day, when I had entered my larger garden alone with two boys [Note: omitted in 2.], at the very entrance I saw the devil in human clothing and human form. He was standing toward the north, uprooting herbs and fruit trees; then, having piled them up with much muttering, he blocked the path. Because he was walking in the likeness and image of a gardener [Note: “I questioned him about why he had blocked the way, and he answered angrily” in 2.], I angrily asked him why he had blocked the way. He replied:

“‘Would that I could block for you the way of eternal life—I, who can heap a greater misfortune upon you in a short time!’

“Wondering at his boldness, because I thought him the keeper of the garden, I said [Note: “I said that I had said this” in 2.]: ‘In what you threaten, you will not harm me in the name of the Lord. Unless you cease from your wickedness, you will heap everlasting destruction upon yourself [Note: “an everlasting end” in 1; “you heap” in 2.].’

“After these words I reached the seat in the garden. Looking around, I did not see him. Wondering greatly that he had so suddenly disappeared completely [Note: “nowhere” in 1.], I asked the boys whether they had seen him. Both said that they had seen no one there except me, but they confirmed that they had heard someone contending with me.

“Then I said: ‘I know, my sons; I know who he is. But I will not fear his threats, nor trust his words, because truth is not in him, as the Lord says [Note: “said” in 2.; the words ‘where “And I perceived” are absent’] (John 8:44).’

“And immediately, departing from there, I recalled this verse in my mind: ‘For I am ready for scourges, and my sorrow is ever before me’ (Psalm 37:18).

“On the following night, at the morning hour [Note: omitted in 2.], this lamentable ruin of the temple occurred [Note: “the lamentable ruin of this temple occurred” in 2.]. Hearing of it, I too was struck with terror in mind, and, I confess, not without tears I repeated that lament of David [Note: “I repeated” in 1.]: ‘And I was scourged all night [Note: ‘all day’ in 2.], and my chastisement was in the mornings’ (Psalm 72:14).

“Therefore, my brothers, since the Lord has deemed me worthy to chastise me by chastising me, I rejoice. According to your exhortation, I shall be patient; and, turning back, I shall do penance for my deeds and words [Note: “I do penance” in 2.], and I shall praise you, my God, so that you may be honored in all things—you who become angry and will be merciful, and forgive all the sins of men in tribulation [Note: “of these men” in 2.].”

After this he ordered the timber and stones to be carried outside the temple [Note: “ordered them carried out, after laying the foundation, for strengthening” in 2.]. When the foundation had been laid, he built it firmly and brought it almost to its former condition in two years. Then he gilded the capitals of the columns and the square stones arranged around the circuit of the monastery, and decorated the entire temple everywhere with various ornaments.

## 16.

Next he rationally restored the provision for the brothers serving God at the episcopal see [Note: “for the brothers serving God there at the episcopal see” in 2.], which had already failed from the most ancient time [Note: “had failed,” plural], and had been almost entirely neglected [Note: “neglected,” plural], and he converted it to excellent use [Note: “renewed it” in 2.]. After everything had been canonically arranged, he ordered all the brothers to be refreshed together in the refectory with their daily food according to the rule [Note: “in the refectory” in 2. A red heading is added: “How he also restored the provisions of the brothers at Nuhusem.”].

Similarly, he mercifully renewed the provision of the brothers at Saint Cyriacus, which through the negligence of invaders had been almost destroyed [Note: “destroyed,” plural], and ordered them [Note: “them,” feminine, in 2.] to be refreshed together [Note: “But now this single place is divided among many. Words of the monk of Kirschgarten.”].

He renewed with remarkable ingenuity all the places belonging to him that had been almost destroyed and deserted through age, and splendidly adorned them with walls and various buildings. He also built the monastery and cloister of Saint Andrew, which had been established outside the wall and had become desolate through neglect, within the city [Note: “which had been built outside the walls and had become desolate through negligence; within …” in 2.]. After venerably arranging the canonical matters pertaining to the brothers’ use, he established a regular life there for the praise and glory of our God [Note: “there, where it now is; previously it was on the hill outside the gate of Saint Andrew, in the suburb. Now nuns or penitent sisters are there. Words of the monk of Kirschgarten, who adds the red heading: ‘How the provost of the major church and other monks came to be, and concerning the teaching of the man of God, how each person ought to remain in his calling.’”].

## 17.

In those days Brunicho [Note: “Brunecho” in 1.], whom we mentioned above [Col. 0523C] [Note: “Chapter 10.”], the venerable provost of that see [Note: “the venerable man, provost of that see” in 2.], seeing the steadfastness of the blessed man—how he rejected worldly pomp [Note: “rejected” in 2.], burned with zeal in God’s service [Note: “burned” in 2.], and, by avoiding human praise, drove it away [Note: “avoided it” in 2.]—came to himself and undertook the monastic life. Through the example of God’s servant he deceived the devil and strove to please God alone with a contrite heart and a troubled spirit.

Likewise, other distinguished men, abandoning the world through the continual teachings of God’s servant, fled the city and submitted themselves to the life of monks. At last the bishop, fearing that the monasteries [Note: “of the canons, as is evident” in 2.] would become deserted, summoned brothers from all the monasteries [Note: “the canons” in 2.] and addressed them in these words:

“I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that everyone who fears God and does justice is acceptable to him—not only a monk, but also a canon and even a layman. It is not good for all who labor in a ship to devote themselves to one task, so that either all are helmsmen and there is no sailor, or all are sailors [Note: “all are sailors and there is no helmsman” in 2.] and there is no helmsman.

“It is wiser, once a helmsman has been appointed, for each person to attend to his own task: some should sail, others sound the depth of the water, others, if necessary, climb the mast [Note: “ascend” in 2.], and still others draw out the bilge water; thus they may all guide the ship in peace.

“Likewise, brothers, we must understand that we cannot all do everything. For if all are monks and canons, where are the laymen? Who then will minister to the monks, or who will serve the canons [Note: “who will serve” in 2.]? But if all are laymen, where then are the praises and services of God? For God’s Church has a diverse household—not only monks, but also canons, and likewise faithful laymen. And all these need the grace of God.

“Therefore, whoever is a canon should not leave his monastery for the monastic life without permission, but should labor in common with the brothers [Note: “in a common life” in 2.]. If he desires to live a stricter life, let him serve God within his monastery by works pleasing to God and restrain himself from evil; thus let him not cease to bring richly marrowed holocausts to God upon the altar of his hidden heart [Note: “offer” in 2.].”

By this judgment he both calmed the minds of the young men and encouraged them to remain afterward in God’s service with a more steadfast mind.

## 18.

Moreover, he firmly ordered each of them, according to the measure of his ability, to present each day studious spoken or written compositions [Note: “diligently” in 2.; “to set before themselves” in 2.]. Since they saw the servant of God devoted to study, learned in the pages of sacred Scripture, and filled with God’s wisdom [Note: omitted in 2.], they did not hesitate to bring him sermons, letters, and various little questions.

One of them, among the other sayings that he often put forward [Note: the intervening words are absent in 2.], composed a question concerning the words about the fast of Moses [Note: “Moses” in 1, almost everywhere.] and Elijah, and [Note: 2 compresses the following: “He put to himself the question whether Moses had taken no food during the forty days. To this the holy man, after many words, added: ‘What wonder if Moses fasted at the command of him in whose kingdom no one has ever fasted and hungered? Do you think that the citizens of heaven, like earthly people sweating at rake or plough, seek bread through toil? By no means. But the unfailing bread of the righteous is God, the Son of God, creator of angels and human beings. Of him it is written: “In the beginning was the Word”; and elsewhere: “I am the living bread.” By this bread the world endures, and the people of Israel lived for forty years in the wilderness. Moses tasted of this bread when he was on the mountain with the Lord. Therefore it is no wonder that he was then so long without bodily food.’ Many other things were done and words spoken there, which I pass over for brevity’s sake, but they are fully contained in his history.”] handed it to him humbly in our presence, as if for an opportunity to dictate.

For he had written as follows:

«Had I not feared the aridity of my mind and intellect, I would in some way have brought before your most merciful lordship certain passages of Sacred Scripture which constrain the smallness of my spirit and compel me to fall into the knot of doubt, so that, instructed by the most learned testimony of your goodness, I might recognize the truth of the matter; for whoever, through the judgments of the sacred Scriptures, falls into the danger of wavering, unless corrected and cleansed by the satisfaction of confession, incurs the guilt of a grave offense. Therefore, deeply grieving over the wound of my conscience and fearing to conceal it any longer, I confidently open it to your most worthy holiness, so that what lies hidden within may be made manifest outwardly. For I present this composition of a written discourse to your holiness, not girded by the boldness of any cleverness, but compelled, God as my witness, by the rarity of a thirsting intellect, so that you may correct me and make me more certain in this investigation, since I know that you bear the likeness and hold the place of those to whom it is said in the Lord’s address: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God” (Mark 4:11).»

When, making a true confession of my conscience, I shall have reached recognition of the truth under your prudent guidance, I both hope and firmly believe that, cleansed from every stain of my guilt, I shall become a participant in the innocence of your holiness, because, if this were not true, the Psalmist would not have said: “With the holy you will be sanctified, and with the innocent you will be innocent” (Psalm 17:26 [18:25]). But because the pain of my ulcer, continually tormenting me, compels me to approach your clemency, I do not cease to express, as best I can and to the extent of my fingernail, the little question for which I composed this heap of trifles, setting aside all circumlocutions, to your prudence, which I do not doubt will come to my aid. [Col. 0527A] [Note: [Col. 0527] “succurrendum” in witness 1.]

In the volumes of Sacred Scripture we read that Moses and Elijah fasted for forty days, but many of us doubt whether they abstained from every kind of food. I know and truly believe that Christ our Lord fasted for the course of forty days and therefore endured a threefold temptation, but whether any human being did this, I doubt; for if Moses, Elijah, or any of the prophets had abstained from every kind of food for forty days, he would not, as I suppose, have escaped the devil’s trial of temptation. For, so to speak, it would be easier for a passible human being to be tested than for the ruler of all creation to be tempted. I now leave this for you to consider, since I tremble to speak further about such matters; for it is written: “For every idle word that people speak, they will give an account of it on the day of judgment” (Matthew 12:36). I had put the question of this investigation to many wise men, but since I have not been instructed, the aforesaid illness has increased a hundredfold. Therefore let your holy wisdom teach me the truth, so that I may not incur the snare of guilt but may obtain the fruit of repentance or true confession, which apostolic wisdom promised by saying: “Confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10:10).

9. When the servant of God had perceived this, on the third day he sent the following words of correction in reply to the young man:

«Because you questioned me, as though in doubt, about the forty-day fast of Moses and Elijah, I do not want you, dear son, to remain in doubt any longer. With God’s help, the matter has a perfectly clear explanation, and I wish to instruct you in it. For, as you yourself confessed, if someone doubts the judgments of the sacred Scriptures, unless he comes to his senses through satisfaction, he incurs the guilt of a grave offense.
