But if, deceived by the aridity of his intellect, the rashness of youth, the obscurity of ignorance, or the trampling-down of negligence, he falls into the danger of wavering, and someone corrects him, he should know that “whoever brings a sinner back from the error of his way saves his own soul from death,” as the apostle James says (James 5:19–20). Therefore we shall save your soul from death if, by carefully examining what we demonstrate, you store it away in a pure mind.

You wrote this: “In Sacred Scripture we read that Moses and Elijah fasted for forty days, but many of us doubt whether they abstained from every kind of food.” You are looking for a knot in a reed; for the person who looks for a knot in a reed wastes his labor. To look for a knot in a reed means to weave the complexity of doubt out of the clearest and truest reasoning and to draw the thickness of the densest fog out of the most serene light.

By “most serene light” I mean Sacred Scripture, in which every believer is corrected by deeds and words; and for this reason it is deservedly called the mirror of life. Sacred Scripture is the explanation of both laws, of the New and the Old Testament. But if someone with an insane mind is not corrected by its most luminous judgments, he is deceived, mocked by the sport of vanity. Everyone is deceived by the sport of vanity who is ensnared by the most vain fault of folly, seeks neither virtue nor flees vice. Therefore every vice must be fled; certainly folly must be fled, for this is the vice of humankind. Conversely, every virtue must be sought; wisdom, indeed, must be sought, for it is the virtue of God. Let the person who desires to know the strong virtue of God seek it with the utmost zeal and greatest diligence. For what is stronger than the virtue of God? What is more luminous than that which the ray of the true God, the sun, illuminates? What is truer than what the hand of Truth itself has written?

For Scripture says: “Moses descended from the mountain, carrying in his hands two stone tablets, both written by the finger of God.” On these tablets it was also inscribed: “Moses, the servant of God, fasted forty days and just as many nights, so that he might merit receiving the Lord’s law.”

What wonder, then, if Moses fasted at the command of him in whose kingdom no one has ever hungered, under whose person the prophet proclaimed these words of correction for correcting the Israelite people: “If I were hungry, I would not tell you, for the world and its fullness are mine” (Psalm 49:12); and again: “Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?” (ibid., 13). He who created all things from nothing never hungered in the kingdom of his glory, never thirsted, and never slept, as Scripture says: “Behold, he who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep” (Psalm 120:4).

Therefore, little son, understand my words by way of example. If one of us had been present at the council of some king or exceedingly powerful emperor, while he looked upon the various riches of his kingdom, by what sweetness of food or drink could he meanwhile have been captivated? He would have seen servants clothed in garments of various kinds; a magnificent house adorned with diverse ornaments; the purest gold decorated with images and precious stones; and the king himself, shining with crown and royal diadem, carefully handling the riches of his kingdom and unraveling the secret matters of his counsel.

And if the slippery and transitory glory of this world delights a human being so greatly that his dominant nature no longer reckons natural things, how much more did the heavenly and eternal glory of the Most High cause Moses, who feared God and followed his commands, to forget worldly things? For he took part in the holy council of the eternal King; he had seen the glory of the Lord—that is, a tabernacle not made with hands, that is, not of this creation—and he had heard the Lord say to him: “I love you above the others, and I know you by name” (Exodus 33:12).

For God led his people through the desert by the hand of Moses for forty years in place of forty days, and spoke with him face to face, as a man is accustomed to speak with his friend, as Scripture says (Exodus 33:11). He changed a day into a year; he fed his people with heavenly nourishment; a human being ate angelic bread.

What is heavenly food, or what is angelic food? What, then, will you say to these things, my son? If you sought a knot, behold, you have found one. Now untie the knot and learn this principle. Do you suppose that the citizens of heaven seek bread in the same way as earthly people, sweating with rake or plow as they labor? By no means. Rather, the unfailing bread of the righteous is God, the Son of God, the creator and lord of angels, of whom it is written: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word” (John 1:1). Behold the angelic bread! “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (ibid., 1:14). Behold, the heavenly food descended, and a human being ate the bread of angels, when the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.

For he himself says: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6:51), the bread through which the world stands and through which the Lord’s people lived for forty years. Moses tasted of this bread already then, when, having been addressed by the burning bush, he replied: “I beg you, Lord, send whom you will send” (Exodus 4:13); and elsewhere he tasted of the same bread when, amid many words of his teaching, he said to the children of Israel: “God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers; you shall listen to him” (Deuteronomy 18:15).

He tasted of this bread when he fasted for forty days, because “human beings do not live by bread alone, but by every word of God” (Luke 4:4). Through this Word all things were created, and everything exists as though from nothing, because God himself is the Word. “The Word was with God, and God was the Word” (John 1:1). In this we understand that God the Father is himself the Son, and that the Son—that is, the Word—is heavenly bread; and that the heavenly bread, that is, the Word, became flesh, as he himself confessed and said: “The bread that I will give is my flesh for the life of the world” (John 6:52).

For he himself is life and the nourishment of angels and human beings, who makes both one. He also satisfied Moses spiritually when Moses fasted bodily for forty days. The devil did not recognize his lofty power, great mercy, and ancient plan when he proposed to him a threefold temptation. For from the beginning he was the accuser of the brothers, the arbiter of wickedness, the inventor of lies, and the most skillful teacher of worthless tricks. He lay hidden in Pharaoh’s heart, harassing Moses through temptations involving various questions.

Thus he recognized Moses as a human being, but did not understand Christ’s divinity veiled in flesh; and therefore he doubted that he was perfect God and human being. Although that poisonous one harassed Pilate’s wife by a vision concerning his redemption, he nevertheless doubted that God was human. For he doubted that there was mercy with God, such that he might have wished to assume humanity and renew or redeem his servants through the marvelous exchange of his divinity. If he had not doubted and had not envied the just man, he would not have stirred up the wretched Jews to disobedience and unbelief against God in this way, nor cried through their mouths, “Let him be crucified.” And because he doubted, he did not know.

Therefore, because he was deceitful and doubtful from the beginning, while his doubt remained suspended he fell into the danger of despair; through the ruin of despair he suffered the passion of eternal damnation; and, cast into the outer darkness, he deservedly endured infernal torments.

As for what you asked about Elijah’s fast, understand it through this account. I think you have also read and understood how, after the curse he pronounced upon the inhabitants of Gilead, Elijah was hidden from King Ahab in the torrent Cherith by God’s command, and was revived and fed by ravens (1 Kings 17). After three years, at God’s command, he showed himself to Ahab, when, zealous for the Lord’s zeal, he ordered the four hundred and fifty priests of Baal to be killed, obtaining rain from God on that same day.

Then, fearing the threats of Jezebel, the furious queen, he fled through the desert and, beneath a juniper tree, fell asleep from weariness of soul. At that time he was twice awakened by an angel, instructed concerning the length of the journey, and refreshed with bread baked under ashes and water; in the strength of that food he walked forty days and as many nights.

Where do you suppose this bread came from, or from what spring was this water drawn? For, as we read, Elijah, taken up by God in a whirlwind into heaven, still lives bodily. But with what bread is he refreshed, or from what spring do you suppose he drinks? I tell you the truth: he who, as I said, is the bread of the righteous undoubtedly grants Elijah nourishment for his satisfaction. The water of his drink flows from the spring of him who said: “Whoever drinks the water that I shall give will never thirst” (John 4:13); and again: “Whoever drinks the water that I give will become in him a spring of water welling up into eternal life” (ibid., 14).

For Elijah is righteous, and therefore was refreshed with the nourishment of righteousness; he lives and lived, as it is written: “The righteous person lives by faith” (Galatians 3:11). Let these few words of correction suffice for you, my son, so that, instructed by these small matters, you may learn to understand greater things perfectly and lightly untie a knot in a similar question. For whatever was written was written for our instruction, so that through the patience and consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope in Christ Jesus our Lord, who lives and reigns as God for ever and ever. Amen.»

At a suitable time for conversation, the aforesaid young man summoned certain of his close associates and, as he himself admitted, lest he alone conceal these delights of the soul by ruminating upon them, distributed them among them with a generous hand. They, however, devouring the head, feet, and entrails, as it is written (Exodus 12:9), shared what remained with the other brothers, and thus the matter came to our knowledge. But since I have delayed by straying farther from the straight path of our journey on account of this, I shall try to return as quickly as possible to the route I began.

20. [Note: [Col. 0529] Witness 2 adds in red: “On the illness of Saint Burchard, bishop.” Witness 2 reads *jugiter* (“continually”) for “therefore,” and “his and our shepherd” for “our pious shepherd”; witness 1 omits “him.”] Therefore, because God chose our pious shepherd for his service, in his customary mercy he took care to chastise him, as we read: “For whom God loves, he corrects, and as a father he takes pleasure in his son” (Proverbs 3:12). [Note: [Col. 0531] Witness 2 reads “the Lord” for “God” and omits “as a father.”] [Note: [Col. 0529] Witness 2: “his own and our shepherd.”] [Note: [Col. 0529] Omitted in witness 1.] Struck by paralytic illness, he was afflicted with the gravest sickness. But he was never overcome or dispirited by this misfortune; with the same expression and the same cheerfulness he remained in the greatest patience.

By this chastisement of God he came to himself [Note: [Col. 0531] Witness 2 reads *se ipse*, “he himself,” for *in se*] and received this salutary thought: namely, that worldly possessions are detestable before God and belong not only to ruin but also to the everlasting ruin of the soul [Note: [Col. 0531] Witness 2 reads “perpetual”]. Therefore he ordered a careful inquiry [Note: [Col. 0531] Witness 2 omits “careful”] to be made throughout the whole household of Saint Peter as to whether anything had been unjustly taken from anyone by his authority, or whether any harm had been done. If anyone reported that an injustice had been done to him, he ordered that what had been taken be restored to him twofold.

His words were so tempered by discretion [Note: [Col. 0531] Witness 2: “discrimination”] that the firmness of his heart could easily be understood by his hearers. Whatever he said, he seasoned with the sweetest examples from the Holy Scriptures [Note: [Col. 0531] Witness 2: “holy men.”]. Justice, legal judgments, or constant sacred reading never departed from his mouth [Note: [Col. 0531] Witness 2: “sacred human reading.”]. It is unnecessary to praise his prudence, since a very great number of people came not only from the palace but also from various regions to understand his counsel [Note: [Col. 0531] Witness 2: “would come together.”].

He was so devoted to frequent fasts [Note: [Col. 0531] Witness 1 reads *frequentatione*, “by frequency,” rather than *frequentationi*, “to the frequency”], almsgiving, vigils, and prayers that few men of our age could equal him. For unless illness compelled him or the greatest necessity forced him, he nourished his life only with bread, vegetables, and fruit. Although everyone continually supposed that he drank wine [Note: [Col. 0531] Witness 2: “having refreshed himself with wine, he drank water. Often…”], he refreshed himself with water.

Very often, after the third or [Note: [Col. 0531] Witness 2 reads “or” (*sive*) for “or” (*vel*)] fourth watch of the night, he silently went around all the streets of the city with a certain intimate companion, whom he strictly forbade to let anyone learn this from him. He inspected every corner and hollow place, and wherever he found poor or sick people, he generously bestowed upon them the comforts of alms.

Every day before dawn he shut himself inside the oratory and remained there until the first hour of the day [Note: [Col. 0531] i.e., “he made himself remain there until the first hour of the day”; witness 2]. What he did inside was known not to us but to God alone. In the daily offices of the Mass, he did not cease to offer sacrifices with tireless devotion for both the dead and the living [Note: [Col. 0531] Witness 2: “solemn rites and offerings.”].

The poor regarded him as a father [Note: [Col. 0531] Witness 2 reads, “for the poor had him as a father”] and frequently came to him from distant places [Note: [Col. 0531] Witness 2: “nearby places.”], and he permitted none of them to depart unconsoled. Whenever the sudden assault of death, the terror or violence of the weather, the savagery of enemies, or the danger of some adversity threatened, he immediately summoned the brothers and overcame it through steadfastness in prayer and fasting.

Behold, before God and his angels I write the truth. Therefore [Note: [Col. 0531] Witness 2 reads “and therefore”], when we were continually gathered together and praising his various virtues, I confess that we already divined what proved true: after his death no one of such brilliant life would be found in this place who resembled him [Note: [Col. 0531] Witness 2 omits “in this place” and reads “similar” (*similem*) for “of his like” (*consimilem*)]. For although he was held by illness, he nevertheless remained unconquered in God’s service.

[Note: [Col. 0531] Witness 2 adds in red: “How he began but did not complete the monastery of Saint Martin.”]

He founded a monastery in honor of Saint Martin. But, after part of the wall had been completed, he was hindered by the frequent demands of royal service [Note: [Col. 0531] Witness 2 reads: “by the brain-racking intricacy of the affairs of regulations and …”], especially by continual illness and various adversities, and, alas, he could not complete it. Thus that monastery remained almost half-finished to this day [Note: [Col. 0531] Witness 2: “remained”; with “Kirsgart” added. Witness 2 then adds: “Nevertheless, Emperor Otto III bestowed certain goods in Bopardia upon that monastery,” followed by the rubric: “On the death of the holy Emperor Henry and the succession of Conrad, whom the Lord Burchard nurtured.”].

21. After these events [Note: [Col. 0531] Witness 1 reads “this”; witness 2 adds “holy.”] Emperor Henry died (13 July 1024), and his body was carried to Bamberg [Note: [Col. 0531] Witness 1 reads “was offered” (*offertur*) for “was carried” (*effertur*); witness 2 reads “and his body was carried to Bamberg.”] and buried there with the greatest honor. After his death, Conrad, the young man whom we mentioned above [Note: [Col. 0531C] Chapter 7], whom the bishop had nurtured and taught in the fear of God [Note: [Col. 0531] Witness 2: “Concerning whom it was said above: the Lord Burchard raised him in the fear of God and taught him.”], by God’s favor took possession of supreme power.

Two years after the king had been raised to the throne of the kingdom (in the year 1025, July), the weakness of the servant of God’s strength began to increase beyond its usual measure [Note: [Col. 0531] Witness 2: “to the utmost.”]. When he was suffering from excessive illness, he withdrew within the city, awaiting the day and hour of his future redemption [Note: [Col. 0531] The words “awaiting the day and hour of his future redemption” are absent from witness 2 but occur below after “was detained.”].

After he had been detained for some time by a serious illness, the king’s envoys came to him and announced that the king would arrive the following week [Note: [Col. 0531] Witness 2: “that he would arrive there.”]. Disturbed by this embassy, the servant of God grieved greatly on account of his illness, because he could neither receive the king with due dignity nor render him the service he owed, given his infirmity [Note: [Col. 0531] Witness 2: “was unable”; “could.”].

Amid these words, he turned to his customary consolation, entered the oratory, and closed the door behind him. There he remained in prayer for an entire day. When evening came, he ordered the disciples to be summoned as usual [Note: [Col. 0531] Witness 2: “to summon them together”]. After the evening praises had been completed, he returned joyfully and was restored to us all, by God’s grace, in good health [Note: [Col. 0531] Omitted in witness 2.]. Thus, throughout the entire time that the king had been with us, he remained strong, as though a reprieve had been obtained.

When the king departed, he went with him to Tribur [Note: [Col. 0533C] “The king was there on 26 July.”] and remained there for three days. Then, having received permission to depart, he foretold, as though joking, in the hearing of many, that he would not see the king again [Note: [Col. 0533] Omitted in witness 1.]. When he came to Worms, he was afflicted beyond measure by dysentery [Note: [Col. 0533] Witness 2 omits “by dysentery”].

22. One day, when he realized that his body was sinking toward death, he summoned the disciples, entered the oratory, and released all those who were indebted to him from the sins they had committed against him [Note: [Col. 0533] Witness 2: “their few offenses.”]; he mercifully absolved those who had been banished or anathematized by him and sent each of them a written absolution.

Then he washed his entire body with perfectly pure water and ordered his neck, beard, and tonsure to be shaved. After putting on clean clothing, he ordered his soldiers, retainers [Note: [Col. 0533] Witness 2: “and”;], clients, and the others who were present to come in to him. When everyone was sobbing with great weeping, the man of God, scarcely able to signal silence with the hand he could move [Note: [Col. 0533] Omitted in witness 2.], said:

«Venerable fathers, beloved brothers, dearest little sons, I now need your help before God. For I grieve greatly that until now I have negligently gone before you, exalted myself above you with excessive pride [Note: [Col. 0533] Witness 2: “above”; “extolled.”], and neither honored nor loved you as was just. But what benefit does that pride now bring me [Note: [Col. 0533] Witness 2: “did it bring me”?], or what help does arrogance give me [Note: [Col. 0533] Witness 2: “what does arrogance add?”]? It now harms me greatly [Note: [Col. 0533] Witness 1: “harmed”; witness 2: “harms.”] and produces many obstacles for me [Note: [Col. 0533] Omitted in witness 2.].

Yesterday I was one of the richest [Note: [Col. 0533] Witness 2: “most learned”;], but now I await what I shall soon become: something like dung and ash. Such is our boasting, such also is worldly dominion [Note: [Col. 0533] Witness 2: “human dominion.”]. I came forth naked from my mother’s womb; naked I shall return there, carrying nothing with me except my sins [Note: [Col. 0533] Witness 2: “my sins”], unless, with God’s mercy urging me on [Note: [Col. 0533] Witness 2: “unless I have done some good”], I have done some good; I hope that I shall find this with God.

Behold, now I am washed; behold, I am about to travel a very long road, prepared to await an exceedingly difficult embassy. From these miseries you can easily recognize how fragile and unstable the livid [Note: [Col. 0533] Witness 2: “mourning”] boasts of worldly things are [Note: [Col. 0533] Witness 1: “are”; witness 2: “may be”], how full of evil, how blind concerning the future [Note: [Col. 0533] Witness 1: “future things.”]. At present I know them as through a mirror, in an enigma, although I am still partly subject to them.

Therefore, to the one whom I have served from the beginning [Note: [Col. 0533] Witness 1 has the corrupt reading “abitro.”], my God, the eternal King, I confidently entrust myself and all that is mine, so that he himself may defend me and lead me with him to that place where my soul will fear no terrifying encounters.»

With such words he admonished us and taught the word of God, speaking not with a human sound; finally, he openly announced the dissolution of his body. When these words had ended, we went outside in the greatest sadness, and all together we mourned and wept over the death of so great a shepherd.

Then the princes who were present entered and carefully searched every corner of the treasury and chamber where they supposed money had been stored [Note: [Col. 0533] Witness 2: “hidden.”]. Finally, overturning chests full of books in hope of finding money, they were deceived by the vain labor of fortune [Note: [Col. 0533] Witness 2: “were disappointed.”]. For apart from the ecclesiastical treasury, they found neither gold nor silver there [Note: [Col. 0533] Witness 2: “found”;], except for only three coins, which the holy man had left in his wanton [Note: [Col. 0533] Witness 2: “in his little purse.”] [Note: [Col. 0533C] That is, a glove, the French *gant*.] when he had distributed the others to the poor.

Therefore his sister, whom we mentioned above [Note: [Col. 0534C] Chapter 12], the venerable abbess, remained in prayer and vigils and did not leave him [Note: [Col. 0533] Witness 2: “did not withdraw.”].

23. When he had been sick for several days with the gravest illness, one night, before daybreak [Note: [Col. 0533] The words “one night” are omitted in witness 2.], the servant of God rose from his bed and prayed for a long time, his eyes and hands directed toward heaven [Note: [Col. 0533] Witness 2: “his eyes and hands directed”;]. Those who were present saw his lips moving, but although they watched carefully, they could not understand at all what he was praying.

Then, lowering himself into bed [Note: [Col. 0533] Witness 2: “placing himself back”], he touched his sister’s right hand [Note: [Col. 0533] Witness 1: “the right hand”; revised by a later hand to “touched”; witness 2, Frankfurt manuscript, and a marginal note in the Hamburg manuscript likewise read “touched”], and said: “Behold, now I see what I desired.” Then he said [Note: [Col. 0533] Witness 2: “he says”]: “The Lord be with you.” When he had said this for the third time, he returned his unstained spirit to our Redeemer, whom he served, whom he loved, whom he sought, and whom he always desired (20 August 1025).

The servant of God had a certain chest, which none of us had ever seen opened. He entrusted its key to his sister, so that whatever she found inside she might keep as an object of love and remembrance of his life. Immediately after her brother’s death, she summoned some of our number, related his words, and then opened the chest.

We found in it a very rough hair shirt and an iron chain, worn on one side as though from use. When we saw these things, we first grieved together, beating our breasts, because we had often sinned negligently against the servant of God [Note: [Col. 0533] Witness 2: “we, the servants of God”; “often beating our breasts”; the phrase “together” is omitted.]. Then, rightly admiring his happy deeds before God, so hidden [Note: [Col. 0533] Witness 1: “upright”] and concealed [Note: [Col. 0533] Omitted in witness 2.], we offered thanks to our God for his life, not without tears.

His soldiers, venerable and illustrious men, were present at his funeral. Carrying his body through all the monasteries, they finally brought it to the principal see. There it was reverently received by all the brothers and was watched over with the customary rites. On the following day it was honorably buried in the same church, in the western choir, namely before the altar of Saint Lawrence [Note: [Col. 0535] Witness 2 ends instead: “In the year of the Lord 1025, the second year of Emperor Conrad. Where are now those who, with poisonous tongues, criticized the holy man’s happy deeds and often belittled and destroyed his works? Now, as we devoutly believe, he reigns with God, Abraham, in those lofty and perpetual joys. Amen.”]

[Col. 0535] A tomb raised somewhat above the pavement was closed by a hemispherical stone, with this inscription added:

“Here lies Buggo, formerly bishop of this place.”

Thus Schannat, *History of Worms*, vol. 1, p. 334.]

24. But where are now those pestilent men who, criticizing the life and deeds of the man of God with poisonous tongues, lied about him and his faithful people through various slanders—many things that it is not even lawful to repeat? O wretched and profane men, forgetful of all honor! O men ignorant of every virtue, stripped of all piety, and fattened only by the gluttony of the belly! O sterile of every goodness, doing nothing like this man, but placing their hope in the world and their salvation in the grave; men who tore apart the deeds of the servant of God with lies but themselves did not know how to do such things; whose god is their belly and whose glory is in their shame, who set their minds only on earthly things and know nothing at all of the things of God.

But this priest of Christ, turned toward God with all his mind and all his strength, carefully concealed whatever good he did, so that Christ alone would know it. He regarded empty praise and likewise the slanders of human beings as of little worth and passed them by with deaf ears, striving only to please God. Therefore we hope and firmly believe that he acquired from God eternal fruit for such deeds and received everlasting rewards in place of worldly things, and that, remaining with Christ, he may possess an eternal priesthood, through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be praise and glory through endless ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0535]

BURCHARD’S LETTER TO ALPERT

(See above under ALBERT, column 451 of this volume.)

[Col. 0537]

THE TWENTY BOOKS OF DECRETALS OF BURCHARD, BISHOP OF THE CHURCH OF WORMS

Collected from the councils and decrees of orthodox Fathers, as well as from the synods of various nations, like a set of commonplaces; in them the entire ecclesiastical office and the ancient observances of the Churches are embraced with lucid brevity. Paris, at the house of Jean Foucher, under the Sign of Florence, on the road to Saint James. — 1549. With the privilege of the Senate.

[Note: [Col. 0537B]

Extract from the Registers of Parliament.

The court, having considered the petition presented to it by Jean Foucher, sworn bookseller in the University of Paris, by which he requested permission to print, or have printed, a book entitled *D. Burchardi, Vuormaciensis episcopi, Decretorum Lib. XX, ex Conciliis et orthodoxorum patrum Decretis*, etc., has permitted and permits the said petitioner to print, or have printed, the said book and to offer it for sale; and forbids all other booksellers and printers of this jurisdiction to print, have printed, or offer for sale the said book, except copies which the said petitioner has caused to be printed, without his authorization and consent, for five years, under penalty of confiscation of the said books and an arbitrary fine. Done in Parliament at Paris on the last day of December 1548.

Collation has been made. Thus signed, DU TILLET.]

BURCHARD, BISHOP OF THE CHURCH OF WORMS, TO HIS MOST FAITHFUL BRUNICHON, PROVOST OF THE SAME CHURCH, GREETING IN THE LORD CHRIST.

[Col. 0537A] For many days indeed—and often in your presence, dearest brother—your affection has earnestly urged me to gather, with vigilant care, some useful work drawn no less from the judgments of the holy Fathers than from the canonical Scriptures and from approved examples of penitents, for the necessary use of those who serve our Church.

You seemed to insist upon this especially because the laws of the canons and the forms of penance in our diocese are so confused and inconsistent among themselves that they appear either wholly neglected, almost entirely deprived of authority, or only moderately established according to ecclesiastical discipline. For this reason it often happens that those who flee to the remedy of penance cannot readily be helped, both because of the confused arrangement of the canons and because of the ignorance of our priests. You did not immodestly ask me whether this was chiefly the reason. And although I think the same, [Col. 0538A] nevertheless, since the judgment of the canons has not expressed a fixed measure of time to be applied to each individual offense of penitents, but has established that this should be left to the judgment of those who grant absolution, salutary remedies of penance are consequently not provided by inexperienced priests according to the character of the offenses; whereas pious priests, instructed by the canonical writings, readily apply them as each person’s weakness requires.

And because the matter stands thus, your affection asked me to offer this little compilation for our younger men to read, so that, at a suitable age, they might learn what either the later age of our contemporaries cannot now attain, or the negligence of our predecessors never reached. You thought it especially fitting that a man should first show himself a disciple, with complete integrity, before rashly presuming upon the authority of a teacher among the people, and that he should learn in the schools what he is to teach those entrusted to his faith.

I have judged this request of yours, dearest brother, entirely just; and for such a pious devotion toward divine religion I give you the greatest thanks, since I continually observe you laboring with no slack concern for the condition of our Church. Yet you will not attribute the fact that I delayed so long to fulfill your frequently repeated exhortation to my laziness or sluggishness. Two causes, in fact, prevented me from promptly complying with your desire. One was brought about by the unavoidable needs of our Church, which arise against us every day like waves. The other comes from the grave cares of secular affairs, to which we are unwillingly dragged by the burden of imperial commands. These two things truly do not permit my mind, which strives toward heavenly things, to rise very far upward. For while the mind is disturbed by many matters, it is [Col. 0539B] too weak to be equal to any one of them.

Nevertheless, complying with your holy requests, with God’s help I gathered into a single bundle synodal precepts and sacred institutions, drawn both from the judgments of the holy Fathers and from canonical writings, from the broadest extent of the world. As best I could, I joined them together as though into a single body and divided them into twenty books, so that whoever reads them diligently will soon perceive that he can obtain no ordinary benefit [Col. 0540A] from them: highly useful for teaching the people, firm because of the authority of Scripture, and honorable as something acquired through study and diligence.

For he does not deserve the name of priest who does not know how carefully the evangelical threat must be weighed; for a blind man cannot be a guide to the blind. Therefore let no one despise this labor of mine as a mere compilation. Certainly, the immense breadth in which the sacred Scriptures are dispersed, together with the negligence and ignorance of our priests, compelled me to labor in this field. To gather material was permitted; but it was unlawful for me alone to enact canons. How many labors and vigils I expended in accomplishing this, God Most High will judge; nothing is hidden from him that I have done for the necessity of our Church.

Therefore, even if this work has not gone beyond the limits of our province, we shall not be troubled at all, provided that it is handled by the hands of our ministers. Moreover, we wish readers to be persuaded of this also: nothing of my own has been added to this work, but each item has been excerpted from divine scriptural testimonies, and with such fidelity that I do not doubt it will possess perpetual authority. The following list indicates from which writings I selected them. Farewell, and support me with your prayers.

## From which authors’ writings these ecclesiastical decrees were collected

[Col. 0539]

[Col. 0539B] From the canons called the Body of Canons.

From the Apostolic Canon.

From councils held overseas.

From councils celebrated in Germany, Gaul, and Spain.

From the decrees of the Roman pontiffs.

From the evangelical and apostolic Scriptures.

[Col. 0540B] From the Old Testament.

From the books of Saint Gregory.

From Jerome, Augustine, Ambrose, Benedict, Basil the Great, and Isidore.

From the Roman Penitential.

From the Penitential of Theodore.

From the Penitential of Bede.

## Index of the individual books of Burchard, Bishop of Worms, briefly showing what each book contains

[Col. 0539]

[Col. 0539C] The first book contains material on the power and primacy of the Apostolic See, of the patriarchs, and of the other primates and metropolitans; on the holding of synods and the summons to synod; on the accused, accusers, and witnesses; on those unjustly dispossessed; on judges; on every appropriate honor and dignity; and on the various business and ministry of bishops.

The second book contains material on the fitting dignity, varied formation, nurture, quality of life, and the various business and ministry of priests, deacons, and the remaining ecclesiastical orders.

The third book contains material on the establishment, worship, and honor of houses of God; on tithes, offerings, and the rights of individuals; on which books are received into the sacred catalogue and which are apocryphal; and on when they are to be introduced.

[Col. 0540C] The fourth book contains the sacrament of baptism and the ministry of those to be baptized and those who have been baptized, and of those to be confirmed and those who have been confirmed.

The fifth book contains material on the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood and on their reception and observance.

The sixth book contains material on homicides committed voluntarily and involuntarily; parricides and fratricides; those who kill legitimate wives and their elders; the killing of ecclesiastical persons; and the observance and penance of each individual.

The seventh book contains material on incestuous unions among blood relatives, on within which degree the faithful may marry and must separate, and on the restoration and penance of each individual.

The eighth book contains material on men and women dedicated to God [Col. 0541A], on those who transgress their sacred commitment, and on their restoration and penance.

The ninth book contains material on un veiled virgins and widows, their abductors and their separation from them; the joining of legitimate marriages; concubines; and the transgression and penance of each individual.

The tenth book contains material on enchanters, augurs, diviners, sorcerers, and the various illusions of the devil; on slanderers, quarrelsome persons, and conspirators; and on the penance of each individual.

The eleventh book contains material on those to be excommunicated and those already excommunicated; on thieves and plunderers; on presumption, contempt, and negligence; and on their reconciliation and penance.

[Col. 0541B] The twelfth book contains material on perjury and its penance.

The thirteenth book contains material on the veneration and observance of the sacred fast.

The fourteenth book contains material on gluttony and drunkenness and on the penance of those guilty of them.

The fifteenth book contains material on emperors, [Col. 0542A] princes, and the remaining laypeople, and on their ministry.

The sixteenth book contains material on accusers, judges, defenders, false witnesses, and the penance of each individual.

The seventeenth book contains material on fornication and various kinds of incest, and on the penance of both sexes and of different ages.

The eighteenth book contains material on the visitation, penance, and reconciliation of the sick.

The nineteenth book, called the *Corrector*, contains corrections of bodies and remedies for souls, and teaches every priest, even a simple one, how and in what way he may come to the aid of each person—ordained or unordained, poor or rich, [Col. 0542B] child, young person, old person, or very old person; healthy or sick; of every age and of either sex.

The twentieth book is called *Speculations*. For it considers divine providence and predestination, the coming of Antichrist and his works, the resurrection, the day of judgment, punishments in hell, and the happiness of eternal life.

# Burchard, Bishop of the Church of Worms: Decretum, Book One

## On the Primacy of the Church

[Col. 0549]

### Chapter I — That in the New Testament, after Christ our Lord, the priestly order began from Peter

[Col. 0549C]

*(From a letter of Pope Anacletus addressed to the bishops of Italy.)* In the New Testament, after Christ our Lord, the priestly order began from Peter, because the pontificate in the Church of Christ was first given to him, as the Lord said to him: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it, and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven.” He therefore was the first to receive from the Lord the power of binding and loosing, and he was the first to bring the people of God to the faith by grace and through the power of his preaching.

### Chapter II — On the privilege entrusted exclusively to blessed Peter in the Lord’s place, and on the distinction of authority that existed among the apostles

[Col. 0549D]

*(From a letter of Pope Melchiades addressed to the bishops of Spain.)* This privilege he entrusted exclusively to blessed Peter, the blessed key-bearer, in his own place; it rightly passed as his prerogative to his see, to be inherited and maintained in future times, just as there was also a certain distinction of authority among the most blessed apostles. And although the election of all was equal, it was nevertheless granted to blessed Peter that he should excel the others and prudently arrange the cases and questions of those matters that came before him as complaints.

We believe that this was arranged in such a manner by God’s ordinance [Col. 0550C] so that all their successors would not claim everything for themselves; rather, the greater cases—such as those of bishops—and the care of more important affairs would always converge upon the one see of blessed Peter, the chief of the apostles. Thus they would receive the conclusion of judgments from the place where they had received the beginning of their institutions, lest they should at any time differ from their own head.

### Chapter III — That the supreme priest should not be called the Roman pontiff, but the bishop of the first see

*(African Canon, canon 6.)* The bishop of the first see should not be called the chief of priests, or the supreme priest, or anything of this kind, but only the bishop of the first see.

### Chapter IV — That the order of priests is divided into two ranks

*(From a letter of Pope Anacletus sent to all bishops [Col. 0550D] and the remaining priests, chapter 18.)* Brothers, the order of priests is divided into two ranks, and just as the Lord established it, it must not be disturbed by anyone. You know that the apostles were chosen and appointed by the Lord and afterward dispersed through the various provinces to preach. But when the harvest began to increase, and he saw that there were few laborers, he commanded seventy disciples to be chosen to assist them.

Bishops occupy the place of the apostles, and priests that of the seventy disciples. Bishops, however, should not be established in castles or small towns, but priests should be ordained and appointed by bishops throughout castles, small towns, and villages, one in each of their respective titles. No more than these two orders of priests has been conferred upon us, nor did the apostles teach any more.

### Chapter V — That bishops who are ordained should not be laymen, bigamists, or husbands of widows, but irreproachable men

*(From a decree of Pope Leo, title 33.)* In cities whose rulers have died, this rule concerning the appointment of bishops is to be observed: the man who is to be ordained, even if supported by the testimony of a good life, must not be a layman, a neophyte, a husband of a second wife, or one who has or has had one wife whom he married as a widow. The election of priests is so exalted that things which in other members of the Church are not counted as faults are nevertheless considered unlawful in them.

### Chapter VI — That when a bishop is being elected, if he has opponents, five bishops should assemble

*(From the African Council, chapter 17.)* The following too must be established: when we have assembled to elect a bishop, if any opposition arises—for such things have occurred among us—those involved should not presume that three bishops are sufficient for the examination of the man who is to be ordained. Rather, two more should be sought, making the number stated above, if they can be found, in the same people over whom he is to be ordained. First, the persons of those who oppose him must be examined; afterward, the charges brought against him must also be investigated. When he has been cleared in public view, only then should he be ordained.

If this accords with the mind of your holiness, let it be confirmed by your dignified reply. All the bishops said: “It is entirely pleasing.”

### Chapter VII — That no one should be ordained bishop against the will of the clergy or people

*(From a decree of Pope Celestine, chapter 18.)* Let no bishop be given against the will of the people; the agreement and desire of the clergy, people, and order must be sought. Only then should someone be chosen from another Church if, among the clergy of the city for which the bishop is to be ordained, no worthy man can be found—which we do not believe will happen.

First, those men must be rejected, so that someone from another Church may deservedly be preferred. Let each person enjoy the fruit of his service in the Church in which he has spent his life through all its offices. No one should stealthily intrude upon another’s service, nor should anyone dare to claim for himself another’s due reward. Let the clergy have the freedom to resist if they see themselves being overburdened. If they recognize that men have been thrust upon them from elsewhere, they should not fear to reject them; if they do not, they ought to have their due reward and free judgment concerning the one who is to rule them.

### Chapter VIII — Which bishops are to be ordained, and that they must first be examined
(From the Council of Carthage, chapter 1.) The man who is to be ordained bishop must first be examined: whether he is naturally prudent, teachable, temperate in conduct, chaste in life, sober, always careful in the management of his affairs, humble, approachable, merciful, literate, instructed in the law of the Lord, cautious in understanding the Scriptures, and trained in ecclesiastical doctrine.

And above [Col. 0552A] all, whether he professes the articles of faith in simple words—that is, affirming that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one Lord, and proclaiming the whole Godhead in the Trinity to be coessential, consubstantial, coeternal, and co-omnipotent, and each person in the Trinity to be fully God, while the three persons together are one God.

Whether he believes that the divine incarnation took place not in the Father or in the Holy Spirit, but in the Son alone: that he who was, in divinity, the Son of God the Father, himself became, in humanity, the son of a human mother; true God from the Father, true man from his mother; possessing flesh from his mother’s womb and a rational human soul; with both natures, namely, that of man and that of God, united in him; one person, one Son, one Christ, one Lord of all creatures that [Col. 0552B] exist, and, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, the Author, Lord, and Creator of all creatures.

Whether he truly suffered the passion of the flesh, truly died the death of his body, rose again in the true resurrection of his flesh, and truly took back his soul, in which he will come to judge the living and the dead.

He must also be asked whether he believes that the New and Old Testaments—that is, the Law, the Prophets, and the Apostles—have one and the same Author and Lord.

Whether the devil became evil not by nature but by his own choice.

He must also be asked whether he believes in the resurrection of this flesh which we bear, and not of another flesh.

Whether he believes that judgment will take place, and that each person will receive either punishments or rewards for what he has done in this flesh.

Whether he does not disapprove of marriage.

Whether he does not condemn second marriages.

Whether he does not condemn the eating of meat.

Whether he communicates with penitents who have been reconciled.

Whether in baptism all sins are forgiven—that is, both the original sin contracted and those voluntarily committed.

Whether anyone can be saved outside the Catholic Church.

When he has been examined on all these matters and found fully instructed, then he shall be ordained bishop.

### CHAPTER IX — That bishops must be examined with the greatest care before they are ordained

(From the Council of Orléans, chapter 12.) Let bishops be advanced to ecclesiastical authority by the judgment of the metropolitans and of those bishops whose sees are adjacent—namely, men who have been tested over a long period both in the word of faith and in the example of upright conduct.

### CHAPTER X — That the people may not themselves conduct the elections of priests

[Col. 0552D]

(From the Council of Braga, chapter 1.) The people may not themselves conduct the election of those who are being summoned to the priesthood; rather, the matter must rest with the judgment of the bishops, so that they themselves may test whether the man who is to be ordained has been instructed in speech, faith, and spiritual life.

### CHAPTER XI — That those are not to be regarded as bishops whom neither clergy nor people elected, and whom the bishops of the province did not consecrate

(Canon 15 of Pope Leo.) No principle permits those to be counted among the bishops who were neither elected by the clergy, nor sought by the people, nor consecrated by the bishops of the province with the judgment of the metropolitan. Therefore, [Col. 0553A] since a dispute often arises over an honor wrongly received, who could doubt that what is not shown to have been conferred cannot in any way be granted by these men either?

If, however, certain clerics were ordained by these false bishops in churches that belonged to their proper bishops, and their ordination was carried out with the consent and advice of the presiding authorities, it may be regarded as valid, so that they may remain in those churches. Otherwise the consecration must be considered void, since it was established neither in the proper place nor secured by proper authority.

### CHAPTER XII — That no one should be ordained bishop except by common agreement

(From the Council of Orléans, chapter 2.) No one is to be ordained bishop unless the clergy and the parishioners have been summoned and have agreed together.

### CHAPTER XIII — Concerning those who assume the governance of churches and despise everyone in the arrogance of pride

[Col. 0553B]

(Origen says:) Some, having assumed a church, are puffed up by divine matters and despise everyone in the arrogance of pride; such men are called dogs rather than rulers.

### CHAPTER XIV — Concerning those bishops who begin to grow proud

(From the sayings of Pope Gregory and the Apostle Paul.) A bishop ought to be humble. For he receives the rank of gentleness, not of pride. Paul says: “Such a man ought to be gentle, not uplifted or proud.”

### CHAPTER XV — That the ordinations of bishops must be carried out by all the provincials under apostolic authority

[Col. 0553C]

(From a letter of Pope Anacletus written to the bishops of Italy, canon 9.) The ordinations of bishops are to be celebrated under apostolic authority by all who are in the same province. Coming together, they are to conduct a careful examination, and to observe a fast with the prayers that accompany it; laying hands upon them together with the holy Gospels which they are to preach, they are to pray on the Lord’s Day at the third hour, and, following the example of prophets and kings, anoint their heads with sacred unction in the manner of the Apostles and Moses. For all sanctification is accomplished in the Holy Spirit, whose invisible power is proclaimed through the holy chrism. In this rite they are to celebrate the solemn ordination.

If they cannot all come together, nevertheless let them give their assent through prayers and letters, so that in spirit they may not be absent from the ordination.

[Col. 0553D]

Moreover, the first archbishop of Jerusalem, the blessed James who was called “the Just” and was named the Lord’s brother according to the flesh, was ordained by the Apostles Peter, James, and John. They thereby gave a pattern to their successors, so that no one may in any way be ordained by fewer than three bishops, with all the others giving their assent, and so that the ordination may be celebrated by common agreement.

### CHAPTER XVI — That no layman may become bishop before thirty years of age and before a year of clerical conduct

(From the Council of Arles, canon 7.) No layman shall receive the honor of the episcopate or presbyterate before a year of clerical conduct or before the age of thirty.

### CHAPTER XVII — Concerning the appointment of laymen as bishops without due consideration

[Col. 0554A]

(From the Council of Sardica, chapter 13.) Bishop Hosius said: “I also consider it necessary that you examine with the greatest care whether perhaps a rich man, a scholar from the forum, or someone from the administrative office is requested as bishop, so that he may not be ordained beforehand unless he has first served in the office of reader and in the ministry of deacon or presbyter. Thus, passing through each rank, let him ascend to the summit of the episcopate if he is worthy.

“For through these promotions, which will necessarily extend over a considerable period, it can be tested with what faith, moderation, seriousness, and modesty he is endowed. If he is found worthy, let him be honored with the divine priesthood. For it is neither fitting nor permitted by reason or discipline that [Col. 0554B] a neophyte should be ordained rashly and lightly as bishop, presbyter, or deacon—especially since the blessed Apostle Paul, the teacher of the nations, appears to have given warning and prohibition against this. Rather, let those be chosen whose life has been examined over a long period and whose merits have been proved.”

### CHAPTER XVIII — That the office of the episcopate must be reached through the ecclesiastical ranks

(From a decree of Pope Celestine sent to the bishops of Gaul, canon 16.) We have learned, dearest brothers, that certain men have been ordained bishops who had not been established through any ecclesiastical orders before reaching the summit of such dignity, contrary to the decrees of the Fathers, through the usurpation of one who acknowledges having done this. Yet the episcopate must be reached through those ranks for which provision has very often been made, so that those [Col. 0554C] initiated into the lesser offices may be strengthened for the greater.

Whoever desires to be a teacher must first be a disciple, so that he may teach what he has learned. Every ordering of life confirms itself by this principle in the direction toward which it aims. He who has given no attention to letters cannot be a teacher of letters. He who has not advanced through each stage of service cannot attain the rank of a higher service.

Among all these offices, is the priesthood alone, I ask, to be considered of lesser value because it is more readily bestowed, although it is more difficult to fulfill?

### CHAPTER XIX — That one who has obtained the episcopate through ambition may not receive lay communion

(From the Council of Sardica, chapter 2.) Bishop Hosius said: “Even if some rash man should appear and perhaps assert, offering such an excuse, [Col. 0554D] that he had received the letters of the people—when it is evident that many could have been corrupted by gifts and payment, people who lacked sincere faith, so that they might cry out in the church and appear to request him as bishop—I consider that these frauds must be condemned altogether, so that such a man may not even receive lay communion at the end of his life. If this pleases all of you, decree it.”

The synod replied: “It pleases us.”

### CHAPTER XX — That no one can be a bishop who was consecrated without the knowledge of the metropolitan

(From the Council of Arles, chapter 6.) Above all, this is clear: the man who has been appointed bishop without the knowledge of the metropolitan must not, according to the great synod, be regarded as a bishop.

### CHAPTER XXI — That bishops may not occupy a position of governance through the Simoniac heresy

[Col. 0555A]

(From the Council of Meaux, chapter 43.) Bishops, kings, all higher authorities, and all their supporters, electors, and those who consent to or carry out ecclesiastical appointments must beware—indeed, must take the greatest precautions—and must forbid, by the power of Christ’s blood, that anyone obtain a position of governance through the Simoniac heresy by any faction, cunning, promise, or advantage, whether by giving directly or through an intermediary.

For among other testimonies the Holy Spirit says through the mouth of Gregory: “Why does he not understand that the blessing bestowed upon him is turned into a curse?” And elsewhere: “Sorrowfully I say it, groaning I proclaim it: [Col. 0555B] the priesthood which has fallen inwardly among you will not be able to stand outwardly for long.”

### CHAPTER XXII — Concerning those who have purchased sacred dignity with money

(From a letter of Pope Gelasius, chapter 5.) Those who are clearly unworthy in merit and have purchased sacred dignity with money must, once convicted, be excluded, because the condemnation of Simon, attested by Holy Scripture, involves equally the giver and the receiver.

### CHAPTER XXIII — On the same matter

(From a letter of Pope Hormisdas, chapter 10.) We therefore join this to what was said earlier: the blessing believed to come from God through the laying on of hands must not be purchased for a price, because Simon, wishing to buy the Holy Spirit with money, was struck down by the Apostle’s condemnation.

### CHAPTER XXIV — That the ordinations of bishops ought not to be long delayed

[Col. 0555C]

(Chalcedon, chapter 25.) Since, as we have learned, certain metropolitans neglect the flocks entrusted to them and delay carrying out the ordinations of bishops, it pleased the holy synod that episcopal ordinations be celebrated within three months, unless some unavoidable necessity should arise that requires the period of delay to be extended. If he does not do this, he shall be subject to ecclesiastical correction. Nevertheless, the revenues of the widowed church are to be kept intact in the hands of its steward.

### CHAPTER XXV — Concerning episcopal ordinations, which must not be long delayed

(From a decree of Pope Damasus, chapter 2.) Since certain metropolitans, refusing to present their profession of faith to the holy apostolic see according to ancient custom, [Col. 0555D] neither request nor receive the pallium, and consequently the consecration of bishops is prolonged, not without danger, for churches deprived of their bishops, it has been decided that any metropolitan who, for more than three months after his consecration, has not sent to the apostolic see to present his profession of faith and receive the pallium shall lose the dignity entrusted to him.

Other metropolitans may, after a second and third admonition, with the advice of the Roman pontiff, assist churches deprived of their bishops by ordaining a bishop. But if the negligence of the bishop-elect causes a widowed church to remain without a bishop for more than three months, he shall be deprived of communion until either he withdraws from the position or ceases to delay presenting himself for consecration. [Col. 0556A] If through his negligence he keeps the church widowed for more than five months, he shall receive the gift of consecration neither there nor elsewhere; rather, he must yield to the judgment of his metropolitan.

### CHAPTER XXVI — When someone is to be ordained by the bishops of a neighboring province

(Canon 5 of Sardica.) Bishop Hosius said: “If it should happen in a province in which there are many bishops that perhaps only one bishop remains, and the people assemble, the bishops of the neighboring province must first approach the bishop who resides in that province and show him that the people are requesting a ruler for themselves. It is just that they themselves should come and ordain the bishop together with him.

“But if, once approached, he remains silent in his letters, makes no response, [Col. 0556B], and dissembles, the people must be accommodated, so that bishops from the neighboring province may come and ordain a bishop.”

### CHAPTER XXVII — That a bishop may not be consecrated without three bishops

(From the Council of Arles, chapter 5.) No bishop may presume to ordain a bishop without the permission of the metropolitan, nor may a metropolitan bishop do so without three bishops of the province. The other bishops of the province are to be notified by letters, so that they may indicate through their reply that they have given their consent. If there is any dispute between the parties, the metropolitan is to agree with the greater party in the election.

### CHAPTER XXVIII — That a bishop may not be ordained by fewer than three, and, if possible, that an archbishop be ordained by all the bishops of the province

[Col. 0556C]

(From a letter of Pope Anicius addressed to the churches established throughout Gaul.)

Concerning the ordinations of bishops about which you wished to consult us, we have found that certain matters were already decreed long ago in the spirit of our predecessor Anacletus. For we know that the blessed James, who was called “the Just” and was also named the Lord’s brother according to the flesh, was ordained bishop at Jerusalem by the Apostles Peter, James, and John.

If so great a man was ordained by no fewer than three Apostles, it is plainly evident that, by the Lord’s institution, they handed down the rule that a bishop ought to be ordained by no fewer than three bishops. As the number of bishops increases, however, more should also be added unless necessity intervenes.

If an archbishop dies and another archbishop is to be ordained, all the bishops of the same province are to come together at the metropolitan see [Col. 0556D], so that he may be elected and ordained by all. For it is proper that the man who is to preside over all of them should be elected and ordained by all of them.

The other bishops of the province, if necessary and with the consent of the rest, may be consecrated as bishops by three at the command of the archbishop. But it is better if the archbishop himself, together with all of them, elects the man who is worthy and if all together consecrate the pontiff.

Although this has been conceded under the pressure of necessity, the rule laid down and proclaimed concerning the consecration of an archbishop—that all his suffragans are to ordain him—may in no way be altered. For he who presides over them must be appointed by all the bishops over whom he presides.

If anything else is presumed, [Col. 0557A] it is undoubtedly without force, because his ordination, carried out otherwise, will be invalid.

### CHAPTER XXIX — Concerning the bishop who ordained another bishop against his will

(From a letter of Pope Simplicius sent to John, bishop of Ravenna, chapter 1.) If anyone observed the standard of ecclesiastical discipline, or if any measure of priestly moderation were preserved in you, such punishable excesses would never have been committed. If no command of your paternal rules could restrain you from them, at least the example of your predecessor of holy memory should have recalled you. Although he had committed a lesser offense in making an unwilling man a presbyter, he nevertheless recognized that such usurpation deserved judgment.

Where did you learn these practices, which you perpetrated against our brother and fellow bishop Gregory—not [Col. 0557B] by election but through envy? You allowed him to be dragged to you by inexcusable violence and harassed, so that you might confer upon him an honor—not through peace of mind but, as must be said, through madness. Such things could not have been done with sound counsel.

We do not wish to exaggerate what happened, lest we be compelled to pass the judgment it deserves. For he deserves to lose his privilege who abuses the power entrusted to him.

### CHAPTER XXX — Concerning the deposition of one whom two bishops presume to ordain

(From the Council of Orange, chapter 20.) Concerning the deposition of one whom two bishops have presumed to ordain, it has been decided in our provinces that, if it should happen anywhere that two bishops consecrate a third, [Col. 0557C], both he and the authors of the act shall be condemned, so that what was established long ago may be observed with greater care.

### CHAPTER XXXI — Concerning the non-ordination of bishops in villages and small cities

(From the Council of Sardica, chapter 6.) Permission must not be given to ordain a bishop either in a village or in a small city for which one presbyter is sufficient. For there is no need for a bishop to be established there, lest the name and authority of bishop be cheapened.

Men invited from another province ought not to make a bishop there, except in cities that have previously had bishops, or in a city that is so substantial or so populous that it deserves to have a bishop.

If this pleases all, the synod replied: “It pleases us.”

### CHAPTER XXXII — On the same matter

[Col. 0557D]

(From a decree of Pope Leo, chapter 49.) With regard to the priestly dignity, we wish the statutes of the canons to be observed above all: bishops are not to be consecrated in just any places or in just any castles, or where there have previously been no bishops. Where the populations and assemblies are smaller, the care of presbyters is sufficient; episcopal governance ought to preside only over larger populations and more populous cities.

Otherwise, what the decrees divinely inspired in the holy Fathers have forbidden would be granted to villages, estates, obscure places, and isolated municipalities: a priestly dignity and honor which ought to be entrusted to more excellent communities, and which would itself be cheapened by the smallness of its numbers.

### CHAPTER XXXIII — Concerning Wamba, king of the Gauls, who established an episcopate in a certain small village contrary to the canons, and how it was annulled

[Col. 0558A]

(From the Thirteenth Council of Toledo, canon 4.) To oppose major institutions and overturn the decrees of the holy Fathers—is this anything other than breaking the bond of Christ’s fellowship and, through the license of usurped command, destroying the order of the Church?

Accordingly, when our venerable and most holy brother Stephen, bishop of the see of Mérida, brought the matter forward, a new affair arising from presumptuous usurpation was placed before us for consideration. It had to be overturned by the judgment of our entire communion in proportion to the audacity with which our wrongdoing was known to have been committed.

He said that he had been driven by royal violence to establish a new episcopal ordination in the monastery of the small village where the venerable body [Col. 0558B] of the most holy confessor Punius rests with due honor. Thus, yielding through indiscreet and excessively easy consent to the unjust commands of Prince Wamba, he introduced a new and unlawful selection of an episcopal see in a place where the canonical constitution rejects this by every argument.

The aforesaid man, prostrate on the ground under the remedy of our instruction, asked that pardon be granted him, and requested that our own judgment should determine what ought chiefly to be done concerning the person who had been ordained there.

But because we knew truly—indeed, as a matter of common knowledge—that the aforesaid prince had acted on the advice of frivolity, and had not only ordered that a bishop be established in the place mentioned, but had also so fixed his determination that he would ordain a bishop in the Praetorian church of Saints Peter and Paul in the suburb of Toledo [Col. 0558C], and likewise do the same in other villages and small settlements, we ordered that whatever the canonical statutes contained on this subject should be brought forward.

Then the following materials were arranged and read in order.

First, the examples from Paul, where he instructed his disciple Titus to establish bishops throughout the cities.

Next, from the Council of Nicaea, title 8, where, among other things, it is prescribed that two bishops must not appear to exist in one city.

Next, from the Council of Laodicea, title 7, where it says: “Bishops ought not to be ordained in villages and small settlements.”

Next, from the Council of Africa, title 2, where Felix, bishop of Sullectum, said: “Even if this pleases your holiness, I submit that dioceses [Col. 0558D] which have never had bishops should not have them. A diocese which once had one should have its own. According to this submission, it is for your holiness to judge what ought to be done.”

Bishop Genecletus said: “If the submission of our father and fellow bishop Felix is acceptable, let it be confirmed by all.”

All the bishops said: “It pleases us.”

Next, from the Third Council of Africa, title 2, where it says that a people which has always been subject to a diocese must not receive another bishop. For Bishop Epigenius said as follows: “A people which has always been subject to a diocese and has never had its own bishop ought not to receive another ruler. Therefore, if what I have said pleases the entire holy assembly, let it be confirmed.”

Bishop Aurelius [Col. 0559A] said: “I do not oppose the submission of our brother and fellow priest, but I declare that I have done this and shall continue to do it.”

Next, from the Council of Sardica, where, among other things, it is prescribed: “Permission must not be given indiscriminately. If suddenly some village or small city, for which one presbyter is sufficient, should wish to have a bishop ordained for itself, so that the name and authority of bishop may be cheapened, those invited from another province must not make a bishop for them in places where there has previously been none.”

Next, concerning the judgment of those who carry out such ordinations, and of those who are ordained contrary to these canonical institutions, from the Council of Turin, in the title where it says: “It has also pleased us that a record of the proceedings be written down for perpetual discipline, concerning what the holy synod decreed regarding Octavius, Ursio, Remigius, and Bishop Trefe.

[Col. 0559B]

“They were called, through envy, to a certain usurpation of the priestly order.” The concession made to them was granted in such a way that, having henceforth been warned by this authority, they would attempt no further usurpation.

“Since they defended themselves in this matter with the excuse that they had not previously been summoned, the holy synod therefore judged that, if anyone henceforth acts against the institutions of the Fathers, the man who has been ordained shall know that he is to be deprived of the honor of the priesthood, and the man who ordained him shall know that he will retain no authority in ordinations or in councils.

“This judgment will prevail not only against the bishop mentioned, but also against all those deceived by a similar error who have carried out such ordinations.”

Applying the effect of this pious work to these strongest rules, we chose in our common [Col. 0559C] decision that, in the aforementioned small village of Aquis, an episcopal see should no longer remain, nor should a bishop ever again be established there.

Conjuldus, however, who appears to have been instituted bishop there contrary to the decrees of the Fathers, shall not be punished by any canonical sentence for his condemnation, because it is clear that he was ordained not through ambition but through the compulsion of the prince.

Therefore, as a humane remedy, we grant him permission to be transferred to another see whose bishop has died. The aforesaid place is henceforth to remain under monastic discipline, no longer relying on an episcopal privilege, but being entirely subject to the rule of an abbot, as it has been until now.

Now, establishing a general edict for the future: if anyone attempts to violate these canonical prohibitions [Col. 0559D] by arranging for a bishop to be elected in places where there has never been a bishop, let him incur anathema in the sight of almighty God. Moreover, both the ordainer and the ordained shall lose the rank of their order, because he has dared to overturn not only the decrees of the ancient Fathers but also the apostolic institutions.

### CHAPTER XXXIV — That a people which has never had a bishop may not have one except by consent

(From the African Council, chapter 61.) It has also been decided that peoples which have never had their own bishops may not receive one unless this has been decreed by the plenary council of the province and by its primate, with the consent of the bishop to whose diocese that church belonged.

### CHAPTER XXXV — That a province must in no way be divided between two metropolitans

[Col. 0560A]

(Council of Chalcedon, chapter 12.) It has come to our attention that certain men, acting contrary to ecclesiastical statutes, have fled to the civil authorities and, through an imperial administrative decree, divided one province into two, so that as a result two metropolitans appear to exist in one province.

The holy synod therefore decrees that henceforth no such attempt shall be made by bishops. Otherwise, whoever undertakes this shall be subject to the loss of his own rank.

Whatever cities have been supported by imperial letters with the honor of the metropolitan name shall enjoy that honor only; the bishop who governs its church shall retain his privileges, without prejudice, of course, to the true privileges of the metropolis.

[Col. 0560B]

### CHAPTER XXXVI — Concerning those bishops who have not been received by those to whom they were ordained or appointed

[Col. 0560B]

(From the Council of Ancyra, chapter 17.) If any bishops have been ordained but not received by the parish to which they had been appointed, and have wished to seize other parishes and to use force against their bishops by stirring up rebellions against them, it has been decided that such men are to be deposed.

If they wish to remain as presbyters in the order in which they had previously served, they are not to be deprived of their dignity. But if they stir up rebellions there against the bishops who have been established, even the honor of the presbyterate shall be taken away from such men, and they shall be marked by condemnation.

### CHAPTER XXXVII — Concerning the bishop who neglects to go to the church to which he has been ordained

(From the Council of Antioch, chapter 17.) If a bishop has received the episcopate through the laying on of hands but neglects to undertake the ministry entrusted to him and refuses to go to the church committed to him, [Col. 0560C], he must be deprived of communion until, compelled, he accepts the office, or until the synod of the priests of that province makes some complete decision concerning him.

### CHAPTER XXXVIII — Concerning the bishop who does not undertake the office entrusted to him

(From the Council of Arles, chapter 6.) If a bishop does not undertake the office entrusted to him, he shall be deprived of communion until he consents and lends himself to his obedience.

But if he proceeds there and is not received, not through his own decision but because of the wickedness of the people, he himself shall remain a bishop, while the clerics of the city shall be deprived of communion because they have failed to discipline the disobedient people.

### CHAPTER XXXIX — Concerning a bishop without a see who invades a vacant church

[Col. 0560D]

(From the Council of Antioch, chapter 16.) If a bishop without a see secretly invades a church without a bishop and rushes upon its people without the council of the entire order, even if the people whom he has led astray desire him, he must be regarded as alien to the Church.

By a complete and perfect council we mean one in which the metropolitan bishop has taken part.

### CHAPTER XL — Concerning a bishop ordained for a church who is not received

(From the Council of Orléans, chapter 10.) If someone who has been ordained is not received in the parish assigned to him, whether because of a dispute among the people or for some other reason, and not through his own fault, he is to retain only the honor of the priesthood, [Col. 0561A], and must presume nothing concerning the property of the church in which he would have served. He must endure whatever the holy council judges concerning him.

### CHAPTER XLI — Concerning those promoted to the episcopate but not received

(From the Council of Antioch, chapter 18.) If a bishop who has been ordained does not go to the parish for which he was elected, not through his own fault but because the people prevent him or for another reason not brought about by his fault, he shall retain both his honor and his ministry, provided that he does not trouble the affairs of the church in which he is known to serve.

He must also observe whatever the complete synod of the province [Col. 0561B] decrees in judgment.

### CHAPTER XLII — That the authority to convene synods has been entrusted by a special power to the apostolic see

(Chapter 8 of Isidore.) The authority to convene synods has been entrusted by a special power to the apostolic see. Nor do we read that any general synod is valid unless it was convened or supported by its authority. Canonical authority bears witness to this; ecclesiastical history confirms it; the holy Fathers affirm it.

### CHAPTER XLIII — That two episcopal assemblies must be held each year

(From a decree of Pope Leo to Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne, chapter 37.) Concerning episcopal councils, we prescribe nothing other than what the holy Fathers wisely established: namely, that two assemblies be held each year, in which judgment may be given concerning all complaints [Col. 0561C] that commonly arise among the various orders of the Church.

If perhaps a dispute should arise among the very men who preside, concerning greater sins—which God forbid—and it cannot be settled by a provincial examination, the metropolitan shall ensure that your fraternity is instructed concerning the entire matter, so that, if the dispute is not resolved by your judgment when the parties have appeared before you, whatever it may be may be transferred to our judgment.

### CHAPTER XLIV — At what time synods are to be held

(From the Council of Antioch, chapter 20.) For the sake of ecclesiastical benefits and the resolution of matters that [Col. 0561D] admit doubt and controversy, it has been most suitably decided that councils of bishops be held twice each year in every province.

The first is to be held after the third week of the Paschal feast, so that the synod may assemble in the fourth week that follows, that is, in the middle of Pentecost, with the metropolitan admonishing the bishops of the province to attend.

The second synod is to be held on the Ides of October, that is, on the fifteenth day of October, which the Greeks call Beretheon.

At these councils presbyters, deacons, and all who consider themselves wronged are to be present and submit their cases to the examination of the synod.

No one may hold councils on his own authority except those to whom metropolitan rights appear to have been entrusted.

### CHAPTER XLV — Concerning the convening of a synod

[Col. 0562A]

(From the Council of Auvergne, chapter 15.) After all that has been promulgated in this council for the correction of our order has been completed, it has pleased us to decree that every year, for the celebration of the council at the metropolitan see, at the time determined by the decision of the ruler or the metropolitan, we shall always come together with devoted zeal of mind.

We must not dissent on the pretext of any request or circumstance. Rather, on the appointed day on which the council has been proclaimed, all the bishops of the province shall assemble at the metropolitan see, and, with God presiding, the council shall be celebrated.

If any bishop, except for an unavoidable cause or necessity, absents himself from the council, he shall be punished by deprivation of communion for one year.

If thereafter he allows a full year to pass without the celebration [Col. 0562B] of a council, he shall remain subject to the judgment of all the bishops of the same province concerning his communion—that is, if he has not been prevented by the authority of the ruler, illness, or an unavoidable cause, but has failed to assemble for the council solely at the impulse of his own will.

### CHAPTER XLVI — Concerning the archbishop who, in a time of peace, neglects to announce a synod for more than two years
