(From the Council of Meaux, chapter 3.) If, within two years of divinely granted tranquility, after the bishops of the province have been admonished, the metropolitan does not announce a synod, and the metropolitan himself delays the summons, he must not celebrate the services for a full year.

If those who have been summoned, and who have not been detained by bodily illness, disdain to attend through their own abuse, they shall be subject to the same sentence.

### CHAPTER XLVII — Concerning bishops summoned to a synod, that they must not disdain to attend

[Col. 0562C]

(From the Council of Laodicea, chapter 40.) Bishops who have been summoned to a synod ought not to despise the summons altogether, but should go immediately and teach and learn those things that concern the correction of the Church and of other matters. The man who despises this will accuse himself, unless he is unable to go because of illness.

### CHAPTER LXVIII — What kind of letters the metropolitan should send to the brothers

(From the Council of Tarragona, chapter 13.) The metropolitan should send letters through the brothers in such a way that they bring to the council not only the presbyters of the cathedral churches but also those of the dioceses, and that they strive to bring with them some of the secular sons of the Church.

[Col. 0562D]

### CHAPTER XLIX — On the same matter

(From the Council of Agde, chapter 36.) If the metropolitan bishop sends letters to the bishops of the province inviting them either to the ordination of a certain brother or to a synod, they must not, after setting everything else aside, delay being present on the appointed day, except because of serious bodily illness or a royal command.

If they are absent, then, as the ancient authority of the canons has prescribed, they shall be deprived of the love of the brothers and of the communion of the Church until the next synod.

### CHAPTER L — Concerning the bishop who neglects to attend the synod
(From the Council of Seville, chapter 10.) But if any of the bishops has neglected to attend the synod, or has thought that the assembly of the brethren should be abandoned before the council is dissolved, let him recognize that he has separated himself from the communion of the brethren; and he may not be received unless he has been absolved at the next synod.

### CHAPTER LI.—Of a bishop who has been unable to come to the synod because of illness

(From the decree of Pope Felix, chapter 11.) If a bishop is ill, or some serious necessity has detained him, let him send a legate in his place to the synod, prepared to accept, without prejudice to the truth of the faith, whatever the synod shall decide.

### CHAPTER LII.—Of bishops summoned to the synod who disdain both to come and to send their representatives

(From the synod held at Althei, chapter 10.) It pleased the holy synod to rebuke with severe admonition those bishops who, summoned from Saxony to the holy council, neither came nor, according to the sacred canons, sent their representatives or vicars, and to reprimand them for the fault of disobedience. Therefore, with fraternal charity, we again invite and summon them to the appointed council. But if—as we do not wish—they should regard this as worthless, refuse to come, and decline to give a proper account of their disobedience, Peter, the envoy of Saint Peter and of the pope, together with the holy synod, forbids them by apostolic authority to celebrate Mass until they come to Rome and give a worthy account before the pope and the holy Church.

### CHAPTER LIII.—A universal council is to be held only from necessity

(From the African Council, chapter 42.) It was decided that there should no longer be a universal necessity for wearying the brethren; rather, whenever common causes demand it—that is, if letters from every part of Africa are brought to this see—a synod is to be convened in the province where convenience recommends it. Causes that are not common, however, are to be judged in their own provinces.

### CHAPTER LIV.—That later bishops should not place themselves before their predecessors

(From the letter of Pope Lucius sent to the bishops of the West, chapter 5.) Let the bishops in each province take care that those ordained later do not place themselves before their superiors, nor undertake anything without consulting them, except insofar as it concerns their own parish. But in all common matters let them pronounce and determine a harmonious judgment, since otherwise their acts will have no force and will not be regarded as ecclesiastical.

### CHAPTER LV.—That bishops should observe the time of their ordination, each showing honor to the other

[Column 0563D]

(From the Council of Chalon, chapter 7.) Likewise, it was decided that, while the primacy of the metropolitan bishop is preserved, the remaining bishops, according to the time of their ordination, should each yield his place to the other who is seated.

### CHAPTER LVI.—Of the order of bishops, so that those ordained later may not dare to place themselves before those ordained earlier

(From the African Council, chapter 53.) Bishop Valentinian said: “If your patience permits, I shall recount what was done in former times in the Church of Carthage and was made known by the signatures of the brethren; I declare that we shall also preserve this. But we know that ecclesiastical discipline has always remained inviolate, so that none of the brethren would ever dare to place himself before his predecessors. Rather, the services of charity were always shown to those who were earlier, and were always gratefully received from those who followed.”

### CHAPTER LVII.—Of doubtful matters arising in councils of bishops

(From the letter of Pope Boniface to the bishops of Gaul.) If a doubt should arise among bishops of the same council concerning ecclesiastical law or other business, their metropolitan, first considering the matter with certain others in the council, shall judge it. If both parties do not accept the judgment, then the primate of that region shall hear the matter between them and shall determine what accords with the ecclesiastical canons and with our laws; neither party shall be able to oppose his decision.

### CHAPTER LVIII.—That bishops sitting in synod should first correct matters pertaining to the amendment of life

(From the Council of Auvergne, chapter 1.) It was first decided that whenever a holy synod is convened according to the decrees of the Fathers, no bishop should dare to bring forward any other matter before the matters pertaining to the amendment of life, the strictness of the rule, and the remedies of the soul have been settled.

### CHAPTER LIX.—If a metropolitan has delayed hearing a provincial bishop in his own case

(From the decree of Pope Alexander.) If a metropolitan has twice been appealed to by any provincial bishop concerning the bishop’s own case, and has delayed hearing him, the bishop shall have leave to pursue his business at the next synod; and whatever shall have been decided by his fellow provincial bishops for the sake of justice must be observed.

### CHAPTER LX.—That bishops should always judge with just judgments

(From the Council of Reims, chapter 19.) Bishops and judges should distinguish judgments, since some matters are reserved for the judgment of the world and others for the judgment of God. For it is written: “Do not judge before the appointed time, until the Lord comes, who will both bring to light the hidden things of darkness and disclose the purposes of hearts; and then each person will receive praise from God.” Let them also remember this: “For with the judgment with which you judge, you yourselves will be judged.”

### CHAPTER LXI.—That the decrees of the canons should be duly observed by all, and that no one should presume to judge them according to his own opinion

(From the Council of Meaux, chapter 11.) Let the decrees of the canons be observed by all without prejudice, and let no one in proceedings or ecclesiastical judgments be guided by his own opinion, but by their authority. In expounding or preaching the divine Scriptures, let everyone also follow the understanding of the holy catholic Fathers and of the most approved teachers; in their writings, as blessed Jerome says, the truth of the faith does not waver.

### CHAPTER LXII.—Of bishops who are at odds

(From the Council of Carthage, chapter 25.) If the fear of God does not reconcile bishops who are at odds, let the synod reconcile them.

### CHAPTER LXIII.—Of the arrogance and pride of metropolitans, and of bishops and other clerics who are injured by a metropolitan

(From the letter of Pope Anicius sent to the bishops established throughout Gaul, chapter 4.) But if any metropolitan should become arrogant and wish to conduct other business without the presence or counsel of all the provincial bishops, except only matters pertaining to his own parish, or should wish to oppress them, let all correct him strictly, so that he may not dare to presume such things thereafter. If he appears incorrigible and disobedient to them, let his contumacy be reported to this apostolic see, which has been commanded to bring all episcopal judgments to an end, so that punishment may be inflicted upon him and the others may be afraid. But if, because of excessive distance, inconvenient timing, or the difficulty of the journey, it is burdensome to bring his case to this see, then let his case be brought before the primate of his province, and let it be judged by him with the authority of this holy see. Similarly, if any bishop regards the metropolitan with suspicion, let him be heard before the primate of the diocese or before this apostolic see.

### CHAPTER LXIV.—That one bishop should not usurp another’s parishes

(From the Council of Carthage, chapter 19.) It was decided that no bishop should usurp another’s parishes, and that no bishop should overstep his colleague in the diocese.

### CHAPTER LXV.—That no metropolitan should hear anyone’s cases without the presence of all the provincial bishops

(From the letter of Pope Hyginus sent to all the faithful, chapter 2.) Moreover, brethren, without prejudice in any matter to the privilege of the Roman Church, no metropolitan should hear anyone’s cases without the attendance of all the other provincial bishops, because proceedings conducted otherwise than in the presence of all of them will be invalid. If he does so, let him be restrained by the brethren.

### CHAPTER LXVI.—That no primate or metropolitan should act concerning the churches or parishes of provincial bishops, or concerning their cases, without the counsel of all of them; and that they likewise should act without his counsel only insofar as their own parishes are concerned

(From the letter of Pope Callistus sent to the bishops established throughout Gaul, chapter 13.) No primate or metropolitan should presume to excommunicate a diocesan church or parish, or to judge or undertake anything concerning it, without the counsel or judgment of its bishop. Rather, let him observe what was established by the apostles, the Fathers, and our predecessors, and confirmed by us: namely, that if any metropolitan bishop attempts to undertake anything outside what pertains solely to his own parish, without the counsel and consent of all the provincial bishops, he shall be liable to the peril of his rank, and what he has done shall be considered invalid and void.

But whatever it is necessary to undertake or arrange concerning the cases of fellow provincial bishops, their churches and clerics, and the needs of their laypeople, let it be done with the consent of all the provincial bishops—not with any pride of condemnation, but with the humblest and most harmonious administration, as the Lord says: “I did not come to be ministered to, but to minister.” And elsewhere: “The one who is greatest among you shall be your servant,” and so forth.

Likewise, let the provincial bishops themselves act with his counsel, except insofar as their own parishes are concerned, according to the decrees of the holy Fathers, so that the holy Trinity may be glorified harmoniously forever with one mind and one voice.

No primate, no metropolitan, and none of the other bishops should enter another’s city or approach a possession that does not belong to him and is the parish of another bishop, or make any disposition concerning it, unless he has been summoned by the one known to possess it to arrange or establish something there, or to judge it—if he wishes to retain the honor of his rank. If he presumes otherwise, he shall be condemned; and not only he, but also those who cooperate with him and consent to him, since just as the arrangement itself is forbidden, so too are its judgment and the disposition of other matters.

### CHAPTER LXVII.—Of a dispute concerning a parish

(From the Council of Auvergne, chapter 3.) If any bishop has possessed the diocese of another bishop for thirty years without any challenge, even though by legal right the diocese appears to belong to the other, an action to reclaim it may not be brought against him. This applies within a single parish; outside it, however, it applies in no way, lest, while the diocese is being defended, the boundaries of the provinces become confused.

### CHAPTER LXVIII.—That bishops who neglect the places belonging to their sees should be admonished by neighboring bishops to correct themselves

[Column 0566C]

(From the African Council, chapter 76.) Likewise, it was decided that those who neglect to win for catholic unity the places belonging to their sees should be summoned by diligent neighboring bishops, so that they may not delay doing so. If they have not accomplished this within six months from the day of the summons, let the places belong to whoever is able to win them.

This is to be understood as follows: if the one to whom they appeared to belong can prove that his deliberate negligence had been chosen by the heretics so that they might remain there with impunity, and that his diligence had been forestalled in order that his care might thereby be prevented, then, once the episcopal judges have learned this, let them restore the places to his see.

But if the bishops between whom the case is being disputed belong to different provinces, let the primate of the province nearest to the place in dispute appoint the judges. If, however, by common agreement they choose neighboring judges, let either one judge be chosen or three. If three are chosen, let them follow either the judgment of all or that of two.

### CHAPTER LXIX.—Of two bishops disputing over the parish of a certain basilica

(From the Council of Seville, chapter 1.) A dispute arose between our aforementioned brothers, Fulgentius, bishop of Astigi, and Honorius, bishop of Córdoba, concerning the parish of a certain basilica, which one of them asserted was Celtacense and the other Reginense. Since the question of the boundary had hitherto been claimed by both sides, although its ancient possession could create no legal prejudice, we did not wish our decision between them to be called into further doubt. Accordingly, after the canons had been produced, the synodal decrees were read, whose authority teaches that desire must be restrained in such a way that no one usurps another’s boundaries.

Therefore, it was decided that men should be sent between the opposing parties to inspect the matter, so that, if the boundary provided with ancient markers should show that the basilica belongs to the diocese of the possessor, it should remain in perpetual ownership of the Church whose right of possession it is. But if a legitimate boundary does not enclose that same basilica, and yet a prescription based on a long period of time is proved to have been raised, the appeal of the present bishop shall have no force, because the objection of thirty years imposes silence upon him.

The edicts of secular rulers also prescribe this, and the authority of the Roman bishops has decreed it. But if the basilica is found to have been unjustly retained within the thirty-year period and beyond another’s boundaries, it shall without delay be restored to the right of the bishop reclaiming it.

### CHAPTER LXX.—Of bishops who dispute over their parishes

(From the African Council, chapter 75.) It was decided that any bishops who judge certain peoples to belong to their sees, yet do not reclaim them by bringing their cases before bishops acting as judges, but invade while another holds them, shall suffer detriment in their case, whether the peoples are unwilling or willing.

If any have already done this, and the dispute between the bishops has not yet been settled but is still being contested, let the one who is shown to have invaded the parish while disregarding ecclesiastical judgments withdraw from it. Let no one flatter himself if he has obtained letters from the primate authorizing him to retain it. Whether he has letters or not, let him approach the one who holds it and receive his letters, so that it may be clear that he has peacefully held the Church belonging to him.

But if the other brings forward some question, let the case be settled by episcopal judges, whether those whom the primates have assigned to them or those neighboring bishops whom they themselves have chosen by agreement.

### CHAPTER LXXI.—That a bishop may in no way ordain clerics in another parish belonging to another diocese

(From the Council of Antioch, chapter 22.) A bishop should not enter another city that is not subject to him, nor approach a possession that does not belong to him, nor presume to perform an ordination there, except perhaps with the counsel and consent of the bishop of the region. If anyone attempts such a thing, his ordination shall be invalid, and he himself shall be restrained by the synod.

### CHAPTER LXXII.—That a bishop should in no way move from one parish to another

(From the same council, chapter 21.) A bishop must not move from one parish to another—neither rushing there entirely of his own will, nor being compelled by force by the people, nor driven by necessity by bishops. Let him remain in the Church that God first allotted to him, and let him not move from it, according to the former regulation established concerning this matter.

### CHAPTER LXXIII.—Of presuming upon another’s diocese

(From the letter of Pope Boniface.) If any bishop, uninvited, comes from one province into another and presumptuously intrudes upon the ordination and appointment of clerics or upon matters that do not concern him, everything established by him shall be void and empty. He himself shall be excommunicated with fitting censure and rejected by the holy council.

### CHAPTER LXXIV.—That a bishop, despising his own city, should not move to another for the sake of ambition

(From the decree of Pope Leo, chapter 38.) If any bishop, despising the smallness of his own city, seeks the administration of a more celebrated place and transfers himself by any means to a larger people, let him indeed be expelled from the foreign see, but let him also lose his own, so that he may preside neither over those whom he desired through avarice nor over those whom he despised through pride. Let each person therefore be content with his own boundaries and not seek to increase himself beyond the measure of his rightful jurisdiction.

### CHAPTER LXXV.—That bishops should by no means invade another’s parish

(From the Apostolic Canons, title 14.) A bishop may not invade another’s parish after abandoning his own, even if he is compelled by many, unless perhaps some reasonable cause forces him—for example, if he could confer greater benefit upon those established there and provide some genuine advantage in the cause of religion. He should not attempt this on his own initiative, but should accomplish it by the judgment of many bishops and with the greatest supplication.

### CHAPTER LXXVI.—Of the same matter

(From the letter of Pope Evaristus addressed to the brethren throughout Egypt, chapter 4.) Priests serve in the Church as Christ’s representatives, and just as Christ is joined to his own bride, that is, the Church, so churches are joined to bishops, each in proportion to his share. Just as a husband should not neglect his wife, but should cherish, guard chastely, love, and prudently govern her, so also a bishop should govern his Church.

And just as a wife who is under her husband’s authority ought to obey, love, and cherish her husband, so much more ought the Church to obey her bishop in all things and love and cherish him as her own soul, because the one is carnal and the other spiritual.

And just as a husband must not commit adultery against his wife, so neither may a bishop commit adultery against his Church—that is, abandon the Church to which he was consecrated without unavoidable necessity or an apostolic or canonical transfer, and join himself to another for the sake of ambition.

And just as a wife may not leave her husband and, while he is alive, enter into marriage with another and thereby commit adultery against him—even if her husband has committed fornication—but, according to the Apostle, must either be reconciled to her husband or remain unmarried, so the Church may not leave her bishop or separate herself from him in order to take another while he is alive. She must either retain him or remain unmarried—that is, she must not accept another bishop while her own is alive and thereby incur the crime of fornication or adultery.

For if she has committed adultery—that is, if she has joined herself to another bishop, or brought another bishop over herself, or caused or desired him to be established—then, through the most severe penance, she must either be reconciled to her own bishop or remain unmarried.

### CHAPTER LXXVII.—Of the transfer of bishops

[Column 0569A]

(From the letter of Pope Antherius sent to the bishops established throughout the provinces of Baetica and Toledo, chapter 14.) Concerning the transfer of bishops, about which you wished to consult the holy apostolic see, know that it is permitted for the common benefit and from necessity, but not according to anyone’s whim or through domination.

Saint Peter, the teacher and prince of the apostles, was transferred from Antioch to Rome for the sake of usefulness, so that he might be more beneficial there. Eusebius, too, was transferred by apostolic authority from a certain small city to Alexandria. Likewise, Felix was transferred from the city in which he had been ordained to Ephesus, by the election of the citizens, because of the teaching and good life that he possessed, with the common counsel of the bishops, the other priests, and the peoples.

A person does not pass from city to city when he does so according to his own whim or ambition, but when he is transferred for some usefulness or necessity, at the urging of others and by the counsel of those of greater authority. Nor is one transferred from a smaller city to a larger one when he does this through ambition or by his own will, but when he has been driven by force from his own see, compelled by necessity, or transferred and enthroned by others humbly, not arrogantly, for the usefulness of the place or the people. For a human being looks at the face, but God looks at the heart.

And the Lord speaks through the Prophet, saying: “The Lord knows the thoughts of human beings, that they are vain.” Therefore, the one who does not change his mind does not change his see, nor does the one who is changed by the counsel and choice of others change his city voluntarily. Thus, the one who does not willingly abandon his own city for the sake of avarice does not migrate from city to city; rather, as has already been said, he has either been driven from his own, compelled by necessity, or transferred to another city by the choice or exhortation of priests and peoples.

For just as bishops have the power regularly to ordain bishops and other priests, so, whenever usefulness or necessity demands it, they have the power, in the manner stated above, both to transfer and to enthrone them.

### CHAPTER LXXVIII.—Of the same matter

(From the Apostolic Canons.) A bishop or presbyter must in no way cast away his own wife under the pretext of religion. If he casts her away, let him be excommunicated. If he persists, let him be deposed.

### CHAPTER LXXIX.—Likewise, from the same source

[Column 0569D]

(From the Council of Sardica, chapter 1.) Bishop Hosius said: “No less an evil than a pernicious corruption must be eradicated utterly, lest any bishop be permitted to move from his own city to another city. The reason why he attempts this is clear, since no bishop has ever been found who moved from a larger city to a smaller one. Hence it is evident that they are inflamed by the ardor of avarice, serve ambition, and seek to exercise domination. If it pleases everyone, let this kind of destruction be punished more harshly and severely, so that such a person may not even have lay communion.”

They all replied: “It pleases us.”

### CHAPTER LXXX.—Of a bishop who is persecuted in his own Church, and that he should flee to another

[Column 0570A]

(From the decree of Pope Callistus sent to the bishops established throughout Gaul, chapter 15.) If any bishop is persecuted in his own Church, he should flee to another and join himself to it, since the Lord says: “If they persecute you in one city, flee to another.” But if a transfer is necessary for the sake of usefulness, let him not undertake it on his own, but let him do so when invited by the brethren and with the authority of this holy see—not for the sake of ambition, but of usefulness.

### CHAPTER LXXXI.—Of a bishop who neglects the principal see of his Church

(From the Council of Rouen, chapter 16.) A bishop must not neglect the principal see of his parish and frequent another Church in his diocese more often.

### CHAPTER LXXXII.—Of bishops who neglect their sees and remain for a long time in their distant possessions

(From the Council of Sardica, chapter 15.) Bishop Hosius said: “Since nothing ought to be overlooked, there are certain of our brothers and fellow bishops who do not reside in the city in which they appear to have been established as bishops, or who at least have only a small holding there. Elsewhere, however, they are known to have suitable estates or relatives to whom they show indulgence.

Permission should extend only so far that they may go to their possessions and arrange or administer the fruits of their labor; after four Sundays—that is, after three weeks—if it is necessary for them to remain, they should stay on their own estates instead. Or, if there is a nearby city in which there is a presbyter, so that they do not appear to spend Sunday without a Church, let them go there. In this way, their domestic affairs will not suffer loss because of their absence, and by not frequently coming to the city in which the bishop resides, they will avoid the suspicion of ostentation and ambition.”

Everyone said that this pleased them.

### CHAPTER LXXXIII.—That a bishop should travel throughout his parish each year

(From the Council of Seville, chapter 4.) Each bishop should travel throughout his parish every year, confirm and instruct the people, prohibit what must be avoided, and usefully urge them to do what ought to be done.

### CHAPTER LXXXIV.—Of bishops who rarely or never visit in person the parishes entrusted to them

[Column 0570D]

(From the Council of Meaux, chapter 5.) Bishops who visit the peoples entrusted to them either rarely or never in person should, in accordance with the evangelical, apostolic, and ecclesiastical order, be rebuked more severely by the provincial bishops, since the Lord says to Moses: “I have appointed you as a watchman to the house of Israel; you shall hear the word from my mouth and announce it to them from me,” and so forth.

### CHAPTER LXXXV.—That bishops should carefully examine their presbyters concerning their ministries

(From the Council of Braga, chapter 2.) It pleased and seemed good to us that bishops, going through the individual Churches and dioceses, should first examine the clerics concerning how they observe the order of baptism and of the Masses, and how they perform each of the offices in the Church. If they find everything correct, let them give thanks to God. But if not, they must teach the ignorant.

### CHAPTER LXXXVI.—That a bishop should travel throughout his parish with only a few companions

(From the Council of Toledo, chapter 5.) When a bishop visits his diocese, he should not be burdensome to anyone by an excessive multitude, nor should the number of his traveling companions ever exceed fifty. Nor should he have permission to remain more than one day in each basilica.

### CHAPTER LXXXVII.—If a bishop cannot visit his parish, let him send men of approved life in his place

(From the same council, chapter 6.) If a bishop, detained by illness or entangled in other occupations, cannot complete the visitation of his diocese, let him send presbyters of approved life or deacons to investigate the revenues of the basilicas, their repairs, and the conduct of those who minister there.

### CHAPTER LXXXVIII.—What kind of minister a bishop should have beside him

(From the Council of Meaux, chapter 3.) Let each bishop strive, as far as he can, to have beside him a man who, according to the most sincere and pure understanding of the catholic Fathers, may continually instruct and train the presbyters of the parishes in faith, observance of God’s commandments, and the doctrine of preaching, lest the house of the living God, which is the Church, remain without the lamp of the divine word.

Let this man also be one whom the love of money does not trouble and whom reprehensible conduct does not make contemptible. Hence, when Moses laid his complaint before God that he could not bear the great burden imposed upon him, he heard the Lord say: “Gather for me seventy men from the elders of Israel, whom you know to be elders and teachers of the people; I will take from your spirit and give it to them, so that they may bear the burden of the people with you and you may not be burdened alone.”

What do we understand by Moses except the high priesthood? What by the seventy men except presbyters? And by the fact that the Lord takes from Moses’s spirit and gives it to them, he plainly shows that those who have been called by the bishop before God to bear the burden of the people with him must desire the same things and cooperate with all their strength in the burden apportioned to them. This is signified by the fact that they receive not another spirit, but the same spirit as Moses.

### CHAPTER LXXXIX.—Of a bishop’s not appointing a layman as his vicar

[Column 0571D]

(From the Council of Braga, chapter 9.) We have learned through a recent proceeding that certain members of our college, contrary to ecclesiastical custom, have appointed laymen as stewards over divine affairs. Therefore, after deliberation, we jointly decide that each of us, according to the decrees of the Fathers of Chalcedon, should appoint a steward from his own clergy.

It is unbecoming for a layman to be the bishop’s vicar and for secular persons to judge in the Church. Within one and the same office, the profession should not be different. This is also prohibited in divine law, where Moses says: “You shall not plow with an ox and an ass together”—that is, you shall not join people of different professions in one office.

Therefore, we must obey both the divine books and the commands of the holy Fathers, establishing that those who are associated with bishops in the administration of the Church must not differ either in profession or in habit. Those whose pursuits and vows are different cannot properly cohere or be joined together.

If, after this, any bishop chooses a lay administration to manage ecclesiastical property, or entrusts its governance without the testimony of a steward, then, truly, as one who despises the canons and defrauds ecclesiastical property, he will be judged guilty before Christ concerning the goods of the poor, and will also remain liable before the council.

### CHAPTER XC.—That during a bishop’s visitation all who are in the parish of the individual mother churches, except the sick, must come to his synod

(From the Council of Rouen, 13, chapter 11.) When a bishop travels through his diocese, the archdeacon or archpresbyter should precede him by one or two days through the parishes he is going to visit. After the people have been summoned, he should announce the arrival of their own shepherd. He must also command and sternly proclaim, with the authority of the holy canons, that all, except the sick, must come without fail to his synod on the appointed day, and that anyone absent without serious necessity will undoubtedly be excluded from Christian communion.

Then, having summoned the presbyters who must provide service to the bishop in that place, he should strive to correct whatever he can among the lesser and lighter matters, so that when the bishop arrives he will not be wearied by easier business or need to remain there longer than the expenses permit.

For the Lord says to Moses concerning such co-workers: “Let them bear the burden of the people with you, and you shall not be burdened alone.” And blessed John the Baptist preceded the Lord’s coming by preaching, saying: “Repent,” and so forth. And again: “Prepare the way for the Lord.”

Since a bishop is seen to act in Christ’s place, he must therefore be received with joy, fear, and the greatest reverence by the peoples subject to him, so that it may rightly be said of them what the Apostle says to his disciples: “I bear witness for you that you received me as an angel of God, as Christ Jesus.”

### CHAPTER XCI.—The decretal constitution of Pope Eutychian concerning what a bishop should investigate in the synod

(From the decree of Pope Eutychian, chapter 9.) A bishop sitting in synod, after an appropriate address, should summon into the midst seven men from the people of that parish, or more, as he sees fit—men mature, honorable, and truthful. After bringing forward the relics of the saints, he should bind each of them by such an oath.

### CHAPTER XCII.—The synodal oath

(From the same decree.) “From this time forward, whatever you know or have heard, or shall later investigate, that has been done or will be done in this parish against the will of God and upright Christianity—if it occurs during your lifetime and comes to your knowledge in any way; if you know or are informed that it is a synodal matter and belongs to the bishop’s ministry—you shall never conceal it from the bishop, or from his envoy whom he has ordered to investigate it, whether because of love, fear, reward, or kinship, whenever he questions you concerning it. So may God help you, and these relics of the saints.”

### CHAPTER XCIII.—The oath of the others

(From the same decree.) “You shall, on your own part, likewise observe the oath which this man has sworn concerning a synodal matter, insofar as you know, have heard, or shall investigate from this day forward. So may God help you,” and so forth.

### CHAPTER XCIV.—After the oath has been given, the bishop shall address those who have sworn as follows

(From the same decree.) “Take care, brothers, to render your oaths to the Lord; for you have not sworn to a human being, but to God your Creator. We, however, who are his ministers, do not desire your earthly possessions, but seek the salvation of your souls. Beware of concealing anything, lest your condemnation result from another person’s sin.”

### The bishop’s first interrogation

(From the same decree.) “Is there in this parish a murderer who has killed a person—whether voluntarily, or for the sake of greed or rapacity, or by accident, or unwillingly, or under compulsion, or in revenge for relatives, or in war, or at a lord’s command, or his own slave?”

### Interrogation 2

“Is there anyone who is a parricide or fratricide, who has killed his father, mother, sister, brother, uncle, or any of his relatives?”

### Interrogation 3

“Is there anyone who has killed a presbyter, deacon, or any cleric, or cut off one of his limbs?”

### Interrogation 4

“Is there any man or woman who has crushed his or her own infant, or suffocated it under the weight of clothing—whether this happened before baptism or after baptism—or whose infant, having become ill, died without baptism through the negligence of the parent?”

### Interrogation 5

“Is there any man or woman who has caused another woman’s fetus to be expelled, or any woman who herself, of her own will, has expelled her own fetus or conception and caused an abortion?”

### Interrogation 6

“Is there any woman who, having conceived in fornication and fearing that it would be discovered, has either thrown her own infant into water or hidden it in the ground—a practice they call ‘morht’ [uncertain reading]?”

### Interrogation 7

“Is there anyone who has killed his wife without legal process or certain proof?”

### Interrogation 8

“Is there any woman who has killed her husband or another person with poisonous herbs or deadly potions, or taught someone else to do this?”

### Interrogation 9

“Is there any man or woman who has done this, or taught someone else to do it, so that a man would be unable to beget children or a woman to conceive?”

### Interrogation 10

[Column 0574A]

“Is there anyone who has killed his own slave without a judge’s authorization, or any woman who, inflamed by jealous rage, has killed her own female slave?”

### Interrogation 11

“Is there anyone who, driven by the devil, has killed himself?”

### Interrogation 12

“Is there anyone who has wounded people in a public war and does not know whether anyone died from that wound? And if anyone is accused of having killed a person, but denies that he did so?”

### Interrogation 13

“Is there anyone who was involved in a plan that a person should be killed, but was not present at the deed, and yet the person was killed through his plan and exhortation?”

### Interrogation 14

“Is there anyone who has cut off hands, feet, the tongue, or testicles, or torn out another person’s eyes?”

### Interrogation 15

“Is there any married man who has committed adultery with another man’s wife, or any wife with another woman’s husband?”

## Question 16

Is there anyone who, while having a wife, has also kept a concubine, whether his own maidservant or another woman?

## Question 17

Is there anyone who has dismissed his lawful wife, joined himself to another, and taken another woman in marriage?

## Question 18

[Col. 0574C]

Is there any woman who has left her own husband and joined herself to another?

## Question 19

Are there any who, after a divorce, have been separated from one another and remain so?

## Question 20

Is there anyone who, without his wife’s consent, has abandoned his lawful marriage and entered a monastery?

## Question 21

Is there anyone who has left his wife, even though she was guilty, without the judgment of the bishop?

## Question 22

Is there any woman who has committed fornication with the knowledge of her husband?

## Question 23

[Col. 0574D]

Is there any unmarried man who has committed fornication with another person’s spouse; or any woman without a husband with another woman’s husband?

## Question 24

Is there any man without a wife who has committed fornication with a woman who has no husband?

## Question 25

Is there any lay virgin who has committed adultery with a young man?

## Question 26

Is there anyone who has failed to marry a betrothed girl and has broken the pledge of the betrothal?

## Question 27

[Col. 0575A]

Is there anyone who has abducted another man’s betrothed and taken her as his own?

## Question 28

Is there anyone who has carried off any woman—virgin or widow—and taken her to himself in marriage; and are there any who consented to this or assisted in it?

## Question 29

Is there anyone who has committed adultery with a Jewish woman; or, if he is a Jew or pagan, with a Christian woman?

## Question 30

Is there anyone who has abducted a nun or a widow consecrated to God and taken her in marriage; or who, with their consent, has committed fornication with them?

## Question 31

[Col. 0575B]

Is there anyone who, while her husband was alive, was accused of committing adultery with his wife, and who is known to have taken that same woman when he had recently died?

## Question 32

Is there any woman who says that her husband is unable to have intercourse with her, and for this reason seeks separation and wishes to take another husband?

## Question 33

Is there anyone who has committed adultery with his spiritual co-mother, or taken her in marriage; and likewise with the girl whom he received from the sacred font, or whom he held before the bishop?

## Question 34

Is there anyone who has taken a close female relative and blood relation [Col. 0575C] in marriage, or committed fornication with her?

## Question 35

Is there anyone who has engaged irrationally—that is, against nature—in intercourse with males and with dumb animals?

## Question 36

Is there any woman who has acted as a procuress?

## Question 37

Is there anyone who permits adulteries to be committed in his house with his own female servants or household slaves?

## Question 38

It must be asked whether there is any thief or sacrilegious person in the same parish who has broken into God’s churches, or stolen anything [Col. 0575D] from the church, or committed robbery openly or theft secretly; or whether anyone is a plunderer, robber, and destroyer of God’s Church?

## Question 39

It must be asked whether anyone is perjured, or whether anyone knowingly and out of earthly greed has sworn falsely; and whether he did so unknowingly, or was compelled by the order of his lord, or to ransom his limbs or his life; and whether anyone has knowingly not only sworn falsely but also led others into perjury?

## Question 40

It must be asked whether anyone has knowingly given false testimony against someone, and what harm anyone suffered because of this testimony.

## Question 41

[Col. 0576A]

It must be asked whether anyone has stolen a free man, another person’s slave, a foreigner, or a newcomer; or whether he has enticed someone by flattery, seduced and sold him, and led him into captivity outside his homeland; or whether anyone has sold a Christian slave to a Jew or pagan; or whether Jews themselves keep Christian slaves in their service or sell them.

## Question 42

It must be asked whether anyone is a magician, soothsayer, enchanter, diviner, or sorcerer; or whether anyone makes vows to trees, springs, or stones, or brings a candle or any other offering there, as though some divine power were present there that could bring about good or evil.

## Question 43

[Col. 0576B]

It must be investigated whether any swineherd, cowherd, hunter, or others of this kind recites diabolical incantations over bread, herbs, or certain wicked ligatures, and either hides these in a tree or throws them at a crossroads or three-way junction, so as to free his own animals from pestilence and destruction and destroy another’s.

## Question 44

It must be investigated whether there is any woman who claims that by certain magic arts and incantations she can change people’s minds—that is, turn hatred into love or love into hatred—or harm or steal people’s property. And whether there is any woman who says that on certain nights she rides with a troop of demons, transformed into the likeness [Col. 0576C] of women, upon certain beasts, and that she has been numbered among their company.

## Question 45

It must be asked whether anyone has eaten the blood of a dead animal, or of an animal torn apart by a beast.

## Question 46

Is there anyone who has sworn something contrary to God, namely, never to be reconciled with his brother—a sin unto death?

## Question 47

Is there anyone who has drunk a liquid in which a weasel, mouse, or some other unclean animal had been killed?

## Question 48

[Col. 0576D]

Is there anyone who has not observed the Lenten fast, the fast of the four seasons, the fast of the Greater Litany, the Rogation fast, or a fast imposed by the bishop on account of any affliction?

## Question 49

Is there anyone who has drunk, eaten, or carried upon himself something by which he believed he could turn aside God’s judgment?

## Question 50

Is there anyone who, on the Kalends of January, did something originating among the pagans, observed the day, the moon, and the months, and hoped that through their effective power something could be changed for the better or the worse?

## Question 51

[Col. 0577A]

Is there anyone beginning any undertaking who has said something, or done something by any magical art, instead of doing everything in the name of the Lord, as the Apostle teaches? For we must not invoke demons for our assistance; rather, when gathering medicinal herbs, we ought to say the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer, and nothing else.

## Question 52

It must also be asked whether women, in their spinning or in arranging their webs, say or observe anything other than—as was stated above—doing everything in the name of the Lord.

## Question 53

[Col. 0577B]

Is there anyone who unjustly withholds offerings—that is, alms belonging to deceased parents?

## Question 54

Is there anyone who, over a dead person during the night hours, sings diabolical songs, and drinks and eats there as though rejoicing over his death; and whether the dead elsewhere are kept under guard during night vigils anywhere but in the Church?

## Question 55

Is there anyone who does not receive communion three times a year—that is, at Easter, Pentecost, and the Nativity of the Lord—unless he has been excluded from communion because of deadly crimes by the judgment of the bishop or priests?

## Question 56

[Col. 0577C]

Is there anyone who does any kind of work on Sunday or on the principal feast days; and whether on those days everyone regularly attends Matins, Mass, and Vespers?

## Question 57

Is there anyone who has treated excommunication as nothing; and whether anyone has shared in communion with an excommunicated person?

## Question 58

Is there anyone who has not observed the measure of penance imposed upon him?

## Question 59

Is there anyone who has dishonored, struck, or cursed his father or mother?

## Question 60

[Col. 0577D]

Is there anyone who has vomited after receiving the Eucharist because of drunkenness?

## Question 61

Is there anyone who has withheld his tithe from God and his saints?

## Question 62

Is there anyone so perverse and alienated from God that he has not come to church even on Sunday?

## Question 63

If swineherds and other shepherds do not come to church on Sunday and do not hear Mass, and likewise on the other feast days?

## Question 64

Is there anyone who does not come to confession, even [Col. 0578A] once a year—that is, at the beginning of Lent—and does not undertake penance for his sins?

## Question 65

Is there anyone who pursues habitual drunkenness, since the Apostle says: “For drunkards shall not possess the kingdom of God”?

## Question 66

Is there anyone who, despising his own priest, goes to a church in another parish, receives communion there, and gives his tithe there?

## Question 67

An inquiry must be made concerning the beggars who go about the parish: whether each person feeds a poor person from his own household.

## Question 68

[Col. 0578B]

It must be asked whether in every parish there are deans appointed throughout the villages—truthful men who fear the Lord—who admonish the others to go to church, to Matins, Mass, and Vespers, and to do no work on feast days; and whether, if anyone transgresses, they immediately report it to the priest—likewise concerning sexual immorality and every evil deed.

## Question 69

Is there anyone who disregards the bishop’s or his own priest’s ban and excommunication?

## Question 70

It must be investigated whether parishioners render due honor to their priest, or whether there is anyone who dishonors him by word or deed and rejects his admonitions.

## Question 71

[Col. 0578C]

Is there anyone who has refused lodging to a foreigner or traveler?

## Question 72

It must be investigated which festivals they observe.

## Question 73

It must be asked whether godparents teach their godchildren the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer, or have them taught.

## Question 74

It must be investigated whether four, five, or more people killed a man.

## Question 75

Is there anyone who contradicts the bishop or his ministers [Col. 0578D] so that peasants or slaves are not beaten naked with rods for the crimes they have committed?

## Question 76

It must be asked whether anyone wishes to regard as his own slave, and dares to sell or give to someone else, a foreigner who fled his homeland because of pagan invasion or persecution, merely because he stayed in his house and served him there as a hired laborer for days or years.

## Question 77

Is there anyone who sells his grain or wine by an unjust measure, although the Lord says: “Let your bushel be just, and your sextarius just”?

## Question 78

[Col. 0579A]

It must also be declared how great a sacrilege it is to demand interest and to seek enrichment from another’s loan, and that the sacred canons command that such people be expelled from the Church.

## Question 79

Is there anyone who, out of greed, has killed a Jew or a pagan?

## Question 80

Is there anyone who, being insane, has killed someone?

## Question 81

Is there anyone who was cutting down a tree, and while engaged in necessary work someone came beneath the tree and was unexpectedly crushed?

## Question 82

[Col. 0579B]

Is there anyone who has pursued conspiracies and plots?

## Question 83

Is there anyone who has presumed to harass the church or a cleric?

## Question 84

An inquiry must be made concerning fugitive and treacherous clerics and laypeople.

## Question 85

An inquiry must be made concerning confraternities and associations of brotherhoods, and how they are conducted in the parish.

## Question 86

It must be asked whether anyone dares to sing obscene and laughter-provoking songs around the church.

## Question 87

[Col. 0579C]

It must be investigated whether anyone, upon entering the church, is accustomed to occupy himself with idle stories and does not listen attentively to the divine words, and whether he leaves the church before Mass is finished.

## Question 88

It must be asked whether men and women offer the oblation—that is, bread and wine—at Masses, and whether married men offer it for themselves and all their household, as is contained in the canon.

## CHAPTER XCV — That Bishops Must Not Read the Books of the Pagans

(From the Council of Carthage, chapter 16.) Bishops are not to read the books of the pagans; but they may read those of heretics when necessity and circumstance require it.

## CHAPTER XCVI — That Bishops Should Adapt Their Preaching to What the Common People Can Understand, According to the Peculiarities of Their Common Language

[Col. 0579D]

(From the Council of Reims, chapter 11.) Bishops should strive to preach the sermons and homilies of the holy Fathers in accordance with the peculiarities of the common language, so that everyone may understand them.

## CHAPTER XCXVII — Rebuke of a Bishop Expounding Pagan Books in the Pulpit, Since the Praises of Christ Cannot Agree with the Praises of Jupiter

(From the letter to Desiderius, Bishop of Gaul, chapter 84.) Since many good things had been reported to us about your studies, such joy arose in our heart that we could hardly bear to deny what your Fraternity had asked us to grant. But afterward it came to [Col. 0580A] us—something we cannot recall without shame—that you were teaching grammar and explaining certain more difficult matters to some people. We received this report with such displeasure and rejected it so vehemently that we turned what had previously been said into groaning and sadness, because the praises of Christ cannot be on the same lips as the praises of Jupiter. How grave and abominable it is for bishops to recite what is not fitting even for a religious layman.

Although our most beloved son, the priest Candidus, later came and, carefully questioned about this matter, denied it and attempted to excuse you, it has nevertheless not departed from our mind. For just as detestable as it is for this to be reported about a priest, so it must be established, by strict and truthful satisfaction, whether it is indeed so. [Col. 0580B] Therefore, if afterward it clearly becomes evident that what was reported to us is false, and it is shown that you do not devote yourself to frivolities and secular literature, let us also give thanks to our God, who did not permit your heart to be stained by the blasphemous praises of the impious; and then, secure and without any doubt, let us consider granting what you ask.

## CHAPTER XCVIII — How Great a Danger Threatens Pastors Who Neglect to Preach the Truth of Christ

(From a decree of Pope Mark, sent to the bishops of Egypt, chapter 3.) Woe to us, who have undertaken the burden of this ministry, if we neglect to preach the truth of our Savior Jesus Christ, which the apostles preached. Woe to us if we suppress the truth by silence, when we are commanded to entrust it to the money-changers [Col. 0580C]—that is, to instruct and teach Christian peoples. What shall we say at Christ’s future judgment if we are ashamed to preach the truth of his word? What will become of us when Christ our God, the just Judge, strictly demands an account of the souls entrusted to us and of the office we have undertaken?

## CHAPTER XCIX — That a Bishop Ought Without Ceasing to Teach and Love His Church

(Chapter 5 of Pope Evaristus, sent to all the brethren throughout Egypt.) A bishop ought, in season and out of season and without ceasing, to teach his Church, and to govern and love it wisely, so that he may abstain from vices and be able to attain eternal salvation. And it ought to receive his teaching [Col. 0580D] with such reverence, and love and honor him, as God’s ambassador and herald of the truth, because, as the Truth bears witness, “Whatever he binds on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever he looses on earth shall be loosed in heaven.”

## CHAPTER C — On the Ignorance to Be Avoided by Everyone, Especially Priests

(From the Fifth Council of Toledo, chapter 25.) Ignorance, the mother of all errors, must especially be avoided by God’s priests, who have undertaken the duty of teaching among the people. For Holy Scripture admonishes priests to read, the Apostle Paul saying to Timothy: “Attend to reading and exhortation.” Let teachers know that they must always persevere in these things. Therefore, let priests meditate on the holy Scriptures [Col. 0581A] and the canons, so that all their work may consist in preaching and teaching, and so that they may edify everyone both by knowledge of the faith and by discipline of conduct.

## CHAPTER CI — That a Bishop Should Compel Those Who Disagree to Be Reconciled

(From the Council of Carthage, chapter 26.) A bishop should strive to urge disagreeing brethren, whether clerics or laypeople, toward peace rather than judgment.

## CHAPTER CII — That Judicial Hearings Must Not Be Held on Sunday

(From the Council of Spalato, chapter 2.) No bishop, or anyone in a lower rank, shall presume to judge cases on Sunday.

## CHAPTER CIII — On the Domestic and Private Conduct of Bishops

[Col. 0581B]

(From the Council of Orléans, chapter 5.) The holy synod decreed that the domestic and private conduct of a bishop must be made impervious to every reproach and suspicion, so that, in accordance with the Apostle, we may provide what is good not only before God but also before all people. Therefore priests and clerics of sound reputation ought to attend upon the bishop in his bedchamber and in all his more private services. They should continually observe their bishop watching, praying, and searching the sacred words, and should be witnesses and imitators of his holy conduct and preachers to the glory of God.

## CHAPTER CIV — That a Bishop Should Conduct Himself Like a Guest

[Col. 0581C]

(From the sayings of Augustine.) A bishop ought to become like a guest and should not have a private house; rather, he ought to be like a guest, as Christ says: “The Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.”

## CHAPTER CV — That Bishops Should Celebrate Mass Frequently

(From the Council of Orange, chapter 3.) We decree that bishops should celebrate Mass not only on Sundays and principal feast days, but, whenever possible, should also frequently offer the daily sacrifices and should not find them burdensome.

## CHAPTER CVI — That a Bishop Corrupted by Payment Must Not Presume to Ordain Another’s Cleric

(From the Council of Hanner, chapter 1.) We forbid all ministers of ecclesiastical rank that no one [Col. 0581D], corrupted by any gift or favor, should presume secretly and furtively to introduce a cleric from another parish for ordination. If he does so, according to the decree of Chalcedon, the intermediary, if he is a cleric, shall fall from his own rank; if a layman or monk, he shall be anathematized.

## CHAPTER VII — That a Bishop Must in No Way Ordain Clerics of Another Parish

(From the Council of Paris, chapter 32.) A bishop shall not appoint priests or deacons subject to another bishop, except perhaps with that bishop’s advice and consent. If anyone attempts such a thing, his ordination shall be invalid, and he himself shall be restrained by the synod.

## CHAPTER CVIII — That No Bishop Should Presume to Enter Another Bishop’s Parish for the Promotion of Ministry

[Col. 0582A]

(From the Council of Antioch, chapter 13.) No bishop from another province shall dare to cross into another province and ordain anyone for advancement in the ministry in its churches, even if some appear to give their consent, unless he comes at the written request of both the metropolitan and the other bishops who are with him, and then proceeds to the act of ordination. But if, without being summoned by anyone, he hastens there in disorderly fashion to conduct ordinations or settle ecclesiastical affairs that do not belong to him, whatever he does shall indeed be invalid. He himself, however, shall suffer punishment for his disorderly movement and irrational boldness, already condemned for this by the holy council.

## CHAPTER CIX — That a Bishop Must Not Audaciously Attempt to Seize the Cleric of Another Church

[Col. 0582B]

(From the Council of Nicaea, chapter 16.) If any bishop audaciously attempts to seize a cleric belonging to another bishop and ordain him in his own church, without the consent of the bishop from whom he departed, such an ordination shall be declared invalid, since it is subject to the rule.

## CHAPTER CX — On Unlawful Ordinations Not to Be Presumed Upon

(From a letter of Pope Simplicius sent to Equitius Florentius, and from the letter of Severus, chapter 1.) The report of your affection has informed us, and the sequence of events has made it even clearer, that Gaudentius, priest of the Church of Offinium, has carried out unlawful ordinations contrary [Col. 0582C] to the statutes of the canons and our commands. We order that all authority over these be entirely removed from him. For we have written to our brother and fellow bishop Severus that, if necessary, he himself, having considered the rules of the Fathers, should perform in the aforesaid Church the office which that man is proved to have abused, so that those who were illicitly advanced by him may be removed from ecclesiastical ministries.

## CHAPTER CXI — On a Blind Bishop Who Had Ordained a Priest and Two Deacons Through His Priest

(From the Council of Braga, chapter 5.) The report of the deacon Gabrensis brought to the attention of our examination the case of certain clerics of that Church. While one was being consecrated to the priesthood and two to the ministry of the Levites [Col. 0582D], their bishop, who was said to be suffering from an affliction of the eyes, reportedly placed his hand only upon them, while a certain priest gave them the blessing contrary to ecclesiastical order. He could have been accused and condemned by the present judgment for such presumptuous audacity, had he not still been in the body when he was overtaken by the summons of death. But because he has now been left to divine judgment, he cannot be accused by human judgment.

As for those who remain, and who received from him not the title of consecration but rather a disgraceful blessing, lest such usurpation provide them with license, we have decreed that they should, after deposition and by equitable judgment, be deprived of the rank of priest or Levitical order which they perversely acquired. Such men [Col. 0583A] were rightly judged to have to be removed, because they were found to have been wrongly appointed.

[Col. 0583A]

## CHAPTER CXII — That a Bishop Must Not Ordain Anyone for Money

(From the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 2.) If any bishop performs an ordination for money and reduces to a price the grace of the Holy Spirit, which cannot be sold, and ordains for money a bishop, priest, deacon, or anyone else numbered among the clergy, he shall be subject to the peril of his own rank; and the person ordained shall gain nothing from that ordination but shall be excluded from the dignity. If anyone acts as an intermediary by giving or receiving payments, then, if he is a cleric, he shall fall from his own rank; but if he is a monk or layman, he shall be anathematized.

## CHAPTER CXIII — That a Gift Must Also Be Avoided from the Tongue

[Col. 0583B]

(From the sayings of Pope Gregory.) There are some who do not receive monetary rewards for ordination, yet bestow holy orders for human favor. Clearly, what they receive freely they do not give freely, because they seek the coin of favor in return for the sacred office entrusted to them. Thus, when Isaiah described a just man, he said: “He who shakes his hands free from every gift.” For one gift comes from service, another from the hand, and another from the tongue. A gift from service is an obedience improperly rendered. A gift from the hand is money. A gift from the tongue is favor. Therefore, the person who bestows holy orders shakes his hands free from every gift when in divine [Col. 0583C] matters he seeks not only no money but also no human favor.

## CHAPTER CXIV — That a Bishop’s Sentence Is Not Valid Unless Confirmed by the Presence of His Clerics

(From the Council of Carthage, chapter 23.) The sentence of a bishop shall be invalid unless it is confirmed by the presence of his clerics.

## CHAPTER CXV — That a Bishop Should Establish the Number of Clerics According to the Income of the Churches

(From the Council of Spalato, chapter 1.) A bishop should not create a multitude of clerics indiscriminately; rather, their number should be regulated according to the merit or income of the churches.

## CHAPTER CXVI — On Foreign Bishops

(From the Council of Arles, chapter 20.) Concerning foreign bishops [Col. 0583D] who customarily come to the city, whom we know to be true bishops: it was agreed that a place should be given to them so that they may offer.

## CHAPTER CXVII — That Bishops Wandering Through Levity Should Be Compelled to Return to Their Own Churches

(From the register of Pope Gregory, to Syagrius, Bishop of Autun, chapter 122.) Since the dignity of a priest seems to excel other dignities, whoever is adorned with it ought to show himself worthy of imitation by all, so that by his example he may harm no one but may rather be able to shape the life of his subjects. For if his conduct disagrees with his name, the more the pontificate elevates him, the more it causes him to fall.

Accordingly, we have learned that a certain bishop named Menas, who went there from the administration of our diocese, has conducted himself with such levity that [Col. 0584A] we are more ashamed of him, and the name of bishop is for him not an honor but a burden. Since it is shameful for us to learn that he does things which we entirely condemn in priests of other provinces, let your Fraternity not permit him to remain there any longer, but compel him to return to us as quickly as possible. Rather, taking every opportunity, send him back, so that, restrained with the vigilance he deserves, he may strive to convert secular habits into the dignity of the priesthood.

For it is sufficiently harmful and destructive if, by imitation of him, those who ought to be built up are instead destroyed. In this matter not only is he found guilty, but so also is anyone who does not resist. For the person who does not join in correcting an erring person, so that the faults may be cut away, seems to consent to the error.

But because it is firmly reported that a certain [Col. 0584B] Bishop Theodore, from the diocese of our most reverend brother Constantius, bishop of the Church of Milan, came there, as is said, to evade discipline, we urge your Fraternity, after investigating him more carefully, to send him back to his own bishop. And because, as we read, “he who rejects discipline is unhappy,” do not tolerate his remaining there under any excuse, so that those who might be deceived by their levity may be freed, and so that you may be able to gain a reward concerning them by preventing them from perishing in this folly.

## CHAPTER CXVIII — How Long a Bishop May Remain in Another City

(From the Council of Sardica, chapter 14.) Bishop Hosius said: You must also establish this: when someone comes from one city to another and, moved [Col. 0584C] more by ambition than devotion, wishes to remain for a long time in another city. For it may happen that the bishop of the place is not so well instructed or learned; and the one who has arrived may begin to despise him and frequently preach in order to dishonor and weaken his standing, so that on this pretext he does not hesitate to leave the Church assigned to him and transfer to another.

Therefore, define a period of time. For it is inhuman not to receive a bishop, but if he remains too long, it is harmful. In the preceding council, our brothers established for everyone that if any layman did not hold an assembly in the city where he lived for four Sundays—that is, for three weeks—he should be deprived of communion. [Col. 0584D] If these regulations were established concerning laypeople, much more is it neither permitted nor fitting for a bishop, unless some very serious necessity detains him, to be absent from his own Church longer than the period stated above. Everyone said that this pleased them.

## CHAPTER CXIX — On Receiving Bishops Who Suffer Persecution

(From the same council, chapter 22.) Bishop Hosius said: At the suggestion of our brother and fellow bishop Olympius, this too was approved: if anyone has suffered violence and been unjustly expelled for the sake of discipline and the Catholic confession, or in defense of the truth, and, fleeing danger, has come innocent and devout to another city, he must not be forbidden to remain there for as long as he is either able to return or receives redress for his wrong. For it is harsh [Col. 0585A] not to receive one who is suffering persecution; rather, abundant goodwill and humanity must be shown to him.

The entire synod said: The Catholic Church, spread throughout the whole world, shall preserve all that has been established. And those who had assembled subscribed.

## CHAPTER CXX — On Those Who Claim to Be Bishops

(From the Council of Reims, chapter 43.) In certain places there are Scots and other erroneous men who claim to be bishops and ordain many negligent persons as priests and deacons without the permission of their lords or masters. Since their ordination very often falls into the heresy of simony and is subject to many errors, we unanimously decreed that it must be made invalid in every possible way.

## CHAPTER CXXI — How Foreign Bishops Are to Be Received

[Col. 0585B]

(From a regulation of Pope Gregory to all the bishops throughout Illyricum, chapter 42.) The most excellent man Jovinus, our son, is known to have informed us in his letters that, after sacred writings had been sent to him, he had been ordered that bishops whom the fury of hostility had driven from their own places should be joined, for the support and expenses of this present life, to those bishops who still reside in their own places.

Although an imperial command urges your Fraternity to do this, we nevertheless have a greater command from the eternal Prince, by which we are compelled to carry it out with even greater fear: that, when circumstances require, we should love in the provision of material assistance not only our brothers and fellow bishops but even those whom we endure as opposed to us.

It is therefore [Col. 0585C] necessary that in this matter you first show yourselves obedient to the heavenly Prince and also comply with imperial commands, so that you may willingly receive our brothers and fellow bishops, whom the constraints of captivity and various necessities oppress, to be consoled and associated with you in ecclesiastical support. This is not so that through sharing the episcopal throne they may possess its dignity, but so that, according to the Church’s ability, they may receive sufficient food and sustenance.

For in this way we are shown to love both our neighbor in God and God in our neighbor. We grant them no authority whatsoever in your churches, but we strongly urge you to keep them sustained by your assistance.

## CHAPTER CXXII — On Unknown Bishops and Priests, Who Must Not Be Permitted to Minister Before Synodal Examination

[Col. 0585D]

(From the Council of Rouen, chapter 8.) In accordance with canonical caution, we decree that all unknown bishops or priests who arrive from anywhere are not to be admitted to ecclesiastical ministry before synodal examination.

## CHAPTER CXXIII — That a Bishop Expelled by Hostility Should Transfer to Another Vacant Church

(From a regulation of Saint Gregory to Bishop Agnellus, chapter 135.) The care of pastoral office admonishes us to appoint proper priests over Churches that have been deprived of them, who must govern the Lord’s flock with pastoral concern. [Col. 0586A] Therefore, we have deemed it necessary to appoint you, John, bishop of the city of Lisbon, which has been taken captive by enemies, to appoint you as a cardinal priest in the Church of Squillace, so that you may fulfill, in view of future recompense, the care of souls once entrusted to you; and although you have been driven from your own Church by the threat of the enemy, you should govern another Church that is without a pastor.

This is to be done in such a way that, if it should happen that you make that city free from the enemies and, with the Lord’s protection, it is restored to its former condition, you should return to the Church in which you were previously ordained. But if the aforesaid city continues to be oppressed by the calamity of captivity, you must remain in this Church in which we have also incardinated you.

## CHAPTER CXXIV — On Bishops, to Whom All People Ought Rightly to Obey

[Col. 0586B]

(From a decree of Pope Clement, chapter 15.) He commanded all rulers of the earth and all people to obey bishops, bow their heads, and become their hearers, so that all might alike be shown to be faithful and co-workers in God’s law, lest it be said of them: “All who fight against you shall be confounded and ashamed, and the men who oppose you shall be as though they did not exist, and shall perish. You will seek them and will not find them—your rebellious men; they shall be as though they did not exist, and like destruction shall be the men who fight against you.”

Thus he showed that all who oppose them were condemned and infamous until they had made satisfaction; and unless they were converted, he commanded that they be excluded from the thresholds of the Church.

## CHAPTER CXXV — That Bishops Are the Keys of the Church and Have the Power to Shut Heaven and Open Its Gates

[Col. 0586C]

(From the same, chapter 37.) He taught that everyone ought to preserve the holy Church undefiled, and said that bishops are its keys. For they have the power to shut heaven and open its gates, because they have been made the keys of heaven. He taught that no one ought to remove them, because they are the eyes of the Lord, and whoever touches them touches the pupil of his eye.

He said that the Lord himself taught how great a punishment is deserved by anyone who scandalizes them, when he says: “Whoever scandalizes one of these little ones who believe in me, it would be better for him that a millstone be hung around his neck and that he be drowned in the depth of the sea.”

## CHAPTER CXXVI — That the Lord Chose Bishops to Glorify Him, and That All Rulers of the Earth Ought to Obey Them and Bow Their Heads

[Col. 0586D]

(From the same, chapter 29.) The Lord chose bishops to glorify him and to sow and proclaim the divine commandments. He said that they must not be hindered or disturbed, because whoever harms them harms the one whose embassy they perform. He urged them to preach continually and to announce the Lord’s commandments without ceasing. He indicated that they should display their good works before people and maintain a good conscience before God.

## CHAPTER CXXVII — On Bishops, Who Ought to Love One Another
(From the same chapter 30.) He taught that the Lord had appointed bishops to act in the place of the apostles [Col. 0587A], and indicated that presbyters ought to occupy the place of the other disciples; and he preached that if anyone scandalized any one of these, the gravest punishment ought to be inflicted upon him. He instructed that all should love and assist one another, and that no one should withdraw himself from helping his brother.

### CHAPTER CXXVIII — That one bishop must not trample upon another bishop

(From the Council of Arles, chapter 13.) No bishop should trample upon another bishop, nor presume to slander or wrong him. If he does so, he shall be subject to the peril of his rank.

### CHAPTER CXXIX — Concerning bishops who have withdrawn themselves from their brothers’ assistance

(From the decree of Pope Alexander, sent to all the bishops, chapter 30.) Whoever belongs to your college and withdraws himself from your assistance will be shown to be more a schismatic than a priest. “Behold,” says the Prophet, “how good and how pleasant it is when brothers dwell together.” But those who withdraw themselves from their brothers’ support do not dwell together; and, what is worse, they prepare ambushes or set snares for their brothers.

Again, shortly afterward: We, therefore, who desire both to be called and to be disciples of the Lord, ought to bear the Lord’s cross, to suffer with our brothers, and not to prepare any ambushes or pits for them; for whoever digs a pit for his brothers deserves retaliation. Do not be deceived, brothers, for God is not mocked. For this reason the Lord entrusted his Church to you: so that you might labor for all and not neglect to bring help to all who are oppressed. Hence the Lord also speaks through the Prophet, saying: “Thus says the Lord: Judge judgment in the morning, and rescue those oppressed by force from the hand of the slanderer, lest perhaps my indignation go forth like fire, and be kindled, with no one to extinguish it.” You, therefore, who have been placed by the Lord on the highest watchtower, ought to watch over and restrain those who stir up seditions and scandals against their brothers, lest you perish together with them.

### CHAPTER CXXX — Concerning bishops who have gnawed one another as with a dog’s tooth

(From the same source, to the same recipients, chapter 18.) But if, God forbid, you become discordant and begin to tear one another with a dog’s tooth, you will not merely fail to overcome them; you will also harm yourselves, be overcome by them, and perhaps perish disastrously [Col. 0587D].

### CHAPTER CXXXI — Concerning bishops who desire to harm their brothers

(From the decree of Pope Boniface.) Just as everyone who loves his brother is from God, so everyone who hates his neighbor is from the devil. For it is by love alone that it is discerned from whom a person has been begotten, as John says: “By this the children of God and the children of the devil are revealed. Everyone who does not do justice is not from God, and does not love his brother. For this is the announcement that you heard from the beginning: that you should love one another.”

And a little later: “Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer. And you know that no murderer has eternal life abiding in him” [Col. 0588A]. Behold, one is rightly shown to be a murderer who separates himself from brotherly fellowship. For even if he does not raise his hand to kill, nevertheless, because he is cruel in his willingness to harm, he is already regarded by God as a murderer. The other lives, while this man is already convicted as a killer.

Since, therefore, blessed Paul the Apostle agrees with these commands in harmonious preaching, saying, “Let not the sun go down upon your anger,” and, “Do not give place to the devil,” reports have reached us that the discord of certain priests has become so fiercely obstinate that not only does the setting of the sun fail to recall them from anger, but not even the passage of many years inclines them again toward the good of charity. Indeed, in their hearts Christ, the sun of righteousness, has set so completely that they can scarcely return to the light of charity.

Accordingly, we decree that the offerings of these and of similar quarrelsome brothers are in no way to be received, in accordance with the definition of the ancient canon. Concerning the persons of those who are at odds, however, we specially prescribe that, before true reconciliation has bound them together, none of them may dare approach the Lord’s altar or receive the grace of holy communion. Instead, they shall make satisfaction through penance for twice as long a period as they served discord.

But if one of them, while the other remains contemptuous, hastens to restore charity, he shall from the time at which he is shown to have hastened toward concord be received within the Church as a peacemaker. Nevertheless, the preceding judgment shall remain in force: the time he spent in anger must be repaid twofold in penitential satisfaction.

### CHAPTER CXXXII — That no one should bring a complaint against his bishop without first repeatedly appealing to him concerning the same matter

[Col. 0588C]

(From the decree of Pope Alexander, sent to all the orthodox, chapter 2.) If anyone believes that he has a just complaint against a bishop or the administrators of a church, he must not first approach primates or other judges before he has approached personally and familiarly those whom he considers to have injured him—not once, but very frequently—so that he may receive from them either his justice or an explanation.

If he acts otherwise, he shall be deprived of communion by both those persons and others, as a contemptor of the apostles and the other Fathers.

### CHAPTER CXXXIII — That bishops are to be judged by the Lord alone

(From the decree of Pope Clement, chapter 38.)
