He said that bishops were to be judged or removed by the Lord alone, and not by others, because they belong to him, not to another. “Who is it,” he asked, “who judges another’s servant?” For if human beings do not tolerate such things, neither does the God of gods and Lord of lords tolerate them in any way.

Therefore he also said that the prophets were his witnesses, through whom the Lord speaks, saying: “Behold, I have refined you, but not as silver; I have chosen you in the furnace of poverty. For my own sake, for my own sake I will act, so that I may not be blasphemed; and I will not give my glory to another.”

### CHAPTER CXXXIV — That it must be greatly feared and foreseen lest bishops be offended

(From a chapter of Pope Evaristus, sent to all the brothers throughout Egypt.) This sentence must be greatly feared, brothers, and you must take care not to offend those who possess such great authority from the Lord [Col. 0589A]. Therefore they ought rather to be obeyed, loved, and honored with the utmost reverence, not slandered, torn apart, or expelled, but borne with and loved, since the Lord himself says: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever rejects you rejects me.”

For this reason we write these things to you and to all the faithful, brothers, so that you may guard yourselves against such offenses and leave your descendants not a bad but a good example, since injury done to bishops concerns Christ, whose office they perform.

### CHAPTER CXXXV — Concerning bishops accused by all their own people, so that their accusations are not to be received

(From a letter of Pope Callistus, chapter 1.) Callistus, bishop of the Catholic Church of the city of Rome, sends greetings in Christ to his brother and fellow bishop Benedict.

No one should receive accusations against a teacher, because children ought not to rebuke their fathers, nor servants tear apart their masters. All those whom teachers instruct are therefore their children; and just as children love their earthly fathers, so these people ought to love their spiritual fathers.

Those who do not live well do not believe rightly, or else rebuke and slander their fathers. Teachers, therefore, who are also called fathers, are to be borne with rather than rebuked, unless they have erred in the true faith.

No teacher, therefore, is to be accused in writing, nor is he to respond except to a faithful and legitimate accuser who also leads an irreproachable life and conduct. For it is unworthy that a teacher should answer a foolish, ignorant, and reprehensibly living person according to his folly, as Scripture says: “Do not answer a fool according to his folly” [Col. 0589C].

A person who does not believe rightly does not live well. Whoever is faithful desires no evil. If anyone is faithful, let him take care not to speak falsely or lay snares for anyone. A faithful person always acts faithfully, whereas an unfaithful person craftily lies in wait and tries to destroy the faithful and those who live piously and justly, because like seeks its like.

An unfaithful person is dead within a living body. Conversely, the words of a faithful person preserve the lives of those who hear them. A Catholic teacher, and especially a priest of the Lord, must be neither entangled in any error nor violated by any scheme or desire, as Holy Scripture says: “Do not follow your lusts, and turn away from your own will.”

### CHAPTER CXXXVI — That bishops are not to be rebuked by their own flocks unless they have erred in the faith

[Col. 0589D]

(From a letter of Pope Anacletus, written to all the priests of Christ, chapter 1.) If a teacher or pastor of the Church has deviated from the faithful, he is to be corrected by the faithful. But for reprehensible conduct he is rather to be tolerated than harshly disciplined, because the rulers of the Church are to be judged by the Lord, as the Prophet says: “God has stood in the assembly of the gods; in the midst he distinguishes among the gods.”

Therefore each faithful person, if he sees or learns that his people are rising up against their pastor or that the clergy are devoting themselves to slander, ought to strive with all his strength to eradicate this vice and correct it prudently. Nor should he presume to involve himself in any of their affairs if they appear incorrigible, before they have been reconciled with their teacher [Col. 0590A]. For priests and all the other faithful alike ought to exercise the greatest care concerning those who are perishing, so that through their reproach they may either be corrected from their sins or, if they appear incorrigible, be separated from the Church.

### CHAPTER CXXXVII — On the same matter

(From the decree of Pope Clement, chapter 17.) If bishops themselves have deviated, they are not to be rebuked or reproved by these people, but are to be borne with, unless they have erred in the faith. These people, therefore, are over those others, not those others over them, because a greater cannot be reproved or judged by a lesser.

Let no one exalt himself against his teachers and masters, because a disciple neither ought nor can be above his master. Let no one wish to be called holy before he is holy; rather, let him first become holy, so that he may be called so more truthfully [Col. 0590B]. The commandments of the Lord and of teachers and masters must be fulfilled daily by deeds, and one must pray in Christ’s name for one’s enemies.

### CHAPTER CXXXVIII — On the same matter

(From a letter of Pope Eusebius, chapter 20.) It is necessary that rulers be feared by their subjects, and that the subjects be corrected by them, so that those who do not fear divine judgments may fear to sin through human apprehension.

Those who corrupt the life and morals of teachers are worse than those who seize the possessions and estates of others. The latter take away things outside us, even if they are ours; but those who slander us and corrupt our morals, or who arm themselves against us, actually deceive us ourselves. Therefore they are justly infamous and deservedly expelled from the Church [Col. 0590C].

### CHAPTER CXXXIX — On the same matter

(From the decree of Pope Gaius, chapter 7.) The sheep entrusted to their pastor ought neither to rebuke him, unless he has deviated from the true faith, nor accuse him in any way. For the deeds of pastors are not to be struck down by their sword, even though they may appear rightly subject to rebuke.

### CHAPTER CXL — Concerning bishops who have been defamed and torn apart and driven from their own cities

(From the decree of Pope Evaristus, sent to all the brothers throughout Egypt, chapter 18.) We have heard that certain bishops among you have been defamed and torn apart, driven from their own cities, and unable to be established as bishops elsewhere except in cities of no small importance [Col. 0590D]; and that others have been appointed in their places while they are still alive.

Therefore we write these things to you so that you may know that this is not permitted, but that the rightful bishops must be recalled and restored in full. Those, however, who hold their betrothed women—whom we understand, according to the established wording, to be their wives—in adulterous disgrace, we order to be expelled as adulterers, made infamous, and barred from ecclesiastical honors.

If you have any complaint against them, it must be investigated after these matters have been dealt with and settled by the authority of this holy see.

### CHAPTER CXLI — That a bishop who has been stripped of his possessions is not to be judged

(From the decree of Pope Felix, sent to the bishops throughout Egypt, chapter 10.) No bishop who has been stripped of his possessions, or driven by force or error from his own see, may be accused, summoned, judged, or condemned according to canonical institution until everything taken from him has been legally restored, he has peacefully enjoyed his honors for a year or more, and he has been regularly restored to his own see.

### CHAPTER CXLII — On the same matter

(From the decree of Pope Stephen, sent to all bishops, chapter 6.) No bishop, while he has been stripped of his possessions or driven from his own see for any reason, is to be accused; nor may any crime be charged against him before he has been completely restored, everything taken from him by whatever means has been legally returned, and he has been regularly restored to his own see and former status [Col. 0591B].

Thus all possessions, everything unjustly taken from him, and all revenues must be entirely restored to the bishop concerned by the primates and the synod before an accusation is undertaken.

For not only ecclesiastical laws but also the laws of the world prohibit this. Nor should any of them, or any administrators or defenders of the churches, be accused before he has himself been approached charitably, twice or three times, by those who consider themselves injured or who wish to correct them for some error, so that they may receive from them either a friendly correction or a just explanation.

Whoever presumes to do otherwise shall be barred from the thresholds of the Church until he has offered due satisfaction.

### CHAPTER CXLIII — On the same matter

[Col. 0591C]

(From the decree of Pope Sixtus, sent to the bishops of Spain, chapter 6.) Having considered these matters in this way, and together with the decrees of the other bishops, as those responsible for the care of all, we decree, on account of the preeminence of this see, that no pontiff may presume to excommunicate or judge a bishop who has been stripped of his possessions or driven from his see. For there is no privilege by which one already stripped naked can be stripped again.

If anyone presumes to act otherwise, let him know that the censure of this see, together with all its members, will not fail to reach him; and as he has acted, so shall he receive. If well, well; if gravely, gravely; if most wickedly, most wickedly. For the laborer is worthy of his wage.

### CHAPTER CXLIV — That accused bishops may freely appeal to the apostolic see, and several other matters to be observed concerning judgment

[Col. 0591D]

(From the decree of Pope Julius, sent to the eastern bishops, chapter 18.) All bishops who are attacked or accused in certain more serious cases should, whenever necessary, freely appeal to the apostolic see and flee to it as to a mother, so that they may be piously supported, defended, and delivered by it, as has always been the case.

Ancient authority deriving from the apostles, their successors, and the canons has reserved to its disposition all the greater ecclesiastical cases and the judgments of bishops. Since bishops are blamed for having acted toward their brothers otherwise than the pope of that same see wished, it has been determined that a bishop accused or judged by his fellow-provincial bishops may freely appeal and approach the pontiff of the apostolic see, who shall arrange for the case to be reconsidered either by himself or through his representatives.

While the pontiff is handling his case in a renewed judgment, no other bishop is to be substituted, appointed, or ordained in his place. For although the fellow-provincial bishops are permitted to examine the pontiff’s case, they are not permitted to decide it without consulting the Roman pontiff, since it was said by the Lord to the blessed Apostle Peter, and by no other: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven.”

If anyone believes that he is being oppressed by his own metropolitan, let him be judged before the primate of the diocese or before the pope of the apostolic universal Church.

We unanimously exclude accusers and accusations that the laws of the world do not admit, lest impiety be carried out without strict proof, since the judgment’s sentence is rightly determined by the choice of the judge.

If anyone believes that he has a personal case against a bishop or the administrators of a church, he must not first approach judges before returning to those persons in a spirit of charity, so that, admonished through familiar conversation, they may remedy the matters brought forward as complaints. If he acts otherwise, he shall be deprived of communion.

Henceforth no pontiff may presume to excommunicate or judge a bishop stripped of his possessions or driven from his see, because there is no privilege by which one already stripped can be stripped again.

With equal force we decree that an accuser who, in the absence of his opponent, has presented a case is not to be believed before both sides have been heard [Col. 0592C]; nor are accusers or witnesses to be admitted who are not suitable.

It has been determined that if an accused or condemned bishop appeals to the Roman pontiff, whatever the pontiff himself justly decides is to be established.

We also judge all those who arm themselves against the Fathers to be infamous; nor are those who associate with their enemies to be admitted either for accusation or testimony.

It has been determined that in every accusation of clergy, the person, faith, life, and conduct of the slanderers must first be examined. For faith must precede all a person’s actions, since one who is doubtful in faith is unfaithful.

No credence at all is to be given to those who do not know the faith of truth and do not lead a life of upright conduct, since such people easily and indiscriminately tear apart and accuse those who live rightly and piously. Their suspicion must therefore first be examined and corrected [Col. 0592D]. Nor is credence to be given to suspect accusers or to those emerging from the households of enemies.

### CHAPTER CXLV — If a bishop is attacked by anyone, the case is to be settled by bishops as judges

(From the Council of Spalatum, chapter 8.) If any bishop is attacked by anyone, or if he brings forward some dispute, the case is to be settled by bishops as judges—whether those whom the primates assign to them or those whom they themselves choose from among their neighbors by common agreement.

### CHAPTER CXLVI — Concerning bishops chosen as judges by common agreement

(From the same council, chapter 9.) It is not permitted for anyone to challenge the bishops whom common agreement has chosen as judges. Whoever is proved, through contumacy, unwilling to obey the judges, once this has been established before the bishop of the first see, shall receive letters ordering that none of the bishops communicate with him until he obeys.

### CHAPTER CXLVII — That fellow-provincial bishops are not to tolerate foreign judgments

(From the decree of Pope Fabian, sent to Bishop Hilary, chapter 26.) We prohibit foreign judgments by a general sanction, while preserving the authority of the apostolic see in all matters. For it is unworthy that one who ought to have provincial judges chosen by himself should be judged by outsiders, unless an appeal has been made.

Therefore, if any bishop is accused of specific crimes, he ought to be heard by all the bishops who are in the province, because an accused person ought not to be heard anywhere except in his own forum [Col. 0593B].

### CHAPTER CXLVIII — Concerning an accused bishop who considers the judge suspect

(From the decree of the same pope sent to the same bishop, chapter 27.) If any bishop considers the judge suspect and sees that he is being oppressed, let him freely appeal to the apostolic see.

The appellant is not to be subjected to any affliction or the wrongful custody of detention. Rather, the appellant must be permitted to relieve the cause of his appeal by the remedy of appeal. It is also permitted to appeal in criminal cases; nor is the right of appeal to be denied to one whom the sentence had destined for punishment.

### CHAPTER CXLIX — If a bishop is detained on a criminal charge and cannot assemble many, he is to be heard by twelve bishops

[Col. 0593C]

(From the Council of Carthage, chapter 12.) Bishop Felix said: I propose, according to the statutes of the ancient councils, that if any bishop—something we do not wish—has fallen under some accusation and is under such pressing necessity that he cannot assemble many, then, so that he does not remain under accusation, he should be heard by twelve bishops; a presbyter by six bishops together with his own bishop; and a deacon by three.

### CHAPTER CL — Concerning an accused bishop when the fellow-provincial bishops disagree about his accusation

(From the Council of Antioch, chapter 14.) If a bishop is judged concerning specific crimes, and it happens that the fellow-provincial bishops disagree about him—some considering him innocent after judgment and others regarding him as guilty—the holy synod has determined, for the resolution of this ambiguity, that the metropolitan bishop should summon other judges from a neighboring province, who will remove the dispute, so that their decision together with that of the fellow-provincial bishops may establish what appears just [Col. 0593D].

### CHAPTER CLI — That no layman may bring a charge against a bishop

(From the decree of Pope Sylvester, chapter 1.) It has been established by the agreement and subscription of all that no layman may bring any charge against a bishop or anyone in orders.

Nor may a presbyter bring an accusation against a bishop, a deacon against a presbyter, a subdeacon against a deacon, an acolyte against a subdeacon, an exorcist against an acolyte, a reader against an exorcist, or a doorkeeper against a reader [Col. 0594A].

Nor shall a prelate be condemned except on the testimony of seventy-two suitable witnesses.

### CHAPTER CLII — That enemies cannot be accusers

(From the decree of Pope Anacletus, sent to all bishops, chapter 37.) Those who have recently become enemies cannot be accusers or witnesses, lest, being angry, they wish to cause harm, or, having been injured, wish to take revenge.

In the case of accusations and witnesses, therefore, their disposition must be investigated and found free from suspicion.

### CHAPTER CLIII — That bishops are to be judges of accused bishops

(From the decree of Pope Damasus, chapter 3.) We decree that wise bishops who desire what is right and just are to be judges of accused bishops.

### CHAPTER CLIV — How an accused bishop is to be examined before patriarchs or primates, and by how many witnesses he must be convicted

[Col. 0594B]

(From the decree of Pope Zepherinus, sent to all the bishops established throughout Sicily, chapter 2.) When patriarchs or primates examine an accused bishop, they must not pronounce a final sentence before he either confesses himself guilty, supported by apostolic authority, or is convicted by innocent and regularly examined witnesses who are not fewer in number than those disciples whom the Lord commanded to be chosen for the assistance of the apostles.

### CHAPTER CLV — Concerning patriarchs and primates

(From the decree of Pope Clement, chapter 9.) In those cities in which, among the pagans, their chief flamens and principal teachers of the law once existed [Col. 0594C], primates of bishops or patriarchs are to be appointed. They are to handle the judgments of the other bishops and, whenever necessary, the more important matters concerning the faith, and, according to the Lord’s will and as the holy apostles established, they are to decide matters so that no one may be unjustly endangered.

### CHAPTER CLVI — Concerning the summons of an accused bishop

(From a letter of Pope Damasus to Stephen and to the Council of Africa.) The summons to a synod of a person who is being prosecuted must, according to the canonical decrees of the Fathers, be made through reasonable written notice, with a suitable and canonical period allowed.

For unless he has been canonically summoned at the proper time and in canonical form, even if he comes to the assembly under any necessity, he shall in no way be required to answer his adversaries unless he wishes to do so voluntarily [Col. 0594D]. For if the laws of the world do not permit this, how much less do the divine laws?

### CHAPTER CLVII — That primates must not pronounce a sentence of condemnation against an accused bishop before he either confesses himself guilty or is canonically convicted by innocent witnesses

(From a letter of Pope Felix sent to Bishop Paternus, chapter 4.) Primates examining an accused bishop must not pronounce a sentence of condemnation before he either confesses himself guilty, supported by apostolic authority, or is regularly convicted by innocent witnesses examined canonically.

Otherwise we decree that the condemnation of the bishops is null and unjust and must therefore be reconsidered by the synod, so that assistance may be provided to the oppressed in every matter [Col. 0595A].

### CHAPTER CLVIII — What a primate ought to be and what he ought to do

(From a letter to Gennadius, Patrician and Exarch of Africa.) Instruct the council of Catholic bishops to take care that it does not appoint a primate on the basis merely of the rank of his place, setting aside the merits of his life, since before the Lord it is not a more distinguished rank but the conduct of a better life that is approved.

The primate himself should not reside indiscriminately throughout the villages, as is customary, but in one city, according to their choice.

### CHAPTER CLIX — That the bishops of each people should know who is first among them

(From a letter of Pope Anacletus, sent to all the bishops [Col. 0595B].) The blessed apostles also established among themselves that the bishops of each people should know who was first among them, so that the greater concern of the others might belong to him.

For there was also a certain distinction among the blessed apostles. Although all were apostles, it was granted by the Lord to Peter—and they themselves wished the same among them—that Cephas should preside over all the other apostles; that is, that Peter should hold the primacy of the apostolate. They handed down this same form to be observed by their successors and by the other bishops.

This was established not only in the New Testament but also in the Old. Hence it is written: “Moses and Aaron among his priests”—that is, they were first among them.

Although this order has been established, no one should seek what belongs to himself, but what belongs to another. Hence blessed Paul the Apostle says: “Let each one please his neighbor for good, for edification.” And, as the Savior himself said to his disciples: “The greater among you will be your servant.” And so forth.

### CHAPTER CLX — That an accused bishop is not to be deprived of communion unless he refuses to come on the appointed day

(From the Council of Carthage, chapter 19.) Bishop Aurelius said: Whoever is accused among the bishops, let the accuser bring the case before the primate of that province. The person against whom the charge is made is not to be suspended from communion unless he fails to appear to state his case on the appointed day of the judges chosen for the matter, after being summoned by letter—that is, within one month from the day on which it is established that he received the letter.

If he proves that there were genuine reasons of necessity that plainly prevented him from appearing, he shall have a full opportunity to state his case during the following month. But after the second month he shall not communicate until he has been examined.

If he refuses to appear before the universal council within the period of a year, so that his case may be settled there, he shall be judged to have pronounced the sentence of condemnation against himself. During the time when he does not communicate, he is not to communicate in his own church or parish either.

His accuser, however, if he has never failed to appear on the days appointed for stating the case, is not to be removed from communion. But if he has at any time failed to appear, withdrawing himself, then, once the bishop has been restored to communion, the accuser himself is to be removed from communion. Even so, he is not to be deprived of the opportunity to pursue the case if he proves that he did not refuse to appear on the appointed day but was unable to do so [Col. 0596A].

It has also been determined that when he begins to act in the judgment of the bishops, if the accuser is a culpable person, he is not to be admitted to bring an accusation unless he wishes to assert his own cases, though not ecclesiastical ones.

### CHAPTER CLXI — Concerning Bishop Maximus, defamed by various crimes and summoned repeatedly to the synod, but neglecting to come and offer his defense

(From a letter of Pope Boniface to the bishops of Gaul.) Boniface, bishop, to Patroclus, Remigius, Maximus, Hilary, Severus, Julian, Castorius, Leontius, Constantine, John, Montanus, Marinus, and the other bishops established throughout Gaul and the seven provinces.

The clergy of the city of Valence have approached us, presenting a petition and the charges which the entire province asserts that Maximus committed [Col. 0596B]. Although the investigation had been delegated so many times, he had always evaded the appointed judgments and, without being troubled in conscience, had not hastened—if he was innocent—to have himself cleared after all obstacles had been removed. We have learned of these matters so often from the contents of our own documents.

By contrast, he has shown these allegations against himself to be true, because, since they were innumerable, the provincial investigation was delegated by my predecessors for the purpose of refuting them. He is also said to have avoided the assembly and to have been entirely unwilling to appear.

No one doubts that a guilty person evades judgment in this way, just as an innocent person seeks judgment in order to be acquitted. But the crafty evasion of those who think matters must be handled by cunning schemes will never acquire the name of innocence.

Anyone who thinks he can evade judgment through delays confesses everything. Nevertheless, the man who is said to be such will at some time come forward. It does him no good to have hidden and evaded judgment so often, since, wherever he flees, his own acts and offenses pursue him with the charges brought against him, if they are true.

I ought by now to pronounce a sentence worthy of the acts for which he has been accused in our judgment—acts by which he thought to mock the investigation and the judgment, repeatedly avoiding them. But lest anyone perhaps judge this premature and say that nothing had been reserved for him, absent though he is and though we have sought him, we preferred to postpone the matter by allowing an interval of time, especially since his accusers also asserted this.

The more secretive he is concerning his intentions and character, the more he must be condemned for committing such things while presenting himself so slowly before the appointed judgment [Col. 0596D]. They accuse him of having long been enveloped in the darkness of the Manichaeans and of an infamous sect.

Since he could not cleanse his mind of its sordid depravity, they brought forward the synodal records of his deeds and, presenting the acts attributed to him, charged that, enveloped on every side in crimes, he had shown no concern for his own recovery. In his madness and insane recklessness, they said, he had even subjected himself to interrogation before the tribunal of a secular judgment—something most shameful even in a person of low station.

They assert, producing the records, that he had incurred the penalties of homicide. They lament with the greatest grief that, after such grave and numerous offenses, this man still claims for himself the name of bishop in his hiding places, bringing disgrace upon his own city [Col. 0597A], and wishes to pollute the holy name by claiming it for himself.

Therefore, dearest brothers, since he refused to present himself to be heard and perhaps cannot defend himself when convicted by his accusers, we judge that, once finally presented, he should be struck by an appropriate sentence pronounced by episcopal judgment.

Although, when these matters have been demonstrated to him, we know that he will regard the loss of this title as nothing—since he is said never to have possessed the modesty of the priesthood and not to have guarded his position even for a brief time—we have granted a delay and decreed that the judgment must take place within your province. You are to assemble a synod before the day of the Kalends of November, so that, if he wishes to be present, he may answer the charges if he has confidence; but if he neglects to appear, he is not to gain a delay of sentence by his absence.

For it is evident that a person confesses his crime when, after judgment has been granted and delegated so many times, he does not use the opportunity to clear himself. It makes no difference whether everything stated is proven in a present examination, since his repeated absence itself is established as tantamount to a confession [Col. 0597B].

We shall send letters throughout all the provinces so that he cannot plead ignorance as an excuse, but will be compelled to come to the province and present himself there before the appointed judgment.

Whatever your charity decides should be decreed in this case, once it has been reported to us, must necessarily be confirmed by our authority, as is fitting.

### CHAPTER CLXII — Concerning an accused bishop who contemptuously refused to come when summoned to the synod

(From the synod held at Altheim, chapter 10.) Richwin, the bishop who invaded the Church of Strasbourg contrary to the sanctions of the holy canons, was invited by our letters to the holy synod. Since he contemptuously refused to come and did not even send his representative, I, John, the vicar of the apostolic see, by the authority of Saint Peter and at the command of the present holy synod, summon him again and order him to come to the council—that is, to the assembly announced at Mainz in May by his metropolitan bishop—to appear before the venerable Archbishop Heriger and his fellow bishops, and there give a just account of his disobedience and perversity.

But if he negligently considers even this matter of little importance, let him withdraw from his own rank until, coming to Rome, he gives an account before the lord pope and the holy Church.

### CHAPTER CLXIII — Who are primates, and who metropolitans

[Col. 0597D]

(From the chapters of the Council of Nicaea, which were added by Pope Felix.) Let those, and no others, be primates who were established in the Nicene synod. The others who hold metropolitan sees are called archbishops, not primates, while in all things the dignity of the apostolic see is preserved, a dignity granted to it by the Lord himself and afterwards confirmed by the holy Fathers.

### CHAPTER CLXIV — That persons accused must be denied leave to accuse before they have cleared themselves of the charge; and concerning intimates, voluntary confessors, and those who were enemies yesterday, the day before, or earlier

(From the decree of Pope Stephen, sent to all bishops, chapter 11.) Persons accused must be denied leave to accuse before they have cleared themselves of the charge by which they are pressed; for their confession against others is not to be believed while they are implicated in crimes, unless they have first proved themselves innocent, since the declaration of an accused person against anyone is dangerous and must not be admitted. Intimates, voluntary confessors, and those entangled in crimes must not be admitted; nor those who were enemies yesterday, the day before, or earlier.

### CHAPTER CLXV — That accusations against teachers are not to be accepted, and that judgments by outsiders are not to be held

*(From chapter 17 of Pope Eusebius.)* Although these statements might generally suffice, whether to avoid errors or to preserve what is catholic, nevertheless we know that it was established by the apostles and their successors that accusations against teachers [Col. 0598B] ought not to be accepted, that judgments by outsiders are not to be held, and that no one ought to be bound by the sentence of any judge other than his own.

### CHAPTER CLXVI — That no one should accept accusations against a teacher

*(From chapter 3 of the Council of Spalato.)* Let no one entertain accusations against a teacher, because one whom God has reserved for his own judgment cannot be condemned by human examination.

### CHAPTER CLXVII — That no one should accuse a bishop before secular authorities

*(From chapter 1 of Pope Felix’s letter sent to the bishops of Egypt.)* Let no one accuse a bishop before secular arbiters, but before the highest primates.

### CHAPTER CLXVIII — That bishops are not to be summoned before a secular court

[Col. 0598C]

*(From Pope Boniface’s letter to the bishops of Gaul.)* No bishop, whether in a civil or a criminal matter, is to be produced or brought before any judge, whether civil or military. For any magistrate who dares to order this shall be punished by condemnation and loss of his belt of office.

### CHAPTER CLXIX — That a bishop is not to be accused by criminals

*(From chapter 18 of Pope Felix’s letter sent to the bishops mentioned above.)* Whenever a bishop is accused of specific crimes, if the accusers are such as ought to be received lawfully and canonically, then, once a legitimate synod has been convened at the proper time, he is to be heard canonically by all the bishops who are in the province. But if the accusers are not legitimate, the bishop is not to be harassed; for priests ought to be summoned to offer sacrifice, not to engage in litigation. Nor should those who are called the thrones of God be disturbed by the plots of wicked men, but should serve Christ freely.

### CHAPTER CLXX — That no bishop should be summoned to judgment outside his province

*(From chapter 18 of Pope Julius’s decree sent to the bishops of the East.)* No bishop is to be summoned to judgment outside his province. Rather, after he has been canonically summoned to a suitable place at the synodal time, he is to be heard by all the bishops of his province, because they ought to pronounce a concordant and canonical sentence concerning him. For if this has been granted to those of lower rank, both clergy and laity, how much more ought it to be observed concerning bishops? If, however, he regards the metropolitan or the judges as suspect, or perceives them to be hostile, he is to be judged before the primate of the diocese or before the pontiff of the Roman see.

### CHAPTER CLXXI — Concerning the accusers and witnesses of bishops

*(From chapter 17 of Pope Calixtus’s decree to the bishops established throughout Gaul.)* Therefore, all who are suspect in the true faith are by no means to be admitted as accusers of priests or of those whose faith is not in doubt; rather, they are to be regarded as doubtful witnesses. The testimony of those whose faith is doubted must therefore be weakened, and no credence at all is to be given to those who do not know the true faith.

In judgment, therefore, it must be investigated what sort of conduct and faith belong to both the accuser and the accused. Those who are not of upright conduct and faith, and whose life is open to accusation, must not be permitted to accuse others. Those whose faith, life, and liberty are unknown, and persons of low standing, are not to be admitted to such an accusation.

The persons of the accusers must be examined individually. Without a written document they are difficult to receive, but with a written document they are never to be admitted, because no one can be accused by writing. Rather, each person must bring his accusation in his own voice and in the presence of the one whom he wishes to accuse; no accuser is to be believed in the absence of the person whom he wishes to accuse.

Likewise, witnesses are not to give testimony through any written document, nor are they to testify concerning other causes or matters, except those which they are known to have seen enacted in their presence. The blood relatives of an accuser are not to testify against the accused, nor are his associates or those who come from his household. But if they wish and agree mutually, relatives may testify among themselves, but not against others.

Neither accusers nor witnesses who are suspect are to be admitted, because the affection of kinship, familiarity, or domination usually obstructs the truth.

### CHAPTER CLXXII — On the same matter

*(From chapter 10 of Pope Damasus’s decree sent to Stephen and all the bishops of Africa.)* The accusers and witnesses of bishops concerning whom you have consulted must be free from every disgrace, suspicion, and manifest blemish, and must be fully instructed in the true faith—such persons as divine authority commands to be chosen for the priesthood. For, as the authority of the ancients teaches, priests cannot be accused, nor can testimony be given against those who neither ought nor are able to be advanced to the same honor.

### CHAPTER CLXXIII — Who are infamous persons

*(From Pope Stephen’s letter to Hilary.)* We call those persons infamous who are branded with infamy on account of some fault—that is, all who reject the rule of Christian law and despise ecclesiastical statutes. Likewise, thieves, sacrilegious persons, and all ensnared in capital crimes; violators of tombs; those who willingly violate the religious statutes of the holy Fathers, of the apostles and their successors; and all who take up arms against the Fathers—all who throughout the world are marked with infamy.

Likewise, incestuous persons, murderers, perjurers, robbers, sorcerers, poisoners, adulterers, those who flee from wars, those who seek to occupy places unworthy of them, those who unjustly seize the resources of the Church, those who slander or accuse their brethren without proving their charges, those who provoke the minds of princes to anger against the innocent, all who have been anathematized or expelled from the Church for their crimes, and all whom ecclesiastical or secular laws pronounce infamous.

Nor are slaves to be admitted before lawful emancipation; nor penitents; nor bigamists; nor those who serve in the civil administration; nor those who are physically incomplete; nor those who lack a sound mind or understanding; nor those who are disobedient to the decrees of the saints.

None of these may be advanced to the sacred orders. Neither these persons, nor freedmen, nor suspects, nor those who lack the true faith or worthy conduct, can accuse the highest priests.

### CHAPTER CLXXIV — Concerning an accused bishop, the admission of accusers, and the summons

*(From chapter 9 of Pope Felix’s decree sent to the bishops established throughout Gaul.)* If a bishop is accused by accusers who ought to be admitted, then, after they have approached him charitably so that he might correct the matter itself, if he refuses to correct it, his case is to be referred canonically—not earlier, but then—to the highest primates.

They must regularly convene a council in a suitable place within the province and at the appropriate season, namely autumn or summer, so that he may be heard together by all the bishops of that province. He too, having been regularly summoned, ought to be present, unless illness or some other serious necessity prevents him. For no one has permission to accuse him beyond the boundaries of the province before a hearing has been requested.

If this rule is violated in any way, they have decreed that, before his proper place and all his rights have been restored to him according to law, he is in no way to be accused or charged by anyone; nor is he to answer anyone concerning such matters unless he chooses to do so voluntarily.

But after he has been restored, as prescribed, and all his rights have been restored to him according to law, a substantial period is to be granted for him to consider his case. Afterwards, if necessary, he is to come when regularly summoned to the hearing and, if the matter appears unjust, he is to answer the accusations of the accusers with the support of his brethren.

For no principle permits anything to be alleged against him while his property, or the property of the Church, or his possessions are temporarily held by rivals or by anyone else. Nothing, whether major or minor, can in any way be alleged against him while he is deprived of his churches, possessions, or powers.

### CHAPTER CLXXV — On the condemnation of bishops who accuse a bishop without the authority of the apostolic see

*(From chapter 8 of Pope Julius’s letter sent to the bishops of the East.)* If, from this day forward, anyone presumes to condemn a bishop and expel him from his own see contrary to the judgment of this holy see, let him know that he is irrecoverably condemned and will be deprived forever of his own honor.

Know also that those who have been expelled or condemned without the judgment of this see are, by the authority of this holy see, to be restored to their former communion and returned to their own sees. For this was granted to this holy see earlier, from the time of the apostles, and afterwards was confirmed unanimously by all in the aforementioned Council of Nicaea because of the assaults of wicked men, the persecutions of heretics, and the schemes of those who plotted against their brethren, so that each individual might take greater care not to dare to perpetrate such acts.

### CHAPTER CLXXVI — That an accused or judged bishop may freely appeal to and approach the Roman pontiff

*(From chapter 1 of Pope Victor’s decree to all the brethren of Alexandria.)* It has been resolved that a bishop accused or judged by the bishops of his province in any matter may freely appeal and approach the pontiff of the apostolic see, who, either personally or through his representatives, shall arrange for his case to be reheard.

While the pontiff is conducting his case in a retrial, no other bishop is to be placed or ordained in his position. For although the bishops of the province may examine the case of the accused bishop, they are not permitted to decide it without consulting the Roman pontiff, since the Lord said to the blessed apostle Peter alone, and not to another: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven.”

### CHAPTER CLXXVII — That no written accusation is to be accepted in the absence of the accused

[Col. 0601C]

*(From chapter 8 of Pope Stephen’s letter sent to all the bishops.)* No written accusation is to be accepted when both the accuser and the accused are absent. Rather, if the accuser is a legitimate and suitable person, he must speak in his own voice and in the presence of the one whom he wishes to accuse, because no one who is absent can be accused or accuse another.

Nevertheless, no man of the aforementioned order may be accused, nor is he obliged to answer his accusers, before he has been regularly summoned by his primate and has been given an opportunity to defend himself or to investigate the charges, so that he may clear himself of the crimes.

### CHAPTER CLXXVIII — That more difficult cases are to be referred to the summit of the Roman see, to be settled by apostolic judgment, since all the churches are governed by the authority of that see

[Col. 0601D]

*(From chapter 14 of Pope Anacletus’s letter sent to all the bishops.)* If more difficult cases should arise among you, refer them to the summit of this holy see, as to the head, so that they may be settled by apostolic judgment. For the testimonies quoted above declare that God wills this and has established it in this way.

This apostolic see has been made by the Lord the hinge and the head, and it was established by no other. Just as a door is governed by its hinge, so, by the authority of this holy see and by the Lord’s ordering, all the churches are governed.

### CHAPTER CLXXIX — That all bishops may appeal to the Roman see when placed in need

*(From chapter 9 of Pope Damasus’s decree sent to Stephen and the bishops of Africa.)* All ought to appeal to it, if necessity requires, and to be supported by its assistance. For, as you know, it is not canonical for a synod to be held without its authority. Nor can a bishop be definitively condemned except in a legitimate synod, at the proper time, convened by apostolic summons. Nor is any council ever read to have been ratified unless it was supported by apostolic authority.

### CHAPTER CLXXX — Concerning the adjournments to be granted to bishops who are accused, and what they ought to be

*(From chapter 15 of Pope Felix II’s letter to the brethren of Egypt.)* Concerning the adjournments of bishops about which you have consulted, we find different rules established by the Fathers. Some ordered that a year and six months be granted, so that they might repel the schemes of the ignorant, prepare their responses, confirm their witnesses, and seek councils of bishops and friends. Others prescribed a year, with which many agree.

I have found no period shorter than six months. For if these concessions have been granted even to laymen, how much more should they be granted to the priests of the Lord? Our predecessors and the other holy Fathers have often prohibited anyone from harassing the priests of the Lord with accusations not arising from the root of charity:

“Be still,” they say, “and do not persecute those who serve God perfectly. By their prayers earthly wars are quieted, the attacks of departing angels are driven away, and through the constant practice of prayer they confound all demons, the corrupters.”

Adjournments are not to be granted for a brief period, but for a long interval, so that the accused may prepare himself, meet with all those in the provinces who share his communion, prepare witnesses, and fully arm himself against his plotters.

The judges and accusers must be such as are entirely free from suspicion and desire to pronounce their judgment from the root of charity.

### CHAPTER CLXXXI — Concerning the bishop of Centuria who refused to conduct his case in a synod

*(From chapter 54 of the African Council.)* Concerning Quodvultdeus of Centuria: when his adversary had requested to be admitted to our council, he was asked whether he wished to plead against him before the bishops. At first he promised to do so, but on the following day he replied that this did not please him and departed.

It was resolved by all the bishops that no one should communicate with Quodvultdeus until his case had reached whatever conclusion it could reach. For no Christian could rightly think that his episcopate should be taken from him before the outcome of his case had become clear.

### CHAPTER CLXXXII — The judgment concerning a bishop who, after being expelled from office for a crime, later invaded the bishopric like a plunderer

*(From chapter 17 of the register sent to John, bishop of First Justiniana.)* When evils that ought to be cleansed by penitential tears are increased by further excesses, correction must be applied to offenders with correspondingly greater severity, so that they may recognize their crime at least through the punishment that avenges it, and so that fear may restrain others from unlawful acts against ecclesiastical protection.

Our most beloved bearer of this letter, Nemesion, came to us and reported—as the copies of the records that he brought here also contained—that Paul, bishop of the city of Doclea, having fallen, among his other evils, into a bodily crime, had been accused by his own clergy. After an inquiry had been held, the truth had become clear—something we cannot say without grief—and, moreover, after he had been convicted, he had presented the document in which he confessed that the matters of which he had been accused were true.

For this reason, he said, Paul had been deposed by episcopal sentence, and he himself had been ordained bishop in his place with the consent of your fraternity. But now the same Paul had come with the assistance of secular judges, entered the bishopric like a plunderer, violently seized the Church’s property, expelled Nemesion, and brought him almost to the point of the greatest injury and death.

Since the wickedness of so great a crime must neither be concealed nor treated lightly, let your fraternity carefully investigate all these matters. If the truth is as we have been informed, let it compel the aforesaid Paul by strict enforcement to restore everything he has taken, without any delay or excuse.

If, however, he says that he took nothing belonging to the Church but only his own property, although it was serious and unjust that he did not seek this from you or from his metropolitan, but rashly presumed to act by force, nevertheless, if he took anything of his own, it must be established under your fraternity’s examination whether his claim is true.

It must also be carefully investigated whether he wickedly dissipated anything from the Church’s property; he is to be compelled by every means to make good and satisfy for this, or for what he has now taken.

If he attempts to delay, he is to be sent to a monastery until he restores everything that he has dissipated or taken from the substance of the Church, so that at least under compulsion he may return what he was not afraid to take unlawfully.

But if, contrary to our belief, after his deposition he should presume to speak shamelessly and with a perverse mind about the episcopate, or should again aspire to it by any presumption, let your fraternity’s firmness be wholly aroused against his insolence. Deprived of communion in the Lord’s body and blood, he is to be confined in a monastery to perform penance until the day of his death, so that he may learn through worthy lamentation to correct the stains of the crime he committed, which he desires rather wickedly to increase to the destruction of his soul.

Our aforesaid most beloved brother Nemesion is without doubt to be restored to his place and to the office of the episcopate. You must take care that he does not again suffer disturbance or hardship on this account. For this is evidently beneficial not only for his protection but also for the correction of others, so that the presumption of wicked men may never again dare to attempt anything against the statutes of the sacred canons or ecclesiastical discipline.

### CHAPTER CLXXXIII — Why the holy apostles and their successors wished the accusation of priests to be difficult

*(From chapter 19 of Pope Fabian’s decree sent to the bishops of the East.)* Reflecting on such matters, the holy apostles and their successors, filled with the Spirit of God, foreseeing wicked men and considering the simple, did not wish the accusation of priests to be easy—or even possible—lest they be overthrown or removed by the wicked.

For if this were readily granted to secular and wicked men, either no priests or scarcely very few would remain, since it has always been, and still is—and, what is worse, is excessively prevalent—that the wicked persecute the good and the carnal harass the spiritual.

Therefore, as stated above, they decreed that priests should not be accused; or, if this could not be avoided, that their accusation should be made extremely difficult and should not be undertaken by those who, as was said above, were not to presume it. Nor were bishops to be expelled from their own sees or churches.

### CHAPTER CLXXXIV — If an expelled bishop should dare to enter the city

[Col. 0604B]

*(From Pope Boniface’s letter to the bishops of Gaul.)* If an expelled bishop dares to enter the city from which he was expelled, or to leave the place in which he was ordered to reside, we command that he be delivered to a monastery established in another province, so that the one who sinned in the priesthood may be corrected while living in a monastery.

### CHAPTER CLXXXV — Concerning bishops who wish to choose successors while they are still alive

*(From chapter 23 of the Council of Antioch.)* A bishop is not permitted to appoint another as his successor, even if he has reached the end of his life. If anything of this kind is done, such an appointment is to be invalid.

The ecclesiastical law containing this provision is to be observed: this is not to be done except with the synod and judgment of the bishops, who, after the death of the bishop who has rested, have the power to advance the one who proves worthy.

### CHAPTER CLXXXVI — That no one is to be appointed over a bishop while he is alive

*(From chapter 13 of the Council of Auvergne.)* No other bishop is to be placed or appointed over a bishop while he is alive, except perhaps in the place of one whom a capital crime has removed.

### CHAPTER CLXXXVII — That a bishop may not choose a successor

*(From chapter 8 of the Council of Spalato.)* A bishop is not permitted to establish another as his successor in his place before the end of his life. If anyone attempts to usurp this right, such an appointment shall be invalid.

It must therefore not be done except with the counsel and judgment of the bishops, who, after the departure of the predecessor, have the power to choose one who is worthy.

### CHAPTER CLXXXVIII — That the canons nowhere prescribe a successor for a bishop on account of illness, and how this may be done if he requests it because of his infirmity

*(From the register of Pope Gregory, to Anatolius, deacon of Constantinople.)* Your affection has written to me that, because my most reverend brother John, bishop of First Justiniana, suffers from a head illness, I should order a bishop to succeed him, lest perhaps—God forbid!—while that city lacks the rights of a bishop, it perish at the hands of an enemy.

Indeed, nowhere do the canons prescribe that a bishop should succeed another because of a bishop’s illness. It is wholly unjust that, if bodily infirmity falls upon him, the sick man should be deprived of his honor.

But it should be suggested that, if someone is ill in his administration, a steward be sought for him who can manage all his affairs and preserve his place in the governance of the Church without deposing him. Thus neither almighty God will be offended nor will the city be found to have been neglected.

### CHAPTER CLXXXIX — Concerning the bishop of Ariminum who suffered from a head illness and in whose place another was appointed

*(From chapter 238 of the register of Saint Gregory the pope.)* Your fraternity has long known that, because the bodily illness hindering the priest whom we ordained has made this evident, the Church of Ariminum has until now been deprived of pastoral and priestly governance.

Moved by the prayers of the inhabitants of that place, we repeatedly urged him that, if he felt himself improved from the head illness by which he was afflicted, he should, with God’s help, return to his Church. After granting him adjournments, we have awaited him for four years.

When we urged him more insistently, in response to the prayers of the clergy and citizens and to our own petitions, that, if he were able, he should return to them with the Lord’s help, he submitted a written petition asking us that, since because of the illness by which he is afflicted he is entirely unable to undertake the governance of that Church or the office he had assumed, we should ordain a bishop for that Church.

Therefore, since the responsibility imposed upon us for all the churches compels us to ensure that pastoral care is not absent from the flock of the faithful for too long, compelled by their prayers and by his renunciation on account of his own inability, we have judged that a bishop ought to be ordained for the Church of Ariminum.

After issuing the customary instructions, we did not cease admonishing the clergy and people of that Church to come together in harmonious deliberation to choose an overseer for themselves. We therefore urge your fraternity to summon to you the man whom all have chosen with one accord, as they themselves are known to have requested from us.

Examine him carefully in every respect. If, with the Lord’s assistance, the things that in the [uncertain: “context of the Eptaticus”] have been punished by death are not found in him, and if his life also pleases you through the report of trustworthy persons, send him to us together with the written record of your decree and a letter of testimony, so that, with the Lord’s arrangement, he may be consecrated by us as bishop of that Church.

### CHAPTER CXC — Concerning a bishop who has fallen into mental weakness through illness

[Col. 0605D]

*(From chapter 2 of the Council of Orange.)* If a bishop falls into illness or into some weakness of the senses, or loses the use of speech, a presbyter is not to be permitted to perform the duties that properly belong to bishops. Rather, let him summon a neighboring bishop, to whom he shall entrust whatever must be done in the Church.

### CHAPTER CXCI — Concerning a bishop who repeatedly fell into insanity because of a head illness

*(From chapter 233 of the register, to Bishop Etherius.)* Although it is very painful for us to speak of what we are saying, and fraternal compassion urges us more than it permits us to determine anything from what we have heard, nevertheless the responsibility of the governance we have undertaken strikes our heart with a pressing goad. It requires us to provide great care for the churches and, before their welfare can perish, to determine with God as our guide what ought to be done.

It has therefore reached us through the report of certain persons that a bishop has suffered such an attack of the head that one can hear him groaning and weeping over what he habitually does with an alienated mind.

Therefore, lest, while the shepherd languishes, the flock—God forbid!—be exposed to the teeth of the prowler to be torn apart, or the interests of that Church perish, we must deal with the matter through prudent foresight.

Since necessity arising from illness, not crime, removes a living bishop from his office, no reason permits another to be ordained in his place unless he himself refuses. But if he is accustomed to have intervals of illness, he should, by submitting a written petition, acknowledge that because of the illness overturning him he can no longer undertake this ministry, and should request that another be ordained in his place.

When this has been done, another who is worthy is to be solemnly elected by all and ordained bishop, but in such a way that, for as long as the present bishop remains alive in this world, his proper expenses are supplied to him from that same Church.

If, however, he never returns to the function of a sound mind, a faithful person of commendable life is to be chosen who can be suitable for governing the Church, can consider the welfare of souls, restrain the disorderly under the bonds of discipline, manage ecclesiastical affairs, and show himself mature and effective in all things. This man is also to be consecrated in his place while the bishop who is now ill is still alive.

### CHAPTER CXCII — Concerning bishops restored by the Roman pontiff

[Col. 0606C]

*(From chapter 7 of Pope Sixtus II’s decree entrusted to the brethren established throughout Spain.)* Know that the brethren whom you unjustly condemned out of earthly fear have been justly restored by us. By the authority of Saint Peter, the apostolic authority, we command that everything taken from them be restored to them in full, unless you and your princes wish to be separated from our fellowship and from the members of the Church.

For by God’s just judgment the power to persecute his saints is often given to sinners, so that those who are helped and led by the Spirit of God may become more illustrious through the exercise of hardships. Those who do this, however, will in no way escape punishment, because, as the Lord says: “Woe to the one through whom scandal comes.” And although, according to the Savior’s sentence, scandals must come, nevertheless woe to the one through whom they come!

It is also a sin rashly to judge the hidden matters of another’s heart, and it is unjust to condemn through suspicion one whose works are seen to be only good, since God alone is the just judge, the true examiner, of things unknown to man.

Hence it is written: “Let us not judge uncertain matters until the Lord comes, who will both illuminate what is hidden in darkness and disclose the purposes of hearts.”

And although such things may be true, they are not to be believed unless they are established by certain judgments, unless they are proved by manifest evidence, unless they are made public in judicial order. No one, therefore, can be condemned by human examination whom God has reserved for his own judgment.

All these matters must be guarded against with the greatest care, lest we appear to be presumptuous.

### CHAPTER CXCIII — Whether priests of the Lord may presume, or be compelled, to swear as the common people customarily do

[Col. 0607A]

*(From Pope Cornelius’s decree.)* We have not learned that an oath is to be demanded from bishops or from the other orders except concerning the true faith, nor have we found that they swore voluntarily.

The holy apostle James, therefore, strongly prohibiting oaths, says: “Above all, my brethren, do not swear, either by heaven or by earth or by any other oath. Let your speech be, ‘Yes, yes; No, no,’ so that you may not fall under judgment.”

### CHAPTER CXCIV — Concerning a bishop covered by an evil rumor, but cleared and absolved by an oath

*(From the register to the emperor Justin, chapter 170.)* It is characteristic of the envy of the ancient enemy that, when he is unable, because God resists him, to deceive those whom he cannot induce to perpetrate wicked acts, he tears them apart for the moment by falsely fabricating reports about them.

Since, therefore, an evil rumor had spread certain allegations against our brother and fellow bishop Leo that were contrary to the priestly calling, we had them investigated through a lengthy and strict inquiry, and we found no fault in him concerning the matters that had been reported.

But lest it appear that anything had been omitted and some doubt remained in our heart, we further required him to give a solemn oath at the most sacred body of blessed Peter. When he had done so, we rejoiced greatly because his innocence shone forth clearly in this matter.

For this reason, let Your Glory receive the aforesaid man with every expression of charity and show him the reverence due to a priest. Let no doubt remain in your hearts concerning matters that have now been purged. You ought so devotedly to adhere to the bishop mentioned above in all things that you may appear properly and fittingly to honor God in his person, since he is God’s minister.

### CHAPTER CXCV — Correction of a bishop who had a concubine

*(From Pope Gregory’s register to Andrew, bishop of Tarentum, chapter 179.)* Whoever, conscious of his guilt, strives to appease the eternal Judge through suitable repentance will look upon the Judge’s tribunal without fear.

We have learned with manifest certainty that you had a concubine, concerning whom some contrary suspicion has also arisen. But since judgment ought not to be absolute in uncertain matters, we have chosen to entrust this to your conscience.

Therefore, if, while established in the sacred order, you remember that you were defiled by intercourse with her, do not presume in any way to approach the ministry after laying aside the honor of the priesthood. Know that you will minister at the peril of your soul and will undoubtedly render an account to our God if, conscious of such a crime, you wish to conceal the truth and remain in the order in which you are.

We therefore exhort you again: if you recognize that you have been deceived by the craft of the ancient enemy, hasten to overcome him through suitable repentance while it is still possible, lest you be counted as his companion on the day of judgment—which we do not desire.

But if you are not conscious of this guilt, you must remain in the order in which you are.

Furthermore, because you assigned a woman from the matriculae to be cruelly beaten with clubs, and although we do not at all suppose that she died from this after eight months, nevertheless, since you refused to have regard for the dignity of your order, we decree that you abstain from the administration of the Masses for two months.

During that period, being suspended from your office, you ought to weep over what you have done. For it is very fitting that, since the examples of worthy priests do not move you toward the tranquil uprightness of this life, the medicine of correction should at least compel you.

### CHAPTER CXCVI — Concerning a bishop cleared and absolved by oaths

*(From the register to Brunhilda, queen of the Franks, chapter 132.)* As for our most reverend brother and fellow bishop Mena, after investigating the matters that had been said about him and finding him guilty of nothing, and after he had satisfied us under oath at the most sacred body of the blessed apostle Peter, demonstrating that he was separate from the charges brought against his reputation, we permitted him to return, purged and absolved.

For just as it was right that, if he had been guilty in any respect, we should canonically punish his fault, so it was not right that, with innocence assisting him, we should detain him longer or afflict him in any way.

### CHAPTER CXCVII — How an elderly bishop is to be rebuked, and how his wicked counselors are to be excommunicated

*(From chapter 37 of the register.)* The apostle Paul, preacher of the almighty Lord, says: “Do not rebuke an elder.” But this rule of his is to be maintained when the elder’s example does not draw the hearts of the young to destruction.

Where, however, an elder provides the young with an example leading to destruction, there he must be struck with a strict rebuke. For it is written: “The snare of the young is you all.” And again the prophet says: “The sinner who is a hundred years old is accursed.”

Such wickedness concerning your old age has reached my ears that, unless we still weighed the matter humanely, we would already have struck it with a fixed curse.

For it was reported to me that, on the Lord’s Day, before celebrating the solemn Masses, you went to plow the field of the bearer of this letter, and that after plowing it you celebrated the solemn Masses. After the solemn Masses, you did not even fear to uproot the boundaries of his property.

What punishment ought to have followed this action is known to all who hear of it. We were uncertain about such great perversity, but when our son Cyriacus, the abbot, was questioned by us, he stated that, while he was a member of the choir, he had learned that this was so.

Because we are still sparing your gray hairs, we exhort you: come to your senses at last, old man, and restrain yourself from such levity of character and perversity of action. The nearer you become to death, the more watchful and fearful you ought to be.

Indeed, the sentence of punishment ought to have been hurled against you, but because we know your simplicity together with your old age, for the time being we remain silent.

We decree that those by whose counsels you did these things are excommunicated for two months, but in such a way that, if anything humanly should happen to them during those two months, they are not to be deprived of the blessing of the viaticum.

From now on, however, be cautious concerning their counsels, and carefully guard yourself, lest, if you become a disciple in evil to those to whom you ought to have been a teacher in good, we spare neither your simplicity nor your old age any longer.

### CHAPTER CXCVIII — Concerning the purification of Pope Leo
(Juramentum Leonis papae.) **The Oath of Pope Leo.**

Beloved brothers, it has been heard and reported in many places how evil men rose up against me, sought to spread this abroad, and brought serious charges against me. For this reason that most merciful and serene lord, King Charles, came to this city together with his priests and nobles. Therefore I, Leo, pontiff of the holy Roman Church, judged by no one and compelled by no one, but of my own free will, [Col. 0609B] clear myself in your presence before God and his angels, who knows my conscience, and before blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, in whose presence we stand: namely, that I neither committed nor ordered to be committed those criminal and wicked acts which they charge against me.

God is my witness, before whose judgment we shall come and in whose presence we stand. I do this of my own free will in order to remove evil suspicions—not as though this practice were found in the canons, or as though I intended to impose this custom or decree upon my successors in the holy Church, or upon our brothers and fellow bishops—but so that you may more effectively cut away rebellious thoughts.

**CHAPTER CXCIX.—If anyone from the ecclesiastical order has been condemned by a synod and dares to undertake anything concerning the sacred ministry**

[Col. 0609C]

(From the Council of Antioch, ch. 4.) If any bishop condemned by a synod, or any presbyter or deacon condemned by his own bishop, should dare to undertake anything concerning the sacred ministry—whether a bishop according to the previous custom, or a presbyter or deacon—it shall in no way be permitted for him to have either hope of restoration in another synod or an opportunity for making satisfaction. Moreover, all who communicate with him are to be cast out of the Church, especially if, after learning that a sentence had been pronounced against the persons mentioned, they should attempt to communicate with them.

**CHAPTER CC.—If someone from the ecclesiastical order has been excommunicated and presumes to communicate, he condemns himself**

[Col. 0609D]

(From the African Council, ch. 29.) It was likewise resolved by the entire council that whoever has been excommunicated for his own negligence—whether a bishop or any cleric—and, during the time of his excommunication, presumes to receive communion before a hearing, is judged to have pronounced the sentence of condemnation upon himself.

**CHAPTER CCI.—Concerning ordained men, if any of them should prove to be a striker**

(From the Council of Mainz, ch. 6.) Those by whom the sacraments of the Lord are administered may not exercise judgment involving bloodshed. Therefore such an excess must be prohibited with the greatest care. Nor may they, driven by impulses of indiscriminate presumption, presume either to pronounce by their own judgment what deserves death [Col. 0610A] or to inflict mutilations upon any persons themselves, or order them to be inflicted. If anyone, forgetful of these precepts, should perpetrate such an act either against members of his own Church or against any persons, he shall be deprived both of the honor and rank of the order he has received and confined in the prison of perpetual condemnation. Nevertheless, communion must not be denied to him when he departs this life, on account of the Lord’s mercy.

**CHAPTER CCII.—Concerning bishops who strike with their own hand**

(From a decree of Pope Boniface.) A bishop must not strike anyone with his own hands. For this ought to be foreign to a priest.

**CHAPTER CCIII.—Concerning a bishop who neglects to correct himself and those entrusted to him**

[Col. 0610B] (Gregory says.) He who has neither governed himself properly, nor cleansed away his own offenses, nor corrected the crime of his children, ought to be called a shameless dog rather than a bishop.

**CHAPTER CCIV.—On the same subject**

(From the sayings of Jerome.) As lye flowing through wet ashes washes but is not itself washed, so good teaching, through a wicked teacher, washes the souls of believers from the filth of sins.

**CHAPTER CCV.—Concerning the wicked shepherd whose sheep flee from him**

(From the sayings of Augustine.) Just as sheep flee from the voice of a shepherd whom they do not know and seek deserted places, so do they flee the fold of a wicked shepherd.

**CHAPTER CCVI.—Concerning one who casts away from himself the nobility of God**

(Gregory says.) Adam, the first man, was expelled from paradise on account of sin; [Col. 0610C] that is, whoever casts away from himself the nobility of God should be deprived of the nobility of his position.

**CHAPTER CCVII.—That not all who occupy the places of saints are sons of saints**

(Jerome says.) It is not easy to stand in the place of Peter and Paul and occupy the chair of those who reign with Christ, because it is said here: “Those who occupy the places of saints are not the sons of saints, but those who perform their works.”

**CHAPTER CCVIII.—That no one ought to boast either of lineage or of position**

(Gregory says.) We who preside must make ourselves known not by the dignity of our positions or lineage, but by nobility of character; not by the splendor of cities, but by purity of faith.

**CHAPTER CCIX.—Concerning priests who provide bad examples to their sheep**

(From the sayings of Augustine.) No one does greater harm in the Church [Col. 0610D] than one who acts perversely while bearing the name or rank of holiness and priesthood. For no one dares rebuke this offender, and the offense is greatly extended as an example when, out of reverence for his rank, a sinner is honored.

**CHAPTER CCX.—That the bishop should have care only of ecclesiastical affairs**

(Apostolic Canon 30.) The bishop shall have charge of all ecclesiastical affairs and shall administer them as though God were observing him. He may not take anything whatever from them for himself or grant to his own relatives what belongs to God. If they are poor, he shall provide for them as for the poor, lest, on their account, the affairs of the Church be plundered.

**CHAPTER CCXI.—Concerning the use of the pallium, so that metropolitans may not use it presumptuously**

[Col. 0611A]

(From a decree of Pope Honorius, ch. 3.) If any metropolitan should presume to wear the pallium in the streets or during litanies, and not only on the principal festivals and at the times appointed by the apostolic see, and solely for the celebration of Mass, let him lose that honor. And, as blessed Pope Gregory writes to John, bishop of Panormus, and to Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna, because he defends a heavy yoke and a burden upon his neck—not for ecclesiastical dignity but for a certain worldly dignity—let him lose the dignity granted to him, which he abuses. For by right he deserves to lose the privilege who boldly usurps what is unlawful.

**CHAPTER CCXII.—That a bishop cannot bequeath the property of his Church by testament unless he first exchanges it with his own property**

[Col. 0611B]

(From the Council of Agde, ch. 6.) If any bishop, having made a testament, should bequeath anything belonging to ecclesiastical property, it shall otherwise have no validity unless he has supplied an equal amount from the resources of his own property.

**CHAPTER CCXIII.—Concerning a bishop who indiscriminately gives the property of his Church to his relatives**

(From the Council of Seville, ch. 10.) Bishops must avoid blame in distributing Church property among their relatives and must observe the measure of discretion.

**CHAPTER CCXIV.—On the same subject**

(From the same council, ch. 5.) Since many bishops, out of love for their relatives, buy estates [Col. 0611C] and slaves from the property entrusted to them, either in their own name or in the name of some friend, and arrange for these to pass into the rights of their relatives, thereby undermining ecclesiastical rights and darkening the priestly ministry—indeed, causing it to be disparaged and despised by those subject to them—it was resolved by all that this kind of greed should henceforth be avoided.

We have decreed that this rule shall be fixed and remain forever: a bishop may, according to canonical authority, do whatever he wishes with property of his own right, which he acquired either before his episcopate or, certainly, during his episcopate by hereditary succession, and may grant it to whomever he wishes. But whatever property he acquires after becoming a bishop from the resources of the Church, whether in his own name or in another’s and under any arrangement, we decree that it shall pass not to his relatives but to the rights of the Church over which he presides.

**CHAPTER CCXV.—That a bishop must not presume to alienate anything from the property of a widowed Church**

[Col. 0611D]

(From a decree of Pope Martin, ch. 20.) If any bishop, compelled by no ecclesiastical necessity, should presume to sell anything from ecclesiastical property, whether within his clergy or where there happens to be no presbyter, he shall be compelled to restore the property itself to the Church. His case shall be heard by the judgment of the bishops, and, as guilty of theft or robbery, he shall be deprived of his honor.

**CHAPTER CCXVI.—Concerning those who disdain to attend the funerals of priests**

(From the Eighth Council of Toledo, ch. 31.) Matters required by propriety are often left undone through the negligence of certain people. Therefore, since it is known from the canons what dignity [Col. 0612A] is to be preserved at the funeral of a dying bishop, we add only this through the tradition of ancient custom: if any priest, after being summoned according to the decrees of the Council of Valencia to come and bury the body of a deceased bishop, should delay through sluggishness, then, upon the clergy’s appealing against him before the synod or the metropolitan bishop, he shall have absolutely no permission for one year either to celebrate Mass or to communicate.

Presbyters and other clerics who held a position of greater honor in that Church whose priest has died, if they are found slow to summon the neighboring bishop with every concern for the funeral of one already dead or of a chief priest who is about to die, or if they are proved to have neglected this through any kind of mental distress, [Col. 0612B] shall be assigned to penance in monasteries for the entire year.

**CHAPTER CCXVII.—That whatever is left to a bishop should be reckoned as transferred to the resources of the Church**

(From the Council of Agde.) As for bishops established in the highest priesthood, if something is given to them by outsiders, or is left or donated to them together with the Church or separately: since the donor is shown to offer this for the redemption of his soul, not for the benefit of the priest, it shall be reckoned not as the bishop’s own property but as something transferred to the resources of the Church. For it is just that, just as the priest possesses what has been left to the Church, so the Church should possess what is left by the priest.

**CHAPTER CCXVIII.—That no bishop should go to war except with the council of the other bishops and the prince**

[Col. 0612C]

(Chapter of Emperor Charles, approved at Aachen concerning bishops.) Charles, by the grace of God king and ruler of the kingdom of the Franks, devoted defender of and helper in all things to the holy Church and the apostolic see:
