At the urging of all our faithful, and especially of the bishops and other priests, and after consultation with them, we entirely prohibit all servants of God from bearing arms, fighting, or going to the army or to war, except only those who have been selected for divine ministry—namely, for fulfilling the solemn celebrations of Mass and carrying the patronage of the saints—that is, one or two bishops together with presbyter-chaplains. Each prince [Col. 0612D] shall also have one presbyter with him who can judge those confessing their sins and assign penance.

**CHAPTER CCXIX.—On the same subject**

(Chapter of the same ruler.) A second time, for the sake of more complete observance, instructed by apostolic authority and the admonition of many bishops, and also taught by the rules of the holy canons, after consultation with all our nobles, correcting ourselves and giving an example to our posterity, we wish no priest to go to war except only two or three bishops, chosen by the others for blessing, preaching, and the reconciliation of the people, together with priests selected to accompany them—men who know well [Col. 0613A] how to assign penance to the people, celebrate Masses, care for the sick, administer anointing with sacred oil and holy prayers, and take particular care that no one departs from this world without viaticum.

**CHAPTER CCXX.—Concerning one who brings a false letter from the apostolic bishop**

(From the Council of Tribur, ch. 30, attended by King Arnulf.) In memory of blessed Peter the apostle, let us honor the holy Roman and apostolic see, so that the one who is the mother of our priestly dignity may be the teacher of ecclesiastical discipline. Therefore humility must be maintained with gentleness, so that, even if a yoke scarcely tolerable is imposed by that holy see, we may accept and endure it with devout dedication.

But if anyone—whether presbyter or deacon—[Col. 0613B] is convicted of having brought a false letter from the apostolic bishop, or something else that was not properly issued from there, by plotting some disturbance, lying in wait for our ministry, acting in bad faith, and lacking sincere humility toward the apostolic see, the bishop shall have authority to thrust him into prison or some other custody until, by letter or through suitable envoys from his own side, he appeals to the apostolic dignity, so that it may deign, through its holy delegation, to decide above all what the Roman law prescribes should be determined concerning such matters according to due order. Thus both he may be corrected and a limit may be imposed upon the others.

**CHAPTER CCXXI.—Concerning accused bishops**

(From a decree of Pope Felix, ch. 4.) If the primates cannot privately reconcile the accusers of bishops with the bishops, [Col. 0613C] then, at the proper time, they shall summon them canonically to a synod convened according to law, not within an unreasonably short period, and shall first inform them in writing of what is being brought against them, so that they may arrive prepared to respond.

For if they have been expelled or stripped of their property by force or fear, they can neither be canonically summoned to a synod nor be required to answer their rivals before they have been canonically restored and all their property has been legally returned to them.

**CHAPTER CCXXII.—That ecclesiastical affairs must not be conducted in the same way as secular affairs**

(From a decree of the same pope, ch. 16.) Ecclesiastical affairs must not be conducted in the same way as secular affairs. Once someone summoned by law has appeared and begun to contend in a public court, [Col. 0613D] he may not withdraw before the case has been completed. In ecclesiastical matters, however, it is permitted to withdraw after the case has been stated, if this should be necessary or if one sees that one is being excessively burdened.

**CHAPTER CCXXIII.—That, while the pope is alive, no one may elect another**

(From a decree of Pope Symmachus, ch. 3.) If any presbyter, deacon, or cleric, while the pope is alive and without consulting him, should attempt to endorse someone for the Roman pontificate, promise him by a written memorandum, give an oath, or promise any support; or if they should deliberate and decide the matter in private gatherings, let him be deprived of the dignity of his position and of communion.

**CHAPTER CCXXIV.—Concerning the bishop’s seat**

[Col. 0614A]

(From the Council of Carthage.) In the Church, when the presbyters are assembled, the bishop shall sit in the more exalted place.

**CHAPTER CCXXV.—Likewise concerning the ordination of a bishop**

(From the sayings of Archbishop Theodore.) At the ordination of a bishop, the one who ordains must celebrate Mass, and the one being ordained likewise.

**CHAPTER CCXXVI.—What the priests of God ought to avoid**

(From the Council of Tours, ch. 1.) Whatever pertains to the allurements of the ears and eyes, by which the strength of the spirit is believed capable of being softened—such as certain kinds of music and various other things—all priests of God must abstain from these. For through the allurements of the ears and eyes, a multitude of vices [Col. 0614B] is accustomed to enter the soul. They must also flee in their own souls the outrageous jokes of shameful and obscene actors, and preach to the other priests that such things must be avoided.

**CHAPTER CCXXVII.—Concerning the inheritance of a bishop and of other ecclesiastics**

(From the Council held at Altheim, ch. 37, attended by King Conrad.) It was also established there concerning bishops, presbyters, and clerics that, if an inheritance has come to them from the Lord King, from another prince, or from a friend, or has fallen to them by hereditary succession, or if they have acquired one, they may, while alive, donate it to whomever they wish: as a remedy for their soul, to whatever Church they choose, or to their relatives or [Col. 0614C] friends.

But if they should die before firmly completing the gift, everything shall be permanently consecrated to the altar at which they serve and transferred to its ownership. The same was decreed concerning presbyters.

Hildibert, archbishop of Mainz, subscribed. Robert, archbishop of Trier, subscribed. Unni, archbishop of Hamburg, subscribed. Adaluvard, bishop of Verden, subscribed. Richwyn, bishop of Strasbourg, subscribed. Noting, bishop of Constance, subscribed. Unewan, bishop of Paderborn, subscribed. Udalric, bishop of Augsburg, subscribed. Bernhard, bishop of Halberstadt, subscribed. Rumald, bishop of Minden, subscribed. Eberis, bishop of Minden, subscribed. The abbots also, together with the other men of the sacred [Col. 0614D] order, subscribed.

**CHAPTER CCXXVIII.—That bishops must not presume to neglect the people entrusted to them for the sake of their own repose**

(From the Council held at Saint-Médard in the presence of King Charles, ch. 5.) Care must be taken that bishops, withdrawing to more remote places for the sake of their own repose and neglecting their ministry, do not abandon their own cities. Instead, they should either travel throughout their dioceses with effective diligence in their office, or live canonically and religiously in their own cities with their clergy. They must also compel the presbyters entrusted to them to be adorned, according to their ministry, with instruction, chastity, sobriety, and hospitality.

**CHAPTER CCXXIX.—Concerning bishops who demand payment for their service without visiting their dioceses**

[Col. 0615A]

(From the Council held at Tribur in the time of King Arnulf, ch. 26.) A complaint of the people was brought before the holy synod: certain bishops were unwilling to travel throughout their dioceses during the year in order to preach or confirm, yet they demanded that those responsible for providing the lodging they ought to have used during their journey redeem it with another payment.

This double disgrace of negligence and greed was a matter of great horror to the holy synod. They decreed that no one should henceforth exercise such a device of greed and that bishops should be more diligent in visiting their flocks.

**CHAPTER CCXXX.—Concerning the purgation of bishops**

(From the Council held at Altheim in the presence of King Conrad [Col. 0615B], ch. 16.) For the love of God and of one’s neighbor, for the honor of the catholic faithful, and especially because of the multitude of scandals that must be eliminated and utterly uprooted, as well as the disturbances that have recently arisen and continue to arise, we have decreed that all should know that we bishops, by God’s mercy, are in no way such as we are said to be. We therefore wish to follow and imitate the example of blessed Pope Leo, who, swearing upon the four Gospels, cleared himself before the people—while nevertheless preserving canonical authority.

**CHAPTER CCXXXI.—Concerning one who has been made a bishop from a monk**

(From the same council, held in the presence of King Conrad, ch. 36.) The synod has established and rationally confirmed, according to the holy Fathers, that a monk whom canonical [Col. 0615C] election releases from the yoke of his profession under the monastic rule, and whom sacred ordination makes a bishop from a monk, may thereafter have the right to claim his paternal inheritance as a lawful heir.

But whatever he had acquired or appeared to possess, he must leave to the monastery, subject to the discretion of his abbot, whom he had had according to the rule of Saint Benedict. After he has been ordained bishop, he must restore to the altar at which he is consecrated and installed whatever he is able to acquire, according to the sacred canons.

**CHAPTER CCXXXII.—Concerning one accused of some heresy, who must recite in the sacred assembly the formula of this profession**

(From Cyril’s letter to John of Antioch.) I, N., by this document which I have written with my own hand, profess that I follow [Col. 0615D] the holy judgment of the Fathers of the Council of Nicaea, numbering three hundred and eighteen, and the universal council of Chalcedon, whose definition the apostolic see confirmed. This was also set forth by the letter of the most blessed Pope Leo, addressed to Flavian, of holy memory, bishop of the city of Constantinople, in a preaching of the clearest truth.

I confess one and the same perfect Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God the Father: the same perfect in divinity, the same perfect in humanity, truly God and truly man. The same one, consisting of a rational soul and flesh, consubstantial with the Father according to divinity and the same consubstantial with us according to humanity, like us in all things [Col. 0616A] except sin: begotten of the Father before the ages according to divinity; but in these last days, for us and for our salvation, the same one born from the Virgin Mary, who bore the same God according to humanity.

I confess one and the same Christ, Son of God, the only-begotten Lord, known in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, and without separation. The distinction of the natures is in no way removed because of the union; rather, the proper character of each nature remains intact, and the two have come together into one person, not into two.

But I declare that those who do not believe in one and the same only-begotten Son, God, true Lord Jesus Christ, as the prophets formerly taught concerning him and as Christ the Lord himself instructed us through his own person, are worthy of eternal anathema together with Nestorius and Eutyches [Col. 0616B] and their followers.

**CHAPTER CCXXXIII.—Concerning bishops who were condemned and later reconciled**

John Chrysostom was judged by two synods of orthodox bishops, but was restored again. Marcellus, bishop of Ancyra in Galatia, was deposed, but afterward recovered his own episcopate. Asclepius was judged by a synod and later recovered his Church. Lucian, bishop of Adrianople, condemned by Pope Julius, recovered the Church of his episcopate. Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem, was deposed and afterward reconciled to his Church.

Likewise, Pope Sixtus [Col. 0616C] condemned Polychronius, pontiff of the same Church of Jerusalem, and then reconciled him himself. Pope Innocent condemned Photinus the bishop, but afterward restored him to his proper place in his Church. The bishop Misenus, condemned by Pope Felix, was both admitted to communion and restored to his Church by his successor, Pope Gelasius. Leontius was deposed while he was a presbyter, but afterward became patriarch in Antioch.

Pope Gregory IV consecrated as bishop of the holy Church of Signia Theodosius, whom his predecessor Eugenius had deprived of the honor of the presbyterate. Bishop Ibas was judged, but the holy synod canonically restored his Church to him. Pope Nicholas reconciled both Rothad, bishop of the holy Church of Soissons, who had been condemned by a synod attended by King Charles, and Soffrenus, bishop of Piacenza [Col. 0616D], who had rightly been rejected.

**Concerning the transfer of bishops**

Since many bishops have migrated and been transferred from one city to another because of the needs or advantages of the times, their names are as follows:

Peregrines was ordained bishop at Petrae, but because the citizens of that city refused to receive him, the bishop of the Roman city ordered him to be enthroned in Corinth, the metropolis. After its bishop had died, he presided over that Church for as long as he lived.

Alexander, bishop of Antioch, transferred Dositheus, bishop of Seleucia, to Tarsus in Cilicia. Reverentius was transferred from Argos in Phoenicia to Tyre [Col. 0617A]. John was transferred from Gordylion to Proconnesus and presided over its Church. Palladius was transferred from Helenopolis to Aspona. Alexander was transferred from another Helenopolis to Adrianople.

Gregory of Nazianzus was first bishop of the Cappadocian city called Sasima; afterward, with the consent of blessed Basil and the other bishops, he was installed at Anzianzus. Meletius first presided over the Church of Sebastia and afterward was appointed bishop of Antioch. Theusebius was transferred [Col. 0618A] from Apamea in Asia to Eudoxiopolis, formerly called Salembria.

Polycarp was transferred from the city of Pristena in Mysia to Nicopolis in Thrace. Hierophilus was transferred from Trapezopolis in Phrygia to Platinopolis in Thrace. Optimus was transferred from Agardamia in Phrygia to Antioch in Pisidia. Silvanus was transferred from Philippopolis in Thrace to Troas.

[Col. 0617] **END OF BOOK ONE.**

**[BOOK TWO.]**

**TABLE OF CHAPTERS OF BOOK TWO.**
[Col. 0617B] **CHAPTER I.** On the ordination of presbyters and the remaining orders. **II.** What presbyters must necessarily learn and know. **III.** On the same matter. **IV.** That ordinations must not be performed except in a definite and religious place. **V.** That Abraham was the first to be called a presbyter, and why presbyters are so named. **VI.** That no one from the ecclesiastical order should be ordained without a specified assignment. **VII.** That ordinations should not be celebrated in the presence of the congregation. **VIII.** That crowds may not conduct the election of those to be advanced.

[Col. 0617C] **IX.** That it is not permissible to ordain a bishop or presbyter before thirty years of age. **X.** On presbyters who are ordained before thirty years. **XI.** That deacons must not be ordained before twenty-five years. **XII.** That the Old Law commands that Levites should not serve in the tabernacle before the age of twenty-five. **XIII.** On presbyters who have been advanced without examination. **XIV.** On one who has deliberately mutilated one of his own limbs. **XV.** On clerics who are made lame by a surgical incision. **XVI.** On those who envy the advancement of their brothers.

[Col. 0617D] **XVII.** That rioters must not be ordained. **XVIII.** That an illiterate person, or one impaired in some limb, must not be advanced. **XIX.** On the sons of concubines. **XX.** That those entangled in demonic or similar afflictions must not handle sacred things. **XXI.** That no one of servile condition may be ordained unless he has first obtained freedom from his own masters. **XXII.** On the same matter. **XXIII.** On the property of those who are granted freedom by their own masters. **XXIV.** That a slave must not be ordained without his master’s knowledge. **XXV.** On those who receive freedom from their masters in such a way that no service is retained from them.

[Col. 0618B] **XXVI.** On slaves to be ordained according to ecclesiastical commands, and how they ought to be made freeborn. **XXVII.** On the same matter. **XXVIII.** On the same matter. **XXIX.** On the same matter. **XXX.** Model document of freedom for one’s own slave. **XXXI.** On the ordination of slaves. **XXXII.** On the slaves of churches. **XXXIII.** That penitents and bigamists must not be advanced. **XXXIV.** That the possessed must not only not be admitted to the clergy, but, if discovered, must be removed from office. **XXXV.** That no one from among penitents may be ordained. **XXXVI.** On administrators and procurators, and whether they ought to be ordained.

[Col. 0618C] **XXXVII.** That no penitent may be admitted to the clergy. **XXXVIII.** That a layman who marries a second wife must not become a cleric. **XXXIX.** That no bishop may presume to retain another bishop’s parishioner. **XL.** That one ordained by another bishop must not remain in the clergy. **XLI.** On a certain bishop who had ordained another bishop’s cleric against that bishop’s will. **XLII.** That no one may receive another’s cleric without the consent of his bishop. **XLIII.** That no bishop may receive another bishop’s cleric without letters from his own bishop. **XLIV.** On presbyters and deacons who travel without letters from their bishop.

[Col. 0618D] **XLV.** On the same matter. **XLVI.** That each person ordained should receive letters from the one who ordained him. **XLVII.** That every ordained person should remain in the places for which he was ordained. **XLVIII.** On a presbyter who confesses that he sinned before ordination. **XLIX.** On the same matter. **L.** That no presbyter may celebrate Mass without priestly vestments. **LI.** That a cleric must not withdraw from office amid temptations. **LII.** That every presbyter should bless water in his church on each Sunday.

[Col. 0619A] **LIII.** Also on the blessing of water. **LIV.** That special Masses must not be celebrated on solemn feast days. **LV.** On the ministry of presbyters, or what has been entrusted to them. **LVI.** That each presbyter should have his own cleric. **LVII.** That the faith of presbyters must first be examined. **LVIII.** On the same matter. **LIX.** What must first be preached concerning how they ought to believe. **LX.** On the same matter. **LXI.** On the same matter. **LXII.** That every presbyter should teach his parishioners the Creed.

[Col. 0619B] **LXIII.** On the same matter. **LXIV.** On love of God and neighbor. **LXV.** On the crimes by which people are assigned to the devil. **LXVI.** That no one should leave the congregation while the priest is speaking. **LXVII.** On the same matter. **LXVIII.** On the same matter. **LXIX.** On prayers after the address. **LXX.** That every presbyter should admonish the people on feast days what prayers they ought to pour out to God. **LXXI.** That presbyters should admonish their congregations to permit cowherds and swineherds to come to Mass on the principal feasts.

[Col. 0619C] **LXXII.** On the presbyters’ admonition. **LXXIII.** How each person ought to pray. **LXXIV.** On children, and how they ought to obey their parents. **LXXV.** On those who celebrate the principal festivals in the villages. **LXXVI.** On the same matter. **LXXVII.** That presbyters should announce to their congregations which days of the year are to be observed as holidays. **LXXVIII.** That when presbyters announce the festivals, they must not forget the vigils. **LXXIX.** That everyone should respond devoutly to the priests’ greetings at Mass. **LXXX.** That no ordained person should wander through holy places while abandoning the care of his own church.

[Col. 0619D] **LXXXI.** How Sunday is to be venerated. **LXXXII.** Also on Sunday. **LXXXIII.** On the same matter. **LXXXIV.** On the same matter. **LXXXV.** On the same matter. **LXXXVI.** On the same matter. **LXXXVII.** On the same matter. **LXXXVIII.** That no one should kneel on Sundays. **LXXXIX.** That presbyters should privately bless faithful people who desire it, and that every presbyter should have authority to confer blessings among families, in the fields, and in private houses.

[Col. 0620A] **XC.** That presbyters must not give the episcopal blessing over the congregation. **XCI.** That no presbyter may receive another presbyter’s parishioner against that presbyter’s will. **XCII.** On another presbyter’s parishioner. **XCIII.** On ordained persons and the other faithful, that they must do nothing without the permission of their bishop. **XCIV.** On the same matter. **XCV.** On the same matter. **XCVI.** That it is not permissible for a cleric to be enrolled simultaneously in the churches of two cities. **XCVII.** On ordained persons, that they must not be transferred from city to city contrary to canon law. **XCVIII.** On the same matter. **XCIX.** That presbyters must not be sent to different places on embassies while abandoning the care of souls.

[Col. 0620B] **C.** That presbyters ought to read continually. **CI.** That presbyters must not go about without their books of hours. **CII.** That a cleric should earn his livelihood by an honorable craft. **CIII.** On the same matter. **CIV.** What presbyters ought to do after completing the morning office. **CV.** On the same matter. **CVI.** What great danger it is for someone who does not know how to govern his own life to become a judge of another’s life. **CVII.** That presbyters should lodge near their churches. **CVIII.** That a presbyter who takes a wife must be deposed. **CIX.** On the same matter.

[Col. 0620C] **CX.** On the same matter. **CXI.** On the same matter. **CXII.** On the same matter. **CXIII.** That female servants must be removed from the presbyters’ storeroom. **CXIV.** That deacons, like bishops and presbyters, must abstain from marital relations. **CXV.** On the same matter. **CXVI.** On the same matter. **CXVII.** On those lacking self-control. **CXVIII.** On ordained persons, if they are caught in fornication, perjury, or theft. **CXIX.** On ordained persons, if they practice usury. **CXX.** On the same matter. **CXXI.** On the same matter.

[Col. 0620D] **CXXII.** On the same matter. **CXXIII.** On the same matter. **CXXIV.** On the same matter. **CXXV.** Also on usurers. **CXXVI.** What usury is. **CXXVII.** On the same matter. **CXXVIII.** On the same matter. **CXXIX.** That no one from the ecclesiastical order may enter taverns for the sake of eating or drinking. **CXXX.** That no one from the sacred order may enter taverns for the sake of food or drink. **CXXXI.** On the same matter. **CXXXII.** That those to whom it is not lawful to marry should avoid the weddings of others.

[Col. 0621A] **CXXXIII.** That a presbyter ought not to dine at the wedding of a bigamist. **CXXXIV.** On the same matter. **CXXXV.** On the same matter. **CXXXVI.** That no cleric may be received in another city without letters of recommendation. **CXXXVII.** On the same matter. **CXXXVIII.** On fugitive clerics, that they must not be received by others. **CXXXIX.** That foreign clerics must not be received without letters from their bishop. **CXL.** That clerics must not remain in another city unless the bishop of the place has first investigated their character. **CXLI.** On clerics and monks who wander without letters from their bishop.

[Col. 0621B] **CXLII.** On the same matter. **CXLIII.** That when the poor and needy depart, assistance should be provided to them through letters of peace. **CXLIV.** That clerics who follow their superiors into other provinces must not minister without a *formata* letter. **CXLV.** That a cleric may not lease another’s property or involve himself in secular business. **CXLVI.** That no layman may presume to involve his presbyter in managing an estate. **CXLVII.** On those presbyters who, contrary to canonical statutes, become estate managers and involve themselves in other business not permitted to them, and on vices that must not be admitted. **CXLVIII.** No cleric—not even a subdeacon—is permitted a carnal marriage.

[Col. 0621C] **CXLIX.** On rulers who are accustomed to assign their priests to judging legal cases. **CL.** On those who intend to serve God, that they must not undertake the administration of households. **CLI.** Also, whether it is permissible for someone from the clergy to become a manager of private persons’ affairs. **CLII.** That if any ordained person, living within the city walls, does not come to the daily sacrifice, he is not to be regarded as a cleric. **CLIII.** On the same matter. **CLIV.** That all the priests of the Lord ought to be taught, so that they may instruct others and make progress themselves. **CLV.** That each presbyter should give an account of his ministry to his bishop every year.

[Col. 0621D] **CLVI.** That every presbyter must compel his subjects to learn the faith. **CLVII.** What profession presbyters or deacons ought to make to their bishop when they are appointed in the parishes. **CLVIII.** No monk who is not a priest, nor any layman, however learned, is permitted to preach. **CLIX.** That parish clerics should learn the canons from their bishops. **CLX.** That no priest is permitted to be ignorant of the canons. **CLXI.** On parish presbyters, when they assemble, that they must not dare to become drunk. **CLXII.** On the same matter.

[Col. 0622A] **CLXIII.** On the same matter. **CLXIV.** On the same matter. **CLXV.** That clerics, as well as religious men, must not begin banquets before the third hour. **CLXVI.** On presbyters, that they should be hospitable. **CLXVII.** On the same matter. **CLXVIII.** That presbyters should admonish their congregations to be hospitable. **CLXIX.** That divine reading should always be combined with priests’ meals. **CLXX.** On clerics living intemperately. **CLXXI.** On vulgar or buffoonish clerics. **CLXXII.** On the same matter. **CLXXIII.** That a cleric must not become a guarantor. **CLXXIV.** That a cleric must not grow a beard. **CLXXV.** On clerics who swear by created things.

[Col. 0622B] **CLXXVI.** On clerics who are found to occupy themselves with flattery and betrayals. **CLXXVII.** On ordained persons who are accustomed, contrary to ecclesiastical commands, to cause annoyance in the ruler’s ears. **CLXXVIII.** On those who oppose their bishops lest they promote them to greater honor in their Church. **CLXXIX.** On a presbyter deposed for a particular crime, if he presumes to do anything concerning the ministry forbidden to him. **CLXXX.** On a condemned presbyter or deacon who has become troublesome to the emperor’s ears. **CLXXXI.** On a presbyter who, by evil examples, has allowed people to suspect evil of him.

[Col. 0622C] **CLXXXII.** On the same matter. **CLXXXIII.** If a cleric has a case against another cleric, he must not resort to secular courts. **CLXXXIV.** On presbyters who are defamed by their congregations, and how they ought to clear themselves. **CLXXXV.** If any ordained person has been condemned by his bishop, no one may defend him. **CLXXXVI.** On a presbyter accused by the people. **CLXXXVII.** On clerics convicted and confessing, if they neglect to clear their case within a year: thereafter their plea must not be heard. **CLXXXVIII.** That no ordained person may presume to swear an oath to a layman.

[Col. 0622D] **CLXXXIX.** If a presbyter or deacon is caught in fornication, perjury, or theft, he must be suspended from office. **CXC.** On ordained persons, if any one of them has been a striker or assailant. **CXCI.** On presbyters who are degraded because of their negligence. **CXCII.** On ordained persons, if they have been unjustly degraded. **CXCIII.** On ordained persons who despise their own bishop. **CXCIV.** If a presbyter, puffed up against his bishop, creates a schism, he must be anathematized. **CXCV.** On those who attack one of the ordained with a false accusation.

[Col. 0623A] **CXCVI.** That the accuser must present to his bishop, before the accusation, the charge against the accused in writing. **CXCVII.** That no ordained person may bring a complaint before a synod except in writing. **CXCVIII.** On accusers of clerics: if they cannot prove one of the charges brought, they must not be admitted to the others. **CXCIX.** If a criminal case has been brought against a bishop or presbyter, how they ought to clear themselves. **CC.** That clerics must not be compelled by foreign judges. **CCI.** One who makes an unjust accusation and fails to prove it must be publicly punished with flogging and deported into exile.

[Col. 0623B] **CCII.** If someone accuses a cleric and cannot substantiate the charge by testimony, the accuser must receive the punishment of the accused. **CCIII.** Just as laymen do not admit clerics in secular matters in their own accusations, so neither may laymen be admitted in accusations against priests. **CCIV.** No one may accept the testimony of a layman against a cleric. **CCV.** On ordained persons, if they are accused and ought to clear themselves through witnesses. **CCVI.** To whom the property of a deceased presbyter should belong. **CCVII.** On presbyters who die without a will. **CCVIII.** On clerics who wear lay clothing.

[Col. 0623C] **CCIX.** On the same matter. **CCX.** On clerics who stroll idly through market fairs. **CCXI.** That no one from the clergy may carry military weapons. **CCXII.** That all clerics should place their confidence more in God’s protection than in weapons. **CCXIII.** On those from the ecclesiastical order who hunt or play with hawks. **CCXIV.** On the servants of God: all woodland wandering with dogs and hawks must be forbidden to them. **CCXV.** That the bishop should reconcile quarrelling clerics by his authority. **CCXVI.** On clerics who break out into mutual slaughter.

[Col. 0624A] **CCXVII.** On the same matter. **CCXVIII.** On the offices and ministries of the seven deacons, together with the subdeacons and ministers of the subsequent orders, which must be observed. **CCXIX.** On the fixed number of deacons. **CCXX.** On the same matter. **CCXXI.** That deacons must not sit in the presence of presbyters. **CCXXII.** On deacons who put themselves before presbyters. **CCXXIII.** That exorcists should lay hands on the possessed. **CCXXIV.** On the honor appropriate to all the orders. **CCXXV.** On priests who do not know how to fulfill their ministry and do not wish to learn, and who must therefore be removed from office.

[Col. 0624B] **CCXXVI.** That those found under the discipline of no bishop must not be counted among the clerics. **CCXXVII.** Model of the *formata* letter composed and commended by the holy Fathers at the Council of Nicaea. **CCXXVIII.** On one who conceals his brother’s flight. **CCXXIX.** On those who mistreat their presbyters. **CCXXX.** That the name of the pope should be recited in the holy Churches. **CCXXXI.** That a presbyter or deacon who is not a canonically enrolled cleric but lives in the villages must never celebrate the principal festivals except in cities.

[Col. 0624C] **CCXXXII.** That presbyters should be granted the authority to preach in their own congregations. **CCXXXIII.** On clerics who are killed in a quarrel. **CCXXXIV.** On clerics who have been freed by their masters. **CCXXXV.** On presbyters who flee the parishes in which they have been appointed. **CCXXXVI.** On presbyters accused of a capital crime who have no colleagues by whom they can clear themselves. **CCXXXVII.** On the preaching of presbyters. **CCXXXVIII.** On ecclesiastical persons, if they desire to possess secular powers. **CCXXXIX.** That truthful and God-fearing men should be appointed deans in cities and public villages.

**End of the Index of Chapters.**

**BURCHARD, BISHOP OF THE CHURCH OF WORMS, BOOK TWO OF THE DECREES: ON THE SACRED ORDERS**

[Col. 0625]

**ARGUMENT OF THE BOOK**

[Col. 0625A]

This book encompasses the ordination, appropriate dignity, quality of life, offices, and ministries of presbyters, deacons, and the remaining ecclesiastical orders.

**CHAPTER I.—On the ordination of presbyters and the remaining orders**

(From the Council of Nantes, chapter 3.) When a bishop intends to perform ordinations, all who wish to enter the sacred ministry must be summoned to the city on the Wednesday before the ordination itself, together with the archpresbyters who are to present them. The bishop must then send from his side priests and other prudent men, knowledgeable in divine law and experienced in ecclesiastical decrees, [Col. 0625B] who are to investigate carefully the life, lineage, homeland, age, education, and place of upbringing of those to be ordained: whether they are well educated and instructed in the law of the Lord. Above all, they must determine whether they firmly hold the Catholic faith and are able to affirm it in simple words.

Those to whom this task is entrusted must take care that they do not, either out of favor or enticed by desire for any payment, depart from the truth and present to the bishop’s hands someone unworthy or insufficiently suitable to receive the sacred orders. If they do so, and the person who has approached the altar unworthily is removed, those who have attempted to sell the gift of the Holy Spirit, already condemned before God, will lose their ecclesiastical dignity. Therefore they must be carefully examined for three consecutive days, and on Saturday those who have been found approved are to be presented to the bishop. [Col. 0625C]

**CHAPTER II.—What presbyters must necessarily learn and know**

(From the sayings of Augustine.) What things are necessary for priests themselves to learn are these: the sacramentary, the lectionary, the antiphoner, the baptismal book, the computus, the penitential canon, the Psalter, and homilies for the Sundays throughout the year, suitable for each feast. If any one of all these is lacking, the title of priest will scarcely remain in him, because the evangelical threats are extremely perilous, as it is said: “If the blind leads the blind, both fall into a pit.”

**CHAPTER III.—On the same matter**

(From a letter of Pope Zephyrinus sent to the brothers throughout Egypt, chapter 10.) Perform the ordinations of presbyters and [Col. 0626A] Levites solemnly at the appropriate time and before many people standing present, and appoint reputable and learned men to this work, so that you may greatly rejoice in their fellowship and assistance.

**CHAPTER IV.—That ordinations must not be performed except in a definite and religious place**

(From the Council of Meaux, chapter 6.) Those who request ordination must on no account be ordained except in a definite and religious place; or they must at least remain for one year in a city, so that certainty may be gained concerning their life, conduct, and learning.

**CHAPTER V.—That Abraham was the first to be called a presbyter, and why presbyters are so named**

(From a letter of Pope Anacletus sent to all the bishops established throughout Italy, chapter 22.) Moreover, Moses too is commanded [Col. 0626B] to choose presbyters, that is, elders. Hence it is said in Proverbs: “The glory of old men is gray hair.” This gray hair signifies wisdom, concerning which it is written: “The gray hair of human beings is prudence.”

Although we read that people lived nine hundred and more years from Adam to Abraham, no one else is recorded as having first been called a presbyter—that is, an elder—except Abraham, who is shown to have lived considerably fewer years. Therefore presbyters are not named on account of decrepit old age, but on account of wisdom.

The beginning of the priesthood was Aaron’s, although Melchizedek first offered sacrifice to God, and after him Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. But these men did so by spontaneous choice, not by priestly authority.

**CHAPTER VI.—That no one from the ecclesiastical order should be ordained without a specified assignment**

[Col. 0626C]

(From the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 6.) No one should be ordained absolutely as a presbyter or deacon, nor anyone to any ecclesiastical rank, unless the name of the church of a city, estate, martyr-shrine, or monastery to which the person being ordained is assigned is specifically pronounced. As for those who are ordained absolutely, the holy synod decreed that such laying on of hands is to be considered invalid, and that they may nowhere minister, to the injury of the one who ordained them.

**CHAPTER VII.—That ordinations should not be celebrated in the presence of the congregation**

(From the Council of Laodicea, chapter 4.) Ordinations ought not to be celebrated in the presence of the congregation.

**CHAPTER VIII.—That crowds may not conduct the election of those to be advanced**

(From the same council, chapter 13.) Crowds must not be permitted to conduct the elections of those who are to be advanced to the priesthood. [Col. 0627A]

**CHAPTER IX.—That it is not permissible to ordain a bishop or presbyter before thirty years of age**

(From the Council of Agde, chapter 7.) No metropolitan should presume to ordain a bishop or presbyter before thirty years of age—that is, before he reaches the age of a fully mature man—lest, because of age, they be held in some error, as has sometimes happened.

**CHAPTER X.—On presbyters who are ordained before thirty years**

(From decrees of Pope Fabian sent to the eastern peoples.) If anyone has not completed thirty years of age, he must in no way be ordained a presbyter, even if he is very worthy, because the Lord himself was baptized in his thirtieth year [Col. 0627B] and then began to teach. Therefore the person who is to be ordained must be consecrated only upon reaching this lawful age.

**CHAPTER XI.—That deacons must not be ordained before twenty-five years**

(From the Council of Carthage, chapter 16.) It was decided that before twenty-five years of age neither deacons should be ordained nor virgins consecrated, and that a lector should not greet the people.

**CHAPTER XII.—That the Old Law commands that Levites should not serve in the tabernacle before the age of twenty-five**

(From the Council of Toledo, chapter 20.) In the Old Law, Levites are commanded to serve in the tabernacle from their twenty-fifth year onward, an authority that the holy Fathers followed in the canons. We, forgetful of the commandment of the divine law and of the councils, make children and boys Levites before the lawful age, before experience of life. Therefore, so that this may not continue to be done by us, we are admonished by the judgments of divine law and the canons: Levites should be consecrated at twenty-five years of age, and presbyters ordained at thirty, so that, in accordance with the apostolic command, they may first be tested and then minister, having no crime. [Col. 0627C]

**CHAPTER XIII.—On presbyters who have been advanced without examination**

(From the Council of Nicaea, chapter 9.) If some presbyters have been advanced without examination, or, when examined, have confessed their sins, and people, stirred up against the canons, have attempted to lay hands upon those who confessed, the rule does not admit such men, because the Catholic Church defends what is irreprehensible. [Col. 0627D]

**CHAPTER XIV.—On one who has deliberately mutilated one of his own limbs**

(From a decree of Pope Innocent, chapter 28.) Accordingly, the canons do not admit to the clergy one who has deliberately cut off part of his finger. But if this happened to someone accidentally, he must not be expelled, even if he is found among the clergy.

**CHAPTER XV.—On clerics who are made lame by a surgical incision**

(From the Council of Lérida, chapter 20.) If a cleric, while suffering from an illness, is made lame by a surgical incision, we do not deny him advancement to the sacred orders.

**CHAPTER XVI.—On those who envy the advancement of their brothers**

[Col. 0628A]

(From the African Council, chapter 54.) A cleric who envies the advancement of his brothers must not be promoted as long as he remains in that vice.

**CHAPTER XVII.—That rioters must not be ordained**

(From the same council, chapter 67.) Rioters must never be ordained clerics, nor usurers, nor those who take revenge for injuries done to them.

**CHAPTER XVIII.—That an illiterate person, or one impaired in some limb, must not be advanced to the sacred orders**

(From a letter of Pope Gelasius, chapter 16.) No one should presume to advance to the clergy those who are illiterate or impaired in any part of the body. For the legal precepts have decreed that one who lacks learning cannot be suitable for sacred duties, and that nothing defective should be offered to God at all. The same applies to those who mutilate themselves. [Col. 0628B]

**CHAPTER XIX.—On the sons of concubines**

(From the Council of Orléans, chapter 10.) Concerning those who have children by concubines, have subsequently set aside legitimate wives, and, after their wives’ deaths, publicly take concubines as partners, we have judged that this rule should be observed: just as we do not remove those who have already been ordained clerics through ignorance, so we decree that such persons must not be ordained in the future.

**CHAPTER XX.—That those entangled in demonic or similar afflictions must not handle sacred things**

(From a letter of Pope Gelasius, chapter 19.) We have plainly discovered that unlawful practices have burst forth to such an extent that the sacred mysteries are entrusted to those entangled in demons and similar afflictions. And a little later: If divine law has in no way permitted someone wounded or disabled in body to touch holy things, how much less is it fitting for those struck in mind—which is worse—to be stewards of the heavenly gift. [Col. 0628C]

**CHAPTER XXI.—That no one of servile condition may be ordained unless he has first obtained freedom from his own masters**

(From the Council of Tribur, chapter 25.) No one of servile condition may be advanced to the sacred orders unless he first obtains lawful freedom from his own masters. The charter of this freedom must be publicly read from the ambo before the ordination; and if no one objects, they may be duly consecrated. A slave who has not been canonically consecrated, however, after falling from his rank, is to remain in the condition in which he was before attaining that rank. [Col. 0628D]

**CHAPTER XXII.—On the same matter**

(From a decree of Pope Leo, chapter 1.) People are admitted indiscriminately to the sacred order who possess no dignity of birth and no dignity of character to support them; those who have been entirely unable to obtain freedom from their masters are advanced to the height of the priesthood, as though servile baseness had a rightful claim to this honor. It is believed that such a person can be approved by God even though he has not yet been able to approve himself to his master.

And a little later: The person who is to be enrolled in the divine army must be free from others, so that he may not be dragged away by any bonds of necessity from the Lord’s camp, in which his name is enrolled.

**CHAPTER XXIII.—On the property of those who are granted freedom by their own masters**

[Col. 0629A]

(From the Council of Toledo, chapter 2.) Concerning their possessions, or personal property, since they are granted freedom by their own masters so that they may be advanced to the ecclesiastical orders, it has been decreed that whatever they possessed before freedom remains under the authority of their masters, who may decide whether they wish to grant it to them or retain it for themselves.

**CHAPTER XXIV.—That a slave must not be ordained without his master’s knowledge**

(From the Council of Orléans, chapter 5.) If a slave is ordained a deacon or presbyter while his master is absent or unaware, although the bishop knows that he is a slave, and the slave remains in clerical office, the bishop must compensate his master with double restitution. But if the bishop did not know that he was a slave, those who give testimony or who requested that he be ordained must likewise be held liable for similar restitution. [Col. 0629B]

**CHAPTER XXV.—On those who receive freedom from their masters in such a way that no service is retained from them**

(From the Council of Toledo, chapter 73.) Whoever receives freedom from his masters in such a way that the patron retains no service from him, if he is free from a capital crime, must be received as a free man into the clerical order, since he is known to have been liberated by direct manumission. Those, however, who have been manumitted with service retained remain bound to their patrons’ servitude; they must in no way be advanced to the ecclesiastical order, lest their masters, whenever they wish, make slaves out of men who are clerics.

**CHAPTER XXVI.—On slaves to be ordained according to ecclesiastical commands, and how they ought to be made freeborn**

[Col. 0629C]

(From the Council of Reims, chapter 1.) Ecclesiastical authority plainly admonishes—and royal majesty also gives its assent to canonical religion—that whenever a church chooses to advance someone from its own household to the sacred orders, he must be solemnly confirmed, in the presence of canonical priests and noble laymen, by the signature and manumission of the person to whom he is subject, under a deed of freedom.

Therefore I, Burchard, by God’s assent bishop of the Church of Worms, establish by this authoritative deed, at the altar’s horn and in the presence of noble men, that a certain servant of our Church, named Eberhard, who has been offered to the sacred orders, shall from this day and time onward remain fully freeborn and secure from every bond of servitude, as though he had been begotten or born of freeborn parents. Let him proceed to whichever status he canonically chooses, so that henceforth he owes neither us nor our successors any service of an injurious condition; rather, throughout all the days of his life, under a certain and complete freedom, like the others who possess the same freedom, he shall by this title of manumission and freedom remain always fully freeborn and secure.

As for the personal property he possesses, or may henceforth acquire, let him freely do with it whatever he wishes, according to canonical authority. And so that this charter of freedom may possess inviolable firmness, we have confirmed it with our own hand. [Col. 0630A]

**CHAPTER XXVII.—On the same matter**

(From the Council of Toledo.) The aforementioned charters of freedom must contain not only the name of the person who requests that they be made, but also, arranged in order, the names of the priests and noble laymen who were present there, together with signs impressed by their own hands. For without their attestation, a document deprived of the authority of witnesses is considered worthless.

They must also have the place, day, year, ruler, and indictions noted at the end or in the margin in this form: “Done in that city, in the house of Saint Peter, on that Kalends, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation ___, while ___ was reigning, under that king, and while that bishop was presiding in the see of the aforesaid [Col. 0630B] city, or in that monastery, in that indiction. In the name of God, successfully. Amen.” For Roman authority says: “Whatever laws have been issued without a date and consul are invalid.”

**CHAPTER XXVIII.—On the same matter**

(From the same council.) Laymen must also be instructed so that they know that they may by no means manumit in another place their own slaves whom they have decided to enroll in the Lord’s army, except in the holy Church, according to the procedure set out above. For how can clerics obtain freedom outside the Church, when they are strangers to secular law? And since they are forbidden to proceed to a secular court, how can they be released from the yoke of servitude by a secular judgment?

But perhaps someone will say: “A person is not permitted to become a cleric unless, before undertaking clerical office, he has attained the dignity of freedom.” Indeed, he speaks truly. And therefore whatever can be weakened or criticized must be guarded against. [Col. 0630C]

**CHAPTER XXIX.—On the same matter**

(From the same council.) Not only those who are to be advanced to the clerical order must be manumitted in the Church, but also those whom anyone wishes to emancipate for the remedy of his soul, because it is so written in the compact of the Franks.

**CHAPTER XXX.—Model document of freedom for one’s own slave**

(From the same council.) Let anyone who releases the bond owed to him and the service that is properly due have no doubt that a reward will come to him from the Lord in the future.

Therefore I, ___, in the name of God, for the remedy of my soul, or for eternal recompense, in the church of Saint Peter, or of that saint, in the presence of the bishop or of the priests assembled there, and of noble laymen, before the horn of this church’s altar, by this charter of release and freedom absolve my slave ___ from every bond of servitude, so that from this day onward he may be and remain freeborn, as though he had been born or begotten of freeborn parents.

Let him proceed to whichever status he prefers, or which canonical authority permits him, and let him live a free life like other freeborn persons. To none of my heirs or prospective heirs, nor to any other person, shall he owe any service of servitude or service arising from freedom, except to God alone, to whom all things are subject, or for whose love I have devotedly offered him to his service.

As for his personal property, whether his master has given it to him or, with God’s help, he may henceforth acquire it through his labor, let him possess it forever as granted, so that he may do with it whatever pleases him, according to ecclesiastical sanctions.

If anyone—which I do not believe will happen—whether I myself, one of my heirs, or any opposing person, attempts to act against this charter of freedom or in any way seeks to violate it, let him first incur the wrath of God, be excluded from the thresholds of God’s holy Church, and moreover pay sixty solidi to the person against whom he brought the suit; nor shall he be able to establish the claim he is pursuing. Rather, this present freedom, confirmed by my hands or those of other good men and supported by attestation, shall remain unshaken forever. [Col. 0631A]

**CHAPTER XXXI.—On the ordination of slaves**

[Col. 0631B]

(From the same, chapter 82.) Concerning the ordination of slaves, who are indiscriminately promoted everywhere to ecclesiastical orders: it was agreed that this must conform to the sacred canons, and it was decreed that henceforth no bishop should presume to promote them to sacred orders unless they had first obtained freedom from their own masters. If any slave, fleeing or hiding from his master, or by employing hired or bribed witnesses, or by any other cunning or fraud, should attain ecclesiastical orders, it was decreed that he be deposed and that his master receive him. But if a grandfather or father, migrating from one homeland [Col. 0631C] to another, should beget a son in that same province, and the son, brought up there, should be promoted to ecclesiastical orders, while it remained unknown whether he was a slave, and afterward his master should come and legally claim him, it was decreed that, if his master wished to grant him freedom, he should remain in his order. But if the master wished to drag him away from the Lord’s encampments by the chain of slavery, he should lose his order, because, according to the sacred canons, a person remaining of servile status cannot exercise the dignity of the priesthood.

### CHAPTER XXXII.—Concerning the slaves of churches

[Col. 0631D]

(From the same council, chapter 33.) Concerning the slaves of churches, it has been decreed by common agreement that the archbishops established in the several provinces should follow our authority; their suffragans, however, should keep a copy of it with them. Whenever someone from the household of the Church is found suitable for ordination, this authority itself shall be read before the people in the pulpit and before the priests and the entire clergy beside the altar’s horn, and, as contained in our authority, he shall obtain freedom, with every form of cunning excluded; only then shall he be promoted to ecclesiastical orders.

### CHAPTER XXXIII.—That penitents and digamists are not to be promoted

(From the Council of Aurelian, chapter 3.) Let digamists, penitents, and husbands of repudiated women not be promoted to the priesthood.

### CHAPTER XXXIV.—The possessed are not only not to be admitted to the clergy, but, if discovered, are to be removed from office

[Col. 0632A]

(From the Council of Orange, chapter 6.) The possessed are not only not to be admitted to any clerical order, but those who have been ordained are also to be removed from the office imposed upon them.

### CHAPTER XXXV.—That no one is to be ordained from among the penitents

(From the Council of Carthage, chapter 68.) No penitent, however good, is to be ordained a cleric. If this should have occurred through the bishop’s ignorance, he is to be deposed from the clergy, because he did not disclose at the time of his ordination that he was a penitent.

### CHAPTER XXXVI.—Whether agents and administrators should be ordained

[Col. 0632B]

(From the same, chapter 9.) Magnus, bishop of Astuaga, said: “What does your affection think? Should administrators, agents, or even guardians of orphans be ordained?” Bishop Gratus said: “If, after all their affairs have been relinquished and their accounts rendered, the conduct of their lives has been found in every respect satisfactory, they ought, if requested, to be honored with the praise and dignity of the clergy. For if they have been ordained by anyone, without due consideration, before being released from business or official responsibilities, the Church is disgraced.” All said: “Your holiness has rightly established everything; therefore this is also our judgment.”

### CHAPTER XXXVII.—That no penitent is to be admitted to the clergy

(From the First Council of Toledo, chapter 1.) It was also agreed that penitents should not be admitted to the clergy, except that, if necessity or need should require it, they may be assigned among the doorkeepers or among the readers, but in such a way that they do not read the Gospels or the Apostle. Those who have already been ordained as subdeacons are to remain among the subdeacons, but they are not to lay on hands or touch the sacred things. We call someone a penitent who, after baptism, whether for homicide or for various grave crimes and sins, has performed public penance in sackcloth and has been reconciled at the divine altar.

### CHAPTER XXXVIII.—A layman who has married a second wife is not to become a cleric

(From the Council of Aurelian, chapter 8.) If any layman, after his wife, has relations with another woman of whatever status, he is in no way to be admitted to the clergy.

### CHAPTER XXXIX.—That no bishop should presume to retain another’s parishioner

[Col. 0632D]

(From a decree of Pope Hadrian, chapter 15.) No bishop should presume to retain, ordain, or judge another bishop’s parishioner without his consent. For just as his ordination will be invalid, so also will his judgment, since we hold that no one is bound by the sentence of any judge other than his own. For he who could not ordain him cannot in any way judge him.

### CHAPTER XL.—That one ordained by another bishop is not to remain in the clergy

(From the Council of Mainz, chapter 4.) A cleric ordained by another bishop, without his own bishop’s request or consent, is not to remain in the clergy.

### CHAPTER XLI.—Concerning a certain bishop who had ordained another bishop’s cleric against his will

[Col. 0633A]

(From the Council of Africa, chapter 42.) Bishop Epigonius said: “This has been established in many councils, and now it must be confirmed by your prudence, most blessed brothers: no bishop should seize for himself another’s cleric against the will of the one whose cleric he is. I speak of Julian, who, ungrateful for the benefits of God bestowed upon him through my insignificance, has proved so rash and audacious that he has taken the man who was baptized by me when he was a very needy boy, who had been entrusted to me by the same person, and whom I supported and raised for many years. As I have said, it is established that he was baptized in my church by the hand of my insignificance. He had begun to serve as a reader in the diocese of Mepalia [Col. 0633B], indeed he had read there for nearly two years; but, I do not know through what most monstrous contempt, this same Julian seized him—he is said to have usurped him, without consulting me, as though he were a citizen of his own place, Vazaritani. For he also ordained him a deacon. If this is permitted, let this license be openly granted by you, most blessed brothers. If not, let such shamelessness be restrained, lest he intrude upon anyone’s communion.”

Bishop Numidius said: “If Julian appears to have done this without requesting or consulting your dignity, we all judge that it was done unjustly and unworthily. Therefore, unless Julian corrects his error and, with satisfaction, restores to your people the same cleric whom he had dared to ordain, let him, because he has acted against the statutes of the council, receive from us a judgment on his obstinacy, separated from our fellowship.”

Bishop Epigonius [Col. 0633C] said: “Our brother and colleague Victor, a father in age and most senior in rank, a praiseworthy man, wishes this petition to be made general for all.”

### CHAPTER XLII.—That no one should receive another’s cleric without his bishop’s consent

(From the Council of Carthage, chapter 20.) No one should dare either to retain another’s cleric or to promote him in the church entrusted to him unless his own bishop grants permission. The designation “clerics,” however, includes readers, psalmists, and doorkeepers.

### CHAPTER XLIII.—That no bishop should receive another’s cleric without letters from his bishop

(From the same council, chapter 6.) Bishop Privatus of Begesila said: “I submit to your holiness that you decree it unlawful for anyone to receive another’s cleric without letters from his bishop, or to retain him, and that no one should take a layman from another’s congregation for himself in order to ordain him without the knowledge of the one whose congregation he belongs to.”

Bishop Gratus said: “Observing this preserves peace. For a similar rule was established at the council of holy Sardica, that no one should appropriate a man belonging to another’s congregation. But if necessity should arise, let him ask his colleague and obtain his consent.”

### CHAPTER XLIV.—Concerning priests and deacons who travel without letters from their bishop

(From the Council of Agde, chapter 5.) Let no one offer communion to a priest, deacon, or cleric who travels without letters from his bishop.

### CHAPTER XLV.—Concerning the same matter

[Col. 0634A]

(From the Council of Laodicea, chapter 41.) A priest or cleric ought not to travel without canonical letters.

### CHAPTER XLVI.—That every ordained person should receive letters from his ordaining bishop

(From the Council of Milevis, chapter 14.) It was then agreed that everyone ordained henceforth by bishops should receive letters from those who ordained them, signed by their hand and stating the year and day of the Lord, so that no dispute might arise concerning what was earlier or later.

### CHAPTER XLVII.—That every ordained person should remain in the places for which he was ordained

(From the Council of Orléans, chapter 2.) Those who have been ordained ministers in any places are to remain in those same places.

### CHAPTER XLVIII.—Concerning a priest who confesses that he sinned before ordination

(From the Council of Chalon, chapter 5.) If a priest sinned before ordination and, after ordination, confesses that he had previously gone astray, he is not to offer the sacrifice, but, for the sake of religious observance, may retain the name of priest. But if he did not confess it himself and was publicly convicted by another, he is not even to retain the privilege of bearing the name of priest. The same is to be observed concerning deacons: if a deacon himself confesses, he is to retain the order of subdeacon.

### CHAPTER XLIX.—Concerning the same matter

(From the Council of Neocaesarea, chapter 8.) If a priest, overtaken by bodily sin, is promoted and confesses that he committed an offense before ordination, he is not to consecrate the offerings, but may remain in the other duties because of his good zeal. If he does not confess it himself and cannot be openly accused, he is to be left to the judgment of his own authority.

### CHAPTER L.—That no priest should celebrate Mass without priestly vestments

(From the Council of Reims, chapter 4.) No priest should presume in any way to celebrate Mass without an amice, alb, stole, fanon, and chasuble. These sacred vestments are to be perfectly clean and kept in a bright, clean place within the church. A priest should never go outside the church wearing them, because the divine law forbids this.

### CHAPTER LI.—That a cleric should not withdraw from his office amid temptations

[Col. 0634D]

(From the sayings of Augustine.) A cleric who withdraws from his office amid temptations, or acts negligently, is to be removed from that office.

### CHAPTER LII.—That every priest should bless water in his church on each Sunday

(From the Council of Nantes, chapter 5.) On every Sunday each priest, in his own church and before the solemn celebration of Mass, is to prepare blessed water in a clean vessel suitable for so great a mystery. The people are to be sprinkled with it as they enter the church, and the church’s courtyard is likewise to be sprinkled as he goes around it with crosses, while he prays for the souls resting there. Anyone who wishes may take some of this water in small vessels and sprinkle it over his dwellings, fields, vineyards, livestock, their fodder, and also his food and drink.

### CHAPTER LIII.—Further concerning the blessing of water

(From a letter of Pope Alexander sent to the brothers throughout Egypt.) “We bless water sprinkled with salt for the people, so that all who are sprinkled with it may be sanctified. We command all priests to do the same. For if the ashes of a heifer, when sprinkled, sanctified and cleansed the people, how much more does water sprinkled with salt and consecrated by divine prayers sanctify and cleanse the people? And if, through salt sprinkled by the prophet Elisha, the barrenness of the water was healed, how much more does water consecrated by divine prayers remove the barrenness of human things, sanctify and cleanse the contaminated, multiply other goods, turn away the devil’s snares, and defend a person from the deceits of phantoms?”

### CHAPTER LIV.—That private Masses are not to be celebrated on solemn days

(From the sayings of Augustine.) “This too must be observed: private Masses celebrated by priests on solemn days are not to be performed publicly in such a way that through them the people are drawn away from the public solemn Mass, which is canonically celebrated at the third hour. For among certain people there is a very bad custom: on Sundays or on any festivals they immediately celebrate a Mass which, even if it is for the dead, a person leaves after hearing, and then spends the entire day, from early morning, serving drunkenness and feasting rather than God.

“The people are to be admonished not to approach food before the public service has been completed, but all are to assemble at the public holy mother church to hear the solemn Mass and the preaching. Priests are to celebrate Mass at the third hour, so that the people are not drawn away from the public solemnity. The priests who are in the vicinity of the city or in the city itself, and the people, as we have said, are to gather together for the public celebration of Mass, except for women consecrated to God, whose custom is not to go out in public but to remain enclosed within the monastery’s cloisters.”

### CHAPTER LV.—Concerning the ministry of priests, or what has been entrusted to them

(From the sayings of the same author.) “You priests must truly know and always remember that we, to whom the care of governing souls has been entrusted, will have to render an account for those who perish through our negligence; but for those whom we have won through words and examples, we shall receive the reward of eternal life. For the Lord has said to us: ‘You are the salt of the earth.’ And if the faithful people are God’s food, we are the seasoning of that same food.

“Know that your rank is subordinate and almost joined to our rank. For just as bishops in the Church take the place of the apostles, so priests clearly take the place of the Lord’s other disciples. The former hold the rank of Aaron, the high priest; the latter, that of his sons. Therefore you must always remember so great a dignity, remember your consecration, remember the sacred anointing that you received into your hands, so that you neither degenerate from that dignity, nor make your consecration void, nor pollute by sinning the hands smeared with sacred ointment. Instead, preserving purity of heart and body and offering your congregations an example of good living, provide those over whom you preside with guidance toward the heavenly kingdoms.”

### CHAPTER LVI.—That each priest should have one cleric

(From the Council of Nantes, chapter 9.) Every priest who governs a congregation is to have a cleric who sings with him, reads the Epistle and the reading, can maintain a school, and admonishes his parishioners to send their children to the church to learn the faith; he himself is to instruct them with complete chastity.

### CHAPTER LVII.—That the faith of priests must first be examined

[Col. 0636B]

(From the Council of Mâcon, chapter 3.) First of all, the faith of priests must be examined: how they believe and teach others to believe. Examples are also to be set forth there, so that the Creator may be understood, however slightly, from the creature.

### CHAPTER LVIII.—Concerning the same matter

(From the sayings of Augustine.) “We urge you to be ready to teach our congregations. Let the one who knows the Scriptures preach the Scriptures. But let the one who does not know them at least tell the people what is most familiar to them: that they turn away from evil, do good, seek peace, and pursue it, because the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous and his ears are toward their prayers. But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil, to destroy their memory from the earth.

“Therefore no one will be able to excuse himself by saying that he does not have a tongue with which he can edify someone. As soon as he sees anyone going astray, let him, according to his ability and strength, draw him back from error—whether by reproving, entreating, or rebuking—and exhort him to accomplish a good work.”

### CHAPTER LIX.—What should first be preached concerning how people ought to believe

(From the Council of Rouen, chapter 1.) First of all, it must be preached to everyone generally that they believe the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit to be one almighty God, who made all things, and that there is one deity, substance, and majesty in three persons: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

### CHAPTER LX.—Concerning the same matter

(From the same, chapter 2.) It must also be preached how the Son of God was incarnate from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary; how, for the salvation of the human race, he suffered, was buried, rose again on the third day, and ascended into heaven; and how, at the end of the world, he will come to judge all people according to their own works. It must be preached how the wicked will be sent with the devil into eternal fire, while the righteous will be with Christ in eternal life.

### CHAPTER LXI.—Concerning the same matter

(From the same, chapter 3.) It must also be preached that all people will rise again in their own flesh.

### CHAPTER LXII.—That every priest should teach his parishioners the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer

[Col. 0637A]

(From the Council of Reims, chapter 8.) Every priest is either to teach the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer to all his parishioners himself, or to instruct others to teach them. When they come to confession during Lent, he is to have each person recite these from memory, and he is not to give anyone holy communion before that person knows how to recite them from the heart. For no one can be saved without knowledge of these. In the one, Christian faith and belief are contained; in the other, what we ought to pray and ask from God is expressed.

“That no one can be saved without faith, the Lord showed when he said: ‘Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved.’ But no one can believe what he does not know or hear. For Paul says: ‘How will they believe in him whom they have not heard?’ Nor is faith alone in the heart sufficient unless it is also expressed in words, as the same Apostle testifies: ‘With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.’

“Let no one plead dullness of understanding or weakness of intellect. These matters are so simple that no one is so slow or barbarous that he cannot learn them and pronounce them in ordinary words; and they are so great that anyone who is able fully to grasp their meaning may believe that they are sufficient for his everlasting salvation.

“This too must be observed: no one should lift an infant from the sacred font at baptism before that same person has recited the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer before the priest. Then the priest is to announce to all the sponsors that, when their godchildren reach the age of understanding, they are responsible for teaching them these same things.”

### CHAPTER LXIII.—Concerning the same matter

(From the Council of Chalon, chapter 4.) It must be ordered that the Lord’s Prayer, in which all necessities of human life are contained, and the Apostles’ Creed, in which the Catholic faith is contained in its entirety, be learned by everyone, both in Latin and in the vernacular, so that what they profess with their mouths may be believed and understood in their hearts.

### CHAPTER LXIV.—Concerning love of God and neighbor

(From the same, chapter 5.) It must also be preached that people love God and their neighbor; concerning faith and hope in God; concerning humility, patience, chastity, kindness, mercy, almsgiving, and confession, so that they forgive their brothers from the heart. Those who do these things and the like will obtain the kingdom of God.

### CHAPTER LXV.—Concerning the crimes by which people are assigned to the devil

(From the same, chapter 4.) It must also be preached for which crimes people are assigned to the devil, which the Apostle enumerates as follows: fornication, uncleanness, debauchery, service of idols, sorceries, enmities, quarrels, rivalries, anger, disputes, dissensions, factions, envy, murders, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these. Those who do such things will not obtain the kingdom of God; therefore these practices must be prohibited with every effort.

### CHAPTER LXVI.—That no one should leave the congregation while the priest is speaking

[Col. 0638A]

(From the Council of Carthage, chapter 24.) When a priest is speaking in the church, anyone who leaves the congregation without serious necessity is to be excommunicated.

### CHAPTER LXVII.—Concerning the same matter

(From the Apostolic Canon.) All the faithful who gather in the church for solemn sacred rites and hear the writings of the Apostles and the Gospel, but do not remain in prayer until the Mass is completed and do not receive holy communion, are rightly to be deprived of communion as people who stir up disturbances in the Church.

### CHAPTER LXVIII.—Concerning the same matter

(From the preceding.) All Christians who enter the church of God and hear the holy Scriptures, but do not join the people in prayer and, through a kind of lack of self-control, turn away from receiving holy communion, are to be removed from the Church until they show the fruits of penitence through confession.

### CHAPTER LXIX.—Concerning prayers after the address

(From the Council of Laodicea, chapter 19.) First, after the addresses of the bishops or priests, prayer is to be offered separately over the catechumens; after the catechumens have gone out, prayers are to be made over those who are doing penance. When these too have approached the priest’s hand and departed, three prayers of the faithful are to be completed, the first in silence, and the second and third with the customary acclamations.

### CHAPTER LXX.—That every priest should admonish the people on feast days what prayers they ought to pour out to God

[Col. 0638C]

(From the Council of Orléans, chapter 3.) On Sundays or feast days, after the sermon delivered to the people during the solemn celebration of Mass, the priest ought to admonish them that, according to apostolic instruction, all should together pour out prayers to the Lord for various needs: for the king and their bishop, for the rulers of the Churches, for peace, for pestilence, for the sick who lie in bed in that parish, and for those recently deceased. In these prayers, the people are to recite the Lord’s Prayer silently, each person individually. The priest, however, is solemnly to complete the prayers appropriate to each admonition. After this, the sacred offering is to be celebrated. For the Apostle says: “I urge, first of all, that prayers, supplications, thanksgivings, and the rest be made.”

### CHAPTER LXXI.—That priests should admonish their congregations to permit herdsmen and swineherds to come to Mass on the principal feast days

(From the Council of Rouen, chapter 5.) Priests must admonish the congregations subject to them to ensure that herdsmen, swineherds, other shepherds, and ploughmen who live continually in the fields or woods and therefore live, as it were, like animals, at least on Sundays and other feast days either attend or are permitted to attend Mass. For Christ redeemed these people too with his precious blood.

“If they neglect this, they should know without doubt that they will have to render an account for their souls. When the Lord came into this world, he did not choose orators and the nobility, but took fishermen and uneducated people as his disciples, to show by deed what he affirms in words in the Gospel: ‘What is exalted among human beings is abominable before God.’ And, without prejudice to the higher meaning, the birth of our Redeemer was first announced by an angel to shepherds.”

### CHAPTER LXXII.—Concerning the admonition of priests

(From the Council of Orléans, chapter 4.) Priests are to admonish the people to give alms and offer prayers for the various afflictions that we continually suffer because of our sins.

### CHAPTER LXXIII.—How each person ought to pray

[Col. 0639B]

(From the same, chapter 6.) The people are also to be instructed that each day, if they cannot pray more often, they should pray at least twice—namely, morning and evening—reciting the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer, or “You who formed me, have mercy on me,” or also, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner.” They should give thanks to God for the provisions of daily life, because he deigned to create them in his own image and separate them from the animals. When this has been done and they have worshiped God alone, their Creator, they should invoke the saints, asking that they deign to intercede for them with the divine majesty.

Those for whom a basilica is nearby are to do these things in the basilica. Those who are traveling, or who for any reason are in the woods or fields, are to do the same wherever the morning or evening hour finds them, knowing that God is present everywhere, as the Psalmist says: “His dominions are in every place.”

### CHAPTER LXXIV.—Concerning how children ought to obey their parents

(From the Council of Auvergne, chapter 3.) The faithful sons and daughters of the holy Church of God are to be admonished to show obedience to their parents, as the Lord says: “Son, honor your father.” Parents too are to be admonished to behave moderately toward their sons and daughters, as the Apostle says: “And you, parents, do not provoke your children to anger.”

They must also be told that, even if parents wish, out of natural affection, to spare their children’s offenses, the Lord nevertheless does not allow these children to remain unpunished unless they submit to penance. Yet it is lighter for children to endure whatever punishments their parents impose than to incur the wrath of God.

### CHAPTER LXXV.—Concerning those who celebrate the principal festivals in villages

(From the Council of Orléans, chapter 8.) It must also be announced that no citizen may celebrate the solemnities of Easter, the Nativity of the Lord, or Pentecost in a village, except one whom illness is proved to have detained there.

### CHAPTER LXXVI.—Concerning the same matter

(From the Council of Agde, chapter 5.) The citizens are also to be taught that, unless illness prevents them, they should celebrate Easter, the Nativity of the Lord, and Pentecost in the cities with their bishops, for the sake of receiving communion or a blessing. Those who neglect this are to be deprived of communion.

### CHAPTER LXXVII.—That priests should announce to their congregations which days are to be kept as holidays during the year

[Col. 0640A]

(From the Council of Lyon, chapter 4.) It must also be announced that they should know the times for keeping holidays throughout the year: namely, every Sunday from evening to evening, lest they be caught up in Judaism. The following days are to be kept as holidays during the year: the Nativity of the Lord; Saint Stephen’s Day; Saint John the Evangelist’s Day; the feast of the Innocents; the octave of the Nativity of the Lord; the Theophany; the Purification of Saint Mary; Holy Easter with the whole week; the Rogation Days for three days; the Ascension of the Lord; the holy days of Pentecost; the feast of Saint John the Baptist; the feast of the twelve Apostles, especially that of Saints Peter and Paul, who enlightened the world by their preaching; Saint Lawrence’s Day; the Assumption of Saint Mary; the Nativity of the Virgin Saint Mary; the dedication of the basilica of Saint Michael the Archangel; the dedication of any oratory; All Saints’ Day; Saint Martin’s Day; and those festivals that individual bishops, in their dioceses, have approved together with the people. The latter are to be announced only to those living nearby, not generally to everyone.
