The remaining festivals throughout the year are neither to be imposed as holidays nor prohibited. Whenever an appointed fast has been announced, however, it is to be observed by everyone.

### CHAPTER LXXVIII.—That priests, when announcing festivals, should not forget the vigils

(From the Council held at Compiègne, chapter 1.) When priests announce the sacred festivals to the people, they are also to urge them in every way to observe the fast of the vigils wherever it is required.

### CHAPTER LXXIX.—That everyone should respond devoutly to the priests’ salutations at Mass

(From the Council of Orléans, chapter 2.) It must also be made known that appropriate responses to the priests’ salutations are to be learned. Not only clerics and women dedicated to God are to offer a response to the priest, but the entire congregation must respond with one harmonious voice.

### CHAPTER LXXX.—That no ordained person should wander through holy places while abandoning the care of his church

(From the sayings of Augustine.) It must be forbidden for any ordained person, or anyone awaiting ordination, to leave his parish for another, or to go to the thresholds of the Apostles for the sake of prayer, while abandoning the care of his church, or to go to the palace to present a petition. If he does so, neither such ordination nor such departure has any validity.

This is also to be announced to all the faithful: those who wish to go to the thresholds of the blessed Apostles for the sake of prayer should confess their sins at home and then depart, because they must be bound or released by their own bishop or priest, not by a stranger.

### CHAPTER LXXXI.—How Sunday is to be venerated

(From the Council held at Compiègne, chapter 2.) We have decreed that every Sunday is to be observed with complete reverence from evening to evening, and that people abstain from unlawful work. There is to be no market on those days, nor a court in which anyone is judged to death or punishment, nor oaths are to be sworn, except for the making of peace.

### CHAPTER LXXXII.—Further concerning Sunday

[Col. 0641A]

(From the Council held at Saint-Médard, in the presence of Emperor Charles, chapter 5.) We also establish, according to what the Lord commanded in the Law, that servile work not be performed on Sundays, as my father commanded in his synodal edicts: men are not to engage in rural labor, work in the vineyards, plough or reap in the fields, cut hay, or build fences; they are not to grub up roots in the woods, cut down trees, work in quarries, build houses, or labor in gardens; they are not to assemble at courts, markets are not to be held, and hunts are not to be conducted.

### CHAPTER LXXXIII.—Concerning the same matter

(From the same council, chapter 6.) Three kinds of carting are permitted on Sunday: military carts, carts carrying provisions, and compulsory transport; and, if it should happen to be necessary, the body of anyone may be taken to the grave.

### CHAPTER LXXXIV.—Further concerning the same matter

(From the same council, chapter 7.) Women are not to perform textile work on Sunday, nor cut out garments, sew, or card wool. It is not permitted to beat flax, wash clothes, or shear wethers, so that honor and rest may in every way be rendered to Sunday. Instead, they are to assemble from every direction for the solemn celebration of Mass and praise God for all the good things he has deigned to bestow upon us on that day.

### CHAPTER LXXXV.—Further concerning the same matter

(From the same council, chapter 8.) We have decreed that every Sunday is to be observed with complete reverence and that people abstain from unlawful work. There is to be no market on those days, nor a court in which anyone is judged to death or punishment, nor oaths are to be sworn, except for the sake of peace.

### CHAPTER LXXXVI.—Concerning the same matter

(From the same council, chapter 9.) No market is to be held anywhere on Sunday.

### CHAPTER LXXXVII.—Concerning the same matter

(From the same council, chapter 10.) No bishop, priest, or cleric should dare on Sunday to pursue the business of any case or undertaking, except only what is necessary for the completion of the solemn rites established for God.

### CHAPTER LXXXVIII.—That no one should kneel on Sundays

(From the Council of Nicaea, chapter 20.) Since there are some who kneel on Sundays and during the days of Pentecost, so that everything may be observed harmoniously in the various places, the holy council has agreed that from Easter until the octave of Pentecost people should pay their vows to the Lord standing.

### CHAPTER LXXXIX.—That priests should bless faithful people who privately desire it, and that every priest should have authority to give blessings among households, in the fields, and in private homes

(From the Council held at Regia, chapter 4.) Priests are to bless faithful people who privately desire it. Among these minor deliberations, it was also ordered that every priest should have authority, according to the desire of the faithful, to give blessings among households, in the fields, and in private homes.

### CHAPTER XC.—That priests should not give the episcopal blessing over the people

[Col. 0642A]

(From the same, chapter 47.) A priest is altogether forbidden to pour the episcopal blessing over the people in the Church or to reconcile a penitent in the Church.

### CHAPTER XCI.—That no priest should receive another’s parishioner against his will

(From the Council of Nantes, chapter 5.) No priest is to receive another priest’s parishioner for Mass against that priest’s will, unless the person is traveling or has a court hearing there.

### CHAPTER XCII.—Concerning another priest’s parishioner and those who maintain an irreconcilable quarrel among themselves

(From the same, chapter 19.) On Sundays and feast days, before celebrating Mass, priests are to ask the congregation whether another parishioner is present in the church who, in contempt of his own priest, wishes to hear Mass there. If they find one, they are immediately to expel him from the church and compel him to return to his own parish.

They are likewise to ask whether there are any people at odds with one another who maintain an irreconcilable quarrel. If any are found, they are immediately to be reconciled. If they refuse to accept peace, they are to be expelled from the church until they return to charity. For we cannot offer a gift or offering at the altar unless we are first reconciled with our brother. When these matters have been completed, the priests are properly to celebrate the solemn Mass.

### CHAPTER XCIII.—Concerning ordained persons and the rest of the faithful, who must do nothing without their bishop’s permission

(From a letter of Clement sent to all the faithful, chapter 22.) Therefore all the faithful, and especially all priests, deacons, and the rest of the clergy, must take care to do nothing without the permission of their own bishop. No priest is to celebrate Mass in his parish without the bishop’s order; he is not to baptize or do anything pertaining to the bishop without his permission.

Likewise, the rest of the people, both great and small, are to do whatever must be done with his permission. They are neither to leave their parish without his permission nor presume to remain there when arriving from elsewhere. Their souls have been entrusted to him; therefore they must [do] everything according to his counsel and nothing without consulting him. For all who obey their bishops appear to obey God as well. But those who do not obey them undoubtedly exist as guilty and rejected.

### CHAPTER XCIV.—Concerning the same matter

[Col. 0642D]

(From a letter of the same author, chapter 36.) For he taught that no presbyter ought to do anything in the parish of another bishop without that bishop’s permission. By the Lord’s institution, he taught that all presbyters must obey their own bishops in everything without delay. He taught that no one should desire or presume upon what belongs to another, but that each person should be content with what is his own and with those entrusted to him. He also instructed that no one should do anything to another that he would not wish done to himself.

### CHAPTER XCV — On the same matter

(From the Council of Arles, chapter 2.) Concerning presbyters or deacons who are accustomed to abandon the places in which they were ordained and transfer themselves to other places, it was decreed [Col. 0643A] that they should minister in those same places. But if they wish to transfer from the places they have abandoned to another place, they are to be deposed.

### CHAPTER XCVI — That a cleric may not be enrolled simultaneously in the churches of two cities

(From the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 10.) It is not permitted for a cleric to be enrolled simultaneously in the churches of two cities: both in the church in which he was ordained at the beginning and in the church to which he has fled as though to a more important one, out of a desire for empty glory. Those who do this must be recalled to their own church, in which they were first ordained, and there alone must they minister.

### CHAPTER XCVII — Concerning ordained persons, that they may not be transferred from city to city contrary to the canons

(From the Council of Nicaea, chapter 15.) Because of the great disturbances and seditions that occur, it was decreed that the custom which appears to have been admitted contrary to the rule in certain regions should be entirely abolished, so that no bishop, presbyter, or deacon may be transferred from city to city. If anyone, after the decree of the holy and great council, attempts to do such a thing and commits himself to such an undertaking, the act is to be considered wholly invalid, and he is to be restored to the church in which he was ordained bishop, presbyter, or deacon.

### CHAPTER XCVIII — On the same matter

(From the same council, chapter 16.) All who rashly and dangerously depart from the Church—presbyters or deacons, or whoever is entirely subject to the rule—without keeping the fear of the Lord before their eyes and without recognizing the ecclesiastical rule, must by no means be received into another church. Rather, every compulsion necessary should be imposed upon them so that they return to their own parishes. If they do not do so, they must be deprived of communion.

### CHAPTER XCIX — That presbyters should not be sent about to various places on missions, with the care of souls abandoned

(From the Council of Arles, chapter 3.) It has been decreed that presbyters, as has hitherto been done, should not be sent indiscriminately to various places, either by bishops, by other prelates, or even by laypeople, lest, because of their absence, both the dangers to souls and the duties of the churches in which they have been appointed be neglected.

### CHAPTER C — That presbyters ought to read continually

(From the sayings of Augustine.) Presbyters, you ought to be assiduous in reading and persistent in prayer, because the life of a righteous man is instructed by reading, adorned by prayer, and fortified against sin by continual reading, in accordance with the one who said: “I have hidden your words in my heart, so that I may not sin against you.” These are the weapons—namely, reading and prayer—by which the devil is conquered. These are the instruments by which eternal blessedness is acquired. By these weapons vices are restrained; by this nourishment virtues are fed.

But whenever reading is suspended, manual labor should follow, because idleness is the enemy of the soul. The ancient enemy, when he finds someone unoccupied with reading or prayer, easily drags him into vices. Through the practice of reading you will learn how both to live yourselves and to teach others. [Col. 0644A] Through the practice of prayer you will be able to benefit both yourselves and those to whom you are joined in charity. Through manual labor and mortification of the body you will both deny nourishment to vices, assist your own needs, and have something with which to extend aid to those suffering necessity.

### CHAPTER CI — That presbyters should not go without oraria

(From the Council of Mainz.) Presbyters should use oraria without interruption, on account of the distinction of priestly dignity.

### CHAPTER CII — That a cleric should seek his livelihood through an honorable craft

(From the Council of Africa, chapter 51.) Any cleric instructed in the word of God should seek his livelihood through an honorable craft.

### CHAPTER CIII — On the same matter

[Col. 0644B] (From the same council, chapter 3.) A cleric should provide himself with food and clothing by a craft or by agriculture, provided only that this does not impair his ecclesiastical office.

### CHAPTER CIV — Concerning what presbyters ought to do after completing the morning office

(From the Council of Nantes, chapter 60.) In the morning, after completing the morning office, the presbyter should discharge the obligation of his service by singing Prime, Terce, Sext, and None. This should nevertheless be done in such a way that afterward, at the appropriate hours and when the signals indicate, these offices may, as circumstances permit, be completed publicly either by himself or by the students. Then, when the hours have been completed and the sick have been visited, if he wishes, he may go out fasting to rural labor, so that he may again assist the needs of pilgrims and guests, or of various travelers, and also of the sick and the dead, [Col. 0644C] until the appointed hour, according to the season and the opportunity.

### CHAPTER CV — On the same matter

(From the sayings of Benedict.) The Prophet says: “Seven times a day I have praised you.” This number seven will be fulfilled by us if, at the times of Matins, Prime, Terce, Sext, None, Vespers, and Compline, we perform the offices of our service, because the Prophet spoke of these. Concerning the nocturnal vigils he likewise says: “At midnight I rose to confess to you,” and so forth. Therefore, at these times let us offer praises to our Creator concerning the judgments of his justice.

### CHAPTER CVI — What a great danger it is for someone who does not know how to govern his own life to become judge of another’s life

[Col. 0644D] (From the sayings of Augustine.) Presbyters must be admonished to consider that whatever is given by the faithful is a redemption for sins. Therefore, they should not glory in using such expenditures, but rather fear what was said in the Old Testament concerning priests: that they ought to bear the iniquity of the people. For this reason, with great fear they should be solicitous for those whose gifts they share, because it is a great danger for one who does not know how to maintain the discipline of his own life to become judge of another’s life.

### CHAPTER CVII — That presbyters should lodge near the church

(From the Council of Meaux, chapter 5.) Presbyters must not in any way be allowed to lodge just anywhere, nor should they themselves presume to do so in any manner; rather, they should diligently remain near their own churches, because of the sacred mysteries and ministries to be provided to the faithful. They should not be permitted to live elsewhere. Nor should women have any kind of dwelling in places to which presbyters have access. If they disregard this, they are to be judged transgressors, as are those who act contrary to the prohibitions. [Col. 0645A]

### CHAPTER CVIII — Concerning a presbyter: if he takes a wife, he is to be deposed

(From the Council of Neocaesarea, chapter 1.) If a presbyter takes a wife, he is to be deposed from the order. If, however, he commits fornication or adultery, he must be expelled still more severely and brought to penance. Similarly, if a deacon falls into the same sin, he is to be removed from the order of ministry.

### CHAPTER CIX — On the same matter

[Col. 0645B] (From the Council of Nicaea, chapter 3.) The great synod altogether forbade a bishop, presbyter, deacon, or anyone at all who belongs to the clergy to have a woman brought in to live with him, unless perhaps she is his mother, sister, or aunt, or one of those persons alone who give no occasion for suspicion.

### CHAPTER CX — On the same matter

(From the decree of Pope Siricius, chapter 12.) We do not permit any women to be in the houses of clerics except those whom the Council of Nicaea allowed to live with them solely for reasons of kinship.

### CHAPTER CXI — On the same matter

(From the same source, chapter 4.) The bishops decreed concerning presbyters who indiscriminately permit women to live with them and are consequently marked by suspicion of ill repute: if, after being admonished, they do not correct themselves, they are to be struck as contemptors of the sacred canons by canonical censure.

### CHAPTER CXII — On the same matter

(From the Council of Agde, chapter 3.) For the preservation of life and reputation, we command by a special ordinance that no cleric be joined to any strange woman by any form of consolation or familiarity. Not only must a strange woman not enter his house, but he himself must not have the authority to visit a strange woman. He may freely live only with his mother, sister, or niece, if he has or wishes to have such relatives; concerning these relationships, it is impious to suspect anything other than what nature establishes.

### CHAPTER CXIII — That female servants should be removed from the presbyters’ storerooms

[Col. 0645D] (From the Council of Reims, chapter 3.) It was decreed that female servants or freedwomen should be removed from the storeroom, from confidential service, and from the same residence in which the cleric lives.

### CHAPTER CXIV — That deacons, like bishops and presbyters, should abstain from marital relations

(From a letter of Pope Leo, chapter 17.) The law of continence is the same for ministers of the altar as for bishops and presbyters. When they were laymen or readers, they were lawfully able both to marry and to beget children; but when they reached the aforementioned ranks, what had been lawful for them began to be unlawful. Therefore, so that the carnal may become a spiritual marriage, they ought neither to dismiss their wives nor, as though they did not have them, to live with them in such a way that both the charity of marriage is preserved and marital acts cease. [Col. 0646A]

### CHAPTER CXV — On the same matter

(From the Council of Tours, chapter 6.) Since no place must be given to the devil, we have decreed that this must especially be guarded: no cleric should have familiarity with strange women, nor give people any opportunity for evil speech or thought. For frequently, through this indecent occasion, it happens that the devil, who lies in wait like a lion in his den, exults over the ruin of God’s servants. If any cleric, after his bishop’s prohibition, presumes to persist in these associations, he is to be held separated from communion.

### CHAPTER CXVI — On the same matter

[Col. 0646B] (From the Council of Nantes, chapter 10.) It must be prohibited and forbidden in every way that any priest keep in his house those women whose presence may give rise to suspicion, as is also contained in the canon—not even those whom the canons permit: his mother, aunt, or sister. For, at the devil’s instigation, a crime is frequently found to have been committed even with such women, or even some of them to have been hindered (*impedisse quas illarum*; the transmitted wording is uncertain). But if anyone has one of these women in such need that she requires a presbyter’s support, he should have a house for her in a village or town far from the presbyter’s residence, and there provide her with what is necessary.

Nevertheless, according to the authority of the canons, this must be prohibited in every way: no woman may presume to approach the altar, minister to the presbyter, or stand or sit within the screens.

### CHAPTER CXVII — Concerning the incontinent

(From the Apostolic Canons, chapter 22.) Concerning presbyters and deacons, divine law prescribes that those placed in such offices who are incontinent should be deprived of every ecclesiastical honor and should not be admitted to a ministry which must be fulfilled by continence alone.

### CHAPTER CXVIII — Concerning ordained persons, that they must not have intercourse with women

(From the same source.) Moreover, the Church must hold firmly to what is worthy, chaste, and honorable: that priests and Levites do not have intercourse with women, because they are occupied with the daily necessities of the ministry. It is written: “Be holy, for I, the Lord your God, am holy.”

### CHAPTER CXIX — Concerning ordained persons, if they practice usury

[Col. 0646D] (From the same source.) A bishop, presbyter, or deacon who exacts usury from debtors must either desist or certainly be condemned.

### CHAPTER CXX — On the same matter

(From the Council of Nicaea, chapter 17.) Since many persons subject to the rule pursue avarice and shameful profits, forgetting the divine Scripture which says, “He who has not given his money at interest,” the holy and great synod rightly judged that, if anyone is found after this decree receiving interest, or conducting business by some device or in any manner, or demanding the *hemiolia*, that is, one-and-a-half times the amount, or pursuing anything of this kind for the sake of shameful profit, he is to be cast out of the clergy and regarded as outside the rule. [Col. 0647A]

### CHAPTER CXXI — On the same matter

(From a letter of Pope Leo, chapter 4.) We have also thought it necessary to warn that, just as no cleric should attempt to practice lending at interest in his own name, so neither should he do so in another’s name.

### CHAPTER CXXII — On the same matter

(From the Council of Tarragona, chapter 3.) Whoever wishes to belong to the clergy must not engage in the pursuit of buying more cheaply or selling more dearly.

### CHAPTER CXXIII — On the same matter

(From a letter of Pope Leo, chapter 3.) We have also thought that this should not be passed over: we grieve over those who, seized by desire for shameful profit, practice usury and wish to grow rich through interest. This, we grieve to say, affects not only those established in clerical office, [Col. 0647B] but also laypeople who desire to be called Christians.

### CHAPTER CXXIV — On the same matter

(From the Council of Carthage, chapter 16.) It was likewise decreed that if a cleric lends money, he should receive money; if he lends a commodity, he should receive the same kind of commodity, in the quantity that he gave.

### CHAPTER CXXV — Further concerning usurers

(From the Council of Orléans, chapter 3.) Presbyters must not only themselves abstain from shameful profits and usury, but also instruct the peoples subject to them to abstain.

### CHAPTER CXXVI — What usury is

(From the Council of Agde, chapter 1.) Usury is when more is demanded than is given. For example, if you give ten solidi and demand more; or if you give one modius of grain and exact something additional.

### CHAPTER CXXVII — On the same matter

(From the decree of Pope Julius, sent to usurers, chapter 125.) Whoever, at harvesttime or vintage, purchases grain or wine not out of necessity but from greed—for example, if he buys one modius for two denarii and stores it until it can be sold for four, six, or more denarii—we call this shameful profit.

### CHAPTER CXXVIII — On the same matter

(From a letter of Pope Leo.) In what way does it excuse or condemn the merchant, since there is both honest and shameful profit? Nevertheless, for the penitent it is more beneficial to endure losses than to be bound by the dangers of commerce, because it is difficult for sin not to intervene in the exchange between buyer and seller. [Col. 0647D]

### CHAPTER CXXIX — That no one from the ecclesiastical order should enter taverns for the sake of eating or drinking

(From the sayings of Augustine.) The statutes of the canons prohibit anyone from the ecclesiastical order from daring to enter taverns for the sake of taking food or drink, unless compelled by the necessity of travel. If anyone violates these prohibitions, he is to be corrected with the severest discipline as a contemner of the holy canons.

### CHAPTER CXXX — That no one from the sacred order should enter taverns for the sake of food or drink

(From the Council of Carthage, chapter 25.) Clerics must not enter taverns for the sake of eating or drinking, unless compelled by the necessity of travel. [Col. 0648A]

### CHAPTER CXXXI — On the same matter

(From the Council of Laodicea, chapter 24.) Those devoted to the sacred mystery—from presbyters down to deacons, and the rest of the ecclesiastical order, namely subdeacons, readers, singers, exorcists, and doorkeepers—and also those numbered among the continent and the monks, ought not to enter taverns.

### CHAPTER CXXXII — That those who are not permitted to marry should avoid the weddings of others

(From a letter of Pope Leo, chapter 19.) Those who have no permission to marry should avoid banquets at other people’s weddings.

### CHAPTER CXXXIII — That a presbyter ought not to dine at the wedding of a bigamist

[Col. 0648B] (From the Council of Neocaesarea, chapter 7.) It is not fitting for presbyters to dine at the wedding of a bigamist. Since a bigamist requires penance, what presbyter could, on account of a banquet, give approval to such a wedding?

### CHAPTER CXXXIV — On the same matter

(From the sayings of Augustine.) Presbyters, deacons, subdeacons, and those below them who are not permitted to take wives should also avoid banquets at other people’s weddings. Nor should they join gatherings where love songs and obscene songs are sung, or where shameful bodily movements are displayed in dances and choreographed performances, lest hearing and sight, assigned to sacred mysteries, be polluted by the contagion of indecent spectacles and words.

### CHAPTER CXXXV — On the same matter

[Col. 0648C] (From the decree of Pope Martin, chapter 1.) Priests and clerics must not watch any spectacles at weddings or banquets; rather, before entering such spectacles, they ought to rise and depart from there.

### CHAPTER CXXXVI — That no cleric should be received in another city without letters of commendation

(From the Apostolic Canon.) If any cleric or layperson travels to another city and is received without letters of commendation, both the person who received him and the person who was received are to be deprived of communion.

### CHAPTER CXXXVII — On the same matter

(From the Council of Antioch, chapter 27.) No strangers are to be received without letters of peace, that is, letters of commendation.

### CHAPTER CXXXVIII — Concerning fugitive clerics, that they should not be received by others

[Col. 0648D] (From the Council of Orléans, chapter 2.) The Council of Antioch, and likewise that of Chalcedon, prescribes that fugitive clerics and strangers are to be received by no one and are not to be ordained unless they have letters of commendation and the permission of their own bishop or abbot.

### CHAPTER CXXXIX — That foreign clerics should not minister without letters from their own bishop

(From the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 13.) Foreign clerics and readers must nowhere minister in another city without letters of commendation from their own bishop.

### CHAPTER CXL — That clerics should not remain in another city unless the bishop of the place has examined their circumstances

(From the Council of Carthage, chapter 35.) Clerics must not remain in another city unless the bishop of the place, or the presbyters of the places concerned, have examined the legitimacy of their reasons. [Col. 0649A]

### CHAPTER CXLI — Concerning clerics and monks who wander without letters from their bishop

(From the same council, chapter 36.) Clerics or monks must not have permission to wander about without letters of commendation from their bishop.

### CHAPTER CXLII — On the same matter

(From the same council, chapter 37.) Clerics must not have permission to wander about without letters of commendation from their bishop; the same provision of this judgment is also to be observed in the case of monks.

### CHAPTER CXLIII — That aid should be given to the poor and needy when they travel, through letters of peace

(From the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 11.) We have decreed that all poor persons and those in need of assistance, when they travel, should, after verification, be commended only by letters of peace, whether letters or ecclesiastical letters, and not by letters of commendation, because letters of commendation are properly granted only to persons of higher rank. [Col. 0649B]

### CHAPTER CXLIV — That clerics who follow their superiors into other provinces may not minister without a *formata*

(From the Council of Meaux, chapter 2.) Those who come with their superiors from other provinces into another province must not be permitted to minister without a *formata*. Even if they bring one and are found fit to minister, they must be instructed how reverently and diligently they should perform the sacred ministry and in which places they ought to act. [Col. 0649C]

### CHAPTER CXLV — That a cleric may not lease the possessions of others or involve himself in secular business

(From the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 3.) It has come to the holy synod’s attention that certain persons who appear to have been chosen for the clergy, for the sake of shameful profits, become lessees of other people’s possessions and take secular business under their management. They slight God’s ministry, run about through the houses of secular people, and, because of greed, assume responsibility for patrimonies. Therefore the holy council decreed that henceforth no one—neither bishop, cleric, nor monk—may lease possessions or involve himself in secular business, apart from the care of ecclesiastical affairs.

### CHAPTER CXLVI — That no layperson should presume to involve his presbyter in estate management

[Col. 0649D] (From the Council of Meaux, chapter 6.) It must likewise be commanded that no layperson presume to involve the presbyters of his churches in shameful estate management, or, in the Apostle’s words, in secular and dishonorable business; nor should anyone presume to take them along with him against authority, thereby forcing them to neglect the ministry entrusted to them. If anyone presumes to violate these prohibitions, he is to be excommunicated.

### CHAPTER CXLVII — Concerning those presbyters who become estate managers contrary to the statutes of the canons and involve themselves in other unauthorized businesses and vices that must not be tolerated

(From the same council, chapter 5.) We have likewise judged that strict and severe measures must henceforth be taken against those presbyters who, contrary to the statutes of the canons, become estate managers, enter taverns, [Col. 0650A] pursue shameful profits, serve usury in its various forms, visit other people’s houses dishonorably and immodestly, are not ashamed to devote themselves to feasting and drunkenness, and run indiscriminately through various markets. Their illicit and indecent conduct must not bring the priestly ministry into contempt or make them a scandal to those for whom they ought to be an example.

### CHAPTER CXLVIII — No cleric, not even a subdeacon, is permitted carnal marriage

(From a letter of Pope Leo, chapter 4.) While those outside the clerical order are free to devote themselves to the partnership of marriage and the begetting of children, nevertheless, for the display of perfect purity of continence, not even subdeacons are permitted carnal marriage, so that those who have wives may be as though they did not have them, and those who do not have wives may remain unmarried. If this is rightly observed in this order, which is fourth from the highest, how much more must it be observed in the first, second, or third, so that no one may be considered suitable for Levitical or priestly honor, or for episcopal excellence, if he is found not yet to have restrained himself from sexual pleasure?

### CHAPTER CXLIX — Concerning rulers who are accustomed to appoint their priests to judicial functions

(From the Council of Toledo, chapter 31.) Rulers often entrust their affairs to priests against persons liable to charges of treason. Since priests have been chosen by Christ for the ministry of salvation, they should consent to become judges for kings where clemency from punishment is promised by oath, but not where a sentence involving danger is being prepared. If any priest, contrary to this common decree, acts as an investigator in the dangers of others, let him be guilty before Christ of shed blood, and before the Church let him lose his own rank.

### CHAPTER CL — Concerning those who intend to serve God, that they should not undertake the administration of households

(From the Council of Carthage, chapter 7.) Bishop Nicasius of Evastitum said: “I believe that my proposal pleases your holiness, and that you disapprove of those who serve God and are attached to the clergy taking up the management, administration, or stewardship of households.”

### CHAPTER CLI — Likewise, whether it is permissible for someone from the clergy to become a manager of private property

[Col. 0650D] (From the same council, chapter 14.) It was likewise decreed that bishops, presbyters, deacons, or clerics should not be managers or stewards of private persons, nor seek their livelihood through any shameful or dishonorable business, because they ought to remember that it is written: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular business.”

### CHAPTER CLII — That if any ordained person living within the city walls does not come to the daily sacrifice, he is not to be regarded as a cleric

(From the Council of Toledo, chapter 5.) If a presbyter, deacon, subdeacon, or any cleric assigned to the Church is within a city, or in a place where there is a church, whether in a fortress, village, or town, and does not come to the church for the daily sacrifice, he is not to be regarded as a cleric if, after being corrected, he does not reform himself. [Col. 0651A]

### CHAPTER CLIII — On the same matter

(From the Council of Vannes, chapter 1.) A cleric who lives within the city walls and is absent from the morning hymns on a given day without illness is to be held outside communion for seven days.

### CHAPTER CLIV — That all the priests of the Lord ought to be instructed, so that they may instruct others and make progress themselves

(From a letter of Pope Anacletus sent to all the faithful, chapter 10.) Therefore all who exercise the Lord’s priesthood ought to be instructed, so that they may both instruct others and make progress themselves. For it is written: “Those who are learned will shine like the splendor of the firmament, and those who instruct many in righteousness like the stars for everlasting eternities.” And elsewhere: “But the people who know their God will prevail and act, and those who are learned among the people will instruct many.” The Truth itself declares and says: “Blessed is the one who is not scandalized because of me.” Without doubt, the person scandalized against God is the one who does not teach correctly and who scandalizes his bishop or priest. [Col. 0651B]

### CHAPTER CLV — That each year individual presbyters should render an account of their ministry to their own bishop

(From the Council of Mainz held by Archbishop Riculf of that see, chapter 3.) Each presbyter must every year render an account of his ministry to his bishop, concerning both the Catholic faith and baptism, and every aspect of his ministry.

### CHAPTER CLVI — That every presbyter should compel his subjects to learn the faith

[Col. 0651C] (From the Council of Gangra, chapter 5.) Let priests continually admonish the Christian people to learn the Creed, which is the seal of faith, and the Lord’s Prayer. We wish those who neglect to learn these things to receive appropriate discipline, whether through fasting or another form of correction. Therefore it is fitting that they send their children to school, or to monasteries, or outside to presbyters, so that they may correctly learn the Catholic faith and the Lord’s Prayer and be able to teach others at home. Whoever cannot do so otherwise should learn it in his own language.

### CHAPTER CLVII — What profession presbyters or deacons ought to make to their bishop when they are appointed to parishes

(From the Fifth Council of Toledo, chapter 27.) When presbyters or deacons are appointed to parishes, they ought to make a profession to their bishop that they will live chastely and purely in the fear of God, so that, while such a profession binds them, they may maintain the discipline of a holy life. [Col. 0651D]

### CHAPTER CLVIII — No non-priest monk or layperson, however learned, is permitted to preach

(From a letter of Pope Leo.) Concerning the matters attempted unlawfully in the aforesaid council through presumption against the venerable canons of Nicaea, we wrote to our brother and fellow bishop, the bishop of the see of Antioch. We added what you had reported to us through our representatives concerning the insolence of certain monks of your religious community, and we established this specifically: apart from God’s priests, no one may dare to preach, whether monk or layperson, even if he boasts of possessing knowledge of any kind. [Col. 0652A]

### CHAPTER CLIX — That parish clerics should learn the canons from their bishops

(From the Council of Orléans, chapter 6.) Parish clerics should receive from their bishops the necessary canonical statutes to read, lest they themselves or the peoples be able later to excuse themselves by claiming ignorance of what has been decreed for their salvation.

### CHAPTER CLX — That no priest is permitted to be ignorant of the canons

(From a letter of Pope Celestine, chapter 20.) Celestine to all the bishops established throughout Apulia and Calabria. No priest may be ignorant of his canons, nor do anything that could conflict with the rules of the Fathers. For what matter worthy of preservation will remain among us if the standard of the decretal constitutions is broken at the whim of certain persons by permission granted to the peoples? [Col. 0652B]

### CHAPTER CLXI — Concerning parish presbyters, that when they gather they must not dare to become drunk

(From the Council of Nantes, chapter 10.) When presbyters gather for the anniversary of a deceased person—whether on the thirtieth, seventh, or third day—or for any other summons to an assembly, no one among them may presume to become drunk. Nor may anyone presume to drink in honor of the saints or of the soul itself, or compel others to drink, or gorge himself through another’s drinking. They must not presume to make disorderly applause or laughter, recite empty stories, or sing; nor may anyone allow indecent jokes, or a bear, or dancing women to perform before them. Nor may they consent to have the demons’ masks, commonly called *Talamascas*, carried before them, because this is diabolical and prohibited by the sacred canons. [Col. 0652C]

### CHAPTER CLXII — On the same matter

(From the same source, chapter 11.) When presbyters gather for some banquet, the dean or one of the senior members should begin a verse before the table and bless the food. Then they should sit according to rank, showing honor to one another, and bless the food and drink by turns. One of their clerics should read something from Holy Scripture. After the meal, they should likewise sing a holy hymn, following the example of the Lord, who is said to have done this at the supper. Thus all the presbyters should conduct themselves, especially in such places, [Col. 0652D] so that their ministry is not brought into disgrace.

### CHAPTER CLXIII — On the same matter

(From the same source, chapter 12.) Above all, each presbyter must take care, if he wishes to rejoice in his status, not to provoke or incite his father or anyone else to anger and quarrel on any pretext, much less to a fight or killing, by any word; nor, if provoked, should anyone rush into such conduct. For at such feasts and drinking parties the devil always intervenes.

### CHAPTER CLXIV — On the same matter

(From the same source, chapter 4.) When presbyters gather together on the Kalends, after the divine mystery and the necessary conference have been completed, they should sit at the tables there not for a full meal but for something like lunch, so that they do not burden one another with such dishonorable banquets; for this is both indecent and burdensome. Often, returning late to the church, they incur greater harm from criticism and contract greater mutual weariness than the benefit they gain there.

Paul criticized the Corinthians for gathering improperly to eat the Lord’s supper. Likewise, those who gather under the pretext of the Lord’s supper—that is, for a conference about the word—and who in reality come together for the sake of their bellies are considered blameworthy before God and human beings. Therefore, after everything has been completed, whoever wishes may break bread together with charity in his brother’s house, together with the brothers; and each should make the others drink one cup, taking care especially not to touch the cup more than three times, and then return to the churches. [Col. 0653B]

### CHAPTER CLXV — That clerics and religious men should not begin banquets before the third hour

(From the Council of Carthage, chapter 12.) Clerics and religious laypeople ought not to begin banquets before the sacred third hour of the day. Nor should clerics ever eat bread before a hymn has been sung, and after the meal they should give thanks to God the author.

### CHAPTER CLXVI — Concerning presbyters, that they should be hospitable

(From the Council of Nantes, chapter 3.) The presbyter should care for guests, especially the poor and weak, as well as orphans and pilgrims, and should daily invite them to his meal as far as possible [Col. 0653C] and provide them lodging.

### CHAPTER CLXVII — On the same matter

(From the same source, chapter 5.) In order to remove every opportunity for robbery, we wish presbyters—who ought to extend a good example of charity to everyone—to be hospitable, in accordance with the Lord’s and the Apostle’s command, and to show kindness to travelers. For through hospitality certain people pleased God by receiving angels as guests. And the Lord will say to the elect on the day of judgment: “I was a stranger, and you welcomed me.” Job also says: “My door was always open to the traveler.”

### CHAPTER CLXVIII — That presbyters should admonish their peoples to be hospitable

(From the council held at Auvergne.) It was decreed that presbyters should admonish their peoples to be hospitable, refuse lodging to no traveler, and, so that every opportunity for robbery may be removed, sell nothing to passersby at a higher price than they could obtain in the market. If they wish to sell at a higher price, the travelers should report this to the presbyter, and at his command they should sell to them humanely.

### CHAPTER CLXIX — That divine reading should always accompany the priests’ meals

(From the Council of Africa, chapter 6.) Out of reverence for God and the priests, the entire holy synod decreed that, since idle stories are often inserted during meals, a reading from the divine Scriptures should be included at every priestly banquet. Through this, souls are built up toward the good [Col. 0654A] and unnecessary stories are prevented.

### CHAPTER CLXX — Concerning clerics living intemperately

(From the Council of Carthage, chapter 62.) Clerics who sing amid their banquets are to be removed from office.

### CHAPTER CLXXI — Concerning buffoonish clerics

(From the same source, chapter 80.) If any cleric or monk speaks buffoonish, joking, or laughter-provoking words, he is to be corrected most severely.

### CHAPTER CLXXII — On the same matter

(From the same source, chapter 60.) Buffoonish clerics and those who jest with indecent words are to be removed from office.

### CHAPTER CLXXIII — That a cleric should not become a guarantor

(From the same source, chapter 70.) A cleric who engages in acting as a guarantor is to be cast out.

### CHAPTER CLXXIV — That a cleric should not grow a beard

[Col. 0654B] (From the same source, chapter 44.) A cleric must grow neither long hair nor a beard.

### CHAPTER CLXXV — Concerning clerics who swear by creatures

(From the same source, chapter 61.) A cleric who swears by creatures is to be rebuked most severely. If he persists in the vice, he is to be excommunicated.

### CHAPTER CLXXVI — Concerning clerics who are found to devote themselves to flattery and betrayals
(From the same council, chapter 56.) A cleric who is found to devote himself to flatteries and betrayals shall be degraded from office.

### CHAPTER CLXXVII — Concerning ordained clergy who customarily cause annoyance in the ears of princes, contrary to ecclesiastical commands

(From the Council of Antioch, chapter 11.) If any bishop, presbyter, or anyone subject to an ecclesiastical rule approaches the emperor without the advice and letters of the bishops of the province, and especially of the metropolitan, he must be rejected and removed not only from communion but also from the honor of which he appears to be a participant, because he has attempted to cause annoyance in the ears of the revered prince, contrary to the laws of the Church. If, therefore, a necessary cause demands that someone approach the prince, this must be done with the deliberation and advice of the metropolitan and of the other bishops who reside in the same province; they must also support the departing man with their letters.

### CHAPTER CLXXVIII — Concerning those who oppose their bishops lest they promote them to higher honor in their Church

(From the African Council, chapter 31.) It was likewise decreed that, whenever any clerics or deacons, for the needs of the Churches, have not obeyed their bishops when the bishops wish to promote them to a higher honor in their own Church, they must not minister there in the rank from which they refused to depart.

### CHAPTER CLXXIX — Concerning a presbyter deposed for a definite crime who presumes to perform anything from the ministry forbidden to him

(From the Council of Toledo, chapter 6.) If any presbyter has been degraded by his bishop, or suspended from office for definite crimes, and through contempt and pride has presumed to perform something from the ministry forbidden to him, and afterward, having been corrected by his bishop, has persisted in his definite presumption, he shall in every way be excommunicated and expelled from the Church. Whoever communicates with him shall likewise know himself to be excommunicated. The same rule must be observed concerning excommunicated clerics, laymen, or women. If anyone should despise all these measures, and the bishop is quite unable to correct him, he shall be condemned to exile by the judgment of the king.

### CHAPTER CLXXX — Concerning a condemned presbyter or deacon who has caused annoyance in the ears of the emperor

(From the Council of Antioch, chapter 12.) If a presbyter or deacon has been condemned by his own bishop, or if a bishop has perhaps been condemned by a synod, and has caused annoyance in the ears of the emperor, the council must return to the hands of the bishops, and they must bring before many bishops whatever they judge to be just; they must await their investigations and judgments. But if, disregarding these things, they cause annoyance to the emperor, they are to be considered worthy of no pardon, to have no opportunity for satisfaction, and to be entirely deprived of hope of future restoration.

### CHAPTER CLXXXI — Concerning a presbyter who, by evil examples, has allowed evil suspicions to arise about himself

(From the Council of Agde, chapter 4.) If any presbyter, negligent of his life, has by evil examples allowed evil suspicions to arise about himself, and the people, bound by the bishop through an oath or the ban of Christianity, have exposed his infamy, while definite accusers of his crime are lacking, he shall first be admonished privately by the bishop, and then in the presence of two or three witnesses. If he does not reform, the bishop shall admonish him publicly with a rebuke in the assembly of presbyters. If he still does not correct himself, he shall be suspended from office until he makes worthy satisfaction, lest the faithful people suffer scandal because of him. But if there are no legitimate accusers who attempt to prove his crimes by manifest indications, and he denies them, then, if he is able, he shall clear himself of the crime together with seven companions of his own order. A deacon, however, if accused of the same crime, shall defend himself with three companions.

### CHAPTER CLXXII — Concerning the same matter

(From the Council of Tribur, chapter 21.) If any presbyter has a dispute arising from a complaint against a layman, or a layman against a presbyter, it shall be settled at the bishop’s command, without respect of persons. The layman shall clear himself by oath, if necessary; but the presbyter shall be questioned in place of an oath by the holy consecration, because priests ought not to swear for a trivial reason. Shall the hand by which the body and blood of Christ are consecrated be polluted by an oath? Far be it! For the Lord says in the Gospel to his disciples, whose place we occupy, unworthy though we are, in the holy Church: “Do not swear at all. Let your speech be, ‘Yes, yes; no, no.’ Whatever is more than these is from evil.”

### CHAPTER CLXXXIII — If a cleric has a case against another cleric, he must not resort to secular courts

(From the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 9.) If any cleric has a case against another cleric, he must not abandon his own bishop and hasten to secular courts; rather, the action must first be examined before his own bishop, or, certainly, by that bishop’s advice, before those whom both parties choose, and judgment shall be conducted there. But if anyone acts otherwise, he shall be subject to canonical correction.

### CHAPTER CLXXXIV — Concerning how presbyters who are defamed by their congregations ought to be cleared

(From the Council of Hilerda, chapter 10.) If any presbyter is defamed by the people entrusted to him through an evil reputation, and the bishop is unable to establish the matter by legitimate witnesses, the presbyter shall be suspended from office until he makes worthy satisfaction, lest the faithful people suffer scandal because of him. Worthy satisfaction consists in this: that, after proper assurance concerning the accusation brought against him, he is shown to be innocent to those by whom he is believed guilty. We are taught that this was established for us by our forefathers.

But, whether according to the canons or at the bishop’s discretion, he shall join seven colleagues to himself and swear, with the holy Gospel placed before him, that the holy Trinity and Christ, the Son of God, who did and taught what the Gospel contains, and the four holy Evangelists who wrote it, may so help him that he did not commit the aforesaid act in the manner alleged against him. Having been cleared by this satisfaction, he may thereafter carry out his ministry securely.

Some of the earlier fathers report that Pope Saint Leo made this satisfaction in the basilica of the holy apostle Peter, before the most reverend Emperor Charles, the clergy, and the people; and that immediately afterward the revered prince exercised worthy vengeance against the adversaries of that same holy pope.

### CHAPTER CLXXXV — If someone from among the ordained has been condemned by his bishop, so that no one may defend him

(From the African Council, chapter 29.) It should also be requested that they deign to decree that, if a cleric of any rank has been condemned by the judgment of bishops for any crime, it shall not be permitted for him to be defended either by the Churches over which he presided or by any person, under penalty involving the loss of money and honor; and they shall order that neither age nor sex is to provide an excuse.

### CHAPTER CLXXXVI — Concerning a presbyter accused by the people

(From a letter of Gregory.) Concerning a presbyter or any priest accused by the people: if there are no certain witnesses who can speak the truth about the crime brought against him, an oath shall be required, and he shall produce as a witness one to whom all things are naked and open, in support of the purity of his innocence; and thus he shall remain in his own rank.

### CHAPTER CLXXXVII — Concerning clerics convicted and confessing: if they neglect to clear their case within a year, no further hearing shall be granted to them

(From the African Council, chapter 46.) It was again decreed that, whenever clerics have been convicted and confessed to some crime—whether out of consideration for those whose modesty is being spared, or because of the reproach of the Church, or because of the insolent attacks of heretics and pagans—if they should wish to appear on behalf of their case and assert their innocence, they must do so within the year of their excommunication. But if they neglect to clear their case within the year, thereafter their voice shall be heard no more at all.

### CHAPTER CLXXXVIII — That no one from among the ordained presume to swear to a layman

(From the Council of Reims, chapter 5.) No one from the ecclesiastical order shall swear anything to any layman concerning sacred matters or over the holy Gospels; instead, he shall simply speak with purity and truth: “Yes, yes; no, no.” But if there is something that laymen bring against him, it shall be referred to the bishop in whose territory he is; and, according to what those of the same order judge, he shall either be corrected or cleared.

### CHAPTER CLXXXIX — If a presbyter or deacon is caught in fornication, perjury, theft, or homicide, he shall be suspended from office

(From the Apostolic Canon.) A presbyter or deacon who has been caught in fornication, perjury, theft, or homicide shall be deposed, but shall not be deprived of communion. For Scripture says: “The Lord does not judge twice for the same thing.”

### CHAPTER CXC — Concerning the ordained, if any one of them has been a striker

(From the Council of Agde, chapter 3.) If anyone consecrated in any ecclesiastical rank has become a striker, he shall be rebuked most severely. If he does not reform, he shall be deposed.

### CHAPTER CXCI — Concerning presbyters who are degraded because of their negligence

(From the Council of Mainz, chapter 40.) It has been reported to us that presbyters who have been canonically degraded because of their negligence live in secular circumstances after losing their rank and neglect the good of performing penance. Therefore we decree that, after losing their rank, they shall be sent to a monastery, whether canonical or regular, for the sake of performing penance. If any circumstance prevents this, wherever they may be, they must not cease doing penance. But if, after losing their rank, they wish to live secularly and neglect to perform penance, they shall be separated from communion with the Church.

### CHAPTER CXCII — Concerning the ordained, if they have been unjustly degraded

(From the same council, chapter 28.) If a bishop, presbyter, or deacon has been unjustly removed from his rank and is found innocent in a second synod, he cannot become what he was unless he receives back his lost rank before the altar from the hands of the bishops. If he is a bishop, he shall receive the stole, ring, and staff; if a presbyter, the stole and chasuble; if a deacon, the stole and alb; if a subdeacon, the paten and chalice. Likewise, the other ranks shall receive, for their restoration, the things they received when they were ordained.

### CHAPTER CXCIII — Concerning the ordained who despise their own bishop

(From the Council of Antioch, chapter 5.) If any presbyter or deacon, despising his own bishop, separates himself from the Church, gathers people separately, and establishes an altar, and does not heed the bishop when admonished, nor wish to consent or obey when summoned once and again, he shall be condemned in every way and shall obtain no further remedy.

### CHAPTER CXCIV — If a presbyter, puffed up against his bishop, makes a schism, he shall be anathematized

(From the Council of Carthage, chapter 11.) All the bishops said: If any presbyter has been corrected by his bishop, he ought certainly to complain to neighboring bishops, so that his case may be heard by them and through them he may be reconciled to his bishop. But if he does not do this and—God forbid!—inflated by pride, judges that he must separate himself from communion with his bishop, and, making a schism with some others, offers sacrifice to God separately, he shall be held anathema and shall lose his position. If he has no just complaint against the bishop, an inquiry shall be made.

### CHAPTER CXCV — Concerning those who attack one of the ordained with a false accusation

(From the same council, chapter 5.) If anyone attacks a bishop, presbyter, or deacon with false accusations and is unable to prove them, communion is not to be given to him except at the end.

### CHAPTER CXCVI — That the accuser must present to his bishop, before the accusation, the charge against the accused in writing

(From the Council of Orléans, chapter 10.) Moreover, this must be observed in every way by the whole ecclesiastical order: no one shall presume to accuse a fellow brother in a council or synodal assembly unless he has first written out in due order, and signed with his own hand, the accusation itself and the causes of the dispute, and has presented it to the bishop or the holy synod, so that the controversies of the litigants may be ended justly and canonically. For, as Roman authority testifies, no one may be made an accused person or brought to judgment unless a formal written accusation has been made, because just as punishment binds the person convicted of a crime, so it binds the accuser if he has not proved what he alleged.

### CHAPTER CXCVII — That none of the ordained shall lodge a complaint in a synod except in writing

(From the Council held at Saint-Médard, chapter 9.) Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, said to his accusers:

“What is your petition, brothers?”

“We ask,” they said, “that mercy be shown to us by your fatherly authority concerning the exercise of the ecclesiastical orders to which we were formerly promoted by Lord Ebo and from which we have been suspended by your authority.”

Bishop Hincmar said: “Do you have a written petition of complaint or request, as ecclesiastical tradition requires?”

They replied that they had no written petition in their hands.

Bishop Hincmar said: “The authority of ecclesiastical laws is such that in cases concerning official proceedings it always requires a written document. Thus, the person who approaches the sacred font is ordered to give his name; the person promoted to the highest priesthood is elected by a decree strengthened by the hands of all; the ordained person is ordered to receive letters from those who ordained him; the person who is cut off from ecclesiastical fellowship for any offense is either received or expelled by a written petition; and the person who is accused, excommunicated, or reconciled is ordered to be accused or reconciled in writing.

“The same is required in other matters of this kind, to such an extent that, as blessed Gregory writes in his memorandum to John the Defender, drawing on Roman laws: ‘A sentence issued without writing does not even deserve to have the name of a sentence.’

“Therefore, brothers and sons, according to ecclesiastical authority you must set forth your complaint in the form of a written petition, sign it with your own hands, and present it to the holy synod, so that a suitable and canonical answer may be given to you.”

Then those brothers composed a petition, subscribed their names to it, and presented it to Bishop Hincmar, who at that time presided over the synod together with Wevilo, archbishop of Sens, and Amalric, likewise archbishop of Tours, in the presence of the glorious King Charles.

### CHAPTER CXCVIII — Concerning accusers of clerics: if they cannot prove one of the charges, they shall not be admitted to the others

(From the African Council, chapter 75.) It was likewise decreed that, whenever many crimes are brought against clerics by accusers, and the accusers are unable to prove one of those charges—the one with which they began—they shall thereafter not be admitted to the others.

### CHAPTER CXCIX — Concerning a bishop or presbyter, if a criminal charge has been brought against him: how he ought to clear himself

(From the Council of Worms, chapter 8.) If a criminal charge—homicide, adultery, or sorcery—has been brought against a bishop or presbyter, he must celebrate Mass in each case, say the Secret publicly, and receive communion, thereby showing himself innocent of each charge brought against him. If he does not do this, he shall be regarded as excluded from the thresholds of the Church for five years.

### CHAPTER CC — That clerics shall not be compelled by foreign judges

(From the decree of Pope Hadrian, chapter 38.) In cases involving clerics, this rule shall be observed: they must in no way be bound by a sentence issued by anyone other than their own judge.

### CHAPTER CCI — An unjust accuser who does not prove his charge shall be publicly punished with blows and sent into exile

(From the Rule addressed to Anthemius, Campanian subdeacon, chapter 201.) Since crimes inflicted upon the innocent, and especially upon sacred orders, ought to be punished more severely than the guilty themselves, consider carefully, all of you who sat in the case of Deacon John, how Hilary, his accuser, came to receive no punishment under your decision.

Nor should you consider this a sufficient excuse: that, as though you wished to judge, our brother and fellow bishop Paschasius alone is said to have brought the matter before you. For if zeal for uprightness had flourished among you, it would have been easier for many to persuade one reasonably than for one, without cause, to delay many.

Therefore, since such great wickedness must not pass without worthy vengeance, we wish our aforesaid brother Paschasius to be admonished to deprive that same Hilary of the office of the subdiaconate, which he unworthily holds, and to have him publicly punished with blows and deported into exile, so that the punishment of one may serve as the correction of many.

### CHAPTER CCII — That if anyone accuses a cleric and cannot prove the charge by witnesses, the accuser shall receive the accused person’s punishment

(From the Council of Braga, chapter 8.) It was decreed that, if anyone attacks a cleric with an accusation of fornication, in accordance with the command of the Apostle Paul he must produce two or three witnesses. If he cannot establish by the witnesses presented what he has said, the accuser shall receive the excommunication imposed on the accused.

### CHAPTER CCIII — Just as laymen do not admit clerics in secular matters for their accusations, so they themselves shall not be admitted in accusations against priests

(From the Council of Orléans, chapter 5.) All the bishops acclaimed in the third session: “It is certainly fitting that, just as laymen do not admit priests or clerics in their accusations or secular judgments, so they themselves shall not be admitted in accusations against priests or clerics, or in ecclesiastical business, unless they are voluntarily approved; for it is inappropriate that those who reject these men should be admitted by them.”

### CHAPTER CCIV — No one shall accept the testimony of a layman against a cleric

(From the Council of Tribur, chapter 4.) No one shall accept the testimony of a layman against a cleric.

### CHAPTER CCV — Concerning the ordained, if they are accused: by how many witnesses they ought to clear themselves

(From the Council of Carthage, chapter 20.) If presbyters or deacons are accused, their own bishop, joined by a legitimate number of colleagues from neighboring places whom the accused themselves request from him—that is, six together with the presbyter in the name of the presbyterate, and three in the case of the diaconate—shall investigate their cases, observing the same procedure concerning days and postponements, removal from communion, and examination of the persons involved, both the accusers and those accused. The cases of the other clerics may be heard and concluded by the bishop of the place alone.

### CHAPTER CCVI — Concerning the property of a deceased presbyter: to whom it belongs

(From the Council of Tribur, at which King Arnulf was present, chapter 23.) It was brought before the holy council that certain laymen behave wickedly toward their presbyters, claiming shares for themselves from the property of dying presbyters as though from their own slaves. We therefore forbid by canonical authority that this happen any longer. Rather, just as they have been made free in order to receive rank and perform the divine office, so nothing shall be demanded from them except the divine office. No one shall appropriate anything from the priests’ peculium; instead, let it all be divided into four portions: one for the bishop, another for the altar, a third for the poor, and a fourth for relatives. If the relatives are not suitable, the bishop shall receive that portion and distribute it diligently for the use of the Church. Whoever presumes to act against these provisions shall be anathematized.

### CHAPTER CCVII — Concerning presbyters who die without a will

(From the same council, chapter 14.) If anyone of ecclesiastical rank dies without a will and without kindred, his inheritance shall devolve upon the church where he served. The same applies to nuns.

### CHAPTER CCVIII — Concerning clerics who use lay clothing

(From the same council, chapter 27.) Clerics shall not use lay clothing—that is, a mantle, tunic, or cape—nor costly and unsuitable footwear or other vain novelties; rather, clothed in a religious and becoming habit, let them conduct themselves.

### CHAPTER CCIX — Concerning the same matter

(From the Council of Carthage, chapter 45.) Let a cleric demonstrate his profession also by his dress and bearing, and let him not seek distinction through unsuitable garments or footwear.

### CHAPTER CCX — Concerning clerics who idle about at markets

(From the same council, chapter 48.) A cleric who strolls about at a market or in the forum, not in order to buy something, shall be degraded from his office.

### CHAPTER CCXI — That no one of the clergy shall bear military arms

(From the same council, chapter 48.) Whoever appears to belong to the clergy shall not take up military arms or go about armed, but shall display the title of his profession through religious conduct and religious dress. If they disregard this, as despisers of the sacred canons and profaners of ecclesiastical holiness, they shall be punished by loss of their own rank, because they cannot serve God and the world at the same time.

### CHAPTER CCXII — That all clerics should place greater confidence in God’s protection than in arms

(From the Council of Orléans, chapter 9.) Presbyters and deacons must by all means be told not to bear arms, but rather to place greater confidence in God’s protection than in arms.

### CHAPTER CCXIII — Concerning those of ecclesiastical order who hunt or sport with hawks

(From the Council of Meaux, chapter 8.) It is not permitted for a bishop, presbyter, or deacon to keep hunting dogs, hawks, or things of this kind. If anyone of such persons is repeatedly found to persist in this inclination, if he is a bishop, let him suspend himself from communion for three months; a presbyter for two months; and a deacon shall be suspended from every office and communion for one month.

### CHAPTER CCXIV — Concerning servants of God: that all wandering in the woods with dogs and hawks be forbidden

(From the Council of Orléans, chapter 3.) We forbid all servants of God hunting and wandering in the woods with dogs, and forbid them to possess hawks and falcons.

### CHAPTER CCXV — That a bishop shall reconcile discordant clerics by his authority

(From the African Council, chapter 59.) Let a bishop bring discordant clerics to concord either by reason or by authority; let the synod condemn the disobedient after a hearing.

### CHAPTER CCXVI — Concerning clerics who break out into mutual violence

(From the Council of Lérida, chapter 6.) If any clerics break out into mutual violence, let them be punished more strictly by the bishop, according as the dignity of their offices has suffered disgrace in such an offense.

### CHAPTER CCXVII — Concerning the same matter

(From the same council, chapter 7.) If a brother has dared to lay hands upon a brother, let him receive lawful discipline.

### CHAPTER CCXVIII — Concerning the observance of the offices and ministries of seven deacons, with subdeacons and ministers of the following orders

(From the letter of Pope Fabian, chapter 2.) There shall therefore be seven deacons in the city of Rome, one for each of the seven regions of the city, as we have received from the Fathers. With the subdeacons, acolytes, and ministers of the following orders, they shall perform the ministries assigned to them through each week, on Sundays, and on the solemnities of feasts; they shall be ready at every hour for the divine office and for whatever is enjoined upon them. Likewise, according to what is appropriate, this is to be done in each city among you, so that the divine office may be performed diligently and solemnly, without any delay or negligence.

### CHAPTER CCXIX — Concerning the fixed number of deacons

(From the Council of Neocaesarea, chapter 14.) There should be seven deacons according to the rule, even if the city is very large. The book of the Acts of the Apostles likewise indicates this.

### CHAPTER CCXX — Concerning the same matter

(From the Council of Bishops who assembled at Ancyra and Caesarea, chapter 9.) There should be seven deacons according to the rule, although the city is large. The book of the Acts of the Apostles shall be the authority for this rule.

### CHAPTER CCXXI — That deacons shall not sit before presbyters

(From the Council of Laodicea, chapter 20.) A deacon ought not to sit in the presence of a presbyter, but shall sit at the presbyter’s command. Likewise, honor shall be accorded to deacons by those who serve them, that is, subdeacons and all clerics.

### CHAPTER CCXXII — Concerning deacons who set themselves before presbyters

(From the Council of Toledo, chapter 39.) Some deacons break out into such pride that they set themselves before presbyters and presume to stand first in the first choir, while the presbyters are placed in the second choir. Therefore, so that they may acknowledge presbyters as superior to themselves, both these and those shall stand in both choirs.

### CHAPTER CCXXIII — That exorcists shall lay hands on the possessed

(From the Council of Carthage, chapter 90.) Every day exorcists shall lay hands on the possessed.

### CHAPTER CCXXIV — Concerning the honor due to all orders

(From the decree of Pope Sylvester, chapter 4.) Thus, brothers, divine authority commands and affirms that, from the subdeacon down to the reader, all are subject to the cardinal deacon of the city of Rome, representing honor in the Church alone. But to the pontiff, presbyter, deacon, subdeacon, acolyte, exorcist, reader, abbot, and monk shall render service in every place, whether in public or within the bosom of the Church.

### CHAPTER CCXXV — Concerning priests who do not know how to fulfill their ministry and are unwilling to learn: that they are to be removed from office

(From the Council of Orléans, chapter 6.) Priests who do not rightly understand how to fulfill their ministry, do not strive according to their ability to learn in accordance with the command of their bishops, or are despisers of the canons, are to be removed from their own office until they have fully corrected these matters.

### CHAPTER CCXXVI — That those found under the discipline of no bishop shall not be counted among clerics

(From the Council of Paris, chapter 10.) Clerics or priests who are governed under the discipline and supervision of no bishop are in no way to be regarded as such. The ancient custom of the Church called such persons acephali, that is, “without a head.”

### CHAPTER CCXXVII — Model of a letter of authorization, composed and approved by the holy Fathers at the Synod of Nicaea

(From the decree of the Council of Nicaea.) In the name of the Father π, and of the Son γ, and of the Holy Spirit α. To Walter, bishop of Speyer: I, Burchard, devoted servant of the flock of Christ of the holy Church of Worms, offer in God the blessedness of supreme happiness. Although the holy Catholic Church is ready to follow the evangelical teachings which say, “He who receives a prophet in the name of a prophet shall receive a prophet’s reward; and he who receives a righteous man in the name of a righteous man,” and so forth; and although the Apostle commands us to pursue hospitality and to share in the needs of holy men: nevertheless, because of those who have their conscience seared, who call themselves simple though filled with the devil’s cunning, who say that they travel from place to place for a work of piety though their own wickedness makes them fugitives, and who say that they have been admitted to sacred ministry though they have not been, the holy Fathers have decreed that no bishop shall receive or enthrone in his church an unknown cleric belonging to another diocese unless he has from his own bishop the letter called in the canons a formata.

We therefore make known to your fatherhood that our present brother, the bearer of these letters, named Ecmannus, was not expelled from us on account of his wickedness. Rather, at the request of our brothers, because he was of our household and was baptized by us, we granted him freedom, received canonically from the horn of the altar, and ordained him to the rank of presbyter. We have also made for him these letters of dismissal or commendation, and send him to your beloved brotherhood, so that he may be able to remain in your diocese under your sacred rule and protection.

I, Burchard, humble bishop, in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and in the unity of the holy Church, in which Peter was given the right of binding and loosing, absolve Ecmannus, presbyter of the city of Worms, in the tenth indiction; and I grant you permission to enthrone him in whatever church of your diocese you wish. We have therefore resolved to secure this letter on both sides with Greek letters and have judged that it should be confirmed with the seal-ring of our Church. May Christ preserve your brotherhood safe for us. π. γ. α. π. β. ε. ζ. ξ. α. κ. η. θ. Given at Worms, on the Ides of March, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1012, the tenth indiction.

### CHAPTER CCXXVIII — Concerning one who conceals a brother’s flight

(From the sayings of Basil.) If anyone learns that a person, unable to bear ecclesiastical discipline, intends to flee, and does not immediately report him, he should not doubt that he has made himself a participant in that person’s destruction. He is to be separated from the assembly of the brothers for as long as the other can be recalled.

### CHAPTER CCXXIX — Concerning those who mistreat their presbyters

(From the Council of Clermont, chapter 7.) If anyone dishonors his own presbyter or offers him insult in word or deed, let him be barred from the thresholds of the Church until he makes satisfaction through fitting penance. For the Apostle says: “Let the presbyters who rule well be held worthy of double honor.” Elsewhere he likewise says: “Obey your leaders; be subject to them,” etc.

### CHAPTER CCXXX — That the pope’s name shall be recited in holy churches

(From the Council of Vaison, chapter 3.) This also seemed right to us: that the name of the lord pope, whoever presides over the apostolic see, be recited in our Churches.

### CHAPTER CCXXXI — That a presbyter or deacon who is not a canon but lives in villages shall celebrate the principal feasts nowhere except in cities

(From the Council of Clermont, chapter 6.) If any presbyter or deacon is known not to be a canon in a city but to live in small villages, serving the holy office in oratories and celebrating the divine mysteries, we admonish him not henceforth to celebrate the chief feasts—the Nativity of the Lord, Easter, Pentecost, and any other principal feasts. He shall celebrate the aforesaid feasts nowhere but with his bishop in the city. All lay citizens who are older in age shall likewise come into the cities to their bishops on the said feasts and there hear the divine mysteries celebrated. If any, with wicked rashness, disregard these provisions, let them be excluded from communion.

### CHAPTER CCXXXII — That presbyters shall be granted authority to preach among their congregations

(From the Council of Vaison, chapter 6.) For the edification of all churches and the benefit of all the people, it also pleased us to grant presbyters authority to preach, not only in cities but also in every parish. If a presbyter is unable himself to preach because some infirmity prevents him, let the homilies of the holy Fathers be recited by approved deacons.

### CHAPTER CCXXXIII — Concerning clerics killed in a quarrel

(From the Council of Tribur, at which King Arnulf was present, chapter 50.) Any cleric who dies in war, in a quarrel, or in games of the heathen shall not be commended by offering or prayer, but shall fall into the hands of the Judge; he is not, however, to be deprived of burial.

### CHAPTER CCXXXIV — Concerning clerics made free by their masters

(From the council held at Altheim, at which King Conrad was present, chapter 38.) No cleric shall be promoted to the rank of presbyter unless this is done as written in the canons. For if anyone, out of love for God, chooses one of his slaves, teaches him letters, grants him freedom, makes him a presbyter through intercession with the bishop, and gives him food and clothing according to the Apostles, but that man afterward, lifted up in pride, refuses to celebrate Mass for his masters, observe the canonical hours, and chant psalms, and refuses to obey them justly, saying that he is free and wishing to become, as though freely, whatever man he wishes, the holy synod anathematizes this and judges that he is to be barred from holy communion until he comes to his senses and obeys his master according to the canonical precepts. But if with obstinate mind he also despises this, let him be accused before the bishop who ordained him and be degraded; and let him become the slave of that same master, as he was born. Whoever afterward keeps such a man with him, after learning the aforesaid matter concerning him, and does not return him to his master or cast him out from himself—whether bishop, count, cleric, or layman—being bound in fellowship with that anathema, shall pay the penalty of excommunication.

### CHAPTER CCXXXV — Concerning presbyters who flee the parishes in which they have been placed
