(From the Council of Chalon, chapter 41.) A presbyter who leaves his proper place and migrates to another shall by no means be received unless he states the reason for his migration and proves, under witnesses, that he lived innocently in the parish in which he was ordained. He shall also have letters bearing the names of the bishop and city impressed in lead; once these are recognized, and he is found to be such a person as may be trusted, let him be received.

### CHAPTER CCXXXVI — Concerning presbyters accused of a capital crime who do not have colleagues with whom they can clear themselves.

(From the Council of Tribur, attended by King Arnolph, chapter 6.) On presbyters accused of the crime of fornication or of some other capital offense, who have no colleagues with whom they can clear themselves, and how, if they should happen to fall, they are to make satisfaction. In judging such cases one must incline neither to the right nor to the left, but walk along the straight path. For it is written in the Council of Neocaesarea: “If a presbyter [Col. 0665D] takes a wife, let him be deposed from the order. But if [Col. 0666A] he has committed fornication or adultery, he must be expelled still further and reduced to penance.”

### CHAPTER CCXXXVII — On the preaching of presbyters

(From the Council of Tribur, attended by King Arnolph.)

We command you that each of you, every two or three weeks, on Sundays or on the festivals of the saints, should endeavor, after the Gospel has been read, to instruct the people entrusted to him in the church committed to his care with saving teachings drawn from Sacred Scripture, and should order them not to leave the church before the final praise—namely, “Benedicamus Domino,” or “Ite, missa est”—has been pronounced by the presbyter or deacon.

### CHAPTER CCXXXVIII — On ecclesiastics who desire to hold secular offices

[Col. 0666B] (From a letter of Pope Gregory addressed to Secundinus, a servant of God living in seclusion.)

It is certain that you would not appoint a commander over an army unless his labor and fidelity pleased you, and unless the excellence and diligence of his former life had shown him to be suitable. But if the command of an army is entrusted only to men of this kind, from this comparison with a good and worthy office it may be understood what sort of commander of souls he ought to be. Yet it is shameful and embarrassing for us to say that priests seize for themselves military command, although they have never witnessed the beginning of religious warfare.

### CHAPTER CCXXXIX — That truthful and God-fearing men be appointed deans in cities and public villages

(From the Council of Rouen, chapter 9.)

So that the people may be admonished [Col. 0666C] to attend without fail on Sundays and feast days at vespers, the nocturnal vigils, and Mass, and so that truthful and God-fearing men may be appointed as deans in cities and public villages, who will admonish the sluggish and negligent to hasten to God’s service without excuse; and so that the deans themselves may be bound by oath not to conceal the negligent and transgressors from the priests, despite any intervening consideration—whether affection, fear, kinship, or a gift—but to disclose their particular faults to them. It will be the priests’ task to correct their vices with zeal and divine love, together with the discipline that is due, just as the priests themselves do not wish to incur the sentence of just condemnation for the errors of others. And let feast days be celebrated from vespers to vespers, with due honor and without servile labor.

[Col. 0665] **END OF BOOK TWO.**

# BURCHARD, BISHOP OF THE CHURCH OF WORMS, DECRETALS, BOOK THREE: ON CHURCHES

## Argument of the Book

[Col. 0673B]

This book treats the establishment, worship, and honor of the houses of God; tithes and offerings; and the rights of individuals. It also shows which books have been received into the sacred canon and which have been rejected as apocryphal.

### CHAPTER I — What the Church is

(From the decree of Pope Julius, chapter 5.)

“Church” is Greek; in Latin it is translated as *convocation*, because it calls everyone to itself. It is called “Catholic,” that is, “universal,” because it has been established throughout the whole world, or because, being catholic—that is, general—it exists for instruction in the same doctrine.

### CHAPTER II — On the primitive Church

(From the decree of Pope Melchiades, chapter 8.)

No one who reads the divine Scriptures is unaware that, at the beginning of the nascent Church, the disciples gathered together with the multitude of believers, among whom there was one heart and one soul. They sold their estates and possessions, brought the proceeds, and these were distributed to each according to his need. The apostles foresaw that the future Church would be among the gentiles, especially because the Lord had foretold to them: “Go into all the world and preach the Gospel”; and because they knew that they themselves would be expelled from Judaea and scattered among the gentiles, while the Church would be gathered from an unformed people. For this reason they acquired no estates in Judaea, but only the proceeds, to support the needy. But when the Church grew amid the storms and adversities of the world, it advanced so far that not only the gentiles, [Col. 0673D] but even the Roman rulers, who held the monarchy of nearly the whole [Col. 0674B] world, came to the faith of Christ and to the sacraments of baptism.

### CHAPTER III — That priests used to hand over to the churches, for the common benefit, the fields they had been accustomed to sell

(From the decree of Pope Urban, chapter 2.)

When the priests, Levites, and the other faithful saw that they could provide greater benefit if they handed over to the churches over which bishops presided the inheritances and fields that they were selling—since from their revenues they could provide more and finer things for the faithful living a common life, both in the present and in the future, than from their sale proceeds—they began to hand over to the mother churches the estates and fields they had been accustomed to sell, and to live from their revenues.

### CHAPTER IV — At what time religious men consecrated themselves to the Lord, building basilicas on their own estates

[Col. 0674C]

(From the decree of Pope Melchiades, chapter 12.)

From that time onward, religious men consecrated to the Lord not only the possessions and estates that they had owned, but also themselves, building basilicas on their own estates in honor of the holy martyrs throughout the cities, and countless monasteries in which assemblies of those serving the Lord might gather. Finally, kings, governors, and magistrates not only granted this permission, but themselves also gave their own possessions throughout all the kingdoms of the earth, so that the needy, who possessed nothing in the world, might be fed; churches might be built and restored; and provisions might be granted without necessity to those who rightly served God and His Church, and to His servants.

### CHAPTER V — That Constantine was the first of the emperors to grant permission for building churches

[Col. 0675A]

(From the same source, chapter 10.)

Among these, the most religious Constantine, the first of the emperors openly to embrace the true faith, granted permission throughout the whole world, among those living under his Empire, not only for people to become Christians, but also for churches to be built, and he decreed that estates should be granted. Finally, this same prince instituted immense gifts and the construction of the temple of the first see, that of the blessed Peter, chief of the apostles, to such an extent that he abandoned the imperial seat where the Roman rulers presided and granted it for the benefit of blessed Peter and his successors.

### CHAPTER VI — That no one should build a church unless the bishop of the place has designated the site

(From the Council of Orléans, chapter 3.)

No one should build a church before the bishop of the city arrives, publicly fixes a cross there, and marks out the churchyard; and before that, he who wishes to build must specify what will suffice for lights, guardianship, and the wages of the guardians. After the donation has been displayed, let him build the house. Once it has been consecrated, let him sprinkle its churchyard with holy water.

### CHAPTER VII — On one who desires to build a church on his own estate

(From the Council of Worms, chapter 6.)

Whoever wishes to build a church on his own property may do so if he has the consent and approval of the bishop in whose parish it will be. Nevertheless, the bishop must take the greatest care that the older churches do not lose their right or their tithe because of the new churches, but that payment always be made to the older churches.

### CHAPTER VIII — That all churches should be under the authority of the bishop in whose territory they are situated

(From the Council of Orléans, chapter 1.)

It has been decided, according to the rule of the earlier canons, that all basilicas built in various places, or established day by day, should remain under the authority of the bishop in whose territory they are situated.

### CHAPTER IX — That ancient churches should not be stripped of their possessions on account of new ones

(From the Council of Meaux, chapter 8.)

Churches established in ancient times should be deprived neither of tithes nor of any possession, so that these may be assigned to new oratories.

### CHAPTER X — On churches and altars concerning which there is some doubt about their consecration, that they be consecrated

[Col. 0675D]

(From the same council, chapter 45.)

Let churches or altars whose consecration is uncertain be consecrated, and let superfluous altars be destroyed.

### CHAPTER XI — If an altar has been moved, that the church be consecrated again

(From the decree of Pope Hyginus, chapter 4.)

If the altar has been moved, let the church be consecrated again. If the walls have been altered but not the altar, let it be exorcised only with salt.

### CHAPTER XII — If a church has been violated, that it be consecrated again

(From the same source, chapter 6.)

If a church has been violated by homicide or adultery, let it be cleansed with the greatest care and consecrated again.

### CHAPTER XIII — That it is not permitted to dedicate a church where a pagan has been buried

[Col. 0676A]

(From the Council of Orléans, chapter 7.)

It is not permitted to consecrate a church where a pagan has been buried, nor to celebrate Masses in it; rather, the body must be cast out and the place cleansed.

### CHAPTER XIV — That it is not permitted to consecrate an altar in a church in which corpses have been buried

(From the same source, chapter 6.)

In a church in which the corpses of the dead are buried, it is not permitted to sanctify the altar. But if it was consecrated previously, Masses may be celebrated in it.

### CHAPTER XV — That places once dedicated should remain so forever

(From the Council held at Aachen, chapter 4.)

Places once dedicated to God, or once made monasteries, should remain so forever and may not thereafter be made secular dwellings.

### CHAPTER XVI — On places formerly consecrated and now neglected, that they be restored again

(From the same source, chapter 6.)

It has been decided that places consecrated long ago and now defiled by filth should, as far as possible, be restored to their former condition.

### CHAPTER XVII — That no one presume to erect another altar except one consecrated by the bishop

(From the decree of Pope Hormisdas, chapter 10.)

Let no presbyter erect another altar in a consecrated church except one sanctified by the bishop of the place or with his permission, so that there may be a distinction between what is sacred and what is not sacred, and so that no one may pretend that there has been a dedication when there has not. If he does so, let him be degraded if he is a cleric; if he is a layman, let him be anathematized.

### CHAPTER XVIII — That the possessed sweep the floors of churches

[Col. 0676C]

(From the Council of Carthage, chapter 91.)

Let the possessed sweep the floors of the houses of God.

### CHAPTER XIX — On monasteries once consecrated

(From the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 24.)

Monasteries once dedicated, with the counsel of the bishops who govern the cities, must remain monasteries forever, and the property belonging to them must be reserved for the monasteries; they may not thereafter be made secular dwellings. Those who permit this to happen will be subject to the judgments of the canons.

### CHAPTER XX — On those who presume to claim the endowment of a church for themselves

[Col. 0676D]

(From the Council of Toledo, chapter 19.)

Many, contrary to the provisions of the canons, request that the churches they have built be consecrated in such a way that they consider the endowment they have bestowed upon the churches not to belong to the bishop’s administration. This action was displeasing in the past and is prohibited in the future; rather, everything must belong, according to ancient custom, to the administration and authority of the bishop.

### CHAPTER XXI — On destroyed churches and how they ought to be restored

(From the decree of Pope Hyginus, chapter 5.)

With regard to destroyed churches, where there are either more than necessary or churches larger than can be restored from the property belonging to them, the bishop’s foresight should determine a way by which they may continue to exist.

### CHAPTER XXII — That there cannot be several baptismal churches within one boundary

(From the Council held at Aachen, chapter 5.)

There cannot be several baptismal churches within one boundary, but only one, together with its subordinate chapels. If a dispute arises concerning the boundary between two mother churches, let the people of both discern the matter; and if they do not agree, let the dispute be decided by the judgment of God.

### CHAPTER XXIII — That regular monasteries may neither be sold nor exchanged except with another monastery

(From the decree of Pope Silverius, chapter 1.)

No king or any other person may lawfully transfer a monastery into private ownership, except to another monastery; exchange it, except with another monastery; or sell it by any contrivance whatsoever. Divine, apostolic, and canonical authority has also sanctioned this under penalty of anathema. If it is done, it will have no force, but the monastery itself must be restored to its former condition.

### CHAPTER XXIV — That no one may transfer the land of one church to another unless it is exchanged

(From the Council of Lyon, chapter 5.)

Neither a bishop nor an abbot may transfer the land of one church to another, even if both are under his authority. If they wish to exchange their lands, however, they may do so with the consent of both parties.

### CHAPTER XXV — That altars, unless they are made of stone, should not be consecrated with chrism

(From the Council of Épaone, chapter 10.)

If altars are not made of stone, they should not be consecrated with an anointing of chrism. [Col. 0677C] For the celebration of the divine offices, their provincial bishops must also observe the order maintained by the metropolitans.

### CHAPTER XXVI — That a monastery may be moved to another place for improvement

(From the decree of Pope Boniface, chapter 6.)

If anyone wishes to move his monastery to another place for its improvement, let him do so with the counsel of the bishop and his brothers, and let him leave a presbyter in the former place for the ministry of the church.

### CHAPTER XXVII — That a church should not be dedicated without Mass

(From the decree of Pope Evaristus, chapter 4.)

All basilicas should always be consecrated with Mass.

### CHAPTER XXVIII — That a bishop should prohibit no one from entering a church and hearing the word of God

[Col. 0677D]

(From the Council held at Valencia, chapter 16.)

A bishop should prohibit no one from entering a church and hearing the word of God, whether gentile, heretic, or Jew, up to the Mass of the catechumens.

### CHAPTER XXIX — That the people who have assembled for Mass should not depart before it is finished

(From the Council of Arles, chapter 1.)

Likewise, when the people have assembled in God’s name to celebrate Mass, they should not depart before the solemnity of the Mass has been completed; and, when the bishop is absent, they should receive the priest’s blessing.

### CHAPTER XXX — On those who possess ecclesiastical benefices

(From the Council of Mainz, chapter 42.)

Whoever possesses an ecclesiastical benefice must give every assistance toward restoring the roofs of the church or repairing the churches themselves, and must pay the ninth and the tenth.

### CHAPTER XXXI — On churches established among barbarians

(From the Council of Constantinople, chapter 6.)

The churches of God established among barbarian peoples ought to be governed and administered according to the custom observed by the Fathers.

### CHAPTER XXXII — On the churches of the Arians

(From the decree of Pope John I, addressed to the bishops throughout Italy.)

Wherever you find churches of the Arians, consecrate them as catholic churches without any delay through divine prayers and works. For when we were at Constantinople, both on behalf of the Catholic religion and in the interest of King Theodoric, at the urging and encouragement of the most devout and Christian Justin, the orthodox emperor, who was uprooting the Arians, we consecrated as catholic churches all those in those regions that we were able to find, with the Lord’s assistance.

### CHAPTER XXXIII — On abandoned diocesan churches

(From the Council of Tarragona, chapter 9.)

Taught by the experience of many circumstances, we have found that some diocesan churches have been abandoned. Therefore we have decreed by this constitution that the order of ancient custom be preserved, that dioceses be visited by the bishop each year, and that, if any basilica should be found abandoned, it be repaired by his arrangement. For we know that the rulers established, in accordance with ancient tradition, that bishops should receive a third part of everything.

### CHAPTER XXXIV — How a bishop may properly join an abandoned church to another church

(From the register of Gregory, sent to Bacauda, bishop of Formiae.)

Temporal necessity presses us, and the decrease in the number of persons requires us to assist abandoned churches with a wholesome and prudent arrangement. Therefore, since we have learned that the Church of Minturnae has been utterly abandoned, both in clergy and people, and since we foresee that your request concerning it—that it be joined to the Formian Church, in which the body of the blessed martyr Erasmus rests and over which your Fraternity presides—is pious and entirely just, we have deemed it necessary, taking into consideration both the desolation of that place and the poverty of your church, to grant by the authority of this decree to the right and authority of your church the revenues of the aforesaid Church of Minturnae, and whatever by ancient or modern right, or by privilege, could or can in any way belong to it. From the present time, you are to care for it as you would for your own church and arrange its affairs according to your authority, so that what until now might have perished may henceforth contribute to the benefit of the poor of your church and to the advancement of its clergy.

### CHAPTER XXXV — That paintings should not be made in a church

(From the Council of Elvira, chapter 2.)

It has been decided that paintings should not be made in a church, lest what is worshiped and adored be depicted on the walls.

### CHAPTER XXXVI — Likewise, on painting

(From a letter of Gregory addressed to Secundinus, a servant of God living in seclusion.)

It is one thing to adore a picture and another to learn through the history represented in a picture what ought to be adored. For what Scripture provides to readers, painting provides to uneducated people who look at it: in it the ignorant see what they ought to follow; in it those who do not know letters read. Thus, especially for the gentiles, a picture takes the place of reading. You, who live among the gentiles, ought to have paid close attention to this, lest, while being inflamed by proper zeal but without caution, you generate a scandal in fierce hearts.

Therefore what had been placed in the churches not for adoration but solely for the instruction of the minds of the ignorant ought not to have been broken. And because antiquity, not without reason, permitted histories of the saints to be painted in venerable places, if you had tempered your zeal with discretion, you could undoubtedly both have obtained beneficially what you intended and gathered rather than scattered the flock that had been assembled, so that the untarnished name of shepherd might stand out and the guilt of a scatterer might not weigh upon you.

### Chapter XXXVII — That a bishop must not demand any gift as a matter of obligation for consecrating a church

*(From the Council of Worms, chapter 1.)* It has been decided that whenever a bishop is invited by one of the faithful to consecrate a church, he must not demand any gift from the founder as though it were owed by obligation; but if the founder himself offers something of his own accord, it must not be refused. Nevertheless, each bishop must remember that he should not dedicate a church until he has first received confirmation, by a written deed of donation, of the endowment of the basilica and of the support required for its service. For it is no less reckless to consecrate a church without lamps or without substantial support for those who are to serve there than it would be to consecrate a private house as a church. [Col. 0679C]

### Chapter XXXVIII — That it is not permissible to consecrate a church in which the bodies of unbelievers have been buried

*(From the Council of Cologne, chapter 23.)* It is not permissible to consecrate a church in which the corpses of unbelievers have been buried. Nevertheless, it appears suitable for consecration—[provided that] the bodies have first been removed, the walls scraped, or the wood washed, and the building reconstructed. If it had previously been consecrated, Masses may be celebrated in it, provided that those buried there were faithful. [Col. 0679D]

### Chapter XXXIX — For what purposes the wood of a dedicated church is to be used

*(From the decree of Pope Hyginus, chapter 3.)* The wood of a dedicated church must not be used for any other work except another church; alternatively, it is to be burned in the fire or used for the benefit of the brothers in a monastery. It must not be employed for the works of laymen.

### Chapter XL — What a bishop should do if several heirs contend over one church

*(From the Council of Tribur, chapter 20.)* If several heirs contend over a church held in common, the bishop must order the sacred relics to be removed and the church to be closed until, by common agreement and with the bishop’s counsel, they appoint a presbyter there and provide for his support. [Col. 0680A]

### Chapter XLI — On the same matter

*(From the decree of Pope Gregory, chapter 5.)* With regard to churches divided among co-heirs, consideration must be given to whether, according to the bishop’s provision and admonition, the co-heirs are willing to retain and honor them. If they oppose this, it must remain within the bishop’s authority to decide whether to allow the churches to continue in that condition or to remove the relics from them.

### Chapter XLII — On churches divided among heirs

*(From the Council of Metz, chapter 1.)* It has been reported to the holy synod that churches established on private estates are divided among heirs, and that such hostility arises from this division that a single altar is split into four parts, each part having its own presbyter—something that cannot occur without discord and hostility. Therefore it has seemed good to us that churches of this kind should not be divided among heirs. If they fall into dispute and hostility arises among them, so that a priest cannot canonically perform his office there, the bishop of the city must order that the solemn celebration of Masses be suspended there entirely until they return to harmony and, by common agreement and counsel, that church has a priest canonically appointed who can freely perform his ministry there. [Col. 0680B]

### Chapter XLIII — That each presbyter is to have a single church

*(From the decree of Pope Dionysius, chapter 4.)* Concerning the parish churches about which you wished to consult the Apostolic See—how they are to be guarded and assigned to priests—we can communicate nothing better to Your Charity than that you should follow what we know has recently been done in the Roman Church: we have assigned individual churches to individual presbyters and established that each should possess his own jurisdiction. Thus no one should invade the boundaries or jurisdiction of another’s parish, but each should be content with his own boundaries and guard the church and people entrusted to him in such a way that before the tribunal of the eternal Judge he may render an account of everything entrusted to him and receive glory, not condemnation, for his actions. You and all bishops should follow this rule, dearest brother, and make what is written to you known to all whom you can, so that this instruction may be not particular but general. [Col. 0680C–D]

### Chapter XLIV — On the same matter

*(From the Council of Reims, chapter 2.)* Let each presbyter be content with the one church to which he has been ordained, and let no one presume to minister in two churches.

### Chapter XLV — On the same matter

*(From the same council, chapter 8.)* Just as there ought to be one presbyter in each church, so that church itself, which is called his bride or wife, cannot be divided among several presbyters; rather, it shall have only one priest, who will govern it chastely and sincerely. Therefore we forbid anyone to presume to divide a church between two or more persons, because the Church of Christ ought to be a wife and bride, not a prostitute, as Pope Callistus testifies. [Col. 0681A]

### Chapter XLVI — That each presbyter is to be content with one church

*(From the same council, chapter 11.)* It has been decreed that each church is to have its own presbyter wherever, with the bishop’s provision, circumstances permit this to be done.

### Chapter XLVII — On the same matter

*(From the Council of Nantes, chapter 8.)* Just as a bishop can have no more than one city and a man one wife, so a presbyter can have only one church. Therefore no presbyter should presume to have several churches if he wishes to remain in good standing.

### Chapter XLVIII — On the same matter

*(From the Council of Meaux, chapter 10.)* If anyone from the priestly order, despising a lesser church, has ambitiously and improperly sought a more eminent one, the canonical judgment against him is to be maintained: namely, that he lose both. [Col. 0681B]

### Chapter XLIX — On the same matter

*(From the decree of Pope Callistus, chapter 4.)* Just as another man’s wife is not permitted to be adulterated by anyone, or judged or disposed of, except by her own husband while he lives, so neither is the bishop’s or presbyter’s wife—who is unquestionably understood to be his church or parish—permitted, while he lives, to be judged or disposed of by another, or to be enjoyed through another’s intercourse. Hence the Apostle says: “A wife is bound by the law as long as her husband lives; but when her husband dies, she is released from the law concerning her husband.” In the same way, the church, which is called the priest’s wife, is bound to him while he lives. When he has died, let her marry in the Lord—that is, according to the rule. For if she marries another while he lives, she will be judged an adulteress. [Col. 0681C]

### Chapter L — On the sacred orders

*(From a letter of Isidore.)* Isidore, bishop, to the holy and meritorious blessed brother Lantfred, bishop.

Having read the letters of Your Holiness, I rejoiced to learn from their report of your desired well-being. As for the matters which your eloquent message sought to explain in what follows, I give thanks to God that you devote yourself to the concern of pastoral office and inquire how ecclesiastical offices are to be ordered. Although everything is known to your prudence, since you consult me in brotherly affection, I shall explain, insofar as I am able, what belongs to each of the Church’s ranks. [Col. 0681D]

The psalmist’s office is to sing, to recite praises and responsories, and to perform whatever belongs to the art of singing. The doorkeeper is responsible for the keys of the church, so that he may close and open the temple of God, guard everything inside and outside, receive the faithful, and exclude the excommunicated and unbelievers.

The reader is responsible for proclaiming the readings and preaching to the people what the prophets foretold. The exorcist is responsible for memorizing the exorcisms and placing his hands, during exorcism, upon the possessed and catechumens. The acolyte is responsible for preparing the lamps in the sacristy. He carries the candle and prepares the stands for the eucharistic chalice.

The subdeacon is responsible for carrying the chalice and paten to the altar of Christ, handing them to the levites, and serving them; he also holds the ewer, basin, and towel and presents them before the altar to the bishop, presbyter, and levites for washing their hands. [Col. 0682A]

The deacon is responsible for assisting the priests and ministering in everything performed in the sacraments of Christ—namely, in baptism, chrism, the paten, and the chalice—and for bringing and arranging the offerings on the altar. He also prepares and clothes the Lord’s table, carries the cross, and preaches the Gospel and the Apostle. For just as readers have been commanded to preach the Old Testament, so deacons have been commanded to preach the New. He is also responsible for the office of prayers and for reciting the names. He prompts ears toward the Lord, urges prayer, cries out, and announces peace. [Col. 0682B]

The presbyter is responsible for confecting the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood on God’s altar, saying the prayer, and blessing God’s gifts. The bishop is responsible for the consecration of basilicas, the anointing of the altar, and the preparation of the chrism. He distributes the offices and ecclesiastical orders mentioned above; he blesses sacred virgins; and although each person performs his own particular function, he is nevertheless the organizer of all.

These are the orders and ministries of the clergy. They are distributed, however, by pontifical authority under the care of the archdeacon and the oversight of the chief cantor and treasurer. The archdeacon commands the subdeacons and levites, to whom these ministries belong. The arrangement for clothing the altar, the care of incense, the necessary supervision of the sacrifice, the assignment of which levite is to read the Apostle and the Gospel, which is to recite the prayers or sing the responsory on Sundays or feast days, as well as the care and organization of the parishioners and the resolution of disputes, belong to his charge. He advises the priest about preparing the diocesan basilicas. By the bishop’s command he investigates the parishes and reports to the bishop the ornaments and property of the parish basilicas, as well as the records of ecclesiastical liberties. He receives the money collected from Communion, conveys it to the bishop, and distributes to the clergy their proper shares. [Col. 0682C]

### Chapter LI — On newly discovered churches or saints

*(From the Council of Cologne, chapter 5.)* Churches or saints newly discovered without authority are not to be venerated unless approved by the bishop in whose territory they are located, while canonical authority concerning this and all churches remains in force. [Col. 0682D]

### Chapter LII — That each church is to have a complete manse free from service

*(From the Council of Worms, chapter 18.)* It has been decreed that one complete manse, free from every service, is to be assigned to each church. The presbyters established there are not to perform any service from the tithes, the offerings of the faithful, the houses, the courtyards or gardens situated beside the church, or the aforesaid manse, except ecclesiastical service. If they possess anything more, they are to render from it the service owed to their superiors.

### Chapter LIII — That no one is to compel a presbyter to pay a tax from the church’s endowment or manse

[Col. 0683A]

*(From the Council of Meaux, chapter 8.)* In accordance with synodal commands, we have decreed that no mortal is to compel any presbyter to pay a tax from church land, a manse, or slaves, or from anything that anyone may have given to the church for a burial place, or from the tithes and offerings of the faithful. No one of any order or rank is to take anything from these resources or demand any temporal payment. If anyone does so, let him be deprived of Communion until he has made satisfaction.

### Chapter LIV — On altars erected indiscriminately in the countryside

*(From the African Council, chapter 50.)* It has likewise been decided that the altars erected here and there in fields and along roads as memorials of martyrs, in which no body or relics of martyrs are shown to have been deposited, are to be demolished by the bishops who preside over those places, if this can be done. If popular disturbances prevent it, the people are nevertheless to be warned not to frequent those places, so that those who think rightly may not be held there by any superstition. In general, no memorial of martyrs is to be accepted as genuine unless either a body or certain relics are present, or the origin of some habitation, possession, or martyrdom is transmitted with thoroughly trustworthy evidence. Altars erected anywhere on the basis of dreams or empty revelations, as it were, of random persons are to be rejected in every way. [Col. 0683B]

### Chapter LV — That no profane person is to defame the dignity of martyrs

*(From the Council of Carthage, chapter 3.)* Let no profane person defame the dignity of the martyrs; nor are the bodies of sufferers, which were ordered to be committed to burial solely through ecclesiastical mercy, to be treated so that persons driven headlong by madness or set apart by such a sin are called martyrs, without regard to reason or to the proper time at which martyrdoms are celebrated. [The transmitted Latin is syntactically uncertain in this clause.] If anyone, to the injury of the martyrs, adds madness to their glory, it is agreed that, if he is a layman, he is to be brought to penance; but if he is a cleric, he is to be deprived of his dignity after admonition.

All said: “Your holiness will rightly stand.” This has also been established by the individual councils. [Col. 0683C]

### Chapter LVI — That the solemn celebration of Mass is to take place not everywhere, but in places consecrated by the bishop

*(From the Council of Tribur, chapter 4.)* We judge that the solemn celebration of Mass is to take place not everywhere, but in places consecrated by the bishop or wherever he has permitted it. We also grant that if, as has happened very extensively on account of our sins, churches have been burned and destroyed by Normans, Slavs, Hungarians, wicked Christians, or in any other way, Masses may meanwhile be celebrated in chapels with a consecrated altar-board until the churches themselves can be restored. For those on a journey, if there is no church, we grant permission to celebrate the solemnity of Mass in the open air or in tents, provided that a consecrated altar-board and the other sacred objects required for this office are present; otherwise we forbid it entirely. [Col. 0683D–0684A]

### Chapter LVII — On not celebrating Mass except in a consecrated place

*(From the decree of Pope Felix IV, sent to all bishops.)* I have gratefully received the letters of Your Holiness, which you sent to the Apostolic See concerning certain questions, as to its head, so that you might receive answers from the source from which the whole Church’s religion took its beginning. I have taken care to answer you briefly.

With regard to the consecration of churches and the celebration of Mass, it is clear to all who know the precepts of the New and Old Testament that these things must not take place anywhere except in places consecrated to the Lord, unless there is great necessity. We read that Moses made the tabernacle at the Lord’s command and consecrated it, together with its table and altar, its bronze vessels and implements, for the completion of divine worship. We know that he consecrated these things not only with divine prayers but also, at the Lord’s command, anointed them with holy oil. [Col. 0684B]

How these things were done, and how no one other than priests, consecrated by sacred anointing and dedicated to the Lord in holy garments, and levites handled, carried, raised, and set them down, is found in the very ordinances written by Moses at the Lord’s command in the law of the Lord. We also find how David, the most devout of kings, enlarged the worship of God and wished to build the Lord’s temple, but was forbidden because of the great amount of blood he had shed, although he himself had gathered the funds. His son Solomon completed, at the Lord’s command and with his help, what David had wished to do, and consecrated the temple, the altar, and the other things required for divine worship. [Col. 0684C]

### Chapter LVIII — On the same matter

*(From a letter of Pope Felix IV sent to all bishops.)* The Jews therefore held consecrated, with divine prayers, the places in which they sacrificed to the Lord, and they offered gifts to the Lord only in places dedicated to God. If the Jews, who served the shadow of the law, did these things, how much more must those to whom the truth has been revealed—and to whom grace and truth have been given through Jesus—build temples for the Lord and adorn them as best we can, and devoutly and solemnly consecrate them, with their altars, vessels, vestments, and the other implements required for divine worship, through divine prayers and sacred anointings. [Col. 0684D]

We must celebrate Masses and offer sacrifices only in places consecrated to the Lord by bishops, not by chorepiscopi, who have often been forbidden to do so, except, as stated above, when the greatest necessity requires it. Nor, unless the greatest necessity compels us, are these things to be done in houses, because the sacred canons prohibit sacrifices from being offered in houses. Rather, in divine tabernacles dedicated by pontiffs through prayers and on tables consecrated to the Lord and anointed with sacred oil by pontiffs, they are to be offered in the supreme necessity mentioned above, and not according to anyone’s preference or laziness.

It is better not to sing or hear Mass than to do so in places where it ought not to be celebrated, unless, as has often been stated, the greatest necessity arises, because necessity has no law. Hence it is written: “See that you do not offer your burnt offerings in every place that you see, but in the place that the Lord your God will choose.” And in Exodus it is read: “You have seen that I have spoken to you from heaven. You shall not make gods of silver for yourselves, nor shall you make gods of gold for yourselves. You shall make an altar of earth for me, and you shall offer upon it your burnt offerings and your peace offerings—your sheep—in every place where there shall be a memorial of my name.” [Col. 0685A]

Just as no priests other than those consecrated to the Lord ought to sing Masses or offer sacrifices upon the altar, so it is not permissible to sing Masses or offer sacrifices anywhere except in the aforesaid places consecrated to the Lord. If it is read in chapter 26 of the Council of Laodicea that those who have not been ordained by bishops cannot exorcise either in churches or in houses, how much more are the ministries of the higher ranks impermissible unless performed by those consecrated to those ranks, whether the offices are carried out or sacrifices offered.

As was briefly stated above, offerings must not be offered in houses; this is prohibited in the same council, chapter 59, as follows: “It is not proper for offerings to be celebrated in houses by bishops or presbyters.” [Col. 0685B]

The solemn anniversaries of the dedication of churches and of priests are to be celebrated solemnly each year, with the Lord himself providing the example. When he came to celebrate the feast of the dedication of the Temple with the rest of the people, he gave all an example that it should be done, as it is written: “The feast of Dedication took place at Jerusalem; it was winter, and Jesus was walking in the temple in Solomon’s portico.” That the Dedication is to be celebrated for eight days, you will find in the Book of Kings, after the dedication of the temple had been completed.

Concerning the consecration of churches, whenever there is doubt and there is neither certain Scripture nor reliable witnesses by whom the consecration is known, know without any hesitation that they are to be consecrated, lest such hesitation cause deterioration; for an act whose performance is unknown cannot be shown to have been repeated. [Col. 0685C]

Brothers, these testimonies of Scripture, consulted by apostolic authority in response to your questions, should suffice as a brief answer. Nevertheless, you must take care, and all must be instructed, that nothing unlawful be done.

### Chapter LIX — That it is not permissible to celebrate Mass except in places consecrated by the bishop of the city

[Col. 0685D]

*(From the decree of Pope Clement, chapter 22.)* Therefore, while placed here—that is, in the present life—you must recognize the will and command of God, and where the place for acting and sacrificing is. It is not permissible to sacrifice or celebrate Mass in other places except those in which the proper bishop has ordered it, or which have been duly consecrated by the bishop who properly governs the city. Otherwise these things are neither to be done nor rightly celebrated, as the New and Old Testament teach us. The Apostles received these matters from the Lord and handed them on to us. We teach them and command you and everyone to observe and teach them without reproach to those who are obliged to act accordingly.

### Chapter LX — On the same matter

[Col. 0686A]

*(From the Council of Laodicea, chapter 58.)* Offerings must not be celebrated in houses by bishops or presbyters.

### Chapter LXI — On the same matter

*(From the Council of Orléans, chapter 4.)* We have heard that certain laymen order their own presbyters to celebrate Masses in their houses, and that amid the barking of dogs and packs of prostitutes the mysteries of holiness are polluted rather than consecrated. Therefore we command that no presbyter presume to sing Mass outside a church. Only if the necessity of a journey requires it do we permit him to celebrate Mass in a tent or in the open air, in a clean place far removed from every impurity—and even then never without a consecrated altar-board. [Col. 0686B]

### Chapter LXII — On the repair of a church

*(From a letter of Pope Vigilius.)* Concerning the structure of any church, if it has been damaged and must be restored, and if the solemnity of consecration is to be repeated in a place where no relics are present, we judge that it causes no impediment if a small amount of exorcised water is sprinkled there. For we know that the consecration of any church in which an altar of the Holy Spirit is not installed consists only in the celebration of Masses. Therefore, even if a basilica of the saints has been renewed from its foundations, without any doubt, once the solemn celebration of Mass has taken place in it, the sanctification of the entire consecration will have been completed. But if the relics it possessed have been removed, it will receive again the reverence of sanctification through their replacement and the solemn celebration of Masses. [Col. 0686C]

### Chapter LXIII — That Masses are not to be celebrated before the third hour of the day

*(From a letter of Pope Telesphorus, chapter 6.)* Masses are not to be celebrated before the third hour of the day, because it is read that at that same hour the Lord was crucified and the Holy Spirit descended upon the Apostles, except on the night of the holy Nativity.

### Chapter LXIV — That Masses may be celebrated each day for the faithful departed

*(From the Council of Chalon, chapter 39.)* It has also seemed good to us that at every solemn celebration of Mass the Lord be entreated, at the appropriate place, for the spirits of the departed. Just as no day is excluded on which the Lord is not entreated for the living and for whatever needs may arise, so likewise no day should be excluded on which prayers are not poured out to the Lord in the solemn celebration of Masses for the souls of the faithful. [Col. 0686D]

From ancient times, therefore, the holy Church has maintained this custom: that the spirits of those who rest be commended to the Lord both in the solemn celebration of Masses and in other prayers. Blessed Augustine says: “Prayers for the spirits of the dead must not be omitted; we commend that they be offered for all within the Christian and catholic fellowship.” The Church also receives the dead under a general commemoration, without naming them individually, so that those who lack parents, children, or any relatives or friends to offer these things for them may receive them from the one common pious mother.

### Chapter LXV — That a Mass for the dead is to be sung for all Christians

[Col. 0687A]

*(From the statements of Dionysius the Areopagite and Augustine.)* Dionysius the Areopagite says that anyone who offers Masses for an evil man commits blasphemy against God. Augustine says that it should be done for all Christians, because it either benefits them or benefits those who offer or request it on their behalf.

### Chapter LXVI — That the arrangements for Mass made in the metropolitan church are to be observed in the other churches of the province

*(From the Council of Gerona, chapter 6.)* Just as the arrangements for Mass are made in the metropolitan church, so, in the name of God, they are to be observed in all the churches of the province, both the order of the Mass itself and the custom of psalmody and ministry.

### Chapter LXVII — That prayers and prefaces not approved by a council are not to be celebrated

[Col. 0687B]

*(From the African Council, chapter 64.)* It has also been decided that the prayers approved in a council—whether prefaces, commendations, or impositions of hands—are to be celebrated by everyone. No others at all are to be uttered contrary to the faith; rather, whatever has been discussed with the more prudent is to be said.

### Chapter LXVIII — That no presbyter is to presume to sing Mass alone

*(From the Council of Nantes, chapter 30.)* The holy council has decreed that no presbyter presume to sing Mass alone. To whom does he say, “The Lord be with you,” or “Lift up your hearts,” or “Let us give thanks to the Lord our God,” when there is no one to respond? Or, in the Canon, “and of all who stand around,” when no one is present? Or whom does he invite to prayer when he says, “Let us pray,” when there is no one to pray with him? [Col. 0687C]

Either these expressions must be entirely omitted, in which case the sacrifice will not only be incomplete, but whoever he is will incur that dreadful sentence: “If anyone takes away from this, may God take away his share from the book of life”; or, if he whispers these words to walls, it will be ridiculous.

Therefore that dangerous superstition must above all be eradicated from monasteries of monks. Superiors must see to it that presbyters in monasteries and other churches have assistants in the celebration of Masses. If anyone transgresses these provisions, let him be suspended from office.

## Here begin the decrees of Pope Pelagius II, successor of Benedict and predecessor of Pope Gregory

### Chapter LXIX — On the prefaces which the holy Roman Church both praises and firmly maintains

*(From the decree of Pope Pelagius.)* Pelagius, bishop of the Roman Church and of the Apostolic See, to all the bishops of the regions of Germany and Gaul.

When, in the name of God, we had convened in the Roman Church a synod of bishops and of the other fellow priests and faithful of God, and were carefully discussing ecclesiastical statutes as they had been handed down by the Apostles and the holy Fathers, your letters arrived. To give them greater authority, living voices also came forward, requesting that we send you in writing the order of the prefaces which the holy Roman Church has maintained until now. [Col. 0688A]

We rejoiced greatly at your good will and zeal. Carefully rereading the sacred Roman order and the sacred constitutions of our predecessors, we found that only these nine prefaces are to be received into the sacred catalogue—those which the distant past has preserved until now in the Roman Church:

1. One for the Paschal season in white vestments.
2. Another for the Ascension of the Lord.
3. A third for Pentecost.
4. A fourth for the Nativity of the Lord.
5. A fifth for the Appearance of the Lord.
6. A sixth for the Apostles.
7. A seventh for the holy Trinity.
8. An eighth for the Cross.
9. A ninth, to be said only for the fast of Lent.

The holy Roman Church holds and preserves these prefaces. We command you to maintain them. [Col. 0688B]

### Chapter LXX — On priests, if an attack of illness occurs during the time of Mass

*(From the Eighth Council of Toledo, chapter 2.)* Nothing established according to the orders is to be rashly presumed against them, nor are matters held in the highest reverence to be dissolved by even the slightest touch of presumption, since they have merely been commanded to be done and are not known to have been interrupted, lest the increase of weakness deprive nature of the strength of health. Provision is made not only for human frailty but also for the sacred mysteries of God, with attentive care.

We have therefore judged it appropriate that, when the holy mysteries are being consecrated by priests during the celebration of Mass, if any attack of illness occurs by which the mystery of consecration already begun cannot be completed, it be permissible for a bishop or presbyter to complete the consecration as part of the office already begun. For nothing is appropriate as a supplement to mysteries already initiated except the completion of the blessing by either the priest who began or the one who follows, since they cannot be considered perfect unless they are completed according to the order of perfection. [Col. 0688C]

Since we are all one in Christ, diversity creates no contradiction where the unity of faith displays the effectiveness of success. Let all clergy of every order understand that this provision has been granted or assigned to them, and, as stated above, that others immediately succeed those who precede them to complete the rite.

Nevertheless, lest what is provided because of bodily weakness be turned to the ruin of presumption, no one is to celebrate Mass after food, drink, or any small amount of consumption; and no minister or priest, once he has begun, is to presume entirely to abandon incomplete offices without an evident outbreak of distress. If anyone presumes to violate these provisions, he shall incur the sentence of excommunication. [Col. 0688D]

### Chapter LXXI — On the same matter

*(From the decree of Pope Anacletus.)* When priests sacrifice, they must not do this alone, but must have witnesses with them, so that they may be shown to offer sacrifice perfectly to God in places consecrated to the Lord. For the authority of the divine law says: “See that you do not offer your burnt offerings in every place that you see, but in the place that the Lord your God will choose.”

### Chapter LXXII — On presbyters afflicted by demons and various disorders, who are not permitted to handle sacred things

[Col. 0689A]

*(From the decree of Pope Pius, chapter 6.)* It has rightly been determined by the rules of our predecessors that those entangled in demonic attacks and other disorders are not permitted to handle the sacred mysteries. With the agreement of reason, we have commonly defined this provision: no one who is seized and thrown to the ground by demons, or who is carried away by attacks of distress in any manner, may dare to minister at the sacred altars or, without investigation, intrude upon the divine sacraments. The exception is those who, afflicted by bodily ailments but without such attacks, are demonstrably thrown to the ground.

Even these men, however, are to be suspended from the office, order, and place of their ministry until, after the passage of one year, they are found, through the discernment of the bishop, to be free from demonic attacks. [Col. 0689B]

### Chapter LXXIII — On the same matter

*(From the decree of Pope Soter, chapter 8.)* Each person must carefully heed the warning of the divine oracle which says: “Woe to the one who is alone, because when he falls he has no one to raise him up.” We must earnestly fear and guard against the possibility that during those hours and times when psalms are sung to the Lord or sacrifice is offered, a harmful attack or any bodily illness may overtake someone engaged alone in the divine offices—an event that might suddenly cause his body to collapse or confuse his mind through alienation or terror.

Therefore, taking precautions against such occurrences, we have judged it necessary to establish that, wherever the availability of time, place, or clergy permits, anyone singing to God and offering sacrifice is to have behind him the assistance of a nearby companion. Thus, if by some accident the person who has come to perform the offices is disturbed or thrown to the ground, he will always have behind him someone who can carry out his part without fear and complete the office that has been begun. [Col. 0689C]

### Chapter LXXIV — On presbyters who are accustomed to celebrate Masses alone

*(From the same decree, chapter 10.)* It has also been established that no presbyter presume to celebrate the solemnity of Mass unless he himself, as the third person, has two others present who respond to him. Since he says in the plural, “The Lord be with you,” and in the Secrets, “Pray for me,” it is entirely appropriate that a response be made to his greeting.

### Chapter LXXV — On those who reject the offerings of married presbyters

[Col. 0689D]

*(From the Council of Agde, chapter 8.)* If anyone decides that a married presbyter ought not to offer on account of his marriage, and for that reason abstains from his offering, let him be anathema.

### Chapter LXXVI — That presbyters are to receive Communion whenever they celebrate Mass

*(From the Council of Rouen, chapter 2.)* It has been reported to us that certain presbyters, after celebrating Mass, refuse to receive themselves the divine mysteries which they have consecrated and hand the Lord’s chalice to little women who bring offerings to the Mass, or to certain laymen who do not know how to distinguish the Lord’s body—that is, how to discern spiritual food from bodily food.

The faithful know how contrary this is to all ecclesiastical religion. Therefore we forbid all presbyters to presume to do this in the future. Instead, the presbyter himself must receive it reverently and hand what is to be collected to the deacon or subdeacon, who are ministers of the altar. He must also see to it that he gives Communion to them with his own hand. [Col. 0690A]

He must not place the Eucharist in the hands of any layman or woman, but place it only in the person’s mouth, saying: “May the body and blood of the Lord benefit you for the forgiveness of sins and for eternal life.” If anyone transgresses these provisions, since he despises almighty God and, insofar as it lies with him, dishonors him, let him be removed from the altar.

### Chapter LXXVII — On the same matter

[Col. 0690B]

*(From the letter of Pope Anacletus, chapter 12.)* After the consecration has been completed, let all who do not wish to be deprived of the thresholds of the church receive Communion. For so the Apostles established, and so the holy Roman Church maintains. If they neglect this, let them be degraded.

### Chapter LXXVIII — On the same matter

*(From the Council of Orléans, chapter 10.)* It has been heard that some presbyters celebrate Mass and do not receive Communion, although this is expressly read to have been forbidden in the canons of the Apostles. Or how can he rightly say, if he has not received Communion: “We have received the sacraments, Lord”? And so forth.

### Chapter LXXIX — On the same matter

*(From the same council, chapter 11.)* If any bishop, presbyter, deacon, or anyone from the priestly catalogue, after the offering has been made, does not receive Communion, let him either state his reason and, if it is reasonable, obtain pardon; or, if he gives no reason, let him be deprived of Communion as one who has become a cause of injury to the people. [Col. 0690C]

### Chapter LXXX — That nothing is to be done in a church except that for which it was established

*(From the statements of Augustine.)* In an oratory, nothing at all is to be done except the worship of God through prayer and psalmody, so that the name may always correspond to the work devoted to it.

### Chapter LXXXI — On the same matter
*(From the sayings of Benedict.)* The oratory shall be what it is called, and nothing else shall be done or stored there except what is appropriate to the divine mysteries.

**CHAPTER LXXXII.—On the same matter.**

*[Col. 0690D]*

*(From the Council of Laodicea, canon 28.)* It is not proper for an agape, that is, a communal banquet, to be held in divine dwellings, namely, in churches; nor is it proper to eat within the house of God or to spread couches there.

**CHAPTER LXXXIII.—That no one shall hold banquets in a church.**

*(From the Council of Carthage, canon 28.)* No bishops or clergy shall hold banquets in a church, unless perhaps, while passing through, they are refreshed there because hospitality requires it. The people also shall be restrained from such banquets as far as possible.

**CHAPTER LXXXIV.—That no one shall establish taverns in a church.**

*(From the Council of Tours, canon 2.)* It has been reported to the holy synod that certain priests establish taverns in the churches entrusted to them—which is sacrilegious *[Col. 0691A]*—and there have wine sold by tavernkeepers, or permit it to be sold. Thus, where only prayers, the divine word, and the praise of God ought to resound, there are feasting and drunkenness, laughter and applause, obscene words, quarrels, and disputes. How contrary this is to God, the Lord Jesus demonstrates. When he found sellers and buyers in the temple, and money-changers sitting there, he made a whip of cords and drove them all from the temple. If he drove out even those things that appeared to be lawfully sold in the temple and were bought for the purpose of being offered to the Lord in that same temple, what do you think will happen to such a pestilential presumption and contempt for God? And if not only priests but also all clerics are commanded not to enter taverns, *[Col. 0691B]* who could tolerate the making of God’s churches into taverns? Therefore the synod absolutely forbids this from ever happening again. If it is done, the priest shall be deposed, and laymen, deprived of communion, shall be expelled from the church that they have dishonored.

**CHAPTER LXXXV.—On the same matter.**

*(From the same council, canon 3.)* If the house of God is called a house of prayer, it ought to be what it is called; nothing else ought to be done or stored there. For where the Lord’s body is consecrated, the presence of angels is undoubtedly present. Where the relics of the saints are stored and venerated, nothing dishonorable should appear that might offend the eyes of those who come to pray; nothing should be seen there that pertains to temporal profit. Everything should be holy, everything clean, and everything pertain only to *[Col. 0691C]* ecclesiastical ministry.

**CHAPTER LXXXVI.—That everyone may pray in his own house.**

*(From the Council of Orléans, canon 3.)* Every member of the faithful may have an oratory in his own house and pray there, but it is not permitted to celebrate Mass there.

**CHAPTER LXXXVII.—That obscene songs shall not be performed around churches.**

*(From the Council of Carthage.)* We absolutely prohibit the performance of an obscene and lustful song around churches and in church atriums; such conduct must be avoided everywhere.

**CHAPTER LXXXVIII.—That relics of the saints shall not be placed in rural oratories.**

*[Col. 0691D]*

*(From the Council of Epaon, canon 25.)* Relics of the saints shall not be placed in rural oratories, unless perhaps a cleric of some parish happens to live nearby and regularly serves the sacred pledges by singing psalms.

**CHAPTER LXXXIX.—That an episcopal see, if necessary, may be transferred to another place.**

*(From a letter of Gregory to John, bishop of Billiètræ.)* The circumstances of the times advise that episcopal sees, which were formerly established in particular cities, be transferred to other places of the same diocese that we consider safer, so that their inhabitants may now live there and the danger of the barbarians may more easily be avoided. Therefore we command you, John, our brother and fellow bishop of the city of Billiètræ, to transfer your see from now on to the place called Renatus, at Saint Andrew’s, the apostle, *[Col. 0692A]* so that you may be freer from hostile attack and may arrange there the customary celebration of the solemn feasts.

**CHAPTER XC.—On the transfer of holy places.**

*(Augustine says.)* Holy places are to be transferred for three reasons. First, when the necessity caused by persecutors has made their locations burdensome. Second, when the difficulty of the locations has become excessive. Third, when they are burdened by association with wicked people.

**CHAPTER XCI.—That when martyrs are transferred, their honor sometimes moves with them and sometimes remains in the place.**

*(From the sayings of Jerome.)* It should be noted that when some of the martyrs are transferred, their honor migrates with them; when others are transferred, however, their honor does not cease to remain in their places.

**CHAPTER XCII.—That the blood of martyrs consecrates a place, not the place the blood.**

*[Col. 0692B]*

*(From the sayings of Augustine.)* The blood of martyrs consecrates a place; the place does not consecrate the blood. If someone says, “The church is mine,” you should say to him what is written in the Song: “My dove is one, and my beloved is one.” And say to him: “Is it fitting for the son to be killed in the bosom of his mother and nurse?” Yet understand that only the nurse was polluted and, because of that pollution, consecrated, while the son was dead.

**CHAPTER XCIII.—What a basilica is.**

*(From the sayings of Saint Isidore.)* Basilion was a king of the Greeks. Hence also the term *basilica*, meaning “royal,” because in the earliest times only kings were buried in one; *[Col. 0692C]* for that reason it acquired this name. Nowadays, however, other people are either burned by fire or buried beneath a heap of stones.

**CHAPTER XCIV.—Concerning those who make the house of God contemptible.**

*(From the Council of Gangra, canon 5.)* If anyone teaches that the house of God is contemptible, and that the assemblies held in it are contemptible, let him be anathema.

**CHAPTER XCV.—On the same matter.**

*(From the same council, canon 6.)* If anyone holds assemblies separately outside the church and, despising the church, wishes to usurp what belongs to the church without a priest attending in accordance with the bishop’s decree, let him be anathema.

**CHAPTER XCVI.—That the chalice and paten shall be made of gold or silver.**

*[Col. 0692D]*

*(From the Council of Reims, canon 5.)* The Lord’s chalice, together with the paten, shall be made of silver if it cannot by every means be made of gold. Priests must not, at the prompting of avarice, plead poverty or inability, since a fourth part of everything belonging to the church is to be spent on the construction and maintenance of that church. The people also are to be admonished to offer something as a gift to the Lord, just as the ancient people under Moses are recorded to have done for the Lord’s tabernacle. If anyone is so poor that he cannot do otherwise, he should at least have a tin chalice. A chalice must not be made of bronze or brass, because, through the power of wine, it produces verdigris, which provokes vomiting. No one shall presume to sing Mass with a wooden or glass chalice.

**CHAPTER XCVII.—On the observance due to Christ’s table.**

*[Col. 0693A]*

*(From the same council, canon 5.)* Care must be taken that Christ’s table—that is, the altar where the Lord’s body is consecrated, where his blood is received, where the relics of the saints are stored, and where the priest offers the prayers and vows of the people before God—be honored with every form of veneration and most carefully covered with the cleanest linens and cloths. Nothing should be placed upon it except reliquaries containing the relics of the saints and the four Gospels. After Mass, the chalice with the paten, the book of the sacraments, and the priestly vestments shall be stored under lock in a clean place.

**CHAPTER XCVIII.—That the corporal shall be of the purest linen and of a single material.**

*[Col. 0693B]*

*(From the same council, canon 3.)* The corporal upon which the sacred offering is sacrificed shall be made of the cleanest and purest linen. No more precious or inferior material of another kind shall be mixed into it. It shall never remain on the altar except during the time of Mass, but shall either be placed in the sacramentary or stored with the chalice and paten in a very clean place. When it is washed by a priest, deacon, or subdeacon, it shall first be washed in the church, in a place and vessel prepared for this purpose, because it has been stained by the Lord’s body and blood. After this, it shall be prepared by the washer in a clean place.

**CHAPTER XCIX.—That the sacrifice of the altar shall not be celebrated on silk or dyed cloth.**

*[Col. 0693C]*

*(From a letter of Pope Eusebius, canon 51.)* Here, among the other matters previously mentioned, after consultation with everyone, we have decreed that no one should presume to celebrate the sacrifice of the altar on silk or dyed cloth, but on pure linen consecrated by the bishop—linen produced and woven from earthly flax—just as the body of our Lord Jesus Christ was buried in a clean linen shroud.

**CHAPTER C.—That women shall not approach the altar or undertake the duties assigned to men.**

*(From the Council of Laodicea, canon 43.)* Women must not enter the altar area or touch those things that have been assigned to the duties of men.

**CHAPTER CI.—On the same matter.**

*(From a decree of Pope Gelasius, canon 16.)* We have nevertheless heard with indignation that such contempt for divine things has arisen that women are asserted to minister at the sacred altars and to perform for a sex to which it does not belong everything assigned exclusively to the service of men.

**CHAPTER CII.—That laymen shall not sit beside the altar.**

*[Col. 0693D]*

*(From the Council of Mainz, canon 13.)* Laymen must not presume to stand or sit beside the altar where the holy mysteries are celebrated, among the clergy, either at vigils or at Masses. Only the portion separated from the altar by the screen shall be open to clerics who sing psalms. For prayer and communion, however, the holy of holies shall be open, as is customary, to laymen and women.

**CHAPTER CIII.—Concerning those priests who presume to sit in church while the Gospels are being read.**

*(From a letter of Pope Anastasius I addressed to the bishops of Germany and Burgundy.)* Anastasius, bishop, sends greetings in the Lord to all the bishops of the German and Burgundian regions. Your affection, dearest brothers, has required that we answer your inquiries on the authority of the apostolic see. Although, because of certain other occupations, we were hastening to do so not at length but briefly, nevertheless, if it should again be necessary because of these or other needs to send word to us as to the head, do not hesitate to do so in a spirit of charity, for we regard your requests as acceptable both now and then.

*[Col. 0694A]*

You have informed us that certain priests sit in church when the Gospels are read and listen to the words of the Lord and Savior while seated rather than standing, claiming that they received this practice from the tradition of their ancestors. We command, by apostolic authority, that you permit this to happen in no way hereafter. While the holy Gospels are being read in church, priests and everyone else shall not sit, but shall stand reverently in the presence of the Gospel, listening attentively to the Lord’s words and faithfully adoring them.

**CHAPTER CIV.—That no one shall presume to give a chalice, paten, or priestly vestment as security to a tavernkeeper.**

*[Col. 0694B]*

*(From the Council of Reims, canon 11.)* No priest shall presume to give as security a chalice, paten, altar pall, priestly vestment, or ecclesiastical book to a tavernkeeper, merchant, or any layman or woman, unless the most just necessity compels it. The holiness of the sacred ministry is so great that, without prejudice to the deeper understanding of the mystery, the Lord even prohibited through the prophet that a priest should go out to the people wearing the sacred vestments; instead, upon returning from divine converse, he should leave them within the sanctuary. If the sacred canons forbid someone from entering taverns to drink, and one consecrated to the sacred ministry is not even permitted to touch unclean things, *[Col. 0694C]* how much less should he offer them as security? Thus the holy Pope and martyr Stephen taught Saint Hilary in his decretal letters.

**CHAPTER CV.—That no one shall presume to use a chalice, paten, or any sacred vessel for other purposes.**

*(From the Council of Orléans, canon 9.)* No priest or layman shall presume to turn a chalice, paten, or any sacred vessel dedicated to divine worship to other personal uses. Whoever drinks from the sacred chalice anything other than the blood of Christ received in the sacrament, or uses the paten for any function other than the ministry of the altar, must be deterred by the example of Belshazzar, who, when he used the Lord’s vessels for common purposes, lost his life together with his kingdom.

**CHAPTER CVI.—That bishops may, with the counsel of the clergy, assist their household in time of need from the treasury of their church.**

*[Col. 0694D]*

*(From the Council of Auvergne, canon 5.)* Bishops may, in the presence of priests and deacons, distribute from the treasury of the church to the household and the poor of that same church, according to canonical institution and in proportion to their need.

**CHAPTER CVII.—That corpses shall not be covered with the altar pall.**

*(From the same council, canon 30.)* The body shall never be covered, while it is being carried to the tomb, with the covering of the Lord’s body or of the altar, lest the altars be polluted by the sacred veil while bodies are being honored.

**CHAPTER CVIII.—That divine ministry shall not be provided for wedding adornment.**

*[Col. 0695A]*

*(From the same council, canon 8.)* Divine ministries shall not be supplied for wedding adornment, lest, being polluted by the touch of the wicked or by the pomp of worldly luxury, they appear unworthy of the service of the sacred mystery.

**CHAPTER CIX.—That the church shall in no way be overrun by secular power.**

*(From the Apostolic Council, canon 31.)* If a bishop, using secular powers, obtains control of the church through them, he shall be deposed and separated, together with all who communicate with him.

**CHAPTER CX.—Concerning priests who have acquired their churches for a price.**

*[Col. 0695B]*

*(From the Council of Mainz, canon 5.)* Whoever has obtained a church for a price, since he is known to have acted against the discipline of ecclesiastical rule, and whoever has expelled for money another priest lawfully ordained to that church and has claimed it for himself in this way, shall be deposed in every respect.

**CHAPTER CXI.—That no layman shall presume to expel a priest from his church.**

*(From the same council, canon 29.)* Laymen shall not expel priests from churches or appoint them without the consent of their bishops.

**CHAPTER CXII.—Again, concerning those who take churches away from priests.**

*(From the Council of Chalon, canon 42.)* It has been discovered that many people, rashly following their own will—and, what is more serious, driven by greed—give or take away churches from priests without the consent of the bishops. *[Col. 0695C]* Therefore, with the canonical rule preserved, no one shall give a church to any priest without the bishop’s consent. If he has obtained it lawfully, he shall lose it only because of serious fault and with canonical severity before the bishop.

**CHAPTER CXIII.—That no one shall demand any gift from a priest on account of a church.**

*(From the Council of Mainz, canon 30.)* No one at all shall demand gifts from priests as a condition of recommending a church.

**CHAPTER CXIV.—On the same matter.**

*[Col. 0695D]*

*(From the Council of Rouen, canon 5.)* It has been decreed and absolutely prohibited that, if any priest is found to give or to have given gifts to a cleric or layman, or to provide any money so that he may seize another priest’s church or purchase a vacant church, he shall be expelled from the clergy for this greed, robbery, or presumption motivated by shameful profit, and shall be outside the rule.

**CHAPTER CXV.—That priests shall admonish the people to prepare altar linens.**

*(From the Council of Reims, canon 4.)* Priests shall preach throughout their parishes to the women, instructing them to prepare linens for the altars.

**CHAPTER CXVI.—That bishops shall determine what priests ought to do for their lords on behalf of their churches.**

*(From the Council of Arles, canon 3.)* Bishops shall determine what honor priests ought to render to their lords on behalf of their churches.

**CHAPTER CXVII.—On the same matter.**

*[Col. 0696A]*

*(From the Council of Orléans, canon 10.)* No priest shall give gifts to anyone at the entrance of a church.

**CHAPTER CXVIII.—Concerning priests who possess nothing when they are ordained.**

*(From the Council of Reims, canon 6.)* It must be investigated whether, when a priest who possessed no patrimony was advanced to ecclesiastical orders, he later purchased estates, and to whose legal ownership they belong; for, according to canonical authority, they ought to belong to the church to which he was promoted from a state of having nothing.

**CHAPTER CXIX.—On the same matter.**

*(From the Council of Orange, canon 54.)* When a priest holds a diocese, he shall draw up a document transferring to the name of the church whatever he has purchased; otherwise he shall withdraw from the administration of the church he holds. *[Col. 0696B]*

**CHAPTER CXX.—On the same matter.**

*(From the Council of Carthage, canon 47.)* It has been decided that bishops, priests, deacons, and any clergy who are ordained while possessing nothing, but who during their episcopate or clerical service acquire fields or any estates in their own name, shall be held liable as guilty of invading the Lord’s property, unless they have transferred those same possessions to the church to which they are enrolled. If, however, something comes to them through someone’s personal generosity or through inheritance from their family, let them do with it as they wish.

**CHAPTER CXXI.—On the same matter.**

*(From the same council, canon 48.)* Each priest shall leave to his own church the property he acquires after the day of his consecration.

**CHAPTER CXXII.—On the same matter.**

*(From the Council of Toledo.)* Moreover, if a priest acquires anything after ordination, the rule established in the canons concerning consecrated persons who possess nothing is to be observed.

**CHAPTER CXXIII.—Concerning priests who acquire property from church revenues, build structures there, and place women there.**

*[Col. 0696C]*

*(From the Council of Reims, canon 10.)* It must be investigated whether any priest has acquired property under another name from church revenues, or from the offerings and vows of the faithful; whether he has built structures there, or placed there things belonging to the church; whether he has permitted women to frequent the place; or, what is more disgraceful, whether he has kept such women there to practice their weaving *[Col. 0696D]* and manage the household, while the priest frequently comes and stays there; and whether, contrary to the decrees of the canons, he commits this evil. For just as a priest must not practice usury in his own name, so neither may he do so in another’s name; still less may he defraud ecclesiastical resources, since this is sacrilege and is equal in crime to the thief Judas, who carried away and stole the sacred offerings.

**CHAPTER CXXIV.—On preserving a custom that is not contrary to the faith.**

*[Col. 0697A]*

*(From a letter of Pope Pius.)* You asked through our secretary Hilary that all the customs of former times be preserved for you—customs that long antiquity has maintained from the beginnings of the ordinances of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, down to the present. In accordance with the sequence of our reply, we praise the custom, provided that it is recognized as usurping nothing contrary to the Catholic faith.

**CHAPTER CXXV.—That ecclesiastical statutes handed down by the apostles and the other teachers of the church shall be preserved intact.**

*(From a decree of Pope Innocent, canon 1.)* Innocent to Decentius, bishop of Gubbio, greetings. If the priests of the Lord wished to preserve intact the ecclesiastical institutions as they were handed down by the blessed apostles, there would be no difference or variation in those rites and consecrations. But since each person considers it necessary to observe not what has been handed down but what seems right to him, different practices appear to be maintained or celebrated in different places and churches. *[Col. 0697B]* As a result, scandal arises among the people, who, not knowing that ancient traditions have been corrupted by human presumption, think either that the churches do not agree with one another or that contradiction has been introduced by the apostles or apostolic men.

For who does not know or recognize that what was handed down by the chief of the apostles, Peter, to the Roman Church and is preserved to this day ought to be observed by all?
