Nothing should be added or introduced that lacks authority or appears to have taken its example from elsewhere, especially since it is clear that throughout Italy, Gaul, Spain, Africa, Sicily, and the intervening islands, no one established churches except those whom the venerable apostle Peter or his successors appointed as priests. Let them read whether, in these provinces, another apostle is found or reported to have taught. If they do not read of one, because they find none anywhere, they ought to follow what the Roman Church preserves, since there is no doubt that they received their beginning from it. Otherwise, while pursuing foreign assertions, they may appear to neglect the source of their institutions.

*[Col. 0697C]*

There is no doubt that your affection has often come to the city and met with us in church, and that you have learned what custom is observed there both in consecrating the mysteries and in carrying out the other sacred rites. I would consider this sufficient for the instruction or reform of your church, if I had been certain that your predecessors had observed anything deficient or different—unless you had said that we should be consulted about certain matters. *[Col. 0697D]* We therefore answer these questions not because we believe that you are ignorant of anything, but so that, with greater authority, you may instruct your people, admonish those who depart from the institutions of the Roman Church, or not delay to identify them, so that we may know who introduces novelties or thinks that the custom of a church other than the Roman Church ought to be observed.

**CHAPTER CXXVI.—That ecclesiastical customs are to be held as law.**

*(Augustine says to the priest Casulanus.)* In matters concerning which divine Scripture has established nothing certain, the custom of the people of God or the institutions of our ancestors are to be held as law. Those who despise ecclesiastical customs are to be restrained just as transgressors of the divine laws are.

**CHAPTER CXXVII.—Again, on observing ecclesiastical customs.**

*[Col. 0698A]*

*(From the sayings of Basil, canon 27.)* We have received some of the customs of ecclesiastical institutions from Scripture, and others through apostolic tradition, confirmed by succession in the mystery. Who, having even a little experience of the sacred Scriptures, would hesitate to acknowledge that these have equal force and produce the same effect of piety? If we attempt to regard the customs of the church, handed down by the Fathers not through written Scripture, as worthless, it will plainly become evident how much harm religion will suffer through those who despise them.

To begin there: which writing taught the faithful to mark themselves with the sign of the saving cross? Which writing commended the many things arranged over the bread and the cup, together with the words of extended prayer and consecration? For we say not only what is contained in the Gospel or what the apostle has handed down in secret, but we also add many other things, contributing, as it were, great force to the completion of the mysteries. *[Col. 0698B]* Which writing taught us to pray facing east? We bless the baptismal font and the oil of anointing. In addition, we immerse those whom we baptize three times, anoint them with oil, and instruct them through words to renounce Satan and his angels.

From where, then, do these practices and many others of the same kind come, unless they have been observed in the mysteries by the Fathers through a tacit and mystical tradition, with greater reverent care according to ecclesiastical custom than if they had been published in writing?

**CHAPTER CXXVIII.—What must be done in cases for which definite judgments are not found in the canons.**

*[Col. 0698C]*

*(From a decree of Pope Innocent, canon 18.)* In cases concerning which no authority for loosing or binding appears in the books of the Old Testament, the four Gospels, or all the writings of the apostles, have recourse to the divine writings in Greek. If nothing is found there either, turn to the Catholic histories of the Catholic Church written by Catholic teachers. If nothing is found in them, examine the canons of the apostolic see. If not there, carefully recall the examples of the saints. If, after all these have been examined, the nature of the question still cannot be clearly investigated, gather the elders of the province and consult them. What is sought from many who think together is more easily found. For the true promiser, the Lord, says: “If two or three of you agree on earth in my name concerning anything whatever they ask, *[Col. 0698D]* it will be done for them by my Father.”

**CHAPTER CXXIX.—That everything offered to God shall be considered consecrated.**

*(From the Council of Orléans, canon 7.)* Everything offered to God is considered consecrated: vineyards, lands, forests, implements, clothing, livestock, and other possessions, as well as whatever is undoubtedly offered to Christ, their bridegroom, for the churches.

**CHAPTER CXXX.—On the same matter.**

*(From the Council of Rouen, canon 3.)* All tithes of the earth, whether from crops or from the fruits of trees, belong to the Lord and are sanctified to him. Oxen, sheep, and goats that pass under the shepherd’s rod: whatever comes as the tenth shall be sanctified to the Lord. Neither the good nor the bad shall be selected, *[Col. 0699A]* nor shall one be exchanged for another. If anyone makes an exchange, both what he exchanges and what is received in exchange shall be sanctified to the Lord and shall not be redeemed.

But because many are now found unwilling to give tithes, we decree that they be admonished according to the Lord’s command once, a second time, and a third time. If they do not amend their conduct, they shall be bound by the chain of anathema until they make satisfaction and offer suitable correction.

**CHAPTER CXXXI.—That the tithe shall in no way be neglected.**

*(From the Council of Mainz, canon 35.)* We admonish and command that the giving of tithes to God not be neglected in any way. God himself established that they be given to him; for it is to be feared that whoever takes away from God what is owed to him may perhaps have his own necessities taken away by God because of his sin. *[Col. 0699B]*

**CHAPTER CXXXII.—Concerning those who refuse to give tithes.**

*(From the Council of Chalon, canon 18.)* Certain brothers have also complained that there are bishops and abbots who do not allow tithes to be given to the churches where those tenants hear Mass. Therefore this holy assembly decreed that bishops and abbots shall arrange for tithes to be brought from the fields and vineyards that they possess for their own support or that of their brothers. Their households, however, shall give their tithes where their children are baptized and where they hear Mass throughout the entire year.

**CHAPTER CXXXIII.—That tithes ought to be demanded from all Christians as a debt.**

*(From the Council of Mainz, canon 8.)* Abraham indicates by his deeds, and Jacob by his promises, that tithes are to be given to God and to God’s priests. The law then established this, and all the holy teachers recall it. *[Col. 0699C]* It was certainly fitting that the Israelites give the Lord tithes of their livestock, crops, and all their money, since he had freed them from the ten plagues with which he struck the Egyptians and, in the final plague, destroyed all their firstborn; he also granted his own people the favor of despoiling Egypt after they had obtained its wealth.

Concerning these tithes, the venerable teacher Augustine says: “Tithes are demanded as a debt. What if God were to say: ‘You are mine, human being; the earth that you cultivate is mine; the seeds that you sow are mine; the animals that you tire are mine; the warmth of the sun is mine? Since everything is mine, you who contribute the lesser share owed me only the tenth. Yet I reserve *[Col. 0699D]* nine parts for you; give me the tenth. If you do not give me the tenth, I will take away the nine. If you give me the tenth, I will multiply the nine.’”

Since the Jewish people observed the commandment of tithes with such diligence that, as the Lord himself testifies, they gave tithes even of the smallest vegetables—rue, mint, and cumin—why should the evangelical people not fulfill the same command with greater zeal, since they have a greater number of priests and a purer worship of the sacraments?

Therefore tithes must be given so that God, pleased by this devotion, may more abundantly provide what is necessary, as we showed above; and so that priests and ministers of the church, relieved of the care and concern for bodily necessities without which this life cannot be lived, may be freer *[Col. 0700A]* for meditation on divine law, the administration of teaching, and the willing completion of spiritual service. They must also be given so that the people’s offering may be sacrificed to the Lord in daily oblation and, according to canonical statutes, contribute to the support of the poor and the restoration of churches. For, according to the canons, four parts are to be made from the offerings of the faithful: one for the bishop, another for the clergy, a third for the poor, and a fourth reserved for the restoration of churches.

**CHAPTER CXXXIV.—Concerning those who refuse to give the tithe unless it is redeemed from them for a price.**

*[Col. 0700B]*

*(From the Council of Metz, canon 3.)* Concerning tithes that the people refuse to give unless they are redeemed from them by some gift, bishops must prohibit this from being done.

**CHAPTER CXXXV.—That the tithe shall be called God’s census.**

*(From the Council of Agrippina, canon 6.)* Likewise, the tithe given by the faithful is to be called God’s census and must therefore be returned in full. According to the Council of Toledo, one third of it ought to belong to the bishops. We do not wish to use this authority, however, but only to receive each year a fourth part, in accordance with the custom of the Roman pontiffs and the practice of the holy Roman Church. If anyone is found to be contentious about this, whether cleric or layman, he shall be deprived of communion and judged by synodal censure.

**CHAPTER CXXXVI.—To whom the offerings of parish churches ought to belong.**

*[Col. 0700C]*

*(From the Council of Toledo.)* Concerning what is offered to parish churches—lands, vineyards, slaves, livestock—the provisions of the ancient canons shall be observed, so that everything remains in the bishop’s power. Of what is offered at the altars, one third shall faithfully be brought to the bishops and two thirds to the clergy. As for tithes, according to some, one third is to be given each year, or the whole in the third year. Nevertheless, following the Romans, the bishops shall receive each year a fourth part, or the whole in the fourth year.

**CHAPTER CXXXVII.—That four portions are to be made in every church from both revenues and offerings.**

*[Col. 0700D]*

*(From a letter of Pope Gelasius, canon 27.)* Four portions are to be made from both revenues and the offerings of the faithful, insofar as the resources of each church permit, as was reasonably decreed long ago. One shall belong to the bishop, another to the clergy, a third to the poor, and a fourth shall be applied to the buildings.

Just as it is the priest’s responsibility to ensure that the full amount mentioned is paid to the ministers of the church, so the clergy must understand that they should demand nothing presumptuously beyond the sum assigned to them. As for what has been allocated to ecclesiastical buildings, the visible restoration of holy places should demonstrate that it has truly been devoted to this work; for it is sacrilegious if, while sacred buildings are left without support, the bishop converts to his own profit the funds designated for them.

Likewise, although he may appear to demonstrate that he has distributed according to divine accounting the portion assigned to the poor, nevertheless, in accordance with what is written—“so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven”—it ought also to be proclaimed through present testimony and not be concealed from the praises of a good reputation. *[Col. 0701A]*

**CHAPTER CXXXVIII.—Again, that four portions are to be made from the tithes.**

*[Col. 0701B]*

*(From the Council of Nantes, canon 6.)* Priests must be instructed and likewise admonished so that they understand that the tithes and offerings they receive from the faithful are the provisions of the poor, guests, and pilgrims, and that they must use them not as their own but as entrusted to them. They must know that they will render an account of all these things before God and that, unless they faithfully administer them to the poor and to those mentioned above, they will suffer loss.

The canons holyly establish how they are to be distributed: namely, that four portions be made from them. One is to relieve the church building, another is to be distributed to the poor, a third is to belong to the priest and his clergy, and the fourth is to be reserved for the bishop, so that whatever he orders from it may be done with prudent counsel.

**CHAPTER CXXXIX.—Where disputes arising among Christians ought to be settled.**

*(From a decree of Pope Marcellus, canon 3.)* Whatever disputes arise among Christians, they shall bring them to the church, and ecclesiastical men shall settle them. If they refuse to obey, they shall be excluded from the thresholds of the holy church until they obey.

**CHAPTER CXL.—Concerning those who attempt to retain or take away the offerings of their parents, bequests, or what they themselves have given to churches.**

*[Col. 0701C]*

*(From the council held at Valence, canon 4.)* Clerics or laymen who persist in retaining offerings given by their parents or left by testament, or who think that what they themselves have given to churches or monasteries should be taken away, shall, as the holy synod has decreed, be excluded from the churches as murderers of the poor until they return what they have withheld.

**CHAPTER CXLI.—Concerning those who make God their heir.**

*(Saint Isidore says.)* Augustine says in his book *On Heirs*: “Do not increase your money under the appearance of piety by saying, ‘I am preserving these possessions for my children.’ Why do you not rather preserve them for the one who made you from nothing, who feeds you, and who preserves your children? Will you not store up treasure more suitably for your Creator than for your children?” Likewise, the same writer says: “With what face do you ask an inheritance from Christ when you have defrauded Christ of your inheritance? He who said: ‘Store up treasures for yourselves in heaven’?”

**CHAPTER CXLII.—Concerning those who deny or reluctantly return the offerings of the dead.**

*(From the council held at Valence, canon 4.)* Those who either deny the offerings of the dead to the churches or return them reluctantly shall be excommunicated as murderers of the needy.

**CHAPTER CXLIII.—On the same matter.**

*(From a decree of Pope Urban, canon 4.)* The possessions of the faithful are called offerings because they are offered to the Lord. They must therefore not be converted to uses other than ecclesiastical purposes or the support of the Christian brothers and needy mentioned above, since they are the vows of the faithful, the prices of sins, and have been handed over to the Lord for the completion *[Col. 0702A]* of the aforesaid work. If anyone, God forbid, acts otherwise, let him beware lest he receive the condemnation of Ananias and Sapphira and become guilty of sacrilege, as did those who defrauded the proceeds of the aforesaid possessions; they are mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles cited above.

**CHAPTER CXLIV.—On the same matter.**
(From the Council of Gangra, canon 7.) If anyone wishes to receive or give the offerings of the Church outside the Church, without the knowledge of the bishop or of the person entrusted with such duties, and is unwilling to act with his counsel, let him be anathema.

## CHAPTER CXLV — On the same matter

(From the same council, canon 8.) If anyone gives or receives offerings apart from the bishop or the person appointed by him to distribute mercy to the poor, [Col. 0702B] let both the giver and the recipient be anathema.

## CHAPTER CXLVI — That all churches and tithes should remain under the authority of the bishops

(From the Council of Chalon, canon 1.) It was decreed in the holy Council of Chalon that all churches, with their endowments and tithes and all their possessions, should remain under the authority of their own bishop and should always belong to his administration and disposition.

## CHAPTER CXLVII — That possession for thirty years is legally secure

(From the Fifth Council of Toledo, canon 35.) Just as possession of another’s diocese is terminated by thirty years’ possession, so the assembly of a territory does not admit such a claim. Therefore, basilicas newly founded will unquestionably belong to the bishop whose assembly they are established to be part of.

[Col. 0702C]

## CHAPTER CXLVIII — That the rural parishes of individual churches should always remain undisturbed

(From the Council of Chalcedon, canon 17.) We have decreed that the rural parishes or estates of individual churches should remain undisturbed for those bishops who are known to retain them, especially if they have held and administered them without force for thirty years. But if a dispute concerning them has arisen within the thirty-year period, we have decreed that those who claim to have been wronged may bring the matter before the holy synod of the province and contest it there.

## CHAPTER CXLIX — That possession for thirty years, if it has remained undisturbed, should not be altered

(From a letter of Pope Gelasius, chapter 11.) It has also seemed good to add that if—God forbid—the resources of a church, as well as its dioceses, are possessed by other bishops, they should assert for themselves the right established by the thirty-year law, [Col. 0702D] since after thirty years no one is permitted to appeal concerning something that the period prescribed by law excludes.

## CHAPTER CL — The same, concerning things possessed for thirty years

(From the Council of Mâcon, canon 7.) Concerning church property that they have possessed for a period of thirty years without any interruption, no testimony should be accepted; rather, it should be held in the same manner in which property belonging to the imperial treasury is customarily held.

## CHAPTER CLI — Concerning those who make cemeteries out of churches

(From the Council of Meaux, canon 9.) In these regions there was formerly a custom of burying the dead in the Church, and places dedicated to divine worship and prepared for offering sacrifices to God [Col. 0703A] were often made into cemeteries, or *polyandria*. Therefore, we wish this practice henceforth to cease, so that no one may be buried in a church unless perhaps he is a priest, or some other just person who, by the merit of his life, acquired such a place for his dead body by living in a manner worthy of it.

Bodies that were buried in churches in ancient times should by no means be cast out, unless they belong to pagans. Rather, the tombs that are visible should be sunk deeper into the ground, and, after a pavement has been laid over them so that no trace of the tombs remains visible, reverence for the Church should be preserved. But where there is such a multitude of corpses that this is difficult to do, let that place be regarded as a cemetery, after the altar has been removed from it and established in another place where sacrifice may be offered to God reverently and in purity.

## CHAPTER CLII — Concerning those who request burial in holy places

[Col. 0703B]

(Augustine says.) Those whose sins have not been forgiven cannot be helped after death by holy places. For when people burdened by grave sins arrange to be buried in holy places, it remains for them to be judged for their presumption, so that the holy places do not free them, but the guilt of their rashness accuses them.

## CHAPTER CLIII — On the same matter

(Gregory says in his *Dialogues*.) When the dead are not burdened by grave sins, it benefits them to be buried in churches because their relatives, whenever they come to those sacred places and see the tombs of their deceased kin, remember them and offer prayers to the Lord for them. But when people burdened by grave sins are buried in churches, their bodies are placed there not so much [Col. 0703C] for absolution as for a greater accumulation of condemnation.

We can demonstrate this more clearly if we briefly relate what happened in our own days. The venerable Felix, bishop of Porto, was born and raised in the province of Sabina. He testified that a certain nun had lived in that same place. She had maintained bodily continence, but she did not avoid shamelessness of speech and foolish talk.

After she died, she was buried in the church. That same night, the custodian of the church saw in a vision that she had been led before the sacred altar and cut in two lengthwise: one part of her was consumed by fire, while the other remained untouched. When he arose in the morning and told the brothers what he had seen, [Col. 0703D] he wished to show them the place where she had been consumed by fire. The burning of the flame appeared before the altar on the marble as though that woman had actually been burned there by bodily fire.

From this it is plainly understood that those whose sins have not been forgiven cannot, after death, be helped by holy places to escape judgment.

## CHAPTER CLIV — On the same matter

(Again Gregory.) John, a distinguished man who holds the office of prefect in this city, whose truthfulness and seriousness we know, testified to me that the patrician Valerian had died in a city called Brixa. The bishop of that city, having received payment, provided him with a place in the church where he was to be buried.

This Valerian had remained frivolous and morally slippery into [Col. 0704A] extreme old age and had refused to put an end to his depravity. On the very night on which he was buried, the blessed martyr Faustinus, in whose church his body had been interred, appeared to the church’s custodian and said: “Go and tell the bishop to throw out from here the stinking flesh that he has placed here, because, if he does not, he himself will die on the thirtieth day.”

The custodian was afraid to report this vision to the bishop, and when he was warned again, he still avoided doing so. On the thirtieth day, the bishop of that city returned to bed healthy and unharmed in the evening, but died a sudden and unexpected death.

## CHAPTER CLV — On the same matter

(Again Gregory.) The venerable father Venantius, bishop of Luna, is still living among us, as is [Col. 0704B] the distinguished Liberius, a most noble and truthful man. They testify that they know, and that their own people witnessed, the event they relate as having recently occurred in the city of Genoa.

There, they say, a man named Valentinus, a defender of the Church of Milan, died. He was extremely morally slippery and wholly given over to every kind of frivolity. His body was buried in the church of the blessed martyr Syrus.

In the middle of the night voices arose in that church, as though someone were being forcibly driven and dragged out of it. The custodians ran toward the voices and saw two exceedingly frightful spirits. They had fastened Valentinus’s feet with some kind of fetter and were dragging him out of the church while he shouted and cried out loudly.

Terrified, the custodians returned to their beds. [Col. 0704C] In the morning they opened the tomb in which Valentinus had been placed, but did not find his body. As they searched outside the church to discover where it had been thrown, they found it placed in another tomb, with its feet still bound just as they had been when it was dragged from the church.

From this, Peter, understand that when those weighed down by grave sins arrange to be buried in a holy place, they must also be judged for their presumption, so that the holy places do not free them, but the guilt of their rashness even accuses them.

## CHAPTER CLVI — On the same matter

(Again Gregory.) The multitude of all who live in this city also bears witness to what happened here. A certain leading member of their profession died [Col. 0704D] and was buried by his wife beside the church of the blessed martyr Januarius, near the gate of Saint Laurence.

On the following night, his spirit began to cry out from that same grave, in the hearing of the custodian: “I am burning, I am burning.” After he had uttered these cries for a long time, the custodian reported them to his wife.

She sent men of that profession who could make a careful examination to the church, wishing to learn what condition his body was in within the tomb from which such cries were coming. When they opened the tomb, they found the clothing completely intact; it is still preserved in that church as evidence of the matter. But they found no trace at all of his body, as though it had never been placed in that tomb.

From this it must be inferred with what [lacuna; surviving text: *ulti*] he was condemned, since even his flesh had been cast out of the church. [Col. 0705A] What benefit, then, do holy places provide for those buried in them, when those who are unworthy are divinely expelled from those same holy places?

## CHAPTER CLVII — That the bodies of the dead should not be buried in a church

(From the Council of Braga, canon 4.) It has also seemed good that the bodies of the dead should in no way be buried inside a basilica, but, if necessary, outside, beside the wall of the basilica. For if the cities of Gaul have preserved until now this very firm privilege—that in no way should the body of any dead person be buried within the circuit of the city walls—how much more ought reverence for the venerable martyrs to be maintained?

## CHAPTER CLVIII — On the same matter

[Col. 0705B]

(From the Council of Meaux, canon 10.) No one should presume to bury any dead person in a church as though by hereditary right, unless the bishop or priest has judged that person worthy on account of the quality of his conduct and life. Nor should anyone cast the bones of any dead person out of his tomb or violate anyone’s burial in any way through rash presumption. Rather, let each person be permitted to await the coming of his Judge in the grave prepared and granted to him by God.

## CHAPTER CLIX — That no one should demand any payment for burying the bodies of the dead

(From the Council of Nantes, canon 11.) In accordance with the authority of the canons, it must be prescribed that no payment be demanded for tombs or for burying people. An exception may be made if the person being buried, while alive, ordered that something from his property be given to the church in whose [Col. 0705C] atrium he is buried, or if, after his death, those entrusted with distributing his alms freely wish to give something from his possessions.

Nevertheless, the priests and those in charge of places and villages must under no circumstances demand anything from them. It must also be prohibited, in accordance with the institutions of our predecessors, that anyone be buried inside the church; burial should take place in the atrium, portico, or side chambers of the church. No one may be buried inside the church or near the altar where the body and blood of the Lord are consecrated.

## CHAPTER CLX — Concerning the burial of married couples, especially those united in their first marriage

(Jerome says.) Hebron is said to be the city of three men because three patriarchs were buried there in a double cave with their three wives: [Col. 0705D] Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebecca, Jacob and Leah—apart from Adam himself and his wife Eve.

Tobit says to his son: “When God takes my soul, you shall bury my body, and you shall honor your mother all your days; and when she has completed her time, you shall bury her beside me in one tomb.”

## CHAPTER CLXI — On the same matter

(The same author again.) “Those whom one marriage joined, let one tomb join, because they are one flesh; and what God has joined, let no human being separate.”

## CHAPTER CLXII — On the same matter

(Augustine says.) Let every woman follow her husband, both in life and in death.

[Col. 0706A]

## CHAPTER CLXIII — Let burial not separate those whose minds had been one

(Again Augustine.) The sister of Saint Benedict was buried in the tomb that he had prepared for himself, so that those whose minds had always been one in the Lord would not have their bodies separated by burial. Thus those joined in their first marriage, since they are one and the same flesh, should be buried in one tomb.

## CHAPTER CLXIV — Concerning the immovable property of the Church

(From the council held at Senlis in the presence of King Louis, canon 5.) No one is permitted to alienate immovable property of the Church—whether a house, field, garden, or rural dependent—or to bind it to creditors by way of a special mortgage. The term “alienation” includes a condition, donation, exchange, [Col. 0706B] and perpetual emphyteutic contract.

But all priests without exception must abstain from such alienation, fearing the penalties threatened by the Leonine constitution.

## CHAPTER CLXV — On the same matter

(From the same council, canon 6.) If a ruler wishes to grant an immovable property to holy places and receive another immovable property from them, thereby making an exchange, he may do so if permitted by the imperial pragmatic sanction promulgated by him.

## CHAPTER CLXVI — Concerning the precarious grants of widowed churches, that they should have no force

(From the council held at Beauvais, at which Emperor Louis was present [the text reads *intereat*, apparently for *intererat*], canon 10.) Precarious grants and exchanges made during the periods when churches were without bishops, by those who had [Col. 0706C] occupied the bishops’ sees, are to be rescinded. If such transactions must be made, they are to be carried out with ecclesiastical or civil authority.

## CHAPTER CLXVII — On the same matter

(From the same council, canon 11.) No one should presume to make precarious grants from church property unless, for an appropriate contribution from his own property, he receives twice as much from the property of the Church, solely in his own name, if he wishes to hold both his own and the Church’s property in usufruct.

But if he has presently relinquished his own property, he may take three times as much from church property for usufruct, solely in his own name, because each person ought to manage such property as a steward of another’s possessions, not as a liberal donor of his own.

## CHAPTER CLXVIII — On the same matter

[Col. 0706D]

(From the same council, canon 12.) No authority may compel anyone to make a precarious grant of property dedicated to God and his saints, since both reason and established practice hold that no one is required to make a benefaction from his own property to someone to whom he does not wish to give it, contrary to utility and reason.

## CHAPTER CLXIX — On the same matter

(From the same council, canon 13.) Precarious grants are to be renewed every five years, in accordance with ancient custom and authority.

## CHAPTER CLXX — Concerning the donation, sale, or exchange of church property

(From the council held at Valence, canon 50.) A bishop’s donation, sale, or [Col. 0707A] exchange of church property is invalid without the approval and subscription of the clergy.

## CHAPTER CLXXI — Concerning exchanges of church property

(From the council held at Beauvais, canon 5.) Exchanges of church property are to be carefully avoided, and, if they must in any way be made, they are to be examined with the greatest precision. Those made without consultation, which a former bishop unlawfully permitted or which were unlawfully committed by others, are to be corrected by his successor, in accordance with the canonical decree of Pope Hilary.

## CHAPTER CLXXII — On the same matter

(From the Council of Mâcon, canon 4.) It has been decreed by the holy synod, and imperial authority declares, that no person should presume to exchange ecclesiastical property or ecclesiastical dependents [Col. 0707B] without royal permission and consent.

## CHAPTER CLXXIII — Concerning ecclesiastical dependents

(From the council held at Quierzy, canon 2.) No one may exchange ecclesiastical dependents except for their liberation—namely, so that the dependents given in exchange for an ecclesiastical person remain in the service of the church, while the ecclesiastical person who is exchanged enjoys perpetual freedom.

For what has once been consecrated to the Lord can no longer be transferred to human uses. For the Law says: “If anyone changes it, both what he changes and what has been changed shall be sanctified to the Lord.”

## CHAPTER CLXXIV — On the same matter

(From the same council, canon 3.) It seems unjust and impious [Col. 0707C] that dependents whom faithful men or women have consecrated to God and his saints for the remedy of their souls should again be reduced to secular servitude through the price of any payment or the transaction of any exchange, since canonical authority permits runaway slaves to be sold only.

Therefore, all rulers of churches must take the greatest care that the almsgiving of one person does not become the sin of another. It is also absurd that a slave who dies under ecclesiastical dignity should be subject to human servitude.

## CHAPTER CLXXV — Concerning royal warrants relating to precarious grants

(From the council held at Saint-Médard, canon 11.) Neither reason nor authority permits royal warrants concerning ecclesiastical precarious grants to be issued in any manner. Since [Col. 0707D] it is judged unworthy to confirm such warrants in ecclesiastical law, the royal majesty must be approached only at the request of an ecclesiastical ruler.

That guardian of the Church must also take the greatest care not, perhaps forgetful of his rank and ecclesiastical communion, to request the issuance of a royal warrant against authority for the sake of any favor. If he does so, he must not be heard. But if he obtains such a warrant, it must be rescinded through royal discretion and episcopal judgment, and the unjust petitioner must be suitably corrected for his unjust appeal to the ruler.

## CHAPTER CLXXVI — Concerning a bishop who wishes to manumit a church dependent

(From the Fifth Council of Toledo, canon 68.) A bishop who [Col. 0708A] wishes to manumit a dependent belonging to the Church, without retaining ecclesiastical protection, must offer before the council of the church over which he presides two persons of equal merit and property, with priests subscribing to the exchange, so that the decision concerning the exchange may be found valid and just.

Only then may he grant free manumission without the Church’s protection, because he has already acquired for his own right the person whom he intends to hand over to freedom. Such a freedman must be denied the right to accuse or testify against the Church to whose jurisdiction he belonged. But if he presumes to do so, it is decreed that, while the exchange remains in force, he be recalled into the Church’s own servitude.

## CHAPTER CLXXVII — Concerning priests who leave their property to the Church

[Col. 0708B]

(From the same Fifth Council, canon 69.) The consensus of the entire council determined that priests who either leave their own property to the Church or, possessing nothing, acquire some estates or households for their churches may manumit certain members of those church households, in proportion to the property contributed, as the ancient canons decreed.

They must remain, together with their property and descendants, if they are freeborn, under the protection of the Church, carrying out the duties assigned to them as far as they are able.

## CHAPTER CLXXVIII — That priests should not presume to sell church property

(From the Council of Carthage, canon 33.) It has also seemed good that priests should not sell the property of the church in which they have been appointed [Col. 0708C] without the knowledge of their bishops, just as bishops may not sell church estates without the knowledge of the council or of their priests.

Therefore, when there is no necessity, neither a bishop may appropriate the property of the mother church, nor a priest the property of his own title.

## CHAPTER CLXXIX — That no ordained person should presume to sell anything from the Church’s possessions

(From the Council of Braga, canon 30.) If a priest or deacon is found to have sold anything from the alms of the Church, since he has committed sacrilege, it has been decreed that he is not to be counted among the Church’s ordained ministry. Nevertheless, the matter is to be left to the bishop’s judgment, whether he is worthy or unworthy of being restored to his rank.

## CHAPTER CLXXX — Concerning priests who alienate anything belonging to their title

[Col. 0708D]

(From the same council, canon 31.) Any priest who attempts in any way permanently to alienate gold, silver, or gems belonging to the property of his title, or garments, if there are any, or any movable objects added for divine adornment, is to be punished by loss of his rank, whether he is the donor, alienator, or seller.

## CHAPTER CLXXXI — On the same matter

(From the same council, canon 32.) If a bishop, compelled by no necessity of ecclesiastical accounting, presumes to sell anything from church property among his clergy, or where there happens to be no priest, he must be compelled to restore the property itself to its own church. After being heard in the judgment of the bishops, he is to be deposed and, as one guilty of theft or brigandage, deprived of his office.

[Col. 0709A]

## CHAPTER CLXXXII — That the offering of church property grants as much remedy of pardon to the donor as it prepares harm for the founder

(From the Council of Toledo, canon 33.) The entire extent of church property grants a remedy of pardon to the one who gives it, just as it rightly prepares harm for the one who defrauds it. Therefore, no priest or minister should take anything from church property that the faithful donate in any place and attach it to his own right or to the unity of his own see.

Rather, so that the security of this matter may be stronger, the relatives of those who built or enriched the church may legitimately exercise this good-intentioned vigilance: if they foresee a priest or minister defrauding anything from the property donated, they should either restrain him through an honorable agreement of admonition or report such conduct to the bishop [Col. 0709B] or judge for correction.

If the bishop attempts such conduct, they should ensure that it is brought to the attention of his metropolitan. If the metropolitan does so, they should not delay bringing it to the ears of the king.

The heirs themselves, however, may not assert power over these properties as though they were their own by right, nor commit robbery, fraud, or any kind of violence. If anyone presumes to violate these admonitions, he will restore what he has wrongly seized with disgrace and will suffer a sentence of excommunication for a year.

## CHAPTER CLXXXIII — Concerning clerics who alienate documents by which the Church’s possession is secured

(From the Council of Agde, canon 5.) If any cleric [Col. 0709C] presumes, through a culpable and punishable obstinacy, either to suppress or deny documents by which the Church’s possession is secured, or perhaps to hand them over to its adversaries, he must repay from his own resources whatever loss the Church has suffered through the absence of the documents, and he must be deprived of communion.

Those who, to the Church’s detriment, have impiously solicited and received warrants and testimonies of the holy Church from traitors are to be struck by the same sentence.

## CHAPTER CLXXXIV — Concerning freedmen who have withdrawn from the Church’s protection

(From the Fifth Council of Toledo, canon 71.) Freedmen of the Church who, leaving its protection, have attached themselves to any other persons, are, if they refuse to return after being admonished, to have their manumission declared invalid, because through contempt of [Col. 0709D] obedience they are held to have acted ungratefully.

## CHAPTER CLXXXV — Concerning the Church’s freedmen

(From the same Fifth Council, canon 70.) Since their patroness, the Church, never dies, the Church’s freedmen must never withdraw from her protection, nor may their descendants do so, as the earlier canons decreed.

And lest their freedom fail to appear in future offspring, and their descendants, possessing natural free status, withdraw themselves from the Church’s protection, both the freedmen and those born from them must make a declaration to their bishop. In it they must acknowledge that they have been made free from the Church’s household and must not abandon its protection, but must offer it service or obedience according to their ability.

[Col. 0710A]

## CHAPTER CLXXXVI — Concerning freedmen manumitted by various persons and commended to the Church’s protection

(From the same Fifth Council, canon 72.) Freedmen who have been manumitted by various persons and entrusted to the Church’s protection are to be defended by priests against everyone’s insolence, as the regulations of the ancient Fathers established—both in the status of their freedom and with respect to the property they are known to possess.

## CHAPTER CLXXXVII — Concerning those manumitted in the Church

(From the Council of Orange, canon 6.) If anyone attempts to force those manumitted in the Church, or commended to the Church by testament, into servitude, personal service, or a tenant’s condition, he is to be restrained by ecclesiastical punishment.

## CHAPTER CLXXXVIII — Concerning fugitive ecclesiastical slaves

[Col. 0710B]

(From the same Council of Toledo.) Fugitive ecclesiastical slaves who have abandoned their homes or households, and who cannot be held even if they have been recalled, may likewise be sold by the bishop, if he wishes, or if they have deserved such treatment.

## CHAPTER CLXXXIX — Concerning bishops who contribute nothing to their churches but nevertheless presume to make freedmen from the Church’s household

(From the same council.) Bishops who contribute nothing of their own property to the Church of Christ should not presume to make freedmen from the Church’s households, to their own condemnation. For it is impious that someone who has not contributed his own possessions to the Church of Christ should inflict loss upon the Church.

Accordingly, a successor bishop shall recall such freedmen to the Church’s right without any opposition.

[Col. 0710C]

## CHAPTER CXC — Concerning those who flee to the Church because of some offense

(From the Council of Orléans, canon 10.) At the First Synod of Orléans under King Clovis, at which twenty-four bishops sat, this was established concerning those who flee to the Church because of their offenses: the rule decreed by the ancient canons and established by Roman law must be observed.

They may not be removed at all from the Church, from the Church’s atria, from the bishop’s house, or from the cloister, since these places are regarded as granting immunity. Nor may they be handed over to another person unless, after oaths have been sworn upon the Gospels, they have been secured against death, bodily injury, and every kind of punishment, so that they may reach an agreement concerning satisfaction with the person against whom the criminal offense was committed.

If someone is convicted of violating the oath he has sworn, he is to be separated not only from communion with the Church and all [Col. 0710D] clerics, but also from the company of Catholics, as guilty of perjury. But if he refuses to settle with the person against whom he is accused, despite the latter’s efforts to reach an agreement, and the accused leaves the Church out of fear, he is not to be pursued by the Church’s clerics.

## CHAPTER CXCI — Concerning a ravisher who flees to the Church with the woman he has abducted

(From the same council, canon 2.) Concerning ravishers of women, we have judged that the following must be established: if a ravisher takes refuge in a church with the woman he has abducted, and it is established that the woman suffered violence, she must immediately be freed from the ravisher’s power and returned to her parents. The ravisher, with immunity from death or punishment granted, is to be allowed to depart freely.

But if the woman’s [Col. 0711A] parents refuse to obey the ecclesiastical authorities, let them be excommunicated.

## CHAPTER CXCII — Concerning a slave who flees to the Church from his master because of any fault

(From the same council, canon 3.) If a slave who has fled to the Church because of any fault receives an ecclesiastical oath from his master concerning the fault committed, he must immediately be compelled to return to his master’s service.

After he has been handed over to his master upon the giving of the oath, if he is proved to have suffered any punishment for the same fault of which he is accused, he is to be regarded as excluded from communion and from the company of Catholics, as stated above, for contempt of the Church and violation of faith.

But if a slave defended by the Church because of his fault has obtained from the clergy [Col. 0711B] an oath from his master guaranteeing immunity, then, if he refuses to leave, the master may seize him.

## CHAPTER CXCIII — On the same matter

(From the same council, canon 5.) It was likewise decreed at the Synod of Mâcon that those who flee from their enemies, whether into a church, the atrium of a church, the bishop’s house, or the cloister of regular religious, must not be removed from there until they have first received, upon sacred objects, security from their persecutors against death, bodily injury, and every kind of punishment.

This applies even if they are slaves of those who pursue them, so that they may reach an agreement concerning satisfaction with the person against whom they have committed the offense. If the person who first swore upon sacred objects is later convicted of violating his oath, he is to be deprived of communion as guilty of perjury until he makes satisfaction.

## CHAPTER CXCIV — On the same matter

[Col. 0711C]

(From the Council held at Thionville, canon 11.) No one should dare to remove an accused person fleeing to a church, the atrium of a church, the workshops or buildings of regular brothers, the bishop’s court, or the bishop’s house, since these places are regarded as granting immunity in the ancient canons. Nor should anyone hand him over from there to punishment or death, so that the honor of God and his saints may be preserved above all.

The rulers of the churches should strive to secure peace, life, and bodily safety for him by oath. Nevertheless, he must make lawful satisfaction for whatever wrong he has committed. If the pursuer refuses to obey the masters of the Church, he is to be restrained canonically.

## CHAPTER CXCV — On the same matter

(From the Council of Orange, canon 5.) Those who have fled to the Church [Col. 0711D] must not be handed over, but must be defended by the reverence due to the place and by intercession. If anyone believes that the clerics’ dependents who have fled to the Church should be seized as his own dependents, let him be struck throughout all the churches by the strictest condemnation.

## CHAPTER CXCVI — Concerning the immunity of the Church

(From the Council of Tribur, canon 30.) If anyone engages in a fight or commits homicide in the atrium of a church, whatever is to be paid as compensation for the violated immunity shall be paid to the altar, regardless of whose church it is.

## CHAPTER CXCVII — Concerning those fleeing to the Church

(From the Council of Metz, canon 2.) If anyone, being stubborn or proud, has no fear of God or reverence for the holy churches, and forcibly removes from the atrium or porticoes attached in any way to a church his [Col. 0712A] slave who has fled, or anyone whom he himself has persecuted, thereby showing contempt for almighty God, he shall pay 400 solidi to the bishop as compensation for the violated immunity and shall himself be subjected to public penance according to the bishop’s judgment.

This is so that the honor of God and reverence for the saints may be upheld, and so that the Church of God may always remain inviolable.

## CHAPTER CXCVIII — What should be read in the Church of God

(From the Council of Orléans, canon 3.) Nothing else is to be read or sung in the Church except those things that are of divine authority and that the authority of the orthodox Fathers has sanctioned. Let them not venerate false names of angels, but only those taught by prophetic and evangelical Scripture: Michael, Gabriel, and Raphael.

## CHAPTER CXCIX — That those who read infamous books should be excommunicated

(From a decree of Pope Hadrian, canon 2.) Those who are found reading or singing infamous and unknown books in the Church are to be excommunicated.

## CHAPTER CC — Concerning those who conceive secretly

[Col. 0712B]

(From the Council of Mâcon, canon 6.) It has been decreed in this holy council that every priest publicly announce in his parish that if any woman, having been secretly seduced, conceives and gives birth, she must on no account, under the compulsion of the devil, kill her son or daughter.

Rather, by whatever means she can manage, she should have the child carried and placed before the doors of the Church, so that on the following day, when it has been brought before a priest, it may be received and nourished by some faithful person. In this way she will escape the guilt of homicide [Col. 0712C] and, what is more serious, of parricide. For anyone who kills a son or daughter is held to be a parricide in every respect.

## CHAPTER CCI — Concerning infants born of adultery and exposed at the Church

(From the Council of Arles, canon 5.) If an infant exposed before a church is taken in by anyone out of compassion, that person must submit a written declaration, so that, if the child who has been taken in is not sought and identified within ten days, the person who collected it may have it securely.

But anyone who, after the stated period, brings a claim against the child is to be condemned as a homicide by ecclesiastical discipline, as the authority of the Fathers has decreed.

## CHAPTER CCII — On the same matter

[Col. 0712D]

(From the Council of Vaison, canon 9.) Concerning exposed infants, since a complaint has arisen from everyone that they are now exposed not to mercy but to dogs, although fear of accusations causes even the unhappy human mind to shrink from the commands of mercy, the following is to be observed:

In accordance with the statutes of the most faithful Augusti and most pious rulers, whoever takes in an exposed child must notify the Church and record the notification. Likewise, on the Lord’s altar-day, the minister must announce that the exposed child has been taken in by the Church, so that within ten days from the day of exposure, anyone who proves that he recognizes the child may reclaim it.

He must, at that time, give the person who collected the child whatever recompense he can for the mercy shown during those ten days; or, if he wishes, he may possess the child permanently with God’s favor. If anyone who exposed a child collected in this manner subsequently [Col. 0713A] claims it or brings an accusation, he is to be regarded as a homicide.

## CHAPTER CCIII — Concerning the avarice of priests

(From the Council of Toledo, canon 33.) Avarice is the root of all evils, and even the minds of priests are seized by its thirst. Many of the faithful, out of love for Christ and the martyrs, build basilicas in the bishops’ parishes and record offerings. The priests take these offerings and convert them to their own uses.

As a result, the worshipers of holy places decline when they lose their stipends. As a result, the ruins of collapsing basilicas are not repaired, because priestly avarice takes everything away.

For this reason the present council has decreed that bishops govern their dioceses in such a way that they presume to take nothing from the rights of those dioceses. Rather, in accordance with the authority of earlier [Col. 0713B] councils, they are to receive a third both of the offerings and of the tithes, tributes, and produce.

If they presume to take anything more, it is to be restored through the council, with the founders themselves making the appeal—or, if they have already departed from this world, their relatives.

Let the founders of basilicas know, however, that they have no authority over the property they contribute to those churches. In accordance with the institutions of the canons, just as the church itself belongs to the bishop’s administration, so does its endowment.

## CHAPTER CCIV — Concerning those who burn churches

(From a decree of Pope Julius.) If anyone burns a church with fire, let him do penance for fifteen years, diligently restore the church, and distribute his own price among the poor.

## CHAPTER CCV — Concerning a certain cleric tormented by the devil
[Col. 0713C]

*(From the Dialogues of Pope Gregory.)* At that same time, a certain cleric of the Church of Aquino was tormented by a demon. The venerable Constantius, bishop of that church, had sent him through many places of the martyrs so that he might be healed. But the holy martyrs of God refused to grant him the gift of healing, in order to demonstrate how great was the grace in Benedict. Thus he was brought to Benedict, the servant of almighty God, who, pouring out prayers to Jesus Christ the Lord, immediately drove the ancient enemy from the possessed man.

After he had been healed, Benedict gave him this command: “Go, and after this do not eat meat, and never presume to approach a sacred order. But on whatever day you presume to violate the sacred order, you will immediately be handed over again to the devil’s jurisdiction.” The cleric therefore departed healthy, and, as a recent punishment commonly terrifies the mind, he observed for a time what the man of God had commanded.

When, however, after many years, all his former superiors had departed from this life, and he saw his juniors being advanced above him in the sacred orders, he set aside the words of the man of God, as though he had forgotten them through the passage of time, and approached a sacred order. At once the devil who had left him seized him again, and did not cease tormenting him until he drove his soul from him.

### CHAPTER CCVI — Concerning ecclesiastical property that was sold by presbyters after the death of a bishop

*(From the Council of Ancyra, canon 14.)* Concerning those things that belong to the Church, whatever the presbyters sold while there was no bishop, it was decided that, with the transaction rescinded, they should be restored to ecclesiastical ownership. It will be for the bishop to judge whether the price should be recovered or not, because the revenue from the properties that were alienated will often have returned a larger sum than the price paid.

### CHAPTER CCVII — Concerning one who rejects the offering of a presbyter who had a wife

*(From the Council of Gangra, canon 4.)* Whoever separates himself from a presbyter who had a wife, on the grounds that, while he is ministering, one ought not to receive an offering from him, let him be anathema.

### CHAPTER CCVIII — That ecclesiastics are not permitted to approach the cemeteries of heretics

*(From the Council of Laodicea, canon 8.)* Ecclesiastics are not to be permitted to approach the cemeteries of heretics, or those places which they call martyria, for the sake of prayer or healing. If any of this sort are faithful, they are to be deprived of communion for a fixed period; but penitents who confess that they have sinned ought to be received.

### CHAPTER CCIX — That one ought not to accept eulogies from heretics

*(From the same council, canon 32.)* One ought not to accept eulogies from heretics, since they are curses rather than blessings.

### CHAPTER CCX — That no Christian ought to go to false martyrs

*(From the same council, canon 34.)* No Christian ought to abandon the martyrs of Christ and go to false martyrs—that is, to those of the heretics, who are known themselves to have been heretics. For these have been alienated from God. Therefore, let those who approach such persons be anathema.

### CHAPTER CCXI — That popular psalms ought not to be recited in the Church

*(From the same council, canon 59.)* Popular psalms ought not to be sung in the Church, nor books read apart from the canon, but only the sacred volumes of the New or Old Testament.

### CHAPTER CCXII — Concerning those who abominate the assemblies held at the shrines of martyrs

*(From the Council of Antioch, canon 20.)* If anyone, out of a proud disposition, abominates the assemblies that are held at the shrines of the martyrs, and at the same time curses the services performed there together with their memorials, let him be anathema.

### CHAPTER CCXIII — That food should be supplied by exorcists to the possessed sitting in the house of God

[Col. 0714D]

*(From the Council of Carthage, canon 91.)* When possessed persons are sitting in the house of God, their daily food is to be supplied by the exorcists at the appropriate time.

### CHAPTER CCXIV — That sacred vessels ought to be handled by no one except sacred persons

*(From a decree of Pope Sixtus, canon 49.)* Let your wisdom know, dearest brothers, that in this holy apostolic see it has been decreed by us and the other bishops, and by the other priests of the Lord, that sacred vessels are to be handled by no one except persons consecrated and devoted to the Lord. For it is utterly unworthy that the sacred vessels of the Lord, whatever they may be, should serve human uses, or be handled by anyone except men serving and devoted to the Lord, lest, angered by such presumptions, the Lord inflict a plague upon his people, and those who have not even sinned suffer evil or perish; for the just very often perishes on account of the wicked.

Take care, brothers, that you do not henceforth permit such things to be done in your churches, lest the flock redeemed by the precious blood of Christ—God forbid!—fall into destruction.

### CHAPTER CCXV — Concerning consecrated women who have presumed to handle sacred vessels and altar cloths

*(From a decree of Pope Soter, canon 46.)* It has been reported to the apostolic see that women consecrated to God, or nuns, among you touch sacred vessels and sacred cloths and carry incense around the altars. No rightly minded person doubts that all these things are full of reprehension and blame. Therefore, by the authority of this holy see, we judge that you must cut off all these practices completely, as soon as possible; and, lest this plague spread more widely, we command that it be removed throughout all the provinces.

### CHAPTER CCXVI — Concerning sacred vessels, altar cloths, and church veils: what is to be done if they have been consumed by age

*(From a letter of Pope Clement, canon 56.)* This is how one ought to proceed concerning sacred vessels: if an altar cloth, a bishop’s chair, a candlestick, or a veil has been consumed by age, it is to be given to the fire, since it is not permitted that things which have been in the sanctuary be treated improperly; rather, everything is to be committed to the fire. Their ashes are also to be brought into the baptistery, where there is no passage, or they are to be thrown into the wall or into pits in the pavement, lest they be defiled by the feet of those entering.

But the cloths and veils that have been soiled in the service of the sanctuary are to be washed inside the sanctuary by deacons together with humble ministers. The coverings of the Lord’s table are not to be carried outside the sanctuary, lest perhaps the dust of the Lord’s body fall improperly when the linen cloth is carried out, and this become a sin for the person doing it. Therefore, we command the ministers to guard them carefully in the sanctuary. Let the cloths be washed in one basin and the veils in another.

## HERE BEGIN THE DECREES CONCERNING BOOKS TO BE RECEIVED OR NOT TO BE RECEIVED, WRITTEN BY POPE GELASIUS WITH SEVENTY VERY LEARNED BISHOPS IN THE APOSTOLIC SEE OF THE CITY OF ROME

*(From the decree of Pope Gelasius concerning books to be received.)*

### CHAPTER CCXVII — Concerning the order of the books of the Old Testament

[Col. 0715D]

One book of Genesis. One book of Exodus. One book of Leviticus. One book of Numbers. One book of Deuteronomy. One book of Joshua. One book of Judges. Four books of Kings. One book of Ruth. Two books of Chronicles. One book of Psalms. Five books of Solomon. One book of Job.

[Col. 0716A]

One book of Tobit. One book of Ezra. One book of Esther. One book of Judith. Two books of Maccabees.

### CHAPTER CCXVIII — Concerning the order of the prophets

One book of Isaiah. One book of Jeremiah, together with his *Cinoth*, that is, his Lamentations. One book of Ezekiel. One book of Daniel. One book of Hosea. One book of Amos. One book of Micah. One book of Joel.

[Col. 0716B]

One book of Obadiah. One book of Jonah. One book of Nahum. One book of Habakkuk. One book of Zephaniah. One book of Haggai. One book of Zechariah. One book of Malachi.

### CHAPTER CCXIX — Concerning the order of the books of the New Testament, which the holy Roman Church holds and which the universal Church observes

Four books of the Gospels. One book according to Matthew. One book according to Mark. One book according to Luke.

[Col. 0716C]

One book according to John. One book of the Acts of the Apostles.

Fourteen epistles of Paul.

One epistle to the Romans. Two epistles to the Corinthians. One epistle to the Galatians. One epistle to the Ephesians. One epistle to the Philippians. One epistle to the Colossians. One epistle to the Thessalonians. Two epistles to Timothy. Two epistles to Titus. One epistle to Philemon. One epistle to the Hebrews. One book of the Apocalypse of John.

### CHAPTER CCXX — The order of the seven canonical epistles

[Col. 0716D]

Two epistles of the apostle Peter. One epistle of the apostle James. Three epistles of the apostle John. One epistle of the apostle Jude the Zealot.

*(From a decree of the same pope.)* After the prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic Scriptures, on which the Catholic Church has been founded by the grace of God, we also thought it necessary to make this known: although all the Catholic churches spread throughout the world are one bridal chamber of Christ, nevertheless the holy Roman Catholic and apostolic Church was not placed before the other churches by synodal decrees, but obtained primacy through the evangelical voice of our Lord and Savior:

“You are Peter,” he says, “and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. And I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven.”

She was also granted the fellowship of the blessed apostle Paul, the chosen vessel. Contrary to the chatter of heretics, he was not crowned at a different time, but at one time and on the same day, suffering martyrdom with Peter in the city of Rome under Caesar Nero; together they consecrated the aforesaid holy Roman Church to Christ the Lord, and by their presence and venerable triumph placed it before all the cities in the whole world.

The first see, therefore, is the Roman Church, the see of the apostle Peter, having neither stain nor wrinkle nor anything of this kind.

[Col. 0717B]

The second see is at Alexandria, consecrated in the name of blessed Peter by Mark, his disciple and evangelist. Sent by the apostle Peter into Egypt, Mark preached the word of truth and completed a glorious martyrdom.

The third see, at Antioch, is honored in the name of the same most blessed Peter, because he lived there before coming to Rome, and there the first name of the new people, the Christians, arose.

And although no one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus, nevertheless, for our edification, the same holy Roman Church does not prohibit the acceptance of these Scriptures also, after those of the Old and New Testament that we have regularly received:

The holy Council of Nicaea of three hundred and eighteen Fathers, held under the authority of the emperor Constantine Augustus, in which the heretic Arius was condemned.

The holy Council of Constantinople, held under the authority of the elder emperor Theodosius Augustus, in which the heretic Macedonius received the condemnation he deserved.

The holy Council of Ephesus, in which Nestorius was condemned, with the agreement of the most blessed Pope Coelestine, under the authority of Cyril, bishop of the see of Alexandria, and of Bishop Arcadius, sent from Italy.

The holy Council of Chalcedon, held under the authority of the emperor Marcian and Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, in which the Nestorian and Eutychian heresies, together with Dioscorus and his associates, were condemned.

We have also decreed that any councils instituted by the holy Fathers up to the present, beyond the authority of these four, are both to be preserved and received.

Now what follows concerns the works of the holy Fathers that are received in the Catholic Church:

The works of the blessed Cyprian, martyr and bishop of Carthage.

Likewise, the works of the blessed Gregory, bishop of Nazianzus.

Likewise, the works of Basil, bishop of Cappadocia.

Likewise, the works of the blessed Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria.

Likewise, the works of the blessed John, bishop of Constantinople.

Likewise, the works of the blessed Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria.

Likewise, the works of the blessed Cyril, bishop of Alexandria.

Likewise, the works of the blessed Hilary, bishop of Poitiers.

Likewise, the works of the blessed Ambrose, bishop of Milan.

Likewise, the works of the blessed Augustine, bishop of Hippo Regius.

Likewise, the works of Jerome, presbyter.

Likewise, the works of Prosper, a most religious man.

[Col. 0718A]

Likewise, the letter of the blessed Pope Leo sent to Flavian, bishop of Constantinople. If anyone disputes its text down to a single jot and does not receive it reverently in every respect, let him be anathema.

Likewise, we decree that the works and treatises of all orthodox Fathers who in no respect deviated from fellowship with the holy Roman Church, nor separated themselves from its faith or preaching, but by the grace of God remained participants in that communion until the last day of their lives, are to be read.

Likewise, the decretal letters that the most blessed popes sent from the city of Rome at various times for the consolation of various Fathers are to be received with reverence.

Likewise, concerning the acts of the holy martyrs, which shine with the manifold torments of their sufferings and the wondrous triumphs of their confessions: what Catholic would doubt that they endured great things in their struggles, and that they bore everything not by their own strength but by the grace and help of God?

Nevertheless, according to ancient custom, they are not read in the holy Roman Church with its distinctive caution, because the names of those who wrote them are entirely unknown, and because they are thought to have been written by unbelievers with either superfluous statements or material less suitable than the order of events required—such as the passions of Cyricus and Julitta, of George, and of others of this kind, which are reported to have been written by heretics. Therefore, as has been said, lest even a slight occasion for mockery arise, they are not read in the holy Roman Church.

Nevertheless, together with the aforesaid Church, we venerate with complete devotion all the martyrs and their glorious struggles, who are known more to God than to human beings.

Likewise, we receive with all reverence the *Lives of the Fathers*—Paul, Antony, Hilarion, and all the hermits—which the most blessed Jerome wrote.

Likewise, concerning the acts of the blessed Sylvester, prelate of the apostolic see: although the name of the person who wrote them is unknown, we have learned that many Catholics in the city of Rome read them, and, because of their ancient use, many churches imitate them.

Likewise, the writing concerning the discovery of the Lord’s cross, and the other writing concerning the discovery of the head of the blessed John the Baptist, are indeed recent accounts, and some Catholics read them. But when these come into the hands of Catholics, let the statement of the apostle Paul precede them: “Test everything; hold fast to what is good.”

Likewise, Rufinus, a religious man, produced very many books of ecclesiastical works and also interpreted some writings. But because the most blessed Jerome censured him in certain matters concerning freedom of choice, we hold those views that we know the aforesaid blessed Jerome held. This applies not only to Rufinus, but also to all whom the frequently mentioned man rebuked out of zeal for God and reverence for the faith.

Likewise, we receive some works of Origen, which the most blessed Jerome does not reject, for reading. But all the rest, together with their author, we declare must be rejected.

Likewise, we do not declare the *Chronicle* of Eusebius of Caesarea, and his books of Ecclesiastical History, wholly to be rejected, on account of their exceptional knowledge of matters useful for instruction, although in the first book of his narrative he was lukewarm and later wrote one book in praise and defense of the schismatic Origen.

Likewise, we highly praise Orosius, a most learned man, because he arranged for us a history greatly necessary against the calumnies of the pagans and composed it with remarkable brevity.

Likewise, we place before the rest with distinguished praise the *Paschal Work* of the venerable Sedulius, which he wrote in heroic verse.

Likewise, we do not disdain the laborious work of Juvencus, but marvel at it.

The remaining works written or set forth by heretics and schismatics the Catholic and apostolic Roman Church in no way receives. Of these, we believe that a few which come to mind, and which Catholics must avoid, should be listed below.

### CHAPTER CCXXI — Concerning knowledge of the apocryphal books condemned by the holy Fathers to eternal damnation

[Col. 0719B]

*(Likewise from the same decree.)* First of all, we confess that the Synod of Rimini, convened by the emperor Constantius, son of the emperor Constantine, under the authority of the prefect Taurus, was condemned from that time and for ever.

Likewise, the eight apocryphal books called the *Itinerary of the Apostle Peter*, or of Saint Clement.

The *Acts* in the name of the apostle Andrew: apocryphal.

The *Acts* in the name of the apostle Thomas: apocryphal.

Another *Acts* in the name of the apostle Peter: apocryphal.

The *Acts* in the name of the apostle Philip: apocryphal.

The Gospels in the name of Thaddeus: apocryphal.

The Gospels in the name of Barnabas: apocryphal.

The Gospels in the name of the apostle Peter: apocryphal.

The Gospels in the name of Thomas, which the Manichaeans use: apocryphal.

The Gospels in the name of Bartholomew: apocryphal.

The Gospels in the name of the apostle Andrew: apocryphal.

The Gospels falsified by Lucianus: apocryphal.

The Gospels falsified by Hesychius: apocryphal.

The book concerning the infancy of the Savior: apocryphal.

The book concerning the Nativity of the Savior, and concerning Mary or the midwife: apocryphal.

The book called *The Shepherd*: apocryphal.

All the books composed by Leucius, the disciple of the devil: apocryphal.

The book called *The Foundation*: apocryphal.

The book called *The Treasure*: apocryphal.

The book concerning the daughters of Adelgenesis: apocryphal.

The cento concerning Christ, compiled from Virgilian verses: apocryphal.

The book called the *Acts of Thecla and Paul*: apocryphal.

The book called *Nepos*: apocryphal.

The book of Proverbs written by heretics and bearing the name of Saint Sixtus: apocryphal.

[Col. 0719D]

The revelation called the *Revelation of Paul*: apocryphal.

The revelation called the *Revelation of Thomas*: apocryphal.

The revelation called the *Revelation of Stephen*: apocryphal.

The book called the *Transitus of Saint Mary*: apocryphal.

The book called the *Penance of Adam*: apocryphal.

The book concerning a giant named Ogia, who is said by heretics to have fought with a dragon after the Flood: apocryphal.

The book called the *Testament of Job*: apocryphal.

The book called the *Penance of Origen*: apocryphal.

The book called the *Penance of Saint Cyprian*: apocryphal.

The book called *Jamnes and Mambres*: apocryphal.

The book called the *Lot of the Apostles*: apocryphal.

The book of the apostle Lusa: apocryphal.

The books called the Canons of the Apostles: apocryphal.

[Col. 0720A]

The book called the *Physiologus*, written by heretics and bearing the name of blessed Ambrose: apocryphal.

The history of Eusebius Pamphilus: apocryphal.

The works of Tertullian, or of Africanus: apocryphal.

The works of Postumianus and Gallus: apocryphal.

The works of Montanus, Priscilla, and Maximilla: apocryphal.

All the works of Faustus the Manichaean: apocryphal.

The works of another Clement of Alexandria: apocryphal.

The works of Cassian, presbyter of Gaul: apocryphal.

The works of Victorinus of Poitiers: apocryphal.

The works of Faustus of Riez in Gaul: apocryphal.

The works of Frumentius: apocryphal.

The letter of Jesus to Abgar: apocryphal.

The letter of Abgar to Jesus: apocryphal.

The passion of Quiricus and Julitta: apocryphal.

The passion of George: apocryphal.

The writings called *Solomon’s Contradiction*: apocryphal.

All phylacteries written not, as they pretend, with the names of angels but rather with the names of demons: apocryphal.

These and similar works—which Simon Magus, Nicolaus, Cerinthus, Marcion, Basilides, Ebion, Paul of Samosata, Photinus and Bonosus, who fell away through a similar error; Montanus with his most obscene followers; Apollinaris, Valentinus or Manichaeus, Faustus, Sabellius, Arius, Macedonius, Eunomius, Novatus, Sabbatius, Callistus, Donatus and Eustathius, Nibianus, Pelagius, Julian of Eclanum, Coelestinus, Maximianus, Priscillian of Spain, Lampedius, Dioscorus, Eutyches, Peter and the other Peter, one of whom corrupted Alexandria and the other Antioch; Achatius of Constantinople with his associates—

[Col. 0720C]

and all the heresies that they or their disciples, or schismatics, taught or wrote, whose names we do not retain, are not only rejected but also expelled from the entire Catholic Roman Church. Together with their authors and the followers of those authors, we confess that they have been condemned for ever under the unbreakable bond of anathema.

### CHAPTER CCXXII — When and at what times the books of the Old and New Testament are to be read

In Septuagesima they begin the Heptateuch, continuing until the fifteenth day before Easter. On the fifteenth day before Easter they begin Jeremiah, continuing until the Lord’s Supper.

On the Lord’s Supper they read three lessons from the Lamentation of Jeremiah: “How solitary sits the city,” and so forth. And three from the treatise of Saint Augustine on Psalm 63: “Hear, O God, my prayer when I plead.” And three from the Apostle, where he says to the Corinthians: “When you come together into one place.” The second lesson begins: “Likewise, after he had supped.” The third: “Concerning spiritual gifts, brothers, we do not want you to be ignorant.”

On Good Friday, three lessons are read from the Lamentation of Jeremiah; three from the treatise of Saint Augustine on Psalm 63; and three from the Apostle, where he says in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “Let us hasten to enter into that rest.” The second lesson: “For every high priest.” The third: “Concerning which we have much to say.”

On Holy Saturday, three lessons are read from the Lamentation of Jeremiah; three from the treatise of Saint Augustine on Psalm 63: “Hear, O God, my prayer when I plead”; and three from the Apostle, where he says in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “Christ, standing as high priest.” The second lesson: “For where there is a testament.” The third: “For the law, having a shadow of the good things to come.”

On the Lord’s Easter, homilies appropriate to that day are read. During the week, homilies are read. At the octave of Easter they begin the Acts of the Apostles, the canonical epistles, and the Apocalypse, continuing until the octave of Pentecost.

At the octave of Pentecost they begin Kings and Chronicles, continuing until the Kalends of August. On the first Sunday of August they begin Solomon, continuing until the Kalends of September. On the first Sunday of September they begin Job, Tobit, Esther, and Ezra, continuing until the Kalends of October.

On the first Sunday of October they begin Maccabees, continuing until the Kalends of November. On the first Sunday of November they begin Ezekiel, Daniel, and the Minor Prophets, continuing until the Kalends of December. On the first Sunday of December they begin the prophet Isaiah, continuing until Christmas.

On Christmas Eve they first read three lessons from Isaiah. The first lesson begins: “At the first time the land of Zebulun was lightened.” The second: “Be comforted.” The third: “Rise up, rise up.” Then sermons or homilies appropriate to that day are read.

On the feast of Saint Stephen, homilies concerning that day are read. On the feast of Saint John, likewise. On the feast of the Innocents, likewise. At the octave of the Lord, homilies concerning that day are read.

On the first Sunday after Christmas, the epistles of Paul are begun, continuing until Septuagesima.

At Epiphany, three lessons from Isaiah are read. The first lesson begins: “All you who thirst.” The second: “Arise, shine.” The third: “Rejoicing, I will rejoice.” Then sermons or homilies appropriate to that day are read.

### CHAPTER CCXXIII — Concerning the vessels in which the sacred mysteries are celebrated

*(From the Council of Tribur, attended by King Arnulf, canon 9.)* The vessels in which the most holy mysteries are celebrated are chalices and patens. When Boniface, martyr and bishop, was asked whether it was lawful to celebrate the sacraments in wooden vessels, he replied: “Formerly golden priests used wooden chalices; now, on the contrary, wooden priests use golden chalices.”

Zephyrinus, the sixteenth Roman bishop, decreed that Masses be celebrated with glass patens. Then Pope Urban XVIII made all the sacred vessels of silver. In this matter, as in the other forms of worship, the adornment of the churches increased more and more with the passage of time.
