In our own days, since we are servants of the head of the household, so that the adornment of Mother Church may not be diminished but rather increased and enlarged, we decree that henceforth no priest presume in any way to celebrate the sacred mystery of the body and blood of Jesus Christ our Lord in wooden vessels, lest God become angry precisely through that by which he ought to be appeased.

### CHAPTER CCXXIV — Concerning a church encumbered by several co-heirs

*(From the same council, attended by King Arnulf, canon 32.)* Whenever a church is encumbered by several co-heirs, concord and unanimity are to be secured on every side, lest the service of God be diminished on account of disputes and the care of the people be conducted irreligiously.

But if it should happen that the co-participants disagree concerning it, refuse to care for it under one presbyter, and consequently begin frequently to engage in quarrels and disputes both among themselves and among the clergy—for, according to the Apostle, God’s servants ought not to quarrel—the bishop is to remove the relics from there and place them honorably in a secure location with great care. He is also to close the doors of that church and seal them.

No one is to celebrate the sacred mystery there until all, in harmonious unanimity, choose one presbyter who is suitable to care for the most holy place and to preside usefully over God’s people.

### CHAPTER CCXXV — Concerning altars in which sacred relics are not found

*(From the African Council, canon 50.)* Altars in which the bodies or relics of martyrs are not found are to be demolished by the bishops of that place.

### CHAPTER CCXXVI — On the altar at which the bishop celebrates Mass, a presbyter must not presume to celebrate another Mass on that day

*(From the Council of Urbicum.)* On the altar at which the bishop has sung Mass, no presbyter may presume to celebrate Mass on that day.

### CHAPTER CCXXVII — That incense is to be placed upon the offering of the Lord’s body and blood

*(From the Council of Rouen, canon 1.)* We have decreed that, at the time when the Gospel is read and the offertory has been completed, incense is to be placed over the offering, namely in memory of the death of our Redeemer.

### CHAPTER CCXXVIII — That whenever the presence of a new congregation fills the basilica to which the people have gone, a subsequent sacrifice is to be offered

*(From a letter of Pope Leo sent to Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria, canon 2.)* So that our observance may agree in all things, we also wish this to be maintained: when a more solemn festival has summoned a larger gathering of people, and such a multitude of the faithful has come to it that one basilica cannot contain them, the offering of the sacrifice must unquestionably be repeated. Otherwise, if only those who arrived earlier were admitted to this devotion, those who subsequently gathered might appear not to have been received, whereas it is entirely in keeping with piety and reason that whenever the presence of a new congregation fills the basilica to which the people have gone, the subsequent sacrifice should be offered.

For it is necessary that part of the people be deprived of their devotion if, while the custom of only one Mass is maintained, they cannot offer the sacrifice unless they have assembled during the first part of the day.

### CHAPTER CCXXIX — That no presbyter presume to usurp title upon title

*(From the Council of Nantes.)* If any presbyter dies, a neighboring presbyter is not to obtain that church from the senior layman by any prayer or gift, because the title previously existed as an established institution; nor is he to obtain a chapel without consulting the bishop.

If he does so, let him receive the sentence determined and pronounced against him, just as canonical authority has decreed concerning a bishop: if, through ambition, he seeks a greater city, he is to lose the one he held and in no way obtain the one he attempted to usurp.

### CHAPTER CCXXX — That a bishop or presbyter, after beginning Mass and saying the prayer, must not dare to leave the altar of God before completing the ministry begun, unless some illness intervenes

*(From a decree of Pope Zacharias, canon 14.)* When a bishop or presbyter has entered to celebrate the solemnities of Mass, he must in no way dare to withdraw after saying the prayer, unless some illness intervenes, so that the solemnities of the Mass may be completed by another bishop or presbyter. Rather, the one who makes the beginning must complete it to the end.

For it is written: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved.” But if anyone presumes to act contrary to what we have established, let him be suspended from the sacred body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ.

### CHAPTER CCXXXI — That no bishop or presbyter may presume to go to celebrate the solemnities of Mass with a staff or to stand at the altar of God with his head covered

*(From a decree of the same pope, canon 13.)* No bishop, presbyter, or deacon may presume to enter to celebrate the solemnities of Mass with a staff or to stand at the altar of God with his head covered, since the apostle Paul also forbids men to pray in the Church with their heads covered. If anyone rashly presumes to do so, let him be deprived of communion.

### CHAPTER CCXXXII — That the bodies of saints are not to be transferred from place to place

[Col. 0723C]

*(From the Council of Mainz, canon 51.)* Henceforth no one is to presume to transfer the bodies of saints from place to place without the advice of the ruler, or the permission of the bishops and the holy synod.

### CHAPTER CCXXXIII — Who may be buried in a church

*(From the same council, canon 52.)* No dead person is to be buried inside a church except a bishop, an abbot, a worthy presbyter, or a faithful layman.

### CHAPTER CCXXXIV — That all the faithful ought to do nothing in church except pray

*(From the Council of Tours, canon 38.)* Priests ought to admonish the faithful that, when they gather at the church, they enter it without noise or disturbance. While they remain there for the sake of prayer, they must not engage in empty conversations among themselves. During the time when the solemnities of Mass are celebrated, they must abstain completely not only from idle and useless words but also from harmful thoughts.

### CHAPTER CCXXXV — That divine clemency is to be entreated with knees fixed upon the ground, except on the greater solemnities

*(From the same council, canon 37.)* It must be known that, except on Sundays and on those solemnities when the holy and universal Church customarily prays standing in remembrance of the Lord’s resurrection, we ought, with knees fixed upon the ground, humbly to ask for the clemency that will benefit us and for the forgiveness of our sins. The Lord himself gave us an example of this in the Gospel.

The book of the Acts of the Apostles also bears witness that the martyr Stephen and the apostle Paul did the same. From this it is shown that a Christian ought humbly to prostrate himself upon the ground, lest it perhaps be said to him: “Why should earth and ashes be proud?”

### CHAPTER CCXXXVI — That it is not permitted to kiss the dead

*(From the Council of Agde, canon 3.)* It is not permitted to kiss the dead, nor to wrap their bodies in the cloths placed upon the altar for the sacrifice, nor to place them upon the bier.

### CHAPTER CCXXXVII — Where the faithful ought to be buried

[Col. 0724B]

*(From the Council of Tribur, attended by King Arnulf, canon 15.)* Because of the urgent necessity that then arises, and which is at that time greatest, it remains that, wherever the means and the circumstances of the time permit, the burial of the dying should be carried out near the church where the bishop’s seat is located.

But if this appears impossible because of the length of the journey or the difficulty of some nearby obstacle, let the earth of his burial await him where a holy community of canons, monks, or nuns dwells together, so that, commended to his Judge by their prayers, he may come before him and receive, through their intercessions, the remission of sins that he does not obtain through his own merits.

But if this too is judged unsuitable and difficult, let him be buried where he paid his tithe while alive.

### CHAPTER CCXXXVIII — That priests should devote a period of time to prayer before celebrating the sacrifice

*(From a decree of Pope Innocent, canon 26.)* For Paul writes to the Corinthians, saying: “Abstain from one another for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer.” He certainly commanded this to laypeople, and much more to priests, whose continual duty is both to pray and to offer sacrifice; they ought always to abstain from such intercourse.

If a priest has been defiled by carnal desire, with what shame would he perhaps presume to offer sacrifice, or with what conscience or merit could he believe that he would be heard, when it has been said: “All things are clean to the clean, but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is clean”?

### CHAPTER CCXXXIX — Concerning laymen who have their own churches

[Col. 0724D]

*(From the Council of Reims, in the presence of the emperor Louis, canon 5.)* If laymen have their own chapels, it is contrary to reason and authority that they themselves should receive the tithes and feed dogs or their concubines from them. Rather, the presbyters of the churches should receive them and use them to provide for the restoration of the churches, the lights, and the reception of guests and the poor, and should earnestly implore mercy for the holy Church and for the stability of the kingdom of God.

### CHAPTER CCXL — Concerning the churches of monks

*(From the Council at Conflans, attended by Kings Henry and Charles, canon 6.)* It has also been established that the churches of whatever monks are situated in the individual parishes of bishops are, as is fitting, to be divinely subjected to episcopal governance, and that they diligently provide the bishops with the services owed in the exercise of ecclesiastical care. The monks themselves are unquestionably to obey their bishops in all things.

### CHAPTER CCXLI — Concerning those who, when they wish to give places belonging to their property somewhere, must recognize that they cannot assign the tithe elsewhere
*(From the same council, at which Kings Henry and Charles were present, chapter 8.)* [Col. 0726A]

If, however, any layman or cleric, or any person of either sex, has delegated property or possessions of his or her own to be donated somewhere, that person shall have no power to withdraw from them the income from tithes lawfully assigned to the former church. But if anyone attempts to do so, such a transfer shall be deemed wholly invalid, and the offender shall be compelled by ecclesiastical censure to make satisfaction.

[Col. 0725] **END OF THE THIRD BOOK.**
