# BURCHARD, BISHOP OF THE CHURCH OF WORMS, DECRETALS, BOOK FOUR: ON THE SACRAMENT OF BAPTISM AND CONFIRMATION

[Col. 0727]

## SUMMARY OF THE BOOK

[Col. 0727C]

This book treats of baptism and confirmation, and of the matters that are to be observed concerning them.

## CHAPTER I — What baptism is

*(From the decree of Pope Fabian, chapter 5.)*

[Col. 0728C]

“Baptism” is interpreted from Greek into Latin as *tinctio*, “dipping” or “immersion.” It is called *tinctio* because there a person is changed for the better by the spirit of grace and becomes something altogether different from what he was, being baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0729A]

Just as every statement stands on three witnesses, so this sacrament is confirmed by the threefold number of the divine names: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER II — That, except at Easter and Pentecost, baptism is not to be administered unless someone is in danger of death

*(From a letter of Pope Leo, chapter 11.)*

Since it is most plainly evident that these two seasons—namely Easter and Pentecost—are the proper times in the Church for those chosen for baptism, we admonish your affection not to mix any other days with this observance. For although there are other festivals on which much reverence is owed in honor of God, we must nevertheless preserve the mystical and reasonable pattern of the principal and greatest sacrament. This does not prohibit the permission by which help is given through baptism at any time to those in danger.

Thus we offer our free prayers for these two festivals, [Col. 0729B] joined and related to each other, on behalf of those who live in safety and peace, while in danger of death, in the peril of siege, amid the constraints of persecution, or in fear of shipwreck, we deny no one, at any time, this unique protection of true salvation.

## CHAPTER III — At what time baptism should be celebrated, and that those who are baptized may be found faithful, not unbelieving

*(From the decree of Pope Victor, sent to the brothers established throughout Alexandria, chapter 2.)*

Catholic baptism should indeed be celebrated at Easter and Pentecost. Nevertheless, if necessity demands it or the danger of death threatens, pagans coming to the faith may be baptized in any place or at any moment, wherever the occasion arises—whether in a river, [Col. 0729C] in the sea, or in springs—provided that the confession of Christian belief has been clearly made.

Careful attention must also be paid to what they have promised in baptism, so that they may be found faithful, not unbelieving. Those, however, who are stained by the mark of unbelief become infamous and are in no way counted among the faithful.

## CHAPTER IV — On the two seasons for baptism

*(From the decree of Pope Gelasius, chapter 10.)*

No one should suppose that he may confidently be baptized indiscriminately at any time, except at the Easter festival and the venerable sacrament of Pentecost—apart only from the onset of the most serious illness, in which it is to be feared that, as the danger of the disease increases, the sick person may perhaps depart, overtaken by death without the remedy of salvation [Col. 0729D].

## CHAPTER V — Again, at what time baptism ought to be administered

*(From the decree of Pope Siricius, chapter 2.)*

There follows the reprehensible and correctable disorder of people being baptized at whatever time each person pleases. We say this with agitation: our fellow priests presume to do this not by reason of any authoritative principle but solely through rashness, so that, indiscriminately and freely, countless communities, as you report, receive the mystery of baptism at the festivals of Christ’s birth, of his manifestation, and likewise of the apostles and martyrs. Yet this privilege is claimed specifically for the Lord’s Easter, together with Pentecost, both by us and by all the churches.

## CHAPTER VI — On the same matter

[Col. 0730A]

*(From the council held at Compendium, chapter 3.)*

Baptism is not to be celebrated outside the times established by the canons, that is, at Easter and Pentecost. For the sacred canons prohibit this in every way unless some danger has arisen, to such an extent that they even exclude from ecclesiastical orders those who are baptized at another time and do not admit them to the clergy.

## CHAPTER VII — On the same matter

*(From the Council of Worms, chapter 10.)*

Let every member of the faithful know that the sacrament of holy baptism is to be administered only at the Easter festival and at Pentecost, except to those whom the danger of death compels us to assist with such remedies, lest they perish eternally.

## CHAPTER VIII — That catechumens should come twenty days before baptism for the cleansing of exorcism

[Col. 0730B]

*(From the Council of Braga, chapter 3.)*

We command this in every respect, as the ancient canons also command: catechumens are to come twenty days before baptism for the cleansing of exorcism. During those twenty days, according to canonical instruction, they are both to be taught and consecrated.

## CHAPTER IX — That all who come for baptism must present their faith to the bishop or priest on Maundy Thursday

*(From the Council of Laodicea, chapter 46.)*

Those who come to baptism must learn the faith and present it to the bishop or priests on the Thursday of Holy Week.

## CHAPTER X — That all who are to be baptized must first undergo exorcism

[Col. 0730C]

*(From the decree of Pope Celestine sent to the bishops of Gaul, chapter 12.)*

We also contemplate, not without attentive consideration, what the holy Church uniformly does throughout the world concerning those who are to be baptized. Whether infants or adults come to the sacrament of rebirth, they do not first approach the font of life until the unclean spirit has been driven from them by the exsufflations of the clergy, so that it may then truly become apparent how the ruler of this world is cast out.

## CHAPTER XI — That those who have given their names for baptism should abstain from meat and wine

*(From the Council of Carthage, chapter 85.)*

Those preparing for baptism should submit their names while abstaining from wine and meat, and should frequently examine their baptism through the laying on of hands.

## CHAPTER XII — That neophytes should abstain for a certain time from richer foods and from conjugal relations

*(From the same council, chapter 87.)*

Neophytes should for some time abstain from richer banquets, spectacles, and conjugal relations.

## CHAPTER XIII — That every priest should possess a baptismal vessel

*(From the Council of Meaux, chapter 7.)*

Every priest who is unable to possess a stone font should have a suitable vessel devoted solely to the duty of baptizing; it must not be carried outside the church. Likewise, separate vessels should be kept for washing the corporal and for the altar cloths, and nothing else should be done in them.

## CHAPTER XIV — That no priest should presume to baptize except in cities, unless illness makes it necessary

[Col. 0731A]

*(From the same council, chapter 48.)*

No priest should presume to baptize except in cities and at the appointed times, unless illness or a definite necessity requires it; and those places are to retain their proper authority and privileges.

## CHAPTER XV — How baptism is to be given to one who wishes to become a believer

*(From the decree of Pope Clement, sent to all the faithful, chapter 62.)*

If anyone wishes to become a believer and desires to be baptized, let him cast off his former evils and henceforth become, through his own deeds, an heir of heavenly blessings on account of good works. Let him approach his priest, give him his name, and hear from him the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven. Let him devote himself to frequent fasts [Col. 0731B] and test himself in all things, so that, after completing three months, he may be baptized on a feast day.

Let each person be baptized in running water, with the name of the threefold blessedness invoked over him. Let him first be anointed with oil sanctified by prayer, so that, consecrated in this way, he may finally receive a place among the saints.

## CHAPTER XVI — On martyrs who suffered martyrdom without baptism

*(From the sayings of Augustine.)*

Although a catechumen has died in good works, we do not believe that he possesses life, except if the sacrament of martyrdom has been completed. The baptized person confesses his faith before the priest and responds when questioned. The martyr does the same before his persecutor: he confesses [Col. 0731C] his faith and responds when questioned.

After his confession, he is sprinkled with martyrdom [reading uncertain], or indeed with blood, or immersed in fire. The baptized person receives the Holy Spirit through the laying on of the bishop’s hands; the martyr becomes a dwelling place of the Holy Spirit, since it is not he himself who speaks but the Spirit who speaks in him.

The baptized person shares in the Eucharist in remembrance of the Lord’s death; the martyr dies together with Christ himself. The baptized person confesses that he will renounce the deeds of the world; the martyr has himself renounced life. All sins are forgiven to the former; in the latter they are extinguished.

## CHAPTER XVII — That the sacrament should not be given to catechumens at Easter

*(From the Council of Carthage, chapter 5.)*

It was also decided that during the most solemn days of Easter the sacrament should not be given to catechumens, except salt alone. For if the faithful do not alter the sacrament during [Col. 0731D] those days, neither ought catechumens to alter it.

## CHAPTER XVIII — On removing catechumens from the baptistery

*(From the Council of Orange, chapter 17.)*

Catechumens are never to be admitted into the baptistery unless they themselves are being baptized.

## CHAPTER XIX — On separating and instructing catechumens

*(From the same council, chapter 18.)*

Catechumens are to be separated, as far as possible, from the blessing of the faithful, even among the household ranks, and are to be instructed so that they may present themselves separately to be signed or blessed.

## CHAPTER XX — On catechumens who sin

[Col. 0732A]

*(From the Council of Neocaesarea, chapter 6.)*

If a catechumen enters the church and stands among those who are being instructed, and is then found to be sinning, if he kneels, let him remain to hear the teaching, so that he may not sin further. But if he sins even after hearing it, let him be expelled.

## CHAPTER XXI — On those who have recently been baptized, that they should not be promoted

*(From the Council of Laodicea, chapter 3.)*

Those who have recently been enlightened through baptism should not be promoted to the priestly order.

## CHAPTER XXII — On priests who do not baptize in the Trinity according to the Lord’s command

*(From the Apostolic Canon.)*

If any bishop or priest does not baptize according to the Lord’s command in [Col. 0732B] the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, but in three beginningless principles, or in three sons, or in three Paracletes, let him be deposed.

## CHAPTER XXIII — On the same matter

*(From the same source.)*

If any bishop or priest does not perform the threefold immersion of the one mystery, but immerses once in baptism, which is said to be given in the Lord’s death, let him be deposed. For the Lord did not say, “Baptize in my death,” but, “Go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”

## CHAPTER XXIV — That, if necessary, one sponsor may serve at baptism and confirmation

*(From the decree of Pope Hyginus, chapter 10.)*

For a catechumen, at baptism, and at confirmation, one father may [Col. 0732C] serve if necessity compels it. This is not, however, the Roman custom; rather, one person receives each person separately.

## CHAPTER XXV — That one male or female sponsor should come forward to receive the infant

*(From a decree of Pope Leo at Saint-Médard.)*

No more than one person, whether man or woman, should come forward to receive an infant from baptism. The same is also to be done at confirmations.

## CHAPTER XXVI — That one who has not been baptized or confirmed should receive no one from baptism

*(From the Council of Mainz, chapter 2.)*

At baptism or in the chrism, one who has not himself been baptized or confirmed cannot receive another as a child.

## CHAPTER XXVII — That no one should become a sponsor unless he believes correctly

[Col. 0732D]

*(From the Council of Paris, chapter 2.)*

No one should receive another from the sacred font unless he knows the Lord’s Prayer and the Creed according to his own language and understanding, and recites them before the priest, so that all may understand the pact that they have made with God.

## CHAPTER XXVIII — That priests should ask sponsors whether they know the Creed

*(From the Fourth Council of Worms, chapter 1.)*

Let priests announce that neither men nor women should receive godsons or goddaughters from the sacred font unless they have memorized the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer.

## CHAPTER XXIX — On reciting the Creed publicly in all churches eight days before Easter

*(From the Council of Agde, chapter 1.)*

It was also decided that the Creed should be publicly delivered [Col. 0733A] in all churches to the candidates for baptism on one day, namely eight days before the Lord’s Resurrection.

## CHAPTER XXX — On sick pagans, if they desire baptism

*(From the same council, chapter 3.)*

If pagans in illness desire that hands be laid upon them, and if they have lived an honorable life in some respect, it was decided that hands should be laid upon them and that they should be made Christians.

## CHAPTER XXXI — On baptizing a pregnant woman

*(From the Council of Neocaesarea, chapter 6.)*

A pregnant woman should be baptized whenever she wishes. For she communicates nothing of this to the child being born, since each person’s intention is declared in confession.

## CHAPTER XXXII — On baptizing sick infants

[Col. 0733B]

*(From the Council of Eliberitanum, chapter 5.)*

Concerning infants who have recently been born from their mother’s womb, it was decided that, if they are sick, as commonly happens, and do not desire their mother’s milk, they should be baptized even on the very day on which they were born, if they are brought forward.

## CHAPTER XXXIII — On those who are baptized during illness

*(From the Council of Neocaesarea, chapter 12.)*

If someone has been baptized during illness, he should not be ordained a priest. For his faith was not voluntary but arose from necessity, unless afterward his devotion and faith appear commendable, or a shortage of men compels it.

## CHAPTER XXXIV — On those who deny that newborn infants should be baptized

*(From the African Council, chapter 66.)*

It was also decided that [Col. 0733C] whoever denies that newborn infants are to be baptized from their mothers’ wombs, or says that they are indeed baptized for the remission of sins but draw nothing of original sin from Adam that might be expiated by the washing of regeneration—so that it would follow that the form of baptism for the remission of sins is understood in them as not true but false—let him be anathema.

For the Apostle’s statement, “Through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin, death, and so death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned,” cannot be understood otherwise than as the Catholic Church, spread throughout the world, has always understood it.

Because of this rule of faith, even infants, who have not yet been able to commit any sin in themselves, are [Col. 0733D] truly baptized for the remission of sins, so that through regeneration what they have drawn from generation may be cleansed in them.

## CHAPTER XXXV — On baptizing the sick

*(From the Council of Laodicea, chapter 47.)*

Those who receive baptism during illness must, after recovering, learn the faith thoroughly and know of what gift they have become participants.

## CHAPTER XXXVI — On the sick who desire baptism and subsequently lose their speech

*(From the African Council, chapter 12.)*

The sick should be baptized if they cannot respond on their own, provided that those attending them at their own peril testify that this was their will. Reconciliation should also not be denied to actors, performers, and other persons of this kind.

## CHAPTER XXXVII — On not baptizing the dead

[Col. 0734A]

*(From the Council of Carthage, chapter 6.)*

Care must be taken lest the weakness of the brethren come to believe that the dead can also be baptized, when it observes that the Eucharist cannot be given to them either.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII — On baptizing one who suddenly loses speech, if he has witnesses

*(From the Council of Orange, chapter 11.)*

One who suddenly loses speech may be baptized and receive penance, as established, if he has testimony concerning his previous will in the words of others, or if those present can discern it from his gestures.

## CHAPTER XXXIX — On those baptized among heretics in the name of the Holy Trinity

*(From the Council of Rouen, chapter 3.)*

There is one baptism, but it is in the Catholic Church, whose members we have become, [Col. 0734B] where there is one faith and where baptism is given in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

Therefore those who have been baptized among heretics who baptize in the confession of the Holy Trinity, and who come to us, are to be received as baptized, so that the invocation or confession of the Holy Trinity may not be annulled. But they are to be fully taught and instructed in the meaning of the Holy Trinity and in the mystery maintained in the holy Church. If they consent to believe or agree to confess, they are to be strengthened, after the integrity of their faith has been purified, through the laying on of hands.

If they are dull-witted children who cannot grasp instruction, those who present them should answer on their behalf according to the custom of baptism. They are to be questioned in such a way that those answering know what they ought to say, and thus they are to receive [Col. 0734C] the laying on of hands.

## CHAPTER XL — On the same matter

*(From the Council of Worms, chapter 5.)*

Whoever has been baptized by heretics in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit must in no way be rebaptized, but must be cleansed solely through the laying on of hands.

## CHAPTER XLI — That baptism received in the Trinity must not be repeated

*(From the Council of Carthage, chapter 1.)*

Baptism received in the Trinity must not be repeated. Therefore, if it pleases you, let us first consider the title concerning those who have been rebaptized. I ask your holiness to bring forth the convictions of your minds concerning one who descends into the water, is questioned according to the faith of the Gospel [Col. 0734D] and the teaching of the apostles, and confesses a good conscience toward God through the resurrection of Jesus Christ: is he permitted to be questioned again in the same faith and immersed again in water?

All the bishops said: “Far be it, far be it!” We decree rebaptization unlawful, and wholly alien to sincere faith and Catholic discipline.

## CHAPTER XLII — On those who do not know with what faith they were baptized

*(From the decree of Pope Leo sent to the bishops established throughout Sicily, chapter 29.)*

As for those about whom you have written—who know that they were baptized but declare that they do not know what faith those who baptized them held—since they received the form of baptism in some manner, they are not to be baptized. Rather, through the laying on of hands and [Col. 0735A] the power of the Holy Spirit, which they could not receive from heretics, they are to be joined to the Catholics.

## CHAPTER XLIII — On the priest who did not know grammar but nevertheless baptized in the Trinity

*(From a letter of Pope Zacharias to Boniface, archbishop of Mainz.)*

Virgil and Sedonius, devout men living in the province of the Bavarians, have visited us by letter. Through it they reported that your revered fraternity had instructed them to baptize Christians again. On hearing this, we were greatly troubled and fell into a certain astonishment, if the matter was as stated.

They reported that there was in the same province a priest ignorant of Latin grammar. When he was baptizing, unable to speak Latin correctly, he said [Col. 0735B]: “I baptize you in the name of *Patria* (‘fatherland’) and *Filia* (‘daughter’), and of the Holy Spirit.” For this reason your revered fraternity considered rebaptizing them.

But, most holy brother, if the one who baptized them did not introduce an error or heresy, but, solely through ignorance of Roman speech, distorted his pronunciation while baptizing, as we have said, we cannot consent that they be baptized again. For your holy fraternity knows very well that whoever has been baptized by heretics in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit must in no way be rebaptized, but must be cleansed solely through the laying on of hands.

Therefore, most holy brother, if the matter is as it has been reported to us, do not preach anything of this kind to them any longer. Rather, as the holy Fathers teach and proclaim, let your holiness [Col. 0735C] strive to preserve them.

## CHAPTER XLIV — On those who have some doubt about their baptism, that they should be rebaptized

*(From the decree of Pope Leo sent to Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne, chapter 27.)*

If no indications exist among relatives or members of the household, and none among clergy or neighbors, by which those under inquiry can be shown to have been baptized, action must be taken so that they may be reborn, lest they plainly perish. In cases where it is not shown that something was done, reason does not permit it to be regarded as a repetition.

Those who can remember coming to church with their parents may recall whether they received what was given to their parents. But if even this is beyond their memory, it seems that what is not known to have been conferred should be conferred [Col. 0735D] upon them, because there is no rash presumption where there is diligent piety.

## CHAPTER XLV — On infants who cannot have reliable witnesses, and are therefore not to be regarded as baptized

*(From the African Council, chapter 39.)*

It was also decided concerning infants that whenever entirely reliable witnesses cannot be found to testify without doubt that they have been baptized, and when, because of their age, they are not competent to answer concerning the sacraments entrusted to them, they are to be baptized without any hesitation, lest this uncertainty deprive them of the cleansing of the sacraments. For the Moorish envoys consulted our brothers about this, since they redeem many such children from the barbarians.

## CHAPTER XLVI — On priests through whose negligence someone has died without baptism

[Col. 0736A]

*(From the decree of Pope Sixtus, chapter 5.)*

Let priests consider how great a danger it is for innocent souls to be excluded from the kingdom of God through their negligence. If there is joy in heaven over one sinner doing penance, what do you think will be the anger and indignation against the one who, through his negligence, closes the gates of paradise to the innocent?

Therefore priests must take the greatest care lest, through their negligence, they separate from heavenly blessedness the souls for whom Christ’s blood was shed. But if—God forbid—it should happen, let the one through whose neglect it occurred submit himself to severe penitential grief throughout the days of his life.

## CHAPTER XLVII — That no priest should presume to deny baptism to any sick person in his own province or elsewhere

[Col. 0736B]

*(From the decree of Pope Martin, chapter 3.)*

Any priest who, in his own province or in another, or wherever he may be found, refuses to baptize a sick person entrusted to him—whether on the pretext of intending to travel or under some other excuse—and the person consequently dies without baptism, shall be deposed.

## CHAPTER XLVIII — On those who have been rebaptized

*(From the decree of Pope Leo to Nicetas, bishop of Aquileia, chapter 47.)*

Concerning those whom your affection has likewise believed should be referred to us—those who, compelled by fear or led astray by error, have undergone baptism a second time and now recognize that they acted against the sacrament of the Catholic faith—the following moderation must be observed: they are to be received into our fellowship and restored to the unity of communion only through the remedy of penance and the laying on of the bishop’s hand.

The periods of penance are to be established according to your judgment, with due moderation, as you observe the devotion of the converts’ hearts. At the same time, consideration must be given to their advanced age and to the necessities arising from any dangers or illnesses. If anyone is so severely afflicted that, while he is still doing penance, his salvation is despaired of, he must be assisted through priestly solicitude by being granted the grace of communion.

## CHAPTER XLIX — On the case in which a sick infant is brought to any priest for baptism

*(From the decree of Pope Eugenius, chapter 6.)*

If a sick infant is brought from any parish to any priest for the sake of baptism, the [Col. 0736D] sacrament of baptism must not be denied to him. If anyone refuses to grant this gift to one who requests it, and the infant dies without the grace of baptism, let that person know that he will have to render an account for the child’s soul and will be severely corrected before a synod.

## CHAPTER L — On those who have been confirmed or baptized two or three times

*(From the Council of Tarragona, chapter 6.)*

It has been reported to us that some people from the common population have been confirmed twice or three times by bishops who were unaware that the same bishops had already confirmed them. Therefore it has seemed right to us that confirmation, like baptism, should by no means be repeated. Those baptized or confirmed twice or more are decreed to serve not the world [Col. 0737A] but the Lord alone, with the greatest devotion, under a regular or clerical habit.

## CHAPTER LI — On those who have been baptized twice unknowingly

*(From the Penitential of Theodore, chapter 14.)*

Those who have been baptized twice without knowing it do not need to do penance for this, except that according to the canons they cannot be ordained unless some great necessity compels it.

Those who have been baptized again knowingly are to do penance for seven years, as though they had crucified Christ again; they are to do penance on the fourth and sixth days of the week and during three Lents. If it was done because of some defect, they are likewise to do penance. If they thought it was required for purity, they are likewise to do penance for three years.

## CHAPTER LII — On the souls of infants who die without baptism
From a letter of Pope Gregory written to Secundinus, a servant of God confined in retreat [Col. 0737B]. At the end of your letter you asked what answer should be given to those who inquire of your affection concerning the souls of little children who die without the grace of baptism, saying: “If the body is held under original guilt, how will the soul—which is given by God and has not yet consented to the body in any actual offense—be guilty?” But concerning this matter, let your most beloved charity know that among the holy Fathers there has been no small inquiry concerning the origin of the soul: whether it descended from Adam, or whether it is given individually to each person. The question has remained uncertain, and they have acknowledged it to be insoluble in this life.

For it is a grave question, and cannot be comprehended by human beings: if the soul is born together with the flesh from Adam’s substance, why does it not also die together with the flesh? But if it is held bound by sins together with the flesh brought forth from Adam, [Col. 0737C] then, although this is uncertain, it is not uncertain that, unless a person is reborn through the sacred grace of baptism, every soul is bound by the chains of original sin.

For it is written: “No one is clean in his sight, not even an infant of a single day upon the earth.” Hence David says: “I was conceived in iniquities, and my mother bore me in sins.” Hence Truth itself says: “Unless someone is reborn of water and the Holy Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven.” Hence the Apostle Paul says: “As all die in Adam, so also all will be made alive in Christ.”

When, therefore, an infant who has committed no sin cannot be clean in the sight of almighty God, why does the Psalmist, born from a lawful marriage, say, “I was conceived in iniquity”? Why, unless because one who has not been cleansed by the water of baptism is not clean? Why does every human being die in Adam, if he is not held by the chains of original sin?

But because the human race rotted in its first parent as in a root, it raised up dryness in its branches; and from that source every human being is born with sin, from which the first human being chose to remain in sin. I ought to have spoken about these matters more subtly and at greater length; but since both the tumult of cares presses upon me and the bearer of this letter proved importunate in asking to be released, I have spoken briefly about matters on which I owed much. [Col. 0737D]

## CHAPTER LIII — Concerning Those Possessed by an Evil Spirit Who Have Been Baptized

(From the Council of Orange, chapter 13.) Those possessed by an evil spirit who concern themselves with their purification, if they entrust themselves to the care of the clergy and obey their admonitions, are by all means to receive communion: by the power of the sacrament itself they are either to be fortified against the assault of the demon by which they are afflicted, or to be cleansed, since the purification of their life is now being manifested. [Col. 0738A]

## CHAPTER LIV — Concerning Those Possessed by an Evil Spirit and Catechumens Who Are to Be Baptized

(From the same council, chapter 14.) Concerning those possessed by an evil spirit and catechumens, advice regarding baptism is to be given insofar as necessity demands or opportunity permits.

## CHAPTER LV — Concerning Those Who Have Been Rebaptized

(From the Council of Évreux, chapter 14.) The faithful and religious are not to participate in food with those who have been rebaptized.

## CHAPTER LVI — Concerning a Priest Who Rebaptizes Someone Correctly Baptized and Does Not Baptize Someone Incorrectly Baptized by Heretics

(From the Council of Lyon, chapter 47.) If a bishop or priest baptizes again someone who has baptism according to the truth, or does not baptize someone polluted by the impious and not correctly baptized, let him be deposed, as one mocking the cross and death of the Lord and failing to distinguish lawfully between true priests and false priests. [Col. 0738B]

## CHAPTER LVII — That Deacons Should Observe Their Proper Measure

(From the decree of Pope Gelasius, chapter 7.) We likewise establish that deacons are to preserve their proper measure, and we do not permit them to attempt anything beyond the scope assigned by the canons of the Fathers. They are in no way to appropriate to their ministry anything that antiquity decreed to belong properly to the higher orders. Without a bishop or priest, they are not to dare to baptize, unless extreme necessity should perhaps compel them to perform the aforesaid duties when those ministers are situated at too great a distance; this is also often permitted to Christian laypeople. [Col. 0738C]

## CHAPTER LVIII — Concerning an Unordained Person Who Presumes to Baptize as Though Ordained

(From the decree of Pope Hormisdas, chapter 4.) If anyone, being unordained, baptizes or performs any divine office through rashness, let him be expelled from the Church and never be ordained.

## CHAPTER LIX — That Priests Should Admonish the People to Present Their Infants to the Bishop for Confirmation

(From the Council of Worms, chapter 2.) Let priests announce to the people that, as soon as they can, they should have their infants presented to the bishop for confirmation. If they neglect this, both priest and people are to be subjected to canonical discipline.

## CHAPTER LX — That All of Mature Age Should Come Fasting to Confirmation

[Col. 0738D]

(From the Council of Orléans, chapter 5.) Let those of mature age come fasting to confirmation, and let them be admonished to make confession beforehand, so that they may be worthy to receive the gift of the Holy Spirit in purity; for no one will ever be a Christian unless he has been anointed with chrism in episcopal confirmation.

## CHAPTER LXI — Concerning the Two Sacraments, That Is, Baptism and the Laying On of Hands

(Pope Melchiades writes the following to the bishops of Spain, chapter 6.) Concerning the matters about which you asked to be instructed—namely, whether the sacrament of the bishops’ laying on of hands or baptism is the greater sacrament—know that both are great sacraments. And just as one is performed by those of higher rank, that is, by the supreme pontiffs, [Col. 0739A] and cannot be completed by those of lower rank, so it is to be revered and observed with greater veneration. But these two sacraments are so closely joined that they cannot in any way be separated from one another except when death intervenes; and one cannot properly be completed without the other.

## CHAPTER LXII — That All Christians Should Hasten to Confirmation

(From the Council of Worms, chapter 6.) Let all come devoutly to the bishop’s preaching and confirmation, and let them faithfully minister to him and obey him.

## CHAPTER LXIII — Likewise Concerning the Laying On of Hands

(Pope Eusebius writes to the brothers established throughout Campania and Tuscany.) The sacrament of the laying on of hands must also be held in great veneration, [Col. 0739B] since it cannot be completed by others except the supreme priests. Nor is it read or known to have been performed in the time of the apostles by anyone other than the apostles themselves; nor, as has already been said, can it ever be completed or performed by anyone other than those who occupy their place. For if it is rashly attempted otherwise, it is to be considered invalid and void, and will never be counted among the ecclesiastical sacraments.

## CHAPTER LXIV — Likewise Concerning Confirmation

(From the Council of Mainz, chapter 5.) We command that all should come diligently and devoutly to receive, through the bishop’s laying on of hands, the gift of the Holy Spirit; they are faithfully to provide their bishop with whatever is necessary, and all are to obey him in every respect.

## CHAPTER LXV — That All the Faithful, Having Received Baptism, Should Receive Chrism

[Col. 0739C]

(From the Council of Laodicea, chapter 48.) Those who are baptized ought, after the washing, to receive heavenly chrism and to be found participants in the kingdom of Christ.

## CHAPTER LXVI — That All Reborn through the Baptismal Font Should Receive the Gift of the Holy Spirit through the Laying On of Hands

(From the letter of Pope Anterus, chapter 15.) For all the faithful ought, after baptism, to receive the Holy Spirit through the laying on of the bishops’ hands, so that they may be found to be complete Christians.

From the Holy Spirit we receive the means to become spiritual, because the natural person does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God. When the Holy Spirit is poured in, the faithful heart is enlarged for prudence and steadfastness. From the Holy Spirit we receive the ability to distinguish between good and evil, to love what is just, and to reject what is unjust; to resist envy and pride; to withstand lust, various enticements, and shameful and unworthy desires. From the Holy Spirit we receive the ability, inflamed by love and the ardor of glory, to raise our mind from earthly things to heavenly and divine things. [Col. 0739D]

## CHAPTER LXVII — That Bishops Should Perform Confirmations Only While Fasting, Except in Cases of Illness

(From the Council of Meaux, chapter 6.) Let bishops, except in the case of the sick and those in danger of death, impart the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands only while fasting. Just as baptism is to be celebrated by those who are fasting at two times, namely Easter and Pentecost, [Col. 0740A] so it is fitting that the imparting of the Holy Spirit should be celebrated by pontiffs who are fasting.

## CHAPTER LXVIII — That Bishops May Confirm in the Open Country When Necessary; It Is Better, However, to Do So in a Church or Its Courtyard

(From the Council of Reims, chapter 10.) Let a bishop be permitted to confirm in the open country if necessary.

## CHAPTER LXIX — That Only Bishops Should Sign Those Who Have Been Baptized

(From the decree of Pope Innocent sent to Bishop Decentius, chapter 3.) Concerning the signing of infants, it is clear that this may be done by no one other than a bishop; for although priests are secondary priests, they do not possess the summit of the episcopate. That this belongs solely to pontiffs—that they should either sign or impart the Spirit, the Comforter—is demonstrated not only by ecclesiastical custom, but also by that passage in the Acts of the Apostles which states that Peter and John were sent so that they might impart the Holy Spirit to those already baptized.

For when priests baptize, whether outside the presence of a bishop or in the bishop’s presence, they may anoint the baptized with chrism; but it must have been consecrated by a bishop. They may not, however, sign the forehead with that same oil, since this belongs solely to bishops when they impart the Spirit, the Comforter. [Col. 0740B]

## CHAPTER LXX — That Priests Should Not Dare to Sign the Baptized on the Forehead with Chrism

(From the Registries of Gregory to Januarius, bishop of Cagliari, chapter 200.) Priests should not presume to sign baptized infants on their foreheads with chrism. Rather, priests should touch the baptized on the breast, so that bishops may afterward confirm them on the forehead.

## CHAPTER LXXI — Concerning Priests Who Demand Payments for Baptism

[Col. 0740C]

(From the letter of Pope Gelasius, chapter 5.) Let them set no prices for baptizing and signing the faithful, nor seek to harass those being reborn by imposing any kind of charge, since we are commanded to give freely what we have received freely. Therefore let them make no effort to exact anything at all from those mentioned above, lest people, deterred either by poverty or turned away by indignation, disdain to approach the means of their redemption. Let them be certain that those discovered to have committed what is forbidden, or who do not correct their offenses of their own accord, will endanger their own honor.

## CHAPTER LXXII — Concerning Priests Who Presume to Baptize with Old Chrism

[Col. 0740D]

(From the Council of Lyon, chapter 3.) If anyone attempts to baptize with chrism other than the new chrism that he has received through the generosity or authorization of his own bishop—unless death is imminent—it is clear that, through this rash undertaking, he has pronounced upon himself the sentence of his own condemnation.

## CHAPTER LXXIII — That a Priest Should Not Go among His People without Chrism

(From the Council of Vaison, chapter 5.) No priest should ever proceed among the people entrusted to him without chrism, because it has been agreed among us that a person is to be anointed with chrism once in baptism. But anyone who, because of some necessity, has not been anointed with chrism in baptism is to be perfected in the priest’s confirmation.

## CHAPTER LXXIV — Concerning a Priest Who Discovers That He Has Not Been Baptized

[Col. 0741A]

(From the Council held at Compiègne, chapter 5.) If a priest who has been ordained discovers that he has not been baptized, let him be baptized and ordained again, as well as all those whom he previously baptized.

## CHAPTER LXXV — Concerning Priests and What They Should Do on the Lord’s Supper with Chrism, Consecrated Oil, and the Oil for the Sick

(From the Council of Meaux, chapter 1.) Let a priest carry three small vessels with him on the Lord’s Supper: one for chrism, another for the oil with which catechumens are to be anointed, and a third for the sick, in accordance with the apostolic teaching: “When anyone is sick, let him summon the priests of the Church,” and so forth.

## CHAPTER LXXVI — On the Same Matter

[Col. 0741B]

(From the Council held at Valence, chapter 2.) Priests who govern diocesan churches should seek chrism before the solemnity of Easter not from just any bishops, but from their own bishop; and not through a junior cleric, but themselves or through someone of the same order.

## CHAPTER LXXVII — On the Same Matter

(From the Council of Meaux, chapter 5.) Let no bishop or any ecclesiastical minister receive any payment on account of the sacred chrism—neither money nor any small gifts—which are irregularly demanded from priests by the bishops’ ministers.

## CHAPTER LXXVIII — On the Same Matter

(From the Council of Vaison, chapter 10.) In each territory, let priests or ministers seek chrism every year from their own bishops as the Paschal solemnity approaches, not, according to their preference, from nearer bishops; nor through anyone other than themselves or deputies of the same order, since it is dishonorable to entrust the highest matters to inferiors. It is best, however, that the person who will use it in administering it should himself receive it. [Col. 0741C]

## CHAPTER LXXIX — Concerning Priests Who Usually Come to the Cities to Receive Chrism

(From the Council of Meaux, chapter 6.) Concerning priests who were accustomed to come to the cities on the Lord’s Supper to receive chrism, it has been decreed that, among those who live far away, one out of every eight or ten is to be chosen by the archdeacon to carry the chrism he has received carefully to himself and his colleagues. Those who live no more than four or five miles from the city are to come in person, as usual, to receive chrism. They are to be summoned to the city for instruction at another time, outside Lent, on account of the congregations entrusted to them. [Col. 0741D]

## CHAPTER LXXX — Concerning Chrism, Which Must Always Be Kept under Seal

(From the Council of Tours, chapter 3.) Moreover, this must be observed in every way: sacred chrism and consecrated oil must always be kept under lock, lest some unbelieving or unclean person touch that by which we are incorporated into Christ, by which all the faithful are sanctified, and by which kings and priests are anointed; or lest some treacherous person steal it to overturn the judgment of God. We have learned this through experience.

## CHAPTER LXXXI — Concerning How Jews Should Be Examined before Baptism

[Col. 0742A]

(From the Council of Agde, chapter 35.) Since the faithlessness of the Jews frequently returns to its vomit, if they wish to come to the Catholic law, let them enter the threshold of the Church among the catechumens for eight months; and if they are found to be approaching with pure faith, only then should they merit the grace of baptism. But if, by some circumstance, they incur the danger of illness within the prescribed period and are considered beyond hope, let them be baptized.

## CHAPTER LXXXII — Concerning Jews, and That No One Should Use Force to Make Them Believe

(From the Fifth Council of Toledo, chapter 57.) Concerning the Jews, the holy synod has commanded this: henceforth no one is to use force to make anyone believe. “God has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills.” For such people are not to be saved against their will, but willingly, so that the form of justice may remain intact.

Just as a human being perished by obeying the serpent through the choice of his own will, so each person is saved by believing through the conversion of his own mind when called by the grace of God. Therefore they are to be saved not by force but through the free exercise of their will, so that they may convert; they are not to be driven to do so.

But those who were compelled to become Christians long ago, as happened in the time of the most religious prince Sisenand, since it is already established that they have been joined to the divine sacraments, received the grace of baptism, been anointed with chrism, and become participants in the body and blood of the Lord, must also be compelled to hold the faith that they received by force or necessity, lest the name of the Lord be blasphemed and the faith they received be regarded as worthless and contemptible. [Col. 0742B–C]

## CHAPTER LXXXIII — That the Baptized Children of Jews Should Be Separated from Their Association

(From the same Fifth Council, chapter 60.) We decree that baptized sons and daughters of Jews are to be separated from their parents’ association, lest they become further entangled in their parents’ errors. They are to be assigned either to monasteries, to Christian men, or to women who fear God, so that under their way of life they may learn the worship of the faith and, being established in better things, progress both in conduct and in faith.

## CHAPTER LXXXIV — That There Should Be No Association between Hebrews Converted to the Christian Faith and Others Not Yet Baptized

(From the same Fifth Council, chapter 62.) Associations with evil often corrupt even the good; how much more those who are inclined toward vices? Therefore let there henceforth be no association between Hebrews converted to the Christian faith and those who still remain in the old rite, lest they be overturned through participation with them.

Whoever, therefore, from now on among those who have been baptized does not avoid the company of unbelievers is to be given to Christians, while the latter are to be assigned to public beatings. [Col. 0742D]

## CHAPTER LXXXV — Concerning Jews Who Have Apostatized

(From the same Fifth Council, chapter 59.) Many who were formerly brought over from Judaism to the Christian faith are now known to have blasphemed Christ, not only practicing Jewish rites but also carrying out the abominable act of circumcision. Concerning these, after consultation with our most pious and religious lord, King Sisenand, this holy council decreed that such transgressors, corrected by pontifical authority, are to be recalled to the worship of Christian teaching, so that those whom their own will does not reform may be restrained by priestly punishment.

Those whom they circumcised, if they are their children, are to be separated from their parents’ association; if they are slaves, they are to be given their freedom as compensation for the injury done to their bodies. [Col. 0743A]

## CHAPTER LXXXVI — Concerning the Slaves of Jews

(From the same council, chapter 9.) Likewise, if Jewish slaves who have not yet been converted flee to the grace of Christ, let them be given their freedom.

## CHAPTER LXXXVII — Concerning Jewish Slaves Who Flee to Baptism

(From the Council held at Clermont, chapter 30.) Although earlier canons have already decreed that, if pagan slaves belonging to Jews flee to the Church and ask for baptism, and likewise if they flee to any Christians, they are to be freed from their masters’ control once a fair price has been assessed and paid by the faithful, we therefore establish this so that such a just constitution may be observed by all Catholics. [Col. 0743B]

## CHAPTER LXXXVIII — Likewise Concerning Jewish Slaves, Whether Christians or Those Desiring to Come to the Christian Faith

(From the Council of Mâcon, chapter 16.) With God as our author, we decree in this present council that henceforth no Christian slave is to serve a Jew. Rather, upon payment of twelve solidi for each valuable slave, any Christian is permitted to redeem the slave, either for freedom or for service. If the slave desires to become a Christian and is not permitted to do so, the same provision is to apply; for it is sacrilegious that a blasphemer of the Christian religion should hold in bondage what the Lord Christ redeemed by the shedding of his blood.

But if any Jew refuses to comply with what we have established, then, for as long as he delays coming for the stipulated payment, the slave himself is permitted to live with Christians wherever he wishes. [Col. 0743C]

## CHAPTER LXXXIX — Concerning Those Who Desire to Come from Heresy to the Faith

(From the Council of Arles, chapter 9.) If anyone comes to the Church from heresy, let them question him concerning the Creed; and if they see that he was baptized in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, let hands alone be laid upon him, so that he may receive the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER XC — Concerning Jews Who Circumcise a Christian Slave

[Col. 0743D]

(From the council held at the village of Theognis, chapter 4.) If any Jew buys and circumcises a Christian slave, or a slave belonging to any other sect, let that slave be removed from the power of the Jew and remain free.

## CHAPTER XCI — What Saint Gregory Commanded Concerning the Jews

(From Gregory’s Registries to John, Bishop of Terracina.) Joseph, a Jew and bearer of this letter, informed us concerning a certain place where the Jews residing in the fortress of Terracina had been accustomed to gather for the celebration of their festivals. He reported that your fraternity had expelled them, and that, with your knowledge and consent, they had moved to another place for the celebration of their festivals; now they complain that they are again being expelled from that place as well.

If this is so, we wish your fraternity to refrain from such a complaint and to allow them, as was their custom, to gather in the place they obtained, as we have said, with your knowledge. For it is necessary to gather those who disagree with the Christian religion into the unity of faith by admonishing them with gentleness and kindness and persuading them, lest those whom the sweetness of preaching and the anticipated terror of the future Judge could have invited to believe be driven away by threats and terrors.

Therefore they ought to come kindly to hear the word of God from you, rather than tremble before an austerity extended beyond measure. [Col. 0744A–B]

## CHAPTER XCII — Concerning Those Who Were Baptized by Deacons because of the Danger of Death

(From the Council of Tours, chapter 3.) If a deacon governing a congregation baptizes anyone without a bishop or priest because of the danger of death, the bishop must complete them through blessing and confirmation. But if the person departs from this world beforehand, he may be just under the faith by which he believes.

## CHAPTER XCIII — Concerning Those Who Compel Priests to Pay Money for Balsam

(From the Council of Chalon, chapter 5.) Certain brothers said that it had been an ancient custom in their churches for priests to pay two or four denarii for the purchase of balsam to make chrism, or for preparing the church lights. Therefore, by unanimous agreement, we establish that, just as nothing is to be received for dedicating basilicas or conferring orders, so priests who are to receive chrism are likewise to pay nothing for the purchase of balsam or lights.

Accordingly, let bishops purchase the balsam from the resources of the Church, and let each bishop provide the lights in his own churches. [Col. 0744C]

## CHAPTER XCIV — Concerning the Cloth Used for Chrism

(From the council held at Beauvais, chapter 8.) If anyone wishes to smear the chrism cloth again and place it upon another baptized person, this is not absurd.

## CHAPTER XCV — That Catechumens Should Not Eat with the Baptized

[Col. 0744D]

(From the Council of Mainz, chapter 5.) Catechumens ought not to eat with the baptized, nor give them a kiss—how much less with a pagan?

## CHAPTER XCVI — Concerning the Scrutiny to Be Conducted

(From the Roman Council, chapter 15.) Concerning the scrutiny to be conducted, we have decreed that it should be celebrated in episcopal churches and wherever there is a gathering of the people and clergy and circumstances permit.

## CHAPTER XCVII — Concerning the Ministry of Baptism

(From the Council of Mainz, chapter 9.) The matter of the baptistery and of the catechumens has been thoroughly examined, so that priests may more fully understand how to make a Christian through fitting rites.

## CHAPTER XCVIII — That a Man Who Had One Wife before Baptism and Another after Baptism Is Called a Bigamist

[Col. 0745A]

(From the decree of Pope Innocent, chapter 52.) It is then stated that a man should not be called a bigamist if, while a catechumen, he had and lost a wife, and after baptism took another; rather, the woman joined to the new man should be regarded as his first wife. For that marriage, together with the other offenses, was washed away through the sacrament of baptism.

If this is said of only one wife, then certainly, if he had three wives while he was in the old man, the one who is fourth after baptism will be his first wife, according to that interpretation. Likewise, the woman who was taken as the fourth will receive the title “virgin.”

Who, I ask, does not see that this is contrary to the Apostle’s command, which says: “A priest must be the husband of one wife”? But it is objected that in baptism everything performed in the old man was dissolved.

Tell me—I speak with your permission—are only offenses forgiven in baptism? Or also those things that are accomplished according to the Lord’s commands and God’s ordinances? Is taking a wife an offense, or is it not an offense? If it is an offense, then, as I have said with the aforementioned pardon, the author will be at fault, since, when he joined them together in paradise so that they might commit offenses, he blessed them.

But if it is not an offense—for it would be sacrilegious to call an offense what God has joined together—and Solomon added, “For a wife is prepared for a man by God,” how can it be believed that what was completed by God’s authority was forgiven among offenses?

What is to be said about the children of such people? Are those born from the woman who was his wife before baptism not to be admitted to a share in the inheritance? Are they to be called either natural children or bastards, because there is no legitimate marriage except, as you suppose, the one contracted after baptism?

When the Lord himself was asked by the Jews whether it was lawful to dismiss one’s wife, and explained that it ought not to be done, he added: “What God has joined together, let no human being separate.” And lest it be thought that he was speaking about those acquired after baptism, let them remember that he was questioned by Jews and answered Jews.

But this is what I carefully ask: if the wife of the man who was first a catechumen and afterward a believer is one and the same, and if he had children by her while he was a catechumen and afterward had others while he was a believer, are they to be called brothers or not? After their father’s death, are the former to share with the others in the division of the inheritance, when spiritual rebirth is believed to have taken away from them the name of children? [Col. 0745B–D]

Since it is absurd to think and judge in this way, what bad reasoning is there for this to be defended and for an empty opinion to be vaunted rather than supported by some authority, when what the law commanded and God joined together cannot be counted among sins?

Suppose a catechumen devoted himself to virtues, followed humility, maintained patience, gave alms, rescued people destined for death by whatever means, abhorred adultery, and preserved chastity. I ask: if, after becoming a believer, he lost these things because baptism is thought to remove everything the old man had done, [Col. 0746A] let us consider the Gentile Cornelius, who saw a revelation through prayers and almsgiving, and Peter himself likewise saw it. Were these things taken away from him through baptism, on account of which he appears to have been granted baptism?

If this is believed, trust me, there is considerable error. For whatever has been done well and preserved according to the legal commandments cannot perish for those who performed it.

Therefore the bond of marriage, because it is completed by God’s command, cannot be called sin; and what is not sin must absolutely not be believed to have been dissolved among sins. It will consequently be sound to judge that the designation of the earlier wife cannot be erased, since what was completed by God’s will was not dismissed on account of sin.

## CHAPTER XCIX — Concerning Bishops, Priests, and Deacons Who Have Been Rebaptized

[Col. 0746B]

(From the decree of Pope Felix, chapter 1.) There is a common grief and universal lament that we have learned that even bishops, presbyters, and deacons have been rebaptized within Africa. Without doubt this matter has also come to the notice of your holiness: how the devil’s cunning raged against the Christian people in the regions of Africa and, through manifold deception, advanced to such a point that it plunged not only the unwary populace but even the priests themselves into the depths of death. No part of the world has not lamented it; no land has been unaware of it. Therefore, placed in great sorrow, we cannot conceal the peril of souls who are perishing and whose account will be demanded from us.

Accordingly, suitable treatment must be applied to such wounds, lest an untimely readiness to cure benefit those seized by a deadly plague in no way, while a calamity treated too negligently involves both the wounded and those treating them in the guilt of an illegitimate cure. First, therefore, the confession of the person coming to you and requesting a remedy must be carefully examined, as must the character of the deceived person, so that an appropriate treatment may be supplied. It must be investigated whether the person who, wishing to make satisfaction to God through repentance, rightly grieves that he has been rebaptized, joined in this crime voluntarily or approached it under compulsion. Let him know that the one who deceives himself is the one who deceives others, and that by our leniency nothing is taken away from the judgment of the exalted tribunal, before which those things are valid that are pious, true, and just.

The matter of necessity must be handled differently from that of intention. The case of the one who was perhaps enticed by payment to bring about his own ruin is worse. The enemy leaves nothing untried. To prevent him from rejoicing over his capture, those caught in the snare must be helped, and the hunter’s trap must be crushed, so that the one lamenting his fall without disguise may, through both the moderation of justice and the compassionate force of contrition, be admitted to the court from which he had departed. Let him not perhaps be ashamed or reluctant to obey during the appointed times of fasting and lamentation, or to submit to other commands of salutary discipline, because grace is given to the humble, not to the proud. Let whoever seeks to be raised up in Christ therefore lie prostrate in grief over his ruin.

Through the ministry of our administration—which it is fitting for your charity to follow, and which no one has the right either to wish or to be able to surpass—we should treat with priestly rigor and humanity the case of the person who, contrary to apostolic teaching, submitted himself to the most disastrous repetition of baptism, or of the one who has cleverly judged that his own consent should be excused by certain arguments. Thus, with the help of the Lord the judge, the faith—which, unless it is one, is already no faith at all—may be restored in them to salvation, without offense caused by our haste. For when a sinner’s satisfaction is delayed by us, his mind is found more purified for forgiveness, not without praise and joy for us.

Therefore remember that we have this judgment concerning these matters: while preserving a distinction among sinners, not all who have fallen are to be weighed on the same scale, since a greater penalty must be exacted from the one to whom the discipline of the Lord’s house has been entrusted.

To begin, then, with the highest ranks of the Church: those who are shown to have been bishops, presbyters, or deacons, and who—whether perhaps willingly or under compulsion—are clearly known to have suffered the loss of that one and saving bath, and to have stripped off Christ, whom they had put on not only through the gift of regeneration but also through the grace of their ordained dignity—for no one could have approached a second washing unless he had openly denied that he was a Christian and confessed that he was a pagan—must be judged to have committed a deed horrible even to hear or speak of. This is execrable in everyone, but much more so in bishops, presbyters, and deacons.

Yet because the same Lord and Savior is most merciful and wills that no one perish, it is fitting that, if they repent, they remain in penitence until the day of their death and in no way participate in prayer—not only with the faithful, but not even with catechumens. At the time of death, lay communion is to be restored to them. The priest’s care must investigate or carry out this matter with particular diligence in regard to baptism.

Concerning clerics and monks, maidens dedicated to God, and laypeople, we command that the following rule be observed, which the Council of Nicaea established for those who have fallen or once fell: those who, without any necessity or fear and danger of anything, impiously surrendered themselves to heretics to be rebaptized, if they nevertheless repent from the heart, are to remain three years among the hearers. For seven years they are to submit among the penitents to the hands of the priests. For two years more they are not to be admitted to the offerings in any way, but are to join the people only in prayer. They must not be ashamed to bow their necks before God, since they were not afraid to deny him.

If, however, as mortal beings, the end of life begins to press upon them within the limits of the prescribed time, help must be given to the one who implores it. Whether from the bishop who imposed the penance, or from another who can nevertheless establish that it was imposed, or similarly from a presbyter, viaticum must not be denied to one departing from this world.

But children who are still *investes*—a designation deriving from their innocence—whether clerics or laypeople, and likewise similar maidens whose age is supported by ignorance, are to be kept for a certain time under the laying on of hands, and communion is to be restored to them. Their repentance is not to be awaited, since the discipline of punishment does not seize those whom their age excuses.

We have established this so that those who have more or less time remaining in life under the stain of earthly contagion may not, while still in penance, perhaps commit further things requiring penance. If, before the appointed period of penance, someone recovers after receiving the grace of communion, having been given up by physicians or pressed by clear signs of death, we are to observe what the Nicene canons ordained: he is to be counted among those who communicate only in prayer until the period of time prescribed for him has been completed.

Nor do we pass over our catechumens who were baptized under such a profession, since the case is not different, as the same holy canons ordained, from that of one who in any way renounced Christ, whom he had once confessed. They are to remain three years among the hearers; afterward they may pray with the catechumens and receive, through the laying on of hands, the grace of Catholic communion. The sole exception is bishops, presbyters, and deacons, whom, as we have already said, we reconcile only at the time of their death.

As for the rest—that is, clerics, monks, and laypeople of either sex—who are shown to have undergone a repetition of baptism under compulsion and threats, or who claim by some contrivance that they are not bound by the guilt of this crime, we decree that they remain in penance for three years and be received into the fellowship of the sacrament through the laying on of hands. In every respect this must be observed: none of those who, at any age, have been baptized or rebaptized anywhere other than in the Catholic Church is ever to be permitted to enter the ecclesiastical service.

It should be sufficient for them that they have been received into the number of Catholics, since whoever among the bishops violates this rule will appear to bear judgment concerning his own rank and communion, as will the one who does not remove a person whom he knows to have insinuated himself from among these into the clerical ministry.

Above all, care must be taken and every precaution observed that none of our brother bishops or fellow bishops, or even presbyters, in another city or diocese receive a penitent, one placed under a priest’s hands, or one who claims to have been reconciled, without the testimony and letters of a bishop or presbyter. A presbyter in a parish, or a bishop in a city, must not receive such a person without them. If this is neglected through any concealment, the fault also touches the clerics who reside in places where this matter has been insufficiently attended to.

These matters having thus been properly arranged and communicated to your churches by our deliberation, it is fitting that you obey them. Although nothing may seem lacking for the restoration of souls, if anything new has been revealed to anyone—something that may have escaped us—let him confidently make it known, following the blessed apostle Paul, while the earlier speaker keeps silence, because the Holy Spirit breathes where he wills, especially when his own cause is being handled. We shall not be reluctant to listen, nor arrogantly reject anything that has been omitted, but shall order it reasonably.

Given on the Ides of March, in the fourth consulship of Dynamus and Sibidius.

## CHAPTER C. — Concerning one who is ordained through ignorance before being baptized

(From the sayings of Saint Isidore, bishop.) If someone is ordained before being baptized through ignorance, those baptized by him must be baptized, and he himself must not be ordained. But the Roman pontiff judges that it is not the human being who baptizes, but the Spirit of God who supplies the grace of baptism, even if the one who baptizes is a pagan.

## CHAPTER CI. — Concerning those who attempt to sell the grace of the Holy Spirit

(From the Council of Tribur, attended by King Arnulf, chapter 22.) It has been said that in certain places money is customarily given for the reception of chrism, and likewise for baptism and communion. The holy Synod detested this seed of the Simoniac heresy and anathematized it. Henceforth nothing is to be demanded for ordination, chrism, baptism, balsam, burial, or communion; rather, the gifts of Christ are to be given freely, through a free administration.

**END OF BOOK FOUR.**

# BOOK FIVE

## TABLE OF CHAPTERS OF BOOK FIVE

[Column 0749A] I. That every crime is removed by sacrifices offered to God, and what ought to be used in sacrifices and what rejected.  
II. That neither pure water nor pure wine ought to be offered in the Eucharist.  
III. That bread and wine mixed with water be offered in the sacrifice.  
IV. That nothing else be offered in the sacrifice except bread and wine mixed with water.  
V. Concerning the Lord’s passion, to be mingled in the consecration of the body.  
VI. What kinds of offerings are to be brought to the altar not for sacrifice but for simple blessing.  
VII. The same matter.  
VIII. Nothing is to be offered in the sacrifice except what the Lord ordained.  
IX. That presbyters have a clean vessel in which the Lord’s body may be carefully stored.  
X. That the presbyter have the Eucharist ready at hand.

[Column 0749C] XI. As many offerings as suffice for the people are to be offered and none reserved for the next day.  
XII. Offerings are to be renewed from Saturday to Saturday.  
XIII. That, in the presence and at the command of the presbyter, the deacon give communion to the people.  
XIV. That great discernment must be exercised in receiving the Lord’s body and blood.
