# BURCHARD, BISHOP OF THE CHURCH OF WORMS: DECRETALS, BOOK FIVE, CONCERNING THE SACRAMENT OF THE LORD’S BODY AND BLOOD

[Column 0751]

## SUMMARY OF THE BOOK

[Column 0751A]

This book treats with complete thoroughness everything pertaining to the sacrament of the Eucharist, so that you will seek nothing further concerning this subject.

## CHAPTER I. — That every crime is removed by sacrifices offered to God, and what ought to be used in sacrifices and what rejected

(From the decrees of Pope Julius sent to the bishops throughout Egypt.) Since every crime and sin is removed by sacrifices offered to God, what will henceforth be given to the Lord for the expiation of offenses when an error is made in the very offering of the sacrifice? For we have heard that some, seized by schismatic ambition, contrary to divine ordinances and apostolic institutions, consecrate milk instead of wine in the divine sacrifices. Others present to the people a dipped Eucharist as a completion of communion. Some offer in the sacrament of the Lord’s chalice wine that has not been pressed, but give communion to the people with grapes that have been offered. Others preserve throughout the entire year a linen cloth dipped in must, and at the time of the sacrifice wash part of it with water and offer it in this manner.

How contrary this is to evangelical and apostolic teaching, and how opposed to ecclesiastical custom, can readily be proved from the very source of truth from which the ordered mysteries of the sacraments themselves proceeded. For when the Teacher of Truth commended the true sacrifice of our salvation to his disciples, we know that he gave them not milk but only bread and the chalice under this sacrament. It is written in the evangelical truth: “Jesus took bread and the chalice, and, blessing it, gave it to his disciples.”

Let milk therefore cease to be offered in sacrifice, since the clear and evident example of evangelical truth has shone forth: nothing may be offered except bread and wine. As for those who give the people a dipped Eucharist as a completion of communion, they have not received this from any testimony brought forth from the Gospel, where he commended his body and blood to the apostles. The commendation of the bread and of the chalice is recorded separately. For we do not read that Christ gave dipped bread to anyone else, except only to that disciple whom the dipped morsel from the Teacher revealed as the betrayer—not that it signified the institution of this sacrament.

As for giving the people communion from a pressed cluster—that is, from grains of grapes—this is altogether confused. But if necessary, the cluster should be pressed into the chalice and mixed with water, because the Lord’s chalice, according to canonical instruction, ought to be offered mixed with wine and water. For we see the people signified by the water, while the blood of Christ is shown in the wine. Therefore, when water is mixed with wine in the chalice, the people are united to Christ, and the multitude of believers is joined and attached to the one in whom it has believed.

This union and joining of water and wine is so mixed in the Lord’s chalice that the mixture cannot be separated. For if someone offers wine alone, the blood of Christ begins to be without us; but if there is water alone, the people begin to be without Christ. Therefore, when the cluster alone is offered, in which only the power of wine is represented, the sacrament of our salvation—which is signified through the water—is neglected.

The Lord’s chalice cannot be water alone or wine alone unless both are mixed together. And therefore, since from this matter there has already flowed a very extensive and manifold judgment of our predecessors, every such error and presumption must henceforth cease, lest the disorderly structure of the perverse weaken the established truth.

Therefore from now on no one shall be permitted to offer anything else in the divine rites except, according to the judgment of the ancient councils, only bread and a chalice mixed with wine and water. Whoever thereafter acts otherwise than has been commanded shall cease from offering sacrifice until, corrected through a lawful satisfaction of penance, he returns to the duty of his rank, which he lost.

## CHAPTER II. — That neither pure water nor pure wine ought to be offered in the Eucharist

(From the Council of Worms, chapter 2.) In the Eucharist pure water ought not to be offered, as some are misled for the sake of sobriety, but wine mixed with water. For there was also wine in the mystery of our redemption, when he says, “I shall not drink of this fruit of the vine,” and wine mixed with water was what he gave after the supper. But water flowing with blood from his side showed wine pressed from the true vine of his flesh, together with water.

When, therefore, the Teacher of Truth commended the true sacrifice of our salvation to his disciples, we know that he supplied them under this sacrament with bread alone and the chalice. Therefore nothing else ought to be offered except bread and wine mixed with water. The Lord’s chalice ought to be offered mixed with wine and water, because we see the people signified in the water, while the blood of Christ is shown in the wine.

Therefore, when water is mixed with wine in the chalice, the people are united to Christ, and the multitude of believers is joined and attached to the one in whom it has believed. This union and joining of water and wine is so mixed in the Lord’s chalice that the mixture cannot be separated. For if someone offers wine alone, the blood of Christ begins to be without us; but if there is water alone, the people begin to be without Christ. The Lord’s chalice cannot be water alone or wine alone unless both are mixed together.

## CHAPTER III. — That bread and wine mixed with water be offered in the sacrifice

(From the Council of Carthage, chapter 23.) In the sacraments of the Lord’s body and blood nothing more is to be offered than what the Lord himself says, namely, bread and wine mixed with water. Nor is anything more to be offered among the first fruits than wine and grain.

## CHAPTER IV. — That nothing else be offered in the sacrifice except bread and wine mixed with water

(From the African Council, chapter 4.) In the sacraments of the Lord’s body and blood nothing more is to be offered than what the Lord himself handed down, namely, bread and wine mixed with water. As for the first fruits, such as honey and milk, which are customarily offered on one especially solemn day in the mystery concerning infants: although they are offered at the altar, they are nevertheless to have their own blessing, so that they may be distinguished from the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood. Nothing more is to be offered among the first fruits than what comes from grapes and grain.

## CHAPTER V. — Concerning the Lord’s passion, to be mingled in the consecration of the body

(From the decree of Pope Alexander, chapter 5.) In the offerings of the sacraments that are presented to the Lord during the solemn celebrations of Mass, the Lord’s passion must also be mingled, so that the passion of the one whose body and blood are effected may be celebrated. Thus, after superstitious opinions have been rejected, only bread and wine mixed with water are to be offered in the sacrifice.

For, as we have received from the Fathers and as reason itself teaches, neither wine alone nor water alone ought to be offered in the Lord’s chalice, but both mixed together, because both are read to have flowed from his side in his passion.

Truth itself instructed us to offer the chalice and bread in the sacrament when it said: “Jesus took bread and blessed it, and gave it to his disciples, saying: ‘Take and eat; this is my body, which will be given for you.’” Likewise, after he had supped, he took the chalice and gave it to his disciples, saying: “Take and drink from it, all of you, for this is the chalice of my blood, which will be poured out for you for the forgiveness of sins.”

For crimes and sins are erased by these sacrifices offered to the Lord. Therefore his passion, by which we were redeemed, must also be commemorated in them and recited again and again, and these offerings must be presented to the Lord. The Lord will delight in and be appeased by such sacrifices, and he will forgive great sins.

Nothing in the sacrifices can be greater than the body and blood of Christ, nor is any offering superior to this; rather, this surpasses them all. It is to be offered to the Lord with a pure conscience, completed with a pure mind, and revered by everyone. And just as it is superior to the rest, so it must be cultivated and venerated above the rest.

## CHAPTER VI. — What kinds of offerings are to be brought to the altar not for sacrifice but for simple blessing

(From the Apostolic Canons, chapter 4.) Nothing may be offered at the altar except new ears of grain, grapes, and oil for the lamps, and beans and incense for burning, at the time when the holy offering is celebrated.

## CHAPTER VII. — The same matter

(From the decree of Pope Melchiades, chapter 1.) These kinds of things, which according to the constitution of the apostles and their successors may not be offered upon the altar, are to be brought to the priests’ house, blessed by the priests, and, after being blessed with a simple blessing, consumed by the people. Only beans and grapes, new ears of grain, oil, fragrances for incense, and the other things that the apostles established are to be offered upon the altar.

## CHAPTER VIII. — Nothing in the sacrifice except what the Lord ordained is to be offered

(From the Apostolic Canons, chapter 3.) If any bishop or presbyter offers something else in the sacrifice upon the altar besides what the Lord ordained—that is, honey, milk, strong drink instead of wine, prepared foods, birds, animals, or legumes—acting contrary to the Lord’s ordinance, he is to be deposed.

## CHAPTER IX. — That presbyters have a clean vessel in which the Lord’s body may be carefully stored

(From the Council of Tours, chapter 4.) Every presbyter is to have a pyx, or a vessel worthy of so great a sacrament, in which the Lord’s body may be carefully stored as viaticum for those departing from this world. This sacred offering must be dipped in Christ’s blood, so that the presbyter may truly say to the sick person, “May the body and blood of the Lord benefit you,” and so forth.

It must always be kept locked upon the altar because of mice and wicked people. It must also be changed from the seventh day to the seventh day: that is, the presbyter is to consume the former, and another, consecrated on that same day, is to be put in its place, lest, if kept too long, it become moldy, God forbid.

## CHAPTER X. — That the presbyter have the Eucharist ready at hand

(From the Council of Worms, chapter 5.) The presbyter is always to have the Eucharist prepared, so that whenever anyone becomes ill, or a sick child is present, he may immediately give that person communion, lest he die without communion.

## CHAPTER XI. — As many offerings as suffice for the people are to be offered and none reserved for the next day

(From the letter of Pope Clement, chapter 28.) Certainly as many holocausts are to be offered upon the altar as should suffice for the people. If anything remains, it is not to be kept for the next day, but must be consumed with fear and trembling through the diligence of the clergy.

Those who consume the remnants of the Lord’s body that have been left in the sanctuary must not immediately proceed to take ordinary food, nor suppose that they should mix with the holy portion food which, digested through the intestines, is discharged into the privy. If, therefore, the Lord’s portion is distributed in the morning, the ministers who have consumed it are to fast until the sixth hour. If they receive it at the third or fourth hour, they are to fast until evening. Thus, through secret sanctification, the eternal sacraments are to be guarded.

## CHAPTER XII. — Offerings are to be renewed from Saturday to Saturday

(From the Council of Orléans, chapter 4.) This also appears necessary to add: the offerings that are made upon the altar are always to be renewed from Saturday to Saturday. For the bread of the Presence that was placed upon the Lord’s table was always changed from Saturday to Saturday, lest, kept for too long, it become moldy and, as some violently insist, be burned by fire. If anyone, instigated by the devil, presumes to do this, let him be anathema.

## CHAPTER XIII. — That, in the presence and at the command of the presbyter, the deacon give communion to the people

(From the Council of Carthage, chapter 38.) If necessity compels it, the deacon, in the presence of the presbyter and when ordered, is to distribute the Eucharist of Christ’s body to the people.

## CHAPTER XIV. — That great discernment must be exercised in receiving the Lord’s body and blood

(From the letter of Pope Clement, chapter 32.) Great discernment must be exercised in receiving the Lord’s body and blood. Care must be taken lest, if it is delayed for too long, this prove harmful to the soul, since the Lord says: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves.”

If it is received indiscriminately, however, we must fear what the Apostle says: “Whoever eats and drinks the body and blood of the Lord unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself.” According to the same apostle’s word, a person ought to test himself and then eat of that bread and drink of the chalice. He should abstain for several days from the works of the flesh, purify his body and soul, and prepare himself to receive so great a sacrament, following the example of David, who, unless he had confessed that he had abstained from marital relations from yesterday and the day before, would by no means have received the bread of the Presence from the priest.

## CHAPTER XV. — Concerning daily reception of the Eucharist

(From the sayings of Augustine.) I neither praise nor condemn receiving communion of the Eucharist every day. Nevertheless, I urge that communion be received every Sunday. If, however, there is fear and an inclination toward sin, I say that a person is burdened more by receiving the Eucharist than purified by it.

Therefore, although someone may be stung by sin and no longer have the will to sin, if he makes satisfaction through tears and prayers, he may approach the Eucharist confidently in reliance upon the Lord’s mercy, without fear or anxiety. But I say this concerning one who is not burdened by mortal sins.

## CHAPTER XVI. — The same matter

(From the sayings of the same author to Januarius.) Someone may say that the Eucharist ought not to be received every day, while another insists that it should be received daily. Let each person do what he piously believes ought to be done according to his faith.

For Zacchaeus and that centurion did not quarrel with one another, nor did either put himself above the other: one of them joyfully received the Lord into his house, while the other said, “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof.” Both honored the Savior, although not in the same manner; both were wretched because of sins, and both obtained mercy. This serves to show that a great matter took on its own meaning in each person’s mouth according to his own intention.

## CHAPTER XVII. — Laypeople are to receive communion at least three times a year

(From the letter of Pope Fabius, chapter 4.) If they do not do so more frequently, laypeople are at least to receive communion three times a year, unless someone is prevented by some especially serious crime: namely, at Easter, Pentecost, and the Nativity of the Lord.

## CHAPTER XVIII. — Whether one who always sins ought always to receive the Eucharist

(From the sayings of Cyprian and other holy Fathers.) Saint Cyprian said: “The Eucharist is received daily as food for salvation.”

Saint Ambrose said: “If, whenever it is poured out, Christ’s blood is poured out for the forgiveness of sins, I ought always to receive it, since I always sin; I ought always to have the medicine.”

Saint Hilary, bishop, said: “If someone’s sins are not so great that he should be excommunicated, he ought not to separate himself from the medicine of the Lord’s body. Therefore we must fear that one who has long been kept away from Christ’s body may remain alienated from salvation. For it is clear that those who touch his body live, since the Lord himself says: ‘Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves.’ Let the one who has now ceased from sinning not cease from receiving communion.”

## CHAPTER XIX. — That the faithful are to receive communion every Sunday in Lent

(From the sayings of Pope Silverius, chapter 3.) On every Sunday in Lent, except those who have been excommunicated and those who are undergoing public penance, the sacraments of Christ’s body and blood are to be received. On the Lord’s Supper, at the Paschal Vigil, on the day of the Lord’s Resurrection, at Pentecost, and at the Nativity of the Lord, everyone must receive communion without exception.

## CHAPTER XX. — That reception of the Eucharist not be neglected on the Lord’s Supper

(From the decree of Pope Soter, chapter 5.) Some neglect receiving the Eucharist on the Lord’s Supper. Ecclesiastical practice demonstrates that it is to be received on that same day by all the faithful, except those to whom it has been forbidden on account of serious crimes, since even penitents are reconciled on that day in order to receive the sacraments of the Lord’s body and blood.

## CHAPTER XXI. — Concerning actors and magicians: whether they ought to receive communion with the other faithful

(From the letter of Saint Cyprian, bishop, to Eucratius.) Cyprian sends greetings to his fellow brother Eucratius.

Because of your affection and respect, dearest brother, you thought me worthy to be consulted about the actor and magician who has been established among you and still persists in the disgrace of his profession. As a teacher and instructor of boys who are to be trained—or rather ruined—he communicates to others what he has wrongly learned. You ask whether such a man ought to be given holy communion with the other Christians, or whether he should communicate with us.

I think it is contrary both to the divine majesty and to evangelical discipline that the modesty and honor of the Church should be defiled by so disgraceful and infamous a contamination.

## CHAPTER XXII. — How long each person ought to abstain from his wife before holy communion

(From the Council of Elvira, chapter 3.) Every man ought to abstain from his own wife for three, five, or seven days before holy communion.

## CHAPTER XXIII. — That one who does not receive communion at Easter, Pentecost, and the Nativity of the Lord is not to be counted among Catholics

(From the canon of Agde.) Laypeople who do not receive communion at the Nativity of the Lord, Easter, and Pentecost are not to be considered Catholics, nor are they to be counted among Catholics.

## CHAPTER XXIV. — That the altar offering be made every Sunday

(From the decree of Pope Fabius, chapter 5.) We decree that every Sunday an altar offering be made by all men and women, both of bread and of wine, so that through these offerings they may be freed from the burdens of their sins.

## CHAPTER XXV. — The same matter

(From the decree of the same author, chapter 10.) The Christian people must also be continually admonished to make an offering and peace in the Church, because the offering itself is a great remedy for souls, for oneself and one’s own people, and in that peace true unanimity and harmony are displayed.

## CHAPTER XXVI. — Concerning deacons: that they ought not to give communion to presbyters

(From the Council of Nicaea, chapter 18.) It has come to the attention of the great and holy council that in certain places and cities deacons give the grace of holy communion to presbyters. Neither rule nor custom has handed this down: those who do not have the power to offer should not give Christ’s body to those who do offer.

It has also become known that some deacons touch the sacred offerings before the bishops. Let all these practices therefore be cut away, and let the deacons remain within their proper measure, knowing that they are ministers of the bishops but are to be regarded as inferior to presbyters.

Throughout the world, therefore, they are to receive the grace of holy communion after the presbyters, with either the bishop or the presbyter presenting it to them. Nor is it lawful for deacons to sit among the presbyters, because if this is done, it is shown to be contrary to rule and order. If anyone, even after these definitions, refuses to obey, he must cease from the ministry.

## CHAPTER XXVII. — Concerning the blessings to be given to the people by presbyters

(From the decree of Pope Pius, chapter 4.) From the offerings brought by the people that remain after the consecration, or from the loaves that the faithful bring to the Church, or indeed from their own supplies, the presbyter is suitably to have portions cut and kept in a clean vessel. After the solemn celebrations of Mass, those who were not prepared to receive communion are to receive blessings from this every Sunday and on feast days. Beforehand, the presbyter must bless what he is going to give as blessings, using these words:

## CHAPTER XXVIII. — Simple prayer for the blessing

[Column 0758A]

Holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, deign to bless this bread with your holy and spiritual blessing, so that it may be salvation of mind and body for all, and a protection against every disease and all the snares of the enemies. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, the bread of life, who descended from heaven and gives life and salvation to the world, and lives and reigns with you. Through him, etc.

## CHAPTER XXIX. — Concerning the bread that is to be offered

(From the decree of Pope Anitius, chapter 3.) The loaves that you offer to God as a sacrifice are to be made either by yourselves or by your servants, cleanly and carefully, in your presence. It must be diligently observed that the bread, wine, and water without which Masses cannot be celebrated are handled with the utmost cleanliness and care, and that nothing cheap or unapproved is found in them, in accordance with what Scripture says: “Let the fear of the Lord be with you, and do everything diligently.”

## CHAPTER XXX. — Concerning presbyters who give the Lord’s body to women to carry to the sick
(From the Council of Reims, chapter 2.) It has come to our attention that certain presbyters hold the divine mysteries in such contempt that they hand over the sacred body of the Lord to a layman or a woman to carry to the sick; and to those who are forbidden to enter the sanctuary or approach the altar, the Holy of Holies is entrusted. How horrible and detestable this is, every religious person’s prudence recognizes. [Col. 0758C] Therefore the synod entirely forbids such rash presumption from occurring any further; rather, in every case, the presbyter himself is to give Communion to the sick person. If he acts otherwise, he shall be liable to the danger of his rank.

### CHAPTER XXXI — That the Eucharist is not to be given to the dead

(From the Council of Carthage, chapter 6.) It was likewise decided that the Eucharist is not to be given to the bodies of the dead. For it is written: “Take and eat.” Corpses, however, can neither take nor eat; and let not the negligence of presbyters now cause dead persons to be baptized.

### CHAPTER XXXII — That offerings on the greater festivals are to be made equally by all

[Col. 0758D] (From the Council of Mâcon, chapter 50.) In the Synod of Mâcon it was decreed that on all Sundays and on the other festivals, an offering should be presented in the church by everyone who had assembled for Mass, men and women alike, each presenting a single offering. When Mass was finished, they were to receive the offerings from the presbyter. Whoever should presume, through disobedience, to render this decree void shall be struck with anathema.

### CHAPTER XXXIII — That only the ministers of the altar may receive Communion at the altar

(From the Council of Laodicea, chapter 19.) Only ministers dedicated to the sacred order may approach the altar and receive Communion.

### CHAPTER XXXIV — That no one ordained below the presbyterate may hand to another anything consecrated by a presbyter

[Col. 0759A]

(From the decree of Pope Sylvester, chapter 7.) No acolyte or subdeacon is thereafter to hand to others anything consecrated by a presbyter, because a minister and an attendant are different things; unless he merely carries what the priest has placed upon him and blessed with his own mouth.

### CHAPTER XXXV — Concerning those who receive the Sacrifice after having tasted some food

(From the decree of Pope Eutychian, chapter 2.) Whoever receives the Sacrifice after food or after some very slight refreshment—unless it is as viaticum—is to do penance: children for three days, adults for seven, and clerics for twenty days.

### CHAPTER XXXVI — That an unlearned presbyter ought not to celebrate Mass

[Col. 0759B] (From the decree of Pope Fabian, chapter 10.) The Sacrifice is not to be received from the hand of a priest who is unable to perform the prayers, readings, and the other observances in the Mass according to the rite. [The manuscript has *postte* for *potest*, “is able.”]

### CHAPTER XXXVII — That one offering is not to be despised on account of another

(Chapter 17 of Pope Eugenius.) A presbyter must not despise one person’s offering because of another’s.

### CHAPTER XXXVIII — That the offerings of dissenting brethren are not to be received

(From the African Council, chapter 93.) The offerings of dissenting brethren are not to be received either in the sanctuary or in the treasury.

### CHAPTER XXXIX — That the gifts of those who oppress the poor are to be rejected

[Col. 0759C] (From the same council, chapter 94.) The gifts of those who oppress the poor are to be rejected by priests.

### CHAPTER XL — Concerning presbyters who sacrifice

(From the Council of Ancyra, chapter 1.) Presbyters who sacrificed and then again entered the contest, if they did this not through any pretense but in truth, and had not previously pretended, contrived, and persuaded others that they were being subjected to tortures, while being subjected to them only in appearance and dress, were permitted to retain the honor of their own rank. They may not, however, offer, address the people, or perform any priestly functions whatsoever.

### CHAPTER XLI — On the same matter

(From the same council, chapter 12.) Likewise, deacons who have sacrificed are to retain their honor, but must cease from every sacred mystery, whether offering the bread or the chalice, or preaching. If certain bishops are aware of their labor, humility, and gentleness, and wish to grant or remove something further from them, the authority shall rest with those bishops.

### CHAPTER XLII — Concerning presbyters from whom semen often flows during sleep

(Question of Augustine, apostle of the English.) After the pollution that commonly occurs in a dream, may anyone receive the body of the Lord? Or, if he is a priest, may he celebrate the sacred mysteries?

### CHAPTER XLIII — On the same matter

(Reply of Gregory.) The Old Testament, as we already said in the preceding chapter, declares such a person polluted; unless he has been washed with water, he is not permitted to enter the Church until evening. The spiritual people, however, understanding this in another way, will receive it according to the meaning we have stated: the person is, as it were, deceived in a dream when, having been tempted by impurity, he is defiled in thought by true images. But he must be washed with water, so that he may cleanse the sins of his thought with tears; and unless the fire of temptation has first withdrawn, he should recognize himself as guilty, as it were, until evening.

Yet in this same kind of pollution a very necessary discernment is required, and the cause from which it arises must be carefully considered in the mind of the sleeper. For sometimes it results from overeating, sometimes from an excess or weakness of nature, and sometimes from thought. When it occurs through an excess or weakness of nature, this pollution is in no way to be feared; for the mind, which has suffered it unknowingly, is rather to be pitied than blamed for having caused it.

But when the appetite for food is carried beyond measure in taking nourishment, and the receptacles of the bodily fluids are consequently burdened, the mind bears some guilt—not, however, to the point of being forbidden to receive Christ’s body or celebrate the solemnities of Mass, especially when a feast day requires it or necessity compels him to provide the mystery because another priest is absent from the place. In that case, he may sing the Mass after changing his clothes.

If others are present who are able to perform the mystery, pollution caused by overeating ought not to prevent reception of the sacred mystery; but, as I think, he should humbly abstain from offering the sacred mystery, provided that the pollution has not disturbed the sleeper’s mind with a shameful image. For there are some in whom such pollution commonly arises without their mind, even while their body lies in sleep, being defiled by shameful images.

In this matter one thing is shown: the mind itself is not guilty, yet is not free according to its own judgment. Although, while the body slept, it remembers having seen nothing, during bodily wakefulness it remembers having fallen into gluttony.

But if the pollution of the sleeper arises from a shameful thought entertained while awake, the mind’s guilt is evident. It sees from what root that defilement proceeded: what he knowingly thought, he unknowingly suffered. Because of such pollution, he ought to abstain from the sacred mystery on that day.

But one must consider whether the thought fell into suggestion, pleasure, or—what is more serious—consent to sin. For every sin is completed in three ways: by suggestion, pleasure, and consent. Suggestion comes through the devil, pleasure through the flesh, and consent through the spirit. Thus the serpent suggested the first fault; Eve, like the flesh, took pleasure in it; and Adam, like the spirit, consented.

Great discernment is necessary between suggestion and pleasure, and between pleasure and consent, with the mind presiding as its own judge. When the evil spirit suggests sin to the mind, if no pleasure in sin follows, no sin has been committed at all. But when the flesh begins to take pleasure, sin begins to be born; and if the mind also consents deliberately, then sin is understood to have been completed.

Thus, in the suggestion of sin, if the mind is in pleasure, there is nourishment; in consent, completion. It often happens that what the evil spirit sows in thought, the flesh draws toward pleasure, yet the mind does not consent to that pleasure. Although the flesh cannot take pleasure without the mind, the mind itself, resisting the pleasures of the flesh, is nevertheless bound in some way against its will by carnal pleasure, so that it contradicts it by reason and does not consent, yet remains bound by pleasure and deeply laments that it is bound.

Hence that outstanding soldier, trained by heaven, lamented, saying: “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin which is in my members.” If he was captive, he was surely not fighting. Therefore he was both captive and fighting: the law that is in his members was resisting the law of his mind. But if he was fighting, he was not captive. Thus, so to speak, a person is both captive and free: free through righteousness, captive through the pleasure he bears against his will.

### CHAPTER XLIV — Concerning rural presbyters, whether they may dare to offer in the city

(From the Council of Neocaesarea, chapter 13.) Rural presbyters may not offer in the church of a city when the bishop or the city’s own presbyters are present; nor may they give the consecrated bread or present the chalice. If those men are absent and the rural presbyters are summoned to give the prayer, they alone may do so.

### CHAPTER XLV — On the same matter

(From the decree of Pope Soter, chapter 13.) Presbyters who are not fellow clergy may not offer in churches when the bishops or presbyters of the city are present, nor may they give the bread; in the prayer, however, they may give the chalice. If the priests of the city are absent and the presbyters have been invited to the prayer, they alone may do so.

### CHAPTER XLVI — Concerning those who vomit the Eucharist because of drunkenness

(From the Penitential of Bede.) If someone vomits the Eucharist through drunkenness or gluttony, he is to do penance for forty days. Clerics, monks, or deacons are to do penance for forty days; presbyters for seventy; bishops for ninety. If he vomits it because of illness, he is to do penance for seven days.

### CHAPTER XLVII — If anything drips from the chalice of the sacred Blood

(From the decree of Pope Pius, chapter 3.) If something drips from the chalice onto the ground through negligence, it is to be licked up, and the board is to be scraped. If there is no board, the place is to be scraped so that it will not be trodden upon, and the scraped material is to be consumed in fire; the ashes are to be placed beneath the altar, and the priest is to do penance for forty days.

If the chalice spills upon the altar, the minister is to suck up the drop and do penance for three days. If a drop passes through the altar cloth to another surface, he is to do penance for four days; if it reaches a third surface, for nine days; if a fourth, for fifteen days. The linens that touched the drop are to be washed three times by the minister, with the chalice placed beneath them; the water used for the washing is to be consumed and deposited beside the altar.

### CHAPTER XLVIII — Concerning one who vomits the Sacrifice and whose vomit is consumed by dogs

[Col. 0762A]

(From the Penitential of Theodore.) Whoever vomits the Sacrifice and it is consumed by dogs is to do penance for one year; otherwise, he is to do penance for forty days. If he vomits the Sacrifice on the day when he received Communion, then, if it occurs before midnight, he is to perform three fasts; after midnight, two; after Matins, one.

### CHAPTER XLIX — On the same matter

(From the Roman Penitential.) If he vomits the Sacrifice, he is to do penance for forty days. If it is because of illness, seven days. If he throws it into the fire, he is to sing one hundred psalms. If dogs lick such vomit, the one who vomited it is to do penance for one hundred days.

### CHAPTER L — Concerning an aged Eucharist

[Col. 0762B]

(From the Council of Orléans, chapter 5.) Every Sacrifice spoiled by filthy age is to be burned in fire, and the ashes are to be buried beside the altar.

### CHAPTER LI — Concerning those who have not carefully guarded the body and blood of the Lord

(From the same council, chapter 6.) Whoever does not carefully guard the Sacrifice, and a mouse or some other animal eats it, is to do penance for forty days. Whoever loses it in the church, or if part of it falls and is not found, is to do penance for twenty days.

Whoever spills something from the chalice onto the altar while it is being offered is to do penance for six days, or, if the spill is greater, for seven days. Whoever spills the chalice while the solemnity of Mass is being celebrated is to do penance for forty days. If, after Mass has been celebrated, the presbyter negligently fails to consume the Sacrifice, he is likewise to do penance for forty days; and whoever receives the Sacrifice while polluted by nocturnal emission is to do penance for seven days.

A deacon who forgets to offer the offering until the cloth is spread, when the names of the departed are recited, is likewise to do penance. Whoever shows negligence toward the Sacrifice, so that it is consumed by worms and reduced to nothing, is to do penance for three Lents on bread and water. If it is found intact, the worm is to be burned within it and the ashes placed beneath the altar; the negligent person is to make satisfaction for his negligence by four-day periods. If the Sacrifice loses its color together with its flavor, twenty days are to be completed in fasting; if it has clotted, the person who immersed it is to do penance for seven days.

### CHAPTER LII — On the same matter

(From the Roman Penitential.) If the Sacrifice falls from the hands of the person offering it onto the ground and is not found, everything whatsoever that is found in the place where it fell is to be burned, and the ashes are to be concealed as above; the person to whom this happened is to do penance for half a year.

If the Sacrifice is found, the place is to be cleaned with brooms, and the straw is to be burned as above; the ashes are to be stored as above, and the priest is to do penance for twenty days.

### CHAPTER LIII — Concerning a woman who has given birth, and whether she may receive Communion if she wishes

(From the Council of Carthage.) A woman who has given birth may receive Communion if she wishes.

[Col. 0761] END OF THE FIFTH BOOK.
