BURCHARD, BISHOP OF THE CHURCH OF WORMS, DECRETALS, BOOK SIX: ON HOMICIDES

[Col. 0763]

## SUMMARY OF THE BOOK

[Col. 0763D]

This book treats of homicides committed voluntarily and involuntarily, of parricides, of fratricides, of those who kill their lawful wives and their lords, and of the slaughter of members of the clergy; it shows what penance is to be imposed for each of these kinds of homicide.

### CHAPTER 1 — If anyone commits homicide voluntarily, what penance he ought to receive according to the decrees of Pope Melchiades and the statutes of the Council of Tribur

(From the Council of Tribur, chapter 4.) First, he is not to have permission to enter the church; for the next forty days he is to walk barefoot and use no vehicle. He is to wear woolen clothing without undergarments, carry no weapons, and during these forty days take nothing except bread and salt, and drink only pure water.

Before the forty days have been completed, he is to have no communion in food or drink with the other Christians or with any other penitent. No one else is to eat from the food he takes.

After consideration of the person’s status or illness, some mercy may be granted, as seems appropriate, in the form of fruit, vegetables, or legumes—especially if someone committed homicide under compulsion and not voluntarily. Canonical authority is also to forbid him absolutely from having intercourse with any woman during these days, from approaching his own wife, or from sleeping with any man.

He is to remain near the church, weeping over his sins before its doors by day and night. He is not to go from place to place, but remain in one place throughout these forty days. If he happens to have enemies lying in wait for his life, his penance is to be postponed until the bishop has obtained peace for him from his enemies. If he is held by illness so that he cannot do penance worthily, the penance is to be postponed until he is restored to health.

If he is held by a prolonged illness, it shall belong to the bishop’s judgment to determine how he should arrange the healing of the guilty and sick man. When the forty days are completed, he is to wash, receive clothing and shoes, and cut his hair.

### CHAPTER 2 — What he ought to observe in the first year

(From the same council, chapter 5.) In the first year, after the forty days, throughout that entire year he is to abstain from wine, mead, and honeyed beer; from meat, cheese, and fatty fish—except on the feast days celebrated in that bishopric by the whole people.

Unless he is on a long journey, on campaign, detained for a long time at the lord’s court, or prevented by illness, he may redeem Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday by one denarius, or the value of one denarius, or by feeding three poor persons—provided that he uses only one of these three means. Once he has returned home or been restored to health, he is to have no permission to redeem these days.

When the year has been completed, he is to be brought into the church and granted the kiss of peace.

### CHAPTER 3 — What he ought to observe in the second and third years

(From the same council, chapter 6.) In the second and third years he is likewise to fast, except that he has the power to redeem Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday at the aforesaid price wherever he may be. In all other respects he is carefully to observe everything as in the first year.

### CHAPTER 4 — What he ought to observe in the remaining four years

(From the same council, chapter 7.) Four years then remain, during each of which he is to fast for three Lents. He is to observe one before Easter with the other Christians, abstaining from wine, mead, honeyed beer, meat, fat, eggs, and fatty fish.

He is to observe another before the Nativity of Saint John. If anything remains of the forty days, he is to complete them after the Mass of Saint John. He is to fast for the third before the Nativity of the Lord, as stated above.

During the four years mentioned above, he may eat whatever he wishes on Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday; he may redeem Monday and Wednesday at the price already stated; but he is to observe Friday absolutely on bread and water and may not redeem it in any way. When these requirements have been completed, he is to receive holy Communion.

### CHAPTER 5 — Concerning homicides and accusations against bishops and the other orders

(From the council held at Theodone’s estate, chapter 3.) At the council held at Theodone’s estate, where thirty-two bishops were present—Histolphus, archbishop of Mainz, with his suffragans; Hetti, archbishop of Trier, with his suffragans; Ebo, archbishop of Reims, with his suffragans; together with envoys of the other bishops of Gaul and Germany—because of the excessive presumption of certain tyrants who raged against the priests of the Lord, and because of what had recently happened in Gascony concerning Bishop John, who had been murdered disgracefully and unheard-ofly, it was decreed that, by common agreement and humble devotion, the ears of the prince should be entreated, if it pleased his piety, so that the accusation brought against Christ’s priests might be fully decided according to synodal statutes.

It would likewise please the judgment of the bishops if the matter could be settled entirely according to their authority—that is, if canonical judgment were inflicted upon those who, setting aside the fear of the Lord, dared to rage against his ministers.

But if it pleased his piety, according to the chapters of the preceding kings, where their provision mercifully introduced a monetary assessment for offenses, that, for the consolation of holy Church, the matters mentioned above should be determined by money granted by the emperors to the priests for their defense and by penance, according to the judgment of the bishops, then it would please them that the matter be settled in this way, if he wished to approve it.

If anyone assaults, wounds, or cripples a subdeacon, and the subdeacon recovers, let the offender do penance for five Lents, without the intervening years, and pay the bishop three hundred solidi together with the subdeacon’s composition and the episcopal fines. If the subdeacon dies, let the offender do penance for each of the aforesaid Lents together with the following years, and pay the bishop four hundred solidi, together with three times the subdeacon’s composition and threefold episcopal fines.

If anyone assaults a deacon and he recovers, let the offender do penance for six Lents, without the intervening years, and pay the bishop four hundred solidi together with the deacon’s composition and episcopal fines. If the deacon dies, let the offender do penance for each of the aforesaid six Lents together with the following years, and pay the bishop six hundred solidi, together with three times the deacon’s composition and threefold episcopal fines.

If anyone assaults a presbyter and [the presbyter] recovers—*spassaverit*; the printed word is uncertain—let the offender do penance for six Lents, without the intervening years, and pay the bishop six hundred solidi together with three times the presbyter’s composition and threefold episcopal fines. If the presbyter dies, let twelve years of penance be imposed upon the offender according to the canons, and let him pay nine hundred solidi together with three times the composition and threefold episcopal fines.

If anyone lays an ambush for a bishop, seizes him, or dishonors him in any way, let him do penance for ten Lents together with the intervening years, and pay three times the composition for a murdered presbyter. If the bishop is killed accidentally and not voluntarily, let the homicide do penance with the counsel of the bishops of the province.

But if anyone voluntarily kills him, let him eat no meat and drink no wine throughout all the days of his life; let him lay aside the military belt, and remain forever without hope of marriage.

Aistolphus, archbishop of Mainz, said: “If it pleases the princes and their other faithful men, let us ask that this be approved and subscribed.” And it was approved and subscribed both by the prince and by all the others.

### CHAPTER 6 — On the same matter

(From the Council of Tribur, chapter 1. An ecclesiastical chapter at Tribur, approved and subscribed by Charles and the leading men of Gaul and Germany.) It has pleased us and our faithful men that, just as we were admonished and entreated the previous year at Theodone’s estate by the bishops and the other priests and servants of God, the bishops and their ministers—whom God, not human judgment, has preserved—should remain untouched according to the statutes of the holy canons, the holy fathers, and the capitularies of the preceding kings set forth in our presence; and likewise God’s priests and their co-workers, through whose intercessions and supplications holy Church is understood to stand.

We establish that if anyone assaults a subdeacon and he recovers, the offender is to do canonical penance and pay the bishop three hundred solidi. If the subdeacon dies, he is to do penance according to what the canons prescribe and pay the bishop four hundred solidi.

If anyone assaults a deacon and he recovers, he is to do penance according to the canons and pay the bishop four hundred solidi. If the deacon does not recover, he is to do penance according to the synodal decrees and pay the bishop six hundred solidi.

If anyone mistreats a presbyter and the presbyter recovers—*spassaverit*, a doubtful printed reading—let the offender do penance according to the judgment of that bishop and pay the bishop nine hundred solidi. If the presbyter dies, let him do penance as the synod shall judge and pay the bishop twelve hundred solidi.

If anyone lays an ambush for a bishop, seizes him, or dishonors him in any way, let him do penance according to the statutes of the canons and pay three times the composition for a presbyter not killed, together with the *instilis* [reading uncertain] which appear to be written and confirmed in the preceding chapter.

If anyone kills a bishop deliberately, let him do penance according to what was decreed at Theodone’s estate by the thirty-two bishops, and what was there approved and subscribed by us and by the leading men of all Germany and Gaul with benevolent approval; and let him pay the money granted by us to the Church that has been deprived of its bishop.

We have added this from our own authority: if anyone in these matters proves disobedient and contumacious toward the sanctions of the holy canons and our decree concerning bishops, let him first be struck by canonical judgment. Then let him have no benefice in our kingdom, and let his allod be placed under the ban. If he remains under our ban for one year and one day, let it be transferred to our treasury; let him be captured and confined in exile, and there kept and constrained until, compelled, he satisfies God and holy Church—something he had previously refused to do freely.

“And if this pleases all of you, say so.” For the third time all shouted together, “It pleases us.” The emperors and nearly all the princes of Gaul and Germany subscribed, each making his own cross; and the ecclesiastical order, offering praises to God and the princes, sang the hymn *Te Deum laudamus*. Thus the synod was dissolved.

### CHAPTER 7 — On the same matter

(From the Council of Mainz, chapter 24.) Whoever kills a presbyter is to be assigned twelve years of penance according to the canons; or, if he denies it, if he is free, he is to swear with seventy-two compurgators. If he is a slave, he is to clear himself by ordeal over twelve red-hot plowshares. Once convicted of the offense, he is to lack the military belt until the end of his life and remain without hope of marriage.

### CHAPTER 8 — Concerning the killers of priests

(From the Council of Worms, chapter 3.) Whoever voluntarily kills a priest is not to eat meat or drink wine throughout all the days of his life. He is to fast until evening, except on feast days and Sundays; he is not to take up arms or mount a horse; he is not to enter the church for five years, but is to stand before the church doors.

After five years he may enter the church, but he is not yet to receive Communion; he is to stand among the hearers. When the course of twelve years has been completed, permission to receive Communion is to be granted to him, and the restriction on riding is to be remitted. In the other observances, however, he is to remain for three days each week, so that he may deserve to be purified more completely.

### CHAPTER 9 — Concerning deposed presbyters who are then killed

(From the Council of Tours, chapter 3.) It has been reported to us that certain men who had once said they were priests, and who were later degraded because of their sins and, while doing penance, sought the assistance of the saints by traveling through various places, were murdered. We deny all ecclesiastical dignity to their killers until they have discharged worthy penance for their offense according to the judgment of the bishops, because they ought to do penance more severely than other homicides.

### CHAPTER 10 — Concerning presbyters who are killed without the stole

(From the Council of Tribur, attended by King Arnulf, chapter 26.) Presbyters are not to travel unless dressed in a stole or orarium. If they are robbed, wounded, or killed while traveling and are not wearing the stole, the offender is to pay only the ordinary composition. If they were wearing the stole, he is to pay threefold.

### CHAPTER 11 — To whom the composition for a murdered presbyter belongs

(From the same council, chapter 5.) The composition for a murdered presbyter is to be paid to the bishop to whose parish he belonged, in such a way that the bishop shall assign half of his *wergeld* to the needs of the Church over which he presided and distribute the other half justly as alms, because no heir of his seems nearer to us than the one who joined him to the Lord.

### CHAPTER 12 — Concerning those who commit homicide by ambush

(From the Council of Nantes, chapter 2.) If anyone voluntarily and by ambush kills a person, he is to submit himself to perpetual penance. If it is established that the deed was committed publicly, then, if he is a layman, he is to be excluded from Communion in prayer for five years. After five years he is to be admitted only to Communion in prayer, but he is not to offer or touch the body of the Lord. Remaining in this state for fourteen years, he is then to be admitted to full Communion with offerings.

### CHAPTER 13 — Also concerning homicide committed voluntarily

(From the Council of Ancyra, chapter 21.) Those who commit homicide voluntarily are indeed to submit themselves continually to penance, but they are to attain completion near the end of their lives.

### CHAPTER 14 — On the same matter

(From the Council of Paris, chapter 6.) If anyone voluntarily commits homicide—not resisting violence, but using force—and kills an innocent person who is simply going on his way, let him do severe penance until the end of his life; nevertheless, if he has carried out his penance well, the viaticum of Communion is not to be denied him at his death.

### CHAPTER 15 — Concerning involuntary homicide

[Col. 0769B] (From the Council of Ancyra, chapter 22.) Concerning homicides committed involuntarily: the earlier determination orders that, after seven years of penance, completion is to be attained; the second, however, orders that a period of five years be fulfilled.

### CHAPTER 16 — On the same matter

(From the Council of Nantes, chapter 2.) If anyone commits homicide accidentally and unwillingly, let him do penance for forty days on bread and water. After completing these, let him be separated from the prayer of the faithful for two years; let him neither receive Communion nor offer. After two years, let him be admitted to communion in prayer; he may offer, but not receive Communion. After five years, let him be admitted to full Communion. Abstinence from food is to remain at the priest’s discretion.

### CHAPTER 17 — Concerning one who commits homicide at the command of his lord

[Col. 0769C]

(From the same council, chapter 25.) If a free man, at the command of his lord, kills the lord’s slave, let him do penance as for homicide committed voluntarily.

### CHAPTER 18 — Concerning one who kills his own slave

(From the Council of Agde, chapter 62.) If anyone kills his own slave without the knowledge or judgment of a judge, let him mourn and make satisfaction as for homicide committed voluntarily.

### CHAPTER 19 — Concerning a woman who, inflamed by jealous fury, beats her maidservant, who consequently dies

(From the Council of Elvira, chapter 5.) If a mistress, inflamed by jealous fury, beats her maidservant with whips so that the maidservant gives up her life in torment within three days, since it is uncertain whether she killed her intentionally or accidentally, it was decided that, if intentionally, after seven years, and if accidentally, after five years, once the prescribed penance has been performed, she is to be admitted to Communion. If she falls ill during the periods established, she is to receive Communion.

### CHAPTER 20 — On the same matter

(From the decree of Pope Sylvester.) If anyone kills a person publicly doing penance, let him do penance twice over for homicide committed voluntarily, and let him not receive Communion except at the end of his life.

### CHAPTER 21 — Concerning those who accidentally commit homicide while engaged in necessary work

(From the Council of Worms, chapter 5.) It often happens that, while someone is engaged in necessary work and cuts down a tree, someone coming beneath it is crushed. Therefore, if the tree was felled through the will or negligence of the person cutting it, he must submit entirely to penance as a homicide.

But if it happened not through his intention, but through his carelessness—and not, finally, by deliberate judgment, but while he was perhaps occupied with necessary work and the other unexpectedly came beneath the tree and was crushed under it—the person cutting the tree is not held to be a homicide.

### CHAPTER 22 — On the same matter

(From the Council of Tribur, chapter 17.) If two brothers cut down trees in a forest, and, as one tree was about to fall, one brother said to the other, “Beware,” and the other, while fleeing, fell into the crushing fall of the tree and died, the surviving brother is to be judged innocent of his brother’s blood.

### CHAPTER 23 — Concerning those who commit homicides in public war
[Col. 0770B] (From the Council of Mainz, chapter 2.) It is necessary, moreover, to admonish more diligently those who regard homicides committed in war as nothing, excusing themselves on the grounds that there is no need for them to do penance for each individual killing, since it was carried out by order of rulers and brought to an end by God’s judgment. For we know that God’s judgment is always just and deserving of no reproach. Nevertheless, they ought to consider whether those who desire this wicked slaughter can excuse themselves before the eyes of God as though they were innocent—those who, because of avarice, which is the root of all evils and is compared with the service of idols, and because of favor toward their temporal lords, despised the eternal Lord and, scorning his commandments, committed homicide not by accident, [Col. 0770C] but deliberately.

For we read concerning those who killed men unintentionally that God, through the lawgiver, appointed cities of refuge, so that those fleeing to them might be saved from the avenger of their kinsman’s blood and might not die. Hence it is written in Deuteronomy:

“This shall be the law concerning the homicide whose life is to be preserved: Whoever strikes his neighbor unknowingly, and it is proved that yesterday and the day before he had no hatred against him, but simply went with him into the forest to cut wood, and, while cutting the wood, the axe slipped from his hand, or the iron fell from its handle and struck and killed his companion, let him flee to one of the cities mentioned above and live there; nor let the near kinsman of the one whose blood was shed, moved by the goad of grief, strike his soul.”

But concerning one who kills someone deliberately, it is written in Exodus:

“If anyone deliberately and by ambush kills his neighbor, you shall drag him from my altar, that he may die.”

And in Deuteronomy:

“If anyone, hating his neighbor, lies in wait for his life, and, rising up, strikes him so that he dies, and he flees to one of the cities mentioned above, the elders of that city shall send and seize him from the place of refuge and deliver him into the hands of the near kinsman whose blood was shed, and he shall die; nor shall you pity him.”

If, then, someone says that the man whom the Lord judged worthy of death is not guilty, how is he not opposing the law of God by maintaining that what God commanded is null? Yet amid these considerations it must be understood [Col. 0771A] that there is a great difference between a legitimate ruler and a seditious tyrant; between one who endeavors to overthrow the tranquility of Christian peace and one who fights with arms to defend justice against iniquity.

### CHAPTER 24 — Concerning those who have been accused of homicide, if they deny it

(From the Council of Tours, chapter 2.) Whenever it can be shown, according to canonical authority, that someone has committed homicide, a penalty of penance proportionate to the offense shall be imposed upon him. But if it cannot be proved by clear indications that he is a homicide, and he himself is unwilling to confess, the matter shall be reserved for the judgment of almighty God, to whom all hidden things are manifest. The priest shall nevertheless declare publicly to him that he is unworthy of ecclesiastical communion and must remain without it until he confesses the crime committed and strives, through confession and fitting penance, to free himself from this crime.

### CHAPTER 25 — Concerning a madman who has committed homicide

(From the same council, chapter 7.) If someone kills another while insane, and later returns to sound understanding, a lighter penance shall be imposed upon him than upon one who committed such an act while of sound mind. Although penance must be imposed upon him, since his illness is believed to have been the cause of his sin, it shall nevertheless be as much lighter than that imposed upon one who killed someone while sane as the difference established between the sane and the insane, and between the irrational and the rational.

### CHAPTER 26 — Concerning those who commit homicide by poisoning

[Col. 0771C] (From the Council of Elvira, chapter 5.) If anyone kills another by poison—for he could not accomplish this crime without idolatry—communion is not to be granted to him except at the end of his life.

### CHAPTER 27 — Concerning one through whose denunciation someone has been killed

(From the same council, chapter 1.) If anyone of the faithful has acted as an informer, and through his denunciation one of the faithful has been proscribed or killed, it has been decided that he shall receive communion only at the end of his life. If the offense was lighter, he may receive communion within five years. If he was a catechumen, he shall be admitted to baptism after the period of five years.

### CHAPTER 28 — That there are three kinds of murderers

(From a letter of Pope Clement, chapter 16.) He said that there are three kinds of murderers and taught that their punishment would be equal. For he declared that those who kill their brothers are murderers, and likewise their detractors and those who hate them. “For whoever hates his brother kills him”; and the one who slanders is likewise shown to be a murderer.

He urged all people to abstain from carnal desires that wage war against the soul and to display to everyone their good and innocent conduct. He urged them to love one another more earnestly from the heart; to venerate elders and love juniors; and to instruct and arm bishops, their priests, all the other ministers of the Church, and the whole people entrusted to them with divine words and commandments. They should love all these bishops [Col. 0772A] with the full strength of their hearts, as their own eyes—for they are their eyes—and obey their commands in everything, even if the bishops themselves, God forbid, act otherwise than they ought, remembering that dominical command: “Do what they say; but do not do what they do.”

### CHAPTER 29 — That homicides are to be removed from ecclesiastical communion

(From the Council of Agde, chapter 10.) Therefore we have decreed that homicides are to be removed from ecclesiastical communion unless they have cleansed their admitted crimes through the satisfaction of penance.

### CHAPTER 30 — On the same matter

(From the Council of Tours, chapter 7.) Communion is absolutely not to be given to homicides until their crimes have been cleansed through confession and penance [Col. 0772B].

### CHAPTER 31 — Concerning those by whose counsel homicides are committed

(From the sayings of Augustine.) Those who think that only those who kill a person with their own hands are homicides, and not rather those through whose counsel, deceit, and exhortation people are destroyed, dangerously deceive themselves. For the Jews certainly did not kill the Lord with their own hands, as it is written: “It is not lawful for us to kill anyone”; nevertheless, the Lord’s death is imputed to them, because they crucified him with their tongue, saying, “Crucify him.”

Hence one Evangelist says that the Lord was crucified at the third hour, another at the sixth: for the Jews crucified him at the third hour with their tongue, and the soldiers with their hands at the sixth. Therefore whoever hands a man over kills him, the Lord saying: “The one who handed me over to you has the greater sin.”

Hence the Psalmist says: “The sons of men: their teeth are weapons and arrows; their tongues are a sharp sword.” Therefore let those whose counsel causes blood to be shed submit to penance, if they wish to merit pardon.

### CHAPTER 32 — Concerning those who commit homicide in revenge for their relatives

(From the Penitential of Theodore.) Whoever kills a man in revenge for his brother or for other relatives shall do penance as for homicide committed deliberately, since Truth itself says: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay.”

### CHAPTER 33 — Concerning one who kills a Jew out of greed

(From the Council of Mainz, chapter 6.) Whoever kills a Jew or a pagan after premeditating hatred or because of greed, because he has destroyed the image of God and the hope of future conversion, shall do penance for forty days on bread and water.

### CHAPTER 34 — Concerning parricides and fratricides

(From the Council of Tribur, chapter 5.) We decree that parricides and fratricides shall remain for the course of one year praying for the Lord’s mercy before the doors of the church. When the year has been completed, they shall be brought into the church, yet shall stand among the hearers until another year has ended. After these things have been carried out, if the fruit of penance is seen in them, let them partake of the Lord’s body and blood, lest they become hardened through despair.

They shall not eat meat for all the days of their lives. Every day they shall fast until the ninth hour, except on feast days and Sundays. Three days each week they shall abstain from wine, mead, and honeyed beer. They shall not dare to bear arms except against pagans. Wherever they prefer to go, they shall not be transported in any vehicle, but shall proceed on their own feet. If they have wives, they shall not separate from them. We leave the duration of this penance to the judgment of the bishops, so that they may lengthen or shorten it according to the conduct of the penitents.

### CHAPTER 35 — On the same matter

(From the Council of Mainz, chapter 11.) How detestable a crime parricide is, the Lord himself demonstrated in the judgment made between Cain and his brother Abel, when he said to the parricide Cain: “You shall be cursed upon the earth, [Col. 0773B] which has opened its mouth and received your brother’s blood from your hand. When you work it, it shall not give you its fruit; and you shall be a wanderer and a fugitive upon the earth.”

He also placed a mark upon him, so that he might live always trembling, groaning, and as a fugitive, and might nowhere dare to establish a peaceful dwelling. But because in modern times fugitive parricides wander through various places and devote themselves to different vices and the enticements of gluttony, it seems better to us that, remaining in one place, they should chastise themselves with strict penance, if perhaps they may deserve to receive from the Lord’s mercy forgiveness for their crime.

They shall not thereafter be permitted to take up the military belt or to enter into marriage and the bond of wedlock, because the sacred canons do not allow this for them.

### CHAPTER 36 — Concerning those who unintentionally kill their children

[Col. 0773C]

(From the Council of Tribur, chapter 21.) If anyone unintentionally kills his son, let him do penance as for homicide committed unintentionally.

### CHAPTER 37 — Concerning one who kills his lawful wife without judgment

(From a decree of Pope Pius, chapter 26.) Whoever kills his own wife without legal process, or without cause and certain proof, and takes another wife, shall lay down his arms and perform public penance. If he is obstinate and disobedient to his bishop, he shall be anathematized until he submits. The same law shall apply to one who kills his superior.

### CHAPTER 38 — On the same matter

[Col. 0773D]

(From the Council of Mainz, chapter 1.) If a husband kills his wife, or a wife her husband, let an equitable judgment be made concerning them, since the Lord says: “You shall not consider the person of the poor, nor honor the face of the powerful.” And shortly afterward: “You shall hear the small as well as the great, and you shall not accept anyone’s person, because it is God’s judgment.”

Therefore, if either of them denies the charge in such a case, he or she shall be examined according to the same judgment. If the accused denies it and cannot be overcome by clear evidence, then, if free, let him or her swear with twelve others; if a slave, let him or her clear himself or herself by the ordeal of red-hot iron.

But if a dying wife accuses her husband of her death in the hearing of one or two persons, he shall not on that account be considered defeated. If he is free, let him swear with seventy-two others; if a slave, let him clear himself upon twelve red-hot plowshares [Col. 0774A]. The same law shall apply to a husband accusing his wife.

### CHAPTER 39 — On the same matter

(From the Council of Elvira, chapter 85.) If a woman kills her husband with poison on account of fornication, or causes him to be killed by any device, because she has killed her lord and superior, let her renounce the world and do penance in a monastery.

### CHAPTER 40 — On the same matter

(Letter of Paulinus, bishop of Friuli, to Heistulf.) I take care to admonish you with tears and great groaning, my son Heistulf—if indeed you ought to be called a son—you who have so cruelly committed this wretched homicide.

For you killed your wife, a part of your own body, joined to you in lawful marriage, without any cause for her death [Col. 0774B]; she did not resist you, nor in any way plot against your life. You did not find her committing some wicked act with another man; but, incited by the devil and inflamed with impious fury, like a brigand, more savage and cruel than every beast, you killed her with your sword.

And now, after her death, you add iniquity to iniquity, wickedly robbing your own children: you did not spare their mother, and you made your children orphans in order to add the cause of death after her death. Through a single murderer and reprobate witness, you wish to accuse the dead woman. Neither the Gospel nor any divine or human law permits this: that anyone should be condemned or justified even by the testimony of one suitable witness. How much less by this witness, so disgraceful and criminal? While she was alive, she ought not to have been condemned; nor will you be able to excuse yourself after her death.

First, the cause of the accusation ought to have been carefully investigated. Then, if she had been found guilty, she should have received the vengeance of punishment according to the course of the law. For even if it had been true—as God forbid—that she was an adulteress, as that man falsely claimed, after seven years of completed penance you could, if you had wished, have dismissed her on an approved ground; but you should in no way have killed her.

We propose two courses of action to you. After deliberating with two others, choose whichever seems preferable, and have mercy on your soul.

You are placed here in this brief period of time. Do not become your own murderer and perish eternally. Abandon this wicked world, which has drawn you into so monstrous a crime. Enter a monastery, humble yourself under the authority of the abbot, and, aided by the prayers of many brothers, observe with a simple heart everything commanded to you by the abbot, if perhaps the infinite goodness of God may forgive your sins.

Know with certainty that this course is lighter and more beneficial: that under another’s guardianship you should mourn the sins that must be lamented.

The second course is as follows. Lay down your arms and abandon all secular business. Do not eat meat or fat for all the days of your life, except on one day of the Lord’s Resurrection, one day of Pentecost, and one day of the Nativity of the Lord. At other times do penance on bread and water, and occasionally on legumes and vegetables. Persevere always in fasts, vigils, prayers, and almsgiving.

Never drink wine, mead, or honeyed beer, except on those three days mentioned above [Col. 0775A]. Do not take a wife, do not keep a concubine, do not commit adultery; remain perpetually without hope of marriage. Never wash yourself in a bath. Do not mount a horse. Do not conduct your own case or another person’s case in an assembly of the faithful. Never sit at banquets of those rejoicing.

In church, separated from the other Christians, stand humbly behind the door. Commend yourself submissively to the prayers of those entering and leaving. Consider yourself unworthy of communion in the sacred body and blood of the Lord for all the days of your life. At the final end of your life, we permit you to receive it as viaticum, if you have observed this counsel.

There are also many other and harsher things that ought to be added to you according to the weight of so great a crime. But if, with God’s help, you carry out and keep with a perfect heart all the things mercifully prescribed above, we trust that, through God’s immense clemency, you will obtain forgiveness of your sins. And, according to the command of the good and just shepherd, the holy Church will release you on earth from this bond of sin, so that through the grace of him who redeemed her with his blood you may be loosed in heaven.

But if you act otherwise and despise the salutary counsel of holy Mother Church, you shall be your own judge, and you shall remain in the devil’s snare in which you are entangled and held. Your blood shall be upon your own head. We shall remain separated from your fellowship, and you shall remain under an unbreakable anathema until you satisfy God and holy Church.

### CHAPTER 41 — Concerning a wife who arranges her husband’s death

(From the Council held at Verberie, chapter 3.) If a woman has arranged the death of her husband with others, and the husband, defending himself, kills one of them, and if that husband can prove that she was guilty of the plot, then, as it seems to us, he may dismiss the wife; and, if he wishes to take another wife, the woman who plotted shall be subjected to penance and remain without hope of marriage.

### CHAPTER 42 — Concerning a case in which several attack one person

(From the same council, chapter 98.) If four or five men, or even more, quarrel with one man, and he dies after being wounded by them, whoever inflicted the blow shall be judged a homicide according to the decrees of the canons. The others who attacked him, wishing to kill him, shall likewise do penance. Those who neither attacked nor wounded him and were not accomplices by counsel or assistance, but were merely present, shall be free from guilt.

### CHAPTER 43 — On the permissibility of vengeance

(From the sayings of the Apostle, Jerome, Augustine, and Gregory.) Concerning vengeance not being prohibited in the New Testament, Jerome says regarding persons worthy of vengeance: “He who strikes the wicked because they are wicked, and has a cause for killing in order to strike the most wicked, is God’s minister.” Likewise: “Let the law and its ministers restrain and bind enemies.” The Apostle says: “To the king as supreme, and to governors as sent by him for the punishment of evildoers, but for the praise of the good.”

Again Jerome says: “To punish homicides and sacrilegious persons is not the shedding of blood” [Col. 0776A].

Augustine says: “What sort of folly is this—to spare one person and bring everyone into danger? For all are polluted when one person sins.” Hence the law commands: “You shall not permit sorcerers to live.” Hence the Prophet says: “They were killing souls that do not die.”

Hence Gregory says: “He kills one who does not die when he condemns the righteous; and he attempts to give life to one who will not live when he strives to release the guilty from punishment.”

For Elijah inflicted death upon many with his own hand, by killing and by divinely inspired fire. In the New Testament also, Peter terribly punished Ananias and Sapphira.

### CHAPTER 44 — Concerning those who pronounced a capital sentence after baptism

(From the sayings of Pope Innocent, chapter 23.) Inquiry has also been made concerning those who, after baptism, held public office and either administered tortures alone or also pronounced a capital sentence. Concerning these matters we read that nothing was defined by our predecessors. For they remembered that these powers had been granted by God, that the sword had been permitted for the punishment of the guilty, and that God’s minister had been appointed as an avenger in such matters.

How, then, could they condemn an act that they saw had been granted by God the author? Therefore, concerning these matters, we retain the practice preserved until now, lest we seem either to overthrow discipline or to act against the authority of the Lord. Nevertheless, when they render an account, all their deeds shall be taken into consideration.

### CHAPTER 45 — Concerning those who are killed while destroying idols

[Col. 0776C] (From the Council of Elvira, chapter 70.) If anyone breaks idols and is killed at that place, since it is not written in the Gospels, nor is it ever found to have been done under the apostles, it has been decided that he is not to be counted among the martyrs.

### CHAPTER 46 — How one who has killed his mother ought to do penance

(From a letter of Pope Nicholas to Radold, bishop of the holy Church of Argentea Retensis.) Nicholas, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend and holy Radold, bishop of the holy Church of Argentea Retensis.

While the hosts of believers from all parts of the world hasten to the threshold of the prince of the apostles, a certain man named Thiothart came bearing a letter from Your Beatitude, which he delivered to our episcopate. On reading its contents, we learned that he was a matricide; and we grieved greatly over this deed, with many sighs and tears.

Therefore we command and establish by the judgments of the gracious fathers that he remain under the yoke of penance, so that for one year he shall not enter the church, but shall continue praying and entreating God before the doors of the basilica, asking how he may be freed from so great a sacrilege.

When the year has been completed, he shall have permission to enter the church, but he shall stand among the hearers and shall not yet receive communion. When three years have been completed, the grace of sacred communion shall be granted to him. He shall not present offerings until seven further years have passed.

Throughout all these years and periods he shall not eat meat [Col. 0777A], nor dare to drink wine, except on feast days and Sundays and from Easter until Pentecost. Wherever he wishes to go, he shall not be transported in any vehicle, but shall travel on foot. He shall not take up arms except against pagans. He shall fast three days each week until evening.

He shall not separate from his own lawful wife, lest he fall into the abyss of fornication; and we desire that this not happen. But if the end of his life approaches before the course of three years has been completed, let him partake of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ. Otherwise, let what we established above be carried out.

Nevertheless, if you see his conduct and the fountain of his tears blossoming everywhere in fruitful actions and excellent works, let your vigilant care toward him appear more humane [Col. 0777B], and let him be shown mercy in every respect.

We wish you well in Christ.

### CHAPTER 47 — If a cleric commits homicide, he must cease from his order

(From the Council of Tribur, attended by King Arnulf, chapter 11.) If any cleric, even under extreme compulsion, commits homicide, whether he is a priest or a deacon, let him be deposed. We read in the canons of the apostles that a bishop, priest, or deacon who is caught in fornication, perjury, or theft is to be deposed. How much more must one who commits this monstrous crime cease from his order?

For whoever desires to follow Christ ought to walk as he himself walked. When he was cursed, he did not curse in return; when he was struck, he did not strike back; when he suffered for us [Col. 0777C], he did not threaten. And in his Gospel he himself commanded: “If anyone strikes you on one cheek, offer him the other also.”

For we ought not to kill, since the Lord says: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients: You shall not kill; and whoever kills shall be liable to judgment. But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment.” Nor should we repay evil with evil; rather, as the Apostle says in writing to the Romans: “Do not be conquered by evil, but conquer evil with good.”

If any cleric is present where a homicide has occurred, and is proved not to have been polluted by consent, advice, or any guilt in the homicide, this shall not prevent him from remaining consecrated in his rank. If he has not been consecrated, he may advance to promotion, provided that he is otherwise worthy.

### CHAPTER 48 — Concerning one who, while fighting against pagans, kills Christian captives among the enemy

(From the same council, attended by King Arnulf, chapter 34.) The Christians often win a victory and the pagan side is defeated. Since Christian captives are sometimes killed together with the pagans slain—because in the rush of battle they cannot be distinguished—we therefore make a just decree and establish that the perpetrators are to be treated more mercifully. After forty days of penance have been completed with leniency, the bishop shall have the authority and power to weigh the guilt and grant indulgence.

### CHAPTER 49 — Concerning one who deceives a Christian slave and then sells him

(From the Council held at Conflans, attended by the kings Henry and Charles, chapter 7.) It was also asked what should be done concerning one who deceived a Christian slave and then sold him. All replied that the man thereby incurred the guilt of homicide.

[Col. 0777] **END OF BOOK SIX.**

# BURCHARD, BISHOP OF THE CHURCH OF WORMS: DECRETALS, BOOK SEVEN, ON INCEST

[Col. 0779]

## Argument of the book

[Col. 0779B]

This book deals with incestuous unions among blood relatives; it shows at which degree marriages ought to be contracted and dissolved, and what penance ought to be imposed upon those polluted by incest in proportion to the offense.

### CHAPTER 1 — That those born from blood relatives are called infamous

(From a letter of Pope Callistus sent to the brothers established throughout Gaul, chapter 1.) Forbid unions among blood relatives, because both divine laws and the laws of the world prohibit them. The divine laws not only expel those who do these things and those born from them, but also call them accursed. The laws of the world call such people infamous and exclude them from inheritance.

Following our fathers, we too mark them with infamy and judge them to be infamous, because they are stained with the marks of infamy. Nor ought we to receive as witnesses those whom the laws of the world reject.

We call those blood relatives whom the divine and worldly laws call blood relatives and accept into inheritance, whom they cannot reject. The unions of such persons are neither lawful nor capable of lasting, but must be rejected.

Therefore, whoever is not lawfully joined, or is known to have been united without a marriage settlement and without a priest’s blessing, cannot accuse priests or those lawfully joined, nor testify against them, since everyone polluted by the stain of incest is infamous and is not permitted to accuse the persons mentioned above.

Not only, therefore, are such people to be rejected and made infamous, but so are all who consent to them.

### CHAPTER 2 — That no one may take a wife from his own kin

[Col. 0779D]

(From the Council of Worms, chapter 2.) In the unions of the faithful we do not define the number of generations, but we establish this: no Christian may take a wife from his own blood relationship or kinship for as long as the generation is remembered, known, or retained in memory [Col. 0780B].

### CHAPTER 3 — Concerning incestuous persons

(From the Council of Hildesheim, chapter 10.) Concerning those who pollute themselves with incestuous defilement, it has been decided that as long as they persist in that detestable and unlawful cohabitation of the flesh, they shall be admitted in the church only as far as the Mass of the catechumens. With them, moreover, no Christian ought to take food, as the Apostle commanded.

### CHAPTER 4 — On the same matter

(From the Council of Agde, chapter 8.) We reserve absolutely no pardon for incestuous unions unless they have remedied the adultery by separation. If they are unwilling to remedy it, let them be anathematized.

### CHAPTER 5 — On the same matter

(From the Council of Orléans, chapter 1.) While incestuous persons remain in that detestable and abominable crime, they shall be regarded not among the faithful Christians but among the gentiles or catechumens. That is, they shall not take drink or food with Christians, but shall do so alone; they shall not kiss them, nor be greeted by them.

But if they prove disobedient to their priests and refuse to separate themselves from so abominable a crime and return to public penance, they shall be counted among those endangered by an unclean spirit, or even among those of whom Truth himself says: “If he does not listen to you, let him be to you as a gentile and a tax collector.”

If one of them is overtaken by death, let the other do severe penance as long as he or she lives and remain without hope of marriage.

### CHAPTER 6 — That no member of the faithful may approach a close blood relative

(From the Second Council of Toledo, chapter 5.) We also salutarily decree that this must be guarded against: no member of the faithful should desire to be joined in marriage to a close blood relative for as long as he recognizes the lines of affinity through the succession of the family, since it is written: “No man shall approach his close blood relative to uncover her nakedness.” And again: “The soul that does any of these things shall perish from the midst of his people.”

Those whose unlawful union is prohibited shall certainly have the freedom to enter a better marriage.

### CHAPTER 7 — That a man is not to be joined equally in marriage to his own blood relatives and those of his wife

(From the decrees of Pope Julius.) A man is equally not to be joined in marriage to his own blood relatives or to the blood relatives of his wife.

### CHAPTER 8 — That the kinship of the man and woman is to be considered in the same way in the union

[Col. 0781B] (From the Council of Mâcon, chapter 3.) The consanguinity that must be observed in the man himself must likewise be guarded by the law of marriage in the wife’s kinship, because it is established that the two have become one flesh; both kinships must be regarded as common to them, as it is written: “The two shall be one flesh.”

### CHAPTER 9 — At which degree one must abstain

(From the sayings of Saint Isidore.) In his *Etymologies*, Isidore asserted that one must abstain from consanguinity as far as the seventh generation and then enter into a lawful marriage. I think he did this because, when tracing the sequence of genealogy, he judged that knowledge of blood relationship should be preserved as far as one could carry the order of counting. Thus he decreed that marriage might be resumed when the reckoning of the order of kinship had come to an end, in order to invoke lineage and confirm the right of friendship [Col. 0781C].

### CHAPTER 10 — In which branch of consanguinity lawful marriages may take place

(From the sayings of the same author.) Blessed Isidore speaks as follows concerning consanguinity:

“Its sequence is divided into seven degrees in this way. Son and daughter—that is, brother and sister—form the trunk itself. When these have been separated from one another, the following branches proceed separately from the root of that trunk: nepos and neptis (grandson and granddaughter), the first; pronepos and proneptis (great-grandson and great-granddaughter), the second; abnepos and abneptis (great-great-grandson and great-great-granddaughter), the third; adnepos and adneptis, the fourth; trinepos and trineptis, the fifth; and trinepotis nepos and trinepotis neptis, the sixth.

When this consanguinity, gradually dividing itself through the orders of descent, has withdrawn as far as the final degree and has ceased to be close kinship, then for the first time the law admits it into the bond of marriage and, in a certain sense, recalls the one who was fleeing.

Consanguinity was established as far as the sixth degree of descent so that, just as the generation and condition of humanity are completed in the six ages of the world, so the kinship of the family might end at the same number of degrees.”

### CHAPTER 11 — That consanguinity must be preserved as far as the seventh degree

(From a letter of Pope Gregory sent to the bishops of Gaul.) We decree that each person must observe his lineage as far as the seventh generation, and that, as long as they recognize one another as close relatives by affinity, we forbid them to approach the marital union. If they do so, let them be separated.

### CHAPTER 12 — On the same matter

(From the council held at Thionville, chapter 8.) No member of the faithful shall take his blood relative as a wife as far as the line of affinity—that is, as far as the seventh generation—or pollute her in any way with the stain of incest. If anyone rashly presumes to do this, let him undergo punishment for incest and perform public penance according to the canonical degrees.

### CHAPTER 13 — On the same matter

(From the Council of Lyon, chapter 10.) No one shall take wives from among his blood relatives as far as the seventh degree, nor without a priest’s blessing. Those who were previously unmarried should dare to marry only after being blessed by a priest [Col. 0782B].

### CHAPTER 14 — On the same matter

(From the Council of Orléans, chapter 10.) We permit no person of either sex to take a wife from the closeness of his or her own blood relationship or that of the spouse as far as the seventh degree of descent, or to be stained by the mark of incest.

### CHAPTER 15 — On the same matter

(From the Council of Cologne, chapter 6.) All the names of relationships are contained within seven degrees; beyond them neither affinity is found nor can succession be extended further.

### CHAPTER 16 — On the same matter

(From the Council of Meaux, chapter 7.) Concerning affinity of blood through the degrees of kinship, it has been decided that it must be observed as far as the seventh generation. For the law of inheritance also sanctions, through its legal definitions, that the succession of heirs extends as far as the seventh degree; they would not succeed unless succession were owed to them through the descent of kinship.

### CHAPTER 17 — That blood relatives are to be separated when two or three witnesses give testimony

(From the Council of Hildesheim, chapter 20.) Every controversy concerning ecclesiastical matters is to be settled according to divine law on the testimony of two or three witnesses. The Lord is witness, when he said: “Let no one stand against another alone, but let every word stand by the mouth of two or three witnesses.”

## Chapter 18 — On the Same Matter

(From the Council of Chalon, canon 5.) We likewise prohibit anyone from contracting marriage in the fourth, fifth, or sixth generation. Wherever this is found to have occurred after the prohibition was issued, the parties shall be separated.

## Chapter 19 — What Saint Gregory Permitted to Augustine, Preacher to the English, on Account of the Tenderness of the New Faith

(From the letter of John, bishop of Constantinople, to Felix, bishop of Sicily.) When Pope Gregory was asked by Augustine, bishop of the English nation, in which generation the faithful ought to marry, he replied by way of dispensation as follows:

“Certain law in the Roman commonwealth permits either a brother and sister, or the son and daughter of two full brothers or of two sisters, to unite; yet, as we have learned by experience, offspring cannot grow from such a marriage. Therefore it is necessary that the faithful should now be permitted to join together in the fourth or fifth generation.”

## Chapter 20 — That Saint Gregory Granted This Permission Specially to the English, Not Generally

(The same John says.) But after a long time, when Felix, bishop of Messina in Sicily, asked whether Gregory had written to Augustine that marriages contracted in the fourth generation among the English should by no means be dissolved, the most humble Father Gregory gave, among other things, this explanation:

“You should know that what I wrote to Augustine, bishop of the English nation—your foster son, as you remember—concerning consanguineous unions, I wrote specifically to him and to the English nation, which had recently come to the faith, so that they would not, out of fear, withdraw from the good which they had begun; it was not written generally.

The entire city of Rome is therefore my witness, and I did not write these instructions to them with the intention that, once they had been firmly rooted in the faith, they should not be separated if they were found within their own consanguinity, or that they should unite within the line of affinity—that is, as far as the seventh generation. Rather, since they were still neophytes, it was necessary first to permit them things that were unlawful, to instruct them by words and examples, and afterward reasonably and faithfully to exclude such practices.

For, according to the Apostle who says, ‘I gave you milk to drink, not food,’ we permitted them to observe these things for the time being—not their successors—so that the good which had been planted with a still-weak root would not be scorched, but might gain some strength and be preserved until perfection.

I, John, have therefore taken care to mention these matters so that those who, on the occasion of this new dispensation, bring charges of unlawful marriages against that most learned man may understand that he did not generally approve unions in the fourth generation, but permitted them as a pardonable concession.”

## Chapter 21 — That Outsiders Should Not Cause Separation between Consanguineous Persons Except in Necessity

(From a decree of Pope Fabian, chapter 8.) No outsider shall accuse persons related by blood, nor shall he establish consanguinity in a synod; rather, those relatives to whom the matter belongs shall do so: the father, mother, brother, sister, paternal uncle, maternal uncle, paternal aunt, maternal aunt, and their offspring. If the entire line of descendants has died out, the bishop shall make canonical inquiry among the oldest and most truthful persons who know the same relationship. If the relationship is established, the parties shall be separated.

## Chapter 22 — On the Same Matter

(From the Roman Council. Gregory.) If anyone takes his niece in marriage, let him be anathema.

## Chapter 23 — On the Same Matter

(The same Gregory.) If anyone takes his first cousin in marriage, let him be anathema.

## Chapter 24 — On the Same Matter

(Again, the same Gregory.) If anyone takes in marriage a woman from his own kindred, or one whom his relative had had, let him be anathema.

## Chapter 25 — The Oath Concerning Kinship: How It Is to Be Investigated

[Col. 0784A]

“Concerning the kinship which is said to exist between that man N. and this woman, his wife, N., whatever you know or have heard from your neighbors or from your older relatives, you shall not conceal from your bishop—or from his messenger whom he has ordered to investigate this matter—by any means, whether on account of love, fear, payment, or kinship, whenever he questions you about it. So may God help you, and these relics of the saints.”

## Chapter 26 — The Oath of the Witnesses

“This oath which this man has sworn concerning the kinship reckoned between that man N. and his wife N., you shall observe insofar as you know or have heard. So may God help you, and these relics of the saints.”

[Col. 0784B]

## Chapter 27 — The Oath Concerning Separation from an Incestuous Union

“From this day forward, by no means shall you associate yourself with this woman, your kinswoman N., with whom, contrary to the law and to your proper Christian faith, you have committed adultery and incest. You shall not associate with her either in marriage or in adultery; you shall not eat or drink with her at one table, nor remain with her under one roof, except perhaps in a church or some public place where no evil suspicion can arise, so that there, in the presence of suitable witnesses, you may speak together for a definite necessity.

Nor shall you take another wife, unless, after you have completed your penance, permission has been granted to you by your bishop or by his messenger. So may God help you, and these relics of the saints.”

[Col. 0784C]

## Chapter 28 — Saint Isidore Set Out These Chapters on the Seven Degrees of Consanguinity after Careful Investigation and Arranged Them More Clearly in the Figure Depicted Below

### Chapter 1: On the Seven Degrees

(Isidore, On the Seven Degrees of Consanguinity.) In the first degree, the ascending line contains the father and mother; the descending line contains the son and daughter. No other persons are joined to them.

### Chapter 2

In the second degree, the ascending line contains the grandfather and grandmother; the descending line contains the grandson and granddaughter. On the transverse line are the brother and sister, and these persons are counted in duplicate.

The grandfather and grandmother are reckoned both through the father and through the mother. The persons in the following degrees are likewise doubled according to the nature of those who stand in each degree and according to the same order.

These persons in the second degree are called double because there are two grandfathers and two grandmothers, paternal and maternal. There are likewise two kinds of grandchildren: those born from a son and those born from a daughter. The brother and sister belong to the transverse line—that is, they are either the father’s brother or the mother’s brother, because one is called a paternal uncle and the other a maternal uncle. These too are doubled in the same order.

### Chapter 3

In the third degree, above are the great-grandfather and great-grandmother; below are the great-grandson and great-granddaughter; obliquely are the son or daughter of the brother or sister.

There are the paternal uncle and paternal aunt—that is, the father’s brother and sister—and the maternal uncle and maternal aunt—that is, the mother’s brother and sister.

[Col. 0785A]

### Chapter 4

In the fourth degree, above are the great-great-grandfather and great-great-grandmother; below are the great-great-grandson and great-great-granddaughter; obliquely are the grandson and granddaughter of the brother and sister.

There are the paternal cousin and female paternal cousin—that is, the son or daughter of the paternal uncle; the cousin and female cousin—that is, the son or daughter of the maternal uncle or maternal aunt; and the children of the paternal aunt, male and female.

There are also the male and female cousins born of two sisters. To these are added the great paternal uncle and great paternal aunt—that is, the brother and sister of the paternal grandfather—and the great maternal uncle and great maternal aunt—that is, the brother and sister of both the paternal and maternal grandmother.

[Col. 0785B]

### Chapter 5

In the fifth degree, above are the great-great-great-grandfather and great-great-great-grandmother; below are the great-great-great-grandson and great-great-great-granddaughter.

Obliquely are the great-grandson and great-granddaughter of the brother and sister; the fratres patrueles and sorores patrueles (male and female paternal cousins); the amitini and amitinae (male and female children of the paternal aunt); and the son or daughter of a consobrinus or consobrina—a proprius consobrinus or consobrina, that is, a cousin properly so called—the son or daughter of the great paternal uncle, great paternal aunt, great maternal uncle, or great maternal aunt.

To these are added the great-great paternal uncle and great-great paternal aunt. These are the brother and sister of the maternal great-grandfather. There are also the great-great maternal uncle and great-great maternal aunt. These are the brother and sister of the paternal and maternal great-grandmother and of the maternal great-grandfather.

This category can be expressed neither by other degrees than those written here nor by other terms.

[Col. 0785C]

### Chapter 6

In the sixth degree, above are the fourth-generation great-grandfather and great-grandmother; below are the fourth-generation great-grandson and great-granddaughter.

Obliquely are the abnepos and abneptis (great-great-grandson and great-great-granddaughter) of the brother and sister; the fratres patrueles and sorores patrueles (male and female paternal cousins); the amitini and amitinae (male and female children of the paternal aunt); and the consobrini and consobrinae (male and female cousins).

There are the great paternal uncle and great paternal aunt, the great maternal uncle and great maternal aunt, and the nepos and neptis, son or daughter of the proprius consobrinus or consobrina, who are called consobrini.

To these are added laterally the propatrui and proamitae; the son or daughter of the proavunculi and promaterterae; and the adpatruus and adamita.

The adpatruus and adamita are the brother and sister of the paternal abavus; the abavunculus and abmatertera are the brother and sister of the paternal and maternal abavia and of the maternal abavus.

These matters likewise cannot be explained more fully than the author himself has set them out.

[Col. 0785D]

[Col. 0786A]

### Chapter 7

In the seventh degree, those who are related in a direct line above and below are not designated by their proper names. Six persons are contained in the transverse line: the great-great-grandson and great-great-granddaughter of the brother and sister, and the successive sons and daughters of the cousins.

For this reason seven degrees have been established: beyond them, by the nature of things, neither further names can be found nor life among succeeding generations be extended. Within these seven degrees all the names of relationships are contained. Beyond them no affinity can be found, nor can succession be extended further.

## Chapter 29 — On Incestuous Persons Who Despise the Admonitions of Priests

(From the Council of Tours, chapter 41.) Incestuous persons, parricides, and murderers are found among us in great numbers, alas! But some of them refuse to heed the admonitions of priests and wish to persist in their former crimes. Those who will not be recalled by the priests’ life-giving warnings ought to be restrained from such wicked conduct by the discipline of secular power.

[Col. 0786B]

## Chapter 30 — That Marriages Must Not Be Contracted before the Sixth Generation

(From the council held at Confluence (Koblenz), attended by Kings Henry and Charles, chapter 1.) In the year 922 of the Lord’s incarnation, at Confluence (Koblenz), by order of the venerable princes, namely the most reverend Kings Charles and Henry, eight bishops were assembled: Hermann, archbishop of Cologne; Heriger, archbishop of Mainz; Thiedo, bishop of Würzburg; Luitthar, bishop of Minden; Doto, bishop of Osnabrück; Richgouwo, bishop of Worms; Richwin, bishop of Strasbourg; and Unwan, bishop of Paderborn, together with many abbots and other men of the sacred order.

Chapter 1. With our Lord Jesus Christ cooperating and confirming their decisions, they sat in synodal assembly and, after deliberating with the most salutary counsel on many matters useful and beneficial to the holy Church of God, among other things firmly established this as especially necessary and, alas, urgently required in a time when incestuous kinship unions were extremely common through abuse: they were to be avoided with the greatest care. Namely, no Christian should presume to contract marriage within the sixth generation.

[Col. 0786D]

[Col. 0785] End of the Seventh Book.

[Col. 0787] Here follows the figure of Saint Isidore, bishop, concerning the seven degrees of consanguinity.
