# Burchard, Bishop of the Church of Worms: Decrees, Book Eight, on Men and Women Dedicated to God

[Col. 0791]

## Preface to the Book

[Col. 0791C]

This book treats men and women who, after being dedicated to God, have abandoned their sacred commitment, and also their penance.

## Chapter 1 — On Those Whom One or Both Parents Have Given to the Holy Religious Life

(From the Eleventh Council of Toledo, chapter 6.) Since the effect of lax practice has sometimes caused the honorable decree of the constitution to waver, when what is held by the authority of an indissoluble sanction is thought capable of being dissolved without knowledge, it is therefore fitting that whatever arises as an uncertain matter should be clearly rejected, so that thereafter nothing remains whose certainty may waver.

Accordingly, if, while their children are of any minor age, either one or both parents give children of either sex the religious tonsure or the clothing proper to religion, and, although unwilling or unaware that they have received it, do not promptly renounce it in their children, but allow those children to retain such things either in their presence or before the Church and publicly in the assembly, those children shall never afterward be permitted to return to secular dress. Once it has been established that they have at some time had the tonsure or religious clothing, they shall immediately be recalled to religion, its observance, and its habit, and compelled to serve under the strict discipline of this observance.

[Col. 0791D]

While the parents are of sound mind, they may give their children to religion only up to the children’s twelfth year. After that, it shall be lawful for the children to assume the religious observance, whether the individual vow is made by their parents’ will or by their own devotion.

Whoever is discovered to have committed a transgression by abolishing the tonsure or assuming secular clothing shall receive the penalty of excommunication and shall always remain attached to religion.

[Col. 0792C]

## Chapter 2 — On Virgins Who Have Voluntarily, and Not under Compulsion from Their Parents, Assumed the Religious Habit

(From the decree of Pope Leo, chapter 17.) Girls who, not compelled by their parents’ authority but by their own voluntary judgment, have assumed the commitment and habit of virginity, transgress if they afterward choose marriage, even if the grace of consecration has not yet been conferred upon them. They would certainly not have been deprived of that grace had they remained in their commitment.

[Col. 0792D]

## Chapter 3 — On Those Who Have Tonsured and Veiled Themselves before the Lawful Age

(From the Council of Mainz, attended by Emperor Charles and Archbishop Riculf, in the cloister of Saint Alban, chapter 20.) If anyone has been tonsured before the lawful age without the consent of his parents, and if those parents have not, within a year, lodged a complaint with the ruler, their own bishop, or the lord’s messenger, he shall remain in the clergy.

But if someone has been made a cleric by force after the lawful age, and no complaint has been lodged within a year with the persons mentioned above, he shall remain in the clergy just as the one mentioned earlier. If, however, the persons named above have lodged a complaint within the year, those who made them clerics shall legally compensate them or their parents for what they have incurred against them.

As for the person tonsured before the lawful age, whether he should remain in the same tonsure shall be in the power of his parents. If the tonsured person was someone’s slave, his master shall legally be compensated for whatever has been done against him concerning his slave. Whether the tonsured person remains in the same tonsure shall be in the power of his master.

But if those who are free, whether before or after the lawful age, have been tonsured in the manner specified above and have advanced to ecclesiastical orders, they shall be compelled to remain in those orders. If a slave tonsured in the manner specified above has advanced to ecclesiastical orders, his master shall be legally compensated, and, once returned to him, the slave shall remain in his order.

The same rule is to be observed concerning girls who are to be veiled.

[Col. 0793B]

## Chapter 4 — On Those Who Have Once Been Assigned to the Clergy or Have Sought the Life of Monks

(From the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 7.) Those who have once been assigned to the clergy or have sought the life of monks shall, we decree, neither enter military service nor attain any worldly dignity. Those who attempt this and do not do penance, and thus refuse to return to what they originally chose for God’s sake, shall be anathematized.

[Col. 0793C]

## Chapter 5 — That Canons Who Live in a Monastery of Monks Should Either Live as Monks or Be Bound by the Canonical Rule

(From the Council of Mainz, chapter 17.) We order that each bishop know, in each monastery, how many canons each abbot has in his monastery, and that both of them take complete care that, if the canons wish to become monks, they live according to the rule; otherwise, they should live entirely according to the canons’ rule.

## Chapter 6 — That a Man Is Made a Monk Either by His Father’s Devotion or by His Own Profession

(From the Council of Toledo, chapter 49.) A man is made a monk either by his father’s devotion or by his own profession. Whichever of these has occurred binds him. Therefore we close off for such persons the avenue of returning to the world and forbid all return to the secular life.

[Col. 0793D]

## Chapter 7 — On Clerics Who Pretend to Be Monks

(From the same council.) Clerics who pretend by habit and name to be monks, although they are not, must be corrected and reformed in every way, so that they may be either true monks or true canons.

## Chapter 8 — That a Monk May Not Change a Voluntary Commitment

(From the decree of Pope Leo, chapter 26.) A monk’s commitment, assumed by his own judgment or will, cannot be abandoned without sin. For what one has vowed to God one must also render. Therefore, whoever has abandoned his profession of solitude and turned to military service or marriage must be cleansed by making satisfaction through public penance. For although military service may be innocent and marriage honorable, abandoning the better choice is a transgression.

[Col. 0794A]

## Chapter 9 — That a Monk May Not Make a Vow without the Knowledge of His Abbot

(From the sayings of Basil.) A monk may not make a vow without the consent of his abbot. If he does vow, the vow must be broken.

## Chapter 10 — On Virgins Who Have Imposed the Veil upon Themselves before Twelve Years of Age without the Knowledge of Their Guardians (Mundburds)

(From the Council of Tribur, chapter 10.) Virgins who, before the age of twelve and without the knowledge of their guardians (mundburds), have placed the sacred veil upon their heads, and whose guardians have consented by remaining silent for a year and a day, shall remain in their holy commitment.

If, however, during that year and day they lodge a complaint on their behalf, their petition shall be granted—unless, perhaps, moved by fear of God, they continue in the religious habit with their permission.

[Col. 0794B]

## Chapter 11 — That Clerics May Not Be Received by Another Church from the Church in Which They Have Once Read

(From the African Council, chapter 57.) It was likewise decreed that whoever has read even once in a church shall not be held by another church for the clerical office.

## Chapter 12 — On Virgins Not Yet Veiled Who Nevertheless Have Professed That They Remain in the Virginal Commitment

(From the decree of Pope Innocent, chapter 20.) Those women who, although not yet covered by the sacred veil, have nevertheless always professed that they remain in the virginal commitment, if they should happen to marry, are to be recalled and must do penance, even if they have not been veiled, because their pledge was held by the Lord.

For if the Apostle said that those who departed from the commitment of widowhood incurred condemnation because they made their first faith void, how much more must this apply to virgins who have attempted to break faith with their earlier promise?

[Col. 0794C]

## Chapter 13 — On Religious Women Who Have Deviated from Their Sacred Commitment

(From the decree of the same pope, chapter 19.) Women who marry Christ spiritually, if they afterward marry publicly or secretly corrupt themselves, are not to be admitted to perform penance unless the man to whom they joined themselves has departed from the world.

For if this principle is observed concerning human beings—that any woman who marries another while her husband is alive is considered an adulteress and is not granted permission to do penance unless one of the two has died—how much more must it be maintained concerning a woman who had previously joined herself to an immortal bridegroom and afterward transferred herself to human marriage?

[Col. 0794D]

## Chapter 14 — On the Same Matter

(From the Council of Toledo.) For sacred men and women who transgress their commitment, the course from the will toward vice is easy, and nature imitates vices. Therefore, whoever among men or women has once put on, or has voluntarily put on, the religious habit, or if a man has been committed to the bridal chamber of the Church, or if a woman is, or has been, assigned to a monastery of girls, shall, in either sex, if a transgressor, be compelled against his or her will to return to the commitment: the man shall be tonsured, and the girl shall enter the monastery.

[Col. 0795A]

If they wish to persist as deserters under any protection, they shall by priestly judgment be regarded as exiles from the assembly of Christians, so that they may have no place in common with them.

The universal synod long ago likewise decreed concerning widows who desert their profession or habit that they are to be condemned by the preceding judgment.

## Chapter 15 — At What Time the Sacred Veil Should Be Imposed upon Holy Virgins

(From the decree of Pope Gelasius, chapter 12.) The sacred veil should not be imposed upon devoted virgins except on the Epiphany, during the Easter octave, or on the feast days of the apostles, and not before the age of twenty-five—unless, as has been said concerning baptism, they are afflicted by serious illness, so that the gift should not be denied to those who request it lest they depart from the world without receiving it.

[Col. 0795B]

## Chapter 16 — On the Same Matter

(From the Council of Milevis, chapter 26.) It was likewise decreed that if any bishop, because the modesty of a virgin is endangered—when a powerful suitor or an abductor is feared—or if she has at some time been troubled by the dangerous fear of death, lest she die unveiled, or if her parents or those responsible for her care require it, veils a virgin before her twenty-fifth year, the decision established concerning that number of years shall not harm him.

## Chapter 17 — On Religious Women Who Presume to Veil Others

(From the decree of Pope Eutychian, chapter 13.) We have nevertheless found in certain places an established practice full of folly and contrary to ecclesiastical authority: some abbesses and some widowed religious women and virgin girls presume, contrary to law, to impose the veil.

As a result, some women who have been veiled unjustly think that they may more freely serve their carnal desires and fulfill their wishes. Therefore we decree that if an abbess or any religious woman, after this definition, should burst into such audacity as to presume to veil either a widow or a virgin girl, she shall be subjected to canonical judgment until satisfaction has been made.

[Col. 0795C]

## Chapter 18 — At What Age Virgins Should Be Veiled

(From the decree of Pope Pius.) Virgins are not to be veiled before the age of twenty-five, except in a case of endangered virgin modesty. They are not to be consecrated at any other time than the Epiphany, during the Easter octave, or on the feast days of the apostles, unless the urgency of death requires it.

[Col. 0795D]

## Chapter 19 — That It Is Not Lawful to Give a Betrothed Girl to Another Man, but That She May Choose a Monastery If She Wishes

(From the decree of Pope Eusebius, chapter 10.) Parents may not give a betrothed girl to another man; nevertheless, she may choose a monastery if she wishes.

## Chapter 20 — That an Unknown Person Should Not Quickly Be Received into a Monastery of Monks

(From the Council of Toledo, chapter 5.) If an unknown person wishes to enter a monastery, the monastic habit shall not be granted to him before three years have passed.

If, within the three years, his master seeks him as a slave, freedman, or tenant, he shall be returned to him with everything he brought, provided that an assurance of immunity from punishment has been received. If he is not sought within the three-year period, he may not afterward be sought, unless he is so far away that he cannot be found. The master of the slave shall receive only what the slave brought into the monastery.

[Col. 0796A]

## Chapter 21 — On Clerics Who Desire the Monastic Commitment

(From the same council, chapter 50.) Clerics who desire the monastic commitment and wish to follow the better life ought to be granted free entry into monasteries by the bishops, and their commitment should not be obstructed when they strive to pass over to the desire for contemplation.

## Chapter 22 — On Sacred Virgins Who Decide to Go to Another Monastery for a Stricter Life

[Col. 0796B]

(From the Council of Tribur, chapter 11.) If sacred virgins decide, for the profit of their souls and for a stricter life, to go to another monastery and resolve to remain there, the synod grants permission. But if they seek another place in order to escape discipline, they shall be compelled to return.

## Chapter 23 — In What Clothing Virgins Should Come for Consecration

(From the Council of Carthage, chapter 11.) When a religious virgin is presented to her bishop for consecration, she shall come in such clothing as she will always use, suitable to her profession and religious status.

## Chapter 24 — That a Slave May Not Become a Monk without the Knowledge of His Master

[Col. 0796C]

(From the Council of Arles, chapter 4.) It was decreed that in monasteries a slave is not to be received to be made a monk without the will of his own master. We decree that whoever transgresses this regulation be suspended from communion, lest the name of the Lord be blasphemed.

## Chapter 25 — On One Who Teaches Another’s Slave to Despise His Master for the Sake of Religion

(From the Council of Braga, chapter 47.) If anyone teaches another’s slave, for the sake of religion, to despise his master and withdraw from his service, he shall be severely rebuked in every respect and compelled to do penance.

## Chapter 26 — On Fugitive Clerics

(From the decree of Pope Leo.) It has been decreed that a fugitive cleric, or a monk who abandons discipline, should be recalled as a contemner.

[Col. 0796D]

## Chapter 27 — On Laypeople Who, after Once Receiving the Tonsure through Religion, Later Become Laymen

(From the Fifth Council of Toledo, chapter 5.) Whoever among laypeople, after receiving penance, has been tonsured and then, transgressing again, has become a layman shall, once apprehended by his bishop, be recalled to the penance from which he departed.

If some who are irrevocable through their power do not return even after admonition, they shall truly be condemned before the Church as apostates by the sentence of anathema.

The same applies to those who, with their parents’ approval, have been tonsured, devoted themselves to religion, and afterward assumed secular clothing. Once apprehended by a priest, they shall be recalled to the religious life after first performing penance. If they do not wish to return, they shall truly be subjected to the sentence of anathema as apostates.

This rule shall also be observed for widows, sacred virgins, and women doing penance who have put on the habit of religious women and afterward either changed their clothing or turned to marriage.

[Col. 0797A]

## Chapter 28 — That a Slave Should Not Be Received into a Monastery without His Master’s Knowledge

(From the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 4.) It is not lawful to receive any slave into monasteries under the pretext of making him a monk without the knowledge of his master.

## Chapter 29 — On Monks and Nuns Who Have Mingled in Sacrilegious Intercourse

[The supplied source ends here, incomplete after this heading.]

(From a letter of Pope Siricius, chapter 6.) We command that immodest [Col. 0797B] and detestable persons—namely, monks and nuns who, having cast aside their resolve to holiness, have joined themselves in illicit and sacrilegious intercourse and, driven to the brink of despair in conscience, have freely begotten children from their unlawful embraces—be expelled from the company of monasteries and from the assemblies of the churches, so that, shut away in their prisons, and lamenting such a great crime in continual mourning, they may be purified and refined in the cleansing fire of their fullness, in order that, at least at the hour of death, they may receive help through the grace of communion, out of regard for mercy alone.

**CHAPTER 30.—That those consecrated to God may not contract marital unions.**

(From the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 16.) A virgin who has consecrated herself to the Lord God, and likewise a monk, may not [Col. 0797C] contract a marital union. If they are found to have perpetrated this, let them be excommunicated. For those who confess, however, we have decreed that the bishop of the same place may grant mercy and humane consideration.

**CHAPTER 31.—Concerning those who have taken nuns in marriage, so that, once separated, they may remain without hope of marriage.**

(From a letter of Pope Paschasius, chapter 11.) Those, therefore, who knowingly have been joined in marriage to religious women, to Christ’s dishonor, shall be separated according to the judgment of Christian zeal; and they shall never be permitted to be bound again by the matrimonial bond. Rather, throughout their lives, they shall be severely afflicted by the lamentations of penance.

**CHAPTER 32.—Concerning virgins who have transgressed.**

[Col. 0797D]

(From a decree of Pope Gelasius, chapter 10.) We have learned that certain men have rashly joined themselves to consecrated virgins and, after a resolve dedicated to God, have entered into incestuous and sacrilegious unions. It is immediately just that such men be cast out from sacred communion and not be received at all except through a public and approved penance; nevertheless, the viaticum shall not be denied to those who are passing from this world, if they have duly repented.

**CHAPTER 33.—That widows should not put on the veil without consulting their bishop, and that presbyters should not presume to veil them, since bishops also may not do so.**

(From the Council of Rouen, chapter 9.) It has been decreed that widows should not veil themselves without consulting their bishop. It has likewise been decreed that if henceforth any presbyter should obstinately transgress the norm of this constitution [Col. 0798A]—namely, if he presumes to veil any widows—he shall incur the danger of his rank, since even bishops are not permitted to do this. Similarly, it has been decreed concerning girls who are virgins, that they are not to be veiled by presbyters: if anyone attempts to do this, let him be condemned as a transgressor of the canons.

**CHAPTER 34.—That widows are to be veiled under no blessing.**

(From a decree of Pope Gelasius, chapter 21.) Concerning veiling widows under no blessing, we have already undertaken to speak at greater length above. If, by their own will, they have trampled with changeable minds upon the chastity of their former marriage, which they had professed, it will be their concern what satisfaction they must offer to appease God. For just as, if perhaps they were unable to remain continent, [Col. 0798B] they were in no way forbidden by the Apostle to marry, so, after deliberation with themselves, they ought to have guarded the pledge of chastity promised to God. We, however, must impose no snare upon such women, but must set before them only exhortations concerning eternal reward and the punishments of divine judgment, so that our conscience may be free of blame and their intention may give an account to God on their behalf. Indeed, one must beware of what the blessed Apostle Paul testifies concerning their conduct and actions; we refrain from explaining it more clearly, lest the unstable sex should appear to be admonished rather than deterred.

**CHAPTER 35.—Concerning widows who once receive the veil of sacred conduct.**

(From the Council of Orléans, chapter 3.) Concerning widows who, by their own free will, receive from the altar the veil of sacred conduct, the holy synod decreed that they must remain in that same [Col. 0798C] resolve. For we do not judge it lawful that, after they have once consecrated themselves to the Lord under the veil and have made offerings among the veiled women, they should again be permitted to lie to the Holy Spirit.

**CHAPTER 36.—Concerning widows: no one is to veil them.**

(From the Council of Mainz, chapter 6.) Let no one attempt to veil widows, as has been established in the decrees of Gelasius, chapter 13, since neither divine authority nor the rule of the canons has granted this. If a widow has professed continence by her own will, as is read in the same chapter 21 of Gelasius, her intention must give an account to God on her behalf. For just as, according to the Apostle, if she could not remain continent she was in no way forbidden to marry, so, after deliberation with herself, [Col. 0798D] she ought to guard the pledge of chastity promised to God. We, however, supported by the authority of the Fathers, enact and freely judge in this sacred assembly that if she has voluntarily placed a veil upon herself, even if it has not been consecrated, and has offered an oblation to God in the church among the veiled women, she must thereafter retain the habit of religious consecration, whether she wishes it or not, even if she wishes to confirm by oath that she placed the veil upon herself on the understanding and for the purpose that she might later remove it.

**CHAPTER 37.—Concerning noblewomen who, after being veiled, delight in remaining at home in luxury.**

(From the council held at Aachen in the presence of Louis the Pious, chapter 6.) Concerning noblewomen who, after losing their husbands, are suddenly veiled and delight in remaining in their own homes, alleging various necessities—women [Col. 0799A] about whom the matter was discussed and settled long ago in other assemblies before your Serenity—we decree that the bishops must admonish and instruct them with greater and diligent care, so that they may attend to their salvation and not, by living so indiscriminately, using their own harmful freedom, and wandering about in various places, incur danger to their souls. Let them always have before their eyes that apostolic saying: “The widow who lives in luxury is dead while she lives.”

**CHAPTER 38.—Concerning those who have taken veiled and consecrated women into marriage.**

(From the Council of Orléans, chapter 23.) If anyone takes into marriage a woman consecrated under the sacred veil and, after a resolve dedicated to God, enters into an incestuous and sacrilegious union, as is read in the constitutions of Pope Gelasius, [Col. 0799B] chapter 20, it is immediately just that he be cast out from sacred communion and not be received at all except through a public and approved penance. If, however, they repent, the viaticum shall not be denied to those passing from this world. At the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 16, those who perpetrate this are excommunicated. To those who confess, mercy is granted by the authority of the bishop.

In the letter of Pope Siricius, chapter 6, it was judged that veiled and consecrated women who, having cast aside their resolve to holiness, secretly joined themselves in sacrilegious intercourse and publicly and freely begot children from unlawful embraces should be expelled from the company of monasteries and from the assemblies of the churches, so that, shut away in prisons, they might lament such a great crime in continual mourning. Therefore, by the word of the Lord and by canonical [Col. 0799C] authority, we command in this holy synod that they be entirely separated and bound by oath never again to live under one roof, to enjoy familiar conversation, or to have any common possession, except in church or in public, from which a suspicion of enticing desire or a scandal arising from a lustful act might justly emerge. If they have anything to divide between them, let them divide it, and let each provide for himself or herself; and let the incestuous man remain without hope of marriage.

**CHAPTER 39.—Concerning widows who have transgressed their professed continence.**

(From the Council of Carthage, chapter 104.) Concerning widows who have transgressed the continence they professed: just as the reward of chastity is good, so it must be guarded with greater observance and injunction, so that if any [Col. 0799D] widows—although still of young age and left by a husband at a mature age—have devoted themselves to God, and, casting aside secular clothing, have appeared in religious dress under the testimony of the bishop and the Church, but afterward have entered into secular marriages, they may, according to the Apostle, incur condemnation, because they are seen to have made void the pledge of chastity that they vowed to God.

Such persons, therefore, shall be separated from the communion of Christians, and they shall not even share a meal with Christians. For if adulterous wives are guilty when they have been subject to their husbands, how much more will widows who have changed God’s religious devotion be marked by the crime of adultery if, by a lustful will, they have corrupted the devotion that they freely and without compulsion offered to God [Col. 0800A] and have proceeded to a second marriage? Even if, after being seized and overpowered by violence, they later consent to remain married to their rapist or violent husband because the pleasure of lust persists, they shall remain subject to the condemnation stated above. Concerning such women the Apostle says: “When they have become wanton, they wish to marry in Christ, bearing condemnation because they have made void their first faith.”

**CHAPTER 40.—On the same matter.**

(From a decree of Pope Zephyrinus, chapter 4.) Widows are not to live in luxury but, according to the Apostle, are to live under the authority of the bishop.

**CHAPTER 41.—On the same matter.**

(The Apostle says.) “Command,” he says, “that widows be irreproachable. Let a widow be chosen who is not less than forty years old, [Col. 0800B] having a testimony of good works, if she has raised children,” and so forth. “Avoid younger widows. For when they have become wanton, they wish to marry in Christ, bearing condemnation because they have made void their first faith, and at the same time they are idle, speaking what they ought not. Therefore I wish younger women to marry, bear children, and be heads of households, giving the adversary no occasion for slander. For some have already turned back after Satan.”

**CHAPTER 42.—Concerning women whose husbands have died, that they should not be veiled quickly.**

(From the Council of Orléans, chapter 5.) Concerning women who lose their husbands, it is agreed that they should not, as hitherto, veil themselves indiscriminately, but should wait thirty days after their husband’s death. After the thirtieth day, with the advice [Col. 0800C] of their bishop—or, if the bishop is absent, with the advice of other religious priests and of their friends—let them choose what they ought to choose. We have also decreed that the prince be petitioned by the sacred assembly to protect, by his authority, those who have performed public penance and women who lose their husbands until they decide what they should do, and that special chapters be drawn up concerning them and inserted into the chapters of secular law.

**CHAPTER 43.—That a profession of widowhood is to be made before the bishop.**

(From the Council of Orange, chapter 6.) We decree that a profession of preserving widowhood, made before the bishop in the secretarium, with the widow’s garment placed upon her before the bishop, is not to be violated, and that a woman who abandons such a profession is deservedly to be condemned.

**CHAPTER 44.—That no one may forbid or command widows or virgins to marry.**

[Col. 0800D]

(From the Council of Toledo, chapter 10.) For the considered purpose of chastity, which ought especially to be advanced by the encouragement of the council, and with our glorious lord King Reccared giving his assent, this holy council affirms that widows who wish to preserve chastity are not to be compelled by any force to marry again. If, before they profess continence, they choose to marry, let them marry those whom they freely choose to have as husbands. The same condition is to apply to virgins: they are not to be compelled to take husbands against the will of their parents or against their own will. But if anyone obstructs the resolve of chastity of a widow or virgin, let him be regarded as an outsider to holy communion and to the thresholds of the church.

**CHAPTER 45.—Concerning widows who abandon their resolve.**

[Col. 0801A]

(From a letter of Pope Gregory sent to Boniface.) Concerning widows who depart from their resolve of widowhood, about whom your affection, dearest brother, wished to consult us, I believe you know from Saint Paul and from many holy Fathers that they have long been condemned unless they convert. We likewise judge that they must be condemned by apostolic authority and barred from the communion of the faithful and from the thresholds of the church until they obey their bishops and, willingly or unwillingly, return to the good work that they began.

Concerning unveiled virgins who have gone astray, we have the following decree from our predecessor, Pope Innocent of holy memory: “Those who have not yet been covered by the sacred veil, but have always pretended to remain in a virginal resolve—although they have not been veiled—[Col. 0801B] if they marry, must perform penance for a considerable period, because their pledge was held by the Lord. For if among human beings a good-faith contract is ordinarily dissolved for no reason at all, how much more will this promise, which she made with God, be unable to be dissolved without punishment?” and so forth.

For if un veiled virgins are punished by such public penance and excluded from the company of the faithful until satisfaction, how much more must widows, who possess more perfect age and more mature wisdom and judgment, who have many times experienced the company of men, who have assumed the habit of religion, and who afterward have apostatized and returned to their former vomit, be expelled by us and by all the faithful from the thresholds of the church and from the company of the faithful until satisfaction, [Col. 0801C] and be handed over to prisons, so that, in accordance with the blessed Apostle Paul, “we may hand such a person over to Satan, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord”?

Concerning such persons the Lord also speaks through Moses, saying: “Remove the evil from your midst.” Concerning them the Prophet also says: “The righteous man will rejoice when he sees vengeance; he will wash his hands in the sinner’s blood.” Concerning such persons, their like, and those who consent to them, it is said: “Not only those who do these things, but also those who consent to those who do them, are guilty.”

**CHAPTER 46.—That veiled widows should not go to marriage.**

(From the decree of Pope Gelasius sent to the bishops of Sicily [Col. 0801D], chapter 9.) We do not permit widows to proceed to marriage who have remained for a long time in a religious resolve. Similarly, we forbid virgins to marry if they have happened to spend many years of their lives in monasteries.

**CHAPTER 47.—Concerning a widow who placed a veil upon herself temporarily under the pretext of religion.**

(From a letter of Pope Nicholas, chapter 5.) Nicholas, bishop and servant of the servants of God, to our most reverend and holy fellow-bishop Adalwin, archbishop of the holy Church of Vivenna.

You asked about a woman who, after her husband’s death, placed a sacred veil upon her head and pretended to be a nun under that veil, but afterward returned to marriage. It seems good to me that, since she wished through [Col. 0802A] hypocrisy to disturb ecclesiastical regulation and did not legitimately remain in her vow, she should do penance for this wicked deception and return to what she promised and began in the sacred ministry.

For if we agree that each person may pretend to perform all ecclesiastical sacraments as he or she wishes and need not truly perform them, the whole ecclesiastical order is thrown into confusion, the rights of the Catholic faith do not stand, and the sacred canons are not properly observed. What benefit did Simon Magus gain from fictitiously receiving sacred baptism and pretending that he would remain in Christianity, when, after his fraud was exposed through the Apostle, what would happen to him was foretold? For he says: “Your money be with you for destruction; for your heart is not right before God. Therefore repent of this wickedness of yours and pray to God [Col. 0802B] that perhaps this thought of your heart may be forgiven you. For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and in the bondage of iniquity.”

Therefore, unless such people repent, we judge that they must be struck with the spiritual sword. For it is not lawful to lie to the Holy Spirit, as Ananias and Sapphira lied and immediately perished.

**CHAPTER 48.—Concerning widows and girls who have assumed the religious habit in their own homes.**

(From the Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 57.) Concerning widows and girls who have changed their habit to a religious one in their own homes, whether by their parents’ action or on their own, if afterward they believe that marriages may be contracted contrary to the institutions of the Fathers or the commands of the canons, let both parties remain suspended from communion for as long as they neglect [Col. 0802C] to correct what they have illicitly perpetrated; and let them be permanently separated from communion and from the meals of all Christians.

**CHAPTER 49.—That Saint Gregory ordered a veiled woman who had transgressed her sacred resolve to be seized.**

(From Gregory’s Register, to Bishop Sepontius.) If you had been a guardian of the religious habit, or knew how to be a bishop, while you were there you would not have allowed the daughter of Tullianus, master of the soldiers, of glorious memory, to cast aside her religious garments and return to secular dress, nor would you have permitted her to send us a perverse letter. But because you are oppressed by excessive laziness and torpor, an illicit matter has now been committed with impunity, to your disgrace.

For, as we have said above, if you had been vigilant, the punishment of the most wicked woman ought to have reached us before her fault. [Col. 0802D] Since, therefore, you are so dull and so negligent that, unless you have experienced canonical correction of life, you do not know how to preserve strictness and discipline in other matters, we shall show you, if it pleases the Lord, at an appropriate time how vigilant you ought to be.

On receiving this present letter, therefore, wake up and, at least now aroused, carry out what, oppressed by sloth, you have delayed until now. Let it be your urgent task to seize the aforesaid woman together with Sergius the defensor and immediately not only to restore her, without any excuse, to the habit she has wickedly despised, but also to thrust her into a monastery where she can be kept under the strictest custody. Show such vigilance concerning her that, through your strict discipline, she may recognize how wicked is the crime she has committed.

If in this matter any layman should attempt, as we do not [Col. 0803A] believe will happen, to resist you by some stratagem, suspend him from participation in the most holy communion and hasten to report it to us, so that, since he did not perceive how execrable his presumption was through his own reflection, he may learn it through the character of his correction.

In all these matters, be so cautious, diligent, and vigilant that neglect does not double your fault, but that your concern may to some extent lessen it.

**CHAPTER 50.—Concerning veiled widows accused of serving the pleasures of the flesh.**

(From the Council of Meaux, chapter 2.) Those women who appear to live as nuns under the veil of religion, but rather live in luxury and are counted as dead in the eyes of God, wandering through the provinces, [Col. 0803B] curious and talkative, if they are accused of serving lust and other pleasures of the flesh, shall, if they can be openly exposed, be compelled by episcopal authority and royal power to reside in such places, under religious supervision, that, if they perform worthy penance, they may also attain fruitful results.

If they cannot be openly exposed, they shall be compelled canonically to purge before the Church the evil reputation of their opinion. They shall also be restrained by episcopal decree and royal power so that thereafter they may live more religiously and conduct themselves in monasteries. Concerning such women the Apostle also says: “When they have committed fornication, they wish to marry in Christ.”

**CHAPTER 51.—That those who have intercourse with consecrated women are to be judged sacrilegious.**

[Col. 0803C]

(From the Council of Arles, chapter 7.) Everyone should know that the bodies of women consecrated to God are, through the vow of their own pledge and the words of the priest, shown by the testimonies of Scripture to be temples consecrated to God; therefore those who violate them are known to be sacrilegious and, according to the Apostle, sons of perdition.

**CHAPTER 52.—Concerning those who abduct consecrated virgins or veiled widows.**

(From the Council of Meaux, chapter 8.) Those who abduct consecrated virgins or veiled widows and, as the crime progresses, take them in marriage shall be subjected to public penance. The women themselves shall be shut away in suitable places of penance and compelled to return to the religious habit. The incestuous man, however, shall remain forever without hope of a marital [Col. 0803D] union, unless he can clear himself by proving that he did not know she was veiled. But if, God forbid, they presume to renew the marriage, they shall be subjected to a more severe punishment and expelled still further. If they should perhaps refuse to obey salutary admonitions, let them be anathematized.

**CHAPTER 53.—That clerics or laymen should speak with consecrated girls in the presence of reputable witnesses.**

(From the Council of Seville, chapter 10.) Let this precaution be observed concerning everyone: laymen must keep apart from private association with virgins and must not be granted familiar permission even to approach the vestibule. Nor should the superior speak with one of them alone; he must do so in the presence of two or three sisters, so that visits may be rare and conversation brief.

**CHAPTER 54.—That veiled women are to observe their habit in monasteries or in their own homes.**

[Col. 0804A]

(From a decree of Pope Eugenius, chapter 28.) Women veiled under the pretext of religion must either live regularly in a monastery or chastely observe the habit they have assumed in their own homes.

**CHAPTER 55.—That younger widows or nuns are not to be neglected by the bishop.**

(From the Council of Carthage, chapter 102.) It is counted as the guilt of the bishop, or of the presbyter who presides over the parish, if younger widows or nuns who are supported by the Church for the sake of their present life are subjected to their familiar associations.

**CHAPTER 56.—That each bishop should make clerics wandering in his diocese return to their own bishop.**

[Col. 0804B]

(From the Council of Mainz, chapter 19.) Let each bishop diligently inquire in his parish concerning presbyters or clerics, asking where they are from. If he finds a fugitive, let him make him return to his own bishop.

**CHAPTER 57.—Concerning wandering clerics.**

(From the same council, chapter 18.) Concerning wandering clerics, or acephali—that is, those who are “without a head,” neither in the service of our Lord, nor under a bishop, nor under an abbot, but living without canonical or regular discipline—as is said of them in the second book of the *Book of Offices*, chapter 3:

“Neither among the laity and the pursuits of secular offices, nor among the clergy, does divine religion claim them; rather, a shameful and wandering life alone embraces them. Since they [Col. 0804C] fear no one, they pursue license to fulfill their pleasure, and are driven like brute animals by freedom and desire, possessing the sign of religion but not the office of religion, like hippocentaurs, neither horses nor men.”

We command that such men, wherever they are found, be immediately placed by the bishops under canonical custody and restraint, and that they in no way be permitted henceforth to live as errant and wandering men according to the desires of their pleasures. But if they refuse to obey their bishops canonically, let them be excommunicated until the judgment of the bishop of that region. If even that bishop is unable to correct them, let them be entirely bound in chains until the synod, so that there it may be determined whether they are to be brought before the judgment of the prince or before a universal synod, [Col. 0804D] under public custody.

**CHAPTER 58.—That nuns are to live in monastic and canonical discipline.**

(From the same council, attended by Emperor Charles and Archbishop Riculph, in the cloister of Saint Alban, chapter 13.) We judge that abbesses, together with the nuns, must live entirely rightly and justly. Those who have made their profession according to the rule of Saint Benedict are to live according to the rule. Otherwise, let them live fully according to canonical discipline, be kept under diligent care, and remain in their cloisters, without permission to go outside. The abbesses themselves, too, are to remain in the monasteries and not go outside without the permission and counsel of their bishop.

**CHAPTER 59.—That nuns must be obedient to their abbess.**

[Col. 0805A]

(From the same council, chapter 14.) Nuns are not to leave the monastery at all, unless their abbess sends them because of some pressing necessity. Those who have no male or female servants may go as far as the middle monastery gate to conduct their business and may conduct it there in the presence of witnesses.

**CHAPTER 60.—Concerning women who change their habit on account of supposed continence.**

(From the Council of Gangra, chapter 13.) If any woman changes her habit on account of supposed continence and, instead of the customary woman’s clothing, adopts a man’s dress, let her be anathema.

**CHAPTER 61.—Concerning one who preserves virginity but condemns marriage.**

[Col. 0805B]

(From the same council, chapter 9.) Whoever, while preserving virginity or pursuing continence, violates marriage as though abhorring it, and does not assume the name of virginity because it is good and holy, let him be anathema.

**CHAPTER 62.—Concerning women who cut their hair on account of religion.**

(From the same council, chapter 17.) If any woman cuts her hair on account of divine worship, as she supposes, although God gave it to her as a reminder of subjection, let her be anathema, as though dissolving the commandment of obedience.

**CHAPTER 63.—Concerning those who wear cloaks on account of supposed continence.**

[Col. 0805C]

(From the Council of Chalon, chapter 12.) If any man, on account of supposed continence, wears a cloak as a garment, believing that by this he possesses righteousness, and despises those who with reverence wear *birri* and other ordinary and customary clothing, let him be anathema.

**CHAPTER 64.—Concerning those who observe virginity and are thereby exalted.**

(From the same council, chapter 10.) If anyone among those who preserve virginity for God exalts himself against married people, let him be anathema.

**CHAPTER 65.—That monks and nuns must not be permitted to live together in one monastery.**

(From the register of Pope Gregory.) We do not permit monks and nuns to have one monastery [Col. 0805D] in any place, nor even those establishments that they call double monasteries, if any such exist. A religious bishop must see to it that the women remain in their own place, while he compels the monks to build another monastery. If there are many such monasteries, let the nuns be separated into some monasteries and the monks into others. The possessions they hold in common are to be distributed according to the rights belonging to them.

**CHAPTER 66.—That the bishop should frequently visit the monasteries of monks and nuns.**

(From the Council of Rouen, chapter 3.) The bishop is to enter frequently into the monasteries of monks and nuns. Sitting with serious and religious persons and in their assemblies, he is to examine their life and conduct carefully and, if he finds anything blameworthy [Col. 0806A], strive to correct it. He is also to investigate the chastity of the nuns with precision. If any woman is found who, having neglected her resolve of chastity, shamelessly joins herself to a cleric or layman, she is to be shut away in private custody, where she may duly repent of what she has done wrong.

He must also prohibit, by the authority of the holy canons, any layman or cleric from having access to their cloisters and private dwellings. Presbyters likewise are not to enter except for Mass; once Mass is completed, they must return to their own churches. Moreover, he must publicly and privately declare how great a sacrilege it is for anyone to presume to violate Christ’s bride. For if the man who violates a human bride is held guilty, how much more does he become guilty of an offense against majesty who corrupts the bride of almighty God?

**CHAPTER 67.—That abbots are to remain under the authority of bishops.**

[Col. 0806B]

(From the Council of Orléans, chapter 4.) Abbots are to remain under the authority of bishops for the sake of religious humility, and if they do anything outside the rule, they are to be corrected by the bishops. Bishops are to visit the monasteries of monks not once but several times a year, and, if anything requires correction, they are to correct it. Monks, however, are to submit to their abbots with all obedience and devotion. If anyone, through defiance, proves disloyal and presumes either to wander from place to place or to possess anything privately, everything he has acquired is to be taken away by the abbots for the benefit of the monastery, according to the rule. Those who have wandered about are to be brought back and restrained under custody wherever they are found, with the help of the bishop, like fugitives [Col. 0806C].

**CHAPTER 68.—Concerning monks who have begotten children.**

(From the sayings of Saint Isidore.) Monks who beget children are to be shut up in prison, lamenting such a great crime in continual mourning, so that, at least at the hour of death, mercy alone may grant them forgiveness through the grace of communion.

**CHAPTER 69.—Concerning nuns who have suffered barbarian violence.**

(From a decree of Pope Leo, chapter 49.) Concerning those who, established in the sacred resolve of virginity, suffered barbarian violence and lost the integrity of their chastity not in intention but in body, it seems to us that this moderation should be observed: they are neither to be cast down to the rank of widows nor counted among sacred virgins who have persevered. If they [Col. 0806D] persevere in all the observances of virgins and preserve the firmness of chastity in mind, communion in the sacraments is not to be denied them, because it is unjust that they should be blamed or marked for what their will did not admit but hostile force took away.

**CHAPTER 70.—Concerning an abbess who complained about soldiers lodging in her cloister.**

(From Gregory’s Register, to Fortunatus, bishop of Naples, chapter 112.) The bearer of this letter, Abbess Agnella, has informed us that soldiers are lodging inside her monastery. We are altogether astonished at the concern shown by your Fraternity: why have you tolerated this patiently and not had it corrected with all speed? Therefore we urge you that even now it be your earnest concern to press [Col. 0807A] those responsible, so that the soldiers may be removed from there without any excuse, that no one may thereafter be granted access there, and that the crafty enemy, finding an opportunity, may not—God forbid!—be able to exult in the deception of the religious habit.

**CHAPTER 71.—That ecclesiastical possessions do not belong to laymen to administer.**

(From the Council held at Compiègne, chapter 10.) It has been established by synodal decree that laymen or secular persons must not think or presume that anything belonging to the men dedicated to God or to the resources of the Church pertains to them, beyond what is due to reverence. It is taught that God has indisputably entrusted the care of administering all such things to the priests. If anyone presumes to act against this, let him be struck with anathema.

**CHAPTER 72.—On the same matter.**

[Col. 0807B]

(From the same council, chapter 3.) No authority is ever recorded as having been granted to laymen, even religious laymen, to administer anything belonging to men dedicated to God or to ecclesiastical resources.

**CHAPTER 73.—That abbots are not to be compelled to attend a synod except for a reasonable cause.**

(From the Council of Tours, chapter 11.) A bishop must not compel an abbot to attend a synod unless some reasonable cause exists.

**CHAPTER 74.—That monastic communities may not be established without the bishop’s approval.**

(From the Council of Épaone, chapter 10.) We prohibit the establishment of new cells or small communities of monks without the bishop’s knowledge.

**CHAPTER 75.—Concerning consecrated virgins who are deprived of their parents.**

[Col. 0807C]

(From the African Council, chapter 11.) If consecrated virgins are deprived of the parents who were protecting them, they are to be protected by the bishop. Where the bishop is absent, they are to be entrusted to the care of more serious women, so that, living together, they may protect one another and not, by wandering about indiscriminately, damage the reputation of the Church.

**CHAPTER 76.—Who is to be placed over religious women.**

(From the Council of Carthage, chapter 97.) The person who is to be placed over religious women is to be approved by the bishop.

**CHAPTER 77.—Concerning what nuns should do in the cloister.**

[Col. 0807D]

(From the Council of Mainz, chapter 6.) Nuns established in a monastery are to devote themselves to reading and singing, and together solemnly celebrate the canonical hours. All are to sleep in the dormitory, except those whom illness prevents, and every day they are to come to the chapter meeting and to the conferences. They are to observe diligently the rule established for them by the holy Fathers.

**CHAPTER 78.—No layman is to enter the cloisters of nuns except to perform work.**

(From the same council, chapter 16.) No vassal of the abbess, nor any servant, cleric, or layman is to enter the cloisters of the handmaids of God, except perhaps when the necessity of performing work arises.

**CHAPTER 79.—The doorkeeper of the cloister is not to be chosen unless she has a good reputation.**

[Col. 0808A]

(From the same council, chapter 15.) A portress is not to be chosen unless she is mature in age, has a good reputation, and is of commendable life.

**CHAPTER 80.—That an abbess may not leave the monastery without her bishop’s permission.**

(From the Council of Gangra, chapter 9.) An abbess is not to leave the monastery at all without the permission of her bishop. Whenever she goes outside, she must take the greatest care of the nuns whom she leads with her, so that no opportunity for sin is given to them.

**CHAPTER 81.—That one abbot should not preside over two monasteries.**

(From the Council of Orange, chapter 54.) We forbid one abbot to preside over two monasteries.

**CHAPTER 82.—That monks should not have godparents.**

[Col. 0808B]

(From the Council of Autun, chapter 5.) Monks or nuns must not presume to have godparents.

**CHAPTER 83.—That women should not teach in an assembly.**

(From the Council of Carthage.) A woman, however learned she may be, must not presume to teach in an assembly.

**CHAPTER 84.—That a woman should neither administer penance nor sit among priests at a meal.**

(From the Council of Reims, in the presence of Emperor Louis, chapter 5.) A woman must not administer penance, nor place the corporal with the offering, nor place the chalice upon the altar, nor stand among the ordained in the church, nor sit among priests at a meal.

**CHAPTER 85.—Concerning women discussing men’s cases.**
### CAP. 85.—Concerning Women Discussing Men’s Cases

(From the Council of Nantes, chapter 8.) Since the Apostle says, “Let women keep silent in the church; for they are not permitted to speak. For it is shameful for a woman to speak in the church,” it seems astonishing that certain women, acting shamelessly and impudently, with brows hardened against divine and human laws, continually attend public assemblies and general meetings, and disturb rather than arrange the affairs of the kingdom and the interests of the commonwealth. For it is indecent—and even reprehensible among barbarian peoples—for women to discuss men’s cases. Matters that they ought to discuss while sitting among their fellow women, concerning their spinning, textile work, and women’s affairs, they instead debate in a public assembly, as though sitting in a courtroom, arrogating to themselves senatorial authority. [Col. 0808D]

This disgraceful presumption seems more chargeable to their supporters than to the women themselves. Therefore, since divine laws, as shown above, contradict this practice, and human laws likewise prohibit it—so that women may pursue nothing publicly except their own case—we forbid it by canonical authority. For the Theodosian Law says: “Women shall in no way have greater power to conduct proceedings than those concerning their own cases, nor shall they undertake to prosecute anyone else’s case.” Accordingly, we prohibit every consecrated virgin or widow from attending general assemblies unless summoned by the ruler or by her own bishop, except perhaps when the necessity of her own case compels her, and then only with the permission and message of her bishop.

### CAP. 86.—That an Abbot May Leave His Position as an Act of Humiliation

[Col. 0809A]

(From the Council of Mainz, chapter 18.) An abbot may, as an act of humiliation and with the bishop’s permission, leave his position. Nevertheless, the brothers shall choose an abbot for themselves from among their own number, if they have one suitable; otherwise, from outside. Nor should the bishop forcibly retain the abbot in his position. The community must choose an abbot for itself after the death of its abbot, or, while he is still alive, if he has departed or fallen into sin. For he cannot appoint any of his relatives or friends without the consent of the brothers.

### CAP. 87.—That a Layman Should Not Recite a Lesson in Church

(From the same council, chapter 19.) A layman should not recite a lesson in church, nor say the Alleluia, except that he may recite psalms and responsories without the Alleluia.

### CAP. 88.—That a Bishop May Not Take Away Monastery Property, Even Though the Abbot Has Sinned Against Him

(From the same council, chapter 20.) A bishop may not take away the property of a monastery, even though the abbot has sinned. Instead, he should send him to another monastery, under the authority of another abbot.

### CAP. 89.—That Monks Should Not Attend Secular Courts

(From the same council, chapter 21.) We then decreed, as the holy Rule says, that a monastery should, where possible, be organized under deans, because those placed in charge often fall into pride and into the devil’s snare. We emphatically require, however, that monks in no way come to secular courts, nor should the abbot himself go there without the permission of his bishop. If necessity requires it, he should go only by the order and advice of his bishop. Nevertheless, he must not presume to initiate any disputes or lawsuits there; whatever must be sought or answered, he should handle through his advocates.

Let abbots and monks remain silent until questioned, and when questioned let them answer with humility and reverence. They should avoid all other complaints. They shall remain in their cloister, and none of them shall go outside unless sent by the abbot in obedience because of necessity. No one shall eat or drink outside without the abbot’s permission, nor attend secular banquets.

### CAP. 90.—Concerning Secular Business

[Col. 0809D]

(From the same council, chapter 22.) We have determined that the ministers of the Lord’s altar and monks must abstain entirely from secular business. There are many kinds of secular business; let us nevertheless briefly indicate some of them. To these belong every form of lust—not only bodily impurity but every carnal desire; whatever a person desires beyond what is just is dishonest gain; accepting or giving unjust gifts for any secular profit; hiring someone for payment; loving disputes, lawsuits, and quarrels; arguing in secular courts, except in the defense of orphans and widows; acting as contractors or agents in secular affairs; being a maker of obscene jokes in word or deed, or taking pleasure in secular humor; loving games of chance; seeking adornment unsuitable to one’s vocation; wishing to live in luxury; pursuing gluttony and drunkenness; possessing unjust weights or measures; conducting dishonest business; pursuing dogs and birds for hunting; and being excessive in any such matters. [Col. 0810A]

Yet lawful business must not be forbidden on account of various necessities, for we read that the holy apostles conducted business, and the Rule of Saint Benedict prescribes that provision be made for through whose hands the business of the monastery is to pass.

We absolutely forbid such things and whatever resembles them to the ministers of the Lord’s altar and likewise to monks. Of these matters the Apostle says: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular business.”

### CAP. 91.—Concerning Clerics Who Have Been Tonsured Unjustly

(From the same council, chapter 23.) Concerning clerics, we decree that those who have hitherto been found tonsured, whether into the canonical or monastic order, without their consent, shall remain as they are if they are free persons. Henceforth care must be taken that no one is tonsured unless he is of lawful age and gives his willing consent, or unless he has his master’s permission or his parents’ consent.

### CAP. 92.—That Bishops and Abbots Should Not Permit Obscene Jests in Their Presence

(From the same council, chapter 24.) Bishops and abbots must not permit obscene jests to be made in their presence. Instead, they should have the poor and needy at table with them; divine reading should be heard there; and they should take their food with blessing and praise of the Lord, according to the Apostle: “Whether you eat or drink, do everything to the praise of God.”

### CAP. 93.—Concerning Those Who, Seduced by a Bishop or Others Out of Greed, Have Been Tonsured

[Col. 0810C]

(From the same council, chapter 25.) This holy assembly has decreed that bishops or abbots who, not seeking the benefit of souls but driven by greed and dishonest gain, have deceived various people by enticement and tonsured them, and by such persuasion have not merely accepted but rather stolen their property, shall be subjected to canonical or regular penance as followers of dishonest gain.

But those who, enticed by empty promises or persuaded by various schemes and thereby deprived of sound judgment, not knowing how to remain masters of their own property, have cut off their hair shall be compelled to persevere in what they have begun. For property known to have been given by the enticed and negligent, and not merely accepted but seized by the greedy and negligent, shall be returned to the heirs who are known to have been disinherited through the folly of their parents and the greed of their instigators. [Col. 0810D]

If it is proved that the ministers of bishops or abbots—anyone in the clergy, that is—did this without the bishops’ or abbots’ knowledge, the bishops and abbots shall be judged for negligence, while the ministers shall be judged for rapacity and greed. But whatever a person justly and reasonably offers to God from his property, the Church must firmly retain.

### CAP. 94.—That an Abbess Should Take Great Care of Her Community

(From the same council, chapter 26.) An abbess must take diligent care of the community entrusted to her. She must ensure that the consecrated women are diligent in reading, the divine office, and the chanting of psalms, and that she lead them in every good work, since she will have to render an account for their souls in the presence of the Lord. She must provide the consecrated women with the necessities of life, lest they be compelled to sin through lack of food or drink. [Col. 0811A]

### CAP. 95.—That Consecrated Women Should Not Presume to Eat or Drink in Their Own Houses with Any Male Person

(From the same council, chapter 27.) Consecrated women must not drink or eat in their own dwellings with any male person, whether cleric or layman, relative or stranger. If this must ever be done, it shall take place in the audience chamber; and they may converse with no male person except there, and then only in the presence of suitable witnesses.

### CAP. 96.—How an Unworthy Abbot Is to Be Removed from His Office

[Col. 0811B]

(From the Council of Tribur, attended by King Arnulf, chapter 15.) If an abbot is not prudent in governance, humble, chaste, sober, merciful, and discerning, and does not demonstrate the divine commands in word and example, he shall be barred from his honor by the bishop in whose territory he resides, together with neighboring abbots and other God-fearing men—even if the entire community, agreeing with his vices, wishes to have him as abbot.

### CAP. 97.—Concerning Clerics Who Have Abandoned Their Tonsure and Taken Wives

(From the same council, in the presence of King Arnulf, chapter 16.) If a cleric, having abandoned his tonsure, takes a wife, and if he is without ecclesiastical rank and was not handed over to any monastery by his parents, then, if he is permitted to have a wife, he must be tonsured again and must not dare neglect his tonsure throughout his life.

But one whom his parents handed over to a monastery, who began to sing and read in the Church, may neither take a wife nor leave the monastery. If he departs, he must be brought back. If he abandons his tonsure, he must be tonsured again; and if he takes a wife, he must be compelled to leave her.

### CAP. 98.—Concerning Girls Who Have Voluntarily Given Themselves to Sacred Religious Life Before the Legal Age

(From the same council, chapter 17.) If a girl voluntarily assumes the sacred veil before she is twelve years old, her parents or guardians may immediately invalidate the act, if they wish. But if they have consented to it by allowing a year and a day to pass without objection, thereafter neither she nor they may change it. Furthermore, if a girl of more mature age, or a young man, chooses to serve God, the parents have no power to forbid it.

### CAP. 99.—Concerning Anyone Who Wishes to Offer His Daughter, Granddaughter, or Female Relative to Almighty God

[Col. 0812B]

(From the same council, chapter 6.) Whoever wishes to offer his daughter, granddaughter, or female relative to Almighty God shall have permission to do so. Otherwise, let her take a husband, raise her children at home, and not presume to send another girl into a monastery for the purpose of being raised there, unless she intends that girl firmly to persevere in that place in God’s service, according to the institutions of the holy Fathers or canonical authority.

### CAP. 100.—Concerning the Same Matter

(From the same council, chapter 7.) We absolutely prohibit anyone from entrusting a son, grandson, or other relative to a monastery of girls for rearing, and no one may dare receive him there.

### CAP. 101.—Concerning an Abbot Who Has Allowed Women to Celebrate Festivities in His Monastery

[Col. 0812C]

(From the Council of Urbicus.) If an abbot permits a woman to enter his monastery or to attend any festivities there, he shall be confined in another monastery for three months, content with bread and water alone.

[Col. 0811] END OF BOOK EIGHT
