# BURCHARD, BISHOP OF THE CHURCH OF WORMS, DECREES, BOOK NINE: CONCERNING UNCONSECRATED WOMEN

[Col. 0815]

## ARGUMENT OF THE BOOK

[Col. 0815A]

This book treats of virgins and widows not consecrated to God; of their abductors and the penalty to be imposed upon them; of legitimate marriage; and of illegitimate intercourse and the penance for it.

### CAP. 1.—That a Wife Is One Thing and a Concubine Another, and That Anyone Who Gives His Daughter in Marriage to a Man Who Has a Concubine Should Not Be Mistaken About This

(From the decree of Pope Leo, chapter 18.) Not every woman joined to a man is the man’s wife, just as not every son is his father’s heir. The bonds of marriage are legitimate among freeborn persons, and especially among equals, since the Lord established this before the beginning of Roman law existed. Thus a wife is one thing and a concubine another, just as a slave woman is one thing and a free woman another.

For this reason the Apostle, in order to make clear the distinction between these persons, cites testimony from Genesis, where it is said to Abraham: “Cast out the slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac.” Since the partnership of marriage was established from the beginning in such a way that, beyond the union of the sexes, it contained the sacrament of Christ and the Church, there is no doubt that the woman in whom the nuptial mystery is not found does not belong to marriage.

Therefore, if a layman from any place gives his daughter in marriage to a man who has a concubine, this must not be understood as though he had given her to a married man—unless that woman is shown to have been made free, lawfully endowed, and honored by a public wedding. For women joined to men by paternal decision are free from blame if the women whom those men kept were not married to them, because a married woman is one thing and a concubine another. [Col. 0815B–C]

### CAP. 2.—What a Legitimate Wife Ought to Be

(From a letter of Pope Leo.) The wife who is to be taken according to law ought to be a chaste virgin, betrothed in virginity, lawfully endowed, handed over by her parents, and received by the bridegroom and the wedding attendants. Thus, according to law and the Gospel, she is to be openly and honorably taken in marriage at a public wedding. She must never be separated for a man’s sake during all the days of her life, except by mutual consent and for the purpose of devoting herself to God; and if she commits fornication, she is to be dismissed. But while the other woman lives, another may not be taken, because adulterers will not possess the kingdom of God. Her penance is to be accepted according to the Scriptures.

### CAP. 3.—That No One Should Celebrate a Marriage Secretly

[Col. 0816A]

(From the decree of Pope Hormisdas, chapter 6.) No believer, whatever his status, should marry secretly. Rather, after receiving a blessing from a priest, he should marry publicly in the Lord.

### CAP. 4.—At What Time Marriages Should Be Celebrated

(From the Council of Lérida, chapter 3.) Marriages should not be celebrated from Septuagesima until the octave of Easter, during the three weeks before the feast of Saint John the Baptist, or from the Advent of the Lord until after Epiphany. If this is done, the parties shall separate.

### CAP. 5.—How the Bridegroom and Bride Are Blessed by the Priest

(From the Council of Valencia, chapter 101.) When the bridegroom and bride are to be blessed, they shall be presented to the priest in the church by their parents or wedding attendants. After receiving the blessing, they shall remain virginal that same night out of reverence for the blessing itself. [Col. 0816B]

### CAP. 6.—That No Marriage Should Take Place Without a Dowry

(From the Council of Arles, chapter 6.) No marriage shall take place without a dowry. The dowry shall be made according to the parties’ means, and no one shall presume to marry or take a wife without a public wedding.

### CAP. 7.—That the Bridegroom and Bride Should Be Blessed by the Priest Before the Wedding

(From the decree of Pope Soter, chapter 5.) The bridegroom and bride shall be blessed by a priest with prayers and offerings; they shall be betrothed and endowed according to law; they shall be guarded by the wedding attendants; and they shall be received publicly and solemnly. They shall also abstain for two or three days, and shall be instructed to preserve chastity between them and to marry at the proper times, so that they may beget children who are not illegitimate but legitimate heirs, for God and for the world. [Col. 0816C]

### CAP. 8.—Concerning a First Marriage

(From the Council of Milan, chapter 2.) In a first marriage the presbyter should celebrate Mass and bless both parties; afterward they should abstain from entering the church for thirty days.

### CAP. 9.—That a Faithful Man Should Not Separate from an Unbelieving Woman

(The Apostle says.) “If any brother has an unbelieving wife and she consents to live with him, he should not dismiss her. And if any woman has an unbelieving husband and he consents to live with her, she should not dismiss her husband.” [Col. 0817A] “For the unbelieving husband is sanctified through the believing wife, and the unbelieving wife is sanctified through the believing husband.”

### CAP. 10.—That There Should Be No Dancing at Christian Weddings

(From the Council of Laodicea, chapter 53.) Christians going to weddings should not applaud or dance. Rather, they should dine or take their meal reverently, as befits Christians.

### CAP. 11.—That No One Should Steal a Widow as a Wife

(Gregory says.) If anyone steals a widow as a wife, or consents to him, let him be anathema. And they all answered three times: “Let him be anathema.”

### CAP. 12.—That No One Should Steal a Virgin as a Wife

(The same author.) If anyone steals a virgin as a wife without having betrothed her, or consents to him, let him be anathema. And they all answered three times: “Let him be anathema!” [Col. 0817B]

### CAP. 13.—Concerning a Stolen Virgin or Widow

(From the decree of Pope Eusebius, chapter 10.) If anyone steals a virgin or widow as a wife without having first betrothed her to himself, let him be anathema.

### CAP. 14.—Concerning Virgins Who Have Not Preserved Their Virginity Before Marriage

(From the Council of Elvira, chapter 5.) If virgins who have not preserved their virginity take as husbands the very men who violated them, they shall be reconciled after one year of penance, since they have violated only the matter of marriage. If they have relations with other men, since they have committed adultery, they shall do penance for five years and then approach communion.

### CAP. 15.—That No One Is Permitted to Have a Concubine

[Col. 0817C]

(From the sayings of Augustine.) Hear, dearest ones, members of Christ and children of the catholic mother Church. Let the faithful hear what I say to those preparing for baptism; let those preparing for baptism hear what I say to the faithful; let the penitents hear what I say to the faithful and those preparing for baptism; and let the catechumens hear what I say to the faithful, those preparing for baptism, and the penitents. Let everyone hear. Let everyone fear, and let no one despise this.

May your hearing be a consolation to me, so that my sorrow may not become a testimony against you. I say to those preparing for baptism: You must not commit fornication. Let your wives suffice for you; you are not permitted to have concubines. Let God hear, if you are deaf; let his angels hear, if you despise this: you are not permitted to have concubines.

Even if you do not have wives, you are still not permitted to have concubines whom you may later dismiss in order to take wives. Your condemnation will be all the greater if you wish to have both concubines and wives. You may not have wives whose former husbands are alive. Likewise, women, you may not have husbands whose former wives are alive. These are adulterous marriages, not marriages by the law of heaven but by the law of the world. Nor may one have a woman who has left her husband by divorce while he is alive. A wife may be dismissed only on account of fornication, but while she is alive one may not take another.

### CAP. 16.—Concerning Those Who Have Had Concubines Before Marriage

(The same Augustine.) What shall we say of the fact that many men are not ashamed, before marriage, to keep concubines attached to themselves, whom they dismiss after several years and then take legitimate wives? Therefore, before God and his angels I testify and declare that God has always forbidden this and has never been pleased with it. Especially in Christian times, it has never been and never will be permitted to have concubines.

### CAP. 17.—Also Concerning Concubines

(From the Council of Arles, chapter 4.) No one is permitted to have two wives at the same time, nor may anyone ever have a concubine.

### CAP. 18.—Whether a Slave Woman Can Become the Legitimate Wife of Her Own Master

(From the decree of Pope Julius, chapter 4.) If anyone grants freedom to his slave woman and joins her to himself in marriage, some people have doubted whether such a marriage should be considered legitimate. Therefore, resolving this ancient ambiguity, we have judged such unions to be legitimate.

For if every marriage is made out of affection, and nothing impious or contrary to the laws can occur in such a union, why should we consider the marriage mentioned above forbidden? You all have one Father in heaven, and everyone—rich and poor, free and slave—will render an equal account for himself and for his soul. Therefore, we do not doubt that all persons, whatever their status, have one law with respect to God. [Col. 0818A–B]

### CAP. 19.—Concerning One Who Has Joined His Male and Female Slaves in Marriage

[Col. 0818C]

(From the Council of Mâcon, chapter 10.) If a master joins his male and female slaves in marriage, and afterward one of them is freed while the other cannot be redeemed from servitude, the marriage is not thereby to be dissolved.

### CAP. 20.—Concerning Those Married Many Times

(From the Council of Braga, chapter 81.) If anyone has been joined in many marriages, let him do penance. The conduct and faith of the penitent, however, shorten the prescribed period.

### CAP. 21.—That Second Marriages Are Not Denied to Laypeople, Although They Are Barred from Entering the Clergy Thereafter

(From the decree of Pope Gelasius, chapter 22.) Just as second marriages are permitted to laypeople, so no one is permitted to enter the clerical order after contracting them. For one thing is the permission generally granted to human weakness, and another ought to be the life dedicated to the service of divine matters. [Col. 0818D]

### CAP. 22.—Concerning Those Who Have Entered into Several Marriages

(From the Council of Neocaesarea, chapter 1.) Concerning those who have entered into several marriages: although a prescribed period is clearly established, their conduct and faith shorten the period.

### CAP. 23.—Concerning Those Who Have Celebrated a Third Marriage

(From the decree of Pope Hormisdas, chapter 2.) No one should take more than two wives, because a third is already excessive.

### CAP. 24.—Concerning Bigamists

[Col. 0819A]

(From the Council of Laodicea, chapter 1.) Those who, according to ecclesiastical rule, have freely and lawfully entered into a second marriage, and have not entered into the marriage bond secretly, should, after a short period has passed, devote themselves to prayers and fasts. We have also decreed that communion should be restored to them as an act of indulgence.

### CAP. 25.—Concerning the Number of Husbands

(From the sayings of Jerome.) Where there is a number of husbands, there ceases to be one proper husband.

### CAP. 26.—Concerning a Freeborn Man Who Has Taken Another Man’s Slave Woman as Freeborn and Later Learns That She Is a Slave

(From the Council at Vermeria, attended by King Pepin, chapter 7.) If a freeborn man takes another person’s slave woman as his wife, believing that she is freeborn, and afterward that woman is found to be in servitude, he should redeem her from slavery if he can. If he cannot, he may take another woman, if he wishes. But if he knew that she was a slave and had approved her as such, he shall thereafter keep her as his legitimate wife. A freeborn woman must act similarly regarding another man’s slave.

### CAP. 27.—Concerning a Freeborn Woman Who Has Taken a Slave as Her Husband

(From the same council, chapter 8.) If a freeborn woman takes a slave, knowing that he is a slave, she shall keep him, because we all have one Father in heaven. There shall be one law for both man and woman.

### CAP. 28.—Concerning Those Lawfully Joined in Marriage, If One of Them Becomes Insane

[Col. 0819C]

(From a letter of Nicholas sent to Charles, bishop of Mainz.) If people contract a marriage while of sound mind, and afterward insanity, madness, or some illness comes upon one of the two, their marriage cannot be dissolved on account of this illness. The same must be understood of those who are blinded or have their limbs cut off by enemies.

### CAP. 29.—Concerning the Lawful Marriages of Slaves

(From the Council of Chalon, chapter 30.) It has been reported to us that certain people dissolve the lawful marriages of slaves by an arbitrary presumption, paying no attention to the Gospel saying: “What God has joined together, let no human being separate.” Therefore, it seems right to us that the marriages of slaves not be dissolved, even if they have different masters. Remaining in one marriage, they shall serve their respective masters. This is to be observed wherever there has been a lawful union and the masters have consented to it. [Col. 0819D]

### CAP. 30.—If Insane Persons Have Contracted Marriage

(From the decree of Pope Fabian, chapter 5.) Neither an insane man nor an insane woman can contract marriage. But if a marriage has been contracted, the parties shall not be separated.

### CAP. 31.—Concerning a Betrothed Girl, and Whether Another Man May Take Her in Marriage

(From a letter of Pope Siricius, chapter 4.) You have inquired concerning the violation of marriage: whether another man may take in marriage a girl betrothed to someone else. We prohibit this in every way, because among the faithful the blessing that a priest bestows upon those who are about to marry is like a kind of sacrilege if it is violated by any transgression. [Col. 0820A]

### CAP. 32.—Concerning Those Who Abduct Another Man’s Betrothed Women

(From the Council of Meaux, chapter 5.) The ancient and synodal judgment concerning those who abduct another man’s betrothed women must be observed. Even if such an event should happen to be found in the Church, so that, for the sake of salvation and religious propriety, the bishops ought to handle the matter somewhat more humanely, as canonical authority teaches—in its own words—“because the earlier definition was harsher, while the later dealt with the matter somewhat more humanely,” we must in no way descend to the greatest indulgence.

The man who takes another’s betrothed woman must not pass without public penance. If she refuses to obey this ruling, she shall be anathematized without any resistance being permitted. Her supporters shall do penance by decree of the bishop, according to the measure of their guilt. If, which we do not wish, anyone in ecclesiastical rank openly reveals himself as consenting to or intervening in such a marriage, he shall be removed from his rank. If afterward he is driven off by plausible suspicions, he must clear himself canonically. [Col. 0820B]

### CAP. 33.—Concerning Those Who Abduct Women

(From the Council of Aachen, chapter 3.) It has been decided that those who abduct, steal, or seduce women may in no way have them as wives, even if the women later agree with them, or if they endow them, or take them in marriage with the consent of their parents. If anyone wishes to have a wife, he must take her canonically and lawfully, not abduct her. Whoever abducts, steals, or seduces a woman shall never have her as his wife. [Col. 0820C]

### CAP. 34.—Concerning the Same Matter

(From the Council of Meaux, chapter 10.) Those who henceforth presume to abduct virgins or widows shall, according to the synodal judgment of blessed Gregory, be anathematized, both they and their accomplices. The abductors shall remain forever without hope of marriage.

### CAP. 35.—Concerning Those Who Abduct Girls Under the Pretext of Living Together

(From the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 27.) Concerning those who abduct women under the pretext of living together, and those who cooperate with or connive at the abductors, the holy synod has decreed that if they are clerics, they shall fall from their ecclesiastical rank; if they are laypeople, they shall be anathematized.

### CAP. 36.—Concerning Abducted Girls Who Are Not Yet Betrothed

[Col. 0820D]

(From the Council of Chalon, chapter 27.) Concerning abducted girls who are not yet betrothed, the Council of Chalcedon has written: “Concerning those who abduct girls under the pretext of living together, and those who cooperate with or connive at the abductors, the holy synod has decreed that if they are clerics, they shall fall from their ecclesiastical rank; if they are laypeople, they shall be anathematized.”

These words make clear how the authors of this evil are to be condemned. When those who participate, advise, or connive are struck by so great an anathema, then, according to canonical authority, the abductors can in no way lawfully claim the women they have abducted for legitimate marriage.

### CAP. 37.—Concerning Abducted Betrothed Women

(From the Council of Toledo.) Accordingly, it was decided and established by the holy assembly that if anyone abducts another man’s betrothed woman, he shall be punished with public penance and remain without hope of marriage. If she did not consent to the same crime, she shall not be denied permission to marry another. But if afterward the two presume to join themselves to each other, both shall remain under anathema until they have made satisfaction. [Col. 0821A]

### CAP. 38.—Concerning the Same Matter

(From the Council of Ancyra, chapter 10.) Betrothed girls who have afterward been abducted by others are to be rescued and restored to those to whom they had previously been betrothed, even if it is established that the abductors used force against them.

### CAP. 39.—Concerning the Same Matter

(From the Council of Meaux, chapter 65.) If, when this decree has been proclaimed to everyone’s ears, the abductors do not yet have the women they abducted joined to them in marriage with the consent of their parents under the aforementioned form of betrothal or dowry, they shall be separated from their union and subjected to public penance. The abducted women shall be legally restored to their parents.

After public penance has been completed, if age and lack of self-control require it, they may be joined in a legitimate marriage agreed upon by both sides. For in these matters we are not establishing a rule; rather, to use the words of the great Leo, we are judging what is more tolerable.

If one of the married parties dies, the survivor who has performed public penance must not presume to marry again, unless perhaps the bishop foresees that some indulgence may be granted in order to remove a more serious offense. [Col. 0821B]

### CAP. 40.—Concerning Those Who Are Joined in Marriage but Cannot Have Intercourse

[Col. 0821C]

(From a letter of Gregory to John, bishop of Ravenna.) You asked about those who are joined in marriage but cannot have intercourse, whether the man may take another woman or the woman another man. It is written: If a man and woman join together in marriage, and afterward the woman says of the man that he cannot have intercourse with her, then, if she can prove by lawful judgment that this is true, she may take another man; but if he takes another woman, they are to separate.

### Chapter 41.—On the same matter.

(From the council held at Verberie in the time of King Pippin, chapter 17.) If a woman declares that her husband has never had intercourse with her, they shall proceed to the ordeal of the cross. If the matter proves true, they shall separate, and she may do [Col. 0821D] what she wishes.

### Chapter 42.—On the same matter.

(From the council held at Compiegne, chapter 20.) If someone has taken a wife and has had her for some time, and the woman says that he has not had intercourse with her, while the man says that he has, the man’s assertion shall prevail, because the man is the head of the woman.

### Chapter 43.—On the same matter.

(From the council of Tribur, chapter 3.) If a man has married a woman but is unable to have intercourse with her, and his brother secretly violates her and makes her pregnant, they shall separate. But, taking the man’s weakness into consideration, mercy shall be shown to them so that they may marry, only in the Lord.

### Chapter 44.—On the same matter.

[Col. 0822A]

(From a letter of Gregory.) Concerning those who, because of what they call a cold nature, say that they cannot unite with one another in carnal intercourse: If this man cannot use her as a wife, let him have her as a sister. But if they wish to sever the marital bond, let both remain unmarried; for if he was naturally unable to be joined to her, how will he be suited to another?

Therefore, if the man wishes to take another wife, the evident reason is that, with the devil kindling the fuel of hatred, he has come to detest her and is therefore trying to dismiss her through the falsehood of a lie. But if the woman makes the complaint and says, “I wish to be a mother and bear children,” let both of them, with seven of their relatives touching the sacred relics, declare under oath that they were never joined through carnal [Col. 0822B] intercourse and thereby made one flesh. Then the woman may apparently contract a second marriage. I say this humanely, because of their bodily weakness. The man, however, who is of a cold nature must remain without a wife. But if he also takes another partner, then those who swore shall be held guilty of perjury; and after completing penance they shall be compelled to resume their former marriages.

### Chapter 45.—On married people who desire to abandon worldly life.

(From the sayings of Bishop Basil.) If a married man wishes to enter a monastery, he must not be received unless he has first been released by his wife’s professing chastity. For if, while he is alive, she marries another through lack of self-restraint, she will unquestionably be an adulteress; nor is the conversion [Col. 0822C] before God acceptable of such a man whose abandonment of the marriage bond is followed by its violation. Thus they may follow Christ without guilt, leaving the world, if they have agreed together in an equal resolve to live chastely.

### Chapter 46.—On the man who has permitted his wife to take the veil.

(From the council of Reims, chapter 3.) A man who has permitted his wife to take the veil must not take another wife; he too must convert.

### Chapter 47.—On a woman who has assumed the veil without her husband’s permission.

(From a decree issued at Compiegne, chapter 6.) If a woman has placed the veil upon her head without her husband’s permission, then, if it pleases the husband, he shall receive her again into marriage.

### Chapter 48.—On a man who has undertaken monastic life without his wife’s consent.

[Col. 0822D]

(From Gregory’s Rule to Hadrian the notary, chapter 80.)

Agathosa, bearer of this letter, has complained that her husband has entered the monastery of the abbot Urbicius against her will. Since this undoubtedly reflects upon that abbot’s guilt and brings him into disrepute, we instruct Your Experience to investigate carefully, lest perhaps he entered with her consent or she herself promised to change her way of life. If you discover that this is so, see that he remains in the monastery and compel her to change as she promised.

But if neither of these things is true, and you find that the aforesaid woman has committed no act of fornication—the only crime that permits a man to leave his wife—then, lest his conversion become an occasion of perdition for the wife left [Col. 0823A] in the world, we wish you to restore her husband to her, or, if he has already been tonsured, to restore him nonetheless, with every excuse set aside. For if, except on account of fornication, a man is in no way permitted to leave his wife, then, once man and woman have become one body through marital union, one party cannot convert while the other remains in the world.

### Chapter 49.—On Queen Thietbirga, who had wished to withdraw from royal dignity for the sake of religion.

(From a letter of Pope Nicholas to King Charles.) Queen Thietbirga wrote to us that she wished to be released from royal dignity and from the marriage bond, and desired to be content with a solitary private life. We wrote to her that this could happen in no other way unless her husband, Lothair, chose the same life.

And a little later: Thietbirga must not be compelled to answer again concerning the dispute already settled. What has once been well decided and determined by the interposition of oaths must not be reconsidered, except perhaps where greater authority is involved.

### Chapter 50.—On King Lothair, who was holding his wife in custody.

(The same author.) But, as we have learned from the report of many people, King Lothair is preparing to convene an assembly and is planning to subject Queen Thietbirga to his own examination and judgment. If he can, through the tricks of his falsehood, present her as though she were not his lawful wife, he wishes to remove her from him entirely. Otherwise, he wishes to receive her as his own [Col. 0823B] wife but then accuse her as though she had committed adultery, drive his own man and Thietbirga’s man to single combat, and, if the queen’s champion falls, put her to death without delay. We believe that Your Prudence has already recognized how contrary these plans are to every divine law and to the law of the holy Fathers.

### Chapter 51.—On the single combat that Lothair planned against his wife Thietbirga.

(The same author.) We do not accept single combat as part of the law, since we do not find that it was commanded. Although we read that some have undertaken it—for example, holy David and Goliath, as sacred history records—we nowhere find that divine authority has sanctioned it anywhere as a legal requirement. Those who follow this and similar practices appear merely to be tempting God.

### Chapter 52.—If a woman accused of adultery is to undertake a lawful contest with her husband, she must first be restored temporarily to her own authority.

(The same author.) Furthermore, whether judgment is to be conducted concerning the marriage bond or the crime of adultery, no reason permits Thietbirga to enter into a conflict or lawful contest with Lothair unless she has first been freely restored for a time to her own control and associated with her own relatives. A place must also be provided among them where no violence from a crowd need be feared and where it is not difficult to produce the witnesses or other persons required in such disputes both by the holy canons and by the venerable Roman laws.

We have said this [Col. 0824A] to show what legal contest Lothair supposes he can undertake, when he brings before judgment the woman whom he daily harasses and crushes within his own chambers, taking her out whenever he wishes and returning her to confinement whenever he wishes; and when she has been brought out, punishing her unless she confesses what he himself has ordered. She must therefore be entrusted to her own freedom, liberated from every oppression and authority of the man with whom she is to contend, allowed freely to use her own resources, and kept away from suspicious persons, so that she may seek to prove herself free from the charges brought against her.

### Chapter 53.—On the same matter.

(The same author.) Therefore, with the greatest care, strive to cherish and love your wife Thietbirga as your own flesh, and watch vigilantly that you do not consent to her departure from you in any way. [Col. 0824B] If she wishes to leave you, rebuke her—or rather correct her—and strive in every respect to recall her from such an intention.

But if she seeks separation out of love of chastity and demands release from the marriage bond, it is certain, as the Apostle says, that “the woman does not have authority over her own body, but the man does.” Yet if you yourself, pursuing chastity under the pretext of religion, wish to dissolve the marriage, we grant permission only if this is done sincerely. For although it is written, “What God has joined, let no human being separate,” God, and not a human being, separates them when, for the sake of divine love and by the consent of both spouses, marriages are dissolved.

If you wish to do this in that manner, we freely permit it and readily give our consent. Otherwise, we forbid your mutual separation. [Col. 0824C]

### Chapter 54.—On those who have fled to other provinces or followed their lords and left their wives at home.

(From the council held at Verberie, chapter 6.) If someone, compelled by unavoidable necessity, flees to another duchy or province, and his wife, although she is able and capable, refuses to follow him out of love for her parents or her possessions, she must remain unmarried for as long as her husband, whom she did not follow, lives. But if the man, compelled by necessity, remains in another country and has no hope of ever returning to his own homeland, and cannot remain continent, he may take another wife, though with penance.

### Chapter 55.—On women who, after their husbands were captured or led into captivity, married other men.

[Col. 0824D]

(From a letter of Pope Leo, chapter 42.) Women who, after their husbands had been captured and led into captivity, married other men, believing their husbands to have been killed, must, when their former husbands return from captivity, be joined to them, so that what each person lawfully possessed may be restored, each may receive what is his or hers, and the marriage bonds may be renewed.

### Chapter 56.—That the man who appears to have taken the wife of a captive is not to be judged guilty.

(The same author, chapter 43.) Nor is the man who took the wife of a husband believed no longer to be alive to be judged guilty or regarded as an invader of another’s legal right. For although many things belonging to [Col. 0825A] those who were led into captivity could pass into another’s possession, it is entirely just that, when the captives return, their own property be restored to them.

If this is rightly observed concerning slaves, fields, houses, and possessions, how much more must it be done in restoring marriages, so that what was disturbed by the necessity of war may be restored through the remedy of peace?

### Chapter 57.—If women refuse to return to their former husbands, they are to be deprived of ecclesiastical communion as impious.

(The same author, chapter 45.) But if some women have been so captivated by love of their later husbands that they prefer to remain with them rather than return to their lawful marriage, they are rightly to be branded, so that they are deprived of ecclesiastical communion. [Col. 0825B] From a matter that could be excused, they have chosen the contamination of crime, showing that, through their lack of self-restraint, they preferred what a rightful release could have atoned for.

Let marriages therefore return voluntarily to their former state of restoration, and let what necessity compelled in no way be turned into a reproach for evil intent. For just as those women who refuse to return to their husbands are to be regarded as impious, so those who return to an affection begun by God are rightly to be praised.

### Chapter 58.—If husbands returning from captivity are not offended by their wives’ lapse and wish to receive them in marriage, they have full liberty to do so.

(The same author, chapter 44.) Therefore, if husbands return after a long captivity and remain so devoted to their [Col. 0825C] wives that they wish them to return to their marriage, what necessity brought about must be overlooked and judged blameless, and what fidelity demands must be restored.

### Chapter 59.—On a man who dismissed his wife while still a pagan.

(From a decree of Pope Eutychian.) If a pagan man dismissed his pagan wife before baptism, after baptism it shall be in his power either to have her or not to have her.

### Chapter 60.—If a baptized person’s wife refuses to convert.

(From a decree of the same author.) Likewise, if one of the married couple has been baptized while the other is a pagan and does not wish to follow, let it be as the Apostle says: “If the unbeliever departs, let him depart.”

### Chapter 61.—On a man who had taken a virgin as wife before baptism.

[Col. 0825D]

(From the council of Meaux, chapter 2.) If someone had a virgin as wife before baptism, he cannot, while she is alive, have another after baptism. Baptism dissolves crimes, not marriages.

### Chapter 62.—On women who, without any intervening cause, left their husbands.

(From the council of Elvira, chapter 7.) Likewise, women who, without any prior cause, left their husbands, joined themselves to another man, and wished to remain in that state shall not receive communion even at the end of life.

### Chapter 63.—On a woman who left an adulterous husband and took an adulterer.

(From the same council, chapter 9.) Likewise, a faithful woman who [Col. 0826A] leaves a faithful adulterous husband and marries an adulterer must be prohibited from marrying him. If she does marry him, she shall not receive communion until the man she left has departed from this world, unless perhaps the necessity of illness compels communion to be given.

### Chapter 64.—That neither a man dismissed by his wife nor a woman dismissed by her husband may join themselves to another.

(From the council of Carthage, chapter 63.) It has been decided that, according to evangelical and apostolic discipline, neither a man dismissed by his wife nor a woman dismissed by her husband may join themselves to another, but must remain as they are or be reconciled to one another. If they disregard this, they must be brought to penance.

### Chapter 65.—On the man accused of committing adultery with another’s wife while her husband was alive and recognized as having taken her after his death.

[Col. 0826B]

(From the council of Meaux, chapter 69.) A man accused of having committed adultery with another man’s wife while her husband was alive, and recognized as having taken her shortly after that husband’s death, must in every respect be subjected to public penance. Concerning him, the rule stated above shall also be observed after penance, if appropriate, unless perhaps some impediment exists—for example, if the woman is found to have killed the husband who died, or if kinship or any other criminal act prevents the marriage.

If this is proved, they must remain perpetually in penance, without any hope of marriage. But if he denies that he ever committed adultery with the woman while her husband was alive, and neither of them is found guilty of the aforementioned homicide, and neither can be convicted by proven witnesses, let them lawfully clear their reputations [Col. 0826C] and enter into marriage, provided that no other circumstance, as we have said, prevents it.

### Chapter 66.—On the same matter.

(From the council of Tribur, chapter 3.) It has been reported to the ears of the holy priests that a certain man violated another’s wife through fornication and, moreover, while her husband was alive, gave the adulteress an oath that he would marry her after her lawful husband’s death, if he survived. This was indeed done. We therefore prohibit and anathematize such a marriage.

### Chapter 67.—On a man who has a wife and has committed adultery repeatedly.

(From the council of Elvira, chapter 4.) If a faithful man who has a wife has committed adultery not once but repeatedly, he must be summoned at the hour of death. [Col. 0826D] If he promises that he will cease, communion shall be given to him. But if, after being restored, he commits adultery again, it has been decided that he must no longer mock others by receiving the communion of peace.

### Chapter 68.—If an absolved layman sins with an absolved laywoman.

(From the council of Meaux, chapter 7.) If a layman has intercourse with a laywoman—that is, if both are free from the law of marriage—they shall do penance for three years. The more frequently and negligently they have committed such sins, the more both the duration and the severity of the penance shall be increased.

### Chapter 69.—On a wife who commits adultery with her husband’s knowledge.

(From the council of Mainz, chapter 9.) If a wife commits adultery with her husband’s knowledge and consent, it has been decided that communion must not be given to either of them even at the end of life. But if he dismisses her, they separate, and they perform worthy penance, they may receive [Col. 0827A] communion after ten years.

### Chapter 70.—On a man without a wife who commits adultery with another man’s wife.

(From the council of Nantes, chapter 6.) If a man who has no wife commits adultery with another man’s wife, or if a woman who has no husband commits adultery with another woman’s husband, the person who violated the marriage bond must do penance for seven years, as stated above. The person who is not bound by the law of marriage must do penance for five years.

For penance cannot be equal for those who could have satisfied their lust through the embrace of their spouses and those who, lacking a spouse and driven by the heat of lust, fell into fornication.

### Chapter 71.—On married people who separate for some definite reason in order to remain unmarried.

[Col. 0827B]

(From the sayings of Augustine.) The Apostle Paul says: “To those who are married I give this command—not I, but the Lord—that a wife should not separate from her husband; but if she does separate, let her remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband.”

It may happen that she separates for the reason permitted by the Lord. Or, if a woman is permitted to dismiss her husband even on account of fornication, while a husband is not, what shall we answer concerning the later statement: “And let the husband not dismiss his wife”? Why did he not add, “except on account of fornication,” which the Lord permits, unless he wishes the same rule to be understood—namely, that if he dismisses her for the reason of fornication, which is permitted, he must remain without a wife or be reconciled to his wife?

And a little later: The Lord permitted a wife to be dismissed on account of [Col. 0827C] fornication, but because he permitted it, he did not command it.

### Chapter 72.—On those who, after a divorce, have joined themselves to others in marriage.

(From a decree of Pope Innocent, chapter 26.) Your Belovedness also asked about those who, after a divorce, have joined themselves to others in marriage; it is clear that they are adulterers on both sides. Those who, while their wives were still alive, hastened to another union, although the marriage may appear to have been dissolved, cannot fail to be regarded as adulterers. Moreover, the persons to whom such men have joined themselves likewise appear to have committed adultery, according to what we read in the Gospel: “Whoever dismisses his wife and marries another commits adultery.”

Therefore all such persons must be excluded from the communion of the faithful. Nothing of this kind, however, can be decreed concerning their parents or [Col. 0827D] relatives, unless they appear to have encouraged the unlawful union.

### Chapter 73.—If someone’s wife has been violated and her husband plots to have her killed for that reason.

(From the council of Tribur, chapter 46.) If someone’s wife has been violated and her husband therefore plots to destroy her by a capital sentence, and she, threatened by the danger of death, flees to a bishop and seeks help, the bishop must nevertheless labor with the greatest effort, if possible, to prevent her being killed. If he cannot, he may in no way return her, when she has offered herself to him for protection, to the man seeking to kill her. Rather, with careful diligence, he must send her to whatever place she herself chooses, so that she may live safely.

But if the husband should later find her and demand her, he may, according to worldly law, exercise whatever power he has over what he wishes to do to her. [Col. 0828A] Let him, however, hear Saint Augustine saying: “Since the man receives his name from strength and the woman from softness—that is, weakness—why does each man wish his wife to be victorious against the most savage beast of lust, when he himself falls defeated at lust’s first assault? For whatever is not permitted to women against the Catholic faith is not permitted to men either.”

But if that woman, terrified by fear, flees from the place to which the bishop assigned her, and her husband demands her from the bishop once, twice, or repeatedly, then, if he can secure her life, the bishop must seek her out and restore her to him; otherwise, he must not restore her at all. The husband, however, must in no way take another wife as long as she lives.

### Chapter 74.—If someone fornicates with another man’s wife while her husband is alive.

[Col. 0828B]

(From the council held at Altenburg in the presence of King Conrad, chapter 5.) By common decree, according to the provisions of the canons, we define and rule in advance that if someone fornicates with another man’s wife while her husband is alive, then, after the husband’s death, access [Col. 0828B] to an unlawful union with her must be closed to him by synodal judgment, so that he may not later marry the woman whom he previously polluted by adultery. For we neither wish nor consider it consistent with the Christian religion that anyone should marry a woman whom he previously polluted through adultery.

### Chapter 75.—On a free man who took a free woman as wife and afterward made himself a slave.

(From the council of Tribur, attended by King Arnulf, chapter 8.) It was reported to the holy synod that a certain free man took a free [Col. 0828C] woman as wife and, after fathering children, made himself a slave on the pretext of some divorce. The question was whether he was necessarily bound to keep the woman and, if he kept her, whether she too ought to be subjected to servitude under secular law.

It was judged that the wife must by no means be dismissed, but that, on account of Christ’s law, the woman must not be reduced to slavery, since he made himself a slave without his wife’s consent, whereas she had accepted him as her free husband.

### Chapter 76.—On married people whose laws are different.

(From the same council, chapter 15.) A certain nobleman from Francia took a noblewoman from Saxony as his wife according to Saxon law. He kept her for many years and fathered children by her. But because the Saxons and Franks do not use the same laws, he alleged that he had not betrothed, taken, or endowed [Col. 0828D] her according to his own law—that is, Frankish law. After dismissing her, he took another wife.

The holy synod decreed that he, as a transgressor of evangelical law, must be subjected to penance; he must separate from his second wife and be compelled to take back the first.

### Chapter 77.—Why husbands who receive communion do not cohabit with adulterous wives.

(From a decree of Pope Innocent, chapter 24.) It has also been desired to know why husbands do not remain with adulterous wives, while wives appear to remain in the company of adulterous husbands. Christian religion condemns adultery equally in both sexes. But women do not readily accuse their husbands of adultery, and their hidden sins therefore escape punishment. Husbands, on the other hand, customarily denounce adulterous wives more freely before priests. Thus communion is denied to women [Col. 0829A] when their crime is exposed, whereas, when the men’s offense remains hidden, no one readily excludes them on the basis of suspicion; they too, of course, will be removed if their disgrace is uncovered. Since the cause is therefore sometimes equal, when proof is lacking, the basis for punishment comes to rest.

### Chapter 78.—That Christians ought not to contract marital rights with heretics.

(From the council of Laodicea, chapter 31.) It is not right to celebrate marriage bonds with any heretics, nor to give them sons or daughters, but rather to take sons or daughters from them, provided that they allow themselves to become Christians.

### Chapter 79.—Examination at judgment.

[Col. 0829B]

Concerning what has been charged against me in this synod: that I committed adultery or fornication together with this woman—which I did not do and for which I do not acknowledge myself guilty—may God help me at this judgment.

### Chapter 80.—Separation from the incestuous union.

From this day forward, with this woman with whom [Col. 0830A] you committed adultery or fornication, for which you undertook discipline or penance, you shall no longer commit adultery or fornication. Nor shall you take another wife unless, after completing your penance, permission has been granted to you by the bishop or by his representative. So may God help you.

### Chapter 81.—Reconciliation of married people.

From this day forward, you shall keep your wife, N., whom you unjustly dismissed, in the manner in which a husband ought rightly to have his wife: with love and due discipline. You shall not separate her from you through any evil contrivance, nor shall you take another wife while she lives. So may God help you.

### Chapter 82.—On the same matter.

[Col. 0830B]

From now on, you shall keep and embrace your husband, whom you unjustly dismissed, and you shall be subject and obedient to him in service, love, and fear, in the manner in which a wife ought rightly to be subject to her husband. You shall never separate yourself from him, nor, while he lives, join yourself to another man, whether in marriage or adultery. So may God help you.

[Col. 0829] END OF BOOK NINE.
