# The Tenth Book of the Decrees of Burchard, Bishop of the Church of Worms: On Incantators and Augurs

[Col. 0831]

## Summary of the Book

[Col. 0831C]

This book treats incantators, augurs, diviners, those who use lots, and various illusions of the devil; also slanderers, quarrelsome people, conspirators, and the penance of each of them.

### Chapter 1.—That bishops expel diviners and sorcerers from their parishes.

(From the council of Ancyra, chapter 1.) Bishops and their ministers must strive with all their strength to eradicate entirely from their parishes the harmful art of divination and sorcery, invented by the devil. If they find any man or woman practicing such wickedness, they must expel that person from their parishes after subjecting them to public disgrace.

For the Apostle says: “Avoid a heretic after one and a second warning, knowing that such a person is perverted.” [Col. 0831D] Those are perverted and held captive by the devil who, having abandoned their Creator, seek aid from the devil. Therefore the holy Church must be cleansed of such a plague.

Nor should this be omitted: certain wicked women, turning back after Satan and seduced by demonic illusions and phantasms, believe and profess that during the hours of night they ride with Diana, the pagan goddess, or with Herodias and an innumerable multitude of women, upon certain beasts, pass over great stretches of land in the silence of the dead of night, obey her commands like a mistress, and are summoned on certain nights to serve her. [Col. 0832C]

Would that these women alone had perished in their faithlessness and had not dragged many others with them into the destruction of unbelief. For an innumerable multitude, deceived by this false opinion, believes these things to be true; and by believing them departs from the true faith and returns to the error of the pagans, imagining that some divinity or divine power exists outside the one God.

Therefore priests must preach with all insistence to the people in the churches entrusted to them, so that they may know that these things are entirely false and that such phantasms are inflicted upon the minds of unbelievers not by a divine but by a malignant spirit.

Indeed, Satan himself, who transforms himself into an angel of light, when he has seized the mind of some little woman and subjected her to himself through unbelief [Col. 0832D] and lack of faith, immediately transforms himself into the appearances and likenesses of various persons. Deceiving in dreams the mind he holds captive, displaying now joyful, now sorrowful, now familiar, now unfamiliar persons, he leads it through every sort of byway.

And when only the spirit undergoes this experience, the unbelieving mind supposes that it has happened not in the soul but in the body. Who is not carried outside himself in dreams and nighttime visions, seeing while asleep many things that he had never seen while awake? Yet who is so foolish and dull as to suppose that all these things, which take place only in the spirit, also occur in the body? [Col. 0833A]

The prophet Ezekiel saw the visions of the Lord in the spirit, not in the body. The Apostle John likewise saw the mysteries of the Apocalypse in the spirit, not in the body, and heard them, as he himself says: “Immediately,” he says, “I was in the spirit.” And Paul does not dare to say that he was caught up in the body.

It must therefore be publicly announced to everyone that whoever believes such things and things like them loses the faith; and whoever does not have the true faith in God belongs not to God but to the one in whom he believes—that is, the devil.

For it is written concerning our Lord: “All things were made through him.” Therefore whoever believes that anything can be done, or that any creature can be changed for better or worse, or transformed into another form or likeness, except by the Creator himself, who made all things and through whom [Col. 0833B] all things were made, is without doubt an unbeliever and worse than a pagan.

### Chapter 2.—On tree worshippers.

(From Gregory’s Rule.) It has come to our attention that certain people—something impious even to say—worship trees and perpetrate many other unlawful acts against the Christian faith. We are astonished that Your Fraternity has delayed correcting this through strict punishment.

Therefore, by this letter, we exhort you to have such people sought out through careful investigation; and, once the truth is known, inflict such punishment upon them that God may be appeased and their punishment may serve others as an example of correction.

### Chapter 3.—On idol worshippers.

(From the same author, chapter 5.) We exhort Your Fraternity to keep especially vigilant pastoral watch over worshippers of idols, haruspices, and those who use lots, and to speak publicly among the people against such persons. By persuasive admonition, recall them from this stain of sacrilege by reminding them of the divine judgment and the danger of the present life.

But if you find that they do not wish to amend and correct themselves from such practices, we wish you to seize them with fervent zeal. If they are slaves, chastise them with blows and tortures by which they may be brought to correction. If they are free, they are worthy of confinement and must be directed strictly in penance, so that those who disdain to hear words that bring healing and recall them from the danger of death may at least be brought back to the desired health of mind through bodily suffering.

### Chapter 4.—On the same matter.

[Col. 0833D] (From the same source, chapter 18.) It has come to our attention that you have prosecuted certain enchanters and lot-casters, and you should know that we have found your concern and zeal altogether pleasing. But we were displeased to learn that you doubted lest we might be deceived by them, contrary to your own experience, when you ought to be certain and know that this will contribute more to your commendation before us than be counted against you as a fault. Therefore, let it be your diligent concern to seek out such persons carefully, and correct all whom you find to be enemies of Christ with such strict punishment that we may form a better judgment of your experience and that you may commend yourself to our God—which is what you must strive for above all.

### CHAPTER 5 — Concerning those who seek divinations

[Col. 0834A]

(From the Council of Ancyra, chapter 23.) Those who seek divinations and follow the custom of the pagans, or who admit such persons into their houses to inquire into something by magical art or for the purpose of expiation, shall remain under the rule of five years, according to the established degrees of penance.

### CHAPTER 6 — Concerning those who observe pagan ritual

(From the Council of Braga, chapter 6.) If anyone, following pagan custom, admits diviners and practitioners of magic into his house, supposedly to drive out evil or discover magical spells, let him do penance for five years.

### CHAPTER 7 — Concerning those who serve auguries and incantations

[Col. 0834B] (From the Council of Carthage, chapter 89.) Anyone serving auguries or incantations is to be separated from the assembly of the Church. Likewise anyone adhering to Jewish superstitions or festivals.

### CHAPTER 8 — On the same matter

(From the Roman penitential.) Whoever serves auguries or divinations, or believes that certain human beings are senders of storms; or if any woman has practiced divinations or diabolical incantations, let her do penance for seven years.

### CHAPTER 9 — Concerning those who observe lots

(From the same source.) Let all who observe auguries or lots—the so-called false lots of the saints—or divinations from any writings, or who have made or fulfilled a vow at a tree, stone, or any object other than a church, be excommunicated. If they come to penance, clerics shall do penance for three years, and laypeople for one year and six months.

### CHAPTER 10 — Concerning the trees that the common people worship

(From the Council of Nantes, chapter 8.) Bishops and their ministers must strive with the greatest diligence to ensure that the trees consecrated to demons, which the common people worship and hold in such veneration that no one dares cut off a branch or shoot from them, are uprooted and burned. The stones, too, which people deceived by the demons’ illusions venerate in ruined and wooded places, where they make and fulfill vows, must be dug up from their foundations and thrown into a place where they can never again be venerated by their worshipers. Everyone must be told how great a crime idolatry is, and that whoever venerates and worships these things as a god denies his God and renounces Christianity; such a person must therefore undertake penance as though he had worshiped idols. Everyone must also be forbidden to make a vow or to carry a candle or any gift elsewhere when seeking something for his welfare, except to the church of the Lord his God. For it is written: “Vow and pay your vows to the Lord your God.” We know, indeed, how great were the threats the Lord made through his prophets against the ancient people who sacrificed in sacred groves and offered sacrifices on high places. If anyone transgresses these commands, he has lost the faith and is worse than an unbeliever. Therefore, in every way [Col. 0835A] he must be cut off from the fellowship of the holy Church and, unless he has done worthy penance, must not be received back.

### CHAPTER 11 — Concerning those who observe days and months

(From the sayings of Ambrose.) The Apostle says: “You observe days, and months, and seasons, and years; I fear that I may have labored among you without purpose.” They observe days who say, “I think one must not set out tomorrow.” For they think that nothing should be begun after tomorrow, and thus they are usually deceived even more. They observe months who examine the course of the moon, saying, “On the seventh moon agricultural tools ought not to be made; on the ninth moon a purchased slave ought not to be brought home.” Through such practices adversity more easily tends to arise. They observe seasons when they say, “Today is the beginning of spring, and therefore it is a festival.” And again: “It is an unlucky day; it is not permissible to leave the house.” They observe years when they say, “The Kalends of January are the new year,” as though the year were not completed every day. This superstition must be far from the servants of God. If anyone is exposed in this unbelief, clerics shall do penance for one year, and laypeople for half a year.

### CHAPTER 12 — Concerning those who sacrifice to demons

(From the penitential of Theodore.) Concerning those who sacrifice to demons, we have the regulations of Bishop Theodore, in which it is written: Those who sacrifice to demons in small matters shall do penance for one year; those who do so in great matters shall do penance for ten years.

### CHAPTER 13 — Concerning those who observe pagan traditions

(From the Council of Braga, chapter 20.) Christians are not permitted to observe pagan traditions or worship the elements, the moon, or the course of the stars, or to consider the empty deceit of signs when building a house or arranging marriages. For it is written: “Whatever you do in word or deed, do everything in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, giving thanks to God.” But if anyone does so, let him be corrected with the utmost severity and do canonical penance.

### CHAPTER 14 — Concerning little women who place their infants in a furnace or on a roof for their health

(From the penitential of the priest Bede.) If any woman places her son on a roof or in a furnace for the sake of curing fevers, let her do penance for one year.

### CHAPTER 15 — That it is not permitted to practice wicked observances of the Kalends

[Col. 0835D] (From the decrees of Pope Martial.) It is not permitted to practice the wicked observances of the Kalends or devote oneself to idleness, nor to encircle houses with laurel or the greenery of trees. All such observance is pagan.

### CHAPTER 16 — Concerning those who presume to celebrate the Kalends of January according to pagan ritual

(From the decree of Pope Zachary, chapter 11.) If anyone presumes to celebrate the Kalends of January according to pagan ritual, or to do anything additional because it is the new year, or to prepare tables with stones or foods in his houses, and to lead singers and choruses through the alleys and streets, let him be anathema.

### CHAPTER 17 — On the same matter

(From the Council of Rouen.) If anyone does anything on the Kalends of January that was invented by pagans, and observes the day, the moon, and the months, and hopes that through the effective power of the hours something may be changed for better or worse, let him be anathema.

### CHAPTER 18 — Concerning herdsmen, cattlemen, or hunters who practice their incantations

(From the same source, chapter 4.) It must be investigated whether any swineherd, cattleman, hunter, or another such person recites diabolical songs over bread, herbs, or certain abominable bindings, and hides these things in a tree, or throws them at a crossroads or a three-way junction, in order to free his own animals from pestilence and destruction and bring loss upon another’s. No believer can doubt that all these things are idolatry; therefore they must be utterly exterminated.

### CHAPTER 19 — That Christian women must not observe superstitions in their spinning and weaving

[Col. 0836B] (From the Council of Braga, chapter 10.) Christian women are not permitted to observe superstition in their spinning and weaving; rather, let them call upon God as their helper, who gave them the wisdom to weave.

### CHAPTER 20 — That the gathering of herbs must not be performed with incantations

(From the same source, chapter 21.) When medicinal herbs are gathered, it is not permitted to observe any practices or incantations, except only with the divine Creed and the Lord’s Prayer, so that God and our Lord may be honored.

### CHAPTER 21 — Concerning those who light torches at trees or springs

(From the same source, chapter 22.) If, in the parish of any presbyter, unbelievers light torches or venerate trees, springs, or stones, and he neglects to root this out, he must recognize that he has committed sacrilege, whether as the perpetrator or as the instigator of the matter. If, after being admonished, he neglects to correct it, let him be deprived of communion.

### CHAPTER 22 — That diviners are to be beaten and expelled from the cities

(From the Council of Arles, chapter 11.) Diviners who claim to know the future are to be beaten and expelled from the city.

### CHAPTER 23 — Concerning those who use amulets

(From a decree of Gregory.) If anyone consults fortune-tellers, soothsayers, or enchanters, or uses amulets, let him be anathema.

### CHAPTER 24 — Also concerning little women who practice incantations

[Col. 0836D] (From the Roman penitential.) If a woman has practiced divinations or diabolical incantations, let her do penance for one year, or for three Lents, or for forty days, according to the nature of the offense.

### CHAPTER 25 — Concerning those who eat, drink, or carry something upon themselves in order to overturn God’s judgment

(From the Council of Tribur, chapter 4.) If anyone eats, drinks, or carries something upon himself by which he thinks he can overturn God’s judgment, and he is convicted of this, let the same sentence be imposed upon him as is imposed upon magicians, fortune-tellers, and enchanters.

### CHAPTER 26 — Concerning those who seek the future in tablets or books

(From the penitential of Theodore.) The future must not be sought by lot in tablets or books, and no one must presume to cast lots in the Psalter, the Gospel, or any other work, or to practice any divinations by means of any objects. If anyone does so, let him do penance for forty days.

### CHAPTER 27 — Concerning those who seek the lots of the saints

(From the Council of Agde, chapter 3.) Nor must we pass over the matter that especially attacks the faith of religion: certain clerics or laypeople devote themselves to auguries and, under the name of a fictitious religion—which they call “the lots of the saints”—profess knowledge of divination, or promise the future through examination of any writings. Any cleric or layperson found consulting or teaching such things is to be expelled from the Church.

### CHAPTER 28 — Concerning those magicians who hope that they can pervert human minds

[Col. 0837B] (From the Roman penitential.) Magicians, enchanters, senders of storms, and those who disturb human minds through the invocation of demons are to be rejected as accursed; and if they wish to amend their ways, clerics shall do penance for three years, and laypeople for one year.

### CHAPTER 29 — On the same matter

(From the Council of Agde, chapter 4.) It must be investigated whether there is any woman who claims that by certain magical practices and incantations she can change human minds—that is, turn hatred into love or love into hatred, or damage or steal away people’s possessions. And if there is any woman who claims that, together with a troop of demons transformed into the likeness of women, she rides on certain beasts on appointed nights and has been counted among their company, such a woman must be beaten in every manner and expelled from the parish.

### CHAPTER 30 — Concerning those who invoke demons to accomplish their vanities

(From the penitential of the priest Bede.) Whoever, out of curiosity about the future, consults either an invoker of demons, or the diviners whom they call fortune-tellers, or the soothsayers who gather auguries, shall be removed from every clerical office and do penance for three years; laypeople shall do penance for two years.

### CHAPTER 31 — Concerning those who celebrate nocturnal sacrifices to demons

(From the Roman penitential.) Whoever celebrates nocturnal sacrifices to demons, or by any art invites demons through incantations to fulfill his wishes, shall do penance for three years.

### CHAPTER 32 — Concerning those who make vows at trees or springs

[Col. 0837D]

(From the Council of Agde, chapter 5.) It must be investigated whether anyone makes vows at trees, springs, or certain stones as though at altars, or carries there a candle or any gift, as though some divinity were present there that could bring about good or evil.

### CHAPTER 33 — Concerning those who practice their cries and magical rites when the moon is eclipsed

(From the Council of Arles, chapter 5.) Whoever practices this when the moon is eclipsed, believing that through his cries, magical rites, and sacrilegious practice he can defend himself; and whoever attempts to have diviners, enchanters, or even diabolical amulets, diabolical characters, herbs, or juices administered to their own people or to themselves; or presumes to honor Thursday in honor of Jupiter, or the Kalends of January according to pagan custom, shall do penance for five years if a monk, four years if a cleric, and two years if a layperson.

### CHAPTER 34 — Concerning those who practice their vanities during wakes

(From the same source, chapter 3.) Laypeople who keep watch at a funeral should do so with fear, trembling, and reverence. No one there should presume to sing diabolical songs or perform the games and dances that the pagans invented under the instruction of the devil. For who does not know that it is diabolical—not only alien to the Christian religion but also contrary to human nature—to rejoice, sing, become drunk, and dissolve one’s face in laughter there, setting aside all piety and the feeling of charity, as though exulting over a brother’s death, where mourning and lamentation ought to resound in tearful voices for the loss of a dear brother? We read in many places that the fathers of the Old and New Testaments lamented the deaths of holy men with weeping; nowhere, however, do we read that anyone rejoiced over those who had departed from the world. Indeed, all Egypt wept for the patriarch Jacob for seventy days. And when Joseph and his brothers carried their father into the land of Canaan for burial, they celebrated the funeral rites at the threshing floor of Atad, situated beyond the Jordan, and filled seven days with great and intense mourning. Their mourning was so great that the place received its name from it. We also read concerning blessed Stephen that devout men buried him—or took care of his burial—and made great lamentation over him. [Col. 0838C] Therefore such foolish merriment and destructive songs must be prohibited by God’s authority. If anyone wishes to sing, let him sing “Kyrie eleison” (“Lord, have mercy”); otherwise, let him be completely silent. If he does not wish to be silent, let the presbyter restrain him the following day in such a way that the others will be afraid.

### CHAPTER 35 — On the same matter

(From the Council of Meaux, chapter 10.) It was decided that women should be forbidden to keep vigil in a cemetery, since they often secretly commit crimes under the pretext of prayer and religion.

### CHAPTER 36 — Concerning banquets held according to pagan ritual

(From the African Council, chapter 27.) It must also be requested that, since banquets contrary to the divine commandments are held in many places—banquets drawn from pagan error, so that Christians are now compelled by pagans to celebrate them, whereby a second persecution seems secretly to be inflicted in the times of Christian emperors—such practices be ordered to be prohibited and, under penalty, forbidden in cities and estates. This is especially necessary since in some cities they do not shrink from committing such acts even on the feast days of the most blessed martyrs and in the sacred places themselves. On those days, too—shameful though it is to say—criminal dances are performed through the alleys and streets, so that the honor of matrons and the modesty of innumerable women who come devoutly to the most sacred day are assaulted by the wanton, and so that access even to the holy religion itself is nearly avoided.

### CHAPTER 37 — On the same matter

[Col. 0839A]

(From a decree of Pope Leo.) If they have merely taken part in a banquet of the pagans and eaten sacrificial foods, they can be cleansed by fasts and the laying on of hands, so that thereafter, abstaining from food offered to idols, they may participate in the sacraments of Christ. But if they have either worshiped idols or been defiled by murders or fornications, they must not be admitted to communion except through public penance.

### CHAPTER 38 — That the faithful must not presume to eat meals in cemeteries

(From the Council of Braga, chapter 70.) Christians are not permitted to carry meals to the tombs of the dead and sacrifice to the dead.

### CHAPTER 39 — Concerning those who perform dances and transform themselves into other forms

[Col. 0839B]

(From the same source, chapter 80.) If anyone has performed dances before the churches of the saints, or has transformed his face by wearing women’s clothing, or a woman by wearing men’s clothing, let him do penance for three years, after promising to amend.

### CHAPTER 40 — That incantations and magical arts are the devil’s snares

(From the sayings of Augustine.) Priests should warn the faithful peoples that they must know that magical arts and incantations can provide no remedy for any human illness, can heal nothing in sick or disabled animals, or even in those near death, but are snares and ambushes of the ancient enemy, by which that treacherous one strives to deceive the human race. If anyone practices these things, let a cleric be degraded and a layperson anathematized.

### CHAPTER 41 — Concerning those who seek health not from the Savior but from his creature

(Augustine, in *The City of God*.) “All wisdom is from the Lord God, and it has always been with him and exists before the age. Who can count the sand of the sea, the drops of rain, and the days of the age? Who has measured the height of heaven, the breadth of the earth, and the depth of the abyss? Who can investigate the wisdom of God, which precedes all things? Wisdom was created before all things, and the understanding of prudence is from eternity. The fountain of wisdom is the Word of God on high, and its entrance is the eternal commandments.””

For whoever wishes to have health without the Savior, and thinks that without true wisdom he can become prudent, is not healthy but sick, not prudent but foolish; he will labor in continual illness and, foolish and senseless, remain in harmful blindness. Accordingly, every inquiry and every remedy sought from diviners and magicians, or from the demons themselves in the worship of idols, should be called death rather than life. Those who pursue such things, unless they correct themselves, are heading toward eternal destruction, as the Psalmist says: “All the gods of the nations are demons.” Through deceived human beings they daily desire to deceive others, so as to make them participants in their own destruction. Thus this vanity of magical arts, handed down from evil angels, prevailed for many ages throughout the whole world through a certain knowledge of future and infernal things; and through their inventions arose soothsaying, augury, and those things called oracles, as well as necromancy.

### CHAPTER 42 — On the same matter

(From the sayings of the same author.) Nor is it surprising that the illusions of magicians developed such great magical powers that they even resisted Moses with signs very similar to his, turning rods into dragons and water into blood. It is also reported in pagan books that a certain very famous enchantress, Circe, changed the companions of Ulysses into beasts. We also read of the sacrifice that the Arcadians offered to their god Lycaeus: whoever partook of it was changed into the form of a beast. But all these things were fabricated more by magical illusions than accomplished in the reality of things.

Therefore, so that these errors may be made plain to the ignorant, we think it appropriate first to speak, according to the tradition of our ancestors, about their nature and their inventors. Magicians are those who, because of the magnitude of their crimes, are commonly called malefactors. By God’s permission they shake the elements, disturb the minds of people who place little confidence in God, and kill without the taking of any poison, solely through the violence of a spell. Hence Lucan also says: “The mind, polluted by no poisonous gore, perishes when bewitched.”

For, having summoned demons, they dare to set them in motion, so that each may destroy his enemies by evil arts. They also use blood and often touch the bodies of the dead with their victims. Necromancers are those whose incantations make the dead appear to rise, foretell things, and answer questions. *Necros* is the Greek word for “dead,” while *mantia* means “divination.” To raise them, blood is added to the corpse. For demons are said to love blood; therefore, whenever necromancy is performed, blood is mixed with water, and they are more easily provoked by the color of blood.

Hydromancers are so called from water. Hydromancy consists in summoning the shadows of demons by gazing into water, seeing their deceptive images, and hearing certain things from them there. When blood has been added, they are said to consult the underworld.

### CHAPTER 43 — On the same matter

(From the sayings of the same author.) Accordingly, this kind of divination is said to have been brought from the Persians. Varro, however, says that there are four types of divination: earth, water, air, and fire. From this, they say, come the names geomancy, hydromancy, aeromancy, and pyromancy.

Diviners are so called as though they were “full of God.” They pretend to be full of divinity and, by a certain fraudulent cunning, conjecture the future for human beings. There are two kinds of divination: art and frenzy.

Enchanters are so called because they perform their art through words. Arioli—“soothsayers”—are so called because they utter abominable prayers around the altars of idols and offer deadly sacrifices, receiving responses from demons through these ceremonies. Haruspices are so called as though they were “observers of hours.” They watch days and hours in conducting business and activities, and attend to what a person should observe at each particular time. They also examine the entrails of animals and foretell the future from them.

Augurs are those who attend to the flights and voices of birds and report other signs or unforeseen observations that occur to people. They are also called auspices. For auspices are the signs observed by travelers. They are called *auspicia*, as though from “observations of birds,” and *auguria*, as though from “the chatter of birds,” that is, the voices and tongues of birds. Indeed, *augurium* is almost *avigerium*, “what birds carry.”

There are two kinds of auspices: one concerns the eyes, the other the ears. The flight of birds belongs to the eyes; their voice to the ears. Pythonesses are named from the Pythian Apollo, because he was the originator of divination. Astrologers are so called because they practice augury from the stars. Genethliacs are named from their consideration of birth days. For human births are described through the twelve signs of heaven, and they attempt to foretell the character, actions, and events of those being born from the courses of the stars—that is, they interpret under which sign a person was born or what effect it has on the life of the one being born. These are the people commonly called mathematicians.

The Latins call this type of superstition *constellations*, that is, the configurations of the stars and how they stand when each person is born. At first, the interpreters of the stars were also called magi, as we read concerning those who announced the birth of Christ in the Gospel. Later, only mathematicians were called by this name; knowledge of this art was permitted up to the Gospel, so that after Christ was born no one might thereafter interpret anyone’s birth from heaven.

Horoscopes are so called because they observe the hours of human births and their unequal and differing fates. Sortilegers are those who, under the name of a fictitious religion, profess the knowledge of divination through certain things they call the lots of the saints, or promise the future through inspection of any writings. Salisators are so called because, whenever any part of their limbs leaps, they predict that something prosperous or sad is thereby signified for them.

### CHAPTER 44 — Concerning the accursed remedies that physicians employ in their incantations

(From the sayings of the same author.) To all the matters mentioned above also belong the bindings of accursed remedies that the medical art recommends, whether in incantations, characters, or any objects that are hung up or tied. In all these things there is the art of demons, arising from a pestilential association between human beings and evil angels. Therefore everything of this kind must be avoided by a Christian and utterly rejected and condemned with every possible curse.

Auguries concern birds. The Phrygians were the first to invent them. Mercury is said to have been the first to invent *praestigium*, “illusion,” so called because it dims the sharpness of the eyes. A certain Strages is said to have first handed down the art of haruspicy to the Etruscans. He dictated haruspicy from the hours and afterward disappeared. For, according to a fabulous tale, while a peasant was plowing, this man suddenly sprang from the clods and dictated haruspicy, dying on the very day he did so. The Romans translated his books from the Etruscan language into their own.

By such portents, human curiosity is mocked through the devil’s deception when people shamelessly desire to know what they have no right to investigate by any rational means. Therefore power is given to unclean spirits so that, through those suited to them—namely, wicked people—they may deceive those who reject the truth and believe falsehood. In accordance with Paul’s statement: “They will not endure sound doctrine, but according to their own desires they will heap up teachers for themselves, itching in their ears; and they will turn their hearing away from the truth and turn instead to fables.” Burdened with sins, they are led by various desires, always learning and never arriving at knowledge of the truth.

As Jannes and Jambres resisted Moses, so these people resist the truth: they are corrupted in mind, rejected with regard to the faith, but they will make no further progress. Their foolishness will be manifest to all, just as theirs was.

No one should therefore believe that anyone can accomplish anything by magical arts without the permission of God, who either does everything that happens by a just judgment or permits it to happen by his will. The magi mentioned above are read to have performed things similar to those of Moses. Moses threw down his rod, and it became a dragon; they too each threw down their rods, and these became dragons, but Aaron’s rod swallowed their rods. Therefore neither the magicians nor the evil angels, through whose ministry these things were done, were creators of dragons. For throughout all the elements of the world there are hidden seminal principles in corporeal things; when a temporal and causal opportunity is supplied, they burst forth into their proper forms according to their own modes and limits.

Thus the angels who perform such things are not called creators of animals, just as farmers are not to be called creators of crops, trees, or anything that grows from the earth, although they know how to provide certain visible opportunities and causes for these things to be born. What the magicians do visibly, the angels do invisibly. God alone is the one Creator, who implanted the causes themselves and the seminal principles in things.

Moreover, some people think it necessary to ask how Scripture can say that the Pythoness raised the prophet Samuel for conversation with Saul, the most wicked king, if Pythonic divination is to be counted among the errors of magical art. They can be answered as follows: it would be wholly unworthy to accept the story according to its literal words. For how could a man holy by birth and righteous in the works of his life be drawn forth by magical art? Or, if he was not drawn forth, did he consent? Both alternatives are contrary to what we should believe of a righteous man.

Justice would have no support if a man voluntarily lost the spiritual merit he had acquired while living in the flesh. This is wholly absurd, because one who departs from righteousness in this way remains righteous. Rather, this is Satan’s illusion, by which he pretends to have even good people in his power, so that he may deceive as many as possible. The Apostle shows this among other things when he says: “Satan himself transforms himself into an angel of light.”

In order to produce the error in which he would glory, he disguised himself in the appearance and under the name of a righteous man, so that he might falsely suggest that the hope they proclaimed to the worshipers of God was of no benefit, when he pretended that the righteous who had departed from this life were in his power. Yet some are deceived by the fact that he did not lie about the death of Saul and his son, as though it were a great thing for the devil to foresee bodily death before its arrival, when certain signs commonly appear to those who are about to die, since God’s protection seems to have been removed from them. How much more could the devil foresee it, whom the prophetic oracles testify to be exalted by angelic majesty and concerning whose greatness the Apostle says: “Or do you not know the height of Satan?”

What is surprising, then, if he was able to foresee an imminent death, when this is the very means by which he deceives and wishes to be worshiped in God’s place? Saul had become so foolish in his madness that he fled to the Pythoness. Having been corrupted by the cause of his sin, he turned to the very things he had condemned.

But if anyone thinks, because of the historical account and the matters expressed in its words, that nothing should be omitted lest the account’s meaning be empty, he may rightly do so, provided that he does not force this matter into the truth of the event, but relates it to Saul’s perception and understanding. For Saul had become rejected and could not have had sound understanding. The historian described Saul’s mind and Samuel’s appearance, expressing what was said and seen while leaving aside whether it was true or false.

For what does he say when Saul heard in what form the figure had been raised? “He understood,” it says, “that this was Samuel.” It reported what he understood; but because he did not understand correctly, he worshiped an apparition contrary to Scripture. Thinking that the aerial being was Samuel, he worshiped the devil, so that Satan might obtain the fruit of his deception. For this is what he strives for: to be worshiped as God.

If Samuel had truly appeared to him, surely the righteous man would not have permitted himself to be worshiped, since he had taught that the Lord alone must be worshiped. And how could a man of God, who was with Abraham in refreshment, say to a man deserving Gehenna, “Tomorrow you will be with me”?  In these two points, careless Satan carefully prepared the subtlety of his deception: he permitted himself to be worshiped under Samuel’s appearance and name, contrary to the law; and he falsely told a man burdened with sins—although there is a great difference between sinners and the righteous—that he would be with the most righteous Samuel.

The statement may appear true, but let us leave aside the name of Samuel, since Saul was going to be with the devil. He passed over to the one whom he worshiped. Thus the devil always reveals himself while hiding beneath a disguise, when he fabricates things that are abhorrent to the persons through whom he tries to deceive.

But if anyone opposes us and says, “How do those things come to pass that the diviners foretell as future? Or how can they provide healing to the sick or bring illness upon the healthy, if they possess no power or strength of their own?”—let him receive this answer from us: this is precisely why no one ought to believe them: because sometimes what they foretell comes to pass, or they appear to heal the sick or harm the healthy. This happens by God’s permission, so that those who hear or see these things may be deterred, and so that it may become evident what kind of faith or devotion they have toward God.

As we read in Deuteronomy, Moses commanded the people of God by the word of the Lord, saying: “If a prophet arises in your midst, or someone who says that he has seen a dream, and he foretells a sign or portent, and what he has spoken comes to pass, and he says to you, ‘Let us go and follow other gods whom you do not know, and let us serve them,’ you shall not listen to the words of that prophet or dreamer; for the Lord your God is testing you, so that it may become clear whether you love him or not. Follow your God with all your heart and with all your soul; fear him, keep his commandments, and hear his voice. You shall serve him and cling to him,” and so forth.

Here he clearly wished it to be understood that even those things spoken by diviners not according to God, if what they say happens, are not to be accepted; nor are the things they prescribe to be practiced or the things they worship to be worshiped. God does not show that these events occur outside his power; rather, when someone asks why he permits them, he explains the reason for the testing: to determine their love, whether they possess it toward their God. This knowledge is intended for them, not for him, who knows everything before it happens.

### CHAPTER 45 — Concerning the nature of demons

[Col. 0844B]

(From the writings of the same author.) It must be understood that the nature of demons is such that, through the perception of an aerial body, they easily surpass the perception of earthly bodies; and, because an aerial body is more mobile, they surpass not only the running of any human beings or beasts but even the flight of birds, incomparably, in speed. Endowed with these two qualities, insofar as an aerial body is concerned—namely, keenness of perception and swiftness of movement—they announce or foretell long beforehand things already conceived, which human beings, because of the slowness of their earthly perception, find astonishing. Moreover, through the very long period over which their lives extend, demons have acquired a far greater experience of things than can come to human beings because of the brevity of life.

Through these capacities, which the nature of an aerial body possesses, demons not only foretell the future but also perform many wonders. Since human beings cannot say or do such things, some judge demons worthy of serving and honoring with divine honors, being especially incited by the vice of curiosity through their love of false and earthly happiness and of temporal superiority. But those who cleanse themselves of such desires, and do not allow themselves to be carried away so as to be struck down and seized by them, but seek and love something that is always the same, through participation in which they may be blessed, first consider that demons are not thereby to be preferred to them because they prevail through a keener bodily sense—namely, that of the air, that is, of a subtler element. For even among earthly bodies they do not think that beasts should be preferred to themselves merely because those beasts perceive many things more keenly: for example, a clever dog, because it finds a hidden animal by its exceptionally sharp sense of smell and leads a human being to capture it—not through a more prudent understanding of the mind but through a sharper bodily sense; or a vulture, because, when a corpse has been thrown out, it flies to it from a great distance after having foreseen it; or an eagle, because, flying high, it is said to foresee from a great distance a fish swimming beneath the waves and to seize it by striking down heavily with extended feet and talons. Nor do they prefer to themselves the many other kinds of living creatures that wander among herbs harmful to their health while grazing, without touching anything by which they would be injured, whereas a human being has learned only with difficulty, through experience, to avoid them and fears many harmless things because they are unfamiliar.

From this it is easy to infer [Col. 0845A] how much keener perception may exist in aerial bodies; yet no sensible person would therefore judge demons, who possess this quality, preferable to good human beings. We say the same concerning the swiftness of bodies. By this superiority, too, human beings are surpassed not only by birds but also by many four-footed animals, so that, in comparison with them, human beings must be considered leaden. Yet they do not for that reason think those kinds of animals preferable to themselves, since they rule them—not by bodily force but by reason—capturing and taming them and reducing them to the use and advantage of their own will.

As for that third power of demons, namely, that through their long experience of things they have learned how to foresee and foretell many events, those who diligently take care to distinguish such matters from the truth of the truest light despise it. They do not therefore think wicked old men who have had greater experience, and are for that reason supposedly more learned, superior to virtuous young men. Nor do they think physicians, sailors, or farmers whom they have seen to be of depraved will and unjust character preferable merely because the physicians foretell much about illnesses, the sailors about storms, and the farmers about kinds of trees and fruits, in such a way that to the inexperienced they seem to divine.

But since demons not only foretell certain things but also perform certain things, because of the excellence of their bodies, why should this not be despised by the prudent, when many wicked and ruined human beings exercise their bodies in such a way, and possess such abilities through various arts, that those who do not know these things and have never seen them can scarcely believe them even when they are recounted? How many marvels have tightrope walkers and other theatrical performers accomplished! How many have craftsmen, and especially mechanics, accomplished! Are they therefore better than good human beings endowed with holy piety?

We have mentioned these matters so that anyone who considers them without obstinacy or the vain hostility of resistance may also reflect that, if human beings can accomplish so much with the denser underlying material—whether of their own bodies or of earth, water, stones, wood, and various metals—that those who cannot do such things often call them divine in astonishment at their abilities, although some of those human beings are more powerful in their arts and some of the others are better in character, then demons, through the capacity and ease afforded by a most subtle body—that is, an aerial body—can accomplish things much better and greater, even though they are unclean and perverse spirits of wicked will, especially swollen with the arrogance of pride and manifest evil.

How much power the element of air possesses, by which their bodies prevail in visibly working, moving, changing, and turning about many visible things, would take too long to demonstrate now; and we think that this will readily occur to anyone who considers it even moderately carefully.

### CHAPTER 46 — On the Divination of Demons

(From the writings of the same author.) Since the question concerns the divination of demons, it must first be understood that they generally foretell things that they themselves are going to do. They often receive the power both to inflict diseases and, by corrupting the air itself, to make it unhealthy, and to persuade the perverse and those who love earthly advantages to commit evil deeds; concerning such people they are certain that, when they offer such persuasion, they will consent.

They persuade them in wondrous and invisible ways by penetrating, through the subtlety of their bodies, the bodies of people who do not perceive them, and by mingling with their thoughts through certain imaginary visions, whether the people are awake or asleep. Sometimes, however, they foretell not what they themselves do but what they foresee will happen through natural signs—signs that cannot enter into human perception. For a physician is not therefore to be regarded as a diviner merely because he foresees what someone ignorant of his art cannot foresee. What is surprising, then, if, just as a physician foresees good or bad future health from the condition of the human body, whether disturbed or regulated, so a demon foresees future storms from an affection and arrangement of the air known to it but unknown to us?

Sometimes they also learn with complete ease the dispositions of human beings—not only those expressed in speech but even those conceived in thought—when certain signs are impressed upon the body by the mind; and from this they foretell many future things to others who do not know that these dispositions have been formed. For just as an agitated movement of the mind appears in the face, so that even human beings recognize externally something of what is taking place within, it should not be considered incredible that even gentler thoughts give certain signs through the body, which cannot be perceived by the duller senses of human beings but can be perceived by the keener senses of demons.

By this and similar abilities demons foretell many future things, although they are far removed from the height of that prophecy which God works through holy angels and prophets. For if they foretell anything concerning God’s disposition, they hear it in order to foretell it; and when they proclaim what they hear from that source, they do not deceive. Angelic and prophetic oracles are indeed utterly truthful.

Yet people take it indignantly that demons also hear and proclaim some such things, as though it were improper that what is spoken so that it may become known to human beings should be concealed not only by the good but also by the wicked. We see, moreover, that among human beings themselves the precepts of a good life are sung alike by the just and the perverse; and this does not hinder but rather helps to increase the knowledge and fame of the truth when even those who contradict it by their wicked conduct proclaim whatever they know about it.

In their other predictions, however, demons are often both deceived and deceivers. When they foretell their own plans, something may suddenly be commanded from above that confounds all their counsels. It is as though some human beings subject to various authorities were to arrange something which they thought their superiors would not forbid, and promised that they would carry it out; but those who possess greater power, following some higher decision, were suddenly to prohibit the whole arrangement that had been devised and prepared.

They are also deceived when they foresee things through natural causes, as physicians, natural philosophers, and farmers do—although they foresee them far more keenly and with much greater ability because of the more perceptive sense of their aerial body and their alertness. For these things too are suddenly and unexpectedly changed by angels who piously serve the supreme God, according to another disposition unknown to the demons. It is as if something external were to befall a sick person and cause him to die, although the physician, on the basis of the preceding signs of health, had promised that he would recover.

Or it is as if some sailors, having foreseen from the condition of the air a wind long set in, had predicted it, but the Lord Christ, sailing with his disciples, commanded it to cease so that he might rest, and a great calm came about. Or it is as if a farmer, skilled in the nature of the soil and the qualities of seeds, promised that a certain vine would bear fruit that year, but an unforeseen disturbance of the heavens dried it up. In the same way, many things connected with the predictions of demons, which are foreseen as future through lesser and customary causes, are altered when those causes are obstructed by greater and hidden causes.

They also deceive deliberately and out of an envious will to deceive, because they rejoice in human error. But so that they may not lose the weight of their authority among their worshipers, they arrange for blame to be assigned to their interpreters and to those who interpret their signs whenever those interpreters have either been deceived or lied.

Sometimes, indeed, those wicked spirits—mockers and enemies of human beings and of their salvation—customarily foretell the failure of their own worship and the ruin of idols, so that they may appear to know beforehand what will happen in particular kingdoms or places and what adverse event may befall their faction. Those who read the histories of the pagans are not ignorant of this.

What is surprising, then, if, when the destruction of temples and images was already imminent—something which the prophets of the supreme God had foretold long beforehand—the demon Serapis disclosed this impending event to one of his worshipers, so that, as it were, while withdrawing or fleeing, he might commend his supposed divinity? For these spirits are driven out, or even dragged away and separated from their places after being bound by superior commands, so that God’s will may be done concerning the things in which they were worshiped—God who had foretold long beforehand through all nations that this would happen and had commanded that it be brought about through his faithful servants.

Why should the demon not be permitted to foretell what it already knew was threatening it? This prediction both bore witness to the prophets by whom these things had been written and made clear to the prudent how watchfully the demons’ deception and their worship must be avoided. Although they had remained silent for so long in their temples about events that they could not have failed to know from the prophets, once those events began to draw near they wished, as though to foretell them, to avoid appearing ignorant and defeated.

### CHAPTER 47 — On the Same Matter

(From the writings of the same author.) Since the event had been foretold and written down so long beforehand, let us—leaving other matters aside—mention what the prophet Zephaniah says: “The Lord will prevail against them; he will destroy all the gods of the nations of the earth, and they will worship him, each from his own place, all the islands of the nations.”

Either they did not believe that these things would happen to them because they were worshiped in the temples of the nations, and therefore did not wish to repeat them frequently through their seers and fanatics; or, since they knew with complete certainty that these things would happen, they remained silent about them in their temples so that even then they would not begin to be abandoned and despised by intelligent people, since the prophets testified to them that their temples and images would be destroyed and prohibited them from being worshiped.

But now, after the time had come when the prophecies of the prophets of the one God were to be fulfilled, who calls these beings gods and commands most insistently that they be worshiped? Since they were not permitted even to proclaim this fact, which they themselves had discovered, it became clearer from this that previously they had either not believed these things at all or had been afraid to announce them to their worshipers; but at the end, as though they had nothing else to do, they wished to display their divinity even there, where they were already being exposed as having long pretended to possess the power of divination.

Nevertheless, even these statements, which they scarcely ever utter and then only secretly, ought not to move us. If something was wrung from some demon so that it disclosed to its worshipers what it had learned from the utterances of the prophets or from angelic oracles, why should this not happen, since such a disclosure is not an attack but a testimony to the truth?

For there is one thing alone that ought to be demanded from those fanatics: something which they have never previously proclaimed and which they will never afterward attempt to proclaim, unless perhaps they fabricate it—namely, that their gods, through their seers, dared to foretell or declare anything against the God of Israel. Their most learned authors, who were able to read and know all those writings, sought more to discover who this God was than to deny him.

This God, whom none of them dared to deny to be the true God—for even if anyone denied him, he would not only suffer the punishments he deserved but would also be convicted by manifest results—this God, then, whom, as we have said, none of them dared to deny to be the true God, openly foretold through his seers, that is, through his prophets, that they were false gods and must be entirely abandoned, and openly commanded that their temples, images, and rites be overthrown; and he openly fulfilled this through his power and truth.

Who, then, is so foolish that he would not choose to worship rather the one whose worship is not prohibited by those whom he used to worship? Once he begins to worship him, he will certainly no longer worship those whom the one he worships forbids to be worshiped.

We mentioned shortly beforehand, and now repeat, that the prophets of this God foretold that the nations themselves would worship him after the false gods whom they had formerly worshiped had been destroyed. “The Lord,” he says, “will prevail against them, and he will destroy all the gods of the nations of the earth, and they will worship him, each from his own place, all the islands of the nations.”

Here “islands” does not mean islands alone; rather, all the nations situated in them worship God. Nor is this surprising, since elsewhere he does not mention islands but the entire inhabited world, saying: “All the ends of the earth will remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations will worship in his presence, for the kingdom is the Lord’s, and he will rule the nations.”

That these things were to be fulfilled through Christ is sufficiently clear from many other testimonies and from that very psalm from which we have cited the passage. For when, shortly before, he himself spoke through the prophet of his future passion, saying: “They pierced my hands and my feet; they counted all my bones; they themselves looked upon me and observed me; they divided my garments among themselves, and upon my clothing they cast lots,” shortly afterward he adds the passage we have cited: “All the ends of the earth will remember and turn to the Lord,” and so forth.

Moreover, the testimony I previously introduced—where it says, “The Lord will prevail against them, and he will destroy all the gods of the nations of the earth”—by the use of the word “prevail” sufficiently shows that this too was foretold: namely, that the pagans would first attack the Church and persecute the Christian name with all their strength, so that, if possible, it might be utterly removed from the earth.

And because the Lord was to overcome them through the endurance of the martyrs, the greatness of miracles, and the faith that followed among the peoples, it was therefore said: “The Lord will prevail against them.” It would not be said that he would prevail against them unless they resisted him by attacking him.

Thus it was also prophesied in the Psalm: “Why did the nations rage, and the peoples devise vain things? The kings of the earth stood forth, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ.” Shortly afterward it says: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession.”

By these and similar prophetic testimonies it is shown to have been foretold—and we see it being fulfilled through Christ—that the God of Israel, whom we understand to be the one true God, would be worshiped not only in that one people called Israel but among all nations, and that he would remove all the false gods of the nations both from their temples and from the hearts of their worshipers.

And now these few who have remained still dare to defend their former vanities against the Christian religion and against the true worship of God; let them perish with a great noise. For this too was foretold concerning them in the Psalms, where the prophet says: “You have sat upon the throne, judging righteousness. You rebuked the nations, and the wicked perished; you blotted out their name forever and ever. The enemies’ swords have failed, and you have destroyed their cities. Their memory has perished with a noise, but the Lord remains forever.”

All these things must therefore be fulfilled. Nor should the fact that the few who have remained still dare to display their empty doctrines and mock Christians as though they were utterly ignorant move us, while we see the things that were foretold being fulfilled in them.

From the time when the nations raged and the peoples devised vain things against the Lord and against his Christ—when the blood of the saints was being shed by them and the Church was being devastated—until the present time and thereafter, their numbers diminish daily.

But we, whom God’s oracles make exceedingly strong against their insults and proud mockery, dare and rejoice to see this matter also fulfilled. For through the prophet he addresses us as follows: “Hear me, you who know judgment, my people, in whose heart is my law: do not fear the reproaches of human beings, and do not be overcome by their insults; do not regard it as a great thing that they despise you. For as a garment, so they will be consumed by time, and as wool, so they will be eaten by the moth; but my righteousness remains forever.”

It is therefore necessary to pay attention and to take every precaution lest, in our times, when we see the Christian religion spread throughout the whole world, those few who still remain, through the negligence of teachers and the inertia of instructors, confuse the rite of the true worship of God. Corrupted by demonic illusions, they may practice false divinations among God’s people, seducing the rustic and uneducated, so that, abandoning the truth itself—which is the light of the world and enlightens every human being coming into this world of darkness—they seek knowledge of future things and seek the salvation either of their souls or even of their bodies from deceivers of human beings.

For by such transgressions God is especially provoked and stirred to vengeance. Thus through Ezekiel he threatens, saying: “Woe to the foolish prophets who follow their own spirit and see nothing. Your prophets, Israel, were like foxes in the deserts. Have you not seen a vain vision and spoken a lying divination, saying, ‘Thus says the Lord,’ when I have not spoken?

“Therefore thus says the Lord God: Because you have spoken vanity and seen lies, behold, I am against you, says the Lord God. And my hand will be against the prophets who see vanity and divine lies. They will not be in the council of my people; they will not be written in the inscription of the house of Israel, nor will they enter the land of Israel.”

Addressing the teachers through the same prophet and rebuking their inertia, he speaks as follows: “You did not go up to the breach, nor did you build a wall for the house of Israel, that you might stand in battle on the day of the Lord.”

And again: “Woe,” he says, “to the shepherds of Israel who fed themselves. Are not flocks fed by shepherds? You ate the milk, clothed yourselves with the wool, and slaughtered what was fat, but you did not feed my flock. You did not strengthen what was weak, heal what was sick, bind up what was broken, bring back what had been cast away, or seek what was lost. Instead, you ruled them with harshness and power.

“And my sheep were scattered because there was no shepherd, and they became food for all the beasts of the field; they were scattered.”

Hence Jeremiah says: “From the least to the greatest, all pursue greed; from prophet to priest, all practice deceit. And they healed the brokenness of the daughter of my people to their disgrace, saying, ‘Peace, peace,’ when there was no peace. They were confounded because they committed abomination.

“Therefore thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Behold, I will feed this people with wormwood, and I will give them water of gall to drink. I will scatter them among nations whom neither they nor their fathers knew, and I will send the sword after them until they are consumed.”

How displeasing to almighty God is the negligence of shepherds and the error of their subjects is shown not only by prophetic testimonies but also by the deeds of the ancients. For in the Book of Kings we read how an evil spirit deceived Ahab, king of Israel, through false prophets, so that he perished because he believed them; and how Ahaziah, his son, when he was sick, sent messengers to consult Beelzebub, the god of Ekron, asking whether he could live and recover from his illness.

For this reason the prophet Elijah, sent by God, rebuked him, saying: “Because you sent messengers to consult Beelzebub, the god of Ekron—as though there were no God in Israel from whom you could inquire about his word—therefore you shall not come down from the bed upon which you have gone up, but you shall certainly die.”

And he died according to the word of the Lord that Elijah had spoken, and he did not obtain the recovery he had sought.

Therefore all people must take the greatest care in every way—rulers and subjects, great and small, priests and laity—that no one be seduced by such a deception, fraud, or wickedness of the ancient enemy, so that we should wish to learn the truth from liars and seek a remedy for our illness from those who cause destructive diseases and death.

Rather, let us hasten with devoted hearts to the living God, who gives life to all, imploring him through sacred prayers, fasts, and almsgiving that, in his goodness, he may care for his servants, rescuing us from all our enemies and teaching us to do his will. For he is the Lord our God; may he also grant us his good Spirit, who will lead us along the right path and revive us in his righteousness, so that, under his instruction, we may offer him acceptable service throughout all the days of our life and, after this life, by his grace, may deserve to possess everlasting blessedness.

### CHAPTER 48 — On Priests and the Other Ecclesiastical Orders Who Consult Magicians, Soothsayers, or Diviners

(From the Council of Toledo, chapter 29.) If any bishop, priest, deacon, or anyone from the clerical order is discovered consulting magicians, haruspices, diviners, lot-casters, or those who profess any art, or anyone practicing similar things, let him be deposed from the dignity of his office, enter a monastery, and, being devoted there to perpetual penance, pay the penalty for the sacrilege he has committed.

### CHAPTER 49 — On Those Who Perform Incantations Against the Evil Eye

(From the Council of Chalon, chapter 5.) If anyone has recited an incantation against the evil eye, or any kind of incantation except the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer, both the one who sings it and the one for whom it is sung shall perform three Lenten periods of penance on bread and water.

### CHAPTER 50 — That One Afflicted by a Demon May Carry Stones or Herbs Without Incantation

(From the writings of Jerome.) A person afflicted by a demon may possess stones or herbs without an incantation.

### CHAPTER 51 — That Those Who Curse Shall Not Possess the Kingdom of God Unless They Correct Themselves

(The Apostle says.) The Apostle says: “Nor shall those who curse possess the kingdom of God.” If anyone has committed this sin, let him perform penance as great as the crime he committed, so that he may not be separated from the kingdom of God.

### CHAPTER 52 — On Those Who Murmur

[Col. 0852A]

(From the Council of Mainz, chapter 8.) If anyone has become a murmurer, let him beware lest he incur the punishment of those who murmured, concerning whom the Apostle says: “Nor murmur, as some of them murmured and perished by the destroyer.” In proportion to the measure and character of the sin, let him do penance by the judgment of the priest, for the Apostle’s sentence is fully expressed in this matter.

### CHAPTER 53 — On the Same Matter

(From the same source.) Whoever has become quarrelsome or murmuring shall do penance according to the judgment of his superior, in accordance with the character of his fault.

### CHAPTER 54 — On the Same Matter

(The Apostle says.) The Apostle says: “Do everything without murmuring.” Whoever murmurs is to be separated from the unity of the brothers, and his work is to be rejected.

### CHAPTER 55 — On Quarrelsome Persons

(From the decree of Pope Hilary, chapter 15.) If anyone appears to be quarrelsome—for the Apostle says, “We have no such custom, nor has the Church of God”—let him be censured until he is corrected.

### CHAPTER 56 — On Those Who Have Been Lewd in Speech

(From the Penitential of Theodore.) If anyone has been lewd in speech, let him be cleansed by three days of penance.

### CHAPTER 57 — On Those Who Have Become Dissident Through Hatred

(From the writings of Saint Isidore.) If anyone has become discordant and contentious, and has separated himself through hatred, let him remain, as the canons command, excluded from the assembly and fellowship of the Church until he returns to concord.

### CHAPTER 58 — On One Who Hates Someone and Does Not Wish to Return to Peace

[Col. 0852C]

(From the same source.) If anyone hates another so much that he does not wish to return to peace, let him be excommunicated and separated from the Church, as the holy Fathers established, until he is reconciled.

### CHAPTER 59 — On the Same Matter

(From the decree of Pope Fabian, chapter 3.) If anyone who has been offended refuses to be reconciled when the one who offended him offers satisfaction, let him be afflicted by the severest fasts until he receives the satisfaction with a joyful heart.

### CHAPTER 60 — On the Same Matter

(From the same source.) If anyone does not wish to be reconciled with his brother whom he hates, let him do penance on bread and water until he is reconciled with him.

### CHAPTER 61 — On the Same Matter

[Col. 0852D]

(From the Council of Agde, chapter 7.) It was also decreed that, as frequently happens, whoever has separated from another after a prolonged lawsuit and cannot be recalled to peace despite prolonged efforts shall be expelled from the assembly of the Church by the most just excommunication.

### CHAPTER 62 — On Those Who Love Quarrels and Fights

(From the same source, chapter 5.) If anyone has loved quarrels or fights, or has openly insulted his brother, let him perform prolonged penance according to the judgment of the ruler and the measure of his sin.

### CHAPTER 63 — On Those Who Are Ready and Eager to Slander

(From the same source, chapter 10.) If anyone is ready and eager to slander, saying what is not true, let him do penance for six days on bread and water, separated from fellowship with his brother.

### CHAPTER 64 — On Those Who Have Conspired Against Their Bishops

(From a letter of Pope Callistus to all the bishops of Gaul.) We have heard that the crimes of conspiracies are flourishing in your regions, and it has been reported to us that the peoples are conspiring against their bishops. The cunning of any such crime is not only hateful among Christians but also among pagans, and is forbidden by law among outsiders. Therefore the laws not only of the Church but also of the world condemn those guilty of this crime—and not only those who conspire but also those who consent to them.

Our predecessors, together with a very large number of bishops, ordered that any of those who are established or serve in the priestly order or as clerics should be deprived of the honor they hold; and they ordered that the rest be deprived of communion and expelled from the Church—not only those who carried out the act but also those who consented to it.

### CHAPTER 65 — On the Same Matter

(From the Council of Tongeren, chapter 5.) Whoever deceitfully lays his hand upon the Christ of the Lord—that is, upon his bishop, father, and shepherd—commits sacrilege. Whoever devastates and burns the Church of God also commits sacrilege. Therefore it pleased the holy synod that such a person should do penance in one place, namely, in a monastery, throughout all the days of his life.

### CHAPTER 66 — On Clerics Who Curse

(From the Council of Carthage, chapter 57.) A cleric who curses is to be compelled, especially by the priests, to ask forgiveness. If he refuses, let him be degraded, and let him never be restored to office without satisfaction.

### CHAPTER 67 — On Those Who Slander Their Superiors

(From the writings of Bishop Basil.) If anyone slanders the person who presides over him, let him do penance for seven days, separated from the assembly of the Church, like Mary, the sister of Aaron, who slandered Moses.

### CHAPTER 68 — On Clerics or Monks Who Swear Together or Conspire Against Their Bishop

[Col. 0854B]

(From the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 19.) If any clerics or monks are found to have sworn together or conspired, or to have laid snares for bishops or clerics, let them be completely removed from their proper rank.

### CHAPTER 69 — On the Same Matter

Therefore, if clerics or monks are found to have sworn together, or through a conspiracy to be contriving an accusation against bishops or clerics, let them lose their proper rank.

[Col. 0853] END OF THE TENTH BOOK.

[BOOK ELEVEN.]
