# THE ELEVENTH BOOK OF THE DECREES OF BURCHARD, BISHOP OF THE CHURCH OF WORMS: ON EXCOMMUNICATION

[Col. 0855]

## ARGUMENT OF THE BOOK

[Col. 0855C]

This book treats of excommunication, its neglect and contempt, thieves and robbers, and despisers and plunderers of sacred buildings.

### CHAPTER 1 — On the Seat of Bishops: Why They Ought to Sit Higher Than the Others in Church
From the letter of Pope Urban. Since the bishops’ seats are found established in the church on high and prepared upon a throne, their very arrangement teaches that the Lord has given them oversight, and the power of judging, loosing, and binding. Hence the Savior himself says in the Gospel: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven.” And elsewhere: “Receive the Holy Spirit: whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven [Col. 0855D] them; and whose sins you retain, they are retained.” Therefore, dearest brothers, we have set these matters forth so that you may understand the authority of your bishops, venerate the Lord in them, love them as your own souls, refrain from communicating with those with whom they do not communicate, and do not receive [Col. 0856C] those whom they have expelled. For the sentence of a bishop is greatly to be feared, even if he binds unjustly—though he ought above all to take care that he not do so.

## Chapter 2—When a bishop has determined to excommunicate or anathematize someone for definite and manifest crimes, he ought, after the reading of the Gospel, to address the clergy and people as follows

(From the Council of Rouen, chapter 3.) Let your charity know, my brothers, that a certain man named N., at the devil’s urging, setting aside the Christian promise that he professed in baptism, has turned through apostasy back to Satan, whom he renounced, and to all his works. He does not fear laying waste and plundering Christ’s vineyard—that is, his Church—violently oppressing and killing Christ’s poor, whom he redeemed with his precious blood, [Col. 0856D] and seizing their goods.

Although he ought to have been a son of this Church of ours, which by God’s authority we preside over—since in it he was reborn through water and the Holy Spirit and was numbered among God’s adopted sons—nevertheless, [Col. 0857A] by imitating the devil, he is now a son of the devil. We are therefore concerned lest, through pastoral negligence, any of the sheep entrusted to us should perish, for which we would be compelled to render an account before our Lord Jesus Christ, the chief Shepherd, at the dread judgment, according to his terrible warning to us: “If you do not announce his iniquity to the wicked man, I will require his blood from your hand.”

We sent him our priest and letters of admonition once, twice, and a third time, canonically inviting him to amendment, satisfaction, and penance, and correcting him with paternal affection. But he—alas!—because the devil hardened his heart, despised these salutary admonitions and, persisting in the wickedness he had begun, disdainfully refuses to make satisfaction to the Church of God whom he has injured, puffed up by a spirit of pride. [Col. 0857B]

Concerning such transgressors and violators of the holy religion and of the peace that Christ gave and left to his disciples, we possess the Lord’s and the Apostles’ commands, by which we are instructed what we ought to do with such transgressors. For the Lord says in the Gospel: “If your brother sins against you, rebuke him.” Brothers, whoever sins against the holy Church sins against each one of us. For if the holy Church is one body, whose head is Christ, and we individually are members of one another; and if, when one member suffers, all the members suffer with it, then without doubt he sins against us who injures our members.

The Lord therefore commands that a brother—that is, a Christian—who sins against us should first be rebuked privately, then reproved with witnesses, [Col. 0857C] and finally confronted publicly in the assembly of the Church. If he despises these three admonitions and charitable corrections and refuses to make satisfaction, the Lord says: “Let him be to you as a heathen and a publican”—that is, a gentile and pagan—so that he is no longer regarded as a Christian but as a pagan.

And elsewhere the Lord commands that a member which is loosened from its framework, separated from the bond of charity, and causes the whole body to stumble be both cut off and cast away, saying: “If your eye, hand, or foot causes you to stumble, tear it out and cast it from you.” And the Apostle says: “Remove the evil person from among you.” And again: “If anyone is named a brother, and is a fornicator, or adulterer, or murderer, or robber, with such a person you may not even eat.”

John also, the beloved disciple of Christ above the others, [Col. 0857D] forbade greeting such a wicked man, saying: “Do not even say ‘Hail’ to him, nor receive him into your house. For whoever says ‘Hail’ to him shares in his evil works.” Therefore, fulfilling the Lord’s and the Apostles’ commands, let us cut off from the body of the Church with the sword of excommunication the rotten and incurable member that does not accept medicine, lest the remaining members of the body be infected, as by poison, with so deadly a disease.

## Chapter 3—The first excommunication

(From the same council, chapter 4.) Since he despises our admonitions and repeated exhortations; since, summoned a third time according to the Lord’s command to amendment and penance, he has disdained to come; since he has [Col. 0858A] not yet acknowledged or confessed his fault, nor sent a delegation to us to inquire into his case; since he is our parishioner and has not sought pardon; since he persists in the wickedness he began, the devil having hardened his heart; and since, as the Apostle says, “according to his hardness and impenitent heart he stores up wrath for himself on the day of wrath”—

therefore, by the judgment of almighty God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; of blessed Peter, chief of the Apostles; and of all the saints; and by the authority of our mediocrity and the power divinely granted to us to bind and loose in heaven and on earth, we separate him, together with all his accomplices, associates, and supporters, from participation in the precious body and blood of the Lord and from the fellowship of all Christians [Col. 0858B]. We exclude him from the thresholds of holy Mother Church in heaven and on earth, decree him to be excommunicated and anathematized, and judge him condemned with the devil, his angels, and all the rejected, in eternal fire—unless perhaps he comes to his senses, escapes the devil’s snares, returns to amendment and penance, and makes satisfaction to the Church of God whom he has injured.

Let all respond three times: “Amen,” or “So be it, so be it,” or “Let him be anathema.” The priests ought to stand around the bishop and hold burning lamps in their hands, which, at the conclusion of the anathema or excommunication, they must throw upon the ground and trample underfoot.

After this the bishop ought to explain the excommunication itself to the people in ordinary words, [Col. 0858C] so that all may understand how terribly he has been condemned and know that from that hour onward he is to be regarded not as a Christian but as a pagan. Whoever, therefore, communicates with him as though he were a Christian, eats or drinks with him, kisses him, holds familiar conversation with him, unless he is striving to summon him to satisfaction and penance; or receives him into his house; or prays together with him—such a person is likewise, without doubt, to be excommunicated.

Next, letters are to be sent to the priests throughout the parishes, containing the manner of the excommunication. They are to be instructed to announce this excommunication publicly on Sundays, after the reading of the Gospel, to the people entrusted to them, so that no one through ignorance may communicate [Col. 0858D] with the excommunicated man. The excommunication must also be made known to the other bishops. For the Council of Toledo commands that letters should immediately circulate among all the bishops of the province whom they can reach, so that the excommunicated man may be heard. His lord or superior must also be informed of the excommunication.

## Chapter 4—Another form of the excommunication address

(From the Council of Orléans, chapter 1.) You have heard how many and how dreadful were the works of depravity and iniquity that N., instigated by the devil, did not fear to commit, and how, through apostasy, he withdrew with a profane mind from the worship of the entire Christian religion. You have heard how he was canonically summoned to make satisfaction, but delayed coming; how, though [Col. 0859A] frequently admonished to recover from the devil’s snares by which he is held bound, he contemptuously refused to hear the most salutary admonitions with the hardened ears of his heart.

The Lord says in the Gospel concerning such a contumacious brother who refuses to accept ecclesiastical correction: “If he will not hear the Church, let him be to you,” he says, “as a heathen and a publican”—that is, he is no longer to be counted among Christians but among pagans.

Following the teaching of the Lord and Master, Paul reproves the Corinthians for maintaining communion with criminals and wicked men, saying: “You are puffed up, and have not rather mourned, so that the man who has committed such a crime might be removed from among you [Col. 0859B]”—that is, separated from your fellowship. And he adds: “Although absent in body, I am present in spirit; I have already judged, as though present, the man who has done this, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, when you are gathered together, and my spirit is with the power of my Lord Jesus, to deliver such a one to Satan for the destruction of the flesh.”

And shortly afterward: “I wrote to you not to associate with fornicators.” He immediately adds: “If anyone who is called a brother”—that is, a Christian—“is a fornicator or a robber, with such a person do not even eat.” And elsewhere: “Remove the evil person from among you.” Also: “If the unbeliever departs, let him depart.”

For one diseased sheep contaminates the entire flock; a little leaven corrupts the whole lump; and often one rotten member infects the whole body. Therefore, let so destructive a plague be torn out by the roots from the body of the Church [Col. 0859C].

## Chapter 5—The second excommunication

(From the same council.) Instructed, therefore, by the Lord’s and the Apostles’ commands, by the judgment of the Father, and of his Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, and of the Holy Spirit, and by the authority and power granted by God to the Apostles and their successors, together with you we exclude the aforesaid wicked man from the thresholds of holy Mother Church and separate him from every Christian fellowship and communion. We decree that he is separated forever—that is, both in the present age and in the future.

Let no Christian say “Hail” to him or presume to kiss him. Let no priest dare celebrate Mass with him or give him the most holy body and blood of the Lord. Let no one associate with him in [Col. 0859D] fellowship or in any business. If anyone associates with him and shares in his evil works, let him know that he has been struck by a similar anathema—except those who associate with him for the purpose of recalling him from error and summoning him to make satisfaction, provided that he should come to his senses, be turned by God’s grace to the remedy of penance, and humbly make worthy satisfaction to the Church of God whom he has injured.

## Chapter 6—The third excommunication

(From the Council of Tours, chapter 2.) Following canonical institutions and the examples of the holy Fathers, we separate from the bosom of holy Mother Church the violators of the churches of God—namely, robbers, plunderers, and murderers—N., in the name of the Father and of the Son and by the power of the Holy Spirit, and by the authority divinely granted [Col. 0860A] to bishops through Peter, chief of the Apostles. We condemn him with the anathema of perpetual malediction.

Let them be accursed in the city and accursed in the countryside; accursed be their granary and accursed the remnants of their goods; accursed be the fruit of their womb and the produce of their land. Accursed be those who enter and accursed those who depart. Let all the curses come upon them which the Lord threatened through Moses to send upon the people who transgressed the divine law. Let them be *anathema maranatha*—that is, “may they perish at the second coming of the Lord.”

Let no Christian say “Hail” to them. Let no priest presume to celebrate Mass with them or give them holy Communion [Col. 0860B]. Let them be buried with the burial of an ass, and let them lie as refuse upon the face of the earth. And just as these lamps, thrown today from our hands, are extinguished, so may their lamp be extinguished forever—unless they should come to their senses and make satisfaction to the Church of God whom they have injured through amendment and fitting penance.

## Chapter 7—The fourth excommunication

(From the Council of Orange, chapter 5.) Following canonical institutions and the examples of the holy Fathers, we expel the violators of the churches of God, N., by God’s authority and by the judgment of the Holy Spirit, from the bosom of holy Mother Church and from the fellowship of all Christians, until they come to their senses and make satisfaction to the Church of God.

## Chapter 8—The reconciliation of an excommunicated person

[Col. 0860C]

(From the same council.) When an excommunicated or anathematized person, moved by penance, asks for pardon and promises amendment, the bishop who excommunicated him must come before the doors of the church, together with twelve priests, who must stand around him on either side. Those to whom injury or harm was inflicted must also be present. There, according to the divine laws, the harm committed ought to be repaired, or, if it has already been repaired, confirmed by their testimony.

Then the bishop must ask whether he is willing to undertake penance, as the canons prescribe, for the crimes he committed. If, prostrated upon the ground, he asks pardon, confesses his fault, begs for penance, and promises caution concerning the future, then the bishop shall chant the seven Psalms [Col. 0860D] with these prayers:

“Lord, have mercy.”  
“Our Father.”

Save your servant,

my God, who hopes in you.

Send him help, Lord, from the sanctuary,

and protect him from Zion.

The enemy will accomplish nothing against him,

and the son of iniquity [text incomplete/uncertain].

Be for him, Lord, a tower of strength,

against the face of the enemy.

Lord, hear my prayer,

and let my cry come to you.

The Lord be with you,

and with your spirit.

[Col. 0861A]

### Prayer

Let us pray. Grant, we beseech you, Lord, that this servant of yours may bear worthy fruits of penance, so that, having obtained pardon for his offenses, he may be restored harmless to your holy Church, from whose integrity he had strayed by sinning. Through the Lord.

### Another prayer

We beseech your majesty, holy Father, almighty and eternal God, who always seek not the death but the life of sinners: look upon your weeping servant; attend to him as he lies prostrate; turn his lamentation into the joy of your mercy; rend the sack of his sins and clothe him in saving gladness, so that, after the long hunger of his pilgrimage, he may be satisfied from the holy altars and, having entered the king’s chamber, may bless the name of your glory forever in his court [Col. 0861B]. Through the Lord.

Then the bishop, taking him by his right hand, shall lead him into the church, restore him to Communion and Christian fellowship, and say this prayer:

Merciful God, gracious God, who according to the multitude of your mercies blot out the sins of the penitent and, by the pardon of remission, remove the guilt of past crimes: look upon this servant N. and graciously hear him as he asks with wholehearted confession for the remission of all his sins. Renew in him, most merciful Father, whatever has been violated through the devil’s deceit, within the unity of the body of your Church. Have mercy, Lord, on his sighs; have mercy on his tears [Col. 0861C]; and admit him, who has confidence in nothing except your mercy, to the sacrament of reconciliation. Through our Lord.

After this, let him impose penance upon him according to the measure of his fault and send letters throughout the parish, so that all may know that he has been received into Christian fellowship. Let him also make this known to the other bishops. No bishop, however, may presume to excommunicate or reconcile another bishop’s parishioner without the knowledge or consent of that person’s own bishop.

## Chapter 9—That bishops should not be hasty in excommunicating anyone

(From a letter of Pope Evaristus, chapter 3.) Almighty God, although all things are naked and open to his [Col. 0861D] eyes, did not wish to judge the evils of Sodom merely upon hearing them, but first to ascertain whether the things reported were indeed manifest. Thus he says: “I will go down and see whether they have fully acted according to the cry that has come to me, or whether it is not so, that I may know.”

By his example we are warned never to be hasty in pronouncing a sentence, or rashly and carelessly to judge matters that have not been investigated, in whatever way they may be presented.

## Chapter 10—The same matter

(From the Synod of Meaux, chapter 3.) No bishop is to deprive anyone of ecclesiastical communion without a certain and manifest cause of sin. No bishop is to place anyone under anathema without the knowledge of the archbishop or of his fellow bishops, except where [Col. 0862A] canonical authority so teaches; for anathema is an eternal condemnation to death and must be imposed only for a mortal crime and upon one who cannot otherwise be corrected.

## Chapter 11—The same matter

(From the Council of Agde, chapter 4.) If bishops, setting aside priestly moderation, presume to excommunicate the innocent or those guilty only of minor offenses, and perhaps refuse to receive those hastening toward grace, they are to be admonished by letters from the neighboring bishops of whatever province. If they refuse to show mercy, they are to be suspended from communion with their brethren until the next synod, and there they must give an account, lest perhaps, while the sin of the excommunicator persists, the excommunicated person be overtaken by death.

## Chapter 12—That no one should take it grievously if his parishioner has been excommunicated by another bishop for a definite offense

[Col. 0862B]

(From the Council at Compiègne, chapter 5.) It was also decided, for the common benefit and pressing necessity, that no bishop should take it grievously if another bishop excommunicates his parishioner on account of plundering.

## Chapter 13—Concerning those residing in a parish who commit something against God, and how often they must be summoned by the bishop to amendment

(From the Synod of Meaux, chapter 3.) The bishop in whose parish someone has committed an injustice shall summon him once, twice, and, if necessary, a third time, through his messenger, by his own admonition and canonically, to amendment or settlement and to penance, so that he may make satisfaction to God and to the Church [Col. 0862C] whom he has injured.

If he despises and scorns the bishop’s admonition and most salutary invitation, let the bishop strike him with the pastoral rod—that is, with the sentence of excommunication—so that he is separated from communion with the holy Church and with all Christians until he gives suitable satisfaction and makes worthy amendment. The same bishop must make this excommunication known to his lord, to all his fellow bishops, and to all his parishioners, so that they do not receive him until he has made worthy satisfaction.

## Chapter 14—The same matter

(From the same council, chapter 6.) A bishop who, through any gift, favor, or negligence, delays admonishing or excommunicating those who act against God and the peace of the Church [Col. 0862D]—so that he may either receive them when they return or expel them from the Church when they remain contemptuous—is to be regarded as excommunicated by the college of the others until he publishes a sentence either of their amendment or of their condemnation.

## Chapter 15—That it is one thing to sin against God and another to sin against a human being

(From the sayings of Augustine.) It must be considered that the Lord says: “If your brother sins against you.” It is one thing to sin against us and another to sin against God. If someone sins against us, it is not a matter left to our own judgment. For it is written: “If a man sins against a man, God may be appeased on his behalf. But if he sins against God, who will pray for him?”

Yet, conversely, we are gentle and [Col. 0863A] merciful when God is dishonored, and we pardon an offense against God without penalty and without appropriate penance, as though it were within our power to determine his willing or refusing—while we do not even tolerate what is committed against us, not even a word of insult lightly spoken, passing without punishment.

Let us therefore pardon, for God’s sake, what has been done against us; but what has been committed against God, since we cannot pardon it, let us punish according to the constitution of the holy Fathers and canonical authority.

## Chapter 16—The same matter

(From the Synod of Meaux, chapter 5.) Those who seize ecclesiastical possessions and are known not merely to retain them against authority but also cruelly to lay them waste—for some strip the Church’s resources [Col. 0863B] through various exactions and revenues, while they also mercilessly afflict, devastate, and oppress the poor, neighbors, and those dwelling around them—are to be punished with public penance for a criminal and public sin, as rapacious persons who, according to the Apostle, are excluded from the kingdom of God.

If they refuse to do this, an apostolic and terrible sentence is to be pronounced against them, which says: “If anyone is named a brother and is a robber, let no one presume even to eat with such a person.” For it is unjust and sacrilegious that this should be done, as Pope Symmachus, and after him blessed Gregory, writes to the subdeacon Sabinus: “If anyone attempts, through the efforts of an evil will, to retain for his own advantage what has been left to venerable places, according to the statutes of the canons he must be excluded from all ecclesiastical communion [Col. 0863C] as a sacrilegious person, until he undertakes to correct by worthy satisfaction what he has committed.”

## Chapter 17—That whatever is offered to the Lord is the Holy of Holies

(From a decree of Pope Boniface, chapter 5.) No one may be permitted to be ignorant that everything consecrated to the Lord—whether it is a human being, an animal, a field, or anything whatsoever—once it has been consecrated, is the Holy of Holies belonging to the Lord and pertains to the right of priests.

Therefore, because everyone who removes, devastates, invades, or seizes what belongs to the Lord and to the Church, to whom such things belong, will be inexcusable, he is to be judged a sacrilegious person until he makes amendment and satisfaction to the Church; and if he refuses to make amendment, he is to be excommunicated.

## Chapter 18—Concerning those who take away or plunder Christ’s monies

[Col. 0863D]

(From a letter of Pope Anacletus sent to all the faithful.) “Whoever takes something away from a father,” he says, “is an accomplice of a murderer.” Without doubt, our Father is God, who created us. Our mother, however, is the Church, which spiritually regenerated us in baptism. Therefore, whoever takes away, plunders, or fraudulently withholds Christ’s monies and the Church’s is a murderer, and before God is counted as a murderer. Whoever takes away the Church’s possessions commits sacrilege and must be judged as a sacrilegious person.

## Chapter 19—The same matter

(From a decree of Pope Lucius, chapter 10.) By apostolic authority we anathematize, [Col. 0864A] expel, and condemn from the thresholds of holy Church those who plunder ecclesiastical property and possessions, and we judge them to be sacrilegious, together with all who consent to them; for not only those who do such things but also those who consent are judged guilty.

Augustine says: “Whoever steals and plunders anything from the Church is comparable to Judas the betrayer.”

## Chapter 20—The same matter

(From the Council of Gangra, chapter 8.) Whoever gives or receives altar offerings apart from the bishop or his representative—both the giver and the receiver—let him be anathema.

## Chapter 21—The same matter

(From the Council at Saint-Médard, chapter 1.) If anyone wishes to seize or give Church offerings outside the Church, without the knowledge of the bishop or of the person to whom such [Col. 0864B] duties have been entrusted, let him be anathema.

## Chapter 22—The same matter

(From a decree of Pope John, chapter 10.) Let those who violate monasteries, places consecrated to God, and churches, and remove deposits or anything else from them, pay ninefold compensation and restore the immunity threefold, and, as sacrilegious persons, be subjected to canonical judgment.

## Chapter 23—Concerning those who regard the house of God as contemptible

(From the Council of Mainz, chapter 7.) Whoever, lifted up by the arrogance of pride, regards the house of God as contemptible, and dishonestly treats possessions consecrated to God and established under the protection of royal immunity for the honor of God; or presumes to violate them; or rashly commits arson or devastation [Col. 0864C]—let him, as an invader and violator of the Church of God, which is the house of the living God, be cut off from communion with all the faithful.

## Chapter 24—The same matter

(From the same council, chapter 6.) If anyone, with wicked cunning, removes, defrauds, invades, retains, or steals gifts of any kind belonging to the Church, collected under the titles of the holy Scriptures, and, immediately admonished by the priest, does not return what was given to God, let him be expelled from communion with the Catholic Church.

## Chapter 25—That what has been taken away must be restored with multiplication

(From a decree of Pope Eusebius, chapter 4.) It is also decreed in the ancient statutes of the Church that whoever invades another’s property must not go unpunished but must restore everything with multiplication [Col. 0864D]. Hence it is also written in the Gospel that if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I restore fourfold.

## Chapter 26—That arsons and plunderings of ecclesiastical property must be repaired under the law of immunity

(From a letter of Pope Gregory to Constantina, queen of Gaul.) Since I know that Your Devotion diligently considers the heavenly life and the remedy of your soul, I judge that I would be gravely at fault if I kept silent about what ought to be suggested for fear of almighty God and did not diligently admonish your Holiness concerning ecclesiastical peace.

The recent complaint of our brother and fellow bishop Julian greatly saddened me, especially since his estates—that is, those of the Church—were plundered by the most wicked robbers and burned in nightly fires, after the manner of thieves [Col. 0865A]. These same wicked men, in accordance with the decrees of our predecessor Boniface, have refused to make amends under the law of immunity. The secular laws also have wished to treat this matter in the same way, as the common law testifies, in which it is written:

“If anyone, armed, comes into another’s village to commit wrongdoing with as many as four men, the leader, through his unlawful presumption, shall pay 900 solidi, while each of his followers shall pay 80 solidi. But if they set fire there, they shall pay ninefold, and shall restore the plunder fourfold.”

If the secular laws have wished to uphold such justice, why should the divine law be inferior, when, in the presence of Truth himself, Zacchaeus was praised for restoring fourfold whatever he had defrauded anyone of?

And since it is the highest good in kings to cultivate justice, to preserve each person’s rights, and not to permit what belongs to power to be done to subjects, but to ensure that what is equitable is observed—which we are entirely confident that you both love and strive to uphold—we therefore send Peter, our fellow bishop, from the bosom of the holy Roman Church [Col. 0865B] to Your Excellence in November of the present year, in the second indiction, so that, with the brothers of that province gathered together, immunity, unlawful presumption, and sacrilege may receive, by canonical authority and your royal dignity, such an ending that henceforth the members of the devil, wicked sons, will not presume to do such things in the holy Church while you also reign there.

## Chapter 27—How ecclesiastical property ought to be restored

[Col. 0865C]

(From a decree of Eusebius, chapter 8.) It is also established in secular laws that whoever steals another’s property must restore elevenfold what was taken to the person whose property was seized. And it is written in the divine law: “Cursed is everyone who moves his neighbor’s boundary marker”; and all the people say, “Amen.”

Such things, therefore, must not be presumed without vengeance or practiced without condemnation. Pursue peace, not anyone’s harm or injustice, among yourselves and toward all. Therefore, if anyone plunders ecclesiastical offerings or anything consecrated to God, or consents to those who do so, let him be judged sacrilegious, restore the harm fourfold, and perform canonical penance.

## Chapter 28—That the plunderers of churches are sacrilegious

[Col. 0865D]

(From the Council of Mainz, chapter 3.) The plunderers of churches are sacrilegious. Hence the following was also decreed in the Council of Agde, under its fourth chapter: “To steal something from a friend is theft; but to defraud, remove, or steal from the Church is sacrilege.” All who act against the law, plunder the Church’s property, or harass churches and priests contrary to the divine ordinances are called sacrilegious and are unquestionably to be regarded as infamous and sacrilegious.

## Chapter 29—The same matter

(From a letter of Pope Pius sent to the Italian brothers.) It has been reported to the Apostolic See that there are disputes and rivalries among you, and that certain people apply to human uses estates devoted to divine purposes, withdraw them from the Lord God [Col. 0866A] to whom they were given, and make them serve their own purposes.

Therefore, this insult of usurpation must be removed by everyone, lest estates assigned to heavenly purposes be harassed by certain invaders. If anyone presumes to do this, let him be regarded and judged as a sacrilegious person.

We have also heard that the very men who do these things persecute and defame clerics and the priests of the Lord, adding evil to evil and becoming worse, without understanding that the Church of God consists in its priests and grows into a temple of God. Just as the person who devastates the Church of God and strips and invades its estates and gifts becomes sacrilegious, so also the one who persecutes its priests is guilty of sacrilege and is judged sacrilegious.

## Chapter 30—Concerning those who mutilate limbs, commit plunderings, or burn houses

[Col. 0866B]

(From a decree of Pope Eutychian.) If anyone mutilates limbs or burns houses, or orders it to be done, or consents to one who does it, let him know that he is deprived of the Church until he has made legal or amicable restitution for these things to each person before the bishop of the city and the other citizens. If, after being summoned a second and third time, he does not make amends for everything of which he is accused, let him be separated from the entire fellowship of Christians as a heathen and a publican.

## Chapter 31—That it is not permitted to pray with an excommunicated person

(From the sayings of Saint Isidore.) No one may pray or speak with an excommunicated person, except concerning matters pertaining to that same excommunication [Col. 0866C]; nor may anyone eat with him.

## Chapter 32—The same matter

(From the sayings of the same author.) If any brother speaks with an excommunicated person, whether openly or secretly, he immediately incurs with him the common penalty of excommunication.

## Chapter 33—The same matter

(From the sayings of Bishop Fructuosus.) Let no one speak with an excommunicated person, comfort him through any compassion or mercy, or presume to encourage him in opposition or pride.

## Chapter 34—The same matter

(From the Council of Antioch, chapter 2.) It is not permitted to communicate with excommunicated persons, nor with those who gather in [Col. 0866D] houses while avoiding the prayers of the Church, where prayer ought to be offered together. If anyone from the clergy is found communicating with excommunicated persons, let him also be deprived of communion.

## Chapter 35—The same matter

(From the Apostolic Canon.) If anyone prays together with an excommunicated person, even in a house, let him be deprived of communion.

## Chapter 36—The same matter

(From the Council of Nicaea, chapter 5.) Concerning those deprived of communion, whether from the clergy or from the lay order, a regular sentence is to be maintained by the bishops in each province, so that those who are expelled are not received by others. It must also be investigated whether the bishop appears to have excluded someone from communion through faintheartedness [Col. 0867A], contention, or any other vice.

## Chapter 37—The same matter

(From the Council of Antioch, chapter 6.) If anyone has been deprived of communion by his own bishop, he is not to be received by other bishops until he has been reconciled with his own bishop.

## Chapter 38—The same matter

(From a decree of Pope Callistus, chapter 3.) Let no one receive those excommunicated by priests before a proper examination of both parties; let no one communicate with them in prayer, food, drink, or a kiss, nor say “Hail” to them. For whoever knowingly communicates with excommunicated persons in these or other prohibited matters is himself, according to the institution of the Apostles, to be subjected to a similar excommunication [Col. 0867B].

## Chapter 39—The same matter

(From the Council of Antioch.) It is not permitted to communicate with those who are excluded from communion, nor to enter their houses and pray with them, who do not participate in the Church’s prayer; nor may one who has been excommunicated from one church be received into another. If any bishop, priest, deacon, or even anyone enrolled in the canon is seen communicating with those excluded from communion, he too must be deprived of communion, as one who confounds the rules of the Church.

## Chapter 40—The same matter

(From a decree of Pope Fabian sent to the bishops of Gaul.) If anyone willingly communicates with an excommunicated person by word, prayer, food, or drink, let him perform forty days of penance [Col. 0867C] on bread, salt, and water. But whoever communicates with them in murders or disgraceful deeds will be guilty of the wrath and vengeance of almighty God, whom he despises, because all these things have been forbidden to him by the divine voice. According to the Apostle, one must obey God rather than human beings; and according to the offense committed, let him perform worthy penance in accordance with the decrees of the canons. If he refuses to do penance, let him be excommunicated.

## Chapter 41—The same matter

(From the Council of Meaux, chapter 10.) Concerning those who are separated from communion because of their offense, it was decided that wherever they have been excluded, they are to receive communion in that same place.

## Chapter 42—The same matter

(From the Council of Rouen, chapter 3.) There are some who [Col. 0867D], because their offenses require it, are excommunicated by their own bishop but are received into communion by other ecclesiastical or lay persons through presumption. The holy Council of Nicaea, together with the Councils of Chalcedon, Antioch, and Sardica, entirely forbids this from being done.

## Chapter 43—The same matter
(From the Council of Carthage, chapter 9.) Augustine, bishop and legate of the province of Numidia, said: “May you deem it worthy to establish that if any persons have been expelled from the Church on account of the merit of their crimes, and have nevertheless been received into communion either by some bishop or presbyter, that person too shall be held liable to an equal crime with them, since they have evaded the regular judgment of their own bishop.” [Col. 0868A] All the bishops said: “It pleases all of us.”

### CHAPTER 44.—On the same matter

(From the same council, chapter 73.) Whoever communicates or prays with an excommunicated person: if he is a layman, let him be excommunicated; if a cleric, let him be deposed.

### CHAPTER 45.—On those who belong to another parish and commit plundering

(From the Council of Meaux, chapter 2.) Concerning those who possess a benefice or inheritance within a parish, but belong to the parish of another bishop, and travel from place to place committing robberies and plundering, it was decided that they should be excommunicated and should not leave the parish before they have made worthy amends for what they committed. Their excommunication is to be reported to their lord and [Col. 0868B] to their own bishop, so that they do not receive them before they return to the place where they committed the robbery and fully make amends for everything.

### CHAPTER 46.—On those who defend offenders

(From the sayings of Bishop Basil.) Whoever agrees with sinners and defends another offender shall be accursed before God and human beings and shall be corrected with the severest rebuke. Hence a certain most holy Father also says: “If anyone has consented to another’s error, let him know that he is to be judged guilty in the same way with him and excommunicated.”

### CHAPTER 47.—On those who have neglected to pursue their case within a year

(From a decree of Gelasius, pope, chapter 2.) Whoever, therefore, within the space of a year, has not conducted his case, whether civilly or publicly, before those who excommunicated him, should be considered to have closed the way of a hearing against himself. But if they die with an obstinate spirit, without communion, we reserve their case for divine judgment according to the decision of our predecessor, blessed Leo; since we did not communicate with them while they were alive, we cannot communicate with them when they are dead.

### CHAPTER 48.—On the same matter

(From a decree of the same pope, chapter 13.) Those who have attempted to receive communion before a hearing must in no way be restored to communion until they have lamented their guilt through penance, except when the urgency of death compels it. Whoever knowingly communicates with an excommunicated person, and thereafter even prays with him in the same house, [Col. 0868D] and provides hiding places for his defense so that he may not be brought face-to-face to make satisfaction, must recognize that he is deprived of communion in the body and blood of the Lord until he receives penance from the person who excommunicated him, and must do penance for his offense according to the canons.

### CHAPTER 49.—That the names of excommunicated persons are to be recorded and posted on the church doors

(From a decree of Pope Honorius, chapter 11.) Let all bishops take care to make the names of the excommunicated known equally both to neighboring bishops and to their own parishioners, and, once these names have been placed in a public location before the church doors, impress them upon all who assemble there, so that by this twofold diligence ecclesiastical hearing may everywhere be denied to the excommunicated and every excuse may be removed from everyone.

### CHAPTER 50.—On a bishop who dies before absolving a condemned person

[Col. 0869A]

(From the Council of Epaon, chapter 10.) If a bishop is taken away by death before the absolution of a condemned person, a successor may absolve the person who has been corrected or is doing penance.

### CHAPTER 51.—On those who die excommunicated

(From the same council, chapter 11.) If an excommunicated person has died who had already confessed, possessed a good testimony, and was unable to come to a priest because death overtook him at home or on the road, let his relatives make an offering for him at the altar and give a ransom for captives.

### CHAPTER 52.—On the same matter

(From a letter of Pope Leo, chapter 21.) The case of such persons [Col. 0869B] must be reserved for God’s judgment, in whose hand it lay that the death of such people was not delayed until the remedy of communion. But we cannot communicate with those with whom we did not communicate while they were alive.

### CHAPTER 53.—On thieves and thefts

(From Augustine’s sayings.) The Lord said to Moses: “Let each person receive from his neighbor, and from his female neighbor, silver and gold vessels and garments,” and so forth. No one should think that he may take an example from this for stripping his neighbor, for God commanded it—he who knew what each person ought to suffer. Nor did the Israelites act on their own, but they rendered service to God when he commanded, just as an executioner kills the one whom the judge has ordered to be killed.

### CHAPTER 54.—On the same matter

[Col. 0869C]

(From the sayings of the same author.) To take something secretly is punishable; to seize it openly is subject to a much greater punishment. To take something from an unwilling person, whether secretly or publicly, has its own prohibition. For by the name “theft” almost every unlawful appropriation of another’s property is understood. The one who prohibited theft did not permit robbery; rather, he wished robbery to be understood under the name of theft. For he signified the whole by a part: everything that is taken.

### CHAPTER 55.—On the same matter

(From the sayings of Jerome.) A thief is judged not only in great matters but also in small ones. For it is not what was taken by theft that is considered, but the thief’s intention: just as in fornication, fornication does not become different because the woman is beautiful or deformed, a slave or freeborn, poor or wealthy; whatever she may be, it is one and the same fornication. So in theft, however much anyone may have taken, he incurs the crime of theft.

### CHAPTER 56.—On the same matter

(From Theodore’s Penitential.) If anyone has stolen food, clothing, or livestock out of necessity, because of hunger or nakedness, let him do penance for three weeks; if he returns what he took, he is not to be compelled to fast.

### CHAPTER 57.—On the same matter

(From the Council of Orléans, chapter 8.) If anyone commits public robbery or theft, let him perform public penance for it, according to the decrees of the holy canons. But if he has acted secretly, let him do penance with the counsel of priests, since, as the Apostle says, robbers will not possess the kingdom of God unless they truly repent of it. Whoever has taken anything from ecclesiastical property is to be judged more severely, because although the punishment of thieves and robbers pertains to the counts, penance nevertheless belongs to the bishops.

### CHAPTER 58.—On the same matter

(From Theodore’s Penitential.) If anyone has committed capital theft—that is, has carried off four-footed animals or broken into houses—let him do penance for seven years and return what was stolen. But if anyone has committed theft of lesser things once or twice, let him return what he took and do penance for one year. Or if anyone has violated a tomb, let him do penance for seven years, three of them on bread and water.

### CHAPTER 59.—On the same matter

(From the Council of Tribur, chapter 5.) If thieves and robbers are killed while stealing or plundering, it was judged that no prayer should be offered for them. If they have been captured or wounded and have confessed to a presbyter or deacon, we do not deny them communion.

### CHAPTER 60.—On the same matter

(From the Council of Orléans, chapter 1.) If a thief or robber caught in the act of plundering could have been captured without danger, yet is killed, then, because they were created in the image of God and baptized in his name, their killers are not to enter the Church for forty days. They are to wear woolen clothing and abstain from forbidden foods and drinks, from the marriage bed, the sword, and riding on horseback. On Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday they are to eat, in moderation and alternately, some kind of legumes or vegetables, fruit, and small fish, with a moderate amount of beer. But if truthful witnesses establish [Col. 0870C] that they killed the members of the devil while freeing themselves and their own property, without intending hatred, and that the victims could not be captured, we impose penance for homicide upon them, unless they themselves wish to do something dictated by humanity. If the offender is a presbyter, he is not to be deposed, but is nevertheless to do penance throughout all the days of his life.

### CHAPTER 61.—On the same matter

(It is said in Exodus.) If a thief breaking into a house, or digging through it, is discovered and dies after receiving a wound, the person who struck him is not guilty of bloodshed. But if he does this after sunrise, he has committed homicide, and he himself shall die. If he has nothing with which to make restitution for the theft, he shall be sold. If what he stole is found with him alive—whether an ox, a donkey, or a sheep—he shall restore double.

### CHAPTER 62.—On a slave who flees from his master

(From a letter of Jerome.) From Jerome’s letter to Pacasius of Alexandria. You asked concerning a slave who has fled from his master: if he should die during that flight, whether it is permitted to pray for him or not. We have not found this prohibited in the divine books, but we know that the apostles firmly commanded that slaves be subject to their masters in all fear—not only to the good and moderate, but also to the harsh. The Council of Gangra likewise states: “If anyone, under the pretext of divine worship, teaches a slave to despise his own master and to withdraw from his service, let him be anathema.” Hence it is understood that if the one who teaches a slave to despise his master and withdraw from his service deserves anathema, how much more does the one who despises the Lord and refuses to submit to his service? Yet there is a distinction between the one who does this through pride and the one compelled by necessity because of his master’s cruelty.

### CHAPTER 63.—On clerics if they are caught demolishing tombs

(From the Fifth Council of Toledo, chapter 45.) If a cleric is discovered demolishing tombs, because this crime is punished by the public laws with blood as sacrilege, it is necessary that the person exposed in such wickedness be removed from the clerical order and assigned to three years of penance.

### CHAPTER 64.—On clerics or monks if they commit theft

[Col. 0871B]

(From the Council of Agde, chapter 2.) If a cleric or monk commits theft—which can more properly be called sacrilege—we have decreed that the following rule shall be observed: if he is a young man, he is to be beaten with rods, and, guilty of so great a crime, is never to undertake ecclesiastical office. But if someone already ordained is discovered in this crime, let him be deprived of the dignity of his rank. For him, in view of the lightness of his act, it may suffice, once the satisfaction of penance has been completed, to receive communion alone.

### CHAPTER 65.—On those who have stolen something from the ministry of the Church

(From the Roman Penitential.) If anyone has stolen anything in any manner from the ministry of the Church, let him do penance for seven years.

### CHAPTER 66.—On monks who have been accused of theft, and how they ought to clear themselves

[Col. 0871C]

(From the Council of Worms, chapter 10.) It often happens that thefts are committed in monasteries of monks. Therefore we establish that when the brothers themselves must clear themselves of such accusations, Mass is to be celebrated by the abbot, or by someone else in the presence of the brothers; and when the Mass has been completed, all are to receive communion with these words: “May the Body of the Lord be my proof today.”

### CHAPTER 67.—On those who defend colonists from punishment by the rod

(From the Council of Elvira, chapter 9.) The holy synod decreed that a bishop and the bishop’s ministers shall have authority to beat colonists with rods for their crimes, out of fear for the others, so that the criminals themselves may be corrected and may do penance, even unwillingly, lest they perish eternally. But if the lords of those colonists take offense unjustly and wish to inflict some revenge on that account, or presume to defend the same colonists so that they are not disciplined, let them know that they are to be struck by the sentence of ecclesiastical excommunication.

### CHAPTER 68.—On bishops who had been accused before the Roman see of communicating with excommunicated persons

(From the council held at Altheim, which King Conrad attended.) In the fifth year of the reign of Conrad, the most devout and most Christian king, a holy general synod was assembled at Altheim in the district of Rhaetia, in the presence of Peter, venerable bishop of the holy Church of Horta and envoy of Lord Pope John. Its purpose was, in whatever way possible, to uproot the devilish seeds that had arisen in our regions, to calm the most wicked schemes of certain perverse people, and to eliminate and cleanse them.

After completing a three-day fast and celebrating the sacred litanies in the customary manner, we assembled in the Church of Saint John the Baptist and sat down in mourning. At last the aforesaid envoy of Saint Peter and of Lord Pope John produced a document written in apostolic letters, in which we were admonished, accused, and instructed concerning everything pertaining to the true religion of the Christian faith. We humbly accepted all these matters, as was just and proper; we carefully considered them and embraced them entirely with devoted affection.

Therefore we proclaimed in a tearful voice the evangelical command and most salutary instruction by which the Pharisees and scribes were rebuked: “Cleanse first what is within.” And again: “First remove the beam from your own eye.” And that prophetic saying: “The ruin of the people is evil priests.” Weighing these words, examining ourselves through discussion, and casting ourselves to the ground in the midst of holy penance with worthy fruit, we lamented our countless negligences and most serious sins. Then, at the urging of Lord Peter, angry with ourselves and our vices, with the assistance and mercy of the Holy Spirit, we gathered together the chapters set out below, establishing them for the correction both of ourselves and of the Christian people.

### CHAPTER 69.—On bishops who lead their subjects astray by communicating with excommunicated persons

[Col. 0872C]

(From the same council, chapter 6.) We know that it is written by sacred authority: “Whoever communicates with an excommunicated person shall be excommunicated.” We bishops, presbyters, and clerics confess that we have sinned culpably in this matter; with God’s help, we desire both to amend and avoid it in the future, and we command this.

### CHAPTER 70.—On the same matter

(From the same council, chapter 7.) It pleased the holy synod to remove this error from the Church as impious, because we have received the care of souls from the Lord, not of money. For this reason we shall render an account to God and, by his mercy, receive eternal reward or just condemnation.

### CHAPTER 71.—That bishops should not be a bad example to the people

[Col. 0872D]

(From the same council, chapter 8.) Bishops and priests ought to offer themselves as a good example to the peoples and demonstrate it not only in words but also in deeds. For this reason we establish that from now on we shall in no way communicate with excommunicated persons contrary to the sacred statutes, and we judge ourselves so that we may not be judged by the Lord in the future. We desire to follow the words and statutes of Pope Saint Gregory, and we wish to perform worthy penance secretly in a monastery, since we cannot do so publicly; and in the future, with God’s favor, we wish in every way to avoid the things mentioned above.

We establish the same law for presbyters, deacons, and the entire clergy: if they do not wish to be removed from their rank, let them faithfully observe it and preach to others that they observe it.

### CHAPTER 72.—On the correction of bishops who have communicated with excommunicated persons

[Col. 0873A]

(From the same council, chapter 9.) By apostolic authority we confirm the words and commands of the holy canons, and we forbid anyone to communicate with an excommunicated person or pray with him in church for as long as he remains excommunicated. As for the laymen who, as they say, followed us in error and by following our example, we correct them—and ourselves—by chastening ourselves through penance, preaching and opening for them the way of life, so that they may recover from the snares of the devil in which they are held captive because of our evil examples and may return through penance to the true mother, the Church.

### CHAPTER 73.—On those who despise the ban imposed by bishops

[Col. 0873B]

(From the Council of Tribur, attended by King Arnulf, chapter 8.) Let no one despise or transgress a ban imposed by bishops. Let him know and dread the statement in the letter of Blessed Clement, written against such a person: “If all people—both of the greater and lesser orders, and the remaining peoples of every tribe and language—do not obey you bishops, they shall be not only infamous but also exiles from the kingdom of God and from the fellowship of the faithful, alienated from the thresholds of God’s holy Church.” And let them hear the Lord himself saying in the Gospel: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you despises me.”

Therefore, considering the evangelical and apostolic authority, seeking not the profit of money but the gain of souls, we establish and confirm [Col. 0873C] that if, after the definition of this holy council, anyone is found to have violated a ban imposed by bishops, he shall be corrected for forty days, taking only bread, salt, and water.

### CHAPTER 74.—For what reasons anyone should be bound by the bond of anathema

(From the same council, chapter 30.) The same synod asked for what reasons any person ought to be bound by episcopal authority with the bond of anathema. By the unanimous judgment of all, it was decreed that this should be done for these three offenses: when someone contemptuously refuses to come to a synod after being canonically ordered to do so; or, after coming there, refuses to obey priestly commands; or, before the examination of his case has been completed, presumes to flee and depart from the synod.

### CHAPTER 75.—On those who practice theft and robbery

[Col. 0873D]

(From the same council, chapter 31.) Thieves and robbers bear witness that the tranquility of God’s holy Church is disturbed and fraternal peace attacked. They walk among us covered with sheep’s wool but depart alienated with a wolf’s mind, driven by a savage intention to seize the property of the churches and tear apart the Lord’s flock by plundering it. Concerning them the Savior says in the Gospel: “Whoever does not enter the sheepfold through the door is a thief and a robber.” And he adds: “The thief comes only to steal, slaughter, and destroy.”

Although by this he designates heretics who steal the faith from the Church, nevertheless, by the persecution of thieves and robbers he shows that the peace of the Churches is disturbed. The Apostle says of such people to the Philippians: “Beware of dogs; beware of evil workers.” He called them dogs because they have no shame; evil workers because they do nothing that accords with piety. And the Lord says through the prophet Isaiah: “I am the Lord, loving judgment and hating robbery.”

Therefore, loving what the Lord loves and hating what he hates, we establish and judge that if, after these evangelical, apostolic, and prophetic words and the definition of the most peaceful synod, anyone is found practicing theft or robbery and deserves to suffer death in that very devilish act, no one may presume to pray for him or give alms on his behalf. Let the alms given for him not come into the remembrance of clerics or the poor, but become accursed and defiled.

Blessed Augustine [Col. 0874B] pronounces a terrible sentence concerning such people, saying: “No one faithfully redeems you after your death, because you were unwilling to redeem yourself.”

But if that thief or robber escapes wounded and is thought to be despairing while awaiting death, and begs to be reconciled to the sacred mysteries through the condition of his body and the devout intention of his mind, and, while life remains, confesses to God and the priest his amendment and conduct, we do not deny him the grace of communion.

### CHAPTER 76.—On those who are hanged on the gallows

(From the Council of Mainz, chapter 5.) Some brothers asked about those who are hanged on the gallows for their crimes after making confession to God: whether their corpses should be brought to the churches, offerings made for them, and Masses celebrated, or not. We answer them: If communion is to be given at the end, according to canonical command, to all who make some confession of their sins and do worthy penance, why should the canons deny it to those who undergo the ultimate punishment for their sins and confess, or desire to confess? For it is written: “God does not judge twice for the same thing.”

### CHAPTER 77.—On bishops who have communicated with excommunicated persons

(From the Council held at Erfurt, attended by King Henry, chapter 9.) The holy synod, with the counsel of the most serene prince, decreed that if henceforth any bishop, forgetful of his office, knowingly communicates with an excommunicated person—whether in greeting, prayer, close fellowship, food, or drink—he is to be considered excommunicated both by the prince and by everyone else until he is heard at the next synod and compelled to make satisfaction to God and the Church.

### CHAPTER 78.—On clerics who flee from their churches, and slaves who flee from their masters

(From the council held at Altheim, attended by King Conrad, chapter 27.) Saint Gregory says: “We judge that a cleric who flees from his own church, or a slave who flees from his own master and is unwilling to return, is to be deprived of communion until he returns to his own church or to his master.” [Col. 0875A] And again: “By apostolic sentence we decree that a fugitive cleric be restored to his bishop, or a fugitive slave to his master, [Col. 0876A] or be excommunicated together with those who have communicated with him.”

[Col. 0875] END OF THE ELEVENTH BOOK.

[THE TWELFTH BOOK.]

[Col. 0875]
