# BURCHARD, BISHOP OF THE CHURCH OF WORMS, DECRETALS, BOOK TWELVE: ON PERJURY

[Col. 0875]

## ARGUMENT OF THE BOOK

[Col. 0875C]

This book treats of oaths and perjury, of the readiness to swear and its danger, and of the breaking of wicked oaths.

### CHAPTER 1.—That the many kinds of oaths be eradicated

(From the Council of Meaux, chapter 10.) Let everyone be attentively informed how detestable and hateful to God is the confusion of multiple oaths and perjuries, through which many souls of the faithful are known to have been lost throughout this entire kingdom. For this evil is so great that at the shrines of martyrs, where the illnesses of various people are healed, perjurers—even when they do not visibly appear to be suffering—are seized by demons through God’s just judgment. As Saint Gregory says, the sick come to the bodies of these saints and are healed, while perjurers are tormented by demons.

### CHAPTER 2.—On those who take the name of God in vain

[Col. 0876C]

(From Jerome’s sayings.) We have it written in the law of the Lord: “You shall not swear falsely by my name, nor profane the name of the Lord your God,” and, “You shall not take the name of your God in vain.” Therefore everyone must be admonished carefully to avoid perjury, not only at the altar or before the relics of the saints, but also in ordinary speech.

It must likewise be guarded against that anyone should honor gold more than the altar, lest the Lord say to him: “Fool, which is greater, the gold or the altar that sanctifies the gold?”

### CHAPTER 3.—On those who commit perjury through greed

(From the Roman Penitential.) If anyone has sworn falsely through greed, let him sell all his possessions and distribute them to the poor; then, entering a monastery, let him submit himself to continual penance.

### CHAPTER 4.—On those who commit perjury at the command of their masters

[Col. 0877A]

(From a decree of Pope Pius, chapter 2.) If a soldier, compelled by his master, knowingly swears falsely, both are to be perjurers: the master because he gave the order, the soldier because he loved his master more than his soul. If he is free, let him do penance for forty days on bread and water, and for the following seven years. If he is his slave, let him do penance for three Lents and the appointed fast days.

### CHAPTER 5.—On those who swear falsely by the hand of a bishop, or by a consecrated or unconsecrated cross

(From Theodore’s Penitential.) Whoever swears falsely by the hand of a bishop or by a consecrated cross shall do penance for three years. But if he swears falsely by an unconsecrated cross, let him do penance for one year. Whoever has been deceived and, in ignorance, has sworn falsely, but later learns the truth, shall do penance for three Lents.

### CHAPTER 6.—On those who commit perjury to save their life

(From the Roman Penitential.) If anyone, compelled to save his life, or for any cause or necessity, swears falsely, because he loved his body more than his soul, let him do penance for three Lents. Others judge that he should do penance for three years, one of them on bread and water.

### CHAPTER 7.—On those who have confirmed unjust vows by an oath

(From the Council of Toledo, chapter 9.) It is necessary that one who swears wickedly perform worthy penance, because he has taken the name of the Lord in vain contrary to his command. For it is written in Exodus: “The Lord will not hold innocent the one who takes the name of the Lord his God in vain.” And in Leviticus: “You shall not swear falsely by my name, nor profane the name of the Lord your God; I am the Lord.”

Nevertheless, let him absolutely not do the evil that he had sworn to perform, because foolish vows must be broken.

### CHAPTER 8.—On the same matter

(From a decree of Pope Fabian, chapter 11.) Whoever knowingly swears falsely shall do penance for forty days on bread and water and for the following seven years; he shall never be without penance, shall never be admitted as a witness, and thereafter shall receive communion.

### CHAPTER 9.—On the same matter

(From a decree of Pope Pelagius, chapter 11.) If anyone swears falsely and knowingly leads others into perjury, let him do penance for forty days on bread and water and for the following seven years, [Col. 0877D] and never be without penance. If others were aware of it, let them likewise do penance; but if not, let each of them do penance as for perjury committed unwillingly.

### CHAPTER 10.—That God receives oaths according to the meaning intended by the person to whom they are sworn

(From the sayings of Saint Isidore.) Just as one who does not speak cannot lie, so one who does not desire to swear cannot swear falsely. An oath must therefore be avoided and used only in absolute necessity. It is not contrary to God’s command to swear, but when we make a habit of swearing, we incur the crime of perjury. Therefore the person who fears swearing falsely never swears.

Many people delight in constantly swearing while they speak, although only this ought to be in their mouth: “Yes, yes; no, no.” Anything beyond this comes from evil. Many swear falsely in order to deceive, using the credibility of an oath to make their words credible; thus, while swearing falsely and lying, they deceive the unwary. Sometimes we too are deceived by false tears, and people are believed while they weep who ought not to have been believed.

Often we intend to speak without an oath, but because of the disbelief of those who do not believe what we say, we are compelled to swear, and by such necessity we acquire the habit of swearing. Many are slow to believe and are not moved to faith by words. But those who compel people speaking to them to swear commit a serious offense.

Whatever verbal device someone uses in swearing, God, who is witness to the conscience, receives it according to the meaning understood by the person to whom the oath is sworn. [Col. 0878B] The person who both takes God’s name in vain and deceitfully ensnares his neighbor is guilty in two ways.

An oath that is carelessly made concerning an evil deed is not to be kept, as when someone promises an adulteress perpetual fidelity to remain with her. It is more tolerable not to fulfill an oath than to persist in the disgrace of sexual immorality.

To swear is an act of that providence of God which has established not to uproot its decrees. God’s repentance, however, is a change in circumstances. Not to repent means not to revoke decrees, as in the saying: “The Lord swore and will not repent,” that is, he will not change what he has sworn.

### CHAPTER 11.—On those who knowingly swear falsely

(From Theodore’s Penitential.) If anyone suspects that he is being led into perjury and nevertheless swears with his consent, let him do penance for forty days and for the following seven years, and never be without severe penance.

### CHAPTER 12.—That everyone ought to swear fasting

(From a decree of Pope Cornelius, chapter 5.) It also seems honorable and just to us that anyone who dares to swear in holy matters should do so fasting, with all honesty and fear of God, and that children under fourteen years of age should not be compelled to swear.

### CHAPTER 13.—On the same matter

(From the Council of Orléans, chapter 10.) The holy synod also decreed that, except for the making of peace, all the faithful should approach the sacred mysteries fasting.

### CHAPTER 14.—What penance perjurers ought to receive

[Col. 0878D]

(From a decree of Pope Eutychian, chapter 26.) It must also be preached that the faithful should beware of perjury and abstain from it with the utmost care, knowing that it is a great crime prohibited in the Law, the Prophets, and the Gospel. We have heard that some regard this crime as insignificant and impose on perjurers a kind of light penance.

They must also know that penance for perjury ought to be imposed of the same kind as for adultery, fornication, voluntary homicide, and the other criminal vices. But if anyone, after committing perjury or any criminal sin, is unwilling to come to confession because he fears lengthy penance, he is to be expelled from the Church—removed from communion and the fellowship of the faithful—so that no one may eat or drink with him, pray with him, or receive him into his house.

### CHAPTER 15.—On those who swear by God’s hair or head, or use blasphemy in another way against immortal God

(From a decree of Pope Pius, chapter 5.) If anyone swears by God’s hair or head, or uses blasphemy in another way against God, then, if he belongs to the ecclesiastical order, let him be deposed; if he is a layman, let him be anathematized. If anyone swears by created things, let him be punished most severely and do penance according to the judgment of the synod.

If anyone fails to expose such a person, there is no doubt that he too will be restrained by divine condemnation. And if a bishop neglects to correct these matters, let him be rebuked by the synod.

### CHAPTER 16.—On Herod’s oath

[Col. 0879B]

(From Jerome’s sayings.) Herod promised the dancing girl under oath that he would give her whatever she asked of him. If he says that he acted because of the oath, suppose she had asked for the death of his father or mother: would he have done it or not? Therefore, what he would have rejected in the case of his own family, he ought to have rejected also in the case of the prophet.

### CHAPTER 17.—On those who have confirmed everlasting hatred among themselves by an oath

(From the Council of Hildesheim, chapter 6.) Whoever binds himself by an oath to quarrel with someone and never return to peace in any way shall, for perjury, be separated from the body and blood of the Lord for one year and shall absolve his guilt through fasts and almsgiving. Let him return quickly to charity, which covers a multitude of sins.

### CHAPTER 18.—On those who have sworn carelessly

[Col. 0879C]

(From a decree of Pope Soter, chapter 3.) If it should happen that we have sworn something carelessly, and keeping it would lead to a worse outcome, let us recognize that it must be changed by more salutary counsel. It is better for us to swear falsely under pressing necessity than, by keeping the oath, to turn aside into another and greater crime.

### CHAPTER 19.—How priests ought to swear
(From a letter of Pope Cornelius, chapter 3.) Cornelius, bishop, sends greetings in the Lord to Rufus, his fellow bishop. Your affection, dearest brother, requires that, on the authority of the apostolic see, we should respond to your inquiries. Although we were hastening to do this not at length but briefly, because of certain difficulties which, through the sins that impede us, have come upon us, nevertheless we entrust to your diligence the task of searching more widely and investigating through the remaining institutions of the holy Fathers. For an exhausted mind, weighed down by burdens and difficulties, cannot accomplish as much good as one that is delighted and released from oppression. We have not therefore placed these matters before you in order to deny your holiness these and other things which we recognize to be necessary, but so that what is found here in lesser measure may be sought out more fully.

We have not learned that an oath has hitherto been required of high priests or of the other ministers of God, except on behalf of the true faith, nor have we found that they swore of their own accord. Therefore the holy apostle James, expressly prohibiting oaths, says: “Above all things, my brothers, do not swear, neither by heaven nor by earth nor by any other oath. Let your speech be ‘Yes, yes; No, no,’ so that you may not fall under judgment.” [Col. 0879D]

And the Lord says in the Gospel: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients, ‘You shall not swear falsely; rather, you shall fulfill your oaths to the Lord.’ But I say to you, do not swear at all, neither by heaven, because it is God’s throne, nor by earth, because it is the footstool of his feet, nor by Jerusalem, because it is the city of the great King, nor by your head, because you cannot make one hair white or black. Let your speech be ‘Yes, yes; No, no.’ Whatever is more than these is from evil”—that is, both from the one who demands an oath and from the one who swears.

These things, dearest brother, the Lord himself prohibits: namely, that one ought not to swear. The apostles above all, all of them; the holy men, our predecessors, who presided over this holy universal apostolic Church; the prophets; and the other holy teachers scattered throughout the world to preach—all forbid oaths to be made. If we began to enumerate their examples or insert them in this little document, the hour of the day would fail before their examples of prohibitions in this matter could be set down. Following them, we affirm the laws of the holy apostles and their successors, and prohibit rash oaths from being made.

Hence the Lord himself wrote with his own hand on the stone tablets that he gave to Moses: “See that you do not take the name of the Lord your God in vain,” and so forth. For each person ought to keep his own conscience pure before God and remember: “The mouth that lies kills the soul.” The Apostle also says: “Speak the truth, each one with his neighbor, because we are members of one another.” And elsewhere: “Do not lie to one another.”

These are the precepts of the Savior; these are the institutions of the prophets; these are the teachings of the holy Fathers. Whoever treats them as vain is an enemy of his own soul, because no one does anything against the prophets, against the Apostle, or against the Gospel without danger.

## Chapter 20 — At what time it is permitted to swear

(From the council held at Saint-Médard, chapter 4.) The holy synod decreed that, from Septuagesima until the octave of Easter, and from the Advent of the Lord until after the consecrated days, as well as during the fasts of the Four Ember Seasons, on the Greater Litany, and on the days of Rogations, [Col. 0880A] and on Sundays, no one may presume to swear over the holy things, except concerning reconciliation and the restoration of peace.

## Chapter 21 — Concerning those who violate the king’s oath

(From the sayings of Augustine.) If a layman profanes by violating the oath that he swore to the king and his lord, and afterward acts perversely and deceitfully toward his kingdom and plots against his life by any device or ambush—because he commits sacrilege, laying his hand upon the Lord’s Anointed—let him be anathema unless he corrects his offense through an appropriate satisfaction of penance, as the holy synod has established: namely, that he abandon the world, lay down his arms, enter a monastery, and do penance all the days of his life. Nevertheless, at the end of his life he shall receive communion with the Eucharist. [Col. 0880B] But if a bishop, presbyter, or deacon commits this crime, he shall be degraded.

## Chapter 22 — Concerning one who hears the voice of a perjurer and gives his consent

(It is written in Leviticus:) “The person who sins and hears the voice of an oath-breaker, and is a witness—whether he has seen it himself or knows of it—if he does not report it, shall bear his iniquity.”

## Chapter 23 — Concerning the Apostle’s calling the Holy Spirit to witness

(The Apostle says:) “I speak the truth in Christ; I do not lie, my conscience bearing witness with me in the Holy Spirit.”

## Chapter 24 — On the same matter

(From the sayings of Jerome.) Jerome says: “I call Jesus and his holy angels to witness.” [Col. 0881A]

## Chapter 25 — That a rash decision ought to be revoked

(From the Irish council, chapter 1.) A rash decision is praiseworthily revoked; this is not transgression but the correction of rashness.

## Chapter 26 — On the same matter

(From the same council, chapter 3.) If a girl still of childish age, living in her father’s house without his knowledge, binds herself by an oath, and if her father, as soon as he hears of it, objects, her vows and oaths shall be invalid, and she will more easily be corrected.

## Chapter 27 — On the same matter

(From the Council of Orléans, chapter 2.) The oath of a son or daughter, made without the father’s knowledge; the vows of a monk, made without the abbot’s knowledge; and the oaths of a child are invalid.

## Chapter 28 — That lying must be avoided in every way

[Col. 0881C]

(Gregory says:) “Do not deny, my son, the grace of God, lest you fall from good into evil, from humility into lying. For lying must be avoided in every way, whether it appears to be uttered for evil or even for good; because every lie is not from God but, as the Savior says, is from evil.”

## Chapter 29 — Also concerning oaths

(From the Council of Toledo.) For when we are compelled to swear falsely, we indeed offend the Creator, but merely stain ourselves; whereas when we fulfill harmful promises and proudly despise God’s commands in order to injure our neighbors with impious cruelty, we slaughter ourselves with the still more cruel sword of death. There we are struck by a double weapon of guilt; here we are slaughtered threefold. It remains, therefore, that our judgment should proceed in the direction where the way of mercy has opened. This way is so acceptable to the Lord that he desires it more than venerable sacrifices, as he himself says: “I desire mercy and not sacrifice.”

Having granted this permission for clemency, we commit the exercise of mercy itself to the authority of the glorious prince, so that, because God has opened to him an entrance to compassion, he too may not refuse the remedies of kindness. These remedies should be regulated by princely discretion in such a way that mercy is granted to those men without the people or the country suffering from them any danger or loss whatsoever.

Let it suffice that these matters have been moderated out of consideration for mercy. But oaths exacted up to now, or that may hereafter be required, for the safety of royal power or for the establishment of the people and the country, we decree must be observed indissolubly, with every care and vigilance, while the religious prohibition of mutilation of limbs and the death sentence is entirely set aside. Yet, lest the crafty wickedness of perverse minds at some time provoke us into the guilt of perjury, or claim that this judgment proceeds contrary to the rule of holy faith, we have taken care to attach to this discussion both oracles of divine authority and the testimony of the Fathers who preceded us.

Thus he said through Jeremiah: “Suddenly I will speak against a nation and against a kingdom, to uproot and destroy it. If that nation repents of its evil against which I have spoken, I too will repent of the evil that I had thought to do to it.” [Col. 0882A]

And through Ezekiel: “If,” he says, “I tell the righteous man that he shall live, and, trusting in his righteousness, he commits iniquity, all his righteousnesses shall be forgotten, and in the iniquity that he has committed, in that he shall die. But if I tell the wicked man, ‘You shall surely die,’ and he repents, he shall surely live and shall not die.”

If, then, our conduct thus changes the divine judgment, why should the abundant tears or distress of the wretched not, through mercy, moderate so harsh a vengeance? For this reason, the vengeance often promised to the Israelite people is suspended, and the destruction of the Ninevites is calmed by a change in the divine judgment.

For Saint Ambrose, in the third book of *On Duties*, says the following: “The disposition must therefore be pure and sincere, and each person must speak plainly. Let him possess his own vessel in holiness, lest he mislead his brother by a deceptive use of words. Let him promise nothing dishonorable, nor seek to have anything dishonorable promised to himself. It is more tolerable not to fulfill a promise than to do what is shameful.

“Very often people bind themselves by the sacrament of an oath, and, although they themselves recognize that the oath ought not to have been made, nevertheless, out of regard for it, they do what they promised, as we wrote above concerning Herod, who shamefully promised a reward to the dancing girl and cruelly paid it. Shameful was the promise of a kingdom for a dance; cruel was the gift of a prophet’s death in observance of an oath. How much more tolerable would perjury have been in such a case than observance of the oath? And shortly afterward, distinguishing the case of Jephthah: ‘Miserable is the necessity that is discharged by parricide.’” [Col. 0882B]

“It is better not to vow what the person to whom it is promised would not wish to be fulfilled. And a little later: ‘Not all promises, therefore, must always be fulfilled.’ Indeed, the Lord himself, as Scripture indicates, frequently changes his judgment.”

The most holy man Augustine, sharp in the acuteness of his inquiry, outstanding in his skill of discovery, flowing in his power of argument, graceful in the flower of his eloquence, and fertile in the fruit of wisdom, relates the following in his writings:

“There are altogether two kinds of lies in which there is not great guilt, though they are nevertheless not without guilt: when we jest, or when we make promises. The first kind, in jesting, is therefore not most harmful because it does not deceive. The person to whom it is said knows that it was said as a joke. The second kind is a lie uttered while retaining some measure of benevolence.”

Again, elsewhere he says: “Let truth not take away mercy; he will not walk in the way of the Lord, in which mercy and truth have met one another.”

Hence blessed Pope Gregory says in the books of the *Moralia*: “When the mind is caught between lesser and greater sins, if no escape without sin is open at all, the lesser sins must always be chosen. For one who is enclosed by the circuit of walls so that he cannot escape throws himself into flight where the wall is shorter.”

Hence Isidore also says: “It is more tolerable not to fulfill an oath than to remain in the shameful act of fornication.” Likewise, in the *Synonyms*: “In evil promises, break faith. In a shameful vow, withdraw from the resolution rashly undertaken, so as not to carry it out. An impious is the promise that is fulfilled through crime.”

Therefore it is necessary that one who swears wrongly should perform worthy penance, because he has taken the name of the Lord in vain contrary to his command. For it is written in Exodus: “The Lord will not hold him guiltless who takes the name of the Lord his God in vain.” And in Leviticus: “You shall not swear falsely by my name, nor profane the name of your God: I am the Lord.”

Nevertheless, he must absolutely not do the evil that he had sworn to perform, because foolish vows must be broken.

[Col. 0883] **END OF THE TWELFTH BOOK**

**THE THIRTEENTH BOOK OF THE DECRETALS OF BURCHARD, BISHOP OF THE CHURCH OF WORMS: ON FASTING**

[Col. 0883]

## SUMMARY OF THE BOOK

[Col. 0883D]

This book treats the observance and usefulness of fasting, especially the fast of Lent, the Four Ember Seasons, and the other fasts established by the Church, as well as those who violate them.

## Chapter 1 — On the observance of Lent

[Col. 0884D]

(From a letter of Pope Gregory.) Lent must be observed with the greatest care, so that during it the fast may in no way be broken, except by one whom illness has prevented from fasting, apart from Sundays, which are exempted from abstinence. [Col. 0885A] For these are the tithes of the year.

From the first Sunday of Lent until Easter of the Lord, six weeks are counted, which amount to forty-two days. When the six Sundays are subtracted from these days of abstinence, no more than thirty-six days remain in abstinence. For example: if the year is reckoned as 365 days, while we afflict ourselves for thirty-six days, we give God, as it were, the tithes of the year.

And in order that the sacred number of forty days may be completed—the number our Savior consecrated by his holy fast—the four days at the beginning of the preceding week are added to complete the forty days: namely, Wednesday, which is designated as the beginning of the fast, followed by Thursday, Friday, and Saturday. Unless we add these four days to the preceding thirty-six, we do not have forty days of abstinence. [Col. 0885B]

We are also commanded by almighty God to give the tithes of all our possessions. Therefore, in order that every tithe may rightly be paid by us to God, let us take the tithe of the year and cleanse ourselves in it by confessing our sins, correcting ourselves, fasting, keeping vigil, praying, and giving alms; let us tithe our flesh, so that we may reach holy Easter with confidence.

## Chapter 2 — On the fast of the Four Ember Seasons

(From the Council of Mainz, chapter 2.) We decree that the four seasons of the year be observed by everyone with fasting: in March, during the first week; in June, during the second; in September, during the third; and in December, during the fourth—the week that is complete before the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity—namely Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday. Let everyone come to the church at the ninth hour, with litanies, for the solemn celebration of Mass.

## Chapter 3 — At what time we should kneel at Mass

(From the Council of Orléans, chapter 14.) Presbyters shall announce to the people that they should kneel during the solemn celebration of Mass only in Lent and during the fast of the Four Ember Seasons. On Sundays, by contrast, and on the other feast days, from vespers to vespers they shall not kneel, but shall pray standing and bowed. No one should presume to pray with only one knee pressed to the ground, as the Jews are read to have done in mockery of the Lord during his Passion; rather, he should fix both knees to the ground. For the Apostle says: “I bend my knees before the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

## Chapter 4 — Concerning those who despise an imposed fast

(From the Council of Mainz, chapter 5.) If anyone, out of pride, despises an imposed fast and refuses to observe it with the other Christians, the Council of Gangra commands that he be anathematized.

## Chapter 5 — On the same matter

(From the Council of Gangra, chapter 19.) If any of those who devote themselves to continence, without bodily necessity, proudly breaks the fasts handed down for the common good and observed by the Church, driven by the impulse of his own thoughts, let him be anathema.

## Chapter 6 — How the Greater Litany is to be observed

[Col. 0886A]

(From the Council of Mainz, chapter 6.) It pleased us that the Greater Litany should be observed by all Christians on one day, the seventh day before the Kalends of May, as we have found established in the Roman Church and as our holy Fathers established it: not riding, not dressed in costly garments, but sprinkled with ashes and clothed in sackcloth, unless illness prevents this.

## Chapter 7 — On the fast of the Rogations

(From the Council of Orléans, chapter 6.) When, because of their sins, the peoples of Gaul were being cruelly slaughtered by the fury of wolves, and no remedy for this scourge could be found, the bishops of Gaul are said to have gathered at the city of Vienne and jointly decreed that they should observe a three-day fast. When the Lord mercifully removed the pestilence, these days became an annual observance, to be celebrated throughout the provinces of Gaul before the day of the Lord’s Ascension.

Let us also observe these days with the greatest reverence and devotion, with abstinence from meat and humility of heart—not so that we may escape the fury of visible wolves, but so that we may be able to overcome the temptations of invisible wolves, that is, of unclean spirits.

During these days no one should wear costly clothing, because we ought to mourn in sackcloth and ashes. Drunkenness and overeating, which occur among the common people, must be prohibited. No one should presume to ride, but everyone should walk barefoot. Women should by no means lead dances; rather, all together should sing “Kyrie eleison” and implore God’s mercy with contrite hearts—for sins, for peace, for pestilence, for the preservation of the crops, and for other necessities. For these are days of abstinence, not of rejoicing.

## Chapter 8 — That on the Lord’s Supper and on the other days of Lent the fast is not to be broken

(From the Council of Laodicea, chapter 50.) It is not proper to break the fast during Lent on Thursday of the final week, nor to pass through the whole of Lent without reverence; rather, it is more fitting to honor the whole of Lent with strict fasting.

## Chapter 9 — That on Holy Saturday the fast is not to be broken before nightfall

(From the Council of Orange, chapter 2.) On Holy Saturday, that is, on the vigil of Easter, the fast must not be broken before nightfall, except by children or the sick, nor on Good Friday itself; for the Lord’s Supper, Good Friday, and Saturday pertain to those forty days. Nor are the divine mysteries to be celebrated on these two days, since the canons command that on these two days—Good Friday and Saturday—the sacraments are not to be celebrated at all.

## Chapter 10 — That the feasts of the saints’ births should not be celebrated during Lent

(From the Council of Laodicea, chapter 51.) The feasts commemorating the birthdays of martyrs should not be celebrated during Lent; rather, their holy commemoration should fittingly take place on Saturdays and Sundays.

## Chapter 11 — That almsgiving should be practiced on fast days

[Col. 0887A]

(From the Council of Chalon, chapter 5.) On fast days almsgiving must be practiced, and whatever food or drink a person would have consumed, had he not fasted, he should distribute to the poor. For to fast while reserving the food of the midday meal for the evening is an increase not in reward but in food.

## Chapter 12 — That the mealtime should be preserved during Lent

(From a decree of Pope Silverius, chapter 1.) Many who think they are fasting during Lent eat as soon as they hear the signal for the ninth hour. They should in no way be considered to be fasting if they eat before the evening office has been celebrated. [Col. 0887B]

For one must go to Mass, and, after hearing the solemn Mass and the evening offices, one should give alms and then approach food. If, however, someone is constrained by necessity and cannot come to Mass, he should, once the evening hour has been reckoned and his prayer completed, end his fast.

## Chapter 13 — That there should be no quarrels on fast days

(From the sayings of Pope Liberius.) On these fast days there should be no lawsuits and no quarrels; rather, one must persist in the praises of God and in necessary work. For through the prophet the Lord reproves those who engage in quarrels and lawsuits during Lent and those who demand debts from their debtors, saying: “Behold, on the day of your fast your own desires are found, and you demand all your debts. Behold, you fast for quarrels and contentions, and you strike with an impious fist.”

## Chapter 14 — That married people should abstain from their spouses on those consecrated fast days

(Also from the same source, chapter 5.) During these most sacred days of Lent one must abstain from one’s spouse and live chastely and piously, so that these days may be spent with heart and body sanctified, and so that one may thus reach the holy day of Easter. For a fast is almost worthless if it is defiled by marital intercourse and is not commended by prayers, vigils, and almsgiving.

## Chapter 15 — Concerning those in the clergy who detest eating meat

(From the Council of Ancyra, chapter 13.) It was decided that those in the clergy, presbyters or deacons, who abstain from meat should at least touch it, and then, if they wish, refrain from eating it. But if they detest it so greatly that they do not consider even vegetables cooked with meat fit to eat, they must withdraw from the order, as people who do not accept the rule.

## Chapter 16 — On the vigils of the saints

(From the Council of Orléans, chapter 1.) When presbyters announce the sacred festivals to the people, they must also urge them in every way to observe the fasts of the vigils.

## Chapter 17 — On the same matter

(From the sayings of Pope Eusebius, chapter 10.) Fasts established by priests in the Church are not to be broken without reasonable necessity.

## Chapter 18 — Concerning what should be done if famine, pestilence, or an irregularity of the weather occurs

[Col. 0888A]

(From a decree of Pope Liberius, chapter 2.) If famine, pestilence, irregularity of the weather, or any other kind of tribulation occurs, the mercy of the Lord must immediately be entreated through fasts, almsgiving, and supplications.

## Chapter 19 — That no one should fast on Sunday as an act of abstinence

(From the Council of Gangra, chapter 18.) If anyone fasts on Sunday on account of a supposed continence or out of obstinacy, let him be anathema.

## Chapter 20 — On the same matter

(From the Council of Tours, chapter 57.) If anyone, because of a public penance received from a priest or on account of some necessity, fasts on Sunday as though out of religious devotion, like the Manichaeans, let him be anathema.

## Chapter 21 — That secular courts should not be held on Sundays, principal feasts, or fast days

(From the council held at Erfurt, which King Henry attended, chapter 2.) In accordance with canonical ordinance, we decree that secular courts should in no way be held on Sundays or other principal feasts, or on those days on which the prescribed fasts are observed. Moreover, the holy synod decreed that no judicial authority should have permission, on its own authority, to summon Christians to court on the days mentioned above: from seven days before the Nativity of the Lord until the octave of Epiphany; from Quinquagesima until the octave of Easter; and from seven days before the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist. This is so that they may have freer opportunity to visit the church and devote themselves to prayer.

## Chapter 22 — That the fast should be observed without luxurious food

(From the sayings of Jerome.) “I do not speak of weeks; I do not speak of doubled fasts. But at least let us pass each individual day without luxurious food.”

## Chapter 23 — That the daily fast should not be without some refreshment

(From the sayings of Pimen, the hermit.) “Let your fasts be daily, and let your refreshment avoid satiety. For it does you no good to carry an empty stomach for two or three days if it is then overloaded. When fasts are repaid with overeating, the filled mind immediately grows sluggish; and when the earth of this body is watered, it produces thorns and thistles.”

## Chapter 24 — On the same matter

(Also from the same source.) “Let your fasts be pure, continuous, and moderate—that is, to hunger every day and to eat every day.”

## Chapter 25 — That fasting heals the wounds of the sinner

(The Apostle says:) “Do not continue to drink only water, but use a little wine for the sake of your infirmities.” For it heals the wounds of the sinner, and fasting sanctifies those who have been healed.

## Chapter 26 — Concerning a certain Alcibiades who had imposed upon himself the heavy yoke of fasting

(From Eusebius’ *Ecclesiastical History*.) There was a certain Alcibiades among those who were held in bonds for Christ. [Col. 0889A] He led a sufficiently arduous and austere life, refusing to take any food, but using only bread and salt with water. When he wished to maintain this rigor of life even while he was in prison, it was revealed to a certain servant of God named Attalus that Alcibiades was not acting rightly toward God’s creatures and wished to leave others an example of stumbling.

When he learned this, Alcibiades began to accept everything with thanksgiving. For the same Spirit that revealed these things to Attalus in order to instruct him persuaded Alcibiades to follow them.

## Chapter 27 — Concerning one who imposes a fast upon himself under the pretext of religion without the command of his bishop or presbyter

(From the council held at Erfurt in the presence of King Henry, chapter 5.) We absolutely forbid anyone, except with the consent of his own bishop or of the bishop’s envoy, to impose a fast upon himself under the pretext of religion by selecting one day in preference to the others. We disapprove of what has been done and prohibit it from being done in the future, because it is recognized as having more to do with divination than with fulfilling Catholic law.

## Chapter 28 — That no Christian who seeks holy places out of reverence should there be constrained by the ban of any public authority

(From the same council.) We command that no Christian who seeks a church out of reverence, remains there, and returns from it should be constrained there by the ban of any public authority, lest, while he hastens to the church for the sake of prayer, he be prevented by such a ban from devoting himself earnestly to the salvation of his soul.

[Col. 0889] **END OF THE THIRTEENTH BOOK**

[Col. 0889]

**THE FOURTEENTH BOOK OF THE DECRETALS OF BURCHARD, BISHOP OF THE CHURCH OF WORMS: ON GLUTTONY AND DRUNKENNESS**

[Col. 0889]

## SUMMARY OF THE BOOK

[Col. 0889C]

This book treats the detestable vices of gluttony and drunkenness and explains what penalty should be imposed on those entangled in these vices.

## Chapter 1 — That gluttony is greatly opposed to Christians

(From the sayings of Benedict.) Nothing is so contrary to a Christian person as gluttony and drunkenness, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “See that your hearts are not weighed down by gluttony and drunkenness.”

## Chapter 2 — That the evil of drunkenness must be avoided altogether

(From the decree of Pope Eutychian, chapter 9.) We command Christians to beware in every way of the great evil of drunkenness, from which all vices spring. Whoever refuses to avoid it, we decree, must be excommunicated [Col. 0889D] until he makes an appropriate correction.

## Chapter 3 — That bishops and their ministers should not be burdened by gluttony and drunkenness

[Col. 0890C]

(From the decree of the same pope, chapter 9.) Bishops and ministers of God ought not to devote themselves excessively to feasts and drunkenness, but should consider the sentence of the Lord, who says: “Take heed lest your hearts be weighed down by gluttony and drunkenness.” Let them take food and the necessary nourishment in moderation, so that, according to the Apostle, they may be sober and ready for the service of the Lord.

## Chapter 4 — On the same matter

(From the Council of Chalon, chapter 10.) Priests must maintain sobriety and preach to the faithful that it should be maintained, because one who fills himself with unmixed wine to the point of losing his reason cannot freely preach sobriety. The same must be observed concerning feasting and the other plagues pertaining to gluttony.

## Chapter 5 — On the same matter

(From the Apostolic Canons, title 42.) A bishop, presbyter, or deacon who devotes himself to dice and drunkenness must either stop or be condemned. A subdeacon, lector, or cantor who does the same must either stop or be deprived of communion. The same applies to a layman.

## Chapter 6 — On the same matter

(From the same source, chapter 43.) If a bishop or any ordained person is habitually drunk, he must either stop or be deposed.

## Chapter 7 — What sort of guests should attend the banquets of priests

(From the decree of Pope Eusebius, chapter 10.) A bishop ought to be content with moderate banquets [Col. 0891B] and should not pressure his guests to eat and drink; rather, he should always provide an example of sobriety. Every inducement to disgrace must be removed from his banquet: no theatrical entertainments, no empty chatter of performers, no foolish talk of fools, and no tricks of buffoons should be admitted.

Let strangers, the poor, and the weak be present, so that, blessing Christ from the priestly table, they may receive a blessing. Let sacred reading be recited, followed by exhortation in the living voice, so that the banqueters may rejoice that they have been refreshed not only by bodily food but also by the nourishment of spiritual words, and so that God may be honored in all things, through Jesus Christ our Lord.

## Chapter 8 — On the same matter

[Col. 0891C]

(From the penitential of Theodore.) If any priest becomes drunk through ignorance, let him do penance for seven days on bread and water; if through negligence, for fifteen days; if through contempt, for forty days. A deacon or monk, according to his order, as it is written, and the other clerics and ministers according to their order, shall do penance at the judgment of the priest.

Laymen, as people without vows, if they become drunk, are to be reproved by the priest, who shall tell them that drunkards will not possess the kingdom of God and that drunkenness leads to destruction; he shall compel them to do penance.

Whoever makes a person drunk out of hospitality must be sharply reproved and do penance for seven days; if he did so out of contempt, for thirty days. No Christian should compel another Christian to drink more than is sufficient for nature. If he does so, let him do penance according to what is contained in the penitential.

## Chapter 9 — On the same matter

[Col. 0891D]

(From the sayings of Bishop Fructuosus.) If anyone endowed with ecclesiastical ordination, or a monk, is found to be drunk, let him do penance on bread and water for three months.

## Chapter 10 — On the same matter

(From the decree of Pope Eutychian, chapter 13.) You must take care both to abstain from drunkenness yourselves and to preach that the peoples subject to you should abstain. You must neither go through taverns drinking or eating, nor travel through houses or villages out of any kind of curiosity, nor hold banquets with women or with any unclean persons—unless perhaps a head of household invites you to his home and wishes to rejoice with you in spiritual joy together with his wife and children, to receive the refreshment of your words, and to offer you bodily refreshment as an act of charity.

For whenever any of the faithful refreshes you with bodily food, you ought to refresh him in return with spiritual food.

## Chapter 11 — Let one who has been drunk do penance according to his order

(From the Council of Agde, chapter 10.) Accordingly, anyone who is established to have been drunk shall, according to his order, either be removed from communion for a period of thirty days or be subjected to corporal punishment.

## Chapter 12 — That it is not permissible to become drunk with wine, but that it must be avoided

(From the sayings of Augustine.) Flee wine as though it were poison, [Col. 0892B] lest drunkenness overcome you and, stripping you of your virtues, leave you naked. For wine, as Holy Scripture says, causes even the wise to apostatize.

Consider Noah, a wise and holy man: how, through drunkenness, he lay asleep exposed naked. Consider also the patriarch Lot, who, through drunkenness, shamelessly had intercourse with his daughters.

Hence blessed Basil says: “Many have been seized by demons through wine; and drunkenness is nothing other than a most manifest demon.” Hence the prophet says: “Fornication and drunkenness take away the heart.” For drunkenness produces agitation, gives birth to madness of mind, and kindles the flame of lust.

As the Apostle testifies: “Do not become drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery.” But if anyone acts contrary to these statutes of the saints, let him perform worthy and lengthy penance, because drunkenness is one of those sins that separate a person from the kingdom of God, as the Apostle Paul says: “Neither will drunkards possess the kingdom of God.”

## Chapter 13 — Concerning those who vomit because of drunkenness
(From the Roman Penitential.) Whoever vomits because of drunkenness, if he is a priest or deacon, shall do penance for forty days. If he is a monk, he shall do penance for thirty days; if a cleric, twenty days; if a layman, fifteen days.

## CHAPTER 14. On the Same Matter

(From the Penitential of the priest Bede.) If a layman vomits because of drunkenness, he shall abstain from meat, wine, and beer for three days.

## CHAPTER 15. On Those Who Arrogantly Make Others Drunk

(From the same source.) If anyone wickedly makes another person drunk, he shall do penance for forty days. But if he has made a habit of it, he shall be deprived of communion until he has done worthy penance and promised amendment. [Col. 0892D]

## CHAPTER 16. That Drunkenness Must Be Avoided

(From the decree of Pope Clement, chapter 35.) The prophet strictly prohibited drunkenness and declared that drunkards were dead in body and soul. Concerning them he said by way of example: “Woe to you who rise early to pursue drunkenness and continue drinking until evening, so that you burn with wine. Harp, lyre, tambourine, flute, and wine are in your banquets, but you do not regard the work of the Lord, nor consider the works of his hands.” And again: “Woe to those who are mighty at drinking wine and strong men at mixing drunkenness, who acquit the wicked for gifts and deprive the righteous of his justice. Therefore, just as a tongue of fire devours stubble and the heat of the flame consumes it, so their root shall become like refuse, and their shoot shall rise like dust. For they have cast away the law of the Lord of hosts and blasphemed the word of the Holy One of Israel. Therefore the fury of the Lord was kindled against his people; he stretched out his hand against them and struck them. The mountains were shaken, and their corpses lay like dung in the middle of the streets. In all this his anger has not turned away, but his hand is still stretched out.” [Col. 0893A]

## CHAPTER 17. Again on Drunkenness

(Saint Isidore says:) Food produces surfeit, and drink produces drunkenness. Drunkenness gives rise to mental confusion, fury of heart, and the flame of lust. It so alienates the mind that a person does not know where he is. Hence he does not even perceive the evil committed through drunkenness. It is true what is said according to the prophet: “Fornication and drunkenness would take away the heart.” Fornication, as Solomon says, makes the wise man foolish. Drunkenness, as in the case of Lot, captures the senses and reason. Hence also in Proverbs: “Let those who are powerful and prone to anger,” it says, “not drink wine, lest, when they have drunk, they forget wisdom.” Many regard it as praise to drink much and not become drunk. Let them hear the prophet speaking against them: “Woe to those who are mighty at drinking wine and strong men at mixing drunkenness.”

Isaiah rebukes those devoted to much wine and living luxuriously, saying: “Woe to you who rise early to pursue drunkenness and continue drinking until evening, so that you burn with wine.” Of such people it is also said elsewhere: “Woe to you, city whose king is young and whose princes eat in the morning.” For many, from morning until sunset, serve drunkenness and the pleasures of gluttony, and do not understand why they were born; held captive by beastlike custom, they devote the whole day only to luxury and banquets. The prophet Joel cries out to those who serve drunkenness, saying: “Awake, drunkards, and weep; howl, all you who drink wine to excess.” By this testimony he does not merely say, “Weep, all you who drink wine,” as though drinking were altogether forbidden, but adds “to excess,” which refers to pleasure-seeking and wasteful indulgence. For the Apostle teaches Timothy how much is sufficient for necessity, saying: “Use a little wine.” [Col. 0894A]

People are made drunk not only by wine but also by other kinds of drink, which are prepared in various ways. Hence the Nazirite, who consecrated himself to the Lord, was commanded not to drink wine or strong drink; both overturn the state of the mind and make people drunk. Both equally produce the flesh’s wantonness. Some who practice abstinence, just as they eat bread by weight, also take water in measured amounts, asserting that abstinence is likewise appropriate for bodily chastity.

[Col. 0893] END OF THE FOURTEENTH BOOK.

[THE FIFTEENTH BOOK.]

[Col. 0893]
