# BURCHARD, BISHOP OF THE CHURCH OF WORMS, DECRETALS, BOOK FIFTEEN: ON LAYMEN

[Col. 0895]

## SUMMARY OF THE BOOK

[Col. 0895B]

This book establishes a treatment of laymen of every condition, both those who rule—such as emperors, kings, and princes—and those subject to their authority.

## CHAPTER 1. Bishops, Since They Hold the Care of the People Entrusted to Them by God, Should Not Tolerate Oppressors of the Poor

(From the Fifth Council of Toledo, chapter 32.) Bishops should not doubt that the care of protecting and defending the people has been entrusted to them by God. Therefore, whenever they see judges and powerful men acting as oppressors of the poor, they should first rebuke them with priestly admonition; and if they refuse to amend, they shall be anathematized.

## CHAPTER 2. On Those Who Have Plundered Episcopal Territories

[Col. 0895C] (From the Council of Carthage, chapter 8.) If anyone has stripped another person of his property and, when admonished by the bishop, has not restored it, he shall be excommunicated.

## CHAPTER 3. That Bishops Should Admonish the Authorities Not to Oppress the Poor

(From the Council of Orléans, chapter 4.) Judges or authorities who oppress the poor, if they do not amend after being admonished by their bishop, shall be excommunicated.

## CHAPTER 4. On the Same Matter

(From the Council of Mainz, chapter 8.) Bishops shall have authority to foresee, rule, govern, and administer ecclesiastical affairs according to the authority of the canons. We wish laymen to obey bishops in their ministry, for the governance of the churches of God, the defense of widows [Col. 0895D] and orphans, and the preservation of their Christian faith; and we wish them to obey the bishops in these matters, while bishops cooperate with counts and judges in administering justice, so that a just law may in no way be perverted by anyone’s lie, false testimony, perjury, or bribe.

## CHAPTER 5. On Laymen Who Unjustly Harass the Church or a Cleric

(From the Council of Agde, chapter 32.) If any layman attempts, on a pretext of accusation, to harass the Church or a cleric, and is convicted, he shall be barred from the thresholds of the Church and from the communion of Catholics unless he has done worthy penance. [Col. 0896B]

## CHAPTER 6. That Despisers of the Canons Should Be Excommunicated

(From the Council of Carthage, chapter 15.) Laymen who despise the canons shall be excommunicated; clerics shall be deprived of their rank.

## CHAPTER 7. On Transgressors of the Divine Laws

(From the council held at Lauriacum, chapter 10.) If anyone is found to be a public transgressor of divine law, or a despiser of the holy canons because of manifest crimes, or an opponent of the constitutions of the holy Fathers, and if he delays obeying episcopal admonitions, he shall be anathematized.

## CHAPTER 8. That Neither the Emperor Nor Any Powerful Person May Do Anything Against the Divine Command

[Col. 0896C]

(From the decree of Pope Hadrian, chapter 16.) Therefore, neither the emperor nor anyone who guards piety may presume to do anything against the commands of God, nor do anything that conflicts with evangelical, prophetic, or apostolic rules. An unjust judgment or an unjust decree ordered by judges through fear of the king or by royal command shall have no validity; nor shall anything stand that has been done against evangelical, prophetic, or apostolic teaching and constitution, or against the constitutions of the holy Fathers. Whatever has been done by unbelievers or heretics shall be wholly annulled.

## CHAPTER 9. That No One Should Presume to Act Against the Canons

(From the Council of Tibur, chapter 10.) Constitutions contrary to the canons and decrees of the Roman bishops, or to good morals, shall have no force. [Col. 0896D]

## CHAPTER 10. On Imperial Law

(From the decree of Pope Pius, chapter 3.) The law of the emperors is not above the law of God, but beneath it.

## CHAPTER 11. When Canonical Matters Are Being Discussed, Laymen Should Not Be Present Unless They Are Religious

(From the Council of Chalon, chapter 6.) When matters that are canonical are being discussed, or when matters governed by a rule are being examined, no laymen ought to be present except religious persons, and only those who are summoned in their own person. [Col. 0897A]

## CHAPTER 12. That Laymen in a Synod Should Not Dare to Teach Unless the Clergy Command It

(From the Council of Carthage, chapter 118.) Laymen present at a synod with the clergy should not dare to teach unless the clergy themselves command it.

## CHAPTER 13. That the People Are to Be Taught, Not Followed

(From the decree of Pope Celestine, chapter 22.) The people are to be taught, not followed; and if they do not know what is permitted and what is not permitted, we ought to admonish them, not give them our assent. Whoever attempts to do what is forbidden will feel canonical censure.

## CHAPTER 14. On One Who Comes Against the Bishop’s Decree

[Col. 0897B] (Gregory says:) If anyone comes against the bishop’s decree, let him be cast out of the Church.

## CHAPTER 15. The Emperor Should Be Admonished to Obey the Decrees of the Apostolic See

(From a decree of Pope Anastasius.) In particular, out of love for your empire and for the blessedness that the kingdom can attain, we proclaim in fulfillment of our apostolic office that, as is fitting and as the Holy Spirit dictates, obedience should be given to our admonitions, so that your commonwealth may obtain every good, as is promised in Exodus: “If you listen to the voice of the Lord your God, do what is pleasing before him, obey his commands, and keep all his justice, I will not bring upon you any disease that I brought upon the Egyptians. For I am the Lord, who heals you.” And there again the most powerful trumpet is sounded: “And now, Israel, what else does the Lord your God ask of you except that you fear the Lord your God, walk in all his ways, love him, and serve the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your mind? Keep the commandments and judgments of the Lord your God that I shall command you.”

When I offer these reminders repeatedly, may your piety not disregard them, keeping before your eyes the words of the Lord in the Gospel: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you despises me; and whoever despises me despises him who sent me.” For the Apostle, echoing our Savior, also says: “Therefore, whoever despises these things does not despise man but God, who gave his Holy Spirit in us.” The breast of your clemency is the sanctuary of public happiness, so that through your diligence—since he has commanded you to preside on earth as his representative—evangelical and apostolic commands may not be resisted with harsh pride, but that what brings salvation may be fulfilled through obedience. [Col. 0897D]

## CHAPTER 16. A General Admonition to Kings

(From the Register to Adilberch, king of the Franks, chapter 264.) For this reason almighty God brings good men to rule over peoples: through them he may bestow the gifts of his power upon all over whom they have been placed. We know this has happened among the English, over whom your glory has therefore been set, so that the good things granted to you may, through heavenly favor, also be restored to the people subject to you.

Therefore, glorious son, carefully preserve the grace divinely given to you; hasten to extend the Christian faith among the peoples subject to you; multiply your zeal for righteousness in their conversion; attack the worship of idols and overthrow the buildings of pagan shrines. Build up the character of your subjects in great purity of life by exhorting, frightening, correcting, and displaying examples of good works, so that you may find in heaven the Rewarder whose name and knowledge you have spread on earth. He himself will also make the name of your glory more glorious among your descendants, since you seek and preserve his honor among the nations.

Thus the most devout emperor Constantine once, recalling the Roman commonwealth from the perverse worship of idols, subjected it with himself to our almighty God Jesus Christ, and with his subject peoples turned his whole mind toward him. As a result, that man surpassed the name of the ancient rulers by his own praises, and advanced so far beyond his predecessors in reputation as he surpassed them in good works.

Therefore let your glory now hasten to instill knowledge of the one God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, in the kings and peoples subject to you, so that you may surpass the ancient kings of your nation in praise and merit. And when you have wiped away even the sins of others among your subjects, you will be all the more secure concerning your own sins before the terrible judgment of almighty God.

Moreover, we wish your glory to know that, as we recognize from the words of the almighty Lord in sacred Scripture, the end of the present world is already near, and the kingdom of the saints is coming, which can never be ended by any conclusion. As that end of the world approaches, many things are impending that have not previously occurred: disturbances of the air, terrors from heaven, storms contrary to the order of the seasons, wars, famines, pestilences, and earthquakes in various places. Yet not all these things will occur in our own days; they will follow after our days.

Therefore, if you recognize any of these things occurring in your land, do not let your minds be disturbed in any way. For these signs are sent before the end of the age so that we should be concerned for our souls, fearful of the hour of death, and found prepared in good works for the coming judgment. [Col. 0898C]

## CHAPTER 17. Another Admonition to Rulers

(From the Register to Justin, governor of Sicily, chapter 2.) What the tongue says is attested by the conscience, because formerly, when you were entangled in no positions of rank, I loved you greatly and revered you greatly. The very modesty of your bearing compelled certain efforts to ensure that you should be loved even by one unwilling to love you. When I heard that you had come to administer the praetorship of Sicily, I rejoiced greatly; but when I discovered that a certain hostility had begun to creep in between you and the clergy, I was deeply saddened.

Now, since both you are occupied with the care of administration and I with the concern of this governance, we can rightly love one another in a special way only insofar as we do no harm to the common good. Therefore, by almighty God, at whose dread judgment we shall be required to render an account of our deeds, I beg that your glory always keep his regard before your eyes and never admit anything from which even a small disagreement might arise between us.

Let no profits draw you toward injustice. Consider how short life is, and reflect upon the Judge to whom you will one day go, you who exercise judicial power. Therefore one must carefully observe that we leave all profits behind here and carry with us to judgment only the account of how we administered our gains. We should therefore seek those advantages that death cannot take away, but that the end of this present life will reveal as lasting forever. [Col. 0899A]

## CHAPTER 18. Likewise, an Exhortation to Rulers

(From Gregory’s Register to Gennadius, patrician and exarch, chapter 73.) If the success of your military actions had not resulted from the merit of faith and from devotion to the Christian religion, it would not be especially astonishing, since we know that such things were also granted to ancient commanders in war. But since, by God’s gift, you anticipate future victories not through carnal foresight but rather through prayers, it is astonishing that your glory proceeds not from earthly counsel but from God’s gift from above.

There the eloquent report of your merits does not remain silent: it would say that you frequently seek war, not from a desire to shed blood, but to enlarge the commonwealth in which we see God worshiped, so that the name of Christ might spread everywhere through subject peoples by the preaching of the faith. For just as your outward works of virtue make you eminent in this life, so also the adornments of your inward character, proceeding from a pure heart, glorify you in the future life through participation in heavenly joys.

## CHAPTER 19. How Kings Should Strive to Avenge the Sins of Priests and the People

(From Gregory’s Register to Brunhild, queen of the Franks, chapter 272.) Since it is written, “Justice exalts a nation, but sin makes peoples miserable,” a kingdom is believed to be established when the fault that has been recognized is quickly corrected.

Many reports have therefore reached us, and we cannot repeat them without great anguish of heart: certain priests in those regions behave so shamelessly and wickedly that it is disgraceful for us to hear of it and grievous to report it. Therefore, lest after the reputation of this wickedness has extended this far, the depravity of others wound either our soul or your kingdom with the dart of sin, we must rise ardently to avenge these things, lest the ill repute of a few become the destruction of many. For bad priests are the cause of the people’s ruin. Who would interpose himself as an advocate for the sins of the people if the priest who ought to plead for them commits worse offenses?

But since neither concern moves anyone to pursue those of whom this report is made, nor zeal to exact vengeance, let your letters come to us, so that, if you command it and with the assent of your authority, we may send a person who, together with other priests, should investigate these matters carefully and correct them according to God. For the things we have mentioned must not be concealed: whoever can correct something and neglects to do so undoubtedly makes himself a partner in the offense.

Therefore, care for your soul; care for the nephews whom you wish to reign happily; care for the provinces. Before our Creator shakes out his hand to strike, consider most diligently the correction of this crime, lest he strike more harshly later because he now waits longer and more mercifully. Know that you will offer our God a great sacrifice of appeasement if you quickly cut away the stain of so great a crime from your territories.

Given on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, in the fourth indiction.

## CHAPTER 20. On the Same Matter

(From Gregory’s Register to Tenderic, king of the Franks, chapter 273.) The letter that reveals your heart has shown, through its abundant and brilliant language, how prudence shines in you together with royal power, so that there can be no doubt about whatever the reputation of your excellence has reported.

And since you have indicated that our exhortation has pleased your royal mind through its praise, so that you may diligently establish and preserve in every respect whatever you recognize as pertaining to the worship of our God, the reverence of the churches, and the honor of priests, we once again urge you, for your own reward, to order a synod to be assembled and, as we wrote previously, to have bodily vices among priests and the depravity of the Simoniac heresy condemned by the decision of all the bishops and cut away from the boundaries of your kingdom. Do not permit them to obtain more through money than the Lord’s commands prescribe.

For since all greed is the service of idols, whoever does not carefully guard against it in the granting of honors, especially ecclesiastical honors, is subjected to the destruction of unbelief, even if he appears to retain the faith that he neglects. Therefore, just as you strive to be vigilant against external enemies, so also be vigilant against the inward adversaries of souls, so that by faithfully resisting the enemies of our God you may both reign happily here under his protection and later, guided by his grace, come to eternal joys.

## CHAPTER 21. That It Is a Consolation to Many if Prudent Men Adhere to Kings

(From Gregory’s Register to Asclepiodotus, patrician of the Angles, chapter 271.) It is a consolation to many that prudent men such as you are should adhere to kings. For when they understand that a place has been granted to them for the benefit of their souls, it is certain that they do not prefer other grounds for reward wherever they find them.

## CHAPTER 22. That Adversaries of Kings Should Be Excommunicated

(From the council held at Lauriacum, chapter 13.) If anyone presumes, with a stubborn and inflated spirit, to contradict or resist royal authority—which, according to the Apostle, is from God—and refuses to obey its just and reasonable commands according to God and ecclesiastical authority, let him be anathematized.

## CHAPTER 23. On Those Who Do Not Obey the Ruler

(From the Council of Toledo.) It is written in the Book of Kings: “Whoever does not obey the ruler shall die.” The Council of Agde, however, commands that such a person be anathematized.

## CHAPTER 24. On Those Found Culpable in the Adversity of Their Own People or Country

(From the same source.) Therefore synodal reason persuaded us to decree that any layman who, by going over to foreign regions, is subsequently found to have acted harmfully in the adversity of his own people, country, or royal authority shall be condemned by perpetual excommunication, and communion shall never be granted to him except at the end of his life.

## CHAPTER 25. That No One Should Presume to Choose Another King While the Ruler Is Alive

(From the same council, seventh council, chapter 17.) Although a judgment on this matter was promulgated in the earlier council held in the first year of our most glorious ruler, it pleases us nevertheless to preserve it again as is fitting.

Therefore, while the king is alive, no layman of any rank or dignity, nor anyone consecrated to the episcopate, priesthood, or diaconate, nor anyone devoted to any other clerical office, shall in any action or deliberation designate a future king against the welfare and, without doubt, the will of the living king. By flattering or persuading others through that same hope, he shall neither draw them to himself nor himself assent to another.

For Christians must regard it as unjust and utterly detestable to anticipate the future by illicit means and to arrange what is to come while ignorant of their own life. If anyone has already devised such things by an unjust deliberation, supposing that priestly moderation permits him to do so, then, if he seeks pardon, he must promptly strive to make this known to the ears of the present ruler. But if he persists and refuses to disclose the contrivances of his deliberation, let him be punished with the most severe anathema. [Col. 0901C]

## CHAPTER 26. That No One Should Plot the King’s Destruction

(From the same source, chapter 18.) In the preceding universal synod, provision was indeed made for the safety of our rulers, but we wish to repeat what was rightly enacted and to strengthen the salutary ordinances with worthy authority.

Therefore we call God and every order of angels to witness, as well as the company of prophets and apostles, the choir of all martyrs, the whole catholic Church, and the assembly of the years of Christ: let no one plot the king’s destruction; let no one attack the ruler’s life with murder; let no one deprive him of the reins of government; let no one, with tyrannical presumption, usurp the height of the kingdom for himself; let no one by any scheme join his hand to the hands of conspirators against him.

If anyone should become presumptuous in any of these matters through reckless daring, let him, struck by divine anathema, be held condemned by eternal judgment, without any possibility of remedy.

## CHAPTER 27. On the Faithful of Kings

(From the same source.) Therefore the holy council decreed that all who, in faithful obedience and sincere service, have obeyed the will or commands of the ruler, and who have devoted their whole intention to guarding his safety or watching over the kingdom, shall not, through an unjust cause, be driven away by his successors either from their rank or from their former possessions. [Col. 0902A]

Rather, they should now be moderated according to each ruler’s judgment for the benefit of each individual, just as he sees them to be necessary for the country; and his kindness should be distributed to them so that favor and authority may remain with them in other matters also. Thus they may lawfully enjoy whatever they have justly acquired, with the freedom to leave it to their descendants or to bestow it upon whomever they choose.

But if anyone has proved faithless toward the royal person or useless in the matters entrusted to him, let it be established that such regulation lies in the hand of your clemency and at the discretion of your power. For it is plainly lawful to exercise the right of authority, since the governance of all things is known to have been delegated by heavenly judgment.

If, after the ruler’s departure, anyone is found to have been faithless during his life, let him lose whatever he possessed among the acquisitions granted by that ruler; it shall be confiscated and distributed to the faithful. [Col. 0902B]

## CHAPTER 28. On the Offspring of Kings

(From the same source, chapter 16.) Just as the insolence of wicked kings is always hateful and detestable to their subjects, so the prudent usefulness of good kings becomes beloved by their peoples. Who, then, could tolerate—or see as a Christian one who errs in this way—someone attempting to strip royal offspring or descendants of their possessions or deprive them of their dignities?

To prevent this from happening, let our judgment concerning the sons of the ruler be generally proclaimed; that is, let suitable decrees be issued by us concerning the descendants of the present most excellent King Chintila, so that the whole of his kingdom may preserve toward all his posterity what the synod held in this Church last year decreed. Namely, let his sons be shown benevolent and steadfast affection, and, wherever the opportunity arises, let protections be granted as appropriate supports, so that they are not defrauded by any cunning device of property rightfully expended [the reading is uncertain], of what was secured through their parents’ dignity, of gifts from rulers, of anyone’s outlays, or even of what is owed on grounds of piety; nor let anyone provide grounds for injuring them through any scheme.

For it is fitting that, since through his rule we possess security, we should grant peace to his descendants by decree of the council.

## CHAPTER 29. That Whatever an Agitated Mind Does, It Considers Just

(From Gregory’s Register to the Emperor Maurice Augustus, chapter 213.) He is guilty before almighty God who is not pure in everything he does and says toward the most serene lord. But I, an unworthy servant of your piety, speak in this petition neither as a bishop nor as a servant by right of public office, but by the right of a private person, because, most serene lord, you were already my lord at the time when you were not yet lord of all.

The useful vigilance of rulers, and the praiseworthy caution, is that in which reason governs everything and anger claims nothing for itself. Power must therefore be restrained under reason, and nothing should be done before the agitated mind has returned to tranquility. For in a time of agitation, anger considers whatever it has done to be just.

## CHAPTER 30. That Laymen Should Compel the Priests Who Hold Their Churches to Do Nothing Other Than the Divine Office

[Col. 0903A]

(From the sayings of Augustine.) I admonish you, beloved, to fear God and honor priests, giving them the reverence due to holiness, so that, with your assistance, they may be able, undisturbed and secure, to proclaim what brings salvation and preserve ecclesiastical rule and vigor, and so that all clerics may be subject to their bishops and be taught by them.

For the Lord has commanded: “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.” I give you the apostolic command that no layman should hold a cleric in his own service; rather, the cleric should serve in mind and heart the one whose seal he bears upon his head, being instructed in the things commanded by his own bishop.

For it is a detestable and unjust deed for a cleric to be found at games, or to spend his life with hawks or in hunting, and, wounded by so many theatrical occupations, to approach the episcopate, priesthood, or any priestly office—not filled with good qualities but with evil vices. For it is written: “You who love the Lord, hate evil.”

We also exhort your Christian community that, in accordance with the institutions of the holy canons, no priest coming from elsewhere should be received into churches founded by you unless he has been consecrated by the bishop of your church or is received by him through a letter of recommendation. For many, lying to themselves and repeatedly taking flight as servants of someone, announce themselves to their masters as if they were consecrated priests, although they are not. They are ministers of the devil, not of God, and so are those who receive them, for it is written: “You saw a thief, and you ran with him,” and so forth. [Col. 0903C]

## CHAPTER 31. That Jews Should Not Be Placed over Christians

(From the Council of Meaux, chapter 3.) Jews should not dare, in an administrative capacity as stewards and agents, to govern a Christian household, nor should anyone command this to be done by them. If anyone presumes to act against this provision, then, if he is a bishop, priest, or deacon, he shall be removed from his own rank; if he is a monk, he shall be deprived of communion. The same shall apply to a layman. If they persist in disobedience, they shall be anathematized.

## CHAPTER 32. That the Holy Church Has One Father in Heaven

[Col. 0903D] (From the Council of Chalon, chapter 51.) Since it is evident that people of different conditions exist in the Church—nobles and commoners, slaves, tenant farmers, resident dependents, and other such classes—it is necessary that all who are placed over them, whether clerics or laymen, act toward them mercifully and treat them compassionately, whether in exacting labor from them, receiving taxes, or collecting certain debts. They should know that these people are their brothers and have one Father, God, to whom they cry: “Our Father, who art in heaven”; and one holy mother, the Church, which gives them birth from the undefiled womb of the sacred font.

Therefore, the most merciful discipline and appropriate governance must be applied to them. The following sentence is corrupt in the supplied text: “Disciplinae in disciplina te vivendo, auctorem suum offendunt” (“the disciplinae, by living in disciplina, offend their maker”). Governances, deprived of their superiors’ assistance in the daily provisions of life, languish. [Col. 0904A]

## CHAPTER 33. On One Who Suffers Tribulations for the Catholic Faith

(From the Council of Carthage, chapter 43.) A catholic Christian who suffers tribulations for the catholic faith, for ecclesiastical matters, and for the Christian religion is to be honored by priests with every honor; food and support are also to be provided for him through a deacon.

## CHAPTER 34. On Heirs Who Do Not Fulfill the Testator’s Instructions, Which the Bishop Is to Fulfill

(From the Council of Mainz, chapter 1.) If heirs do not fulfill the testator’s instructions, all property left to them shall be canonically placed under interdict by the bishop of that place, together with its fruits and other profits, so that the wishes of the deceased may be fulfilled. [Col. 0904B]

## CHAPTER 35. That Laymen, However Religious, Should Not Administer Ecclesiastical Affairs

(From the same source, chapter 5.) Laymen, however religious, shall never be granted the authority to administer anything concerning ecclesiastical resources.

## CHAPTER 36. On Those Who Ask Kings for Church Property

(From the Council of Lyon, chapter 11.) Those who ask kings for Church property and, driven by appalling greed, seize the substance of the needy shall have whatever they obtain declared invalid and shall be excluded from the communion of the Church whose resources they desire to take away.

## CHAPTER 37. What Is to Be Done If the Bishop Has Appointed an Ecclesiastical Court and the Count a Secular Court on the Same Day
[Col. 0904C] (From the Council of Tribur, attended by King Arnulf, chapter 9.) When a bishop, governing the Church entrusted to him by the Lord God, has gone throughout his diocese on visitation, decreed that a canonical assembly be held, and invited the people entrusted to him to attend it, and when the count, knowing that the bishop has summoned an assembly for that same day—or not knowing it—has summoned an assembly with his own people and ordered them by public ban to come there, everyone shall postpone the count’s assembly, and the count himself and the same people shall hasten after the bishop, knowing that they are not there to contend in seditious strife, but to watch over the Catholic faith—not to gather heaps of money, but to gather the gain of souls.

Hence, in the same letter of blessed Clement: “It is your task, who perform the Lord’s embassy, to teach the peoples; theirs, however, is to obey you in God.” And in the letter of Pope Alexander, the successor of Evaristus: “If anyone hinders your embassy, he turns aside the advancement not of one person but of many. And just as he harms many, so he must be reproved by many; and because he hinders God’s cause and disturbs the order of the Church, let him therefore be excluded from its thresholds.” Accordingly, let no count, no judge, and no one at all, whether established in clerical or secular rank, hinder the embassy of bishops or presume to disturb it.

For the sake of unanimity and concord between bishops and counts, it was further resolved that if a bishop, remaining at home, wishes to hold an assembly of the people, and the count nevertheless summons an assembly on that very same day, the one who announced it first shall prevail. The dignity and authority of the bishop are nevertheless preserved.

CAP. 38.—On kings who rule well

(From the sayings of Saint Isidore.) Whoever rules well in temporal affairs within this world reigns forever without end and passes from the glory of this world to eternal glory. But kings who exercise their rule wickedly descend, after their gleaming garments and the brightness of their jewels, naked and miserable, to be tormented in hell. Kings are so called from acting rightly; therefore, by doing right, the name of king is retained, and by sinning it is lost.

Holy men, too, are called kings in the sacred writings because they act rightly, govern their own thoughts well, and regulate by rational discernment the impulses that resist them. Accordingly, those are rightly called kings who know how to govern and moderate both themselves and their subjects well.

Some turn the very name of rule toward the monstrousness of cruelty. When they have reached the summit of power, they immediately fall into apostasy, and raise themselves with such swelling pride of mind that they despise all their subjects in comparison with themselves and do not recognize those whom they have been permitted to govern. To such men Ecclesiastes appropriately says: “I have appointed you ruler; do not exalt yourself.”

When the kings of the world regard themselves as higher than others, let them nevertheless recognize that they are mortal. Let those who are exalted in this world not gaze upon the glory of their kingdom, but attend to the work they will carry with them to hell. If, then, they will lose the glory of this present time, let them do those things which, after the end, they will possess without end.

While the Apostle says, “There is no authority except from God,” how is it that the prophet says of certain authorities: “They have reigned, but not from me”? It is as though he said: “Not with me favorably, but with me angered.” Hence, farther on, through the same prophet, he says: “I will give you a king in my fury.”

From this it is more clearly evident that both good and evil authority are ordained by God—good authority when he is favorable, evil authority when he is angry. When kings are good, they are a gift of God; when they are evil, they are the result of the people’s crime. For the life of rulers is arranged according to the merit of the peoples, as Job testifies: “He makes a hypocrite reign because of the sins of the people.” For when God is angry, peoples receive such a ruler as they deserve for their sin.

Sometimes kings are changed because of the wickedness of the people, and those who previously seemed good become wicked after receiving the kingdom.

CAP. 39.—On the same matter

(From the sayings of the same author.) Whoever uses the power of kingship rightly ought to conduct himself toward everyone in such a way that, the more he shines in the loftiness of honor, the more he humbles his own mind, setting before himself the example of David’s humility. David did not become swollen with pride over his merits; rather, humbly abasing himself, he said: “I shall walk in humility and appear lowly before God, who chose me.”

Whoever uses the power of kingship rightly shall establish the pattern of justice more by deeds than by words. Such a man is lifted up by no prosperity and disturbed by no adversity. He does not rely on his own strength, nor will his heart depart from the Lord. He presides over the height of kingship with a humble spirit. Iniquity does not delight him, nor does greed inflame him. Without defrauding anyone, he makes a poor person rich, and what he could have extorted from the peoples by virtue of his power he often grants through the mercy of compassion.

God gave rulers authority for governing peoples, and he wished them to rule over those with whom they share the same condition of being born and dying. Therefore, authority ought to benefit peoples, not harm them; it ought not to oppress them by domination, but to assist them through condescension. In this way the distinction of power truly becomes useful, and they use God’s gift for the protection of Christ’s members.

The faithful peoples are Christ’s members. When rulers govern them excellently by the power they have received, they certainly render a good return to God, the giver. A good king returns more readily from wrongdoing to justice than he turns from justice to wrongdoing, so that you may know that the one is a lapse and the other a settled purpose. It ought to be his settled purpose never to depart from the truth; and if he should happen to stumble through a lapse, he must rise again immediately.

CAP. 40.—On the patience of kings

(From the sayings of the same author.) A just ruler often knows how to overlook even the errors of wicked men—not because he consents to their iniquity, but because he awaits a suitable time for correction, when he may either amend or punish their vices.

Many are exposed as guilty of conspiracy against rulers. But God, wishing to test the rulers’ clemency, permits those men to harbor evil thoughts, while he does not abandon the rulers. From the wickedness of the former he brings good to the latter, when the rulers pardon with extraordinary patience the faults committed by those men.

To repay evil with evil is an exchange of justice. But whoever adds clemency to justice does not repay the guilty with evil for evil; rather, he bestows good upon those who have caused offense.

CAP. 41.—On the offenses of kings, or examples concerning them

(From the sayings of the same author.) It is difficult for a ruler to return to what is better if he has become entangled in vices. Sinning peoples fear a judge. Kings, however, unless they are restrained solely by fear of God and dread of Gehenna, rush freely headlong and, through the precipice of license, fall into every crime of vice.

The higher a person’s position, the greater the danger in which he lives; and the higher he stands in the honor of splendor, the greater his sin if he transgresses. For “the powerful will suffer powerful torments.” To the one entrusted with more, more is required of him, including a corresponding measure of punishments.

Kings easily build up or overthrow the lives of their subjects by their own examples. Therefore a ruler ought not to transgress, lest the unpunished license of his sin become a pattern of sinning. For a king who falls into vices quickly shows the way to error. Thus we read of Jeroboam, who sinned and caused Israel to sin.

Whatever his subjects perpetrate by his example is attributed to him. Just as some follow the deeds pleasing to God of good rulers, so many readily imitate their wicked examples. Many, however, exist as wicked under wicked rulers more from necessity than from choice, while obeying their commands.

Some are as ready to follow kings into evil as they are sluggish to imitate them in good. Often good rulers are justified precisely where wicked kings sin, when they correct the greed and wickedness of their predecessors. For they truly share in their predecessors’ sins if they retain what those predecessors seized.

Whoever follows another’s sin must necessarily follow that person’s punishment. The punishment of one whose error and vice someone shares will not be unequal.

CAP. 42.—That kings are bound by the laws

(From the sayings of the same author.) It is just that a ruler obey his own laws. He should then consider his laws worthy of being observed by everyone when he himself shows them reverence. Rulers are bound by their own laws, lest they suppose that they may condemn in themselves the rights which they establish for their subjects.

Their authority has a just voice if they do not permit themselves to do what they forbid to the peoples. The powers of this world are subject to the discipline of religion. Although they possess the summit of kingship, they are nevertheless bound by the bond of faith, so that they proclaim Christ’s faith through their laws and preserve that proclamation of faith through good morals.

CAP. 43.—On the discipline of kings in the Church

(From the sayings of the same author.) The rulers of this world sometimes hold within the Church the heights of authority they have acquired, so that through that same authority they may protect ecclesiastical discipline. Otherwise, powers would not be necessary within the Church except so that what a priest cannot accomplish by the word of teaching, authority may command through the terror of discipline.

Often the heavenly kingdom advances through the earthly kingdom, so that those placed within the Church who act against the faith and discipline of the Church may be crushed by the severity of rulers. The ruling power may impose upon the necks of the proud the very discipline which the Church’s usefulness is unable to enforce, and may grant them the strength of authority by which they may deserve to render a good account.

Let the rulers of this world recognize that they must render an account to God for the Church which they have received from Christ to protect. Whether the peace and discipline of the Church are increased through faithful rulers or dissolved, he will demand an account from them who entrusted his Church to their authority.

CAP. 44.—Why God distinguished some for freedom and others for servitude

(Also from the same author.) Because of the sin of the first man, a divinely imposed punishment was inflicted upon the human race in the form of servitude, so that to those whom he sees not suitably fitted for freedom he mercifully assigns servitude. Although this distinction arose through the sin of human origin, God nevertheless, being just, distinguished human lives by making some slaves and others masters, so that the license of slaves to do evil might be restrained by the power of their rulers.

For if all had been without fear, who would have restrained anyone from evil? For this reason rulers and kings were also chosen among the nations, so that by their terror they might restrain peoples from evil and subject them by laws to right living.

As regards the rationale of punishment, there is no partiality with God. He chose the lowly and despised things of the world, and things that are not, to destroy the things that are, so that no flesh—that is, no carnal power—might glory before him.

For there is one Lord, who gives equal counsel to masters and slaves. Subjection in servitude is better than exalted freedom. Many are found freely serving God while placed under wicked masters: they are subject to them in body, yet superior to them in mind.

[Col. 0907] END OF THE FIFTEENTH BOOK.

That no one should readily accept the accusation of a person who readily litigates and accuses. 33. That a bishop should excommunicate accusers of their brothers. 34. On those convicted of bringing false charges against their brothers. [Col. 0910A] 35. On those witnesses who attempt to accuse someone from the sacred order, and that the best and most faithful persons should be chosen as witnesses. 36. That no secular person should presume to use force against anyone from the clergy. 37. That husbands may accuse their wives on suspicion.

End of the table of chapters.

BURCHARD, BISHOP OF THE CHURCH OF WORMS, DECRETALS, BOOK SIXTEEN: ON ACCUSERS AND WITNESSES

[Col. 0909]

SUMMARY OF THE BOOK

[Col. 0909B]

This book teaches what sort of persons judges, accusers, and witnesses ought to be, and what penance is to be imposed upon judges who judge for favor, upon slanderers, and upon false witnesses.

CAP. 1.—On the rulers of Churches, that they should not be hasty in pronouncing judgments

(From the sayings of Pope Gregory.) The rulers of Churches and those who exercise public judgments must take the greatest care that, in pronouncing judgments, they are in no way hasty, driven by levity or fury. Rather, after the cases have first been carefully examined, when the matter that was unknown has been fully brought to light, let divine and human law then be applied, and, with all partiality toward persons removed, let a definitive judgment be pronounced according to what has been established there.

For this reason Moses always reported the people’s complaints to the Lord after entering the tabernacle, and proposed judgments according to what the Lord commanded. In this way he clearly instructed us to pronounce a sentence of condemnation or justification not from our own heart, but from divine command.

CAP. 2.—That counts and judges should not accept gifts in judgment

(From the Council of Chalon, chapter 21.) Counts and judges must take the greatest care to judge justly and never accept gifts or persons in judgment, as the Lord says: “You shall not accept a person or gifts, because gifts blind the eyes of the wise and alter the words of the just.”

They ought also to have just ministers, whom they call deputies and centurions, lest the people be burdened by their greed or rapacity and, losing their possessions, be reduced to poverty.

The witnesses, however, should be thoroughly approved and few in number. Among the many, such persons should be selected whose good faith cannot be doubted. The commonwealth is greatly harmed by the greed and falsehood of wicked witnesses.

CAP. 3.—On those who bring an accusation but do not prove it true

(From the Council of Orange, chapter 4.) Whoever brings an accusation should know that he must truly prove it, so that the case may be ended where the crime is alleged to have occurred; and whoever has not proved what he alleged must himself suffer the punishment he sought to inflict.

CAP. 4.—What sort of persons should come forward as witnesses

(From the Council held at Theodone’s Villa, chapter 3.) Homicides, evildoers, thieves, sacrilegious persons, robbers, poisoners, adulterers, those who have committed abduction, those who have given false testimony, and those who have resorted to diviners and magicians are in no way to be admitted either for accusation or for testimony.

CAP. 5.—That an innocent person should not be stained by the harm caused by accusers

(From the decree of Pope Felix, chapter 15.) It is right that the life of an innocent person should not be stained by the harm caused by accusers, to such an extent that whoever is accused by anyone should not be assigned to punishment before the accuser is presented and the judgment of the canons has been sought. If the person is found unworthy to accuse, judgment should not be rendered upon his accusation.

CAP. 6.—That no one should be designated guilty before he is convicted

(From the decree of Pope Hadrian, chapter 2.) A judge examining a criminal case should not pronounce a final sentence before either the accused himself confesses or he is convicted by suitable witnesses.

CAP. 7.—That priests ought to accuse their parishioners in synod

(From the Council of Mainz, chapter 6.) It has been decreed in holy council that priests may both accuse and testify against the people of their parishes. If they neglect this duty, they will be subject to the peril of their rank.

CAP. 8.—On those convicted of inducing someone to give false testimony

(From the Council of Aachen, chapter 9.) If anyone is convicted of inducing someone to give false testimony or commit perjury, or of soliciting someone through any kind of corruption, he himself shall not receive communion until the end of his life.

CAP. 9.—That a concluded case should not be reopened

[Col. 0911A]

(From the Council of Mainz, chapter 7.) An accusation cannot be reopened concerning crimes for which the accused has been acquitted.

CAP. 10.—On those who have not been summoned before their own judges

(From the decree of Pope Eusebius, chapter 20.) Let the person against whom proceedings have been brought state his case before his own judge; if proceedings have not been brought against him before his own judge, let him remain silent if he wishes. Whenever the defendant appeals, let a delay be granted.

CAP. 11.—That no infamous person may accuse a religious Christian

(From the decree of Pope Felix, chapter 7.) No infamous or sacrilegious person may ever, in any matter whatever, give testimony against a religious Christian, even if that person is humble and servile; nor may he bring a Christian to trial concerning any matter, action, or formal accusation.

CAP. 12.—On the false witness, who should not depart unpunished

(From the sayings of Augustine.) “A false witness,” Solomon says, “will not go unpunished.” Whoever gives false testimony against his neighbor, his lamp will be extinguished on the last day.

Whoever conceals the truth through fear of any power provokes God’s anger against himself, because he fears a human being more than God. A lying witness is liable to three persons: first to God, whose presence he despises; then to the judge, whom he deceives by lying; finally to the innocent person whom he harms by false testimony.

If false witnesses are separated from one another, they are quickly found to be liars. Both are guilty: the one who conceals the truth and the one who tells a lie, because the former does not wish to help, while the latter desires to harm. Blessed is the person whose testimony is found acceptable in God’s sight.

CAP. 13.—That no one should be judged in his absence

(From a letter of Pope Zephyrinus sent to the bishops of Sicily.) No one should be judged in his absence, because human and divine laws forbid this. For no one of them—that is, of the accusers—should be bound by a sentence not pronounced by his own judge, because the laws of the world also command this.

CAP. 14.—On the same matter

(From the decree of Pope Hadrian, chapter 4.) Let the judges of the Church beware of pronouncing judgment while the person whose case is being examined is absent, because the judgment will be invalid; indeed, they will incur guilt for the matter before the synod.

CAP. 15.—That no one should at the same time be accuser, judge, and witness

(From a letter of Pope Alexander, chapter 7.) No one should at the same time be accuser, witness, and judge. No one should ever presume to be simultaneously accuser, judge, and witness, because in every place of judgment four persons must always be present: namely, the appointed judges, the accusers, the defenders, and the witnesses.

CAP. 16.—That false testimony is a capital crime

(From the Council of Agde, chapter 8.) Let false witnesses know that if false testimony were not a capital crime, the Lord would never have counted it among the principal crimes in the Gospel. For he says: “From the heart proceed murders, adulteries, thefts, false testimonies.”

Therefore a false witness must repent and be excommunicated in the same way as an adulterer, a thief, and a homicide.

CAP. 17.—That false witnesses are to be removed from communion unless they repent

(From the Council of Orléans, chapter 5.) False witnesses are to be removed from ecclesiastical communion unless they cleanse away the crimes they have committed by the satisfaction of repentance.

CAP. 18.—That a false witness should be punished according to the crime he alleged

(From the Council of Elvira, chapter 10.) A false witness shall be excluded according to the nature of the crime he alleged. If what he alleged was not a capital offense, and if he has proved what he had long concealed, he shall be excluded for two years. But if he has not proved it before the assembly of clerics, it has been decided that he shall be excluded for five years.

CAP. 19.—On free men if they are accused in synod

(From the Council of Tribur, chapter 10.) If a nobleman or free man is accused in synod and denies the charge, and if they know him to be faithful, let him clear himself with twelve free men. But if he has previously been caught in theft, perjury, or false testimony, he shall not be admitted to the oath; rather, like one who is not free, he shall clear himself by boiling water or red-hot iron.

CAP. 20.—That witnesses whom the accuser has brought from his own household should not be admitted to testify

(From the same council, chapter 5.) Witnesses are not to be admitted to testify if they have been barred from being admitted for accusation, or if the accuser himself has brought them from his own household. No one under fourteen years of age is to be admitted as a witness.

CAP. 21.—That no cleric should presume to accuse another cleric before a secular judge

(From the Council of Meaux, chapter 8.) No cleric should presume in any way to accuse another cleric before a secular judge or drag him into court to answer a case. Rather, every clerical matter should be concluded either before the bishop of the cleric concerned or before priests in the presence of the archdeacon.

If any cleric delays fulfilling this requirement, then, if he is junior, he shall receive one blow fewer than forty. If he is of higher rank, he shall be punished by thirty days of confinement.

CAP. 22.—That no secular judge should presume to coerce any member of the clergy

(From the Council of Paris, chapter 10.) No judge shall, without the knowledge of the bishop, personally coerce or presume to condemn any priest, deacon, cleric, or junior member of the Church. If he does so, he shall be separated from the Church to which he is known to have inflicted an injury, until he acknowledges and amends his guilt.

CAP. 23.—That all cases should be examined by the authority of truth

(From the sayings of Augustine in the book *The City of God*.) All cases must first be examined by the authority of truth: who the persons are, whose they are, how they are, and what sort they are; whether educated or uneducated, small or great, known or unknown; whether they have been discovered through the custom of a long time or a short time, or through the practice of an ancient enemy. The judge must discern all these matters with impartiality.

CAP. 24.—On clerics convicted of false testimony

[Col. 0913A]

(From the Council of Epaon, chapter 76.) It has been decreed that if a cleric is convicted of false testimony, he shall be considered guilty of a capital crime and degraded from the order of his office.

CAP. 25.—On judges

(From the sayings of Saint Isidore.) It is a fault of rulers when, against God’s will, they place wicked judges over faithful peoples. For just as it is the people’s fault when their rulers are evil, so it is the ruler’s fault when the judges are unjust.

A good judge knows how neither to harm citizens nor to fail to benefit everyone. To some he offers the correction of justice, to others kindness. He who undertakes judgments without partiality toward persons does not weaken justice through the flame of greed, nor does he seek to take from another what he would wish for himself.

Good judges undertake justice solely to attain eternal salvation; they do not distribute it in exchange for gifts received. By not seeking temporal advantages from just judgment, they are enriched with an eternal reward.

Everyone who judges justly carries a balance in his hand, bearing justice and mercy in its two pans. Through justice he delivers the sentence for sin; through mercy he tempers the punishment of sin. By this balance he corrects some matters according to equity and pardons others through compassion.

Because he sets God’s judgments before his own eyes, he always acts with fear and trembling in every matter, lest he stray from the path of justice and fall, and lest he be condemned precisely where he is not justified.

CAP. 26.—On wicked judges

[Col. 0913C]

(From the sayings of the same author.) No foolish or wicked person ought to be a judge. The fool, through sloth, does not know justice; the wicked person, through greed, corrupts the very truth he proclaims.

The poor are torn apart more grievously by wicked judges than by the bloodiest enemies. No plunderer is so greedy for another’s property as an unjust judge is for his own.

Robbers lie in ambush at hidden and secluded approaches; these men openly rage through the greed of rapacity. Enemies aim only at the blood of others; judges, like the most cruel executioners of citizens, extinguish the lives of their subjects through oppression.

There are many who destroy; there are few who govern peoples by the restraint of laws. Often judges are good, but they have rapacious ministers. Their likeness, as someone says, is painted and described as that of a *scylla*: human in appearance, but fitted about and surrounded by doglike heads.

The same thing happens to certain authorities: their humanity is disturbed by the inhumanity of wicked associates. Wicked judges often, for the sake of greed, delay or pervert judgments. They do not conclude the cases begun by the parties until they have emptied the purses of those who are litigating.

When they judge, they do not desire cases but gifts. Just as they are negligent in examining the cases of litigants, so they are diligent in pursuing their financial ruin.

Wicked judges, in the words of the Prophet, are like evening wolves: they leave nothing for the morning. That is, they think only about the advantages of the present life, not about the future. This life is understood as evening, while the future is understood as morning. He rightly says “like wolves,” because in the manner of wolves they seize everything and scarcely leave anything for the poor.

CAP. 27.—On verbose and haughty judges

(From the book *The Offices* by Saint Isidore.) Verbose and haughty judges, wishing to appear wise, do not examine cases but assert their own views. Thus they disturb the order of judgment, since, not content with their own office, they presume upon another’s.

Some, when they begin to judge, become angry and turn the very sentence of judgment into madness. Of such men the prophet rightly says: “They turn judgment into fury.” Whoever judges in anger changes judgment into fury and pronounces sentence before understanding the case.

Fury in a judge cannot reach an investigation of the truth, because his mind, disturbed by fury, is alienated from examining justice. An angry judge cannot fully observe the examination of a judgment, because the darkness of fury prevents him from seeing.

But whoever examines a case after putting away fury rises more easily, through serenity of mind, to contemplate the truth, and without any disturbance reaches an understanding of equity.

CAP. 28.—On the reward of remuneration

(From the same author.) Whoever judges rightly while expecting a reward of remuneration commits fraud against God, because he sells for money the justice he ought to distribute freely.

Such people misuse good things, because they judge justly for the sake of temporal profit. They are moved toward the truth not by the defense of justice but by love of reward. If the hope of money is taken away from them, they immediately withdraw from confessing justice.

The acceptance of money is a betrayal of truth. Hence it is said of the just man: “He who shakes his hands free from every gift shall dwell on high.”

A rich man quickly corrupts a judge with gifts. But a poor man, having nothing to offer, is not only contemptuously refused a hearing but is also oppressed against the truth. Justice is quickly violated by gold, and the accused fears no guilt which he thinks he can redeem with money. The love of profit gains more influence over the censor’s mind than the equity of judgment.

There are three kinds of acceptance of gifts by which human vanity wages war against justice: the favor of friendship, flattery of praise, and the physical acceptance of a gift. The mind is more easily perverted by a material gift than by the favor of gratitude and praise.

Human judgment is turned aside in four ways: by fear, greed, hatred, and love. By fear, when through dread of someone’s power we are afraid to speak the truth; by greed, when we are corrupted by the reward of some gift; by hatred, when we strive against an adversary and are corrupted by hatred of him; and by love, when we seek to favor a friend or relative. For these four reasons equity is often violated.

CAP. 29.—On oppressors of the poor

(From the same author.) Oppressors of the poor will then be judged worthy of a more severe sentence when they have prevailed against those whom they sought to harm more cruelly. They will be condemned to future punishment in proportion to the strength with which they prevailed here against the lives of the wretched.

Let judges and those who govern peoples hear that, because of the temporal troubles they inflict upon the common people, they will be burned in eternal fire, as the Lord testifies through the prophet Isaiah: “I was angry with my people,” he says, “and I gave them into your hand. You showed them no mercy; you made your yoke exceedingly heavy. Descend, sit in the dust, keep silent, and enter into darkness. Evil will come upon you and you will perish; misery that you do not know will suddenly fall upon you.”

We ought to grieve more for those who do evil than for those who suffer evil. The former advance toward evil by doing wrong; the latter are corrected from evil by suffering it.

Through the evil wills of some, God accomplishes many good things in others. The will of wicked people can in no way be fulfilled unless God grants them the power. For when, by God’s permission, people accomplish the evil they desire, he is said to do it who permits it.

Hence it is written through the prophet: “If there is evil, has the Lord not done it?” Nevertheless, because the wicked desire evil by their own will, God, through his good will, grants them the power to accomplish it, since from our evil he himself accomplishes many good things.

Some resist God’s will and, without knowing it, carry out God’s purpose. They should know that all things are so subject to God that even those who think they are resisting his ordering fulfill his will.

For this reason, in this life the good are judged by the wicked, so that in the other life the wicked may be judged by the good. It may also be that the good have temporal affliction here and eternal reward there.

The wicked are therefore necessary, so that whenever the good offend, they may be chastised by them. Hence the Lord testifies that Assyria is “the rod of my fury.” But whenever this occurs, it proceeds from God’s indignation, so that through them God may rage against those whom he desires to correct by chastising them.

God acts with a most just will; they, however, often act with a cruel intention. Thus the prophet says concerning that same Assyria: “But he does not intend this; his heart is set on destroying”—that is, a harsh divine fury is to come upon those who persecute and use violence against the faithful.

God promises his people, for their consolation, that he will judge in this way: “Against those who judged you, I will judge; I will feed your enemies with their own flesh, and they shall become drunk, as it were, with their own blood mingled together.”

The wickedness of the evil has a certain usefulness: it tears apart God’s beloved by its conduct, and thus the life of the impious is wasted on itself, while the life of the just, though also afflicted, makes progress. The wicked, through the exercise of tribulation, teach the just to hate the present life and desire the future one.

Sometimes the perversity of the wicked benefits the good, when their malice instructs them and temporal hardship drives them to seek the kingdoms of heaven.

This is demonstrated by the example of the Israelite people. They were treated more harshly in Egypt precisely when the time had come for Moses to call them to the promised land, so that they might depart from the evils they suffered in Egypt and hasten toward the promised homeland.

When the wicked see the steadfastness of the just amid their persecutions, they waste away in confusion of mind. When they display adversity but do not conquer, they are finally confounded by the madness of their own perversity.

Fools are always zealous against the good. When prosperity shines upon them, they boast arrogantly of their own merits and disparage the afflictions of the good and just. When adversity befalls them, they immediately turn through weakness of spirit to blasphemy.

Some simple-minded people, not knowing God’s dispensation, are scandalized by the advancement of the wicked and say, in the words of the Prophet: “Why does the way of the wicked prosper? All is well with those who transgress and act wickedly.”

Those who say this should not wonder when they see the temporal and fleeting happiness of wicked people; rather, they should consider their final destiny and how great eternal punishments await them afterward, as the prophet says: “They spend their days in prosperity, and suddenly they descend to hell.”

CAP. 30.—That a judge should not forestall litigants with his judgment so long as they still have something to present concerning the case

[Col. 0916B]

(From the decrees of Pope Eleutherius to the churches established throughout Gaul, chapter 3.) A judge should not prematurely forestall litigants with his decision, unless, after everything has been completed, they have nothing further to propose in the case. The action should be examined until the truth of the matter is discovered. It is necessary to question them frequently, lest something be inadvertently omitted that ought to be added. Time for investigation must be granted in no small measure, lest anything seem to be hurriedly undertaken by either party, since many things arise through fraud. Nevertheless, nothing should be done without a legitimate and suitable accuser. For our Lord Jesus Christ knew that Judas was a thief [Col. 0916C]; but because he was not accused, he was not expelled, and whatever he did among the apostles remained valid by reason of the dignity of his ministry. For if the laws of the world require accusers, how much more do ecclesiastical regulations? They teach, after all, what earthly and human things are, and what ecclesiastical and heavenly things are.

### CHAPTER 31.—That the accusers, judges, witnesses, and accused must not be the same persons.

(From the sayings of Pope Damasus, chapter 19.) Accusers and judges must not be the same persons; rather, accusers by themselves, judges by themselves, witnesses by themselves, and the accused by themselves, each in his own properly ordered role. For a formal written accusation must always be made first, so that the false accuser may receive the punishment of retaliation. For before the written accusation no one ought to be judged [Col. 0916D] or condemned, since even the laws of the world preserve this same principle. In all these matters true equality must always be maintained, so that they may receive, according to the truth of what was done, the due reward or penalty of accusation, judgment, and testimony.

### CHAPTER 32.—That no one should readily accept the accusation of one who readily litigates and accuses.

(From the Council of Worms, chapter 2.) No one should accept the accusation of a person who frequently litigates and is ready to accuse without careful and thorough examination.

### CHAPTER 33.—That a bishop should excommunicate accusers of their brothers.

(From the Council of Orléans, chapter 1.) A bishop should excommunicate those who accuse their brothers; and if they correct their fault, he should restore them to communion, but not to the clergy.

### CHAPTER 34.—Concerning those who have been convicted of bringing false charges against their brothers.

[Col. 0917A]

(From the Council of Agde, chapter 6.) It was decreed that those who have been convicted of bringing capital charges against their brothers should not receive communion until death, unless they repent with worthy satisfaction.

### CHAPTER 35.—Concerning witnesses who attempt to accuse someone from the sacred order, and that the best and most trustworthy persons should be chosen as witnesses.

(From the Council of Mâcon, chapter 5.) It pleased the holy assembly that witnesses should not be hired for money to give testimony, and that the best and most trustworthy persons should be chosen as witnesses, so that the person against whom they are required to testify might not be able to bring any disgrace upon them, and that no one should give testimony unless fasting.

### CHAPTER 36.—That no layman should presume to use force against anyone of the clergy.

[Col. 0918A]

(From the council held at Theodonsville, chapter 10.) Whoever, whether a judge or a layman, presumes to inflict an injury upon a presbyter, deacon, anyone else of the clergy, or one of the junior clergy, without a hearing before the bishop, archdeacon, or archpresbyter, is to be regarded as anathema.

### CHAPTER 37.—That husbands may accuse their wives on suspicion.

(From the Council of Paris, chapter 3.) Husbands are permitted to accuse their wives even on suspicion, and they, more than others, may both accuse and defend in cases of adultery.

[Col. 0917] END OF THE SIXTEENTH BOOK.

[BOOK SEVENTEEN.]
