# BURCHARD, BISHOP OF THE CHURCH OF WORMS, BOOK SEVENTEEN OF THE DECREES: ON FORNICATION

[Col. 0919]

## SUMMARY OF THE BOOK

[Col. 0919B]

This book encompasses various kinds of fornication and incest, and teaches what correction and penance are owed to those entangled in these vices.

### CHAPTER 1.—Concerning a woman who fornicated with two brothers.

(From the Council of Neocaesarea, chapter 2.) If a woman marries two brothers, she is to be excluded until death. Nevertheless, at the time of death, out of mercy, if she promises that, once restored to health, she will dissolve the bonds of this union, she may obtain the fruit of repentance and be granted communion. But if the man or woman dies while involved in such a marriage, the penance during the life that remains will be difficult [Col. 0919C].

### CHAPTER 2.—Concerning the same matter.

(From the decree of Pope Martin, chapter 9.) If any woman has married two brothers, or if any man has taken two wives, they are to be separated from communion until death. At death, they may receive the viaticum as an act of mercy.

### CHAPTER 3.—Concerning the man who fornicated with two sisters, one of whom had been his wife.

(From the Council of Orléans, chapter 6.) Whoever has slept with two sisters, one of whom was previously his wife, must have neither of them; nor may those adulterers ever be joined in marriage.

### CHAPTER 4.—Concerning the man who, unknowingly, fornicated with his wife’s sister.

(From the Council of Tribur, chapter 8.) While the wife was absent [Col. 0919D], her sister went into the husband’s bed. Thinking that she was his wife, he slept with her. Concerning this, it was determined that, if he truly proves with certainty that he committed this crime unknowingly, he should perform the penance assigned to him, and he may be permitted to retain his lawful marriage [Col. 0920B]. The woman is to be afflicted with worthy punishment and deprived of marriage forever.

### CHAPTER 5.—Concerning the same matter.

(From the same council, chapter 9.) If anyone has fornicated with two sisters, and one sister did not know that the other had previously been violated by the same man—or if he himself did not recognize that she was the sister of the woman whom he had previously violated—then, if they repent worthily and are unable to remain continent, marriage is not to be denied them after seven years. But if they knew, they must abstain from marriage until death.

### CHAPTER 6.—Concerning the same matter.

(From the same council, chapter 10.) If a man has fornicated with two sisters, the man must do penance for the days of his life [Col. 0920C]. But the sister who did not know about the other sister may have permission to marry.

### CHAPTER 7.—Likewise, concerning the man who fornicated with two sisters, neither of whom was his wife.

(From the same council, chapter 11.) Likewise, concerning two sisters: if he remained in adultery with one and publicly took the other, he must not have a woman until the day of his death, while the one who did not know may take a husband.

### CHAPTER 8.—Concerning the man who fornicated with two sisters, with his stepmother, with his sister, with his paternal or maternal aunt, with the daughter of his paternal or maternal uncle, with the daughter of his paternal or maternal aunt, with his niece, with his spiritual co-mother, or with the spiritual daughter whom he received from the baptismal font or held before the bishop.

(From the Council of Mainz, chapter 3.) If anyone has fornicated [Col. 0920D] with two sisters, or with his stepmother, or with his sister, or with his paternal aunt, or with his maternal aunt, or with the daughter of his paternal uncle or maternal uncle, or with the daughter of his paternal or maternal aunt, with his niece, or with his spiritual co-mother [Col. 0921A], or with his spiritual daughter, whether one whom he received from the font or held before the bishop—and if any woman has fornicated in a similar manner—he must abstain from entering the house of God for one year, and during that year use only bread, water, and salt, except on Sundays and feast days. He must carry no weapons, give no kiss, and receive the sacrifice only as viaticum.

For the following six years he may indeed enter the house of God, but he must not use meat, wine, or beer except on feast days. The regulations concerning weapons, kisses, and the sacrifice remain as written above. Thereafter, for two years, whenever he eats meat, he must abstain from every drink by which he could become drunk. If he drinks such a beverage, he must not eat meat, except on the principal feast days. Concerning weapons, the kiss, and the sacrifice, he must observe the rule already stated [Col. 0921B].

From then until his death, unless it is one of the aforementioned feast days, he must abstain from meat; he must properly observe three appointed fast days each week and three Lents each year. Concerning weapons, the rule is as stated above, and he must never be joined in marriage.

The same penance is to be imposed on those guilty of parricide, fratricide, or the killing of a blood relative, and also on those who voluntarily kill an innocent person through deceit and greed, an act they call *morchidum*.

### CHAPTER 9.—Concerning the man who, having taken a mother as his wife, fornicated with his stepdaughter.

(From the same council, chapter 2.) If anyone has married a widow and afterward fornicated with his stepdaughter, or has slept with two sisters, or if any woman [Col. 0921C] has married two brothers, or has fornicated with a father and son, we order that such unions be anathematized and dissolved, and that the persons never again be joined in marriage, but they must be subjected to severe discipline.

### CHAPTER 10.—Concerning the same matter.

(From the Council held at Verberie, chapter 10.) If anyone has fornicated with his stepdaughter, he may have neither the mother nor the daughter; neither she nor he may ever join themselves to others at any time. Nevertheless, his wife, if she wishes and cannot remain continent, may marry another, provided that, after learning that her husband had committed adultery with his daughter, she had no carnal relations with him.

### CHAPTER 11.—Concerning the man who fornicated with his stepmother.

[Col. 0921D]

(From the same council, chapter 21.) If anyone has slept with his stepmother, neither of them may enter into marriage. But her husband may, if he wishes and cannot remain continent, take another wife. Similarly, the man who has slept with his stepdaughter or with his wife’s sister may remain married.

### CHAPTER 12.—Concerning the man who fornicated with his stepdaughter while the mother was unaware.

(From the same council, chapter 4.) If a man has fornicated with mother and daughter, while the mother was unaware of the daughter and the daughter of the mother, he must never take a wife. But the women may take husbands if they wish. If, however, the women knew this, they must remain without husbands forever.

### CHAPTER 13.—Concerning the man who violated a woman whom his brother later took as wife.

[Col. 0922A]

(From the same council, chapter 5.) If a man has fornicated with a woman and his brother, unaware, has afterward married her, the brother must do penance because he concealed the crime from his brother, and after penance he may marry. But the woman must do penance until death and remain without hope of marriage.

### CHAPTER 14.—Concerning the same matter.

(From the same council, chapter 6.) If one brother has fornicated with a woman and the other brother, unaware, has slept with the same woman, the woman must do penance for the days of her life; but after penance, the brother who was ignorant of the crime may take a wife if he wishes.

### CHAPTER 15.—Concerning the same matter.

[Col. 0922B]

(From the Council of Mâcon, chapter 5.) It was reported that a certain man had violated a woman whom his brother afterward took as his wife. They decreed that the man who violated her and concealed from his brother that she had been violated by him should be punished with stricter penance, because he had doubled his sin. Such a marriage ought to be dissolved, and the woman must never be given permission to marry. Out of mercy, however, marriage may be granted to the others, but with penance.

### CHAPTER 16.—Concerning the woman with whom both father and son fornicated.

(From the Council of Tribur, chapter 6.) A certain man fornicated with a woman; afterward, his son, unaware of what his father had done, violated the same woman. When the father learned this [Col. 0922C], he confessed concerning himself and his son. They determined that, for those who had fallen in this way, it was better to permit lawful marriages with worthy penance than for them perhaps to commit an even worse offense. But the fornicating woman must remain without hope of marriage.

### CHAPTER 17.—Concerning the man who fornicated with his brother’s wife.

(From the same council, chapter 12.) If anyone has slept with his brother’s wife, the adulterer and the adulteress must remain without marriage for the days of their lives. But the man whose wife she was may take another wife if he wishes.

### CHAPTER 18.—Concerning the man who violated his son’s betrothed.

(From the same council, chapter 13.) If anyone has violated his son’s betrothed and afterward his son has married her, the father must thereafter have no wife [Col. 0922D], nor may the woman have a husband; the son, who was unaware of his father’s crime, may take another wife.

### CHAPTER 19.—Concerning the man who fornicated with a wife, her mother, and her stepdaughter.

(From the Council of Mainz, chapter 6.) If anyone has married a widow and afterward fornicated with her stepdaughter, or with two sisters; or if a woman has fornicated with two brothers, or with a father and son; if anyone has polluted his brother’s widow, his niece, his stepmother, his daughter-in-law, his cousin, his uncle’s daughter, his uncle’s widow, or his stepdaughter, we order that the persons be separated and never again joined in marriage.

### CHAPTER 20.—Concerning the married man who fornicated with the daughter of his maternal aunt, maternal uncle, paternal aunt, or paternal uncle.

[Col. 0923A]

(From the Council of Tribur, chapter 1.) It was asked whether, if anyone had slept with the daughter of his maternal aunt, paternal aunt, maternal uncle, or paternal uncle and was married, he might continue to use his marriage, or, if unmarried, whether he might take a wife. It would be just, according to certain statutes of our predecessors, that such persons abstain from marriage forever. But, out of consideration for human frailty, it seemed appropriate that after penance they should not be entirely deprived of marriage; nevertheless, so enormous a fornication must be punished with the greatest severity, as the holy Pope Nicholas and other Roman pontiffs decreed, lest those driven to despair sin even more abundantly.

### CHAPTER 21.—Concerning a father and son, or an uncle and nephew, if they fornicated with the same woman.

[Col. 0923B]

(From the Council of Mainz, chapter 5.) It was asked what should be done if a father and son, two brothers, or an uncle and nephew had fornicated with the same woman. It is clear that this must be punished with severe vengeance, since it is found to be a grave crime. For every act of adultery is forbidden, as it is written, “You shall not commit adultery”; how much more so when the woman is a relative, or the wife or concubine of a relative?

Hence it is written in Leviticus: “If anyone commits adultery with another man’s wife, both the adulterer and the adulteress shall surely be put to death. Whoever sleeps with his stepmother or with his daughter-in-law, and whoever takes both daughter and mother, and whoever takes [Col. 0923C] his sister, shall be put to death.” If, then, the Law ordered the disgrace of incest to be punished by a sentence of death, how will the incestuous person escape penance for sin in the Gospel, where supreme justice prevails? Hence the Apostle says: “Anyone who has violated the law of Moses dies without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses. How much worse punishment, do you think, does the one deserve who has trampled upon the Son of God, regarded as profane the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified, and insulted the Spirit of grace?”

Therefore Theodore judged that one who had committed incest ought to do penance for twelve years; others prescribed fifteen, others ten, and others seven. But, following the footsteps of the ancient fathers, we moderate the period of penance only for those who have performed penance devoutly and with tears [Col. 0923D]; the rest must observe the appointed period.

### CHAPTER 22.—Concerning the same matter.

(From the Council held at Verberie, chapter 4.) If anyone has held his stepson or stepdaughter before the bishop for confirmation, he must be separated from his wife and never take another. The same applies to a woman.

### CHAPTER 23.—Concerning those who receive their children from baptism in order to separate from their spouses.

(From the Council of Chalon, chapter 4.) It was also reported to us that certain women, through negligence, and others deceitfully, in order to separate from their husbands, had held their own sons before bishops for confirmation. We therefore deemed it right that if any woman, through negligence or by some deceit, has held her son before the bishop for confirmation in order to carry out her deception [Col. 0924A], she should do penance throughout her life, but should not be separated from her husband.

### CHAPTER 24.—Concerning the same matter.

(From the Council of Mainz, held in the monastery of Saint Alban in the presence of Emperor Louis, chapter 10.) Concerning what you asked—whether the man who takes his goddaughter as wife, the man who has intercourse with his spiritual co-mother, and the man who baptized his son, whose wife received him from the font, for the purpose of causing a marital separation, may afterward remain in such unions—the following answer is to be given.

If anyone has taken his goddaughter or spiritual co-mother in marriage, we have judged that they must be separated and punished with severe penance. But if one or both lawful spouses deliberately [Col. 0924B] arrange for their son to be received from the font in order to cause a separation, we give this counsel: if they wish to remain unmarried, that is good. But otherwise, severe penance must be imposed upon the schemer, and they should remain together; and if the transgressing spouse outlives the other, he or she must be punished with the harshest penance and remain without hope of marriage.

### CHAPTER 25.—Concerning the same matter.

(From the Council of Tribur, chapter 8.) No one should receive his own son or daughter from the baptismal font, nor take his goddaughter or spiritual co-mother as wife, nor marry the woman whose daughter he has held before the bishop for confirmation. Where this has occurred, the persons must be separated.

### CHAPTER 26.—Concerning the same matter.

(From the Council of Mainz, chapter 5.) How detestable and abominable a crime it is for any Christian to violate his goddaughter [Col. 0924C] is testified by Saint Pope Gregory in his Dialogues, where he relates that a certain man polluted his goddaughter and, because he neglected to do penance, was suddenly seized by a miserable illness and died; after he had been buried, not only his body but also the entire tomb was consumed by invisible fire.

### CHAPTER 27.—Concerning women who fornicate with one another by some device.

(From the Penitential of Theodore.) A woman who fornicates by any device, either with herself or with another woman, must do penance for three years.

### CHAPTER 28.—Concerning nuns, if they fornicate with one another.

(From the same source.) If one nun has fornicated with another nun by some device, they must do penance for seven years [Col. 0924D].

### CHAPTER 29.—Concerning a woman if she has fornicated with another woman.

(From the Council of Ancyra, chapter 8.) If a woman has fornicated with another woman, she must do penance for three years. The woman who mixes her husband’s semen into food so that she may thereby obtain more of his love must likewise do penance.

### CHAPTER 30.—Concerning those who have behaved unnaturally.

(From the Council of Ancyra, chapter 15.) Concerning those who have behaved unnaturally, or are behaving so—that is, those who have polluted themselves with animals or males—the synod decreed that all who committed such a crime before the age of twenty, after completing fifteen years of penance, may be admitted to the communion of prayers; then, after remaining in this communion for five years, they may finally receive the sacrament of the offering. Their life during the time of penance must also be examined, and they are to obtain mercy accordingly. If they have clung to these crimes insatiably, they must spend a longer period in penance.

But all who, after the age of twenty and while having wives, have fallen into this sin are to be admitted to the communion of prayer after doing penance for twenty-five years. After remaining in it for five years, they may receive the sacrament of the offering. But if, while having wives and being over fifty years of age, they have committed such an offense, they may receive the grace of communion at the end of their life [Col. 0925A].

### CHAPTER 31.—Concerning the same matter.

[Col. 0925B]

(From the same council, chapter 16.) The holy synod ordered that those who have lived unnaturally and polluted others with the leprosy of an unjust crime should pray among those possessed by an unclean spirit.

### CHAPTER 32.—Concerning those who sin with animals.

(From the Penitential of Theodore.) Concerning one who sins with an animal, some prescribe ten years, some seven, some three, and some three hundred days of penance, according to the quality of the person.

### CHAPTER 33.—Likewise, concerning those who fornicate with quadrupeds.

(From the Roman Penitential.) If people are found who sin against nature with quadrupeds or males, they must be restrained by harsh and strict penance. Therefore bishops or presbyters who impose the judgment of penance must strive by every means to cut out this evil by the roots [Col. 0925C].

### CHAPTER 34.—Concerning those who fornicate as the Sodomites do.

(From the Penitential of Theodore.) Whoever has fornicated as the Sodomites do must do penance as follows: if he is a slave and is punished with beatings, two years; if he is free and married, ten years; if he is unmarried, seven years. Boys are to do penance for one hundred days if the practice is habitual. A married layman, if he practices it habitually, must do penance for fifteen years. If he is in holy orders and practices it habitually, he must be degraded and do penance as a layman. Whoever has fornicated with his natural brother must abstain from all flesh because of such a filthy union, or do penance for fifteen years; if he is a cleric, he must be expelled.

### CHAPTER 35.—Concerning clerics or monks who are pursuers of males.

[Col. 0925D]

(From the sayings of Basil.) A cleric or monk who pursues adolescents or boys, or who is caught in a kiss or some other shameful circumstance, is to be publicly beaten and deprived of his tonsure. After being disgracefully shaved, his face is to be smeared with spittle. Bound with iron chains, he is to be confined in the distress of prison for six months, and on three days of every week he is to be fed barley bread at evening.

After this, for another six months, he is to live separated under the custody of an elder spiritual person in a small enclosure, devoted to manual labor and prayer and subject to vigils and tears. He must always walk under the custody of two spiritual brothers and must thereafter be joined to no young men in private conversation or counsel.

### CHAPTER 36.—Concerning the same matter.

[Col. 0926A]

(From the sayings of Saint Isidore.) If anyone from among the young men, or any person under suspicion, has played with children, he must be worn down by prolonged penance.

### CHAPTER 37.—Concerning the same matter.

(From the sayings of the same author.) If any brother is caught playing with boys and forming friendships with persons of immature age, he must be admonished three times to remember decency and the fear of God. If he does not stop, he must be corrected with the utmost severity.

### CHAPTER 38.—Likewise, concerning intercourse with animals.

(From the Roman Penitential.) If anyone has sinned through intercourse with any animal, he must submit in humility for fifteen years at the door of the church. After this, having been received into the communion of prayer [Col. 0926B] for another five years, he must do penance, and thus receive the grace of the sacrament. Others must be asked what kind of life he led during his penance, and he may then obtain the mercy of communion. But if, after the age of twenty, while having a wife, anyone has succumbed to this sin, he must submit to humility for twenty-five years and spend five years in prayers, and thus receive communion.

### CHAPTER 39.—Concerning a bishop who has fornicated according to nature.

(From the Penitential of Theodore.) Likewise, in the canons of the apostles it is judged that a bishop, presbyter, or deacon who has been caught in fornication, perjury, or theft is to be deposed, but not deprived of communion, because God does not judge the same matter twice.

If a bishop has committed natural fornication, the synod decreed [Col. 0926C] that he should do penance for ten years and seek pardon from the Lord with many tears and almsgiving.

A presbyter who, without a monk’s vow, sins with a girl or prostitute must do penance for three years, and during three Lents, on the second, fourth, and sixth days of the week and always on Saturday, he must do penance on dry food. If he sins with a servant of God or with a male, fasting is to be increased: seven years, if the practice is habitual.

Similarly, deacons who are not monks are to do penance for two years, as are monks without rank. If they are monk-deacons, they are to do penance for seven years. Monks with rank are to do penance for seven years.

Likewise, if a bishop without a monk’s vow has sinned with a girl or prostitute, he must do penance for ten years. If a cleric without a monk’s vow has fornicated with such a girl [Col. 0926D], he must do penance for one year; if frequently, two years. With a canoness, two years; if frequently, three years. If he has fathered a son by her, four years; others say seven.

Theodore said: A monk who commits fornication must do penance for seven years. Bede likewise said: A monk who seeks fornication but does not find it must do penance for half a year. The Roman Penitential likewise says: A monk who fornicates with a prostitute or girl must do penance for three years; with a nun, seven years.

Likewise, a private layman who pollutes his neighbor’s wife must do penance as an adulterer. If he sins with a virgin, both must do penance for one year. With a servant of God, four years; if he fathers a child by her, seven years.

Likewise, if anyone has sinned as the Sodomites do, some say that he must do penance for ten years [Col. 0927A]; one who practices it habitually must be expelled. But if they are in holy orders, they must be degraded and do penance as laymen.

A man who has fornicated between the thighs must do penance for one year; if he repeats it, two years. If he has fornicated in the rear, three years; boys, two years. Whoever has fornicated with an animal or beast of burden must do penance for ten years. There must be discrimination according to the kind of animals or human beings, as we said above.

Likewise, a bishop who sins with quadrupeds must do penance for ten years and lose his rank; a presbyter, five years; a deacon, three; a cleric, two.

### CHAPTER 40.—Concerning a priest who has been polluted by obscene speech or a lustful gaze.

(From the Roman Penitential.) A priest who has been polluted by obscene speech or a lustful gaze, but did not wish to fornicate, must do penance for ten days [Col. 0927B]. If a presbyter has kissed a woman out of desire and emitted semen, he must do penance for twenty days. A deacon, ten days; likewise a monk. A cleric, seven. A layman, four.

Likewise, if a presbyter has emitted semen through thought, he must do penance for seven days; if he has touched himself with his hand, three weeks. If a bishop has emitted semen through thought, he must do penance for four weeks. If a deacon has touched himself with his hand and emitted semen, thirteen days; a monk likewise. Otherwise, if he is a cleric, twenty days—how much more, then, those of the other ranks?

If he is polluted through a mental assault, he must do penance for seven days, or until the thought is overcome. If he has been polluted involuntarily in sleep, he should rise and sing seven penitential psalms, namely: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger”; “Blessed are those”; “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger” [Col. 0927C]; “Have mercy on me, O God”; “Lord, hear”; “Out of the depths”; “Lord, hear”—or each person according to his strength—and in the morning sing thirty psalms.

One who wished to sin in sleep, or who was polluted involuntarily, should sing fifteen psalms. One who sinned without being polluted should sing twenty-four psalms.

### CHAPTER 41.—Concerning the same matter.

(From the Penitential of Theodore.) Likewise, one who sins in sleep and is polluted through thought should sing twenty-five psalms. One who sins in sleep without thought should sing twelve psalms. If he emits semen in a church while asleep, he should sing the Psalter, or do penance for three days. If he voluntarily emits semen in a church through an evil thought, then, if he is a cleric, fourteen days [Col. 0927D]; a deacon, twenty-five; a presbyter, forty; a bishop, fifty; a monk, thirty.

### CHAPTER 42.—Concerning those who are polluted through seductive embraces of women.

(From the Penitential attributed to Bede.) Whoever is polluted through the seductive embraces or a kiss of a woman must do penance for twenty days. Whoever has touched the flesh of that woman immodestly must do penance for three months. Whoever is polluted through obscene speech must do penance for seven days. A presbyter who has kissed a woman out of unclean desire must do penance for twenty days. If he has been polluted, forty days. Whoever is polluted in a church during sleep must do penance for three days. Whoever is voluntarily polluted in sleep should rise and sing seven penitential psalms, and during the day thirty [Col. 0928A]. Whoever wished to sin in sleep but was not polluted should sing thirty-four psalms.

### CHAPTER 43.—Concerning clerics who have emitted semen through evil thoughts.

(From the Roman Penitential.) If a cleric has emitted semen without touching himself, through evil pleasures, he must do penance for seven days. If he touches himself with his hand, he must do penance for twenty days. A deacon, thirty days; a presbyter, four weeks.

If a presbyter has emitted semen through thought, he must do penance for seven days; a monk likewise. Whoever voluntarily emits semen in a church must do penance, if he is a cleric, for fourteen days; if a monk or deacon, thirty days; if a presbyter, forty; if a bishop, fifty days.

### CHAPTER 44.—Whether a woman should be separated from her husband if, through negligence and by accident, she received her son from the baptismal font.

[Col. 0928B] *(From a decree sent by Pope Deusdedit to Bishop Gordianus.)* Deusdedit, bishop of the holy Roman and apostolic Church, to Gordianus, co-bishop of the Hispanic Church, and most beloved brother.

Your deacon has come to us, bringing a letter from Your Holiness, stating that certain men and women, on the past Easter Saturday, because of the great influx of people, unknowingly received their own children from the sacred font. You wish to know whether, on account of such an accident, the men and women ought to return to their proper marital relations, or not.

We, saddened by this matter, sought the statements of our predecessors. We found in the archive of this apostolic see that such things had already occurred in the Church of Isauria and of the Ephesians, [Col. 0928C] and likewise at Jerusalem, as well as in other Churches whose bishops and citizens had asked this apostolic see whether the men and women might return to their proper marriage beds.

The holy fathers of blessed memory, Julius, Innocent, and Celestine, together with an assembly of many bishops and priests, wrote and confirmed in the Church of the blessed chief of the apostles that, under no circumstances, should women or men who had received children for any reason take one another back in marriage, but should separate, lest, with the devil’s persuasion, such a sinful fault grow throughout the world and the error of all increase.

You know that just as there are seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, so there are seven gifts of baptism: from the first nourishment of consecrated salt and entrance into the holy Church [Col. 0928D] up to the confirmation of the Holy Spirit through chrism. From this first gift of the Holy Spirit until the seventh, no Christian ought to take his spiritual co-mother in marriage; and whoever presumes to do so shall be bound forever by the bond of anathema, unless he performs worthy penance.

But when the women have been separated from their own husbands on account of the unlawful act, we order that they receive the whole dowry which they received on the day of their marriage, and that after one year has been completed they may take another husband, if they wish. The same applies to the man with respect to his wife.

## CHAPTER 45. On a man who has a spiritual co-father whose wife is not his spiritual co-mother, and whether, after that co-father’s death, he may marry his widow

*(From the Council of Tribur, attended by King Arnulf, chapter 47.)* If a man has a spiritual co-father whose son he received from the sacred baptismal font, and whose wife is not his spiritual co-mother, he may, after his spiritual co-father’s death, marry that man’s widow, provided that they have no consanguineous relationship. For why should those not be joined whom no carnal proximity, nor any relationship arising from birth, separates spiritually?

## CHAPTER 46. Whether a man may marry the daughter of his spiritual co-mother

*(From the same council, chapter 48.)* We neither define this matter by canonical institution nor reject it by any established precedent; but, because some hold different opinions about it, we mention something here. If someone should happen, through circumstances and the accidental course of events, to marry the daughter of his spiritual co-mother, let him retain her, after more mature deliberation has been taken, and let him honorably pursue a lawful marriage.

## CHAPTER 47. On a certain man who violated his spiritual goddaughter

*(From Gregory’s Dialogues.)* The venerable man Maximianus, bishop of Syracuse, who for a long time presided over my monastery in this city, used to relate that something terrible had happened in the province of Valeria. He said:

A certain curial official received at baptism, on the most holy Easter Saturday, a young girl who was someone’s daughter. After returning home from the fast, he became drunk on a great quantity of wine, asked that this same goddaughter remain with him, and that night did to her what is forbidden even to mention: he ruined her.

When he had risen in the morning as a guilty man, he began to consider going to the bath, as though washing in the bathwater could cleanse away the stain of his sin. He therefore went and washed, but then began to tremble as he entered the Church. On the one hand, if he stayed away on so great a day, he was ashamed before men; on the other, if he went, he feared God’s judgment.

Human shame therefore prevailed. He went to the Church, but trembling and afraid he began to stand there, constantly apprehensive about the moment when he might be handed over to the unclean spirit and tormented before all the people. Yet, while he was terribly afraid, nothing adverse happened to him during that celebration of the Mass. He went out joyfully and entered the Church the following day with confidence.

For six successive days he proceeded joyfully and securely, thinking that the Lord had either not seen his crime or, having seen it, had mercifully dismissed it. On the seventh day, however, he died suddenly. When he had been committed to burial, a flame came out of his grave for a long time before all who saw it, and burned his bones until it consumed the whole tomb; the earth that had been heaped upon the grave appeared to have been dug away.

By doing this, almighty God showed what his soul suffered in secret, whose body the flame also consumed before human eyes. In this event, too, he graciously granted us who hear it an example of fear, so that from this consideration we may understand what a living and conscious soul suffers for its guilt, if even insensible bones are burned by so great a punishment of fire.

## CHAPTER 48. On a certain brother who was attacked by the spirit of fornication

*(From the sayings of the hermit Paphnutius.)* A certain father was suffering affliction from the spirit of fornication. He went to a highly esteemed elder and begged him, saying:

“Take care for me, most blessed father, and pray for me, because the passion of fornication is attacking me severely.”

When the elder heard this, he prayed fervently day and night, entreating the Lord’s mercy for him. The same brother came again and asked the elder to pray for him still more intently. In the same way, the blessed elder prayed for him with every concern and with even greater intensity.

But when the elder frequently saw the monk coming to him and begging him to pray, he became very sorrowful and wondered why the Lord did not hear his prayers. That same night, however, the Lord revealed to him what was happening with the monk: negligence, relaxation through sloth, and bodily pleasures in his heart. This was shown to the holy elder in the following way.

He saw the monk sitting while the spirit of fornication played before him in various female forms, and the monk himself took pleasure together with it. He also saw an angel of the Lord standing there and greatly indignant against that same brother, because he did not rise or prostrate himself in prayer before the Lord, but rather delighted in his thoughts.

These things were therefore revealed to the holy elder. He understood that the monk’s fault and negligence were the reason his prayers were not being heard. Then the elder said to him:

“It was your fault, brother, because you take pleasure together with evil thoughts. It is impossible for the unclean spirit of fornication to depart from you while others pray and entreat God for you, unless you also undertake labor yourself through fasting, prayer, and many vigils, begging with groaning that he grant you his mercy and the help of his grace, and that the Lord Christ provide you with the ability to resist evil thoughts.

“For physicians who prepare and administer medicines for human bodies, although they do everything with the utmost care, accomplish nothing by their treatment, diligence, and concern if the sick person does not abstain from harmful foods or from other things that customarily aggravate illnesses.

“The same thing happens with diseases of the soul. Even if the holy fathers, who are spiritual physicians, pray with complete devotion and from their whole heart for the mercy of Christ our Lord and Savior on behalf of those who ask to be helped by their prayers, their prayers will not benefit them unless those people themselves, with complete devotion of mind, act both in prayer and in every spiritual work that is pleasing to God.”

## CHAPTER 49. On a brother’s betrothed, if the brother violates her

*(From the Council of Tribur, attended by King Arnulf, chapter 10.)* A certain man betrothed and endowed a woman, but was unable to have intercourse with her. His brother secretly corrupted her and made her pregnant. It was decreed that, although she could not have become married to the lawful husband, the brother could nevertheless not have as his wife the woman betrothed to his brother. But the adulterer and the adulteress shall undergo a certain punishment for fornication, while lawful marriages shall not be denied to them.

## CHAPTER 50. If someone moves from one bishopric to another and violates a female relative or commits some capital crime

*(From the same council, chapter 42.)* If someone moves entirely from one bishopric to another, and—God forbid—it happens that he violates the daughter of his sister, paternal aunt, maternal aunt, maternal uncle, or paternal uncle, or commits some capital crime, the bishop in whose diocese he then resides, and under whose jurisdiction he is accused of such a crime, shall have the right and power, according to canonical authority and our synodal ordinance, to restrain the wicked man and soften him toward penance. For through whom can the truth of the matter be examined better than through the one under whom he lives and desires to live?

## CHAPTER 51. On women who conceive in the absence of their husbands and destroy the fetus

[Col. 0931B]

*(From the Council of Elvira, chapter 3.)* If a woman conceives through adultery while her husband is absent and kills the child after the crime, it has been decided that communion should scarcely be granted to her even at the end of her life, because she has doubled her crime.

## CHAPTER 52. On women who have sought to kill children wrongly conceived

*(From the Council of Hilerda, chapter 5.)* Those who have sought to kill children wrongly conceived through adultery, whether before or after birth, or who have crushed them in their mothers’ wombs with some potion, shall be granted communion, in either sex, after the passage of seven years, provided that throughout their entire lives they persist in tears and humility.

## CHAPTER 53. On women who secretly kill their offspring

[Col. 0931C]

*(From the Council of Arles, chapter 6.)* Certain women, as we have heard, who conceived through fornication and feared that the crime they had secretly committed might become known, killed the infants they had borne and covered them with heaps of earth, or threw them into the water. How great a crime this is is attested by the canons of the Councils of Ancyra, Elvira, and Hilerda.

Accordingly, those councils decree that communion should scarcely be granted to such women even at the end of life. But treating them more humanely, it was decided that such women should be admitted to communion after ten years of penance.

## CHAPTER 54. On the same matter

Concerning women who commit fornication and kill their offspring, or who take measures against themselves to expel what has been conceived in the womb: the ancient ruling removes them from the Church until the end of their lives. We now define the matter more humanely, so that they are granted ten years of penance according to the previously established stages.

## CHAPTER 55. On the same matter

*(From the Council of Orléans, chapter 10.)* If anyone has suffocated an infant, let him perform penance for three years, one of them on bread and water. If a cleric has done this, let him perform penance for four years, one of them on bread and water.

## CHAPTER 56. On the Sodomitic sin

*(From the Roman Penitential.)* A bishop who commits natural fornication shall perform penance for twelve years; a priest, ten; a deacon, nine; a subdeacon, eight; a cleric, seven; and a layman, six years.

A carnal brother who commits fornication with his carnal brother shall abstain from all flesh for fifteen years. If he has put semen into his mouth, let him perform penance for seven years; others say that he ought to perform penance until the end of his life.

Men who fornicate between the thighs shall perform penance for one year; if they repeat the act, two years. If they fornicate between the legs, and are boys, let them perform penance for one year; if they are men, two years. If it has become habitual, the priest shall increase the measure of penance according to his judgment.

A man who pollutes himself shall first perform penance for ten days, and, if he repeats it, twenty days. If he holds an ecclesiastical rank, penance shall be added.

A boy of fifteen years shall perform penance for forty days. Whoever desires in his mind to fornicate but is unable to do so shall perform penance for ten days. Whoever has been polluted through obscene speech or through sight, yet did not wish to sin bodily, shall perform penance for twenty days. If he has been violently polluted by an assault of thought, let him perform penance for twenty days. Whoever is long tormented by a thought, resisting it gently, shall perform penance for six days, or for as long as the persistence of the thought demands.

It has been decreed that boys who fornicate among themselves are to be beaten. Boys who merely speak among themselves about this matter and transgress the regulations of the elders shall receive three “superpositions” [a prescribed additional penance]. Those who give a non-simple kiss shall receive five superpositions. Those who give a seductive kiss without pollution shall perform penance for five days. If there is pollution without an embrace, they shall receive ten superpositions.

Those over twenty years of age who commit the same act shall live for forty days separated from the table and excluded from the Church, on bread and water.

The youngest boys who imitate fornication and provoke one another, but have not been polluted, shall be flogged because of their immaturity. If they do so frequently, the punishment shall be increased.

Boys under twenty who pollute one another with their hands and confess shall perform penance for twenty days before receiving communion. If they repeat the act after penance, they shall perform penance for one hundred days. If they do so more frequently, they shall be separated and perform penance for one year.

A boy assaulted by an older person, if under ten years of age, shall fast for one week; if he consented, twenty days; if he is a passive partner, he shall perform penance for one year.

Whoever has been voluntarily polluted in sleep shall rise and sing seven psalms on bended knees. Whoever wished to sin in sleep shall sing twenty psalms. If he was polluted involuntarily, he shall sing fifteen psalms and, at the end of each psalm, say three times: “O God, attend to my help,” and the rest.

Whoever has emitted semen while sleeping in a church shall fast for three days.

A bishop who commits fornication against nature shall be degraded and perform penance for twelve years. A priest or deacon who commits fornication against nature shall, after first making the vow of a monk, be degraded and perform penance for five years; let them ask forgiveness at every hour and undergo superposition each week, except during the fifty-day periods.

After the superposition, let them use bread without measure and a dish somewhat enriched with butter, and let them live in this way on Sundays. On the other days, let them be refreshed with a measured portion of rusk-like bread, vegetables enriched with a little butter, a few eggs, and cheese, and with as much water as is sufficient if they are laborers.

Their bed should not contain much hay. During the three Lents of the year, let them add something according as their strength permits, always mourning their guilt from the depths of their heart. Let them most willingly accept obedience, which surpasses all things.

After a year and a half, let them receive the Eucharist and come to peace; let them sing the psalms with the brothers, lest the soul, deprived for so long of heavenly medicine, perish completely.

If a monk had previously held a lower rank, let him perform penance for three years, but let him not be burdened by a measure of bread. If he is a laborer, let him take one Roman sextarius of milk, another of thin gruel [reading uncertain], and as much water as is sufficient for the burning of thirst.

If a priest or deacon without a monastic vow has sinned in this way, let him perform penance like a monk without rank, and afterward let him receive his rank again. But if, after such a sin, a priest or deacon wishes to become a monk, let him perform penance for a year and a half with an unqualified resolve of exile. Nevertheless, the abbot, with the counsel of his bishop, shall have the authority to regulate this matter, if the penitent’s obedience is pleasing to God and to the brothers to whom this matter has been entrusted.

## CHAPTER 57. On those who cause conception to be expelled

*(From the Council of Worms, chapter 30.)* If anyone, in order to satisfy lust or from a meditation of hatred, does something to a man or woman, or gives something to drink, so that he or she cannot beget or conceive and offspring may not arise from it, let him be held as a murderer.

## CHAPTER 58. On those who suffocate their infants

*(From the Council of Mainz, chapter 6.)* If anyone suffocates his infant or smothers it beneath the weight of clothing, and this happened after baptism, let him perform penance for forty days on bread and water and abstain from his spouse during that time. Afterward let him perform penance for three years on the appointed weekdays and observe three Lents each year.

But if the infant was suffocated before baptism, let him perform penance for the next forty days as above. Afterward let him complete five years.

## CHAPTER 59. On a father and mother who find their children dead in their care

*(From the Council of Paris, chapter 5.)* Concerning infants who are found dead with their father and mother, when it is not apparent whether the infant was killed or suffocated by the father or mother, or died a natural death: the parents ought not therefore to be secure or to remain without penance. Nevertheless, consideration should be given to compassion in their case, where not intention but the outcome of death was the cause.

But if it is not hidden from them that they themselves were the killers, they must know that they have sinned gravely, as is confirmed by the Council of Ancyra. Some judge that their penance ought to be three years, one of which must be spent on bread and water, while throughout the time of their penance they must guard themselves from all lust.

## CHAPTER 60. On women who have caused an abortion

*(From the Roman Penitential.)* If a woman voluntarily causes an abortion, let her perform penance for three years.

[Col. 0933] **END OF THE SEVENTEENTH BOOK.**

# [BOOK EIGHTEEN]

[Col. 0933B]

## TABLE OF CONTENTS

[Col. 0933C]

This book teaches that the sick are to be visited by priests and what is required for such a visitation.

When a priest hears that someone in his parish is ill, he should go to him quickly. After entering the room, he should sprinkle blessed water over the sick person and throughout the room, with the antiphon “You shall sprinkle me, O Lord,” and the verse “Let God arise, and let his enemies be scattered,” and so forth.

Then he should say the prayer “O God, who have granted such great grace to your priests.” Afterward he should sing seven psalms with prayers for the sick. Then he should sing the Litany.

After this he should order everyone to withdraw from the room. Approaching the bed on which the sick person lies, he should address him gently and kindly, so that he may place all his hope in God, patiently endure God’s scourge, and believe that these things have come about for his purification and correction; so that he may confess his sins, promise amendment if the Lord grants him life, promise penance for the faults committed, arrange his possessions while his senses and reason are still sound, redeem his sins through almsgiving, forgive those who have sinned against him, and hold the right faith and belief.

If he does not know the faith whole and entire, the priest ought to teach it to him. He should also teach him never to despair of God’s mercy. When the sick person’s mind has been relieved by such and similar exhortations, the priest should give a blessing and question him individually and in order.

When the priest enters the house in which the sick person lies, he should first say:

“Peace to this house.”

“And to all who dwell in it.”

Afterward salt and water shall be blessed, and the house shall be sprinkled with the antiphon:

“Bless, O Lord, this house and all who dwell in it, because you, O Lord, have said: ‘Peace to this house.’ Bless, O Lord, those who fear you, small and great. Blessed are you by the Lord, who made heaven and earth.”

After this the seven penitential psalms are to be sung, followed by the Litany. When it is completed, the following shall be sung:

“Our Father.”

“And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil. Amen.”

“Save your servant,

my God, who hopes in you.

Send him help, O Lord, from the sanctuary,

and protect him from Zion.

May no harm befall him from the enemy,

and may the son of iniquity not add to his injury.

Be for him, O Lord, a tower of strength

against the face of the enemy.

May the Lord preserve him, give him life, and make him blessed [Col. 0935B] upon the earth, and not deliver him into the soul of his enemies. May the Lord bring him help upon the bed of his illness. You have turned his entire bed in his sickness. O Lord, hear my prayer.

Psalm: ‘Have mercy on me, O God.’”

Then follows the prayer.

“Let us pray.

“Almighty and merciful God, we ask your immense compassion: at the entrance made in your name by our humility, may you deign to visit this servant of yours N., lying exhausted in this dwelling, with saving care. Just as you deigned, O Lord, to visit Tobiah and Sarah, Peter’s mother-in-law, and the centurion’s boy, so may this man, having recovered his former health of soul and body, render thanksgiving to you in your Church.

“Through the Lord.”

Then a more private place shall be given to him for confession. Above all, he shall be questioned about the catholic faith. The priest shall say:

“Do you believe in God the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit?”

**Response:** “I believe.”

“Do you believe that these three persons are one God?”

**Response:** “I believe.”

“Do you believe that in this very flesh in which you now are, you will rise on the day of judgment and receive either the good or the evil that you have done?”

**Response:** “I believe.”

“Do you wish to forgive those who have sinned against you?”

**Response:** “I do.”

“Do you wish to amend the sins you have committed, if you recover?”

**Response:** “I do.”

Afterward he shall be anointed. After the confession, the profession of faith, and the anointing, the antiphon shall be said:

[Col. 0935D]

“In your truth hear me, O Lord.”

Psalm:

“O Lord, hear my prayer;

give ear to my supplication.

Then: ‘Lord, have mercy,’ and ‘Our Father,’ with the following prayers:

‘Arise, O Lord God; let your hand be exalted; do not forget the poor.

For the poor man has been abandoned to you;

you will be the helper of the orphan.

The Lord has heard the desire of the poor;

your ear has heard the preparation of their heart.

Make your mercies wonderful,

you who save those who hope in you.

But you dwell in the holy place,

the praise of Israel.

They cried to you and were saved;

they hoped in you and were not put to shame.

Do not deliver, O Lord, to the beasts the soul that confesses to you;

do not forget the soul of your poor man forever.’”

Afterward let the following prayers be said.

“Let us pray.

“O God, who granted your servant Hezekiah ‘er qui nos’ years of life [the number is corrupt in the supplied text], may your power likewise raise your servant N. from the bed of illness to salvation.

“Through Christ.”

Another:

“Look upon your servant N., O Lord, suffering in the weakness of his body, and refresh the soul which you created, so that, corrected by chastisements, he may immediately perceive that he has been saved by your medicine.

“Through Christ.”

Another:

“O God, who always rule your creation with devoted affection, incline your ear to our supplications, and mercifully look upon your servant N., suffering from adverse bodily health. Visit him with your salvation and grant him the medicine of heavenly grace.

“Through Christ.”

Another:

“O God, who have bestowed upon the human race remedies of salvation and gifts of eternal life, preserve in your servant N. the gifts of your virtues, and grant that he may feel your healing not only in his body but also in his soul.

“Through.”

Another:

“O God of the heavenly powers, who by the power of your command drive away every sickness and every illness from human bodies, graciously be present to this servant of yours N., so that, his illnesses driven away and his strength restored, he may immediately bless your holy name in renewed health.

“Through the Lord.”

[Col. 0936C] Another:

“Holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, who strengthen the frailty of our condition by the gracious infusion of your power, so that our bodies and limbs may be invigorated by the saving remedies of your compassion, look mercifully upon this servant of yours N., so that, every bodily necessity of illness being removed, the grace of his former health may be perfectly restored in him.

“Through the Lord.”

Another:

“Let us pray, brothers, to our Lord for our brother, whom the harshness of his present illness grievously afflicts, that the Lord’s compassion may deign to heal him with heavenly medicines; that he who gave life may also give health.

“Through.”

Another:

“Holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, who are the way, and the truth, and the life, hear and preserve your servant N., whom you have given life and redeemed at the great price of the holy blood of your Son.

“Through that same Son.”

If the sick person is in despair, reconcile him by means of the following prayers, so that when he recovers he may perform penance according to the statutes of the canons and the holy Fathers and according to the character of his offense.

### Reconciliation of the sick person

“Grant, we ask, O Lord, to this servant of yours N. a worthy fruit of penance, so that, having obtained forgiveness for his offenses, he may be restored unharmed to your holy Church, from whose integrity he had departed by sinning.

“Through.”

Another:

“Almighty and everlasting God, in your compassion forgive the sins of this servant of yours N., who confesses them, so that the guilt of his conscience may not harm him more toward punishment than the compassion of your pardon benefits him toward forgiveness.

“Through.”

Another:

“Hear our prayers, O Lord, and spare the sins of those who confess to you, so that the one whom the guilt of conscience accuses may be absolved by the indulgence of your mercy.

“Through our Lord Jesus Christ.”

# BURHARD, BISHOP OF THE CHURCH OF WORMS, BOOK EIGHTEEN OF THE DECREES: ON THE VISITATION OF THE SICK

[Col. 0937D]

## CHAPTER 1. That final conversion is to be judged more by the mind than by the time

*(From a decree of Pope Celestine, chapter 20.)* True conversion to God in those who are at the point of death is to be judged more by the mind than by the time, as the Prophet asserts in these words: “When you have turned and groaned, then you will be saved.”

Since the Lord is the examiner of the heart, penance must not be denied at any time to one who asks for it, since that person binds himself to the Judge to whom he knows that all hidden things will be revealed.

## CHAPTER 2. That every faithful person at the point of death ought to be anointed with sanctified oil

*(From a decree of Pope Calixtus.)* The blessed apostle James wrote in his Epistle:

“If anyone among you is sick, let him bring in the priests of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord; and the prayer of faith will save the sick person.”

The apostles are also read to have done this in the Gospel, and now the custom of the Church maintains that the sick are anointed by priests with consecrated oil and healed with prayer accompanying it.

Not only priests may use this sacred oil in their own illnesses; as Pope Innocent describes, all Christians may likewise use the same oil to anoint themselves or their relatives in time of need. Nevertheless, this oil may be prepared only by bishops.

For when he says “with oil in the name of the Lord,” he means oil consecrated in the name of the Lord; or certainly because, when they anoint the sick person, they must also invoke the Lord’s name over him.

“And if he is in sins, they shall be forgiven him.”

Many are punished with bodily illness or even death because of sins committed against the soul. Thus the Apostle says to the Corinthians, because they had been accustomed to receive the Lord’s body unworthily:

“For this reason many among you are weak and sick, and many sleep.”

Therefore, if the sick are in sins and confess them to the priests of the Church, and strive with a perfect heart to abandon and amend them, they shall be forgiven. For they cannot be forgiven without confession and amendment. Hence the text rightly adds:

“Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, so that you may be saved.”

## CHAPTER 3. On those who confess their sins during illness because of fear of death

*(From the Council of Nantes, chapter 2.)* A sick person who confesses his sins because the necessity of death presses upon him shall be reconciled by the priest on this condition: that, if the Lord grants him life and restores his health, he perform penance according to the character of his offense and according to the statutes of the canons and of approved penitentials.

## CHAPTER 4. On those who, in a time of necessity, desire both penance and reconciliation

*(From a decree of Pope Leo, chapter 9.)* To those who, in a time of necessity and danger, under urgent pressure, implore the aid of penance and immediate reconciliation, neither satisfaction is to be forbidden nor reconciliation denied. For we cannot impose measures or define times upon the Lord’s mercy, with whom conversion suffers no delay, as the Lord says through the Prophet:

“When you have turned and groaned, then you will be saved.”

And elsewhere:

“First declare your iniquities, so that you may be justified.”

Likewise:

“For with the Lord there is mercy, and abundant redemption with him.”

In administering God’s gifts, therefore, we must not be difficult, nor neglect the groans and tears of those who accuse themselves, since we believe that the very affliction of repentance has been granted through God’s inspiration, as the Apostle says:

“Lest perhaps God may grant them repentance, so that they may recover from the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive for his will.”

## CHAPTER 5. On the same matter

*(From a decree of Pope Innocent, chapter 22.)* It has also been asked what should be observed concerning those who, having devoted themselves throughout the whole period after baptism to the pleasures of unrestrained living, at the very end of their lives ask simultaneously for penance and reconciliation through communion.

The earlier practice concerning them was stricter; the later practice, through the intervention of mercy, is more lenient. For the earlier custom held that penance should be granted to them but communion denied. Since persecutions were frequent in those times, communion was rightly denied and penance granted, lest the easy granting of communion should make people secure about reconciliation and fail to recall them from falling. Thus, so that everything might not be entirely denied, the severity of the time made the practice more lenient.

But after our Lord restored peace to his Churches, when terror had been removed, it was decided that communion should be given to those departing this life, both out of mercy, as a viaticum for those about to depart, and lest we appear to follow the harshness and severity of the heretic Novatian, who denied pardon.

Therefore final communion shall be granted together with penance, so that such people, with the permission of our Savior, may be rescued from eternal destruction even at the end of their lives.

## CHAPTER 6. On those who are approaching death, so that they may not be deprived of the final and necessary viaticum

*(From the Council of Nicaea, chapter 13.)* Concerning those who are approaching death, the ancient and regular law shall still be observed: if anyone is departing from the body, he must not be deprived of the final and necessary viaticum.

But if someone who was considered hopeless, after receiving communion and becoming a participant in the offering, should recover, he shall be among those who receive only the communion of prayer.

In general, to anyone at the point of death who asks that the grace of communion be granted to him, the bishop ought reasonably to give it from the offering.

## CHAPTER 7. That penance can abolish sins, even if someone performs penance at the final breath of life

[Col. 0939D]

*(From the Council of Mainz, chapter 2.)* We unhesitatingly believe that penance can abolish sins, even if the person who committed them performs penance at the final breath of life, and even if his sins are disclosed by public lamentation. For God’s purpose, by which he decreed to save what had perished, stands unshaken.

Therefore, because his will does not change, whether through amendment of life when time is granted, or through humble confession when life is immediately ended, forgiveness of sins is to be confidently expected from him who does not desire the death of the sinner, but desires that he turn from destruction through repentance and be saved by the Lord’s mercy, so that he may live.

If anyone thinks otherwise about God’s most just compassion, he is not a Christian but a Novatian.

## CHAPTER 8. On the lapsed who are at the point of death, so that, if they ask, they ought to be helped with the gift of viaticum

[Col. 0940A]

*(From a letter of Pope Siricius.)* Whoever has fallen through carnal weakness, when he begins to depart to God, shall, if he asks, be helped through the grace of communion as a viaticum.

## CHAPTER 9. On sick persons who, while requesting penance, lose the use of speech before the priest arrives
(From a letter of Pope Leo.) Thus assistance must be given to the needs of such persons, so that neither the opportunity for penance nor the grace of communion is denied them, if they are found to seek it, even after losing the power of speech, by signs indicating sound understanding. But if they have been so weakened by illness that they cannot at that moment indicate what they had requested shortly before, the testimony of the faithful standing by should benefit them. Nevertheless, they should receive both the benefit of penance and of reconciliation.

### CHAPTER 10.—On the same matter

(From the Council of Carthage, canon 81.) If someone who has requested penance during an illness becomes speechless because, while the priest summoned to him was coming, he was overcome by his sickness, those who heard him should give testimony; he should receive penance; and, if he is believed to be about to die immediately, he should be reconciled by the laying on of hands, and the Eucharist should be poured into his mouth. If he survives, the witnesses mentioned above should inform him that his request has been fulfilled, and that he is subject to the laws of penance, for as long as the priest who administered the penance shall have determined.

### CHAPTER 11.—On the same matter

(From a decree of Pope Eusebius, canon 10.) If someone requesting penance is deprived of the use of his tongue when the priest arrives, it has been established that, if he has reliable witnesses that he himself had requested penance, and if he can make some sign of his will by certain movements, the priest should do everything prescribed above concerning the sick penitent: that is, he should say the prayers, anoint him with holy oil, give him the Eucharist, and, after he has died, provide for him as for the other faithful.

### CHAPTER 12.—On those who have repented in their final illness and have immediately been reconciled

[Col. 0940D]

(From the sayings of Augustine.) Certainly, whoever, placed in the final extremity of his illness, receives penance, is immediately reconciled, and then departs from the body—I confess to you that we do not deny him what he asks, but neither do I presume to say that he has departed well from this life. Whether he has departed securely, I do not know. We can give penance; we cannot give security. Do I say that he will be condemned? But neither do I say that he will be freed. Do you wish to be freed from doubt? Do you wish to escape what is uncertain? Do penance while you are healthy. For if you do true penance while you are healthy, and the final day finds you, you hasten to be reconciled. If you act in this way, you are secure. I say that you are secure because you did penance at a time when you were able to sin. But if you wish to do penance when you are no longer able to sin, your sins have abandoned you, not you your sins.

### CHAPTER 13.—On those who are in danger, so that, after consulting the bishop, a presbyter may reconcile them

(From the Council of Carthage, canon 4.) Bishop Aurelius said: “If anyone is in danger and asks to be reconciled to the divine altars, and the bishop is absent, the presbyter must certainly consult the bishop and, on his instruction, reconcile the person in danger.” We ought to strengthen this matter with salutary counsel.

### CHAPTER 14.—On the sick who are in danger of death

[Col. 0941A]

(From the Penitential of Theodore.) From the sick who are placed in danger of death, a sincere confession of sins should be sought through presbyters. The measure of penance, however, should not be imposed upon them, but should be made known; and the burden of penance should be lightened through the prayers of friends and the practice of almsgiving. If they should perhaps depart this life, they should not become bound—excluded from communion or from fellowship in forgiveness. If, having been rescued from this danger by God, they recover, they should carefully observe the measure of penance imposed by their confessor. Therefore, in accordance with canonical authority, lest the door of mercy appear closed to them, they should be strengthened by ecclesiastical prayers and consolations, together with the holy anointing with oil, and refreshed with the communion of the viaticum, according to the statutes of the holy Fathers.

### CHAPTER 15.—On a certain man who had denied Christ, and how he was freed by the viaticum at the end of his life

[Col. 0941C]

(Dionysius says this in his Ecclesiastical History.) In his Ecclesiastical History, Dionysius, writing in reply to Fabianus, relates the following story. There was a certain man in Alexandria, one of those who had fallen away. He had often begged to be received, but had not obtained his request. Then he was overcome by illness, so that he lay completely without a voice for three days. On the fourth day, it is said, when he had recovered his breath a little, he called his little daughter to him and said: “How long will you keep me here? I beg you, let one of the presbyters come quickly, so that I may be released.” After saying this, he again remained without a voice.

The boy quickly went to the presbyter, at night. The presbyter was ill and could not come. Nevertheless, because it had been ordered that no one should deny the comforts of reconciliation to those who had fallen away when they were at the point of death—and especially to those who were known previously to have requested it—he gave the girl a small portion of the Eucharist.

While the girl was still returning, before she entered the house, Serapion said again: “Have you returned, my child? Although the presbyter could not come, nevertheless carry out what you were commanded, so that I may depart.” When he received the Eucharist, as though certain chains and bonds had been broken, he breathed forth his spirit in greater joy. From this it is clear that no one should be deprived of the aid of this good gift.

### CHAPTER 16.—That presbyters should reconcile penitents for hidden sins by order of the bishop

(From a decree of Pope Evaristus, canon 4.) Presbyters are to reconcile penitents for hidden sins by order of the bishop and, as we stated above, absolve and communicate the sick.

### CHAPTER 17.—If a penitent departs from the body during penance and desires reconciliation

(From the Council of Orange, canon 3.) It has been decided that those who depart from the body as penitents should receive communion without the reconciling laying on of hands, since this was sufficient consolation for one who was dying, according to the definitions of the Fathers, who called such communion an appropriate viaticum. If they survive, they should remain in the order of penitents, so that, after the necessary fruits of penance have been demonstrated, they may receive legitimate communion with the reconciling laying on of hands.

### CHAPTER 18.—That penance should be remitted to penitents on the Thursday before Easter, but earlier if they fall into the danger of death from illness

[Col. 0942B]

(From a letter of Pope Innocent, canon 7.) Concerning penitents who are performing penance either for graver offenses or for lesser ones, Roman custom shows that, if no illness intervenes, it should be remitted to them on the Thursday before Easter. In other respects, it is the priest’s responsibility to judge the weight of the offenses, so that he may attend to the penitent’s confession and to the weeping and tears of the one who is correcting his life, and order the penance to be remitted when he sees that adequate satisfaction has been made. Certainly, if someone falls ill and reaches the point of danger, his penance should be relaxed before Easter, lest he depart from this world without communion.

### CHAPTER 19.—On those who have not believed that sins are remitted in the Church

[Col. 0942C]

(From the sayings of Augustine.) Whoever, not believing that sins are remitted in the Church, despises the generosity of the divine gift and closes his final day in this obstinacy of mind is guilty of that unforgivable sin against the Holy Spirit, in which Christ remits sins.

### CHAPTER 20.—That the sick may take food at any hour

(From the Council of Mainz, canon 23.) The sick may take food and drink at any hour, whenever they desire.

### CHAPTER 21.—On those priests who have denied penance to the dying

[Col. 0942D]

(From a decree of Pope Julius.) If any presbyter has denied penance to the dying, he will be guilty concerning their souls, because the Lord says: “On whatever day the sinner is converted, he shall live and shall not die.” For true conversion can occur at the final moment, because the Lord is an examiner not only of time but also of the heart—just as the thief, through his confession, deserved to be in paradise at the final hour after a single moment.

### CHAPTER 22.—That final penance is to be denied to no one

(From a decree of Pope Celestine, canon 15.) We have learned that penance is being denied to the dying, and that the desires of those who, at the time of their death, wish assistance for their souls are not being granted. I confess that we shudder to find anyone so impious as to despair of God’s mercy, as though he could not come to the aid of one who runs to him at any time, and free a person endangered beneath the burden of sins from the weight by which that person desires to be released.

What else, I ask, is this than to add death to one who is dying, and, through one’s cruelty, to kill his soul by preventing it from being set free? Yet God, ever ready to come to our aid and inviting the sinner to penance, proclaims: “On whatever day he is converted, his sins shall not be reckoned against him.” And again: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but only that he should turn and live.”

Whoever, therefore, denies penance at the time of death and despairs of the mercy of God deprives a person of salvation; he does not believe that God can be sufficient to aid the dying even in a single moment. The thief hanging at Christ’s right hand would have lost his reward if the penance of a single hour had not helped him. While he was undergoing punishment, he repented, and through the profession of a single statement he earned a dwelling in paradise, promised by God.

### CHAPTER 23.—On penitents who have received the Eucharist during illness

(From the Council of Carthage, canon 78.) Penitents who have received the viaticum of the Eucharist during illness should not believe themselves absolved without the laying on of hands, if they survive.

### CHAPTER 24.—On penitents who have died suddenly

(From the same source.) The offering for those who, after receiving penance, die in the good course of life without communion is to be accepted, and their funerals, as well as their subsequent commemoration, are to be attended to with ecclesiastical observance.

[Col. 0943] END OF THE EIGHTEENTH BOOK.

# BURCHARD, BISHOP OF THE CHURCH OF WORMS, DECRETALS, BOOK NINETEEN: ON PENANCE

[Col. 0949]

## ARGUMENT OF THE BOOK

[Col. 0949A]

This book is called the Corrector and the Physician because it fully contains remedies for the correction of bodies and souls, and teaches every priest, even a simple one, how he may assist each person—ordained or unordained, poor or rich, child, young person, old person, aged person, healthy or sick, of every age and of either sex.

### CHAPTER 1.—At what time presbyters of the parishes, by canonical authority, should compel those who are at odds to make peace and those who have sinned to do penance

(From the Roman Penitential.) During the week before the beginning of Lent, the presbyters of the parishes should summon the people to them, reconcile those who are at odds by canonical authority, settle all quarrels, and then first assign penance to those who confess. Thus, before the beginning of the fast, all who have confessed should have received their penance, so that they may say more freely: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.”

### CHAPTER 2.—How priests should admonish and instruct the people entrusted to them during the time of penance

(From the sayings of Augustine.) Presbyters should admonish the people subject to them that everyone who feels himself wounded by the deadly injury of sin should hasten, on the Wednesday before Lent, to the life-giving mother, the Church. There, having simply confessed with complete humility and contrition of heart what he has wrongly committed, he should receive the remedies of penance according to the measure prescribed by canonical authorities.

Not only the person who has committed something mortal, but every person who recognizes that he has stained with the blemish of sin the undefiled tunic of Christ, which he received in baptism, should hasten to come to his own priest and humbly confess with purity of mind all the transgressions and sins by which he remembers having incurred God’s displeasure. Whatever is imposed upon him by the priest, he should heed carefully and observe most cautiously, as though it had been spoken by the mouth of almighty God himself.

When bishops or presbyters receive the confessions of the faithful, they should humble themselves and pray with sighs of sorrow and tears, not only for their own offenses but also for the fall of their brother. For the Apostle says: “Who is weak, and I am not weak?”

Therefore, when someone comes to the priest to confess his sins, the priest should tell him to wait a little until he enters the church or his own room for prayer. If there is no suitable place for this, he should say this prayer in his heart.

### CHAPTER 3.—The prayer that the priest should say to those coming to penance

Lord, almighty God, be merciful to me, a sinner, so that I may be able to give you fitting thanks: you who, because of your mercy, have made me, unworthy as I am, a minister of the priestly office, and have appointed me, insignificant and humble, as a mediator to pray and intercede with our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, for sins and for those returning to penance.

Therefore, Lord and Ruler, who desire all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, who do not desire the death of sinners but that they should turn and live, receive my prayer, which I pour out before the sight of your mercy, for your male and female servants who have come to penance. Give them the spirit of compunction, so that they may recover from the snares of the devil by which they are held bound, and may return to you through fitting satisfaction.

Through the same Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, etc.

### CHAPTER 4.—On confession, penance, reconciliation, and the questioning of those who desire to confess their sins, and the order for assigning penance to them

[Col. 0950C]

Then the priest should first question him gently and kindly about how he believes concerning the faith, and should say:

(From the Roman Penitential.) Do you believe in God the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit?  
**Answer:** I believe.

Do you believe that these three persons are one God?  
**Answer:** I believe.

Do you believe that in this very flesh in which you now are, you will rise on the day of judgment and receive either good or evil according to what you have done?  
**Answer:** I believe.

Are you willing to forgive the sins of those who have sinned against you, since the Lord says: “If you do not forgive people their sins, neither will your Father forgive you your sins”?  
**Answer:** I am willing.

And inquire carefully whether he is incestuous or unfaithful to his lord. If he does not wish to abandon incest, you cannot give him penance; but if he does wish to do so, you can.

After these preliminaries, the priest should address the penitent affectionately in these words:

Brother, do not be ashamed to confess your sins, for I too am a sinner, and perhaps I have committed deeds worse than yours. I admonish you for this reason: as blessed Gregory says, it is a customary vice of the human race both to commit sin by falling and, after committing it, to expose it not by confessing but by denying it, and then to multiply it by defending what has been proved against us.

Although, at the devil’s prompting, we are not afraid to perpetrate shameful crimes, we are ashamed, at his same persuasion, at least to confess in words the very things we have accomplished in deed without any shame; and before a human being who is like us and perhaps subject to the same passions, we are embarrassed to say what, before God who sees everything, we did not fear to commit without any inward shame—a detestable refusal.

Let us therefore freely confess what we committed without compulsion. If we conceal our crimes, they will be revealed by the one who is both the accuser and the instigator of sin. He himself incites us to sin; he himself accuses us after we have sinned.
