Each girl holds a separate rod in her hands; they lead the aforesaid girl, dragging the herb behind her, into the nearest river, and sprinkle the girl with the same rods. Thus, by their incantations, they hope to obtain rain. Then, after turning the same naked girl around from the river to the village with her footprints reversed and changed in the manner of a crab, they bring her back among them. If you have done this or consented to it, you must do penance for twenty days on bread and water.

### CHAPTER 6. On the admonition concerning the eight principal vices and their kinds

(From the *Penitential of Theodore.)* I shall now explain to you the eight principal vices. If you feel yourself struck, touched, and wounded by them, take care not to conceal them from me: pride, vainglory, envy, anger, [Col. 0977A] sadness, avarice, gluttony of the belly, and lust. If you recognize yourself as guilty of these, undertake penance, for all vices arise from them.

From pride, which is the beginning of every sin and the queen of all evils, arise every disobedience, every presumption, every obstinacy, disputes, heresies, and arrogance.

From vainglory arise boasting, arrogance, indignation, discord, desire for empty glory, and hypocrisy.

From envy arise hatred, whispering, detraction, rejoicing at the misfortunes of one’s neighbor, and distress at his prosperity.

From anger arise quarrels, swelling of the mind, insults, shouting, indignation, presumption, blasphemies, shedding of blood, murders, the desire for revenge, and [Col. 0977B] remembrance of injuries.

From sadness arise malice, rancor of spirit, faintheartedness, bitterness, despair, sluggishness, wandering of the mind, and often also no enjoyment whatever of the present life.

From avarice arise envy, thefts, robberies, murders, lies, perjuries, plunder, violence, unrest, unjust judgments, contempt for future truth, forgetfulness of blessedness, and hardness of heart.

From gluttony of the belly spreads foolish merriment, buffoonery, frivolity, empty talk, bodily uncleanness, instability of mind, drunkenness, lust, and dullness of perception.

From lust are generated blindness of mind, lack of consideration, unsteadiness of the eyes or precipitancy of the whole body, [Col. 0977C] immoderate love of oneself, hatred of God’s commandments, attachment to the present age, and dread and despair concerning the future.

### CHAPTER 7. Likewise, on the virtues by which these same vices can be overcome, and on the conclusion of penance

Therefore, if you have been proud until now, humble yourself in the sight of God. If you have loved vainglory, consider whether, for the sake of passing praise, you may lose an eternal reward. If the rust of envy has consumed you until now—which is the greatest sin and detestable above all, since the envious person is compared with the devil, who envied the first man the gift that he himself had lost through his own fault—do penance, and count the progress of others as your own. If sadness overcomes you, meditate on patience and long-suffering. If the disease of avarice weighs upon you, consider that it is the root of all evils and is compared with idolatry; therefore you ought to be generous. If anger troubles you, that anger which rests in the bosom of fools, you must rule your spirit and drive it away from you through tranquility of mind. If gluttony of the belly draws you toward devouring, pursue sobriety. If lust afflicts you, vow chastity.

Then let the penitent prostrate himself on the ground and say with tears:

“In these and in all other vices by which human frailty can sin against God and its Creator—whether by thinking, speaking, acting, taking pleasure, or desiring—I acknowledge and confess that I have sinned in all things and am guilty in the sight of God above all people. I humbly beseech you, priest of God, to intercede for me and for my sins with the Lord and our Creator, so that I may deserve to obtain pardon and forgiveness for these and all my crimes.” [Col. 0978A]

Then let the priest prostrate himself on the ground with the penitent and chant the following psalms.

First, let him say the whole of Psalm 37, “O Lord, rebuke me not in thy fury”; afterward let him say, “Let us pray,” and chant Psalm 102, “Bless the Lord, O my soul”; and again let him say, “Let us pray,” and chant Psalm 50, “Have mercy on me, O God.” After this let him chant Psalm 53, “O God, in your name,” and say, “Let us pray,” and chant Psalm 51, “Why do you glory in wickedness?”

Then let him say the following prayers.

[Col. 0978B] O God, whose forgiveness no one does not need, remember your servant N., who has been stripped bare by the slippery frailty of an earthly body. We beseech you: grant pardon to the one who confesses; spare the one who supplicates, so that the one accused by his own merits may be saved by your mercy. Through the Lord.

Holy Lord, Father, almighty and eternal God, who through Jesus Christ your Son, our Lord, have deigned to heal our wounds: we humbly entreat and ask you to incline the ear of your kindness to our prayers. You who also forgive all crimes and pardon every sin, grant to this servant of yours, Lord, pardon in place of punishment, joy in place of sorrow, and life in place of death, so that, trusting in your mercy, we may deserve to attain eternal life. Through the same Lord.

[Col. 0978C] Almighty and merciful God, who have placed the forgiveness of sins in prompt confession, come to the aid of those who have fallen and have mercy on those who confess, so that those whom the chain of their offenses binds may be released by the greatness of your mercy. Through him.

I beseech you, Lord, by the majesty of your clemency and mercy, that you deign to release the debts of your servant N., who confesses his sins and crimes, grant him pardon, and forgive the guilt of his past crimes. You who brought the lost sheep back upon your shoulders, who were appeased by the prayers and confession of the publican: may you also deign to be appeased toward this servant of yours, Lord. Look kindly upon him in response to his prayers, so that he may remain acceptable in confession, and so that his weeping and petition may earnestly implore your perpetual [Col. 0978D] clemency. Restored to the holy altars, may he again be devoted to eternal hope and heavenly glory. You who live and reign.

Then add:

May almighty God be your helper and protector, and may he grant forgiveness for your past, present, and future sins. Amen.

### CHAPTER 8. A salutary antidote for souls

(Compiled from the writings of the Prophet, Gregory, Jerome, Augustine, and three penitentials.) That practice which was followed in the days of our fathers never abandoned the right paths. They established that penitents and mourners should overcome their passions and vices by the medicine of eternal salvation. For, [Col. 0979A] just as the diversity of diseases causes physicians of bodies to prepare diverse medicines or potions, so the diversity of sins causes diverse medicines for penitents. Likewise, judges in secular cases render different judgments; when they are good, they weigh and consider rightly how they should judge between the wretched and the rich, and between one case and another.

How much more, then, ought the priests of God to weigh and administer diverse medicines for invisible souls among human beings, lest, through a foolish physician, the wounds of souls putrefy and become worse. As the Prophet says: “My wounds have become corrupt because of my foolishness.” O foolish physician, do not deceive your own soul and that of the other person, lest you receive a twofold punishment, or sevenfold, or a thousandfold. Hear Christ saying: “If the blind lead the blind, both fall into the pit.” And if you think, [Col. 0979B] “Another person neither hears nor sees me, so as to judge me,” do you not understand that God, the just and strong judge, sees and hears, brings hidden things into the open, and repays each according to his works?

And again: Truly, there are some who resemble blind dogs running toward the corpses of the dead, or resemble flying ravens, who are raised to the priesthood not for God but, rather, because they yearn for earthly honor, blind to divine wisdom. Gregory Nazianzen said of such men: “I fear this: that dogs are pursuing the pastoral office, especially when they have prepared no discipline for themselves.”

For Ezekiel says: “Woe to the shepherds of Israel who fed themselves and not the flock. They drank the milk, clothed themselves with their wool, and ate what was fat; [Col. 0979C] what was broken they did not bind,” and so forth. Again Ezekiel says: “Woe to the priests who eat the sins of my people,” that is, taking their offerings for themselves and not praying for them; eating the sacrifices and not reproving them. When they hear that people are dying, they rejoice and prepare themselves for plunder, like ravens for the corpses of the dead.

Now therefore, brothers, whoever wishes to bear the name of priest should first think of God, so that he may learn what is necessary for him before the bishop’s hand touches his head: namely, the Psalter, the Lectionary with the Gospels, the book of the Sacraments, the Baptistery, the computus with the cycle and the commendations of souls, the martyrology, and homilies to be preached to the people throughout the year. This is for the simpler sort; [Col. 0979D] if any one of the things mentioned above is lacking, the name of priest will not properly belong to him.

In addition to these, he should have his *Penitential*, arranged both according to the authority of the canons and according to the sound judgments of the three penitentials: that of Bishop Theodore, those of the Roman pontiffs, and that of Bede. Many useful things are found in Bede’s *Penitential*, but many others have been inserted by others that agree neither with the canons nor with the other penitentials. A wise physician should select the better elements, so that he may investigate the distinctions among all cases, without which a proper judgment cannot stand. For it is written: “In nothing should you appear undiscerning, but distinguish what, where, how long, when, and in what manner you ought to do it.”

Therefore not everyone is to be weighed on one [Col. 0980A] and the same scale, although they may be bound by the same vice. There must be discernment among them: between rich and poor, free and slave; infant, child, youth, adolescent, elderly person; dull-witted, ignorant, layman, cleric, monk, bishop, priest, deacon, subdeacon, lector, whether in an order or without an order; married or unmarried; foreigner or native; virgin, widow, canoness, nun; disabled, sick, healthy; one fornicating with animals, or with human beings against nature; continent or incontinent; acting by choice, necessity, or accident; sinning publicly or secretly; and according to the degree of contrition with which each of these matters is corrected, so that places and times for doing penance may also be distinguished.

[Col. 0980B] We have collected all these things from the canons, from the judgments of the holy Fathers, from Jerome, Augustine, Gregory, Theodore, Bede, and from the true Roman *Penitential*. And, so that no one may be forced to perish, we entrust these matters to knowledgeable and understanding physicians of souls, to be moderated.

In Jesus son of Sirach it is said: “In judging, be merciful, like a father to orphans.” Saint James likewise says: “Judgment without mercy will be shown to the one who has not acted mercifully; but mercy triumphs over judgment.”

Saint Augustine says concerning those who perform true penance: they do so in fasting and weeping, in almsgiving and prayers, and by not committing again what they have done; and if they do so, they nevertheless do not persevere in it. For God said: “You thought evil: I forgave. You spoke evil: I forgave. You did evil: I forgave. I do not forgive persevering in evil.” Therefore, do not forgive those who persevere in evil, but judge them with a strict judgment according to the canons and the established rules of the elders, so that the others may have fear.

### CHAPTER 9. The penance of that year which is to be fasted on bread and water is to be observed in this manner

(From the Roman *Penitential.*) The penance of one year, during which one must fast on bread and water, must be as follows: each week let him fast on bread and water for three days, namely Monday, Wednesday, and Friday. For three days—namely Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday—let him abstain from wine, mead, honeyed beer, meat, fat, cheese, eggs, and every fatty fish. He may eat small fish if he can obtain them. If he cannot, let him eat only one kind of fish, and legumes, vegetables, and fruit, if he wishes, and let him drink beer. On Sundays and at the Nativity of the Lord, for those four days; on the Epiphany of the Lord, for one day; at Easter, through the eighth day; at the Ascension of the Lord and Pentecost, for four days; and at the Mass of Saint John the Baptist, of Saint Mary, of the Twelve Apostles, of Saint Michael, of Saint Remigius, of All Saints, of Saint Martin, and at the feast of whatever saint is celebrated in that bishopric—on these aforesaid days let him share charity with the other Christians, that is, let him use the same food and drink as they do. Nevertheless, let him always avoid drunkenness and distension of the belly in all things.

### CHAPTER 10. This is the second year after the year that is observed on bread and water, and it is to be fasted after that year

This year is also to be assigned to those who deliberately kill ecclesiastics, who habitually commit the Sodomitic crime, who habitually sin against nature, who deliberately commit murders in churches, burn churches, commit adultery in churches, or perpetrate other things of this kind.

(From the same source.) The penance of that year must be as follows: two days each week, namely Monday and Wednesday, let him fast until evening, and then let him refresh himself with dry food—that is, bread and dry but cooked legumes—or raw fruit or vegetables. Let him choose and use one of these three, and let him drink beer, but soberly. On the third day, namely Friday, let him observe the fast on bread and water. Let him also fast through three Lents: one before the Nativity of the Lord, the second before Easter, and the third before the Mass of Saint John. If he cannot complete the entire Lent before the Mass of Saint John, let him complete it afterward.

During these three Lents, let him fast two days each week until the ninth hour and eat dry food, as noted above, and let him fast on Friday on bread and water. On Sundays and at the Nativity of the Lord, for those four days; on the Epiphany of the Lord, for one day; at Easter, through the eighth day; at the Ascension of the Lord and Pentecost, for four days; and at the Mass of Saint John the Baptist, of Saint Mary, [Col. 0981C] of the Twelve Apostles, of Saint Michael, of Saint Remigius, of All Saints, of Saint Martin, and at the feast of whatever saint is celebrated in that bishopric—on these aforesaid days let him share charity with the other Christians. Nevertheless, let him always avoid drunkenness and distension of the belly in all things.

### CHAPTER 11. On those who cannot fast and fulfill what is written in the *Penitential*

(From the same source.) Whoever can fast and fulfill what is written in the *Penitential* should do so and give thanks to God. But for whoever cannot, by the mercy of God we give this counsel, so that no one need despair or perish, either himself or anyone else.

### CHAPTER 12. On redeeming that year which he ought to fast on bread and water

[Col. 0981D]

(From the same source.) For one day on which he ought to fast on bread and water, let him chant fifty psalms on bent knees in the church, if this can be done. Otherwise, let him do the same in a suitable place, feed one poor person, and on that day, except for wine, meat, and fat, let him eat whatever he wishes.

### CHAPTER 13. Another method

(From the same source.) If he is such that he cannot remain on his knees for so long, let him do this: inside the church, if possible; otherwise, standing attentively in one place, let him chant seventy psalms in order, feed a poor person, and on that day, except for wine, meat, and fat, let him eat whatever he wishes.

### CHAPTER 14. Likewise, another method

[Col. 0982A]

(From the same source.) Whoever bends his knees one hundred times in church—that is, if he asks pardon one hundred times—should do this in the church, if possible; this is most just. If it cannot be done there, let him do the same secretly in a suitable place. If he does this, then on that day, except for wine, meat, and fat, let him eat whatever pleases him.

### CHAPTER 15. Likewise, another method

(From the same source.) Whoever does not know the psalms and ought to do penance for one day on bread and water may redeem it by three denarii if he is rich, and by one denarius if he is poor; and on that day, except for wine, meat, and fat, let him eat whatever he wishes.

### CHAPTER 16. Likewise, another method

(From the same source.) For one day on which he ought to do penance on bread and water, let him feed three poor people. And on that day, except for wine, meat, and fat, let him eat whatever pleases him.

### CHAPTER 17. Likewise, another method

(From the same source.) Some say that twenty *palmatae* (palm-strikes) are equivalent to one day.

### CHAPTER 18. On redeeming one week which he ought to fast on bread and water

(From the same source.) For one week on which he ought to fast on bread and water, let him chant three hundred psalms on bent knees in the church. If he cannot do this, let him chant three Psalters attentively in the church or in a suitable place. After he has chanted the psalms, except for wine, meat, and fat, let him eat whatever he wishes.

### CHAPTER 19. On redeeming one month which he ought to fast on bread and water

[Col. 0982C]

(From the same source.) For one month on which he ought to fast on bread and water, let him chant one thousand two hundred psalms on bent knees.

(From the same source.) If he cannot do this, let him chant, without genuflection, sitting or standing in the church if possible, or otherwise in one place, one thousand six hundred and eighty psalms. Each day, if he wishes and does not want to abstain, let him refresh himself at the sixth hour, except on Wednesday and Friday, when he is to fast until the ninth hour. Let him abstain from meat, fat, and wine for the entire month. After chanting the aforesaid psalms, let him eat other food. In this way the whole of that year is to be redeemed.

### CHAPTER 20. On those who cannot fast and do not know the psalms: how they can redeem one year which they ought to fast on bread and water

[Col. 0982D]

(From the same source.) Whoever does not know the psalms and cannot fast should, for one year during which he ought to do penance on bread and water, give twenty-two solidi as alms to the poor and fast every Friday on bread and water. Let him also observe three Lents: namely, forty days before Easter, forty days before the feast of Saint John the Baptist, and forty days before the Nativity of the Lord. If anything remains before the feast, let him complete it afterward.

During these three Lents, whatever is prepared for his mouth as food or drink, of whatever kind it may be, let him estimate its price, or what its price could be, and distribute half of that price as alms to the poor. Let him pray continually and ask God that his prayer and his alms may be acceptable before God.

### CHAPTER 21. Likewise, the redemption of that year during which he ought to do penance on bread and water

(From Theodore’s *Penitential.*) Likewise, whoever cannot fast and observe what is written in the *Penitential* should do what Pope Saint Boniface established. For one day on which he ought to fast on bread and water, let him ask the priest to sing a Mass for him—unless there are capital crimes which must first be washed away through confession and tears. Then let him himself be present and hear the Mass, and let him devoutly offer bread and wine with his own hands into the priest’s hands. Let him answer attentively as much as he understands to the greetings and exhortations of the priest, and let him humbly beseech God that the offering which he and the priest have offered to God for him and for his sins may be mercifully received by almighty God through his angel. On that day, except for wine, meat, and fat, let him eat whatever he wishes. In this way let him redeem the remaining days of the year.

### CHAPTER 22. On those who cannot fast but have the means by which they can redeem it

(From the same source.) If someone is unable to fast but has the means with which he can redeem it, let him give twenty solidi for seven weeks if he is rich. If he does not have enough to give that much, let him give ten solidi. If he is very poor, let him give three solidi.

Let no one be troubled because we have ordered twenty solidi or [Col. 0983C] less to be given. If he is rich, it is easier for him to give twenty solidi than for a poor person to give three. But each person should consider to whom he ought to give it: whether for the redemption of captives, upon the holy altar, to God’s servants, or to the poor as alms.

### CHAPTER 23. On those who cannot fulfill what is written in the *Penitential*

(From the same source.) Whoever cannot do penance in the manner described above should do this: if he ought to fast for three continuous years but cannot fast, he can redeem it as follows. In the first year let him distribute twenty-six solidi as alms; in the second year let him distribute twenty solidi as alms; in the third year, eighteen solidi. This makes sixty-four solidi.

Powerful people ought to give more, because from the one to whom more is entrusted, more will be demanded. And those who commit illicit acts ought also to abstain from lawful ones, and they ought to afflict the body with fasts, vigils, and frequent prayers. For a joyful flesh draws one toward guilt, but afflicted flesh brings one back to pardon.

### CHAPTER 24. On those who cannot fast and have no means by which they can redeem it

(From the *Penitential of the priest Bede.*) Whoever cannot fast and has no means of redemption, but knows the psalms, should, for one day on which he ought to fast on bread and water, chant three times “Blessed are the undefiled,” through “When I was in trouble I called upon the Lord.” And six times: “Have mercy on me, O God.” Let him prostrate himself on the ground seventy times and, at each genuflection, chant the “Our Father.”

Whoever does not know the psalms should, for one day on which he ought to fast on bread [Col. 0984A] and water, prostrate himself on the ground one hundred times and say the “Our Father” at each genuflection.

### CHAPTER 25. On the redemption of seven years

(From the Roman *Penitential.*) Likewise, by another method: twelve periods of three days, each with three completed Psalters and three hundred *palmatae* (palm-strikes) for each Psalter, excuse one year of penance. Similarly, twenty-four periods of two days, with three completed Psalters and three hundred *palmatae* for each Psalter, excuse two years.

Twenty-five psalms with an equal number of *veniae* during the night, together with three hundred *palmatae*, excuse a period of two days. One hundred psalms with *veniae* during the night, together with three hundred *palmatae*, excuse a period of three days. One hundred and twenty special Masses, each with three Psalters and three hundred *palmatae*, excuse one year. [Col. 0984B] One hundred solidi given as alms excuse one year.

### CHAPTER 26. That at the beginning of Lent all public penitents should come into the city and present themselves to their bishop before the doors of the church barefoot and clothed in sackcloth

(From the Council of Agde, chapter 9.) At the beginning of Lent, all penitents who undertake or have undertaken public penance should present themselves to the bishop of the city before the doors of the church, clothed in sackcloth, barefoot, with their faces cast down toward the ground, proclaiming by their clothing and countenance that they are guilty.

The deans should be present there—that is, the archpriests of the parishes, namely the priests of the penitents—who must carefully observe their conduct and, according to [Col. 0984C] the measure of their guilt, impose penance through the prescribed stages. After this, let the bishop lead them into the church and, prostrate on the ground with all the clergy, chant the seven penitential psalms with tears for their absolution.

Then, rising from prayer, as the canons command, let him lay hands upon them, sprinkle them with holy water, first cast ashes upon them, then cover their heads with sackcloth, and with groaning and frequent sighs declare to them that, just as Adam was cast out of paradise, so they too are cast out of the church because of their sins. After this let him order the ministers to drive them outside the church doors.

The clergy should follow them with the Responsory: “By the sweat of your face you shall eat bread,” and so forth, so that, seeing the holy church shaken and [Col. 0984D] moved by their crimes, they may not regard penance lightly. At the Lord’s holy Supper, however, they are to be presented again at the thresholds of the church by their deans and their priests.

### CHAPTER 27. That penitents, when they seek penance, should receive the laying on of hands

(From the same source, chapter 7.) At the time when penitents seek penance, they should receive from the priest the laying on of hands and sackcloth upon their heads, as has been established everywhere. But if they have not cut their hair or changed their clothing, they should be cast out.

### CHAPTER 28. By what authority the measure of penance should be imposed on those confessing their sins

(From the Council of Mainz, chapter 10.) The measure and duration of penance for those confessing their sins should be imposed by priests either according to the establishment of the ancient [Col. 0985A] canons, the authority of the sacred Scriptures, or approved ecclesiastical custom.

For those who impose certain light and unusual forms of penance upon people guilty of serious sins, “sew pillows,” in the prophetic expression, “under every elbow,” and “make cushions under the head of people of every age” in order to capture souls. But discernment must be maintained between those who sin publicly and those who sin secretly. Whoever sins publicly ought to be publicly punished by penance and, according to the order of the canons, excommunicated in proportion to his desert and then reconciled.

### CHAPTER 29. That the diversity of sins produces a diversity of penances

(From the sayings of Augustine.) The diversity of sins produces a diversity [Col. 0985B] of penances. Physicians of bodies likewise prepare different medicines so that they may treat wounds differently from illness, tumors, putrefactions, blindness, fractures, and burns.

So spiritual physicians must heal the wounds of souls by different kinds of treatment. But since it belongs to few to know, examine, treat, and heal everything thoroughly, and to restore people to a complete state of health, we therefore earnestly admonish every learned priest of Christ to arrange everything not according to his own judgment but according to the statutes of the canons and the traditions of the Fathers. Let him consider the condition of each person wishing to do penance: sex, age, poverty, cause, status, person, [Col. 0985C] and the very heart of the penitent; and according to these matters, as seems appropriate to him, let him judge each case as a wise physician.

### CHAPTER 30. That the fruits of penance are many

(From the sayings of the same author.) The fruits of penance are many, and through them one reaches the expiation of crimes. Eternal salvation is not promised merely through that simple name, “penance,” as in the apostolic saying: “Repent and be converted, so that your sins may be blotted out.” Nor will anyone be saved merely because of that bare groaning or that bare name of penance, as in the prophetic saying: “When you have turned and groaned, then you will be saved.” Rather, through true confession, the counsel of an understanding priest, the affection [Col. 0985D] of charity, and the fruit of almsgiving, the mass of sins is overthrown.

### CHAPTER 31. Why the canons do not prescribe precisely the time and measure of penance for every crime

(From the sayings of Jerome.) The canons do not prescribe with sufficient clarity the measure of time for doing penance, specifying for each crime how each matter should be corrected. Instead, they establish that it should be left to the discretion of an understanding bishop. For before God the measure of time is not as valuable as the measure of sorrow, nor abstinence from food as much as the mortification of vices.

For this reason they command that the periods of penance be shortened according to the faith and conduct of penitents, and they judge that they should be prolonged on account of [Col. 0986A] negligence. Nevertheless, for certain sins forms of penance have been imposed, according to which other sins are to be assessed, since through these same forms it is easy to estimate the punishment and severity of the canons.

### CHAPTER 32. On those who hasten to fulfill the penance imposed upon them

(From the Roman *Penitential.*) If you see someone who approaches penance and stands firmly and constantly in penance, immediately act more leniently toward him. If he is able to fast what has been imposed upon him, do not forbid him, but allow it. Those who hasten to discharge the burden owed by them quickly are more worthy of praise, because fasting is a burden owed and is therefore to be loved by those who do penance. If he fasts and completes what the priest has commanded him, [Col. 0986B] he will be purified from his sins.

But if he returns again to his former habit of sin, he is like a dog that returns to its own vomit. Therefore every penitent ought not to fast only what the priest has commanded him; even after he has completed what was ordered, he ought to fast as much as seems proper to him.

For if he does what the priest has commanded him, only those sins that he confessed will be forgiven. But if afterward he fasts of his own will, he will acquire a reward for himself and the kingdom of heaven.

Therefore, whoever fasts the entire week for his sins should eat and drink whatever is suitable for him on Saturday and Sunday. Nevertheless, let him guard himself against gluttony and drunkenness, because every lust arises from drunkenness. Therefore blessed [Col. 0986C] Paul prohibited it, saying: “Do not become drunk with wine, in which there is lust”—not because lust is in wine, but because it is in drunkenness.

### CHAPTER 33. That whenever people approach penance, priests ought to share with them in fasts and prayers

(From Theodore’s *Penitential.*) Whenever Christians approach penance, we impose fasts, and we too ought to share with them in fasting for one or two weeks, or as much as we can, so that it may not be said to us what the Lord said to the Jewish lawyers: “Woe to you lawyers, who burden people and place heavy and unbearable burdens upon their shoulders, while you yourselves do not touch those burdens with one of your fingers.”

No one can lift up [Col. 0986D] a person falling under a burden unless he bends down to extend his hand to him. Nor can any physician heal the wounds of the sick unless he shares in their foul odors. Likewise, no priest or bishop can heal the wounds of sinners or remove sins from souls without diligent care and tearful prayer.

Therefore, dearest brothers, it is necessary for you to be concerned for sinners, because we are members of one another. And so, if we see someone lying in sins, let us hasten to call him to penance through our teaching. Whenever you give counsel to a sinner, give him penance at the same time, immediately specifying how much he ought to fast or redeem his sins by almsgiving, lest perhaps you forget what he has already told you and it become necessary [Col. 0987A] to question him again; perhaps he will then be ashamed to confess his sins again and will be found subject to further judgment.

### CHAPTER 34. That a person sometimes sins through a movement of the mind and sometimes through the frailty of the flesh
(From the Council of Chalon, chapter 32.) We also saw that this required correction: some people, when confessing their sins to priests, do not do so fully. Since it is established that a human being consists of two substances, namely soul and body, and since sin is committed sometimes through a movement of the soul and sometimes through the weakness of the flesh, the sins themselves must be investigated with careful diligence, so that confession may be complete in both respects—that is, so that they confess both what was done through the body and what was committed in thought alone. The confessor of sinners must therefore be instructed to require confession concerning the eight principal vices, without which life in this world is difficult, since a person sins at their instigation either in thought or, what is more serious, in deed. Hatred, envy, pride, and the other plagues of the soul of this kind injure all the more dangerously because they spread more subtly.

### CHAPTER 35 — That penance must be imposed without respect of persons

(From the Council of Carthage, chapter 74.) A priest must impose the laws of penance upon one who seeks penance, without respect of persons.

### CHAPTER 36 — Concerning incest committed secretly

(From the sayings of Augustine.) If someone has secretly committed incest and has secretly made confession to a priest, the canonical remedy that he would have had to undergo had his crime been made public must be indicated to him. But because the deed remains hidden, the priest should give him counsel by which he may advance the salvation of his soul through secret penance: namely, that he sincerely confess from his heart that he has grievously sinned, and strive to cleanse himself through fasting, almsgiving, vigils, and sacred prayers with tears, and thus trust that, through the mercy of God, he may attain the hope of forgiveness.

### CHAPTER 37 — That a distinction must be observed between those who do penance publicly and those who do so secretly

(From the Council of Mainz, chapter 21.) A distinction must be observed between penitents: those who ought to do penance publicly and those who ought to do so secretly.

### CHAPTER 38 — Concerning those who neglect penance

(From the Council of Carthage, chapter 75.) More negligent penitents are to be received more slowly.

### CHAPTER 39 — That priests ought to receive a penitent from the heart with great joy

(From the sayings of Bishop Basil.) A penitent ought to be received from the heart in the manner the Lord showed when he said: “He called his friends and neighbors together, saying: Rejoice with me, because I have found my sheep that was lost.”

### CHAPTER 40 — That the periods of penance are to be determined at the bishop’s discretion according to the differences among sins

(From the African Council, chapter 10.) For penitents, the periods of penance are to be determined at the bishop’s discretion according to the differences among sins; and a presbyter is not to reconcile a penitent without consulting the bishop, except when the bishop’s absence makes necessity compelling. If any penitent has committed a public and notorious crime that has disturbed the whole Church, hands are to be laid upon him before the apse.

### CHAPTER 41 — Concerning those who have ceased sinning and have done perfect penance, so that communion may be granted to them during their penance

(From the Council of Laodicea, chapter 2.) Concerning those who have sinned through various crimes but, persevering in prayer, have achieved complete conversion from their evil ways: according to the character of the offense, after the period of penance has been completed, communion is to be granted to such persons because of the mercy and goodness of God.

### CHAPTER 42 — Concerning the fallen: how they ought to be corrected and consoled with brotherly affection, so that they may not fall into the devil’s snares and despair

(From a letter of Pope Callistus.) But if someone has fallen in any manner, let us bear with him and correct him with brotherly affection, as the blessed Apostle says: “If someone is overtaken in any offense, you who are spiritual should instruct such a one in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself, lest you also be tempted. Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ.”

Moreover, holy David did penance for deadly crimes and nevertheless remained in honor. Blessed Peter also shed very bitter tears when he repented of having denied the Lord, yet he remained an apostle. And through the prophet the Lord promises sinners, saying: “On whatever day the sinner turns and groans, I will remember none of all his iniquities any longer.”

Those who think that priests, after falling, cannot serve the Lord if they have done worthy penance, or enjoy their honors if thereafter they lead a good life and faithfully preserve their priesthood, are in error. Indeed, those who think this not only err, but also appear to scatter and drive away the keys entrusted to the Church, of which it was said: “Whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven.” Otherwise, this judgment is either not the Lord’s or it is not true.

We, however, firmly believe that both the Lord’s priests and other faithful people can, after worthy satisfaction, be restored to their honors, as the Lord testifies through the prophet: “Will one who sleeps not rise again? And will one who has turned away not return?” And elsewhere: “I do not desire,” says the Lord, “the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live.”

The prophet David, doing penance, said: “Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and strengthen me with a governing spirit.” For after his penance he taught others and offered sacrifice to God, giving an example to teachers in the holy Church that, if they have fallen and have done worthy penance, they can both offer sacrifice and teach others.

### CHAPTER 43 — Whether those who have fallen in the sacred orders can be restored

(From the Register of Pope Gregory, to Secundinus, a servant of God living in seclusion.) Your Holiness asked us to write back to you concerning rising again to priestly office after a fall, since you say that you have read different canons and different judgments on this matter—some allowing restoration and others denying that it can occur.

Beginning with the Council of Nicaea, we venerate this council together with the other four, because the later councils, following it, agree unanimously in all their judgments. We therefore follow the Fathers who preceded us, since, with God as our author, we do not depart from their sacred teaching.

Beginning at the head and proceeding down to the fourth minister of the altar, we understand this rule to be observed: since the greater precedes the lesser, just as he is greater in honor, so he should be greater in guilt; and the greater the fault of the one who precedes, the greater the punishment that should be imposed upon him. Thus afterward his penance may be believed fruitful. For what benefit is there in sowing wheat without gathering its fruit, or in building a house without dwelling in it?

After worthy satisfaction, we believe that a person can return to honor, as the prophet says: “Will one who falls not rise again? And will one who has turned away not return?” He also says to the sinner: “On whatever day you turn and groan, then you will be saved.”

Hence the Psalmist says: “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me. Do not cast me away from your presence, and do not take your Holy Spirit from me.” When he asked not to be cast away by God because of the guilt of his fall, the king and prophet—shaken with fear because he had seized another man’s wife—added, after the prophet had pointed out his crime and he had done penance: “Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and strengthen me with a governing spirit.”

For if he himself had not done worthy penance before God, he would never have preached to others. He says: “I will teach the wicked your ways, and the ungodly will turn back to you.” When the prophet saw that his sins had been cleansed through penance, he did not hesitate to rebuke the sins of others by preaching; and thus he sought to offer himself as a sacrifice to God when he said: “A troubled spirit is a sacrifice to God.”

These things would be sufficient, but every judgment is more readily believed the more strongly it is confirmed by testimonies from sacred Scripture. Concerning this the prophet says: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live.” To sinners it is said: “On whatever day the sinner turns and groans, all his iniquities are consigned to oblivion.”

If our Redeemer, who came not to destroy sinners but to justify them, leaves the offenses of sinners in oblivion, who among human beings would reserve them for condemnation, when the Apostle says: “If God justifies, who is the one who condemns?”

Returning to the fountain of mercy, let us bring forward the Gospel judgment: “There will be more joy,” he says, “over one sinner doing penance than over ninety-nine righteous people who have no need of penance.” He left the ninety-nine sheep that had not strayed and carried the lost sheep back to the sheepfold on his shoulders.

If a wandering sheep, once found, is carried back to the fold on the shepherd’s shoulders, why should this man not be restored after penance to the Church’s ministry?

What, then, is more serious: to commit a carnal offense—an offense in which not many but few are found—or to deny the Son of God out of fear? We know that the blessed chief of the apostles, Peter, whose body we unworthy ones now sit beside, fell into this very sin. But denial was followed by penance, and penance by mercy, because the Lord did not cast him out of the apostolate, though he had foretold that Peter would deny him.

Let these words, dearest son, be sufficient for you, so that when you see a man wiping away his offenses with tears, you may not doubt that he will obtain mercy in the presence of the Divinity. For no one who returns after sinning is despised by the one who came to redeem sinners with his blood.

For this reason blessed Augustine, also writing to the deacon Peter concerning faith, says: “Penance can be useful to every human being in this life, whenever a person undertakes it—however wicked or advanced in years he may be—if with his whole heart he renounces his former sins, sheds before God not only bodily tears but also tears of the heart for them, and strives to wash away the stains of evil deeds through good works. He will immediately receive forgiveness for all his sins.”

For the Lord promises this to us in prophetic speech, saying: “If you turn and groan, you will be saved.” And elsewhere it is said: “Son, you have sinned; do not sin again, but pray concerning your former sins, that they may be forgiven you.” Prayer for sins would never have been prescribed to one who had sinned if forgiveness were not to be granted to the one who prays.

Penance benefits the sinner only if he performs it within the Catholic Church, to which God, in the person of blessed Peter, granted the power of binding and loosing, saying: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven.”

Therefore, whenever a person of any age performs true penance for his sins and, with God’s illumination, reforms his life, he will not be deprived of the gift of forgiveness. For, as God says through the prophet, he does not desire the death of the one who dies, but rather that he turn from his evil way and that his soul live.

Nevertheless, no one should remain longer in his sins under the hope of God’s mercy, since even in the body no one wishes to remain sick longer in the hope of future health. Such people, who neglect to turn away from their iniquities and promise themselves forgiveness from God, are sometimes overtaken by God’s sudden wrath, so that they find neither time for conversion nor the benefit of forgiveness.

Therefore sacred Scripture kindly warns each of us, saying: “Do not delay turning to the Lord, and do not postpone it from day to day; for his anger will come suddenly, and at the time of vengeance he will destroy you.”

Blessed David also says: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.” Blessed Paul agrees with him in these words: “See to it, brothers, that perhaps there is in any one of you an evil heart of unbelief, causing him to depart from the living God. But exhort one another each day, as long as it is called ‘Today,’ so that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin.”

A person lives with a hardened heart if he does not turn back, despairing of forgiveness for his sins, or if he hopes for God’s mercy in such a way that he remains until the end of his present life in the perversity of his crimes.

Therefore, loving God’s mercy and fearing his justice, let us neither despair of the remission of sins nor remain in sin, knowing that the justice of the most just Judge will exact from every human being those debts that the mercy of the most merciful Redeemer has not forgiven. For just as mercy receives and absolves those who turn back, so justice will reject and punish those who remain hardened.

These are the people who sin against the Holy Spirit and receive no forgiveness of sins either in this age or in the age to come.

On this subject Isidore, bishop of Seville, wrote the following reply to Bishop Masso’s inquiry: “As your venerable Fraternity subsequently made known in your letters, no diversity of decrees is to be understood in such judgments: in one place it is read that, after penance, the rank of honor is to be restored following a bodily fall; elsewhere it is read that, after such an offense, the former rank of order is by no means to be restored; elsewhere, that after such an offense the merit of the former order is by no means to be restored.

“This difference is distinguished in the following way. The canon commands that those return to their former ranks of office whose satisfaction through penance, or worthy confession of their sins, preceded their restoration. On the other hand, those who are not corrected from the vice of corruption and who, with a kind of superstitious presumption, even attempt to defend the very carnal offense they have committed receive neither their rank of honor nor the grace of communion.

“Thus the two judgments must be reconciled in such a way that those who have earned reconciliation through penance by the mercy of God must be restored to their place of honor. Nor is it without reason that those known, through the amendment of penance, to have received the remedy of life attain the status of the dignity they had acquired.

“So that this may not remain more ambiguous, let it be confirmed by the judgment of divine authority. The prophet Ezekiel, under the figure of faithless Jerusalem, showed that after the satisfaction of penance the former honor could be restored. ‘Be ashamed,’ he says, ‘O Judah, and bear your disgrace.’ And shortly afterward: ‘You and your daughters, return from your iniquity.’

“By saying ‘Be ashamed,’ he showed that after the shame—that is, after the deed of sin—one must feel shame, and for the crimes committed must lower one’s shamefaced brow to the ground, because one had perpetrated a deed deserving of shame. Then he commanded that the disgrace of his deposition be borne, mourning humbly over what he had done in sin. Thus, according to the prophet, he can be restored to his former state.”

### CHAPTER 44 — That the soul, nobler than many nations and more precious than many cities, must be mourned, and that one must not despair of forgiveness

(Excerpt from a book of John of Constantinople to Theodore, chapter 59.) “Who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes?” This is said more appropriately by me now than it was then by the prophet of God. For although it is not many cities or an entire nation that must be lamented, the soul must nevertheless be mourned, since it is nobler than many nations and more precious than many cities.

If one person who does God’s will is better than a multitude of wicked people, then you too were once better than the multitudes of the Jews. Therefore no one should wonder if I now use longer lamentations and pour out more bitter tears than the prophet poured out then.

I do not mourn, as I said, the destruction of a captured city, nor do I lament the captivity of a worthless crowd; rather, I mourn the fall of a distinguished soul and the destruction of the temple in which Christ dwells. This lamentation for the distinguished soul that I mourn is all the harsher and more bitter because it is also more genuine.

That is why I weep without relief: because I know; and I mourn without ceasing whenever I remember. When will I see you once more rejoicing in the state of your former glory? Even if this appears impossible among human beings, with God all things are possible.

He is the one who raises the needy from the dust and lifts the poor from the dungheap, to place him with the princes of his people. He is the one who makes the barren woman a joyful mother of children.

Do not doubt, then, and do not despair that you can be changed for the better. If the devil had such power that he could lead you from the lofty heights of the virtues into the depths of evil, how much more can God restore you to the summit of goodness and not merely return you to what you were, but make you far more blessed than you previously appeared?

Only do not lose heart and do not cut off your hope of good things. Please, do not let what usually happens to the impious happen to you. It is not the multitude of sins that brings the soul to despair, but impiety. It belongs to the impious to despair of salvation, not to sinners.

Therefore divine mercy promises, saying: “There will be joy in heaven before the angels of God over one sinner.” And shortly afterward: To those who stand, if they fall, it threatens punishment; to those who have fallen, it promises mercy so that they may desire to rise. It frightens the former, lest they presume upon their good works; it strengthens the latter, lest they despair in their evils.

You are righteous: fear anger, lest you fall. You are a sinner: rely on mercy, that you may rise.

And just as a very heavy fall, pressing upon the neck of the soul, continually forces it to look downward toward the earth and does not allow it to raise its eyes upward to God, so too [the text is defective: “of a manly soul its own weight”], as the Prophet says: “As the eyes of a maidservant are upon the hands of her mistress, so our eyes are toward the Lord our God, until he has mercy on us.”

For that woman in the Gospels who found the drachma she had lost called her friends and neighbors together to congratulate her. I too will call together your friends and mine, and I will ask our neighbors to assemble—not to rejoice, but to mourn with me; not to celebrate, but to lament; and, raising our voices together to heaven, to utter a great cry of mourning, saying to them:

“Wail with me, friends; mourn and pour out fountains of tears—not because I have lost an immense weight of gold, or talents of gold, but because a friend dearer than all these things, more precious than all gold and jewels and every noble possession, has somehow fallen into the very depths of perdition.”

Do not despair over your fall, lest you fall. Whoever despairs of another receives forgiveness; but whoever despairs of himself receives none, because he is not master of another person’s mind.

Thus, when the soul once begins to despair of its salvation, it no longer understands how or into what evils it is being precipitated. Those who have been seized by despair likewise become unbearable and run through every path of wickedness.

Rise, rise, I beg you; awaken at last, and lay aside this demonic drunkenness. Spare all those who despair because of your despair, lest they think they are walking in the way of virtue if they do not see you return to it.

Consider, I beg you, how great a sorrow now possesses the choir of all the holy brothers, how great a joy and exultation comes to unbelievers, and how greatly their authority for rushing into lust is diminished. After this, no one who has been cast down by any fall will fail immediately to desire to rise and hasten immediately to restore himself.

### CHAPTER 45 — That no one should withdraw from consoling a wounded brother

(Also by John of Constantinople to the same Theodore, concerning the fall of Bacharius, chapter 60.) Where is the mercy of the Christian religion, which our teacher taught to be better than sacrifice? Look: a brother lies struck down by the enemy, perhaps still breathing, and you return as though you had suffered no wound, without even attempting to bring consolation for his injury?

Do not be without fear, brothers. The enemy struck the stronger man so that he might have easier access to the others. Why, then, do you despise the wounded man, or treat him as though, in your opinion, he were already dead?

Better was Rizpah, Saul’s concubine, who guarded the bodies of the dead whom David had struck in vengeance for the Gibeonites. Clothed in sackcloth—that is, haircloth—she guarded them until water from heaven sprinkled them, that is, until a spark of heavenly mercy descended for their forgiveness.

Better was Judas Maccabaeus, who believed that prayer should even be made for dead brothers, whom condemned gifts from the city of Jamnia had overthrown through idolatry.

Why, I ask, would our physician place so many kinds of remedies among the compartments of his books if none of his plasters could heal the wound inflicted by the enemy? If you wish, let us open our medical school and examine from the beginning the catalogue of wounds and the kinds of medicines.

At the very entrance of that school we meet the ancestors of the human race, struck by the poisonous tooth of the serpent. They were not immediately given over to the punishment of death, but were expelled from the delights of paradise—that is, from the freedom of the Church and communion in the sacred ministry—

### CHAPTER 46 — On the same subject

(Also by the same author.) Hence you see how we are stained by the contagion of sin. Please, most blessed man, let us not overwhelm our brother, sunk in the depths of a pit under the power of an unjust ruler, with the stones of despair.

Let us imitate that Ethiopian who rescued the holy Jeremiah, cast into a pit by an unjust king, by taking the assistance of thirty men and sending him old rags and ropes.

Do not be quick to abandon the fallen and ruined. Extend your hand to your fallen brother, who, ashamed of the disgrace of sin, neither dares to raise himself nor lift his eyes.

Fulfill the law of Moses. Your brother’s donkey has fallen beneath its burden—that is, the flesh has been overcome by sin. Bend down, humble yourself, and lift it from its ruin.

Why are you ashamed to associate with a sinful man? Consider him who says: “Do not be excessively righteous.”

Our teacher judged the man wounded by robbers not only worthy of care, but also led him to his inn and sheepfold. You too, therefore, gather up the brother whom the devil, like a robber, has struck. Entrust him to the innkeeper—that is, to the blessed bishop—who, if he spends anything on him, will receive more from the Lord.

### CHAPTER 47 — On the same subject

(Also by the same author.) The Gospel teaching says: “If your brother sins against you, rebuke him privately. If he listens to you, you have gained your brother,” and the other words contained in this command.

Consider what it says: “Let not the sons of the uncircumcised rejoice.” The sons of the uncircumcised are worldly people, living in the error of their foreskin and in paganism. They rejoice when they hear of the fall of Christ’s soldier.

Let the sin therefore be concealed, and let correction be applied. Let us provide the linen cloths of consolation and the remedies of heavenly hope. But let the sinner who has confessed his sin remain below, within the tomb of his secrecy, restrained by shame, where he is torn by the worm of conscience; the worm binds up all the corruptions of sins within him until he emits from himself no stench of a disgraceful reputation.

### CHAPTER 48 — On the same subject

(From a letter of John of Constantinople to Theodore.) How, I ask, can we despair of the Lord’s mercy, when he even reproved Pharaoh for not deigning to repent, saying: “I crushed the arms of Pharaoh, king of Egypt, and he did not entreat that healing be given him and strength restored to him to grasp the sword”?

That remarkable Solomon, who deserved to be joined to God’s attendant—that is, to the wisdom of God—fell into the embraces of foreign women and, ensnared in the bonds of lust, polluted himself even with the horror of sacrilege, because he fashioned an image of Cathmos, the Moabite idol.

But because he acknowledged the guilt of his error through the prophetic voice, he was never deprived of heavenly mercy. Perhaps you will say: “In neither Testament do I read that he repented or obtained mercy.”

### CHAPTER 49 — That no one is to be admitted to the clergy after penance

(From the decree of Pope Siricius, chapter 14.) We ought also to have foreseen this: just as no cleric is permitted to undertake penance, so after penance and reconciliation no layman should ever be permitted to attain the honor of the clergy. For although they may have been cleansed from the contagion of all sins, they ought not to receive the instruments for administering the sacraments if they were previously vessels of vices.

### CHAPTER 50 — Gelasius discovered that men entangled in serious crimes had been admitted to the clergy, and that clerics involved in grave vices had not been removed from office

(From the decree of Pope Gelasius, chapter 18.) We have also discovered that certain men entangled in dreadful crimes, with all discernment set aside, not only do not undergo the necessary penance for atrocious deeds, but, without any correction whatsoever having followed, strive for the divine ministry and its honor.

Some who have been established in the very orders are not expelled even though they commit serious crimes, although the Apostle cries out: “Do not lay hands quickly on anyone, nor share in the sins of others,” and although the venerable decrees of our predecessors declare that such men, even if they have slipped through, must be driven out—both those who sinned before [their admission] and must be deposed and expelled, and transgressors who have forgotten their sacred profession and must unquestionably be removed far away by the holy superior.

### CHAPTER 51 — Concerning those who imprudently travel to the shrines of the saints under the pretext of religion

(From the Council of Chalon, which Emperor Charles attended, chapter 45.) There is also great error among certain people who imprudently travel to Rome, Tours, or certain other places under the pretext of prayer.

There are presbyters, deacons, and others established in the clergy who, living negligently, think that they are cleansed from their sins and ought to exercise their ministry if they reach the places mentioned.

There are likewise laymen who think that they may sin or may have sinned with impunity because they visit these places to pray.

There are some powerful people who, in order to acquire revenue, obtain many things under the pretext of a Roman or Touraine journey, oppress many poor people, and make it appear that what they do from pure greed they do for the sake of prayer or visiting holy places.

There are poor people who do this either to have greater material for begging—their number includes those who wander about everywhere and falsely claim that they are going there—or because they are so foolish as to think that they are cleansed from sins merely by seeing holy places, without considering what blessed Jerome said: “It is not seeing Jerusalem, but living well in Jerusalem, that deserves praise.”

Concerning all these matters, the emperor’s judgment is to be awaited as to how they should be corrected. But those who have confessed their sins to the priests in whose parishes they are located, and who have received from them counsel concerning the penance they must undertake, if they desire to visit the thresholds of the apostles or any of the saints by devoting themselves to prayer, distributing alms, regulating their conduct, and reforming their lives, deserve every commendation for their devotion.

### CHAPTER 52 — Concerning every sinner: however often he falls, he must rise that many times

(From the sayings of a certain hermit named Sosius.) A certain brother repeatedly questioned Abbot Sosius in these words: “What shall I do, Father, since I have fallen?”

He answered him: “Rise.”

When the brother admitted that he had risen and then fallen again, he replied: “Rise again.”

When the brother reported that he had often risen and often fallen, while the old man continued to use the same saying, he cried out: “Do not stop rising.”

The brother said to him: “How long can I rise, Father? Explain.”

The old man said: “Until you either die, overcome by a good work or by an evil one. For in whatever work a person is overcome, in that work he will be judged.”

### CHAPTER 53 — That it is right for every person to rebuke himself

(From the sayings of a certain hermit named Pimen.) A certain brother asked Abbot Pimen: “What does the Apostle mean when he says, ‘All things are clean to the clean’?”

He said to him: “If someone can arrive at an understanding of this saying, he will see himself as lower than the whole of creation.”

The brother said: “How can I consider myself lower than a man who is a murderer?”

The old man replied: “If a person can arrive at this saying of the Apostle and sees someone who has perhaps killed another, he says to himself: ‘This man has committed only that one sin; but I commit murder every hour, killing myself.’”

When the brother asked how this could happen, he replied: “This alone is a person’s righteousness: that he rebuke himself. For he is righteous when he condemns his own sins.”

### CHAPTER 54 — That no one should condemn a brother before God has judged him

(From the sayings of a certain hermit.) Abbot Isaac once came to a monastery and saw there a negligent brother. In anger he ordered him to be expelled from the monastery.

As he was returning to his dwelling, an angel of the Lord came and stood before the door of his cell, saying: “I do not permit you to enter.”

He begged that his fault be revealed to him. The angel replied: “God sent me, saying: ‘Go and tell Isaac: Where do you command us to send the brother who sinned?’”

At once he did penance, saying: “I have sinned, Lord; forgive me.”

The angel said to him: “Rise; may the Lord forgive you. But do not do this again—condemn no one before God has judged him.”

“Human beings have taken judgment upon themselves and do not leave it to me,” says the Lord.

This was said because, if it should happen that one of those who are perfect sins even in a small matter, he is not to be exposed immediately.

### CHAPTER 55 — That rightful obedience is rewarded with rightful gifts

(From the sayings of a certain hermit.) One of the Fathers, while in ecstasy, saw four orders before God. The first order consisted of sick people who gave thanks to God. The second consisted of those who practiced hospitality and served in it. The third consisted of those who practiced solitude. The fourth consisted of those who, for God’s sake, were subject in obedience to the Fathers.

That fourth order, which displayed obedience, was superior to the other three; it wore a golden necklace and possessed greater glory than the others.

The old man said to the one who showed him this in ecstasy: “All the others have some rest in fulfilling their own wills. But the one who practices obedience abandons every will of his own and depends entirely upon the will of the Father who commands; therefore he has obtained greater glory than the others.”

### CHAPTER 56 — Concerning those who sin deliberately and promise themselves a certain impunity for sinning because of the distribution of alms

(From the Council of Chalon, chapter 36.) We also thought that this should not be passed over: certain people sin deliberately and promise themselves a kind of impunity because they distribute alms.

Almsgiving extinguishes sin, according to the saying: “Water extinguishes a burning fire, and almsgiving extinguishes sin.” But this applies to sins committed through necessity, chance, or any kind of weakness. Those deeds that are committed deliberately in order to satisfy someone’s lust, precisely so that they may be redeemed by almsgiving, can by no means be redeemed in this way. For those who do this appear to hire God for a payment, so that they may be permitted to sin with impunity.

A person should not sin in order to give alms; rather, he should give alms because he has sinned. The mind and body that lust drew into guilt must be led back to forgiveness by affliction and contrition.

### CHAPTER 57 — Concerning those who, after completing penance, return to their former wallowing places

(From the decree of Pope Siricius, chapter 10.) Your affection has rightly believed that the apostolic see should be consulted concerning those who, after completing penance, return like dogs and pigs to their former vomit and wallowing places, and again seek military service, frivolous pleasures, new marriages, and forbidden sexual relations. Their declared lack of self-restraint was exposed by the children born after their absolution.

Concerning such people, because they no longer have recourse to penance, we have decided that they are to be joined to the faithful within the Church only in prayer, and are to attend the celebration of the sacred mysteries, although they do not deserve to do so. They are to be excluded from the banquet of the Lord’s table, so that, corrected at least by this discipline, they may chastise their own errors and provide an example to others, so that they may be withdrawn from obscene desires.

Nevertheless, because they fell through carnal weakness, we wish to assist them with the provision for the journey when they begin to depart to the Lord, through the grace of communion. We decree that the same rule is to be observed concerning women who, after penance, have bound themselves to such pollutions.

### CHAPTER 58 — Concerning a female penitent who, after her husband’s death, has presumed to marry another

(From the Council of Arles, chapter 2.) Female penitents who, after the death of their husbands, presume to marry others, or who live with an outsider in a suspicious or forbidden intimacy, are to be kept away from the thresholds of the Church together with that man. It has also been decided that this is to be observed concerning men who are under penance.

### CHAPTER 59 — That in imposing penance there is to be no respect of persons
(From the Council of Cabillon, attended by the Emperor Charles, chapter 34.) Since, as the Apostle testifies, there is no acceptance of persons with God, and since this must be observed in all judgments, it must be guarded against all the more carefully in this judgment of penance, so that no priest ever judges otherwise, whether out of favor or hatred toward anyone, than what he has found in the sacred canons, or what, according to the authority of the holy Scriptures and ecclesiastical custom, seems more correct to him. [Col. 0998A] If, then, physicians who try to apply medicine to bodies do not, out of regard for any person, spare those whom they wish to heal the cautery, the knife, or any other harsh instrument, how much more must this be observed by those who are physicians not of bodies but of souls. For penance is not to be measured by the length of time, but by fervor of mind and mortification of the body. God does not despise a contrite and humbled heart.

### CHAPTER 60.—Those who deceive themselves by thinking that their sins can be remitted without worthy penance

(From the sayings of Augustine.) Whoever, therefore, says that anyone can receive forgiveness from God for evil deeds without worthy penance is entirely mistaken; and, while hastening to deceive others after having been deceived, he is bound by a double guilt: namely, that of his own error and that of deceiving another.

### CHAPTER 61.—That each person must labor until he possesses Christ

(From the sayings of Gregory.) A person must labor until he possesses Christ. But whoever has once obtained him no longer labors. Nevertheless, the Lord permits his elect to labor so that they may remember the tribulations of their labor and thereby guard themselves, fearing that they might lose such great labors. For this reason God also led the children of Israel around through the desert for forty years, so that, remembering their tribulations, they would not turn back.

### CHAPTER 62.—That no bishop or presbyter should receive another’s penitent without letters from his bishop

[Col. 0998C]

(From a letter of Pope Felix, chapter 2.) Above all, care must be taken and every precaution must be adopted lest any of our brother bishops or fellow priests, or even any presbyter, receive in another’s city or diocese a penitent, or one placed under the hand of a priest, or one who says that he has been reconciled, without the testimony and letters of the bishop or presbyter to whose parish he belongs.

### CHAPTER 63.—That, according to the canons, penitents should not receive Communion until they have completed their penance

(From a decree of Pope Pius, chapter 2.) Penitents must not receive Communion before the completion of their penance.

### CHAPTER 64.—That one who refuses to repent of a committed sin is to be regarded as a pagan and a publican

[Col. 0998D]

(From the sayings of Augustine.) Toward one who does not repent of a committed sin, we must conduct ourselves as the Lord commanded when he said: “Let him be to you as a pagan and a publican”; and as the Apostle commands: “Withdraw from every brother,” he says, “who walks disorderly, according to the tradition that I delivered to you.”

### CHAPTER 65.—That one who remembers having committed unlawful acts ought to abstain even from lawful ones

(From the sayings of Pope Gregory.) Whoever remembers having committed unlawful acts should strive to abstain even from lawful ones, so that by this he may make satisfaction to his Creator: one who has committed what was forbidden ought to cut himself off even from what was permitted.

### CHAPTER 66.—That no one should return to secular military service after performing penance

[Col. 0999A]

(From a letter of Pope Leo, chapter 25.) It is wholly contrary to ecclesiastical regulations to return to secular military service after performing penance. Since the Apostle says, “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs,” whoever wishes to entangle himself in worldly military service is not free from the snares of the devil.

### CHAPTER 67.—Those who, abandoning their religious purpose, return to the world

(From the Council of Arles, chapter 3.) Those who, after undertaking holy religion, apostatize and return to the world, and afterward do not seek the remedies of penance, must not receive Communion without penance. We also order that they not be admitted to clerical office, and that no such person presume, after penance, to wear secular clothing. If he presumes to do so, he is to be regarded as alienated from the Church.

### CHAPTER 68.—That no religious or holy person is without sin

(From the sayings of Augustine.) No holy and true person is without sin; nevertheless, for this reason he does not cease to be just or holy, since he holds holiness in his intention. We do not acquire holiness by the powers of nature, but by the assistance of our purpose through God’s grace. Therefore all the saints rightly declare themselves sinners, because in truth they have something to lament—if not the reproach of conscience, then certainly the instability and changeability of a transgressing nature.

### CHAPTER 69.—That penitents ought to abstain from banquets and ornaments

[Col. 0999C]

(From a decree of Pope Lucius, chapter 5.) Penitents ought to abstain from banquets, ornaments, and white clothing; and those who are at enmity are to be expelled from the church until they return to peace.

### CHAPTER 70.—That a presbyter should not reconcile a penitent unless his bishop orders it

(From the African Council, chapter 30.) A presbyter must not reconcile a penitent without consulting the bishop, except when the bishop’s absence makes necessity compel it.

### CHAPTER 71.—That no one in ecclesiastical orders should receive the remedy of penance by the laying on of hands

[Col. 0999D]

(From a decree of Pope Leo to Rusticus, chapter 16.) It is foreign to ecclesiastical custom that those consecrated to the presbyteral dignity or the diaconal rank should receive, for some crime of theirs, the remedy of penance through the laying on of hands. This undoubtedly derives from apostolic tradition, according to what is written: “If a priest has sinned, who will pray for him?” Therefore such fallen persons must seek God’s mercy through private withdrawal. If their satisfaction is worthy, it will also be fruitful.

### CHAPTER 72.—That those in orders found guilty of grave sins should not receive the laying on of hands as lay penitents

(From the Council of Carthage, chapter 27.) It was likewise confirmed that, if presbyters or deacons should at any time be convicted of some other grave fault for which it is necessary to remove them from ministry, no laying on of hands should be performed upon them as penitents or as faithful laypeople, nor should those who have been rebaptized be permitted to advance to the clerical rank.

### CHAPTER 73.—Whether clerics who sin through bodily misconduct can be restored

(From a letter of Saint Isidore to Masson.) No diversity of decrees is to be understood in such judgments, where in one place it is read that, after penance, the rank of honor is to be restored following bodily misconduct, while elsewhere it is said that after such an offense the dignity of the former order is by no means to be restored. This difference is distinguished in the following way. The canon ordered those to return to their former offices whose satisfaction in penance, or worthy confession of their sins, had preceded it. But those who are not corrected by bodily vice, and who, with a kind of superstitious audacity, even strive, with a kind of superstitious audacity, to justify the very carnal offense they commit, are to receive neither the rank of honor nor the grace of Communion.

### CHAPTER 74.—Those who serve at God’s altar, if they suddenly fall through the grievous weakness of the flesh

(From the Council of Everdun, chapter 5.) If those who serve at God’s altar suddenly fall through the lamentable weakness of the flesh, and, with the Lord looking favorably upon them, perform worthy penance, so that, having mortified the body, they offer God the sacrifice of a contrite heart, it shall remain in the power of the bishop either not to suspend those who are truly afflicted for long, or to separate the negligent from the body of the Church for a longer period. They are nevertheless to resume their places in their offices in such a way that they cannot thereafter be promoted to higher offices. But if they return like dogs to their vomit and lie immersed like pigs in the mire, they are not only to lose the dignity of their office, but are also to receive holy Communion only at the end of life.

### CHAPTER 75.—That married persons ought to abstain from their wives during Lent

(From the Council of Elvira, chapter 5.) Whoever has intercourse with his wife during Lent before Easter and refuses to abstain from her shall do penance for one year, or shall give twenty-five solidi to the Church, or distribute them to the poor. If it happened through drunkenness and without habitual practice, he shall do penance for forty days.

### CHAPTER 76.—Those who presume to eat meat during the days of Lent

[Col. 1000D]

(From the Council of Toledo.) Whoever presumes to undertake the eating of meat during the days of Lent shall not only be guilty with respect to the Lord’s Resurrection but shall also be excluded from the holy Communion of that day. This shall be added to his punishment: throughout the cycle of that year he shall abstain from all eating of meat, because he forgot the discipline of abstinence on holy days.

### CHAPTER 77.—Of the brother whose sin is not unto death, and of sin unto death

(From the Epistle of John the Evangelist.) Whoever knows that his brother is committing a sin not unto death should ask for him, and God will give him life. If anyone sins unto death—because there is sin unto death—I do not say that anyone should pray for him.

### CHAPTER 78.—That it is difficult for one who sins grievously to remain in his rank

[Col. 1001A]

(From the sayings of Jerome.) Whoever does not preserve the dignity of a divine rank should be content to save his soul, for it is difficult to return to the rank in which he formerly stood.

### CHAPTER 79.—The same matter

(From the sayings of Bishop Basil.) Whoever sins while holding a rank ought to be excommunicated, because the dignity of this title is great. Nevertheless, after penance he can redeem his soul; but it is difficult to return to his former rank.

### CHAPTER 80.—The same matter

Whoever has fallen from his rank should, after penance, be content to baptize, to give Communion to the sick, and only to minister at the altar.

### CHAPTER 81.—The same matter

(From the sayings of Saint Isidore.) In the Gospel, Isidore identifies the overseer of Ephesus, that is, the priest, in accordance with Malachi, who says: “The lips of a priest guard knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts.” The lampstand is understood as the doctrine of the priest, or the honor of the authority that he bears. The priest’s lampstand—that is, the gifts of honor—is completely moved, according to John, when, after sins have been committed, the crimes are not mourned and penance is neglected. For he does not say, “Because you have fallen, I will move your lampstand,” but, “Unless you do penance, I will move your lampstand.”

### CHAPTER 82.—That the canonical discipline orders a penitent priest to return to his former state after seven years

[Col. 1001C]

(The same source.) The canonical discipline has ordered a penitent priest to return to his former state after seven years—not through the fulfillment of his own will, but rather according to the judgment of divine justice.
