And just as nothing is hidden from his wisdom, so his arrangement directs and governs everything. For no creature is hidden in his sight. [Col. 1028D–1029A]

### CHAPTER 40. — On the creation of the angels

(The same author.) “In the beginning God created heaven and earth and water from nothing.” While darkness still concealed the water itself and the earth hid the water, the angels and all the heavenly powers came into being, so that God’s goodness would not be idle but would have beings in whom he could display his goodness throughout the many ages beforehand. Thus this visible world was made and adorned from the things that had been created. [Col. 1029A]

### CHAPTER 41. — That nothing is incorporeal and invisible except God alone

(The same author.) Nothing in nature should be believed incorporeal and invisible except God alone. He is believed incorporeal because he is everywhere, fills all things, and holds them together. He is invisible to all creatures because he is incorporeal. [Col. 1029A]

### CHAPTER 42. — That every creature is corporeal

(The same author.) Every creature is corporeal: the angels and all the heavenly powers are corporeal, although they do not subsist in flesh. We believe intellectual natures to be corporeal because they are circumscribed locally, as is the human soul, which is enclosed in flesh, and the demons, who belong to the substance of angelic nature. [Col. 1029A–B]

### CHAPTER 43. — That all intellectual natures are immortal

(The same author.) We believe intellectual natures that lack flesh to be immortal, since they have nothing that can fall and require resurrection after its fall. [Col. 1029B]

### CHAPTER 44. — That the apostate angels possessed free choice before their fall

(Gregory, in his *Moralia*.) Each thing tends toward something else by as many steps as it is subject to movements of change. The only nature that cannot be comprehended does not know how to move from its state; it cannot be changed from what is always the same. For if the substance of the angels had been created by its Author with an unchangeable movement, it would never have fallen from the citadel of its blessedness.

Almighty God, however, wondrously created the nature of the highest spirits good but changeable, so that those who did not wish to remain might fall, while those who persisted in their condition would be all the more worthy in it because they stood by their own choice. They would thus become more deserving in God’s sight to the degree that they fixed the movement of their mutability through the steadfastness of their will. [Col. 1029B–C]

### CHAPTER 45. — Why the angelic spirits sinned irrevocably

(From the same work.) The angelic spirits sinned irrevocably for this reason: they were able to stand all the more firmly because the admixture of flesh did not hold them back. The human being, however, deserved forgiveness after guilt because through a fleshly body he received something by which he was inferior to himself. Hence, in the sight of the Judge, this very weakness of the flesh is an argument for compassion. [Col. 1029C–D]

### CHAPTER 46. — That guardian angels are placed over human beings

(Gregory says in his *Moralia*:) That angels preside over human beings is attested by the prophet through the angel’s words: “The prince of the kingdom of the Persians resisted me.” That angels are administered through the powers of higher angels is testified by the prophet Zechariah, who says: “Behold, the angel who was speaking with me was going out, and another angel was going out to meet him, and he said to him: Run, speak to this young man, saying: Jerusalem shall be inhabited without a wall.” [Col. 1029D–1030A]

### CHAPTER 47. — That individual angels are given as guardians to individual human beings

[Col. 1030A]

(From the sayings of someone in the *Life of the Fathers*.) Abba Paul the Simple had been granted the gift of seeing the old men who entered the church and, from their very faces, perceiving the thoughts of each one, whether they were evil or good.

When he came to the church and the old men entered, he saw them entering with radiant faces and joyful spirits, and their angels likewise with them in gladness. But he saw one man with a black and gloomy body, demons pulling him from both sides, a bridle fastened in his nostrils, and his holy angel following far behind him in sadness.

Blessed Paul began to weep most bitterly and beat his breast, sitting before the church because of the man he had seen in such a state. All the other old men, seeing him weeping in this way, began to ask him to enter the assembly with them if he had seen anything concerning them. He, however, refused to enter and continued to weep because of the man he had seen in this condition.

A short while later, when the assembly had ended and the people were leaving, he again looked carefully at everyone’s faces to see whether they were leaving as they had entered. He saw the man whom he had previously seen black and gloomy leaving the church with a radiant face and a bright body; the demons followed him at a distance, while his holy angel was near him, cheerful and rejoicing greatly over him. [Col. 1030A–B]

### CHAPTER 48. — That the right hand of God is the portion of the elect angels, while his left hand is the portion of the reprobate angels

(Gregory says in his *Moralia*:) What, then, does it mean that the army of heaven is said to stand at his right and left? God, who is within all things in such a way that he is also outside all things, is enclosed by neither right nor left. Rather, God’s right hand signifies the portion of the elect angels, while God’s left hand signifies the portion of the reprobate angels.

For it is not only the good who minister—those who help—but also the others who condemn; that is, not only those who raise up people returning from guilt, but also those who weigh down those unwilling to return. Nor should it be understood that the phrase “the army of heaven” cannot refer to the reprobate portion of the angels. We call the birds that we know to be suspended in the air “the birds of heaven.” Concerning these same spirits Paul says: “Against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places.” And, naming their leader, he says: “According to the prince of the power of this air.” [Col. 1030C–D]

Therefore the army of angels stands at God’s right and left, because the will of the elect spirits agrees with divine compassion, while the disposition of the reprobate, serving its own wickedness, obeys the judgment of his severity.

Hence a deceptive spirit is immediately described as springing forward among them, through whom King Ahab was deceived in accordance with his deserved punishment. For it is not right to believe that a good spirit wished to serve deceit by saying: “I will go out and be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.” But because King Ahab was worthy, through his preceding sins, to be condemned by such a deception, so that the one who had often fallen willingly into guilt might at some point be seized unwillingly for punishment by hidden justice, permission is given to the evil spirits. Those whom they willingly strangle in the snare of sin, they also drag unwillingly into the punishment of sin. [Col. 1030D–1031A]

Therefore, what is described there—that the army of heaven stood at God’s right and left—is represented here by the statement that Satan was present among the sons of God. Behold, angels stood at God’s right, those who are called the sons of God; behold, angels stood at his left, because Satan was also present among them. [Col. 1031A]

### CHAPTER 49. — That unclean spirits wander in the space between heaven and earth

(Gregory says in his *Moralia*:) We have already said shortly before why we also call them the birds of heaven. We know that the unclean spirits who fell from the ethereal heaven wander in the space between heaven and earth. They envy human hearts ascending to heavenly things all the more because they see themselves cast down from heavenly things through the impurity of their pride. [Col. 1031A–B]

### CHAPTER 50. — Whether peace is preserved in the heights

(From the same work.) In the midst of these matters, it is worth asking: if the highest peace is preserved in the heights, what does it mean that the angel says to Daniel: “I came because of your words, but the prince of the kingdom of Persia resisted me for twenty-one days; and behold, Michael, one of the chief princes, came first to help me”? And shortly afterward: “Now I shall return to fight against the prince of Persia. When I was going out, the prince of the Greeks appeared, coming.”

Who else does he call the princes of the nations except the angels who could resist him as he departed? What peace, then, can exist in the heights if even among the angelic spirits themselves, who always stand before the sight of truth, there is a struggle of combat?

But because particular angelic ministries have been assigned to govern particular nations, when the conduct of their subjects causes the assistance of the spirits placed over them to contend against one another, the spirits who preside are said to come against one another. The angel who spoke to Daniel is recognized as having authority over the captives of the Israelite people established in Persia; Michael, however, is found to be appointed over those who had remained from that same people in the land of Judea.

Hence the same angel shortly afterward says to Daniel: “There is no one who helps me in all these matters except Michael, your prince.” Concerning him he also says what we quoted above: “And behold, Michael, one of the chief princes, came first to help me.” Since he is said not to be present together with him but to come to his aid, it is plainly recognized that he was placed over the people who were being held captive in another region. [Col. 1031B–D]

### CHAPTER 51. — That the devil’s will is always unjust, but his power is never unjust

(From the same work.) It must be understood that Satan’s will is always unjust, but his power is never unjust, because he has his will from himself but his power from the Lord. What he himself desires to do unjustly, God permits to happen only justly.

Thus it is rightly said in the Books of Kings: “An evil spirit from the Lord rushed upon Saul.” Behold, the one and the same spirit is called both the Lord’s and evil: the Lord’s, namely, through the permission of just power; evil, through the desire of an unjust will.

Therefore he should not be feared, since he can do nothing except by permission. The only power that ought to be feared is that which, when it permits the enemy to rage, is served both by the exercise of its just judgment and by his unjust will.

He asks that his hand be extended a little, because it is external things that he seeks to crush. For Satan does not think that he has accomplished anything significant unless he wounds the soul, striking it so as to drive it back from that homeland. [Col. 1031D–1032A]

### CHAPTER 52. — That God speaks to the devil in four ways, and the devil to God in three ways
(Gregory, in his *Moralia*:) It should be understood that, as we learn in this passage, God speaks to the devil in four ways, and the devil to God in three. God speaks to the devil in four ways: he rebukes his unjust ways, sets before him the righteousness of his elect against him, permits him to test their innocence by granting him permission, and sometimes forbids him even to dare to tempt them.

He rebukes his unjust ways, as has already been said: “Where have you come from?” He sets before him the righteousness of his elect against him, as he says: “Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him upon the earth?” He permits him to test their innocence by granting him permission, as he says: “Behold, all that he has is in your hand.” Again, he prohibits him from tempting him when he says: “Only do not extend your hand against him.”

The devil, however, speaks to God in three ways: when he either makes his ways known, or accuses the innocence of the elect with fabricated charges, or asks that their same innocence be tested. He makes his ways known when he says: “I have gone around the earth and traversed it.” He accuses the innocence of the elect when he says: “Does Job fear God for nothing? Have you not fenced him in, and his house, and all his possessions on every side?” He asks that their same innocence be tested when he says: “Extend your hand and touch all that he possesses, unless he blesses you to your face.”

### CHAPTER 53 — That there is no palm of victory without the labor of combat

(From Gregory’s *Dialogues*.) Without the labor of combat there is no palm of victory. How, then, are they victorious, unless they have struggled against the snares of the ancient enemy? For the malignant spirit is always present at our thought, speech, and action, in case he should find something by which he might stand as an accuser at the judgment of the eternal Judge.

Would you like to know how he is always present in order to deceive? Some who are now with us bear witness to the matter I am about to relate. A man of venerable life, named Stephen, was a presbyter of the province of Valeria and was closely related by kinship to our deacon and steward of the church, Boniface. One day, having returned home from a journey, he spoke carelessly to his servant and ordered him, saying: “Come, devil, take off my shoes.”

At these words, the straps of his sandals immediately began to come undone with great speed, so that it plainly appeared that the one whom he had named—the devil—had obeyed him in removing his shoes. As soon as the presbyter saw this, he was overcome with great fear and began to cry out loudly: “Go away, wretch, go away! I was not speaking to you, but to my servant.”

At his words the devil immediately departed, so that the straps were found already loosened for the most part, though some remained fastened. From this incident it may be inferred how the ancient enemy, who is already present in bodily actions, assails our thoughts with exceedingly great snares.

### CHAPTER 54 — On the creation, nature, and ministry of the angels, and on the fall of the apostates

(Saint Isidore speaks thus in his book *On Ecclesiastical Offices*.) The name “angel” denotes an office, not a nature. According to their nature, they are called spirits. When they are sent from heaven to announce things to human beings, they are called angels from that very act of announcing. By nature they are spirits. They are called angels when they are sent.

The nature of angels is mutable, but everlasting love makes them incorruptible. We say that angels are immutable by grace, not by nature. For if they were immutable by nature, the devil certainly would not have fallen. The contemplation of the Creator therefore supports the mutability of their nature in them.

Thus the apostate angel was deprived of his status, because he wished to preserve his strength not from God but from himself. Angels were made before every other creature, when it was said: “Let there be light.” Scripture says of them: “Wisdom was created before all things.” They are called “lights” because they participate in the eternal Light; they are called “wise” because they cleave, as if kindled, to Wisdom. Although they are mutable by nature, divine contemplation does not permit them to change.

Angels were created before the whole creation of the world, and before the creation of all the angels the devil was formed, as it is written: “He is the beginning of the ways of God.” Hence, in comparison with the angels, he is called an archangel. He was created first in the order of precedence, not by a greater duration of time.

We know that the devil held primacy among the angels, and that from this confidence he fell, so that he slipped without restoration. The prophet announces the excellence of this preeminence in these words: “The cedars were not higher than he in the paradise of God; the fir trees did not equal his summit. No tree of paradise was likened to him, because God made him more beautiful.”

The condition of an angel differs from the condition of a human being. The human being was created in the likeness of God. But the archangel who fell was called the seal of God’s likeness, as the Lord testifies through Ezekiel: “You were the seal of likeness to God, full of wisdom, perfect in beauty; you were in the delights of the paradise of God.” For the more subtle his nature was, the more fully was he formed in the likeness of divine truth.

It is clear that the devil fell from heaven before the human being was created. For as soon as he was made, he burst into pride and was hurled down from heaven. According to the testimony of Truth, he was a liar from the beginning and did not stand in the truth, because as soon as he was made, he fell. He was indeed created in the truth, but because he did not stand, he immediately fell from the truth.

By one fall of pride, when through arrogance they compared themselves with God, both the human being and the devil fell. But the human being returned to repentance when he recognized himself to be inferior. The devil, however, was not content merely to have fallen because he considered himself equal to God; moreover, he declares himself superior to God, according to the apostle’s words concerning Antichrist: “He opposes and exalts himself above everything that is called God or worshiped.”

The devil will no longer ask forgiveness because he is not moved to repentance. His members, however, often ask forgiveness through hypocrisy, though on account of their evil conscience they do not deserve to obtain it.

Let human misery learn why God is more readily moved to grant forgiveness: because he has compassion on the weak human being. The human being drew the weakness of sin from the lower part of his constitution, that is, from the flesh, by which the enclosed soul is held.

The apostate angels have no forgiveness because they were not burdened by any weakness of bodily frailty when they sinned. Human beings, however, return to forgiveness after sin because from their material origin of clay they have drawn the burden of weakness. Therefore, on account of the weakness of the fleshly condition, the way back to salvation remains open to the human being. As the Psalm also says: “He himself knows our formation”; and again: “Remember, Lord, that we are dust”; and elsewhere: “Remember,” he says, “what my substance is.”

After the apostate angels fell, the others were strengthened in the permanence of eternal blessedness. Hence, after the creation of heaven, the words are repeated at the beginning: “Let there be a firmament,” and the firmament was called heaven. This clearly shows that after the ruin of the angels those who remained acquired the firmness of eternal perseverance and blessedness, which previously they had received in lesser measure.

After the devil’s expulsion, the holy angels were granted the perseverance of holiness and the blessedness that they had previously possessed in lesser measure. Thus it must be understood that the wickedness of the evil serves the humility of the saints: for from the place where the wicked fall, the good advance.

The number of the good angels, diminished after the fall of the evil angels, will be made up from the number of all the elect. That number is known to God alone.

Among the angels there are distinctions of powers, and ministries have been distributed among them according to the dignity of their ranks. Some are placed over others both in the height of power and in knowledge of virtue. Thus some serve the commands of others and obey their orders. Hence, in the book of Zechariah, one angel sends another angel and commands him what he must announce.

Holy Scripture testifies that there are nine distinctions or orders of angels: angels, archangels, thrones, dominions, virtues, principalities, powers, cherubim, and seraphim.

The prophet Ezekiel also describes the number of these orders under the corresponding names of precious stones when he speaks of the apostate angel’s preeminence: “Every stone of your covering was sardius, topaz, jasper, chrysolite, onyx, beryl, sapphire, carbuncle, and emerald.” By this number of stones the orders of the angels are signified.

Before his fall, the apostate angel had these orders, as it were, affixed to him as the ornaments of his garment. When he saw himself brighter than all of them, he immediately swelled with pride and lifted his heart to arrogance.

The angels always rejoice in God, not in themselves. The devil is evil for this reason: he sought not the things of God but his own things. There is no greater iniquity than for anyone to wish to glory not in God but in himself.

The angels of God know all things before they come to pass in reality; and things that among human beings are still future, the angels already know because God reveals them.

The transgressing angels, even after losing holiness, nevertheless did not lose the living perception proper to the angelic creature. For they are powerful in the acuity of foreknowledge in three ways: through the subtlety of their nature, through experience of times, and through revelation by higher powers.

Whenever God is angered with this world by any scourge, apostate angels are sent to carry out vengeance. Yet they are restrained by divine power, lest they do as much harm as they desire.

The good angels, however, are assigned to the ministry of human salvation, so that they administer the concerns of the world and govern all things by God’s command, as the Apostle testifies: “Are they not all ministering spirits, sent for service on behalf of those who are to inherit salvation?”

Angels take from the upper air the bodies in which they appear to human beings, and they assume a solid form from the heavenly element, by which they make themselves more clearly visible to human eyes.

It is believed that individual nations have angels appointed over them. This is shown by the testimony of the angel speaking to Daniel: “I came,” he says, “to announce this to you, but the prince of the kingdom of Persia resisted me.” And later: “No one helps me against them except Michael, your prince.”

It is also established that all human beings have angels, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Amen, I say to you, their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven.” Hence, in the Acts of the Apostles, when Peter was knocking at the door, the apostles inside said: “It is not Peter, but his angel.”

If angels contemplate and see God, why does the apostle Peter say: “Into whom the angels of God desire to look”? Again, if they do not contemplate or see him, how can the Lord’s statement be true: “Their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven”?

Both statements are rightly true. For we truly believe that the angels both see God and desire to see him; they both possess him and hasten to possess him; they both love him and strive to love him.

If they desire to see him in such a way that they do not enjoy the fulfillment of their desire, that desire entails need, and that need is punitive. But every punishment is far from the blessed angels, since punishment and blessedness never coexist.

Again, if we say that they are satisfied by the vision of God, satisfaction ordinarily produces weariness, and we know that they cannot grow weary of the vision of God, which they both desire and possess. What, then, remains except that we believe both things together in a wondrous manner: that they desire and are satisfied?

They desire without labor and are satisfied without weariness. So that desire may not be need, they are satisfied while desiring. And again, so that satisfaction may not be weariness, they desire to be satisfied.

The angels see the face of the Father through satisfaction; but because this satisfaction knows no weariness, they always desire to look upon him in it. Wherever in the holy Scriptures an angel is put in place of God, it is not the Father or the Holy Spirit who is understood, but the Son alone, in accordance with the dispensation of the Incarnation.

Before the coming of the Lord’s Incarnation, there was discord between angels and human beings. But when Christ came, he made peace in himself between angels and human beings. At his birth the angels cried out on earth: “Peace to human beings of good will.”

Through Christ’s Incarnation, therefore, not only was the human being reconciled to God, but peace between angels and human beings was also restored.

The existence of discord between angels and human beings before Christ’s coming is recognized especially from this: when angels were greeted by human beings in the Old Testament, they disdained to return their greeting. But when this was done by John in the New Testament, the angel not only reverently accepted it; he even forbade him to do it.

In the Old Testament the human being is thus despised and is not greeted in return by the angel, because the human being had not yet passed into God. But the human being is received by God and reverently greeted by the angel. For the angel is read to have greeted Mary, and when John greeted the angel, the same angel said to him: “See that you do not do this, for I am your fellow servant and the fellow servant of your brothers.”

From this it is recognized that through the Lord’s Incarnation peace was given back to human beings and to angels.

### CHAPTER 55 — That the number of the citizens above is both finite and infinite

(Gregory, in his *Moralia*.) The number of the citizens above is expressed as both infinite and defined, so that what is numerable to God may be shown to be innumerable to us. Yet it is one thing to attend and another to minister.

Those powers unquestionably attend who do not go out to announce certain things to human beings. Those minister who come to fulfill the duties of messengers, although they too do not withdraw from the innermost contemplation. And because those who minister are more numerous than those who principally attend, the number of those who attend is shown as if defined, while that of those who minister is shown as infinite.

We rightly call the angelic spirits the soldiers of God, because we know that they battle against the powers of the air. Yet they carry out these battles not through labor but by command, because whatever they desire to accomplish against unclean spirits, they are able to do through the help of him who governs all things.

### CHAPTER 56 — That every fault is absolved before death by the gift of the offering

[Col. 1036D]

(From Gregory’s *Dialogues*.) Nor do I think this should be passed over in silence: I recall what occurred in my monastery three years ago. A certain monk named Justus, trained in the art of medicine, was accustomed, while I was established in that monastery, to attend me diligently and to keep watch during my continual illnesses. He was overtaken by bodily sickness and brought to his end. In this affliction he was attended by his own brother, named Copiosus, who even now in this city earns the livelihood of this temporal life by the same medical art.

When the aforementioned Justus knew that he had reached his end, he revealed to his brother Copiosus that he had three gold coins concealed [Col. 1037A]. This could not, of course, be hidden from the brethren; carefully investigating and searching all his medicines, they found the three gold coins hidden in a medicinal preparation. As soon as this was reported to me, I could not bear with equanimity so great an evil in a brother who had lived with us in common; for it had always been the rule of that monastery that all the brethren should live in common, so that none of them might be permitted to have anything of his own.

Then, struck by excessive grief, I began to consider both what I should do for the purification of the dying man and what provision I should make for the example of the living brethren. Therefore, having summoned to me Preciosus, the superior of that monastery, I said: “Go, and let none of the brethren join himself to that dying man; nor let him receive a word of consolation from the mouth of any of them. But when, lying at death, he asks for the brethren, let his own fleshly brother tell him that he is abhorred by all the brethren because of the coins he kept secretly, so that at least in death bitterness may pierce his mind because of his fault and cleanse him from the sin he committed.

“But when he has died, do not lay his body with the bodies of the brethren. Instead, make a grave for him anywhere in the dung-heap, throw his body into it, and cast over him there the three gold coins which he left, all crying together: ‘May your money be with you unto perdition’; and then cover him with earth.” In these two measures I wished one to benefit the dying man and the other the living brethren: that the bitterness of death might make him free from guilt, and that so great a condemnation of avarice might prevent them from being implicated in that fault.

This was done. For when he came to death and anxiously sought to commend himself to the brethren, and none of the brethren deigned to approach or speak to him, his fleshly brother told him why he was abhorred by all. He immediately groaned deeply over his guilt and departed from the body in that sorrow. He was buried as I said. But all the brethren, disturbed by the same sentence, began one by one to bring forth to the common stock every last and trifling thing which they had always been regularly permitted to possess, and they greatly feared lest they might have anything in their possession for which they could be reproved.

When thirty days after his death had elapsed, my heart began to have compassion on the dead brother, to weigh his punishments with grievous sorrow, and to seek some remedy for his deliverance. Then I summoned to me Preciosus, the superior of our monastery, and said sadly: “It is a long time since that brother who died has been suffering in fire. We ought to bestow some charity upon him and help him, insofar as we can, to be delivered. Go, therefore, and from this day for thirty consecutive days take care to offer sacrifice for him; and let no day at all be omitted on which the saving Victim is not immolated for his absolution.” He immediately departed and obeyed.

While we were occupied with other concerns and were not counting the days that had elapsed, that same dead brother appeared by night in a vision to his own brother Copiosus. When Copiosus saw him, he asked: “What is it, brother? How are you?” He replied: “Until now I was badly off; now I am well, because today I received communion.” Copiosus went at once and told this to the brethren in the monastery. The brethren carefully counted the days and found that it was the day on which the thirtieth offering had been completed for him. Since Copiosus did not know what the brethren were doing for him, and the brethren did not know what Copiosus had seen concerning him, when at one and the same time he learned what they did not know, and they learned what he had seen, the vision and the sacrifice agreed together. The matter was made plain: through the saving Victim, the brother who had died escaped punishment.

### CHAPTER 57 — That the sacred offering can benefit souls after death, if their sins are not indissoluble

[Col. 1038B]

(From Gregory’s *Dialogues*.) If sins are not indissoluble after death, the sacred offering of the saving Victim is accustomed to help many souls even after death, so that sometimes the souls of the dead themselves seem to request it. For the aforementioned Bishop Felix asserts that he learned from a presbyter of venerable life, who lived until two years ago, dwelt in the diocese of the city of Centumcellae, and presided over the church of Saint John situated in the place called Tauriana, that this presbyter was accustomed to bathe, whenever bodily need required it, in a place where hot waters produce abundant vapours.

On entering there one day, he found an unknown man ready to serve him, to remove his shoes from his feet, receive his garments, provide him with towels as he came out from the heat [Col. 1038C], and perform every service with great attentiveness. After this had happened frequently, the presbyter, going to the baths one day, thought within himself: “I ought not to appear ungrateful to the man who so devotedly attends me whenever I bathe; I must bring him something as a gift.” Then he took with him two loaves of the offering.

As soon as he reached the place, he found the man and, as usual, made use of his service in every respect. He bathed; and when, now dressed, he wished to leave, he offered to the man attending him what he had brought with him as a blessing, asking him kindly to accept what he offered through charity. The man replied sadly and sorrowfully: “Why do you give these things to me, Father? This bread is holy, and I cannot eat it. For I whom you see was once the master of this place, but because of my sins I was assigned here after death. If you wish to help me, offer this bread for me to almighty God, that you may intercede for my sins; and then know that you have been heard when you come here to bathe and do not find me.”

At these words he disappeared; and by vanishing, the one who seemed to be a man made known that he was a spirit. The presbyter afflicted himself for him in tears throughout a whole week, offered the saving Victim daily, and afterward returned to the bath, where he did not find him. From this it is shown how greatly the immolation of the sacred offering benefits souls, when the spirits of the dead themselves request it from the living and indicate by signs that they appear to have been absolved through it.

### CHAPTER 58 — That it is more blessed for each person to depart free from here than to seek freedom after death

(Gregory says in his *Dialogues*:) It is shown to all that, if sins are indissoluble, even for the dead the Victim of the sacred offering can be of no benefit toward absolution. But it must be known that the sacred Victim benefits those dead persons who, while living here, obtained that the good things done here by others for them might help them even after death. Meanwhile, it must be considered that the safer course is for each person himself while living to do the good which he hopes will be done after death by others. For it is more blessed to depart free than to seek freedom after bonds.

### CHAPTER 59 — That no one ought to pray for a sin that is unto death

[Col. 1039B]

(Gregory, in his *Moralia*.) A sin is carried even to hell when it is not amended before the end of this present life by correction and repentance. Concerning this sin John says: “There is a sin unto death; I do not say that anyone should pray for it.” A sin is unto death because forgiveness for a sin not corrected here is sought in vain. Of this it is further said: “Let mercy forget him.” The mercy of almighty God is said to forget the person who has forgotten the justice of almighty God. Whoever does not now fear him as just will not afterward be able to find him merciful.

### CHAPTER 60 — That all souls of the elect should be believed to be in heaven, and souls of the wicked in hell

[Col. 1039C]

(From Gregory’s *Dialogues*. Peter asks; Gregory replies.) I see that my inquiry has now been answered sufficiently, but there is still something that troubles my mind with a question. Since it was said above that the souls of the saints are already in heaven, it surely remains that the souls of the wicked too are to be believed to be nowhere but in hell; and I do not know what truth holds concerning this matter. For human estimation does not admit that the souls of sinners can be tormented before judgment.

“If you have believed, on the satisfactory authority of sacred utterance, that the souls of saints are in heaven, you must in every respect believe that the souls of the wicked are in hell. For by the recompense of eternal justice, through which the righteous already rejoice, it is necessary in every respect that the unrighteous be tormented. For just as blessedness gladdens the elect, so it must be believed that from the day of their departure fire burns the reprobate.” [Col. 1039D]

### CHAPTER 61 — That, as there is no end to the joy of the good, so there is no end to the torments of the wicked

(From Gregory’s *Dialogues*. Peter asks; Gregory replies.) “Do we then, I ask you, say that those who have once been plunged there will burn forever?”

“It is altogether certain and unquestionably true: just as there is no end to the joy of the good, so there is no end to the torments of the wicked. For when Truth says, ‘These shall go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life,’ because what God promised is true, what he threatened will undoubtedly not be false.”

### CHAPTER 62 — That it is not as some maintain: that God threatened eternal punishment to sinners in order to correct them from evil

[Col. 1040A]

(From Gregory’s *Dialogues*. Peter asks; Gregory replies.) “What if someone says that God threatened eternal punishment to sinners in order to restrain them from committing sins?”

“If what he threatened is false, so that he might correct them from injustice, then what he promised is also false, so that he might call them to righteousness. But who, even if mad, would presume to say this? And if he threatened what he was not going to fulfil, then while we wish to affirm him merciful, we are compelled—an impious thing to say—to proclaim him deceitful.”

### CHAPTER 63 — Why sins committed with an end are punished without end

(From the same. Peter asks; Gregory replies.) “I should like to know how it is just that a fault committed with an end should be punished without end.”

“This would rightly be said if the strict Judge weighed not human hearts but deeds. The wicked sinned with an end because they lived with an end. For assuredly, if they could, they would have wished to live without end, so that they might be able to sin without end. They show that they always wish to live in sin, since they never cease to sin while they live. Therefore it belongs to the great justice of the Judge that those who in this life never wished to be without sin should never be without punishment.” [Col. 1040B]

### CHAPTER 64 — That God is merciful and does not feed on the torment of the wretched, but is just and therefore is not sated forever by vengeance on the wicked

(From the same. Peter asks; Gregory replies.) “But no just person feeds on cruelty, and a sinning servant is ordered to be beaten by a just master in order that he may be corrected from wickedness. For he is beaten for this purpose, that he ought to amend himself. But if the wicked handed over to the fire of Gehenna are never brought to correction, to what end will they burn forever?”

“Because almighty God is merciful, he does not feed on the torment of the wretched; but because he is just, he is not sated forever by vengeance on the wicked. Yet all the wicked assigned to eternal punishment are indeed punished for their own wickedness, and nevertheless they will burn for something: namely, so that all the righteous may both see in God the joys which they receive and behold in the wicked the punishments which they escaped, so that they may know themselves to be debtors to divine grace all the more eternally, the more eternally they see the evils punished which they overcame with his help.” [Col. 1040C–D]

### CHAPTER 65 — Whether, before the restoration of their bodies, the souls of the righteous are received into heaven

(From the same. Peter asks; Gregory replies.) “What you say pleases me; but I should like to know whether now, before the restoration of bodies, the souls of the righteous can be received into heaven.”

“We can neither affirm this of all the righteous nor deny it of all. For there are souls of certain righteous persons that are delayed from the heavenly kingdom in certain dwelling places. What else is indicated by the loss involved in this delay except that they had something less than perfect righteousness? Nevertheless, it is clearer than light that the souls of perfect righteous persons are received into heavenly seats as soon as they leave the prison of this flesh. Truth itself bears witness to this, saying: ‘Wherever the body is, there the eagles will be gathered’; for where our Redeemer himself is in body, there also the souls of the righteous are undoubtedly gathered.

“And Paul desires to be dissolved and to be with Christ. Therefore one who does not doubt that Christ is in heaven does not deny that Paul’s soul is in heaven. He also says concerning the dissolution of his body and the dwelling-place of the heavenly homeland: ‘We know that if our earthly house of this habitation is dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands but eternal in heaven.’” [Col. 1041A]

### CHAPTER 66 — That on the day of judgment the righteous will rejoice in the glory of both soul and body

(From the same. Peter asks; Gregory replies.) “If, therefore, the souls of the righteous are now in heaven, what is it that they receive on the day of judgment as the recompense for their righteousness?”

“In them, of course, this increases at judgment: now they enjoy the blessedness of souls alone, but afterwards also that of bodies, so that they may rejoice in the very flesh in which they bore pains and torments for the Lord. For this twofold glory it is written: ‘In their land they shall possess double.’ Hence also, concerning the souls of the saints before the day of resurrection, it is written: ‘To each of them white robes were given, and they were told to rest yet a little while, until the number of their fellow servants and brethren should be fulfilled.’ Those, therefore, who now have received single robes will have two robes at judgment, because now their condition concerns souls alone, but then they will rejoice in the glory of souls and bodies together.” [Col. 1041B–C]

### CHAPTER 67 — Whether the good recognize the good in the kingdom, and the wicked the wicked in punishment

(From the same. Peter asks; Gregory replies.) “I should like to know whether the good recognize the good in the kingdom, and the wicked the wicked in punishments.”

“The answer to this question is displayed more clearly than light in the Lord’s words which we have already set forth above. When it had been said: ‘There was a certain rich man, clothed in purple and fine linen, who feasted splendidly every day; and there was a certain beggar named Lazarus, lying at his gate full of sores, desiring to be filled with the crumbs that fell from the rich man’s table, and no one gave him any; but dogs also came and licked his sores,’ it was added that Lazarus died and was carried by angels into Abraham’s bosom, while the rich man died and was buried in hell.

“Lifting up his eyes while he was in torments, he saw Abraham afar off and Lazarus in his bosom. He cried out: ‘Father Abraham, have mercy on me and send Lazarus, that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue.’ Abraham said to him: ‘Son, remember that you received good things in your lifetime, and Lazarus likewise evil things.’ The rich man, now having no hope of salvation for himself, turns to securing the salvation of his own people, saying: ‘I ask you, father, to send him to my father’s house, for I have five brothers, that he may testify to them, lest they also come into this place of torments.’

“By these words it is plainly declared that both the good recognize the good and the wicked recognize the wicked. For if Abraham had not recognized Lazarus, he would not have spoken to the rich man in torments about Lazarus’s past affliction, saying that he had received evil things in his lifetime. And if the wicked did not recognize the wicked, the rich man in torments would not have remembered even his absent brothers. For how could he be unable to recognize those who were present when he took care to pray even in remembrance of those absent?

“In this matter, something also is shown which you did not ask: both the good recognize the wicked, and the wicked know the good. For the rich man is recognized by Abraham when it is said, ‘Remember that you received good things in your lifetime’; and the elect Lazarus is recognized by the reprobate rich man, who asks that he be sent by name, saying, ‘Send Lazarus, that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue.’ In this recognition, the measure of recompense for each party increases: the good rejoice more because they see those whom they loved rejoicing with them; and the wicked, while they are tormented with those whom in this world they loved despite God, are consumed not only by their own punishment but also by theirs.

“Yet something more wonderful happens in the elect: they not only recognize those whom they knew in this world, but they recognize as though seen and known the good whom they never saw. For when they see the ancient fathers in that eternal inheritance, those whom they always knew in their deeds will not be unknown to them through sight. For since all there behold God in a common brightness, what can they not know there, where they know him who knows all things? [Col. 1042C]

“A certain man among us, venerable in life, very religious and praiseworthy, died three years ago. As other religious persons who were present testified, at the hour of his departure he began to see the prophet Jonah, and Ezekiel and Daniel as well. Saying that they had come to him and lowering his eyes in reverent service to them, he was taken from the flesh. From this it is plainly understood what knowledge there will be in that incorruptible life, if this man, still placed in corruptible flesh, recognized the holy prophets whom he certainly had never seen.

“It also frequently happens that a departing soul recognizes those with whom it is to be assigned to one dwelling place because of equality either of sins or even of rewards; this many see at their departure, who will be equals either in the kingdom or in punishment.” [Col. 1042D]

### CHAPTER 68 — Whether purgatorial fire should be believed to exist, which after death purges souls from sins
(From the same work. Peter’s question and Gregory’s answer.)

I should like to learn whether a purgatorial fire is to be believed to exist after death.

In the Gospel the Lord says: “Walk while you have the light.” Through the prophet he also says: “In an acceptable time I heard you, and on the day of salvation I helped you.” The apostle Paul, explaining this, said: “Behold, now is the acceptable time,” and so forth. Solomon likewise says: “Whatever your hand is able to do, perform it diligently, for there is neither work, nor reasoning, nor knowledge, nor wisdom in the underworld, where you are hastening.” David also says: “For his mercy endures forever.” From these statements it is plainly established that each person appears at judgment in the condition in which he departs from this life.

Nevertheless, it is to be believed that before the judgment there is a purgatorial fire for certain minor faults, since the Truth says that “if anyone speaks blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, it will not be forgiven him, either in this age or in the age to come.” In this statement it is understood that certain faults can be forgiven in this age and others in the future. For when forgiveness is denied in one case, it follows plainly that it is granted in certain others.

Yet, as I have said, this must be understood of small and very minor sins: such as habitual idle talk, immoderate laughter, or the sin involved in managing one’s household affairs—things that are scarcely done without fault even by those who know how faults ought to be avoided—or an error of ignorance in matters that are not grave. All these things continue to burden a person after death if they have not been forgiven while he still lived in this life.

For when Paul says that Christ is the foundation and adds: “If anyone builds upon this foundation with gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, or stubble, each one’s work will be revealed by fire; if anyone’s work is burned, he will suffer loss, but he himself will be saved, yet as through fire”—although this may be understood of the fire of tribulation imposed upon us in the present life—nevertheless, if anyone takes these words as referring to the fire of future purification, it must be considered carefully. He said that the person who builds with wood, hay, and stubble can be saved through fire, not the one who builds upon this foundation with iron, bronze, or lead—that is, greater and therefore harsher sins, already insoluble at that time—but with wood, hay, and stubble, that is, the smallest and lightest sins, which the fire easily consumes.

This, however, must be known: even there no one will obtain any purification, not even from the smallest faults, unless he has earned it through good works while he is still living in this life, so that he may obtain it there.

### Chapter 69 — That there is one fire of Gehenna, but that it does not torment everyone in the same way

(From the same work. Peter’s question and Gregory’s answer.)

I ask you: Is one fire of Gehenna to be believed to exist, or should as many fires be thought to have been prepared as there are varieties of sins?

There is indeed one fire of Gehenna, but it does not torment all sinners in the same way. Each person will feel there as much punishment as his guilt requires. For just as many people stand beneath one sun in this world, yet do not feel the heat of that same sun equally—one burns more intensely and another less—so there is not one uniform mode of burning in that one fire. What bodily differences accomplish here, differences of sins accomplish there: they have a fire that is not different in kind, yet it burns each of them differently.

### Chapter 70 — How many kinds of offering are to be made for the dead

(From the sayings of Augustine.)

There are four kinds of offering. For the very good, there are thanksgivings: that is, thanks are given to God because they lived well. For those who were not very good, offerings are made so that complete forgiveness may be granted. For those who were not very evil, propitiations are made so that their damnation may become more tolerable. For the very evil, such offerings are not aids to the dead, but only consolations for the living.

### Chapter 71 — Why the souls of the saints do not pray for their enemies when they see them burning in eternal fire

(From the same work. Peter’s question and Gregory’s answer.)

Where, then, is their holiness, if they will not pray for their enemies when they see them burning there?

They were certainly told: “Pray for your enemies.” They pray for their enemies at the time when they are able to turn their hearts toward fruitful repentance and save them through that conversion. For what else should be prayed for concerning one’s enemies than what the Apostle says: “That God may grant them repentance for the acknowledgment of the truth, and that they may recover from the snare of the devil, by whom they are held captive for his will”?

But how will anyone then pray for those who can no longer in any way be changed from iniquity to works of righteousness? The reason, therefore, why prayer is not then offered for those condemned to eternal fire is the same reason that even now prayer is not offered for the devil and his angels, who have been assigned to eternal punishment.

For the same reason holy people do not now pray for human beings who have died unbelieving and ungodly: they refuse to have the merit of their prayer annulled before the sight of the just Judge on behalf of those whom they already know to have been assigned to eternal punishment.

If even now the righteous who are living do not pity unjust people who have died condemned, although they themselves know that they are still undergoing in their flesh something subject to judgment, how much more strictly will they then regard the torments of the wicked, when, stripped of all corruption of life, they will cleave more closely and firmly to justice itself?

For their minds are so absorbed by the right of strict judgment, through their adherence to the most just Judge, that they have no desire at all for anything that differs from the subtle exactness of his eternal rule.

### Chapter 72 — That, just as life is spoken of in two ways, death also is to be understood in two ways

(From the same work. Peter’s question and Gregory’s answer.)

There is no longer anything that ought to be answered against the evident reasoning. But this question now troubles my mind: how can the soul be called immortal when it is clear that it dies in perpetual fire?

Because life is spoken of in two ways, death also must be understood in two ways. One thing is that we live in God, and another is that we live in the fact that we have been formed or created. In other words, one thing is living blessedly, and another is living essentially.

The soul, therefore, is understood to be both mortal and immortal. It is mortal because it loses blessed life; but it is immortal because it never ceases to live essentially. It cannot lose the life belonging to its nature, not even when it has been condemned to perpetual death. There it will lose blessedness, but it will not lose existence. Consequently, it is always compelled to suffer both death without dying, and being dead without one who has died, and an end without an end.

### Chapter 73 — That the elect and the reprobate are led, amid torments, to common places

(From the same work. Peter’s question.)

Even if examples were lacking, the words of the Truth would satisfy us concerning the fact that both the elect and the reprobate, whose condition in their works has been similar, are led to common places.

The Truth itself says in the Gospel, for the sake of the elect: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places.” If there were no difference in the eternal blessedness of their rewards, there would be one dwelling place rather than many. There are therefore many dwelling places, in which distinct orders of the good rejoice together on account of their fellowship in merit; yet all the laborers receive one denarius, which is distributed among many dwelling places, because the blessedness they receive there is one, while the quality of their reward differs according to the diversity of their works.

The Truth, announcing the day of his judgment, also says: “Then I will say to the reapers: Gather the weeds and bind them into bundles to burn.” The reapers are the angels. They bind the weeds into bundles for burning when they join those who are alike with their counterparts in similar torments, so that the proud burn with the proud, the lustful with the lustful, the greedy with the greedy, the deceitful with the deceitful, the envious with the envious, and the unbelieving with the unbelieving.

When, therefore, those who are alike in guilt are brought to similar torments, the angels who assign them to places of punishment bind them, as it were, into bundles of weeds for burning.

### Chapter 74 — That there are many dwelling places in the house of God

(Gregory says in his *Moralia*:)

In the Gospel the Truth says: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places.” Yet in those many dwelling places there will in some manner be a harmonious diversity of rewards, because such power exists in that peace which joins us together that each person rejoices in having received in another what he himself has not received.

Thus, although they did not labor equally in the vineyard, all alike receive the denarius. There are indeed many dwelling places with the Father, and yet laborers of unequal merit receive the same denarius, because there will be one blessedness of joy for all, although the exaltation of life will not be the same for everyone.

### Chapter 75 — That the one whom guilt once drags to punishment is not afterward brought back to pardon by mercy

(Gregory says in his *Moralia*:)

“As a cloud is consumed and passes away, so the one who descends to the underworld does not ascend.” A cloud is lifted to higher places, but when it has become dense it is driven by the wind so that it runs; it is dispersed by the heat of the sun so that it vanishes.

Such, indeed, are human hearts. Through the intellect received from reason they rise to higher things; but when driven by the breath of an evil spirit, they are dragged here and there by the movements of their perverse desires. Yet under the strict scrutiny of the heavenly Judge, they melt as if under the sun’s heat, and, once handed over to places of punishment, they do not return again to the exercise of action.

The holy man, expressing the rise and decline of the human race, says: “As a cloud is consumed and passes away, so the one who descends to the underworld does not ascend.” It is as though he were saying openly: “The one who advances toward destruction through pride fails while running upward.” Once guilt has dragged him to punishment, mercy does not afterward bring him back to pardon.

### Chapter 76 — That God is called jealous, angry, repentant, merciful, and foreknowing

[Column 1046A]

(Gregory says in his *Moralia*:)

How, then, is God jealous, since he is touched by no mental anguish in guarding our chastity? How is he angry, since he is moved by no disturbance of spirit in punishing our vices? How is he repentant, since he does not at all regret having done what he once did? How does he have mercy, since he does not have a sorrowful heart? How is he foreknowing, when only things that are going to happen can be foreknown?

And we know that nothing is future for God, before whose eyes past things are not absent, present things do not pass away, and future things do not arrive. Whatever was or will be for us is present in his sight; and everything that is present can be known rather than foreknown.

Yet he is called jealous, angry, repentant, merciful, and foreknowing. Because he guards the chastity of each soul, he is called jealous in human terms, although he is not touched by mental anguish. Because he strikes down faults, he is said to be angry, although he is moved by no disturbance of mind. Because he himself is unchangeable yet changes what he wills, he is said to repent, although he changes the matter and not his plan.

When he comes to the aid of our misery, he is called merciful, although he helps the miserable without ever becoming himself a sorrowful heart. And because he sees the things that will be future for us, although they are always present to him alone, he is called foreknowing, although he does not foresee as future what he sees as present.

### Chapter 77 — Why God permits his elect to die in such a way that their holiness is not displayed during their lifetime

[Column 1046C]

(From the same work. Peter’s question and Gregory’s answer.)

What is this, I ask you: the almighty God permits those whom he will not allow to remain hidden after death, when their holiness will be revealed, to die in such a way? For it is written: “Whatever death overtakes the righteous, his righteousness will not be taken away from him.”

The elect, who are undoubtedly moving toward eternal life—what harm does it do them if they die painfully for a short while? And perhaps there is sometimes some fault of theirs, though a very small one, which ought to be cut away in that same death.

Thus it happens that the reprobate receive power against the living, but when those people are dying, what is more gravely avenged upon the reprobate is that they received power for their cruelty against the good. So the same executioner who was permitted to strike the venerable deacon while he was alive was not permitted to rejoice over him when he was dead.

The sacred writings also testify to this. For the man of God sent against Samaria ate on the way through disobedience, and a lion killed him on that same journey. But immediately it is written there: “The lion stood beside the donkey and did not eat from the corpse.”

From this it is shown that the sin of disobedience was forgiven in death itself, because the same lion that dared to kill him while alive did not dare to touch him once killed. The one who had permission to kill did not receive permission to eat from the corpse of the slain, because the man who had been guilty in life, his disobedience having been punished, was already righteous through death.

The lion, therefore, which first killed the sinner’s life afterward guarded the corpse of the righteous.

### Chapter 78 — That for the wretched there is death without death

(Gregory says in his *Moralia*:)

For the wretched there is death without death, and an end without ending: death lives, the end always begins, and the dead do not know how to come to an end. Thus death destroys but does not extinguish; pain torments but does not in any way dispel fear; the flame burns but does not at all drive away the darkness.

### Chapter 79 — That in the underworld the fire does not shine for the consolation of sinners, but shines in order to torment them more

(Gregory says in his *Moralia*:)

Although the fire there does not shine for consolation, nevertheless it shines for a purpose, so that it may torment them more. For the reprobate will see, with the flame illuminating their torment, all their followers with whom they sinned, those whose love led them into wrongdoing. Thus those whose life they loved carnally, against the commands of the Creator, will afflict them by their destruction as well, increasing their damnation.

### Chapter 80 — On the same subject

(Gregory says in his *Moralia*:)

Just as fire knows how to burn for the elect as a consolation, yet does not know how to burn as punishment, so, conversely, the flame of Gehenna neither shines for the reprobate as a gracious consolation nor fails to shine for their punishment. It will shine for the eyes of the condemned as punishment, with no charity, and will show how they are tormented, increasing their pain.

What is surprising if we believe that the fire of Gehenna contains punishment together with both darkness and light? We know this by experience, because even now a harsh flame shines obscurely. Then the devouring flame will burn those whom carnal pleasure now pollutes. Then the bottomless chasm of the underworld, standing open without limit, will swallow those whom empty pride now exalts.

Those who here, through whatever vice, fulfilled the will of the cunning persuader will then, as reprobates, arrive at torments with their leader. Although the nature of angels and human beings is vastly different, one punishment will nevertheless entangle those whom one guilt binds together.

### Chapter 81 — That the human soul is immortal in such a way that it both can and cannot die

(Gregory says in his *Moralia*:)

Since, then, this state of our immortality perishes not so as to be evil, but so as not to be, it must be asked what it is that is desired to perish, not so as not to be, but so as to be evil.

The human soul, or the angelic spirit, is immortal in such a way that it can die, and mortal in such a way that it cannot die. For it loses blessed life, whether through vice or through punishment; but it does not lose essential life either through vice or through punishment.

It falls away from the quality of living, but even when dying it does not experience the destruction of its entire existence. In brief: it is immortally mortal and mortally immortal.

### Chapter 82 — That the fire of Gehenna is corporeal and needs no other material except the torment of the reprobate

(Gregory says in his *Moralia*:)

The fire of Gehenna has been expressed in remarkably few words. Corporeal fire, in order to remain fire, requires corporeal fuel. When it must be kept burning, it is undoubtedly nourished by piled-up wood; it cannot exist unless kindled and replenished.

The fire of Gehenna, however, although corporeal and corporeally burning the reprobate cast into it, is not kindled by human effort and is not nourished by wood. Once created, it endures unquenchable; it does not need kindling and does not lack heat.

Thus it is rightly said of this wicked person: “Fire that is not kindled will devour him.” For the justice of the Almighty, foreknowing future things, created the fire of Gehenna from the very beginning of the world. It will once begin to be the punishment of the reprobate, but it will never end its burning even without wood.

It must also be known that all the reprobate, because they sinned both in soul and in body, will there be tormented equally in soul and in body.

### Chapter 83 — Why the soul cannot be seen either while remaining in the body or while departing from it

What is surprising, Peter, if you did not see the soul departing, when you do not see it even while it remains in the body? When you are speaking with me now, do you believe me to be without a soul simply because you cannot see my soul within me? The nature of the soul is invisible, and so it leaves the body invisibly just as it remains invisibly in the body.

Peter: I can infer the life of the soul remaining in the body from the body’s movements, since unless the soul were present in the body, the body’s limbs could not move. But I do not see through what movements or actions the soul’s life exists after the flesh, so that I might infer from visible things what I cannot see.

### Chapter 84 — That no one ought to doubt that those things are invisible which minister to the invisible God

(From Gregory’s *Dialogues*.)

Just as the soul’s power gives life to and moves the body, so divine power fills all the things it has created. By inspiring, it gives life to some; to others it grants that they live; to others it grants only that they exist.

Since you do not doubt that God is true, creating and ruling, filling and encompassing, transcending and sustaining, unbounded and invisible, you likewise ought not to doubt that he has invisible attendants. Those things that minister ought to tend toward the likeness of the one whom they serve, so that it should not be doubted that those who serve the invisible are themselves invisible.

What else, then, do we believe these to be except the holy angels and the spirits of the righteous? Just as, by considering the movement of the body, you mentally discern the life of the soul remaining in the body, so you must discern from above the life of the soul leaving the body, because that which must remain in the service of the invisible can live invisibly.

Peter: Everything has been said rightly; but my mind shrinks from believing what it cannot see with bodily eyes.

### Chapter 85 — That no visible things can be seen or known except through invisible things

(From Gregory’s *Dialogues*.)

When Paul says: “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen,” it is truly said that what cannot be seen is believed. What can be seen can no longer be believed.

Yet, to bring you briefly back to yourself: no visible things are seen except through invisible things. Your bodily eye sees all corporeal things, but the corporeal eye itself would not see anything corporeal unless an incorporeal reality sharpened it for seeing. Remove the mind, which is not seen, and the eye that was seeing remains open in vain.

Take the soul away from the body, and certainly the eyes remain open in the body. If, therefore, they saw by themselves, why do they see nothing when the soul departs? Understand from this, then, that visible things themselves are seen only through invisible things.

Let us also place before the eyes of the mind the building of a house, the lifting of immense masses, and the hanging of great columns from machines. Who, I ask you, performs this work? Is it the visible body that drags those masses with its hands, or the invisible soul that gives life to the body?

Remove what is not seen in the body, and immediately all the visible bodies of metal that seemed to move remain motionless. From this it must be considered that even in this visible world nothing can be ordered except through an invisible creature.

For just as almighty God, by breathing into or filling rational beings, gives life to and moves invisible things, so those invisible things themselves, by filling them, move and gradually give life to the bodily things that are seen.

Peter: I confess that I have gladly been overcome by these arguments, and am now compelled to believe that these visible things scarcely exist at all, since previously, assuming the role of one who was weak in faith, I doubted invisible things. Everything you say therefore pleases me; yet, just as I recognize the soul’s life while it remains in the body from the body’s movement, so I desire to recognize the soul’s life after the body through certain manifest things that bear witness to it.

### Chapter 86 — That an incorporeal spirit is afflicted in the underworld by corporeal fire

(From Gregory’s *Dialogues*.)

If the incorporeal spirit of a living human being is held in the body, why should the spirit, although incorporeal, not also be held after death by corporeal fire?

Peter: In every living person the incorporeal spirit is held in the body because it gives life to the body.

### Chapter 87 — That an incorporeal spirit can give life and can be held where it is tormented by corporeal fire

[Column 1049D]

(From Gregory’s *Dialogues*.)

If, Peter, an incorporeal spirit can be held in that which it gives life to, why should it not also be held punitively where it is subjected to death?

We say that the human spirit is held through fire, so that it is in the torment of fire by seeing and feeling. It suffers fire precisely by seeing it; and because it sees itself being burned, it is burned.

Thus an incorporeal reality burns an incorporeal reality, since invisible burning and pain are drawn from visible fire. Through corporeal fire, therefore, the incorporeal mind is tormented by an incorporeal flame as well.

We can also gather from the evangelical sayings that the burning of souls is endured not only by seeing but also by experience. For the voice of the Truth says that the rich man, having died, was buried in the underworld. That his soul was held in fire is indicated by the rich man’s voice when he begs Abraham, saying: “Send Lazarus, so that he may dip the tip of his finger in water to cool my tongue, for I am tormented in this flame.”

Since the Truth declares that the sinful rich man was condemned in the fires, what wise person can now deny that the souls of the reprobate are held in fires?

Peter: Behold, reason and testimony incline the mind toward belief; but when it is released again, it returns to its rigidity. For I do not know how an incorporeal reality can be held and afflicted by a corporeal reality.

### Chapter 88 — That apostate spirits are to be believed incorporeal

(From Gregory’s *Dialogues*.)

Tell me, I ask you: Do you suppose that the apostate spirits, cast down from heavenly glory, are corporeal or incorporeal?

Peter: What wise person could say that spirits are corporeal?

### Chapter 89 — That the fire of Gehenna is to be believed corporeal

(From Gregory’s *Dialogues*.)

Do you acknowledge that the fire of Gehenna is corporeal or incorporeal?

Peter: I have no doubt that the fire of Gehenna is corporeal, since it is certain that bodies are tormented in it.

### Chapter 90 — On what is written, “No one has ever seen God,” and how it is to be understood

(Gregory says in his *Moralia*:)

“No one has ever seen God.” Yet when I consider the fathers of the Old Testament, I recognize that many of them, as the history of sacred reading itself bears witness, saw God.

Jacob saw the Lord and said: “I have seen the Lord face to face, and my life has been preserved.” Moses saw the Lord, of whom it is written: “The Lord spoke to Moses face to face, as a man is accustomed to speak to his friend.” Job saw the Lord, saying: “I heard you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you.” Isaiah saw the Lord, saying: “In the year when King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord seated upon a high and exalted throne.” Micaiah saw the Lord, saying: “I saw the Lord sitting upon his throne, and all the army of heaven standing before him on his right and on his left.”

What, then, does it mean that so many fathers of the Old Testament testified that they had seen God, while it is said of this wisdom, which is God: “It is hidden from the eyes of all the living,” and John says: “No one has ever seen God”? It plainly means that, so long as one lives here in mortal existence, God can be seen through certain images, but cannot be seen through the very form of his nature.

Thus the soul, breathed upon by the Spirit’s grace, sees God through certain figures, but does not reach the very power of his essence. Hence Jacob, who testified that he had seen God, saw here only an angel. Hence Moses, who speaks face to face with God, as a man speaks with his friend, says in the very course of his speech: “If I have found favor in your sight, show yourself to me plainly, so that I may see you.”

Certainly, if the one with whom he was speaking was not God, he would have said, “Show me God,” and not, “Show yourself to me.” But if the one with whom he was speaking face to face was God, why did he ask again to see the one whom he was seeing?

His request shows that he thirsted to behold through the splendor of God’s unbounded nature the one whom he had already begun to see through certain images, so that the heavenly essence might be present to the eyes of his mind in such a way that no created and temporal image would intervene between him and the vision of eternity.

The fathers of the Old Testament therefore saw the Lord, and yet, in John’s words, “No one has ever seen God.” In accordance with blessed Job’s statement, the wisdom that is God is hidden from the eyes of all the living, because those who remain in this mortal flesh could see him through certain bounded images, but cannot see him through the unbounded light of eternity.

Yet the eternal brightness of God can be seen by some who still remain in mortal flesh, provided that they grow through immeasurable power and the sharpness of contemplation.

### Chapter 91 — On the twofold punishment of the condemned

(From the sayings of Isidore.)

The punishment of the condemned in Gehenna is twofold: sorrow burns their mind, and flame burns their body. In accordance with the correspondence between them, they are punished both in mind and in body for what they conceived in mind and accomplished through the body.

The fire of Gehenna has light for one purpose and does not have it for another. It has light for condemnation, so that the impious may see the source of their sorrow; it does not have light for consolation, so that they may not see anything in which they could rejoice.

The furnace of the three young men provides an apt comparison as an example of the fire of Gehenna. Just as that fire did not burn for the punishment of the three young men but burned to consume the bonds with which they were tied, so the fire of Gehenna will shine upon the wretched to increase their punishments, so that they may see the source of their sorrow; but it will not shine for consolation, so that they may not see anything in which they could rejoice.

There is a great distinction between the misery of this life and the misery of future unhappiness. There, misery exists because of the torment of pain, and darkness because of the withdrawal of light. Of these two, one—misery—exists in this life, while the other does not. In the underworld, however, both exist.

### Chapter 92 — On the punishments of the ungodly

(From the sayings of the same author.)

Just as bundles of wood are tied together with similar pieces for burning, so on the day of judgment those guilty of similar faults will be joined to their counterparts, so that punishment may constrain them equally, as if into a bundle, those whom similar conduct made alike in evil.

Just as each saint will be glorified at the future judgment according to the measure of his virtues, so each ungodly person will be condemned according to the measure of his crimes. Nor will there be no order of condemnation in the punishment to come. Rather, there will be a distinction of punishments according to the quality of the crimes, as the prophet confirms.

Punishment is also added to the dead on account of the punishments of their loved ones. Thus, as the Gospel discourse proclaims concerning the rich man in the underworld, so, for the increase of Judas’s punishment, the Psalm also says: “May his children be continually shaken and beg.”

The ungodly will be punished more harshly at the judgment by the pain of their minds because they will see that the righteous have earned the blessedness of glory.

The devil must be cast down in the sight of all, when, before the eyes of all good angels and human beings, he is to be sent into eternal fire together with those who are of his party. When the devil is lifted up in order to be condemned, many of the elect who are to be found in the body when the Lord comes to judgment will be shaken with fear, seeing the ungodly punished by such a sentence.

They will be purified by that terror, because if any sin from the body still remains in them, they will be purified by the very fear with which they see the devil condemned. Hence Job says: “When he is lifted up, the angels will fear, and, terrified, they will be purified.”

The prophet teaches that many among those who now appear to be elect and holy can perish on the day of judgment: “The Lord called judgment upon the fire, and it devoured the great abyss and consumed a portion of the house.” A portion of the house will be devoured, because the underworld will also swallow those who now boast in the heavenly commandments.

Of them the Lord also says: “Many will say to me on that day: ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name? Did we not cast out demons in your name? Did we not perform many mighty works in your name?’ Then I will declare to them: ‘I never knew you. Depart from me, you workers of iniquity. I do not know who you are.’”

### Chapter 93 — On the Antichrist

(From the sayings of the same author.)

Everyone who does not live according to the rule of his profession, or who teaches otherwise, is an Antichrist. Many will not see the times of the Antichrist, yet will be found among the members of the Antichrist.

Before the Antichrist comes, many of his members have gone before him and, by the merit of their wicked actions, have preceded their own head, in accordance with the Apostle’s statement that he is already working the mystery of iniquity, even before he is revealed.

The greatness of the signs in the time of Antichrist will cause even the elect, if it is possible, to be led into error. But if they are elect, how can they be led into error? They will therefore enter briefly into the error of wavering because of the multitude of prodigies; nevertheless, they will not be cast down from their stability by the force of terrors and signs.

For this reason the phrase “if it is possible” is inserted: the elect cannot perish, but, quickly recovering their senses, they will restrain the error of their hearts through religious faith. They know that the Lord foretold that, when the adversaries do these things, the saints are not to be disturbed.
