When the Antichrist comes, he will already be performing wondrous prodigies and signs, so that a certain scruple may also arise in the hearts of the elect. Yet reason will quickly prevail in them, because they will know that the same signs are performed for the deception of the reprobate and the testing of the elect.

At that time the saints will be glorious through patience, not through miracles, just as the earlier holy martyrs were. For they endured persecutors who were also performing prodigies. Consequently, they will endure a harsher war, because they will fight not only against persecutors but also against those who flash with miracles.

Under the times of the Antichrist, the Synagogue will serve against the Church more harshly than it would have persecuted Christians at the Savior’s own coming. Although the devil, even while bound, has already exercised great cruelty against the martyrs, he will be more cruel under the times of the Antichrist, when he will also be released.

For if he could do so much while bound, how much will he do when released? The nearer the devil sees the end of the world, the more cruelly he carries out persecutions. Since he sees that he is about to be condemned immediately, he multiplies his associates, with whom he may be consigned to the fire of Gehenna.

The shorter the time the devil sees remaining to him before his condemnation, the more violently he is stirred to persecution, by divine justice permitting it, so that the righteous may be glorified, the wicked disgraced, and the severity of the devil’s sentence of condemnation increased.

### Chapter 94 — That before the day of judgment even the elect will fall in the coming of the Antichrist

(Gregory says in his *Moralia*:)

“In his days the last will be struck with amazement, and terror will invade the first.” For then such unrestrained iniquity will rage against the righteous that even the hearts of the elect will be struck by no small fear. Hence it is written: “So that, if it were possible, even the elect would be led into error.”

This is said not because the elect will fall, but because they will tremble amid great terrors. At that time the last and the first elect are said to have a contest of righteousness against him. Those who are found elect at the end of the world will be struck down in death, while those who arose from the earlier parts of the world—namely Enoch and Elijah—will be brought back into the midst and will suffer his cruelty while still in their mortal flesh.

The last are amazed and the first are afraid at his strength, released with such great power. Although, insofar as he is lifted up by the spirit of pride, they despise all his temporal power, nevertheless, insofar as they themselves are still in mortal flesh, in which they can be tormented temporarily, they shudder at the very punishments they endure courageously.

Thus at one and the same time there is in them both steadfastness from virtue and fear from the flesh. Although they are elect, so that they cannot be overcome by torments, nevertheless, because they are human beings, they fear the very torments that they overcome.

### Chapter 95 — On the Antichrist
(Gregory says in his *Morals*): For he sees that at the end of the world Satan, entering into the man whom Holy Scripture calls the Antichrist, will be raised up with such arrogance, with such power of rule, and with such great signs and wonders displayed as evidence of holiness, that his deeds cannot be reproved by human beings; for the signs of displayed holiness will also be joined to the power of terror. And he says: “Who can rebuke his way before him?” That is, what human being would dare to rebuke one whose very appearance he fears to endure? Nevertheless, not only Elijah and Enoch, who are brought back into the midst of the world for his reproach, but all the elect also rebuke his way, when they despise him and resist his wickedness with strength of mind.

## CHAPTER 96. Likewise, concerning the Antichrist

(Gregory says in his *Morals*): In this passage “the man who is wise in human things” is mentioned; but since “all” are more than “innumerable,” we must ask why he is said to draw innumerable before him and all after him, unless it is because the ancient enemy, then entering the reprobate man, drags beneath the yoke of his dominion all whom he finds to be carnal. Even now, before he appears, he draws innumerable people, though not all the carnal; for every day many are recalled from carnal works to life, and return to the state of righteousness, some through brief repentance and others through prolonged repentance. Even now he seizes innumerable people, although he does not display to human beings the astonishing signs of his falsehood. But when he has performed marvelous portents before the eyes of the carnal, then he will draw after him not innumerable people but all, because those who delight in present goods submit themselves to his power without resistance.

But, as we have said, since drawing every human being is more than drawing innumerable people, why is it first said that he draws everyone, and afterward, as an increase, that innumerable people are subjected to him? Reason would require that what is less should be stated first, and afterward, as an increase, what is greater. We must understand, however, that in this passage saying “innumerable” is more than saying “all.” He draws every human being after him because, in three and a half years, he binds under the yoke of his condemnation all whom he finds engaged in the pursuits of carnal life. But he drew innumerable people before him because, through the course of five thousand and more years, although he could by no means draw all the carnal, there are nevertheless far more people whom he has seized before him over so long a period than all those whom he will find to be seized within so short a time. Thus it is rightly said that he draws every human being after him and innumerable people before him, because he will take less then, when he has taken everyone, and now he plunders more, when he does not invade the hearts of everyone.

## CHAPTER 97. That at the end of time all Israelites must be converted through the preaching of Elijah

[Col. 1054C]

(Gregory says in his *Morals*): But at the very end all the Israelites hasten to the faith once they have learned Elijah’s preaching; and they return to the protection of the one whom they had fled. Then that exceptional banquet is celebrated through the gathering together of many peoples.

## CHAPTER 98. Why in this life things are often bad for the good and good for the wicked

(Gregory says in his *Morals*): Since divine judgments are exceedingly hidden, why are things sometimes bad for the good and good for the wicked in this life? They are more hidden when things are good here for the good and bad for the wicked. For when things are bad for the good and good for the wicked, this can perhaps be understood: the good, if they have committed some offenses, receive their due here, so that they may be more fully freed from eternal condemnation; and the wicked find here the good things that they do for this life, so that afterward they may be led on to torments alone. Hence it is said to the rich man burning in hell: “Remember, son, that you received good things in your lifetime, and Lazarus likewise evil things.”

But when things are good here for the good and bad for the wicked, it becomes very uncertain whether the good receive good things for this reason—that, being encouraged, they may grow toward something better—or whether, by a just and hidden judgment, they receive here the reward for their works, so that they may be emptied of the rewards of the life to come. And it is uncertain whether adversity strikes the wicked for this reason—that, by correction, they may be protected from eternal punishments—or whether their punishment begins here, so that, when completed, it may eventually lead them to the final torments of Gehenna.

## CHAPTER 99. That all unbelievers too must rise, for torment, not for judgment

[Col. 1055A]

(Gregory says in his *Morals*): All unbelievers too rise, but for torment, not for judgment. Their case is not then examined, since they approach the sight of the strict Judge already bearing the condemnation of their unbelief. Those who retain the profession of faith but do not possess the works of that profession are rebuked so that they may perish. But those who held neither the sacraments of faith hear no rebuke from the Judge at the final examination; because they are already condemned by the darkness of their unbelief, they do not deserve to be rebuked by the denunciation of the one whom they had despised.

At least those hear the words of the Judge who held the words of his faith; these, in their condemnation by the eternal Judge, do not even receive his words, because they did not wish to preserve his reverence even in words. The former perish according to the law, because, placed under the law, they sinned; to the latter, in their destruction, nothing is said from the law, because they did not attempt to possess anything belonging to the law.

## CHAPTER 100. That all human beings must rise

(Augustine says): There will be a resurrection of all human beings. If there will be a resurrection of all, then all die, so that the death given in Adam may rule over all his sons; and that privilege may remain in the Lord which is said especially of him: “You will not allow your holy one to see corruption.” We have accepted this understanding, handed down by the greatest multitude of the Fathers.

Yet, because there are other equally Catholic and learned men who believe that, while the soul remains in the body, those who are to be found alive at the Lord’s coming will be changed into incorruption and immortality—and that this will be reckoned for them as resurrection from the dead, namely, that they lay aside mortality through transformation, not through death—whoever accepts either view is not a heretic, unless he becomes a heretic through contention. For it is enough, according to the law of the Church, to believe that the resurrection of the flesh takes place from death.

## CHAPTER 101. On the same subject

(Also Augustine.) When we say in the Creed that at the Lord’s coming the living and the dead will be judged, this does not mean, as Diodorus thinks it signifies, that only the righteous and sinners will be judged; rather, it says that the living are those who will be found in the flesh. For they are believed either to die for this purpose, or to be changed, as others maintain, so that, immediately raised or transformed from the dead, they may be judged.

## CHAPTER 102. That apostate angels and wicked human beings, after torments as though purified by punishments, will not be granted the fellowship of the righteous

(Also Augustine.) After the resurrection and judgment, let us not believe in the future resurrection which Origen raves about: that demons or wicked human beings, after torments as though purified by punishments, may either return to the angelic dignity in which they were created, or that the unjust may be granted the fellowship of the righteous, on the ground that this would accord with divine goodness, lest anything among rational creatures perish, but that they might be saved in some manner. Rather, let us believe in the Judge and just Requiter of all things, who said: “The wicked will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life,” so that they may receive the fruit of their works. And again: “Go into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels.”

## CHAPTER 103. That the resurrection must take place at the age of perfect youth, which needs no further growth

(From the sayings of Isidore.) The beginning of the peace of the saints exists in this life, but not its perfection. Then, however, there will be the fullness of peace, when, with the weakness of the flesh absorbed, they have been strengthened for the contemplation of God. The resurrection of the dead, as the Apostle says, will take place “unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ”—that is, in the age of youth which needs no further growth and which, without any decline toward weakness, is in its perfection full and vigorous on both sides.

Although faithful people are now called by the name “children of God,” nevertheless, because they suffer this servitude of corruption, they are still bound under the yoke of servitude. They will receive the full freedom of the children of God when this corruptible nature has put on incorruption. Now God is known through a mirror; but in the future each elect person will be presented face to face, so as to contemplate the very form that he now strives to see through a mirror. In this life the Church of God is completed from the number of the elect, who belong on the right, and the reprobate, who will go to the left; but at the end of the age the weeds will be separated from the wheat.

## CHAPTER 104. That the strict Judge, coming to judgment, sees the sinner in order to strike, not in order to save

(Gregory says in his *Morals*): When the Lord comes to judgment, he sees the sinner in order to strike, but he does not see him in order to recognize him for the granting of saving grace. He examines his faults, but does not acknowledge the life of those who perish.

## CHAPTER 105. That God comes to judgment seeing in order to strike, and not seeing in order to save

(Gregory says in his *Morals*): The strict Judge will come to judgment, “not seeing in order to save, seeing in order to strike,” because the one whom in the present life he does not regard with the mercy of his dispensation, he later destroys by regarding him in accordance with justice. For now every sinner, while he does not fear, lives, blasphemes, and prospers; for the merciful Creator, who wishes to correct him by waiting, does not wish to punish him by looking upon him, as it is written: “You overlook the sins of human beings for the sake of repentance.”

But then the sinner does not endure when he is looked upon, because when the strict Judge examines his merits minutely, the guilty person cannot endure the torments. This also accords with the voice of the righteous, whose minds are always anxious and intent upon the coming examination. They fear everything they do, carefully considering before what kind of Judge they will stand. They behold the power of his majesty and weigh the guilt by which their own weakness is bound. They enumerate the evils of their own works and set against them the good things of the Creator’s grace. They consider how strictly he judges evil deeds and how minutely he weighs good works; and they know without doubt that they would perish if they were judged with mercy removed. For even the fact that we appear to live justly is itself guilt, if, when he judges our life, divine mercy does not excuse it before him.

## CHAPTER 106. That on the day of judgment the two orders are divided into four

(From the sayings of Isidore.) There are two distinctions, or orders, of human beings at the judgment: the elect and the reprobate. These, however, are divided into four.

There is one order of the perfect, consisting of those who judge with God, and another consisting of those who are judged. Nevertheless, both will reign with Christ. Likewise, the order of the reprobate is divided into two: those who are evil within the Church are to be judged and condemned; but those who will be found outside the Church are not to be judged, but only condemned.

The first order, therefore, consists of those who are judged and perish; it is opposed to the order of the good, consisting of those who are judged and reign. The second order consists of those who are not judged and perish; it is opposed to the order of the perfect, consisting of those who are not judged and reign. The third order consists of those who are judged and reign; it is opposed to the order consisting of those who are judged and perish. The fourth order consists of those who are not judged and reign; it is opposed to that contrary order consisting of those who are not judged and perish.

The wicked person is punished with a double sentence: either here, for his merits, he is struck with blindness of mind so that he does not see the truth, or at the end he is condemned so that he may pay the penalties he deserves.

## CHAPTER 107. That the book of life is the very vision of the coming Judge, because when anyone sees him, he will immediately understand whatever he has done

(Gregory says in his *Morals*): “The books were opened, and another book was opened, which is the book of life; and the dead were judged according to what was written in the books.” The book of life is the very vision of the coming Judge. In it, as though written, is every commandment, because whoever sees him immediately understands, with his conscience bearing witness, whatever he has not done.

The books are also said to have been opened because the life of the righteous is then seen, in whom the heavenly commandments are discerned as impressed through their works. “And the dead were judged according to what was written in the books,” because, in the life of the righteous displayed as though in the opening of books, they read the good that they themselves refused to do, and are condemned by comparison with those who did it.

Therefore, so that each person, seeing them then, may not mourn what he failed to do, let him now pay attention to what he may imitate in them—something that certain people never cease to do.

## CHAPTER 108. Concerning the glory of the saints after judgment

[Col. 1058A]

(From the sayings of Isidore.) In the future, the heart of the righteous will not be made sorrowful by compassion for the condemned, where the joy of the saints in contemplating God will be so great that sorrow will be given no entrance. Just as white, compared with black, is the more beautiful color, so the rest of the saints, compared with the condemnation of the wicked, will be more glorious. As justice surpasses injustice, so virtue surpasses vice. The glory of the saints therefore increases when the wicked are condemned to their deserved punishment.

After the resurrection, the ascent to heaven has been promised to the saints in the flesh, Christ saying to the Father: “I will that where I am, they also may be with me.” For if we are members of the head, and Christ is one in himself and in us, then wherever he has ascended, we too will ascend.

## CHAPTER 109. That when judgment has ended, the new age and the new earth begin

[Col. 1058B]

(From the sayings of the same author.) As blessed Augustine says, once judgment has been completed and brought to an end, this heaven and earth will then cease to exist, when the new heaven and the new earth will begin to exist. For this world will pass away through a transformation of things, not through complete destruction. Hence the Apostle also says: “For the form of this world is passing away.” The form, therefore, passes away, not the nature.

## CHAPTER 110. Against those who say that, if the conflagration of the world will occur after judgment, the saints could then exist without being touched by the flames of the fire

(From the sayings of the same author.) Blessed Augustine resolves this question. He says: Perhaps someone will ask: If this world will burn after judgment has taken place, before the new heaven and the new earth are established in its place, where will the saints be during the time of its conflagration, since, having bodies, they must exist in some bodily place?

We can answer that they will be in the higher regions, where the flame of that fire will not rise, just as the floodwaters did not rise there. Their bodies will be of such a kind that they may be wherever they wish to be. But, having been made immortal and incorruptible, they will not fear the fire of that conflagration any more than the three living men, whose corruptible and mortal bodies were able to live unharmed in the blazing furnace.

[Col. 1057] END OF BOOK XX.

[Col. 1057]

# COUNCIL HELD AT SALEGUNSTAT

[Col. 1057D] In the name of God, I, Aribo, archbishop of the see of Mainz, although unworthy, together with our other brethren and fellow bishops—Burchard of Worms, Werenhar of Strasbourg, Bruno of Augsburg, Eberhard of Bamberg, and Meginhard of Würzburg—have convened a synod at Salegunstat. In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1023, indiction 5, on the second day before the Ides of August, and in the twenty-first year of the reign of our lord Henry II, and the sixth year of his empire, so that, through the common counsel and deliberation of the aforesaid brethren, the many disagreements concerning the divine offices and synodal laws, as well as the divergence of our individual customs, might be brought together into one through honorable agreement. Therefore, because of those lamentable disagreements, these chapters were enacted by the common decree of the council.

## CHAPTER 1. Concerning abstinence from meat and blood at the times specified below

(In the council held at Salegunstat.) All Christians are to abstain from meat and blood for fourteen days before the feast of Saint John the Baptist, except when prevented by illness or when the solemnity of some feast celebrated with distinction in that diocese intervenes. The same is to be observed before the Nativity of the Lord, on the vigil of Epiphany, on the vigils of all the apostles, on the vigil of the Assumption of Saint Mary, on the vigil of Saint Lawrence, and also on the vigil of All Saints. To these aforesaid vigils they are to add one hour for taking nourishment, except in cases of illness and unless someone wishes, by his own vow, to observe a greater abstinence.

## CHAPTER 2. Concerning the observance of the fast of the four seasons

(From the same council.) Concerning the uncertain fast of the four seasons, we establish this rule for certainty: if the Kalends of March fall on Wednesday or earlier in the week, the fast is to be celebrated in that same week. But if the Kalends of March fall on Thursday, Friday, or Saturday, the fast is to be deferred to the following week.

Likewise, if the Kalends of June fall on Wednesday or earlier, the fast is to be celebrated in the following week. If they fall on Thursday, Friday, or Saturday, the fast is to be reserved for the third week. It must be understood that, if the fast of the month of June should fall on the vigil of Pentecost according to the rule stated above, it is not to be celebrated there, but in the very solemn week of Pentecost. Then, on account of the solemnity of the Holy Spirit, the deacons are to wear dalmatics, the Alleluia is to be sung, and “Let us bend the knee” is not to be said.

The same arrangement has been established for the fast of September: if the Kalends of September fall on Wednesday or earlier, the fast is to be celebrated in the third week; if they fall on Thursday, Friday, or Saturday, the fast is to be observed in the fourth week.

In December the following is to be observed: the fast is to be celebrated on the Saturday immediately before the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord, because if the vigil falls on Saturday, it is not appropriate to celebrate the vigil and the fast together.

## CHAPTER 3. At what times lawful marriages are to be prohibited

[Col. 1059D]

(From the same council.) Concerning lawful marriages, it has been decided that no Christian should take a wife from Advent until the octave of Epiphany, or from Septuagesima until the octave of Easter; nor during the fourteen days noted above before the feast of Saint John the Baptist; nor on the aforesaid days of fasting, or on the nights preceding all solemn days.

## CHAPTER 4. That a priest who drinks after cockcrow should not dare to celebrate Mass on the following day unless necessity compels him

(From the same.) It was also decreed in the same council that no priest who drinks after cockcrow on summer nights should celebrate Mass on the following day, and likewise during winter, unless necessity compels him.

## CHAPTER 5. That a priest should celebrate no more than three Masses in one day

(Also from the same.) It was likewise decreed that no priest should presume to celebrate more than three Masses in a day.

## CHAPTER 6. That no one should throw the corporal into a fire to extinguish a conflagration

(From the same.) Complaint was also made in the holy council about certain exceedingly foolish priests who, when they saw a fire, threw into it, with rash presumption, the corporal consecrated with the Lord’s body, in order to extinguish the fire. Therefore it was decreed, under penalty of anathema, that this must not happen again.

## CHAPTER 7. What is to be done if two persons are accused of adultery, one denies it and the other confesses

[Col. 1060B]

(From the same.) It was asked what should be done if two people were accused of adultery, one confessed and the other denied it. It was also decreed by the holy council that the one who denied it should clear himself by a credible judgment, while the one who confessed should perform worthy penance.

## CHAPTER 8. That no one should carry a sword into a church

(From the same.) It was also decreed in the same council that no one should carry a sword into a church, except a king.

## CHAPTER 9. That evil conversations should not take place in a church or in the church courtyard

(From the same.) The holy synod also decreed that a bad practice which has now taken root among almost everyone should be entirely prohibited: namely, that people arrange to hold their conversations in the courtyard of a church and then conduct them inside the very great church itself, where only prayers and divine offices ought to take place.

## CHAPTER 10. Concerning the Gospel, “In the beginning was the Word,” and private Masses, so that they may not be celebrated at improper times

(From the same.) Certain laypeople, especially married women, have the custom of reciting every day the Gospel, “In the beginning was the Word,” and of saying special Masses—that is, Masses of the Holy Trinity or of Saint Michael. Therefore it was decreed in the same council that this should not be done thereafter except at its proper time, and unless one of the faithful wishes to hear it out of reverence for the Holy Trinity, not for any divination. If they wish Masses to be sung for them, they should hear the Mass of that day, either for the salvation of the living or for the dead.

## CHAPTER 11. Concerning the reckoning of consanguinity

(From the same council.) Some people wish to count the generations of consanguinity in such a way that brother and sister are the first degree. But the holy synod decreed, as the ancient Fathers also decreed, that this should not be so; rather, nephew and niece—that is, the son of a brother and the daughter of a sister—are to be reckoned as the first degree.

## CHAPTER 12. That lay buildings should not be placed in the church courtyard

(From the same.) It was also decreed that the buildings of laypeople adjoining churches should be removed, and that no buildings should be placed in the church courtyard except those of priests.

## CHAPTER 13. That no layperson should entrust his church to a priest without the permission of his bishop

(From the same.) It was likewise decreed that no layperson should entrust his church to any priest without the consent of the bishop. Rather, he should first send him to his bishop or the bishop’s representative, so that it may be established whether he is such in learning, age, and conduct that the people of God may be entrusted to him.

## CHAPTER 14. What is to be done if two persons are accused of adultery

(From the same.) The holy synod also decreed that if two people are accused of adultery, both deny it, and they ask that permission be granted for one of them to clear both by divine judgment, then, if one of them falls in this ordeal, both are to be held guilty.

## CHAPTER 15. That the proclaimed fast is to be observed most carefully by all

(From the same.) It was also decreed that everyone should observe with the greatest care the proclaimed fast wherever it is celebrated in any diocese; and if anyone wishes to redeem any one of the eight prohibited things, he should provide food for one poor person that same day, according to his means.

## CHAPTER 16. Concerning those who are going to Rome

The holy synod also decreed that no one should go to Rome without the permission of his bishop or his representative.

## CHAPTER 17. That the *carina* should not be divided for a penitent

It was also commanded under penalty of anathema that no priest should presume to divide the *carina* for any penitent, unless illness intervenes.

## CHAPTER 18. Concerning those who refuse to receive penance from priests

Because many people are deceived by such great foolishness of mind that, accused of some capital crime, they refuse to receive penance from their own priests, relying especially on the expectation that the pope (*apostolicus*) will forgive all their sins when they go to Rome, the holy council decreed that such indulgence should not benefit them. Rather, they must first complete the penance assigned to them by their own priests according to the measure of their offense; and then, if they wish to go to Rome, they must receive from their own bishop permission and letters to be carried to the apostolic authority concerning these matters.

## CHAPTER 19. That no penitent should move from place to place while fasting his *carina*

[Col. 1062B]

It was also decreed in the same council that no penitent should move from one place to another while fasting his *carina*, but should remain where he received his penance, so that his own priest may provide testimony for him. If, however, he cannot fast because of hostile ambushes, his priest should most carefully entrust him to one of his fellow priests, in a place where he can fast peacefully.

## CHAPTER 20. That no priest should admit any penitent into the church

It was also decreed in the same council that no priest should presume to admit into the church anyone who, because of some offense, is not permitted to enter it, except at the command of the bishop.

[Col. 1061]

# HOW THE SYNOD IS TO BE INITIATED

[Col. 1061C] At the appropriate hour, whenever it seems right to the bishop or his representative, everyone is to be expelled from the church. With all the doors barred, doorkeepers are to stand at the one entrance through which the priests must enter. A chair is to be placed in the middle, and upon it sacred relics and a plenary book (*plenarium*) with a stole are to be placed. Then all the assembled priests are to enter and sit according to the time of their ordination. After them, reputable deacons whom the order requires to be present are to enter. Thereafter laypeople of good conduct are to be admitted. Then the bishop is to enter, if he wishes or if necessity requires it; and if the bishop is not present, his representative is to do the same.

When he or his representative enters the synod, he should first greet the clergy and people, and, turning toward the east, say in a moderate voice:

“God, visitor of the humble, who consoles us with fraternal love, extend your grace to our assembly, so that through those in whom you dwell we may perceive your coming among us. Through our Lord Jesus Christ.”

Then a deacon, proceeding with a subdeacon, a censer, and two candle-bearers, is to read the Gospel:

“When it was evening on that day, the first day of the week, and the doors were shut.”

Then the bishop or his representative is to say:

“Holy Mary, and all the saints and elect of God, intercede for us sinners with the Lord our God, that we may deserve to be helped, protected, and healed by him, who lives and reigns forever.”

Afterward he is to say twice:

“God, attend to my assistance.”

“Lord, hasten to help me.”

Then he is to say a third time:

“God, attend to my assistance.”

The clergy responding:

“Lord, hasten to help me,” with “Glory to the Father,” and the Kyrie eleison, and the Lord’s Prayer, with these prayers:

“Lord, do not remember our former iniquities.”

“Help us, O God our Savior.”

“Be for us, O Lord, a tower of strength.”

[Col. 1063A] “Lord, hear my prayer.”

“The Lord be with you.”

“Let us pray. Hear us, O God our Savior, and order our days in your peace, so that, freed from every disturbance, we may serve you in tranquil obedience. Through our Lord Jesus Christ.”

Then, for all the orders and also for the welfare of the pope and of the bishop of that see, they are to say these psalms:

“Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy.”

“Save me, O God, by your name.”

“Have mercy on me, O God; have mercy on me.”

“May God have mercy on us.”

And the Lord’s Prayer, with the prayers:

“Let your priests be clothed with righteousness.”

[Col. 1063B] “Remember your congregation.”

“Save us, O Lord our God.”

“That we may give thanks to your holy name.”

“Our help is in the name of the Lord.”

“Lord, hear my prayer.”

“The Lord be with you.”

“Let us pray. Almighty and everlasting God, by whose Spirit the whole body of the Church is sanctified and governed, hear us as we supplicate you for all its orders, so that, by the gift of your grace, you may be faithfully served by all its ranks. Through the Lord.”

Then he is to say:

“God, shepherd and ruler of all the faithful, look favorably upon your servant whom you have willed to preside as shepherd over your Church. Grant him, we ask, by word and example to prosper those over whom he presides, so that together with the flock entrusted to him he may attain eternal life. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son.”

When these things have been completed, they are to sing the seven penitential psalms, with the Kyrie eleison and the Lord’s Prayer, with these prayers:

“I said, O Lord, have mercy on me.”

“Turn, O Lord; how long?”

“Let your mercy, O Lord, be upon us.”

“Lord, hear my prayer.”

“The Lord be with you.”

“Let us pray. Look favorably, we ask, O Lord, upon our days, and in your mercy free us from our sins and graciously rescue us from every adversity. Through the Lord.”

[Col. 1063D] After this, everyone is to leave except the priests and the other suitable clerics. When silence has been made, the bishop or his representative is to say this prayer:

“The Lord be with you.”

“Let us pray. Be present with us, we ask, holy Lord Spirit, who find us held fast by the enormity of sin but specially gathered in your name. Come to us and deign to enter our hearts; teach us what we should do, show us where we should walk, and bring about what we should accomplish. Be the salvation, prompting, and effecting power of our judgments. You alone, with God the Father and his Son, possess the glorious name. Do not allow us, who love the equity of supreme truth, to be disturbers of justice. Do not let ignorance draw us to the left, nor favor bend us, nor acceptance of a gift or person corrupt us. Rather, join us effectively to yourself by the gift of your grace alone, so that we may be one in you and deviate from the truth in nothing. Thus, gathered in your name, may we hold fast to justice in all things with a moderation shaped by compassion, so that our judgment may dissent from you in nothing here, and in the future we may obtain eternal rewards for good conduct. Through.”

Then the deacon, bringing the book of canons into the midst, is to proclaim the chapters concerning the conduct of councils—that is, those from the Council of Toledo. When the titles have been completed and everyone is seated in order, this exhortation is to be read by the bishop or, if he wishes, by the deacon:

“Behold, most holy brothers: after offering the preceding prayers to God, I address your brotherhood with a pious exhortation, and I adjure you by the divine name to intend, with the greatest reverence, to carry out whatever has been said to you by us concerning God, the sacred orders, or our conduct. If perhaps any one of us has understood something differently from what was said, let him, without any contentious scruple, bring the matter about which he has doubts back for discussion among us all, so that, with God’s help, he may either be taught or teach.

“Then I adjure you in like manner that none of you, when judging, accept a person or, driven by any favor or gift, depart from the truth. Rather, reconsider whatever is brought before the assembly for judgment with such great compassion that neither contentious disagreement may find a place among us for the subversion of justice, nor, again, may the vigor of our order grow sluggish in the pursuit of equity or in the exercise of careful attention.”

[Col. 1064C] After this exhortation, any of the clergy who wishes may bring forward a complaint. They are also to be admonished that no one should come to the synod without fasting, or withdraw from the common assembly before the general dismissal takes place. Thus the synod of the first day is to be concluded.

On the second day, when the bishop or his representative enters the synod, he is to stand in his place and say:

“The Lord be with you.”

“Let us pray. God, who reveals signs of your presence to us through your servants, send upon us the spirit of charity, so that at the arrival of our brothers and fellow servants your gift of generosity toward us may increase. Through.”

Afterward the Gospel is to be read as on the preceding day:

“The Lord appointed also seventy-two others.”

[Col. 1064D] Then the bishop or his representative is to say the prayers as on the preceding day:

“Holy Mary, and all the saints,” and so forth.

Then all are to prostrate themselves and sing these psalms for the safety of our king and of the other leaders of his kingdom:

“O Lord, how many are those who trouble me!”

“May the Lord hear you in the day of tribulation.”

“O God, we have heard with our ears.”

With the Kyrie eleison and the Lord’s Prayer, with these prayers:

“O Lord, save the king.”

“Be for him, O Lord, a tower of strength.”

“Save your people, O Lord.”

“Let there be peace in your strength.”

“Arise, O Lord; help us.”

[Col. 1065A] “Lord, hear my prayer.”

“O Lord God of hosts, convert us.”

“The Lord be with you.”

“Let us pray. God, ruler of all kingdoms and especially protector of the Christian empire, grant to your servant, our king, knowingly to cultivate the triumph of your power, so that he who is prince by your institution may always be powerful by your gift. Through.”

“Let us pray. Extend, O Lord, the right hand of heavenly assistance to your servants, so that with their whole heart they may seek and deserve to obtain the things they rightly ask. Through.”

Then, for the sick and for the salvation of the whole Church, they are to sing these psalms:

“Blessed is the one who understands.”

“The Lord is our refuge.”

[Col. 1065B] “O Lord, God of my salvation.”

With the Kyrie eleison and the Lord’s Prayer, with these prayers:

“The Lord has chastised and disciplined them.”

“May the enemy accomplish nothing against them.”

“Arise, O Lord; help us.”

“Lord, hear my prayer.”

“The Lord be with you.”

“Let us pray. God, singular protection of human weakness, show the power of your help to your sick servants, male and female, so that, aided by the support of your mercy, they may deserve to be restored to your holy Church. Through.”

Afterward a homily of Gregory is to be read by the deacon, beginning with these words:

“The harvest indeed is plentiful,” up to “they scarcely recognize themselves to be fathers.”

Then, if the clerics have no complaint to bring forward, let the laypeople be admitted. With them also listening, a reading from the Council of Nicaea is to be recited:

“Judges should discern laws and judgments only when fasting.”

Any layperson who has a complaint is to bring it forward. Thus the synod of the second day is to be concluded.

On the third day, when the bishop or his representative enters the synod as on the other days, he is to say:

“The Lord be with you.”

“Let us pray. Protect us, we ask, O Lord, your servants, with the supports of mind and body; nourish us with spiritual food, and in your mercy make us secure from all enemies. Through our Lord Jesus Christ.”

After this the Gospel is to be read:

“Jesus went about the cities and villages.”

Then, for the faithful departed, let these psalms be sung:

[Col. 1066A] “Attend to my words, O Lord.”

“O Lord, not in your wrath. The lesser [psalm].”

“To you, O Lord, I have lifted up my soul.”

With the Kyrie eleison and the Lord’s Prayer, together with these prayers:

“Grant them eternal rest, O Lord.”

“The righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance.”

“From the gate of hell.”

“The Lord be with you.”

Let us pray. Grant, we ask, O Lord, that the souls of your servants and handmaids, all who rest in Christ, may find fellowship with eternal light—those who, placed in this light, have attained your sacrament. Through our Lord.

After this, for the irreligious, let these psalms be sung:

[Col. 1066B] “To you, O Lord, I will cry.”

“I will bless the Lord.”

“O God, the nations have come.”

With the Kyrie eleison and the Lord’s Prayer, together with these prayers:

“Let peace be within your strength.”

“Show us, O Lord, your mercy.”

“O God, when you have turned, you will revive us.”

“O Lord, hear my prayer.”

“The Lord be with you.”

Let us pray. O God, who abandon the unbelieving and justly grow angry with the irreligious, mercifully turn your people back to you, we ask, so that those who continually offend you through the hardness of an irreligious mind may, by the inspiration of your mercy, be converted to earn the sacred offices. [Col. 1066C] Through our Lord.

If there are any questions or complaints, let them be brought forward; and thus the synod shall be dismissed on the third day.

On the fourth day, when the bishop enters the synod, he shall proceed as follows: first, candelabra with burning candles shall be carried before him; these shall be followed by a subdeacon carrying the Gospel, with two crosses, one on either side. Then the deacon. Finally, the bishop, clothed in episcopal vestments and a cope, shall enter; and, having entered, he shall stand in his seat and say:

“The Lord be with you.”

Let us pray. Bending the knees of our hearts before you, O Lord, we ask that we may fulfill the good which you seek in us—that is, that as we walk with you in ready attentiveness, we may exercise the subtle [Col. 1066D] judgment of difficult discernment, and, loving mercy, may shine forth through works pleasing to you. Through our Lord Jesus Christ.

Afterward, as usual, let the Gospel be read:

“Looking upon his disciples, Jesus said to Simon Peter: ‘If he should sin…’”

# APPENDIX TO BURCHARD

[Col. 1067]

## STATUTES OF THE CANONS CONCERNING THE OFFICE OF PRIESTS, BY AN UNCERTAIN COMPILER

(In Canisius, *Ancient Readings*, Basnage’s edition, vol. III, p. 396.)

## JACOB BASNAGE’S OBSERVATION ON THIS COLLECTION OF CANONS

Burchard compiled a very extensive Collection of Canons, which he had embodied in very many books. An anonymous writer abridged it, or rather excerpted from Burchard’s books those matters that concerned the office of priests. At what time this anonymous writer lived is uncertain; but since it is established that Burchard did not die until the year 1026, it was not permissible to place his abridger before the end of the eleventh century, although he may perhaps have lived much later. For there is nothing that can indicate his date.

## HERE BEGIN THE STATUTES OF THE CANONS CONCERNING THE OFFICE OF PRIESTS

[Col. 1067]

## FROM BOOK II OF BURCHARD

[Col. 1067A]

(From the Council of Reims, chapter 4.) Let no priest presume in any way to celebrate Mass without an amice, alb, stole, fanon, and chasuble. Let these sacred vestments be perfectly clean and be kept in a bright, clean place within the church. Nor may a priest ever leave the church wearing them, because divine law forbids this.

From the Council of Nantes, chapter 5: On every Sunday, before the solemn celebration of Mass, each priest shall bless water in his church, in a clean vessel suitable for this mystery. The people shall be sprinkled with the water inside the church; and, going around the church’s courtyard with crosses, he shall sprinkle it likewise. He shall pray for the souls resting there. Whoever wishes may take some of this water in his own vessel and sprinkle it in his house, in the fields, over livestock, or wherever he wishes.

Pope Alexander decreed that water mixed with salt should be blessed for the people; and he commanded all priests to do the same.

From the sayings of Augustine: Private Masses are not to be celebrated publicly on feast days, lest through them the people be drawn away from the public solemn celebrations of Mass; [Col. 1068A] for among some people there is a most improper custom on Sundays and other feast days of celebrating Mass immediately, so that anyone who hears it—even if it is for the dead—then departs. The people should be admonished not to approach food before the public office has been completed and celebrated canonically at the third hour, but to assemble for the public Mass, in order to hear the preaching.

From the Council of Nantes, chapter 8: Every priest who governs a people shall have a cleric who sings with him.

Every priest shall teach the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer to all his parishioners; and when they come to confession during Lent, he shall first require each one to recite them to him from memory. No priest shall give holy Communion to anyone unless [Col. 1068B] that person has recited them from the heart.

From the Council of Carthage, chapter 4: If, while the priest is speaking in the church, anyone leaves the auditorium without serious necessity, let him be excommunicated.

(From the Council of Orléans, chapter 2.) The Canons of the Apostles likewise prescribe that the three Rogation days before the Lord’s Ascension [be observed], so that not only clerics and women dedicated to God, but the entire people, may answer the priest’s greeting with one voice.

[Col. 1069A] (From the sayings of Augustine.) Let no ordained person leave his own parish for another, nor go to the thresholds of the apostles for the sake of prayer while abandoning the care of his church, nor go to the palace to make an appeal. If he does so, such ordination or departure is of no effect.

(From a council held at Reggio.) This also must be announced to all the faithful: those who wish to go to the thresholds of the blessed apostles for the sake of prayer must confess their sins at home and then set out, because they are to be bound or loosed by their own bishop or priest, not by a stranger.

(From the same council, chapter 4.) Priests shall privately bless faithful persons who desire it.

From the Council of Vienne, chapter 20: No one shall kneel on Sundays, nor from Easter until the octave [Col. 1069B] of Pentecost. Priests may not give a blessing over the people on Sundays or on other feast days when the people are assembled in the church.

(From the Council of Nantes, chapter 300, 18.) If some persons are in disagreement, they shall immediately be reconciled by the priest or expelled from the Church; once this has been done, Mass shall be celebrated.

(From the Council of Mainz.) Priests shall use stoles (*oraria*) without interruption, on account of the distinction of priestly dignity.

(From the African Council.) A cleric shall provide himself with food and clothing by an honorable craft or by agriculture, provided only that he does not neglect his office.

(From the Council of Nantes, chapter 60.) In the morning, after completing Matins, the priest shall discharge the duty of his service by singing Prime, Terce, Sext, and None. He shall do so in such a way that afterward, at the appropriate hours and at the appointed signals, these offices shall, as far as possible, be completed publicly either by him or by the schoolboys.

From the Council of Toledo, chapter 6: If any ordained person living in a city and in the place where there is a church does not come daily to the sacrifice, he shall not be regarded as a cleric.

(From the Council of Vienne, chapter 1.) If a cleric living in a city is absent from the morning hymns on a given day without illness, he shall be considered excluded from communion for seven days.

(From the Council of Nantes, chapter 11.) At a priests’ meal, a verse shall be said before the table, and the food shall be blessed by one of the senior members. Then they shall eat, blessing food and drink in turn, while a cleric reads; likewise, after the meal, they shall sing a hymn.

(From the African Council, chapter 6.) At every priestly meal, a reading from the divine Scriptures shall be interspersed.

(From the Council of Carthage.) A cleric shall neither grow his hair long nor wear a beard. If he swears by a creature, he shall be corrected most severely; if he persists in the fault, he shall be excommunicated.

(From the Council of Tribur.) We decree that every priest shall, every two or three weeks, on Sundays or the feasts of the saints, endeavor to instruct the people entrusted to him in his church, after the Gospel has been read, with teachings drawn from Holy Scripture.

[Col. 1070A] From the Council of Laodicea, chapter 20: Deacons shall not sit in the presence of priests unless at their command. The same applies to the other ranks.

(From the Council of Valence, chapter 6.) If a priest is unable to preach because of illness, homilies of the holy Fathers shall be read by an approved deacon.

## FROM BOOK III OF BURCHARD

(From the Council of Arles, chapter 1.) The people assembled for the celebration of Mass shall not depart before the priest’s blessing.

(From the decrees of Pope Hyginus, chapter 3.) The timbers of a consecrated church shall not be used for any other work except another church; otherwise they are to be burned in the fire, or given for the benefit of the brothers in a monastery.

Examples of Isidore to Bishop Lamfrid [Ludifred]: [Col. 1070B] The office of the psalmist is to sing; to pronounce blessings and praises at the sacrifice, responsories, and everything belonging to the office of singing.

The keys of the church belong to the doorkeeper, so that he may close and open God’s temple; guard everything inside and outside; receive the faithful; and exclude the excommunicated and unbelievers.

The reader’s duty is to proclaim the readings and preach to the people what the prophets foretold.

The exorcist is to retain the exorcisms by heart and, in exorcising, lay hands upon the possessed and the catechumens. The acolyte is responsible for preparing the lights in the sacristy. He carries the candle; he prepares the *surgesta* [sic in the manuscript] for the Eucharistic chalice.

The subdeacon is to carry the chalice and paten to the altar [Col. 1070C] of Christ and hand them to the levites; he is also to serve them, and to carry the pitcher and water, the cloth and towel, and provide water for the bishop, priest, and levites to wash their hands before the altar.

The deacon is to assist the priests and minister in everything they do in the bishop’s sacraments, and in baptism, chrism, the paten, and the chalice; also to bring in the offerings, and to preach the Gospel and the Apostle. For just as the Old Testament is entrusted to readers, so the New Testament is commanded to be preached by deacons. The office of prayers and the recitation of names also belongs to him. He admonishes the people to have their ears turned toward the Lord; he urges them to cry out; he gives the peace and announces the peace.

The priest’s duty is to prepare the sacraments of the Lord’s body and [Col. 1070D] blood on the altar, to say the prayer, and to bless God’s gifts.

The bishop is responsible for the consecration of basilicas, the anointing of the altar, and the preparation of the chrism. He distributes the foregoing offices and ecclesiastical orders, and he blesses sacred virgins.

These are the orders and mysteries of the clergy; nevertheless, they are distributed under pontifical authority, under the care of the archdeacon and the supervision of the chief officer and treasurer. The archdeacon commands the subdeacons and levites; responsibility for the levites’ dressing of the altar belongs to him, as does responsibility for incense and the sacrifice. Any of the levites may read the Epistle and the Gospel; any may say the prayers or sing the responsory on Sundays or other feast days [Col. 1071A] and perform the remaining duties. Thus far Bishop Isidore concerning ecclesiastical orders.

From the decrees of Pope Felix: Mass is not to be celebrated except in places consecrated by a bishop, unless extreme necessity compels it. From the same source: The dedications of churches shall be solemnly celebrated every year.

From the Council of Orléans, chapter 3: When the necessity of travel compels it, we permit Mass to be celebrated in a tent or under the open sky, in a clean place. But this may in no way be done without a consecrated altar stone.

From the letter of Pope Telesphorus, chapter 6: Mass must not be celebrated before the third hour of the day, because at that same hour the Lord was crucified and the Holy Spirit descended upon the apostles. The night of the Lord’s Nativity is excepted.

[Col. 1071B] From the Council of Chalon, chapter 39: It seemed good to us that at all solemn celebrations of Mass the Lord be entreated, in a suitable place, for the spirits of the dead.

Dionysius the Areopagite says that anyone who offers Masses for an evil man blasphemes God.

Augustine says that this should be done for all Christians, because it benefits either them, or those who offer the sacrifice, or those who repent.

From the African Council, chapter 64: Prayers and prefaces are not to be celebrated except those approved in a council.

From the Council of Nantes, chapter 30: The holy council decreed that no priest shall presume to celebrate Mass alone, because he ought to have someone standing beside him and answering him. If anyone transgresses this, he shall be suspended from office.

[Col. 1071C] From the decrees of Pope Pelagius, chapter 8: Only the following prefaces are to be received: one for the Paschal season in white vestments; another for the Lord’s Ascension; a third for Pentecost; a fourth for the Lord’s Nativity; a fifth for the Lord’s manifestation; a sixth for the apostles; a seventh for the Holy Trinity; an eighth for the cross; and a ninth, to be said only for the Lenten fast. Holy Roman Church holds and preserves these prefaces. We command you to retain them.

From the Ninth Council of Toledo, chapter 2: If, during the time of Mass, after the priest has begun to consecrate the sacred mysteries, a sudden illness prevents him from completing what he began [Col. 1071D], the bishop or priest shall be free to complete the consecration of the service begun. For repeated mysteries cannot be considered complete unless they are completed in due order. Let all the clerical orders likewise understand that this provision has been made or granted to them, so that others may immediately succeed those who preceded them for the sake of completion. Nevertheless, let what is provided for the sake of nature or illness not be turned into the destruction of presumption. No one shall celebrate Mass after food or drink, or after taking anything at all, however small; and no minister or priest, unless an evident occurrence of distress intervenes, shall presume entirely to abandon an unfinished service once he has begun it. Whoever rashly presumes to do this shall suffer the sentence of excommunication.

[Col. 1072A] From the decrees of Pope Anacletus, chapter 11: After the consecration has been completed, all who wish to avoid exclusion from the thresholds of the churches shall communicate. Thus the apostles established it, and the holy Roman Church maintains it; if they neglect this, they shall be degraded.

(From the Council of Rouen, chapter 1.) Every priest celebrating Mass shall communicate, and shall hand the divine mysteries to the deacon or subdeacon, who are ministers of the altar, to be gathered up. He shall also take care to communicate them with his own hand. He shall not place the Eucharist in the hands of any layman or woman, but only in the mouth; whoever transgresses this shall be removed from the altar.

From the Council of Laodicea, chapter 29: Agapae are not to be held in churches, nor shall people eat or spread couches there.

From the Council of Reims, chapter 6: The chalice and paten, unless made of gold, must in every respect be made of silver. Nevertheless, let the very poor have a tin chalice. A chalice of bronze, brass, wood, or glass is in no way to be used.

From the same council: Nothing shall be placed on the altar except reliquary chests containing the relics of saints and the four Gospels.

From the Council of Mainz: Laymen shall not presume to stand or sit among the clergy within the screens, either at vigils or at Masses.

Examples of Pope Anastasius: By apostolic authority we command that, while the holy Gospels are being recited, no one shall listen to the Lord’s words while sitting.

[Col. 1072C] From the Council of Auvergne: Concerning the covering of the Lord’s body or of the altar: when the body is carried to the tomb, it shall never be covered with the altar covering; nor shall the altars be polluted with the sacred veil while bodies are being honored; nor shall things belonging to the divine ministry be supplied for the pomp of weddings.

Augustine to the priest Casulanus: In matters about which divine Scripture has established nothing certain, the custom of the people of God or the institutions of our ancestors are to be held as law. And just as transgressors of divine laws are restrained, so contemptuous violators of ecclesiastical customs must be restrained.

(From the Council of Orléans, chapter 3.) Nothing shall be read or sung in the church except what is of divine [Col. 1072D] authority and what the authority of the orthodox Fathers has sanctioned.

From the Council of Laodicea, chapter 59: In church it is not permitted to read books other than those of the Old and New Testament.

(From the decree of Pope Sixtus.) Sacred vessels shall be handled by no one except sacred persons.

Examples of Pope Soter: Consecrated women, or nuns, shall in no way presume to touch sacred vessels or sacred cloths, or to carry incense around the altars.

Examples of Pope Clement: The altar cloth, chair, candlestick, and the *udum* [sic], worn out by age, shall be burned, and the ashes shall be stored in a clean place near the church.

From the decrees of Pope Gelasius: The holy Church accepts the deeds of the holy martyrs [Col. 1073A], although they are not read in the Roman Church because their authors are unknown.

From the Council of Rouen, chapter 2: We have decreed that after the Gospel, when the offertory has been completed, incense shall be placed over the offering.

(From the Council of Urbicum.) Examples of Pope Leo, chapter 2: Whenever the church to which people have gathered has been filled by the presence of a new congregation, the offering of the sacrifice must unquestionably be repeated, lest any of those who have assembled there be deprived of their devotion. Nor may a priest presume to celebrate Mass on that day at the altar where the bishop has sung Mass.

From the nineteenth decree of Pope Zacharias: [Col. 1073B] After a bishop or priest has entered for Mass and said the prayer, unless some illness intervenes, he must in no way dare to leave the altar of God before completing the service he has begun.

(From the Council of Tours, chapter 37.) It must be understood that, except on Sundays and on those solemnities when the holy Church customarily prays standing in memory of the Lord’s resurrection, we ought to pray humbly with our knees fixed to the ground, following the example of Jesus, Saint Stephen, and the apostle Saint Paul.

Concerning the sacrament of baptism, from Book IV of the same work, according to the decree of Pope Leo, Pope Victor, Pope Gelasius, and Pope Siricius: Baptism is not to be administered at any time except on Holy Saturday of Easter and at Pentecost, unless it is advanced because of danger of death.

[Col. 1073C] From the decrees of Pope Celestine, chapter 12: When infants or young people come to the sacrament of regeneration, they shall not first approach the font of life until the unclean spirit has been driven from them by the exorcisms and exsufflations of the clergy.

From the Council of Meaux, chapter 7: Every priest who cannot have a stone font shall have a suitable vessel solely for the purpose of administering baptism; it shall not be carried outside the church.

(From the decree of Pope Hyginus, chapter 10.) Likewise, separate vessels shall be kept for washing the corporal and the altar cloths; nothing else shall be done in them.

In the catechumenate, in baptism, and in confirmation, one sponsor may be appointed if necessity compels it. This is not, however, the Roman custom: one is received for each.

From the decrees of Pope Leo: No more than one person, whether man or woman, shall come to receive an infant from baptism. The same shall be done in confirmations.

From the Council of Mainz, chapter 2: In baptism or chrismation, no one who has not himself been baptized or confirmed can receive another as a son.

From the Council of Paris, chapter 2: No one shall receive anyone from the sacred font unless he knows the Lord’s Prayer and the Creed according to his own language and understanding, and recites them before the priest.

Examples of Pope Zacharias to Archbishop Boniface: Those baptized by a priest ignorant of grammar, who so mangles the Latin language as to say, “In the name of the Fatherland, and of the Daughter, and of the Holy Spirit,” should not be rebaptized.

[Col. 1074A] From the decrees of Pope Martin and Pope Eugenius: Wherever a sick person is brought to any priest for baptism, whether in his own parish or in another’s, he shall baptize him; if he does not, he shall be deposed.

From the decrees of Pope Hormisdas, chapter 3: If anyone who is not ordained baptizes or presumptuously performs any divine office, he shall be expelled from the Church and shall never be ordained. [The printed reading is *non ordinatur* (“he is not ordained”), apparently redundant; CAN. reads *non ordinatus* (“one not ordained”).]

From the decrees of Pope Gelasius, chapter 7: Deacons shall not dare to baptize without a bishop or priest, unless extreme necessity compels them because those persons are perhaps located far away for the aforementioned offices. This is also generally permitted to Christian laymen.

[Col. 1074B] From the Council of Tarragona, chapter 6: It has often been decreed against those confirmed a second time: They are to leave the world and live or serve God alone, just like those baptized twice.

From the decrees of Orléans, chapter 5: Let all adults come fasting to confirmation, and let them first be admonished to make confession, so that they may be able to receive the gift of the Holy Spirit in purity. For no one will ever be a Christian unless he has been chrismated through episcopal confirmation.

Pope Melchiades to the bishops of Spain, chapter 6: Baptism and the laying on of hands are both great—that is, sacraments—but the laying on of hands is worthy of greater veneration, since it is to be received from pontiffs alone. [Col. 1074C] These two are nevertheless so closely joined that they cannot in any way be separated from one another unless death intervenes, and one cannot properly be completed without the other.

From the Council of Lyon, chapter 3: No one shall presume to baptize with any chrism other than the new chrism received through the gift or permission of his own bishop, unless death intervenes first.

From the Roman Council, chapter 20: We decree that the scrutiny be conducted wherever there is a bishop, wherever the people and clergy are assembled, and wherever circumstances permit.

From the Council of Tribur, chapter 22: It has been decreed that henceforth nothing shall be demanded for ordination, chrism, [Col. 1074D] baptism, balsam, burial, or communion.

## FROM BOOK V OF BURCHARD’S DECREES, CONCERNING THE EUCHARIST

From the decree of Pope Julius to the bishops of Egypt: Some people, as though to complete communion, give the people a dipped Eucharist; but they have not accepted as Gospel testimony the passage where the Lord entrusted his body and blood to the apostles. The giving of the bread and the giving of the chalice are mentioned separately. For we do not read that Christ gave dipped bread to anyone except that one disciple whom the dipped morsel from the Master revealed as the betrayer; it did not signify the institution of this sacrament.

[Col. 1075A] From the Council of Tours, chapter 4: Every priest shall have a clean vessel in which the Lord’s body is carefully kept, or in which it is kept as viaticum for those departing from the world. This sacred offering, however, must be dipped in the blood of Christ, so that the priest may truthfully say to the sick person: “The body and blood of the Lord,” and so forth. It shall always be kept locked on the altar because of mice and wicked people. It shall always be changed every seventh day and consumed by the priest. On that same day, a newly consecrated offering shall be substituted in its place, lest, if kept longer, it become moldy—which God forbid.

From the Council of Orléans, chapter 4: It also seems necessary to add that the offerings placed upon the altar shall always be renewed from one Saturday to the next [Col. 1075B], like the loaves of the Presence, lest, being kept too long, they become moldy; as some think, they should be burned in the fire. If anyone, instigated by the devil, presumes to do otherwise, let him be anathema.

From the Council of Carthage, chapter 38: If necessity compels it, the deacon, in the presence and at the command of the priest, shall distribute the Eucharist to the people.

Saint Ambrose urges daily reception of the Eucharist.

Saint Hilary, bishop, says that no one should be separated from the medicine of the Lord’s body except one burdened by such sins that he ought to be excommunicated.

[Col. 1075C] From the decrees of Pope Sylvester, chapter 4: Every person shall receive the Eucharist on Sundays during Lent, except the excommunicated and those doing public penance. On Maundy Thursday, at the vigils of Easter, at Pentecost, and at the Nativity of the Lord, absolutely everyone must communicate.

From the Council of Elvira, chapter 3: Every person must abstain from his own wife for three, five, or seven days before holy Communion.

From the canon of Agde: Lay people who do not communicate at the Nativity of the Lord, Easter, and Pentecost are not to be regarded as Catholics.

A priest who entrusts the Eucharist for delivery to a sick person to a layman or woman—persons who are not permitted to enter the sacristy or approach the holy of holies—shall be subject to the danger of losing his rank. For the priest himself must communicate the sick person personally.

[Col. 1075D] (From the Council of Laodicea, chapter 19.) Only ministers appointed to the sacred order may approach the altar and communicate.

(From the decree of Pope Sylvester, chapter 7.) No acolyte or subdeacon shall give to others something already consecrated by a priest, except that he may carry what the priest has placed upon him.

(Pope Fabian, chapter 10.) The sacrifice must not be received from the hand of a priest who cannot perform the prayers, readings, and other observances of the Mass according to the rite.

(From the Council of Carthage, chapter 23.) The offerings of brothers who are in disagreement shall be received neither in the sacrifice nor in the treasury.

(From the same council.) The gifts of those who oppress the poor must be rejected by priests.

[Col. 1076A] (From the responses of Saint Gregory to Augustine, archbishop.) An illusion in sleep sometimes arises from gluttony, sometimes from an excess of nature or from illness, and sometimes from thought. If the illusion arises from nature, it is not to be feared, because it is more grievous that the mind, unaware, should have suffered this than that it should have caused it. In the case of an illusion caused by gluttony, the mind indeed bears some guilt, but not enough to prohibit receiving the Eucharist or celebrating Mass if a feast day requires it and the priest himself cannot have a substitute. In that case, after changing his garments, let him sing Mass. [Col. 1076B] If, however, the priest has a substitute, an illusion caused by gluttony should prohibit him not from receiving but from offering the sacred mystery—provided that the sleeper’s mind was not disturbed by an obscene imagination. For there are people who frequently experience such an illusion, yet whose minds are not defiled by obscene images in sleep, although when awake they remember having fallen into gluttony. If, however, an illusion of the sleeper arises from an obscene thought entertained while awake, then, because the mind unknowingly endured what it had thought, he must abstain from the sacred mystery that day. But the thought itself must be weighed: was it a suggestion, a delight, or consent? Suggestion comes through the devil, delight through the flesh, and consent through the spirit. Thus, when the unclean spirit suggests sin, if the flesh takes no delight in it, the sin is in no way committed. But if the flesh begins to take delight, sin begins to arise. If the mind consents to the delight, then sin is certainly completed.

[Col. 1076C] Nevertheless, it often happens that the mind resists the flesh, which is taking delight through a diabolical suggestion.

(From a Penitential.) Whoever vomits the sacrifice shall do penance for forty days. If this happens because of illness, seven days; if he throws it into the fire, he shall sing one hundred psalms. If dogs lick such vomit, the person who vomited it shall do penance for one hundred days. Whoever fails to guard the sacrifice properly, and an animal eats it, shall do penance for forty days. Whoever loses it in the church, or if part of it falls and is not found, shall do penance for twenty days. Whoever spills anything from the chalice upon the altar shall do penance for six or eight days. Anyone who receives the sacrifice while polluted at night shall do penance for seven days.

[Col. 1076D] (From the Roman Penitential, concerning the sacrifice; from a certain Penitential.) If the sacrifice falls to the ground and is not found, everything whatsoever that is found in the place where it fell shall be burned, and the ashes shall be stored beside the altar. The person to whom this happened shall do penance for half a year. If the sacrifice is found, the place shall be cleaned with brooms, the straw shall be given to the fire, and the ashes stored as above; the priest shall do penance for twenty days. If the chalice drips onto the altar linen, the drop itself shall be absorbed, and the linen moistened by it shall be washed over the chalice; the washing water shall be drunk beside the altar [Col. 1077A] or stored there. If the chalice drips elsewhere, the place itself shall be licked clean, the scraped-off material shall be consumed by fire, and the ashes shall be stored beside the altar.

## FROM BOOK VIII OF BURCHARD

(From the Apostolic Council according to Medard.) A layman shall not recite a reading in church or say the Alleluia, but only psalms and responsories without the Alleluia.

From Book XII of the same work, concerning oaths: The holy synod decreed that from Septuagesima until the octave of Easter, and from the Advent of the Lord until after the consecrated days, as well as during the fasts of the Four Ember Seasons, on the Greater Litany, on Sundays, and on the Rogation days, no one shall presume to swear upon sacred things except concerning reconciliation and peacemaking. [Col. 1077B] The soul that sins and hears the voice of one swearing falsely, or sees it, or is privy to it, and does not punish it, shall bear the iniquity.

(From the Council of Orléans, chapter 13.) Concerning fasting, from Book XIV of the same work: Priests shall announce to the people that during Lent and the fast of the Four Ember Seasons they are to kneel only at Mass. On Sundays, by contrast, and on other feast days, they shall not kneel from vespers to vespers, but shall pray standing and bent forward. No one shall presume to pray with one knee pressed to the ground, as the Jews did while mocking the Lord.

[Col. 1077C] (From the Council of Laodicea, chapter 51.) Martyrs’ feast days should not be celebrated during Lent; rather, their holy commemoration shall take place on Saturdays and Sundays. Nor shall the Lenten fast be broken before the end of the evening office. Whoever fasts on Sunday as though for continence shall be anathema.

(From the decree of Pope Callistus, chapter 15.) No one shall receive those excommunicated by priests before a just examination of both parties. No one shall share prayer, food, drink, or a kiss with them, nor even greet them; for whoever knowingly associates with excommunicated persons in these or other prohibited matters is himself subject, according to the institution of the apostles, to a similar excommunication.

[Col. 1077D] (From Book XVII of the same work; from the Roman Penitential.) If a priest is defiled by obscene speech or a lustful gaze, although he did not wish to fornicate, he shall do penance for five days. Whoever is polluted by an assault of the mind shall do penance for seven days. Whoever is voluntarily polluted in sleep shall rise and, kneeling, sing seven psalms of penance.

If he merely wished to sin in sleep, he shall sing twenty psalms. If he was polluted involuntarily, he shall sing fifteen psalms and, at the end of each psalm, say three times: “O God, attend to my help,” etc. Whoever, while sleeping in a church, emits semen shall fast for three days.

(From the Council of Carthage and the decrees of Pope Eusebius.) Concerning a penitent who became mute before the priest’s arrival, from Book XIX of the same work: If someone requests penance but, when the priest arrives, has lost the use of speech, he shall be reconciled and the Eucharist shall be administered to him [Col. 1078A], provided that he has suitable testimony that he had requested penance.

From Book XIX of the same work: Married people must observe chastity for the twenty days before the Nativity of the Lord, on every Sunday, during all the appointed fasts, on the feast days of the apostles, and on the principal and public festivals. If they do not, they shall fast for twenty days on bread and water.

(Augustine.) Some people, after lunch and when full, presume to receive the sign of peace from the priest offering it to the people. Whoever presumes to do this shall do penance for three days on bread and water.

For anyone who confesses a secret incest, the canonical remedy should be prescribed that he would have had to undergo if his crime had been public. But because the offense remains hidden [Col. 1078B], he should be admonished to do penance secretly, as far as he can.

(From the Penitential of Theodore.) Some say that sins should be confessed to God alone, as do the Greeks; and this is also the view of the righteous. Others say they should be confessed to priests, as does almost the whole holy Church. For we must follow the Apostle’s instruction: “Confess your sins to one another.”

(From the Council of Lleida, chapter 10.) Ordained persons who, after or before ordination, have fallen into capital crimes—that is, theft, fornication, perjury, and similar offenses—shall be degraded if their crimes are public. If they are secret, they may retain their rank, provided that they confess secretly to a priest and strive worthily to repent according to his counsel.

[Col. 1078C] (From the Council of Toledo.) Ordained persons whose sins are secret may retain their proper rank if they have secretly confessed to a priest and have done worthy penance according to his judgment.

(From a Roman Penitential.) Just as no one ought to offer the sacrifice except bishops [and] priests, to whom the keys of the kingdom of heaven have been entrusted, so no others ought to usurp the judgment of penitents. If necessity arises and no priest is present, the deacon shall receive the penitent for communion.

(From the Council of Elvira.) During the three Lents of the year, on Sundays, and on Wednesdays and Fridays, married people must abstain; nor may they have intercourse on those days, or while the wife is pregnant, from the day the child first moves in the womb until the birth, and after the birth for thirty-three days if it is a son, but fifty-six if it is a daughter.

[Col. 1078D] (From the letter of Pope Leo, chapter 11, to all bishops.) The confession of penitents must not be made public. That penance is sufficient which is first offered to the Lord and then to the priest, who comes as intercessor for the offenses of penitents. More people can be led to repentance if the conscience of the one confessing is not made public to the ears of the people.

(Callistus, pope, to all bishops.) We receive criminals whom the laws of the world put to death for penance, with mercy going before us, under the mark of infamy. We cannot erase the very infamy with which they are stained; but we desire to heal their souls through public penance and satisfaction to the Church [Col. 1079A], because manifest sins are not to be cleansed by secret correction.

(Also, Saint Gregory to Felix, bishop of Sicily.) Manifest sins likewise are not to be cleansed by secret correction; rather, those who openly do harm must be rebuked publicly, so that, while they are healed by open reproof, those who had sinned by imitating them may be corrected. While one is reproved, many are amended. It is better that one be condemned for the salvation of many than that many be endangered through one person’s license. For it is better that the wicked be corrected openly than that the good perish on their account.

(From the Decretals of Pope Melchiades and the Council of Tribur, chapter 4.) Concerning the penance of those who voluntarily commit homicide: first, they must not be permitted [Col. 1079B] to enter a church. For the next forty days they shall go barefoot and use no vehicle. They shall wear woolen clothing without undergarments, carry no weapons, and during these forty days take nothing except bread and drink only pure water. They shall have no communion in food or drink with the other Christians or with any other penitent until the forty days have been completed. No one else shall eat from the food that he takes. Yet, taking account of the person’s condition or illness, some indulgence may be granted out of mercy with fruit, vegetables, or legumes, as seems appropriate—especially if he committed the homicide under compulsion and not voluntarily. He must also be strictly forbidden, by canonical authority, during these days to have intercourse with any woman, to approach his own wife, or to sleep with any man [Col. 1079C]. He shall remain near a church and weep over his sins before its doors day and night. He shall not move from place to place but remain in one place during these forty days.
