If he should have enemies lying in wait for his life, his penance is meanwhile to be postponed until the bishop has secured peace for him from his enemies. If he is held by illness so that he cannot perform penance properly, the penance is to be postponed until he is restored to health. If he is held by a long illness, he shall do penance according to the bishop’s judgment, in whatever manner the bishop decides to heal the guilty and the sick person. (From the decrees of the same.) When the forty days have been completed, he shall wash with water, receive clothing and footwear, and have his hair cut.

What he must observe in the first year. In the first [Col. 1079D] year, after the forty days, throughout that entire year he shall abstain from wine, mead, and honeyed beer, from meat, cheese, and fatty fish, except on feast days celebrated in that diocese by the whole people. If he happens to be on a long journey, or in the army, or detained for a long time at the lord’s court, or held by illness, he may then redeem Tuesday and Saturday by giving a denarius, or the value of a denarius, or by feeding three poor people—yet in such a way that he uses only one of the three alternatives. That is, he may drink either wine, or mead, or honeyed beer. After he has returned home or been restored to health, he shall have no permission to redeem the fast. When the year has been completed, he shall be brought into the church, and the kiss of peace shall be granted to him.

(From the same, chapter 6.) In the second and third years he shall fast in the same way [Col. 1080A], except that on Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday he may redeem the fast at the aforesaid price wherever he is. He shall carefully observe all the other requirements, as in the first year.

(From the same, chapter 7.) Four years then remain, during each of which he shall fast for three Lents: one before Easter with the other Christians, abstaining from wine, mead, and honeyed beer, from meat and blood, eggs, and fatty fish; a second beginning on the third day after Pentecost; and before Christmas he shall fast as stated above. In the four years mentioned above, on Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday he may have whatever he wishes; and on Monday and Wednesday he may redeem the fast at the price already mentioned. He shall observe Friday strictly, with bread and water, and shall not redeem it in any way [Col. 1080B]. When these things have been completed, he shall receive Holy Communion. Nevertheless, as long as he lives, he must never cease doing penance.

(Also, Pope Pius, chapter 10.) Penitents must not receive Communion before the completion of their penance.

Concerning parricides, incestuous persons, and fratricides. Pope Nicholas to Charles, archbishop of Mainz, and his suffragans: Concerning parricides, brother, we command that they persevere for the space of one year in praying for the Lord’s mercy before the doors of the basilica. When the year has been completed, they shall be brought into the church, but shall stand among the hearers until the period of another year has come to an end, whenever they come to hear the solemn celebrations of Mass or other sacred offices. When these things have been carried out, if you see in them the fruit of penance, let them partake of the body and blood [Col. 1080C] of the Lord, so that they may not be hardened by the darkness of despair. They shall not eat meat on any day of their lives. Every day they shall fast until the ninth hour, except on feast days and Sundays. They must not presume to take wine or cooked food, except against pagans. Wherever they wish to go, they shall not be conveyed by any vehicle but shall strive to travel on foot. We leave the duration of this penance to the judgment of the bishops, so that, according to their manner of life, you may either lengthen or shorten it. They shall not be separated from their wives, if they have wives; but if they have none and are unable to remain continent, they shall take legitimate wives, lest they fall into the abyss of fornication. If, before the courses of the two years mentioned above have ended, the end of their lives should come, the viaticum must not be denied them [Col. 1080D].

If anyone has fornicated with two sisters, or with those persons whom Sacred Scripture forbids, and has performed worthy penance but has been unable to maintain chastity, he may take a legitimate wife. The same applies to a woman who has fallen into such a crime, lest she be brought into the chaos of fornication. But this is ordained only concerning laymen and laywomen.

If anyone has fornicated with his spiritual godmother, he is struck, as you know, by the blows of anathema. Likewise, we promulgate that the man be struck who has committed the crime of fornication with the woman whom he received from the sacred baptismal font, or with the woman whom he held before the bishop while she was being anointed with sacred chrism [Col. 1081A]. Nevertheless, if he has a legitimate wife, he must not dismiss her. In this matter your Holiness has also taken care to ask whether, if someone’s wife has committed adultery, her husband may, according to secular law, kill her. The holy Church of God is never bound by secular laws. It has no sword except the spiritual and divine one; it does not kill but gives life.

(Concerning various forms of homicide.) Pope Nicholas to Luitpert, archbishop of Mainz: If someone kills a pagan, not in war, nor from a determination born of hatred, nor for the sake of greed, since he is committing no slight offense, it is fitting that the homicide do penance, since the ancient people had been strictly commanded not to wage war even against foreign nations unless they had rejected the peace that was offered. If someone, while stretching a bow to test the string, kills his son when an arrow leaps out accidentally and not by intention, he must do penance as the Council of Ancyra decreed, as for homicide voluntarily committed [Col. 1081B]. A more severe penance ought indeed to be imposed because the victim was his son; but the closer he was in fleshly relationship, the sharper the grief over his death arose in his heart. For this was not done voluntarily. If a madman kills someone, penance must be imposed on him, since the illness itself is believed to have been the cause of the sin; nevertheless, it should be lighter than that imposed on one who commits such a deed while sane, in proportion to the difference that is acknowledged between the sane and the insane, and between the rational and the irrational.

If someone cuts down a tree and a person is crushed beneath its fall, the tree-cutter must do penance as a homicide if it happened through his intention or negligence. But if it occurred neither by his intention, nor through any wrong of his, nor, finally, with his knowledge, but while he was perhaps occupied with necessary work the unsuspecting person came beneath the tree and was crushed unexpectedly, the tree-cutter is not to be compared with a homicide [Col. 1081C].

(From the letter of Paulinus, bishop of Fano, to Aistulf.) Concerning the man who killed his wife: We propose two courses to you. Either enter a monastery, humble yourself under the authority of the abbot, and, assisted by the prayers of many brothers, observe with a simple heart everything that the abbot orders you, if God’s infinite goodness may forgive your sins. This course, as you should know with certainty, is lighter and more salutary: that you mourn your sins under another person’s supervision [Col. 1081D]. The second course is as follows: lay down your weapons and abandon all secular affairs. Never eat flesh or blood, except on the holy day of Pentecost, on one day of the Lord’s Resurrection, and on Christmas Day. At other times do penance on bread and water, occasionally with legumes and vegetables.

Persevere at all times in fasts, vigils, prayers, and almsgiving. Never drink wine, mead, or honeyed beer, except on the days mentioned above. Do not marry; do not keep a concubine; do not commit adultery; remain perpetually without hope of marriage. Never bathe in a bathhouse [Col. 1082A]; do not mount a horse; do not pursue your own case or another’s in an assembly of the faithful. Never sit at banquets of those who are rejoicing. In church, separated from the other Christians, stand humbly behind the door; commend yourself earnestly to the prayers of those entering and leaving; consider yourself unworthy of the Communion of the sacred body and blood of the Lord for all the days of your life. At the final end of your life, if you have observed this course, we grant it to you as a viaticum.

(From a chapter of Pope Nicholas, or of the bishop of Worms.) How one who kills a priest must do penance: Whoever voluntarily kills a priest must not eat meat or drink wine. Every day he shall fast until evening, except on feast days and Sundays. He must not take up arms or mount a horse. For ten years he must not enter a church [Col. 1082B]. After five years he may enter a church, but he must not receive Communion; he shall stand among the hearers. When the course of nineteen years has ended, permission to receive Communion and release from the prohibition against riding shall be granted to him. In the remaining observances, however, he shall continue three days each week, so that he may deserve to be more perfectly purified.

(From a chapter of Pope Nicholas, or of the Council of Worms.) Concerning one who accidentally crushes his child: If anyone inadvertently crushes his child, or suffocates him after baptism under the weight of clothing, let him do penance for forty days on bread and water, vegetables, and legumes, and abstain from unmixed wine. Afterward let him do penance for three years on the prescribed weekdays. In the fourth year let him observe three Lents. But if it happened before baptism, let him do penance for forty days [Col. 1082C] and observe the prescribed discipline after five years.

(From the Decrees of Pope Eutychian.) Concerning those who mutilate people or burn houses: If anyone mutilates limbs or burns houses, or orders it to be done, or consents to the person doing it, let him know that he is deprived of the Church until he has legally or amicably made satisfaction concerning these matters before the bishop of the city and the other citizens. But if he does not amend after the second and third summons, in which he is accused, let him be separated from the entire fellowship of Christians as a pagan and a publican.

(From a decree of the same pope, chapter 26.) That perjury is to be equated with other crimes: It must be preached [Col. 1082D] that the faithful beware of perjury and abstain from it with the utmost care, knowing that this is a great crime, prohibited in the Law, the Prophets, and the Gospel. We have heard, however, that some regard this crime as insignificant and impose, in a way, a light form of penance for perjury. They ought to impose such penance for perjury as they impose for adultery, fornication, voluntarily committed homicide, and the other criminal vices. If anyone, having committed perjury or any criminal sin, refuses to come to confession because he fears a long penance, he must be expelled from the church, from Communion, and from the fellowship of the faithful, so that no one may eat or drink with him, pray with him, or receive him into his house.

(From the Decrees of Pope Pelagius XI.) Concerning the same matter [Col. 1083A]: If anyone perjures himself and knowingly leads others into perjury, let him do penance for forty days on bread and water and for the following seven years, and never be without penance. The others, if they were aware of it, shall likewise do penance. But if they acted individually, let them do penance as for perjury not committed voluntarily—

(From the Decrees of Pope Pius, chapter 2.) If anyone is compelled by his lord to perjure himself, both are perjurers. Whoever knowingly perjures himself under compulsion from his lord: both are perjurers, the lord and the soldier—the lord because he commanded it, the soldier because he loved his lord more than his soul. If he is free, let him do penance for forty days on bread and water and for the following seven years. If he is a servant, let him do penance for three Lents and the prescribed weekdays.

(From the Decrees of Pope Soter.) Concerning rash oaths that must not be kept [Col. 1083B]: If it should happen that we have sworn something too rashly, and keeping it would lead to a worse outcome, we must recognize that it should be changed by wiser counsel; and, when necessity presses, it is better for us to perjure ourselves than, by keeping the oath, to turn aside into a greater crime.

(Saint Ambrose, *On Duties*, book III.) On the same matter: Many people often bind themselves by the religious obligation of an oath; and, although they themselves recognize that they ought not to have made the promise, nevertheless, out of regard for the oath, they do what they promised—as we wrote above concerning Herod, who disgracefully promised a reward to the dancing girl and cruelly paid it: disgraceful, because a kingdom was promised for a dance; cruel, because the death of a prophet was [Col. 1083C] given as the price of an oath. How much more tolerable would such perjury have been than the oath! And shortly afterward: Therefore, not every promise must be fulfilled.

(From the Council of Nevers.) Concerning rash oaths that must not be kept: A rashly made declaration may rightly be rescinded; this is not transgression but correction of rashness.

(From Pope Gregory in his *Moralia*.) That it is better to perjure oneself than to fulfill a sworn abomination, when the mind is constrained between lesser and greater sins: If there is absolutely no way to escape without sin, the lesser sins must always be chosen. For one who is enclosed by the circuit of walls and cannot escape throws himself toward flight wherever he finds the shorter wall.

(Saint Isidore.) On the same matter: An oath by which evil is rashly promised must not be kept [Col. 1083D]. For example, if someone promises an adulterous woman perpetual fidelity to remain with her. It is more tolerable not to fulfill an oath than to remain in the disgrace of sexual immorality.

(Also Isidore, in his *Sentences*.) Likewise: In evil promises, rescind your pledge. In a shameful vow, take care not to do what you rashly vowed. A promise that is fulfilled through crime is impious.

(From the Council of Toledo.) [Col. 1084A] It is necessary that one who has sworn wrongly perform worthy penance, because he has taken the name of God in vain against God’s command. For it is written in Exodus: “The Lord will not hold him innocent who takes the name of his God in vain”; and in Leviticus: “You shall not swear falsely by my name, nor profane the name of the Lord your God: I am the Lord.” Nevertheless, he must not do the evil that he had sworn to do; for foolish vows must be broken.

(Saint Isidore.) That God regards an oath in the same way as the person to whom it is sworn: However cleverly someone swears by his words, God, who is the witness of the conscience, accepts it in the same way as the person to whom the oath is sworn. He will be guilty in two ways, because he both takes God’s name in vain and deceives his neighbor.

(From the Council of Orléans, chapter 10.) Except for the sake of peace: The holy synod also decreed that, except for the making of peace, all the faithful should approach the sacraments fasting.

(From the Council of Orléans, chapter 2.) Oaths of a son or daughter made without the father’s knowledge, vows of a monk made without the abbot’s knowledge, and the oaths of a child are invalid [Col. 1084B].

Concerning invalid oaths: Children under fourteen years of age are not to be compelled to swear. Whoever receives the sacrifice after food or after even the smallest taste of food, except as a viaticum, shall do penance: children for three days, adults for seven, and clerics for twenty days.

(From the Decrees of Pope Cornelius, chapter 5.) If anyone gives or receives Communion from the hand of a heretic, and does not know that the Catholic Church forbids it, then, after subsequently learning of it, let him do penance for a full year. But if he knows and neglects the prohibition, and afterward performs penance, let him do penance for ten years. Others judge seven years, and more humanely, five years. (From the Decrees of Pope Eutychian, chapter 2.) If anyone permits a heretic to celebrate his Mass in a Catholic church [Col. 1084C], and does not know, let him do penance for forty days; if he did so out of reverence for him, let him do penance for a full year; but if he did so for the condemnation of the Catholic Church and of Roman custom, let him be cast out of the Church as a heretic, unless he has penance. If he has withdrawn from the Catholic Church into a gathering of heretics and persuaded others, then afterward performed penance, let him do penance for twelve years: three years outside the church, six among the hearers, and two more outside Communion. Concerning such persons, the canon says that in the tenth year they are to receive Communion without an offering. If a bishop or abbot orders his monk to have Masses said for dead heretics, it is neither lawful nor expedient to obey them. If it happens to a priest, when he has sung Mass and another has recited the names of the dead, that he names heretics together with Catholics, and he realizes it after Mass, let him do penance for a week. If he did it knowingly, let him do penance for a full year. If anyone arranges a Mass for the death of a heretic and, out of reverence for him, keeps his relics there, and does not know the distinction of the Catholic faith, then, after subsequently understanding fully what he has done, he must burn the relics there in a fire and do penance for a year. But if he knows and neglects the distinction, let him, being thoroughly moved to repentance, do penance for ten years. If anyone withdraws from the Catholic faith without any necessity and afterward accepts penance with his whole heart, let him do penance for three years outside the church among the hearers, according to the Council of Nicaea; for seven years in the churches among the penitents; and for two further years outside Communion.

# IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1027. ADELBOLD, BISHOP OF UTRECHT.

[Col. 1085]

# HISTORICAL NOTICE ON ADELBOLD

(From R. P. Bernard Pez, *Introductory Dissertation* in volume III of the *Newest Treasury of Anecdotes*, p. III.)

[Col. 1085A] Adelbold, born of noble lineage, was first a counselor to Emperor Henry II, called the Saint. Then, seriously reflecting in his heart upon the mockeries of fortune and the vanity of the world, he renounced his dignities and professed himself a monk in the Benedictine monastery of Lobbes. After cultivating there for some time the studies of piety and of the liberal arts, he was finally appointed in 1008 to succeed Ausfrid in the bishopric of Utrecht. He administered that province with great distinction until 1027, when he departed to the greater number on 27 November. We have condensed this account from the *Chronicle of Utrecht* of John of Beka, chapter 17, from Trithemius, Possevinus, Oudinus, and others, while not being unaware of the many difficulties to which the whole story is subject. Certainly Sigebert, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 138, says only this about Adelbold: “Adelbold, a former cleric of Lobbes and bishop of Utrecht, wrote a Life of the second Emperor Henry and left to posterity several monuments in both branches of learning.” On the words “a former cleric of Lobbes,” the learned Aubert Miraeus has this scholion: “Thus Adelbold, before his episcopate, was not a monk but a cleric of Lobbes.” Students of ecclesiastical antiquity should note that formerly at Lobbes, as also [Col. 1086A] among the Vedastines and Amandines, not only monks but also clerics resided. Certainly the college of the clerics, or canons, of Lobbes had its seat in the church of Saint Ursmer, which is now parochial, until the year of Christ 1409, when it moved from there to Binche, a town of Hainaut two miles distant from Lobbes. But whatever the situation may be concerning the canons or clerics of Lobbes, it is nevertheless far more probable that Adelbold was a monk of Lobbes rather than merely a cleric. Indeed, in the preface to his little work *On the Thickness of the Sphere*, he himself admits that he was a scholar, certainly at Lobbes. But who does not know that the study of letters flourished especially among the monks of Lobbes toward the end of the tenth century, and that nothing was more common than for clerics to share the schools of the monks, especially schools so celebrated and nearby—indeed almost joined to them? Therefore Adelbold was a monk and scholar of the monastery of Lobbes, a common teacher both of the monks and, if there were any, of the clerics, as very often happened in our other monasteries.

[Col. 1085]

# HISTORICAL AND LITERARY NOTICE

(From Pertz, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, *Scriptores*, volume IV, p. 679, in the prefaces to the *Life of the Emperor Saint Henry II*, edited by G. Waitz, Ph.D.)

[Col. 1085C] Adelbold, bishop of Utrecht, as Alpert attests [Note: [Col. 1085C] *On Various Times* I, 5.], set forth in one substantial volume, in polished language, the deeds performed by the emperor Henry II. This history, however, seems to have remained unknown to most people throughout the Middle Ages [Note: [Col. 1085C] What Sigebert reports *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 138, and in the *Chronicle* under the year 1024, he drew from Alpert; Sigebert was followed both by Alberic and other chroniclers and by Trithemius. Concerning the Saxon Annalist, see below.]; and those who later attributed to Adelbold the *Life of Henry* written by someone from Bamberg were far from the truth [Note: [Col. 1085C] Vossius, *On History* II, 42, p. 359, and many others [Col. 1086C].]. Gretser published another fragment of a Life [Note: [Col. 1086C] See *On Saint Henry II*.] from a Vienna manuscript, whose marginal note contained this: “The Life of the first Emperor Henry, written, as is believed, by Adelbold, bishop of Utrecht.” Relying on this authority, Gretser, though not without some hesitation, and those who later discussed the matter, treating it as established beyond doubt, ascribed to Adelbold [Note: [Col. 1086C] Leibniz, *Scriptores Rerum Brunsvicensium* I, Preface, no. 20; Sollerius, *Acta Sanctorum*, July III, p. 723; Rivet, *Literary History* VII, p. 252, and others.] the book that everyone has extolled with the highest praises and regarded as an exceptionally precious monument of antiquity.

Yet, when the matter was examined more carefully, we discovered that almost the entire work was copied from Thietmar [Col. 1087A]; I believe Stenzel was the first to point this out [Note: [Col. 1087C] I have already said elsewhere that what Gontzen brought forward to the contrary (*Geschichtschreiber*, p. 145) is of no importance.]. I say that Thietmar’s narrative was copied, not in such a way that it reproduces every word, but so that nearly all the events were drawn from him and reported in the same manner, order, and sense. The author of the *Life* omitted certain things, but did not add a single more important matter of his own [Note: [Col. 1087C] You will search Thietmar in vain for only those things that are related concerning Otto III’s body being brought back to Germany, together with certain matters of lesser importance.]. In many places, however, he enlarged, embellished, and, as it seemed to him, illuminated Thietmar’s narrative; but, led on by this endeavor, he committed no small number of errors, sometimes sufficiently ridiculous, and, unless I am greatly mistaken, invented many things from his own imagination in order to make the history more elegant and arrange it with a certain artistry. For he used a cultivated and ornate style, varied the narrative with antitheses and moral and philosophical sayings, and, while neglecting the facts, took the greatest care with the language [Col. 1087B]. In his preface, indeed, our author said that usefulness and truth should be demanded of a writer of history: usefulness, so that readers may be instructed by the events; truth, so that the author may not, through flattery, conceal the truth or present falsehoods. But it is easy to understand that he himself pursued the former more earnestly. Everywhere he raises Henry too extravagantly with praise, narrates his election with unmistakable partiality, and afterward embellishes many things in his favor [Note: [Col. 1087C] For example, chapter 7, the words he attributes to the king; chapter 13, concerning Hermann’s submission; chapter 38, concerning the king’s disposition.]. For this reason, the things that here and there he added as though from his own knowledge, although they are not important [Note: [Col. 1087C] For example, in chapter 17, the number of each army; in chapter 34, the material inserted concerning Helmiger the chaplain.], seem to me to possess rather weak authority.

Since this is so, it may reasonably be doubted whether this book can be attributed to Adelbold, a man outstanding in his age who was often employed by Henry in public affairs [Col. 1087C] [Note: [Col. 1087C] Thietmar VI, 50; Alpert II, 3, 10, 13, 21; Balderic, *Chronicle of Cambrai* III, 14, 17; Sigebert under the year 1004. The claim made by Trithemius (*Chronicle of Hirsau* I, p. 150) that Adelbold was Henry’s chancellor is plainly false. Beka, *Chronicle of Utrecht* (Utrecht edition, 1643, p. 37), calls him Henry’s proconsul; the *Great Chronicle of Belgium* (Pistor III, p. 105), an outstanding counselor of the emperor.]. Moreover, it is not easy to understand how Adelbold, whose work was already known to Alpert around the year 1021 [Col. 1088A], could have obtained Thietmar’s history, completed in 1018 and apparently not even then conveyed to foreigners. The note cited above from the manuscript, written by a later hand, will have little authority—unless one says that, since Adelbold wrote a *Life of Henry*, this work, which alone besides the Bamberg *Life* survives, must principally be attributed to him. If everything else argues against it, at least the style seems to fit him extremely well.

For Adelbold, educated in the monastery of Lobbes, which at that time excelled in the study of letters, under Notger, bishop of Liège [Note: [Col. 1087D] *Deeds of the Bishops of Liège* II, 26, appendix in Martène, *Collection* IV, p. 865. Sigebert, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 138, calls Adelbold a cleric of Lobbes.], and under the celebrated abbot Heriger, who “under his own name and that of Adelbold wrote a dialogue on the Church’s disagreement concerning the Advent of the Lord [Col. 1088B]” [Note: [Col. 1087D] Sigebert, same work, chapter 137], greatly excelled in knowledge, learning, and the literary disciplines that flourished at that time in Lotharingia—grammar, philosophy, and mathematics. As a scholar he went to Rome and there, apparently, sent a letter on the thickness of the sphere to Gerbert, already elected pope [Note: [Col. 1087D] Pez, *Thesaurus* III, II, p. 87.], and, prompted by the writings of Berno of Reichenau, inquired at what time the feast of the Lord’s Advent should be celebrated [Note: [Col. 1087D] Berno’s letter to Aribo, Martène, *Collection* I, p. 387.]. Elected bishop of Utrecht in 1010 [Note: [Col. 1087D] *Annals of Hildesheim*.], he devoted himself to public affairs, waged many very serious wars [Note: [Col. 1087D] Alpert related these events at greater length; see Thietmar VIII, 13, 15; Balderic, *Chronicle of Cambrai* III, 7, 14, 15.], restored churches and monasteries, and won great renown for himself throughout the kingdom [Note: [Col. 1087D] A clear testimony to this exists in a letter written by a monk of Tiel to Adelbold (*Acta Sanctorum*, February III, p. 546): “When I was considering writing certain miracles by which our Lord Jesus Christ, through the merits of Saint Walburga, has graciously deigned to illuminate his Church in our own times, you, most distinguished of bishops, Adelbold [Col. 1088C], came to my mind. You were worthy of the honor that I should dedicate these writings to your name, because nothing can ever be done, said, or written so appropriately but that [the edition reads: ‘when’] you surpass it by your own excellence in everyone’s judgment. Your outstanding wisdom is known to all, and everywhere you are proclaimed a man of supreme virtue and counsel. By everyone’s judgment it is also proved that, not only at home but even in the imperial camps, you perform the duties of the most excellent and capable man. If, however, these things that we say about you seem doubtful to anyone, let him look at Utrecht, enlarged and adorned by you through various works, and at the new monastery of Saint Martin founded and organized there by you with marvelous ingenuity and brought almost to completion in a few years with marvelous speed, so that these things seem not to have been constructed by building but, as it were, to have suddenly appeared there through wishful thought. Let him know that no flattery whatsoever can be spoken about you. Therefore, if I have expanded anything ineptly, I have decided to place it under your correction and defense, believing that through your authority it may be defended and ennobled. But if anyone still attempts to detract from your extensive prudence, let him also look at our place at Tiel, already flourishing in divine matters, which, as I promised I would discuss, had been deprived of every support by the earlier bishops but has been restored by you alone, through pious consideration, almost to its former condition. You also restored the estates long held by invaders, which devout men had formerly entrusted there for the worship of God. From these things it is easily gathered that you do not seek earthly advantages but strive to please God alone.”]. In the final years of his life he assumed the monastic habit and for some time even resigned the administration of his diocese, although he later resumed it [Note: [Col. 1088D] *Life of Poppo of Stavelot*, chapter 33, in Mabillon, *Acta* VI, I, p. 585.]. He died [Col. 1088C] in 1027, on 27 November [Note: [Col. 1088D] *Chronicle of Egmond*, in Kluit, *History of the County of Holland* I, I, p. 45.].

[Col. 1089A] Besides the *Life of Henry*, Sigebert reports that he “left several monuments in both branches of learning” [Note: [Col. 1089C] *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 138.]. Among these, Guibert of Gembloux mentions a nocturnal chant in praise of Saint Martin, to whom the principal church of Utrecht was dedicated, and a book on the triumph won by that same saint over the Danes [Note: [Col. 1089C] Heda quotes his words, *History of Utrecht*, p. 109.]. Trithemius lists books on the praises of the Holy Cross and on the praises of Saint Mary [Note: [Col. 1089C] *Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 312; *On Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict* II, 164; *Chronicle of Hirsau* I, p. 150.]. I have already mentioned the mathematical little work that he wrote [Note: [Col. 1089C] From the Tegernsee manuscript used by Pez, Gerbert published under Adelbold’s name a work on music (*Writers on Music*, pp. 304–312), but I have doubted whether it can be attributed to him. His name was written into the manuscript by a later hand.]. Another philosophical work remains unpublished in the Paris library [Note: [Col. 1089C] No. 7361. It begins: “The little work of Adelbold, bishop of Utrecht, on the words of Boethius: ‘O you who govern the world with everlasting reason,’ which neither Hermes nor Plato could unravel, since they were too much philosophers.” I possess a copy of this work made by our Bethmann; it lacks a preface. A book of the same or similar subject is found in other libraries; see Rivet, *Literary History* VII, pp. 257–258.]. Heda, however, without justification [Note: [Col. 1089D] Neither the style nor the subject supports this, nor do the manuscripts.], attributes to him the shorter *Life of Saint Walburga* [Note: [Col. 1089D] P. 110. He seems to have been led into error by the letter written to Adelbold concerning Saint Walburga (no. 18). Through misunderstanding it, he says that the bishop’s brother lived near Tiel. Rivet accepted both errors, *Literary History* VII, pp. 253, 256.], and also published from the Utrecht cartulary a charter—clearly false—in which Adelbold is said to enumerate the vassals of the bishopric [Note: [Col. 1089D] Neither the bishops said to have subscribed—Anno of Cologne, Eberhard of Trier, and Adelbert of Hamburg—were seated in Adelbold’s time, nor did the vassals mentioned—the duke of Brabant, the count of Guelders, the count of Cleves, the count of Bentheim, and so forth—exist at the beginning of the eleventh century.].

[Col. 1089B] But if we compare the genuine works with the Life of Henry that we have before us, we surely detect the same manner of expression, the same method of artfully connecting sentences, precisely the same authorial character, and indeed, not merely once, almost the same words [Note: [Col. 1090C] Compare chapter 2: “Nor is it tedious for me to say this, nor superfluous for others to hear it”; and the letter to Gerbert, § 4: “If it is not tedious for you to hear, it will not be burdensome for me to say.”]. It is necessary [Note: [Col. 1090C] You may recognize this even in the brief fragment quoted by Guibert of Gembloux: “This jewel (he is speaking of Saint Martin) shines in heaven, flashes on earth, is honored everywhere, and is loved everywhere. Whoever has purchased it will rejoice in an everlasting treasure. Whoever possesses it will lack no good thing. O sons of men, acquire this treasure for yourselves and possess this everlasting light, and nothing will be lacking to you.”]—a conclusion that almost moves me myself to undermine the arguments advanced above—to contend that Adelbold was the author of the Life, although I cannot assert this with certainty, nor yet deny it. The bishop of Utrecht visited Saxony frequently in these years [Note: [Col. 1090C] At that time Bishop Adelbold was staying in Saxony with Emperor Henry, Balderic III, 17.—In 1013 he was at Gruona (Life of Meinwerk, ch. 21); in 1016, at Dortmund (ibid., ch. [Col. 1090D] 134; the charter in Schaten, *Annales Paderbornenses* I, pp. 417–418); in 1018, at Paderborn (Life of Meinwerk, ch. 164; Schaten I, p. 429); in 1019, at Goslar (Life of Meinwerk, ch. 165; Schaten, p. 432), and afterward at Ermeneswerethe (Life of Meinwerk, ch. 173).], where it may be believed that he obtained a copy of Thietmar’s History. The fact that he followed this book, whether it was communicated to him by Thietmar himself [Note: [Col. 1090D] Thietmar nowhere indicates that he had met Adelbold.] or by someone else, as a “reliable reporter” [Note: [Col. 1090D] Adelbold’s preface], and that during the early years of Henry he added almost nothing of his own, must be explained [Col. 1089C] by the fact that during those years he lived in a monastery, devoted to study [Col. 1090A] and removed from public affairs. Nor is it surprising that a man trained in philosophical and poetic disciplines, when writing history, should have cared more for verbal ornament and for entertaining his readers than for bare and simple truth, since even in our own times we see the same thing happening every day. Certainly, concerning the events that afterward took place in the Rhineland provinces, in which he himself was largely involved, he should be thought to have written more accurately and from personal knowledge. This is also suggested by Alpert, when he says that the siege of the city of Metz, which Thietmar omitted, was described at greater length by Adelbold [Note: [Col. 1090D] I, 5. Conversely, it may appear that Adelbold omitted the account of the Burgundian expedition of 1016 narrated by Alpert, II, 14.]. We cannot help lamenting that these writings have been lost [Note: [Col. 1090D] Compare Leibniz, *SS. R. Br.* II, preface, p. 19.].

The Saxon Annalist, who, so far as I know, was the only person in the Middle Ages to use this Life, whether he possessed a more complete text [Col. 1090B] or only a similar fragment, is not so easy to determine, since among the words of Thietmar that he copied it is scarcely possible to recognize any other narrative drawn from the same source. Nevertheless, after reading the Annalist’s book carefully, I would affirm that nothing of this kind is found in it. Certainly, neither concerning that siege of Metz nor concerning the events that afterward took place in Lorraine, whether under Bishop Theoderic or under Adelbold himself, is anything found there that could have been taken from Adelbold. If he had possessed a book dealing with these matters, that careful and copious historian would surely not have neglected it. It therefore appears that he already possessed this Life of Henry in a form lacking its conclusion; but whether he read it under the name of Adelbold, who does not even mention his death, may reasonably be doubted.

[Col. 1091]

# THE LIFE OF SAINT HENRY, EMPEROR, BY ADELBOLD

(See above, in the entry for Saint Henry the Emperor under the year 1024, col. 87 of this volume.)

[Col. 1091]

# ADELBOLD’S LIFE OF SAINT WALBURGA

[Note: [Col. 1091B] The title prefixed in our manuscript is: “The Life of the most blessed, most beloved of God, and paradoxical Walburga.”]

(In Bollandus, *Acta Sanctorum*, February, vol. III, February 25, from manuscripts of Utrecht and three others, collated with Capgrave, *Historia Sanctorum*, printed 175 years ago by Surius and in breviaries.)

## CHAPTER ONE. The deeds of Saint Walburga, her death, and the translation of her body

[Col. 1091A]

### 1

After the nation of the English, dear to God, had been converted from the error of paganism to the truth of Christianity through the apostolate of the memorable Pope Gregory, many from among them crossed beyond their maritime homeland and came as far as the empire of the Franks [Note: [Col. 1091B] “The empire of the Franks” is used broadly for all the territories in Gaul, Belgium, and Germany that had been subject to the dominion of Charlemagne and his descendants]. In their number was Saint Boniface. When he had arrived here in this foreign province [Note: [Col. 1091B] Saint Boniface first landed in Frisia, then subject to the Franks, and labored for three years—Beka says thirteen—as Saint Willibrord’s co-worker in the diocese of Utrecht and in the conversion of the Frisians; his feast is celebrated on June 5], he acquired for himself, as it were, a native country, when he obtained the episcopal see of Mainz through his merits [Note: [Col. 1092B] He had for many years been appointed bishop for the conversion of the nations, and at length Mainz was assigned to him; at that time the city was called the metropolis of the Franks. Consult Serarius’s note 23 on the Life of Saint Boniface, book III of the *Rerum Moguntiacarum*]. From the woodland of that same island of England [Note: [Col. 1092B] Some manuscripts read “of England”] three most fruitful trees sprang forth here among us: namely, the two brothers Willibald and Wunibald, born of the same mother, together with their sister Walburga, most dear to God and to men. The elder of them, Willibald, after the aforementioned Boniface had ordained him, was advanced to the episcopate of the Church of Eichstätt. There, leading an angelic life, he finally departed most blessedly—he did not die, but went forth. The other, dedicating himself entirely to Christ’s service and utterly rejecting all worldly things, chose for his dwelling the place called Heidenheim. There, fortified by unceasing prayers, strengthened by hope, and armed with faith, he brought to a most vigorous completion, until the departure of his soul, the monastic way of life that he had undertaken together with his brother; and, going before many who followed him [Note: [Col. 1092B] In the Utrecht manuscript and two of Trier: “he encouraged them by rewards to live well”; but in the earlier Leuven Legend, Surius, altering the style, writes: “and by his example led many to strive to live well”], he exhorted them to the rule of virtuous living.

### 2

After their departure [Note: [Col. 1092B] So all the manuscripts, together with Capgrave and the readings of the Morin breviaries. Surius, however, corrected it to: “But when Wunibald had departed this life, she of the female sex …” The earlier Life by Wolfhard agrees with this], their sister Walburga, the glory of all womankind after Saint Mary, making herself an example worthy of imitation to all whom she could, was appointed head of the monastery of that same community of girls at the aforementioned place of Heidenheim, ever most effective in obtaining whatever she asked from Christ.

Once, after evening had been completed there, as she was returning from the church to her lodging, it happened that a certain custodian of the church, named Guomerand [Note: [Col. 1092B] Other manuscripts have Gaumeradus and Goumeradus; Surius has Conmeradus], foolishly refused Walburga a light to guide her as darkness fell. Maintaining invincible patience in the face of this insult, she ate with the community of nuns and, after the divine praises had been completed, went to the dormitory. Then immediately, in a wondrous manner, such a great blaze of light shone there [Col. 1092B] that it seemed to penetrate the floor of the dwelling, and it remained until the morning praises.

All the consecrated virgins were astonished, and, rejoicing, ran to the bed of their most religious mother-superior and told her of the immensity of the heavenly radiance. She burst into tears, raised her eyes and hands to God, and said:

> “To you, Lord Jesus Christ, whom I, your humble handmaid, resolved to serve from my cradle, I give thanks for this gift bestowed upon me. You have deigned to console me, unworthy as I am, with the aid of your light, for the exercise of the minds of your handmaids who are joined to me, and you have dispelled the darkness of foul horror by the rays of your mercy. I ascribe this not at all to my own merits, but to the merits of my brothers—namely, your servants” [Note: [Col. 1093D] Wolfhard has: “to the prayers of my devoted brother and your servant.”].

### 3

After the death of the most blessed Bishop Willibald, the brother of Saint Walburga [Note: [Col. 1093D] So all the manuscripts, together with the Leuven Legend and Capgrave. Surius, deleting the word “bishop,” inserted Wunibald, whom we said died in 761; he seems to have believed that Saint Willibald survived Saint Walburga], she became thereafter, as is recognized to be characteristic of the female sex [Note: [Col. 1093D] Surius: “seized by immoderate grief”], intolerably impatient. Then, one evening, without anyone from her household knowing, she left the monastery and came to the house of a certain rich man. She stood alone before his door like a stranger and an unknown woman.

When the master of the house saw her, not knowing who she was, he was distressed, together with all his household, lest the swift ferocity of his dogs tear her to pieces. He ordered her to identify herself at once. Then she replied:

> “By no means do I fear that the dogs you fear will touch me with a cruel tooth; they will not be able to bite Walburga—for that is my name. He himself who brings me unharmed here to your house will be able to lead me unharmed back to the place from which I came; and he will grant healing comfort to your household, if you believe with complete faith that he is the physician of physicians.”

When he heard this, the distinguished man immediately sprang up from the place where he had been sitting. Troubled in spirit, he asked why so noble a girl and servant of almighty God had taken her stand at his door. He then received her with every mark of veneration and provided her with every service that was her due.

At the hour of nighttime rest, when she was asked where she wished to sleep, she replied that she wished to rest nowhere else but in the room in which his daughter lay, worn down by a grave illness almost unto death [Col. 1093C], and whose funeral arrangements her father and mother were already preparing. While they lamented in excessive grief, she entered the room and spent the entire night sleepless, pouring out prayers to the Lord throughout the night. On the following day the girl recovered in complete health.

When the parents saw this miracle, they gave manifold thanks to almighty God, who kills and makes alive, strikes and heals. They presented the virgin, most beloved of God and men, with many gifts and commended themselves to her most sacred prayers. But she rejected the preciousness of the gifts, loving Christ alone above all things, and returned to the monastery. And the more she discovered divine mercy to be active within her, the more, day by day, she adapted herself to the excellence of a stricter life [Col. 1093D] [Note: [Col. 1093D] The Trier and Saint-Maximin manuscripts have: “excellent mercy.”].

### 4

After these two miracles, among others known to us, had been accomplished in her life, the most blessed virgin, strengthened in God and having utterly overcome the world with its desires, became an example of every religious virtue to all who followed her. At length she triumphed over this world and died, going most blessedly to paradise to receive the prize of her triumph [Note: [Col. 1093D] In the *Historia Sanctorum*, or *Legenda*, printed at Cologne in 1483 and Leuven in 1485, the following is inserted: “It is also read that, in order to preserve the purity of her chastity, she always so abhorred the touch of men during her life that even after death, when a certain man touched her body in order to bury it, it immediately began to shake and tremble as a testimony to her former preservation of purity.”]. She was buried with the greatest honor in the same monastery in which she had always served Christ as a handmaid.

### 5

Not long afterward, when the pastors of the same church in which Saint Walburga was buried had died, it happened that Otgar, a venerable man, obtained the see of the Church of Eichstätt. Since he had treated with less honor than was proper the same monastery in which the body of the blessed virgin lay buried, the holy virgin is said to have addressed him one night in a vision in these words:

> “Why, O Bishop Otgar, worthy of God, have you hitherto wished to keep so negligently the monastery in which my body is buried? For I am trampled daily by the drunken feet of the servants who gather there, and I am crushed beneath common footsteps. You will soon learn that I shall disclose to you some sign by which you may understand that you have not acted rightly toward me and the house of God, so that, if you recognize yourself thereafter to be guilty, you may deserve forgiveness.”

That this was not false was proved by the outcome shortly afterward. For as soon as the walls of that structure had been raised and the projecting framework of beams was to be set upon the walls the following day, the northern wall suddenly collapsed to the ground during the night and struck no small terror into both the household and all who lived around it.

When morning came and everyone had assembled in fear at the sight, the custodian of that church, named Reginfrid, conveyed the news by the swiftest messenger to the aforementioned Bishop Otgar [Note: [Col. 1094D] The Antwerp manuscript has: “by an intermediary.”]. When he heard this, he immediately understood that the vision he had seen had been fulfilled [Note: [Col. 1094D] The Utrecht manuscript has: “the vision he had heard”], and he hurried there. With the greatest speed, together with his most devout fellow-countrymen, he restored and dedicated the church.

After a year had passed, the bishop mentioned above ordered his archpriests Walco and Adhalung, together with a certain nun named Liubila [Note: [Col. 1094D] Surius has: “Walco and Alung, with Hubila”], to go there, dig up the body of Saint Walburga with the utmost care, and carry it with the ringing of bells, the singing of hymns, and every mark of reverence to the monastery at Eichstätt. They completed this with the rejoicing of all the people on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October [September 21] [Note: [Col. 1094D] The Utrecht manuscript has “on the eighth day before the Kalends”]. By order of the same bishop, three days later, on the eighth day before the Kalends of October [September 24] [Note: [Col. 1094D] The same manuscript has “on the fifth day before the Kalends”], they also took the remains of Saint Walburga’s brother Wunibald from that same church and transferred them to the same place.

## CHAPTER TWO. A portion of Saint Walburga’s relics given to Abbess Liubila. Gluttony and other illnesses removed

[Col. 1095A]

### 6

But after the most blessed Walburga had deigned to visit the territory of Eichstätt in person, it later happened that the aforementioned nun Liubila was so oppressed by relatives who greatly envied her that, both violently and cunningly, she was almost driven from the same maternal inheritance. In her salutary anxiety, she took counsel and asked Ercambald, bishop of the Church of Eichstätt, that the relics of Saint Walburga be granted to her, so that, if she prevailed in obtaining her maternal inheritance, she might forever dedicate it to Christ and to his virgin Walburga.

Because this request had its beginning from God, it deserved also to have from him the happiest conclusion. Therefore, in the year 893 from the Incarnation of the Lord, while Arnulf was reigning, the tomb of the most blessed virgin Walburga was opened—the tomb in which she had been placed during the episcopate of Otgar, and for whose burial, because it had been inadequately cared for by that bishop, he had been severely rebuked in a vision, as has already been related.

### 7

[Note: [Col. 1095D] The following miracles have been selected from Wolfhard. The first is narrated by him in book III, chapter 3; it occurred in the year 895, two years after the translation of the body.]

A miracle occurred, unheard-of throughout the ages and established by many clear testimonies. A certain maidservant of a household, named Fritherada [Note: [Col. 1095D] The Antwerp manuscript has Fricherada; Surius has Friderada], who served her master and his wife more assiduously and familiarly than the others, was suddenly seized by the distress of an illness. After being miserably afflicted by it for two days, she recovered somewhat; but afterward such a great gluttonous appetite grew in her that she could not in any way be satisfied, but could scarcely even be refreshed.

At first her relatives supplied her with a very large quantity of food, and when she desired greater provisions day by day, they began anxiously to consider what they should do with her. For she had not yet regained the use of walking, but crawled miserably on little stools. Then, with the counsel of her own parents and relatives, she asked her mistress that she might be permitted to visit the oratory of the aforementioned virgin.

When permission was granted, she came and earnestly offered her prayers. On the third day she received the use of her disabled feet. When the master of the household and his wife heard this, they hastened there in great joy and gave the same maidservant to Saint Walburga as her permanent property, to serve there [Col. 1095D]. But the aforementioned abbess Liubila retained her, allowing her to remain there for some time, and after a few days returned her unharmed to her masters.

### 8

But as soon as she had returned, she was seized by her former illness. When her mistress saw that it had not been good counsel to remove her in any way from the monastery after her healing, she brought her back in haste and entrusted her to the church’s personal service. She immediately recovered; but she was tormented by an intolerable appetite for food [Note: [Col. 1096D] The Antwerp manuscript adds: “every day.”].

Since she was extremely distressed by this and ashamed, she prudently took counsel and confessed it to a certain Thiedild, the monastery’s administrator, so that she might be relieved of this insatiable gluttony by her prayers. Thiedild pitied her affliction and devised a salutary remedy: she had her receive a portion of blessed bread from a venerable priest named Reimund [Note: [Col. 1096D] Other manuscripts have Remundus, Himundus, Immundus, and Mundus].

As soon as she tasted it, her appetite began gradually, in a wondrous manner, to diminish and disappear, just as it had previously grown. At length, for nearly half a year, she was able to eat nothing but cheese and drink only a very small amount of milk. Afterward, her desire for bodily nourishment so entirely failed that, if she ever attempted to taste anything, she immediately vomited it up.

When she became convinced that she could taste nothing at all without immediate vomiting [Col. 1096B], she asked the aforementioned handmaid of God, Thiedild, to provide her with none of the sustenance of life, since everything she provided was lost. Then Thiedild, astonished at a matter unheard-of throughout the ages—namely, that any body could live so long without nourishment—was greatly troubled about what should be done with her.

At length she sent her to another church of that monastery, situated nearby, and entrusted her to one of her companions who had been appointed administrator there. Receiving her, the woman watched over her with the greatest care and kept her with her for nearly six weeks. During that time it was absolutely certain that she ate or drank nothing.

### 9

When this period had ended, the aforementioned Thiedild came to visit her and learned what had happened. Then the handmaid of God, Thiedild, began to exhort her in various ways and with soothing words, saying:

> “Do not, my dearest daughter, do not deceive yourself through such obstinacy. Rather, hasten to return to your senses and, taking thought for yourself, receive some nourishment. But if you are being deceived by some illusion, confess it, daughter, and do not be ashamed. I firmly believe that, if you do so, you will soon be helped by the prayers of our lady.”

When she heard these words, she was ashamed because of the excessive reproach [Note: [Col. 1096D] The Antwerp and Saint-Maximin manuscripts add: “she remained silent”]. She tried to taste something, but could not. Yet, so that she might not appear to disregard the persuasive words of God’s handmaid who was exhorting her, she asked that some of the poorer-quality cider be offered to her.

When she unwillingly tasted a very little of it, that small amount immediately burst out through her nose and eyes, so that she at once became blind. Then she was brought back to the monastery, and after not much time she recovered her sight [Col. 1096D]. But she persisted in the same abstinence that had previously held her, to the astonishment of all.

When the aforementioned mother-superior and the entire community of girls were greatly astonished at this cause, never before heard of, they took counsel and approached the venerable bishop to whose diocese the monastery was subject. They narrated to him in order everything that had happened from the beginning, asking what his wisdom might discern and determine concerning this incredible sign.

When he heard this, the bishop was astonished. Since he could not believe it at all, he feared that, deceived by some thousandfold [Col. 1097A] stratagem of the devil, she might be deluding human sight and that nourishment might somehow be secretly supplied to her in hidden places. He therefore took counsel with his associates and summoned from Saint Walburga’s monastery a highly religious priest. By episcopal authority he repeatedly ordered him to take the maidservant in question into his keeping and watch over her with the utmost care, lest any deception mislead human eyes.

He did so and reported to the bishop that he had himself most diligently verified the matter, just as it had previously been related. Then the bishop, every doubt having been removed, believed, as though compelled by the evidence. Thus, even then, she had remained for three years from the Mass of Saint Martin until that day. Yet she performed whatever had been assigned to her, in accordance with her strength.

Whenever she attempted to receive the Eucharist [Col. 1097B], however, unless she went to sleep with the utmost haste, she immediately vomited. Therefore, whatever now appears impossible to human weakness should be believed to be entirely easy for the divine majesty.

### 10

Afterward, therefore, the very prudent Ercambald was sent there with other archpriests and men of good merit. He ordered the little body of the blessed virgin to be dug up and, once found, carefully handled. While they fulfilled the excavation with great trembling and with divine praises, they discovered the relics of the most holy virgin, exceedingly worthy of love, as if moistened by a thin liquid.

Although they were merely dewy, not even a single tiny particle was able in any way to adhere to the hands of those touching them. A portion of the sacred virgin’s body was then removed from the monastery at Eichstätt, according to the bishop’s instructions. At this, an extremely turbulent grief and lamentation arose among the people of Heidenheim, who mourned as though their entire lady had been taken from them [Col. 1097C].

Meanwhile, as such great pledges of the desired gift were being carried with the joyful celebration of the rejoicing crowd to the place called Movenheim, a certain boy who happened to be epileptic met the bier bearing the sacred burden. Bending beneath it, he received the very healing he had sought. Then suddenly, as all who were passing by testified, such a powerful fragrance of perfume spread through that place that the nostrils of those going before or following the bier could scarcely endure it.

## CHAPTER THREE. Various miracles accomplished through the aid of Saint Walburga

[Col. 1097D]

### 11

After the relics of the most holy virgin had been placed above the sacred altar of the aforementioned monastery, it happened on the following night that Abbess Liubila was present there. While she had been held there for three nights and, suffering from severe gout, had given herself over to sleep, a cleric of venerable white hair appeared before her, Willibald, as is believed, the bishop and brother of Saint Walburga, who had long before possessed property at that same place by hereditary right.

Addressing her, he said:

> “Liubila, why are you sleeping? Why do you not rise and go to the church?”

She replied:

> “Why must one go to the church now, when the morning bells have not yet sounded? I cannot in any way go there on foot unless I am led by the hands of others.”

He said:

> “Go more quickly, and do not delay, because Willibald has entered the church with a great throng and wishes carefully to ask you how you are keeping his holy sister, who has been buried there.”

At once she rose as though suffering no inconvenience at all. Leaping from place to place, she entered the basilica toward which she had set out and gave thanks to divine mercy and to the blessed virgin for the health she had received.

### 12

A certain poor man, crippled from birth and appearing almost like some kind of monster, had joined the many who fled to Saint Walburga’s protection, seeking both food and the comfort of healing. One night, while he was asleep, the most blessed virgin appeared to him and ordered him to go to the church.

When he replied that he dreaded the severity of the cold and therefore did not dare even to rise from his resting place, she answered him in gentle words:

> “Go, poor little man, quickly. I shall protect you from the severity of this cold by which you are now afflicted and provide warmth for your limbs. As a small payment for the health restored to you, you will have to hang up at the church the little stools [Note: [Col. 1097D] The Trier manuscripts add: “after your health has been restored”] that you still use because of your bent limbs.”

Although he went to the church most reluctantly and remained there for a little while, he returned anxiously to his lodging. When morning came, he went back there, threw himself before the bier of the blessed virgin, and around the third hour suddenly began, quivering, to roll and stretch himself out on the pavement. The little stools, without which he had never been able to move from his place, were thrown before the altar as though torn from his hands by divine power.

Thus, with all his limbs restored, he rose and walked. Recovering his strength, he afterward served in that same church, vigorous and unharmed, for the remainder of his life.

### 13

A certain woman named Reginsundis was brought to the same monastery. All her limbs were so weakened that she could not be moved anywhere except either by a vehicle or by two people carrying her with their arms bent together.

Her people laid her down before the altar on which the virgin’s bier was kept, and she immediately received healing, so that without anyone’s guidance she could move on her own with the greatest vigor wherever she wished, glorifying Jesus Christ and the merits of the sacred virgin.

### 14

A certain woman from a village called Stofohem, named Geyla, came on the annual feast day of the dedication of that church, when everyone in the region was celebrating. She alone, with a presumptuous spirit, treated the day as insignificant. She entered her winter hut and began weaving with the fingers of her right hand at the *curciboldus*, which she had previously set upright for weaving.

But when she had twice transferred from the *glomex* or *tramea* that she held in her hand [Note: [Col. 1098D] Wolfhard has “a ball of thread or a woof”] into the loom, the ball of thread became miserably lodged in her hand, while her entire arm swelled. The women who were present tried to unravel the enclosed ball of thread thread by thread [Note: [Col. 1099D] The Saint-Maximin manuscript has: “the ball of thread”; the same manuscript and the Antwerp manuscript have: “limb by limb”] [Note: [Col. 1099D] Wolfhard, book I, relates how this same woman was healed after repeatedly invoking Saint Walburga.].

### 15

A certain man named Ercambald had already completed thirty-seven weeks [Note: [Col. 1099D] The Utrecht manuscript has “thirty”; Wolfhard has “twenty-seven”] during which he had been unable to eat or drink any kind of food or beverage at all. Nevertheless, he had not been deprived of the ability to walk, except that he went wherever he wished in a feeble condition.

With only the rare yolks of eggs and a very small amount of legume as support, he scarcely sustained his precarious life. He bore a body exceedingly lean and weak, a little body whose life was burdensome to him, and he took no pleasure whatsoever in tasting wine or cider.

As he was sleeping uneasily, a gentle voice addressed him:

> “Why, languishing in idleness and neglecting the remedy for your health, do you despair so completely of your life? Come, then: do what I now advise. Confident of recovering your condition, go quickly to the monastery at Mouvenhem, and there you will be helped through the merits of the blessed virgin. When you arrive there swiftly, you will find three nuns standing beside the altar who will give you consecrated blood of the Lord to drink from the chalice [Note: [Col. 1100D] Wolfhard says: “They will offer you a drink from the consecrated chalice of the altar.”]. When you have received it from them, the pleasure of eating and drinking will immediately return to you and flourish without any doubt.”

Awakened by the impulse of this most salutary voice, he was brought with the greatest speed to the monastery mentioned. Rising from prayer there, he found three women standing beside the altar and fulfilled the vision he had seen [Col. 1099C]. As soon as he tasted from the sacred chalice, a great desire to eat and drink came upon him. Thus, having recovered the remedy of eating, drinking, and bodily health in every respect, he returned home unharmed in great rejoicing and remained in the same good health until the end of his life.

### 16

An exceedingly wondrous event occurred, and, unless it were confirmed by the knowledge of many people, it would be highly unbelievable—an unprecedented sign recently manifested in the world, although nothing is impossible for the divine majesty.

As a very great crowd of people from everywhere streamed together to the basilica of Saint Walburga, there appeared among them an unknown exile, standing or lying there in the garb of a pilgrim. Among the others, he prayed with particular attentiveness and urgency. When Abbess Liubila saw him and was astonished that he prayed among the others with greater sorrow and perseverance, she ordered him to be summoned before her. She questioned him with great curiosity as to who he was and from where he came.

He replied:

> “I give thanks to almighty God, who, through the merits of the most holy virgin Walburga, has deigned to free me, the most unworthy of sinners, from the scandal of the greatest shame. Both you who are present here now and everyone else ought to hear from me, rather than from others, how wondrous this matter is. And lest anyone suspect that I wish to deceive divine knowledge, I call God to witness—nothing can be hidden from him—before whose altar I stand, unworthy though I am, and Saint Walburga, whose aid I was compelled to seek. I shall relate in this miracle nothing fictitious but only a true account, insofar as human weakness permits.”

### 17

In the preceding year [Note: [Col. 1100D] The year 894, as established in book II, chapter 2 of Wolfhard, where these events are narrated], when the severity of famine had afflicted many people, it happened that two poor men, fleeing from place to place and from region to region, were suffering the same harshness of hunger. Then it happened that a third poor man from a distant region joined them.

When they asked him where he was going and where he wished to go, he replied that, as many are known to wish, he intended to seek the protection of Saint Walburga [Col. 1100B]. Then they said to him:

> “If you desire to go there, take us as companions on the same journey and in the same consolation, so that, together crossing the dangers of such a long distance, we may strengthen one another with mutual assistance. For we too are preparing to go to the same place. Constricted by extreme lack of food and still walking while fasting, we can scarcely move forward except with faltering steps.”

Their simple fellow traveler replied:

> “Come, brothers. Commending the length of our long journey to the Lord Jesus Christ, let us lay aside our distress. And since the time for the midday rest is approaching, let us seek a suitable little place where we may break our fast and rest briefly.”

When they had found one and reclined there, and the first companions complained that they had no provisions with them, the third companion who had joined them said [Col. 1100C] [Note: [Col. 1100D] The Utrecht and Trier manuscripts have “the provider”]:

> “Now, as we rest from our weariness, let us eat from my little supply of food. Afterward let us sleep in such a way that the third may keep watch safely for the two, so that, refreshed by this twofold renewal of nourishment and rest, we may complete the journey we have begun in the Lord.”

They deceitfully approved this good counsel. One of the two companions then assumed an imaginary sleep; but the third who had joined them assumed a deadly and final one. For immediately they rose up against the innocent man and wickedly killed him.

### 18

When this had been carried out, what were the most impious men to do with the dead body? Hemmed in by difficulties, at last one of them fitted the horrible burden upon his own shoulders [Col. 1100D] and began to search for some remote or hidden place in which he might expose the dead man. At last, having found such a place, as he tried to set down the body he had embraced, he began to be more tightly constricted by the corpse, so that by no effort could he separate the weight of the dead from himself.

What could the most wretched man do? Anxiously striving to go wherever he wished, he carried about with him, firmly glued to his person, an unyielding betrayer of his crime, instilling horror in everyone. Meanwhile, as he wandered laboriously from place to place [Col. 1101A], a certain acquaintance of his met him. But when the man saw the burden of such horror, he grew pale and almost lost consciousness; recovering himself at last, he asked why he had become the bearer of so dreadful a mass.

The other, trusting him as a familiar friend, related to him the whole sequence of this wicked contrivance and showed, out of compassion for his misfortune, that he wished somehow to remove from himself the weight by which he was so miserably oppressed. Then the friend, thinking that he could easily help him, drew the sword he was carrying and wished to cut off, joint by joint, the arms of the dead body that were vigorously embracing the neck of his living companion, so that he might rescue his friend from the violence of this unheard-of disgrace.

But—an astonishing and wondrous thing, and one to be praised in the Lord Jesus Christ!—as soon as his hands touched the conjoined limbs of that dead man in order to cut them off, the body of the one doing the cutting was glued to those two limbs as though by the most tenacious bitumen.

Immediately, however, moved by divine mercy, and recalling his crimes with tears, he prayed that God’s boundless clemency, through the intercession of Blessed Walburga, might deign to have mercy on him, the most wretched and excessively criminal of men. While he prayed in this manner, repeatedly making vows to Saint Walburga and lamenting greatly, the body was detached from him, and he proceeded with complete freedom, consoled by an exceedingly easy gait, raising his eyes and hands and continually glorifying God everywhere, as well as the holy virgin.

### 19

He then accompanied him, still bearing the terrible burden of the corpses, as far as the bank of the Rhine. When he had halted there for a little while [Col. 1101C], the aforesaid wretched man, afflicted by the weight of such a burden and by shame and confusion, preferring to suffer death rather than endure longer the loathing of a detestable and ungrateful life, climbed into the bed of the Rhine and, in order thereby to obtain for himself and for the weight of the corpse congealed to him an unknown burial, threw himself with all his force into the whirlpool of that abyss.

[Note: [Col. 1101C] Wolfhard gives the following account differently.]

But the Rhine, presuming that the filth of so great a crime was not its proper prey, without any delay vomited the parricide, alive with his corpse, back onto the bank. His fellow traveler, astonished and greatly terrified, and rejoicing exceedingly at his deliverance, just as he had wept over the other’s misfortune, finally abandoned the pitiable man with his pitiable burden and hurried at a swift pace to the monastery of Saint Walburga. There he truthfully related to everyone, in order, the sequence of what had happened, and he most gladly wished to affirm it, if permitted, with the confirmation of a solemn oath.

It is said that the aforesaid man, held captive by the corpse, often wished to approach the aid of Blessed Walburga the virgin [Col. 1102B], but was never able to reach the boundaries of her church, so that it might be clearly shown by what bond of guilt he was bound: he was restrained at such a distance that he could in no way reach the monastery of Saint Walburga.

Many people who were present at that time saw him with the mass of the burden so often mentioned. Hence it is clear that what was confirmed as true by the testimony of so many people cannot possibly be false.

### 20

These signs and prodigies, therefore, now committed to writing here—wonders that divine majesty performed in that extraordinary lifting from the tomb of the body of the virgin beloved by God and human beings—are greatly worthy of praise and admiration. Yet even now, throughout the various provinces of the whole Frankish kingdom, which are made illustrious by the pledges of that same virgin’s relics [Col. 1102C], many more and greater deeds worthy of proclamation are performed daily through Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, be everlasting glory forever and ever. Amen.

## On the Method of Finding the Thickness of a Sphere

### Notice of R. P. Bernard Pez on the Following Little Work

*Isagogical dissertation in vol. III of the latest* Thesaurus Anecdotorum, p. III.

The little work *On the Thickness of the Sphere*, addressed to Sylvester II, formerly Gerbert, was prompted in Adelbold by a rather difficult passage of Macrobius’s commentary on the *Dream of Scipio*. Macrobius says there that it had been discovered among the most expert geometers that, in two circles, if the diameter of one is twice the diameter of the other, the thickness of the circle whose diameter is doubled is eight times the thickness of the circle whose diameter is half as great, and so forth.

While Adelbold carefully explains this doctrine, he nevertheless refers the whole matter to Sylvester:

> “In all these matters,” he says, “if I am mistaken, I beg you to lead me back to the path of truth. If I am following the right path, I nevertheless ask that the path which holds me, doubting, in darkness may shine forth, illuminated by the authority of your assent.”

From this we learn how highly Adelbold valued Sylvester’s learning. Adelbold must have composed this work before the year 1003, which was Sylvester’s last year. This was supplied to us from a six-hundred-year-old parchment manuscript of the Tegernsee library by the most reverend and distinguished Father Alphonsus Hueber, an ascetic of Tegernsee, whom we have praised elsewhere. There is another manuscript of the same period at Saint Peter’s, in duodecimo, from which we have edited the same little work. Finally, the distinguished Edmond Martène, in his *Gallican Literary Journey*, part II, p. 92, testifies that at the abbey of Cheminon in the diocese of Châlons he saw a work of Adalbold addressed to Pope Sylvester, *On the Circle*, etc.; this is without doubt our very work.

## Adelbold, Bishop of Utrecht, of the Order of Saint Benedict: Little Book on the Method of Finding the Thickness of a Sphere, Addressed to Sylvester II, Supreme Pontiff

Now published for the first time from the manuscript codices of the celebrated monasteries of Tegernsee and Saint Peter’s at Salzburg, through the work of the most reverend Father Alphonsus Hueber, ascetic of Tegernsee.

*(In R. P. Bernard Pez, latest* Thesaurus Anecdotorum, *vol. III, part II, col. 85.)*

### Preface

[Col. 1103A] To the lord Sylvester, supreme pontiff and philosopher, Adelbold the scholar sends perpetual health and happiness.

It is a serious fault to disturb a man occupied with public affairs by private requests. Yet I trust in your ingenuity that you can at once serve the commonwealth and satisfy me in what I seek. Nevertheless, I act rashly and sin knowingly in approaching such a great man, as a young man approaching a fellow scholar. But confession of sin, I say, not only seeks pardon; it demands it.

Perhaps you think that I am sinning in such a way that I do not wish to repent of having sinned, and therefore that my confession, lacking the fruit of repentance, ought neither to seek pardon nor to demand any remission. To this I shall reply that, if I offend your kindness by this request [Col. 1103B], I shall regret having approached you more deeply than you could believe. Therefore I shall judge that pardon ought to be granted to one who is sorrowful and repentant, who confesses that he has sinned, and who thereafter wishes to abstain from such a sin—especially by one who holds the place of him who said: “I do not say to you seven times, but seventy times seven” (Matthew 18:22).

But if I do not offend you, and instead seek what I shall obtain through your goodwill—since I shall rejoice that my acquisition will benefit both me and many others—I fear that the questions I have already sent to your authority, because they have not been resolved, have offended either me or you; or I hope that something great will come from the delay in their resolution [Col. 1103C]. I shall propose nothing else, so that either I may grieve more deeply over what I fear, and the magnitude of my grief may move you to pardon; or I may rejoice more greatly over what I hope, and the fullness of my joy may implore a future reward for you.

As for what I now wish to propose, I seem to see by what reasoning it can be examined and brought all the way to understanding. But I await your diligence in determining it, so that the authority of so great a man may make my instruction either a correction or a completion.

[Col. 1104A] I shall now explain what the matter is, and by what images I am both deceived concerning it and held in certainty, so that, once the wound of my hesitation has been opened, the medicine of certainty may be supplied by you.

### § I

Macrobius, when speaking in his commentary on the *Dream of Scipio* about the size of the heavens, the earth, the sun, and the moon, and their rounded spherical shape, says that it was discovered among the most expert geometers that, in two circles, if the diameter of one is twice the diameter of the other, the thickness of the circle whose diameter is doubled is eight times the thickness of the circle whose diameter is half as great.

To find the diameter from the circle, the circle from the diameter, and the area from the diameter and circle, and therefore to compare diameter with diameter, circle with circle, and area with area, is easy for those accustomed to deal with such matters. But how can someone compare thickness with thickness who has not yet grasped what thickness is? For knowledge of two things does not precede their comparison; it follows it. Thus someone cannot understand that one thickness is eight times another if he does not know from what the thickness of each circle is formed.

I shall explain what I have understood so far—not, as they say, to teach Minerva her letters, but to show what I think—so that, if I am mistaken, your acumen may lead me back to the right path; and if I am holding the right path while stumbling, I may lean upon the assent of your authority. But in order to reach what I desire, I shall begin with matters more widely known.

### § II

I take a diameter of seven feet. From this I determine the circle as follows. I triple it, and add one-seventh of it to that triple; thus I obtain a circle of twenty-two feet. When half the diameter, which is three and a half, is multiplied by half the circle, which is eleven, the area of the same circle comes to thirty-eight and a half feet. Behold, I have the diameter, the circle, and the area!

But in order to find the thickness, I cube the same diameter and make a cube of such a kind that it touches the sphericity of the sphere at its sides, but projects beyond it at its angles and along the lines running from angle to angle.
