From such a cube it is necessary to cut away the thickness that extends from the sphericity to the angles and lines, so that, after this has been cut away, only the solidity of the sphere remains.

I make this cutting in the following way. I divide the sum of the entire cube by twenty-one. From this I take the twenty-first part of the cube, which is sixteen; I multiply it by ten, and obtain the excisions of the cube. Then I multiply it by eleven, and obtain the sphericity of the sphere. That is, of these twenty-first portions of the cube I assign ten to the excisions and leave the remainder to the thickness [cod. Petr. *thicknesses*] [Col. 1105B] of the sphere.

The same result would follow if I multiplied the sum of the entire cube by eleven and subtracted from that product one twenty-first part [Petr. *multiplied*]. For this twenty-first part is as large as the eleven twenty-first parts that were removed from the simple cube.

### § III

To make what we are saying clearer, we shall assign two thicknesses in definite numbers, so that we can compare the assigned quantities with one another—not because these figures are more correct, or because we suppose that you are ignorant of them, but so that, once our paths have been shown to your diligence, we may thereafter be guided by you and know how not to go astray.

I seek the thickness of a circle whose diameter is seven feet as follows. I cube the diameter and say: seven times seven makes forty-nine. Again, seven times forty-nine makes 343. Behold the cube of the square whose every side is seven feet; this cube entirely encloses the sphericity of the sphere.

To cut away the projecting portions, I proceed as follows. I take one twenty-first of 343, which is sixteen and SS. If I multiply this by ten, I obtain 163 and SS, namely the excesses of the cube. If I multiply it by eleven, I obtain 179 and SS, namely the thickness of the sphere.

To make what we are saying still more evident, we draw the circle beneath the square [Tegern. *we draw beneath*], so that what is seen on a plane may be more easily understood in thickness [Petr. *may be understood*].

[Col. 1105D]

[Col. 1106A] Behold: in this sphere the diameter is seven feet, the circle twenty-two, the area thirty-eight and a half, and the solidity 179 and SS. It is not surprising that the cube in its excesses contains nearly half the thickness, since this square, when laid out on a plane, retains scarcely a third in its projections. For in this quadrature, since each side is seven feet, it will have an area of forty-nine according to the measurement of its sides [Tegern. *division*]. Since the circle has taken thirty-eight and a half of this for itself, the square retains only ten and a half in its cut-off portions.

### § IV

Why this seems to me to be so, I shall explain, if it is not tedious for you to hear it; it will not be burdensome for me to say it. Here is the point: the square, if raised sevenfold in height [Col. 1106B], yields 343 feet, carrying upward with it its excesses and the area of the circle. For seven times ten and a half—that is, the excesses—make seventy-three and a half; and seven times thirty-eight and a half—that is, the area of the circle—make 269 and a half. But seventy-three and a half plus 269 and a half yield 343.

Therefore to raise the square in height is nothing other than to carry its excesses and the area of the circle upward with it. If, then, someone cuts away from that cube, which had arisen from an area of forty-nine feet, seven times ten and a half—that is, seventy-three and a half—he has not yet polished the spherical sphericity; rather, he has formed, after the manner of a grain-measure, an equal area drawn from an equal area, namely 269 and a half feet.

From this form we must remove not half—lest it be sharpened on both sides in the manner of a spinning top—but a third part, which is 89 and SSS, in order to polish the sphere. Yet this third part, although not entirely of rounded form [Petr.: “But this third is not so much of a rounded form as of number, that is, etc.”]—that is, 89 and SSS together with seven excesses, namely 73 and a half—nevertheless yields the same as the ten twenty-first parts that were removed from the entire cube in order that the sphere might be rounded on every side. These ten twenty-first parts would almost reach half the cube, were it not for the forty-second part of the same cube, which prevents this [Tegern. *were prevented*].

### § V

It is now easy to see why, when the square does not overcome its circle by a third of itself [Petr. *not in a third*], the cube exceeds the spherical sphericity by nearly half of itself. [Col. 1106D] This grain-measure form, rounded by cutting away the cube’s sides everywhere, although it cannot be made completely so, may nevertheless be represented to some extent, so that what the dullness of language conceals may be revealed by the truth of the picture.

[Col. 1107A] Behold, it can be seen how much must be cut away from the middle after the pointed parts have been removed from the cube [Tegern. *grain-measure*], so that the pure sphericity of the sphere may remain.

It seems that enough has now been said about how the thickness of a sphere is formed from a diameter of seven feet. Let us now posit another sphere, arising from twice the diameter. Let the diameter be fourteen. I cube this: fourteen times fourteen times fourteen makes 2744. This is the cube enclosing the sphere. If I take one twenty-first part of it, which is 130 and SS, and multiply it by ten, I obtain 1306 and SS; and this is the amount by which the cube exceeds the sphere [Petr. *and in these the cube*]. But if I multiply it by eleven, the result is 1437 and SS; this is the thickness of the sphere.

If someone wishes to construct this sphere by the same methods by which we constructed the former—namely, to reduce it from the cube to the form of a grain-measure, and from the grain-measure form to its [Col. 1107B] own sphericity—he will be able to round not only this sphere but all spheres arising from any diameter in the same manner.

But let both circles be drawn, the one whose diameter is seven feet and the one whose diameter is fourteen, so that the number assigned to each solidity may demonstrate how much the larger exceeds the smaller.

[Col. 1108A]

The diameter and circle of the larger sphere are joined to the diameter and circle of the smaller in a twofold proportion; the area is fourfold, while the thickness is eightfold. For twice seven and twice twenty-two—the diameter and circle of the smaller—make fourteen. And fourteen, which is the diameter of the larger, together with four times thirty-eight and a half, which is the area of the smaller, makes 154, which is the area of the larger; and eight times 179 and SS, which is the solidity of the smaller, yields 1437 and SS, which is the solidity of the larger.

### § VI

I would now have no doubt that this is the method of finding spherical thickness, if it were peculiar only to spherical thickness that, when doubling occurs in the diameter, an eightfold quantity is found in the solidity. But I find this same cause and ratio in all cubes. For if I make one cube from two and another from four, since four is twice two, the cube of four will be eight times the cube of two, and the area of four will be four times the area of two. And this is found not only in cubes but also in the depths of wells.

In all these matters, if I am mistaken, I beg you to lead me back to the path of truth. If I am following the right path, I nevertheless ask that the path which holds me, doubting, in darkness may shine forth, illuminated by the authority of your assent.

## Adelbold’s Charter Concerning Vassals, or Those Bound by Faith to the Church and Bishop of Utrecht

*(Heda, Utrecht Chronicle, p. 282.)*

[Col. 1107C] In the name of God. Amen.

I have judged it worthwhile to insert the following matters in writing, lest what the present age does remain hidden from posterity. Therefore I wish it to be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God, both present and future, that I, Adelbold, solely by the grace of God the unworthy bishop of the holy Church of Utrecht, when the free feudal vassals of the Church of Utrecht demanded their fief from me, was shown by them letters of my predecessors, the bishops of Utrecht, containing what goods and what kinds of goods they and their ancestors had held from the Church of Utrecht. Having seen these letters, I had the following matters committed to writing.

The duke of Brabant is a free feudal vassal of the Church of Utrecht, and holds in fief the stone-built town at Tiel, together with its estates, households, serfs, woods, waters, [Col. 1109A] fisheries, pastures, meadows, and the willow plantation situated beside the aforesaid town of Tiel, and everything belonging to that town.

Likewise, he holds the whole of Campinia as far as Tournoutervoerde, with serfs, woods, and fields; and his office is that which is called, and is in fact, the steward of the bishop of Utrecht.

Likewise, the count of Gelre is also a free feudal vassal of the Church of Utrecht, and holds in fief the county of Zutphen, with many estates, serfs, meadows, woods, waters, watercourses, and rights of jurisdiction. Likewise, Emmerich with its appurtenances, half of which belongs to him and the other half to the bishop of Utrecht. Likewise, a large part of the Batavian district, with male and female serfs and rights of jurisdiction. Likewise, Tielerwaard and Bommelerwaard, with many serfs, homesteads, lands, cottages, houses, [Col. 1109B] fields, meadows, waters, watercourses, and jurisdiction. The office of the said count is that which is called, and is in fact, the huntsman of the bishop of Utrecht.

Likewise, the count of Holland is a free feudal vassal of the bishop of Utrecht, and holds in fief the county of Holland and the land of Kennemerland, with lands, homesteads, woods, fields, meadows, pastures, serfs, waters, watercourses, and jurisdiction, except for the tithes of the said lands, and the land of Waterland and West Frisia, which belong entirely to the bishop and Church of Utrecht. The said count of Holland is called, and is in fact, the marshal of the bishop of Utrecht.

Likewise, the count of Cleves is a free feudal vassal of the Church [of Utrecht] and holds in fief, in the Batavian district above the Rhine, a large part of the lands [Col. 1109C] and homesteads, with cottages, houses, serfs, fields, meadows, and pastures; and on the other side of the Rhine, and in certain other places, lands, homesteads, cottages, houses, woods, and fields. Likewise, Woudrichem, with its arable lands and fields, waters and watercourses, and [Col. 1110A] jurisdictions, is held by him; and he is called, and is in fact, the chamberlain of the bishop of Utrecht.

Likewise, the count of Bentheim is a free feudal vassal of the Church, and holds in fief the burgraviate, or prefecture, of Utrecht, with very many homesteads, lands, islands, fields, serfs, woods, meadows, pastures, waters, watercourses, and jurisdiction, in many places of the city and diocese of Utrecht. He is called, and is in fact, the doorkeeper of the bishop of Utrecht.

Likewise, the lord of Cuke is a free feudal vassal of the Church, and holds in fief many lands, islands, and tithes, with cottages, houses, woods, fields, meadows and pastures, waters, watercourses, and jurisdiction in various places of the diocese of Utrecht. He is called, and is in fact, the cupbearer of the bishop of Utrecht.

[Col. 1110B] Likewise, the lord of Ghoer is a free feudal vassal of the Church of Utrecht, and holds in fief the castle of Ghoer and the land called Ameide, with many lands, homesteads, cottages, houses, woods, fields, serfs, meadows, pastures, waters, watercourses, movable and immovable goods, and everything belonging to the said districts of Ghoer and Meyde. He is called, and is in fact, the standard-bearer of the bishop of Utrecht.

All the aforesaid feudal vassals of the Church are bound to attend the general synod of the bishop of Utrecht in person. They received their fiefs from me as an act of homage and rendered their fealty before the lord Henry II, the most invincible Roman emperor and Augustus, in the presence of Aribo, archbishop and archchaplain; Anno of Cologne, Everhard of Trier, and [Col. 1110C] Adelbert of Hammelburg, archbishops; Udalric, vice-chancellor; and many other bishops, counts, and faithful men of the kingdom.

Done at the castle of Tulpiac, in the year of the Lord 1021, on the fourth day before the Nones of January. Amen.

## Adelbold’s Music

*(D. Martin Gerbert, ecclesiastical writers on music, I, 303, from the Tegernsee codex of the eleventh or twelfth century.)*

### Notice

In the Tegernsee codex of the eleventh or twelfth century, from which Bernard Pez published Adelbold’s little work *On the Thickness, or Circle, of the Sphere*, I found, written in a more recent hand, the title *Adelbold’s Music to Pope Sylvester*. Sylvester occupied the Roman see from the year 999 to 1003. Indeed, Adelbold the scholar dedicates that celebrated little work to “the lord Sylvester, supreme pontiff and philosopher”; immediately after it, without interruption in the writing, there follows what we now publish under his name and what concerns our present subject.

## On Music

[Col. 1109]

### How Musical Consonances Can Be Judged with Certainty

[Col. 1109D] In order that the ratio of consonances may be established without uncertainty, this can be achieved by means of the following very brief and simple instrument. Let there be a carefully stretched rule.

Upon it let two hemispheres, which the Greeks call *magades*, be placed, so that a line drawn from the curve of the one designated E to that designated B forms right angles around itself. Likewise, let a line drawn from the curve designated F to the point designated C form right angles around itself. Let these hemispheres be equally polished on every side, and let other equal ones be prepared for the same purposes.

Over these let an equal string be stretched throughout, namely the one designated E, A, F, D. If, then, I wish to discover what the consonance of a fourth is, I shall proceed in this way. From the point E, where the string touches the hemisphere, to the point F, where on the other side the other string is again joined to the other hemisphere [Col. 1111A], I divide the space F–E into seven parts. At the fourth of the seven parts I place the point designated K. Thus K is in the sesquitertian ratio to F.

If, then, I place a hemisphere above at K equal to the upper hemispheres, and strike E–K and K–F alternately with a plectrum, the interval of a fourth will sound; but if I strike both simultaneously, I recognize the consonance of a fourth.

If we wish to produce a fifth, I divide the whole into five parts, assign three to one portion and two to the other, and, having placed the hemisphere according to the method stated above [Col. 1112A], I examine consonances and dissonances.

Likewise, if I wish to test the consonance of an octave, I cut the whole into three parts, distributing them into one and two; striking the two either together or alternately, I recognize which of the two is consonant and which dissonant.

The triple proportion, which arises from mixed consonances, is produced as follows: if we divide the whole by divisions into four parts and divide the entire length of the string into three and one, the hemisphere placed at the three will produce the dissonance and consonance of the triple proportion.

## Division of the Notes of the Monochord through Three Genera

[Col. 1111B] In order that the mixed description may proceed through the three genera, and that the proper multiplicity of strings may be assigned to all of them, so as to preserve the proportions of tones and dieses, a number was devised that could fulfill all these requirements. Let the *proslambanomenos* be represented by 9,216, and let the lowest be 2,304; the proportions of the remaining sounds will be woven into the halves of these numbers.

We proceed from the lower end and indicate all the names of the strings not only by their names but also by letters attached to them. But since the division into three genera must be made, and the number of strings exceeds the number of letters, when the letters run out we repeat them in the following manner: when we have reached Z, we designate the remaining strings as follows [Col. 1111C]: twice A, AA; twice B, BB; and twice C, CC.

Let the first and greatest number, therefore, occupying the place of the *proslambanomenos*, be 9,216. [Note: In this musical treatise it is sufficient to note generally that numbers placed before hundreds always denote thousands.] Let the entire extent of the string run from A to LL. This A is the *proslambanomenos*, 9,216. I divide it in half at O, so that the whole A is twice the quantity designated O. Likewise, let O be twice the quantity designated twice II, the *nete hyperboleon*.

Thus let A be 9,216, and O half of this, 4,608, at the *mese*, so that the *proslambanomenos* may correspond to the consonance of the octave. The quantity designated twice II is half of the *mese*, so that the *proslambanomenos* may be four times the *nete hyperboleon* and may sound with it the consonance of two octaves. Let it be II, 2,304.

[Col. 1111D]

If, therefore, I remove an eighth from 2,304—that is, 288—and add it to the same number, I obtain 2,592. This will be HH, 2,592, which, as the *paranete hyperboleon*, has the interval of a tone from the *nete hyperboleon*.

Again, from HH, namely 2,592, I remove an eighth, which is 324, and add it to the quantity from which the eighth was taken. The result is 2,916, and I obtain FF, the diatonic *trite hyperboleon* [Col. 1112B], in the diatonic genus, 2,916. It is separated by a tone from the diatonic *paranete hyperboleon*, but by two tones from the *nete hyperboleon*.

The same FF will be the chromatic *trite hyperboleon* in the chromatic genus, and in the enharmonic genus the enharmonic *paranete hyperboleon*. This is more easily recognized when we have described the first three tetrachords of the three genera, beginning from the *nete hyperboleon*.

Since, if I subtract two sesquioctave proportions from a sesquitertian proportion, the smaller semitone remains, I take a third of the quantity designated II, namely the *nete hyperboleon*. This is 768. I add it to the same quantity, obtaining 3,072, which is the *nete diezeugmenon*, DD, a smaller semitone from the *trite hyperboleon*.

Since the *nete diezeugmenon* contains the consonance of a fourth up to the *nete hyperboleon*, while the diatonic *trite hyperboleon* lies two tones from the *nete hyperboleon*, the interval that remains between the *nete diezeugmenon* and the *trite hyperboleon* is a smaller semitone.

Since, therefore, we have completed the hyperboleon tetrachord of the diatonic genus, the chromatic and enharmonic tetrachords must now be supplied in the following way. Since the *paranete hyperboleon* is one tone from the *nete hyperboleon* in the diatonic genus, three semitones away in the chromatic genus, and two tones away in the enharmonic genus, if we take the distance between the diatonic *paranete hyperboleon* and *nete hyperboleon*, and add half of it to the diatonic *paranete hyperboleon* [Col. 1112D], we shall obtain a number three semitones distant from the *nete hyperboleon*. This will be the chromatic *paranete hyperboleon*.

I therefore subtract from 2,592—the diatonic *paranete hyperboleon*—2,304—the *nete hyperboleon*. There remain 288. I divide these, obtaining 128, and add the same quantity to 2,310; the result is 2,438. This will be the chromatic *paranete hyperboleon*.

[Note: [Col. 1111D] That an error has been committed here is clear from the fact that half of 288 is 144, not, as is stated here, 128. Therefore, in accordance with the explanation given immediately below [Col. 1112D], it should be read as follows: “I therefore subtract from 2,592—the diatonic *paranete hyperboleon*—2,304—the *nete hyperboleon*. There remain 288. I divide these, obtaining 144, and add the same quantity to 2,592; the result is 2,736. This will be the chromatic *paranete hyperboleon*.”]

Again, since the diatonic or chromatic *trite hyperboleon* is two tones distant from the *nete hyperboleon*, and in the enharmonic genus the *paranete hyperboleon* is two tones distant from the *nete hyperboleon*, the enharmonic *paranete hyperboleon* will be identical with the diatonic or chromatic *trite hyperboleon*.

But since the *trite hyperboleon* of the diatonic and chromatic genera preserve a smaller semitone up to the *nete diezeugmenon*, while the enharmonic tetrachord consists of two whole tones and a diesis plus a diesis—the latter being halves of the smaller semitone—I take the distance between the *nete diezeugmenon* and the enharmonic *paranete hyperboleon*.

Since the *nete diezeugmenon* is 2,738 and the *paranete hyperboleon* is 2,310, their distance will be 428. I take half of this, namely 214, and add it to 2,310; the result is 2,524. This will be EE [Col. 1113B], the enharmonic *trite hyperboleon*.

[Note: [Col. 1113D] As is clear from the foregoing, another error has entered the calculation here. It should therefore be read: “Since the *nete diezeugmenon* is 3,072 and the *paranete hyperboleon* is 2,916, their distance will be 156. I take half of this, namely 78, and add it to 2,916; the result is 2,994. This will be …”]

Thus the hyperboleon tetrachord has been described according to the three genera. We have appended below its diagram.

### Diagram No. I

Ratio of the description arranged above.

Three tetrachords, therefore, have been described for us according to this method. For every tetrachord produces the consonance of a diatessaron. Thus nete hyperboleon and nete diezeugmenon contain, in the three genera—that is, diatonic, chromatic, or enharmonic—the symphony of a diatessaron. The consonance of a diatessaron, moreover, consists of two tones and a minor semitone. This same interval has been divided in the foregoing tetrachords according to the three genera.

In the diatonic genus, the first paranete hyperboleon—that is, II. D. XC. II—has, in relation to nete hyperboleon, that is, II. CCC. IIII, the distance of a tone, which we have marked with this notation: T.[o] Again, trite hyperboleon of the diatonic genus, which is II. DCCCC. XVI, has in relation to paranete hyperboleon of the diatonic genus, which is II. D. XC. II, the difference of a tone, which we have marked with the similar notation T.[o]. Nete diezeugmenon, however, that is, III. LXX. II, in relation to trite hyperboleon, that is, II. DCCCC. XVI, forms a semitone, which we have marked with this notation: T.[s]. The entire interval between nete diezeugmenon and nete hyperboleon thus consists of two tones and a semitone.

But these same two tones and semitone are divided in the chromatic genus as follows. The second genus, which is chromatic, has been described in this manner. Paranete chromatica hyperboleon, which is II. DCC. XXX. VI, compared with nete hyperboleon, which is II. CCC. IIII, contains the interval from paranete hyperboleon of the diatonic genus to nete hyperboleon, which is one tone—that is, two semitones, a greater and a lesser. And the interval from paranete hyperboleon of the diatonic genus to nete hyperboleon has again been divided. Thus it has been made [Note: [Col. 1113D] The following must be supplied: “Thus it has been made so that a minor semitone was added to two semitones, which is,” etc.] a tone, but not a complete one, only a half-tone, because, as was demonstrated at length above, a tone cannot be divided into two equal parts. We have therefore marked this interval of three semitones—that is, a tone and a semitone—in this way: T.[s] T.[s] T.[s].

Again, paranete chromatica hyperboleon in relation to trite hyperboleon retains part of a tone, namely the semitone that remained from the two tones contained between trite hyperboleon diatonica and nete hyperboleon. When four semitones have been subtracted, the remaining interval of the entire tetrachord is a semitone, contained between nete diezeugmenon and trite hyperboleon. This tetrachord therefore consists of two tones and a semitone, divided once into an interval of three semitones and twice into intervals of two semitones; and these three intervals are contained by four strings.

In the enharmonic genus, the chief point is the ease of recognizing [Note: [Col. 1114D] For the sense to be complete, the following must again be supplied: “the ease of recognizing this, for paranete hyperboleon is distant from nete hyperboleon by two complete tones,” etc.] that paranete hyperboleon is distant from nete hyperboleon by two complete tones, which we have marked in this way: T.[o] T.[o]. There therefore remains, from the two tones and semitone of the entire tetrachord, one semitone, contained between nete diezeugmenon and paranete hyperboleon enharmonia. This we divided into two dieses, with trite hyperboleon placed in the middle, and we marked the interval of a diesis in this way: Q.

Thus the tetrachord of hyperboleon has been described for us. Having completed it, let us proceed to diezeugmenon. There is no need to linger over the same explanations in the remaining cases, since the description given here can also serve as an example for the others.

## Division of the Netes of Diezeugmenon of the Monochord According to the Three Genera

Nete diezeugmenon, therefore, which is III. LXX. II, if I take half of it, gives I. D. XXX. VI; added to the same number, this makes IIII. DC. VIII. [Note: [Col. 1114D] This is mese, which bears the ratio 3 to nete diezeugmenon.] We marked this meanwhile with the letter O. But if from that same nete diezeugmenon, namely III. LXX. II, I subtract a third part, that is I. XX. IIII, and add it to the same number, the result will be IIII. XC. VI, which will be called paramese, marked below with the letter X.

Nete diezeugmenon, therefore, namely III. LXX. II, in relation to mese, namely III. DC. VIII, stands in a sesquialteral ratio; consequently, it will produce the consonance of a diapente. The same nete diezeugmenon, namely III. LXXII, in relation to paramese, namely IIII. XC. VI, which is also composed in a sesquitertian ratio to it, retains the consonance of a diatessaron.

If, therefore, from nete diezeugmenon, III. LXX. II, I subtract an eighth part, namely CCC. LXXX. IIII, and add it to the same number, the result will be III. CCCC. L. VI. This will be paranete diezeugmenon diatonic, marked with two C’s, bearing to nete diezeugmenon the proportion of a tone. From this, again, I subtract an eighth part, namely from III. CCCC. L. VI, which is CCCC. XXX. II; if I add this to the same number, the result will be III. DCCC. LXXX. VIII. This will be Y, trite diezeugmenon diatonic.

But since nete diezeugmenon bore a sesquitertian proportion to paramese, while trite diezeugmenon diatonic is two tones distant from nete diezeugmenon, a minor semitone will be contained between trite diezeugmenon and paramese. The diatonic genus, therefore, has also been completed in this tetrachord and pentachord in such a way that the tetrachord from nete diezeugmenon to paramese has the consonance of a diatessaron, while the pentachord from nete diezeugmenon to mese has the consonance of a diapente.

[Col. 1115B] We shall now construct the enharmonic and chromatic genera in the following manner. I take the difference between nete and paranete diezeugmenon diatonic, namely III. LXX. II and III. CCCC. L. VI. Their difference is CCC. LXXX. IIII. I divide this, obtaining C. XC II. If I take this and add it to paranete diezeugmenon diatonic, namely III. CCCC. L. VI, the result is III. DC. XL. VIII. This is paranete diezeugmenon chromatic, marked with the doubled letter B. It is distant from nete diezeugmenon by a tone and a semitone, that is, by three semitones; and in relation to trite diezeugmenon, formerly diatonic but now chromatic, namely III. DCCC. LXXX. VIII, it contains the semitone remaining from the tone divided between paranete diezeugmenon diatonic and trite diezeugmenon diatonic.

Another semitone remains from the tetrachord between trite diezeugmenon chromatic and paramese. This is what remains from the consonance of the diatessaron between nete diezeugmenon and paramese after subtracting the two tones contained by nete diezeugmenon chromatic and trite diezeugmenon chromatic.

What is trite diezeugmenon diatonic in the diatonic genus and trite diezeugmenon chromatic in the chromatic genus is called paranete diezeugmenon enharmonic in the enharmonic genus. For it is distant by two complete tones from nete diezeugmenon, and is marked AA. There is no separate string between nete diezeugmenon and paranete enharmonic diezeugmenon; for that reason it is called paranete.

We divide the semitone between paranete enharmonic diezeugmenon and paramese—that is, between AA and X—in the following way, so that two dieses are produced. I take the difference between paranete enharmonic diezeugmenon and paramese, namely III. DCCC. LXXX. VIII and IIII. XC. VI; this is CC. VIII. I divide it, obtaining C. IIII. I add these to paranete, which is III. DCCC. LXXX. VIII; the result is III. DCCCC. XC. II. This will be trite diezeugmenon enharmonic, marked with Z.

I have therefore added below the description of this tetrachord according to the three genera, and have joined to it the tetrachord of hyperboleon arranged above, so that there might be one description of both and the form of the entire arrangement might gradually emerge.

## SCHEMA No. 2

### Division of the Netes of the Monochord According to the Three Genera

The preceding description has shown how the two tetrachords joined to one another but separated from mese are situated according to the three genera. We must now come to the tetrachord called synemmenon, which is joined to mese.

Since we have stated that there is a diapente consonance between nete diezeugmenon and mese—and a diapente consonance consists of three tones and a semitone—and since there are three tones in this pentachord, one between nete diezeugmenon and paranete diezeugmenon diatonic, another between paranete diezeugmenon diatonic [Col. 1116B] and trite diezeugmenon diatonic, and the third between paramese and mese, with the remaining semitone between trite diezeugmenon diatonic and paramese; and since the tetrachord from nete diezeugmenon and paramese is separated from mese by the tone between paramese and mese, if from the pentachord extending from nete diezeugmenon to trite synemmenon [Note: [Col. 1115D] Read: “to mese.”] we subtract one tone—namely, the tone contained between nete diezeugmenon and paranete diezeugmenon diatonic—we can join another tetrachord to mese, so that it becomes synemmenon, that is, joined, as follows.

Since paranete diezeugmenon diatonic, which is designated by the number CC, is III. CCCC. L. VI, adding its third part produces mese. This number, in the tetrachord of diezeugmenon, marked with the two letters CC, was distant by a tone from nete diezeugmenon in the diatonic genus and was called paranete diezeugmenon diatonic.

In the synemmenon tetrachord—that is, the tetrachord of the joined strings—let nete synemmenon be established in the three genera, marked with the letter V. Let an eighth part be subtracted from it, namely CCCC. XXX. II, and added to the remainder; the result will be III. DCCC. LXXX. VIII. This is paranete synemmenon diatonic, marked with the letter T.

Again, from paranete synemmenon diatonic, namely III. DCCC. LXXX. VIII, an eighth part, namely CCCC. LXXX. VI, is subtracted; if this is added to the number from which it was taken, the result will be IIII. CCC. LXX. IIII. This is trite synemmenon diatonic, namely Q.

But since nete synemmenon in relation to mese—that is, III. CCCC. L. VI in relation to IIII. DC. VIII—has a sesquitertian proportion, which is that of a diatessaron, while trite synemmenon in relation to nete synemmenon—IIII. CC. LXX. IIII in relation to III. CCCCC. L. VI—has the proportion of two tones, the proportion of a semitone remains between trite synemmenon diatonic and mese. This tetrachord is therefore joined to mese; for that reason it is called synemmenon, as though continuous and joined.

The proportion of the diatonic genus has therefore been established in this way; the division of the chromatic genus is as follows. I take the difference between nete synemmenon and paranete synemmenon diatonic, namely III. CCC. L. VI and III. DCCC. LXXX. VIII. Their difference is CCCC. XXXII. I divide this so that a semitone may be produced; the result is CC. XVI. I add this to III. DCCC. LXXX. VIII, so that three semitones may be produced; the result is IIII. C. IIII. This is paranete synemmenon chromatic, with the letter S placed above it.

From this point, therefore—that is, from paranete synemmenon chromatic—to trite synemmenon, formerly diatonic but now chromatic, there is a semitone; and from trite synemmenon chromatic to mese there is another semitone. But since two complete tones are contained between nete synemmenon and trite synemmenon, that which is trite synemmenon diatonic or chromatic is, in the enharmonic genus, paranete synemmenon enharmonic, having the total IIII. CCC. LXX. IIII and marked R. From this point to mese there is a semitone.

I divide this semitone into two dieses as follows. I take the difference between paranete synemmenon enharmonic and mese, namely IIII. CCC. LXX. IIII and IIII. DC. VIII; this is CC. XXX. IIII. I divide it, obtaining C. XVII. I add this to paranete synemmenon enharmonic, namely IIII. CCC. LXX. IIII; the result is IIII. CCCC. XC. I, marked with the letter P. This is trite synemmenon enharmonic. The semitone contained between paranete synemmenon enharmonic and mese—that is, between IIII. CCC. LXX. IIII and IIII. DC. VIII—is therefore divided by trite synemmenon enharmonic, namely III. CCCC. XCI.

Thus the method of this tetrachord too has been set out. Now it must be represented in a diagram; nevertheless, it is joined to the others—hyperboleon and diezeugmenon—so that the orderly progression of the arrangement may gradually be completed.

## SCHEMA No. 3

[Col. 1117C]

From what has been said above, therefore, I do not think that it is necessary to labor at length over the remaining cases. For the other tetrachords, those of meson and hypaton, must also be extended according to the model of these.

First, then, we shall describe the diatonic tetrachord of meson in the following order. From mese, which is O. IIII. DC. VIII, I take a third part, namely I. D. XXX. VI. I join this to the same number; the result is VI. C. XL. IIII. This is hypate meson, retaining the consonance of a diatessaron in relation to mese. It will be divided into two tones and a semitone as follows.

I take an eighth part of mese, namely IIII. DC. VIII, which is D. LXX. VI. I join this to the same number; the result is V. C. LXXX. IIII. This is lychanos meson diatonic, marked M. An eighth part of it is again taken, namely DC. XL. XIII. I add this to the same number; the result is V. DCCC. XXXII. This is parhypate meson diatonic, marked I, bearing a tone in relation to lychanos meson diatonic, but distant by two tones from mese. A semitone therefore remains between hypate meson diatonic and parhypate meson diatonic, that is, between VI. C. XL. IIII and V. DCCC. XXX. II.

We divide this same tetrachord of mese and hypate meson in the chromatic genus according to the following method. I take the difference between mese and lychanos meson diatonic, namely IIII. DC. VIII and V. C. LXXX. IIII; this is D. LXX. VI. I divide it in half; the result is CC. LXXX. VIII. I add this to the larger number, namely V. C. LXXX. IIII; the result is V. CCCC. LXX. II. This is lychanos meson chromatic, marked N.

Two semitones therefore remain: one between lychanos meson chromatic and parhypate meson chromatic, that is, between V. CCCC. LXX. II and V. DCCC. XXX. II; and another between parhypate meson chromatic and hypate meson, that is, between V. DCCC. XXX. II and VI. C. XL. IIII.

We divide the enharmonic genus as follows. Since what was parhypate meson diatonic and parhypate meson chromatic was distant by two tones from mese and had the value V. DCCC. XXX. II, in the enharmonic genus this will be lychanos meson enharmonic, marked with the letter L, likewise bearing two tones in relation to mese.

The remaining semitone between lychanos meson enharmonic and hypate meson—that is, between V. DCCC. XXX. II and VI. C. XL. IIII—we divide into two dieses as follows. I subtract the difference between V. DCCC. XXX. II and VI. C. XL. IIII; this is CCC. XII. I divide it in half; the result is C. L. VI. I add these to V. DCCC. XXX. II; the result is V. DCCCC. LXXX. VIII. Let this be parhypate meson enharmonic, marked K.

There are therefore two dieses: one between lychanos meson enharmonic and parhypate meson enharmonic, that is, between V. DCCC. XXX. II and V. DCCCC. LXXX. VIII; and another between parhypate meson enharmonic and hypate meson, that is, between V. DCCCC. LXXX. VIII and VI. C. XL. IIII. The tetrachord of meson has therefore been divided; it should be placed in the diagram so as to be joined to the tetrachords described above.

## SCHEMA No. 4

We must now divide the tetrachord of hypaton according to the three genera.

I take half of hypate meson, namely VI. C. XL. IIII; this gives III. LXX. II. If I add this to the same number, the result is VIIII. CC. XVI. This is proslambanomenos, retaining the consonance of a diapente in relation to hypate meson. But if from the same hypate meson, namely VI. C. XL. IIII, I subtract the part that is II. XL. VIII and add it to the same number, the result is VIII. C. XC. II. This is B, hypate hypaton.

Hypate meson therefore has the consonance of a diapente in relation to proslambanomenos, but that of a diatessaron in relation to hypate hypaton. From hypate meson, therefore, namely VI. C. XL. IIII, let an eighth part be subtracted; this gives DCC. LX. VIII. If this is added to the same number, the result is VI. DCCCC. XII. This is E, lychanos hypaton diatonic, bearing the proportion of a tone to hypate meson.

Again, let an eighth part be subtracted from VI. DCCCC. XII; this is DCCC. LX. IIII. If this is joined to the same number, the result will be VII. DCC. LXX. VI. This is C, parhypate hypaton diatonic, retaining a tone in relation to lychanos hypaton and a distance of two tones from hypate meson diatonic. A semitone therefore remains between parhypate hypaton diatonic and hypate hypaton, that is, between VII. DCCC. LXX. VI and VIII. C. XC. II. Such is the tetrachord of hypaton in the diatonic genus.

We divide the chromatic genus according to the following method. I take the difference between hypate meson and lychanos hypaton diatonic, namely VI. C. XL. IIII and VI. DCCCC. XII; this is DCC. LX. VIII. I divide it in half, so that two semitones may be produced; the result is CCC. LXXX. IIII. I add this to VI. DCCCC. XII, so that three semitones may be produced; the result is VII. CC. XC. VI. This is F, lychanos hypaton chromatic, distant by three semitones from hypate meson.

One semitone therefore remains, between lychanos hypaton chromatic, namely VII. CC. XC. VI, and parhypate hypaton chromatic, namely VII. DCC. LXX. VI. [Note: [Col. 1119] Here the following addition seems necessary: “and another between parhypate hypaton, that is, between VII. DCC. LXX. VI and VIII. C. XC. II, that is, hypate hypaton.”]

The enharmonic genus remains, whose division follows the preceding model. Since parhypate hypaton diatonic or parhypate hypaton chromatic, marked with VIII. DCC. LXX. VI units, is distant by two tones from hypate meson, it will likewise be lychanos hypaton enharmonic in the enharmonic genus, differing from hypate meson by two complete tones.

A semitone therefore remains from the consonance of the diatessaron, between lychanos hypaton enharmonic and hypate hypaton, that is, between VII. DCC. LXX. VI and VIII. C. XC. II. We divide it into two dieses as follows. I take the difference between lychanos hypaton enharmonic and hypate hypaton, namely VII. DCC. LXX. VI and VIII. C. XC. II; this is CCCC. XVI. I take half of it, namely CC. VIII. I add this to VII. DCC. LXX. VI; the result is VII. DCCCC. LXXX. IIII. Let this be D, parhypate hypaton enharmonic.

There are therefore two dieses: one between lychanos hypaton enharmonic and parhypate hypaton enharmonic, that is, between VII. DCC. LXX. VI and VII. DCCCC. LXXX. IIII; and another between parhypate hypaton enharmonic and hypate hypaton, that is, between VII. DCCCC. LXXX. IIII and VIII. C. XC. II.

The final tone is contained between proslambanomenos and hypate hypaton, that is, between VIIII. CC. XVI and VIII. C. XC. II. The tetrachord of hypaton has therefore been divided according to the three genera: diatonic, chromatic, and enharmonic.

# In the Year of Our Lord 1027: Saint Romuald, Abbot and Founder of the Camaldolese Order

[Col. 1119]

## Historical Notice on Saint Romuald

*(From Fabricius, Bibliotheca Latina of the Middle and Lower Ages)*

Romuald, founder of the Camaldolese order, was born at Ravenna into a noble family of dukes and was educated in the liberal arts. He sought the desert and endeavored to correct the looser discipline of the Order of Saint Benedict. He died in the year 1027 at the age of 120.

His Commentary on the Psalms is preserved in manuscript at the Camaldolese monastery. On its cover are written these words:

“This Psalter was written and glossed in his own hand by the most holy and most blessed Romuald, as God had commanded him, when he was caught up into paradise while celebrating Mass in the desert of Sytria, as blessed Peter Damian, cardinal priest, writes in his Life.”

Joannes Mabillon reports this in his *Itinerary of Italy*, page 179. Romuald also composed an exposition of several prophetic canticles. Add Possevinus, volume II of the *Apparatus*, page 256.

[Col. 1119]

## Mabillon’s Prefaces to the Life of Saint Romuald Written by Saint Peter Damian

*(Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict, volume VIII, page 277)*

[Col. 1119C]

### 1

Romuald, or Romald—as he is consistently written in the earliest monuments of the Camaldolese Hermitage—had Peter Damian as the first writer of his Life. Nearly three lustra after Romuald’s death had passed, as Peter himself asserts in the prologue, when he undertook this work.

He did not carry it out with such accuracy and diligence that he failed to omit many things deliberately—not only miracles, as he himself admits in the prologue, but also sayings and deeds, some of which Peter records in other writings of his. It is surprising how lightly, or not at all, he treats the institution both of the Camaldolese congregation or order and of the primary eremitical order, from which the order itself derived its name.

More is read on this subject in the lengthy sermon on the Life of the same Romuald published in 1433 by Jerome of Prague, a Camaldolese hermit distinct from the heretic of the same name. Joannes Bollandus illuminated both authors with learned commentaries in volume II of February. A summary of the same Life exists in Saint Antoninus, Peter of Equilinum, Gononus, and others; also in the *Camaldolese History* composed by Augustine of Florence. The same Life was written in Spanish by Giovanni Castagnizza, a monk of Valladolid, and later rendered into Italian and even French.

Here it will be enough to present Peter Damian, whose text we saw in a manuscript of the monastery of Salem in Swabia. Leo of Ostia also discusses Romuald in book II, chapters 18, 19, and 24 of his *Chronicle of Cassino*.

### 2

Besides the book on the Life of Romuald written by Peter Damian, he reports certain matters concerning him in other writings. First, in chapter 16 of opusculum 15, where he is discussing discretion:

“For we too approve,” he says, “what blessed Romuald is often reported to have said to his disciples: ‘So long as any brother does not leave his cell, let him also, as an exercise of discretion, be permitted to eat meat, if such unavoidable necessity should appear to threaten,’” and so forth.

And in chapter 9 of opusculum 49:

“Nor should you ineptly apply what the man of God Romuald often said to his disciples: ‘Brothers, when you take refreshment in the company of others, while the rest are intent upon food, abstain at the very beginning of the meal; and when they have already been satisfied to some extent, begin your own meal, so that you may both escape the charge of hypocrisy and observe the rule of sobriety without giving offense.’”

Finally, in chapter 3 of opusculum 49:

“Once, when blessed Romuald was returning from a conversation with the countess Sibylla, he is said cunningly to have said to the disciple accompanying him: ‘What an elegant and handsome face that woman has—if only, alas, she were not afflicted by the loss of one eye.’

“The disciple replied: ‘God forbid, master! Just as her face is certainly beautiful, so too, as I have cleverly observed, her eyes are no less sound.’

“The master immediately rebuked him with the sharpest severity: ‘And who taught you to look into women’s faces?’

“Then, realizing that he had been trapped, the disciple blushed, moved to repentance, and solemnly vowed that in future he would be more cautious.”

### 3

Peter Damian’s account of the beginnings of the Camaldolese order, whose founder was Romuald, is entirely obscure. The holy man came to the place during the pontificate of Theodald, bishop of Arezzo, in whose diocese the Camaldolese Hermitage is situated. Theodald began to hold the see in the year 1023, as is clear from the documents presented below.

In the first document, the same Theodald grants Campo-Malduli—as he writes it—to Peter, prior of the holy Hermitage, in the year 1027, and indeed after Romuald’s death, as we learn from his authentic document. We have found no document older than this in the archive of Fonte Buono, where the charters and diplomas of Camaldoli are preserved.

It is useful to excerpt something from this document:

“Theodald, vicar of Saint Donatus—for the bishops of Arezzo commonly call themselves this. Let all the faithful know that, out of love for the pious memory of our father, the lord Romald, the most renowned hermit, by common counsel with our clerical brothers we give . . . to the lord Peter, venerable hermit, for the use and support of the brothers living the eremitical life under him and of their successors, the hermits, a certain church in the midst of the Alps, belonging to the episcopal jurisdiction of Saint Donatus. At the request of the aforesaid lord Romald, the hermit, we consecrated it under the honor and name of Our Lord Jesus Christ, Saint Savior.

“It stands in the territory—namely, a day’s journey from Arezzo—at the foot of the Alps dividing Tuscany from Romagna, in a place called Campo-Malduli, with the boundaries marked out as follows. On the first side runs a stream called the Black Stream, opposite which another stream called the Tellito emerges; both flow together into the basin of a certain river. On the second side is a road descending from the highest ridges of the Alps. On the third side are wild mountains and uncut ridges of the Alps. On the fourth side are thickets plunging down into the aforesaid Black Stream.

“Within these fixed boundaries lies the place called Campo-Malduli, a beautiful and pleasant field, where there are seven pure springs and delightful green spaces. The lord Romald, the pious father of hermits, chose this place and foresaw that it would be highly suitable and appropriate for the individual cells of brothers serving God in the contemplative life. Having built there a basilica of Saint Savior, he marked out and separated five cells, together with their little shelters, and assigned individual hermit brothers to the individual cells, so that, removed from worldly cares and anxiety, they might devote themselves solely to divine contemplation. To them he also gave the venerable lord Peter, the hermit, as a faithful minister and teacher.

“To him, together with our successors, so that we too may have a share in eternal life with the aforesaid holy man Romald, we give and grant the aforementioned place,” and so forth.

“Given in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1027, in the fifth year of the pontificate of the lord Theodald, bishop, in the month of August, indiction 10. Executed in the cloister of the canons.”

Bucelinus mentions Peter the prior, said to have been surnamed Dagninus, with the title “blessed” in the Benedictine Menology on November 2, the date on which he is said, on the authority of commonly circulated sources, to have died in 1051.

The second document is one in which the same Theodald grants “all the tithes of all things acquired by selling and buying, belonging to all the citizens of Arezzo, urban and suburban,” to “our dearest brothers,” as he says, “the hermits who are and who will be in our hermitage called Campo-Malduli, at the church of Saint Savior. The holy father Romald, of blessed memory, entrusted them to us to be provided for and governed.”

“Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of June, in the year from the incarnation of the Lord 1033, in the tenth year of the pontificate of the lord Theodald, bishop, indiction 1.”

Moreover, that the first grant of this hermitage was made by Bishop Theodald is proved by Immo, also called Herenfredus, his successor, in letters issued in 1037, in which there is a distinguished eulogy of the Camaldolese; by the emperor Henry II, who in 1047 confirmed the donation of all the goods that the venerable Theodald had granted to the hermits living in the place called Campo-Amabile; and finally by Guido, monk and sinner, though unworthy, by the grace of God bishop of the see of Arezzo, as the heading of the charter states. Guido confirms the privileges offered to the Camaldolese Hermitage by the venerable lord John, prior of that place, and everything that his predecessors Theodald, Immo, Constantine, and Gregory had granted to the same place.

“Given in the year from the Lord’s incarnation 1116, under King Henry, in the month of October, indiction 10.”

Butanus, bishop of Arezzo, in a letter addressed to the lord Azo, archimandrite of the Camaldolese church, approves in 1132 everything that had been bestowed on the same place by Bishops Theodald, Constantine, Walter, and Guido.

From these facts it is understood that Theobald was the first to make a donation of the Camaldolese Hermitage to Romuald, who consequently was not admitted there before the year 1023. More recent writers say that the place was given to Romuald by Maldulus. I fear, however, that this is not certain. For at that time the place depended on the Church of Arezzo, and it was occupied by Bernardinus, son of Sidonius, as is confirmed by Bishop Gregory, who confirms to the venerable father Martin the goods of the Camaldolese Hermitage that Bernardinus, son of Sidonius, or his father, held from the church of Saint Donatus.

“Given in the Camaldolese Hermitage on the third day before the Ides of October, in the year from the Lord’s incarnation 1016, indiction 15, in the second year of the pontificate of the same Gregory.” A seal was attached to this letter.

### 4

In the thirteenth century the number of cells in that hermitage had grown to nearly thirty, as attested by William, bishop of Arezzo, who exhorts the diocesan people subject to him to provide assistance for repairing the buildings of the holy hermitage, in which, he says, there are twenty-eight cells. These letters were issued in 1246.

The number had diminished by the time of Jerome of Prague, that is, in 1433, when he composed a sermon on blessed Romuald in which he says:

“This holy hermitage of Camaldoli is in Italy, in the regions of Romagna, a day’s journey from the city of Arezzo. There are twenty-four separate cells of hermits. Some hermits are open, while others are enclosed. Nevertheless, all the hermits fast throughout the entire year for three days each week on bread and water, sitting barefoot on the ground, except during the two Lents, in which the hermits are given only one dish on Sunday and Thursday. The enclosed hermits recite the entire Psalter every day, while the open hermits always recite half,” and so forth.

We visited this place in the holy week of 1686 and saw the hermits there with great edification. For other matters relating to the Camaldolese order, consult the History of Augustine of Florence. Anselm of Havelberg praises the original fervor of this institution in book I of the *Dialogues*, volume XII of the *Spicilegium*, page 112.

### 5

Peter Damian does not state in what year Romuald ceased to live on earth, nor does any other writer of that period—at least none known to us. Baronius and some other more recent writers assign his final year as 1027, which seems the date that should be retained.

At any rate, it is certain that Romuald did not live beyond this year, from letters of Theodald, bishop of Arezzo, issued after his death in 1027, indeed in the month of August, and therefore about one month after Romuald’s death, which occurred on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July. In fact, Romuald’s death can scarcely be placed before the year 1027. For he did not come to the Camaldolese Hermitage before 1023, the first year of Theodald’s pontificate, by whom he was received.

Peter Damian assigns Romuald an age of 120 years in number 101; this is likewise confirmed by number 77, so that it is not probable that the number of years is corrupt. Baronius does not accept so great an age, because Romuald entered the monastery of Classe in the twentieth year of his age, as is read at the end of the Life, under Honestus, archbishop of Ravenna, who entered this see in 971, according to Rubeus.

Peter Damian indeed states in chapter 2 of opusculum 19 that Honestus succeeded Peter, who had voluntarily relinquished the dignity of archbishop, while Otto I was first governing the empire. Therefore either Romuald’s age must be corrected, or he entered the monastery of Classe when he was older, or—and this may perhaps be more probable—he entered before the pontificate of Honestus, if it is to be admitted that there was not two but one archbishop of Ravenna bearing this name in the tenth century.

Yet since Romuald’s father was still alive in 982, it seems to us that Romuald’s age should rather be corrected.

[Col. 1124C]

### 6

“Five years after the holy man’s death,” writes Peter Damian at the end of the Life, “permission having been granted to the monks by the apostolic see, an altar was constructed above his venerable body.”

This therefore occurred while Pope John XX was seated. Yet the same Peter makes no mention of Pope John in chapter 1 of opusculum 51, where he argues against the monk Teuzon, who spoke of Romuald’s sanctity with insufficient modesty, that Romuald’s holiness had been approved by the apostolic see.

Peter’s words from that passage should be brought here:

“When, in the course of a dispute over a certain point, Saint Romuald was brought forward as a witness, the question immediately arose whether Romuald had at that time existed as a saint, or whether he was now received in paradise. Although this question concerning the holy man was being raised against the faith of the entire Church of our provinces, nevertheless, to support the position of our side, we called upon as witnesses those saints whose most celebrated and ancient reputation could not waver even among ordinary and ignorant people—namely, Leo and Gregory, once illustrious bishops of the Roman see. One of them promulgates the authoritative decrees of the canons; the other waters the Church with the clear and profound springs of heavenly eloquence.”

I believe, however, that by these names he designates not Leo IX and Gregory VI, but Leo I and likewise Gregory I. Peter used the authority of these men in asserting the authority of the Roman see concerning the canonization of saints against Teuzon.

[Col. 1125A] 7. The feast of Romuald is celebrated on February 7, the day of his translation from the town of Jesi to the city of Fabriano, situated in the March of Ancona. This translation took place in 1481, during the generalship of Peter Delfino, who discusses it in an unpublished letter to Benedict, abbot of Saint Michael’s at Murano:

“Concerning the body of the most holy Romuald, which at the beginning of my generalship was secretly taken by three of our monks from the ancient sarcophagus at Valdicastro and transferred to the town of Jesi, and which afterwards, by order of the pontiff, was restored to the people of Fabriano, I do not doubt that you have learned many things from the aforementioned citizen—and especially where it ought to remain and be preserved: in Fabriano, at the monastery of Saint Blaise, where it now is, or in the monastery of Valdicastro, where it had previously lain. I judged, for sound reasons, that it should remain at Fabriano. For it is certain that it can be kept more safely in the city, lest it be stolen again; and the people of Fabriano had promised that, if it were left there, they would do much in honor of the sacred relics. Thus, after learning from the people of Fabriano that this matter had been entrusted by the supreme pontiff to the cardinal of Saint George, legate in the Picenian territory, I deemed it necessary to meet him at Macerata, etc. From Ancona, May 16, 1481.”

This preliminary notice is sufficient.

[Col. 1125]

## LIFE OF SAINT ROMUALD, ABBOT, BY SAINT PETER DAMIAN

(See below, among the works of Saint Peter Damian, at the end of volume 144 of the *Patrologia*.)

[Col. 1125]

## FRAGMENT OF AN EXPOSITION OF PSALM 68 ATTRIBUTED TO THE HOLY ROMUALD

(*Annales Camaldulenses* I, 237, from an eleventh-century parchment of the monastery of Saint Michael at Murano.)

I have become a stranger to my brothers and a sojourner to the sons of my mother.

[Col. 1125B]

**The voice of Christ.** Here he calls the Jews “brothers,” because they were joined to him by blood relationship. He became a stranger to them when they refused to believe in him; for although he himself was descended from Abraham according to the flesh, they, devoted to evil deeds, were separated from the patriarch’s lineage, as he says in the Gospel: “If you were Abraham’s children, you would do the works of Abraham.” He added: “And a guest to the sons of my mother.” Let us call a guest anyone who, having obtained access to our house, dwells there [for a time] and is received not by the name of kinship but as a stranger. He calls the Synagogue his mother, since he arose from it when he deigned to be born among the Jewish people.

For zeal for your house has consumed me, and the reproaches of those who reproached you have fallen upon me.

[Col. 1125C]

**The voice of Christ.** Because they made it a den of thieves. They cast upon him the insult of those who reproached you when they called him both a Samaritan and one who had a demon, and said: “If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross,” and so forth. Zeal for God’s house consumed him when, after making a whip, he overturned the seats of those selling doves and the tables of the money-changers, teaching that the holy temple was one thing and the business of commerce another. What followed from this zeal is powerfully added: “And the reproaches of those who reproached you have fallen upon me.” For after they had been rebuked, as unworthy, with saving admonitions, they hurled reproaches upon him like a massed volley of weapons, returning quarrels in place of holy admonitions. [Col. 1126B]

And I covered my soul with fasting, and it became a reproach to me.

He attempted to bring reproach upon him when Satan tested him, saying: “Say that these stones should become loaves.” We call it fasting whenever we abstain from bodily foods and do not satisfy our hunger by eating anything. In this sense the Lord Christ is said to have fasted, because he could find none of the faith of human beings for which he was greatly hungry. “I covered,” he said, as though he had wrapped his soul in some mantle of sadness. It follows: “And it became a reproach to me.” The good are always a reproach to the evil, because they do not consent at all to their crimes, while by their zeal for what is good they distance themselves from those with whom they have no fellowship. For the reproach is attested by the blows, scourging, and spitting that the Lord and Savior suffered from the frenzied crowd. [Col. 1126C]

And I put on sackcloth as my garment, and I became a byword to them.

**The voice of Christ.** Mourning or weeping is shown by sackcloth, such as he used at the death of Lazarus. He became a byword to the Jews when, as he wept, they said: “See how he loved him”; while others said: “Could not he who opened the eyes of the man born blind have caused this man not to die?” Sackcloth signifies sorrow, and the tears that the Lord, moved by the weakness of the human race, shed when he was about to raise Lazarus. For nowhere is the Lord recorded as having used sackcloth. He also became a byword to the Jews when he seemed to teach the carnal people through various comparisons, as we read in the Gospel: “The Lord spoke a parable to the crowd”; and in another psalm: “I will open my mouth in parables.” A parable is a comparison made, through some likeness, between things that differ in nature, in accordance with the manner of divine providence, so that those who could not grasp heavenly things might perceive what they heard through earthly analogies. [Col. 1127A]

Those who sat at the gate spoke against me, and those who drank wine sang against me.

That is, the scribes and Pharisees, who, possessing the key of knowledge, neither entered nor allowed others to enter; they distinguished cases while sitting in public judgment. “And those who drank wine sang against me,” for they were filled with the wine of iniquity. They devised how they might kill him. Hear, then, how he teaches those who foolishly sang: “Sing wisely,” he says. [Col. 1127B] Or they were drunk with wine when they covered his head and said: “Prophesy to us, Christ; who is it that struck you?” Those who mingle with human gatherings in diligent curiosity sit at the gates. He says that his Passion was a public story for the Jewish people, so that no one who took part in such conversation would be excluded from it.

Thus far he has spoken of the reproaches and insults of the Jews. Now, as it seems to me, he speaks of the faithful: “And those who drank wine sang against me.” Those sing to the Lord who are guided by commendable conduct and render in their deeds what they receive as heavenly commands through admonitions.

But I address my prayer to you, Lord; it is the time of favor, O God.

[Col. 1127C]

**The voice of Christ to the Father.** I am not overcome by these sufferings, because I am with you in prayer: “But I address my prayer to you, Lord.” While the Jews were saying to me, “Crucify him, crucify him,” I spoke while praying for them: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.” “It is the time of favor, O Lord.” “This is the Son, my Son, in whom I am well pleased.” He has reached the third section, where, in opposition to the curses of the Jews, the heavenly Teacher sets the holiness of his prayer, suggesting that human quarrels should be met not with inflamed strife but with devout prayers.

Let us now see what the time of favor is. It is the time of favor when, through the benefit of his incarnation, he delivered the world, which was in peril, from the impending destruction. This is the time of favor, of which the Apostle also says: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation.” [Col. 1127D]

In the abundance of your mercy hear me; in the truth of your salvation look upon me.

So that, after the true death, the truth of the resurrection might be demonstrated. It was no small mercy that prevailed over so great a burden of sin (sic). The multitude of sin was indeed great, but that mercy was much greater and prevailed; and when the aforementioned time of mercy had brought salvation to the world through the Passion, it followed that he should also pray for the resurrection that he had truly promised through the prophets. He therefore prays to the Father not according to the nature of divinity, in which he is coequal with him, but according to the assumed weakness of humanity, in which he is lesser than the Father.

Deliver me from the mire, that I may not sink; rescue me from those who hate me, and from the depths of the waters.

[Col. 1128A]

He speaks openly here of the Jews; the printed text is corrupt here (“qui cum nunc quam dilexerunt” [sic]), before it continues: “And from the depths of the waters.” Let us take care to beseech the Lord ourselves in the same words in which we know that our Head prayed. This point must be examined carefully: why above he said that he had been fixed in the mire, while here he asks that he be kept from remaining stuck in it. He was indeed fixed in the mire when he was held by the weakness of the flesh he had assumed; hence he also accepted death on the cross. Here, however, he appropriately asks that his soul be made free from muddy desires—that is, from the desires of this world. This is rightly received on behalf of the members, because he who had no stain of sin could not cling to the mire.

“Deliver me from those who hate me”: this manifestly refers to the Jewish people. When Christ rose, their hatred was frustrated and vanished. For what he said, “From the depths of the waters,” unquestionably refers to that people, because it was deep in the malignity of its counsel and turbulent with seditions.

Let not the tempest of water overwhelm me, nor the deep swallow me, nor let the pit close its mouth over me.

The voice of Christ insofar as he is human. May the tempest of the Passion not hold him in the depth of the infernal abyss. “Nor let the deep swallow me”: although he descended through death, may he not be devoured by it. “Nor let the pit close its mouth over me”: the entrance of hell, or the devil. For he asks not to be submerged by the waves—that is, by the fiercest storm of this age, which swallowed souls like a sea when it had enveloped them in the fault of depravity. He says: “Nor let the deep swallow me.” Sin is certainly a deep, which with a kind of voracity devours the souls of the ungodly, so that those who despair of the wickedness of their deeds cannot return to repentance. “Nor let the pit close its mouth over me.” A pit is a depth excavated farther into the earth. Allegorically, sinners truly fall into it when they do not withdraw themselves from a vicious will; and it presses upon them to close its mouth when they persist in the worst disposition until the time of their death.

Hear me, Lord, for your mercy is kind; according to the abundance of your compassion, look upon me.

[Col. 1128D]

**The voice of Christ to the Father, on behalf of the flesh.** According to human weakness he asks these things, saying: “You who redeemed others through my Passion, look upon me with the mercy that goes before me.” For he says: “Hear me, Lord,” and adds the reason why he should be heard—not because humanity deserves it, but because the Lord’s mercy is kind and always ready to do good, when it is devoutly sought and entreated with the utmost purity. And, wishing to explain that kindness, the devout teacher added: “According to the abundance of your compassion, look upon me.” He always returns to that point, showing how it is a patron to the weak, to whom all sins yield, however numerous they may be proved to be.

### BOOK TWO OF THE DECRETALS — ON THE SACRED ORDERS

625  

Summary of the book.—This book encompasses the ordination, appropriate dignity, quality of life, duties, and ministries of presbyters, deacons, and the remaining ecclesiastical orders. 625  

Index of the chapters of Book Three. 665  

### BOOK THREE OF THE DECRETALS — ON CHURCHES

673  

Summary of the book.—This book treats the establishment, worship, and honor of the houses of God; tithes and offerings; and the rights of each person. It also shows which books have been received into the sacred catalogue, and which have been rejected as apocryphal. 673  

Index of the chapters of Book Four. 725  

### BOOK FOUR OF THE DECRETALS — ON THE SACRAMENT OF BAPTISM AND CONFIRMATION

727  

Index of the chapters of Book Five. 749  

### BOOK FIVE OF THE DECRETALS — ON THE SACRAMENT OF THE BODY AND BLOOD OF THE LORD

750  

Summary of the book.—This book treats everything pertaining to the sacrament of the Eucharist so fully that you will find nothing lacking concerning this subject. 751  

Index of the chapters of Book Six. 763  

### BOOK SIX OF THE DECRETALS — ON HOMICIDE

763  

Summary of the book.—This book treats homicides committed voluntarily and involuntarily; parricides; fratricides; those who kill their legitimate wives and their elders; and the slaughter of clerics. It shows what penance is to be imposed for each of these kinds of homicide. 763  

Index of the chapters of Book Seven. 777  

### BOOK SEVEN OF THE DECRETALS — ON INCEST

779  

Summary of the book.—This book concerns incestuous intercourse between blood relatives. It shows within which degree marriages may be contracted or must be dissolved, and what penance should be imposed, according to the offense, upon those defiled by incest. 779  

Here follows Saint Isidore the bishop’s diagram of the seven degrees of consanguinity. 788  

Index of the chapters of Book Eight. 788  

### BOOK EIGHT OF THE DECRETALS — ON MEN AND WOMEN CONSECRATED TO GOD

791  

Summary of the book.—This book establishes a treatment of men and women who, having been dedicated to God, have abandoned their sacred undertaking, and of the penance owed by such persons. 791  

Index of the chapters of Book Nine. 811  

### BOOK NINE OF THE DECRETALS — ON WOMEN WHO HAVE NOT BEEN CONSECRATED

815  

Summary of the book.—This book treats virgins and widows who have not been consecrated to God; those who abduct them and the punishment to be imposed upon such abductors; legitimate marriage; and illicit intercourse and the penance due for it. 815  

Index of the chapters of Book Ten. 831  

### BOOK TEN OF THE DECRETALS — ON ENCHANTERS AND AUGURS

831  

Summary of the book.—This book treats enchanters; divinatory augurs; diviners by lot; various deceptions of the Devil; those who utter curses; quarrelsome persons; conspirators; and the penance due to each of them. 843  

Index of the chapters of Book Eleven. 853  

### BOOK ELEVEN OF THE DECRETALS — ON EXCOMMUNICATION

855  

Summary of the book.—This book treats excommunication and its neglect and contempt; thieves and robbers; and those who attack and plunder sacred buildings. 855  

Index of the chapters of Book Twelve. 875  

### BOOK TWELVE OF THE DECRETALS — ON PERJURY

875

### BOOK THIRTEEN OF THE DECRETALS — ON FASTING

883  

Summary of the book.—This book concerns the observance and usefulness of fasting, especially the Lenten fast, the fasts of the four seasons, and the other fasts established by the Church, as well as those who violate them. 883  

Index of the chapters of Book Fourteen. 889  

### BOOK FOURTEEN OF THE DECRETALS — ON GLUTTONY AND DRUNKENNESS

889  

Summary of the book.—This book establishes a treatment of the detestable vices of gluttony and drunkenness, and teaches what punishment should be imposed upon those entangled in these vices. 889  

Index of the chapters of Book Fifteen. 893  

### BOOK FIFTEEN OF THE DECRETALS — ON THE LAITY

895  

Summary of the book.—This book establishes a treatment of laypeople of every condition, both those who rule—such as emperors, kings, and princes—and those subject to their authority. 895

909

Index of the chapters of Book Seventeen. 917  

### BOOK SEVENTEEN OF THE DECRETALS — ON FORNICATION

919  

Summary of the book.—This book encompasses fornication and various kinds of incest, and teaches what correction and penance are owed by those entangled in these vices. 919  

### BOOK EIGHTEEN OF THE DECRETALS — ON VISITING THE SICK

933  

Summary of the book.—This book teaches that the sick are to be visited by presbyters and explains what is required for such a visitation. 933

### BOOK NINETEEN OF THE DECRETALS — ON PENANCE

949  

Summary of the book.—This book is called *Corrector* and *Physician*, because it fully contains medicines for the correction of bodies and souls. It teaches every priest, even a simple one, how he may come to the aid of each person—whether ordained or without orders, poor or rich, child, young person, old person, or decrepit; healthy or sick; of every age and of either sex. 949

### BOOK TWENTY OF THE DECRETALS — ON CONTEMPLATION

1017  

Summary of the book.—This book is called *The Watcher*. For it considers divine providence and predestination; the coming of the Antichrist; his works; the resurrection; the day of judgment; the punishments of hell; and the blessedness of everlasting life. 1017
